Meta faces $40 bn data privacy penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:37:19 UTC
21:37:19 KST

Meta faces $40 bn data privacy penalty
Meta Platforms is facing between $35 billion and $40 billion in civil penalties from the US state of New Mexico, Reuters has reported. At the upper end, the fine would rank as the largest financial penalty ever imposed on a US corporation.
The case stems from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal, which erupted after a whistleblower revealed that the British political consulting firm had obtained data from tens of millions of Facebook users without their consent through a third-party app.
The data was used to profile voters and target them with political messaging, including during Donald Trump’s successful 2016 presidential campaign. Cambridge Analytica filed for bankruptcy months later, while Facebook faced billions of dollars in fines and compensation claims over its handling of user data.
It comes a week after a jury found the Facebook parent company liable for misleading statements about the privacy of users’ data.
The jury in Santa Fe found that Meta had willfully deceived consumers, resulting in more than 43 million breaches of the state’s consumer protection law. The violations were deemed to have affected the state’s entire population of some two million people.
Attorneys for Meta and New Mexico clashed over the appropriate penalty, with the company arguing that the up to $40 billion sought by the state did not match the conduct at issue in the trial, Reuters reported Wednesday. The news agency said that Judge Francis Mathew is expected to rule later this month on how much Meta must pay.
The ruling marks Meta’s latest major legal defeat in New Mexico. In March, another Santa Fe jury found the company liable for 75,000 violations related to child safety and ordered $375 million in penalties. A local judge later deemed Meta’s platforms a “public nuisance” and ordered it to pay additional $567 million. The corporation has said it will appeal.
Meta’s legal exposure stretches beyond the state of New Mexico. In August, it agreed to pay roughly $17 billion to settle claims brought by dozens of US states and territories that it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the associated risks. The deal also included claims stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, but New Mexico did not join the settlement, allowing its case to proceed to trial.
Meta, which operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, is not alone in facing scrutiny over Big Tech’s data practices. Last month, TikTok and its parent company ByteDance agreed to pay $400 million to settle US allegations that the platform illegally collected children’s personal data without parental consent. Google, Apple, Netflix and other tech giants have also been involved in privacy-related litigation.

TOKYO, October 2. /TASS/. Japan is currently not considering new sanctions against Russia and is focused only on extending the existing restrictions, Muneo Suzuki, a member of the upper house of parliament from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, told TASS.

EU says Ukraine no longer requires additional funds in 2026
EU and Ukrainian representatives concluded during a joint meeting on 1 October that Ukraine currently has no need for additional international funding in 2026.
Source: Paula Pinho, Chief Spokesperson of the European Commission, on Friday 2 October, as reported by a European Pravda correspondent in Brussels
Details: The European Commission reported that it had concluded, together with Ukraine, that there is no external financing gap in 2026.
Quote from Pinho: "We had never said that there was a financial gap. This is what we were hearing from reports [from the Ukrainian side – ed.]... yesterday we came to a conclusion, together with our Ukrainian friends, that there is no financial gap."
Details: She emphasised that this is fully in line with what the European Commission had stated earlier when answering questions about Ukraine's additional financial needs.
Quote from Pinho: "When asked, and you had been asking us a number of times about this reported gap, and we were saying we need to sit down with our Ukrainian partners and assess if indeed there is a gap and to what extent."
Background:
- In a joint statement on 1 October, the EU and Ukraine announced that they had found opportunities to provide funding for the Ukrainian budget and defence in 2026.
- On 2 October, the European Commission allocated a regular €2.9 billion tranche to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility mechanism; part of the funds was provided through a €90 billion support loan.
- On 24 September, it was reported that Ukraine would soon receive almost €3 billion after the Council of the EU approved the eighth regular payment under the Ukraine Facility.
- On 29 September in Brussels, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that the EU was fulfilling its share of the commitments and indicated that it expected Kyiv to do the same. In particular, she called on the Ukrainian authorities to unite for a "reform drive" in exchange for funding.

Kickbacks through charitable foundations: the ESBU is investigating a scheme involving the purchase of medical equipment, in which Bogomolets National Medical University figures
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:36:18 EEST
21:36:18 KST

Kickbacks through charitable foundations: the ESBU is investigating a scheme involving the purchase of medical equipment, in which Bogomolets National Medical University figures
Kyiv • UNN
The ESBU is investigating possible overpricing of medical equipment for the National Medical University and hospitals. According to the investigation, losses to the budget amounted to UAH 5.6 million.
The embezzlement of budget funds in the procurement of medical equipment involving Bogomolets National Medical University is being investigated by the Territorial Office of the Economic Security Bureau in Vinnytsia region, reports UNN.
The investigation began at the beginning of 2025. It concerns the procurement of medical equipment manufactured by Karl Storz. According to the investigators, the prices specified in the tender documentation were artificially inflated. Bogomolets National Medical University is among the customers of the equipment.
Criminal proceedings were initiated under Parts 4 and 5 of Article 191 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — misappropriation, embezzlement, or seizure of property through abuse of official position, including on an especially large scale.
According to the detectives, the scheme was organized by officials of Karl Storz Ukraine LLC — the official and sole distributor in Ukraine of products manufactured by the German company KARL STORZ SE & Co. KG. The aim, investigators allege, was to embezzle budget funds allocated for expensive medical equipment and consumables.
Apparently, the first episode in the case was the investigation into embezzlement at the Podilsk Oncology Center. Subsequently, investigators uncovered an entire network of dealers who, according to law enforcement officials, acted under the control of Karl Storz Ukraine. These included Livin, Medprovider, Ksenko, and Yasmed. In addition to the Podilsk Oncology Center, they entered into agreements with the Sumy Regional Oncology Center, the Zhytomyr Regional Hospital, the Ladyzhyn City Hospital, and Bogomolets National Medical University.
The investigation established that between June and December 2024, the budget suffered losses totaling UAH 5.6 million as a result of artificially inflating equipment prices and creating discriminatory conditions for participation in tenders.
According to a court ruling, in April 2024 the medical university signed a contract worth more than UAH 4 million with Ksenko LLC. According to the investigators, before the procurement was announced, the head of NMU (the surname is not given in the publicly available court ruling, but it likely refers to the university's rector, Yuriy Kuchyn) allegedly discussed its specifications with a representative of Karl Storz Ukraine. Among the items seized from the distributor during the investigation were four Ksenko payment instructions from 2024.
Apparently, this concerns a tender for the procurement of equipment for operating units (a set for ENT surgical procedures, not containing medicinal products and intended for repeated use), in which the aforementioned company Ksenko was the sole participant.
The court rulings contain information about the mechanism used by the participants in the scheme: first, representatives of Karl Storz Ukraine and representatives of the customer institutions coordinated the tender and the specifications of the procurement item. The procurement customers then “tailored” the technical requirements to a specific manufacturer, narrowing the range of participants and making it possible to artificially inflate the price. Under such conditions, victory in the tender for “their participants” became guaranteed. Subsequently, according to the investigators, a “kickback” amounting to 5–10% was transferred to controlled charitable foundations. The detectives believe that the participants in the scheme withdrew the remaining unlawfully obtained funds in cash from bank tellers and handed them over to representatives of Karl Storz Ukraine and the customers during personal meetings.
Interestingly, after the aforementioned tender worth more than UAH 4 million, NMU concluded four more agreements with Ksenko worth a total of more than UAH 2 million. Also, in April 2024, the university signed an agreement with another company from among the dealers listed above — Livin LLC — to procure a steam sterilizer and operating lights worth more than UAH 2.5 million. Livin was the sole participant in the tender. According to our information, these agreements do not appear in the Eсonomic Security Bureau's criminal proceedings.
We remind you
The State Audit Service began monitoring two procurements by Bogomolets National Medical University due to possible violations.
It concerns the renovation of two university dormitories in the capital. Journalists’ investigation indicates a possible overpricing of construction materials.

The European Commission on Friday announced the disbursement of €2.9 billion ($3.2 billion) to Ukraine to help meet the country's financing needs, maintain public administration and support reforms amid the ongoing war.
The payment includes €800 million ($899 million) being provided for the first time under the Ukraine Facility component of the EU's Ukraine Support Loan, according to a statement.
"With today's disbursement, we are helping safeguard Ukraine's financial stability and supporting investments that will underpin its future recovery," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The bloc said total EU support provided under Ukraine's reform plan will exceed €32 billion ($36 billion) following the latest payment, including contributions from EU member states and partner countries.
For the remainder of 2026, Ukraine has €33.7 billion ($37.9 billion) in financial support available, including €29.3 billion ($32.91 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan and €4.4 billion ($5 billion) in budget support under the initial Ukraine Facility.
Of the €29.3 billion available under the Ukraine Support Loan, €16.6 billion ($18.6 billion) is earmarked for Ukraine's defense industrial capacity and €12.7 billion ($14.3 billion) for budget support.
The European Commission also reiterated its commitment to delivering the €90 billion ($101 billion) Ukraine Support Loan planned for 2026 and 2027, along with the remaining funds under the initial Ukraine Facility.

Ex-UN director who protested Gaza famine challenges dismissal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:35:05 UTC
21:35:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Ex-UN director who protested Gaza famine challenges his dismissal
A former senior UN food agency official has said he has launched an appeal against his dismissal, alleging it was motivated by his stance on Israel imposing hunger on Gaza, in a case that has exposed tensions within the Rome-based organisation.
Benjamin Davis, 62, a Spanish American director at the Food and Agriculture Organisation, was informed his employment would end on 30 September at the request of Director-General Qu Dongyu, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The papers cited breaches of international civil service standards which require staff to act with impartiality. Davis rejected the allegation.
"I feel it’s a terrible injustice. I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking up about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food which is the most basic of human rights," he told Reuters. He said he had filed an appeal.
The FAO did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Davis' allegations or on the grounds for his dismissal.
Davis, said he had worked at the FAO for 26 years on a renewable contract, and that his dismissal was linked to staff activism against Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
He was one of hundreds of employees who have joined moments of silence for hunger victims in Gaza where an international hunger-monitoring system used by UN agencies determined famine in August 2025.
He also authored a report on food availability in the Palestinian enclave in May 2025.
The dispute burst into public view this week when Qu, speaking at a FAO conference, defended the dismissal of an unnamed staff member whom he accused of having "played the political game".
"We will not allow you to play the game here of human rights," Qu said.
Debate over staff activism
The remarks prompted fresh debate about whether UN employees are able to express views on humanitarian crises without jeopardising their careers.
A large crowd of staff gathered at FAO headquarters in Rome on Wednesday to applaud Davis as he departed, according to UN officials and video seen by Reuters.
Under UN rules, staff are allowed to express political opinions but must ensure these do not adversely affect their official duties or UN interests.
Davis, who was head of the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division, said he was concerned that other employees would face retaliation over their participation in the Gaza moments of silence.
The case, now with the FAO's internal justice process, could later be escalated to a UN tribunal which has the authority to award damages in employment disputes.

UFORCE, a Ukrainian defense company, says it fielded 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO's largest unmanned-systems exercise in Portugal, Militarnyi reported. The firm's crews acted as both mock enemy and allied forces alongside Ukraine's Navy during the 31 August–25 September drills. The turnout more than doubled the company's presence at last year's exercise, when it brought five vessels.
Ukraine began the all-out war without large warships, yet uncrewed boats drove Russia's Black Sea Fleet out of its main base on the Black Sea—a result that now pulls far larger navies to the same ranges to test the weapon for themselves.
Ukraine brings its sea-drone playbook to Portugal's NATO exercise
UFORCE joined REPMUS 26, the Portuguese Navy's annual exercise, co-organized with NATO, where member states try out robots and drones built for combat at sea. This year the company widened its presence sharply, UFORCE said on LinkedIn. Across the scenarios, its crews ran strikes, reconnaissance, and defense.
At the center sat the MV7, an uncrewed boat UFORCE showed in every setup it offers. Across its configurations, the MV7 carried interceptors, FPV drones, other kinetic weapons, and electronic-warfare gear. Crews launched flying drones straight off the decks while the boats sat on the water, all run by a single control program.
The company brought three systems to REPMUS for the first time: the Nemesis SeaStrike drone, which launches from the MV7, the MV11 boat, and a supply vessel called L11. UFORCE teams worked beside Ukraine's Navy throughout. Portuguese President António José Seguro inspected the MV7 on the pier, the company said.
Not Ukraine's first visit
Ukraine was at REPMUS last year, too. At REPMUS 2025, a Ukrainian-led "enemy" team beat NATO's side across all five drill scenarios and, in one, landed enough mock strikes on a NATO frigate to have sunk it in a real battle. Ukraine also brought the upgraded Magura v7.2 to that year's drills.

Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
Zelensky also said in the interview that Ukraine is unable to use all of its F-16 fighter jets during Russian attacks because around half of the aircraft are undergoing scheduled maintenance and repairs in Europe.
F-16s, which Ukraine first received in the summer of 2024, are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used to intercept Russian missiles and drones during aerial attacks on Ukraine. They could also be deployed to launch missiles and bombs against Russian positions along the front line.
The lengthy maintenance periods leave some aircraft unavailable when they are particularly needed for air defense. Kyiv wants to move some F-16 maintenance work to Ukraine to allow the jets to return to service faster.
Zelensky also said Ukraine faces a budget shortfall that is limiting the development and mass production of critical defensive weapons.

Greens see red-hot anger as an opportunity to take on Hanson, Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:33:41 UTC
21:33:41 KST

analysis
Greens leader sees red-hot anger as an opportunity to take the battle to Hanson, Labor
David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.
The new leader wants to harness the anti-establishment anger rife in Australia, declaring the Greens will fight and ultimately seek to "replace" Labor.
That won't be easy at a time when the populist right is capturing much of the voter anger here, though Shoebridge is not alone in seeing widespread economic frustration as an opportunity for the left.
Insurgent political movements in Britain, the United States and Germany have built support around everyday frustrations like rent, wages and living costs, and directed voters' anger toward inequality and concentrated wealth rather than the targets favoured by their opponents on the right.
Zack Polanski took the Green party in the UK and explicitly embraced "eco-populism" to achieve extraordinary membership growth and a surge in the polls.
In New York, Zohran Mamdani defeated an establishment Democrat and won the mayoral election by relentlessly translating socialism into rent, buses, childcare and groceries.
While a revitalised Die Linke party in Germany has almost doubled its vote through young supporters with a pitch on rent, wages and inequality.
All three have embedded climate, minority rights and other progressive causes inside a simple economic story.
Their circumstances and politics differ significantly, but each has demonstrated the potential for the left to turn economic dissatisfaction into electoral support.
If some of that sounds familiar, it's because the strategy is hardly new to Australians.
Long before Polanski or Mamdani became globally recognised names, the Greens here were trying to harness economic frustration with a pitch centred on inequality and the cost of everyday life.
Particularly under former leader Adam Bandt, the Greens consciously broadened beyond environmentalism.
Housing, inequality, free childcare, dental in Medicare, taxing billionaires and corporations and cost of living were all brought to the fore.
The strategy delivered the party four lower house seats and a 12.25 per cent primary vote nationally in 2022.
But three years later the Greens got a taste of just how fragile success can be.
Greens' changing strategy
The 2025 loss of three lower house seats — including Bandt's — showed the limits of a strategy that had produced spectacular gains, even as the party's national vote barely moved.
The Greens' attempts to extract concessions from the Albanese government on housing and climate were ultimately presented by Labor as blocking progressive outcomes rather than achieving them.
When Larissa Waters became leader of the party last year, she instead promised to be "firm but constructive" with Labor — to "get shit done".
The party's strategy basically went from "Labor isn't good enough so fight them and force them further left" to "Labor isn't good enough so negotiate and show voters what Greens leverage delivers".
But that leverage has yet to translate into a significant boost in the polls.
Shoebridge has now swung the emphasis back towards confrontation, though in a dramatically different political environment.
"We're not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them," he said.
He's also vowed to fight One Nation but blamed Labor for the rise of the populist right party.
Radical change, but how?
Meanwhile, Shoebridge's rivals for the leadership have ended this week emphasising markedly different priorities.
The rare, contested ballot against Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young on Wednesday exposed a party still grappling with how to translate its ambitions into greater political power.
While they broadly share a vision of radical change, there is a live argument about who the Greens should fight and what voters should hear from them first.
Faruqi used a post-ballot statement to suggest she had not sought the deputy role so she could have the freedom to pursue "bold politics and radical action" from outside the leadership team.
Expressing her disappointment at the result, Faruqi appeared to imply she would have succeeded had the party held a membership-wide vote for the leader.
Her reaction contrasted starkly with Hanson-Young, who not only managed to congratulate Shoebridge but also kept her sights trained firmly on the populist right.
She cast the Greens as a progressive force to take on Pauline Hanson, rather than sharpen the fight with Labor.
It's been a week of free advice from outside the party room, too, with ousted MP Max Chandler-Mather also calling for a membership ballot — something Shoebridge has guaranteed would happen by 2028.
Meanwhile, Bandt told the Insiders On Background podcast the Greens could either choose "division and fear" or to "offer hope", working to "get good things done for people, for nature for climate".
When pushed on the idea that using the power of government to achieve those goals sounded "quite different" to the pitch from Shoebridge, Bandt replied, "well, that's right".
Loading
Opponents, allies and message
There is strong agreement inside the Greens about the problems they want to solve. But consensus on who exactly is their main opponent, which allies they need and what message will grow the party's support remains elusive.
For now, Labor and the Greens have a relatively reliable path to passing legislation through the Senate when they agree.
That arithmetic could look very different after 2028.
Shoebridge evidently believes there are gains to be made in chipping away at Labor, perhaps even more so if Labor is preoccupied fighting One Nation.
But it's unlikely Anthony Albanese would ever lose focus on a perennial political foe to his left.
That makes the Greens' message as important as the opponents they choose.
Each leadership hopeful offered a different strategy for success and while Shoebridge prevailed on the day, the battle for the future of the party is ongoing.

Switzerland's President Guy Parmelin says he will quit government at end of year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:31:18 UTC
21:31:18 KST

A winegrower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced on Friday that he will quit the government at the end of the year, in a sudden move after more than a decade of ministerial service.
Switzerland's presidency rotates annually among the seven members of the government, called the Federal Council, of which Parmelin was the longest-serving minister.
Parmelin told a press conference in Bern that he had informed ministerial colleagues of his decision to step down on 31 December.
"By then, it will have been 11 years since I was elected to this role, and the time has come for me to make way for new energy in these times of great uncertainty," he said, admitting to feeling "a certain weariness" while insisting he was not stepping down for medical reasons.
Tariff tussle with Trump
A pragmatist, Parmelin seemed to make more headway with US President Donald Trump than his predecessor Karin Keller-Sutter.
Trump shocked Switzerland in August 2025 when he announced 39% duties on imports of Swiss goods, among the highest in his global tariff blitz.
Parmelin, the economy minister, went to Washington three times in a bid to reduce the rate.
Eventually, Switzerland and the United States announced a declaration of intent to cut tariffs to 15%, with the Swiss vowing to invest $200 billion (€178 billion) in the United States.
A winegrower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Parmelin was previously president in 2021 and took centre-stage as Switzerland hosted a summit in Geneva between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Joe Biden.
The president of the Swiss Confederation is first among equals on the Federal Council, chairs its meetings and typically represents the country in major domestic and international matters.
The position goes to whoever has had the longest run on the council without being president.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will become president in 2027.
Parmelin joined the Federal Council in 2016 as defence minister and has held the economy brief since 2019.
The Federal Council seven seats are shared 2-2-2-1 among the four main political parties under a decades-old tacit agreement known as "the magic formula."
Parmelin's successor will come from the SVP. Candidates have until 23 October to come forward and parliament will choose on 9 December.

US Navy to buy 30 medium drone warships from three firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:30:56 BST
21:30:56 KST

The US Navy plans to buy 30 Medium Unmanned Surface Vessels (MUSVs) from Galliano Marine Services, HII and Saronic Technologies after completing the first phase of at-sea testing, with the first vessels due for delivery before the end of fiscal year 2027, according to the service.
Each of the three companies has been awarded a production Other Transaction Authority agreement covering 10 vessels, at an average procurement cost of $40 million per boat. Across the three agreements, that amounts to roughly $1.2 billion. Three other firms that took part in the prototype phase, Leidos, PAC MAR and Sea Machines, were judged to have completed the work set out in their prototype agreements and will each receive a $15 million award under the terms previously agreed.
All six companies will be accepted onto the Maritime Marketplace hosted by Drones.mil, the Navy said, making them eligible for follow-on production agreements from acquisition authorities across the Department of War. On 23 September the service also released a Phase II Integration and Testing Call for Solutions, which it says is intended to widen the pool of offerings and meet future MUSV mission sets.
According to the Navy, Phase I testing assessed the vessels’ ability to perceive and understand the surrounding maritime environment, their autonomous navigation in line with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, and their capacity to carry out long-duration missions.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in the release: “Our warfighters don’t have time to wait on bureaucracy while our adversaries pace forward.” He added: “Our message to the defense industrial base is simple: build fast, deliver on time, and match the urgency of the threat. This MUSV award is a prime example of how we are streamlining acquisitions to ensure our Sailors and Marines have the capabilities they need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The Navy’s interest in medium-sized uncrewed surface vessels dates back several years, with earlier efforts including DARPA’s Sea Hunter, the Overlord programme and a 2020 MUSV prototype contract awarded to L3Harris. The three production awardees take different approaches. HII has developed its ROMULUS family of autonomous vessels, Saronic has expanded from small autonomous boats towards larger designs, and Galliano Marine Services comes from the Gulf Coast offshore vessel sector.
The Chief of Naval Operations was quoted in the release as describing MUSVs as part of the hedge strategy set out in the service’s Fighting Instructions. “They give commanders a Tailored Offset — additional capacity and capability that can be rapidly adapted to the threat, distributed across the battlespace, and placed at risk without placing Sailors at unnecessary risk,” the CNO said. “Just as importantly, MUSVs give us a platform for rapidly integrating new sensors, weapons, and other mission payloads as technology and operational requirements change. This is about moving beyond experimentation and putting reliable, combat-relevant capability into the hands of our Sailors at the speed the Fleet requires.”
Fielding will be led by the Direct Reporting Program Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems, working alongside the Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center, which is responsible for developing tactics, training and operational experience for the vessels. Under the Navy’s Containerized Capability Campaign, the service intends to use modular payloads so commanders can fit sensors, weapons and other mission equipment to the boats according to the task at hand.

Katelynas urges EU to work more closely with origin countries on migrant returns  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:06 UTC
21:29:06 KST

VILNIUS - Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas urged the European Union to cooperate more closely with third countries on the return of illegal migrants.
"In the area of returns, we must move from discussions to results. If a decision is made that a person has no right to stay in the European Union, states must have realistic opportunities to implement it. This requires both stronger political pressure and closer cooperation with countries of origin," Katelynas said on Friday.
He also stressed the importance of identifying migration risks and responding to them before they reach the European Union's external borders.
Katelynas made the remarks at the European Union Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg.
Interior ministers discussed the situation in the Schengen area, migration management, the return of people illegally present in the European Union, as well as drug-related violence and intimidation and preparedness to respond in a timely manner to emerging migration and security threats.
During the debate on Schengen, Katelynas highlighted the importance of stronger protection of the European Union's external borders, closer cooperation between law enforcement authorities and the use of modern technologies.
According to the interior minister, Europe must pay more attention to prevention rather than simply reacting to crises that have already arisen.
The council also stressed that the response to drug crime and related violence and intimidation must include not only law enforcement measures but also stronger prevention and assistance to victims.
Katelynas also drew attention to hybrid threats posed by Russia, cyberattacks, disinformation and the malicious use of drones, calling for stronger mutual information exchange and greater investment in preparedness for such threats.
Lithuania promises to raise these issues during its presidency of the European Union Council in the first half of 2027.

Survey: People lack faith in an adequate state pension  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:05 UTC
21:29:05 KST

TALLINN - As many as 74 percent of people in Estonia do not believe they will receive a state pension sufficient for a normal standard of living, a Norstat survey commissioned by LHV reveals.
Furthermore, for half of Estonia's residents, an adequate retirement income would be twice the current average pension.
Faith in receiving a state pension that allows for a normal standard of living is lowest among those aged 30-39. A striking 81 percent of people in this age group do not consider it likely. The corresponding figure is 68 percent for the 18-29 age group, 77 percent for those aged 40-49, 70 percent for the 50-59 age group, and 71 percent for those aged 60-75.
According to Vahur Vallistu, chairman of the management board of LHV Asset Management, the results reflect higher expectations for quality of life throughout the entire lifespan than before. "An increasing number of people in Estonia know that relying solely on the state pension is likely not the best strategy. A financial buffer for a dignified old age is built over a long period, and smart savers first take advantage of the tax-benefited opportunities of the second and third pillars," he said.
Vallistu added that it is also worth considering increasing personal contributions to the second pillar to four or six percent of one's gross salary to maximize the results of decades-long saving. If possible, one should also consider making regular contributions to the third pillar. "It is consistent and automated investment solutions that most effectively support the growth of wealth in the long term," Vallistu is convinced.
The survey revealed that 48 percent of people in Estonia consider a pension of over 1,500 euros per month necessary for a normal standard of living. A pension in the range of 1,001-1,500 euros is considered as such by 42 percent of respondents. The actual average pension in Estonia is currently 860 euros.
In Vallistu's view, these numbers clearly illustrate the gap between people's expectations and reality. The income of Estonian residents experiences one of the largest drops in the European Union after retirement. While the average pension in the EU constitutes nearly 70 percent of a person's previous income, in Estonia it is about 40 percent.
Vallistu pointed out that, primarily due to the demographic situation, the gap between the average salary and the state pension will only widen. Therefore, it is important to save additionally to the first, or state, pension pillar. "Saving in the second pillar, increasing personal contributions, and investing in the third pillar form a good foundation that allows one to face the future with more confidence," he said.
To start receiving more money in the second pillar monthly as early as next year, an application to increase contributions must be submitted before November 30. To date, more than 123,000 second-pillar savers have already submitted the relevant application. For contributions made to the third pillar by the end of December, a tax refund can be received next year on an amount up to 15 percent of a person's gross income, but not more than 6,000 euros in one year.
The survey was conducted this September by the research firm Norstat. Across Estonia, 1,000 people aged 18-74 were surveyed.

Shortage of refined oil products has reached a critical level  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:05 UTC
21:29:05 KST

TALLINN - Supply disruptions and government interventions to regulate fuel prices are causing sharp fluctuations in gasoline and diesel prices across Europe at a time when the shortage of refined oil products has reached a critical level.
Supply crises in the Middle East and Russia, along with disruptions in refinery operations, have led to a situation in the European fuel market where the market is unstable and fuel stocks are at historically low levels.
The conflict between the US and Iran continues to disrupt refinery operations in the Persian Gulf region, significantly limiting the availability of refined oil products. Russia's decision to extend its diesel export ban has further strained Europe's security of supply. The result is a scarcity of refined oil products at a time when refining margins are at historically high levels.
"Global diesel flow remains 1.3-1.4 million barrels per day lower than a year ago, which has left Europe with a minimal buffer before the autumn refinery maintenance season. It remains to be seen in the near future whether and to what extent the regular autumn maintenance of the plants will be postponed until spring to keep production running in this tense situation," commented Indrek Sassi, head of motor fuel pricing at Circle K.
The production capacity of European oil refineries remains exceptionally high this autumn. TotalEnergies' European plants are operating at full capacity and, according to CEO Patrick Pouyanne, have become a "gold mine." Due to high profit margins, the company postponed maintenance at its Gonfreville plant in northern France until the spring.
To regulate high fuel prices, several European countries have introduced special measures to limit retail prices and ease budgetary pressure. From October 1 until the end of the year, Germany lowered the energy tax on road transport fuels by 14.04 cents per liter and plans to introduce a fuel price cap by January 1, 2027, at the latest.
The Czech Republic will lower the excise duty on diesel fuel from October 1 to 31, limit retail prices for motor fuels, and plans to impose a temporary windfall tax on its only refining company, Orlen Unipetrol.
Italy has introduced price caps through major retailers Eni and IP. For 30 days starting September 28, Eni set the maximum price for diesel at 2.19 euros per liter and for gasoline at 1.99 euros per liter. Since March, the Italian government has approved 15 separate aid packages, costing the state over 2.3 billion euros. Among Estonia's neighboring countries, Latvia has lowered its fuel excise duty to the minimum level allowed by the European Union.
"Last week, the Estonian Association of Transportation Fuels, together with other professional associations, sent a joint appeal to the government to follow the practice of other European Union countries and temporarily reduce the tax burden on fuels. This is to alleviate the energy crisis and prevent a situation where high fuel prices severely impact both households and businesses," said Sassi.
Additional supply restrictions also pose a significant risk to motor fuel prices. U.S. President Donald Trump is still considering a ban on diesel exports to lower domestic prices. According to Goldman Sachs, a complete U.S. ban on diesel exports would raise European diesel prices by three dollars per barrel, or just under 2 percent. Yesterday, Reuters reported that China has halted fuel exports and canceled previously agreed gasoline and jet fuel deliveries for October. In this situation, releasing Europe's strategic reserves could help mitigate the price increases.
"It is expected that European Union leaders will meet on October 15 to discuss the use of emergency reserves, but it must be kept in mind that Europe's gasoline stocks are critically low compared to its diesel stocks," Sassi noted.
According to the European Commission, fuel stocks in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region are below the five-year average but have remained stable in recent weeks.

Eamets: Autumn will not bring relief from inflation  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:28:56 UTC
21:28:56 KST

TALLINN - Raul Eamets, chief economist at Bigbank, stated that inflation accelerated in September and predicts that the autumn will bring no relief.
"This summer, we were getting used to an inflation rate of two percent or less year-on-year, a level the European Central Bank considers reasonable," Eamets said. "However, on Friday, Statistics Estonia released its flash estimate of the harmonised index of consumer prices for September, which showed a year-on-year price increase of 3 percent - double the rate seen in August."
"Looking ahead to the autumn, it's clear we cannot expect a slowdown in price growth. The main reasons are the ongoing oil and gas crisis and the uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. This is compounded by the actions of the Houthis in Yemen, who have successfully blocked shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb strait - a key maritime gateway connecting the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea to the Suez Canal," Eamets explained.
"Today, most cargo ships are sailing around Africa for fear of Houthi attacks. Nearly a quarter of the world's maritime transport passes through these straits, and blocking them increases the cost not only of oil and gas but of all goods transported by sea from Asia to Europe," Eamets said.
"Rising energy prices continue to have the greatest impact on inflation. As autumn progresses, demand for heating and electricity will grow, pushing energy prices even higher. This will be particularly painful for local governments and private consumers who rely on natural gas, as gas prices are already very high and are set to rise further with increasing demand across Europe. Alternative fuels such as wood pellets and firewood have also become more expensive due to increased demand. The rising price of diesel will, sooner or later, translate into higher consumer prices through increased transportation costs. Therefore, we should expect inflation to accelerate this autumn," Eamets added.

Tallinn International Horse Show to Kick Off on Friday  - The Baltic Times

TALLINN – The 23rd Tallinn International Horse Show kicks off on Friday, set to delight audiences this weekend with top-level international equestrian sports and a spectacular show program.
Tickets for Saturday and Sunday are sold out, but a few tickets are still available for Friday. This year, the competition features participants from nine countries: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Brazil, Portugal, Sweden, Uzbekistan, and Ukraine. A total of 150 athletes and over 220 horses will gather at the Unibet Arena. Over the three days, the athletic pairs will complete nearly 600 starts.
The focus of Friday evening is Ladies' Night, beginning at 7 p.m. The event will merge fashion and equestrian sports, with "dancing horses" taking the stage during Riina Laanetu's fashion show, "DRESS the CODE." This will be followed at 7:30 p.m. by a performance from Italian equestrian artist Diego Giona. The evening's program also features top dressage riders. At 9:30 p.m., the Young Stars Dressage will provide a platform for young riders to showcase their talents.
Saturday evening's program is dedicated to both music and athletic spectacle. At 6:15 p.m., ALIKA will perform, followed by the 145 cm open class competition at 7:15 p.m. The day concludes at 9 p.m. with the Six Bar competition, one of the most engaging events for spectators, where horse and rider pairs must clear a series of six fences of increasing height.
Sunday's show program includes a small pony show at 2:45 p.m. and another performance by Diego Giona at 3 p.m. The Tallinn International Horse Show will culminate with the 150 cm Grand Prix, starting at 5 p.m. This event, presented for the Alexela prizes, is a leg of the FEI Jumping World Cup. The Sunday evening Grand Prix brings the highest level of show jumping of the weekend to the Unibet Arena and is one of the most anticipated competitions of the entire event. A closing ceremony will follow the Grand Prix.
This year's Horse Show is supported by over 40 partners and sponsors, with a total prize fund of approximately 112,000 euros.
The Tallinn International Horse Show 2026–2028 project is co-financed by the European Union.

Nine people injured in eight traffic accidents across Estonia in one day  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

TALLINN – Eight serious traffic accidents occurred in Estonia on Thursday, injuring a total of nine people. Three of the incidents involved e-scooters.
The first accident occurred at 8:15 a.m. in Tallinn at the intersection of Vääna Street and Pärnu Highway, where a 60-year-old woman driving a Kia Sportage made a left turn and hit an eight-year-old boy who was crossing the road on a scooter at a crosswalk. The child was taken to the hospital, the Police and Border Guard Board informed BNS.
The second accident took place at 1:40 p.m. on Sõpruse Avenue in Tallinn, where a 17-year-old youth riding an electric scooter lost control of the vehicle and fell. The young man was transported to the hospital.
At 4:12 p.m., an accident happened in Nabala village, Harju County, where a Mercedes driven by a 43-year-old man struck a 76-year-old man who was riding a bicycle. The cyclist was taken to the hospital.
In the evening, at 7:31 p.m., a 30-year-old man riding an electric scooter fell on Raadiku Street in Tallinn and was injured. Paramedics took him to the hospital.
At 8:17 p.m., a Honda motorcycle and a Ford passenger car collided on Narva Highway in Tallinn. The 38-year-old man driving the motorcycle was injured in the accident and taken to the hospital. The 67-year-old woman behind the wheel of the Ford was not injured.
In Kohtla-Järve, Ida-Viru County, a 58-year-old man showing signs of alcohol intoxication fell while riding his bicycle on Toome Avenue at 9:04 p.m. The cyclist required hospital treatment.
At 10:31 p.m. on Tammsaare Road in Tallinn, a 21-year-old man driving a Volvo veered into the oncoming lane and collided with an approaching Škoda passenger car, driven by a 45-year-old man. The Volvo driver was transported to the hospital.
The last accident of the day occurred at 10:41 p.m. on Ehitajate Road in Tallinn, where a BMW driven by a 19-year-old man rear-ended a Mercedes-Benz. Both drivers, the young man in the BMW and the 59-year-old woman driving the Mercedes, were taken to the hospital.

Aboutorabi-Fard said today's world was witnessing fundamental developments and that the voices of dissatisfaction among nations and governments were being heard louder than ever.
Referring to developments at the UN General Assembly, he cited the departure of 77 delegations during the speech by the Israeli prime minister as evidence of what he described as the changing global political landscape.
Aboutorabi-Fard also pointed to the growing political awakening among people worldwide, the Islamic world’s return to its religious and moral identity, the growing strength of the resistance front, and what he described as major victories by Islamic resistance forces against the United States, Israel and Western-aligned powers.

Aboutorabi-Fard said the peoples of the region and the world have witnessed the consequences of “American democracy” for the region, including the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Muslim men, women and children in Afghanistan and Iraq.

The Tehran Friday prayer leader said the U.S.-led system of global power had pursued dominance and warfare under the banner of democracy, freedom and human rights since the beginning of the 19th century.
Aboutorabi-Fard also said the United States had supported authoritarian governments for nearly two centuries and noted that Israel currently received the largest share of U.S. military assistance.
Referring to Iran and the broader resistance front, Aboutorabi-Fard said the resistance of Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Lebanon, Gaza, Palestine, Yemen and other parts of the Muslim world marks the beginning of the end of the U.S. presence in the region.
Aboutorabi-Fard said the United States and its allies had learned this lesson from the Iranian people, as well as from Iran’s police forces, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Army.

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister and Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) founder C Joseph Vijay stopped at a tea shop during his roadshow in Madurantakam on Friday, interacted with people and had tea with them, as he campaigned for his party’s candidate ahead of the October 6 bypoll.A video shared by news agency PTI showed Vijay stepping out of his campaign vehicle and stopping at the tea shop. He was seen interacting with people gathered there and having tea with them.
The chief minister was in Madurantakam to seek votes for TVK nominee Maragatham Kumaravel, who is contesting the bypoll to the Assembly constituency. Vijay’s campaign also saw him drive a tractor through agricultural fields during his visit to a village near the town.
Vijay drives tractor during campaign
Vijay’s motorcade came to a halt near a village when he spotted a farmer operating a tractor by the roadside. The chief minister, dressed in a white shirt and dhoti, got down from his campaign vehicle and walked towards the fields to speak to the farmer, who welcomed him.Vijay then took the driver’s seat and drove the tractor across the slushy fields for a few minutes. He later brought it out onto the main road, where people waiting nearby greeted him.
Vijay is known for driving vehicles at official events. His decision to drive a tractor came amid his campaign for the October 6 bypolls.
Vijay covers over 30 villages in roadshow
The TVK chief held a roadshow across Madurantakam, covering more than 30 villages and a cluster of neighbourhoods in the Assembly constituency, around 100 km from Chennai.
People gathered outside their homes and along roads in villages and semi-urban neighbourhoods to catch a glimpse of Vijay. He waved at them, greeted them with folded hands and sought votes for the party.TVK workers also organised cultural programmes and dance performances at town squares for people waiting to see the chief minister.
Bypolls in Madurantakam, Dharapuram on October 6
The bypolls in Madurantakam and Dharapuram were necessitated after legislators Maragatham Kumaravel and P Sathyabama resigned from their Assembly seats and quit the AIADMK. Both subsequently joined the ruling TVK and have been renominated from their respective constituencies.Opposition parties have accused the ruling party of horse-trading, making it a key issue in the bypoll campaign.Polling for both constituencies will be held on October 6.

Ethiopian gov’t-aligned group claims close to full control of Tigray region
Claim comes as violence flares across northern Ethiopia, provoking diplomatic spats amid a deteriorating humanitarian situation for millions.
Eritrea severs diplomatic ties with Ethiopia in row over Tigray
An armed group aligned with the Ethiopian government has said it is close to gaining full control of the conflict-stricken northern Tigray region.
The commander of the Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) declared on social media late on Thursday that Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces had been wiped out.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises

The claim, which could not be immediately verified by Al Jazeera, came after fighting resumed between Ethiopian federal forces – including the TPF – and an opposition alliance led by the TPLF in September.
Residents told the Reuters news agency on Friday that Ethiopian government forces were closing on the region’s capital Mekelle.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack “in due course”.
Pro-government forces have made quick advances into Tigray since fighting erupted last week. The return of the hostilities follows the apparent collapse of a 2022 peace deal that ended the war between the federal government and forces from the Tigray region.
Seven armed and political groups announced an alliance on September 20 aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s administration and establishing an inclusive transitional government.
The African Union reported last month that Tigrayan forces had seized airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and detained federal personnel, disrupting civilian air services.
Fighting has also spread from southern Tigray to the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions.
The remarks from the commander of the Tigray Peace Forces “shed light on a new phase of this conflict,” reported Al Jazeera Arabic Ethiopia Bureau Chief Mohammed Taha Tawakel.
The federal army is clearly providing full support to the TPF, yet the original TPLF still holds several towns, he said, but maintains a strong link with Eritrea along more than 800 kilometres of frontier.
“That raises the prospect of the conflict increasingly becoming an internal struggle among Tigrayans themselves,” Tawakel noted.
Ethiopian military officials have accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting the Tigrayan-led fighting alliance. That has led to tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt.
The African Union has called for “maximum restraint” between the three countries and for them to “refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace”.
Eritrea and Egypt have denied accusations that they are backing efforts to destabilise Ethiopia.
Meanwhile, the conflict is provoking a worsening humanitarian situation in Tigray.
”The region is home to between six and seven million people, living amid electricity cuts, internet blackouts and a total lack of communications,” Tawakel said.
Some civilians, fearing the fighting could move into major urban centres, have already begun fleeing to Amhara and Afar, he reported.
Aid agencies, including the United Nations, have managed to relocate some operations to newly secured areas, he added, in an effort to maintain a minimum level of humanitarian access.

EU current account surplus drops to $90B in Q2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:27:38 UTC
21:27:38 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The EU current account balance recorded a surplus of €80.2 billion ($90 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, shrinking from the previous quarter, according to official data.
This figure accounted for 1.6% of the bloc's gross domestic product, decreasing from a surplus of €98 billion, or 2% of GDP, in the first quarter, Eurostat announced on Friday.
In the second quarter of 2025, the EU recorded a current account surplus of €91.7 billion, which also represented 2% of GDP.
The surplus in the goods account fell to €62.9 billion in the second quarter, down from €63.6 billion in the previous three-month period.
The services account surplus also dropped to €41.7 billion during the same period, compared to €48.1 billion in the first quarter.
Eurostat data showed the primary income account surplus narrowing to €0.8 billion from €15.7 billion.
The secondary income account deficit decreased to €25.2 billion from €29.3 billion in the preceding quarter.
The capital account deficit widened significantly to €16.2 billion in the second quarter, up from €1.7 billion in the first quarter of the year.

US suspends consular services before Brazil vote, citing security
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 - The United States suspended consular services at its embassy and consulates in Brazil on Friday in advance of that country's presidential election, citing unspecified security concerns.
The State Department did not elaborate on the security issues or link them to Sunday's election. The department did not immediately return a request for more information.
"Consular Services in the US Embassy and Consulates in Brazil will be suspended starting Friday, October 2 due to security concerns," it said in a statement Thursday. "US citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other US diplomatic facilities."
There was no information on when the consular services would resume.
Brazilians will vote for president on Sunday in a race that will determine whether Latin America's largest nation follows the conservative shift that has swept the region or charts its own course.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has warned of foreign interference in the election, including fresh tariffs from Washington. Violent crime has also dominated the list of voter concerns in election polls, prompting candidates to pledge tougher security measures. REUTERS

AKP ‘stands tall,’ Erdoğan says amid fund crisis

21:22:40 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has said his ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) remains strong amid a financial scandal involving investment funds and the resignation of a senior party official.
“Don’t worry, we stand tall. We will stand firm, but we will not become confrontational,” Erdoğan said on Oct. 1 at an AKP event in Istanbul.
His remarks came after AKP deputy chair Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya resigned from her party posts Sept. 26 following allegations involving stock transactions.
“In recent days, some have launched a campaign of attacks against our party, taking advantage of negative incidents on which we have clearly stated our position,” Erdoğan said.
“They are trying every possible way to tarnish this spotless movement. I leave these immoral people, who turn every opportunity they get into a weapon of attack, to the judgment of our nation.”
Sayan Kaya and her husband, İlyas Kaya, have faced allegations of making large gains from shares in shipbuilder Özata Denizcilik shortly before broader turmoil hit financial markets.
“Basing their actions on isolated cases, they have adopted an extremely ugly and irresponsible attitude that also targets our values. They are basely attempting to cast aspersions on millions of our people,” Erdoğan said.
The wider crisis has shaken Türkiye’s financial markets and prompted authorities to investigate alleged irregularities involving investment funds. Türkiye’s Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered the liquidation of 131 funds on Sept. 17, affecting about 455,000 individual investors, according to figures reported by Turkish authorities.
Erdoğan urged AKP supporters to ignore what he described as attacks on the party and continue working.
“Our nation already sees with its wisdom and common sense what is being attempted,” he said. “As always, we are not giving these people any attention; we are getting on with our work.”
He also said the AKP and its nationalist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) would continue their political path with greater strength.
“If we have left our mark on Türkiye’s last 25 years, God willing, we will also leave our mark on the next quarter century and the next 100 years,” Erdoğan said.

The world through the lens of Italian photographer Olivo Barbieri
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:20:48 UTC
21:20:48 KST

Olivo Barbieri says he has been photographing for nearly fifty years. He is reticent about revealing his preferred cameras and lenses, shrouding his methods in an air of mystery: “I have made use of every possibility that technology has successively made available, from 8x10 inch analogue to 150 megapixel digital”.
His New York gallery suggests he has used a large-format analogue camera as a starting point for his magic.
The Italian photographer’s view of Türkiye’s ancient past is part of an exhibition at Borusan Contemporary.
The exhibition running until mid-August next year also features works spanning his stellar career.
His Türkiye photographs, commissioned by Borusan Contemporary under the heading Time Space Geometry, depict nine archaeological sites in Türkiye, including Ephesus, Aphrodisias, Hierapolis and Laodikeia.
Barbieri, born in Carpi, Italy, in 1954, now lives in Modena. He is known in international art circles for challenging how we look at images.
He has photographed around the world, from China to the US, from the Alps to Capri, from New York to Istanbul, and from Niagara Falls to Victoria Falls, always finding something new for viewers to notice even if we think we already know the subject of the photograph.
His Time Space Geometry is one of two exhibitions currently running at Borusan Contemporary, housed in Perili Kosk – or “Haunted Mansion” – and serving as Borusan Holding’s headquarters during the workweek and an art space at weekends.
Rather than hanging in a sterile gallery with bare white walls, Barbieri’s photographs are scattered around office spaces overlooking the Bosphorus.
Borusan Contemporary is concurrently hosting Haunted. A single ticket provides access to both exhibitions.
The exhibition also includes a photograph of Istanbul taken from a helicopter in 2011, part of Barbieri’s site specific_ series.
“Istanbul is an ancient city rich in historical vestiges. It is a place of connection between East and West – or West and East – and a potential point of equilibrium in dialogue with Rome, New York, and Shanghai,” he says.
‘Image of reality’
Curator Firat Arapoglu says Barbieri’s photographs “begin with recognizable subjects—a city, an archaeological site, a mountain, a waterfall—but very quickly turn into questions about perception”.
According to Arapoglu, Barbieri connects the geographically distant locations of the different series he has produced “through a single question: How is the world transformed by the way we look at it?”
Barbieri says it all goes back to the late 1990s, when he was “annoyed” by claims that suggested photography was a depiction of reality, “something that was almost never true”.
So he set out to prove them wrong.
“Using the technique of selective focus, I devised a process that allowed me to indicate the starting point for reading the image, much like a page of text,” he says.
“It was only then that I realised the image of reality was transforming into a scale model, a maquette.”
His technique, perfected over the years, has resulted in “a novel way of interpreting the visible world”. Barbieri says he later started using helicopters “to see what would happen from a floating vantage point”.
When asked what he would say to a visitor encountering Barbieri’s work for the first time, Arapoglu says: “I would first tell the visitor not to concentrate only on what Barbieri has photographed, but on how he makes us look at it. That distinction is fundamental.”
Arapoglu believes that describing Barbieri’s manipulation of “focus, scale, perspective, and colour, particularly through the selective-focus strategies associated with his site specific_ project” simply as a “miniature effect” would be misleading.
He brings up the ancient sites in Türkiye that Barbieri was commissioned to photograph: “What he gives us is not a ‘better view’ of antiquity. He gives us an unfamiliar view of something excessively familiar.”
When asked whether he makes any modifications or corrections to the images before he prints them on a massive inkjet printer, Barbieri says: “I never intentionally alter the form of the object or subject being depicted. These interventions serve only as tools to subliminally emphasize potential hidden meanings within the image.”
He adds: “Very often, I do nothing.”
Does Barbieri have an idea of the final image in his head as he takes a photograph, or does the initial output guide him?
The photographer says: “I always have an ideal image in mind that I want to create, but it is rarely the right one. During the shooting and selection process, I almost always discover something unexpected that surpasses my initial intent.
“This is the most interesting aspect of the practice.”
Olivo Barbieri’s Time Space Geometry exhibition, so named because “the sites depicted were built according to precise mathematical laws”, can be viewed at Borusan Contemporary on Saturdays and Sundays from 10 am to 7 pm.
Barbieri adds that these laws, “in the form of artworks, appear as technological images, algorithms from the past” and are “the necessary completion of the site specific_ project” that he began in 2003.

From Ottoman 'rocket man' to lunar mission: How did Türkiye’s long road into space begin?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:18:01 UTC
21:18:01 KST

On a festive night in 1633, as Istanbul celebrated the birth of Kaya Sultan, the daughter of Ottoman Sultan Murad IV, an inventor known as Lagari Hasan Celebi is said to have mounted a seven-branched rocket packed with gunpowder paste on the shores of the Bosphorus.
When the powder burned out, as the story goes, he opened a pair of wings he had built himself, descended into the sea in front of the Sinan Pasha mansion and swam back to shore.
The episode is recorded by 17th-century Ottoman traveller Evliya Celebi in his Seyahatname, or Book of Travels.
Nearly four centuries on, the “rocket man” gives his name to a satellite and space museum operated by Turksat, Türkiye’s state-owned satellite operator.
Decades earlier, in 1577, the Ottoman astronomer Takiyuddin established the landmark Istanbul Observatory, where he conducted astronomical observations and developed instruments for measuring celestial movements. Equipped with a large armillary sphere, mechanical clocks capable of measuring time in seconds, and other precision instruments of his own design, the facility ranked among the most advanced of its age.
From observatories and early experiments in flight to satellites and human spaceflight, Türkiye’s relationship with the sky has evolved dramatically.
From Oct. 5 to 9, the country’s space program will be on show before the global space community, when the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) opens in the Turkish resort city of Antalya.
It is the first time the annual gathering, organized by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), is being held in Türkiye.
The 1990s brought Türkiye's first major step into satellite communications.
Turksat 1B was launched in August 1994, becoming Türkiye's first communications satellite, followed by Turksat 1C in 1996.
The country's ambitions increasingly shifted from operating satellites made elsewhere toward designing and building spacecraft itself.
RASAT, launched in 2011, was the country's first domestically developed Earth-observation satellite, while GOKTURK-2, launched in 2012, became Türkiye's first high-resolution Earth-observation satellite.
In 2023, IMECE, a high-resolution Earth-observation satellite designed and built by TUBITAK UZAY, the country's space research institute, was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from California. According to the institute, it featured Türkiye's first space-compatible electro-optical camera, along with domestically developed electric propulsion, star trackers, reaction wheels and other key systems.
TURKSAT 6A, launched in 2024, became Türkiye's first domestically developed communications satellite, putting the country among 11 countries with the capability to build their own.
The turning point came on Dec. 13, 2018, when a presidential decree set up the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) under the Ministry of Industry and Technology. Its mandate included preparing and implementing the National Space Program and setting longer-term priorities for space and aerospace science and technology.
That program was unveiled in 2021 with a 10-year vision.
Its goals included reaching the Moon, developing a globally competitive commercial satellite brand, establishing a regional positioning and timing system, creating independent access to space and a spaceport, improving astronomical observation and space-object tracking capabilities, as well as developing a domestic space industry and technology-development zone. A human space mission was also included among the program's objectives.
The first major public milestone arrived sooner than some of the longer-term goals.
In 2024, Alper Gezeravci became the first Turkish citizen to travel to the International Space Station, spending 18 days in orbit as part of Axiom Mission 3. He carried out 13 scientific experiments prepared by Turkish universities and research institutions.
Four months later, Tuva Cihangir Atasever conducted a suborbital research flight, carrying out seven scientific experiments.
The most ambitious item on that list is now within reach.
In mid-September, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir announced that production, assembly and system integration of Türkiye's first lunar spacecraft had been completed.
The roughly 3.5-ton vehicle was developed under the leadership of TUBITAK UZAY as part of the Lunar Research Program, known by its Turkish acronym AYAP. It has been handed over to the Space Systems Integration and Test Center (USET) at Turkish Aerospace (TUSAS) for system-level environmental testing.
According to Kacir, more than 80% of the vehicle was produced domestically, and all of its software was written in Türkiye.
Once testing is over, it will be shipped to the Kennedy Space Center in the US for launch, as the lift-off is planned for the first months of 2027.
After a journey of about two months, the spacecraft is expected to settle into a circular polar orbit some 100 kilometers above the lunar surface and operate there for at least three months. A hybrid propulsion system developed in Türkiye is to handle its maneuvers, including a controlled descent to the surface at the end of the mission.
Kacir said the program, launched in early 2022, had reached 77% completion, with more than 200 engineers contributing.
Noting that only eight countries have so far carried out a Moon mission, the minister said: "With our Lunar Research Program, which we will carry out with our own engineering capabilities, we aim to become the ninth."
Under the 2021 road map, this mission is the first phase. A second phase envisages a launch on a national rocket and a soft landing on the Moon.
Türkiye also wants to be able to put its own satellites into orbit from its own launch site.
Last year, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced that Türkiye plans to build a spaceport in Somalia under agreements signed between the two countries. He made the announcement at a joint news conference in Istanbul with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.
Minister Kacir said feasibility studies had identified Somalia as the most suitable location. He cited its proximity to the equator, its ocean coastline, weather that allows launches year-round and low air and sea traffic.
The feasibility and design work had been completed and first-phase construction had begun, he said, adding that the site would serve both national needs and the commercial launch market.
As for rockets, defense company Roketsan is developing a Micro Satellite Launch System designed to place satellites of at least 100 kilograms into a 400-kilometer orbit.
The country's space ambitions is being backed by a growing budget. Under the 2026 central government budget, Türkiye allocated a record 8.729 billion liras to space and aviation activities this year, up from 5.052 billion liras in 2025.
In December 2025, TUA President Yusuf Kirac was unanimously elected council chair of the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO) for 2026-2027. He is the first Turkish representative to hold the post.
Ankara has also stepped up its space diplomacy. On Aug. 31, Kacir signed the Artemis Accords at NASA headquarters in Washington. That made Türkiye the 71st signatory to the US-led set of principles for peaceful and sustainable exploration of the Moon and beyond.
The signing came just weeks before Türkiye hosts its first International Astronautical Congress.
From Oct. 5 to 9, Antalya will host the 77th International Astronautical Congress, the world’s largest space gathering, marking the first time the event has been held in Türkiye.
Organizers expect more than 10,000 registered participants, including space agency chiefs from around the world, industry executives, engineers, scientists and students. This year's theme is The World Needs More Space.
The event is hosted by Türkiye's national space agency TUA and co-hosted by SAHA, a Turkish defense and aerospace industry cluster.

“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push, that the door was right there,” he said.

Machchhar, who has 17 years of aviation experience – 11 as a captain – described the moment he realised the plane was going down while he was lying injured.
He told Modi that during the ordeal, he had recited a Hindu devotional prayer dedicated to the deity Hanuman.

He said years of aviation experience allowed him to understand what was happening even while he was wounded.

Passengers described rushing into the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane suddenly plummeted – losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.

“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew, ‘Kill me, kill me’,” Netanyahu told US media, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.
The Israeli leader identified the co-pilot as an Omani national and said Israel would check how he had been cleared to work on flights to the country.
“We have constraints that say that you can’t have pilots from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Obviously he was able to go through that,” Netanyahu told Fox News.
Flydubai has suspended flights to and from Israel since the attack, leaving some Israelis stranded in the UAE.
Israel’s flag carrier El Al is planning replacement flights to bring them home but was forced to cancel them on Oct 2, saying the Emirati authorities had not given landing permission.
“As soon as approval is received from the authorities, we are prepared to carry out the special flights to Dubai and return the Israelis home as soon as possible,” El Al said in an online notice. AFP

Global food prices hit four-year high in September: FAO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:16:11 CST
21:16:11 KST

ROME, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Global food prices rose in September to their highest level in nearly four years amid disruptions to logistics and concerns over weather conditions, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said Friday.
The FAO Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points in September, up from a revised 134.0 points in August and reaching its highest level since November 2022.
The FAO benchmarks for cereal, sugar and vegetable oil prices all increased last month, while meat and dairy prices declined.
FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea, combined with climate shocks, were putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities.
If sustained, such pressures could eventually be passed on to consumer food prices, particularly in countries dependent on food and energy imports, Torero said.
Concerns over a severe El Nino weather pattern pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while disruptions to Black Sea trade amid the conflict drove wheat futures to a three-year peak in early September, according to the FAO.
The FAO forecast global cereal production in 2026 at 2.979 billion metric tons, broadly unchanged from its previous forecast. The figure is 2.1 percent below the 2025 level but would still be the second-highest on record.
The FAO also cut its forecast for global cereal trade in 2026/27 by 0.7 percent from September, citing lower expectations for wheat and maize exports amid constrained shipping routes in the Black Sea. ■
