Asian Games | China misses women's football podium after defeat to South Korea
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:16:07 CST
21:16:07 KST

Yuan Cong (C) of China competes during the women's 3rd place match of football between China and South Korea at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Fukuroi of Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng)
SHIZUOKA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China lost 1-0 to South Korea in the women's football bronze medal match after conceding an early goal on Friday, finishing fourth at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
It was China's second-worst result in Asian Games history, better only than its fifth-place finish at the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon, South Korea. It was also the third time China has failed to win a medal in the event.
In the semifinals, China conceded twice from set pieces in a 2-0 loss to the DPR Korea, while South Korea also suffered a 2-0 defeat to Japan.
Just four minutes into Friday's bronze medal match, South Korea earned a free kick on the right. After a series of headers inside the box, Noh Jin-young headed the ball home to give South Korea an early lead.
Both teams struggled to establish control in a scrappy first half. China's best chance came in the 17th minute when Wang Yanwen won possession and crossed into the middle of the box, but Shao Ziqin's shot sailed over the crossbar.
After the break, China head coach Ante Milicic brought on forward Wurigumula to replace midfielder Wang Aifang in an attempt to increase the tempo and strengthen the attack.
In the 70th minute, Wang Shuang cut inside from the right and fired a shot that struck the crossbar. Six minutes later, Shao Ziqin played a diagonal ball behind the defense, sending Wurigumula through on goal, but the forward's shot went wide.
Milicic brought on tall forward Yuan Cong for Wurigumula in the 79th minute as China increasingly resorted to aerial attacks, but failed to create a clear-cut chance.
South Korea came close to doubling its lead in the 88th minute when its forward broke through for a one-on-one opportunity, but China's goalkeeper Xiao Zitong came off her line to avert the danger.
South Korea held on for a 1-0 victory.
China had 10 shots, three on target, and 46 percent possession, compared with South Korea's nine shots, two on target, and 54 percent possession.
Asked about China's repeated concessions from set pieces, Milicic blamed the quality of training, the players' defensive ability and luck.
"When a team concedes in the same way repeatedly, it is inevitable that the defense will become nervous. This has taught all of us a very good lesson about the importance of set pieces. At the same time, we created many chances but failed to turn them into goals," said Milicic.
"If you understand football, we absolutely shouldn't have lost this game. But we were punished by a set piece at the very beginning and failed to take our chances. That's football, and that's the frustrating part. We will learn from this and make sure the same mistakes don't happen again," he added.
Chinese captain Wu Haiyan said: "Failure to finish on the podium this time is a regret. I just told the younger players that I hope this can become a valuable experience for them, because the road ahead may be even tougher for them than it has been for us." ■

France weighs emergency oil release as US pressure mounts ahead of G7 call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:49 UTC
21:15:49 KST

France is set to present a plan to release emergency oil stocks following US pressure, with Paris considering a combined release of crude oil and diesel. President Emmanuel Macron will hold a G7 call on Friday.
France is considering releasing emergency oil stocks to ease soaring diesel prices and address supply concerns, according to three EU diplomats.
The idea was floated at a meeting between the European Commission and EU countries on Friday morning, shortly after French President Emmanuel Macron spoke with US President Donald Trump about the global energy situation.
According to the diplomats, France has not yet made a formal proposal but suggested releasing 50 million barrels of diesel alongside another 50 million barrels of crude oil from the International Energy Agency's (IEA) emergency stocks.
"The US demanded 100 million barrels, but the EU is not accepting, and France proposed the 50 + 50 formula," one EU diplomat told Euronews.
The US has been pressing European countries to release more strategic oil reserves as Washington seeks to contain rising fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, with the Trump administration also considering a diesel export ban.
US energy secretary Chris Wright previously suggested the EU release 120 million barrels from its stockpiles over three months as an alternative to a dramatic US diesel export ban.
Macron has previously described a potential US diesel export ban as "catastrophic", with France among the countries expected to be most affected.
Brent crude prices rose above $100 a barrel on 1 October, driven by the deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East and China's suspension of fuel exports.
Following Friday's energy meeting, the European Commission said the EU was "ready for collective action", while stressing that the IEA would be responsible for organising any potential stock release.
The proposed split between diesel and crude is significant because diesel can reach consumers more quickly, while crude would first need to be refined into fuel.
Any release would also require coordination among countries participating in the IEA's emergency stock system.
A G7 leaders' videoconference will take place on Friday afternoon, with France currently holding the group's presidency.
"The aim is to coordinate measures to help ease price pressures and guarantee supplies of crude oil and refined products — both among G7 nations and globally," the Elysée said.

ZAGREB, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Croatia's inflation accelerated to 4.7 percent year-on-year in September, mainly driven by energy price hikes, the Croatian Bureau of Statistics said on Friday.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.9 percent, up from 0.3 percent in August. Energy prices were the main driver of inflation, rising 20.5 percent year-on-year amid supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Prices of services increased 7.6 percent, while prices of food, beverages and tobacco edged up 0.2 percent.
According to Eurostat, Croatia's annual inflation stood at 4.3 percent in September, up from 3.7 percent in August. Meanwhile, inflation in the euro area as a whole accelerated to 3.8 percent in September from 3.2 percent in August.
Croatia's inflation has been among the highest in the euro area in recent years, but the gap has narrowed in the last few months. Finance Minister Tomislav Coric said earlier that the government expects inflation to match the euro area average in the first quarter of 2027. ■

Kyrgyzstan's first national satellite launched into orbit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:15:36 CST
21:15:36 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Kyrgyzstan's first national satellite was launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the United States, on Oct. 1 local time, according to a statement published by the official website of the president of Kyrgyzstan on Friday.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov attended the satellite's launch ceremony during a working visit to the United States. The satellite was launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket operated by the U.S. company SpaceX, the statement said.
The satellite was launched into orbit as part of a group of spacecraft carried by a single launch vehicle. The satellite will be controlled from a center in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, it said.
Data obtained from the satellite will enable the monitoring of agricultural land, glaciers, water bodies, forests and pastures, as well as changes in natural ecosystems, the statement said.
Satellite technologies will be particularly important for the monitoring and early detection of natural hazards, it added, noting that the data obtained will enable the faster detection of signs of droughts, floods, landslides, mudflows and forest fires, creating additional opportunities for timely response and mitigation of potential damage.
In the future, satellite data will be integrated into the country's government digital systems and used to create spatial maps and analytical models. This will enable the use of objective data in government decision-making, investment planning and monitoring the implementation of state programs, the statement said. ■

America moves guided missile destroyer to Europe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:15:33 BST
21:15:33 KST

The U.S. Navy destroyer USS John Basilone (DDG-122) will move its homeport from Naval Station Mayport, Florida, to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain this autumn, according to U.S. Fleet Forces Command.
The Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer is described by the U.S. Navy as capable of ballistic missile defence, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction operations and integrated air and missile defence. Built by General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine, the ship was commissioned in November 2024, making it one of the newest destroyers in the fleet to be forward deployed to Europe.
At Rota, John Basilone will join the U.S. Navy’s Forward Deployed Naval Forces-Europe, a group of destroyers permanently based in Spain and operating under U.S. Sixth Fleet. The arrangement began in 2014 and 2015 when four destroyers, USS Donald Cook, USS Ross, USS Porter and USS Carney, moved to the Andalusian base as part of the U.S. contribution to NATO ballistic missile defence under the European Phased Adaptive Approach. Their Aegis combat systems and Standard Missile interceptors were intended to provide sea-based protection for Europe against ballistic missile threats from the Middle East.
In June 2022, during the NATO summit in Madrid, Washington and Madrid agreed to increase the number of U.S. destroyers based at Rota from four to six. The expansion has been accompanied by a gradual rotation of ships, with older destroyers returning to the United States and newer hulls taking their place. Ships based at Rota spend more time on station in the Mediterranean, the Black Sea region before 2022, the Baltic and the High North than destroyers deploying from the U.S. East Coast, as they avoid the lengthy Atlantic transit at either end of each patrol.
Naval Station Rota is a Spanish naval base at which U.S. forces operate under a bilateral defence agreement between the two countries. Located near the Strait of Gibraltar, it gives ships quick access to both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and also supports U.S. Navy logistics and maritime patrol aircraft.
The ship’s namesake, Gunnery Sgt. John Basilone, received the Medal of Honor for his actions defending Henderson Field on Guadalcanal in October 1942, when his machine gun section held off repeated Japanese assaults. After returning to the United States to promote war bond sales, he requested a return to combat and was killed on the first day of the landings at Iwo Jima in February 1945. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions there, making him one of the most highly decorated Marines in U.S. history, the U.S. Navy noted. A Gearing-class destroyer, USS Basilone, previously carried his name and served from 1949 to 1977.
U.S. Fleet Forces Command, which announced the move, is responsible for manning, training and equipping more than 125 ships and 1,000 aircraft and supplying combat-ready forces to numbered fleets and combatant commanders around the world.

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board reviews payment schedule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:32 UTC
21:15:32 KST

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, held its second meeting on Oct. 2 to discuss the payment schedule for fund accounts and a draft amendment to the Capital Markets Law.
On Sept. 30, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation.
According to a statement issued after the meeting, the Coordination Board reviewed the work being carried out by relevant institutions on the calculation methodology for net investment amounts under the SPK’s Sept. 30 decisions.
The board also assessed secondary regulations and the payment timetable related to the SPK’s decision on payments.
In addition, the board discussed a draft law amending the Capital Markets Law, which has been under preparation for some time. The statement said instructions had been conveyed to relevant institutions and organizations to finalize the draft.
“The necessary efforts regarding the resolution of problems that have emerged in a specific and limited segment of the fund market will continue swiftly and effectively within the framework of capital markets regulations, with due regard for fairness and justice,” the statement said.
The SPK said on Oct. 30 that payments will be made to investors whose account reconciliations have been completed and will be treated as advances against final liquidation proceeds.
The payments will be calculated based on each investor’s net investment amount determined by the Central Securities Depository (MKK). Investors with net investments below 1 million liras will receive the full amount, while payments for investors with net investments of 1 million liras or more will be capped at 1 million liras.
The liquidation process will begin with money market funds, while other funds will be liquidated according to investor numbers.
According to the SPK, 131 investment funds designated for liquidation hold approximately 826 billion liras in assets across 455,758 investors.
On Oct. 1, Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said in a social media post that stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and the measures being taken would limit the impact of recent developments on the financial system and the real economy.
The measures would also give Türkiye’s capital markets a stronger, healthier and more resilient structure, he said.
Meanwhile, speaking online at S&P Global Ratings’ 6th Annual Global Emerging Markets Conference on Oct. 1, Şimşek said authorities had moved swiftly.
“We acted very quickly. We “quarantined” the troubled portfolio management companies and the relevant funds,” he said.
Şimşek said the main objective was to prevent the problem from spreading to the rest of the financial system.
“Our aim here was to stop the contagion from spreading to the rest of the system, and I believe we have been largely successful in doing so,” he said.
“There has, of course, been a limited impact, but we are not talking about a systemic problem. We will continue to deepen the capital markets,” Şimşek added.

The union alleged that French crews arrived in Porto on Thursday to operate flights in place of striking workers.
The strike, which runs through Tuesday, was called over disputes including schedule stability, seniority-based pay progression and conditions under negotiation for a new enterprise agreement.
A second strike by EasyJet cabin crew is scheduled for Dec. 19-23. ■

EU rejects potential US diesel export ban, warns it could undermine trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:15 UTC
21:15:15 KST

Melike Pala
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The European Commission on Friday rejected any potential US ban on diesel exports, saying such a measure would benefit no one and could undercut the European Union's trust in the US as a "reliable partner."
"We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters in Brussels.
Itkonen said the EU is ready to act collectively through the International Energy Agency (IEA), which she said was responsible for organizing any possible release of oil stocks.
She stressed that the bloc's role is to coordinate member states' positions within the IEA, rather than independently decide on a stock release.
Her comments came after US President Donald Trump said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as his administration considers restricting US diesel exports amid pressure on global refined-fuel supplies.
Itkonen said member states had coordinated their positions at an Energy Union Task Force meeting on Friday and that discussions are continuing with international partners.
She said the EU would remain united in whatever further steps are taken, while declining to specify whether the bloc is considering "retaliatory" measures against Washington.
"We take one step at the time," Itkonen said.
She added the EU currently sees no immediate security-of-supply problem, with oil supplies stable for the time being, but warned that high energy prices are creating an affordability crisis for households and industry.
Paula Pinho, another spokesperson, said France, which holds the G7 presidency this year, intends to convene a video conference of G7 leaders "as soon as possible" to coordinate measures aimed at easing energy price pressures and guaranteeing supplies of crude oil and refined products.
She said EU coordination groups had been closely monitoring energy markets for months and that gas prices in Europe had risen by 140% since the end of February, when the US and Iran launched their war on Iran, while diesel prices had doubled.

Ethiopia: African Union must convene emergency session on Ethiopia as new conflict expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:14:42 UTC
21:14:42 KST

The African Union must convene an emergency session on the situation in northern Ethiopia as the latest armed conflict which broke out in the Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions on 21 September expands, Amnesty International said today.
Since the outbreak of fresh fighting, the organization has continued to receive credible reports of destruction of civilian objects through shelling and air strikes, intensified forced conscription, and other acts that may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law.
“The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
“The starting point is for the Peace and Security Council to urgently convene an emergency session on the situation in Ethiopia. This is especially critical as fears of regionalisation of the conflict are on the rise”.
The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late.
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The fighting between Tigrayan forces and their allies on one side, including Amhara Fano forces, and the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and its allies, on the other, has significantly intensified across southern Tigray and the Northern Amhara and Western Afar regions since it began a week ago. In addition to the extensive use of heavy weaponry, the renewed hostilities have involved intensified aerial attacks across Tigray including in the town of Axum and the regional capital Mekelle.
Amnesty International is particularly alarmed by reports that civilian infrastructure, including several schools, has been damaged or targeted during aerial attacks. Fighting involving heavy weapons in and around the towns of Maychew and Alamata has reportedly resulted in civilian casualties and further endangered critical civilian infrastructure.
The disruption of communication services across Tigray, and parts of Afar and Amhara regions combined with increasing restrictions on civic space by the Ethiopian government, raises serious concerns that grave human rights violations could occur under the cover of darkness, hidden from independent monitoring.
“Disrupting communications in conflict-affected areas is a well-documented pattern in Ethiopia’s armed conflicts. Such restrictions have frequently concealed atrocities and isolated civilians from the outside world. We call on all relevant authorities to immediately restore access to communications services and ensure civilians are not cut off from life-saving information and assistance at this critical time,” said Tigere Chagutah.
The current outbreak of conflict in Tigray and the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions comes on the backdrop of six years of persistent armed conflict across Ethiopia, including in the Oromia region. These armed conflicts have devastated communities across the country with most of the armed actors involved in the fighting linked to serious violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. Yet, despite the scale and gravity of these abuses, meaningful and independent accountability remains largely absent.
Disrupting communications in conflict-affected areas is a well-documented pattern in Ethiopia’s armed conflicts. Such restrictions have frequently concealed atrocities and isolated civilians from the outside world. We call on all relevant authorities to immediately restore access to communications services and ensure civilians are not cut off from life-saving information and assistance at this critical time.
Tigere Chagutah
“Regional and international actors, including the AU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), and the UN, must address the deeply entrenched accountability crisis in Ethiopia. They must take urgent measures to protect civilians from harm, renew efforts to restore independent investigations into serious violations committed by all parties to Ethiopia’s conflicts, and ensure unhindered access for journalists, humanitarian organizations, and human rights monitors,” said Tigere Chagutah.
Background
The Peace and Security Council (PSC) is AU’s standing decision-making body for the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in Africa. During the 2020-2022 armed conflict in Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions, the PSC held its first session on the situation in Ethiopia in November 2021, one year after the conflict began.
The conflict was described by the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE) as ‘one of the deadliest conflicts of the twenty-first century.’ Reports indicate that hundreds of thousands of people died, millions were displaced, and thousands of women and girls were subjected to conflict-related sexual violence and other grave violations.
The conflict was marked by an unprecedented communications blackout as civilians in Tigray were largely cut off from telephone services, internet access, and other forms of communication for more than a year.
Although hostilities formally ended in November 2022, the consequences of the conflict continue to be felt. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people remain unable to return home. Victims of serious violations continue to await truth, justice, and reparations.

RAF Demonstrates NATO First Readiness on Exercise Auxilium Fort
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:13:07 BST
21:13:07 KST

Air power starts long before an aircraft takes off. Behind every sortie is a network of specialists who build, sustain, protect and recover the deployed operating base that makes flying possible.
Exercise Auxilium Fort 26 brought those people together, testing RAF Global Enablement’s ability to deploy, operate and protect air operations in demanding conditions. Running alongside Exercise Cobra Warrior 26-2, the exercise provided a realistic backdrop for RAF personnel and international partners to train together, strengthen interoperability and demonstrate what NATO First in action really means.
From logistics, engineering, communications and catering to medical support, RAF Police, force protection and Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) specialists, teams worked across a deployed operating base to replicate the pressures of modern operations. The exercise covered the full deployed cycle: establishing the operating base, sustaining flying activity, responding to escalating threats, managing incidents and recovering capability.
CBRN scenarios added further complexity, testing how the whole deployed force responds, adapts and continues operating when conditions change. CBRN activity, casualty decontamination, and command decisions demonstrated resilience across the force rather than a single capability in isolation.
International participation was central to the exercise. Personnel from the French Air and Space Force and Service de l’Énergie Opérationnelle trained alongside RAF teams, while Tactical Medical Wing was joined by personnel from the United States Air Force’s 48th Fighter Wing. Observers from the Royal Norwegian Air Force used the opportunity to share lessons, strengthen relationships and build shared understanding across allied forces.
The involvement of the British Army’s 39 Engineer Regiment further demonstrated the value of joint integration, showing how Defence brings specialist capabilities together to support operational output in a challenging environment.
Exercise Auxilium Fort 26 showed that readiness is built by people working as one team and as NATO First.
Training with our allies allows us to share expertise and prepare to operate together when it matters most.
For RAF Global Enablement, enabling air power means more than supporting aircraft. It means deploying at pace, protecting the force, sustaining operations and integrating with partners to keep the RAF ready to fly, fight and win.

Estonia pushes for cybersecurity boost ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:13:00 UTC
21:13:00 KST

Estonia pushes for cybersecurity boost ahead of elections
The government wants to boost investments in cybersecurity, including e‑voting, because attacks against Estonia have become massive. Increasingly, they are also carried out with the help of artificial intelligence.
In March, Estonia faces elections, and voting will again be possible digitally. But technological development has created new risks for the digital state.
"In the past, cybercriminals tried to find security vulnerabilities manually, but now machines do it for them. I must clarify that no fully AI‑based cyberattack has been carried out in Estonia, or at least we have no information about it, but we know of such cases elsewhere in the world," said Information System Authority (RIA) director Joonas Heiter.
Where hacker groups once operated on their own, they now have AI at their disposal, scanning for vulnerabilities on a massive scale. According to Heiter, the number of damaging incidents doubles every year.
But within the government, there is no shared understanding of how to improve the situation. The prime minister said one thing, yet no additional money was added to the state budget.
"The necessary funding exists, and if needed, resources can be shifted within the field," said Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform Party).
"The Justice and Digital Ministry did not receive additional funds. We are making further cuts, but cybersecurity is indeed exceptionally important, so we are looking for coverage from other existing expenses. We will shut something down to improve cybersecurity," said Justice and Digital Minister Liisa‑Ly Pakosta (Eesti 200).
Improving cybersecurity next year would require an additional five million euros. Over four years, more than 20 million.
Pakosta confirmed that even if this money does not come, funding for conducting e‑voting will still be found.
"If necessary, we will take additional money from the government's reserve fund to protect the elections. The elections will be protected. We need both more technology and people who operate that technology," Pakosta said.
If everything truly goes wrong, the election service also has a plan B.
"We are prepared for all special situations, and ultimately there is a plan B that allows us to switch entirely to paper voting if, for any reason, the system can no longer be trusted," said head of the State Electoral Office Arne Koitmäe.

Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

UN rights chief calls for 'decisive shift' toward de-escalation, peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:40 UTC
21:12:40 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday called for a “decisive shift” toward de-escalation and peace in Ukraine, urging renewed negotiations as he warned the war has become a “human rights catastrophe” that is intensifying by the week.
“The conduct of this war to date cannot be allowed to dictate its future. We need a decisive shift towards de-escalation and peace,” Turk told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
He said rebuilding momentum toward negotiations was key, calling for confidence-building measures that could reduce the impact of hostilities on civilians.
Such measures could include an agreement to end attacks on economic targets and energy infrastructure, local ceasefires along the frontlines, enabling civilians to leave Oleshky, and a full exchange of prisoners of war, he said.
Turk urged the international community, particularly states with influence, to take “urgent action to push for a negotiated peace now, before this tragedy becomes even worse.”
The rights chief said his office verified some 15,280 civilians killed and injured across Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026 -- an average of more than 400 every week and 55% higher than during the same period in 2025.
Calling Ukraine a “laboratory for drone warfare,” Turk urged international action to address the “carnage” caused by such weapons worldwide.
He said Russian aerial glide bombs alone killed or injured nearly 2,500 civilians in the first eight months of the year in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia regions, up 62% year-on-year.
Turk also accused Russian forces of increasing attacks on energy infrastructure, supermarkets, food companies and transportation networks.
In Russia, Ukrainian forces have reportedly struck warehouses and logistics centers belonging to major e-commerce companies, as well as oil refineries, he said.
Turk also cited a recent report documenting more than 1,000 cases of conflict-related sexual violence, of which "89% were attributed to Russian authorities and 11% to Ukraine." Most victims were men, particularly in detention, though women and children were also affected, "primarily in occupied Ukrainian territory," according to Turk.
“Alongside peace, there must be accountability,” he said.
The UN rights chief also voiced alarm over human rights violations linked to the presence of fighters from third countries in the war, noting his staff had interviewed "prisoners of war from 29 countries who are held by Ukraine; many said they were deceived into joining the Russian forces."

‘West Bank is Israel’s weak point’: US sanctions pressure grows ahead of Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:37 UTC
21:12:37 KST

Little is expected to change before Israel’s election and the formation of its next government. What follows, according to sources familiar with Israel’s relations with Washington, could depend heavily on the composition of that government.
If the current coalition returns to power, they say, the U.S. approach toward Israel could harden further, potentially including sanctions. They also warn that after the U.S. midterm elections, declining public support for Israel could increasingly translate into concrete congressional action.
“The West Bank is Israel’s weak point in Washington today,” one source familiar with the issue said, citing anger in the United States over settler violence and a growing number of congressional initiatives targeting settlements and individuals involved in them.
Two such initiatives came close to advancing this week.
Six Democratic members of the House of Representatives introduced the Stop the Settlements Act: Joaquin Castro, Madeleine Dean, Don Beyer, Greg Casar, Sara Jacobs and Veronica Escobar.
The legislation would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities involved in establishing or expanding settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, while also banning imports of goods produced there.
According to information provided to Ynet, the initiative has support from nearly 40 Democratic lawmakers, including figures associated with the party’s mainstream rather than only its progressive wing.
Other supporters include Stephen Lynch, Bennie Thompson, Rosa DeLauro, Ro Khanna and Pramila Jayapal.
The bill would require sanctions against foreign actors involved in establishing new settlements or outposts, developing infrastructure for their expansion, construction in the E1 area or facilitating the transfer of civilians into settlements.
Potential penalties include asset freezes, visa restrictions and bans on entry into the United States.
The bill could also apply to individuals involved in maintaining or expanding existing settlements, including through financial and banking sanctions. Under the language described, people who attempt to facilitate such activity or are indirectly involved could also fall within its scope, potentially including officials responsible for planning approvals.
Ministers in the Israeli government, and potentially even the prime minister, could be affected. Provisions concerning infrastructure and E1 construction contain no stated starting date, raising the possibility that they could apply to earlier activity.
U.S. citizens, including settlers with dual citizenship, are exempt. The legislation does not explicitly define the term “settlement,” does not specifically mention East Jerusalem and leaves the final sanctions list to the president.
The proposal is not expected to pass the current Congress, where Republicans hold the majority and President Donald Trump remains in office. Its sponsors, however, are already looking toward the next Congress.
A senior Democratic source told Ynet that the ability of party leaders to prevent such measures from advancing would depend heavily on Israel’s election.
“If the same coalition returns, these proposals will pass Congress,” the source said, presenting that as the source’s assessment of the political trajectory in Washington.
At the same time, a separate resolution led by Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen was narrowly defeated in the Senate this week, 51-47.
The measure invoked Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act and would have required the State Department to submit a report within 30 days on the deaths of nine U.S. citizens in incidents involving Israeli settlers or security forces since 2022, as well as on the detention of Palestinian children.
Had the resolution passed and the administration failed to provide the required report, most covered U.S. security assistance to Israel could have been suspended until the report was submitted.
All Senate Democrats except John Fetterman supported the measure, along with Republican Sen. Rand Paul. Two senators did not vote.
Dr. Kobi Barda, an expert on U.S. politics, reacted to the developments on X: “I don’t even want to think about the blood bath waiting for us after the midterms. I don’t believe we’ve reached the bottom yet.”
Another source of tension is Lt. Gen. Sean M. Salene, the U.S. security coordinator responsible for strengthening security cooperation between Israel and the Palestinian Authority.
According to sources familiar with the matter, Salene has been sending Washington troubling reports about what he views as lawlessness in the West Bank and failures by the IDF and police to address it. Israeli officials dispute that characterization, arguing that information reaching Washington is one-sided and reflects the Palestinian narrative.
The same sources said there is anger within the current U.S. administration over the Israeli government’s handling of the West Bank. They added that U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee should not necessarily be viewed as the best indicator of broader administration policy, arguing that his positions are particularly close to those of the settlement movement.
Another indication cited by the sources is Washington’s muted official response to settlement-related sanctions announced by Britain and other Western governments, as well as British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s accusations of “ethnic cleansing” in parts of the West Bank.
U.S. officials had drafted a statement sharply criticizing the measures, but it was never issued after failing to win support from senior White House and State Department officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would not join the sanctions but stopped short of condemning the countries that imposed them.
For Israeli officials watching Washington, that silence was viewed as a troubling signal.
According to the sources, possible U.S. measures against Israeli military units accused of serious violence against Palestinian civilians also remain under discussion.
The Biden administration previously considered action against the Netzah Yehuda battalion but ultimately declined to impose sanctions after sustained Israeli pressure.
A more severe option described by the sources would restrict the use of U.S.-supplied weapons by particular units or in certain areas.
Another possibility would be placing IDF or police officers on lists of officials with whom the United States would cut contact over alleged involvement, or possible involvement, in settler violence.
“That does not necessarily mean it will happen,” one source said. “But it is on the table.”
The source added that the political situation in Congress surrounding Israel is now “far more serious” than in the past.

Russia’s Drevoch camouflage suit upgraded based on special op experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:34 UTC
21:12:34 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Drevoch camouflage suit has been modernized based on experience gained in the special military operation, enhancing its ability to reduce visibility in the thermal imaging spectrum, the Zavoz.pro company told TASS.
Drevoch was introduced about a year ago as a camouflage suit for units that need to maintain mobility. Unlike capes and ponchos, the suit consists of a jacket and pants and is designed for active movement. Its design allows for movement across rough terrain and through vegetation, while the fine mesh of the base fabric reduces the likelihood of snagging on equipment. "The product was improved based on feedback from Russian service members fighting in the special military operation zone," the company reported.
It noted that one of the main changes was the decision to add a shielding layer made of metallized fabric to the design, which will make the suit easier to use in cold temperatures.
Previously, Drevoch already combined several types of camouflage. For example, its camouflage pattern and three-dimensional 3D texture help conceal a person’s silhouette in the terrain, while the material with infrared properties reduces visibility when observed through night vision devices and thermal imagers.
In addition, Zavoz.pro reported that over a thousand Drevoch suits were delivered during the first year of production. "The upgraded version was released later - about three months ago. During this period, about 500 suits with improved design were delivered," the company stated.

Fakir died due to lack of oxygen says family's lawyer
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:12:15 CEST
21:12:15 KST

Abderrahim Fakir, a 42-year-old Moroccan man who died while being restrained by two policemen in Bologna on July 19, suffocated, the lawyer representing his family, Fabio Anselmo, said Friday after meeting experts commissioned to assess the cause of death. 
    Fakir died after being pinned to the ground face down. 
    Anselmo said the case was like that of Riccardo Magherini, a 39-year-old man who died while being arrested by Carabinieri police in Florence in 2014. 
    Italy was condemned to pay damages by the European Court of Human Rights over Magherini's case earlier this year. 
    "It is a death like that of Riccardo Magherini - hypoxic death due to the prone position," Anselmo said. 
    The lawyer representing the two police officers, who are being probed for manslaughter, said Thursday that toxicology reports showed Fakir had consumed more than a lethal dose of cocaine. 
    Anselmo contested this. 
    "The cocaine is not even a contributing factor; combined with the agitation, it increased the need for oxygen—oxygen of which he was deprived due to the officers holding him in a prone position," he said. 
    The officers' lawyers, Gabriele Bordoni, reiterated the assertion that the cocaine was what killed Fakir. 
    "The primary cause of death by hypoxia is the drug, with the alveolar haemorrhage in the lungs, as I have said ad nauseam for as long as anyone can remember whenever someone claimed that the blood in the lungs was the result of compression," Bordoni said after speaking with his expert witness, medical examiner Matteo Tudini. 
    "Instead, it is the result of excessive cocaine use, which was found at a metabolic level three times higher than the lethal dose". 
    Fakir had recently started treatment for mental-health problems. 
    Fakir was referred to a mental health centre (CSM) after being admitted to the emergency room of Bologna's Maggiore Hospital on June 20 because of a psychiatric issue. 
    He went to the centre in the following days, he was assessed and given an initial diagnosis, and a treatment plan was prepared. 
    He had a follow-up appointment scheduled early in August to continue his treatment. 
    In a video recorded by a local person, Fakir can be held shouting "help" and "enough" as the police try to restrain him, tying his hands and feet together, before he passes out. 
    Other videos have shown that Fakir, who had lived in Italy since he was a child, was in an extreme state of agitation and confusion before the police intervened. 
    Law enforcement had been called to intervene in Bologna's Pilastro quarter because Fakir was suffering from a "psychiatric crisis" and was disturbing the peace and acting erratically, according to initial findings by investigators. 
    He was allegedly threatening people parking a car in a garage. 
    Investigators are also looking into the conduct and four paramedics who were at the scene. 
    Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi has said that he was confident the cops will be cleared of any wrongdoing.

Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:10:00 EEST
21:10:00 KST

Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Russian biker Oleg Lyovushkin, who is linked to a Russian military intelligence officer, may have organised an attempted sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany.
Source: a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the investigation, Lyovushkin presumably organised the attempt to plant explosives at the airport. German investigators believe that Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov was supposed to carry out the plan.
Journalists analysed intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, and also spoke with representatives of Western secret services. According to their data, Lyovushkin and Karshakov arrived in Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect that Lyovushkin conducted reconnaissance of the airport shortly before the attack, after which he instructed Karshakov to execute the plan.
Investigators also found similarities between the incident in Leipzig and other attempted Russian sabotage operations in Poland, Lithuania, and Germany.
Specifically, the explosive device seized in Leipzig was reportedly similar to devices used in other sabotage operations in Europe.
Lyovushkin, who holds a Russian passport and is an avid motorcyclist, is also linked to Denis Smolyaninov, a man Western secret services consider to be one of the coordinators of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
According to Lithuanian intelligence, Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian desk in Russian military intelligence and specialised in psychological operations, among other things. Documents also link him to secret sabotage campaigns in Europe.
It is noted that Lyovushkin and Smolyaninov met back in 2007. Reportedly, they have kin repeated contact over the many years.
German security agencies link the Leipzig attack to GRU Unit 29155, which, according to German intelligence assessments, plays a key role in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
German security agencies assess that the goal of such operations could be to create a sense of insecurity among European society due to its support for Ukraine and to influence the debate on further assistance to Kyiv.
Lyovushkin himself publicly leads an inconspicuous life. He takes part in motorcycle races, travels around Europe, fishes, and skis with his family.
At the same time, journalists claim that this lifestyle may conceal his involvement in Russian sabotage operations in Central Europe.
According to German intelligence, he travelled to Germany via Türkiye this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. Investigators stated that Lyovushkin rented a car at Berlin airport a week before the attack and over the next few days drove it to several locations where weapons were suspected of being stored.
They believe that the explosives used in the operation were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in the cavities of trucks, and were likely temporarily stored along the route.
The journalists say that Lyovushkin's links to the GRU were known at the time he entered the country. However, he was not placed under surveillance upon his arrival.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.
- On 6 September, it was reported that German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser was planning a set of measures to cover protection against drones, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

The UAE’s Technology Innovation Institute (TII) will showcase some 23 demonstrations from its nine applied research centers, as well as sector-specific innovations in energy, marine infrastructure, aerospace and autonomous systems.
The Falcon family of AI large language models (LLMs), especially the Falcon-H1 Arabic model, will be one of the key highlights of the summit.
The event will also address topics like who will control AI amid a rise in autonomous agents and speculative AI policies.

Drone firm linked to Trump sons eyes Ukrainian tech
A US drone company linked to President Donald Trump’s sons wants to bring Ukrainian military technology to America, Reuters has reported, as Kiev pursues billions in arms exports despite multiple corruption scandals in its procurement programs.
Powerus is negotiating with Ukrainian defense firms and wants to manufacture their technology in the US, potentially including long-range attack drones. Its Guardian interceptors, introduced in March, were also jointly developed with Ukrainian partners, according to company president Brett Velicovich.
The company completed a merger with golf course operator Aureus Greenway Holdings on Thursday. Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump hold an indirect investment in Aureus through American Ventures, which regulatory filings projected would own 9.9% of the combined business.
Velicovich, a former US Army Special Operations intelligence analyst, told Reuters he wants Powerus to become a “one-stop solution” for the Pentagon, offering foreign technology with an “American face.”
Company executives and representatives of the brothers say they are passive investors with no operational role. However, Powerus adviser Keith Kellogg, Trump’s former Ukraine envoy, said “it never hurts to have their name on something.”
Powerus has secured a US Air Force contract with a ceiling of $90 million, although purchases are not guaranteed. It has also received an initial Pakistani order for drones and associated support.
Kiev has meanwhile been seeking billions in weapons-export revenue while continuing to rely heavily on Western military and financial assistance. Vladimir Zelensky has announced overseas export hubs and previously touted a proposed US drone agreement worth $10-30 billion.
Kiev’s weapons export ambitions come as multiple corruption scandals have rocked its military procurement system, including programs intended to supply drones to its own forces.
On September 23, Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) announced new charges in a case involving border guard officials and a private supplier. Investigators say a manufacturer won a drone tender by offering a lower price, only for a rival working with officials to demand $1 million to allow the contract and equipment deliveries to proceed.
In a separate investigation, NABU said in August that suspected losses from drone purchases reached approximately $5.7 million. Investigators alleged prices were inflated by 60-90%, competing bids were staged, and illicit proceeds were transferred to company accounts, including abroad.
European officials have also raised concerns over weapons supplied to Kiev disappearing and potentially reaching criminal networks.

Ethiopian forces near Tigray capital, fears grow of wider conflict
Oct 2 - Ethiopian government forces closed in on the capital of the northern rebel stronghold of Tigray on Friday, residents and a diplomat said, as fears grew that fighting could spill into a wider war after Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties.
Banks and shops in the city, Mekelle, were closed with the Ethiopian National Defence Force and allied militiamen reported to be within striking distance, two residents, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Reuters.
Pro-government forces have made quick advances into Tigray since combat erupted last week with a rebel alliance led by the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front, in the worst escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war.
But suspected drone attacks on the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, earlier this week suggested the TPLF and its allies might have better striking capability than previously thought.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military and government did not respond to requests for comment on the reported advance or suspected attacks on Addis Ababa.
ETHIOPIA CLOSES EMBASSY IN ERITREA
Analysts fear the current conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders in an increasingly fragile territory where regional powers are competing for influence. Tigray has Ethiopia's longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west.
Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the opposition alliance - an allegation they have all denied.
On Thursday, Ethiopia said it was closing its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence" and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours.
Eritrea responded by severing all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 and only restored diplomatic relations in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia's federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Relations have since soured, in part over landlocked Ethiopia's public insistence that sea access is vital for its security and economy.
Eritrea says it fears Ethiopia will try to take its Assab port by force. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has said Ethiopia intends to secure sea access through peaceful means.
TPLF THREATENS COUNTER-ATTACK
The federal forces and allied militiamen captured a town about 75 km (50 miles) south of Mekelle, the pro-government Tigray Peace Forces militia said on Thursday. One of the Mekelle residents said they were now within 30 km.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack "in due course".
"We should ensure that Tigray is their graveyard, not their playground," he said in a statement.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's foreign ministry also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, prompting Cairo to respond in kind by expelling an Ethiopian embassy counsellor.
In a statement, the African Union Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise "maximum restraint".
EXPLOSIONS HEARD IN ETHIOPIAN CAPITAL
Ahead of the latest fighting, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other Ethiopian armed groups that say they aim to overthrow Abiy's government.
While the TPLF and allied fighters made some initial gains in the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions, pro-government forces say those have been largely reversed.
Explosions were heard late Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, in what a source linked to the opposition alliance said were drone attacks targeting the ENDF headquarters there and other sites.
Reuters could not independently verify this.
If confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on Addis Ababa, which is hundreds of kilometres from the northern front lines. REUTERS

My Word: The art of resilience - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:59 UTC
21:06:59 KST

If the proverbial picture is worth a thousand words, the Jerusalem Biennale 2026 has too many words to count – many of them prayers, pleas, and thanksgiving.
This is the seventh Jerusalem Biennale since it was founded in 2013, and like its predecessors, it is dedicated to a theme, but individual artists have been literally creative in the way they chose to interpret it.
Jerusalem Biennale founder Ram Ozeri told a press tour last week that he chose the theme “De Profundis,” “Out of the Depths,” or “Mima’amakim” in Hebrew, after the opening words of Psalm 130: “Out of the depths I call You, O Lord.”
It was the psalm many Jewish communities added to their prayers following the horrors of October 7, 2023, the war, and especially the fate of the hostages held in Gaza. Even now, a year after the last living captives returned home, the Hamas-led invasion and mega-atrocity of October 7, when 1,200 were murdered and 251 abducted, continues to haunt us.
Ozeri noted that choosing the Latin “De Profundis” was based on a large bank of works, including the letter by Oscar Wilde in Reading Gaol with the oh-so-quotable: “Where there is sorrow there is holy ground.” Ozeri sees art as a form of prayer, and also as a part of the recovery and healing process – a way of bringing the collective subconscious to the surface.
Displaying works of more than 250 Israeli and international artists in 42 exhibitions across 21 venues throughout the capital, JB2026, running through November 12, is the biggest yet, but was one of the most challenging to assemble.
The Jerusalem Biennale was created to give space to contemporary art, beyond Judaica, mixing with the Jewish and Israeli experience, although not all the artists are Jewish. Despite its starting point in the depths, there is also optimism in JB2026, which Ozeri sees as “creating a dialogue among different communities… celebrating Jewishness rather than hiding it.”
While some artists abroad were afraid of a possible backlash for participating in the event in Israel, others were delighted at the chance to push back against the cultural boycott.
The press tour took place at the Biennale’s main venue at the former National Library at the Hebrew University’s Givat Ram campus. It was a chance to remember the charm of the old building that has been overshadowed since the opening of the new National Library, a nearby architectural gem.
Undoubtedly, the outstanding feature of the building itself is the monumental stained-glass windows created by Mordecai Ardon, three immense panels reflecting Isaiah’s “Vision of Eternal Peace.” Dr. David Sperber and artist Porat Salomon, the curators of the Or Chozer (Reflected Light): An Active Vision exhibition, made good use of Ardon’s work as an impressive backdrop.
Art to bring us out of the depths
There was too much to relate to everything within the constraints of this column, but some sights and insights made a particular impact.
In a combination-confrontation between the old and the new, Isaiah’s Still Waiting, by Andi LaVine Arnovitz, is composed of mounted old-fashioned View-Masters, the black-and-white scenes of the wheel changing with every click of the device, using the light of the windows.
Close to Ardon’s panel depicting the swords turned into plowshares are powerful works by Swiss-born Jerusalem artist Ariane Littman. One component is an “incantation bowl,” reminiscent of the ancient amulets often buried under the entrance to a home as a form of magical protection.
Littman’s bowl is covered with the date 7.10.23, written in spiraling form in red ink. It was the first work she was able to produce, a month and a half after the attack, and she describes it as “a counter-curse of that horrific day.” Next to it, Littman, who works a lot with gauze, has “blood-soaked” (red ink) bandages hanging from meat hooks in a work called “Sanguine Fields.”
Richard McBee has completed 100 paintings in 35 years based on the biblical figures of Abraham and Isaac, and God’s command to the father to sacrifice his son. McBee told the journalists: “After the Holocaust, we Jews are all Isaac,” even more so after October 7, when “the modern world turned its back on Israel.”
The six paintings on display start with the question: “Where is the lamb?” and Abraham’s reply: “God will provide,” and ends with Isaac abandoned, alone, on the mountaintop after the intervention of the angel and the sacrifice of a ram instead. I was struck by the extent to which the “Akeida” was a test of Isaac no less than Abraham.
The One Who Dwells in This House, curated by Shoshana Gugenheim Kedem and Ahuva S. Zaslavsky, is described “as a visual commentary on what it means to grieve, to be marginalized, vulnerable, witnessed, and to return again.”
The curators told the press tour how their Portland, Oregon Jewish community – known for its progressive politics – suffered painful fissures following October 7, like many similar Diaspora communities. A group of local artists grappled with these issues through their Art Lab.
Zaslavsky’s To Move a Mountain II is a work in slow motion. Visitors are invited to scoop soil from a central pile into small linen bags in something that feels like a reverse burial service, while Gugenheim Kedem contemplates loss and grief through works based on burial shrouds.
Abraham’s Children, by artist Mel Brown and curator Ori Z. Soltes, broadens the dialogue even further. Brown described the dilemmas of being a Torah-observant Jew who started working as an artist at a relatively late stage in life. Acutely aware of the Second Commandment not to make a graven image, he produces abstract works on biblical themes.
Together with Soltes’s input, the exhibition extends to include, among others, Muslim artists – including a Turkish father and son in exile, and a painter from the United Arab Emirates. Unlike Christian art, which readily depicts human forms, Muslim and Jewish art have traditionally been non-representational. The result is a reminder of what we have in common.
Czech photographer David Tesinsky, who is not Jewish, said he wasn’t bothered by negative comments and the small number of followers who dropped from his Instagram account. He has seen it in other places he has visited, including Russia, Ukraine, Iran, and Pakistan.
Tesinsky captures street scenes with his camera, and Jerusalemite visitors will recognize places he visited in the capital – including Mahaneh Yehuda, Mea She’arim, and downtown Jerusalem –as part of his The Light Within series.
American artist Rina Nissel Shalhov provides a positive note in her acrylic work, A Sabra is Born. Shalhov, who is married to an Israeli, explained that the desert fruit has become “a symbol of the national pride and patriotism of the Jewish state. The sabra cactus faces tremendous challenges as it struggles to survive in a hostile environment…
“After years of dormancy, the cactus blooms, producing vibrant flowers that eventually transform into bright, vivid fruit. Upon closer inspection, the thick outer skin is covered in prickly bumps and more barbed needles. Only those patient enough to carefully peel back the tough layers will discover the sweetness and complexity hidden within.”
The metaphor is as clear as the blue desert sky above the “prickly fruit” in her painting.
Coming out of the depths, the sky is not the limit: Mexican artist Alejandro Glatt makes a truly uplifting contribution to this year’s Jerusalem Biennale in his Mezuzah to the Moon exhibition. Glatt is as colorful as his artwork and proud of both elements of his Mexican-Jewish identity.
In 2024, a representation of one of his papaya works landed on the moon as part of the Lunaprise mission. Now he aims to similarly elevate one of his striking mezuzot in some form. I can imagine a UN debate on “Jewish colonization” when news of a mezuzah landing on the moon gets out, but as this Biennale proves, the fear of antisemitism should not leave us grounded.
Navigating around Jerusalem at a time of massive construction can feel as challenging as space travel (although Mayor Moshe Lion is credited with helping make this year’s Biennale possible), but planning visits to the multiple venues is a reminder of Jerusalem’s special cultural map.
We have come out of the depths, bearing the scars both physical and emotional, but Glatt’s vision of Jewish art one day landing on the moon left me raising my eyes to the heavens with a sense of hope.

====================================================================================================

AI, fraud, and cyberattacks: What security threats face Israel’s 2026 election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:59 UTC
21:06:59 KST

Israel’s elections may increasingly be surrounded by artificial intelligence, deepfakes, and online disinformation, but the actual process of casting and counting a ballot remains strikingly old-fashioned.
That is intentional, according to attorney Dean Livne, acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
As the country prepares for the 2026 election, the CEC is confronting technologies that were not part of the electoral landscape when Israelis last went to the polls in November 2022.
Generative AI has advanced rapidly since then, creating new opportunities for campaigners, as well as new ways for false information to reach voters.
“What we were doing in 2022... is different from what we’re doing in 2026,” Livne said. “The world is different, and in practice, technological advancement is amazing and surprising.”
But while the technology surrounding elections has changed dramatically, the system responsible for counting the votes remains deliberately physical.
The challenge, he said, is adapting to those technological changes without compromising the integrity of the actual vote.
Local voters still mark a physical paper ballot and place it in a ballot box. From there, the CEC builds multiple layers of verification around that slip of paper.
Livne also emphasized that the results are not simply transmitted from polling stations over the internet.
Instead, once voting ends, they are recorded in a protocol at the polling station. That protocol is then signed by representatives, with the process documented on video.
The physical materials are then transported to a regional election committee.
“And there it goes to a regional judge, who sits and checks whether what happened is really true,” Livne said.
The judge checks the numbers against each other, the number of voters and the number of votes, to ensure that they are consistent.
“It hasn’t happened that there were more votes than the number of voters there; it doesn’t happen, but he still checks it again,” Livne said. “Of course, it’s counted and checked several times.”
Only after those physical checks does the information enter the CEC’s central systems.
And even then, Livne said, the central systems themselves are not connected to the internet.
“It’s up to the security systems of the central polling station, which are secured with military-grade equipment,” he said. “The level of data security and cyber defense that the committee adheres to is unprecedented.”
The public-facing results are separate.
“The only thing that’s available over the internet is a view to the public that is completely separate from our systems, which are not connected to the internet,” Livne said.
The CEC also publishes images of the handwritten protocols alongside the results, allowing the public to compare the physical record with the electronic results.
“So the public can know that what is handwritten on the copy... is what’s in the computer,” Livne said.
The result is a system in which changing a digital number would not, by itself, change the underlying vote. That paper trail also gives the CEC a way to investigate allegations after the fact.
“The moment there is an allegation that, God forbid, there was fraud, the first thing we do is examine the claim,” Livne said. “We examine it on its merits.”
He said that the CEC deploys large teams after elections to examine allegations individually.
“I deploy teams of hundreds of legal professionals immediately after the election to examine every allegation individually,” he said.
The committee has the physical records required to conduct those investigations, he said.
“Because I have all the ballot boxes, all the protocols, and all the photographs, the examination will be very, very fast,” Livne said.
“And there will be an unequivocal answer: Yes or no.”
Livne is confident that most allegations will not withstand that examination.
“And I can already tell you that usually the answer will be no because it is almost impossible to rig elections on that level,” he added.
He then offered a more colorful assessment of the idea that Israel’s elections could be systematically rigged.
“Anyone who believes [these] elections can be rigged can also believe in flat Earth and that birds are CIA drones,” Livne said.
The confidence comes from the number of independent records produced during the voting and counting processes. A claim about a particular polling station can, in principle, be tested against the ballot box, protocol, photographs, signatures, and other documentation generated there.
The information environment around the physical voting process has changed
THE PHYSICAL voting process may have remained largely unchanged, but the information environment around it has not.
Livne said the CEC has been forced to adapt to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, notably generative AI, since the last election.
Israel has amended its election law to address campaign material created or altered using advanced technologies, including AI, and the CEC subsequently established rules for labeling such material.
The issue is particularly significant when artificial content looks real.
As Livne explained, there is a difference between a video that is obviously fictional and one that appears to show a real political figure saying something which that person never said.
The CEC’s response is therefore not limited to labeling requirements. It also wants to make voters more skeptical of what they encounter online.
“Today, whatever you see online or on WhatsApp or anywhere else, doubt if it is true,” Livne said. “Be confused, learn, and come to us.”
The CEC is also preparing for situations in which false information could directly interfere with the election process.
Asked about a hypothetical deepfake released shortly before Election Day showing a major candidate falsely announcing that they had withdrawn from the race, Livne said the CEC would act.
“We deal with the big platforms,” he said.
The committee works with security authorities and the Cyber Agency, he said, and can seek to have false material removed.
The CEC can also warn voters that the material is fake. Livne said that the committee would work to ensure such warnings reached the public.
The CEC’s role becomes more complicated, though, when the threat originates outside the electoral system itself.
Livne declined to discuss specific countries or intelligence assessments, saying that such information is classified. But he described extensive coordination between the CEC and Israel’s security establishment.
“The committee is working in full coordination with the security authorities,” he said, naming the Shin Bet (Israel Security Service), IDF, Israel Police, judiciary, and Prime Minister’s Office.
The CEC, therefore, is protecting a voting process that is deliberately difficult to manipulate electronically, while other government bodies work to identify threats to the broader electoral environment.
That distinction is crucial as technology changes what an election can look like.
Israel is hardly alone in retaining a physical component to elections. Livne noted that much of the world continues to use analog voting or maintains a paper trail because of cyberattack concerns. Even countries using electronic voting can maintain a physical record, which allows the electronic result to be checked.
Israel’s system is particularly suited to paper because voters select a single party list. “With us, you vote very simply,” Livne said. “You vote for one list.”
That makes it possible to keep the voting process relatively simple even as the technological environment surrounding the election becomes increasingly complicated.
The most consequential threats may not necessarily involve the ballot boxes at all
THE IRONY of Israel’s election security system is that the most consequential threats may not necessarily involve the ballot boxes at all.
The CEC has spent decades building layers of protection around the physical vote: paper ballots, signed protocols, photographs, multiple checks, judicial oversight, and an offline central system. But none of those safeguards can tell a voter whether the video they watched on WhatsApp that morning was real.
They cannot determine whether an apparently authentic recording of a candidate was AI-generated. Nor can they stop a voter from making a decision based on deliberately fabricated information before that person walks into a polling station.
That is the increasingly complicated part of election security.
“The world is different,” Livne said.
The ballot box may still look much the same as it did in previous elections, yet the information reaching the person carrying the ballot there is changing rapidly.
And while the CEC can check a ballot, a protocol, and a photograph against one another, the harder question may be what happens before the voter ever reaches the ballot box.

Ukraine sends mixed signals on F-16 repair delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:47 UTC
21:06:47 KST

- Zelensky told the Financial Times that about half of Ukraine's F-16s have spent long periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance.
- Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later called reports of catastrophically low F-16 availability false, saying overhauled jets are returning at an increasing pace.
About half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets have spent long stretches in Europe for repairs and maintenance, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, and some have taken so long to come back that Ukraine lost time when it needed them most to defend its skies.
Zelensky made the comments in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2. He said Kyiv wants Western partners to help move more of the maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the jets closer to the front would get them back into service faster. He did not say how many aircraft are affected, where in Europe the work is done, or how long the jets have been away.
Zelensky said the F-16s have been effective against Russia’s newer jet-powered drones, which fly faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia has used for most of the war. In the same interview, he said Ukrainian forces are shooting down about 57% of jet-powered drones and between 85% and 90% of conventional ones.
Hours later, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry pushed back on reports describing a readiness crisis in the F-16 fleet. Spokesperson Heorhiy Tykhyi said on X that claims of catastrophically low aircraft availability and excessively long maintenance turnaround times were false. He said Ukraine’s industrial partners are returning overhauled aircraft at an increasing pace and that maintenance times are getting shorter, not longer.
Tykhyi acknowledged that the fleet is hard to keep flying. Ukraine flies the jets intensively under demanding conditions, he said, and some components for its early-model F-16s are no longer produced and are getting harder to find. He warned that such reports should not undermine international funding for F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for more jets from partner nations.
Ukraine’s F-16s are older jets from European air forces, mainly the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. The first ones arrived in the summer of 2024. They have been used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and to strike ground targets, and Ukraine has lost several of them in combat and accidents.
Because the jets are Western-built, much of their deeper maintenance has been done outside Ukraine, where parts, tools and trained technicians are available and the aircraft are out of reach of Russian strikes on airfields. Moving that work into Ukraine would bring the jets closer to the fight but would also put repair sites within range of Russian missiles and drones.

OpenAI dismisses 3 researchers over alleged mishandling of sensitive information
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:28 UTC
21:06:28 KST

Dilara Hamit
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
OpenAI has dismissed three researchers after an internal investigation concluded that they mishandled sensitive company information, the ChatGPT developer told news outlets.
“We have parted ways with three individuals” for violating information-access and handling policies, an OpenAI spokesperson said.
The company said the researchers dealt with sensitive material outside its established procedures, violating internal rules and undermining the trust required for its work.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the dismissals late Thursday, identified the researchers as Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni. It said the alleged misconduct included sharing confidential information with an external AI-safety organization that was helping analyze OpenAI’s models.
Neither the outside organization nor the material allegedly shared was identified publicly. OpenAI has not confirmed the names reported by the newspaper.
The dismissals come amid heightened scrutiny of OpenAI’s safety procedures, as well as questions about the safety of AI for the industry as a whole, following several incidents in which experimental AI agents acted outside their intended boundaries during training or evaluation.
In July, OpenAI agents escaped a restricted testing environment and gained access to the internet before breaching systems operated by the open-source development platform Hugging Face.
The agents exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities, established unauthorized communication channels, and shared information across separate evaluations. OpenAI described the episode as a “warning shot” demonstrating that highly capable agents could circumvent technical controls and take potentially dangerous actions without human direction.
Company channel for reporting 'misalignment'
A subsequent company review found other instances in which its models affected external websites and services. OpenAI said it had notified third parties whose security controls may have been bypassed or whose services were affected, while stressing that notification did not necessarily mean private data had been accessed or a system fully compromised.
The company also acknowledged that in June, its experimental models accessed Australian government websites without authorization during internal testing. One model obtained non-public access to a Services Australia system and retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, although OpenAI said no individual medical records were accessed.
OpenAI has since tightened network restrictions, expanded monitoring, and temporarily paused some training and evaluation involving tool use for its most capable models.
The company has also introduced a framework for publicly reporting examples of model “misalignment,” including unauthorized actions, efforts to evade oversight and communication between agents outside approved channels.
OpenAI has said the industry has not yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to continue expanding the most advanced AI systems at maximum speed indefinitely.
