Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:03:20 UTC
21:03:20 KST

Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?
Fines replace jail terms for first-time ‘false news’ offences under a decree rights groups say is still repressive.
Tunisia has softened a cybercrime law that has landed journalists and activists in prison, letting first-time offenders pay fines instead of serving time.
The amendment to Decree 54, which went into effect on Wednesday, sets fines of 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for a first offence of spreading “false news” and related violations.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tunisia swelters as power cuts disrupt water supplies
- list 2 of 3Tunisian protesters demand release of four Sumud activists
- list 3 of 3Tunisia fuel strike highlights growing economic and political anger
The fines replace a five-year prison sentence. However, repeat offenders may still face jail.
Rights and media freedom advocates in Tunisia and abroad have long opposed the decree as repressive, saying it has been wielded against President Kais Saied’s opposition, activists and reporters.
The government, meanwhile, says the decree protects people and public order from attack, and is needed to tackle online crime and disinformation.
So what has changed, how has the decree been used, and why has Tunisia softened it now?
What does the amended law say?
Decree 54, issued by President Kais Saied in September 2022, made it an offence to spread falsehoods by electronic means.
Until this week, anyone convicted of circulating untrue information deemed threatening to public security, or to infringe on other people’s rights, risked up to five years in prison.
The penalties also applied when allegedly doctored content, personal data or untrue allegations were spread to stir up hatred, incite attacks, defame someone, damage their reputation or cause them material or moral harm.
Targeting a public official or a person of equivalent status raised the ceiling to a decade behind bars and a fine of 100,000 dinars (more than $32,000).
Anyone who reoffended faced six months behind bars on top of a 50,000-dinar fine (more than $16,000).
The penalties doubled when the offence was aimed at a public official or someone of equivalent status.
How has Decree 54 been used?
The decree has garnered widespread criticism from Tunisian and international organisations concerned with press freedom.
The law was “one of the potent tools of oppression used by the government to crush dissent, crack down on civic space and arbitrarily restrict the freedom of expression in the country,” Said Benarbia, Middle East and North Africa director of the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ), told Al Jazeera.
Rafik Abdessalem, Tunisia’s foreign minister from 2011 to 2013 and a senior figure in the Islamist Ennahdha party, said the decree had been used “to silence every voice critical of the regime”.
Ennahdha was a leading opposition party under Saied until he initiated a severe crackdown against it, sentencing its leadership, including Abdessalem, to long prison sentences, some in absentia.
The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT) documented that hundreds of journalists, bloggers, opposition politicians, lawyers and activists had been tried under the decree since it came into force in 2022, and declared the situation an “emergency”.
In its latest annual report, the SNJT recorded 14 prosecutions of journalists between April 2025 and April 2026 – six of them under the decree.
In one example, prominent Tunisian lawyer and columnist Sonia Dahmani was sentenced to two years for criticising conditions in Tunisian prisons in a radio interview this May.
She has been charged under the decree in five cases, each relating to remarks she made in media appearances, and had already been sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment after criticising Saied’s policies in 2024.
Another citizen, Saber Ben Chouchane, was sentenced to death after being charged under a number of censorship laws, including Decree 54, for Facebook posts. He was later granted a presidential pardon.
Among international critics of the decree are Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the European Parliament, which has described it as “a tool to interfere with fundamental freedoms” and called for its repeal.
Critics connect it to a larger trend of democratic backsliding in the country since Saied took office, undoing progress the country has made after its 2011 revolution.
In 2021, during his third year in office, Saied suspended parliament, dismissed the government and began ruling by presidential decree – steps his critics have denounced as an autocratic subversion of Tunisia’s democratising political system.
A new constitution, put to a referendum in 2022 that many Tunisians boycotted, later locked in those powers.
In 2024, amid political repression, Saied won a second five-year term with more than 90 percent of the vote. It was the lowest turnout of any election since 2011 at 28.8 percent.
Saied rejects accusations of autocratic rule, saying his actions are legal and are needed to end years of disorder and alleged corruption.
Why now?
Hours before Wednesday’s amendment came into effect, civil society groups spearheaded by Tunisia’s largest labour union unveiled plans for a nationwide march over what they regarded as restrictions on civil liberties.
Seven years after Tunisians elected Saied on promises he would address the country’s poor economic situation and tackle corruption, Tunisians have found themselves facing a cost-of-living crisis and restrictions to their political freedoms.
In the past year, the country has seen a rise in demonstrations by civil society against abuses of power, democratic backsliding and deteriorating living standards. In June, hundreds of protesters in Tunis called for press freedom and for detained critics to be freed. In July, thousands gathered on the fifth anniversary of Saied’s suspension of parliament, urging him to “leave”.
Abdessalem, the former foreign minister, credited popular mobilisation – in the form of marches and gatherings – for forcing the government to back down.
Saied also faced mounting pressure from abroad. In July, a member of the US House of Representatives, Joe Wilson, said he would keep pushing a bill that would impose sanctions on Saied and those closest to him for anti-democratic policies.
Is the amendment enough?
Critics say the amendment does little to address freedom of speech concerns under Saied’s government.
The reduction in penalties was a “positive development”, Benarbia of the International Commission of Jurists said, but what was required was an end to all abusive prosecutions and the release of those arbitrarily detained under the decree.
Even if repealed, a host of other legal measures have been used to harass, imprison and exile Saied’s opponents.
“In short, the punishment has been reduced, but its repressive and punitive character remains unchanged,” Abdessalem told Al Jazeera. The amendment aimed to make the image of Saied’s Tunisia “less bleak” after it has become associated with “trials, arrests and the use of arbitrary decrees,” he said.
Lotfi Hajji, head of Al Jazeera’s bureau in Tunisia, said civil society groups and the journalists’ union were demanding Decree 54 be scrapped altogether, so that journalists could be judged under the 2011 press freedom law instead.
That law was one of the main gains of the revolution, Hajji said, balancing freedom with responsibility. Proposals in parliament since 2024 for a wider overhaul have been ignored.

Ex-UN director who protested Gaza famine challenges his dismissal
GENEVA/ROME, Oct 2 - A former senior UN food agency official has said he has launched an appeal against his dismissal, alleging it was motivated by his stance on hunger in Gaza, in a case that has exposed tensions within the Rome-based organisation.
Benjamin Davis, 62, a Spanish American director at the Food and Agriculture Organization, was informed his employment would end on September 30 at the request of Director-General Qu Dongyu, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The papers cited breaches of international civil service standards which require staff to act with impartiality. Davis rejected the allegation.
JOINED MOMENTS OF SILENCE FOR GAZA
"I feel it’s a terrible injustice. I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking up about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food which is the most basic of human rights," he told Reuters. He said he had filed an appeal.
The FAO did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Davis' allegations or on the grounds for his dismissal.
Davis, said he had worked at the FAO for 26 years on a renewable contract, and that his dismissal was linked to staff activism over the Gaza war.
He was one of hundreds of employees who have joined moments of silence for hunger victims in Gaza where an international hunger-monitoring system used by UN agencies determined famine in August 2025.
He also authored a report on food availability in the Palestinian enclave in May 2025.
The dispute burst into public view this week when Qu, speaking at a FAO conference, defended the dismissal of an unnamed staff member whom he accused of having "played the political game".
"We will not allow you to play the game here of human rights," Qu said.
DEBATE OVER STAFF ACTIVISM
The remarks prompted fresh debate about whether UN employees are able to express views on humanitarian crises without jeopardising their careers.
A large crowd of staff gathered at FAO headquarters in Rome on Wednesday to applaud Davis as he departed, according to U.N. officials and video seen by Reuters.
Under UN rules, staff are allowed to express political opinions but must ensure these do not adversely affect their official duties or UN interests.
Davis, who was head of the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division, said he was concerned that other employees would face retaliation over their participation in the Gaza moments of silence.
The case, now with the FAO's internal justice process, could later be escalated to a UN tribunal which has the authority to award damages in employment disputes. REUTERS

Annual inflation in the euro area accelerated to 3.8% in September 2026 from 3.2% in August, a flash estimate from Eurostat showed on Friday.
Energy recorded the highest annual rate among main inflation components at 18.8% in September, jumping from 14.3% in August, the statistical office of the European Union reported.
Services inflation reached 3.2% in September compared with 3.0% in August, while food, alcohol, and tobacco prices climbed to 1.4% from 1.1%.
Non-energy industrial goods inflation fell to 1.1% from 1.2% in August, while core inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco edged up to 2.5% in September from 2.4%.
Among euro area economies, Lithuania posted the highest annual inflation rate at 6.1%, followed by Bulgaria at 5.6% and Cyprus and Luxembourg at 5.2% each.
Conversely, Malta logged the lowest annual inflation rate at 2.4%, with Finland following at 2.6% and Latvia at 2.9%.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices in the euro area increased 0.6% in September.

A botched sabotage attempt in Leipzig has shed light on a broader Russian campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:01:20 UTC
21:01:20 KST

Had the explosive device at Leipzig Airport detonated on the 4th of August, investigators might not have gained such a clear insight into what European officials regard as a wider campaign of Russian attacks, reports Politico.
In early August, a package at Leipzig Airport struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft and fell onto the tarmac. It contained explosives that failed to detonate, thereby providing investigators with a valuable piece of evidence: the device itself. According to German Federal Police investigation documents, the device was encased in a metal plate featuring several circular indentations.
This was not the first time such an improvised explosive device had been discovered in Europe. Almost two years earlier—on the 20th of August, 2024—police investigators and an explosive ordnance disposal unit visited a cemetery in Kaunas. According to the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, Lithuanian authorities had received information from Poland regarding explosives and a Ukrainian national who had planted them on behalf of Russian special services. Near an old gravesite, hidden beneath artificial flowers and concrete fragments, investigators found a plastic bag containing two tin cans. The labels indicated they contained corn, but an examination revealed that the cans held 968 grams of explosives—equivalent to 700 grams of TNT, or the explosive power of four hand grenades.
In January and June 2025, investigators discovered several more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four of them were attached to metal plates featuring circular indentations; investigators noted that, in the event of an explosion, these would have produced shrapnel. Analysis revealed that all the plates had likely been manufactured using the same equipment.
The explosive devices found at Leipzig Airport bore a striking resemblance to the items discovered in Lithuania.
 However, similarity alone does not prove that the devices were part of the same operation. Nevertheless, two Western security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, indicated that the devices matched others, thereby linking them to a broader Russian campaign. The similarity in execution is one element of a trend that, according to German and European officials, points to a growing sabotage campaign across Europe orchestrated by Russian intelligence services. According to three senior German and European security officials, the primary driver of the campaign is Russia's military intelligence agency (GRU). At its core is Unit 29155, which is linked to destabilization operations targeting European nations.
German authorities have indicated that, as Russian dictator Vladimir Putin seeks ways to diminish military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv, various hybrid operations are to be expected in the future. Gerhard Schindler, the former head of the German Federal Intelligence Service (BND), stated that the goal is to instill a fear of direct military confrontation among the public—thereby casting doubt on support for Ukraine—and that the Russians will consequently intensify military pressure on Ukraine while expanding hybrid operations in the West.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin denied Moscow's involvement in acts of sabotage across Europe and stated that it categorically rejects unfounded accusations regarding an alleged drone incident at Leipzig Airport, as well as other activities aimed at sabotage.
One of the clearest leads involves Olegs Levushkin, a Latvian-Russian dual national
 suspected by German authorities of helping to orchestrate an attack at Leipzig Airport. According to investigative documents and a statement by a high-ranking German official, Levushkin is not a low-level recruit but rather a logistics officer linked to the GRU, with long-standing ties to Russian intelligence services. On social media, Levushkin offers a glimpse into a seemingly ordinary life, showcasing motorcycle trips to Crimea and the Hungarian-Serbian border, visits to the Volgograd monument, and leisure activities such as fishing, skiing, and traveling across Europe with his family.
According to a German intelligence official and investigative documents, investigators believe that in late July, Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin’s Brandenburg Airport to prepare for the Leipzig operation. He rented a car at the airport on the 27th of July. Investigators believe the explosives were brought into Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, concealed in long-haul trucks.
On the 31st of July, the rental car was spotted near Leipzig Airport, and investigators believe Levushkin conducted reconnaissance there prior to the attempted attack. Levushkin has not responded to requests for comment on this information.
Levushkin is believed to have ties to high-ranking GRU officials
 and has maintained a close relationship with GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov for approximately 20 years. The 2025 report by the Lithuanian State Security Department states that Smolyaninov is the head of the GRU’s Ukraine division, specializes in psychological operations, and is linked to sabotage campaigns in Europe orchestrated via Telegram. The 2025 intelligence report notes that Smolyaninov also coordinated the activities of Longifolia, a Russia-linked military company registered in Panama. European investigators suspect several of the company's shareholders of involvement in an operation that saw explosive devices sent to Poland and the UK. One of the packages caught fire en route to Leipzig Airport in July 2024, while another ignited in Birmingham two days later. Lithuanian intelligence agencies link this operation to the GRU, specifically to Unit 29155.
Western governments and investigators have previously linked Unit 29155 to a series of operations in Europe, including explosions at arms depots in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, as well as the poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal in the UK. Lithuanians also link Unit 29155 to recent arson attacks, including those at an IKEA store in Vilnius and a post office in Bucharest.
German officials have blamed the GRU for a failed arson attack on a defense company in Munich,
 while Estonia has stated that an attack on Milrem Robotics in August was orchestrated by Russian intelligence services. European security agencies consulted by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network believe the number of such attacks will rise in the coming months; potential targets include defense companies, critical infrastructure, and individuals supporting Ukraine.
Omar Haijawi-Pirchner, the former head of Austria's domestic intelligence service, stated that the Kremlin views its relationship with Europe as a "systemic conflict." He, too, predicted an increase in the number of such incidents.

America orders 22 more upgraded F-15EX Eagle jets
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:54 BST
21:00:54 KST

The U.S. Department of the Air Force has awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II fighters under Lot 7, keeping all planned aircraft in the batch within the funding Congress provided through budget reconciliation, the service stated.
The contract was finalised before the end of the fiscal year on 30 September, following negotiations between the F-15 Program Office and Boeing that the Air Force described as focused and complex. According to the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate, the agreement takes account of the effects of the 2025 production disruption and wider inflation across the defence industrial base. That disruption was the strike by around 3,200 International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers members at Boeing’s St. Louis-area plants, which began in August 2025 and halted work on the company’s military aircraft lines for around three months.
Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, portfolio acquisition executive for the directorate, said in the release: “Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production.” He added: “The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future.”
The reconciliation funding referenced by the Air Force came through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, which included tens of billions of dollars for defence procurement on top of regular appropriations. The service said the negotiation team worked across programme management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management and logistics to assess the impact of changing production conditions and align the aircraft buy with the money available.
The F-15EX is a two-seat-capable development of the F-15 family, derived from the Advanced Eagle variants Boeing built for export customers such as Qatar and Saudi Arabia. It features a fly-by-wire flight control system, large-area cockpit displays, the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System electronic warfare suite and an open mission systems architecture. The Air Force intends the aircraft to replace its ageing F-15C and F-15D fleet, and the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing at Portland became the first operational unit to receive the type. The service’s planned total has shifted over the life of the programme, falling from 144 to 98 aircraft in the fiscal 2025 budget request.
The Air Force also presented the award as an example of the Secretary of War’s acquisition transformation principles, saying an integrated negotiation team was empowered to elevate issues needing senior-level decisions while keeping accountability for cost, schedule and aircraft numbers.
Col. Jonathan Varoli, system program manager of the F-15 Program Office, was quoted in the release as saying: “The Lot 7 award demonstrates what is possible when the acquisition enterprise moves with purpose, remains accountable to the taxpayer and stays focused on delivering capability to the warfighter.” He continued: “This effort brought together the right expertise, at the right time, to achieve an outcome that strengthens the F-15EX program and supports the future fighter force.”
According to the service, the award sustains near-term production of the F-15EX while the Air Force continues to assess its future requirements and acquisition strategy for the aircraft.

Gut bacteria and digestive metabolites are linked to psychopathic traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

Specific bacteria in the gut and mouth, along with the chemical byproducts of digestion, are associated with traits like emotional detachment and impulsivity. These findings suggest that the microscopic organisms living inside the human body might play a role in shaping complex personality characteristics. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
The human body is home to trillions of microorganisms, collectively known as the microbiome. These bacteria, viruses, and fungi do a lot more than digest food and fight off infections. They communicate directly with the central nervous system through a network of chemical signals, hormones, and immune responses called the gut-brain axis.
Previous research links this biological pathway to mood disorders like depression and anxiety. More recently, researchers have started looking at how the microbiome relates to everyday personality traits and social behavior.
Psychopathy is a personality construct defined by emotional detachment, a lack of empathy, manipulative behavior, and a tendency toward impulsivity. In a clinical setting, it affects roughly one percent of the population. The exact biological mechanisms behind these traits remain poorly understood.
Carolina F.F.A. Costa, a researcher at the University of Porto and the University of Oxford, led a team to investigate this knowledge gap. The researchers wanted to see if the bacteria in the gut and mouth could be tied to subclinical psychopathic traits in the general public.
The researchers recruited 200 adult volunteers from the community in Portugal. The participants were screened to remove individuals who had taken antibiotics in the prior three months, as those medications drastically alter intestinal bacteria. The volunteers completed extensive self-report questionnaires designed to measure their levels of psychopathy, empathy, and anxiety.
These psychological assessments measured several distinct components of personality. The psychopathy survey looked at interpersonal manipulation, affective callousness, an erratic lifestyle, and antisocial behavior. Empathy was measured by testing how well participants could understand the perspectives of others and share their emotional states.
Alongside the psychological assessments, participants provided stool, saliva, and blood samples. The research team used a laboratory technique called DNA sequencing to identify the specific types of bacteria present in the gut and oral microbiomes. They also analyzed the samples for metabolites, which are the small molecules left behind when the body or bacteria break down food.
The researchers first grouped the participants based on their psychological survey scores. A computer algorithm separated the volunteers into four distinct groups characterized by varying levels of psychopathy and anxiety. As expected, participants who scored high in psychopathic traits tended to score lower in overall empathy.
Next, the team examined the bacterial makeup of the participants. They found that the overall richness of the microbiome, meaning the total number of different species present, did not vary among the four psychological groups. Any initial correlations between total diversity and psychopathy were not statistically significant after adjusting for the ages of the participants.
While overall diversity did not differ, the abundance of specific bacterial families did show a relationship with personality traits. In the gut, bacteria from the groups Allisonella and Prevotella, as well as a species called Cloacibacillus evryensis, were positively associated with higher psychopathy scores.
Participants with elevated levels of traits like an erratic lifestyle and emotional callousness had higher amounts of these specific intestinal bacteria. In the mouth, a bacterial species called Treponema vincentii showed a negative association, meaning it was less abundant in individuals with higher psychopathy scores.
Many of these specific bacteria have known biological roles that could influence the brain. Allisonella is known to produce histamine, a chemical that triggers immune responses and inflammation. Chronic inflammation in the body can send stress signals directly to the brain, which often influences mood and behavior.
Cloacibacillus evryensis has the genetic potential to produce gamma-aminobutyric acid in the gut. This specific chemical acts as an inhibitory signal in the central nervous system, helping to regulate impulsivity and self-control. Prevotella has been previously associated with differences in how the brain processes emotional and sensory stimuli.
After identifying the bacteria, the researchers looked at the metabolites in the stool and blood samples. Out of over 200 molecules analyzed, two stood out in the stool samples: glucose and taurine. Both molecules were found at elevated levels in the group of participants who scored high in both psychopathy and anxiety.
When looking at the scores on a sliding scale, higher levels of fecal glucose and taurine correlated positively with traits like antisociality and interpersonal manipulation. Glucose serves as the primary energy source for the body. The digestive tract contains specialized sensors that detect glucose and send metabolic updates to the brain.
Finding elevated glucose in feces suggests a disruption in how energy is extracted from food and absorbed into the bloodstream. Previous studies have noted abnormal glucose metabolism in the brains of individuals with high psychopathic traits, suggesting a potential link between energy use and behavior.
Taurine is an amino acid primarily produced by the liver, and it is involved in brain development and anxiety regulation. It normally binds to bile acids to help digest fats, and gut bacteria eventually separate the taurine from the bile. Finding excess free taurine in stool can indicate that the gut is struggling to absorb nutrients properly, or that specific bacterial populations are overgrown.
Finally, the team cross-referenced the bacterial data with the metabolite data. They found that higher levels of Allisonella in the gut predicted higher amounts of both glucose and taurine. This suggests that specific gut bacteria might be altering energy metabolism in ways that ultimately relate to personality expression.
The researchers note several caveats to their findings. The study relies on observations at a single point in time, meaning it cannot prove that gut bacteria cause psychopathic traits. It is equally possible that the behaviors associated with psychopathy, such as dietary choices or physiological stress responses, alter the microbiome.
The participants were volunteers from the general community rather than individuals with clinical diagnoses. The findings relate to subclinical personality traits, which may not fully represent the severe psychopathy seen in forensic settings.
The psychological data came from self-reported surveys. While these are standard tools in psychology, they are subject to personal bias, as individuals may lack self-awareness or alter their answers to appear more socially acceptable. Future research using animal models could help determine if altering gut bacteria directly changes behavior.
The study, “Gut and oral microbiota composition is associated with psychopathic personality: a cross-sectional study,” was authored by Carolina F.F.A. Costa, Daniel Radford-Smith, Alexandre R.T. Figueiredo, Rita C.M. Ribeiro, Sofia Pinto, Fay Probert, Renata Barros, Paula Serrão, Luisa Barreiros, Marcela A. Segundo, Daniel C. Anthony, Fernando Barbosa, Philip W.J. Burnet, and Benedita Sampaio-Maia.

China’s PLA sets up new military academy colleges for AI, drones and discipline

China stockpiles ASML lithography tools, spurring US calls for complete export ban
DUV tools, though not as advanced as EUV, can be adapted to manufacture 7-nm logic chips and advanced memory for AI processors, report says
Chinese semiconductor plants amassed hundreds of immersion lithography machines worth billions of dollars in recent years, according to former US officials, who urged Washington and its allies to shut down further exports.
Chinese-owned fabs had acquired an estimated 343 immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems by early 2026, said a report published in late September by the Centre for Technology & Statecraft (CTS), a Washington research group established in August.
Co-authored by former US export control official Nicholas Brown and Saif Khan, a former White House and commerce department technology policy adviser, the study adds fresh data to the debate in Washington over whether Western allies should impose a total blockade on immersion DUV tools bound for China.

Rare northern bald ibises take flight in human-led European migration project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

Fifteen new birds have joined a growing flock of bald ibises in northern Spain, guided there by human migration guides in micro aircraft who helped them along the route.
The birds are part of the growing European flock of the northern bald ibis (Geronticus eremita), the charismatic and frankly extraordinary bird that had been extinct on the continent for 300 years.
By the end of the 20th century, the last major population in Morocco had fallen from 9,000 to 250 individuals in the wild. But then captive breeding and reintroduction plans were launched at various sites in Europe, initially in Austria and in Jerez, Andalucía. This most recent project, in Alt Empordà, Catalonia, has just welcomed the birds from Austria, to join an already established flock.
“They are such intelligent birds,” says Bernat Garrigós, a biologist who runs the Alt Empordà project, “very sociable, all with different personalities. They like to check everything that comes into the project with their beaks; your socks, the food, everything.”
There is no fear of humans because, as Garrigós explains, the birds do not really know any predators. They are still curious, and trusting.
“We started working on the project in 2024, and by 2025 we had a first generation flock of nearly 60 ibises,” he says. “They were released in March 26 here [at Torre d’en Mornau, a converted Spanish army stable]. Currently there are two full-time and two part-time staff on the team, plus 20 volunteers, to manage the flock and site.
“The Aiguamolls Park [a protected coastal wetland and nature reserve] is a close collaborator and with whom we maintain a very close, ongoing relationship. The goal is to mitigate risk to breeding, and mortality, until there is have a self-sustaining population.”
In a year or two, and with some luck, Garrigós’ project should have its first breeding pair. Ibises do not breed until they are at least three or four years old. The plan is to establish a breeding colony, with nests on the towers dotted around the stables. The team will help by partially building the nests. Like most teenagers, they need to be shown how to make their beds.
The Alt Empordà group is in constant contact with the projects in Austria and Jerez, and the birds migrate between the groups with the help of the human “foster parents” of the Waldrapp team (Waldrapp is another name for these birds) who guide their path with the help of an ultralight aircraft. With 20 years of experience, they have helped Garrigós’ group avoid many of the mistakes made early on. So far, as a result, the mortality rate has been much lower.
Over the next 10 years, Garrigós is aiming to release his ibises into the Alt Empordà, the plan being a minimum of 50 breeding pairs and about 300 individuals living wild. The comarca, or county, which is about halfway between Austria and Jerez, serves as an excellent stopover point in the migration route. The shared goal for the three projects is to establish colonies across Europe. These colonies will be connected by migrating birds, to form breeding pairs of different lineage and creating a robust gene pool to ensure survival.
The project in northern Spain is one more piece in a broader European effort to save a species that has been among the most threatened in the world. The charisma of the ibis and the passion of the team are essential for promoting environmental education, raising awareness in younger generations and driving the importance of active conservation.
And that charisma is a useful tool for winning over people. Recently, representatives from the Endesa, a large electric utility company, came to visit and were so bowled over by the project that they began retrofitting their pylons to be more visible and less dangerous for birds, with the ibis particularly in mind.
“It’s not enough to stop destroying our environment,” says Garrigós. “We need to make a positive, active effort to prevent extinctions and the destruction of habitats where this and many other species live. In the end, it all comes down to having diverse, resilient ecosystems that provide the ecosystem services necessary for the survival of the ecosystem and of humanity itself.”

Does Philadelphia’s ‘house of horrors’ hold the key to seven missing women?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

A dilapidated house, burned out above the second story, may hold clues to dark tales and – potentially – the darkest of endings as the FBI and police in Philadelphia try to unpick what took place at 417 West Chew Avenue for more than three decades.
Last week, homicide investigators shifted their focus from examining an archive of a million photographs and film recovered from what is known locally as the “house of horrors” to excavating what is in or under the home of Raymond “RC” Horsch, a career criminal, local artist, author and snuff photographer who died last year aged 82, and his son Eugene, 44.
So far, at least seven missing women have been linked to the home in the Olney section of the city, originally a German American neighborhood but now largely African American, Hispanic and Asian. Investigators believe five are dead.
Fifty-eight women seen on film and in photographs recovered from the trash-strewn property have been identified. Of those, 25 have been located but not yet interviewed; 19 have spoken with detectives but declined to cooperate.
Investigators are faced with a difficult task: how to discern from images whether Horsch’s subjects are posing, and what is real and what is staged. Such is the grim nature of snuff photography and the murky exchanges that lie beneath. Investigators have said that the five women appear unconscious, lifeless or injured, but with no bodies the medical examiner cannot issue death certificates.
“We’re going slow and methodical,” a police source said. “Do we think people were killed in the house? Sure. It’s a tough investigation because the guy who had the house was a violent pornographer. Is it art or is it reality?”
Deputy police commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference on 10 September: “Some of this is play-acting. Some of it we believe could be real, but we’re not there yet.”
The five women who police believed to be dead are Blair Tonzelli, 35, missing since 2023; Nicole Fusaro and Maribel Fresses, both 27, who disappeared in 2018; Amy McHale, who disappeared in June 2016 and had been married to Horsch; and Gabrielle Amarando, 22, who disappeared in 2012.
Four miles from the Olney home lies Philadelphia’s Kensington neighborhood, an area notorious for its open-air drug use, prostitution and homelessness, and as a place where people simply disappear from life.
Many women in the community last week recalled some of those identified by investigators. One had connections to the Olney house – her driver’s license was registered there – but declined to discuss the case. Others said they recalled Horsch’s son, Eugene, currently in custody pending federal gun and drug charges, cruising the block in a black BMW. One remembered Fresses as an “Italian princess – sweet and kind”.
Ashley, making her way from a woman’s shelter with a plastic bag of candies, syringes, and a glass bowl for smoking fentanyl or meth, said bleakly: “A lot of girls go missing here. You get dope sick, it makes you crazy, and then you make bad decisions.”
Not all the women who passed through the Olney home were connected to Kensington. Media reports suggest that some met Horsch in Camden, New Jersey, 20 miles away. A woman from the area told ABC Philadelphia she had gone to the Olney home, blacked out from the drugs Raymond Horsch gave her, and woke up with him standing over her, taking pictures.
Police first raided the home in June after Eugene Horsch was stopped in a car in Philadelphia’s Old City neighborhood. Horsch was carrying fake ID indicating he was federal law enforcement and DEA agent. A female passenger was carrying Tonzelli’s identification.
Two handguns and approximately $8,000 worth of illegal drugs were found in the vehicle. According to court documents, Eugene Horsch allegedly said Tonzelli would “never be seen again”. A search of the home turned up an additional illegal firearm, a marijuana grow operation, a fake FBI badge and five urns containing cremated remains.
The arrest of the younger Horsch, who had not been charged in connection with the missing women, shone a spotlight on his father, who was never charged in connection with the disappearances of any of the five identified women. The city’s medical examiner’s office has advised that if images of at least three women recovered from the home “are authentic and have not been altered, the women depicted appear to be deceased”.
Court records show that Raymond Horsch was convicted in 2009 for attempting to lure a nine-year-old girl into his car in Kensington. “Come here, in my car, sexy girl,” Horsch said to her, according to an arrest report. Horsch was found guilty, sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison, and required to register as a sex offender.
But his lawyers sought a new trial and the case collapsed because the girl was too afraid to testify a second time, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. Horsch’s conviction was expunged and the records placed under seal. A judge has ordered them to be preserved.
According to a 1985 psychological examination obtained by the Inquirer, Horsch was a manipulative criminal who was “consumed by anger … grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious, and excessively controlling”.
The profile was commissioned as part of a federal drug manufacturing case. Horsch fled the US with his second wife, Myroslawa Anna Ferkuniak. He was arrested in New Zealand, where he’d been living under the name of Stanley Stokowski, a real California chemist who had a Stanford doctorate.
According to the profile, he spoke in the third person, as if describing “events from someone else’s life”. Michael Yoder, a retired FBI special agent, told the outlet that, judging from the report, “I would say you have a potential serial killer on your hands.”
For a time, Horsch and his young son lived in Pennsylvania’s Berks county, where he opened a barbecue restaurant while also pursuing a career as a fetishistic or “snuff” photographer. In 2009, he was arrested after a marijuana grow operation was discovered in his basement, and he was sentenced to five years in prison.
Raymond Horsch had been offering cash and drugs to women in Kensington in exchange for participating in his violent pornographic films since the early 2000s. He also had access to to a crematorium connected to Kensington’s Garzone funeral home to photograph corpses. In 2007, the business was shut down for selling body parts on the black market.
Horsch wasn’t hiding his access to the morgue – a video exhibited at a “Transgressions” art show in 2014 featured a body being loaded into an incinerator. The exhibition asked visitors to consider if Horsch’s “often transgressive images can possibly be art? Or, as many critics and philosophers claim, are art and pornography completely and forever mutually exclusive?”
Horsch was not reticent about his obsession with women in addiction. He uploaded photos of his subjects to his website featuring women “imagining and acting their own deaths” juxtaposed with real photos of overdose victims. A handwritten note found in the home describes hurting people and makes reference to serial killer Ted Bundy.
Horsch’s films included a documentary, Whore!, and films including Deleted Scenes: A Serial Killer’s Video Journal and Slaves. He starred in and directed Lovers, which was produced by a feminist porn studio. He produced The Erotic Memoirs of a Male Chauvinist Pig, featuring Georgina Spelvin, the star of The Devil in Miss Jones.
He published a two-volume photo book called Eroto~ To the Prurient Interest, showing a woman he referred to as “Anna” in staged “deaths”. 2014’s Empathy included a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman’s body with chemicals.
The home is already a tourist attraction even as investigators still search for evidence. “It was creepy vibes. He’d be out front staring at women, or he’d be in his yard doing some kind of chemist stuff,” recalled Jessica Diaz, 37. A neighbor living opposite the home said he recalled young women coming and going from the home. On occasion, ambulances were called. “They need to tear that house down,” he opined.
With Raymond Horsch dead, and his son Eugene under investigation, it remains possible that no charges will be brought and the best the families of the missing can hope for is a police report. “We have a duty to those families who are all concerned about whether their loved one lost their lives in that house or maybe somewhere else,” said the Philadelphia police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.
But the story of Raymond Horsch is already entering the annals of Philadelphia horror lore. Edgar Allan Poe and Bram Stoker both wrote in the city, and it’s had serial murderers in the past. In the 1980s, Gary Heidnik, an inspiration for the fictional character Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs, imprisoned six vulnerable women in a pit in his basement with the goal of creating a “baby farm”.
Josh Hitchens, a writer and historian known locally as a prominent “purveyor of the macabre”, said that in each case, it was people preying on the vulnerable. “These are often not the people that law enforcement pays much attention to. That’s one of the horrifying things about what’s unfolding now – what Raymond Horsch was doing was apparently known and talked about within the community.”
Hitchens said Horsch is likely to become a point on the horror map of Philadelphia, achieving a measure of recognition in death that his films and writings failed to secure in his life.
“I hope that within that we’re not just talking about Raymond and Eugene Horsch, but the lives of the women are also remembered and given the respect they deserve.”

Tip Toe Is a Harrowing Melodrama of Queerness and Masculinity in a World Gone Mad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans. An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years. Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood, which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence.
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series (BEEF, too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films (Eddington, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years, it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

Cocktail of the. week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

The move into autumn proper leads our taste buds to crave warmth and comfort in equal measure. And what could be more warming and comforting than a spiced vodka and citrus cocktail spiced with nut liqueur? Slice of carrot cake optional.
Have your cake and drink it
Serves 1
For the vodka infusion (for 7-8 serves)
Peel of 1 unwaxed lemon, all white pith removed
375ml good vodka – we use Belvedere
For the drink
50ml lemon peel-infused vodka – see above and method
   15ml hazelnut liqueur – we use Frangelico
   15ml vanilla syrup – homemade or store-bought (Bristol Syrup Co make a good one)
   15ml fresh lemon juice
   15ml fresh orange juice
   15ml fresh carrot juice
   6 dashes foamer, or 1 egg white
4 dashes aromatic bitters (we use Angostura aromatic), or 1 pinch ground cinnamon
1 orange slice, to garnish (or 1 slice carrot cake, to accompany)
The night before, infuse the vodka: put the lemon peel and vodka in a jar, seal and leave to steep overnight. Next day, strain the vodka into a clean jar or bottle, seal and store in a cupboard out of direct light, where it’ll keep almost indefinitely.
To build the drink, measure all the liquids into a shaker filled with ice, shake hard, then double strain into a coupe. Garnish with an orange slice, or serve with carrot cake to nibble on alongside.
- 
  Bruce Dorfling, bar manager, Palé Hall, Bala, Gwynedd, Wales

The True Story Behind Iraq War Reconciliation Drama Atonement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

In April 2003, a family in Baghdad was driving home as U.S. Marines engaged in a firefight with Iraqi forces. The family was caught in the crossfire, and three men were killed. Nearly 10 years after the shattering incident, the two women who survived the attack, having immigrated to the U.S. and settled in Glendale, Calif., sat down with one of the Marines who opened fire on them.
Journalist Dexter Filkins told the story of this encounter in the 2012 New Yorker article “Atonement After Iraq.” The piece details the efforts of U.S. Marine Lu Lobello to speak to Margaret and her daughter Nora Kachadoorian and seek their forgiveness for the attack that killed Margaret’s husband James and their sons Nicolas and Edmund and left Nora with a wound to the shoulder. Lobello reached out to Filkins to help facilitate the meeting.
Lobello’s time with the Kachadoorians informs the climax of Atonement, written and directed by Reed Van Dyk and now in theaters. Their real names have been changed for the film: Filkins becomes Michael Reid (Kenneth Branagh), Margaret is Mariam Khachaturian (Hiam Abbass), and Lobello is Lou D’Alessandro (Boyd Holbrook).
“I cried through most of the article,” recalls Van Dyk, sitting down to discuss the film at a hotel in Toronto, where the film had its North American Premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival. He first read the New Yorker piece the year it was published. “I found it really touching to see and feel in a very detailed way the impact that this one incident in war had had on all of these characters' lives, and I did remember thinking, ‘Boy, this would be a really beautiful film story.’”
From concept to screenplay
At the time, however, Van Dyk was at the beginning of his career and in no position to make that film. Six years later, he won an Oscar for Best Live Action Short Film for DeKalb Elementary, inspired by a school-shooting incident in Atlanta. That brought attention his way, allowing his feature-film ambitions to begin to materialize. “After that,” says Van Dyk, “I immediately reached for my copy of that New Yorker issue, which I still have, and started trying to make this film.”
His first challenge was turning a 12-page article into a two-hour film. “You have this wonderful reportage to work with, and all of the texture and specificity that comes with that,” says Van Dyk. “Then there are all the rooms that Dexter wasn't in. That's where my job comes in. There were three people that the story is centered around, two of whom come to life in Dexter’s article. He’s not much of a character in his own piece, so I had to flesh out this character that Branagh plays.”
It’s a unique story that requires a unique take on a film about war. For one thing, there are hardly any actual scenes of war depicted on screen. Van Dyk’s film uses a single event from the Iraq War as an opportunity to explore the humanity in, and aftermath of, conflict. War movies often seek to enforce the lines of division, but Atonement is more interested in the unexpected ways in which people come together. Van Dyk was keen to explore the humanity in the story, not only from the American perspective, as we so often see in Hollywood films, but from the Iraqi one, too.
“I’m accustomed to seeing Iraqi characters in most Western films about war through sniper scopes. That wasn’t something I was interested in,” he says. Instead, the director wanted to centralize the voices and people that are typically marginalized in American films. “As a writer, I want to know my characters as deeply as I can, and I want to have love for them. The real pleasure of writing was getting to know this Iraqi family, who lived a very different life than I did, and I worked really hard behind the scenes to make that feel real.”
The real-life meeting
The real Lobello first reached out to Filkins in March 2012 on Facebook, saying that he had been trying to get in touch with him for a decade. “You could ease my PTSD,” he added. The two began communicating, and Filkins learned that Lu wanted him to help connect with the Kachadoorians so that he could atone and apologize for the tragedy that transpired that day.
Filkins had previously reported on the Kachadoorians in Iraq, but later lost touch with them. Thankfully, Lobello had already found them, via Facebook. He asked Filkins to facilitate the meeting, hoping he could bridge the gulf between them.
The Kachadoorians were not hesitant to meet Lobello. “If he is asking for forgiveness, then we will give him forgiveness. God ordered us to forgive. He forgives us, so we must forgive others. Even people who killed our dears,” Margaret said.
The meeting took place on a Saturday in July 2012. Lobello was deeply anxious going in, and immediately burst into tears upon meeting Margaret and Nora. Margaret comforted him with a pat on the back. The conversation that followed was tense. As Filkins describes it, the day ended with a sense that a true resolution would never be reached, though progress had been made. While forgiveness was granted, forgetting is impossible, and resentment lingers. There are no easy answers when it comes to grief and war. But something extraordinary did, in fact, happen in the room, just as Van Dyk recreates in Atonement.
Explains the filmmaker: “They begin to see themselves in each other.”
Several days after meeting, Lobello received a Facebook message from Nora. She said she felt happy when he came to visit, and that she felt she got “a third brother,” and “the third son to my mom.”
Holding conflicting truths
In order to capture the emotional depth and intensity of that encounter, Van Dyk conducted extensive research throughout his years writing Atonement. He spoke to as many people involved in the real events as he could, including Lobello and the Kachadoorian family. He spoke to countless marines and Iraqi civilians and traveled to Baghdad with his director of photography, Jon Peter. The visit challenged his perception of the country based on what he’d seen in cinema. “I found it rich with color and rich with spirit, when most films posit the country as something more apocalyptic,” he says. “It was important for us to highlight that richness when we were working on the design and how we were shooting.”
He drew further from books written by Iraqi authors, and marines who’d come back from war. Documentaries also played a key role. He credits the documentary Homeland: Iraq Year Zero by Abbas Fahdel as “the best document of the Iraq War, certainly from the civilian perspective. It became a reference point for all of us.” Restrepo was an important reference when it came to filming the war sequence, and Van Dyk notes that The Act of Killing influenced the way he thought about the psychological and spiritual effects of men who have killed, as well as the moral implications of that experience.
Van Dyk became close with the Kachadoorian family while making Atonement. He’s spent “too many hours to count” with them, and they regularly have dinner together. “Every visit is like a five-hour hang,” he says. It was during one of those visits that Van Dyk had a breakthrough moment that prompted him to revise the movie’s script. “In one of the conversations we had, Margaret said something about Lobello that ended up in the movie: ‘Sometimes I look at him and I see my son, and sometimes I look at him and I see the man who took my son.’ I thought it captured very poignantly the complexity of her experience on that day, and I think it was teaching me too that the film had to hold both visions she had of him.”
As Van Dyk puts it, Atonement “pushes back on the larger narrative we’re absorbing from the media about other countries.” The film’s ultimate aim, like so many great works of cinema, is to give the audience an opportunity to expand their empathy for people they might never encounter in their daily lives.
“It’s rare that there are opportunities to make amends,” says Van Dyk. “Thats what makes this story so different from other stories that unfold during a war. Everyone got to sit down together again. I think there’s something powerful about people willing to hold space with others who were on a completely different side of war, let alone forgive someone.”

APA Member Interview, Rida Jafar
Unknown

Gaza: WHO appeals for massive aid influx ahead of winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Gaza: WHO appeals for massive aid influx ahead of winter
Repeated delays in bringing lifesaving medicines, prosthetics and more from Israel into Gaza risk having devastating consequences on Palestinians who urgently need them in the war-torn enclave, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) said on Friday.
“A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late, doesn't save lives. That's the question that actually matters," said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).
Almost 12 months into a fragile ceasefire agreement between Hamas fighters and Israel marked by ongoing Israeli airstrikes and other military activity, Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains “overwhelming”, according to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA.
Approved aid can only be brought into the Strip via Kerem Shalom in the southern tip of the enclave, while Rafah (also in the south) is open for the limited movement of people including patients requiring medical treatment abroad. At least four other main entry points into Gaza for aid remain closed: Kissufim, Gate 96, Erez and Erez West.
'Dual use' denials
In a call to the Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”, Dr Van De Weerdt also stressed that essential medicines “should not be considered as dual use” – and therefore banned by Israel on the grounds that they could be used by Hamas fighters – “as they are globally accepted standards on medical items anybody needs anywhere to run a hospital or a clinic”.
In the last six months, one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices was rejected four times. "Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again," stressed the WHO official, who noted that medicines "by contrast, move relatively well", with almost 87 per cent approved and just over 1 per cent rejected.
UN aid agencies operating in Gaza still provide critical assistance to families across the Strip in coordination with the Israeli authorities, but this lifesaving work is impeded by a lack of reliable and timely access.
“Our ask is simple and has not changed: we need the unimpeded and predictable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale. We also need a multi-crossing model so that aid isn't forced to trickle down through a limited number of crossings,” the WHO senior official said.
Highlighting the “extraordinary health workers” still risking their lives to help others in Gaza, Dr Van De Weerdt said that too few supplies were reaching them and not enough patients were getting the care they needed and deserved. The already dire humanitarian situation risks getting even worse soon, once autumn ends.
Rodent threat
“As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens. Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone [their] dignity,” the WHO official explained.
As in previous winters in Gaza, the enclave’s residents are expected to face a heightened risk of preventable disease outbreaks, linked to the absence of safe shelter, a lack of clean water and the high number of rats, whose bites transmit infection. The destruction of public health laboratories has complicated the task of identifying potential epidemics, WHO explained.
The development follows a warning from OCHA on Thursday about serious public health risks linked to the accumulation of solid waste in the heart of Gaza City.
Recent gains in improving sanitation in Gaza remain fragile because of a lack of reliable access to heavy machinery and equipment, OCHA explained, “or to engine oil and spare parts required to keep them running. Sustained funding for fuel is also critical.”
Meanwhile, mine action partners reported that they still lack “permissions and equipment” to remove unexploded ordnance hazards identified in the rubble during 37 assessment missions.

UK scraps charges to seat children with parents on flights, and for simple name errors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:58:35 UTC
20:58:35 KST

The new rules, announced by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, have now come into force.
The UK has just announced that airlines will no longer be able to charge parents to secure seats next to their children.
The new rules, which come into force today (2 October), apply to children under the age of 14 with a parent or accompanying adult.
Before the rule change, a parent and child could be charged up to £104 (€122) on a return ticket to book seats next to each other.
Passengers will also be able to correct simple name errors on bookings for free. Previously, some airlines were charging up to £40 (€47) to do so.
“Parents should not have to feel the pinch just to sit next to their child on a flight, or for amending a simple booking error,” UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said.
“That’s why we’re scrapping these unnecessary charges for all airlines – another everyday fix to help put money back in people’s pockets and give households more breathing room.
“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”
Under the EU’s new air passenger rules, which are yet to come into effect, parents must be afforded a seat next to their child provided they are under the age of 14 free of charge. The same is also true for those accompanying a pregnant passenger, or a passenger with a disability or reduced mobility.
The proposed rules, which could come into effect next year, will also allow for free spelling correction or administrative name updates.
Further to this, the regulations would ban airlines from charging checked-in passengers for a printed boarding pass.
Ryanair CEO responds
Ryanair’s outspoken CEO Michael O’Leary has slammed the UK’s move, claiming that no such fees exist. According to Ryanair, passengers have a 24-hour grace period to correct minor spelling mistakes.
“There are no fees for children to sit with their parents on UK airlines, and no fees for making minor spelling changes to bookings,” he said.
“[Alexander’s] press release is designed to cover over the damage that this Labour Govt has inflicted on UK air travel by raising UK APD to £15 (€17.63) per ticket (£60 (€70.53) for a family of 4) in 2026, and her inexplicable failure to sack failing overpaid NATS CEO, Martin Rolfe, from his £1.4m (€1.65m) job despite ‘taking responsibility’ for 4 ATC system collapses in the UK over the last four years, when no other European ATC system has suffered any collapses.”
Unruly passengers to be added to list
At the same time, the UK government has announced it is working with airlines and trade unions to create a new system for sharing information on persistently disruptive passengers.
Last year, more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents were logged by airlines.
The move will allow airlines to see if other carriers have banned passengers in order to extend the ban to their own flights if it is deemed necessary.

For First Time, India Offers Active Role in Brokering Peace in Ukraine
India has, for the first time, offered to play an active role in efforts to broker peace in Ukraine, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated on October 1.
On the same day, RBC-Ukraine reported that Kyiv currently has four international proposals concerning possible ceasefire arrangements, with India presenting the broadest initiative.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have four proposals. The broadest is India’s proposal. For the first time, India has offered to play a role,” Sybiha told journalists.
Türkiye and Egypt have proposed a grain and food-related ceasefire in the Black Sea. Sybiha noted that the issue is particularly important for Egypt, which depends on Ukrainian grain for roughly one-third of its needs.
The US proposal concerns an energy ceasefire previously discussed between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Ukraine has presented partners with its own approach and is prepared for both an energy and Black Sea ceasefire as part of a broader arrangement.

A strike by easyJet cabin crew in Portugal began Friday and is set to continue until Tuesday, with 443 flights from the airline’s bases in the capital Lisbon, Porto, and Faro already canceled, according to the National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel.
Union leader Ana Dias said the canceled flights represent around 80% of scheduled services during the five-day strike, while warning that other flights could also face disruptions.
“Crews arrived in Porto from France, and will probably operate flights to replace the strikers, once again in an illegal manner,” Dias said Thursday, according to the union.
An easyJet official told the Lusa news agency that the airline expects to operate around 55% of its scheduled flights during the strike.
The company said minimum services account for around 22% of its Portugal-based operations, while additional flights to and from Portugal will be operated by aircraft and crews from other European bases.
EasyJet said the operation is being conducted “in full compliance with applicable legislation and regulations.”
The union disputes the use of crews from other bases to replace striking workers, calling the practice illegal and saying it may take the matter to court.
The strike follows disputes over flight schedule stability, pay progression based on length of service, and terms proposed during negotiations for a company agreement.
Another easyJet cabin crew strike is scheduled for Dec. 19-23, potentially affecting travel during the busy Christmas period.

Russia’s Offensive Goes Backward as Ukraine Regains Nearly 300 Square Kilometers Since March
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:57:02 UTC
20:57:02 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Offensive Goes Backward as Ukraine Regains Nearly 300 Square Kilometers Since March
Russia lost ground in September while suffering more than 46,000 casualties—its worst monthly toll of 2026—as Ukrainian counteroffensives erased months of Russian gains, according to ISW.
Russian forces have lost control of nearly 300 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory since March 2026, while suffering their highest monthly casualty rate of the year in September, according to the Institute for the Study of War’s (ISW) October 1 assessment.
ISW said Russia’s territorial gains have slowed dramatically since March, at times becoming negative as Ukrainian forces launched successful counterattacks across several sectors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
After adjusting for the timing of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi, analysts assessed that Russian forces have lost a net 293.59 square kilometers across the front since March. Even when areas of Russian infiltration are included, Moscow expanded its presence by only 174.44 square kilometers over the same period.
ISW assessed that Russia seized 175.54 square kilometers during the month but lost 256.35 square kilometers, leaving Moscow with a net territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers.
When Russian infiltration zones are also counted, the picture becomes even worse: Russian forces entered or seized 143.2 square kilometers while losing 318.38 square kilometers, a net difference of 175.18 square kilometers in Ukraine’s favor.
At least 147 square kilometers liberated around Lyman during Operation Vivaldi became visible in ISW’s September mapping, although Ukrainian forces had actually conducted parts of the operation over several preceding months.
Ukraine deliberately kept much of Vivaldi concealed while the operation was underway, making exact month-to-month comparisons difficult. ISW therefore concluded that Russia likely achieved no net territorial gain at best in September—and probably lost ground overall.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported 46,320 Russian casualties in September, according to ISW—the highest monthly figure of 2026 and the third consecutive month in which Russian losses exceeded 40,000 personnel.
Operation Vivaldi played a major role in reversing Russian gains around Lyman. The Ukrainian counteroffensive eliminated a Russian salient that had threatened the northern approaches to Sloviansk and disrupted Moscow’s plans for a broader maneuver around Ukraine’s Donetsk region defensive belt.
ISW assesses that the consequences may extend beyond the territory already retaken, as Ukrainian positions around Lyman could complicate future Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk from the east.
Earlier, internal Russian military documents revealed battlefield losses, mass unauthorized absences, suicides, and serious disciplinary problems inside Russia’s 127th Motor Rifle Division.

Fire Erupts Near Major Volgograd Refinery After Drone Attack
A drone attack targeted industrial infrastructure in Russia’s Volgograd region overnight, with a large fire visible near major industrial facilities, OSINT channel ASTRA reported on October 2.
Volgograd region Governor Andrei Bocharov claimed the attack was carried out by Ukrainian drones and confirmed that a residential building caught fire in the city’s Krasnoarmeysky district. One person was hospitalized.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, launched in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, have repeatedly disrupted fuel production and contributed to shortages nationwide. UNITED24 Media reported that the campaign had disabled more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity by September, increasing pressure on fuel supplies and refinery operations.
“Tonight, as a result of a massive UAV attack on the industrial infrastructure of the Volgograd region, a fire was recorded in an apartment building on Udmurtskaya Street,” Bocharov stated. “One injured person was hospitalized, the fire has been contained.”
Residents reported numerous explosions across Volgograd and published footage showing drones in flight and air defenses operating. ASTRA initially noted that its OSINT specialist had not independently verified the footage.
Further analysis of eyewitness footage placed the glow from a major fire in the area of the Volgograd oil refinery and the Kaustik chemical plant, which are located close to each other. ASTRA emphasized that the available footage did not make it possible to determine which facility was burning.
The Volgograd refinery, operated by Lukoil, is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with an annual capacity of roughly 14.8–15.7 million tons of crude, or about 5% of Russia’s total refining capacity. It produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, fuel oil, and bitumen, ASTRA noted.
Kaustik is a major chemical producer in southern Volgograd. According to ASTRA, the facility manufactures dual-use basic chemicals considered important to Russia’s military-industrial sector.
Russia’s aviation authority also imposed restrictions at Volgograd airport at around 1 a.m., disrupting flights to and from Moscow. One aircraft was diverted to Samara after several hours of delay, the outlet wrote.
The same Volgograd refinery was already struck on July 31, when drones also hit a major Wildberries logistics hub in the city, and fires broke out at both sites.
