Kaunas launches 45-metre observation wheel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

A 45-metre observation wheel opened to visitors Friday on Nemunas Island in Kaunas, with the city’s mayor saying the attraction was not intended to generate significant revenue for the municipal budget.
Named “Kaunastic”, the wheel began operating at 4:00, according to the Kaunas municipality.
A ride lasts about 15 minutes and includes three rotations. Each enclosed gondola can accommodate up to six passengers, while the wheel has a stated capacity of up to 760 visitors per hour.
Mayor Visvaldas Matijošaitis said the city did not view the attraction as a business venture.
“Whether you build a swimming pool, a sports hall or an ice arena, the goal is not business here,” Matijošaitis told reporters when asked whether the wheel was expected to generate income for the city.
The mayor also acknowledged that the wheel had not yet been coordinated with Lithuania’s Department of Cultural Heritage, saying the municipality had not had enough time to complete the process.
“It is a structure that is, in a way, temporary. Everything is being coordinated now, and perhaps we made some mistakes,” Matijošaitis said. He added that the wheel could be moved within a week if residents decided another location would be more suitable.
He also dismissed concerns about its impact on the surroundings, saying he believed the attraction would not damage the environment or the cityscape.
Tadas Stankevičius, head of Kaunas IN, the municipal institution that commissioned the wheel, said he would be satisfied if 100,000 people visited annually.
“I think we will definitely cover the operating costs. The only question is how long it will take for the investment in the wheel itself to pay off,” Stankevičius said.
Kaunas purchased the wheel in April under a contract worth 4.6 million euros from Dutch engineering company SkyView Creation B.V.
The company will also provide technical maintenance for the first year after installation, LRT reported.
An adult ticket costs 12 euros, while tickets for children, students, seniors and people with disabilities cost 8 euros.
A family ticket costs 35 euros for two adults and two children, or 39 euros for two adults and three children.
A VIP cabin for one or two people costs 50 euros and includes sparkling wine or another beverage. The cabin can accommodate up to four people, with each additional passenger charged 25 euros.
Kaunas IN had previously considered several locations for the wheel, including the Small Oak Park, near the Kaunas County Public Library, Parodos Hill, Vytautas Park and Nemunas Island.

The group found a scent bottle, a zip made in Pennsylvania in the mid-1930s, parts of a pocket knife of the same brand listed in the aircraft inventory, and the heel of a woman's shoe.
Archive research discovered that human remains discovered on the island in 1940 were initially believed to be of Earhart or Noonan — but were lost in the chaos of the Pacific war.
Despite the searches, no one has yet found the "smoking gun" artifact, an item that could only have come from the doomed flight.
Satellite images offer fresh hope
Expedition leader Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), believes the elements may have uncovered incontrovertible evidence.
A powerful tropical cyclone tore through the central Pacific in 2015, shifting geographical features on the island and in its lagoon. Satellite images taken over the following years showed what might be the outline of an aircraft fuselage and wings in shallow water off the Taraia promontory.
"This object in the satellite images is exactly the right size to represent the fuselage and tail of the Electra," the ALI website states. "It also appears to be very reflective and is likely to be metallic. It lies in very shallow water, largely covered by sediment, in a place where the current would bring an object floating into the lagoon through Tatiman Passage, the opening to the ocean and the reef."
Pettigrew's 17-strong team intends to focus all its efforts on the place where the images indicate debris may be located, using drone photography, remote sensing with magnetometers and sonar units. If the initial results are positive, a hydraulic dredge will excavate sediment.
"Once we have a sufficient portion of the object exposed, we should be able to identify it," according to the ALI's expedition plan. "If it is made of aircraft aluminum and has the specific shape and rivet patterns of the Electra, we will know that we have found the remains of Earhart's aircraft."
In search of a 'smoking gun'
Much of the ALI's theory is based on the research and fieldwork carried out by TIGHAR, but its executive director, Ric Gillespie, is not convinced the researchers will find the "smoking gun."
"The object visible in old satellite imagery that Pettigrew believes is aircraft wreckage does not look like aircraft wreckage," Gillespie told DW. "It looks like a dead pandanus tree that was uprooted in a storm and washed up on Taraia."
"Pettigrew thinks the wreckage is no longer visible because it is buried in silt," Gillespie noted. "He has never been to that location and does not understand that the silt there is only a few inches deep."
Teams from TIGHAR searched the same location in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors and drew blanks, he said. Yet Gillespie remains convinced that Earhart was on Nikumaroro.
"I think the aircraft sank immediately after being washed over the reef edge and was smashed to pieces in the surf," he said. "Major components were eventually buried in underwater landslides … or grown over with coral. We have found what there is to find."
Dorothy Cochrane, who has monitored progress in the search for Earhart for more than 35 years as curator at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC, and continues to do so since her recent retirement, says Earhart still holds fascination for so many people "because it is 'the greatest unsolved mystery of the 20th and continuing into the 21st centuries.'"
An alternative scenario
She has a different view of what happened in 1937. She argues that if Earhart was nearly out of fuel while still close to Howland, it would have been impossible to fly another 640 kilometers (400 miles) to Nikumaroro. Cochrane also says that items cited as evidence of a castaway on the island can be explained by other visitors and by a small settlement that existed there for several years.
"I believe that Earhart and Noonan were in the general vicinity of Howland Island, based on the facts of the flight, but just could not find it before they ran out of fuel," she said.
"Howland Island was a tiny speck in the morning light of a vast sea," she said, suggesting Earhart could not establish radio contact to guide her the last few miles to her destination.
Cochrane believes the Electra lies on the seabed near Howland. Others have advanced this theory, and several searches of the area have been carried out in recent years.
If Pettigrew's lead pays off, however, it will conclude aviation's nearly 90-year puzzle.

Washington’s diplomacy in Sudan has backfired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:41:45 UTC
20:41:45 KST

Washington’s diplomacy in Sudan has backfired
Pressure meant to isolate Sudan’s army has instead left Washington isolated and a ceasefire further out of reach.
After more than three years, Washington continues to fumble its way through a response to Sudan’s heart-wrenching war. This past week, it may have inadvertently backed itself into a diplomatic corner that offers no options for either itself or Sudan’s army to exit, putting a ceasefire even further out of reach.
As world leaders gathered in New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Washington pressed hard on the leaders of the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) to sign an unconditional ceasefire that would freeze the conflict and allow unimpeded access for critical aid deliveries.
In the past, the rebel Rapid Support Forces militia, using the ample diplomatic and public relations support from its chief regional backer, has been quick to agree to any deal that puts it on equal footing with the national army it is seeking to unseat. But with no intention or ability to implement the terms of any ceasefire, the RSF’s commitment to peace is likely worth what one would expect from a mercenary army that has committed multiple rounds of genocide. Still, United States officials repeatedly refer to the RSF in diplomatic circles as the more “cooperative party”.
In that light, since earlier this year, Washington’s pressure campaign has been focused on the SAF almost exclusively in the misguided belief that sufficient pressure would bring the army to its knees and cause it to abandon its effort to liberate the millions of Sudan’s civilians trapped under RSF rule. But 20 years of comprehensive US sanctions on Sudan, far more biting and wide-ranging than anything Presidents Donald Trump’s or Joe Biden’s administrations have imposed, should have taught the Trump team that sanctions in Sudan are not instruments to be used tactically. This is a regime capable of withstanding US pressure over the long run.
Nonetheless, a new round of US sanctions against SAF military procurement networks in June was followed by the imposition of chemical weapons sanctions in July despite the lack of any credible attempt to investigate the facts of their use on the ground. Later, in August, the US added to its punitive approach by tabling a new initiative at the UN to impose a countrywide arms embargo, updating the Darfur arms embargo dating from the first Darfur genocide in the early 2000s, which the RSF and its regional backers have flouted on a nearly daily basis since the start of the war.
Washington’s latest move was widely interpreted as an unbalanced attempt to target the army’s supply networks that had recently enabled a number of critical battlefield victories for the SAF and created a shift in momentum in the conflict. But lacking the minimum votes from even half the UN Security Council to expand the embargo in addition to the likely prospect of a Russian veto, the US agreed to a one-month technical extension of the current embargo in the hope that an additional month of lobbying would add supporters to its initiative. It won’t.
The final piece of Washington’s maximum pressure campaign came last week when it chose to tighten its noose around Khartoum by making General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan’s attendance at the General Assembly contingent upon his signing of Washington’s stale ceasefire deal. Acts of diplomatic blackmail are high-risk gambits and, in this case, reflect more Washington’s own deep embarrassment and growing frustration at failing to get a deal signed than the army’s intransigence.
Since Washington first tabled its ceasefire proposal in the days leading up to last year’s UN General Assembly, it has been repeatedly stymied by both sides’ unwillingness to sign. But fighters are going to fight. Especially if they believe that the deal they are meant to sign only allows the other side to regroup and rearm. Indeed, a ceasefire signed in a vacuum that offers neither side a glimpse of their respective futures is more likely to entrench the de facto partition that already divides the country.
That is clearly an outcome that benefits the Rapid Support Forces, which is eager to formalise its rule over large swaths of the country, more than Sudan’s army, which argues that it is fighting to make the country whole again.
The often-repeated belief held by Washington that both sides are continuing to fight because they think they can achieve a total military victory misdiagnoses each side’s motivations. They fight because they believe they have to win to ensure their own survival.
This motivation to fight was only given further fuel by the US Department of State’s hastily issued statement in the midst of the UN’s marathon meetings last week, arguing that, “Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan – they rule through force of arms alone. The conduct of each leader of the warring factions renders them ineligible to govern the country.”
This may be true in the long term, but it is hardly a diplomatically smart tactic to employ if trying to persuade either side to lay down their arms in the near term. Instead, the statement appears intended more as an ex post facto justification for Washington’s latest diplomatic sleight of hand in barring al-Burhan from delivering his country’s address to the UN General Assembly.
Leave aside the breach of international law and diplomatic protocol or the policy inconsistency that saw leaders from military juntas across Africa, not to mention an Iranian delegation, receive visas to New York. Washington’s choice appears to be more than a simple strong-arm tactic to achieve a ceasefire and raises the question of whether it is ratcheting up its pressure even further to the only place left for it to go by trying to bring about more immediate regime change in the country.
Taken alongside the manifold measures this year to punish, isolate and delegitimise Sudan’s army, the argument is hard to ignore. But here too, a US approach that has largely been driven by tactics and not strategy risks making solutions even more difficult to achieve. Already, Washington’s move has left it isolated among the broad Western, Arab and African coalitions that are pressing not merely for a quick ceasefire but for a more comprehensive and lasting peace that will return Sudan to a stable national and regional footing.
Many countries have since expressed quiet disappointment that the US missed an important opportunity for diplomacy, not for al-Burhan to express his views on the war but for the military leader to hear loudly and collectively the calls for peace from dozens of assembled world leaders. Most serious was Saudi Arabia’s warning that it would review its participation in the US-led Quad initiative going forward.
The Trump administration has little progress to show since it announced last summer its ambition to bring peace to Sudan. Instead, the administration appears to be making many of the same mistakes past US peacemaking efforts have made by believing that diplomatic pressure alone will shape battlefield outcomes and aid the cause of peace.
Last week, Washington took this approach to an extreme. But the isolation intended for Sudan’s army has ricocheted back onto Washington. Reversing course and engaging the war’s belligerents are today not merely necessary for the US to save face and maintain a diplomatic coalition it aims to lead, but they are the only thing that will save lives in Sudan.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Global life expectancy nears pre-pandemic level, but healthy years lag behind: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:40:37 UTC
20:40:37 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Global life expectancy has nearly returned to its pre-COVID-19 pandemic level, but healthy life expectancy continues to lag behind, according to the World Health Organization's (WHO) latest estimates released Friday.
Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, close to the 73.4 years seen in 2019, a year before the pandemic hit, WHO's Global Health Estimates showed.
Healthy life expectancy recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level, said the UN agency.
“Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Alain Labrique, the director of WHO's Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI. “The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health.”
The WHO also reported a growing mental health burden. Between 2019 and 2023, the global age-standardized rate of healthy life lost climbed about 20% for depressive disorders and nearly 45% for anxiety disorders.
Together, depression and anxiety accounted for an estimated 110 million years of healthy life lost through premature death and disability in 2023.
Drug use disorders also showed diverging regional trends between 2000 and 2023, with the Americas seeing the largest increases in the risk of mortality and healthy life loss, while the Western Pacific saw substantial declines.
Meanwhile, noncommunicable diseases accounted for 74% of deaths globally in 2023, up from 58% in 2000.
Dementia became the fifth-leading cause of death globally in 2023, up from 19th in 2000, with deaths tripling over the period.

Poland upgrades military electronics plant near Wrocław
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:39:54 UTC
20:39:54 KST

- PIT-RADWAR signed a nearly 21 million zloty contract with Grupa KDM for the first stage of modernizing its Czernica plant.
- The full investment is worth nearly 90 million zlotys and is tied to Poland's San counter-drone program.
Polish state-owned radar maker PIT-RADWAR has signed a contract to start rebuilding its plant in Czernica, near Wrocław, the first step in a nearly 90 million zloty (about $23 million) investment that the company links to Poland’s new counter-drone program.
The first stage is worth nearly 21 million zlotys (about $5.5 million) before tax, and covers construction and modernization work in most of the plant’s production buildings, Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa, the state defense group that owns PIT-RADWAR, said on Oct. 2. The contractor is Polish construction firm Grupa KDM. PIT-RADWAR will also buy about 4.5 million zlotys’ worth of new workshop equipment with its own money, the Polish defense outlet MILMAG reported.
PGZ said the new buildings and machinery will expand PIT-RADWAR’s production, research, assembly and quality control work at the site. The group did not give a completion date for the first stage or say when the remaining stages will be contracted.
The Czernica plant used to be a separate company, Military Communications Works No. 2, which builds military communications and command systems. It was merged into PIT-RADWAR, with the deal finalized early this year, and the modernization is one of the commitments PGZ made during that merger, Portal Obronny reported. The plant integrates communications systems, builds equipment containers and is a key Polish partner of U.S. firm L3Harris, whose military radios the Polish Armed Forces use.
Equipment made in Czernica goes to both Polish and allied forces, PIT-RADWAR chief executive Arkadiusz Miszuk told the Polish Press Agency. He said employment at the plant will grow by about half. The site currently employs about 170 people, and the company expects that to reach about 270 once all the investment is finished, according to Defence24. PIT-RADWAR is hiring mainly engineers, electronics specialists, welders and fitters.
PIT-RADWAR has tied the Czernica plant to San, Poland’s largest counter-drone program. In January, Poland’s Armament Agency signed a deal worth about 15 billion zlotys (about $3.9 billion) with a consortium led by PGZ and Norway’s Kongsberg for 18 batteries of the San system, with private Polish firm Advanced Protection Systems as a key subcontractor. The system is meant to detect, identify and destroy hostile drones and covers more than 700 vehicles. Deliveries are due to finish within two years.
The program followed the September 2025 incursion of Russian drones into Polish airspace.
The Czernica investment is PIT-RADWAR’s second major factory project, after it expanded production at its plant in Kobyłka near Warsaw. That site builds radars and parts for the Patriot air defense system, including identification friend-or-foe antennas for the new LTAMDS radar under an offset deal with RTX’s Raytheon.
PIT-RADWAR is also the technical lead on two of Poland’s biggest radar programs: 24 P-18PL long-range early warning radars ordered in 2023 and a 2025 contract worth up to 5.8 billion zlotys for up to 46 passive location radars for the Narew short-range air defense system.

T-shirts instead of winter coats: what a warm October reveals about winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:39:43 UTC
20:39:43 KST

At the start of October, temperatures of up to 25C give parts of Europe a last taste of late summer. Yet, according to an old farmers' rule, a warm autumn can herald a severe winter. What do the statistics and meteorologists say?
People out and about these days often still do not need a jacket. October is starting with unusually mild temperatures, with around 25 degrees possible in some countries. After the wet, changeable weather many associate with autumn, it almost feels like a belated summer week.
Yet, according to an old farmers' saying, this fine weather is precisely what should give cause for concern: "If October is warm and fair, a harsh winter will follow."
If you take the saying at face value, you should already be digging out scarf, gloves and snow shovel. The friendlier October is meant to be, the harder the winter that follows. But is that really true?
Is a warm October a warning sign?
Farmers' rules once served as a kind of weather calendar. Long before satellites, weather balloons and computer models were available, people spent generations observing how the seasons unfolded. The experience they gained produced rhymes that were easy to remember and meant to provide guidance for farming and everyday life.
The snag is that something which seems plausible over decades is still far from being a reliable link. That is why, when it comes to October and the winter that follows, it is worth looking back – and history provides a fairly spectacular counter-example.
When the farmers' rule missed the mark completely
Autumn 2006 in Germany, for example, was exceptionally warm. Anyone relying on the old rule back then would have braced for a bitterly cold winter.
It turned out exactly the other way round: the winter of 2006/07 became the warmest in Germany since regular weather records began in 1901. The German Weather Service (DWD) calculated at the time (source in German) an average temperature of 4.3 degrees Celsius – 4.1 degrees above the long-term mean. There was no prolonged spell of frost.
December 2006 was also exceptionally mild, and January set a new temperature record. The old rule had produced about the worst forecast imaginable.
Why October does not 'pre-programme' January
Measurement data show that the current impression of a 'summer-like autumn' is not just subjective. According to the German Weather Service, September 2026 in Germany averaged 15.9 degrees, 2.6 degrees above the long-term norm. Rainfall was also significantly below usual levels.
On 30 September, 31 degrees were recorded on the Upper Rhine and 29 degrees in northern Baden. On 1 October temperatures reached 25 degrees in Bavaria and Saxony and 23 to 25 degrees in Berlin and Brandenburg. That does not mean, however, that the whole of October will continue like this. The weather pattern is expected to shift in the coming days, with temperatures falling.
The weather in Germany is shaped by large-scale airflows. In the winter months, factors such as pressure patterns over the Atlantic, the so-called North Atlantic Oscillation and changes in the Arctic atmosphere play a role. The polar vortex can also influence how cold air masses are distributed.
That is why specific weather forecasts over several months are difficult even with modern models. The further ahead you look, the less it is about pinpointing the weather on a particular day and the more it is about probabilities and possible developments.
El Niño and its influence
One factor still makes the outlook for winter 2026/27 interesting: El Niño.
The climate phenomenon in the tropical Pacific is currently developing with unusual strength. According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), there is more than a 90 per cent probability of a very strong El Niño event in autumn and winter 2026/27.
For October to December, NOAA puts the chance at 75 per cent that the intensity of the phenomenon will exceed all previous El Niño events since 1950.
El Niño influences the global climate system, but its effects vary widely from region to region and depend on other atmospheric conditions. NOAA itself stresses that any impacts are not guaranteed.
So will there be snow after all?
A cold winter is of course not ruled out. Even after a very mild autumn, wintry conditions can still set in during January or February.
But as a piece of weather lore from a time before satellites, the old farmers' rule offers no robust forecast. So anyone who sees an ice-cold winter looming just because temperatures reach 20 or 25 degrees at the start of October can afford to relax. A warm October is not a meteorological countdown to frost.

AI generated
LUBLIN – The Polish city of Lublin has revived a Cold War-era air raid shelter as Russia steps up attacks in Ukraine, with one symbolic change reflecting a shift in perceived threats: its emergency exit now faces west, not east.
Poland, once part of the Soviet bloc and now a member of NATO, is on heightened alert after several Russian missile and drone incursions into its airspace. Residents of eastern regions have been issued warnings to seek shelter during Russian air strikes on neighbouring western Ukraine.
The alerts have become an increasingly familiar part of life near the border. Last week, a regional television station interrupted a live broadcast for about 20 minutes after journalists evacuated to a shelter during an air raid warning.
One of the shelters available during recent alerts is a modernised facility beneath the premises of municipal bus operator MPK in Lublin. Built in the mid-1980s at the height of Cold War tensions, it was upgraded to meet current standards.
“It provides shelter for 200 people for up to 72 hours, ensuring access to air, water and electricity independent of external power grids,” Kamil Rzad, a civil defence inspector at MPK Lublin, told Reuters.
Poland repeatedly scrambles aircraft
The upgrades reflect growing efforts to bolster civil defence preparedness during Russia’s war in Ukraine. Yet many residents remain unsure where they would seek refuge in the event of an attack.
The number of shelters is estimated by the government at around 2,000, enough for about 300,000 people. Poland also has more than 86,000 places of refuge offering a lower level of protection, such as basements, underground garages or subway stations, catering for around 23 million people.
“I actually doubt we even have a shelter. I’d probably run to the basement or my own bathroom,” said 77-year-old Elzbieta Woznica.
“For many years I was accustomed to peace and quiet. I couldn’t imagine something like this could happen.”
Prime Minister Donald Tusk this week said Russia’s military campaign in Ukraine was moving ever closer to Ukraine’s border with Poland.
“We are repeatedly forced to scramble our aircraft, night after night and day after day, because Russian attacks near the border have become a constant occurrence,” Tusk told a Cabinet meeting.
“We remain fully focused on ensuring that nothing untoward happens on the Polish side.” REUTERS

Being there from hundreds of kilometers away: Ukrainians are invited to join the fundraiser for vehicles for the front line
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainians are invited to join the fundraiser for vehicles for the front line.
From October 1 to November 11, 2026, EVA customers will be able to add a charitable contribution to their receipt to fund off-road pickups for the 9th Army Corps of the Ukrainian Ground Forces. The new "Be There" fundraiser continues the partnership between EVA and HeroCar to provide the military with wheeled vehicles.
The project launches on the Day of Defenders and Defendresses of Ukraine and offers an opportunity to support the military during regular shopping trips. To do so, customers simply need to tell the cashier at any EVA store the amount they would like to donate. They can also contribute online via the project’s donation jar.
The funds raised will go toward vehicles needed by units of the 9th Army Corps to transport personnel, equipment, and medical supplies.
"Within a day, one pickup in our unit makes 2 to 5 trips and sometimes more, covering between 20 and 300 kilometers—it transports personnel, ammunition, and equipment, and supports rotations and the evacuation of the wounded. When such a vehicle is put out of action, the unit immediately loses several logistical capabilities: transport and rotations slow down, while a vehicle already assigned to another task has to be brought in for urgent evacuation, comments Oleksandr Tsekotskyi, Head of the Civil-Military Cooperation Department of the 9th Army Corps. – The pickups purchased through this fundraiser will help us maintain uninterrupted logistics, conduct timely rotations, and preserve the ability to respond quickly to urgent requests."
HeroCar will be responsible for purchasing, technically preparing, and delivering the pickups. Before being handed over to the military, each vehicle will undergo diagnostics and comprehensive maintenance.
"During our cooperation with EVA, we have managed to build a strategic partnership that enables hundreds of thousands of the chain’s customers to support the military. During this time, as part of our joint projects, the Defense Forces have received more than 160 vehicles. The "Be There" project continues this work and makes it possible to direct assistance toward the current needs of the 9th Army Corps," says Yevheniia But, CEO of the Ruslan Shostak Foundation.
The "Be There" project continues the systematic cooperation between EVA and HeroCar, which has been ongoing since 2023. As part of previous initiatives, the chain and the foundation, with the participation of hundreds of thousands of caring donors, raised more than UAH 26 million and delivered over 160 wheeled vehicles to the military. In particular, over the past year alone, they delivered 119 off-road motorcycles, five medical evacuation vehicles, three pickups for mobile air defense crews, and more.
"With these fundraisers, there is no point at which one can say: the vehicles have been delivered, the need has been met, and we are moving on to another issue. Vehicles at the front wear out, break down, and are lost under shelling. Therefore, returning to the same need is a necessary part of providing assistance. For us, the previous results are also a source of experience. We have a reliable partner and customers who get involved. This is what we are relying on as we launch "Be There." We want the military to feel one simple thing through the project’s name: their request has been heard and is being acted upon," summed up Oleksandra Hnatik, Deputy Director for Reputation Management at the EVA chain.

World food prices rose in September to a nearly four-year high – UN

World food prices rose in September to a nearly four-year high – UN
Kyiv • UNN
The FAO Food Price Index rose to 136 points due to weather risks and disruptions in the Black Sea. The forecast for grain trade was lowered.
World food prices rose in September to their highest level in nearly four years due to logistical disruptions and weather risks that affected agricultural commodity markets, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said. Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
Concerns about a strong El Niño weather event pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while a war-related collapse in Black Sea trade at the beginning of last month drove wheat futures to a three-year high.
The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in international prices for a basket of food commodities, averaged 136.0 points, compared with a revised 134.0 points in August. This was the index’s highest level since November 2022.
The FAO Sugar Price Index rose by 6.1% in September compared with August. This was the third consecutive monthly increase. Adverse weather conditions threaten to reduce supplies in key producing regions.
The benchmark grain price index rose by 5.1% over the month. Additional pressure came from worsening prospects for the U.S. corn harvest and disruptions to grain trade through the Black Sea.
Vegetable oil prices rose by 0.9%. The main factor was an increase in palm oil prices due to strong demand and concerns about production risks in Southeast Asia associated with El Niño.
The overall FAO Meat Price Index fell by 1.1%. This was linked to lower poultry prices, partly due to falling demand in the European Union after new import rules came into force.
Separately, the FAO made almost no change to its forecast for global cereal production in 2026 — 2.979 billion metric tons. This is 2.1% below the record figure of the previous year, but still the second-largest harvest in the history of observations.
At the same time, the FAO cut its forecast for global cereal trade in the 2026/27 marketing year by 0.7% compared with last month’s forecast. The reason given was lower expectations for wheat and corn exports amid restrictions on shipping in the Black Sea.

The 'Flydubai incident' tests resilience of the regional aviation sector
The region's aviation sector is facing an immensely challenging period as rising security risks intersect with higher fuel prices and fluctuating demand at a time when airlines are trying to recover from disruption caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran. Now, the "Flydubai incident" has added a new layer of concern.
A Flydubai aircraft made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, on Wednesday, two days ago. The circumstances and motives behind the incident remain unclear, but it has once again highlighted security concerns linked to aviation in the region.
The number of flights operated by airlines in the region, particularly Gulf carriers, fell to near-zero after the war began on 28 February. Airlines gradually resumed operations, and flights are now close to their pre-war levels.
James Halstead, managing partner at Aviation Strategy, told Reuters that it was difficult to assess the implications of the Flydubai incident while many questions remained unanswered.
He said its likely impact would vary depending on whether it was linked to terrorism or mental health problems, as happened in the 2015 Germanwings crash.
"If the incident is similar to what happened with Germanwings, its impact on Flydubai as an airline is likely to be greater than its impact on travel in the region," Halstead said. "If it is terrorism-related, the picture is different, and its impact is likely to be largely limited to transport to Israel."
Following the incident, Flydubai, which is owned by the Dubai government, suspended its flights to Israel until the ongoing investigations are completed.
Data from FlightRadar24 shows that the number of Flydubai flights has already lagged behind those of other Gulf airlines in returning to pre-war levels.
Reuters quoted aviation analyst John Strickland as saying that Flydubai is considered "one of the main economic and tourism tools in Dubai's portfolio".
He added that the region had demonstrated resilience in the face of new complexities and threats since the war with Iran began.
"We have seen very strong and largely thriving demand in the region," he said, noting that he expected Flydubai to overcome the impact of the incident given its position as a key link between Dubai and regional markets.
"It would surprise me if it had any significant impact," he remarked.
Analysts also expected Flydubai to benefit from its position as a major regional carrier.
In relation to Israel, data from Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport shows that Flydubai is among the 10 largest airlines operating there by passenger numbers.
It is also the main Gulf carrier on the route, according to Reuters.
Flydubai was established in 2008 as a low-cost carrier owned by the emirate's government, complementing Emirates' role by serving regional markets and short- and medium-haul destinations.
However, the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began on 28 February, caused heavy losses for the sector after Gulf flights fell to near-zero levels in its early stages before gradually recovering.
This coincided with a sharp rise in jet fuel prices, one of the highest operating costs for airlines, putting pressure on their profit margins.
Meanwhile, the failure of efforts to reach a peace agreement led to another decline in flight volumes in recent weeks.

Russia Lost Ground Despite Putin’s Claims of Major Advances, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:36:10 UTC
20:36:10 KST

Russian forces have suffered a net loss of controlled territory since March, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), challenging President Vladimir Putin’s claims of accelerating battlefield advances.
In its report published Thursday, Oct. 1, the Washington-based think tank said Russia’s rate of territorial advance declined significantly in March and has since remained low or even negative.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
After adjusting for territory liberated during Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi, ISW calculated that Russian forces had lost control of a net 293.59 square kilometers (113.36 square miles) across the front since March.
A separate calculation that includes areas of Russian infiltration, where Moscow has not established full control, shows a net expansion of Russia’s presence by 174.44 square kilometers (67.35 square miles) over the same period.
September mapping shows Russian losses
ISW’s September mapping recorded Russian gains of 175.54 square kilometers (67.78 square miles) of Ukrainian territory and losses of 256.35 square kilometers (98.98 square miles).
That represents a net Russian territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers (31.20 square miles), equivalent to an average of 2.69 square kilometers (1.04 square miles) per day.
A separate measure that includes areas of infiltration shows a larger net Russian loss.
Under that methodology, Russian forces seized or infiltrated 143.2 square kilometers (55.29 square miles) while losing 318.38 square kilometers (122.93 square miles) – a net loss of 175.18 square kilometers (67.64 square miles).
SBU Nabs 2 Zaporizhzhia Teenagers Accused of Moscow-Backed Assassination Plot
ISW cautioned that the September figures include Ukrainian gains from Operation Vivaldi that occurred over several preceding months but became publicly known only in September.
Ukraine maintained operational secrecy around the counteroffensive, making it difficult for open-source analysts to determine precisely when some territory changed hands.
Operation Vivaldi complicates monthly comparisons
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps conducted Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk region, disrupting Russian plans to advance toward Sloviansk and encircle Ukraine’s fortified defensive belt from the east.
ISW has confirmed the liberation of at least 147 square kilometers (57 square miles) during the operation.
Ukrainian commanders put the figure higher. Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, commander of the 3rd Army Corps, said Ukrainian forces had reclaimed 176 square kilometers (68 square miles), liberated five settlements and captured more than 250 Russian soldiers during the operation’s first three stages.
President Volodymyr Zelensky later said Ukraine was preparing a fourth phase of the counteroffensive.
ISW said Ukraine’s effective operational security would probably make future month-to-month assessments of territorial changes similarly difficult.
Putin claims accelerating advances
ISW’s assessment contrasts with Putin’s description of accelerating Russian advances.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club on Thursday, Putin claimed that Russian forces had brought 1,301 square kilometers (502 square miles) of Ukrainian territory under their control in September alone.
“In September alone, Russia brought 1,301 square kilometers (502 square miles) under control,” Putin said, claiming the figure was 2.5 times the level in previous months.
The Kremlin did not provide independently verifiable evidence supporting the figure.
Putin’s figure is more than seven times the 175.54 square kilometers (67.78 square miles) of Russian gains recorded in ISW’s September mapping.
ISW’s mapping instead recorded a net reduction of approximately 81 square kilometers (31 square miles) in Russian-controlled territory. However, the delayed confirmation of Ukrainian advances means that change cannot be attributed entirely to fighting in September.
The institute has repeatedly accused the Kremlin and senior Russian commanders of exaggerating battlefield advances to portray a Russian victory as inevitable and pressure Ukraine and its partners into accepting Moscow’s demands.
The latest figures continue a trend Kyiv Post reported in May, when Russian forces recorded their first monthly net territorial loss since Ukraine’s 2024 operation in Russia’s Kursk region.

BAE to add jam-resistant GPS to carrier landing system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:34:49 UTC
20:34:49 KST

- BAE Systems received a $16 million contract from Collins Aerospace to upgrade the U.S. Navy's JPALS carrier landing system to M-code GPS.
- The DIGAR-500M receiver will run older SAASM and new M-code signals together, supporting aircraft with and without the upgrade.
BAE Systems will upgrade the GPS inside the U.S. Navy’s carrier landing system to the military’s encrypted, jam-resistant M-code signal under a $16 million contract from Collins Aerospace.
The company will design and develop the M-code GPS solution for the Joint Precision Approach and Landing System, known as JPALS, BAE Systems said on Oct. 1. It will supply its DIGAR-500M anti-jam receiver for the job. The company did not say when development will finish, how many receivers the work covers, or when upgraded systems could reach the fleet.
JPALS guides aircraft onto the decks of aircraft carriers and amphibious assault ships using GPS, in fog, heavy rain and rough seas, without relying on landing radar. All three versions of the F-35 carry it, as do the CMV-22B Osprey and the MQ-25 Stingray unmanned tanker. The system reached initial operational capability with U.S. Marine Corps F-35Bs on amphibious ships in 2018 and with the U.S. Navy on nuclear-powered carriers in 2021.
Raytheon, now part of RTX, built JPALS and delivered all 23 low-rate production units to the U.S. Navy under a $234 million contract awarded in 2019. The system is also installed on Britain’s HMS Queen Elizabeth, Italy’s ITS Cavour and Japan’s JS Izumo. Collins Aerospace, which awarded the BAE Systems contract, is also an RTX business.
BAE Systems already provides the GPS receivers in today’s JPALS. They use an older protected technology called SAASM, short for Selective Availability Anti-Spoofing Module. The new DIGAR-500M will run SAASM and M-code at the same time, so the system can work with aircraft that have and have not yet been upgraded, the company said.
M-code is a military-only GPS signal that is encrypted and built to hold up better against jamming and spoofing, where an enemy broadcasts false signals to throw off navigation. For a carrier landing, where an aircraft depends on precise position data in the final seconds before touchdown, a corrupted signal is a safety problem as much as a combat one.
The DIGAR receiver uses digital beamforming, which lets its antenna electronics focus on satellite signals while tuning out interference. It can track up to 24 steered beams at once, BAE Systems said.
“Integrating M‑Code strengthens JPALS against evolving threats and ensures our warfighters maintain a decisive operational advantage,” said Molly O’Brien, program manager for Airborne GPS at BAE Systems.
The upgrade is a small piece of a much larger and slower effort. The Government Accountability Office has estimated that up to 1 million M-code receivers could be needed across some 700 types of weapon systems, from ground vehicles to destroyers and fighter jets. U.S. Air Force officials now expect operational testing of the chip cards that let ships and aircraft receive M-code to wrap up in fiscal 2027, two decades after the first satellite broadcasting the signal went into orbit, Breaking Defense reported in July.
BAE Systems bought Collins Aerospace’s military GPS business in 2020.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani again sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, calling him “the architect of a horrific genocide” and saying he supports the United States joining the International Criminal Court in The Hague, as well as enforcing the arrest warrants it has issued, including the one against Netanyahu.
Mamdani made the remarks in an extensive interview on the American podcast This Past Weekend, hosted by Theo Von, a well known comedian and podcaster who regularly interviews public figures, politicians, and entertainers.
The conversation initially focused on the cost of living, socialism, and the management of New York City, but toward the end shifted to a lengthy discussion about Israel, Gaza, and Netanyahu’s recent visit to the city.
Von raised the question of whether Netanyahu could have been arrested during his visit to New York and asked whether it had ultimately become clear that the mayor lacked the legal authority to arrest him or prevent him from entering the city.
Mamdani replied that after reviewing the legal framework, it became clear that the relevant authority rested with the federal government.
“If the federal government were to join the International Criminal Court, it could enforce an arrest warrant,” he said.
When Von noted that the United States is not a member of the court, Mamdani replied, “We’re not. But I believe we should join it, and that we should enforce its warrants.”
Accountability, rule of law shaken by not arresting Netanyahu, Mamdani says
The mayor said he viewed the issue as part of a broader principle of accountability and the rule of law.
“The more that people see someone breaking a law or a rule and there being no accountability for it, the more they begin to ask whether those rules have any value at all,” he said.
“We always talk about international law, about the things that began to be created after World War II, about the UN and the idea of multilateralism. A lack of enforcement also undermines their value.”
Mamdani added, “The United States government should join the International Criminal Court. It should enforce every warrant that has been issued. In the case of the prime minister, the warrant was issued over allegations of crimes against humanity and war crimes.”
Von later returned to the question directly.
“But if it were up to you, we would arrest this guy, you think?” he asked.
Mamdani replied, “If it were up to me, the United States government would join the International Criminal Court and honor every arrest warrant it has issued.”
Mamdani says Netanyahu's UNGA speech was attempt to divert attention
Referring to remarks Netanyahu made about him during his speech at the UN General Assembly, Mamdani said that at the time he had been meeting with the prime minister of the Netherlands at an LGBTQ center in Manhattan.
“When I came back from the meeting, they said to me: Oh, by the way, here’s what he said at the UN. It was strange,” Mamdani said.
Asked whether he felt Netanyahu had attacked him personally, Mamdani said, “All of this is an attempt to divert attention from accountability. Mention as many people as possible and try to turn it into an exchange. This is not about me and him. This is about the fact that he is the architect of a genocide.”
Mamdani added pointedly, “If I were the architect of a genocide, I would probably talk about anything else but that.”
Von also asked how anger directed at Israel and its policies could be prevented from turning into hostility toward Jews in the United States.
Mamdani said he was proud that New York has the largest Jewish population of any city in the United States and stressed, “No Jewish person in New York City is responsible for the actions of the State of Israel.”
He said those seeking to assign responsibility should direct it toward decision-makers, the prime minister and the State of Israel, “and also toward our own complicity as American taxpayers, given the billions of dollars we have sent and continue to send in the form of bombs.”
Mamdani said New York City had published a municipal plan that day to combat antisemitism, which he said was intended not only to condemn incidents but also to prevent them.
At the same time, he stressed, “Criticism of the State of Israel, of its policy decisions, of the genocide, is not in and of itself antisemitism.”
Mamdani hosts Gazan Palestinians at official residence
Mamdani argued that despite talk of a ceasefire, civilians in Gaza were continuing to be harmed.
As an example, he cited a claim that the IDF had killed an 11-year-old Palestinian boy the previous week in an area considered safe.
He said he had hosted Palestinian families from Gaza at his official residence, Gracie Mansion, the previous week.
Among them, he described meeting two sisters and their mother, who told him that the strike in which one of the sisters was wounded had killed two of their siblings.
“An elderly grandmother came up to me at the end of the meeting and simply asked, ‘Can you bring my son here?’ I had to tell her that I would try, but as mayor I could not promise it.”
Addressing the future of US policy after the Trump administration, Mamdani said there needed to be a commitment to a different approach.
“How are you going to provide something other than 1,000-pound bombs?” he asked.
Future US policy, he said, should be based on “humanity, not only toward the people we represent at home, but also toward the people we bomb abroad.”

Supreme Court allows Ofer Cassif, Ra'am, Joint List to run in 26th Knesset election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:32:26 UTC
20:32:26 KST

The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that MK Ofer Cassif, Ra'am, and the Joint List may run in the election for the 26th Knesset, overturning the Central Elections Committee's decisions to disqualify them.
At the same time, candidate Sami Abu Shehadeh announced that he was withdrawing his candidacy following the hearing, and the proceedings concerning him were dismissed.
The hearing was held on Thursday following four parallel proceedings brought before the Supreme Court: requests to approve the disqualification of two individual candidates, MK Ofer Cassif and Sami Abu Shehadeh, and appeals filed by the United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List against the Elections Committee's decision to disqualify the two lists in their entirety.
In Cassif's case, the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify him on the grounds of denying the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and supporting the armed struggle of an enemy state or terrorist organization.
By a 7-2 majority, the Supreme Court declined to approve the disqualification and ruled that Cassif may run.
Supreme Court rejects Cassif disqualification
All members of the judicial panel stressed that they disapproved of Cassif's statements and actions, which the court described as "revolting."
Nevertheless, the majority ruled that his actions and statements did not meet the stringent tests established in case law, and that the evidence had not reached the required "critical mass" needed to establish grounds for disqualification.
The two dissenting justices, David Mintz and Alex Stein, took the opposite view, holding that Cassif's conduct and statements established grounds for disqualification based on support for armed struggle against the state and therefore justified barring him from running.
Regarding the two lists that had been disqualified by the Central Elections Committee, Ra'am and the Joint List, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in their favor and accepted their appeals.
The justices found that the material and evidence presented to the Central Elections Committee did not meet the narrow and stringent standards established in case law for barring an entire candidate list from participating in an election.
Sami Abu Shehadeh withdraws candidacy
Meanwhile, Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh announced on Friday that he was withdrawing his candidacy on behalf of the Joint List.
During the hearing, the justices made clear that there was "unanimity that the remarks made by Mr. Abu Shehadeh are painful, outrageous and nauseating."
The judges also indicated to the parties that the emerging outcome was that they would uphold the Central Elections Committee's decision to disqualify him.
The decision surprised many in Arab society and among Joint List activists, who believed Abu Shehadeh, Balad, and the Joint List should have insisted on a reasoned High Court ruling, particularly given that the proceedings had already reached such an advanced stage.

Just one in 10 Germans thinks Merz is up to the job after election wipeout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:31:15 UTC
20:31:15 KST

Support for Merz plunges after CDU’s losses to Germany’s right and left
Chancellor Friedrich Merz hits a record low approval rating after his party suffered defeats in three state elections.
Stuttgart, Germany – Minutes after the results of the first exit polls flashed across German screens, Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) declared in a televised statement at the party’s headquarters that he was going nowhere.
“It’s a disaster,” he said of the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience. I will muster them – as party chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why the world should care about the far right’s rise in Germany
- list 2 of 4The leftist leader with Turkish roots who could become Berlin’s next mayor
- list 3 of 4‘Hope’ rises in Berlin immigrant communities as Left wins amid AfD gains
- list 4 of 4German, Russian foreign ministers hold rare talks amid rising tensions
But pressure on Merz is mounting.
On Thursday, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his work. That is the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
His party crashed out of the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, failing to clear the 5 percent threshold needed to win seats – the first time this has happened since the Federal Republic of Germany was founded in 1949. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came first with more than a third of the vote.
On the same day in Berlin’s state elections, the CDU suffered another major setback. It came second after The Left party, which won 25.7 percent of the vote. The Left now hopes to form a government in the capital although it will need coalition partners.
Just two weeks earlier, the CDU suffered another blow. The AfD won the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, receiving more than 40 percent of the vote, compared with 17 percent for the CDU.
No obvious successor
Merz could face a revolt within his own party, but removing him as chancellor would be considerably harder.
Under Germany’s Constitution, the Bundestag can replace a chancellor only by simultaneously electing a successor with an absolute majority.
Wolfgang Schroeder, a professor of political science at the University of Kassel, told Al Jazeera: “The CDU is in a situation where it can’t really get any further with Merz, but it also doesn’t know how things would work without him. There is no attractive replacement, so there is no alternative.”
A former chairman of the BlackRock investment company’s German supervisory board, Merz had long harboured ambitions of becoming chancellor but was sidelined by then-CDU leader Angela Merkel in the early 2000s. Merkel later became chancellor in 2005. Merz staged an unexpected comeback, finally taking office in May 2025.
At the helm, Merz has drawn criticism for remarks about the country’s “Stadtbild” (cityscape), widely interpreted as a suggestion that there were too many refugees and migrants on the streets. The debate has resurfaced in recent days with prominent CDU figures returning to the issue after the party’s poor election results.
The AfD’s surge is but one factor behind the decline of Germany’s long-dominant conservative party, which has produced six chancellors in its history.
The CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, govern Germany in coalition with the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The government is struggling amid the rising cost of living, deindustrialisation, crumbling infrastructure and a housing crisis in major cities.
Nils Diederich, a professor emeritus of political science at the Free University of Berlin and a former SPD member in the Bundestag, said Merz has failed to make a good impression but argued he is not the main reason for the CDU’s poor results.
“Overall, I see the coalition itself as the main problem,” he said. “The Social Democrats have worn themselves out in the coalition. They have lost their sense of direction and are putting the brakes on reforms. That, in turn, is dragging the CDU down with them.”
Schroeder told Al Jazeera: “It’s possible that the crisis surrounding the chancellor could develop into a fundamental crisis for the CDU and from there into a crisis for the coalition.”
The reform dilemma
In July, the German government announced a package of 34 measures, including reforms to pensions, taxation, bureaucracy and the labour market. Merz originally intended to push through his repeatedly promised reforms by the end of the year.
But the state elections have put the coalition parties under greater pressure to stake out their own positions.
To ease the burden on people in need of long-term care and to plug multibillion-euro deficits, the SPD is calling for a cap on care costs and for people with private health insurance to share the costs. The CDU firmly rejects both proposals on legal and financial grounds.
State premiers from both major parties and the SPD leadership want to retain the option of retiring without a pension reduction after 45 years of contributions, which they see as a reward for a lifetime of work. The conservative bloc’s business wing, however, insists that the provision be phased out.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD is planning new revenue measures to consolidate the budget but faces fierce resistance from CDU state premiers and conservative legislators determined to block any tax increases.
Schroeder warned that the coming months could be difficult.
“The CDU is caught in a dilemma. If Merz continues down the path of reforms that place a burden on society, the likelihood of cooperative governance with the SPD will diminish further. If he goes along with the course the SPD is proposing, pressure within the party will increase.”
Diederich said: “If the reforms fall through, then either Merz or the Social Democrats would have to act and let the coalition collapse.”
The next major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters elect a new parliament in April.

The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped

The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped
These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.
Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.
These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought.
The 2026 midterms offer Democrats the chance to win the Senate, and in turn the ability to put a serious check on Trump's agenda – including blocking any new appointments to the supreme court or his cabinet.
Republicans currently hold a majority with 53 seats out of 100, while the Democrats and their allies hold the remaining 47.
Thirty-five seats are on the ballot this November. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third facing voters at each two-year election cycle.
But in practice, the battle for the Senate is being fought across a very small map.
The Cook Political Report, a prominent US election forecaster, currently lists seven seats as tossups: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.
A further two – North Carolina and Kansas – are leaning Democrat and Republican respectively.
Democrats must win at least four seats that are held by Republicans to gain a majority.

But as Trump's approval ratings fell over the course of the year amid discontent with the Iran war and rising gas prices, Cook shifted several races in Democrats' direction, as did other major forecasters.
A key example of this is Georgia, which is now rated as a likely win for the Democrats.

Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel.

Poland puts AI to work guarding its border with Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:29:40 UTC
20:29:40 KST

- Poland's military and Border Guard are using an AI system called Intelligent Border to analyze camera, drone and sensor data on the Belarusian border.
- The system is being tested on a section of the eastern border several dozen kilometers long as part of Operation Safe Podlasie.
Poland’s military and Border Guard are now using an artificial intelligence system to watch the country’s border with Belarus, pulling feeds from cameras, drones and other sensors into one picture and flagging activity that needs a human’s attention.
Poland’s Operational Command said the system, called Inteligentna Granica, or Intelligent Border, is now working as part of Operation Safe Podlasie, the military mission that supports the Border Guard along the Belarusian frontier. Brig. Gen. Jarosław Chojnacki, the command’s chief of staff, was briefed during a visit to Task Group Podlasie on how the rollout is going and how the system performs in day-to-day border duty, the command said.
The system is being tested on a stretch of the eastern border several dozen kilometers long. Along with AI, the trial covers robotics and autonomous systems, the command said. It did not say which robotic or autonomous systems are involved, how many are deployed, or exactly where the test section runs.
Intelligent Border was developed by the Artificial Intelligence Implementation Center, part of Poland’s Cyberspace Defense Forces, together with the Border Guard. The software recognizes objects, assesses what they are doing and points operators to events that need attention, the cyber command said in July. The aim is to cut the hours soldiers and border officers spend staring at video feeds and to speed up the response when someone tries to cross.
Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that the system would enter operational use in August.
The work is split between the two services. The Border Guard installs, maintains and oversees the cameras and observation equipment and supplies their data. The military builds and runs the analysis. The system draws on an AI platform the cyber forces have developed called AIRON TACTIC, and its results feed into the TAK and JAŚMIN systems already used by troops and officers on the border, the command told Polish outlet CyberDefence24.
Col. Piotr Turek, who heads the AI center, said earlier this year that the Polish Ministry of National Defence is automating the eastern border, citing Intelligent Border as the clearest example, CyberDefence24 reported.
Operation Safe Podlasie began on Aug. 1, 2024, replacing two earlier missions on the eastern frontier. Polish troops have supported the Border Guard on the Belarusian border since 2021, when Minsk began what Warsaw describes as hybrid attacks, including pushing migrants toward Polish territory.
The military mission is large. More than 10,000 troops took part in the operation’s third rotation, with about 5,000 supporting the Border Guard on the Belarusian border each day. On July 30, the 12th Mechanized Division took over the operation from the 18th Mechanized Division, which led the fourth rotation with four task groups along the border.

Non-neutral Ukraine, in whatever form, poses threat Russia — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:28:57 UTC
20:28:57 KST

SIMFEROPOL, October 2. /TASS/. A non-neutral Ukraine, whatever the form, would pose a constant threat to modern Russia, Alexander Irkhin, a professor at the V. I. Vernadsky Crimean Federal University, told TASS in an interview.
Speaking during the plenary session of the 23rd meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club yesterday, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that Ukraine’s neutral status remains one of Russia’s goals. The head of state noted that from the very beginning of the formation of the post-Soviet space and the new Russia, Moscow proceeded on the assumption that Ukraine would be a neutral state.
"At present, any status for Ukraine other than neutrality poses an existential threat to modern Russia. Moreover, Kiev must be not only neutral but also friendly toward Moscow. However, the second component has not yet been raised, as it is no longer of a legal nature," Irkhin noted.
The expert recalled that Ukraine’s neutral status was a prerequisite for the "civilizational divorce" during the dissolution of the USSR. Western elites from that same period agreed with this. "However, after just a few years, this condition began to gradually erode and be re-evaluated. The main reason was the power vacuum that the weak Russian Federation of the 1990s was unable to fill," Irkhin added.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has traditionally met with Valdai participants since the club’s founding in 2004. The first conference took place in Veliky Novgorod in the Novgorod Region in western Russia, near Lake Valdai, from which the event takes its name. Since 2014, the club’s meetings have been held in Sochi. In 2026, the Valdai meeting moved to the Moscow Region due to the large number of participants, who find it more convenient to travel to Moscow.

The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.

The group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, reports said.

It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft.
The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published on Oct. 1, raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the Nov. 3 elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.

Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough.”
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies’ oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.

In 2027 budget, Kremlin readies for long war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:27:30 UTC
20:27:30 KST

Hello and welcome to Vlast! This is a special edition newsletter looking at the record defense spending in Russia’s recently-released 2027 budget.
There is no paywall this time! If you want to support our work, please consider upgrading to paid.
⏳ This newsletter contains 727 words and will take approximately 3 minutes to read. It was translated and edited by Howard Amos.
The Russian government submitted to parliament on Wednesday a 3-year draft budget that included a post-Soviet record for defense spending in 2027. The huge resources being committed suggest that the Kremlin does not expect the war with Ukraine to end any time soon—and may even be preparing to expand the conflict.
“This is an ultra-militarized budget,” an official who worked on the document told Vlast.
Spending on what the government terms “national defense” next year will be significantly higher than expected, according to the draft, amounting to about 17.1 trillion rubles ($196 billion), or 6.9 percent of projected GDP. When spending on “national security” (the police, National Guard, and intelligence agencies) is added, a staggering 44 percent of Russian spending in 2027 (8.8 percent of GDP) will be related to the military and security services. That is an absolute record.
Before the full-scale invasion, Russia’s defense bill was far lower. Between 2011 and 2022, 29 percent of all spending went toward the military and security services (5.3 percent of GDP).
It’s important to remember that real spending in 2027 is likely to be even higher. Over the course of the war in Ukraine, Finance Ministry planners have repeatedly lowballed defense spending. Notably, the budget deficit was almost five times higher than the official target in 2025, and grew 52 percent between January and August this year.
According to the official who took part in drafting the budget, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and warehouses earlier this year influenced the decision to make such big increases. “This was all happening in the spring and summer, precisely when the budget was being prepared,” he said.
The defense spending plans come despite the Finance Ministry expecting a decline in oil and gas revenues this year and next. According to official estimates, oil and gas revenue will be at historic lows: just 16.2 percent of total revenue in 2026 and 16.6 percent in 2027.
Where will the Kremlin get the money for defense?
First, tax increases are planned for next year (although they will not be as big as recent ones). The Kremlin wants to increase taxes on income earned from securities and bank deposits, as well as tax companies that earn extra income from the sale of gold, some base metals, and fertilizers amid higher global commodity prices. Russian mining and fertilizer companies will pay a 30 percent windfall tax, while gold producers will pay 20 percent.
Second, social spending and investment will fall. This clearly shows that the Kremlin does not have enough money to finance both the war and social and economic development projects—and that it is prioritizing the war. In previous years, the authorities had avoided across-the-board cuts to non-military spending.
Finally, almost the entire budget deficit in 2027 (as well as the unplanned increases to the deficit this year) will be financed via government debt. For the first time in modern Russian history, public debt will exceed 20 percent of GDP (it was about 15 percent before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022).
The unveiling of Russia’s budget—which now needs to be rubber-stamped by parliament and then signed into law by President Vladimir Putin—has coincided with increasingly aggressive rhetoric from the Kremlin.
“After everything they [Ukraine] have done, we will think twice about what we need to do in response,” Putin said last month in response to a question about resuming negotiations. And, speaking on Thursday, Putin rejected a proposal from Kyiv and Washington for a halt to mutual energy infrastructure strikes, calling it “absurd.” In recent weeks, Russia has attacked energy facilities, data centers, and other infrastructure across Ukraine. Strikes on Kyiv have been an almost daily occurrence, with regular civilian casualties.
This newsletter was compiled with input from a journalist who wished to remain unidentified for security reasons.

Russia Plans to Cut 90% of Power, Heat and Water in Ukraine’s Biggest Cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:26:11 UTC
20:26:11 KST

Russia is planning a campaign of strikes aimed at cutting electricity, heating, and water supplies to Ukraine’s largest cities this winter, according to a document Ukrainian officials presented to European partners, The New York Times reported.
The ultimate goal is to cut off electricity, heat, and water to major Ukrainian cities, which could lead to a humanitarian crisis. Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa have been identified as the main targets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The plan is to cut electricity supplies to these cities by 90 percent, reduce heating supplies by 90 percent, and severely disrupt the operation of the sewer system.
The newspaper said it obtained a copy of the Russian-language document, dated August. Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented the document to European partners in Paris two weeks earlier, describing it as an intercepted Russian plan, according to two people familiar with his presentation.
It outlines a campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses.
The reported strategy raises concerns about simultaneous failures of essential services as temperatures fall. Alongside attacks on power generation, the document describes strikes on pumping stations and water treatment facilities using dozens of ballistic missiles and glide bombs.
Ukrainian officials expressed concern about limited backup arrangements for severe interruptions to water supplies, according to the report.
‘No Rules Now’: Putin Orders Civilian Attacks, Zelensky Says
One of the document’s most consequential proposals involves forcing Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to shut down by striking the electrical substations connecting them to the national grid.
Those substations are located less than a mile from the reactors, the newspaper reported. The described targets are the plants’ grid connections, rather than the reactors themselves.
The warning comes as Russia renews attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season. A large missile-and-drone barrage this week killed civilians and caused widespread power outages, with Ukrainian officials identifying energy facilities as principal targets.
The New York Times reported that Russian President Vladimir Putin had publicly pledged a major campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure this winter, presenting it as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The campaign is expected to peak in November, according to the report published on Tuesday in The Economist. The publication also described the offensive as an effort to cripple the Ukrainian capital before winter arrives.
Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv’s civilian infrastructure in August and September, according to the report.
