Defense briefing: Russia repeats war aims at UN as frontline clashes fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:25:00 UTC
20:25:00 KST

Defense briefing: Russia repeats war aims at UN as frontline clashes fall
Russia has reiterated at the UN its intention to achieve its war aims in Ukraine at any cost, the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) said Friday
Speaking at the regular Friday defense press conference, Col. Ants Kiviselg said Russia is intensifying its long-range strikes to achieve a deterrent effect, all at a time when Moscow continues to lose more than 10,000 troops per week.
At the same time, the number of combat engagements fell this week – the 240th week of the war – compared with the preceding week. Ukraine too launched its own medium- and long-range strikes.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made the claim that Ukrainian forces lack the means to repel jet-powered drone attacks and to end Russia's blockade of the Black Sea coast.
Col. Kiviselg said Putin had been selective in the truth on this, presenting Russian actions as "countermeasures" to Ukraine's steps while omitting who started the war.
The very fact that Moscow is intensifying its long-range strikes to achieve a deterrent effect shows that Ukrainian strikes on its critical infrastructure and strategic sites have been successful.
More than that, Ukrainian forces have been downing up to 50–60 percent of the much faster jet-propelled drones, Kiviselg noted, and are intensively developing countermeasures. He also noted highlighted spokesman Dmitry Peskov's statements that Russia is closely monitoring which countries help Ukraine produce or supply weapons, and "takes this into account."
Front-line fighting averaged 220 engagements per day last week, as noted down on the previous week and also continuing a gradual decline seen over three weeks. The most intense fighting was in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka areas in Donetsk Oblast, followed by southern Slobozhanske, in Kharkiv Oblast; Lyman in Donetsk Oblast and Huliaipole in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Ukrainian counterattacks took place mainly in the Lyman, Sloviansk (Donetsk Oblast) and Kostiantynivka directions and toward Kupiansk. (Kharkiv Oblast).
Russian forces lost an average of 1,700 personnel per day. Losses remained above 10,000 fighters per week for the fifth consecutive week, and Ukrainian forces have been successful in the Lyman zone, pushing Russian forces further back and improving the situation on the northern flank of the Donbas fortified belt.
Russia's long-range strikes have targeted critical infrastructure, strategic sites, homes, educational, medical and scientific institutions and transport infrastructure in at least 15 Ukrainian oblasts. Since mid-September, Russian forces have tried to hit telecoms companies and data centers to disrupt strategic services and the economy.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said data and technical infrastructure are being protected in several ways, including by moving some infrastructure underground and data to on cloud services.
On September 30, Russian forces carried out a large-scale attack on Kyiv's energy infrastructure, suggesting a possible systematic campaign against Ukraine's energy system. Air raid alerts in September totaled nearly a third of the month in Kyiv, with one hour of alert costing Ukraine around $45 million.
Ukrainian strikes hit military and strategic targets in occupied areas and in Russian regions, destroying 76 air defense systems in September. Ukraine attacked oil refineries in Krasnodar and Perm krais (regions) and in Rostov Oblast, fuel depots in Rostov and Belgorod oblasts, and oil fields in Krasnodar Krai.
Putin signed a law on September 28 classifying as confidential information on companies' exports, including data on products supplied, routes, transshipment points and delivery schedules. Kiviselg said the move is likely aimed at reducing the effectiveness of Ukrainian long-range strikes and hiding the true state of Russia's fuel industry.
On other issues touched on in the press conference, Kiviselg reported Finland and Denmark's security services have issued warnings about possible sabotage in supporting countries; Estonia's own Internal Security Service (ISS) this week said the arson attack on the Milrem Robotics building in Lasnamäe in August was a sabotage act commissioned by Russian special services.
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, has asked allies in recent weeks for more detailed information on Russia-linked incidents and responses, to improve the alliance's threat picture, Kiviselg pointed out.

Ebola death toll in Congo tops 4,000 in fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

British thermal satellite firm doubles its fleet in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:23:44 UTC
20:23:44 KST

- British firm SatVu launched its HotSat-3 thermal imaging satellite on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Oct. 1.
- Once commissioned, HotSat-3 will join HotSat-2, letting SatVu collect thermal imagery anywhere on Earth every 24 hours, day or night.
British company SatVu has launched HotSat-3, a satellite that maps heat on the ground from orbit, giving it a second working spacecraft and the ability to photograph any spot on Earth in thermal infrared once every 24 hours, day or night.
The satellite lifted off on Oct. 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, the London-based company said on Oct. 2. HotSat-3 will now go through commissioning in orbit before it starts commercial work. SatVu did not say how long that will take.
HotSat-3 is SatVu’s third satellite, but only its second operational one. It will work alongside HotSat-2, which launched in March on SpaceX’s Transporter-16 mission and began delivering imagery in June. The company’s first spacecraft, HotSat-1, failed six months after its June 2023 launch.
The satellites carry mid-wave infrared cameras, which detect heat given off by objects instead of reflected sunlight. That lets them work at night and pick out things a normal camera cannot, such as running engines, generators, gas flares, ship wakes and warm cooling water flowing out of power plants. SatVu says its images resolve detail down to 3.5 m (11.5 feet).
For military and intelligence analysts, that means a single image can show whether a vehicle, ship, factory or piece of equipment is running or sitting idle. Repeated images of the same site can show how busy it is and how that changes over days and weeks.
SatVu pitches the data at defense and intelligence users monitoring strategic sites and critical infrastructure, especially at night or in places where reports from the ground are scarce or slow. It also sells to commodity traders and energy analysts, who use heat signatures at refineries and liquefied natural gas plants to spot shutdowns, restarts and changes in output.
“With two operational satellites, we will have double the capacity: customers can collect twice as much imagery, monitor twice as many sites, or return to the same site more often,” said Anthony Baker, CEO and co-founder of SatVu.
HotSat-1, built by Surrey Satellite Technology, returned its first images in October 2023, including wildfires in Canada and urban heat in Las Vegas, before an anomaly halted operations that December. Baker later linked the failure to a likely power circuit problem in the camera. SatVu received a £10 million insurance payout and ordered HotSat-2 and HotSat-3 from the same builder in 2024.
In February, SatVu closed a £30 million ($40 million) funding round that included the NATO Innovation Fund, bringing its total equity funding to £60 million. The company has also received a Defence Innovation Loan from the UK Ministry of Defence through its innovation arm, which Minister of State Luke Pollard said helped attract the private investment.
SatVu says launches for HotSat-4 and HotSat-5 are already booked, and it has contracts covering long-lead parts for HotSat-6. The company has said it plans a constellation of about 10 satellites that could offer up to 20 revisits a day.

‘Containerabad’: Pakistan’s capital and truckers bleed money amid lockdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:22:57 UTC
20:22:57 KST

‘Containerabad’: Pakistan’s capital and truckers bleed money amid lockdown
As Islamabad prepares for another opposition march, drivers and businesses are counting the cost of the barricades.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Two boys scale the rusted corner of a shipping container marked “EVERGREEN” in block white letters. They kick up into handstands, legs steady, without so much as a glance upward, even as traffic passes on the road behind them.
The clip runs 27 seconds, cut exactly to a verse from rap singer Cheema Y’s Punjabi track “Police”, about containers of smuggled goods crossing the border that nobody can account for.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Can Pakistan’s Sohail Afridi win freedom for ex-PM Imran Khan?
- list 2 of 4‘Source of anxiety’: Pakistan cracks down before march to free Imran Khan
- list 3 of 4Pakistan seals roads to Islamabad before protests for Imran Khan’s release
- list 4 of 4Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan’s sisters arrested before planned PTI march
The four-tonne container beneath their feet carries nothing at all. It is one of what transport associations and officials put at between 1,500 and 2,000 heavy steel boxes barricading Islamabad’s roads ahead of an opposition march.
The idea for the video, shared on Instagram six days ago, was the brainchild of 26-year-old Mujaddad Asrar, a callisthenics and parkour athlete. Asrar has been staging shoots like this one on Islamabad’s containers for several years. This clip, along with several others, went out from a friend’s account rather than his own, because the friend has a bigger following, he says.
“It’s like clockwork every year,” he told Al Jazeera. “One lot of containers or another comes right on time, like it’s part of the calendar. It’s basically a fifth season.
“Yeah, these containers have now made Islamabad as Containerabad,” he added, cheerfully.
The containers have been up for nearly four weeks as part of efforts by the country’s government to block an upcoming march on the capital by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The party had planned to set off on September 27 from Peshawar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, then pushed the date back to October 4, citing “strategic reasons.” The march is PTI’s latest attempt to pressure the government into releasing Khan, the country’s most popular political figure according to polls, who has been behind bars for more than three years.
Islamabad has been here before several times in recent years. In August 2024, as PTI petitioned the Islamabad High Court over a cancelled rally permit at D-Chowk, the square where the city’s high-security Red Zone starts, then-Chief Justice Aamer Farooq remarked that the authorities had turned the capital into a “container city”.
Talal Chaudhry, the state minister for interior, however, said the use of containers ahead of the coming protest reflects standard practice rather than overreach.
“Security preparations are based on intelligence assessments and anticipated security requirements, not simply on the date a political event is formally announced,” he told Al Jazeera. “Islamabad is the federal capital, so precautionary security arrangements are often put in place well in advance.”
The price of security
The containers come with a price tag, though no one agrees on what it is.
Islamabad police initially sought roughly 820 million rupees ($2.9m) for a week of security arrangements around PTI’s planned march, according to local media reports. With the march delayed a week, officials now expect the final bill to top 1 billion rupees ($3.6m).
Container rental sits at the centre of that budget: one estimate puts the daily rental for more than 1,500 containers at 46.5 million rupees ($167,000).
While owners maintain they have not been paid for their containers, Chaudhry disputes this.
“What I can say with certainty is that legitimate container rentals are documented and paid through the proper process,” he said.
In a written reply to the National Assembly in March 2025, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi disclosed that the government had spent 1.35 billion rupees ($4.9m) on law-and-order deployments in Islamabad over five years, with a peak of 724 million rupees ($2.6m) in 2022-23.
The reply itemised personnel movement, housing and meals for deployed police, and, in one year, anti-riot equipment, but excluded the period covering the 2024 PTI protest. Nowhere in the government response did the word “container” appear.
Chaudhry rejected the idea that this amounted to an omission. “Container rentals are not necessarily recorded as a separate political-protest expenditure category,” he said. “They are processed through the established administrative and contractual mechanism. Every container hired is recorded, and the corresponding payment is traceable through official accounts.”
Whose containers are these?
The containers fall into two categories: trucks with containers welded on to them owned by individuals, and containers owned by foreign shipping lines sitting on someone else’s vehicle.
Roughly 2,000 vehicles and containers are held across Islamabad, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, according to transporters’ associations, though the figure remains an estimate rather than a definitive number.
Muhammad Owais Chaudhry, a lawyer who heads the All Pakistan Goods Transport Owners Association, represents owners in the first category — those whose trucks and containers have been grabbed by the police.
“If you combine the container and the vehicle, the total cost comes to 30,000 to 40,000 rupees ($108 to $144) a day,” he told Al Jazeera, describing earnings lost per truck-container combination while idle.
“Not a single rupee has been given,” he said of compensation from the government. “No procedure has ever been worked out for how it would be paid. In our history, no transporter has ever received money for any past protests.”
Talal Chaudhry, the state minister, disputes this entirely.
“That is simply not consistent with our records,” he told Al Jazeera. “Containers are hired through a proper contractual mechanism at market rates, and payments are made through official accounts. We have a complete container-by-container record, including payments made in previous years. If there is any legitimate outstanding claim, it will be settled.”
Owais Chaudhry has also pressed officials to buy a fleet of containers outright rather than renting them for every sit-in, adding that the purchase cost of a container is between 400,000 and 500,000 rupees ($1,444 to $1805).
Talal Chaudhry called that a question of policy, not principle.
“The government already has an established rental mechanism that allows containers to be deployed when required without permanently bearing the cost of purchasing, storing and maintaining them,” he said.
One of the vehicles seized belongs to Haji Atlas Khan, provincial general secretary of the All-Pakhtunkhwa Goods Federation.
He was at home in Nowshera district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province when his driver rang one evening in early September to say police had impounded his lorry minutes after it entered Islamabad.
“We didn’t know, and the police didn’t know either, under what authority these vehicles were being seized,” Khan told Al Jazeera.
In the following days, three more of his trucks joined the first at police stations across the capital.
Owais Chaudhry has watched containers seized for sit-ins and protests since 2018, he says. Haji Atlas Khan, in his early 50s, has been in the business for 26 years and has seen his vehicles impounded through several protests and rallies.
But neither has ever waited this long to retrieve a vehicle — and both insist they have never been paid for their losses.
Owais said association officials have met Islamabad’s police leadership and Talal Chaudhry since the crackdown began, but came out of those meetings with “empty promises”.
“Everyone says you’ll get everything,” he said. “But we ask, how, and when?”
Asked about a compensation timeline, minister Talal Chaudhry said the process concerns “the hiring or temporary use of containers, not an indefinite seizure of vehicles”.
Loaded vehicles, he said, were returned immediately, while empty containers taken for security arrangements fall under “the rental arrangement,” with release “coordinated with the relevant authorities.”
None of the drivers or transporters Al Jazeera spoke to recognised that arrangement, received anything in writing, or knew when they might get their vehicles back.
The container ownership has another variable, say sector experts.
“In most cases, the shipping line is the owner of the container,” Mehmood ul Hassan Awan, a Karachi-based customs agent and importer, told Al Jazeera. “We don’t have a single shipping line in Pakistan, only shipping agents.”
Of the roughly 2,000 containers stuck in the three regions, most, he says, belong to foreign shipping lines, each accruing $150 to $300 a day in penalties that flow abroad through the State Bank.
“Those dollars don’t come into our economy,” he said. “They go out.”
Waiting by the trucks
Drivers waiting for release tell a similar story. Owners don’t trust that their trucks and containers will stay safe even in police custody, so they ask drivers to stay near the vehicles — even as they gather dust parked on the streets of Islamabad.
On a strip of open ground near Islamabad’s fruit and vegetable market, Muhammad Naseer and a handful of others sit out the days on a mat laid beside their parked trucks.
Naseer, 48, from Mianwali, on the border of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was hauling an empty container back towards Karachi when police stopped him as he was leaving Islamabad.
“Our container belongs to a shipping line,” he told Al Jazeera. There is a 10-day window to return it, Nasir said, after which “a claim will come.”
One of the trucks nearby belongs to Khan from Nowshera district.
Muhammad Saleem Jaffar, his driver, recalled the night it was stopped: 3am, at a checkpoint near a wholesale market in Islamabad.
He had just dropped off his shipment when police stopped him. Like the others, he, too, has not been told when he might leave.
“No one has ever asked how we are,” he said of the police who come and go from the holding area. “Whether anyone of us is sick, what the loss has been. No one has asked anything at all.”
Conditions have become more difficult.
Driver Farooq Khan, 22, said the single washroom at a nearby fuel pump now draws an hour-long queue, and there has been nowhere to bathe since his container was seized.
The uncertainty extends to when it all ends.
Jaffar said a fellow driver walked to the nearby police post to ask about release, and was first told October 4. Days later, the police told him the date was changed to October 16, with no guarantee attached, he said.
“It could go beyond that too,” Jaffar said.
Asked if he had ever thought about simply walking away from the job, Naseer pointed first to the truck he was minding, worth close to 15 million rupees ($54,000) and entrusted to him by an owner in Karachi.
But he framed it as more than a question of money or debt.
“How can we become disloyal to him, and abandon the vehicle over a little hardship?” he asked.
A wider cost
Back in the city where Asrar and his friends perform atop the containers, the economics take a different shape.
The full cost, says Sajid Amin Javed, deputy executive director for research at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, goes well beyond container rental.
“When we close a hotel and cancel all bookings, it is not the room rent that the hotel loses,” he told Al Jazeera. “It is the signalling it sends to investors, businesses, tourists. Every pillar of state, society bears that cost.”
The impact is not limited to the capital, others say.
“The metropolitan area it forms with Rawalpindi is the third-largest in the country,” said Danyal Adam Khan, an Islamabad-based researcher and urban governance specialist, adding that people from distant provinces too were deeply integrated into the socioeconomic fabric of the city. “When you shut down the capital like this, you cut everyone off.”
For now, the containers remain where they have always ended up: half barricade, half backdrop, and Asrar says the response to his friends’ video online has mostly been good-natured.
“Some people call it showing off,” he said. “Some call it political. We try to stay neutral about it.”
Asrar recalled one police officer who figured they were not damaging anything and stayed to watch. “They were just impressed by it,” he added, speaking of his stunts.
But not everyone has the luxury of treating the containers as a backdrop.
“This is such a government that it doesn’t listen to anyone’s request, anyone’s plea, anyone’s complaint,” Khan, the truck owner, told Al Jazeera. “There’s simply no one we can go to who will hear us.”

UAE for first time calls attempted Flydubai crash a ‘terrorist act’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:20:09 UTC
20:20:09 KST

Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, on Friday described Wednesday’s apparent attempt to crash a Flydubai flight as a “terrorist act,” marking the first time an Emirati official has publicly used the term to characterize the incident while the investigation continues.
His remarks came a day after the investigation was transferred to Abu Dhabi and as Capt. Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot injured in the cockpit attack, publicly recounted the moments in which he fought to regain access to the cockpit as the aircraft plunged.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel had received no specific intelligence warning or indication ahead of the incident and that the investigation into the motive was continuing.
He said investigators currently had no specific information linking Iran to the attack. “We will know very soon whether Iran had anything to do with it, but I cannot say that before the investigation is completed,” Netanyahu said. “We will get to the bottom of this attacker, whether he had accomplices and whether Iran was behind him. I think we will find out very soon. It is too early to say.”
Netanyahu said the suspect was being investigated and that Israel would follow the probe and “may also participate in it.”
Gargash made his remarks on X while responding to Machchhar’s account during a video conversation Friday morning with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
“The Flydubai pilot deserves full appreciation,” Gargash wrote. “Faced with a dangerous terrorist act and a possible disaster, he embodied the true meaning of courage and responsibility. The professionalism and moral integrity he demonstrated under the most challenging circumstances make him a true hero.”
He added: “While avoiding interpretations or promoting conspiracy theories, vigilance and caution remain essential in confronting the dangers of extremism and terrorism.”
Israeli officials have differed in how quickly they have characterized the incident. Netanyahu has been cautious about drawing conclusions about the motive, while Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday evening that the incident was an “attempted jihadist terrorist attack.”
The investigation into the attempted crash was transferred to the UAE on Thursday after both Machchhar and the Omani co-pilot were moved there from Saudi Arabia, where the aircraft made its emergency landing.
Israel had asked to participate as an observer in the investigations in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, but Riyadh did not agree. Following the co-pilot’s transfer to the Emirates, Israeli officials are now relying on close ties and security cooperation with Abu Dhabi in hopes of becoming as involved as possible in the investigation, even if only as observers.
Machchhar appeared publicly from the hospital Friday for the first time and spoke with Modi by video call.
“I had so many injuries that I collapsed. I’ve been a captain for 11 years. I know, even with my eyes closed, what is happening with the aircraft,” he said.
“When I fell, I felt the plane descending, the nose going down, and I knew these were the final seconds. I tried to crawl. I opened the door, and everything else happened immediately after that.”
Machchhar praised the medical treatment he received in both Saudi Arabia and the UAE, adding: “I realized that if I didn’t show courage, 170 passengers would lose their lives.”
Modi praised him in return.
“The entire country is praying for you. The courage, composure and calm you showed saved many lives,” the Indian prime minister said. “The country can proudly say Indians are not people who take lives, but people who are prepared to risk their lives to save others.”
A visibly emotional Machchhar replied: “You are my idol. I never thought I would have the opportunity to speak with you.”

Yemen's coffee industry seeks a comeback amid conflict
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:20:04 CST
20:20:04 KST

SANAA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- In Yemen, coffee is more than a crop. It is part of the country's history and identity, and growers and businesses are seeking to revive the industry amid years of conflict.
The effort was on display Thursday in Sanaa, where farmers, traders and coffee enthusiasts gathered to mark International Coffee Day.
"Coffee is a treasure for Yemen," coffee farmer Sheikh Abed Rajeh told Xinhua at the event. Expanding the sector, he said, could raise incomes for rural communities and give a boost to Yemen's economy.
Mohammed Al-Qasimi, head of the Coffee Unit at Sanaa's agricultural authorities, said around 15 million coffee trees had been planted across the country over the past five years.
Yemen's coffee production has risen from around 17,000 tons to between 42,000 and 45,000 tons in 2025, while output is expected to reach about 50,000 tons in 2026 as cultivation continues to expand, Al-Qasimi said.
An initiative is underway to plant 100 million coffee trees over 10 years, at a planned rate of 10 million trees a year, across Yemen's mountains, slopes and agricultural terraces, he added.
For Yemen, the effort is about more than increasing production. It is also an attempt to reclaim a centuries-old place in global coffee history.
Coffee grown in Yemen's highlands was once shipped through the Red Sea port of Mocha to overseas markets, eventually giving the port's name to one of the world's most familiar coffee terms.
Al-Qasimi estimated that around 250,000 people work across the coffee sector, including farmers, intermediaries and traders, while more than 276 companies, projects and entrepreneurs have entered the industry in recent years.
Yemeni coffee is now sold in Gulf countries, the United States, Europe and Asia, with producers looking to expand into more international markets.
"We are trying to bring Yemeni coffee back to local and international markets," said Ghaleb Al-Emadi, owner of the Haraz Coffee Center. The center has worked since 2016 to promote the identity and distinctive flavor of Yemeni coffee internationally, he said.
Producers are also seeking to capitalize on the premium reputation of Yemeni beans.
At a national coffee auction, a kilogram of coffee sold for as much as 976 U.S. dollars, Al-Qasimi said, underscoring the value that exceptional Yemeni varieties can command.
But getting that coffee to overseas buyers remains a major challenge.
Years of conflict in Yemen have disrupted roads, ports and trade routes, and driven up transportation costs, making it harder for coffee producers to connect directly with international markets.
Al-Qasimi said the cost of sending a one-kilogram coffee sample overseas has risen from around 20 U.S. dollars to as much as 120 U.S. dollars, while delivery times have increased dramatically.
A sample that once reached an overseas customer within three days can now take between 20 and 30 days. Larger shipments that previously arrived within a week can now take three to four months.
"The demand is there. The difficult part is getting our coffee to the customer," Al-Qasimi said. ■

* With "China Haul" emerging as a buzz hashtag on social media platforms worldwide, more foreign visitors are flocking to the country not merely for sightseeing, but also for shopping sprees.
* In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
* Official data showed that foreign nationals made almost 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period of 2026, up 19.5 percent from a year earlier. Visa-free entries accounted for 23.72 million of the total, an increase of 26.8 percent compared with 2025.
BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Andrea Triboldi, an Italian tourist, arrived in China with a long shopping list.
After landing in Shenzhen, a thriving tech hub in southern China, Triboldi and his 11-year-old son couldn't wait to visit a major sci-tech exhibition, which showcased drones and other latest tech products of this city in Guangdong Province.
Prior to the trip, Triboldi had drawn up a shopping list featuring more than 20 Chinese products. "I chose Shenzhen as the first station of our China travel because of its technology. My son is particularly into DJI drones and wants to buy one to take home," he said.
Triboldi is not alone. With "China Haul" emerging as a buzz hashtag on social media platforms worldwide, more foreign visitors are flocking to the country not merely for sightseeing, but also for shopping sprees.
In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
DIVERSE SHOPPING SPREES
"I came here to feel the best technology I have ever seen in the whole world. It's really amazing. We don't have these kinds of drones in Mexico," said Ulises Padilla, an 11-year-old Mexican tourist, in describing his impressions of Shenzhen.
The city is drawing an increasing number of foreign visitors like Padilla. An average of nearly 8,000 foreign buyers have visited Huaqiangbei, Shenzhen's mega electronics marketplace, each day this year. From January through July, sales of artificial intelligence (AI) products surged more than 55 percent from a year earlier in this area. Sales of AI glasses doubled, while sales of drones and robots climbed by 60 to 70 percent during the same period.
Zhang Linwan, an employee of INNO100, a Shenzhen store featuring tech products, said that foreign tourists contribute roughly 40 percent of the store's total sales.
"They show strong interest in exoskeletons, 3D printers and laser engraving machines. At our store, they can also make their own 3D dolls and turn photos of themselves and their families into fridge magnets," the employee added.
Wang Linlin, who works at a DJI flagship store in Shenzhen, described a similar scene. "We've seen a large number of foreign customers recently. They enjoy getting hands-on experience with our products, especially trying out our drones in test flights," Wang revealed.
In Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, Chinese snacks are proving a big hit with foreign tourists. Ivan, a 32-year-old Russian tourist, made a point of visiting Snack Kingdom, a specialty store in the city that offers over 35,000 types of snacks.
He said that not many large snack stores in Russia have such a complete range of products, and the variety is so rich that it's a bit difficult to choose.
Tanzanian tourist Shija Theodora Desderi commented that the store serves not only as a shopping destination but also as a place for entertainment. She compared Chinese snacks with Tanzanian ones, which she described as sweeter, noting that the former taste refreshing and are more organic, containing less sugar and salt.
"From sneakers and cosmetics to trendy toys and daily necessities, my family and friends often have their shopping plans ready before visiting China," said Mok Jin Jin from Malaysia.
She said her mother especially likes a Chinese-made blender and often uses it to make various healthy drinks for the family. The machine's one-touch automatic cleaning feature is particularly appealing, sparing her the hassle of manual cleaning.
APPEALING PRODUCTS PLUS FAVORABLE POLICIES
It is not only the price advantage, but the design, quality and practicality of Chinese products that draw the attention of foreign tourists, according to the Malaysian.
She concluded that behind the "China Haul" phenomenon lies not only China's enhanced manufacturing capabilities, but also profound shifts in Chinese brand design, innovation and consumer experience.
Carlos Alvarado, an international student from Guatemala, is already a seasoned shopper in China. "Chinese products, like clothes, accessories and daily necessities, are not only competitively priced, but also feature trendy designs that are hard to find in stores in my home country," he said.
Moreover, an array of favorable policies, such as visa-free policies and departure tax refunds, has further boosted the shopping frenzy in China.
Official data showed that foreign nationals made almost 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period of 2026, up 19.5 percent from a year earlier. Visa-free entries accounted for 23.72 million of the total, an increase of 26.8 percent compared with 2025.
Before ending her trip to Chengdu, capital city of southwest China's Sichuan Province, Hungarian tourist Annamaria purchased some tea, teacups and teapots as gifts for her mother and younger brother at home.
"I like shopping in China because it's very convenient and there are many choices here," she said, praising the tax refund policy for allowing her to get refunds immediately upon purchase.
"The policy has boosted our sales. Foreign tourists now account for 30 percent of our daily customer flow," said Zhou Man, manager of a Chengdu store of Xiaomi, a Chinese consumer electronics and technology company.
Data from the Ministry of Commerce revealed that the number of overseas visitors applying for departure tax refunds had increased by more than threefold year on year during the first seven months of 2026.
Roger Matute, an international student from Honduras, was impressed by how convenient mobile payment is in China. "I have rarely used cash since I arrived here because it is very easy to pay everything with my smartphone using WeChat or Alipay apps," he said.
A range of favorable conditions, including tax refunds, mobile payments and visa-free policies, have systematically reduced the cost of cross-border consumer transactions, helping to facilitate the "China Haul" trend, according to Gao Li, vice dean of the School of International Business, Tianjin Foreign Studies University, located in north China.
The popularity of "China Haul" essentially stems from a shift in the consumption logic of overseas tourists, who are moving from purchasing foreign cultural symbols to buying Chinese technologies, designs and consumption experiences, said He Yun, an associate professor at the school of public administration of central China's Hunan University.
The trend, she noted, is underpinned by the upgrading of China's manufacturing and cultural and creative industries, a substantial transition from exporting production capacity to exporting brands and lifestyles.
(Video reporters: Hu Rong and Zhang Yujie; Video editors: Hong Liang, Zhu Cong and Zhou Yang) ■

Asian Games | Wang Xiyu wins women's tennis gold to book LA Olympics berth (updated)
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:19:56 CST
20:19:56 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's Wang Xiyu defeated compatriot Zhang Shuai in straight sets to win the women's singles gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games here on Friday, extending China's winning streak in the event to six consecutive editions.
Wang, 25, dominated the opening set, winning all of her first-serve points compared with 50 percent for Zhang. The 37-year-old Zhang, who struggled with unforced errors, was broken twice as Wang took the set 6-2.
Zhang continued to struggle in the second set, holding serve just once as Wang cruised to a 6-1 victory to seal the gold medal.
"Every loss is an opportunity to learn and a chance to become a better player," said Zhang. "Losing to Wang Xiyu is probably the loss that hurts the least. I'm genuinely so happy for her. She is such a kind girl, and even if we weren't playing tennis, we would still be very good friends."
"I'm much older than her, and she treats me like an older sister. We are always talking about how to improve our game," added the veteran.
"Tennis is part of our lives. It's part of who we are. So we are very happy to have the opportunity to compete at the Asian Games alongside our professional careers and win valuable gold and silver medals for our team and our country," Zhang said.
Wang endured a shoulder injury in 2025 that kept her out of competition for nearly six months, sending her ranking tumbling outside the top 200. She was forced to restart her season on the ITF circuit before making a strong comeback at this year's French Open, where she advanced from qualifying to reach the last 16, the best Grand Slam result of her career.
In August, she also reached the round of 16 at a WTA 1000 event in Cincinnati for the first time.
"At first, I was definitely a little disappointed because I had been playing on the WTA Tour for several years, and then I had to work my way back up through ITF tournaments. There was a bit of a gap to overcome," Wang said.
"But they are all competitions. Sometimes, playing in a big tournament doesn't feel all that different from playing in a smaller one. You have to figure out how to face your opponent that day and how to overcome the challenges that come your way. Those are the lessons you have to learn each day.
"By taking it one step at a time and building on each experience, I feel I've learned a lot this year. It has also given me great encouragement for the future. It shows that I'm not afraid to start from zero and that I can get back on my feet after falling down," Wang added.
In the semifinal, Wang came from behind to defeat top-seeded Philippine rising star Alexandra Eala 3-6, 6-3, 6-2.
With her victory, Wang also secured a berth in the women's singles event at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Wang said winning the Asian Games title had given her a significant boost in confidence.
"It makes me believe in myself and believe that I'm on the right path. I need to stay committed and keep moving forward. That takes a lot of courage, as well as a willingness to keep trying, learn from different kinds of failures and constantly improve myself," Wang said.
"I think that's very important, not just in tennis but in life as well."
Asked what areas of her game she still needed to improve, Wang said there was plenty of work to do.
"There are still many areas I need to work on, including my physical fitness, refining my technique and becoming mentally stronger. I think all of these are essential for me to become a better player," she said. ■

Russian strikes undermine production of military products in Ukraine — State Duma deputy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:19:56 UTC
20:19:56 KST

SIMFEROPOL, October 2. / TASS/. Russian strikes on Ukrainian enterprises have shut down the steel industry used to make military products, which will hurt Kiev’s military output, State Duma deputy from the Republic of Crimea, Reserve Major General Leonid Ivlev said in an interview with TASS.
Reuters quoted the Federation of Metallurgists of Ukraine as saying that production in the country, which was one of the world's ten largest steel producers by the beginning of 2022, was stopped after the last enterprises were put out of operation.
"Ukraine's steel industry suffered as a result of targeted missile attacks by Russian troops on key metallurgical enterprises in the country, which effectively led to the cessation of production of various grades of steel, the most important raw materials for the military-industrial complex of the Kiev regime," Ivlev said.
He said that Russia had many times warned that in response to the Ukrainian strikes on its cities and energy companies retaliatory strikes would be launched against Ukraine's infrastructure facilities - ports, air bases, locomotives, warehouses and logistics chains. At the same time, not a single peaceful object was damaged.
Yulia Mendel, Vladimir Zelensky's former spokeswoman, said that in September Ukraine did not produce steel at all for a week, for the first time in 100 years. According to her, the export shutdown already causes losses of $200 million per month.
Steel industry in Ukraine
On September 22, Interpipe Steel pipe rolling plant shut down, and on September 18, Zaporozhstal and Kametstal became idle. Another large metallurgical enterprise, Dneprovsky Metallurgical Plant, stopped operations earlier due to financial problems (in January 2022, the plant stopped working, and in 2026, the process of declaring it insolvent began). Besides, explosions hit it in early September.
Metallurgy annually provides $6.2 billion in foreign exchange earnings for Ukraine (about 13%, second only to agricultural products), ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog paid about 8.5 billion hryvnias ($189 million) annually to the budget, Interpipe Steel - 5.56 billion hryvnias ($123 million), Zaporozhstal - 4 billion hryvnias ($90 million), Kametstal - 2.5 billion hryvnias ($56 million).

September 2026 ranks 2nd hottest on record in France
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:19:32 CST
20:19:32 KST

PARIS, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- September 2026 was the second-hottest September in France since records began in 1900, the national weather service Meteo-France said on Friday.
France's average temperature for the month was 3.1 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 normal, surpassed only by September 2023, when the average temperature was 3.6 degrees Celsius above normal, Meteo-France said.
It was also the fourth consecutive month with a temperature anomaly of more than 3 degrees Celsius, the first time a streak has lasted more than three months, the weather service said.
This month was also the third-driest September on record, with rainfall across France nearly 70 percent below normal.
Meanwhile, sunshine was more than 30 percent above normal, making September 2026 the second-sunniest September on record, Meteo-France said.
The prolonged heat and drought have taken a toll on France's agriculture and broader economy. French Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut said earlier that this summer's heatwaves could cost the French economy between 10 billion and 15 billion euros (11.23 billion to 16.85 billion U.S. dollars). ■

Israel's Balad party leader withdraws from parliament election
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:19:27 CST
20:19:27 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Israel's Balad party, announced Friday his withdrawal from the upcoming parliament election after the Supreme Court indicated the likelihood of upholding his disqualification.
Last week, Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to bar Balad, an Arab party that advocates turning Israel into a "state of all its citizens," from running in the general election on Oct. 27.
The decision followed a petition filed by the Jewish Power party, a far-right Israeli party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The petition focused on an article published by Abu Shehadeh, in which he described Hamas's attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023 as a historically significant event in military, political and strategic terms.
The Supreme Court held a hearing on the disqualification Thursday. During the proceedings, the justices indicated that a majority appeared likely to uphold the committee's decision and suggested that Abu Shehadeh withdraw his candidacy rather than await a formal ruling disqualifying him.
Abu Shehadeh announced his decision to withdraw in a Facebook post. He said he had been subjected to what he described as political persecution, while noting his withdrawal did not constitute a retreat from his political positions or values.
The Supreme Court is also expected to rule on the disqualification of Ra'am, an Arab party led by Mansour Abbas that has pursued a pragmatic approach to Israeli politics and previously joined a governing coalition, as well as that of Ofer Cassif, a Jewish lawmaker from the Hadash party, which advocates Jewish-Arab equality and an end to the Israeli occupation. ■

Sweden's SDP leader Andersson again tasked with forming gov't
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:19:27 CST
20:19:27 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Swedish Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlen on Friday again tasked Social Democratic Party (SDP) leader and former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson with exploring the prospects of forming a new government.
At a press conference, Norlen said developments surrounding the election of the parliament speaker had previously prompted Andersson to return the exploratory mandate, but the distribution of seats in parliament remained the basis for deciding who should be given the task.
Norlen said the new exploratory mandate will formally begin on Oct. 5, and Andersson is expected to report back by Oct. 12. She may request an extension if more time is needed for negotiations.
A vote on a new prime minister will be held in parliament after the exploratory process is completed, Norlen said.
Following the announcement, Andersson said on social media that she welcomed the speaker's decision and would use the coming weekend to consider how to proceed. She also called on all parties to carefully consider their positions.
Sweden holds parliamentary elections every four years. This year's election took place on Sept. 13.
According to the Swedish Election Authority, the SDP won 99 seats, remaining the largest party in parliament. The opposition bloc therefore secured 176 of the 349 seats and a parliamentary majority.
Outgoing Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson tendered his resignation following the election. ■

Parties have declared a total of EUR 2.78 million in election campaign spending  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:19:19 UTC
20:19:19 KST

RIGA - Since the start of the pre-election campaign period, political organizations have reported campaign expenditures totaling EUR 2.780 million with the United List (AS) spending the most, followed by the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) and Latvia First (LPV), the Corruption Prevention Bureau (KNAB) informed LETA.
Since June 6, when the pre-election campaign period officially began in Latvia, through October 1, political organizations have collectively entered into agreements for limited pre-election campaign spending totaling EUR 2,779,923. HOW DO YOU KNOW WHEN A PLUMBING PROBLEM IS AN EMERGENCY?  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:19:01 UTC
20:19:01 KST

Not all plumbing problems need immediate attention. A loose fixture that keeps dripping can wait. But it’s different if a plumbing issue poses a safety risk.
In the following situations, a delay in repairs can be much more than an inconvenience.
Water is flowing at a rate faster than you can contain it
A small drip is one thing. It is a different story when the pipe suddenly bursts open or cracks and begins to release a significant amount of water. Water can quickly infiltrate the:
- Floor
- Walls
- Ceiling
- Other surfaces.
This means more damage.
First, closing the water can help to reduce the immediate damage. But only if it is safe to reach the main water valve. While at it, request emergency plumbing repairs immediately.
Wastewater is coming back through your fixtures
Water can back up through a:
- Toilet
- Shower drain
- Sink.
This is a big emergency. It may indicate a clog in the drainage line.
Please do not continue to use or flush items through the affected fixture. Sending more water into the system will aggravate backup and spread contaminated water throughout the house.
You cannot find a way to stop the water
Sometimes, the source of the leak is visible. But turning off the fixture doesn’t stop it. This happens if:
- The valve fails
- The supply line is damaged
- A fixture breaks.
As a result, water can keep leaking out.
If the source cannot be controlled and water continues to flow, it requires immediate attention. If feasible, turn off the main water valve to the house and avoid unsafe areas.
Water has entered an electrical zone
Water and electricity can be very dangerous together. Never enter an area to investigate a leak if water has leaked onto:
- Wiring
- Electrical panels
- Appliances.
If there is an immediate electrical hazard, contact the appropriate emergency service.
You notice gas around a water heater
If a gas-powered water heater emits a gas odor, it is an emergency. It could indicate:
- A gas leak
- A problem with the appliance.
If you smell gas, avoid:
- Flames
- Switches
- Other possible ignition sources.
Evacuate and notify the proper gas or emergency service from a safe place.
Delaying repairs could put your home at risk
The urgency of a plumbing problem isn't limited to how inconvenient it is. Consider the consequences of this situation persisting for several hours.
Water that infiltrates walls or floors can cause severe damage. A sewage backup can contaminate living areas. A leak may ruin furniture and other valuables.
It is an emergency if it could cause more damage within a short time.
The last words
In these cases, waiting for regular service hours may not be practical. Prompt action may help limit the damage and the scope of the problem.

QEst Hack invites participants to test quantum algorithms on real business problems  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:18:59 UTC
20:18:59 KST

Metrosert, Estonia’s Applied Research Centre and National Metrology Institute, invites Estonian companies as well as students, researchers and other interested participants from the Nordic and Baltic countries to apply for the QEst Hack 2026 quantum hackathon, taking place in Tallinn from 11 to 13 November.
Five companies will be selected for the second edition of QEst Hack in Estonia. Each company will bring a complex business problem and its own data to the hackathon. They will be joined by individual participants and quantum experts from Estonia, Finland and Canada to explore whether quantum algorithms could offer a better way to solve these problems in the future.
According to Kalev Kaarna, a member of the QEst Hack organising team and Business Development Manager in Metrosert’s sales team, Metrosert has consistently contributed to building Estonia’s quantum technology ecosystem and developing the country’s capabilities in recent years.
“Estonia’s neighbouring countries are actively developing this field, and quantum technologies have already become a national technology and innovation priority in many European countries. To keep pace and avoid falling behind, Estonia must start building the necessary knowledge, experience and partnerships now,” Kaarna explained.
“QEst Hack gives both companies and people who may become Estonia’s future quantum technology experts an opportunity to take a major practical step forward. They can work with real company problems and data under the guidance of international quantum experts and gain an understanding of the potential benefits of quantum algorithms. Estonia needs people with this kind of experience and companies that start exploring the field early if we want to be among the frontrunners in applying quantum technologies rather than merely becoming late adopters,” Kaarna said.
Companies can bring a complex optimisation or simulation problem whose current solution is expensive or time-consuming and where even a small improvement could provide a significant competitive advantage. Potential problems may involve logistics and route planning, energy grid balancing, production planning, financial portfolios, material properties or drug discovery.
“A ready-made quantum solution will certainly not emerge in two and a half days. However, a company will gain an initial practical understanding of whether it makes sense to explore solving its business problem with quantum algorithms and what would be needed for the next experiments,” said Kaarna.
Teams will be formed around the participating companies, bringing together their IT, data and business specialists with students, researchers and other individual participants. Participants will receive an introduction to quantum computing and, with support from mentors, test quantum algorithms using a real company problem and a sample of its data.
The inaugural QEst Hack, held last year, was won by Enefit, which continued exploring its problem through a pilot project after the hackathon. According to Kaarel Oja, Head of AI Systems and Prototyping at Enefit, winning QEst Hack 2025 enabled the company to move from a theoretical interest in quantum computing to practical experimentation.
“The hackathon prize – a three-month collaboration with Université de Sherbrooke – enabled us to explore quantum computing applications in the energy sector using real business problems and data, without first having to spend years building new expertise, methodologies and technological capabilities. The collaboration helps us test the potential of quantum computing quickly and systematically, reduce innovation risk and make investment decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions. In essence, working together allowed us to achieve in months what could have taken years to build independently,” said Kaarel Oja.
Companies, individual participants and mentors can apply for the hackathon until 11 October. Participation is free of charge, and the working language is English. Further information and application forms are available on the QEst Hack 2026 website.
QEst Hack 2026 is organised by Metrosert in cooperation with BDA, IBM, IQM, the City of Sherbrooke in Canada and the Institut quantique at Université de Sherbrooke. The hackathon is supported by the Estonian Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.
Metrosert is Estonia’s state-owned Applied Research Centre and National Metrology Institute, operating under the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications. As an applied research centre, Metrosert helps companies develop and test new technologies and strengthen their international competitiveness. As the national metrology institute, Metrosert supports Estonia’s quality infrastructure by maintaining and developing the national measurement standards and ensuring the international traceability of measurements.

Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:18:00 UTC
20:18:00 KST

Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.
The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.
“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.
The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.
“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.
According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.
Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.
Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).
After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.
Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.
In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.
The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.
Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey: Germans unite in frustration over the government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:17:00 UTC
20:17:00 KST

Germans unite in frustration with Merz and his government
October 2, 2026
Ahead of October 3, which marks the reunification of West and East Germany in 1990, pollster infratest dimap asked 1303 eligible voters to assess their personal situation. Twenty percent of those identifying as East Germans, but 44% see personal advantages. Only a quarter said reunification had no major impact on them personally.
More than half of West German respondents said reunification had no major impact on their personal lives. The remaining half is split: 19% said reunification had a positive impact, while 18% said it had a negative one.
Germany held three state elections in September, two of them in eastern states. They were seen as a test of nationwide voter sentiment. The results were particularly devastating for the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In Saxony-Anhalt and the city-state of Berlin, where it had been in government, the CDU dropped by 10% compared to the previous election and lost its hold on power. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party even failed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. This has never happened before in Germany's history.
Chancellor Merz wants to remain in office
Merz has long been unpopular and has seen his support fall even further in the aftermath of the elections. The coalition he leads, comprised of the CDU, the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), is unpopular. Only one in 10 respondents in the survey said they were satisfied with the federal government's work and the chancellor's performance, a historic low. Only 40% of CDU supporters say they are still satisfied with Merz.
Far-right AfD in the lead nationwide
The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the domestic intelligence agency has classified as, in part, far-right extremist, continues to benefit from the voter dissatisfaction with the centrist parties.
If a general election were held now, the CDU/CSU alliance would win only 20% of the vote. That is one of the lowest figures in the party's history and a far cry from the 43.8% it won in the first election after reunification in 1990. The SPD polls at only 13%. This means that the ruling parties together would not even win one-third of the vote and would lose their majority in parliament.
The AfD would remain the strongest political force. It has been polling steadily at 27% nationwide. The environmentalist Greens are up slightly, reaching 16%, while the socialist Left Party has dropped by the same margin, landing at 11%. With this result, it would be a Herculean task to form a majority in the national parliament.
AI, Russia and Donald Trump's policies
The overall situation in Germany gives only one in eight people cause for optimism, while nearly nine in 10 express concern. Voters for the AfD and the Left Party are particularly worried.
Two-thirds of respondents said they're worried that humans could lose control over artificial intelligence, and just as many are worried about the consequences of US President Donald Trump's policies for Germany. Six in 10 expressed concern about climate change, and just over half said they are worried that Russia could attack other countries in Europe.
About one in two respondents fear they will not be able to maintain their standard of living in the future. A similar number are concerned about immigration to Germany.
By far the biggest source of concern for Germans, however, is that political parties cannot find common answers to key political issues.
Social reforms must be fair
Germany is a rapidly aging country. Fewer working people must support an ever-increasing number of retirees.
The aging society also strains the health care system. Since 2015, the number of people in need of long-term care has risen from about 2.8 million to about 6.5 million — and the trend continues to rise.
According to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, only one in six eligible voters believes that the federal government will succeed inmaking the social security systems sustainable for the future.
Not all respondents said they are willing to dig into their own pockets: Voters who tend to support left-leaning parties would be more likely to accept higher social security contributions than benefit cuts. Among AfD and CDU/CSU voters, the opposite is true.
Three-quarters of respondents view the government's proposed reform measures as contradictory. They complain about an ever-increasing burden, even though the government had promised relief.
Sixty-one percent say that cuts should be scaled according to individual financial capacity, even if this would place a heavier burden on some people.
One in two would be more willing to accept cuts if the necessity were explained in a way that made sense. The message to policymakers is clear: reforms require explanation and social balance; otherwise, they lose acceptance.
The welfare state and the health care system are regarded as key achievements in Germany. When asked what works particularly well in Germany compared to other countries, survey respondents most often cited social benefits and medical care. Education, schools, vocational training and universities came in last place.
Energy policy is seen as a problem
High energy prices continue to burden citizens and the German economy. The ongoing crisis in the Persian Gulf is driving oil prices even higher. This is impacting fuel and electricity prices in Germany.
Respondents to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey found that the government is not doing enough to address high energy prices. Three-quarters of them said the government's efforts are insufficient.
A "Tankrabatt" (fuel discount) has again come into effect on October 1: Through the end of the year, the federal government is reducing the energy tax on gasoline and diesel by about 17 eurocents ($0.19) per liter. A similar discount was already in place from early May through the end of June. That cost the government €3.4 billion.
Some of that money ended up in the pockets of oil companies and gas station operators because they did not pass on the full discount. Experts view the measure critically.
Added to this is the fact that fossil fuels are being made cheaper despite shortages, which is controversial from a climate policy perspective. The new fuel discount has received only a lukewarm reception among the public; half of those surveyed in the ARD Deutschlandtrend poll believe it is the wrong approach.
This article was originally written in German.

Inside Washington's tougher position on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:16:59 UTC
20:16:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside Washington's tougher position during the latest talks with Iran
Just a few weeks ago, the administration of US President Donald Trump was prepared to reach a deal with Iran that would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz. But, today, it is rejecting in the current negotiations with Iran what it had been prepared to accept less than three months ago.
On 26 September, Trump publicly rejected a ceasefire proposal from Iran that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for lifting the US naval blockade, ending sanctions on oil exports and resuming nuclear negotiations. He said Iran was losing badly and wanted to reach a deal.
So what changed for the Trump administration?
The United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports on 13 April, before Trump announced on 19 August the start of what he described as the "most crushing economic operation ever"; part of a broad campaign of economic warfare and isolation against Iran, which included sanctions on banks, companies and importers, a ban on Iranian aviation, coordination with foreign countries and threats of sanctions against countries cooperating with Tehran.
Trump and his team believe the United States can achieve more by waiting and tightening the military naval blockade and economic sanctions.
His administration and Treasury Department officials estimate that the amount of Iranian oil available at sea will run out by the end of next week, which will increase Tehran's hardship and may push it to make further concessions.
The US president said earlier this week that he does not know "whether the Iranians will surrender now, but they will surrender".
On Sunday, 27 September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in comments to Fox News that the blockade on Iran was succeeding and that the remaining Iranian oil at sea amounted to no more than an additional 15 million barrels and expected the final shipments to reach China within the next two weeks, adding that "after that, it will have nothing left to bargain with".
Iran already acknowledges that the new sanctions are highly effective, although it has stressed that surrender is impossible.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in comments to Fox News on Sunday, on the sidelines of his attendance at United Nations meetings, "One of the problems we face is that our money is being held in China."
"We cannot even recover our money from countries to which we exported goods," he added.
No shipment of Iranian crude oil has passed outside the US-imposed blockade area since 14 July, according to data from tracking companies.
The figures cited by the US Treasury secretary also match shipping-tracking data.
Data from Kpler, according to what was published by The Wall Street Journal, showed that the amount of Iranian crude oil aboard tankers at sea outside the blockade area stood at 29 million barrels on 1 September, compared with 90 million barrels in mid-July.
It is expected the supply to run out by mid-October and the flow of payments to stop by mid-March next year.
President Trump argues that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to pre-war levels and has again called for Tehran's surrender.
However, Kpler data published by Reuters indicate that total volumes leaving through the strait amounted to about 9.7 million barrels out of a total of about 16.3 million barrels of oil exported by major Middle Eastern oil producers during September, compared with 19.5 million barrels in February.
The remaining volume is being transported through alternative routes.
Paulo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University, told The New Arab that the reason for the notable change and tougher US position is that Washington has found a pressure point that is actually affecting Iran.
"As the blockade continues and its actual effects on the Iranian economy begin to emerge, Washington is no longer prepared to accept what it had previously agreed to," he said.
He further explained that the US realised that the economic blockade and sanctions were actually working, and that they were the strongest pressure tool, with Iran suffering the most, in turn led them to see any negotiations to lift the blockade in return for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of initial talks as "unacceptable at the present time".
Schirach added that months ago, Washington could have accepted a deal that would have reopened the strait to end the war and the impasse that had led to Iran controlling it.
He also noted that the factor of time is now in the US' favour, saying that "the current stalemate serves the pressure on Iran", and that the US blockade is working effectively despite Iranian claims that the domestic situation remains stable.
"The blockade prevents the movement of goods through Iranian ports and prevents Tehran from selling oil as usual, despite the existence of land routes and railways with China," he said.
He pointed to another variable, namely that Washington believes it has, to some extent, secured "the use of the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool".
"The United States has succeeded in escorting oil tankers through the strait so that traffic has become more than 75% of what it was before the war," he added.
Schirach also noted that "global markets have begun to adapt and no longer see the situation as an existential threat, unlike what Tehran had sought by using the strait as a tool to impose its conditions".
He estimated that the chances of reaching an agreement at the current time appear extremely slim, given the wide gap between the two sides' positions.
He pointed out that Washington's current goal is the complete halt of Iran's nuclear programme, while Tehran refuses to completely give up enriched uranium.
Iranian demands go far beyond what Washington can accept, such as the release of frozen assets and the closure of military bases, which he described as "ridiculous".
Although the Iranians have extensive experience in dealing with sanctions and pressure, they have not faced a crisis like the current one or such a large and highly complex and interconnected set of sanctions, according to the US researcher.
He argued that the continuation of the blockade for several more months could put the regime before a genuine survival crisis, and they may rely on land routes through the Caucasus, but this will not compensate for the losses.
Schirach also noted that the United States has "a lack of patience in dealing with long-term conflicts, especially as the current situation affects public opinion and citizens, which could save Tehran before its economy completely collapses".
President Trump shared on his platform on Monday an analysis written by Alexander Stahl, an investor and energy analyst, arguing that Iran had lost the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool and that oil levels had returned to pre-war levels.
However, Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International Studies who specialises in Iranian political economy and the effects of sanctions, wrote on X, pointing to several factors that go beyond the issue of control over the strait alone.
"Yes, Iran may no longer be able to disrupt the flow of energy as effectively as it did during the first phase of the war, but it still retains a significant ability to destroy assets (in the Middle East), including production, refining and distribution infrastructure," he said.
He added that saying Iran had lost control overlooks the fact that it can still escalate and target these facilities if it believes it needs to send a message that it can inflict damage that forces Trump to accept the diplomatic options on the table.
He cited the 2019 attacks on Aramco facilities in Abqaiq and Khurais.
He noted that Trump's unpredictable and volatile approach and his strong insistence on victory in the war could push Iran towards escalation.
He also said that the strait is not the main source of Iranian leverage in this war, but rather Iranian attacks on infrastructure, countries and US bases.
He added that this is being downplayed because acknowledging it would mean recognising the United States' inability to neutralise Iran's capabilities.
He warned that Iran could resort to a "scorched earth" policy if the current situation continues for a long period.
He said, "The US Navy can certainly escort ships at great cost and ensure the continued flow of oil, but the deeper problem remains unresolved, which is the failure of US security guarantees across the Gulf region, and this gives Iran leverage in negotiations."
