EU ‘fully rejects’ US threat to ban diesel exports unless bloc releases more fuel stocks
The European Union on Friday pushed back against a US threat to ban any diesel exports unless the 27-member bloc releases more of its fuel stocks, “fully” rejecting the move, an EU official said. French President Emmanuel Macron will chair a video call with his G7 counterparts Friday to discuss possible measures on global fuel markets.
The EU pushed back hard Friday against US threats to impose a diesel export ban, as Washington pressures Europe to tap its strategic reserves in a bid to bring down fuel prices.
The United States’ war in Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite US President Donald Trump at home with high fuel costs, a key issue in the run-up to midterm congressional elections next month.
“We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner,” European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said.
Read moreEuropean drivers choke on rising diesel prices due to Iran conflict
The 27-nation bloc was ready to work with the International Energy Agency on the possible release of fuel reserves to contain prices, she added, following crisis talks between member states and commission to forge a unified response.
Earlier Friday, French leader Emmanuel Macron spoke to Trump and urged G7 nations to work together on the matter – while also speaking out against any export ban.
“The president stressed that G7 countries had a common interest in acting in a coordinated way, without export restrictions,” Macron’s office said after his exchange with the US leader.
Macron will chair a video call with his counterparts from the G7 from 2.30pm local time (12.30pm GMT) to discuss possible measures on the world markets for crude and refined products, the Élysée Palace said in a statement.
Brussels suggested the talks could take place as early as Friday afternoon.
The flurry of diplomatic activity came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cranked up the pressure on European nations.
“Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” Bessent posted on social media.
“American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage,” he wrote.
Earlier this week, the Executive Director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), Fatih Birol, said European nations were yet to release part of the stocks they had agreed to in an earlier bid to ease prices in March.
“A big chunk of the stocks have been released, but still some remain, both in terms of crude oil and products,” Birol told reporters Tuesday after a meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin.
‘Dramatic consequences’
The 32 members of the IEA agreed last March to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves, their largest release ever.
About a third was yet to come to market, Birol said, adding that further releases were possible with 80 percent of overall IEA stocks “still in our pocket”.
Diesel prices in the United States and Europe have hit record highs due to the US-Iran war, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure also blamed for pushing up prices.
The issue has emerged as a major drag for Trump’s Republican Party in the coming midterm elections, in which it risks losing control of Congress.
Trump on Wednesday floated the possibility of banning US exports of diesel, which is used in trucks and other hauling vehicles – an alarming prospect for the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports.
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers gathering in Milwaukee that the ban would have “dramatic consequences for our economic performance.”
Reports said the Trump administration wants France and Germany in particular to tap their stockpiles of diesel to try to curb prices.
“It is in Europe’s best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers,” a US official told AFP.
At the G20 trade talks, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer struck a conciliatory tone, saying there was an “eagerness on both sides to work together” on the diesel issue.
Average US diesel prices have surged more than 70 percent to $6.39 a gallon since the start of the Iran war, according to the American Automobile Association.

British forces land on Danish territory near Arctic circle
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:52 BST
20:12:52 KST

Royal Marines have deployed to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the Second World War, training with Danish and Faroese forces around the strategically important Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap, according to the Royal Navy.
The deployment formed part of Exercise Lion Protector 2026, a Joint Expeditionary Force activity intended to test how quickly participating nations can respond to events across the High North and the approaches linking the North Atlantic with the Baltic Sea.
Commandos from the UK Commando Force deployed as part of the Allied Reaction Force Special Operations Maritime Task Group, or SOMTG, working with Danish forces and maritime agencies from the Faroe Islands.
Training included maritime interdiction operations, with personnel practising the boarding, inspection and seizure of vessels, as well as small boat operations and coastal landings on steep and difficult terrain.
The Faroe Islands sit between Iceland and Scotland in the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap, an important maritime route connecting the North Atlantic and Arctic. The area has long been closely watched by NATO because Russian naval vessels operating from bases in the north use routes through the wider region to reach the Atlantic.
According to a Royal Navy news update, First Sea Lord and Commandant General Royal Marines General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said: “Defending the Atlantic is fundamental to our economy, national security and way of life. In troubling times, we cannot be complacent.
“The return of the Royal Marines to the Faroe Islands should send an unequivocal message: the UK, alongside Denmark and our other allies in the Joint Expeditionary Force, stand ready to protect the waters, islands and vital routes that keep our nations secure.”
The exercise is the principal 2026 deployment for the UK Commando Force’s Allied Reaction Force Special Operations Maritime Task Group. The formation is designed to provide NATO with forces able to deploy at short notice for missions including recapturing vessels or offshore infrastructure and conducting reconnaissance or raids along coastlines ahead of larger amphibious operations.
The task group includes specialist personnel from across the Royal Navy and UK Commando Force, including boarding teams, pilots, engineers and small boat crews.
During Lion Protector, personnel practised approaching target vessels, using boarding ladders and climbing aboard before carrying out searches and simulated seizures.
Training later moved ashore across the Faroes’ 18-island archipelago, where Royal Marines operated around steep volcanic terrain, established observation posts above maritime routes and conducted cliff ascents. The deployment also has a historical connection. Royal Marines last operated in the Faroe Islands during the Second World War after Germany invaded Denmark in April 1940.
Britain subsequently launched Operation Valentine, with Royal Navy destroyers sent to Tórshavn before around 250 Royal Marines landed from HMS Suffolk. British forces remained on the islands until 1945, when control was returned to Denmark. The Joint Expeditionary Force brings together the United Kingdom, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, with its activities focused primarily on Northern Europe, the North Atlantic, Baltic Sea and High North.
Exercise Lion Protector ran between August and October and was designed to rehearse military response options across the High North and through the Danish Straits into the Baltic Sea. The Royal Navy said the activity was intended to improve the ability of JEF forces to deploy and operate together across the region.
The training takes place ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and International Sea Power Conference aboard HMS Prince of Wales later this autumn, which will bring together defence leaders, industry representatives and policymakers to discuss Euro-Atlantic security.

Overseas operations also contributed to growth this year. Msscorps' US and Japan sites took on more projects and improved operational efficiency, with both moving toward profitability as they benefit from greater scale.
The company has also expanded cooperation with major international AI customers and completed three dedicated facilities. Discussions are underway on three additional facilities, which are expected to begin operations progressively in the fourth quarter.

Kyiv will propose a new law on minority education rights, with a vote expected in October. Budapest has blocked EU accession talks until Ukraine adopts the laws agreed under an 11-point plan on Hungarians in Transcarpathia.

Ties soured sharply under Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv over Ukraine and blocked its progress towards EU membership. His successor, Péter Magyar, has sought to repair relations since taking office in May, but the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine's Transcarpathia region remain a source of tension.
In June, the two countries agreed an 11-point plan to strengthen minority rights. Hungary responded by allowing two negotiating clusters to open in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
But Budapest has blocked further progress, insisting that Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, first pass the legislation required under the deal. The laws are due to be adopted by the end of the year.
"Deputy Prime Minister of Ukraine Vsevolod Chsentsov personally informed me that a bill on the educational rights of national minorities will be submitted to the Ukrainian parliament. We welcome this step," Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on social media.
"Hungary remains interested in the dialogue and in tangible results in the everyday life of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia," she added.
Deal could ease tensions
The breakthrough follows another flare-up between the two governments just two weeks ago.
Magyar and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha clashed over Zelenskyy's C8 regional development initiative, with Sybiha accusing the Hungarian leader of following in Orbán's footsteps after Magyar said Hungary had been included against its will.
A bill covering language and cultural rights is due to go before the Rada later in October. Kyiv has not officially commented on the latest developments.
Ukrainian outlet LIGA.net reported that experts from both countries held intensive talks this week and agreed which parts of the 11-point plan Kyiv can deliver.
Dániel Hegedűs, deputy director of the Institut für Europäische Politik, told Euronews that the move could help reverse recent negative trends in bilateral relations, but that the legislation could still run into obstacles in the Rada.
"Given the absence of stable majorities in the Verkhovna Rada, passing the legislation in October is an ambitious goal and a real test of whether the Ukrainian administration can regain political control over issues of strategic importance to the country's EU integration," Hegedűs said.
Minority deal could unlock Ukraine's EU talks
Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had previously planned to meet, but the Hungarian leader made the talks conditional on progress over minority rights.
Hungarian public opinion also complicates the picture. After years of hostility towards Ukraine under Orbán, conservative voters remain wary of closer ties with Kyiv. But defending ethnic Hungarians abroad is also popular with conservatives, potentially giving Magyar room to strike a deal.
If Ukraine passes the minority package, Hungary could lift its veto on opening more chapters in Kyiv's EU accession talks.
"It remains to be seen whether passage of the law will secure Hungary's support for opening all negotiation clusters or only for some of them," Hegedűs said.
"In the most positive scenario, passage of the minority law and Hungarian support for opening all negotiation clusters could mark a new era in relations between the two countries."
He added that approval of the minority package in Ukraine "would make Budapest's continuation of its blockade harder to sustain and significantly more costly politically at the European level."

Can we detect rainbows on alien worlds?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:10:33 UTC
20:10:33 KST

In some ways, finding exoplanets is amazingly easy.
It doesn’t necessarily take a huge telescope and sophisticated equipment to detect these alien worlds. Characterizing them, however—getting detailed information on their size, orbital period, and more—is usually more difficult.
Studying their atmospheres is currently at the cutting edge of what we can do, because that does indeed take state-of-the-art observatories. For example, astronomers can painstakingly gather a star’s light after it has physically passed through an orbiting planet’s air and look for the subtle signatures of various molecules absorbing some of that light at specific wavelengths.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But it’s not the only way to find and examine an atmosphere. Research published a few years back in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS) indicates another very clever method that astronomers could implement with a future space telescope.
They could look for exoplanetary rainbows.
There’s not a prayer of viewing one directly, alas; just getting a dotlike image of an exoplanet is already quite a task. But, with careful planning, some telltale indicators of rainbows and other optical phenomena can be seen.
To be clear, none of these can be detected with our extant fleet of telescopes. But NASA is currently developing a mission called the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), planned for launch in the early 2040s. This huge telescope will sport an at least six-meter light-collecting mirror and will be fine-tuned to look for Earth-sized worlds orbiting nearby sunlike stars in their habitable zone, the circumstellar region in which a planet can sustain liquid water on its surface.
Using HWO’s capabilities as a baseline, the astronomers responsible for that MNRAS paper investigated the prospects for detecting atmospheric phenomena such as rainbows, Rayleigh scattering and sunglint on exoplanets.
Observing such things, it turns out, is essentially a matter of perspective: They can all be revealed as an exoplanet goes through phases while orbiting its host star, just like the moon does as it orbits Earth. When the planet is between its star and us, we’re looking at its dark, unilluminated half (its “new” phase). As it orbits and appears to move away from the star, it exhibits a crescent phase, growing to appear half full at its farthest separation, then becoming full when it’s on the opposite side of the star from our viewpoint. The phases then occur in reverse order as it moves around the star and returns to its original “new phase” position. With a telescope like HWO, we wouldn’t see such phases directly, instead registering them as periodic brightness changes as a targeted exoplanet waxes and wanes.
The atmospheric phenomena potentially detectable by HWO depend on those phases and the angle between the planet, its star, and the observatory, and therefore are best seen at different times in the planet’s orbit.
Of these, sunglint is the simplest: it’s just the reflection of the sun on a body of water, such as a lake or an ocean. The surface of the water acts exactly like a mirror, bouncing incoming sunlight at an angle away from the sun. You can see this for yourself on a beach when the sun is low, with the bright reflection visible just under the sun in the water. This has also been seen from orbit many times in photos from the International Space Station and, in fact, was seen by the Cassini spacecraft at Saturn when sunlight reflected off lakes of liquid methane on its huge moon Titan.
Sunglint is seen when the angle between the sun, the water and the observer is very low, like at sunrise or sunset. For an exoplanet, it occurs when the planet is nearly between the star and Earth. From our viewpoint, the planet, if we could see it clearly, would be in a crescent phase.
In their MNRAS paper, the astronomers found that in projected HWO observations, the glint would add a small but significant bump in brightness to some planets at and near crescent phase. And because water and most other liquids can’t persist on a planet’s surface without an insulating blanket of air, seeing such a glint could signal the presence of an atmosphere as well.
Rainbows on Earth occur when sunlight passes through raindrops. Different colors of light bounce inside the drops at different angles, so when they emerge they’re spread out. When we stand with the sun at our backs, the drops we’re facing send that light back toward us sorted by color, creating a characteristic prismatic arc in the sky: a rainbow.
If this occurs on an exoplanet, we won’t be able to see it directly. The light in rainbows is polarized, however. This means the waves all align. (For example, they oscillate up and down or left and right.) HWO will likely carry a polarimeter—an instrument designed to let through only the light aligned in one way—and the paper’s authors modeled what it might see. If an exoplanet is at the right phase, HWO’s polarimeter should be able to detect the extra bump in polarized light from potential rainbows (and related phenomena like glories, which have been detected on other planets). The amount of polarization can also reveal how big the rainbow-making raindrops are and possibly even their composition.
Rayleigh scattering occurs when incoming sunlight bounces off molecules like nitrogen in Earth’s atmosphere, and it makes our sky blue. This scattering also polarizes the light; the amount of polarization seen depends on the incoming light’s angle with respect to the observer.
You can see this effect for yourself on a clear, sunny day! Polarized sunglasses are essentially basic polarimeters. They have filters in them with molecules all aligned in one direction (usually vertically); light polarized vertically passes through that filter like a key in a lock, while light polarized in another direction (say, horizontally) does not. The sky’s Rayleigh scattering causes the strongest polarization of sunlight 90 degrees away from the sun: if you rotate your sunglasses around while looking through them, you’ll see the sky darken significantly as you do—the sunglasses block the light when the light’s polarization angle doesn’t match that of the sunglasses. Closer to the sun—though be careful and don’t look too close!—this effect is much smaller. This is the effect astronomers can exploit using HWO to look for signs of an exoplanet’s atmosphere.
Based on simulations using data from real stars HWO might survey, the team of scientists found that polarization signals of rainbows and sunglints should be detectable on a decent fraction of accompanying small, warm rocky worlds, while Rayleigh scattering would register for most of them—presuming they have atmospheres, that is. That’s the whole point: we want to optimize HWO’s ability to detect air on alien worlds, and searching for these optical phenomena would really give it a boost.
A blue sky, a poststorm rainbow and the sun reflecting off the ocean are sights we take for granted here on Earth. But they may be ubiquitous on planets throughout the cosmos. If they are, we may be on the verge of being able to detect them.

Poland is preparing a law on the state’s full readiness in the event of war - media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland’s Ministry of National Defence has drafted a bill to coordinate defence management and speed up the deployment of troops to a state of war. The document is undergoing consultations.
Poland is preparing a bill on the state’s full readiness in the event of war. The bill aims to streamline the national defense management system and accelerate the process of redeploying troops to critical locations. Rzeczpospolita reports on October 2, UNN writes.
Details
The Polish Ministry of Defense has reportedly drafted a bill on national defense readiness. According to the publication, until recently the title itself included the phrase "on the state’s defensive readiness for war." The bill is currently at the stage of interministerial consultations.
The country’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that work on such a bill is ongoing. According to the information, the aim is "to strengthen the defense capabilities of the Republic of Poland, improve cooperation between the armed forces and services responsible for internal security, and adapt existing legislation to modern threats, including hybrid, cyber, and disinformation threats."
"This is the preparation of the state for the pre-war period, which Prime Minister Tusk spoke about some time ago," said a source connected with the presidential center. It is reportedly intended to fill the gap between the functioning of the state in peacetime and the formal introduction of martial law.
Its aim is also to "organize organizational and legal arrangements and increase the readiness of public administration bodies to perform tasks during a state of permanent and full defensive readiness of the state, in particular by clarifying the duties and competencies of the authorities." The Polish Ministry of Defense notes that currently, decisions concerning the preparation of the state for defense and the functioning of the defense management system are scattered across several resolutions of the country’s Council of Ministers issued after the adoption of the Homeland Defense Act in the spring of 2022.
"This regulatory model makes it difficult to ensure regulatory consistency and a unified approach to the performance of defense tasks by public administration bodies and other entities participating in the state’s defense system. Another significant problem is the scope of issues currently regulated at the level of subordinate legislation. Some existing provisions directly concern the tasks, competencies, and responsibilities of public administration bodies and other entities performing defense tasks, which justifies regulating them by law," the Polish Ministry of Defense stated.
The purpose of the law is to increase the readiness of state institutions for the threat of war
The bill aims to streamline the state defense management system and improve the readiness of public administration to perform tasks in a state of permanent and full defensive readiness, that is, even before the official declaration of martial law. Among other things, this will allow the earlier deployment of troops, including allied forces, link Poland’s Defense Response Plan with the NATO Response System, and prepare infrastructure.
The law will also expand the number of organizations participating in the permanent service system and the national defense management system, regulate the rules governing the work of civilian officials in command positions with limited leave to return home, amend the planning of non-war operational activities, and amend documentation concerning defense programs. Amendments will also be made to the rules for training, defense courses, and defense exercises.
According to the Polish Ministry of Defense, "due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm." The publication’s conclusions indicate that the National Security Bureau (BBN) is also awaiting the submission of such a bill.

Eurozone inflation surges to 3.8%, exceeding forecasts
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:09:27 EEST
20:09:27 KST

Eurozone inflation rose more than expected in September as energy costs pushed consumer prices further above the European Central Bank’s target, leaving policymakers to decide whether the latest surge requires another interest rate rise.
Eurostat estimated annual inflation across the 21-country currency bloc at 3.8%, up from 3.2% in August. A Reuters poll had put the expected rate at 3.6%.
Prices rose 0.6% from August, according to Eurostat’s flash estimate.
The annual inflation rate now stands close to twice the ECB’s 2% medium-term target and at its highest level since 2023.
Energy accounted for much of the increase. Energy prices rose 18.8% from September 2025, compared with a 14.3% annual increase in August. They gained 3.9% in September alone.
Other parts of the consumer basket showed smaller increases. Services prices rose 3.2% from a year earlier, compared with 3.0% in August. Food, alcohol and tobacco inflation increased to 1.4% from 1.1%.
Unprocessed food prices rose 4.0%, up from 2.7% in August. Prices for non-energy industrial goods increased 1.1%, down from 1.2%.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%. The limited movement in the measure gives ECB policymakers evidence that the energy shock has not yet spread across prices on the same scale as the headline figure.
The ECB has raised interest rates twice this year. Its latest 25-basis-point increase in September took the deposit facility rate to 2.50%. The Governing Council will announce its next monetary policy decision on 29 October.
Reuters reported that investors expect further increases over the coming year, though market expectations over the timing remain subject to changes in energy prices, inflation data and financial conditions.
The inflation figures varied across the currency bloc. Lithuania recorded the highest annual rate at 6.1%, followed by Bulgaria at 5.6%. Cyprus and Luxembourg each recorded 5.2%, while Greece reached 5.1% and Spain 5.0%.
Malta recorded the lowest rate at 2.4%, followed by Finland at 2.6% and Latvia at 2.9%.
Inflation also accelerated across the eurozone’s four largest economies. Spain recorded 5.0%, Italy 4.1%, France 3.4% and Germany 3.3%. Italy registered a 2.0% monthly increase in consumer prices, the largest September rise among euro-area members.
Eurostat will publish the full September inflation data on 16 October.

Rare defence show where buyers outnumber the sellers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:08:44 BST
20:08:44 KST

A new defence event opening in London next week has attracted 400 military and government end users among around 800 people registered, a balance its organisers say they have not seen before at a defence show.
Nick Waite, product director for Apex Europe, told the UK Defence Journal that the end user turnout has been exceptional. “We’re actually going to have more end users in the room than industry,” he said, adding that in eight years working in the defence trade show and conference industry he had not come across that before.
Apex grew out of research carried out about two and a half years ago with the industry and government partners who attend DSEI, which identified a need for a more targeted conversation than a large trade show can accommodate. The result rests on three things: near-term capability, operational problems rather than platforms, and access for smaller companies.
On the first of those, the cut-off is deliberately tight and rules out most of what a large show puts on display. “The focus is on near-term capability, so we’re looking at technology that can be integrated in the next 12 to 24 months,” Waite said. “The defence landscape has changed dramatically in the last decade. Geopolitical context to that, but also the rate of technological change is driving that. So our ability to find technology and take them from idea through to prototype through to operationally ready, then put into the hands of the operator, that iteration cycle, there’s a requirement for it to be much quicker.”
The second principle is what everything else at the event is organised around, because rather than dividing the event by domain or platform type, it is built around what the organisers call mission sets, six operational problems. “These range from autonomy related operational effects that European and allied forces want to achieve, to deep precision strike, spectrum related topics,” he said. “These are the things that anchor who attends, the topics, the conversations, which lends itself to having an audience which is much more focused than you would get at a traditional trade show.”
Those problems were not settled internally and then announced to the market. “They were chosen based off of research with the user, in short, and validated by speaking to another 20 users to say actually yeah, they’re spot on,” he said, describing a process that drew on the company’s relationships with industry and government alongside a set of advisers, some named publicly and some not.
The format follows from that choice, and each operational problem gets a panel of roughly fifty minutes, with at least a couple of end users on it to set the context and a mix of large, medium and small companies that have delivered against the problem in Britain or elsewhere in Europe. Immediately afterwards comes a run of ten minute capability presentations, mostly taken up by small businesses, responding to the problem that has just been discussed. Working group sessions run alongside for anyone wanting to get further into the detail with peers from industry and from allied nations.
Waite connected all of this to language he heard from the British Army at DVD last week, saying “There was a phrase I heard constantly, which was the way that the British Army was putting out this signal to industry was mission before platform, sharing the mission with industry versus traditionally, it’s okay, here’s my shopping list of strict requirements for this vehicle that we need,” he said. “It’s here’s the problem we’re trying to solve. Come on this journey early and try and help solve it. And that’s what we’re trying to mirror with Apex.”
Asked why Europe needs its own event rather than European delegations travelling to the American original, he said the two sets of priorities are complementary but distinct. “There is a separate need for European and NATO nations to have their own opportunity to lead the conversation in their own right,” he said. “There’s different priority sets, although they do overlap. And alongside that, there’s an industrial base that supports them equally.”
Apex and DSEI sit under the same Clarion umbrella, and the difference between them is one of scale and access as much as content. Nick told me, “DSEI is all halls of the Excel. Apex is much more intimate and focused,” Waite said. “Once you’re in the room, it’s open doors. Everyone eats together, everyone drinks together. There’s no closed doors. It’s all access, all areas within reason.”
Flagship speakers include a number of flag officers, which Nick described as a seal of approval for what the event is trying to do, but the bulk of the audience sits lower down. “If I showed you the attendee list, they’re going to be that SO1 capability, they’re going to be the programme manager level, they’re going to be the people who are responsible for delivering and integrating this capability in the day to day,” he said. “For us, that’s our primary audience from a user perspective. It’s to make sure that there’s an event for that cohort of people who would benefit from a more technical, operationally driven conversation.”
Asked what success looks like for a first outing, he described a single conversation rather than a number. “Success would be X, Y, Z person from UK MOD or a different government saying, hey, really enjoyed the event, I met with six companies I didn’t know existed that have capability that I didn’t know was a thing,” he said.
The multi-domain structure is where he sees the event doing something siloed shows cannot. “Any operational effect that’s trying to be achieved cannot be done by a single service or by a single type of kit nowadays,” he said. “So it’s by being multi-domain and having these multi-domain problems that integration piece across the services and across these problem sets is allowed to happen in a way that doesn’t necessarily happen at traditional events.”
The American event, Apex Defense, enters its third year in January, and Apex Europe returns in 2027 on the Monday and Tuesday of DSEI week, which Nick described as carving out a day and a half for a mission-focused conversation that could not happen alongside the larger show while everyone is already in town.

Syrian students get caught in rift between Druze leaders and Damascus
SWEIDA, Syria Oct 2 - Young people in Syria's Sweida province are unable to progress through school and university due to a deepening rift between the post-Assad Islamist government and the Israel-aligned Druze leaders of the last area outside central control.
Their dilemma reflects deep trauma and lingering instability in the province, where hundreds of Druze were killed last year in sectarian violence by government-linked forces and Israel struck Syria's military, saying it was defending the minority.
Maram Abu Hamra had been pursuing her dream of studying architecture in Syria's northern city of Aleppo but has been back in Sweida for more than a year, too afraid to return to government-held territory.
"Every student had a dream of being an engineer, a doctor, an artist -- or anything that they can achieve. But sadness, fear and resentment took control instead," the 20-year-old told Reuters.
SWEIDA LEADER SAYS DRUZE ARE 'PART OF ISRAEL'
Sweida, home to many of the estimated 700,000 Druze in Syria, lies in the southwest, bordering Jordan. Most of it is now controlled by forces loyal to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hajari, a Druze cleric who declared his community 'part and parcel of the state of Israel' in an August video.
Facing calls from Israeli Druze to help Syrian Druze, Israeli leaders have cited protecting them as a reason for attacking Syria repeatedly.
Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who aims to restore the country's relations with the West after overthrowing longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, has vowed to reunite Syrian territory under a single leadership.
But many Druze, Arabs who follow a branch of Islam seen as heretical by some Sunni Muslims, do not trust assurances that he will protect their rights, citing his earlier links with al Qaeda as well as last year's mass killings.
"What I want to say is that our fear is justified, because there are past incidents that were not that long ago, that were barely a year ago," said Fahed Abu Saad, whose son and daughter missed their final exams this year.
Syrian authorities first cancelled exams for high school and university entry in Sweida last year as a result of the killings. Syrian government troops withdrew from most of Sweida and Hajari barred them from returning, hardening his stance against integration and founding an armed faction called the National Guard.
Hajari's areas are now the only ones outside government control, after Kurdish authorities in Syria's northeast began integrating earlier this year following a lightning government offensive.
Even there, Syria's Kurds are seeking to preserve schooling in their mother tongue.
DEEP DISTRUST LINGERS
Many Druze students studying in other parts of Syria returned to Sweida in 2025.
But this year, student exams were disrupted again, with the government and Druze factions trading blame once more.
In the spring, Damascus offered to send proctors into Sweida to supervise exams, but some Druze saw it as an attempt to redeploy government forces.
Qutaiba Azzam, the government's media relations director for Sweida province, said local factions threatened the proctors, a claim Reuters could not independently verify.
In August, Damascus proposed that students from Hajari-held areas take their exams in a northern part of Sweida province now held by the government.
But that spooked students and their parents.
"It is not allowed for us to be scared that our children go to the northern countryside, but it is allowed for the ministry of education to be scared for its envoys to come here," Abu Saad said.
Some Druze, still shaken by the 2025 killings, fear Hajari's forces would label students as traitors for travelling into government-held territory for the exams.
Government-appointed provincial official Tarek Adwan told Reuters armed factions in Sweida city had attacked buses meant to carry students to their exams, a claim Reuters could not independently verify.
Hajari's office did not reply to repeated requests for comment. Syria's education ministry declined to comment.
Only 150 of 13,700 school students in Sweida managed to take exams this year that they need to progress into high school or university, according to government figures shared on Syria's state news agency.
The rest -- as well as university students like Abu Hamra -- remain in limbo, along with the Sweida province as a whole.
The area has traditionally been fairly autonomous, including during the nearly 14-year civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of Syrians and forced millions from their homes.
Syria's government, Jordan and the United States agreed last year on a seven-step roadmap to resolve the Sweida dispute, but the United Nations said in June that it had made "no progress." REUTERS

Guy Parmelin bows out after a remarkable final act

Guy Parmelin bows out after a remarkable final act
When Guy Parmelin began his second stint as Swiss president, the 66-year-old could reasonably have expected a quiet final year in office. Instead, the political dramas of 2026 gave the usually reserved economics minister an unexpected return to centre stage before his departure in December.
When Parmelin was elected to the Federal Council at the end of 2015, he was virtually unknown to the public. Even during his first few years in office, he rarely sought the limelight. In public opinion polls on popularity and influence within the Federal Council, he consistently ranked in the lower mid-table. In the media, he was sometimes described as a reserved “water-carrier” for his party.
From a winegrower from Bursins, canton Vaud – often perceived as a man of measured judgement – the right-wing Swiss People’s Party politician has, in his second year in the rotating president role, transformed himself into a crisis manager and architect of sustainable economic agreements.
More
Swiss President Guy Parmelin to step down and make way for ‘new blood’
Parmelin enjoyed a level of respect in the final stages of his federal government career, particularly in German-speaking regions and among the conservative business establishment, that extended beyond the confines of his own party.
His down-to-earth and level-headed manner helped him in this regard. Even his command of German, which had been criticised at the start of his term of office, was hardly an issue any more.
The previously uncharismatic speaker developed into a credible statesman serving the Swiss population. Last December, parliamentarians elected Parmelin as Swiss president with a record result of 203 votes.
Turning point in US customs dispute
Among the most enduring images of his presidency was his role during the complex tariff dispute with the US. While relations with Washington had long been strained by unilateral additional tariffs and uncertainties over trade policy, Parmelin’s pragmatic negotiating style – with the support of Swiss State Secretary Helene Budliger Artieda – gave the Swiss export sector some breathing space.
His ability to communicate directly with decision-makers in the US government made it possible to secure concrete relief for Swiss industry. In contrast to last year’s president, Karin Keller-Sutter, Parmelin forged a connection with the inner circle of the US government close to Donald Trump.
More
Incoming Swiss president wants new partnerships but deems the US ‘indispensable’
This success was directly reflected in a rise in his standing in the economic centres of German-speaking Switzerland. Whereas Parmelin was sometimes met with mild scepticism in the past, he is now recognised as a reliable advocate for Switzerland as a business hub. Prominent business leaders have spoken positively about the head of the economics ministry.
The influential financial investor and Partners Group co-founder Alfred Gantner underlined Parmelin’s down-to-earth efficiency and negotiating skills. This praise shows that he has raised his profile over the course of 2026.
At odds with own party on EU dossier
Alongside relations with the US, 2026 was marked by key decisions on European policy. It is not without certain irony that it was Parmelin of all people – as a representative of the Eurosceptic People’s Party – who signed the Swiss-EU bilateral treaty, known as Bilaterals III. However, during a joint appearance with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on March 2, 2026, he could scarcely be persuaded to smile.
In his first year as Swiss president in 2021, Parmelin had been forced to inform EU leaders in Brussels of the unilateral termination of negotiations on a framework agreement. The Federal Council is keen to avoid a second such shock if possible.
More
‘One for all, all for one’ – how the Swiss government makes decisions
Just this week, Parmelin defended the controversial Swiss-EU agreement in the Senate in the face of fierce opposition from his own party. The long-negotiated compromise reached by the social partners on wage protection remained intact – a success for the negotiating team and for Parmelin.
Throughout his years in government, Parmelin has rarely lost his composure; he has dealt with the conflicting views of the Federal Council and those of his party with stoic calm, consistently prioritising the principle of collegiality and the country’s economic stability.
Juggling on the global stage
The economics minister was also pragmatic when it came to diversifying Switzerland’s trading partners. Concluding and modernising free trade agreements was a key priority of his term in office. A milestone was the signing of the free trade agreement with India in March 2024 in New Delhi after 16 years of negotiations – a success of which he was visibly proud.
More
Swiss government confirms free trade deal with India to go into force on October 1
As early as 2021, he had successfully defended the free trade agreement with Indonesia in a referendum. This was followed by agreements with the Mercosur states, Malaysia, Thailand, Chile and Turkey, whilst intensive talks were held with trading partners such as China and Japan on modernising existing treaties.
More
Swiss parliament approves Mercosur free trade deal
In doing so, Parmelin generally managed to strike a balance between the left’s demands for strict sustainability and human rights standards, the centre-right’s calls for deregulation, and the concerns of the domestic agricultural lobby. For the left, however, this was often not enough. Referendums on the Mercosur and Malaysia agreements are likely to be held soon.
Agriculture and cutting red tape
On domestic policy, Parmelin, who is a trained farmer, remained closely connected to his roots. He followed the emotionally charged debates on the future direction of Swiss agricultural policy with empathy for the concerns of the farming and food sectors. Although he introduced new environmental regulations to parliament on several occasions, he did not appear disappointed when lawmakers passed watered-down versions of the bills.
Parmelin was also successful in his fight against two initiatives that sought to ban the use of pesticides in agriculture almost entirely. This vote revealed a significant urban-rural divide. The agriculture minister subsequently sought to close the ranks – and defended certain tighter restrictions on pesticide use in Parliament.
More
Parmelin defends government support for Swiss farmers amid drought
He took seriously the complaints about “too much red tape”, voiced during the farmers’ protests in early 2024, which are also clearly heard among small- and medium-sized businesses. Together with the sector, he pushed forward initiatives to free businesses from administrative burdens.
Calm leadership in times of crisis
Parmelin built his reputation as a stabilising force during previous moments of crisis. His appearance on the world stage during his first year as president in 2021 remains unforgettable, particularly when he hosted US President Joe Biden and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit in Geneva. He appeared relaxed and demonstrated his diplomatic skill by greeting the two statesmen in their own languages, thereby brushing aside ridicule about his limited language skills.
During the pandemic, however, the economics minister also faced criticism. Many businesses would have liked more support from the federal government to compensate for lost revenue resulting from strict Covid-19 measures. Parmelin was also reluctant to come to the aid of so-called “hardship cases”. The state cannot help everyone was his credo and he urged the public to take personal responsibility.
More
Swiss president calls for unity at UN
In the spring of 2022, too, when Russia launched its war of aggression against Ukraine, Parmelin reacted hesitantly. Initially, he was cautious, even opposed, to sanctions against Russia. According to media reports, his department, for example, put the brakes on discussions regarding the Russian oil embargo before bowing to the will of the Federal Council and the federal administration. The system for monitoring compliance with the sanctions also drew criticism of the economics ministry.
Recurring rumours of resignation
There were periods during his tenure when he was less visible in public. These were the times when the media speculated about his resignation. Back pain, a fall in his office and reaching retirement age fuelled such rumours, particularly in the 2023 election year. At the time, Parmelin felt compelled to deny media reports about his possible imminent resignation.
Since then, observers have assumed that Parmelin will announce his resignation after his second term as Swiss president and before the federal elections in autumn 2027. For some time now, the Vaud native has been the longest-serving member of the federal government.
Parmelin’s early years as a cabinet minister have almost been forgotten. Following his election in December 2015 as the successor to Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf, he headed the defence ministry, as many People’s Party ministers have done before him. He immediately made his mark by securing an increase in the army’s budget.

Italy's firefighting planes return home after summer battling blazes across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:07:58 UTC
20:07:58 KST

Western Europe recorded its hottest summer on record, with some 540,000 hectares going up in smoke across the European Union between mid-June and early September.
After a gruelling summer skimming lakes and coastlines to dump thousands of tonnes of water on wildfires burning across a parched Europe, Italy's fleet of bright yellow and red Canadair planes has finally returned home to a base near Rome for maintenance.
Italy operates one of the world's largest fleets of Canadair amphibious aircraft, part boat, part plane, that can respond quickly to a fire because they do not need to land to take on water from lakes, reservoirs or the sea.
This summer brought Italy's fourth-largest fire season since 2006, with 113,800 hectares burned in 645 fires, according to data from the European EFFIS system, keeping the country's 18 water bombers busy.
But the planes were called to tackle wild blazes abroad too, as part of the European Union's shared firefighting resources, with the continent battling a historic fire season.
"At the start of the summer, we deployed to Portugal and Spain, where we faced two quite difficult situations," said Francesco Morgante, a pilot with Avincis, the company that manages the fleet on behalf of Italy's fire service.
Both countries saw devastating fires, threatening cities and tourist hotspots.
"After that, our own country required our full attention, particularly due to the emergency situation in northern Italy, which was quite unexpected and unusual this year," Morgante told the AFP news agency.
The Canadair water bombers are manufactured exclusively by Calgary-based De Havilland.
Italy has the CL-415 model, but like many European countries is awaiting delivery of new-generation aircraft, the DHC-515, which comes with a price tag of around €100 million.
'Ideal tool'
The Canadair is capable of scooping up over 6,000 litres of water in just 12 seconds without landing thanks to two intakes beneath the fuselage and dropping the load in three seconds, making it an "ideal tool" for firefighting, said Morgante.
"It is a versatile, flexible tool capable of tackling medium-to-large fires", and "enables a fire to be contained even when it is already fully developed," he said, from the cramped cockpit of one of the water bombers.
A vast, newly renovated hangar houses planes undergoing inspection, including one with its twin turboprop engines exposed.
The in-depth checks are performed on every aircraft in the fleet over a period of several weeks after summer, Maurizio Tomassi, head of maintenance operations at Avincis, told AFP, adding they hope to complete the maintenance by March.
In the meantime, the closure of the last operational base in Calabria on 31 October will mark the official end of this year's summer season.
'No weather break'
Western Europe recorded its hottest summer on record, with some 540,000 hectares going up in smoke across the European Union between mid-June and early September.
That makes the issue of how many Canadair fleets are available to member states more pressing than ever.
Over the years, there has been "a slow, gradual increase in the need" for the bombers, said Morgante.
"Having a fleet that meets our needs at both national and European levels...is essential," he said.
For pilots, technical staff and operational coordinators alike, this summer will go down in the record books.
"We didn't get that moment when a summer storm rolls in, the temperature drops by three or four degrees, and you get a two-day break before things potentially pick up again, if they pick up at all," Morgante said.
"That weather 'break' simply didn't happen."
Alessandro Sette, the head of the operations room which handles incoming requests from the Italian Civil Protection agency, agreed it has been "an exceptional summer."
"Work started early in the morning because the planes took off at first light...and operations usually wrapped up at dusk, making for long, intense days," he said.
But on this quiet late-September morning, there is no movement on the screen used to track aircraft flight paths.
"Practically all the planes are on the ground," he said with satisfaction.

Supercam S180, S350 UAVs jointly perform missions in special op zone — developer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:05:06 UTC
20:05:06 KST

BAKU, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s latest high-speed Supercam S180 reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and the S350 unmanned system work in conjunction with each other, carrying out the full range of aerial reconnaissance missions in the special military operation, Unmanned Systems Group Spokeswoman Yekaterina Zgirovskaya told TASS at the ADEX 2026 International Defense Exhibition in Baku.
"The combined use of the Supercam S350 and S180 allows for optimal coverage of the entire spectrum of command tasks: autonomous monitoring in the rear and in controlled territories, as well as reconnaissance in the close tactical zone for live monitoring of fire damage," Zgirovskaya said.
She emphasized that the mass use of interceptor drones in the combat zone has altered the tactics for deploying unmanned aerial systems. Now, the effectiveness of aerial reconnaissance is achieved through the proper distribution of tasks among aircraft with different tactical and technical characteristics, depending on the area of operation and the nature of the threats.
Zgirovskaya noted that the Supercam S350 is ideal for detailed reconnaissance behind enemy lines at ranges of up to 150 km and for carrying out missions in the close tactical zone. The UAV remains the primary platform for autonomous surveying of territories, monitoring logistics routes and extended national borders, and surveying coastal areas – including the detection of uncrewed boats.
According to her, the new high-speed Supercam S180 reconnaissance drone is effective for aerial reconnaissance in areas of intense countermeasures. It features a high cruising speed, and thanks to its "afterburner" mode, it can accelerate and evade ramming attacks by interceptor drones. In addition, the drone has its own system for detecting and identifying approaching drones and is capable of operating autonomously without a global navigation satellite system.

Poland introduces new procedures for shooting down objects in airspace
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:05:01 CEST
20:05:01 KST

Poland introduces new procedures for shooting down objects in airspace
Poland's military has completed new procedures allowing simpler identification and shooting down of foreign objects in Polish airspace, Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Wednesday.
The new rules concern Polish pilots involved in missions to protect the country's airspace during Russian attacks on Ukraine. Under the previous peacetime procedures, pilots were required to visually identify an object before shooting it down. The new rules introduce so-called positive identification, based on information from radars and other systems, as well as information provided by Ukraine.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said he had received a report from Operational Commander Gen. Ireneusz Nowak that the procedures were fully ready and were being implemented. "October 1 is always a good time not only to start the academic year, but also to implement new procedures," he said.
The defence minister said the changes did not require legislative amendments and were being introduced at the military level. He said they would establish clear procedures for pilots and other soldiers involved in air defence.
Under current regulations, the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces Branches is responsible for protecting Polish airspace and may decide to shoot down a foreign object that has entered Polish airspace, or authorise fighter pilots to do so.
The change removes the requirement for visual identification, under which a fighter pilot had to approach an unidentified object closely enough to determine its type. The procedure was designed to minimise the risk of mistakenly shooting down a civilian aircraft unable to communicate with the military due to a malfunction.
Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Monday that the changes were necessary because the risk of drones entering Polish airspace had become a regular occurrence. He said such capabilities had previously generally been reserved for wartime or martial law. (PAP)

Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:04:48 UTC
20:04:48 KST

Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.
Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.
In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.
Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.
Transport under pressure
 “This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”
The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.
Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.
On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.
Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.
The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.
Rain needed
 Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.
He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.

Russia’s “Shadow Fleet” Is Growing Again—This Time With New Arctic LNG Tankers
Russia is attempting to expand a new “shadow fleet” of tankers to circumvent British sanctions and maintain revenues from energy exports, The Telegraph reported on October 1, citing the UK Foreign Office.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Moscow is believed to be expanding its network of civilian vessels used to transport fuel and generate revenue that helps finance Russia’s war against Ukraine. The reported effort includes at least two newly built tankers designed to transport liquefied natural gas (LNG) through the Arctic.
According to The Telegraph, the two vessels, each measuring approximately 984 feet in length, entered service earlier this year. Russia is also believed to have acquired several additional ships to strengthen the fleet as NATO countries increasingly seek to target vessels involved in sanctions evasion.
The UK government disclosed the reported expansion as it announced a new package of sanctions against Russia, including measures targeting vessels acquired to support Moscow’s energy exports.
“The Russian state is attempting to build a dangerous new ‘shadow fleet’ to circumvent sanctions and sustain revenues from its gas exports,” the Foreign Office said.
“Today’s package targets several vessels acquired to support that effort, including some that entered service as recently as July this year. By targeting these ships, the UK is increasing pressure on a sector the Russian state sees as critical to its future revenues.”
As part of the package, the UK targeted eight vessels linked to Russia’s efforts to preserve LNG export revenues despite Western sanctions. They include three shadow fleet tankers, two vessels providing bunkering services, and three Russian-owned ice-class ships.
The designated vessels will face shipping and trade restrictions, while sanctioned individuals and entities will be subject to asset freezes and other measures.
The UK measures come amid broader efforts to identify vessels allegedly supporting Russia’s sanctions-evasion network. On September 23, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) identified 38 ships it said were involved in circumventing international sanctions, exporting Russian energy products, and supporting military logistics.
According to HUR, 28 of those vessels are involved in exporting Russian oil, petroleum products, and LNG, providing bunkering services to sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, and transporting Ukrainian grain from temporarily occupied territories.

However, he admitted that the negotiations are "often difficult and complex", adding that the G20 has not expanded its core membership for many years.
"It is a difficult process, but Poland holds strong cards. Our track record of economic growth and our achievements command respect worldwide," Domanski argued, adding that Poland's experience could be highly valuable to the G20.

Brazil's election: Lula or Bolsonaro Jr?

PRESS REVIEW – Friday, October 2: We look at reactions in the French papers after high school blockades turned violent across France. We also look ahead to Brazil's two-round presidential election, which begins this weekend. The electoral campaign culminated with the cancellation of a presidential debate after both President Lula and his rival Flavio Bolsonaro pulled out. Finally, this year's Comedy Wildlife Awards finalists do not disappoint.
There's lots of focus on this week's high school protests in France that turned violent on Thursday. Le Parisien evokes the anger of pupils and talks of a "situation that escalated", with more than 2,000 arrests.
Many of the papers point their finger at the far-left France Unbowed party, whose members have publicly supported the high schoolers. Le Figaro, the right-wing daily, calls them "the proxies" of the protesters and says that behind the demonstrators lurks the "shadow of the France Unbowed party". La Croix is more tempered in its coverage, reminding us that the violence of the protests is still marginal. Libération, the left-wing paper, is one of the few dailies that actually looks at what high schoolers are demanding: more funding for schools, better school facilities and adequate numbers of teachers and personnel. It offers some examples of how bad the situation is for some schools: one maths teacher was absent for three months and in one school, only one toilet was available for 1,200 pupils. Communist paper L'Humanité denounces the police action against protesters on Thursday. Its headline reads "Take your police away first" – a play on words of the word "bac", which also means high-school leaving diploma.
L'Humanité is also focusing on Brazil on its front page. Brazilians head to the voting booths this Sunday for the first round of presidential elections and the election is garnering a lot of attention in the papers there. The election pits incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Jornal do Brasil is focusing on polls that predict Lula will win the first round, but it could be neck and neck for the run-off on October 25. The paper also reports that international observers have arrived in Brazil to observe the correct undertaking of the electoral process.
It has been a bitter electoral campaign, culminating on Thursday with the cancellation of the final presidential debate, set to be hosted by O Globo, after both Lula and Bolsonaro refused to attend. In its editorial, Brazilian daily O Globo explains why it cancelled the debate. The Superior Electoral court authorities refused to leave an empty chair for absent candidates to allow the other candidates to direct questions at them in absentia. As O Globo explains, this is a deep-seated tradition in campaign debates and part of the democratic process. The other grievance was the inclusion of certain candidate from Lula's party who did not meet the requirements necessary to participate in the debates. O Globo says that faced with political interference and violations of the constitution and press freedom, it had no option but to cancel the presidential debate. A columnist for another daily, Folha da Sao Paolo, says the Supreme Electoral Court's meddling with the debate "with such brazenness would have been unthinkable not long ago, something associated with banana republics. Not anymore."

They include an orangutan flipping the bird, a pair of elephant seals necking each other and a macaque learning the hard way that you shouldn't ram into a tree at full speed!

Senior Green party figures privately fear defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.
Attempts to concentrate resources on the byelection have caused internal friction, with the Guardian revealing last month that Polanski wanted the Greens’ annual conference postponed so the party could focus on the contest. That proposal was rejected by its executive.
Polanski, who has never been an MP, maintained there were “still advantages to being a leader outside Westminster”, while also arguing that entering parliament would offer another way of putting pressure on the Labour government.
The byelection has become an early test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can reclaim progressive voters who have moved towards the Greens, and the result may inform the government’s decisions over expanding North Sea oil and gas drilling.
“I see this election as high stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.”
The Guardian has reported the Jackdaw decision is likely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs.
Both projects already hold licences granted under the Conservatives, meaning approval by Labour would not amount to issuing new exploration licences.
Asked whether Burnham’s surge could win back younger and progressive voters from the Greens, Polanski said there were two possibilities. One was that Burnham “means what he’s saying right now” and would actually “implement action today and not tomorrow, and not after the next general election”. In this case, Polanski said, the country would improve as a result of pressure from the Greens and others.
The other, which Polanski called “the more likely scenario”, was that “what we’re getting is talk”. He said Burnham was “promising things after the next general election, but soon we’re going to have a budget that he’s already warning is going to be a difficult budget”.
In this case, he said, “more and more people will start to question why would you vote for the Labour party or get involved with the Labour party when the Green party has been growing for over a year now”.
He added: “You don’t have to accept the half-fat version. You can join the Green party and actually make sure we have the country that Andy Burnham’s talking about, but not taking the action on.”
Arguing that Labour’s climate policy had a gap between rhetoric and actions, Polanski asked: “Does Andy Burnham just not care about the climate crisis? It just feels like such a glaring gap in everything that he’s talked about, not just because of Rosebank and Jackdaw, but in the need to invest in renewables, the need for a clean green revolution, the need for new jobs, and it just feels like this vision is just not there.”
He added: “When are we going to see difficult choices for the super rich and the very, very wealthy? Instead, he’s talking about difficult choices for pensioners. So already, the action is not meeting his ‘hope’ rhetoric, and I think people are already starting to ask questions.”
Referring to arrests of Palestine Action supporters outside the Labour party conference, Polanski said: “Those people on the doorstep, they can see that Ed Miliband stood on stage and told many of us that we were right on Palestine, but just behind him, outside the conference hall, pensioners were still being dragged off, being arrested for holding signs up saying ‘I support Palestine Action’.”
Polanski is facing a separate test of his leadership at the Green party’s annual conference, where members are due to debate a deeply contentious motion declaring “Zionism is racism”.
Asked about criticism from senior Greens who believe he has failed to provide leadership over the issue, he said: “Leadership is about priorities, and this motion isn’t my priority. My priority is the cost of living. My priority is nationalising Thames Water. My priority is ending the genocide that’s happening in Gaza and freeing Palestine.”
Some Jewish Greens have raised concerns about what the motion could mean for their place within the party.
Asked whether he could guarantee that a Jewish member would not face disciplinary action simply for attending a synagogue that identified as Zionist, Polanski said: “I can guarantee that this motion has absolutely nothing to do with disciplinary action against anyone.”

Russia Stops Cyprus-Flagged Cargo Ship Heading to Estonia in Gulf of Finland

Russia Stops Cyprus-Flagged Cargo Ship Heading to Estonia in Gulf of Finland
Russian border guards detained a Cyprus-flagged cargo vessel bound for the Estonian port of Sillamäe while it was passing through Russian territorial waters in the Gulf of Finland, ERR reported.
The vessel, Vasterbotten, was traveling through an area of Russian territorial waters where ships are permitted to transit under an agreement between Estonia, Finland, and Russia. Estonia’s Police and Border Guard Board confirmed that the vessel had been detained.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to vessel-tracking data cited by ERR, Westerbotten appeared to have entered Russian territorial waters before it was stopped. The ship was later allowed to resume its voyage, departing at around 5 p.m. and continuing toward Sillamäe.
The route through Russian waters is covered by an agreement between the three countries because it provides a safer passage for larger vessels than navigating shallower waters on the Estonian side.
Are Piel, head of the Vessel Traffic Management Department at the Estonian Transport Administration, said that while the incident was unwelcome, inspections of vessels within a country’s territorial waters were not unusual.
“Every country has the right to inspect vessels in its territorial sea, and apparently the Russian administration considered it necessary to inspect this vessel as it passed through their territorial sea,” Piel said.
He added that all vessels have the right to innocent passage through another country’s territorial sea, but stressed that this does not prevent the coastal state from inspecting them.
The Estonian Transport Administration said it had received no explanation from Russia regarding the reason for the vessel’s detention.
The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of Russian maritime activities in the region. Russia is working to expand a new “shadow fleet” of tankers in an effort to bypass British sanctions and preserve revenues from energy exports, The Telegraph reported on October 1, citing the UK Foreign Office.
The reported expansion involves a network of civilian vessels used to transport Russian fuel and generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war against Ukraine. The fleet reportedly includes at least two newly built tankers designed to carry liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Arctic waters.

Many Group of Twenty (G20) countries believe it is necessary to consolidate around the most pressing issues and seek consensus, Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov told reporters on Thursday following the G20 meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
"Many expressed the view that it would be wrong to abandon the G20’s standard working format, under which all decisions are made by consensus among all countries, in favor of an approach where certain countries simply sign on to a particular position. Guidance: Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
Guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme for veterans who served under, and were impacted by, the Ban on LGBT personnel in HM Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
Documents
Details
LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Data detailing scheme progress which will be shared on a monthly basis.
Data as of 28/09/26:
Total individual applicants*: 1,780
*Applicants may have more than one case due to there being two payment types.
Total decisions made on cases: 2,309
Value of total payments made: £59,305,000
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme was recommended by the LGBT Veterans Independent Review which was published in July 2023.
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme is a payment scheme open to those who served under and were directly impacted by the Ban on LGBT personnel serving in the Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
This page provides information and guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, including eligibility and how to apply.
Types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments
There are two types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments:
1. LGBT Dismissed or Discharged Payment. This payment is for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged because of the Ban, including officers who were ordered or instructed to resign or retire by their respective Service Board.
2. LGBT Impact Payment. A payment to recognise other experiences of those who served under the Ban, as outlined in the Financial Recognition Payment Types and Tariff Table. (LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme Rules, Annex B).
Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above before starting an application.
How to Apply
Online applications
The Ministry of Defence encourages all eligible applicants to submit their applications online.
An app for the scheme can be accessed on Defence Gateway from 13 December 2024.
This platform will ensure that your data and any uploaded documents are secure. The app dashboard will keep you updated about the status of your application.
The online application process has two steps:
Step 1: Register for a Defence Gateway Account so you can access the online Financial Recognition Scheme application form.
Step 2: Sign in to your Defence Gateway account and submit your Financial Recognition Scheme application form via the Financial Recognition Scheme app.
Hard copy applications
If you would prefer to submit a hard copy (paper) application form, read scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above.
Hard copy application forms can also be obtained from Veterans UK.
Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Help with applying to the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion have partnered with the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme to provide support to veterans who are applying to the scheme.
These charities can assist with completing the application form, provide guidance on writing the necessary evidence and answer any questions applicants may have.
Royal British Legion
- Email: info@britishlegion.org.uk
- Phone: 0808 802 8080
For more information on the support the Royal British Legion can offer, visit Royal British Legion - Applying for restorative measures for LGBTQIA+ Veterans.
Fighting with Pride
For more information on the support Fighting with Pride can offer, visit Fighting with Pride LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme.
Veterans Welfare Service
Additional support is also available from the Veterans Welfare Service (VWS) who provide information, guidance and support to veterans and their families, as well as supporting veterans through a network of case managers across the UK and Republic of Ireland.
To find out more, visit Veterans Welfare Service or contact the Veterans’ Helpline using the details below.
- Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
- Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
- Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Other restorative measures
For information on non-financial restorative measures visit LGBT veterans: support and next steps.
