Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. And normally I’d tell you who today’s guest is but she described herself so delightfully that I want you to hear it in her own words:
Alexis Nikole Nelson: Alexis Nikole Nelson, field botanist, eater of things off ground?
Feltman: Even if you don’t know Alexis by name, you’ve almost certainly seen some of her work on social media as Black Forager. Millions of followers devour her videos about finding and eating wild foods, from fruits to flowers to seaweeds. She’s here today to talk about her debut book, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Nelson: Oh, my gosh, I’m so happy to be joining you.
Feltman: So let’s talk about your new book a little bit and how you got to be writing it. I would love to just go back in time a little bit and hear how you first got into foraging.
Nelson: So I began foraging at, like, the ripe old age of five with my mom. I used to love tagging along when she was working in the garden on the weekends. And I don’t know if you know this, famously, five-year-olds, not the most helpful genre of human. Motor skills not fully downloaded yet. And so whether it was an act of love and sharing knowledge or an act of trying to keep a small child busy, my mom pointed out some onion grass that was growing in our back lawn, and I had never noticed it before.
I asked her when she put it there. She said she didn’t, it was just there on accident, and that there were lots of plants that were just there minding their own business that were also edible and medicinal. And to me, a small child, that blew my mind. I was like, “What do you mean you didn’t put it here? And why isn’t everyone talking about this? Alert the presses. Alert the masses.” And that just sparked my love of knowing all things edible that happened to be growing in my general vicinity, which, you know, has now spread to just a love of the natural world in general.
Feltman: You know, speaking of the love of the natural world and, you know, how foraging feeds that for you, tell me about, you know, what you love about foraging and why it feels so important to share with other people.
Nelson: I think it’s two main things that I really love about it. One is: It’s really meditative. It’s a beautiful way to force your brain to slow down and to notice tiny details about the world around you, to participate in your local ecosystem. And I think that does my brain a whole world of good. I know I’ve been traveling a lot lately, so I haven’t been able to, and I can definitely tell the difference in brain when I am outside in the woods every day and brain when I’m not.
And additionally, I think especially this past summer, we have recognized how fragile some of our food systems are and how maybe we have created such a big food system in which we’re so separated from the food that ends up on our plates that maybe we’ve taken a bridge too far. So it’s really nice to have some things in your pantry, on your dinner plate, that you know the entire trajectory of its travel from being in the ground to being on your plate.
I think it’s a good skill to have. I don’t think it’s ever gonna replace the grocery store for anybody, but there’s something really fulfilling about being responsible for some of the things you’re eating. You know, people who have hobby vegetable gardens will say the exact same thing.
Feltman: So in doing this work publicly including on the Internet, what kinds of questions do you get from the people who are watching what you’re creating?
Have you been surprised at all by what kinds of feelings come up in people when they, they see you sharing stuff about foraging?
Nelson: Yeah, absolutely. I think the two most surprising questions that I still get with some amount of frequency is always a question of where I’m foraging and the legality of me as an individual foraging there.
Feltman: Interesting.
Nelson: And there’s a lot to unpack in that particular question, ’cause sometimes it is really coming from a place of, like, earnest curiosity. A lot of times, some people are also kind of telling on themselves with some of their own inherent biases, and I try to talk through that with people to the best of my ability, ’cause a lot of our feelings about trespass and who has access to wild spaces ends up becoming, like, a classism conversation, I think, a lot faster than people necessarily expect it to.
And I also don’t think a lot of people realize that the origin of a lot of trespass law lies in purposefully cutting off poor people and people of color from being able to access wild foods, be they plants, fungi, fish, squirrels, on land that doesn’t belong to them.
The other question very much in that same vein is “Well, what happens if everyone starts foraging? What’s gonna be left?” People think everyone’s gonna see one of my videos, and then it’s just going to be, like, a cartoon desert with a tumbleweed going by—except maybe no tumbleweed, ’cause, you know, that’s a brassica. Somebody might try to eat that, too. And the first thing that I love to assure people is everyone’s not gonna become a forager.
I know, ’cause I try. I can’t even get my whole family to go foraging with me. And that’s okay. Choose your own adventure, like the books at the library in the ’90s. Choose your own adventure. I am not here to yuck anybody’s yum, and sometimes people are city mice and inside mice, not country mice, and that’s fine.
Second of all, I think, to assume some sort of, like, capitalist intent behind every single person who is foraging is also kind of telling on yourself if that’s the frame of mind you’re going into asking the question with—because I do honestly and earnestly believe that if people were just foraging for the sake of being able to take care of themselves, their family and the community in which they live, and that includes your human neighbors and your not human neighbors, too, then they will make an informed choice while they are gathering.
You know, there are a lot of different global cultures that have rules and rituals to follow, whether that is, you know, some of the Indigenous bands here in the United States taking a moment to pause, lay down tobacco, because that moment of mindfulness helps you from going overboard. You know, globally there’s a lot of also, you know, never take the first thing that you see of a specific species. You know, never take a noticeable amount of a specific species—because not only would that be bad for the thing you’re gathering, but in the long run, it’s also bad for you.
Feltman: Right.
Nelson: You know, foragers are constantly having to be future-focused. We are constantly in a conservationist mindset, not just because we also want to keep having that experience, but we would love people a generation down the road, seven generations down the road, to also get to foster these relationships with our nonhuman neighbors, with the trees and the plants and the fungi and the animals that we happen to be lucky enough to live near.
I think foraging becomes poaching when you start putting money into the equation. I live in a part of the country that is, you know, in the ramp belt. And if you’re not a foodie, a ramp is a very pungent wild onion that is in season for about a month in the Midwest.
Feltman: And people lose their minds.
Nelson: They lose their minds. People lose their ever plant-loving minds over them.
Martha Stewart wrote one article about them two decades ago, and the ramps have not recovered since. And you will see people, in order to be able to stock, like, farmers markets in Manhattan and in order to be able to stock, you know, the kitchens of Michelin-starred restaurants around the country, coming into places like southeast Ohio, coming into West Virginia, and filling up trash bags with this plant that frequently can take nearly a decade to reach maturity. You know, [it] can sometimes take 10 years before it is at a point where it can be procreating, creating seeds. Those seeds take an additional two years then to break down their seed coat and germinate. So you, you do have to be using your noggin when you’re going out and gathering.
And if you’re just gathering enough for you and your family to have a mess of greens for a couple nights in the spring and to pickle a couple jars of bulbs, that’s totally fine. I’m not the person who’s gonna be, like, pick-shaming people for going and gathering ramps. They’re a wonderful springtime treat. But yeah, the second that you put money into the equation and start putting more steps in between the gathering and the consuming of the plant, the muddier the waters become, the less careful the people doing the gathering suddenly start to be because you have this magical dollar sign hovering over your head that you’re chasing.
Feltman: Yeah. So let’s talk about your book. Who is it for, and what are they going to come away with after reading it?
Nelson: My book is for current and future foragers. I think people assume you have to be at my level to be considered a forager, and I think if you just go and dig up the dandelions in your backyard, congratulations, you are a forager. Your laminated name tag will be in the mail shortly, I promise. And I want this book to help people recognize that and also help them recognize that you don’t have to live in the middle of the woods on an expansive piece of land in order to become a forager.
There are so many opportunities. I live in the middle of a city. I love getting—you know, another question I get a lot is “Oh, where do you live where you find all of the”—Columbus, Ohio. We often don’t take stock of the plants that do exist around us. Even if you feel like you’re living in a concrete jungle, odds purslane is still coming up out of the sidewalk cracks. There you go. That’s a snack that you could be foraging. Make sure it’s not in a place where a dog could have peed on it, but you know, that’s still something forageable in the heat of summer, surrounded by nothing but industry and concrete.
Feltman: Yeah, very cool. What are some other of your favorite sort of like gateway-drug foraging things that, like, are more abundant than people realize, that they’re gonna love once they try them, and then they won’t be able to stop picking stuff?
Nelson: Ooh, my favorite is actually a throwback for both of us, Rachel, and that is serviceberries, which secretly have a million names. If I don’t call them by the name that you at home specifically call them, I’m so sorry, but we don’t have time....
Feltman: And you can go listen to my other show,The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week, if you want to hear, still probably not literally every name for the serviceberry, but many more of them.
Nelson: They’re such a popular planting for parks and lining city streets because they’re resilient, their foliage is beautiful in the autumn, and their fruits are so good. Amelanchier arborea is the species that I see used in parks globally the most. I saw an Amelanchier arborea in the middle of Tokyo earlier this year.
So when I say that there is one hiding near you, that is not a joke. Unless you live right around the equator, where it’s a little too toasty for them, you will probably find a park close to you that has these guys, and they are such a springtime treat. You might have to fight some birds for them. I have an uneasy truce with the robins in my neighborhood. They’re like, “You don’t bring out the berry rake, we don’t poop on you. That’s the deal.”
Feltman: Well, and so as an experienced forager, I would also love to hear, to inspire our guests for their future foraging endeavors: What are some of the more surprising or challenging things that you have foraged yourself?
Nelson: Ooh. Well, I was in Glacier National Park last summer and just hanging out on a mountainside, eating alpine strawberries. That was fun and worth it. I mean, that hike did kick my whole butt. But also, if you’ve never had a wild strawberry, I need you to pencil it in for next summer because the amount of flavor that gets packed into one of those little guys is insane. They’re so good.
Feltman: Well, another one that I would love to hear more about, I think you recently did some ocean pickling, uh, which of course, so much interesting science there. So for our listeners who don’t follow you yet online, it would be great if you could tell us a little bit about that one.
Nelson: So I love food history, especially when it comes to things like foraging and fermentation and older food preservation methods. And there is a pretty strong bit of evidence for humans discovering lacto-fermented pickles through preserving things in saltwater, because frequently, so long as it hasn’t rained super recently, ocean water is right around the salinity that you want to make a good sour lacto-fermented pickle—like, high 2 percent to high 3 percent range, enough that you get some good salty flavor but also not so salty that the lactobacteria can’t get really active and create that delicious lactic acid that we love, that wonderful crisp acidity that we love from a good pickle.
So to showcase this, while I was visiting some of my family on Martha’s Vineyard—far away from industry, I promise, that’s always everyone’s biggest fear—I checked the water quality levels before I did this. I gathered up a bunch of seawater, put it through multiple layers of filtration. We filtered out the bits, big and small, brought it up to a rolling boil for just a moment, just to kill off anything too small to be able to be filtered out.
And then I have pickled beets, jalapeños, garlic. They all pickle beautifully. And due to the fact that our ocean water, it’s not just sodium making a salt in the ocean, we also have some magnesium salts in there, too, which I think add to the flavor profile of the pickles. They are pretty slammin’, if I may say so myself. And I love an excuse to sneakily shove some science education into my videos.
Feltman: Amazing. Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat with us. This has been wonderful.
Nelson: Thank you so much for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Monday with our usual science news roundup.

Greece proposes suspending the acceptance of asylum applications during emergencies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:20:51 UTC
19:20:51 KST

On the 1st of October, Greece called on the European Union to allow member states to suspend the acceptance of asylum applications during periods of large-scale migration flows, noting that current rules are inadequate for emergency situations like the one experienced in Ceuta this summer, reports Reuters.
The proposal, submitted during a meeting of EU interior ministers, garnered support from some of the bloc's member states. Dutch Migration Minister Bart van der Brink stated that a legal way must be found to prevent a mass influx of migrants into the asylum system; situations like the one in Ceuta should be treated as a broader management issue rather than an asylum matter. Since the arrival of more than a million people in the EU in 2015—most of them Syrians fleeing war—anti-immigration sentiment has remained a significant factor in politics. Large-scale migrant flows have fueled support for nationalist and far-right parties, and many governments have shifted toward stricter migration policies focusing on border control, deterrence, and the return of migrants. Illegal migration has decreased by 35% this year, and 8% more migrants were returned in the first half of the year compared to the preceding six-month period.
Spain estimated that more than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While the majority have been returned to Morocco, around 10,000 individuals remain on Spanish territory,
prompting governments in several countries to call for a tougher approach.
Several member states have noted that the EU Migration Pact, which entered into force in June, has helped reduce the number of arrivals but lacks sufficient tools to respond to large-scale emergencies—even though the pact does include mechanisms for such situations.

UK diesel price hits record high of £2 a litre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:20:26 UTC
19:20:26 KST

British motorists face more pressure at the pumps after the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre.
The price of a litre at UK forecourts has risen 40.5% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.
The RAC motoring group said on Friday that the average price had reached 200.01p a litre, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.
Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”
The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.
Petrol prices are also continuing to rise, with a litre of unleaded costing 174.1p on average, a 31.5% increase since 28 February, taking the cost of a typical tank to £96, just over £23 more than before the US-Iran conflict.
Earlier on Friday the transport minister Keir Mather sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting the UK was not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The Trump administration has told Germany and France to release their diesel stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.
On Thursday, the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency supplies, and Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said on Friday that Europe was discussing the diesel reserves issue with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the US.
In a video conference with G7 leaders, chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, attenders discussed a proposal from the French government that European nations release 50m barrels of diesel from reserve supplies, and for members of the IEA to release 50m barrels of crude oil, Reuters reported.
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Motorists and small businesses have been struggling with the increasing cost of filling up.
Williams added: “This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders.
“In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”
Capital Economics estimated that a ban on US exports of diesel could raise UK diesel prices from £2 a litre to £3 a litre and push inflation up to 5%, from 3.1% in August.
The fresh high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures.
Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia.
Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait.
Trump has pushed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to cease Kyiv’s drone and missile attacks on Russian refineries so they can help to relieve the global fuel squeeze.
The Middle East war has also pushed up household energy bills. This week the quarterly price cap rose by 4%, meaning a typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year. The cap is forecast to increase by a further 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.
Reports of talks among European nations to potentially release diesel and oil reserves fuelled a 2.5% fall in the price of Brent crude to $99.78 a barrel.
“This highlights that the main stress in the energy market is no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering,” said Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. “But rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia.”

Could the future of AI data centres be in space? Google wants to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:19:48 UTC
19:19:48 KST

The tech giant has launched a prototype satellite carrying its AI chips to explore whether solar powered infrastructure in orbit could one day support large-scale computing.
Google launched a prototype satellite into orbit loaded with its AI chips on Thursday as part of the first phase of a project to explore if space could be the best place for powering large-scale AI infrastructure.
The satellite, built by Planet Labs and launched on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare, is loaded with Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to see how they perform in space and deal with the physical stress of spaceflight, radiation and extreme temperature conditions.
The thinking behind the initiative, aptly named 'Project Suncatcher', is to place satellites in low-earth orbit where they can benefit from near-constant sunlight to capture up to eight times more solar energy than on Earth.
Google wants to see if large-scale machine-learning infrastructure can survive in space and benefit from abundant solar energy.
The amount of energy data centres consume is growing rapidly, driven in no small part by the massive surge in artificial intelligence workloads. Globally, data centres consumed an estimated 415 to 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) last year.
This accounts for 1.5% to 2.5% of the world’s total electricity generation, according to the European Commission, a figure that is set to double by 2030.
Many data centre projects around the world are facing growing public opposition amid concerns that they drive up energy bills; therefore, building data centres in space far away from the general public is an appealing prospect.
Google is not the only company exploring the possibility of sending AI into space. Nvidia-backed startup Starcloud trained an artificial intelligence model from space for the first time last December.
In June, Elon Musk unveiled SpaceX's AI1 satellite, also known as Starmind, a new satellite class designed as a flying GPU (graphics processing unit) cluster rather than a communications relay.
And in September, Mistral announced a partnership with Marlan Space and Loft Orbital to develop artificial intelligence satellite infrastructure, with the first satellite launch this October.
What is Google testing?
The launch marked the first phase of Google's test with a 10-minute climb into low Earth orbit. The spacecraft endured intense vibrations and sustained acceleration of up to 10 times the force of gravity, while the TPU chips on board were hit by brief shocks of between 50 and 100g.
In anticipation of these hardy conditions, the Suncatcher team carried out vibration testing on the satellite to mimic a rocket launch, with the craft and TPU chips passing test.
Now that Google has safely launched the TPU chips into orbit, the next phase of the experiment begins as the team assesses how the TPU chips deal with the higher levels of radiation outside the Earth's atmosphere, as well as solar events and cosmic rays, which can also disrupt electrical systems.
Data centres infamously require an inordinate amount of energy and water resources, but in the vacuum of space this is a different problem entirely. The mission will be an opportunity for the research team to test a number of different solutions, including a combination of heat pipes and radiators to cool the chips.
In future Suncatcher missions, satellites carrying dozens of TPU chips will be tested with the aim of moving from the current approach of low bandwidth across large distances to high bandwidth over extremely short distances to maintain connectivity.
The technology already exists in space. However, Google will test ways of maintaining a high bandwidth connectivity over shorter distances with greater accuracy when it launches further satellites next year.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Giant Samara Oil Hub—Fire Erupts at Europe’s Largest Tank Farm
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil-industry facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 2, as explosions were followed by a fire at what open-source analysts believe was the massive Samara oil pumping and dispatch complex.
Russian outlet ASTRA, after analyzing eyewitness imagery, reported that the blaze likely broke out at the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station, or LPDS Samara.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents across the region reported drones overhead during the night, while a missile alert was declared in the city of Samara at 5:51 am. A particularly powerful explosion was reported at around 6:30 am.
Authorities did not publicly confirm the weapons used in the operation or the immediate cause of the fire.
Reports also tracked a drone flying toward Chapayevsk, roughly 55 kilometers west of the Samara oil facility.
Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+ separately reported a fire at LPDS Samara and published coordinates pointing to the site.
Russian local authorities did not acknowledge damage to the oil complex. Samara’s mayor said only that the city’s ground-based public transportation had been temporarily suspended.
LPDS Samara is part of Russia’s Transneft pipeline network and functions as a major storage, pumping, and crude-blending hub.
The complex covers more than 216 hectares and includes 71 oil storage tanks with a combined capacity exceeding 1.6 million cubic meters. Russian reporting has described the site as the largest oil tank farm in Europe.
The facility also incorporates the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations and a separate crude-blending station.
Four major trunk pipelines converge at the hub, carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan before it moves farther through Russia’s pipeline system.
Previously, Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Krasnodar region, sparking a significant fire at a fuel storage facility operated by wholesale trader Edelweiss-95.

Taiwan's Chen Nien-chin wins Asian Games silver in women's boxing
Unknown

2026-10-02
10:18:01 UTC
19:18:01 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese boxer Chen Nien-chin (陳念琴) won silver in the women's 65-kilogram division at the Asian Games on Friday, losing to India's Parveen Hooda by a 2-3 split decision in the gold-medal bout.
Chen battled back from a first-round deficit to level the fight in the second round, but three of the five judges scored the decisive third round for Hooda, per ETtoday. The silver medal marks the best Asian Games result of Chen's career.
Chen advanced to the final after defeating Thailand's Suwannapheng 5-0 in the quarterfinals to secure a medal. She then edged North Korea's Hwang Hyo-sun 3-2 in a split decision in the semifinals, reaching an Asian Games final for the first time.
Under the 10-point system, each of the five judges scores every round independently, typically awarding 10 points to the winner and nine to the loser. Each judge totals the points across all three rounds to determine the winner on their scorecard.
In the opening round, all five judges scored Hooda 10-9, leaving Chen trailing 0-5 on the scorecards, ETtoday reported. Chen responded in the second round, with all five judges awarding her a 10-9 win to level the fight at 19-19 on every scorecard.
The gold medal came down to the final three minutes, with the five judges split on the decisive round. Two scored it 10-9 for Chen, while the other three gave Hooda the same margin, resulting in a 3-2 split decision in the Indian boxer's favor.
Chen finished with a 29-28 advantage on two scorecards but trailed 28-29 on the other three, according to ETtoday. The decision gave Hooda the gold and Chen the silver, one judge's vote short of her first Asian Games title.

Flydubai hijacking: Israel is a nation of heroes - time for the gov't to show courage too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:56 UTC
19:17:56 KST

Israelis are a nation of heroes. That might sound like a slogan, but every so often something happens that reminds us how true this is.
Of all the extraordinary stories to emerge from Wednesday’s flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the one that stands out is the courage of the passengers who realized something had gone terribly wrong, forced their way into the cockpit, and helped subdue the co-pilot, who had allegedly stabbed the captain and appeared to be trying to bring down the plane.
The aircraft plunged thousands of feet; there was chaos onboard, and the passengers had no way of knowing exactly what was happening or whether they had minutes, seconds, or no time at all.
And they acted. They didn’t wait for someone to rescue them or see if everything would resolve itself on its own. They took the initiative and saved lives: not only of the passengers on board, but whatever else the plane could have taken down with it.
When we remember aircraft that have been hijacked or crashed over the years, it is difficult not to appreciate what happened aboard this flight and how there is something deeply Israeli about it.
It is part of this country’s culture: not to stand by and watch events unfold, but to run headfirst into the fire, battle, or the storm and do whatever can be done to save lives.
We have now heard some testimony from passengers aboard the flight. It is frightening and disturbing, particularly as investigators are still trying to understand what exactly happened and what the co-pilot’s motive was. But there is also something heartwarming in hearing how people responded in those terrifying moments.
They literally took charge, and, when we think about it, it is a characteristic we know all too well. Next week, Israel will mark three years since October 7. That terrible day will be seared into our collective memory as one of the greatest failures and tragedies in Israeli history. But, like with the airplane, it too was filled with stories of some of the greatest courage this country has ever seen.
There are many different kinds of heroism, and there is no need to rank them.
But it is impossible to forget the people who woke up that morning, heard that something incomprehensible was happening in the south, understood that people were in desperate need of help, and got into their cars. They took whatever weapons they had, if they had any, and drove straight into the battle.
They did not know what they would find. They did not know how many terrorists had crossed the border, where the army was, or whether they themselves would make it home. They just went.
That, to a large extent, is the story of Israel: a small country whose people are repeatedly confronted with danger and who, when the moment comes, stand up, fight and lead the charge.
A nation prepared to fight
It is worth thinking about that now, just weeks before Israelis go to the polls on October 27.
This election will help determine the direction Israel takes after three extraordinarily difficult years. And whichever government ultimately emerges, it will inherit a country confronting a series of strategic challenges, almost none of which have truly been resolved.
Hamas still controls part of Gaza and retains weapons and military infrastructure. Hezbollah remains a threat to Israel’s north. And Iran remains locked in confrontation over its nuclear program and its wider regional capabilities.
It is true that three years after October 7, Israel has achieved amazing accomplishments, but victory, as we know too well by now, is not measured only by what an army destroys – it is also measured by what a country builds in its place.
And that is where a striking discrepancy has emerged.
Israel’s leaders have been given an extraordinary gift: a population willing to fight, to endure difficult years, and send its children to war knowing the risks and knowing, painfully, that some will not return.
Consider the family of Israel’s ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter. His son Neria was seriously wounded last week in a ramming attack on Route 443 while serving in the reserves. His brother, Moshe, was killed fighting in Gaza in 2023.
Neria had every reason not to continue serving: his brother had been killed, and his family had already sacrificed enough. He could have remained home with his wife and children. He could have spared his parents the anguish of once again worrying about a son fighting on the front.
But he did not. He continued putting on his uniform. He continued reporting for reserve duty. And he continued serving.
Without people like that, Israel would not survive. But courage cannot only be demanded of soldiers and civilians; it must be demanded of politicians as well.
Political courage is different. It is not about charging a cockpit or running toward gunfire. It is about making difficult decisions, accepting risk, challenging traditional assumptions and, most importantly, telling the public where you actually want to take the country.
That is the question Israelis should be asking as they prepare to vote: What is the vision?
Is the future being offered to us simply one of hunkering down, a kind of super-Sparta, stronger and better armed than everyone around us but condemned to fight one war after another?
Or is there another possibility, one that recognizes the threats Israel faces, takes them seriously, and preserves overwhelming military strength, but also searches for a path toward greater security, stability, and eventually something else?
Israel looking for brave leaders
Last week in New York, for example, the US-backed Board of Peace unveiled an ambitious plan for Gaza. Senior officials acknowledged the enormous obstacles standing in the way, including the unresolved dispute over how Hamas will disarm and how Israel will withdraw.
Considering everything that would have to happen for this plan to succeed, skepticism is more than understandable. Is it ambitious and hard to imagine? 100%.
Three years after October 7, with the situation in Gaza still dire – both for its residents and for Israel’s security – this is a thoughtful plan that offers a real chance to change reality on the ground. Considering all the alternatives, isn’t it worth a shot?
But here is the catch: Israelis were not even in the room.
That is what this election campaign should be about. Instead, too much of Israeli politics remains focused on what candidates are against. This person will sit with that party; that person cannot be trusted; this bloc is dangerous, and that bloc is illegitimate.
But what are these politicians for? Where do they want Israel to be in five years?
What is their plan for Gaza? For Lebanon? For the Palestinians? For Israel’s increasingly strained relationship with parts of the Western world? What does victory realistically look like?
Israelis have demonstrated time and again that they are prepared to take extraordinary risks for this country.
The people who stormed the cockpit this week did not wait to be asked. Neither did the Israelis who drove south on October 7. They saw danger. They understood that someone had to act. And despite having no guarantee of what would happen next, they moved forward.
Israel’s political leaders do not need to storm a cockpit. But they do need to show some of the same courage. Instead of spending the next few weeks telling Israelis what they will never do, whom they will never sit with, and why everyone else is dangerous, they should tell us where they want to take this country.
The Israeli people have already shown that they are prepared to be brave. Now they deserve leaders brave enough to offer them a future.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

====================================================================================================

Flydubai saga captures Israel’s role in a new Middle East - and its old limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:36 UTC
19:17:36 KST

Wednesday’s flydubai saga crammed the new Middle East into a single aircraft.
An Emirati airline carrying Israelis made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia amid war with Iran – and the incident was immediately drawn into an Israeli election campaign dominated by the question of who can keep the country safe.
Talk about one event bringing everything together.
But beyond the frightening drama aboard the plane, the incident also brought something else into focus: how much the region has changed, and where the limits of that change still lie.
Israelis were flying home on an Emirati airline. When their flight turned into a nightmare, they landed in Saudi Arabia, received medical attention and assistance, and were eventually collected by another Emirati aircraft and brought to Israel.
For all the tensions, wars, and political sensitivities, that sequence is worth noting. The absence of Saudi-Israeli diplomatic relations did not prevent the passengers from receiving help or getting home.
Granted, the Saudis refused to let an Israeli aircraft collect them. That matters and is maddening, especially considering the security and intelligence cooperation that does exist between the two countries. But it need not obscure what they did allow, or turn a story of regional cooperation into a tale primarily about rejection.
The new Middle East is imperfect. Wednesday showed, however, that it is also real.
A changing Middle East takes shape
TO APPRECIATE the broader picture, connect the dots from earlier in the week.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, known as MBZ.
According to reports, Netanyahu shared intelligence about Iran’s continued nuclear ambitions, including new construction at the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site, as well as developments involving the Houthis in the Red Sea.
These are issues on which Israel and the Gulf states have overlapping interests. An Iran rebuilding its nuclear capabilities concerns more than Jerusalem. So do the Houthis threatening Red Sea shipping.
But Netanyahu reportedly brought another concern to the meeting, one rooted in Israel’s election campaign.
AP reported that he asked MBZ to deny the Haaretz account that the Emirati leader had warned him about a looming Hamas threat before October 7.
This report has since mushroomed into several accounts of warnings that Netanyahu allegedly received but did not act on before October 7. And all of this has figured prominently in opposition party attacks on him during the campaign. Netanyahu’s office has denied he received any such warning.
The visit thus carried two possible purposes: discussing threats facing the region now and addressing allegations about what Netanyahu knew back then.
That combination is characteristic of this election campaign. Netanyahu wants the public to focus on what he has done to reshape the region since October 7. His opponents want it to focus on what he failed to prevent on that Simchat Torah morning.
A meeting with an important Arab leader can serve the first argument. Reports that the same leader warned him before the attack feed the second.
The UAE confirmed that Sunday’s meeting took place, unlike in May, when it denied Netanyahu’s claim of an earlier visit. That acknowledgment gave him something to point to: evidence that, despite the wars and international criticism, he could still meet a key Arab leader.
The UAE did not, however, deny that a pre-October 7 call had taken place. Netanyahu came away, therefore, with the proverbial half a loaf: confirmation of Sunday’s meeting, but no denial of the earlier warning.
There were also reports that representatives of other Arab countries attended discussions in Abu Dhabi, including Saudi representatives, though the Saudis denied it.
Then, on Tuesday, MBZ’s brother, UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed, traveled to Riyadh and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman.
With the Houthis again threatening Saudi interests, the two Gulf powers had reason to repair ties ruptured by their competing policies in Yemen.
Might the timing – two days after Netanyahu’s meeting with MBZ – have been a coincidence?
It might. But it also might not.
The sequence raises the possibility of wider coordination against threats that concern Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE alike. It does not, however, establish that Netanyahu brokered the Saudi-Emirati rapprochement, or that all three countries agreed on a common policy.
There is enough here to connect some dots. There is not enough to color in the entire picture.
Still, the meetings suggest a region in which governments have reasons to work through their differences because the threats facing them are greater than those differences.
THEN THE flydubai flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai for Tel Aviv.
That flight is the stuff of movies: one pilot stabs another and tries to crash the aircraft before passengers, along with a crew member, intervene and save the day. The plane makes an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Passengers later describe receiving medical attention and assistance there.
For those aboard, this was a terrifying brush with catastrophe. Their survival owed much to the people who intervened and helped bring the aircraft down safely.
What happened next carried its own regional significance: a plane carrying Israelis lands in Saudi Arabia, its passengers receive help, and the UAE sends another aircraft to bring them home.
Each part of that sequence may seem practical and unremarkable on its own. Taken together, however, they describe a regional reality that Israelis should not take for granted.
And that is precisely one of the main achievements of the Abraham Accords: making previously extraordinary things – like a flight from the East on an Arab airline over Saudi Arabia – ordinary.
That does not make Saudi Arabia a party to the Abraham Accords. But it does show that the relationships created by the accords can function in a wider regional setting, even where formal diplomatic ties are absent.
The Saudis nevertheless drew a line, rejecting Israel’s request to send a plane to collect the passengers. Another flydubai plane eventually brought them back home.
That refusal understandably irked Israelis who felt that, after what the passengers had endured, getting them home on an Israeli plane so they felt safe should have overridden political considerations.
Tellingly, Netanyahu chose to stress the Saudi willingness to receive the plane and the hospitality shown to its passengers.
Just a week ago at the UN, he chose to call out by name the leaders of France and Turkey whose words and actions harm the Jewish State, proving he is not shy about doing so when he deems it necessary or politically expedient. He didn’t do so with Saudi Arabia.
There was a practical reason for that restraint: publicly berating the Saudis would hardly strengthen the cooperation that already exists and benefits both sides.
There was also a political reason: Netanyahu has an interest in presenting the region as one in which Israel’s relationships have expanded, even if full normalization with Riyadh remains elusive.
In this case, emphasizing the cooperation also reflected an important part of what happened. The assistance the Saudis did provide showed that the lack of diplomatic relations need not prevent practical help.
But the Saudi refusal to allow Israel to send a plane to retrieve the passengers showed how carefully Riyadh guards the boundary between basic humanitarian help – allowing the plane to land – and a visible gesture toward Israel.
Perhaps the approaching election made the Saudis especially reluctant to allow a scene that Netanyahu could then use in his campaign. An Israeli aircraft retrieving passengers from Saudi soil would have made a striking picture.
It would be a stretch, however, to assume that everything becomes easier after October 27. Saudi reservations about public normalization extend far beyond a reluctance to give Netanyahu a campaign gift.
The limits of regional normalization
THE ATTEMPTED hijacking has also been framed as a test of Israel-UAE ties and the staying power of the Abraham Accords.
That is understandable since the Tel Aviv-Dubai air routes are the accords’ most visible, tangible benefits for the average Israeli. A terrifying incident can shake public confidence in flying that route, and passengers will now understandably want to know what is being done to prevent a recurrence.
But the Israel-UAE relationship will certainly withstand this shock. A relationship that has endured October 7 and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran rests on interests that one attempted hijacking will not shake. If anything, the incident shows the threats both countries face, why they need each other, and how they can help one another.
The regional lesson is broader.
The Saudi refusal showed that significant political barriers to normalization remain, and that Riyadh still insists on keeping its relationship with Israel in the back room rather than bringing it into the front room.
The passengers’ safe return showed, however, that even a relationship confined to the back room can produce practical cooperation when it matters.
The Abraham Accords did not produce a Middle East free of hostility, danger, or diplomatic sensitivities. They did, however, help create a region where Israelis forced to land in an Arab country can receive assistance rather than face unbridled hostility.
Wednesday was a nightmare for the passengers and their families. For the region, however, the response offered something encouraging: evidence that the relationships built up in recent years can deliver practical help when it is needed most.

Taiwan, US organize disaster management forum in New Zealand

2026-10-02
10:17:32 UTC
19:17:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan and the US co-sponsored a Global Cooperation and Training Framework workshop about disaster management in the Pacific in New Zealand, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Friday.
The Sept. 29-30 event in Auckland marked the first time Taiwan and the US cooperated on a workshop in New Zealand. They invited member nations of the Pacific Islands Forum, government officials, and disaster response experts.
In her opening speech, Taiwan envoy in New Zealand Joanne Ou (歐江安) said it was important to learn from past experiences to prepare for natural disasters. The practice will not only reduce the impact of a new disaster, but also help speed up the recovery.
As a frequent victim of earthquakes, typhoons, and flooding, Taiwan is interested in sharing its practical disaster prevention experiences with Pacific island nations, Ou said.
US Charge d’affaires Gabrielle Cowan described the Pacific as one of the regions in the world most likely to suffer major disasters. Regional disaster resilience is the result of generations of communities responding to threats and rebuilding after disasters, she said. Cowan named Taiwan as a model for disaster prediction and public participation in disaster prevention.
The ministry said the workshop deepened international partnerships through the exchange of views and the practical use of resources. The experience helped strengthen the potential of the attending countries to prevent and respond to disasters in the Pacific region.

Taiwan government warns of ‘new method’ of transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:24 UTC
19:17:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Mainland Affairs Council said Thursday that a campaign impersonating a Taiwanese distributor of a documentary on forced organ harvesting in China could represent a “new method” of transnational repression.
Since last year, impersonators of Kuan Chien-chung (管建忠) have made threats to an attorney and two organizations, and authorities have brought him in for questioning for each case, said spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) at a press conference.
Every time a victim reported their case, Kuan had to make a statement to the police, Liang said. “The goal is to have him run around exhausted.”
Kuan heads the Taiwanese distributor that brought the Canadian documentary “State Organs” to Taiwan in 2024. Directed by Raymond Zhang, the film examines allegations of state-sanctioned organ harvesting in China targeting Falun Gong followers.
Liang said Kuan has reported the impersonation incidents to police. The council has also worked with the National Police Agency and Ministry of Justice to consolidate the incidents into a single case, which remains under investigation.
The impersonation campaign followed a series of threats against theaters that screened the film.
In late 2024, as “State Organs” was screened nationwide, several theaters received threats, including bomb threats and warnings that their computer systems would be hacked if they did not stop the screening.

First expedition vessel 'stitched' for Northern Maritime Museum in Arkhangelsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:23 UTC
19:17:23 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 2. /TASS/. The first expedition vessel was 'stitched' using traditional technology for the Northern Maritime Museum in Arkhangelsk, the museum told TASS. The vessel will not be an exhibition object. It will be a boat for voyages.
"The Solombala boat, which is traditional for Arkhangelsk, is not a museum exhibit, it is a real boat built specifically for our museum, it is the first expedition vessel in our history," the museum said. "The boat was "stitched" by boat master Mikhail Tsarev in Maymaks at his home shipyard, commissioned by a philanthropist who wished to remain anonymous, and the boat was donated to our museum."
Solombala is a symbol of Arkhangelsk of the 20th century. The boat carries the name of the Solombala historical island, where Peter the Great founded the country's first shipyard.
The newly-made vessel was named the Soyga after a river in the Arkhangelsk Region's Verkhnetoyemsky District. The river is a tributary of the Northern Dvina River. First voyages are planned for the spring and summer of 2027. Presently, the boat is installed in front of the museum entrance on the Northern Dvina embankment.
The Solombala boats with recognizable rounded hull contours and plywood cabins appeared in Arkhangelsk in the late 1950s. They were known as Solombala leisure boats. The boat was 6.22 m long, the width was 1.65 m, the hull was made of pine planks, the frames were made of oak, and the cabin - of plywood. The speed was about 15 km/h, the boat could carry up to 6-8 passengers. The Solombala Shipyard designed the project based on the development by Mikhail Kuroptev, the shipyard's master. The boat used to be equipped with an SM3-12hp diesel engine, popularly called as "top-foot." A stove for heating was normally installed in the cabin.
The Solombala boats were top popular in the 1960s - 1980s. Despite the good capacity, the carrying capacity and the ease of handling, the wooden vessel required constant maintenance. Therefore, by the beginning of the 21st century, wooden Solombala boats became exotic giving way to light and easily-maintained plastic and metal hulls.
The fresh interest in the Solombala boats emerged after the Pomor Shipbuilding Association's shipyard back in 2021 discovered, digitized and published on the web drawings of the Solombala Shipyard's vessels, including those of the Solombala boat.

How can Jordan respond to Israel’s escalation across the West Bank?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:23 UTC
19:17:23 KST

How can Jordan respond to Israel’s escalation across the West Bank?
Settlement expansion, displacement and growing Israeli control would have direct consequences for Jordan.
It is increasingly difficult to regard what is happening in the West Bank as merely a series of measures that the Israeli government justifies on security grounds or as part of counterterrorism operations. Taken together, the cumulative pattern and expanding scope of these measures point to a broader political and territorial trajectory: one aimed at reshaping the West Bank, imposing new facts on the ground, entrenching Israeli control and advancing the de facto annexation of large parts of the territory while simultaneously subjecting Palestinians to mounting pressure that, directly or indirectly, pushes them from their land.
Israeli, journalistic and research reports have documented the intensification of this trajectory through settlement expansion, land confiscation, restrictions on Palestinian movement, control over water resources and grazing areas as well as military operations and repeated internal displacement in several parts of the West Bank.
Considered individually, each of these measures may appear to be a separate issue. Viewed together, however, they reveal a more consequential development: an effort to re-engineer the geography and demography of the West Bank in ways that undermine the prospect of establishing a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.
The question, therefore, is no longer simply what is happening in the West Bank.
The more urgent question is how can Jordan, the Palestinians, the Arab world and the international community prevent this trajectory from becoming a permanent reality.
Jordan Valley at the heart of the equation
The Jordan Valley assumes exceptional importance in this context, not only because of its geographical and security significance but also because of its agricultural and economic importance and its water resources for the Palestinian people.
Reports concerning the construction of a new Israeli barrier, referred to as the “Crimson Thread”, extending roughly 480km (300 miles) from the Golan Heights to the Red Sea, warrant serious Jordanian, Arab and international scrutiny, particularly if such a project is intended to isolate the Jordan Valley and place as much as 83 percent of its total area under Israeli control.
Such a development could in effect sever the West Bank from Jordan and deprive Palestinians of one of their most important agricultural and water resources.
Borders, walls, roads and settlements cease to be merely physical infrastructure when they are combined with control over land and water. They become instruments for reshaping political and demographic geography and weakening the ability of Palestinians to remain on their land.
This is precisely where the Palestinian issue intersects directly with Jordan’s national security.
Jordan faces a different phase
Jordan cannot treat developments in the West Bank as an exclusively Palestinian matter. At its core, this is an issue of Jordanian national security, regional stability and the future of the Palestinian cause.
Any fundamental change to the geographical or demographic reality of the West Bank will inevitably carry direct consequences for Jordan because of geography, history and proximity. And if the eventual outcome is forced displacement, then, as King Abdullah II has repeatedly made clear, such a scenario would amount to a declaration of war on Jordan.
The policy required of Jordan at this stage, therefore, must be proactive: one that anticipates possible scenarios and prepares for them politically, diplomatically, economically and in security terms.
First: Protect Jordanian national unity
Jordan’s first line of defence is its national unity.
At this stage, it is essential to strengthen the concepts of citizenship and the state, consolidate full equality among Jordanians, and reject any discourse or practice that creates divisions on the basis of origin, region or roots.
The Palestinian cause must remain a national, Arab and humanitarian cause. It must not be allowed to become a source of division within Jordanian society.
Responsibility falls on both the state and society to confront hate speech and incitement, apply the law equally and fairly, and protect the national fabric from attempts to exploit regional turmoil to sow division among Jordanians.
One of the gravest outcomes Jordan must prevent is the transfer of the conflict into its own domestic sphere. Relations among Jordanians of different origins, including those of Jordanian and Palestinian heritage, must never become a vulnerable fault line through which those seeking discord, whether from within the country or from abroad, can operate.
National unity, therefore, is not merely a social value. It is an integral component of Jordan’s national security architecture.
Second: Move from diplomacy of protest to diplomacy of pressure and proportionate action
Jordan has accumulated considerable international credibility and diplomatic capital. The present phase, however, requires Jordan to expand the tools at its disposal.
It is no longer sufficient simply to condemn settlement activity, reject annexation or warn against displacement. What is needed is an Arab, Islamic and international diplomatic front capable of translating political positions into practical measures.
In coordination with Palestine and Arab and Islamic states, Jordan should work to:
- Mobilise countries that reject annexation and settlement expansion.
- Support international legal action.
- Push for concrete measures and sanctions not only against settlements but also against state policies that enable and encourage them.
- Systematically document violations.
- Use Arab political and economic relations with influential states more strategically, expanding economic cooperation with countries that adopt firm positions against the Israeli occupation while recalibrating engagement with those that remain reluctant to take clear positions towards Israeli policies.
- Build an international coalition capable of preventing the imposition of irreversible facts by force.
A comparison with Russia’s war in Ukraine is instructive. When Russia occupied large areas of Ukrainian territory, sanctions were not confined to the territories under occupation; they were imposed on Russia itself. The question, therefore, is why a different standard should apply elsewhere.
The international community does not lack resolutions or statements. What it lacks is the conversion of political will into a tangible cost for those who violate international law.
Third: Establish an Arab and Islamic fund for Palestinian resilience
If the objective is to prevent displacement and enable Palestinians to remain on their land, financial support must become a sustained strategic policy rather than seasonal assistance tied to moments of crisis.
One option would be to establish an Arab, Islamic and international fund dedicated to strengthening Palestinian resilience with a mandate to finance specific projects in the West Bank and Gaza, including:
- Protecting land threatened with confiscation.
- Supporting farmers.
- Developing water resources and irrigation networks.
- Assisting affected families.
- Financing housing projects in vulnerable areas.
- Supporting education and health services.
- Assisting municipalities and local councils.
- Providing alternative sources of income to families who have lost employment as a result of Israeli measures.
Resilience is not merely a political slogan. It is a material reality.
Every Palestinian family who remains on its land, every farmer who continues to cultivate his fields and every village that retains access to its water resources represents part of the effort to prevent displacement.
Fourth: Treat the Jordan Valley as a Jordanian national security issue
Jordan should address developments in the Jordan Valley as a permanent strategic file.
A specialised Jordanian mechanism should be established to monitor:
- Settlement expansion.
- Land confiscation.
- The construction of roads, barriers and walls.
- Demographic changes.
- Control over water resources.
- Population movements and displacement.
- Any measures that could permanently alter the status quo.
These developments should be documented through maps, satellite imagery, statistics and official records so Jordan maintains a comprehensive dossier that can be used politically and legally before the international community.
Struggles over land are not determined by force alone. They are also shaped by documentation, maps, law and the ability to present an authoritative, evidence-based account of what is happening.
Fifth: Strengthen Jordan’s national defence architecture
Strengthening Jordan’s ability to protect its security, borders and national interests is not optional.
Jordan is a country with limited resources, but it possesses significant human and institutional expertise. It can further develop an advanced national defence, civil protection and crisis-management architecture.
This could include strengthening national service and training programmes, enhancing civil defence preparedness, protecting critical infrastructure, reinforcing cybersecurity and border security, and improving disaster and emergency management.
Jordan could also draw on the extensive experience of retired military personnel through structured national programmes under the supervision of appropriate state institutions, thereby strengthening the country’s overall defensive readiness.
The strength Jordan requires is the strength of deterrence, protection and preparedness, not an impulse towards an ill-considered confrontation.
Sixth: Prevent Jordan from becoming an “alternative homeland”
This issue must remain at the centre of Jordanian strategic calculations.
Any project that directly or indirectly leads to the depopulation of the West Bank or pushes large numbers of Palestinians towards Jordan is not merely a humanitarian question. It would carry profound political, security and demographic consequences for the kingdom.
Jordan’s position, therefore, must remain unequivocal: Resolving the Palestinian question cannot come at Jordan’s expense; displacement is not a political solution; and Jordan is not an alternative homeland for the Palestinian people.
At the same time, Jordan must preserve the humanitarian and legal dimensions of its response to any forced developments, so that opposition to displacement does not translate into further suffering for civilians.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Military court centres court listings
Court listings for the military court centres.
Documents
Details
In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.
Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.
In addition to this, the court listings are published using digital signage technology within the reception areas of both military court centres.
Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

Here's How Russia Plans to Pay for the Ukraine War in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Russia plans to raise defense spending to a post-Soviet high next year while cutting civilian programs and increasing taxes, signaling that the Kremlin is bracing for a prolonged war in Ukraine despite saying it is ready for peace talks.
The draft 2027 budget unveiled Thursday allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.2 billion) to defense, 26% more than was earmarked for that year in the previous budget and 375% above the pre-war level of 2021.
Defense would account for roughly a third of federal spending next year, setting a post-Soviet record in nominal ruble terms.
Analysts say that Russia still has the resources to keep fighting, but that households, businesses and public services will bear more of the cost.
Economist Boris Grozovsky said Russia’s wartime economy still has a “considerable” financial cushion.
“But the message is clear: everyone will pay for the war, as much as they can. Wherever a little more money appears, the government will come for it, while handing out as little as possible itself,” he wrote in an analysis published by the exiled outlet IStories.
The published defense allocation does not capture the full cost of the war. Russia has released only planned military spending rather than actual outlays since 2022, while classified budget items make the overall bill difficult to establish.
Soaring war costs have put increasing pressure on state finances. The federal budget deficit reached 5.65 trillion rubles ($67.8 billion), or 2.6% of gross domestic product, in 2025.
The government projects a shortfall of 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.6 billion), or 3.2% of GDP, for 2026 before it narrows to 5.4 trillion rubles ($64.8 billion), or 2.2%, in 2027.
In a forecast published before the draft budget was unveiled, economists at Russia’s largest lender Sberbank put next year’s deficit at 2.7% of GDP, questioning whether the government could deliver the spending restraint and higher non-oil and gas revenues needed to meet its earlier target.
This deficit is high by recent Russian standards, but it is still manageable and remains lower than in many European countries, such as France (5.4% of GDP) and Britain (4.3% of GDP).
The projected deficit does not in itself point to an imminent fiscal crisis, but containing it while increasing military spending is becoming more difficult.
The government plans to borrow 6.1 trillion rubles ($73.2 billion) next year, up from 5 trillion rubles ($60 billion) in 2026, to help finance the deficit.
Yet debt servicing is projected to reach 4.6 trillion rubles ($55.2 billion) in 2027, or 9.4% of total federal spending. Those costs remain high because the Central Bank has kept interest rates elevated to contain stubborn inflation that has been fueled by heavy government spending.
To help close the gap, Moscow is also cutting civilian spending and planning another round of tax increases for a third consecutive year.
The draft reduces allocations for healthcare by 5.5%, education by 5.4% and social programs by 6% compared with the amounts previously budgeted for 2027.
Some of Russia's national projects, government programs targeting priorities like healthcare and infrastructure, will also face cuts going forward.
Funding for the Long and Active Life project, which supports health initiatives, would fall by about 20%, from 181.1 billion rubles ($2.17 billion) in 2026 to 145.9 billion rubles ($1.75 billion) next year.
The allocation for the federal cancer program would drop from 44.9 billion rubles ($538.8 million) to 3.9 billion rubles ($46.8 million).
The proposed tax measures are expected to raise an additional 1.5 trillion rubles ($18 billion).
They include a 22% value-added tax on purchases from foreign online retailers and a customs fee of 100 rubles, or about $1.20, on each parcel worth less than 200 euros.
Tax rates on income from sources including deposit interest, dividends and property sales would rise from a range of 13% to 15% to a range of 13% to 22%. The Finance Ministry has also proposed a one-time windfall tax on mining and metals companies.
The changes to taxes on passive income are expected to raise the most revenue, up to 700 billion rubles ($8.4 billion), followed by levies on online purchases, which would bring in another 500 billion rubles ($6 billion).
Analyst Alexandra Prokopenko said the budget showed defense spending growing faster than overall expenditure, squeezing the funds available for other purposes.
In an analysis for Carnegie Politika, she warned that the government may soon be approaching the limits of how much additional revenue it can raise through taxes to fund the war.
That could increase pressure on the Central Bank to support the wartime economy by cutting interest rates to reduce borrowing costs for the government and businesses, as well as increase debt restructuring for struggling companies, she said.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000, government data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000, government data shows
- Congo's Ebola outbreak has caused over 4,000 deaths and 8,300 confirmed cases, making it the deadliest in the country's history and second largest globally.
- The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola strain, continues to spread rapidly in eastern Congo and has reached seven provinces.
- There are signs of slowing transmission in some areas, but the virus recently appeared in South Ubangi province after a traveller died, showing ongoing risks.
AI generated
DAKAR, Senegal – The number of deaths in Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has surpassed 4,000, government data showed on Oct 2, as the worst epidemic in the country’s history resists containment efforts.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in Congo after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now second only to the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Government figures showed on Oct 1 that the death toll had risen to 4,018, and confirmed cases had reached 8,300 across seven provinces.
Over 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease.
Congo’s government and the UN said in September there were signs that transmission was slowing in some parts of Ituri province, where the outbreak began. But it continues to spread fast across eastern Congo, including in neighbouring North Kivu.
South Ubangi province, located in the northwest of the country, became the seventh province to declare the outbreak in September after a man who had travelled from eastern Congo died of the virus. REUTERS

“We always consider every lead, starting with aliens,” spokesman Andrei Litovka told reporters late on Thursday.
Originally built in the late 18th century and redesigned in 1880 with Italian Renaissance-style facades, the protected heritage building had been scheduled for a major overhaul.
Earlier this year, a local developer secured a 768 million ruble ($9.2 million) loan to restore the site and convert it into a luxury residential development. The project was due to be completed in 2027.

Nike shares dropped Friday, falling for a second straight day after the company reported declining revenue and plans to lay off staff in 2027.
The sportswear giant said Thursday that its fiscal first-quarter revenues were down 4% to $11.2 billion, citing declines in Greater China, which was partially offset by growth in its North America segment. Its net income was $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the previous year.
"We have more work to do in NIKE Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China, and we're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses the right way for the long term," Nike President and CEO Elliott Hill said in the release.
Nike expects revenues to decline in the high-single digits in 2027. Its shares were last down about 6% in morning trading on Friday and have declined nearly 45% since the beginning of the year.
The company also announced its new operating model "Pace," which is expected to deliver $2.5 billion in cost savings by 2031, with plans to lay off more staff starting in 2027.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill said in a separate announcement on Thursday. "Decisions about impacted roles related to this work will begin in calendar year 2027 and beyond."
The program also includes efforts to modernize Nike's global supply chain, organizing into three geographies, establishing a new campus in India, and further streamlining the organization to reduce costs.
'Cost cutting story'
Nike has already carried out layoffs twice since the beginning of the year, including cutting 775 jobs across its U.S. distribution centers in January, and letting go of a further 1,400 employees primarily in its tech division in April.
Citi analysts said in a note Friday that they will remain "neutral" on the company as its sales guidance came in below market expectations.
"Nike is turning into a cost-cutting story, announcing a $2.5bn cost savings program as management is adapting to the reality of significant pressure within Sportswear, Jordan, and China," the Citi analysts said.
They noted that management will offer more detail on its five-year outlook at their investor day, but details around when Pace will actually "move the dial" will only come in 2029.
"It isn't out of the question that Nike can beat some of the guidance they just provided, but there really is no justification (in our view) for Nike to receive a premium multiple versus its growing peers," they added.

EU adds €130 million to drone funding in border security push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:10:44 UTC
19:10:44 KST

The Commission is adding €130 million for drone technology as Brussels steps up border surveillance and prepares to strengthen Frontex’s role.
The EU is putting an additional €130 million into drone technology as part of a broader push to strengthen border security and counter hybrid threats.
The European Commission announced the funding at a meeting of justice and home affairs ministers in Luxembourg – their first in-person talks on migration and border controls since the Ceuta crisis erupted this summer.
"Another important topic today is how we work with new technologies, drones. That is important also for border protection, but also for protecting our critical infrastructure," European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said on Thursday.
In February, the Commission unveiled an action plan on drone and counter-drone security, including a €250 million call for national authorities to invest in land and maritime border surveillance.
The scheme covers up to 90% of project costs, including the purchase of drones and counter-drone systems, their integration into national surveillance networks and other technologies designed to counter hybrid threats.
"Due to the high demand actually and the excellent quality of many proposals in the member states, we will be topping up the initiative with another 130 million," Brunner said.
"I've just visited the counter-drone centre in Munich last week and saw how much progress our authorities throughout the whole Union are making," he added.
Brussels has separately made €170 million available to EU border agency Frontex and national authorities under the Border Management and Visa Instrument to buy uncrewed equipment for border surveillance.
The latest top-up brings EU investment in new border-surveillance technology to more than €500 million, reflecting the growing emphasis on security.
Greece, meanwhile, has proposed temporarily suspending the right to apply for asylum during emergencies involving mass arrivals of irregular migrants. Several member states, including Poland, Germany, Austria and Denmark, back the idea.
Brussels is also expected to strengthen Frontex's role, particularly in crisis management and in monitoring emerging hybrid threats online. The agency's mandate is up for review later this year.
EU leaders are set to discuss the bloc's approach to migration and border management at a European Council summit on 15-16 October.

Russia paid with more than 46,000 casualties, and the front moved the other way, ISW finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:09:54 UTC
19:09:54 KST

Russia lost almost 300 km² of Ukrainian territory on net between March and September 2026, and it likely gained no ground in September despite its heaviest casualties of the year, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi accounts for much of the swing. The think tank notes that Ukraine's secrecy around such counterattacks makes exact monthly tallies hard.
Russia has pressed attacks along the entire front through 2026, accepting mass casualties for marginal ground, and its battlefield year has already been called its worst since 2023. Its losses have been outpacing its recruitment for months.
Russia came out behind in September
Russian forces seized 175.54 km² in September but lost 256.35 km², a net loss of 80.81 km², or minus 2.69 km² a day, ISW calculated. The balance stayed negative when Russian infiltrations into areas Russia does not control are counted: Russia seized or infiltrated 143.2 km² but lost 318.38 km², a net loss of 175.18 km².
The September figures include at least 147 km² near Lyman that Ukraine liberated over earlier months, but that ISW recorded only once details of Operation Vivaldi emerged in September. The operation already disrupted Russia's plan to encircle the Fortress Belt cities from the Lyman and Dobropillia directions.
Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive disrupts Russia’s plan to encircle Donetsk Fortress Belt – ISW
Almost 300 km² lost since March
Russia's rate of seizing territory dropped sharply in March 2026 and has stayed low, or even negative, since, ISW found. After controlling for the gains Ukraine made during Vivaldi, Russia lost control of 293.59 km² net across the front since March. Counting infiltrations, it gained a presence in only 174.44 km² over the same period.
ISW's monthly chart shows net Russian losses of 116.01 km² in April and 281.1 km² in May, modest gains in June, July, and August, and a net loss again in September. Oleksandr Syrskyi, then Ukraine's commander-in-chief, reported in June that Ukrainian forces had recaptured 100 km² in May.
More than 46,000 casualties for no ground
Russian forces suffered 46,230 casualties in September, Ukraine's General Staff reported. It is the third straight month above 40,000 and the highest monthly toll of 2026, by Kyiv's count. Monthly Russian casualties have climbed from 32,980 in April to 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August, ISW's chart shows.
Russia keeps suffering heavy personnel losses while making extremely limited or even net-negative territorial gains, ISW said, and its current force generation system still recruits fewer soldiers than it needs to replace them.
Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says
Ukraine's effective operational security around Vivaldi, likely to continue in future counterattacks, will make meaningful month-to-month assessments of Russian gains and losses hard, the think tank added.
