makelab expands footprint at MADE: bush terminal to unlock tier-one 3D printing
expanding its footprint to brooklyn's made: bush terminal, makelab unlocks the logistics, physical infrastructure, and production capacity needed to serve major tier-one clients.
MAKELAB SCALES INDUSTRIAL FACILITY AT MADE: BUSH TERMINAL
At MADE: Bush Terminal, a reimagined 140,000-square-foot industrial campus on Brooklyn‘s waterfront, on-demand 3D printing studio Makelab has secured a new 3,840-square-foot facility to scale its production capabilities. Key tenants like Makelab are bolstering Sunset Park’s working waterfront as the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) continues to transform the district into a thriving epicenter for industrial design and urban manufacturing. In an exclusive interview with designboom, the Makelab team shares how the new location has transformed their capacity to take on major tier-one clients.
‘Every time you hit a new milestone or a new stage on the growth trajectory, there’s more to figure out. That’s just the nature of manufacturing,’ starts Makelab Co-Founder & CEO Christina Perla. ‘The other day a 53-foot truck came to pick up an order — that could never have happened at our previous location. Limited access restricts the types of companies you can work with, but that truck was sent by our client, a tier-one auto supplier, and it was their only transport option.’
COMBINING INDUSTRIAL DESIGN EXPERTISE WITH 3d printing
When Makelab launched a decade ago, the mainstream design industry treated 3D printing as an effortless alternative to traditional production, a misconception that often led to unprintable screen models and structural failures. As industrial designers, founders Christina Perla and Manny Mota positioned the company not as a push-button vendor, but as an expert partner that grounds ambitious CAD concepts in real-world physics, material properties, and physical usability.
‘Manny and I are industrial designers by trade, so we’re programmed to think about the next step of a part’s lifecycle. When we started almost 10 years ago, 3D printing was painted as this magical thing where if you didn’t know how to make something before, 3D printing could just do it — we were explaining gravity! Walking back from that narrative was a lot of work,’ recalls Perla.
MAKELAB BRINGS TANGIBILITY TO DIGITAL DESIGN PROCESSES
Beside providing the physical infrastructure required to handle complex, high-volume production schedules, the studio’s move to MADE: Bush Terminal reinforces a broader mission: bridging digital workflows with physical manufacturing literacy. Operating within a collaborative waterfront ecosystem, Makelab aims to influence how modern product designers approach fabrication from the very beginning of the creative process.
‘I’ve noticed a shift toward people thinking more about the manufacturing side of product design, which is very smart and much needed. I hope that with the availability of all these tools, designers can better visualize how things actually get made and bring more tangibility to the design process,’ notes Perla.

Egypt expels Ethiopian diplomat in growing rift over GERD: state media
Egypt has declared an Ethiopian diplomat persona non grata and given him 48 hours to leave the country after Addis Ababa expelled an Egyptian diplomat, Egyptian state-linked media said.
The dispute is the latest in a years-long rift between the two countries over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a massive hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile that Egypt sees as a threat to its share of Nile water.
An Egyptian official, quoted by state-linked broadcaster Al-Qahera News late Thursday, described Ethiopia's decision to expel the diplomat as "regrettable and unjustified", saying Cairo had long adhered to a policy of non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries.
The official accused Ethiopia of blaming foreign actors for its "successive internal crises" and said Egypt's decision had been taken "in line with the principle of reciprocity".
Ethiopia has not publicly provided a reason for expelling the Egyptian diplomat.
In addition to the dam, regional security concerns have further strained ties in recent months.
This week, Ethiopia accused Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea of backing a rebel group, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched a major assault against government forces last week, raising fears of a return to Ethiopia's devastating 2020-2022 civil war that killed an estimated 600,000 people.
Egypt has not publicly responded to the allegation, while Sudan has denied it.
On Thursday, Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic ties, accusing each other of fuelling internal conflicts as fighting continued in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region.
Egypt has strengthened ties with Eritrea in recent months.

Women farmers need greater role in agricultural policymaking: RSS leader Ramlal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

RSS leader Ramlal described the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh’s first national conference of women farmers as a symbol of women’s growing role in Indian agriculture
NEW DELHI: RSS leader Ramlal described the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh’s first national conference of women farmers as a symbol of women’s growing role in Indian agriculture and a platform to advocate changes in agricultural policies, according to the PTI report.Speaking at the event, RSS All-India Sampark Pramukh Ramlal said around 5,000 women farmers and office-bearers from across the country, including states such as Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur, travelled to Delhi at their own expense to participate in the All India Women Farmers’ Workers Conclave held at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium on Wednesday.RSS leader Ramlal, who attended the conference, said women farmers should have a central role in decision-making on issues related to sustainable agriculture and the development of rural economies.In a statement, the RSS All-India Sampark Pramukh said "women should receive legal and social recognition not just as agricultural workers but as farmers and agricultural entrepreneurs capable of making independent decisions with self reliance and discernment."He congratulated the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh (BKS) for highlighting women’s empowerment and called on other organisations to draw lessons from such efforts.
Ramlal said the women who travelled to Delhi at their own expense and raised the slogan, “We, the women of India, will bring prosperity”, had added a new sense of pride and dignity to the term “Annadata” (food provider). He said their participation could mark the beginning of a significant transformation towards a healthier and more prosperous future for the country.He noted that women have traditionally played an important role in Indian agriculture, from sowing and harvesting crops to preserving indigenous seeds and rearing livestock.According to Ramlal, women perform nearly 60 to 70 per cent of the physical work associated with agriculture. However, he said they have often been classified in society and official records merely as agricultural labourers or family helpers.The conference, organised under the guidance of the women’s wing of the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, sought to change this perception and ensure women farmers receive recognition, dignity and self-respect, he said.Ramlal said the event, held against the backdrop of the United Nations’ declaration of 2026 as the “International Year of the Woman Farmer”, was more than an organisational gathering but it was more of a manifestation of the women empowerment in Indian agriculture. He described it and a call for changes in agricultural policies.
He said participants discussed the role of traditional farming in achieving the vision of a developed and healthy India by 2047, with “Gau-Krishi-Vanijyam” (cattle, agriculture and commerce) also featuring in the deliberations.Opposition to genetically modified (GM) seeds and gene-editing technology was another key issue discussed at the conference, Ramlal said.The conference identified five key areas: toxin-free farming and cow-based organic agriculture, nutritious food, disease-free living, an addiction-free society and remunerative prices for agricultural produce, he said.Ramlal also urged the Centre and state governments to put women farmers at the centre of policymaking and design schemes according to their requirements. He called for easier access to credit, local processing facilities and better avenues for marketing organic products.He said existing policies often focus on corporate and chemical-based farming, while arguing that women’s participation is crucial to rural development.

AI weapons systems are already here. Algorithms must not decide who lives and dies | Kenneth Roth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:17 UTC
19:00:17 KST

As tech leaders warn about the threats of artificial intelligence, most conjure up images of AI agents running amok, such as hacking systems used to run our critical infrastructure, banks or even militaries. Yet one serious danger is mentioned less frequently – the threat posed by AI–empowered lethal weapons. Fully autonomous versions of these weapons are colloquially known as killer robots.
Israel’s conduct in Gaza shows that, in an important respect, such AI weapon systems are already here. An algorithm has been deciding who lives and who dies.
For more than a decade, governments have been meeting in Geneva to stop the development of autonomous AI weapons. In early September, 128 governments met to approve a report that could serve as the foundation for a binding treaty.
But a collection of lawyers sent by Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin teamed up to water it down. Notably, they weakened a provision that requires humans to review military targets developed by AI before a strike.
Fully autonomous weapons remain the focus; the use of AI to determine targets for conventional weapons is not. At risk is the longstanding quest to maintain a “human in the loop” – that is, meaningful or effective “human control” of AI-empowered weaponry.
For many people, talk of killer robots conjures up images of Arnold Schwarzenegger’s The Terminator. I have often thought about the problem in the context of the Tahrir Square uprising at the height of the Arab spring that led to the ouster of the Egyptian president Hosni Mubarak.
Mubarak’s fate was sealed when the Egyptian army made clear it would refuse to fire on Egyptian protesters. But killer robots would have had no such qualms. If Mubarak had been able to deploy them, he might have stayed in power.
The negotiators in Geneva are not even addressing this problem. The Trump-Putin lawyers made sure that the agreed report referred only to war, not repression.
Today, amid the drone warfare in eastern Ukraine, Russian and Ukrainian troops are experimenting with fully autonomous weapons to overcome jamming of the signals used to control drones. We can expect these nascent deployments to expand.
Yet the “killer robot” metaphor is deceptive. If we look at targeting decisions more expansively, AI has already taken over. In Gaza, the Israeli military is using AI to target Palestinians.
Israel has long monitored phone communications in that territory. After the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israel used an AI system called “Lavender” to uncover patterns that it equated with the phone of a Hamas operative. People whose phones AI determined met these criteria could be killed.
Because it was easier to target suspects at home, a separate automated system called “Where’s Daddy?” tracked them there, meaning that their families were often killed too. There was no pretense that Hamas was using its operatives’ homes for military purposes. It was simply easier for the AI system to find suspected Hamas fighters where they slept. The families were the collateral damage.
Theoretically, a human remained in the loop because an AI-picked target was routed through intelligence officers who approved it and sent it to others who launched the attack. In fact, this human role was nominal.
In the past, Israeli targeting decisions were subject to significant review. But in Israel’s killing spree that followed the Hamas attack, the intense demand for targets took precedence over such review.
Israeli intelligence officers who received the AI selections routinely passed them to the attackers without second guessing. As one officer described: “I would invest 20 seconds for each target at this stage, and do dozens of them every day. I had zero added-value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. It saved a lot of time.”
From computer to killing, the human judgment exercised was perfunctory – a “rubber stamp”. In essence, an algorithm played God.
One Israeli officer suggested the practice might be justified because AI makes better decisions than humans do. It is dispassionate, while people’s judgment can be clouded, such as by the animosity toward all Palestinians that some Israelis felt after the Hamas attack.
As one Israeli soldier explained: “I have much more trust in a statistical mechanism than a soldier who lost a friend two days ago. Everyone there, including me, lost people on October 7. The machine did it coldly. And that made it easier.”
Yet AI algorithms are inevitably affected by human input. How much evidence is required to identify someone as a Hamas fighter? What margin of error is tolerated?
The answer to such questions depends on the judgment of the AI programmers and their commanders – ordinary Israelis who might have devalued Palestinian civilian life in the fury that followed the Hamas attack. Even the Israeli military conceded that about 10% of the human targets slated for assassination were not members of the Hamas military wing at all.
The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, epitomized the heedless attitude toward Palestinian civilians when he said: “It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It’s not true, this rhetoric about civilians were not aware, not involved – it’s absolutely not true. They could’ve risen up, fought against that evil regime.”
That same contempt contributed to the Israeli military’s shocking willingness to tolerate civilian deaths. The Israeli military permitted an anticipated 20 dead for the killing of a mere suspected low-level Hamas fighter.
Under the rule of proportionality, international humanitarian law prohibits a wartime attack if it “may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life … which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated”. Although international law doesn’t specify the number of civilian casualties that are acceptable in a given situation, virtually no legal expert considers Israel’s shocking 20-to-one ratio to be lawful.
These are war crimes. They reflect an appalling devaluing of Palestinian civilian life.
Evoking for me Hannah Arendt’s “banality of evil”, ordinary soldiers became complicit in extraordinary cruelty by trusting what they call the “system”. The essence of that system remained people – the generals who ordered its creation, the military lawyers who excused the unjustifiable, the programmers who tweaked the algorithm, the intelligence officers who passed on the computer-generated targets, and the soldiers who launched the attack.
But part of what made it easier to trust the system was the pseudo-scientific precision of AI. We are all familiar with the breezy, authoritative tone of today’s chatbots. When AI is used for targeting, it brings a similar feigned omniscience to killing.
When inevitably flawed human beings make decisions, they can expect others to challenge them. But AI makes it easier for us to defer to its judgments. That deference risks magnifying the human biases that inevitably infect any AI system.
As we seek to curb killer robots, we should also remain attentive to AI that can lull us into complacency about other targeting. The International Committee of the Red Cross calls it “automation bias”.
To have meaningful human control of AI, we need not just nominal endorsement of its decisions. We need intense questioning of its product, and accountability for commanders when junior officers fall short.
Only that skepticism has any hope of ensuring that soldiers who deploy AI remember that real human beings are at the end of the kill chain they enable. Even in war, people should never be snuffed out by the mechanical application of an algorithm.
- 
  Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Chinese woman, 60, becomes gaming streamer after playing to understand son’s addiction

A 60-year-old woman in southern China has defied public stereotypes surrounding senior citizens by becoming a popular e-game live-streamer.
Zhong Juanjuan, affectionately known as Auntie Juan by internet users, has amassed 527,000 followers on social media. She hosts two daily live-streaming sessions, each typically attracting around 10,000 viewers, as reported by Beijing News.
Zhong, who lives in a suburban area of Meizhou in Guangdong province, only began playing computer games six years ago. Before that, she held various part-time jobs, including sales and childcare, due to her limited educational background, having only completed primary school. She retired about 10 years ago, according to the report.
Once, Zhong viewed e-games as a foe to her family. Two decades ago, when her younger son was a secondary school student, he became addicted to gaming, which resulted in a significant drop in his grades.

OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia.
In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into a New South Wales state government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
The breach, which comes weeks after news of a similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday.
The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach.
The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service.
OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available.
The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office.
“The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences.
“We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.
Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week.
“We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said.
On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date.
The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June.
The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent.
An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools.

YouTube sports strategy targets more live rights -- but not necessarily events
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

YouTube is stalking the sports landscape for live rights.
YouTube would like as many games as it can get its hands on – while also giving users as "clean" of an experience as possible, according to people familiar with the matter.
YouTube has been coy with its sports strategy, acquiring the rights to one NFL game last year for its free, ad-supported platform and buying "NFL Sunday Ticket" rights until the end of the 2029-30 season. Beyond those two moves, YouTube has largely been quiet.
Still, YouTube is an interested buyer in live sports for almost all of the major U.S. sports leagues if it can get bespoke rights that present an easy consumer message, such as all local games or all games in a tournament, said the people, who asked not to be named because the company's plans are private.
YouTube's strategy is distinct from Netflix's — an interesting contrast between the two largest streaming services in the world by users. While Netflix wants individual games or tournaments that it can turn into mini-events, YouTube is more likely to buy games in bulk if there's a clear consumer proposition underlying the rights. In other words, YouTube isn't interested in a swath of games if there's no obvious connection to them.
Sports Business Journal reported earlier this year that YouTube is in advanced talks to be the NBA's new regional sports network solution, buying the rights for 20 to 25 teams for a price tag of potentially more than $1 billion. YouTube is interested in the FIFA Men's World Cup rights, as CNBC first reported in July.
YouTube is still wrestling with the feasibility of this idea if it can't get all of the teams, said the people. YouTube ideally wants both in-market and out-of-market games, the people said. It's also unclear if the NBA is comfortable selling complete rights to one platform.
A big part of YouTube's sports objective relates to building up its premium service. A few weeks ago, YouTube Premium struck a deal to ingest Peacock content within the service for no extra cost.
YouTube Premium, which eliminates YouTube ads and costs $15.99 per month, doesn't necessarily want to strike a bunch of other similar deals and turn the service into an aggregator of other companies' streaming services. But what may interest YouTube executives is buying a chunk of live sports and putting it behind the paywall. In other words, making people pay for YouTube Premium to get access to the games.
YouTube could then use "free" YouTube as its front-of-the-paywall marketing tool to get people to pay the monthly subscription fee for YouTube Premium. For example, it could put a small number of games on ad-supported YouTube to effectively advertise for signing up for the full package in Premium. It also can use its millions of sports-related content creator videos to push live games on Premium.
YouTube hired Justin Connolly away from Disney last year to be its global head of media and sports. Connolly was one of Disney's highest paid executives, having spent 25 years at the company and rising through the ranks to become the company's president of platform distribution, including ESPN and Disney+.
Sunday Ticket's fate
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell told CNBC last month the league could redo its existing packaging of games to better fit the modern media landscape. One way of doing this is to deconstruct "Sunday Ticket," which would give the league many more games to sell in other packages.
YouTube executives are already considering this as a possibility, said the people. YouTube currently spends $2 billion per year on "Sunday Ticket" and could use that money and more to buy a new, premium package of games if the league moved in that direction.
Wolfe Research analysts wrote a note to clients Friday predicting the NFL "will tier its rights in order to maximize the value of premium tiers while setting lower cost tiers to firms with more limited buying power."

Democratic Texas AG candidate vows to probe Deloitte's role in voter registration delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

Nathan Johnson, a Texas state senator and the Democratic candidate for attorney general, announced that, if elected, he plans to investigate Deloitte and other state vendor contracts in the wake of a software error that resulted in a failure to process voter registrations for what he and a Republican state lawmaker say were at least 178,000 Texans.
Johnson, in an exclusive interview with CNBC ahead of the Friday announcement, blamed Texas Republicans for pretending to shrink the state government and outsourcing essential duties to contractors.
Deloitte allegedly installed a software update on the Department of Public Safety's servers in 2025 that led to the error, which was only caught in September with a little over a month to go before the 2026 midterm election. If he becomes attorney general, Johnson said he wants to review the process for outsourcing state functions, as well as the individual contracts themselves.
"I think the voter registration issue is absolutely not the whole story," the Dallas County Democrat said. 
"It's just the leading edge that really ought to cause people to look hard at this larger phenomenon of outsourcing core state functions that really a major government like Texas ought to be able to handle."
Johnson, who has been in the state Senate since 2019, will face off against Republican nominee Mayes Middleton — who is also a state senator — in a bid to replace GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton. An August poll from the Texas Politics Project showed Middleton up 5 percentage points on Johnson. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points.
Deloitte did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
According to the Texas Legislative Budget Board, which keeps an online database of state contracts, Deloitte has six active contracts with DPS at a total value of $84.46 million. Across the state government, Deloitte has 30 active contracts with 16 state agencies totaling $2.02 billion in active value.
Johnson's announcement, shared first with CNBC, comes a little more than a week after The Texas Tribune and VoteBeat reported that the DPS error caused at least 200,000 voter registration applications to go unprocessed. The Secretary of State's office flagged the error when DPS transmitted the entire backlog of registrations in one batch, flooding county registrars in mid-September, ahead of the state's Oct. 5 voter registration deadline.
Texans can use DPS's online driver's license portal to register to vote.
Republicans have also criticized the blunder. Texas state Sen. Paul Bettencourt, a Republican from the Houston area, pointed to Deloitte and the Texas Secretary of State in a post to X on Monday.
"In typical unintended IT upgrade consequences, the DPS vendor Deloitte updated the voter registration system, and those automatic transfers stopped coming thru, and before you ask, YES, the Texas Secretary of State personnel should have also caught the lack of Voter Registrations, but they didn't!" Bettencourt wrote.
Alicia Pierce, a spokesperson for the Texas Secretary of State said the office "is providing grant funding to help offset the cost of additional personnel as counties process these delayed registrations." Pierce said the registrations were sent to counties in time for the Nov. 3 election.
The voter registration issue is not the first botched job by an outside vendor, which Johnson said the state has come to rely on more as Republicans have worked to shrink the government.
In 2023, Deloitte has been asked to administer the Texas Energy Fund, a taxpayer-funded state program to build electric power infrastructure. But the consultant's contracts came under fire a year later after it chose a company whose CEO had been convicted of an "embezzlement scheme" as a finalist for a Texas Energy Fund loan program.
News of the voter registration backlog broke in the lead-up to Texas' midterm elections, which feature some of the most critical races in the country.
Democrats are hoping to win statewide in Texas for the first time since 1994, and have launched spirited campaigns for both governor and Senate. State Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has led Paxton in most recent polls. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the race a "toss up."
It also comes amid growing fears that President Donald Trump could question the results of this year's elections or try to suppress votes by deploying the National Guard or border agents to polling places.
Johnson said he believed the voter registration gaffe was a "genuine error, but not an excusable error."
"There's a lot of talk about election integrity," Johnson said. "But I can't think of a thing that shakes voters' confidence much more than learning that almost 200,000 people applied to vote and didn't have their registrations processed."

Press review: NATO escalates Russia tensions as Putin's envoy, economy minister visit US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. NATO is hindering efforts to reopen dialogue with Russia and discuss Moscow’s legitimate concerns, as Russian President Vladimir Putin discusses nuclear escalation with the West and UN reform at the plenary session of the Valdai forum, among other topics. Meanwhile, his envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Russian Economic Development Minister travel to the United States for talks with senior US officials. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: NATO seen escalating tensions with Russia
NATO is blocking efforts to restore direct dialogue with Russia and discuss its legitimate concerns, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Moscow has warned the alliance that it will use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, in the event of an attempted blockade of the Kaliningrad Region. Russia has called on NATO to end its expansion. However, the bloc's leadership is calling for increased support to Kiev as it shies away from a dialogue on security guarantees. Meanwhile, the EU too is increasingly resembling a military structure.
"Any sensible initiatives regarding the need to restore direct dialogue with Russia and discuss our legitimate concerns at the EU and NATO are being blocked. As long as the erroneous opinion prevails in these structures that taking Russia’s interests into account in any form would be a defeat for the West rather than a condition for ensuring genuine stability and security in Europe, we will not get off the ground," Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs, told Izvestia.
According to Natalya Yeremina, a professor at St. Petersburg State University, NATO is escalating the situation around Kaliningrad to test Russia's military capabilities. The bloc is using non-military means to divert Moscow's attention and gain control of Russian shipping in the Baltic Sea. However, she warned, such actions increase the risk of random incidents, which could lead to more serious consequences later on.
Russia and NATO maintaining only emergency communication channels aggravates the situation. However, the alliance did not use those in the wake of incidents with falling UAVs in Romania and Poland as it immediately blamed Moscow instead. Therefore, restoring a limited technical dialogue between defense agencies could be the first realistic step, Yekaterina Antyukhova, professor with the Department of Global Political Processes at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, told Izvestia. Reviving the political dialogue would be more difficult, as the conditions for this are not yet ripe, she explained.
According to her, NATO is unlikely to abandon its expansionist policy any time soon. For the alliance, this line remains an instrument of bolstering its positions. However, the bloc will hardly expand in the near future, the expert argued. Instead, it may further spread its military and political influence, develop cooperation with partner states, expand joint exercises, and strengthen military cooperation. The Armenian army, for one, has recently started to embrace the alliance’s standards.
The risks of a direct military conflict between Russia and NATO are growing, with the alliance being increasingly drawn into the Ukraine conflict and currently "testing" Moscow in the Baltic Sea. To stabilize the situation, it would be necessary to restore at least a technical dialogue, but Brussels is not currently planning to take Russia’s demands into account.
Vedomosti: Putin talks Kaliningrad, nuclear escalation with West, in Ukraine and at UN
Moscow is not "threatening anyone," while Russia’s recent warnings about the possibility of using nuclear weapons in case of any blockade of Kaliningrad by NATO’s European allies is "a response, not a threat," Russian President Vladimir Putin said on the last day of the forum hosted by the Valdai International Discussion Club on October 1.
Putin was commenting on the exchange of remarks in absentia started by the Russian embassies across Europe and Russia’s Foreign Ministry and continued by NATO countries, its Secretary General Mark Rutte and later concluded by the Kremlin. The exchange came as NATO countries stepped up exercises around Kaliningrad, politicians in Lithuania and Latvia discussed hosting third-country nuclear weapons and Britain, a nuclear power, made a corresponding proposal.
Commenting on global international cooperation, Putin lamented that the UN as its key symbol now operates "far less collegially and democratically." This, he argued, explains justified claims to it, with Russia supporting reform of the global organization, even if the move would require internal consensus. The UN structure should reflect the global diversity, with Asia, Africa and Latin America playing a much more significant role there, while the institutions established in 1945 no longer reflect the global situation, the president added.
Russia’s position regarding UN reform has been quite consistent: it should adapt to today’s realities, and rule out any diktat or moves to impose certain players, while staying true to the key ideas underpinning the global body since 1945, senior research fellow at the Institute for International Studies at MGIMO University Vladimir Pavlov told Vedomosti. According to him, this path or the processes of embracing a new world order will neither be simple nor quick. "The West is trying to retain its global posture or even remain relevant in an already transformed world. Navigating these new realities will not come without crises or be a quick process, so it will be necessary to make compromises and firmly defend the position as a sovereign at times," Pavlov said.
The situation around Kaliningrad, as well as recent statements from Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova and the latest comments from Putin have been a preventive exchange of deterrence signals, Yulia Semke, leading expert with the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Higher School of Economics, explained. Russia is responding to the whole range of abundant military signals and scenarios, as Moscow views them as potentially leading to escalation and cautions against the maximum costs of such an escalation.
"In turn, NATO officials say such Russian signals do not require any change in their strategy. The problem is there is a huge gap between military planning and drills and actual preparations for a blockade, but given the extent of the current mistrust one of the two sides may take the other’s actions for preparations for the worst-case scenario," Semke emphasized.
Vedomosti: Putin’s envoy, Russian economy minister travel to US
One after another, Russian special presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov visited the United States. Their trips came as senior Russian officials took part in G20 meetings against the backdrop of the diesel crisis in the United States and Donald Trump’s ambition to mitigate it.
Meanwhile, there have been no direct contacts on potential sanctions relief, economic cooperation or other meaningful discussions with the US, Reshetnikov told reporters on the sidelines of the two-day G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee on October 1.
Prior to Reshetnikov’s visit, Putin’s special envoy Dmitriev, who also heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), traveled to the US on September 24-29. He visited New York and Washington.
The New York Post and Reuters reported, citing White House officials, that Dmitriev held high-level talks with US officials to continue "constructive discussions", focusing on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and "prospective post-war energy initiatives" between the US and Russia. Reuters specified, citing sources, that Dmitriev had met US Treasury and Department of Commerce officials.
Meanwhile, Trump himself is advocating an energy ceasefire. Moscow halted fuel exports which, in combination with the crisis around Iran, pushed US diesel prices to a record $6.5 per gallon, while diesel and gasoline prices in Europe rose to four-year highs.
The US has continued to use the carrot and stick policy in its contacts with Russia, given the impact its economic agencies may have on politics, Vladimir Vasilyev, chief researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. But the bulk of benefits and rapprochement between Russia and the US will come after de-escalation expected by Trump by December, when the US will host the G20 summit, with Putin invited to attend, the expert maintained.
Dmitriev’s US visits are extremely important and his mandate is quite extensive, Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at HSE University, said. As Trump’s special envoys, not the Department of State, act as US top negotiators, Russia is trying to maintain an equal dialogue, he explained. Suslov described Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov as Moscow’s second-largest counterparty, as he said Dmitriev is nearly "equivalent to [US special envoy Steve] Witkoff."
The US approach to Russia involves proposing economic deals in exchange for political concessions, and Dmitriev’s role as an emissary fits with his position at the RDIF, Nikolay Silayev, Leading Research Fellow at the Institute for International Studies at MGIMO University, argued. The expert noted that Moscow understands that some political positions have no economic price tag attached to them.
Kommersant: Global fuel crisis explained
The large-scale global crisis triggered by chronic fuel, mostly diesel, shortages is getting worse. A sharp supply reduction by major exporters, including Russia, and fierce competition over remaining volumes have pushed petroleum prices to record highs, with no signs of stabilization in sight. Against this backdrop, the US is considering a ban on diesel exports, while EU countries are calling for relaxed rules governing fuel quality.
Diesel costs in the US and the EU have risen to new record highs. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), in the third week of September, average US prices exceeded $6.50 per gallon, an increase of $2.6 year-on-year. In the EU, diesel prices rose to €2.23 per liter, according to data from the European Commission. Prices are climbing amid lower oil and petroleum supplies from the Middle East, as well as ongoing restrictions on diesel exports from Russia, which previously was the world's second-largest supplier with a 9.5% market share.
Dmitry Danilin, a portfolio manager at Alfa-Capital brokerage, told Kommersant that the crisis has mostly affected poorer countries that import fuel and lack the means to subsidize consumer prices. For developed economies, he argued, high fuel prices play the role of an additional consumer tax which curbs demand and increases inflation pressures in the economy due to rising shipment costs.
Olga Osharova, CEO of S+Consulting, noted that rising fuel prices have primarily hit Finland, Denmark, Greece and Germany where fuel costs are rising at an accelerated pace, while supply disruptions at gas stations have been reported in France and other countries.
Amid record fuel prices, US President Donald Trump supported a diesel export ban on September 22. Later, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent specified that both a full and a partial ban are being considered. In theory, the measure would make a significant amount of fuel available for the domestic market: an estimate from S&P Global showed that a full ban would free up 1.48 million barrels per day. At that, according to estimates from Wood Mackenzie quoted by Nikita Gorbun, Director of the Energy and Oil and Gas Practice at Yakov and Partners, a 90-day ban would help replenish available stocks in more than a month.
According to Dmitry Kastatkin, a managing partner at Kasatkin Consulting, if Russia eases its diesel export restrictions, the first additional shipments could take place within a couple of weeks, provided the product, vessels, and buyers are ready. Russian diesel could likely go to Turkey, Brazil, and North and West Africa--regions with established trade ties and infrastructure already available, Kasatkin added. The impact on the European market would be indirect, as Russian diesel will replace US or Indian volumes in other markets, thereby freeing up those supplies for Europe, he concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Houthis prepare to storm Saudi borders
Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement is moving troops to the Saudi borders, Qatari media outlets reported on Thursday. Major preparations are underway in Saada Governorate in northern Yemen, a key Houthi stronghold. Yemen’s central government views these maneuvers as preparations for a large-scale ground offensive. Officials believe that ground clashes between Iranian-backed militants and regular Saudi troops are only a matter of time.
Since Saudi Arabia and its allies launched their large-scale intervention in the Yemeni war in 2015, the Houthis have repeatedly conducted cross-border incursions into the kingdom, which has actively supported the internationally recognized government in the republic. Now, Saudi Arabia is not only looking for assistance in establishing effective protection against combined missile and drone attacks by Ansar Allah among various international players but also weighing a scenario of renewing a large-scale military campaign against the militants, which formally stopped in September 2022 thanks to a UN-led ceasefire. Earlier this month, the Houthis recaptured the western part of the Yemeni coast and occupied a number of islands in the Red Sea as they gained the ability to deliver more precise strikes on maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic waterway that Riyadh relied on for oil transit.
Anton Mardasov, an expert in the Middle East, explained to Nezavisimaya Gazeta that the increased concentration of Houthi forces in Saada, near the border with Saudi Arabia’s Najran Province, will inevitably be interpreted by the Saudi ruling family as evidence of a launching point for an offensive being established there. "Saada, the movement's historic stronghold, is becoming both a potential axis for a ground assault and a means to draw Saudi forces and warplanes away from other fronts in Yemen," he told the newspaper. "The more so that Aramco’s oil infrastructure is located in Najran. At the same time, this Houthi military buildup could serve as an instrument of not only escalating tensions but also for exerting pressure ahead of negotiations," he argued.
Mardasov does not rule out the possibility of the Houthis factoring in the ethno-confessional dimension too as they raise the stakes in their standoff with Saudi Arabia. "For instance, the escalation of tensions in Saada will inevitably affect the Ismaili community in Najran, which enjoys a certain degree of autonomy," he explained to Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The expert noted that Saudi authorities are attempting to contain this threat by offering social guarantees to this religious community, whose members serve in the kingdom's regular army. However, this may prove insufficient, given that Ismailis are barred from holding high-ranking positions in the country. "Consequently, a certain level of discontent has persisted there," Mardasov concluded.

News Analysis: Saudi Arabia once counted on U.S. protection. Now it's pivoting to new alliances
Unknown

News Analysis: Saudi Arabia once counted on U.S. protection. Now it’s pivoting to new alliances
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- After Washington rebuffed calls to strike Houthi rebels, Saudi Arabia is pursuing new maritime and defense alliances.
- Houthi forces have seized territory on the Red Sea coast and threatened Saudi shipping, endangering an export route made more vital by Iran’s stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz.
BEIRUT — For decades, the relationship between Saudi Arabia and the U.S. has centered on an often-mentioned but rarely tested supposition: If the kingdom were attacked, America would come to its rescue.
But recent events have shown that much-vaunted security umbrella to be a leaky one.
Last month, Iran-aligned Yemeni rebels blitzed through Yemen’s coast and threatened to shut down Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea lifeline. But the Trump administration, reluctant to open a new front in its war with Iran, rebuffed Riyadh’s calls to come to its rescue.
That has left the kingdom searching for friends beyond Washington, for allies ready to put rockets where the rhetoric is and assist in a fight Saudi Arabia considers existential.
Over the last few months, as Persian Gulf nations contended with the fallout from the Israel-U.S. war on Iran, Saudi Arabia has supercharged its military-focused diplomacy. In July, it announced a 15-nation maritime alliance to safeguard shipping through the Red Sea, the Bab al Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean, is a new tinderbox in the Iran war.
Soon after came the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a NATO-inspired security pact where any attack on Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would be regarded as an attack against all three.
And this week, Saudi Arabia’s race to rally allies spurred a detente of sorts with its frenemy the United Arab Emirates, with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — the country’s de facto ruler — and defense minister brother receiving the Emirates’ vice president for the first high-level meeting since the two sides fell out over Yemen late last year.
There have even been reports of possible cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Israel against the Houthis, a notable development — if true — for two countries with no formal diplomatic relations.
The Saudi overtures come at a sensitive time for the kingdom. The standoff between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz has largely cut off Saudi Arabia’s main export channel, and attacks on its energy infrastructure are lowering its oil output.
As a result, the kingdom saw a 25% contraction in “oil activities,” according to official economic data, triggering an almost 5% decrease in the country’s gross domestic product between April and June, compared with the first quarter of the year.
That reduction forced painful cuts to Vision 2030, the prince’s signature policy aimed at remaking Saudi Arabia. So-called giga-projects, such as the Line and Trojena, have revised their ambitions downward amid the financial realities of a Saudi Arabia under fire.
Saudi Arabia is gambling on a gargantuan building boom to remake its image and economy, but history offers cautionary tales over such ambitions.
And all that was before the Houthis got involved.
The Houthis had been fighting the Saudis since 2015 in Yemen’s civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people before settling into a stalemate and an uneasy ceasefire in 2022.
But in July, Saudi Arabia attacked the airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, to prevent the landing of an Iranian plane carrying high-ranking Houthi officials. That set off a flurry of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, and the Houthis’ announcement of a blockade against Saudi shipping on the Red Sea — now the main corridor for Saudi energy exports.
Then in September, the Houthis overran Yemen’s coastal cities, snapping up materiel left behind by Saudi-backed government fighters and seizing control of territory near the Bab al Mandab strait.
A few days later, the Saudis accused an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq of coordinating with the Houthis to hit the East-West Pipeline, the vital infrastructure that had allowed Saudi Arabia to reorient its oil from Hormuz to the Red Sea.
All that pushed the Saudi crown prince to turn to the U.S. for help — and he had reason to think it would come: Late last year, the U.S. signed a strategic defense agreement with the kingdom, designated it a major non-NATO ally and agreed to sell it advanced F-35 fighter jets.
Mohammed also has something of a personal relationship with President Trump, who made Saudi Arabia the first stop of his first overseas tour in 2025 after being reelected and boasted that he had garnered almost $1 trillion in Saudi investments into the U.S. economy.
Trump initially seemed receptive to the prince’s entreaties but reportedly pulled back just as U.S. warplanes were set to take off for sorties on Houthi targets. Later, he told Fox News that Washington was “in constant communication with the Houthis and that they’ve agreed not to fight the United States.”
The Houthis have also assured European nations, which have been wary of provoking the rebels’ ire, that they won’t attack their shipping either. Last month, France and the U.K. said they would offer defensive assistance to Saudi Arabia, while Greece is operating U.S.-made Patriot missile batteries in the kingdom.
The Saudi deal stoked surprise and immediate concern across Washington, as well as in Israel, itself a nuclear power that has long feared an atomic arms race could grip the region.
With the U.S. hesitating, the expectation is that Saudi Arabia’s partners in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will form the international cavalry to help, but that has yet to manifest itself on the ground.
This week, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif said his country was “bound” by the pact to defend Saudi Arabia.
“That means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.
Pakistan already has 8,000 troops in Saudi Arabia, along with 16 Chinese-made JF-17 Thunder fighter jets, combat drone squadrons and a surface-to-air missile battery. But it’s unclear whether they have participated in attacking the Houthis.
Turkish officials, meanwhile, say they have “no issues meeting” Saudi Arabia’s “military needs,” especially on technical matters.
The Houthis say any party attacking them will face retaliation.
“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” said Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, in an interview on Iraqi television.
Observers say Saudi Arabia is gearing up for a ground offensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from consolidating their gains on the Red Sea coast and reversing the tide. The plan is for Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters to lead the charge.
“It will be mostly an air campaign for the Saudis, with Yemenis and maybe Pakistanis on the ground, though I doubt the latter will get involved beyond being on the border,” said Bernard Haykel, a professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University.
There is little chance the U.S. would contribute to such a fight with boots on the ground. But it could provide intelligence and logistical support, just as it did during Mohammed’s 2015 foray into Yemen. The U.S. Navy could also launch strikes, as it did when the Houthis blockaded the Red Sea in 2025, before Trump declared a ceasefire.
In any case, although Saudi leaders may not expect Washington to get involved, their fear is that the U.S. will forge another agreement with the Houthis to the exclusion of Riyadh’s concerns, Haykel said.
“The Saudis want a signal that the U.S. is in the background as support if something happens,” he said.
“They’d love to have it in the center of everything. But if they can’t, they want to make it seem like America is fully on board without necessarily being in the battle.”

Press review: NATO escalates Russia tensions as Putin's envoy, economy minister visit US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. NATO is hindering efforts to reopen dialogue with Russia and discuss Moscow’s legitimate concerns, as Russian President Vladimir Putin discusses nuclear escalation with the West and UN reform at the plenary session of the Valdai forum, among other topics. Meanwhile, his envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Russian Economic Development Minister travel to the United States for talks with senior US officials. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: NATO seen escalating tensions with Russia
NATO is blocking efforts to restore direct dialogue with Russia and discuss its legitimate concerns, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Moscow has warned the alliance that it will use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, in the event of an attempted blockade of the Kaliningrad Region. Russia has called on NATO to end its expansion. However, the bloc's leadership is calling for increased support to Kiev as it shies away from a dialogue on security guarantees. Meanwhile, the EU too is increasingly resembling a military structure.
"Any sensible initiatives regarding the need to restore direct dialogue with Russia and discuss our legitimate concerns at the EU and NATO are being blocked. As long as the erroneous opinion prevails in these structures that taking Russia’s interests into account in any form would be a defeat for the West rather than a condition for ensuring genuine stability and security in Europe, we will not get off the ground," Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs, told Izvestia.
According to Natalya Yeremina, a professor at St. Petersburg State University, NATO is escalating the situation around Kaliningrad to test Russia's military capabilities. The bloc is using non-military means to divert Moscow's attention and gain control of Russian shipping in the Baltic Sea. However, she warned, such actions increase the risk of random incidents, which could lead to more serious consequences later on.
Russia and NATO maintaining only emergency communication channels aggravates the situation. However, the alliance did not use those in the wake of incidents with falling UAVs in Romania and Poland as it immediately blamed Moscow instead. Therefore, restoring a limited technical dialogue between defense agencies could be the first realistic step, Yekaterina Antyukhova, professor with the Department of Global Political Processes at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, told Izvestia. Reviving the political dialogue would be more difficult, as the conditions for this are not yet ripe, she explained.
According to her, NATO is unlikely to abandon its expansionist policy any time soon. For the alliance, this line remains an instrument of bolstering its positions. However, the bloc will hardly expand in the near future, the expert argued. Instead, it may further spread its military and political influence, develop cooperation with partner states, expand joint exercises, and strengthen military cooperation. The Armenian army, for one, has recently started to embrace the alliance’s standards.
The risks of a direct military conflict between Russia and NATO are growing, with the alliance being increasingly drawn into the Ukraine conflict and currently "testing" Moscow in the Baltic Sea. To stabilize the situation, it would be necessary to restore at least a technical dialogue, but Brussels is not currently planning to take Russia’s demands into account.
Vedomosti: Putin talks Kaliningrad, nuclear escalation with West, in Ukraine and at UN
Moscow is not "threatening anyone," while Russia’s recent warnings about the possibility of using nuclear weapons in case of any blockade of Kaliningrad by NATO’s European allies is "a response, not a threat," Russian President Vladimir Putin said on the last day of the forum hosted by the Valdai International Discussion Club on October 1.
Putin was commenting on the exchange of remarks in absentia started by the Russian embassies across Europe and Russia’s Foreign Ministry and continued by NATO countries, its Secretary General Mark Rutte and later concluded by the Kremlin. The exchange came as NATO countries stepped up exercises around Kaliningrad, politicians in Lithuania and Latvia discussed hosting third-country nuclear weapons and Britain, a nuclear power, made a corresponding proposal.
Commenting on global international cooperation, Putin lamented that the UN as its key symbol now operates "far less collegially and democratically." This, he argued, explains justified claims to it, with Russia supporting reform of the global organization, even if the move would require internal consensus. The UN structure should reflect the global diversity, with Asia, Africa and Latin America playing a much more significant role there, while the institutions established in 1945 no longer reflect the global situation, the president added.
Russia’s position regarding UN reform has been quite consistent: it should adapt to today’s realities, and rule out any diktat or moves to impose certain players, while staying true to the key ideas underpinning the global body since 1945, senior research fellow at the Institute for International Studies at MGIMO University Vladimir Pavlov told Vedomosti. According to him, this path or the processes of embracing a new world order will neither be simple nor quick. "The West is trying to retain its global posture or even remain relevant in an already transformed world. Navigating these new realities will not come without crises or be a quick process, so it will be necessary to make compromises and firmly defend the position as a sovereign at times," Pavlov said.
The situation around Kaliningrad, as well as recent statements from Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova and the latest comments from Putin have been a preventive exchange of deterrence signals, Yulia Semke, leading expert with the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Higher School of Economics, explained. Russia is responding to the whole range of abundant military signals and scenarios, as Moscow views them as potentially leading to escalation and cautions against the maximum costs of such an escalation.
"In turn, NATO officials say such Russian signals do not require any change in their strategy. The problem is there is a huge gap between military planning and drills and actual preparations for a blockade, but given the extent of the current mistrust one of the two sides may take the other’s actions for preparations for the worst-case scenario," Semke emphasized.
Vedomosti: Putin’s envoy, Russian economy minister travel to US
One after another, Russian special presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov visited the United States. Their trips came as senior Russian officials took part in G20 meetings against the backdrop of the diesel crisis in the United States and Donald Trump’s ambition to mitigate it.
Meanwhile, there have been no direct contacts on potential sanctions relief, economic cooperation or other meaningful discussions with the US, Reshetnikov told reporters on the sidelines of the two-day G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee on October 1.
Prior to Reshetnikov’s visit, Putin’s special envoy Dmitriev, who also heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), traveled to the US on September 24-29. He visited New York and Washington.
The New York Post and Reuters reported, citing White House officials, that Dmitriev held high-level talks with US officials to continue "constructive discussions", focusing on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and "prospective post-war energy initiatives" between the US and Russia. Reuters specified, citing sources, that Dmitriev had met US Treasury and Department of Commerce officials.
Meanwhile, Trump himself is advocating an energy ceasefire. Moscow halted fuel exports which, in combination with the crisis around Iran, pushed US diesel prices to a record $6.5 per gallon, while diesel and gasoline prices in Europe rose to four-year highs.
The US has continued to use the carrot and stick policy in its contacts with Russia, given the impact its economic agencies may have on politics, Vladimir Vasilyev, chief researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. But the bulk of benefits and rapprochement between Russia and the US will come after de-escalation expected by Trump by December, when the US will host the G20 summit, with Putin invited to attend, the expert maintained.
Dmitriev’s US visits are extremely important and his mandate is quite extensive, Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at HSE University, said. As Trump’s special envoys, not the Department of State, act as US top negotiators, Russia is trying to maintain an equal dialogue, he explained. Suslov described Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov as Moscow’s second-largest counterparty, as he said Dmitriev is nearly "equivalent to [US special envoy Steve] Witkoff."
The US approach to Russia involves proposing economic deals in exchange for political concessions, and Dmitriev’s role as an emissary fits with his position at the RDIF, Nikolay Silayev, Leading Research Fellow at the Institute for International Studies at MGIMO University, argued. The expert noted that Moscow understands that some political positions have no economic price tag attached to them.
Kommersant: Global fuel crisis explained
The large-scale global crisis triggered by chronic fuel, mostly diesel, shortages is getting worse. A sharp supply reduction by major exporters, including Russia, and fierce competition over remaining volumes have pushed petroleum prices to record highs, with no signs of stabilization in sight. Against this backdrop, the US is considering a ban on diesel exports, while EU countries are calling for relaxed rules governing fuel quality.

Observers say Saudi Arabia is gearing up for a ground offensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from consolidating their gains on the Red Sea coast and reversing the tide. The plan is for Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters to lead the charge.
“It will be mostly an air campaign for the Saudis, with Yemenis and maybe Pakistanis on the ground, though I doubt the latter will get involved beyond being on the border,” said Bernard Haykel, a professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University.
There is little chance the U.S. would contribute to such a fight with boots on the ground. But it could provide intelligence and logistical support, just as it did during Mohammed’s 2015 foray into Yemen. The U.S. Navy could also launch strikes, as it did when the Houthis blockaded the Red Sea in 2025, before Trump declared a ceasefire.
In any case, although Saudi leaders may not expect Washington to get involved, their fear is that the U.S. will forge another agreement with the Houthis to the exclusion of Riyadh’s concerns, Haykel said.
“The Saudis want a signal that the U.S. is in the background as support if something happens,” he said.
“They’d love to have it in the center of everything. But if they can’t, they want to make it seem like America is fully on board without necessarily being in the battle.”

Kinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:58:19 UTC
18:58:19 KST

Feeld, a UK-based dating app aimed at non-monogamous, queer and kinky users, has reported strong sales growth and paid its largest-ever dividend as it attracts users from more “vanilla” rivals.
Revenues jumped by 32% to £64m following a surge in interest from what it called “open-minded people exploring love, desire, and alternative relationships in a safe, inclusive space”.
Pre-tax profits grew from £9.3m to £11.4m, and the company’s shareholders – including the couple who founded it – shared in a dividend of £3.8m.
Ana Kirova and her partner, Dimo Trifonov, started the business under the name 3nder (pronounced Thrinder), initially targeting couples and singles looking for threesomes.
They were forced to change the company’s name to Feeld owing to a lawsuit from Tinder but it has since experienced rapid growth even as larger rivals have faltered.
Match Group, which owns Tinder and other dating apps such as Hinge and OK Cupid, reported a 5% decline in user numbers earlier this year, amid reports of fatigue with the experience of seeking romance or sex via an app.
But Feeld, which calls itself a dating app “for the curious”, appears to be scooping up some of those users. While this has prompted reports that its edgy image has been watered down by an influx of people with more conventional or monogamous sensibilities, Feeld’s president, Kyle Brennan, said it reflected changing tastes.
“These numbers speak to something bigger than the growth of our business,” said Brennan. “They reflect a broader shift in how people are thinking about connection, with greater openness, curiosity and agency to do things differently.”
Accounts filed at Companies House said rising sales reflected “strong global user growth”, particularly outside the UK, with the rest of the world accounting for £56m of its total £64m in revenues, nearly 90%. Mexico and Spain were Feeld’s fastest-growing regions, while New York, Toronto and Paris led the way among cities, each recording an uplift in user numbers of more than 20%, the company said.
Feeld makes money via the sale of its Majestic memberships, which give users features such as unlimited opportunities to “like” other members, the ability to see who has liked them, and advanced filters to tailor specifications for a potential partner.
It also sells members extra “pings”, a feature that allows members to express interest in someone and send them a message, without having matched with them first.
In 2024, it emerged that some of these features were temporarily vulnerable to manipulation due to security “vulnerabilities” exposed by cybersecurity experts.
Research by the London-based cybersecurity firm Fortbridge found that users could have had sensitive data including messages, private photos and details of their sexuality accessed or even edited.
At the time, Feeld said it had investigated the problems brought to its attention by Fortbridge on 3 March and fixed them by 28 May that year. It said there was no evidence that any customer data had been accessed. It has invested £10.5m in technological upgrades in the past year.
The largest dividend reported in Feeld’s previous accounts was £600,000 in 2024.
As well as its dating platform, Feeld runs in-person social events including a “kinky trivia” night and a “pitch your mate” event, at which guests take to the stage to wax lyrical about why people should date their friends.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

18:57:18 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The UN on Friday allocated $160 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) to support life-saving assistance in 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises.
The allocation is part of a broader effort to reach 87 million people facing the most severe humanitarian needs this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
“We have 87 million people to reach, and no time to waste,” UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said in a statement.
Fletcher stressed that funding alone would not be enough, urging leaders to “exercise political will to open access, remove obstacles and help us reach people whose lives are on the line.”
Of the funding, $150 million will go to Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Cuba, Mali, Niger, the occupied Palestinian territory, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen.
Afghanistan, the occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen are also among 10 crises where Fletcher has called for urgent diplomatic action to secure humanitarian access.
Another $10 million will address the needs of people with disabilities across the 12 crises.
The latest allocation brings total CERF funding provided so far in 2026 to $483 million.

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.
