European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.
Prosecutors seek prison sentence and nightlife ban for Danish man over fatal punch at World Cup event
Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

A majority in the Climate, Environment and Technology Committee at Copenhagen Municipality approved a new plan Monday afternoon.
According to it, the city has moved a step closer to introducing a zero-emission zone in part of Vesterbro, where petrol and diesel vehicles would generally not be allowed to drive.
“It is really good that Copenhagen is now getting its first zero-emission zone. It is good for the climate and for reducing local air pollution,” Kristine Ammitzbøll-Bille of De Radikale, the Danish Social Liberal Party, told TV 2 Kosmopol.
The proposal was originally larger but was changed after 768 consultation responses from residents, businesses and interest groups.
Around 80 percent of the responses were either critical or reserved about the plan.
The revised version exempts all of Vesterbrogade, the area around Copenhagen Central Station, Skelbækgade and part of Halmtorvet.
Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.

Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.
DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ organization, criticized the government’s plan.
Thomas Sørensen, director of DI’s automotive branch, called it an “own goal to let taxes on electric cars rise from the new year.”
According to FDM, Denmark’s main association for car owners, a VW ID.4 Style could cost around DKK 10,300 more in tax, while a Tesla Model Y Long Range with all-wheel drive could face an increase of nearly DKK 28,000.
Mobility Denmark, an industry association representing the automotive sector, also criticized the proposal.
“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.

Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.

Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”

Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.

Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

charlotte perriand’s built-in interiors survive inside 1960 paris tower

charlotte perriand’s built-in interiors survive inside 1960 paris tower
the preserved rooms show how furniture, structure and everyday life were brought together within an early french residential high-rise.
CHARLOTTE PERRIAND’S APPROACH TO DOMESTIC SPACE
Designed by architect Édouard Albert in 1960, the Albert Tower in Paris’s 13th arrondissement contains a surviving apartment interior shaped by Charlotte Perriand, with built-in storage, a kitchen and furniture designed by the influential architect and designer. Now offered for sale, the property provides a rare glimpse into Perriand’s approach to domestic space within one of France’s early experiments in residential high-rise architecture.
The residence occupies a high floor of the tower, with 102.49 square meters of living space and extensive views across the French capital. Its interior includes an entrance hall with built-in closets attributed to Perriand, a separate kitchen, and a living and dining area. The apartment was once home to Swiss designer Ubald Klug and his wife Helena, a ceramicist. Their home was part of the creative circle around designers such as Jean Prouvé, reflecting the experimental spirit of postwar French design.
ÉDOUARD ALBERT’S FLEXIBLE STEEL STRUCTURE
The interior, listed for sale by the real estate agency Architecture de Collection, gains significance from its relationship to Albert’s construction. The Albert Tower uses a regular metal grid of steel tube columns filled with concrete, supporting reinforced concrete slabs and cross-shaped bracing. Designed to combine lightness and transparency, the structure leaves the facade to reveal its underlying construction. With the supporting elements concentrated in pillars, the plan can be reorganized with relative freedom, giving Perriand’s built-in elements a flexible architectural setting.
The kitchen and entrance storage are particularly revealing. Perriand’s designs are built into the rooms, making storage and other everyday functions part of the architecture. The space shows how architects and designers of the period brought furniture, interiors and structure together.
MODERNIST HIGH-RISE LIVING IN PARIS
Albert’s tower, now listed as a historical monument, was conceived as an experiment in bringing high-rise residential construction into the Parisian context. The metal structure of the building, developed through Albert’s research into steel tubes, reflects his interest in linking construction, economy and architectural expression.
The panoramic position of the apartment makes the relationship between structure and domestic life particularly apparent. Its many windows open toward landmarks including the Eiffel Tower, the Invalides, the Val-de-Grâce, the Sacré-Cœur, the Panthéon and Notre-Dame, while its western exposure brings changing light into the rooms.
Yet the more revealing aspect of the property is closer to eye level. The Perriand-designed elements show how the ambitions of postwar modern architecture could extend where things are stored, how a kitchen is organized and how furniture occupies a flexible plan.
project info:
name: Albert Tower apartment
 architect: Édouard Albert
 interior designer / furniture designer: Charlotte Perriand
 location: Paris 13th arrondissement, France
 year: 1960
 living area: 102.49 square meters
 total area: 106 square meters

Meloni asks Brussels for fiscal leeway as energy shock squeezes Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:53:35 UTC
18:53:35 KST

Italian prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging the European Commission again to relax the EU's fiscal rules, saying that higher inflation due to soaring energy prices is squeezing households and businesses, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging Brussels once again to give capitals more room to cushion households and companies from the latest energy-price shock, arguing that European Union fiscal rules are becoming increasingly restrictive as inflation drives up government spending.
In a letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, seen by Euronews, Meloni said the prolonged Middle East crisis has left European energy markets “extremely tight,” with oil prices up almost 80% and gas up to 156%.
"Against this backdrop, the agreed net expenditure paths under the European fiscal framework leave limited room to alleviate the impact on households and firms without resorting to tightening measures at a time of significant downside risks for the economy," Meloni added.
Italy, which is heading to polls next year, holds one of the highest debt-to-GDP ratios in the EU, trailing only Greece, which has recently sought a similar appeal to relax fiscal rules with the Commission.
The Italian leader argues that governments are collecting more tax revenue because prices are higher, but EU fiscal rules make it difficult to recycle that windfall into temporary energy support.
Higher inflation automatically increases indirect tax receipts such as VAT, but using that additional revenue to finance measures that reduce energy costs can count as discretionary fiscal action and run into limits imposed by agreed national spending paths, Meloni noted.
As a solution, the Italian leader is asking Brussels to recognise that some of the additional spending is not the result of governments choosing to spend more, but of inflation mechanically increasing existing obligations.
Meloni wants the Commission to find a way to allow at least part of those additional revenues to be used for "temporary and targeted measures" to reduce the impact of high energy prices — an approach that has been repeatedly recommended by EU officials.
EU budget rules put a limit on how much governments can increase spending, based on the amounts agreed in their budget plans. But when inflation rises more than expected, some government costs automatically go up — such as pensions linked to the cost of living — leaving governments with less room to absorb those extra costs.
The EU’s fiscal framework sets national spending limits in nominal terms, meaning governments cannot simply raise expenditure when inflation comes in significantly above initial forecasts. At the same time, some areas of public spending automatically increase as prices rise.
Meloni said that spending directly affected by inflation exceeding the assumptions underpinning Italy’s budget plan amounts to 20.4% of GDP, while a further 12% of GDP in other expenditure is also expected to come under pressure in 2027.
"We are mindful of the risk of amending newly introduced fiscal rules that pursue a goal we all share, debt sustainability. We are also fully mindful of Italy's commitments under the ongoing excessive deficit procedure and of the need to comply with the corrective net expenditure path," reads the letter.
Meloni called for the issue to be discussed at the upcoming meeting of finance ministers in Brussels on 9 October.

The Italian Embassy in Tokyo is hosting pianist Andrea Molteni
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:53:35 CEST
18:53:35 KST

The Italian Embassy in Japan becomes a concert hall, and Andrea Molteni—one of the most acclaimed Italian pianists of his generation—transforms the diplomatic residence into an ideal bridge between the past and the present, between Scarlatti and Petrassi, between Italy and Tokyo. The concert at the embassy residence follows performances at the Italian Pavilion at Expo 2025 in Osaka and is part of a tour that has included stops at the Miyoshi Kiriri Civic Concert Hall, the Tokyo Bechstein Centrum, and the Kamata Misono Church. For Molteni, performing in a venue that officially represents his country abroad is not only an honor but a specific responsibility. “It’s an extremely important thing that every person of culture—not just a musician—should do,” he explains to ANSA. “It’s not just about bringing Italian music; it’s about finding connections, bringing something new while at the same time seeing it rooted in tradition.” He is referring to the thread linking Goffredo Petrassi and Domenico Scarlatti—a connection the pianist has forged with philological precision. “Petrassi was Morricone’s teacher; he taught all the Italian composers of the 20th century. An absolute genius who wrote works inspired by Scarlatti. We must seek out these kinds of connections, highlighting both the Italian art of the past and that of the present.” The Japanese audience, he says, impressed him with their knowledge and sensitivity. “The hardest thing is finding a balance between one’s personal message and what the audience enjoys,” he admits. “Liszt wrote concert fantasies to entertain—there were no movie theaters back then. This aspect must not be forgotten.” Thus, the program features Bach’s Italian Concerto—“a piece everyone knows, even non-musicians, but one inspired by Italy”—Beethoven’s Sonata, Op. 110, and Brahms’s Variations, Op. 21, all linked by the thread of counterpoint. By Petrassi, he performs the Toccata and the composer’s final work, inspired by a play by Samuel Beckett (Oh les beaux jours), though derived from a sonata by Scarlatti: “A magnificent connection.” The mission, however, is another: to rediscover 20th-century Italian music. “György Ligeti is as well-known as Beethoven and Chopin, but Petrassi is not. Yet he is on the same compositional level. For me, it’s almost a mission; I’ve chosen to discover him within my own country. Having a sense of healthy patriotism is right, especially abroad. I find music that represents my origins. It’s something I almost feel compelled to do.”

Claims about catastrophically low availability and excessively long maintenance of F-16s are false - Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Kyiv • UNN
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi called claims about the low readiness of F-16s and lengthy repairs false. According to him, maintenance is being expedited.
Ukraine’s F-16 fighter fleet is being used intensively and under challenging conditions, but recent reports of catastrophically low aircraft readiness rates and excessively long maintenance periods are false. Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi made the statement on October 2 on X, UNN writes.
Ukraine operates its F-16 fleet intensively and under demanding conditions. We have always recognized that sustaining these aircraft would be challenging, particularly because certain components for this early F-16 variant are no longer in production and are becoming increasingly difficult to source. However, recent reports alleging catastrophically low aircraft availability rates and excessively long maintenance turnaround times are simply false
According to him, "contrary to these claims, our industrial sustainment partners are not only continuing to deliver overhauled aircraft, but are doing so at an increasing pace. Turnaround times are decreasing, not increasing."
"We have full confidence in our industry partners and their ability to further optimize sustainment processes, ensuring the highest possible levels of F-16 readiness and availability during the coming winter months, when these capabilities will be needed most," the Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated.
"Such reports should not undermine confidence in the international funding that supports F-16 sustainment efforts or question the continued need for additional F-16 aircraft from partner nations' inventories," Tykhyi noted.
He emphasized: "We should not allow misinformation to weaken this vital support. The modernization and sustainment of our F-16 fleet remain essential to Ukraine's ability to defend its airspace and protect its people."
Addendum
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson’s statement followed a publication by the WSJ, which claimed that more than half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets are in a state of uncertainty regarding maintenance.

Germany news: Reform row raises fears for Merz's coalition
Published October 2, 2026last updated October 2, 2026
What you need to know

- Merz's Christian Democrats could hold up a Social Democrat-backed tax reform, fueling fears of a coalition collapse

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, October 2, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Nearly half of German long-distance trains late again
Nearly half of Deutsche Bahn's long-distance trains were late in September, as Germany's state-owned rail operator struggles with its aging network.
Just 52.4% of long-distance trains arrived on time, down from 54.2% in August and the third-worst monthly figure this year.
DB blamed extensive construction work and a persistently high number of infrastructure failures, particularly on long-distance routes.
ICE trains between Berlin and Wolfsburg, for example, repeatedly had to slow down because of the poor condition of the tracks.
That section forms part of the Berlin-Hannover route, which has now been closed for a major overhaul. Long-distance trains are being diverted via Braunschweig and Magdeburg, adding around 80 minutes to journeys between Berlin and Hannover. The work is expected to continue until December 2027.
DB considers an ICE or IC train punctual if it is less than six minutes late. Canceled trains are not included in that measure.
A separate passenger punctuality rate, which includes cancellations and counts arrivals of less than 15 minutes late as on time, stood at just 58.6% in September.
The company had targeted a long-distance punctuality rate of at least 60% this year, but says that goal is now unlikely to be reached.
Steinmeier steps into German coalition row — report
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier reportedly intervened in the government's recent dispute over care reform amid concerns about the survival of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition.
News magazine Der Spiegel reported that Steinmeier called Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) on Tuesday.
The intervention by Germany's largely ceremonial head of state was highly unusual.
Der Spiegel said Steinmeier's intervention came after he spoke with Merz on the sidelines of an event in Karlsruhe on Monday. The president reportedly returned to Berlin with the impression that the coalition could collapse and Germany could face a political crisis.
The government on Friday declined to confirm the reported calls and rejected suggestions that the coalition was in crisis.
Deputy government spokesperson Sebastian Hille said the government remained "capable of acting," pointing to Wednesday's cabinet agreement on care reform.
He said the three governing parties were working together "well, constructively and reliably," and accused the media of placing disagreements at the top of a "conflict escalation scale."
Department store Galeria files for insolvency, again
German department store chain Galeria has filed for insolvency for the fourth time in six years, putting the future of some 12,000 employees in doubt.
A spokesperson for the Düsseldorf district court said the application was filed on Friday morning.
Galeria said its 83 stores would remain open for the time being.
The Verdi trade union blamed "outrageous management mistakes" for the latest crisis and demanded rapid answers about what would happen to employees.
"Employees need a plan for the future now, not smoke and mirrors," Verdi retail chief Silke Zimmer said.
Galeria previously filed for insolvency in 2020, 2022 and 2024. Its most recent difficulties followed the collapse of Austrian investor Rene Benko's Signa empire, its former parent company.
A consortium comprising US investment firm NRDC Equity Partners and entrepreneur Bernd Beetz's BB Kapital SA took over Galeria in 2024.
Benko, who once controlled Galeria as well as Berlin's KaDeWe luxury department store, is currently serving a prison sentence for fraud.
Germany's 1,000th player: 'I had no idea'
New Germany international Mika Baur has admitted he was completely unaware that he was making history when he became the 1,000th player to represent the men's national football team.
"I had no idea about it. I found out after the game," the 22-year-old Celtic midfielder said following Germany's 2-0 win over Serbia. "I'm delighted."
Baur came on for goalscorer Tom Bischof in the 77th minute and said the experience was difficult to put into words.
"It's a feeling you have where you hope it doesn't go away," he said.
His phone was flooded with messages when he switched off airplane mode in the dressing room, while his debut shirt is destined for a special place.
"It's going to my parents and will be framed," said Baur, whose father Markus was part of Germany's handball World Cup-winning team in 2007.
Read more about Germany's win over Serbia here: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
German recovery still on shaky ground, trade group warns
Germany's emerging economic recovery remains fragile despite an improving outlook, the country's foreign trade association BGA has warned.
A BGA survey found companies reporting improved business conditions after diversifying supply and distribution routes and adapting to recent crises. However, many firms said red tape was hampering their operations.
"Companies can see light at the end of the tunnel again, but they are still driving with the handbrake on," BGA President Dirk Jandura said.
Leading German economic institutes have raised their growth forecast for this year to 1.3%, up from 0.6% in their spring forecast. The government is also expected to raise its forecast next week.
Debt-financed government spending on infrastructure and defense is a major driver of the expected growth.
Jandura said bureaucracy remained a significant drag, with 82% of companies surveyed naming it as one of the biggest obstacles to competitiveness and 78% saying they had yet to notice any reduction in red tape.
The improvement has also yet to reach the labor market, according to BGA, with more companies in the sector planning to cut jobs than create them.
German university graduates rise 3%
The number of students and doctoral candidates graduating from German universities has risen by 3%, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Some 527,600 people completed a degree in 2025, an increase of 16,000 from the previous year. Women accounted for 53% of graduates, unchanged from 2024.
Almost half of all qualifications were bachelor's degrees, with their number rising 4% to 256,000. Master's degrees increased 1% to 150,800.
The number of master's and state-exam qualifications allowing graduates to enter the teaching profession rose 6% to 32,400.
Law, economics and social sciences accounted for the largest share of qualifications at 41%, followed by engineering at 25%.
Union slams VW over scrapping labor agreements
Germany's IG Metall union has sharply criticized Volkswagen over its latest cost-cutting drive, accusing management of provoking a conflict "that the company cannot afford."
Thorsten Gröger, IG Metall's regional head for Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that VW's approach was "disrespectful toward its own employees" and "irresponsible toward the company itself."
Gröger said worker representatives had listened to a 50-minute presentation from management without hearing "a single word" about plans to terminate key collective bargaining agreements, while the media had already been informed.
He described the move as "unprecedented in the history of Volkswagen" and said employee representatives were prepared for the dispute.
VW says employment conditions need to be revised because of mounting cost pressures.
The carmaker plans to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years, on top of previously announced reductions. Around half of the additional cuts could come in Germany.
The longer-term future of entire VW plants in Emden, Hannover and Zwickau, as well as Audi's Neckarsulm site, also remains uncertain.
German coalition infighting evokes Scholz-era collapse
Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is stepping up pressure on its center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) coalition partners ahead of talks next week on a series of contested economic and social reforms.
CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann said Labor Minister Bärbel Bas, who is also an SPD co-leader, needed to produce legislation on pension reform "so that we can finally negotiate concretely."
Her comments to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) newspaper come as Chancellor Friedrich Merz prepares to bring labor market reforms before the coalition committee next week. Merz said this week that Germany had "some catching up to do" when it came to making the labor market more flexible.
The Handelsblatt newspaper reported that CDU parliamentary leaders were considering withholding support for Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil's income tax reform until Bas submits legislation on pensions and the labor market.
One government official described the increasingly fraught atmosphere as "real traffic-light vibes," according to the Handelsblatt, a reference to the bitter disputes that preceded the collapse of former Chancellor Olaf Scholz's three-party "traffic light coalition."
The CDU argues that reforms agreed by the coalition in July were a package and that the SPD cannot expect its preferred measures to go ahead while delaying concessions it made on pensions and the labor market.
Among the most contentious plans is the proposed abolition of penalty-free early retirement after 45 years of contributions. The measure faces opposition within the SPD as well as from several CDU state premiers.
The coalition committee is due to meet next week as the government tries to resolve disputes not only over pensions and the labor market but also taxation, care funding and other reforms.

US Targets Russia's A7 Network In New Iran Sanctions Push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:52:06 UTC
18:52:06 KST

WASHINGTON -- US authorities designated the A7 financial network as a "significant transnational criminal organization" in the latest step by Western authorities to try and choke the sprawling Kremlin-backed scheme to evade sanctions.
The move, announced by the US Treasury Department on October 1, comes as A7 -- backed by a fugitive Moldovan oligarch and a major Russian Defense Ministry-linked bank -- continues to grow, by some expert accounts, exponentially.
Treasury said the A7 network of companies, known as subagents, disguised payments involving sanctioned entities as legitimate commercial transactions, helping Russian and Iranian entities move money outside traditional banking channels, including to facilitate Iranian oil sales and weapons procurement.
"Treasury is dismantling the financial infrastructure that allows Iran and other adversaries to evade sanctions, move illicit funds, and undermine the integrity of the global financial system," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The measures, which also include sanctions targeting Iran's automotive, rail, manufacturing, and metals sectors, are part of the Trump administration's broader Operation Economic Outcast campaign to cut off Tehran's access to international finance and revenue.
"Today's action targeting A7 continues Treasury's unprecedented efforts to isolate Iran and its financial enablers," Bessent added.
FinCEN, the Treasury bureau responsible for combating illicit finance, said A7's subagents processed more than $17 billion between January 2025 and June 2026.
A7 denied any links to Iran in a statement on October 2, saying it "categorically rejects any allegations that it has worked with Iran or terrorist organizations" and that it was providing "uninterrupted payment settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures."
A7 claimed that as of January it was processing more than 2,000 transactions a day, with a total volume exceeding 7.5 trillion rubles, or about $91.5 billion, according to Treasury.
The network also provided channels for Iranian entities, including the Central Bank of Iran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, to move funds internationally.
Treasury said A7-linked companies were involved in about $140 million in Iranian sanctions-evasion transactions and about $1.6 million in weapons procurement. It also linked the network to Nobitex, Iran's largest digital-asset exchange.
Several A7 entities were already sanctioned by Washington in August 2025.
FinCEN proposed a rule that would prohibit the transmission of funds involving A7's subagents and issued an alert to help financial institutions identify suspicious transactions connected to the network.
Senior US officials, speaking to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity, said the proposed rule would send a strong signal to banks in China, the United Arab Emirates, and Kazakhstan that depend on access to US correspondent banking.
The officials said mapping A7's hundreds of intermediaries would give banks information to monitor, block, and report transactions.
RFE/RL has previously reported on A7's activities, including its operations in Kyrgyzstan. RFE/RL investigations have also examined the roles of Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor and Russia's Promsvyazbank in the network, as well as A7's ruble-backed cryptocurrency.
Officials compared the move targeting rail transit to Washington's earlier targeting of Iran's aviation sector, saying foreign rail operators, terminals, logistics companies, and financial institutions supporting Iranian rail activity could face sanctions.
"If Turkmenistan stops taking Iranian cars at Sarakhs, the China route is closed," one senior US official said, referring to the city on the Iran-Turkmenistan border that is a major transit hub.
Treasury also targeted Iran's two main automotive companies and foreign suppliers of auto parts in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, Indonesia, and Turkey. Two China-based steel companies were among those sanctioned in the metals sector.
Maria Shagina, a senior fellow for geoeconomics and strategy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said A7's designation was notable because the network was built in Russia but was being targeted as part of Washington's campaign against Iran.
"It's quite telling that the US is designating a major evasion network born and bred from Russia via the Iran connection," Shagina told RFE/RL.
She said the decision to target A7's wider network, rather than only the main operation, could disrupt financial links in third countries.

Poland
Unknown Publisher

Mzia Amaglobeli awarded this year's Lech Wałęsa Solidarity Prize
30.09.2026
On 30 September, Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski presented the Lech Wałęsa Solidarity Prize in Warsaw. This year's laureate is a Georgian journalist, Mzia Amaglobeli.
The ceremony gathered representatives of the Polish authorities, foreign guests, and members of Polish, Georgian, and Belarusian civil societies. The gala was inaugurated by the Chair of the Committee, Poland’s former president Lech Wałęsa. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski delivered a laudatory speech about the awardee.
The prize was awarded to Mzia Amaglobeli, a journalist, the founder and chief editor of the Netgazeti news website, established in 2010, and of the Batumelebi newspaper and news portal, established in 2001. Both rank among the oldest independent media outlets in Georgia. Her news services are a symbol of independent journalism: they protect human rights, oppose corruption and the abuse of power.
In August 2025, a court in Batumi sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. When incarcerated, she was subjected to psychological abuse by police officers and denied legal assistance. This is a symbolic sentence against all independent journalists in Georgia.
Irma Dimitradze, Mzia Amaglobeli’s friend who accepted the prize in her name, said:
Many years ago, Mr Wałęsa and the people of Poland had to struggle for democracy against the regime backed by the Soviet Union. Many years later, Mzia and the people of Georgia are once again having to struggle for democracy. [...] The monster is now called the Russian Federation. [...] The propaganda of Russian cognitive operations has caused harm in many, including invisible ways. Yet, there are people like us—Georgians and Poles—who have experienced and can recognise it at first glance. [...] Poland understands us without words. This understanding is important and we are endlessly grateful for it.
In his speech, Poland’s top diplomat Radosław Sikorski stressed that Mzia Amaglobeli’s story reminds us that the defence of human freedom and dignity is not the sole responsibility of states or international organisations—it is the responsibility of each and every one of us.
An authoritarian regime does not begin with people being sent to prison, it begins when fear triggers apathy
- Sikorski said.
Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski also reiterated that the freedom of speech needs protection especially when speech becomes inconvenient. Today, amid rising authoritarian trends, it is particularly important to express solidarity with those who are brave enough to defend democracy.
Our mission to disrupt the established order was accomplished thanks to Solidarity. Today, we are awarding this prize to ensure that the next generation confirms our victory. Only then will we truly win. As I am presenting the prize today, I hope for more. I hope that the next generation will take this path and come up with solutions to modern challenges.
- said Poland’s former president Lech Wałęsa.
* * *
The Lech Wałęsa Solidarity Prize was established in 2014 to mark 25 years of Poland’s independence. In 2024, Minister Radosław Sikorski decided to relaunch the initiative. The prize is awarded for outstanding achievements in promoting and defending democracy and civil liberties.
Previous awardees include Mustafa Dzhemilev, a long-standing chair of the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People who fought for the Tatars’ rights in occupied Crimea; Zhanna Nemtsova, daughter of Boris Nemtsov who has continued her father’s work; Pavel Latushka, one of the leaders of the Belarusian democratic opposition; and a Cuban dissident Berta Soler Fernández.
The prize, organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in cooperation with the Foundation “Lech Wałęsa Institute”, reflects Poland’s commitment to the protection of democratic values.

Man City verdict puts UK-UAE diplomatic relations under strain
- A court found Manchester City guilty of nearly all 115 financial charges, risking penalties like points deduction or expulsion, straining UK-UAE diplomatic and investment relations.
- The UAE has invested over £30 billion in the UK, but the ruling has caused frustration and may affect future large-scale investments and defense cooperation.
- UK officials stress Premier League independence despite political tensions; Manchester City plans to appeal, while the case threatens football governance and bilateral ties ahead of an October summit.
AI generated
A historic legal ruling against Manchester City Football Club has placed diplomatic ties between the UK and the United Arab Emirates under significant strain, with billions of pounds in projected foreign investment at stake.
Over the past five years, the UAE has poured more than £30 billion (S$50.6 billion) into major UK sectors, including defence, life sciences and technology. The two nations are eager to maintain their financial partnership, and an investment summit is pencilled in for October, but frustration on both sides has escalated due to the fallout surrounding the Manchester City case.
In a seismic judgment late last week, Abu Dhabi-owned Manchester City was found guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against it by England’s Premier League after a four-year investigation. The club artificially inflated its financial results by more than £900 million, according to the findings of an independent commission published on Sept 29.
Potential punishments include points deduction, heavy fines or even expulsion from the Premier League.
The ruling is a major blow for the 18-year soft power project, at the top of which is Manchester City’s ultimate owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the brother of the UAE’s president. The Emirati owners, with Khaldoon Al Mubarak as the club’s chairman, have delivered eight premier league titles and transformed the club into a footballing superpower.
Emirati officials have warned the UK government that the severity of the ruling could undermine their appetite for future grand-scale UK commitments, according to people familiar with the matter. They consider the Premier League’s actions to have an influence on the bilateral state relationship, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing undisclosed information.
UK government officials are equally frustrated by the conduct of their UAE counterparts in relation to the scandal, according to other people familiar with the matter. They believe some in the Gulf nation must have been aware of the extent of Manchester City’s wrongdoing, even while insisting there was nothing untoward, said the people, who asked not to be identified talking about private deliberations.
The scandal has also caused splits in the UK government. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s comments thanking Manchester City’s owners for their investment riled his own politicians who want to keep the process independent of government influence.
A spokesman for the UK government declined to comment. The UAE’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The frustration from both sides comes at a crucial time for UK-UAE relations. The current investment partnership is up for discussion ahead of an Abu Dhabi summit to be held in London later in October, with British officials eager to secure more commitments.
Man City ruling may test billion-dollar ties: Mideast money
Under the original five-year agreement, the UAE’s sovereign wealth fund Mubadala, led by Mubarak, committed £10 billion to British industries, though the total has reached nearly £30 billion. That has been a small part of a global commitment: Abu Dhabi, home to wealth funds holding more than $2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) of assets, is planning to invest another $1.4 trillion in the US and has pledged $46 billion in Germany.
Defence is central to UK-UAE talks, with the need for cooperation heightening due to the ongoing US-Iranian war and wider unrest in the Middle East. The UK lent military support to the UAE after the US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic prompted Tehran to retaliate against Washington’s Gulf allies.
Despite both sides agreeing that talks on defence are far more important than football, the Premier League’s judgment has injected political tension into the negotiations. Longer standing issues remain contentious, including the UAE’s alleged role in the Sudanese civil war and the thwarted Emirates-backed takeover attempt of The Telegraph newspaper.
Officials are now trying to smooth over the issue. In a UK media interview on Sept 30, Burnham thanked City Football Group – the owners of Man City – for their investment in Manchester.
“I would be really concerned to lose them,” Burnham said. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.”
The relationship is important to Burnham and fellow senior politicians. Shortly after becoming Prime Minister in July, Burnham spoke to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. They connected over Manchester, where Burnham was mayor before ascending to the top job. Massive Emirati capital injections into urban regeneration across the east of the city helped bolster Burnham’s political profile during his tenure.
UK government officials have privately suggested that Premier League investigations are outside their control, given sporting regulation and judicial matters are not subject to state influence.
“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions,” Manchester City said on Sept 29. The club has until Oct 2 to appeal the decision.
Manchester City has been one of the UAE’s most successful outlets for projecting soft power. Under Sheikh Mansour’s ownership, the club came out of the shadow of crosstown competitor Manchester United and usurped its historically more successful rival as a perennial challenger for league titles. It has attracted a string of star players, notably Sergio Aguero, Kevin De Bruyne and current striker Erling Haaland.
The league has yet to set out sanctions, but the guilty verdict already threatens to upend the Premier League and football in England more widely. Manchester City’s haul of trophies during the period in question potentially opens the door to compensation claims from rival clubs and even fans.
While no prosecutor is known to be looking at criminal charges, false accounting is a crime in England and Wales that carries potential jail terms. Meanwhile, the club’s auditors could face a probe from the Financial Reporting Council. Neither regulator responded to requests for comment.
The UK has long touted its investment links with the UAE. A little over a week before the Manchester City verdict, Burnham posted a video to his almost one million TikTok followers showing him inside a McLaren sports car boasting “that is the sound of Britain making things again”.
Burnham’s comments came as McLaren Automotive announced plans to invest £500 million into the UK, part of a larger commitment from McLaren Automotive shareholder L’IMAD Holding, a sovereign investor of the Government of Abu Dhabi.
But the prime minister’s recent comments backing Manchester City’s owners have riled local lawmakers. They risk undermining legislation aimed at preserving the operational autonomy of the Independent Football Regulator, which is responsible for determining the outcome of the case against Manchester City, Bloomberg reported.
Downing Street later issued a statement saying Manchester City are not “above the rules”. BLOOMBERG

Large volumes of medical supplies for Gaza face wait times of 74 days for Israeli clearance: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:49:19 UTC
18:49:19 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Large volumes of medical supplies meant for Gaza wait a median of 74 days for clearance by Israeli authorities, the World Health Organization said Friday, urging “unimpeded and predictable” access for the much-needed aid.
“Not one hospital in Gaza is fully functional,” Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the occupied Palestinian territory, told reporters in Geneva.
Van De Weerdt said chronic shortages of medicines and medical supplies remain a major obstacle to restoring health services, despite a year having passed since the ceasefire was announced.
"Without those items, no hospital will ever be fully or even partially functional," she said.
According to the WHO's latest analysis, large volumes of medical supplies wait a median of 74 days, roughly 2 1/2 months, for Israeli clearance.
“If the shipment hasn't been approved, then we start that lengthy, cumbersome process all over again with no guarantees for a different outcome,” she said.
Medicines have an approval rate of nearly 87%, while medical equipment – including X-ray machines, sterilization equipment, and spare parts for CT scanners – is regularly rejected, she said, "often with no explanation given."
"Every extra day in storage or in transit brings medicines a day closer to expiry, an equipment closer to being damaged before it ever reaches the person who needs it," she warned.
She also described the security situation in Gaza as “very, very precarious,” saying collecting medical supplies from the Kerem Shalom crossing requires WHO teams to travel through an area controlled by the Israeli military using armored vehicles and personal protective equipment.
The process must be coordinated with Israeli authorities and teams often face delays in receiving the green light, she said, adding that logistical staff can leave early in the morning and return late in the evening with supplies that had been waiting at the crossing.
The WHO called for the “unimpeded and predictable” entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale and the use of multiple crossings.

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Units participating in the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) Echelon 2026 exercise are actively using ground robotic systems to evacuate the wounded and damaged equipment, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"At Russia’s Chebarkul training ground during the Echelon 2026 special exercise involving CSTO logistics forces and assets (collective forces), special attention is being paid to organizing the evacuation and repair of damaged equipment under conditions where enemy unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) pose a threat. Units are practicing the delivery of supplies to the front line using modern equipment--ground robotic systems and UAVs – as well as the evacuation of the wounded and damaged equipment," the ministry stated.

The exercise participants also organize workshops at the disabled vehicle collecting point. Based on experience gained during the special military operation, equipment repair and restoration posts and stations were set up in underground fortifications.
At the welding station, BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles were fitted with additional protection against enemy UAVs and FPV drones. At the missile and artillery weapons repair section, work is underway to restore a D-30 gun. Repairs of motorcycles, quad bikes, special transport vehicles, and ground robotic systems are also being carried out. Spare parts are being printed, in part, using 3D printers.
Contingents of CSTO forces (collective forces) from the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Russian Federation, and the Republic of Tajikistan are participating in the CSTO exercise at the Chebarkul training ground. These include military contingents, special forces’ units of internal affairs bodies, security agencies and special services, authorized bodies in the sphere of emergencies prevention and relief, as well as task groups of the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat.
In total, about 2,000 military personnel and 350 pieces of weaponry, military and specialized equipment are engaged. The maneuvers’ key features include the extensive use of various types of UAVs and robotic systems, as well as combat practice based on experience gained during the special military operation in Ukraine.
