Two opposing demonstrations this Saturday, one by opponents of migration and a separate event organised by migrant rights activists, are set to take place about 50 metres of each other in central Vilnius, prompting police to deploy more than 200 officers to maintain public order.
The demonstrations come after a series of incidents that have intensified debate over migration in Lithuania, including an incident in September when a group of men brought a pig’s head to a mosque in Kaunas and a suspected Quran burning in Vilnius. Both incidents are being investigated by police.
The right-wing National Alliance party plans to hold a protest at 14:00 in Vinco Kudirkos Square, near the government headquarters. The party has called for demonstrations against what it describes as “mass migration”.
Among its demands are reducing migration quotas and deporting foreign nationals who have committed crimes. The party has offered free bus transportation to Vilnius from other parts of Lithuania.
A counterprotest organised by the groups Antifa and Solidarumo grandis (Chain of Solidarity) is scheduled to begin 30 minutes earlier at the same location under the title “Demonstration Against Racism”.
Organisers of the counterprotest say the number of migrants in Lithuania is lower than some politicians claim and accuse politicians of fuelling panic and spreading misleading information.
Vytautas Sinica, parliament member and leader of the National Alliance, said protesters on his side would be urged to behave respectfully but that he expected provocations from Antifa supporters.
“I am surprised that the municipality allowed them to move next to us,” Sinica told LRT RADIO. “We are also hiring a private security service.”
Sinica estimated that about 500 people could attend his party’s protest. He said buses from Klaipėda and Kaunas had already filled their available seats.
“If there are provocateurs, pig heads or posters encouraging violence, we will ask security services and police officers to discipline such people,” he said.
Antifa, meanwhile, rejected insinuations that provocations may come from their side.
“It’s comical to hear warnings in advance that any potential provocations will inevitably come from the anti-racist protest side. The actual chronicle of recent weeks looks somewhat different: Muslim prayers are disrupted with a pig’s head, the Quran is burned in Vilnius, threats against Muslims are made, and law enforcement have launched investigations. So, perhaps before identifying the perpetrators of future provocations, it would be worth taking a moment to look back at the provocations that have already occurred?” reads the commentary received by LRT.lt from Antifa Lithuania.
Meanwhile, the migrant rights organisation Sienos grupė, or Border Group, is organising a separate event nearby at 13:00 called “Wake Up From Hate”.
The organisers said the event was intended as a response to the incident at the Kaunas mosque and the National Alliance protest.
They plan to set up a display showing migration routes, where participants will be able to mark countries to which they or their relatives have migrated. Participants will also be invited to share their personal stories.
“We would not want to create a narrative of conflict or threat in advance,” Emilija Švobaitė, one of the event’s organisers, told LRT. “Our goal is to create a calm space for conversation and to remind people that migration is not an abstract political issue – it is part of the history of many people and families living in Lithuania.”
Police prepare for potential tensions
Vilnius police plan to deploy 235 officers for the events, including officers arriving from other Lithuanian cities. Officers from the Public Security Service will also assist.
Jevgenijus Liepis, head of the Public Order Board at the Vilnius County Police Department, said the proximity of the demonstrations presented an additional challenge but that police were prepared.
“We will take all measures to ensure that participants in both protests can peacefully express their opinions,” Liepis said.
Police are considering additional “technical solutions” to keep the demonstrations safe, although it was not yet clear whether barriers would be erected between the groups.
Police have also been monitoring public communications for signs of planned provocations. Liepis said no such activity had been detected so far.
“At this moment, we are not recording provocations or calls to violate public order,” he said.
The Vilnius municipal government said it could not prohibit either demonstration because both applications complied with the country’s Law on Meetings.
Andžej Dinikis, head of the municipality’s Public Order Group, said organisers had been informed of their responsibilities regarding safety.
He said both groups had initially asked to gather at the same location, in which case authorities would coordinate alternative locations and times.
“If people organise provocations, neither 50 meters nor 5 kilometres will stop them,” Dinikis said.

A Flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac App Could Have Let Hackers Grab Sensitive Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.
The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.
“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”
OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.
The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.
Objective-See Foundation researchers found, though, that there is a trusted component, a script interpreter, that would accept an untrusted script (or list of commands to run) and could then be manipulated to deliver this script into the main ChatGPT process. “They also check the parent and grandparent of that process, but the malicious script just spawns the script interpreter three times and then makes the request so it will satisfy the requirements,” Wardle says.
The vulnerability was “insanely trivial” to exploit, he adds, and his proof of concept only required about a dozen lines of code. In addition to accessing ChatGPT chat logs, the vulnerability could also be used to get ChatGPT to run commands for the attacker, such as accessing a browser or other sensitive applications, with the requests appearing as legitimate instructions issued by the OpenAI software.
Wardle will present analysis of a number of AI macOS application bugs at Objective by the Sea, an Apple-focused security conference in November.
He recently found a flaw, now patched, in the dictation feature of Meta’s new Muse AI assistant that could have been exploited by a local attacker to grab a mishandled authentication token and gain access to user data. And he says that he has already submitted a new vulnerability finding to OpenAI related to the integration between ChatGPT and the company’s new always-on Dots AI assistant. OpenAI is currently reviewing his report.
“AI companies are fixated on adding features right now,” Wardle says. “But as always, the more features, the broader the attack surface. So all of these companies need to be fully focused on security, and from what I can see, it still often seems like an afterthought.”

Overnight on October 2, units of Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka oil refinery in Volgograd, Volgograd region. Explosions and a fire were recorded at the facility.
LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka is one of the largest oil refineries in the Russian Federation. Its refining capacity is about 15 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility produces motor gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuel. It is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
In addition, the Samara linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) in the area of the settlement of Prosvet, Samara region, was hit. A fire was recorded at the facility.
The Samara LPDS is a production facility and a major oil receiving, storage and blending hub. Oil reaches the station via trunk pipelines from Tatarstan, Western Siberia and other oil-producing regions of Russia. The facility blends high- and low-sulfur crude from different fields to produce Urals export-grade crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia's total oil exports. The facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.

Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha Special Operations Center, together with the Unmanned Systems Forces, Special Operations Forces and the Main Intelligence Directorate, struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, as well as the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations near the settlement of Prosvet. Fires were recorded at the facilities following the strikes.
The Volgograd Oil Refinery was also hit in a joint operation with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate. A fire was recorded at the refinery.
NASA's FIRMS satellite service detected fire hotspots near the delayed coking unit and the ELOU-AVT-1 and ELOU-AVT-5 units, which are key processing facilities at the refinery.
As reported, the Transneft hub caught fire in Samara following explosions, while a fire broke out in the area of an oil refinery and chemical plant in Volgograd.

At the age of 100, Zenon Vrublevskyi, a veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, has died
Kyiv • UNN
In Lviv, OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army Zenon Vrublevskyi has died. He survived captivity, Soviet camps, and arrest.
In the 100th year of his life, Zenon Vrublevsky, an OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division, died. This was reported by Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv Regional Military Administration, on Telegram on October 2, UNN writes.
Almost a century of life. And what a life! An OUN underground member, a soldier of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. He experienced captivity and Soviet camps. He fought for Ukraine back when one could pay with freedom or life merely for thinking about its independence
More detailed information about the funeral will be announced later.
Supplement
Zenon Vrublevsky was born in Lviv on March 17, 1927. At the age of 16, he left the gymnasium and secretly, without his parents’ knowledge, volunteered for the Galicia Division. Later, he was the personal driver of Colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic Ivan Rembolovych. During the fighting in the "Brody cauldron," he was taken prisoner and transported to a concentration camp in the Urals. After spending two years there, he managed to escape. In Lviv, he established contacts with the OUN underground.
He was arrested in 1947 and sentenced to 25 years in prison and five years of deprivation of rights, with confiscation of property. He served his sentence in the prisons and camps of Sverdlovsk, Karaganda, Kemerovo, and Vorkuta. After his release, he was forced to live in Vorkuta for several more years. He returned to Lviv in 1960.

Bonds steady as French borrowing costs hit 24-year high and UK 30-year yields top 6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:43:43 UTC
18:43:43 KST

Government bond markets steadied on Friday morning after a sell-off pushed France's 10-year borrowing costs to their highest since 2002, lifted UK 30-year yields above 6% for the first time since 1998 and drove the benchmark US 10-year yield to a 24-year high.
Global bond markets found their footing on Friday morning, with yields slipping back after a turbulent Thursday in which government borrowing costs in Europe and the US hit multi-decade highs.
Yields, which rise when bond prices fall, retreated as Brent crude slipped about 2% to around $99.95 a barrel, tempering fears that the energy shock would keep inflation high and force central banks into more rate hikes.
In the UK, the yield on 30-year government bonds, or gilts, fell to around 5.92% after climbing above 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. The 10-year yield dropped to about 5.37%, below the 19-year high reached earlier this week, while the two-year yield slid more than six basis points to around 4.77%.
Thursday's sell-off also hit British bank shares, with NatWest, Lloyds, HSBC and Barclays falling around 4% to 5%.
The losses deepened after Sky News reported that Chancellor John Healey had summoned bank bosses to a meeting ahead of his 28 October budget, fuelling speculation about new bank taxes.
France in the firing line
France's 10-year yield hit 4.96% on Thursday, its highest since July 2002, before easing to about 4.92% on Friday at about 11 am CEST. The extra yield investors demand to hold French rather than German debt reached over 140 basis points this week, the widest gap since 2012.
That gap jumped 13.9 basis points on Thursday, its biggest daily rise since March 2020, according to Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid.
"The daily moves were reminiscent of the Euro crisis in many respects, with sovereign contagion a big talking point," Reid told clients in a note.
The sell-off came as Paris unveiled a 2027 budget seeking €43 billion in new savings to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP this year to 5% next year. Public debt stands at a post-war record of 119% of GDP, and France plans to borrow a record €340 billion next year.
"Here and there, I hear the prophets of doom promising us worse times ahead. I would like to reiterate here that France's signature is solid," French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said.
France's fiscal watchdog, the High Council of Public Finances, was less upbeat, calling the government's 1% growth forecast for 2027 optimistic and a return below the EU's 3% deficit limit by 2029 very unlikely.
"With a difficult political process ahead, French bonds are likely to remain under pressure, while the threshold for ECB intervention remains high," ING analysts wrote.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polls ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Fresh figuresadded to the inflation worries behind the sell-offas eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, its highest in three years, up from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate published on Friday.
Economists had expected 3.6%, and Spain's annual rate hit 5%.
It was the seventh month in a row above the European Central Bank's 2% target as traders expect the ECB, which raised rates in June and September, to lift its deposit rate by another quarter point to 2.75% by year-end.
US Treasuries retreat from 24-year high
In the US, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.34% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before pulling back to around 5.26%.
Surging energy costs are stoking inflation, while the AI and data-centre boom competes for capital. After a rate hike in September, markets expect at least three more from the Federal Reserve by mid-2027.
"As yields have crept higher, that is going to tighten financial conditions and could increase the risk of a slowdown," said Danny Zaid, portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management.
Overall, the bill is mounting.
Developed economies paid more than $3.3 trillion (€2.9tn) in interest on internationally traded government bonds over the past year, according to the Washington-based Institute of International Finance, which is more than the estimated global spending on defence or AI.

Ousted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has been moved to a military-run hospital in Khartoum for treatment and needs further medical care abroad, his lawyer said Thursday.
Bashir, 82, was ousted by Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2019 after months of mass protests that brought an end to his nearly three-decade rule.
The army and RSF later turned against each other over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the military as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Their dispute erupted into war in April 2023, triggering a devastating conflict that has killed and displaced large numbers of people and left much of Sudan in ruins.
Bashir had been moved from prison to a hospital before the war broke out and was later transferred to the town of Merowe in northern Sudan, where he was placed under military guard.
Bashir was sent to Khartoum for medical tests after developing symptoms that required diagnosis and treatment outside Sudan, his lawyer, Mohamed Alhassan Alameen, told Reuters.
In a statement Wednesday, Bashir’s family said his need for medical treatment outside Sudan "has become critical and urgent, and cannot be delayed any longer," but said they had not received official permission to send him abroad.
It was unclear precisely what condition Bashir was suffering from. Sudan’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several prominent Sudanese Islamist figures also called for his transfer out of the country on social media.
Any such move would likely cause discord within Sudan and could draw international condemnation, as Bashir is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges including genocide. He also faces open cases in Sudan.
During Bashir’s three decades in power, Sudan was listed by the U.S. as a state sponsor of terrorism and was subject to wide-ranging sanctions. Protesters during the popular uprising accused him and his Islamist National Congress Party of widespread corruption and repression.
After his ouster, Bashir was tried on various charges and convicted of corruption and illicit financing, for which he was serving a prison sentence when the war began.

Egypt builds rail link in Sinai, with Israel watching closely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:39:43 UTC
18:39:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt's rail link project in Sinai sets off alarm bells in Israel
Egypt is constructing a new railway to connect the Suez Canal on the Red Sea to the northern Sinai town of Taba near the border with Israel, a project that has raised alarm bells in Israel and prompted calls for tight supervision from Tel Aviv.
The railway, some Israeli media outlets have claimed, would change the demography of Sinai, for years considered a symbol of isolation on the border between Egypt and Israel.
It could also enable the flow of military logistics at high speed, consequently changing the entire regional equation, one Israeli media outlet warned.
Extending over 500 kilometres from al-Ferdan, the world's largest rotating bridge over the Suez Canal, to Taba, the new rail line is Egypt's new attempt to create the infrastructure necessary for the development of Sinai, a territory the size of Israel, Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon combined that has remained largely underdeveloped for decades.
An empty, massive expanse of desert on the Egyptian Israeli border was always viewed as a good sandy buffer against direct contact between the Egyptian and Israeli militaries, bolstering limits to troop deployments on the shared border between the two countries, ones enshrined in the Security Annex of the 1979 peace treaty, analysts said.
But an outsized buffer has come at a heavy cost for Egypt's national security, the same analysts added.
"My belief is that the lack of development in this area for year gave the chance for terrorist groups to take root and grow in it," remarked Gen. Ali Hefzi, the former governor of North Sinai.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that terrorist groups exploited Sinai's sparsely populated geography because of the lack of services in it to expand.
"This is why development is becoming a prerequisite of security in this Egyptian territory," Gen. Hefzi said.
It took the Egyptian army and police a sizeable amount of resources to eradicate a branch of the Islamic State group that popped up in Sinai between 2012 and 2023 and wanted to establish an Islamic caliphate in this territory.
Thousands of Egyptian army personnel and policemen were also either killed or injured over the same decade, during which Egypt tried to uproot the group from Sinai, according to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
Dual goals
Sinai remains generally empty, despite its huge size. Covering almost 6% of Egypt's overall space of 1 million square kilometres, this territory is home to around 600,000 people only.
In the past few years, Egypt accelerated the development of this territory, implementing agricultural and industrial development projects worth tens of millions of dollars.
The same projects also include a new network of roads and educational institutions that try to meet the needs of the territory's residents which have been complaining from the lack of services for years, observers said.
Apart from easing the movement of persons to and from Sinai, the project could also serve as an alternative backup to the Suez Canal for certain types of cargo, thus competing with old Israeli initiatives for a rail link between the Red Sea port of Eilat and the Mediterranean Port of Ashdod, Israeli media declared.
Having been discussed since 1950, the Eilat-Ashdod rail link would be Israel's first attempt to connect the Red Sea with the Mediterranean through an overland route.
According to initial plans, the core section of the project would run from Beersheba/Dimona in southern Israel through the Negev and Arava to Eilat, covering between 180 and 260 kilometres.
The project was approved by the Israeli cabinet in 2012, having received interest from China and other countries for construction and financing.
Egyptian specialists do not underestimate Israeli fears from the new rail link between Suez and Taba sabotaging the planned Eilat-Ashdod link.
The Egyptian project, they say, aims primarily to preserve the competitiveness of the Suez Canal route, contribute to Sinai's development, and protect Egypt's status as an international trade nod at a time of high rivalry.
"The Egyptian project will necessarily negatively affect the planned Israeli project," Wael Qadurra, a former deputy head of the Suez Canal Authority, told TNA.
Egypt's construction of the railway, he added, would make the Israeli project both "useless" and "unfeasible", even as its main objective remains to allow for a speedier transport of goods between Egypt's Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.
Egyptian-Israeli relations at a critical time
The Egyptians are working round the clock to finalise the new Suez-Taba rail link which enjoys support from Sisi and is directly supervised by the minister of transport and the prime minister, according to Israeli media.
The line will pump economic life into Sinai's desert and strengthen Egyptian sovereignty in the region, it adds.
The basic part of the project is in place already, a 100-kilometre line between Suez and the North Sinai town of Bir al-Abd that has returned to work after a five-decade slump since the 1967 Egyptian-Israeli war.
On 30 September, Egyptian Minister of Transport Kamel al-Wazir highlighted the importance of transport and infrastructure projects in Sinai for development in this Egyptian territory.
Commenting on Israeli media reports about the new railway, he added that Egypt has the full right to develop each inch of Sinai.
"Sinai is an inseparable part of the Egyptian homeland," the minister of transport said.
"The primary goal of the road network and the railway [constructed in Sinai] is to serve residents and ease the movement of persons and goods," he told Egyptian television.
The construction of the new rail link comes, meanwhile, at a critical time for relations between Egypt and Israel, analysts said.
These relations are coming under renewed stress against the background of a number of regional developments, including Israel's procrastination to implement the Gaza ceasefire plan which was proposed by US President Donald Trump and approved in Sharm el-Sheikh in October last year, they added.
Israel is also expressing objection to the measures Egypt has taken in Sinai since 2023, including the deployment of additional troops in the border area, in what the Israelis describe as a violation of the Security Annex of the 1979 peace treaty.
However, this tension appears to be only one aspect of complex relations between Cairo and Tel Aviv.
An international newspaper has just revealed that Egypt's former intelligence chief Abbas Kamel visited Israel and met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu days ahead of the October 7, 2023 attacks by Gaza factions to warn him against the imminent attacks.
"Despite political differences and tensions between the two countries, they are capable of maintaining a minimum level of security and intelligence coordination," Gen. Hefzi said. "This coordination is important for finding solutions to problems that emerge between the two sides, not to mention security coordination on the shared border and coordinating aid entry into Gaza."

Eurozone inflation spikes to 3.8%: Is your country on the worst list?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:39:21 UTC
18:39:21 KST

Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, a three-year high above forecasts. Energy drove the spike. See where prices rose fastest.
Eurozone inflation spiked to 3.8% year-over-year in September, marking the highest rate in three years and topping economists' forecasts of a 3.6% rise.
The jump came almost entirely from one corner of the shopping basket.
Energy costs explained close to half of the inflation rate.
The flash estimate from Eurostat showed prices rising 0.6% in September alone compared with August.
The reading is the highest since September 2023, when inflation ran at 4.3%. It is also almost double the European Central Bank's 2% target, the level the ECB considers consistent with stable prices.
Core inflation told a calmer story. Stripping out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, whose prices swing sharply from month to month, it edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%, exactly in line with forecasts.
That gap leaves the ECB with a central question. Is this an energy shock that will fade, or the start of broader price pressure?
Energy prices drove the eurozone inflation spike
Energy prices rose 18.8% from a year earlier, up from 14.3% in August. In September alone, energy prices climbed 3.9%.
Energy carries a weight of about 9% in the euro area inflation basket. At an 18.8% annual rate, it added roughly 1.7 percentage points to the 3.8% headline figure.
Services inflation rose to 3.2% from 3.0%. Services are the largest piece of the basket, accounting for about 47% of the eurozone inflation basket, and cover items such as rents, restaurants, travel and insurance.
Food, alcohol and tobacco prices increased 1.4%, up from 1.1% in August. Within that group, inflation for unprocessed food such as fresh fruit, vegetables and meat jumped to 4.0% from 2.7%.
Non-energy industrial goods, which include cars, clothing and household appliances, rose 1.1%, down slightly from 1.2%. It was the only major category where annual inflation slowed.
Where was eurozone inflation highest?
Lithuania recorded the highest annual inflation rate in the euro area at 6.1%, up from 5.6% in August.
Bulgaria, which joined the euro on Jan. 1, 2026, followed at 5.6%. Cyprus and Luxembourg both posted 5.2%, ahead of Greece at 5.1% and Spain at 5.0%.
In total, six of the euro area's 21 member countries recorded inflation of 5% or more. Ten countries were at or above the 3.8% euro area average.
At the other end, Malta had the lowest rate at 2.4%, followed by Finland at 2.6% and Latvia at 2.9%. Latvia was the only member country where annual inflation eased in September.
Italy and France saw the sharpest moves among big economies
Inflation accelerated in all four of the euro area's largest economies.
Italy posted the biggest increase among them. Its annual rate climbed to 4.1% from 3.2%, and Italian prices rose 2.0% in a single month, the largest monthly increase in the bloc.
France followed, with inflation rising to 3.4% from 2.6%. As a result, French inflation is now higher than Germany's, where the rate rose to 3.3% from 2.9%.
Spain remained the highest of the four. Its inflation rate reached 5.0%, up from 4.6% in August.
What Eurozone inflation means for the ECB
The ECB raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points on 10 September.
The deposit facility rate now stands at 2.50%. It was the ECB's second increase this year, after a similar move in June.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for households and companies. That tends to slow spending. Over time, slower spending eases pressure on prices.
The ECB's September projections see headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028.
Policymakers meet next on 28-29 October in Frankfurt, with the decision due on 29 October. That meeting will not include new staff projections. The next set arrives in December.
The September data put a fresh warning in front of the ECB. Headline inflation is well above target and still rising.
Prediction markets assign a 91% chance of a further ECB rate hike at the end of the month.

I believe that formally recognising such an act would carry significance far beyond the honour bestowed upon one Individual. It would send a powerful message, particularly to our young people, thut courage is not confined to the battlefield or to any particular profession," he added.
Machchhar, a Mumbai-born pilot, was seriously injured after his co-pilot allegedly attacked him and attempted to take control of the aircraft during flydubai flight FZ1073. Despite his injuries, Machchhar continued to act to protect the 174 passengers on board, Deora said in his letter to PM Modi.
The flight, carrying 174 passengers, including 27 children, transmitted emergency signals and rapidly lost altitude before diverting to Prince Sultan Bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.According to accounts of the incident, Machchhar was attacked in the cockpit, after which an Israeli passenger and a crew member managed to enter the cockpit and helped overpower the co-pilot. The UAE has launched an investigation into the incident, with the motive behind the alleged attack still under probe.Deora said Machchhar's actions went beyond the responsibilities of his profession and demonstrated "courage, selflessness and duty" in an extreme situation."The Ashoka Chakra is India's highest peacetime gallantry decoration" and is intended to recognise conspicuous bravery, valour or self-sacrifice other than in the face of the enemy, Deora said, urging the government to consider Machchhar for the honour.The appeal comes after PM Modi spoke to Machchhar over a video call and praised his courage, presence of mind and composure during the ordeal. PM Modi told him that the country was proud of his efforts to protect the lives of those onboard.During the conversation, Machchhar told PM Modi that he recites the Hanuman Chalisa whenever he faces difficulty and had done so during the tense moments aboard the flight. He also described Modi as his "biggest idol".
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also praised Machchhar's actions, saying he helped thwart what could have been a "9/11-like" disaster.In his letter, Deora said formally recognising Machchhar would underline that courage and self-sacrifice are not confined to the battlefield or any particular profession.

Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Cambodia reattaches 2 ancient deity statue heads at Angkor Thom's gate in Angkor complex
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:37:11 CST
18:37:11 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's APSARA National Authority (ANA) has reattached the heads of two ancient deity statues at Angkor Thom's Victory Gate, located within the UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park in Siem Reap province, according to an ANA news release on Friday.
The traditional ritual, part of the Returning Spirits to Their Original Sites campaign, took place on Thursday. The ceremony was attended by Minister of Culture and Fine Arts Phoeurng Sackona and UNESCO Representative to Cambodia Flavio Bonetti, alongside Buddhist monks who were invited to chant and bless the statues.
Sackona highlighted the profound cultural and historical significance of the event. She explained that the Victory Gate served as a vital ceremonial site where Khmer kings traditionally conducted major royal rituals, including coronations and military departures.
The restoration of the deity and asura (demon) sculptures not only enhances the site's beauty but also helps restore an important part of Cambodia's cultural heritage for future generations and visitors, she said.
A total of 108 devas (gods) and asuras line the approach to the Victory Gate, representing the Hindu myth of the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. Over the centuries, particularly during periods of conflict, many of these sandstone heads were lost or scattered both within Cambodia and abroad, the news release said.
Built in the late 12th century by King Jayavarman VII, Angkor Thom was the grand capital of the ancient Khmer Empire. Its enclosure wall extends roughly three kilometers on each side, stands approximately eight meters high, and is surrounded by a moat. Five monumental gates provide access to the ancient city.
Through long-standing cooperation between the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, the ANA, and international partners including UNESCO, many of the missing heads have been recovered. Some were found through archaeological excavations, while others were recovered from international collections.
To date, almost all of the missing heads have been recovered. Only three remain in museums abroad, and efforts are continuing to facilitate their return to Cambodia and, ultimately, to their original locations, the news release said.
Bonetti expressed his appreciation for the ceremony, describing it as an important act of respect for Khmer culture and its World Heritage significance.
The Returning Spirits to Their Original Sites campaign reflects Cambodia's peaceful and secure environment, which allows heritage custodians to successfully reunite these historic sculptures with their original locations. ■

LONDON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- A new scheme allowing prisoners to be released early to prevent prisons from reaching capacity took effect in England and Wales on Thursday.
Around 700 prisoners are estimated to have been released early from prisons in England and Wales on Thursday under the new rules, according to British media. A total of some 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early by June 2027.
Under the new scheme, eligible prisoners will be released after serving a third of their total custodial sentence, rather than after serving 40 or 50 percent of their sentence.
Prisons in England and Wales are struggling with overcrowding. According to the British Ministry of Justice, 87,499 people were incarcerated in prisons across England and Wales as of Monday, representing 98 percent of usable capacity.
Although early released prisoners would be subject to electronic tagging, the policy has nevertheless raised concerns. Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones warned earlier this week that the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance." ■

NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:37:00 EEST
18:37:00 KST

NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
Russia plans to disable Ukraine's energy system in three stages. This is according to a plan published by journalists based on information intercepted by Ukraine.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The plan lays out three stages of attacks.
The first is to disable substations near Ukraine's western borders that import electricity from Europe. The second is to disable hydroelectric power plants. The third is to disconnect Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants: Khmelnytskyi, Rivne and Pivdennoukrainsk.
Russia plans to use up to 1,000 missiles, drones and aerial bombs. The targets include substations, thermal power plants, hydroelectric power plants, boiler houses and other energy infrastructure.
The ultimate goal is to cut major Ukrainian cities off from electricity, heating and water supplies, potentially causing a humanitarian crisis.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa have been identified as the main targets. Russian forces plan to cut electricity supplies to these cities by 90%, reduce heating supplies by up to 90%, and seriously disrupt their sewage systems.
However, The New York Times notes that it is unclear whether Russia will follow the strategy outlined in the plan and whether it would succeed if it did.
Background: Ukrainian officials have said they are concerned that Ukraine does not have a sufficiently developed plan in case of large-scale Russian strikes on water supply systems.

U.S. urges Europe to ‘immediately’ release diesel reserves as Iran war fuels record prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:36:33 UTC
18:36:33 KST

President Donald Trump on Friday said Europe has agreed to release diesel reserves, as the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East have constrained global fuel supplies.
"Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil," Trump said in a Truth Social post. "The process will begin immediately."
Average U.S. diesel prices surged to a record high of $6.50 per gallon late last month, according to AAA, up sharply from a year ago amid supply disruptions fueled by the Iran war and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In a post on social media, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday that America's European partners "should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions."
He added: "America is doing its part. We look to our allies to match their commitments with action."
The U.S. government is currently facing mounting political pressure to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
EU crisis talks
The prospect of the world's largest diesel exporter implementing an outright ban on diesel exports has prompted firm pushback from the U.S. energy industry and raised alarm across the Atlantic. The U.S. supplied around half of the European Union's diesel imports in August, according to the International Energy Agency, underscoring the 27-nation bloc's exposure to a potential U.S. export ban.
EU member states are scheduled to hold crisis talks on Friday, seeking to develop a coordinated response to soaring diesel prices.
Oil prices fell sharply on Friday morning after Reuters reported that European Union member states were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
The report, which cited a single unnamed source familiar with details of the discussion, said France had proposed that EU nations release 50 million barrels of diesel and International Energy Agency members release 50 million barrels of crude oil.
CNBC could not independently verify the report. A spokesperson for the French government and the IEA were not immediately available to comment.
Speaking to reporters in Milwaukee at the G20 trade ministers meeting, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said he had discussed diesel supplies and soaring prices with his U.S. counterpart, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
"We have every interest in working together on lowering the prices, be it on diesel or also other products from oil and gas supplies," Sefcovic said, according to Reuters.
He added that any move from the U.S. to restrict diesel exports would be unexpected and have a negative impact on Europe's economic outlook.
'A global energy problem'
Energy strategists at Macquarie Group said Thursday it is understandable that the U.S. position on the global diesel crisis has taken on an apparent global dimension.
"The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem," Macquarie Group's Walt Chancellor said in a research note.
"So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the Strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs," he added.
The Strait of Hormuz is a major throughway for the global oil trade that saw ship traffic stifled after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. But this week it saw daily exports return to prewar levels.
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

China's longest undersea highway tunnel completes shield tunneling
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:36:31 CST
18:36:31 KST

Constructors make a safety inspection at the construction site of Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Second Tunnel in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, Oct. 2, 2026. China's longest undersea highway tunnel completed all shield-driven excavation work on Friday as a shield machine reached its designated position at a depth of 105 meters beneath the sea surface in Jiaozhou Bay, eastern China's Shandong Province, according to China Railway Construction Corporation Limited. The Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Second Tunnel will connect Qingdao's main urban area with the Qingdao West Coast New Area. The latter is a national-level new area. The 17.48-km project includes a 14.37-km main tunnel section, featuring two main tunnels and a middle service tunnel, with three lanes in each direction and a design speed of 80 km per hour. (Xinhua/Li Ziheng)
BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's longest undersea highway tunnel completed all shield-driven excavation work on Friday as a shield machine reached its designated position at a depth of 105 meters beneath the sea surface in Jiaozhou Bay, eastern China's Shandong Province, according to China Railway Construction Corporation Limited.
The Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Second Tunnel will connect Qingdao's main urban area with the Qingdao West Coast New Area. The latter is a national-level new area. The 17.48-km project includes a 14.37-km main tunnel section, featuring two main tunnels and a middle service tunnel, with three lanes in each direction and a design speed of 80 km per hour.
According to Wang Junping with the China Railway 14th Bureau Group Corporation Limited, the project used a combination of drill-and-blast and shield tunneling methods, advancing from both the east and west shores of Jiaozhou Bay and meeting under the sea.
The main shield section has a maximum depth of 95 meters below the sea surface, and the service tunnel reaches 105 meters, creating high water pressure and requiring stringent sealing and waterproofing.
The team, for the first time, adopted a new muck discharge system, integrating a screw conveyor, rock crusher box and rock crusher, to improve efficiency and reduce blockage risks, Wang said, adding that innovative anti-vibration technology was developed for the shield body to improve stability.
Once completed, the new tunnel will help Qingdao form a multi-level cross-bay transport network together with the existing Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel, Jiaozhou Bay Bridge and Jiaozhou Bay Highway.
China has issued a plan to comprehensively advance the high-quality development of integrated transport services during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the Ministry of Transport announced in July this year. The plan aims to largely establish a modern integrated transport service system by 2030.
Under the plan, China will improve connections among different modes of transport, make passenger transfers more convenient and enhance freight logistics services. It will also promote the integration of transport and tourism, improve services at transport hubs, and strengthen rural passenger transport, freight and delivery services. ■

In northeastern Kansas and northwestern Missouri, flash and river flooding was ongoing Thursday afternoon, the NWS Kansas City office said. Radar estimates indicated widespread rainfall of about 51 to 102 millimeters since Tuesday.
The NWS issued a flash-flood emergency Tuesday after dam operators and county officials reported the imminent failure of McLeod Dam. ■

DTU data breach may affect personal information of 200,000 current and former users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:33:28 UTC
18:33:28 KST

The Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, has suffered a cyberattack in which unauthorized people gained access to its user database.
The university, which mainly educates engineers, announced the breach in a news release Friday.
DTU said the attackers obtained “a larger amount of data,” potentially affecting 200,000 current and former users. They include employees, students, guests and external partners.
The exposed information may include full names and CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. For active users, the database also contains private addresses and telephone numbers.
DTU cannot yet determine exactly which information was obtained or how many people were affected. The university has not identified who may be responsible for the attack.
“This is a serious attack against DTU, and we deeply regret the uncertainty it creates for the people whose information may be affected,” university director Bjarke Bak Christensen said.
“Our first priority has been to clarify the scope, limit the consequences, and ensure that those affected are notified and know how to respond,” he added.
DTU said it contained the attack Friday morning.
According to the university, the attackers compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to enter the database. They gained access to personal information dating to 2003.
The database holds information on about 40,000 active users and 160,000 former users.
DTU has reported the breach to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency, which oversees the handling of personal information. The case has also been referred to other relevant authorities for investigation.
The university warned that CPR numbers and other personal details could potentially be used for identity fraud if they have reached the wrong people.
“The information can also make phishing attempts and other abuse more credible,” DTU said.
The university advised current and former users to be particularly cautious about suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls.
People whose CPR numbers are held by DTU will receive a notification through e-Boks, Denmark’s official digital mail service.

2026-10-02

18:32:32 KST

Disruption caused by the recent bout of severe weather continues, with authorities warning that further problems may arise as conditions remain unsettled.
Civil Protection services, the Region of Crete, local municipalities and the competent authorities in Rethymno are on heightened readiness, as Crete faces a new wave of intense rainfall from Friday afternoon.
This latest deterioration in the weather comes at a particularly difficult time for the regional unit, which is still counting the serious consequences of the previous spell of severe weather.
One person has lost their life, while many areas have suffered extensive damage to roads and infrastructure, landslides, disruptions to public utility networks and access problems for mountain settlements.
Mylopotamos at the epicentre
The situation is especially serious in the municipality of Mylopotamos, which has been placed under a Civil Protection state of emergency because of the scale of the problem.
For Friday, it was decided that all schools and nursery and childcare facilities in the municipality would remain closed, in order to ensure the safety of pupils, teachers and staff.
The worst destruction has been recorded in Zoniana, Livadia, Axos and other parts of mountainous Mylopotamos. In Zoniana, the river overflowed, sending large volumes of water and debris into the settlement and causing significant damage to the road network, retaining walls and other infrastructure.
Serious problems have also been reported in the water supply and sewerage networks, while power cuts and faults in the electricity grid have affected mountain villages. Damage to the sewerage system from Axos to Apladiana is particularly widespread, and both the main road network and rural roads have suffered heavy damage.
Extensive damage
In Kynigiana, part of an uninhabited house collapsed, while in Veni partial collapses were recorded in two more dwellings.
At the same time, the toll in the municipality of Agios Vasileios is tragic. In Karines an 80-year-old livestock farmer was found dead. He had left home on Wednesday night heading for his sheepfold and had been missing ever since.
In Livadia, the worst was avoided when a farm vehicle carrying two people was swept away by the raging waters after part of the road gave way. The couple were freed from the vehicle and taken to PAGNI hospital for precautionary checks, and they are not reported to have suffered any health problems.
The full extent of the destruction has not yet been completely assessed, as the final survey will only be carried out once the severe weather passes.
Heightened readiness across Crete
The Region of Crete, the municipalities, the Fire Service, the Police and Civil Protection services remain on alert so they can respond immediately to any new incidents.
The General Secretariat for Civil Protection is advising citizens to secure any objects that could be swept away by strong winds or water, to check gutters and drains of their homes and to follow instructions issued by the competent authorities.
Particular caution is required near torrents and streams. Crossing them, whether on foot or by vehicle, should be avoided both during heavy rainfall and for a considerable time afterwards, as water levels can suddenly rise.
People are also urged to avoid outdoor activities during thunderstorms and to seek shelter immediately if there is intense lightning activity.
Residents are asked to seek information on the state and passability of the road network from the competent services and the Hellenic Police, and to consult official Civil Protection updates for guidance on self-protection.
Attention remains focused on Crete, with Rethymno at the centre, as local communities struggle to cope with the already serious impact of the severe weather while preparing for a new round of intense phenomena.

Taiwan Army says Clouded Leopard accident caused by driver error
Unknown

18:31:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s 6th Army Corps said a Friday accident involving a Clouded Leopard armored vehicle on Guandu Bridge was caused by driver error, rather than an equipment malfunction.
A Clouded Leopard became stuck on a traffic island on Guandu Bridge at 5:37 a.m. after the driver claimed a sudden malfunction of her seat obstructed her vision and led to the crash, per UP Media. Authorities removed the armored vehicle by 7:47 a.m. and had restored normal traffic flow by 8 a.m.
After the accident, the 6th Army Corps rejected the driver’s claim, saying the crash was caused by improper operation, per NOWNews. The corps said it would reinforce training on pre-mission equipment checks to safeguard personnel and equipment.
The Clouded Leopard is an indigenously designed and built wheeled armored vehicle platform developed with the aim of minimizing damage to the road network, per China Times. The project faced major hurdles during its development and production, including a major procurement scandal in 2015, per Liberty Times.
Prosecutors found that contractors used cheap parts for the chassis system and bribed inspectors, contributing to the vehicle’s low availability rate. Soldiers have complained about recurring malfunctions, including failures of the passenger compartment’s cooling system, the installation of tires with incorrect specifications, and problems with starter motors.
More recently, armor plates rated to withstand rifle-caliber rounds on 50 Clouded Leopards were found to have cracks, including two on the forward-facing plates and 48 on rear ramps, per Tai Sounds. The army identified faulty welding as one cause and addressed the problem by replacing the two forward-facing plates and repairing the rear ramps.
To address maintenance issues affecting the armored vehicle, the army allocated NT$1.5 billion (US$46.5 million) for vehicle maintenance from 2025 to 2029.
The Clouded Leopard is one of the flagship projects of an indigenous defense manufacturing initiative, with roughly 90% of its components produced domestically. The modular design of the Clouded Leopard’s second-generation chassis also allows for the expansion of the vehicle family, with the latest variant carrying a 105 mm gun, per Liberty Times.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US officials increasingly believe China is unlikely to invade Taiwan in 2027, while Taiwan’s defense minister says Beijing’s ambition to annex Taiwan by force remains unchanged.
Previous Pentagon assessments indicated that China aimed to have the capability to invade Taiwan by 2027. However, current and former US officials told Reuters that recent analyses suggest Beijing may be delaying its timeline for military action.
US officials cited two main reasons for the shift. The first is an anti-corruption campaign that has disrupted the PLA’s readiness, while the second is Beijing’s hope that the 2028 presidential election will produce a government more willing to engage in political dialogue with China.
Since Xi took power, a sweeping anti-corruption campaign has removed numerous senior military officers, affecting equipment procurement and operational preparations. US officials told Reuters that the purges have complicated the PLA’s efforts to prepare for a potential conflict across the Taiwan Strait.
Beijing is focused on the presidential election, with some Chinese officials hoping the vote will produce a government more amenable to bringing Taiwan under Chinese control. US officials said Beijing could become more inclined to use force in 2028 or afterward if the DPP wins a fourth consecutive presidential term by potentially reelecting President Lai Ching-te (賴清德).
One US official said the scale and intensity of Chinese military exercises declined in 2025 compared with previous years, although activity increased again this year, Reuters reported. The official added that Chinese military leaders remain dissatisfied with the PLA’s state of readiness.
Beijing has also studied the wars in Ukraine and Iran and recognizes that a campaign against Taiwan would need to achieve a rapid victory to avoid a prolonged war of attrition. However, the operation would be exceptionally difficult, with numerous aspects of the PLA’s preparations still incomplete, the official said.
US assessments of how the 2028 US presidential election could affect Beijing’s calculations remain divided, according to Reuters. Some sources said Beijing may be watching for rising US opposition to overseas military intervention, while others said China sees both US parties as broadly united in support of Taiwan, making the election outcome less relevant to its decision to use force.
Presidential Office Spokesperson Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said Thursday that China has continued using threats of force to pressure Taiwanese to abandon freedom and democracy since Taiwan’s first direct presidential election in 1996, per SET News. Over the past 30 years, she said, Taiwanese have defended their values and way of life without yielding to such threats.
Kuo said Taiwan would continue strengthening its self-defense capabilities and whole-of-society defense resilience under Lai’s leadership. It would also work with the US and other democratic partners to maintain the status quo, deter threats through strength, and preserve peace, she said.
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄), asked about the report Friday, said China’s ambition to annex Taiwan by force has never changed, per UDN.
Koo said the defense ministry and the armed forces must maintain high combat readiness based on early-warning intelligence and assessments of the Chinese military’s posture. “China will never abandon its ambition to annex Taiwan, regardless of which party is in power. This is something the public should understand,” he said.

Climate education moves to front burner for UN's COP31 conference in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:46 UTC
18:30:46 KST

Zeynep Ozturhan
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Quality climate education is "probably the most transformative climate adaptation action," according to an expert, who said the UN climate conference COP31, which will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in November, offers a significant opportunity to bring climate education to the center of the global climate agenda.
Youth and Education is one of the 10 priority areas of the COP31 Action Agenda.
Eric Guilyardi, a climate scientist at CNRS-IPSL -- a research federation that groups nine laboratories focused on Earth sciences and climate -- and president of the Office for Climate Education (OCE), spoke to Anadolu about how education can drive climate action.
A lead author on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report, Guilyardi said climate education is not just about transferring scientific knowledge but about equipping young people with the tools they need to think about what kind of world they want to live in.
"There are many reasons why we need young people worldwide to better understand what climate is, how it works, how we are modifying it through our human activities, and what course of action we can think of to limit the changes we are doing and their impact on societies and ecosystems," Guilyardi said.
Noting that climate education is interdisciplinary by nature, spanning from climate science to the humanities, sports and history, Guilyardi said the subject can "fall through the cracks" depending on how an education system is structured.
Quality climate education is 'most transformative' adaptation action
Underlining that teachers are at the heart of climate education, Guilyardi said quality climate education is "probably the most transformative climate adaptation action."
He noted that education systems and teachers must be equipped with both the science and the associated pedagogy, adding that this was the reason OCE was created to bring together climate scientists and educators.
Emphasizing the importance of adapting content to local realities, cultures and education systems, Guilyardi said: “This is absolutely key. The one-size-fits-all approach doesn't work in this field.”
30 to 80 hours of training needed to change teachers' practice
Noting that many teachers feel "a bit lonely" on climate topics they do not fully master, Guilyardi said changing their professional practice requires between 30 and 80 hours of training.
"This education is very different from just awareness. You're not going to have a two-hour conference and that's it. It's not enough to change your professional practice in the classroom," he said.
Guilyardi announced that the fifth edition of the "Teachers' COP" -- a global platform OCE established five years ago -- will be held at COP31 in Antalya this year.
COP31 dedicates a full day to climate education
Guilyardi said it was "extremely exciting" that COP31 in Türkiye is giving such a prominent place to youth and education with a whole day dedicated to the topic, adding that OCE is contributing to and helping organize the day with Turkish authorities.
He noted that COP31 could create a platform to move quality climate education beyond mere awareness, stressing that equipping teachers to overcome anxiety-inducing narratives around climate is critical.
Education now part of NDCs
Noting that disinformation work that started with the Belém Agenda at last year's COP will continue at COP31, Guilyardi said "prebunking" -- equipping young people with the capacity to discern trustworthy information from disinformation on social networks -- has moved higher on the agenda.
Guilyardi described the fact that education is now part of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) -- at the heart of the Paris Agreement -- as a "game-changer" since the last COP, and said OCE would hold several events at COP31 to help countries seize this opportunity.
'Between 3% and 7% receive quality climate education'
Stressing that awareness of climate change is high but not enough on its own, Guilyardi said awareness must be transformed into action through quality climate education, which is different from mere awareness.
"If we look at the different surveys we've been doing in the 30 countries where OCE is working, we estimate at the moment - it varies among countries -- that between 3% and 7% of the young generation receives quality climate education. So we're very far from having a majority that is equipped with quality climate education."
Recalling that climate now appears in more than 50% of national curricula, which was not the case even five years ago, Guilyardi said things are "changing fast."
Drawing attention to the current disconnect between the climate and education arenas, Guilyard said: "We're trying to bring those two worlds together because they really need each other to address today's challenges."

Gandhi's first birthday in free India was no celebration: What happened on October 2, 1947
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:30 UTC
18:30:30 KST

Freedom was just two months old and the country was still struggling to come to terms with Partition when Gandhi’s 78th birthday approached
NEW DELHI: India wanted to celebrate Mahatma Gandhi on October 2, 1947. Gandhi, however, himself wanted no celebration at all.It was his first birthday in an independent India and, as it turned out, his last. Messages, flowers and greetings poured in from India and abroad. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and others came to meet him. But Gandhi, who turned 78 that day, was consumed by what was happening outside the walls of Birla House.Barely seven weeks had passed since Independence. Partition had displaced millions and triggered widespread communal violence across India and Pakistan.So when people wished Gandhi a long life, his response was not one of celebration."Where did the congratulations come in? Would it not be more appropriate to say condolences?" he asked.Later that day, Gandhi told those gathered for his prayer meeting: "For me today is the day of mourning. I am surprised and also ashamed that I am still alive."
A country in flames
Freedom was just two months old and the country was still struggling to come to terms with Partition when Gandhi’s 78th birthday approached.Gandhi had already spent months confronting the violence.
According to the Gandhi Heritage Portal, he left for Noakhali in November 1946 after communal violence erupted there and later began a barefoot march through affected villages, appealing for peace and Hindu-Muslim unity.His peace mission continued even when India became independent. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that Gandhi stayed in riot-hit Calcutta in August 1947 and spent Independence Day fasting and praying rather than taking part in the celebrations.Violence followed Gandhi to Delhi. According to the Gandhi Heritage Portal, when he reached the capital on September 9, 1947, communal violence and refugee camps had made it impossible for him to stay at his usual accommodation at Valmiki Colony, and he moved into Birla House instead.
From there, Gandhi continued holding prayer meetings and appealing for communal peace as tensions gripped the capital.
What Gandhi did on his 78th birthday
According to historian Brijmohan Heda, October 2, 1947, was remembered by those who visited Gandhi that day as one of the most painful days of his life. While the country prepared to celebrate his birthday, Gandhi showed little interest in the celebrations and spent much of the day in prayer and spinning the charkha.
At the morning prayer, Mirabehn decorated the space around Gandhi’s seat at Birla House with flowers arranged in the shape of an Om, the words 'Hey Ram' and a cross. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Ghanshyamdas Birla and Indira Gandhi were among those present.Lady Mountbatten was among those who visited Gandhi later in the day and brought letters and telegrams sent to him from India and abroad.A special radio programme had also been planned to mark his birthday. When asked whether he would listen to the All India Radio programme, Gandhi made his choice clear. He said he would give greater importance to the 'rentio', the spinning wheel, than to the radio.Later in the evening, Gandhi suffered a bout of coughing. His doctors advised him to take penicillin, but he refused, saying Ramanama: the chanting of Lord Rama’s name was his 'sole remedy'.
'Today nobody listens to me'
Consumed by the bloodshed around him, Gandhi used his prayer meeting address on October 2, 1947, to speak openly about his anguish.“Today is my birthday. I do not celebrate my birthday in the usual way. I would say that on this day we must fast, spin and pray. That, in my view, is the most appropriate way of celebrating one’s birthday,” Gandhi said.
“For me today is the day of mourning. I am surprised and also ashamed that I am still alive. I am the same person whose word was honoured by the millions of the country. But today nobody listens to me,” he added. The remarks are recorded in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi.Gandhi then spoke about the growing hostility towards Muslims and questioned what India would become if the violence continued.“You want only the Hindus to remain in India and say that none else should be left behind. You may kill the Muslims today; but what will you do tomorrow? What will happen to the Parsis and the Christians and then to the British?” he said.“Ever since I came to India I have made it my profession to work for communal harmony, and I wish that though our religions are different we may live in amity like brothers. But today we seem to have become enemies,” Gandhi said.Gandhi also said he had given up his earlier desire to live to the age of 125.“I have now stopped thinking about living for 125 years. I have stopped thinking in terms of 100 or even 90 years. I am entering my 79th year today; but even that pains me,” he said.He ended with an appeal against communal hatred: “If you really want to celebrate my birthday, it is your duty not to let anyone be possessed by madness and if there is any anger in your hearts you must remove it.”After the prayer meeting, Gandhi spoke to Sardar Patel in private and asked what “sin” he had committed to be kept alive to witness such horrors, an exchange also recounted by historian Ramachandra Guha.
'If I’m to die by the bullet of a mad man ...'
Just four months later, Gandhi was assassinated in New Delhi.On January 30, 1948, as he walked towards the evening prayer meeting at Birla House, Nathuram Godse approached him and fired three shots at close range. Gandhi died shortly afterwards. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that he was shot while on his way to the prayer ground and received three bullets.
Gandhi was 78 when he was killed. He had spent much of his life speaking against violence and urging Hindus and Muslims to live together peacefully.Just two days before his assassination, Gandhi had spoken about the possibility of being killed."If I’m to die by the bullet of a mad man, I must do so smiling. God must be in my heart and on my lips," he had said on January 28, 1948, according to a contemporary report published by 'The Hindu'.Four months earlier, on his last birthday, Gandhi had already spoken of losing his desire for a long life.The man who had once hoped to live for 125 years had finally seen India become independent. But on his first birthday in free India, the violence surrounding that freedom left him with little reason to celebrate.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

====================================================================================================

Health Care Workers Are Tired of Cleaning Up Palantir’s Mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.
Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.
“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.
The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.
As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.
Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.
HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”
Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”
Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds.
HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback.
“Being Kicked”
On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.
But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says.
Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology.
Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.)
Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry, a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations. Named after the beat-keeping musical instrument, it uses algorithmic forecasts of patient volumes and staffing needs to automatically build nursing schedules. When Timpani launched in 2023, HCA’s top innovation executive Michael Schlosser told WIRED it would save time and money, as well as eliminate favoritism in assigning shifts.
Schlosser said in a paper this past July that Timpani has drastically reduced the number of hours managers spend on scheduling each month, lowered reliance on costly contract nurses to fill shifts, and increased retention. “The efficiency comes from AI generating stronger initial schedules,” he wrote, adding that over 98 percent “include a mix of skill and experiences.”
HCA’s responsible AI policy emphasizes protecting individuals from “physical” or “emotional” harms, and executives have said they spoke to nurses and took an empathetic approach in developing Timpani. In marketing materials, the company features nurses praising the tool for being easy to use and saving them time. Yet other HCA nurses say they feel ignored and disrespected, and they are not the only health care workers who have raised concerns about Palantir’s push into their industry.
Rayus Radiology, a large US imaging chain, began receiving complaints about scheduling errors earlier this year after it introduced a tool also built on Palantir Foundry, according to internal documents viewed by WIRED. The software is designed to populate scheduling fields from doctors’ orders. But in a number of cases, it linked the requests to the wrong patient profiles, listed tests or scans that didn’t match the orders, or made up personal details about patients. Schedulers who work at Rayus suspect that non-standard forms, illegible handwriting, and insufficient human review contributed to the issues.
Rayus spokesperson Kit Crancer says “the broad characterizations” do not fairly reflect its “processes, safeguards, or commitment to safe, accurate, and timely patient care.” He adds that Rayus uses technology “to support, not replace, appropriate human judgment and oversight.”
A Palantir spokesperson declined to comment using their name, but the company has described its software as merely presenting information in a more helpful manner and emphasized that customers are responsible for the data, policies, and decisionmaking.
Palantir Anxiety
Palantir’s sales have nearly doubled recently to almost $2 billion per quarter, as organizations seek its help analyzing data and automating tasks. Soaring costs and staffing shortages have made health care providers especially eager customers. Cleveland Clinic credited Palantir software with boosting patient capacity by forecasting ER discharges and replacing manual coordination.
But Palantir has also received pushback from civil rights activists over its defense and immigration work, as well as the stated political views of cofounders Peter Thiel and Alex Karp. In the UK, Palantir landed a $440 million contract with the National Health Service to try to cut appointment wait times, but nurses and activists have demanded it be canceled over privacy and security concerns.
At HCA, some nurses also want Palantir gone. While studies show AI-based scheduling holds promise, nurses say Timpani has become a source of anxiety. “Everyone checks immediately and every month you hear, ‘Man, why did it schedule me like that?’” Barker says.
Initially, some local managers could edit Timpani’s schedules. Now, nurses must flag problematic shifts to a centralized team at HCA headquarters in Nashville, which reviews appeals without direct communication or room for explanation, according to nurses. If denied, they try to swap shifts, but the chances of success are about only 50 percent, Barker and Retzloff claim.
Barker, who is a National Nurses United leader at an HCA psychiatric center, claims several colleagues quit over Timpani and that workplace injuries have climbed in the first 12 months with the tool. The center’s union of about 500 nurses filed a grievance over the software, arguing HCA is failing to sufficiently honor scheduling preferences. The matter is likely headed to arbitration.
In Timpani’s early days, HCA’s Schlosser acknowledged health care workers can be slow to adopt tech “because they have people’s lives in their hands.” But he envisioned a future where frontline nurses actively pushed for more tools: “Then it’ll be fun.” Three years later, some nurses see little reason to rejoice.
