France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:17:00 UTC
18:17:00 KST

France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
October 2, 2026
Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent.
"There are over 400 schools and other educational establishments that I know of that will be closed," confirmed French Education Minister Edouard Geffray on broadcaster France 2 late on Thursday night.
The protests against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week.
Student protests in France: damage, injuries, arrests
Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray.
Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently splashed with petrol at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials.
At least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.
In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone.
On Friday, more clashes between student protesters and police were reported in cities across the country, including in Loire, where several officers were injured, and in the capital Paris.
But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response.
"You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris (see main photo above).
"Protest is a fundamental right," read another sign.
Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests.
"What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said.
Geffray was planning to meet with student representatives and trade unions on Friday, saying: "Today will be a day of dialogue."
France: government blames far-left LFI
According to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been initiated by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations.
Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods.
"Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation."
Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!"
"The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced."

“The real way forward is in mobilizing whatever resources and support we can to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal and rebuild a capable and effective state ... with one army and one decision-making (authority),” Salam said at a news conference during a visit to the southern city of Nabatieh.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Oct. 4’s nail-biter election.
A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarization in Latin America’s biggest economy, one of the last major leftist bastions in the region.
The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America.
Trump said on Oct. 1 he was watching Brazil’s election “very closely.”
Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a runoff on Oct. 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat.
“The race is tied but not at a standstill: The final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go,” Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, told AFP.
Many of the nation’s 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised program on Oct. 1 evening.
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil’s beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a Black Madonna, became the focus as rumors erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that “messing” with her was “unacceptable.”
The electoral court ordered on Oct. 1 that posts with the “untrue” claims be taken down.
Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were “cowards” when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while “women learn to receive a touch from a young age,” referring to gynecological exams.
Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being “sexist.”
“It’s really turned into a circus, my vote won’t go to any of them,” said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee.
In another jab during a podcast on Oct. 1, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified “to serve as a building manager.”
Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.
The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.
Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has remained a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

During visit to south, Lebanon PM says scale of war recovery beyond state's capacity
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Friday that rebuilding regions destroyed in the latest Israeli war on Lebanon was beyond the state's capacity, calling for funding as he visited the heavily damaged south.
"I am aware of the magnitude of the crisis" including the destruction, displacement and loss of livelihoods due to Israeli attacks, Salam said in Nabatieh, a major southern city hit hard by airstrikes.
"But the scale of the needs exceeds the capacities of the Lebanese state and its ability to bear these burdens alone," Salam added. "We still need significant funding" for reconstruction, the prime minister said.
Fighting broke out in March during the early period of the US-Israeli war on Iran, as Lebanese militant group Hezbollah shot rockets and Israel unleashed massive airstrikes and a ground invasion.
The fighting followed another war that erupted in 2023 related to Israel's genocide of Gaza.
Lebanon has put the overall death toll from these Israeli wars on the country at more than 8,900.
Hundreds of thousands of people remain displaced, mainly from the south, while Israel maintains troops in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside Lebanon along the border.
Last month, Salam said the estimated total cost of the two wars could exceed $27 billion.
"I am here today to affirm the return to work of state institutions," he said during Friday's visit.
Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, while Lebanon and Israel concluded a US-sponsored framework agreement later that month.
But Nabatieh and surrounding areas in particular have seen continued Israeli attacks.
The Israel-Lebanon deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
Salam said it was important to rally "all the capabilities and support we can to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal" and build a state that is the sole decision maker on war and peace.
"This is the path to avoid finding ourselves once again facing a new war or new pretexts to attack Lebanon, or a new expansion of the (Israeli) occupation," he added.

Ukraine has limited contingency plans for Russian attacks on water supply – NYT

Source: The New York Times, citing its sources

The New York Times notes that Ukrainian officials have privately expressed concern that the country has limited contingency plans for major disruptions to its water supply.

Gaza toddlers evacuated in incubators return home after 2 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:11:26 UTC
18:11:26 KST

Bissan’s life began in the chaos of war, and her first months were marked by separation from the mother she had never known.
Two weeks after the war in Gaza began in October 2023, an Israeli airstrike hit Bissan’s family home in Beit Lahiya, killing a sister she would never meet. The blast severely injured her pregnant mother, Sundus al-Kurd, who was forced to deliver Bissan six weeks early to save their lives.
She was evacuated to Egypt in an ambulance, inside an incubator, with 28 other premature babies.
Seven of those children died in Egypt. Bissan survived.
She spent the next two years growing up in Egyptian hospitals and a care home, away from her parents. Her mother remained in Gaza, holding onto hope that they would be reunited.
Whenever she had internet access, Sundus made video calls to her daughter.
In March this year, Bissan was brought back to Gaza in a U.N.-assisted operation. She was among 11 children from the group evacuated to Egypt in 2023 who were returned to their families.
But the reunion was not what Sundus had imagined.
Bissan did not recognize her.
The toddler would call any woman who showed her affection “mama,” Sundus said. After spending most of her life away from her family, Bissan had to learn who her mother was.
Reuters documented their reunion and followed Bissan and several other children as they rebuilt relationships with their parents.
Returning home has also meant learning to live where the sounds of war remain part of everyday life.
Bissan returned to Gaza as a toddler, but she was coming home to a war zone.
When she first heard explosions, she would freeze in fear for several minutes, Sundus said. Even a balloon popping can still trigger panic.
“Her life changed. Her life became sleeping and waking up to the sound of explosions, to the sound of the numerous attacks and missiles,” Sundus said.
Yet there are moments when fear gives way to childhood curiosity.
Soon after their reunion, Sundus took Bissan to a small zoo in central Gaza. Wearing pink-framed glasses, the girl watched as a blue parrot perched on her mother’s arm.
For Sundus, such moments are part of helping her daughter rediscover childhood.
Not every child returned to Gaza was able to meet a mother who had been waiting for them.
For Ibrahim, the reunion with his mother was already impossible.
His mother, Israa Badr, gave birth to him during the eighth month of pregnancy. After her premature son was evacuated to Egypt, she fell into a deep depression. She died the following month.
Her husband, Jabri Badr, said doctors told the family she had died from overwhelming sadness.
“Ever since he was in her womb, she thought about him, dreamed of holding him, playing with him, and feeling what it was like to be a mother,” he said.
Ibrahim has since been reunited with his father in Gaza. But their separation has left another bond to rebuild.
“He was supposed to call me dad,” Badr said. “Today he doesn’t even say dad, or anything. I tell him to come, and he ignores me.”
Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental health expert, said the children and their parents would need time to reconnect after nearly two years apart.
The separation deprived the children of their mothers’ presence.
“They were deprived not only of their mother’s milk but also of her embrace and the emotional development that comes with it,” Abu Mashayikh said.
For Bissan and Sundus, the bond is returning through everyday routines.
Some days, they walk to Gaza’s Mediterranean shoreline. On a recent afternoon, they held hands along the sand. Bissan smiled as she looked toward the horizon.
Nights are harder.
When explosions shake the area, Bissan wakes up and searches for her mother. Those moments have brought them closer.
Sundus said her daughter is beginning to understand who she is and what it means to have a mother.
“Bissan has begun to understand who mama really is, who her mother really is,” Sundus said. “I am the only person present in her life. I am the one who feeds her, changes her clothes, combs her hair, and plays with her.”
For a child whose life began with an airstrike and who spent her earliest years separated from her family, the bond is still being built.
Each walk, embrace and frightened midnight search is helping Bissan learn the meaning of the word she once used for any woman who showed her kindness: “Mama.”

30% boost to UK military transport aircraft availability under new deal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

30% boost to UK military transport aircraft availability under new deal
MoD extends £190 million contract with Airbus to maintain the RAF's A400M Atlas fleet, boosting aircraft availability while sustaining over 350 UK jobs.
- £190 million contract extension with Airbus to support RAF’s A400 Atlas fleet, retaining more than 350 UK jobs.
- Agreement set to increase the number of mission-capable A400M aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.
- Britain’s air defence will be boosted under new deal.
A 30% improvement in availability for the RAF’s tactical and strategic airlift fleet will be delivered under a £190 million contract extension between the Ministry of Defence and Airbus.
The extension will see Airbus continue its maintenance, repair and support services for the RAF’s A400M Atlas fleet from its UK Support Centre at RAF Brize Norton.
As well as sustaining more than 350 UK jobs, the extended contract is set to deliver a significant boost to operational capability and will increase the number of fully mission-capable aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying.
By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.
The A400M Atlas is a cornerstone of the UK’s air mobility capability, supporting operations ranging from humanitarian relief to rapid troop deployment.
Continued support at RAF Brize Norton ensures the fleet remains ready to meet these demands without interruption, forming part of the government’s wider commitment to strengthening the UK’s defence industrial base and value for money in defence contracts.
Air Cdre Si Young, Head Air Mobility in National Armaments Materiel, said:
  This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future.
It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.
The 31-month extension to the Medium-Term Contract means support services will continue until April 2029, sustaining more than 240 Airbus staff and 110 primary sub-contract staff.
Kata Escott, Managing Director of Airbus Defence and Space UK, said:
  Airbus is proud to be a trusted partner to the Ministry of Defence, and this contract extension reinforces that commitment. The A400M Atlas is the backbone of Air Mobility. Our highly skilled teams work side by side with Royal Air Force personnel and are fully focused on enhancing operational readiness, keeping the fleet mission-ready.
The contract builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

UK is not facing diesel shortage despite fears of Trump export ban, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:09:21 UTC
18:09:21 KST

The government has sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting that the UK is not facing a diesel shortage after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The transport minister Keir Mather said on Friday that the UK has a wide range of sources of the fuel and is in talks with other European countries over the potential release of emergency diesel stockpiles.
“I want to reassure people that they can still go to the pump and fill up with diesel because the supply we have to the UK is inherently resilient,” he said on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. “The flows of diesel into the UK come from a variety of sources, and that is resilient.
“The government’s obligation now is to work really closely with our partners [in Europe] and officials in the US administration to re-stress how important it is to have flows of diesel into the UK. People shouldn’t be concerned about shortages because of the inherent resilience that is built into that system.”
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Earlier this week it emerged that the UK’s biggest refinery, Fawley in Hampshire, is set to shut for up to 10 weeks for planned maintenance. The UK had 18 refineries in the 1980s but now has only four.
On Thursday the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel supplies, after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring prices or face a US supply ban.
The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a record high on Friday, breaking the £2 mark for the first time, according to the motoring body the RAC.
“This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “The average price of a litre of diesel has risen to a record 200.01p and is showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery on to motorists.”
The government has extended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year. Earlier this week the RAC called on the government to extend the freeze into spring.
“We need to give people support where we can,” Mather said on GMB. “The government is not powerless. That is why we have a fuel duty freeze in place at the moment. The chancellor will set out the future of that at the budget, but is very aware of the impact that [high prices] are having on people.”
On Friday, Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said Europe was discussing the question of whether to release emergency reserves of diesel with all members of the International Energy Agency, not only the US.
“This is one of the opportunities that we have; we have used it before, and it is likely that we would use it again,” he told Euronews.

Can AI play a role in reducing inequality?

Can AI play a role in reducing inequality?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
In the debate about how best to regulate artificial intelligence, what about its role in development and aid? Warnings about the potential for exacerbating inequality are rife – but the World Bank argues that the technology could be harnessed for good.
Paschal Donohoe, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer at the World Bank Group, says there are concrete benefits in industries like farming, education and healthcare. "We know that artificial intelligence can play a role in crop productivity. By playing a role in helping farmers better managing what they are planting and harvesting, it has a bigger impact on their productivity and the income they gain. And I saw a very clear example of this in India, where I saw small rice farmers who, through use of artificial intelligence, were given better advice on how rice could be planted and harvested."
He believes developing economies can reap the benefits of AI if it's tailored to their needs – which he refers to as small AI. "That means AI that is more appropriately adjusted to local circumstances, has a higher ability to run offline, will have the ability to operate in environments in which connectivity or electricity may not be at a very high level."
Donohoe says that even as technology transforms daily life, development agencies remain focused on addressing inequality and basic needs like access to clean water, healthcare and education. "By ensuring in dealing with the development of artificial intelligence, that we do not for a moment lose sight of all [those] issues (...) We are recognising the change that is now taking place with AI, and we are making the case that while of course it brings challenges, small AI in particular, harnessed correctly with the right policies around it, can play a positive role."

EU holds crisis meeting as US pressure mounts to release emergency oil stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:05:23 UTC
18:05:23 KST

EU countries and the European Commission are holding talks on Friday that could pave the way for a new emergency oil reserves release, as pressure from Washington mounts. Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Euronews a fresh emergency release is "a possibility".
European countries will meet on Friday to discuss releasing emergency fuel stocks as soaring diesel prices put pressure on governments and the United States urges Europe to act.
Washington has warned European allies to release more diesel supplies or risk a US export ban, a European Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
The talks come as the diesel market tightens ahead of winter, driving up prices for consumers and raising concerns over supplies.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Euronews on Thursday that a new emergency release was "a possibility".
"We are discussing with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the United States, when the right time is to release, because this is one of the opportunities that we have," the Danish commissioner said.
"We've used it before, and we'll likely use it again."
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, confirmed the meeting on Friday.
A spokesperson for Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment said the diesel market was "very tight", resulting in high prices for consumers worldwide.
Ireland is coordinating with EU countries and the European Commission to "take stock of the situation" and "examine appropriate measures" to tackle high prices, the spokesperson said.
The discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency, which coordinated collective action in March to support oil markets following US and Israeli military attacks against Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
IEA chief Fatih Birol has also urged European countries to make use of their diesel stocks.
The reserves have not been tapped since the agency's first emergency oil release in March, when 400 million barrels of oil were put on the market.
Macron speaks to Trump over energy crisis
With pressure mounting, French President Emmanuel Macron held an overnight call with US President Donald Trump to discuss the global energy situation, according to the Elysée.
The French presidency said the two countries shared a "common interest" in coordinated action "without export restrictions".
Macron also discussed the issue with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
The talks stressed "the need to work together to combat rising fuel prices" and "ensure the global availability of refined products", according to the Elysée.
A videoconference of G7 leaders, with France currently holding the presidency, will take place "as soon as possible".
"The aim is to coordinate measures to help ease price pressures and guarantee supplies of crude oil and refined products — both among G7 nations and globally," the Elysée said.
"Coordination efforts are also underway at the European level."
EU holds technical talks on possible emergency release
EU countries will meet on Friday under the Commission's crisis-monitoring and coordination table for energy security.
The forum is used for technical discussions on whether disruptions threaten supplies and what coordinated action may be needed.
An EU source said representatives from France, Germany, Ireland and the UK held a call with the European Commission on 1 October.
The call appears to have preceded Friday morning's technical meeting.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent renewed pressure on European countries on Thursday, urging them to release additional supplies.
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent wrote on X.
"American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage. America is doing its part. We look to our allies to match their commitments with action."
EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the US tone as "rough", saying Washington was not sending "gentle diplomatic messages".
The Trump administration has been considering a 90-day diesel export ban as it seeks to contain domestic fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections.

Energy Department employee arrested by FBI for allegedly trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
Washington — A Department of Energy electrical engineer has been arrested on charges of providing support to the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, including by buying materials for homemade explosives and drones and traveling to Yemen, the Justice Department said Thursday.
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and is due to make his first court appearance Friday. Court records don't list an attorney available to speak on his behalf.
The FBI says Ellaboudy had a goal of helping the Houthis improve their communications capabilities and traveled last September to Yemen, where the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces are now engaged in renewed violence that has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands. The conflict began in 2014 when the Iran-backed rebels took over the capital, Sanaa, forcing the country's government to settle into exile in Saudi Arabia.
Ellaboudy used a passport issued to him when he was working at the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to make his way to Oman, then bordering Yemen, the Justice Department said.
Upon his return to the United States, authorities say, Ellaboudy told Customs and Border Protection officials that he was traveling back from Oman on a work trip and was part of a U.S. government mission to inspect missile defense systems. But investigators interviewed Ellaboudy's supervisor, who reported having no knowledge of any international travel or of an Energy Department missile inspection program that Ellaboudy would have been assigned to, an FBI affidavit said.
Ellaboudy himself was recorded telling FBI informants, whom officials had introduced into the investigation, that he had to be smuggled into and out of Yemen and that he had hoped to reach the country's capital to make government-level connections, the affidavit says. He was ultimately unable to make it to Sanaa, the FBI said.
The FBI says investigators began looking into Ellaboudy after learning that he had purchased precursor chemicals commonly involved in the construction of homemade explosive devices, including acetone and sodium bisulfate, as well as parts used for drones.
During the course of the investigation, the FBI says, he communicated with multiple informants - including one who purported to be a Houthi colonel - and provided advice and assistance on communications equipment.
Ellaboudy is charged under a law that makes it a crime to provide material support to a group designated by the United States as a foreign terrorist organization, of which the Houthis are one.
"These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination," John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's National Security Division, said in a statement.
If convicted, Ellaboudy faces up to 20 years in prison, the Justice Department said.

UK arrests British-Iranian suspect over RAF ‘plot’: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:03:21 UTC
18:03:21 KST

UK arrests British-Iranian suspect over RAF ‘plot’: What we know
Police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’ as sixth man arrested over RAF Fairford incident.
United Kingdom police have arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian man in relation to a security incident at a Royal Air Force (RAF) station near Fairford, England, this week
The man, described by police as a “dual UK/Iranian national” and detained on suspicion of preparing “terrorist” acts, is the sixth person to be arrested in what British authorities said was potentially an Iran-backed plot. The five other people arrested earlier were released on bail on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Bail for RAF base suspects suggests no evidence of ‘terror’, say analysts
- list 2 of 3‘Strong indications’ Iran linked to suspected UK airbase plot
- list 3 of 3US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
The investigation began when British authorities were alerted early on Sunday about unusual activity near the airbase, including oddly parked vans and a group of masked men. After searching the vans, authorities found no weapons or explosives but did recover a “quantity of petrol”.
The RAF station has been used by the United States for military operations, including by bombers during the US-Israel war on Iran.
Here’s what we know about the latest development in the case:
What’s happened?
British counterterrorism police announced the arrest of a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national in Westminster, London, on Thursday. Iran, however, does not recognise dual citizenship, and treats Iranians with a second passport solely as Iranian.
The man was detained on “suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006”, the same offence cited in the arrests of the five other suspects. In line with standard police practice, none of the suspects has been named ahead of any charges being made.
Police said they also conducted searches of two properties in the London area. They appealed to the public for any information that could assist the investigation.
What do we know about the suspect in custody?
The Times newspaper reported that the British-Iranian suspect is being investigated as a possible “recruiter” in the still-opaque plot or as someone otherwise believed to have played a significant role.
The media reported that the man was placed under surveillance after the arrest of the first five men. He has not been named.
What evidence is there that this was an Iran-linked plot?
The UK has pointed to an Iranian connection but has so far kept the reason for that assessment under wraps.
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are “strong indications” of Iran’s involvement in the incident and an “ongoing, complex and serious police investigation” is continuing.
He did not give information on what the suspects may have been planning or what intelligence has led the UK to suspect the involvement of Iran, saying only that he would “update people more in due course”.
In the US, President Donald Trump said the case “might be” Iran-linked and the US had been keeping tabs on the suspects “for a long time”. Trump criticised the UK’s decision to release the first five suspects on bail.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his government had forewarned the UK about a potential “Iranian-sponsored attack” but did not specify if that was related to the same RAF base incident.
Iranian officials have firmly denied any connection to the incident. Deputy Foreign Minister for Political Affairs Majid Takht-Ravanch called the claims “false and ridiculous”.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned British Ambassador Hugo Shorter on Thursday to protest against the allegations.
What happened at RAF Fairford?
Authorities received two early-morning calls on Sunday alerting them to suspicious activity near the Fairford airbase, including three vans parked strangely and a group of hooded, masked men.
Unusually, the first call to the UK’s emergency line was made by one of the suspects who would later be arrested.
Police responded and arrested five British men in their early 20s in the nearby Whelford area, saying they were suspected of explosives offences. Counterterrorism police later took over the investigation and said the men were suspected of preparing “a terrorist act”.
The suspects were released on bail on Monday but remained subject to “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others”, according to the UK’s head of counterterrorism policing, Laurence Taylor.
After searching the vans located near the airbase, police said they found no explosives but did retrieve a “quantity of petrol”.
Why were the men arrested at the scene given bail if this is a major incident?
That’s one of the big unanswered questions.
Under British “counterterrorism” law, police may hold suspects for up to two weeks before charging them. However, if authorities find little evidence to support their initial suspicion of “terrorism”, they have far less time – usually 24 to 36 hours, Chris Phillips, a former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office, told Al Jazeera.
Other security experts told Al Jazeera that police likely released the first five suspects because they did not deem them to be an imminent security risk or found that their potential involvement in any plot was unwitting.
“In cases involving terrorism, suspects can still be released on bail when the authorities feel relatively confident that these individuals do not pose an imminent danger of either carrying out or organising a terrorist attack,” Andrew Silke, professor of criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London, told Al Jazeera.
“Individuals may have been involved unknowingly or in a peripheral manner to potential terrorist activity. This seems possible in the current case,” he added.
Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior RAF officer, agreed that police likely have assessed that the five released suspects do not pose “any immediate danger”.
“We can reasonably assume that police judged that these individuals did not present any immediate danger nor did they have any credible means or intention of creating further danger to the public or to government installations,” Ashraf told Al Jazeera.
However, he said their release on bail should not necessarily be taken to mean the incident in question “was minor or that the Iranian-involvement hypothesis has been rejected”.
What happens next?
British authorities said they are continuing to investigate all aspects of the case, including the possibility of it being a foreign-backed “plot”.
Silke said authorities will likely be thoroughly analysing all suspects’ communications and interactions, looking for information on contacts who may have organised their involvement and for any payment the suspects may have received.
“The authorities can investigate all of these links to establish if they lead back to foreign government sources or agencies,” he said.
Silke added that authorities will also look into any links between the RAF airbase incident and previous plots carried out on British soil.
Phillips said he believes the suspects could have been recruited online by foreign actors to carry out some type of malicious activity, such as “setting fire to something”.
He said both Russia and Iran have allegedly paid “stooges” to carry out such acts in recent years. “At first glance now, it seems that that may be the case, but time will tell,” Phillips added.
Iran and Russia have also previously been accused of orchestrating plots in the UK. Those plots have involved “surveillance, sabotage, arson or physical violence”, MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said last year.

Crop outputs grew up to 100% in China’s big agricultural experiment: scientists
Peking University scientist says solar-activated mineral water improves photosynthetic efficiency across major crops
Large-scale field trials across China show that irrigation water treated with natural minerals radiated by sunlight could dramatically increase the yields of several crops, according to Chinese scientists behind the experiments.
The team said the trials, including on rice, wheat, soybeans, peanuts, sweet potatoes, sugar cane and vegetables, improved photosynthetic efficiency.
Their study, conducted from Heilongjiang province in northeastern China to Hainan province in the south, recorded yield increases of up to 40.6 per cent for rice, 24.7 per cent for wheat and 45.7 per cent for sugar cane, according to the scientists who said one sweet potato trial recorded an increase of 109.5 per cent.
Lu Anhuai, the lead scientist of the team and a professor at the School of Earth and Space Sciences at Peking University, said the approach could offer alternative ways of increasing agricultural production, such as improved crop varieties and fertilisers, by using irrigation water to improve how efficiently plants use sunlight.
“This is a new track,” Lu said in an interview on September 22.

No EU Membership for Ukraine on Jan.1, 2027, Brussels Admits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:02:14 UTC
18:02:14 KST

Ukraine cannot join the EU on Jan. 1, 2027, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said, rejecting President Volodymyr Zelensky’s target as Kyiv struggles to deliver reforms central to accession.
In an interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera published Friday, Oct. 2, Kos said the date was incompatible with a process based on candidates meeting membership requirements.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The date of Jan. 1, 2027, was set by President Zelensky. Accession is based on merit: it’s clear that this date is not possible. I understand that Kyiv and many others see EU membership as a guarantee of security. The war in Ukraine has changed European geopolitics, and one of the consequences is that enlargement is once again a priority, not only for Ukraine but for others as well.”
Her statement specifically addressed Jan. 1, rather than categorically excluding every possible accession date in 2027. Nevertheless, it challenges expectations of imminent membership while Ukraine’s justice and anti-corruption commitments remain largely unfinished.
A September civil-society assessment puts implementation of the Kachka–Kos priority reform plan at just 15%. Meanwhile, the confrontation between former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko and independent anti-corruption investigators has renewed concerns about whether Kyiv is protecting institutions it promised Brussels to strengthen.
The delays also carry a political risk. France elects a new president next year, and a victory for Marine Le Pen could leave Ukraine negotiating with a less supportive government in one of the EU’s most influential capitals.
CCTV Captures Russian Drone Slamming Into Kyiv School With 104 Children Inside – Warhead Fails to Detonate
More political than practical
The prospect of joining in 2027 had never amounted to an agreed timetable for full membership.
As Kyiv Post reported in April, discussions included a form of symbolic or political association that would anchor Ukraine in the EU before it completed the reforms required for full participation.
Under that scenario, Kyiv would receive political recognition while access to key benefits and decision-making rights remained limited. It would not immediately enjoy everything ordinarily associated with membership.
Even that proposal faced skepticism. A diplomatic source in Brussels directly familiar with negotiations told Kyiv Post that political association in 2027 “sounds too good to be true.”
“There should be no illusions about member states,” the source said. “They will defend their interests.”
That warning concerned the willingness of European governments to approve an exceptional arrangement, not simply Ukraine’s ability to complete reforms. A proposal discussed by officials does not become an accession commitment until member states agree to it.
September assessment still puts priority reforms at 15%
Agreed in December 2025, the Kachka–Kos plan sets out 10 priority commitments on justice and anti-corruption, named after then-Deputy Prime Minister Taras Kachka and the enlargement commissioner.
The package is an urgent subset of Ukraine’s broader accession obligations, with implementation expected by the end of 2026. It includes safeguards for anti-corruption investigations, changes to prosecutorial appointments, and continued international participation in judicial selection.
The Membership Check coalition awarded implementation 15 points out of 100 in June, up from nine in its initial assessment. Much of that progress involved preliminary steps rather than completed reforms.
The newer 2026 civil-society shadow report, summarized by Automaidan, still puts implementation at 15% as of September, with roughly three months remaining before the deadline.
Its findings identify insufficient progress in strengthening the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), unfinished judicial reforms, and continuing problems with the independence and transparency of prosecutorial appointments.
The report also notes that 114 EU-related bills were at various stages of parliamentary consideration as of Sept. 15. That demonstrates legislative activity, but pending bills do not establish that the promised safeguards have taken effect.
Kravchenko’s departure
The September confrontation involving Kravchenko illustrates why Brussels’s requirements go beyond passing legislation.
As Kyiv Post reported, Kravchenko announced a notice of suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos after submitting his own resignation amid an investigation into alleged corruption within the Prosecutor General’s Office.
NABU rejected the accusations. Together with SAPO, it described the move as another attack on their independence.
Kravchenko denied wrongdoing and had not been named as a suspect when he resigned. Parliament subsequently approved his dismissal, which Zelensky formalized by decree.
Mykhailo Zhernakov, executive director of the DEJURE Foundation, told Kyiv Post that replacing the prosecutor general without changing the appointment procedure would leave the underlying vulnerability intact.
He called for an open competition involving international experts and legislation restoring safeguards in judicial selection. These commitments belong to the Kachka–Kos plan.
The accession risk lies in recurring interference and unfulfilled safeguards, rather than in an investigation or resignation itself. Independent agencies exposing suspected corruption can demonstrate institutional strength – retaliation against them raises doubts about whether that independence will survive politically sensitive cases.
Opening negotiations is not completing them
Ukraine has made measurable progress through the accession process. It opened the Fundamentals negotiating cluster on June 15 and External Relations on July 14.
But opening a cluster means beginning negotiations over a group of policy areas, not certifying that Ukraine has met their requirements.
The Fundamentals cluster covers the institutions on which the wider process depends, including judicial independence, anti-corruption safeguards, and democratic governance. It opens first and closes last, with progress determining the pace of negotiations elsewhere.
Zhernakov has previously told Kyiv Post that Ukraine’s problem cannot simply be attributed to parliament’s inability to act. Lawmakers have repeatedly assembled large majorities when there was sufficient political backing.
His argument is that the remaining decisions require a willingness to limit political influence over institutions, rather than another declaration supporting European integration.
Elections in France
Ukraine is pursuing those reforms while the political support surrounding accession may change.
President Emmanuel Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term in 2027. A Le Pen victory could weaken the French backing Kyiv currently relies on for military assistance and European integration.
As Kyiv Post’s analysis of the French presidential race explained, Le Pen has changed parts of her position since Russia’s full-scale invasion. She condemned the invasion and supported Ukrainian sovereignty, but continues to oppose deploying French troops and allowing French long-range weapons to strike inside Russia.
However, she still remains an ardent euroskeptic. The continuity with Macron’s pro-EU policy cannot be assumed while the accession of new member states require agreement from every EU country. A less supportive French leadership could slow decisions, demand additional conditions, or withhold support for an accelerated arrangement.
Kyiv’s reforms and Europe’s elections run on different schedules
Kos continues to support gradual integration before full membership, allowing candidates to receive more benefits as they meet requirements. She presents that approach as preparation for accession, rather than a substitute for it.
For Ukraine, such arrangements could deliver practical gains while negotiations proceed. But neither gradual integration nor a political declaration removes the need for independent courts, credible appointments, and anti-corruption agencies capable of investigating powerful officials.
Kyiv cannot impact the outcome of elections across Europe, France included, but without it can and must do its homework. Inaction and obstruction will only leave Ukraine dependent on political goodwill that may be harder to secure next year.

Trans-Caspian Corridor: Europe and Central Asia target faster trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:02:03 UTC
18:02:03 KST

Transit along the Trans-Caspian Corridor currently takes around 35 days, with a target of cutting this to between 15 and 20. Officials say customs, digital systems and predictable border procedures are as important as new railways and ports.
Countries along the Trans-Caspian Corridor, backed by the European Union, are trying to make the route faster and more predictable, with a target of cutting transit times from around 35 days to between 15 and 20.
For cargo moving west from Uzbekistan, the route can run through Kazakhstan to the Caspian Sea, cross by ferry to Azerbaijan, and continue through Georgia and Türkiye towards Europe. It combines railways, roads, ports and maritime links that have to work together across several national transport systems.
Improving how those different parts of the route work together was a central focus of the second National Conference on the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor in Tashkent, where European and Uzbek officials, international financial institutions and transport companies discussed priority investments, project preparation, logistics, digitalisation and faster border procedures.
TRACECA, the intergovernmental commission for the Europe-Caucasus-Asia transport corridor, is among the bodies working with governments along the route to improve cross-border connectivity.
Beyond infrastructure: customs and digital links
Jasurbek Choriyev, Secretary General of TRACECA, told Euronews that infrastructure remains uneven along the route and will require continued investment. But he said the priority over the next four years is improving what TRACECA calls “soft connectivity”.
“Digital connectivity and cross-border facilitation and simplification of procedures will be the number one priority for the next four years that we need to focus on,” Choriyev said.
Pēteris Ustubs, Director for Asia and the Pacific at the European Commission’s Directorate-General for International Partnerships (DG INTPA), pointed to the need for closer coordination across the route.
“We have to look at the corridor in its entirety, making sure that the procedural part of the entire corridor is working as smoothly as possible, making sure that documentation is moved as far as possible to the electronic versions, making sure that customs procedures are harmonised to the maximum,” he said.
Why predictability matters for freight
For logistics companies, a shorter journey is only part of what makes a transport corridor competitive. They also need predictable transit times.
“The transport companies and logistics companies are interested in a very predictable timeline of the corridor, making sure that they know when and how the transport will move around,” Ustubs noted.
EU Ambassador to Uzbekistan Toivo Klaar described cooperation on what he called “soft infrastructure” as just as important as investment in physical links.
He said this meant agreeing on procedures to simplify border crossings and reduce the time needed for clearances and permits. "So that if somebody wants to ship, for example, from Uzbekistan, a container load or a trainload of cargo to Europe, they don't have to apply for individual permits in each country along the route, because there are quite a few," Klaar said. Instead, he added, a single agreed permit and system would make it easier to move cargo along the route.
“That is perfectly possible. It has been done elsewhere, and it is about political will. It is about cooperation,” Klaar added.
Bottlenecks further west
Shorter transit times also depend on removing capacity constraints further west. Choriyev pointed to new railway connections involving Azerbaijan, Armenia, Nakhchivan and Türkiye as examples of how relatively short links can connect larger sections of the route.
The Black Sea presents another challenge. The International Maritime Organisation warned in July of a resurgence in attacks on civilian merchant ships in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Recent attacks have also hit commercial vessels and port infrastructure along Ukraine’s Black Sea coast.
“Black Sea security is a concern now,” Choriyev said, also pointing to ferry links and maritime capacity as potential constraints.
Uzbekistan expands links east and west
For Uzbekistan, the economics of the corridor are closely tied to geography. It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, and Transport Minister Ilkhom Makhkamov says transport accounts for a significant share of the cost of Uzbek products.
Tashkent is also looking beyond its own borders to improve access to international markets. Makhkamov said plans include involvement in Caspian port infrastructure, ferries or barges on the Caspian Sea, infrastructure projects in Azerbaijan and stakes in ports in Georgia and on the Black Sea.
There are capacity constraints at home as well. Passenger and freight trains share parts of Uzbekistan’s railway network, while a planned dedicated high-speed passenger line between Tashkent and Samarkand is intended partly to free up freight capacity.
Hikmatulla Rahmetov, First Deputy Chairman of Uzbekistan Railways, said the project would “decrease the pressure on our cargo flow” and help reduce freight operating costs.
At the same time, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway could bring significantly more cargo into the network from the east. Uzbekistan Railways estimates the route could eventually carry up to 15 million tonnes of freight a year, much of it towards European markets via Uzbekistan.

Monuments in Bucha have 198 names of people unrelated to civilians on them — GFCN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. The 198 names on eight monuments in Bucha do not actually include any civilians, the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) told TASS.
"Using the OSINT (Open Source Intelligence - TASS) method of analyzing news reports and photos, analysts established that the memorial includes eight panels. An analysis revealed that 198 disputed names cannot be classified as what Ukraine calls `civilians who died in the city of Bucha’," the association noted.
Instead, 57 servicemen, including militants from the Azov nationalist battalion (recognized as terrorist and banned in Russia), and 26 unofficial combatants are mentioned there, the GFCN told TASS.
"An analysis revealed that both official Ukrainian servicemen and unofficial participants in the hostilities have their names listed on the plaques for the memorial," it said. Experts found out that the 57 people are official Ukrainian servicemen, members of the Ukrainian army or the Ukrainian Security Service (SBU), territorial defense brigades, police, the National Guard of Ukraine, "including militants from the Azov neo-nationalist battalion." And 26 others include "unofficial participants in the hostilities who targeted Russian servicemen with Molotov cocktails, explosives, and other weapons," the GFCN noted.
Also, the panels of the memorial include the names of civilians who died outside the city and those who left no digital footprint at all, the organization continued. Experts identified the names of 42 people who "died outside Bucha (in Gostomel, Irpen, and other localities) and cannot be positioned as `"killed in Bucha’ as the memorial stated.
"[And there are] 73 names without any digital footprint there: no information about these people is available on the Internet or from official data leaks, which may indicate data fabrication," the GFCN added.
According to the GFCN, despite regular requests from Russia using "official and unofficial channels, the lists of killed civilians in Bucha have not been made public."
"Ukrainian databases, media outlets and government websites were mostly scanned for information. Each point reviewed in the analysis contains links to one or several such resources available to any user or group of researchers for cross-checking," the GFCN explained.
The GFCN comprises experts and fact-checking organizations from around the world. The association was established by TASS news agency, the ANO Dialogue Regions, and the Workshop of New Media to combat disinformation. More than 125 journalists from 55 countries are already working with GFCN, collaborating on fact-checking.

Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

Top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community are calling for a moratorium on the US death penalty after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike left the prisoner alive but in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care.
The recent spate of harrowingly botched executions across US death penalty states reached a new low late on Wednesday when Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, called off the procedure after Pike had been injected with two full syringes of pentobarbital. She is the only person to have survived being administered 5g of the sedative – a massive dose that under normal circumstances is considered fatal.
An hour after the first injection was given, she was overheard by eyewitnesses to be still breathing, choking and struggling, and was found to have a heartbeat. Her lawyers said that her current condition, and the degree to which she may have been brain-damaged through oxygen deprivation, were as yet unknown.
Sandra Babcock, a death penalty scholar at Cornell law school who advises Pike’s legal team, told the Guardian that the events that unfolded were “unimaginably barbaric. They demand accountability.”
She added that at a minimum Lee must now “commute Christa Pike’s death sentence to life imprisonment”.
Another of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, who was present in the death chamber, called Pike’s ordeal “cruel and torturous”. He said he had personally counted seven needles stuck in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of a teenage classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Leading voices on the death penalty in America told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings had to be halted. Bryan Stevenson, an internationally renowned death penalty lawyer and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative in Montgomery, Alabama, said that many warnings had been made in recent months that US executions were flawed and unreliable.
“Nearly a dozen botched executions in recent years should have suspended executions long before now,” he said.
Stevenson said it was time to turn around the threshold question. Instead of asking whether a prisoner deserved to die for the crime committed, the question should be: “Do our governments which tolerate inequality, unreliability and bias deserve to kill?”
He added: “Last night’s tragedy makes clear we should stop the misguided policy of killing people to show that killing is wrong.”
Wednesday night was the second time in five months that Tennessee had failed to carry out an execution. In May, Tony Carruthers survived the death chamber after the execution team were unable to set up an IV line.
He has been given a new execution date for next May.
That followed Alabama, which also failed to execute two death row prisoners, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, having been unable to find a vein. The spectacle of prisoners being sent to their deaths, only to have the executions called off as a result of basic failures in IV procedures, has sent death penalty states scrambling to find alternatives to lethal injections.
In turn, those alternative procedures have become mired in complications and disputes. Miller and Smith were both eventually killed by Alabama using an experimental procedure, nitrogen gas, that veterinarians have banned as inhumane for the euthanasia of cats and dogs.
In June, a federal judge blocked Alabama’s use of nitrogen in executions, ruling it cruel and unusual punishment.
Other states have opted for the firing squad. But recent firing squad executions have been troubled by bullets missing the heart, to the extent that the suggestion has been raised that some of the mis-targeted shots may have been intentional.
Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America after her book Dead Man Walking was turned into a film of the same name, told the Guardian that the events on Wednesday night were the definition of cruelty.
“This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her. She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”
Prejean added that she hoped the agony Pike had endured “would be redemptive for others, and help to wake up the nation”.
As the number of gruesome botched lethal injections rapidly mounts, the central premise that has been held up by supporters – that it is a humane, medicalised and scientific way to kill a person – has come under fire. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta, Georgia, who has reviewed hundreds of autopsies of executed people in the US, said that lethal injections would never deserve the label of medicine.
“This is the impersonation of a medical act. It is the theft of a medical act. So when it goes awry, that is not at all surprising to me.”
Zivot was invited to present as an expert witness at a hearing convened in August by a special master in the Pike case. He warned the senior judge that Pike had a blood condition in which her blood platelets were elevated that rendered her vulnerable to blood clots.
Zivot told the hearing that Pike, as a small woman who had been in solitary confinement on death row for almost 30 years, probably had veins that were of poor quality, small in caliber, and hard to find. “I told them. I warned them,” he said.
The special master rejected almost all the evidence presented to him.
The last time that the US saw a moratorium on executions was in 1972 when the supreme court ruled in Furman v Georgia that capital punishment was capricious and arbitrary in its rendition. The ban was lifted four years later.
Paradoxically, calls for a renewed nationwide pause are reaching fever pitch at precisely the time that pressure to carry out executions is also peaking. Donald Trump has repeatedly exhorted death penalty states and the federal Department of Justice to speed up judicial killings, and his orders are having an effect.
Last year saw the highest number of US executions – 47 across 12 states – in 16 years.
Prejean said that the answer to the growing determination of Trump and the death penalty states to carry out executions was to bring the American people closer to the action. She pointed to Gallup’s findings tracking popular sentiment towards capital punishment.
In 1993, when her book came out, 80% of Americans supported the death penalty for convicted murderers. Now that figure is 52%.
“That’s progress, though not enough. People have good hearts, but they are too removed from the process that is secret and hidden. We have got to bring this to the people, bring them into the execution chamber, so that they too become a witness.”

For too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that? | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

How much can a Labour government change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.
This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.
At last year’s Labour conference, Andy Burnham was widely derided for what was seen as a half-launched and clumsy leadership coup attempt. Much of the media and Starmer’s cabinet reckoned his chances of being prime minister were gone for good. Yet, at this week’s unusually packed and perhaps unwisely optimistic gathering, Burnham’s can-do presence was almost as dominant as Tony Blair’s in his early leadership years: a constant point of reference, from the main hall to the merch stands to leftwing fringe events.
Moreover, Burnham appears to want to use his personal dominance – which may well be briefer than Blair’s, given Labour’s more fragile position in a more fragmented politics – to open up an array of huge issues that his party has long been advised to keep closed. Electoral reform, social care, public intervention in failing privatised utilities, the pension triple lock, even rejoining the EU: announcements about exploring or pursuing all these punctuated his conference speech, in a sequence of softly voiced political shocks.
“Change will be difficult,” he acknowledged. But he insisted: “More of the same isn’t good enough.” At an excited fringe event the night before, his ally Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who in that job and his previous one as energy secretary has pioneered Labour’s unexpected recent interest in confronting difficult problems and dangerous interests, summed up the party’s defiant new mood. “All politics is a risk. Progressive politics is a particular risk,” he said with relish. Burnham might have similar charisma and communication skills to Blair in the 1990s, but New Labour ministers did not dare say such provocative things.
Defenders of that now remote-seeming political culture would argue that avoiding head-on clashes was one of the reasons Blair was twice re-elected. But Burnham, who served in the Blair government at a formative age, does also have a strong conciliatory impulse, such as his frequently stated keenness to cooperate with other parties. However, as with his reluctance to criticise them by name – his conference speech was almost completely free of the usual party-political attacks – this apparent absence of aggression is in one sense the opposite: a determined attempt to break with the ultra-partisan politics of the post-Brexit decade that has excited many journalists but increasingly exhausted and alienated the public.
Burnham might come across as a nice bloke but he is ruthless, wrongfooting opponents and rendering their tactics obsolete, as his supposedly formidable Labour enemies such as Morgan McSweeney learned this year. Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage’s perpetual outrage and tribalism suddenly seem rigid and unreasonable next to Burnham’s talk of hope and national togetherness, and his disarming admission this week that all politicians must do better, that “this country isn’t where any of us would want it to be”.
Labour’s modest but persistent rise in the polls suggests that sufficient voters have had enough of the old high-argument, low-achievement politics to make Labour the leading party again for a period, perhaps up to the next general election and even beyond, when many of his ambitious reforms are actually meant to take place. Of course, proposing, let alone implementing, major changes to the status quo such as loosening the triple lock will also make many voters absolutely furious (even if that policy initially appears popular), and provide regular targets for Labour’s enemies in Westminster and the media. Yet, with the electorate more divided than ever, and the bar for re-election probably set as low as winning over less than a third of voters, being controversial or unpopular matters less for a government than before – provided it holds its nerve and pleases a large enough core of supporters. Burnham’s sweeping attacks on Labour bogeymen such as the privatised utilities seem likely to achieve that. Meanwhile, his cross-party overtures and support for electoral reform may well lure voters and politicians from the Lib Dems and Greens.
Like Pedro Sánchez in Spain, another centre-left premier of similar age who has managed to stay in power for eight years, Burnham is a paradoxical politician: both frank and evasive; opposed to populism and good at populist gestures; prepared to echo the left’s critique of capitalism but also pro-business; a self-styled lone saviour who is able to work in coalitions. Photogenic and politically agile – you could say shameless – Sánchez and Burnham seem better suited to today’s world of flux, short attention spans and deep discontent than the previous generation of stiff social democrats such as Starmer. Perhaps the modern centre-left is finally working out how to govern and reshape the societies that its more popular 1990s predecessor never sufficiently reformed.
For too long, it has been the right that expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. If Burnham’s barely begun administration is to become a significant one – perhaps like that of Harold Wilson, another slippery, charming Labour leader with Merseyside connections – it will need to enact big reforms as well as talk promisingly about them.
Sixty years ago, Wilson won an election landslide, and commemorative items competed with the cult of Burnham on the merch stands at conference in Liverpool. “Wilson’s greatest hits”, said the cover of a souvenir record, “Featuring Creation of the Open University, Equal Pay Act, Abolished Capital Punishment, Race Relations Act, Abortion Act, Decriminalised Homosexuality”. Wilson’s premiership was often unpopular and struggled economically, but it lastingly changed Britain by resolving some contentious social questions. Burnham may have to settle for doing the same.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

A senior South Korean Foreign Ministry official told reporters on Friday that the countries' foreign ministers had been discussing how Kyiv could address Seoul's concerns, including a possible apology, according to South Korean media reports.
Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Sybiha had been in direct contact and were discussing what level of response Seoul was seeking and what Ukraine could accept, while taking into account Ukraine's wartime circumstances and the need to avoid causing either side a loss of face, according to the reports.
The dispute comes at a sensitive time for Lee's administration, which has sought to reduce tensions with North Korea and is also dealing with the political fallout from a recent landmine incident in the Demilitarized Zone that separates the two Koreas.
Cho Han-bum, a senior fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification in Seoul, suggested that possible additional measures could concern support that South Korea already provides to Ukraine, including humanitarian, financial and reconstruction assistance.
"Ukraine has more to lose than South Korea because it is receiving support from Seoul," Cho said.
South Korea has provided humanitarian and financial assistance to Ukraine since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion and in July pledged an additional $100 million in non-lethal support on the sidelines of the NATO summit.
"However, neither side benefits from a prolonged confrontation," Cho said, noting that South Korea relies on Ukraine for information related to North Korea's military activities.
The South Korean presidential office earlier expressed "deep regret" over Ukraine's alleged denial of an agreement on nondisclosure of information concerning the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea.
On September 25, Ukrainian presidential communications advisor Dmytro Lytvyn wrote on Facebook that there had been no nondisclosure agreement and that it would be wrong to conceal where the prisoners were being transferred. In response to a query from Yonhap, the Presidential Office explained that Kyiv had disclosed only the fact of the transfer, without revealing details of the process.

President Murmu gives assent to Gujarat UCC Bill, state becomes second after Uttarakhand

However, the provisions of the bill will not apply to members of Scheduled Tribes (STs).READ ALSO: ‘Sat for 11 seconds’: Mystery shrouds Premanand Maharaj disciple’s death after CCTV footage emergesWhile tabling the bill in the Assembly, chief minister Bhupendra Patel had said that the UCC was among the key reforms that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was determined to implement. Children born from live-in relationships will be considered legitimate children of the couple, while women deserted by their live-in partners will be entitled to seek maintenance, according to the bill.
The legislation bans polygamy and provides for up to seven years' imprisonment for marriages conducted through coercion or force. Divorce through any means other than a court decree will be punishable with up to three years in prison.The bill also allows divorced couples to remarry without conditions and prohibits the practice of `halala' in certain communities.

Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:58:10 UTC
17:58:10 KST

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

Julius Bär announces share buyback worth up to CHF600 million
Julius Bär intends to buy back its own shares worth up to CHF600 million ($725 million). The bank has received approval from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) to do so, after the authority announced on Tuesday that it had concluded its investigation into the Signa debacle.
Julius Bär announced on Friday that the share buybacks are now set to begin in the coming weeks and be completed within a year. The implementation will depend on prevailing market conditions. The shares will be purchased via a secondary trading line on the SIX Swiss Exchange.
At the same time, the asset management bank announced a revision to its capital distribution policy. According to this, between 40% and 60% of the IFRS consolidated profit is to continue to be distributed in future. The aim is to pay a progressive dividend per share, provided no exceptional events occur.
With regard to capitalisation, Julius Bär remains committed to maintaining a “solid capital base” with a target Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 15%. As at mid-2026, the bank’s CET1 capital ratio stood at 18.5%.
The revised capital policy reflects the business’s strong capital-generating nature, according to board chairman Noel Quinn, who is quoted in the press release. Surplus capital will be returned to shareholders, while at the same time maintaining the financial strength and flexibility required to achieve the confirmed financial targets for the current 2026–2028 cycle.
Immediate measures relaxed
On Tuesday, FINMA announced that it had concluded its enforcement proceedings against Julius Bär, which had been ongoing for almost two years, relating to the heavy losses on loans to the collapsed property group Signa, owned by the Austrian investor René Benko.
More
Swiss financial watchdog ends Julius Bär proceedings
At the same time, the supervisory authority had eased or lifted certain emergency measures relating to capital and liquidity that had been imposed during the investigation. In an initial response, Julius Bär had already stated that it had immediately applied to FINMA for authorisation to carry out share buybacks.
