SP to field third candidate in UP Rajya Sabha polls? How move would trigger contest with BJP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:13:46 UTC
17:13:46 KST

The SP has so far announced two candidates, both of whom are assured of win
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) MP Virendra Singh on Friday announced that the party will field a third candidate in the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, despite only two SP candidates being assured of victory.If the SP fields a third candidate, it would set up a contest with the ruling BJP for one seat. Seven BJP candidates are assured of victory. Polling for 10 vacant Rajya Sabha seats from the state is scheduled for October 16.“We will decide our third candidate today and the nomination will be filed by October 5,” Singh told PTI.The Chandauli MP further remarked that the SP would adopt the “same strategy” the BJP used to secure the election of its candidates in the previous Rajya Sabha polls.“We will get all three of our candidates elected through the same route by which the BJP had got its candidates elected in the last Rajya Sabha elections,” Singh added.He also claimed that several BJP MLAs seeking SP tickets for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections were in touch with the Akhilesh Yadav-led party.Singh’s remarks came a day after Akhilesh Yadav declined to confirm whether the SP would field a third candidate, suggesting that the BJP could put up “nine or even 10 candidates.”
The SP on September 30 nominated veteran party leader and Akhilesh Yadav’s uncle, Ram Gopal Yadav, and Reliance Industries executive Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani for the elections. Both subsequently filed their nomination papers in Lucknow.
The arithemtic
The number of first-preference votes required to win a Rajya Sabha seat in Uttar Pradesh depends on the number of vacancies and the number of MLAs eligible to vote. With 10 seats up for election this time, the winning benchmark is likely to be around 37 first-preference votes.The BJP currently has 255 MLAs in the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly, while its NDA allies have another 33, taking the alliance’s combined strength to 288.The SP has 101 MLAs. Three legislators who defected to the BJP are currently unattached, while rebel MLA Puja Pal remains listed with the SP despite having joined the BJP. The Congress, an SP ally, has two MLAs.
In the 2024 Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP won all eight seats it contested, while two of the SP’s three nominees were elected. The SP’s third candidate, Alok Ranjan, lost.Rajya Sabha elections are conducted through proportional representation using the single transferable vote system. Under this system, surplus votes received by winning candidates can be transferred to other candidates based on voters’ subsequent preferences.As a result, if more than 10 candidates enter the fray, the contest could hinge on the distribution and transfer of votes, making electoral arithmetic and strategy crucial.(With PTI inputs)

Modi has ‘very good ideas’ to end Ukraine conflict – Putin
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has “very good ideas” for ending the Ukraine conflict and has repeatedly pressed for its peaceful settlement, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said. 
Modi has refused to take sides in the conflict, despite pressure from the West to isolate Russia. This neutrality has given India the room to discuss the need for a peaceful end to the conflict with both Moscow and Kiev. 
Putin told the annual Valdai Discussion Club meeting on Thursday that Modi raises the Ukraine conflict at every meeting between them, despite their close personal relationship, and has proposed ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. He thanked Modi for those efforts but did not disclose details of the proposals. 
The Russian leader briefed Modi on the ongoing peace initiatives when they met on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi last month, where the Indian prime minister reiterated his call for dialogue and diplomacy and said India stood ready to assist peace efforts.
❗️Putin: PM Modi Has Very Good Ideas for Finding Mutually Acceptable Solutions in Ukraine Conflict
‘We are grateful to the Prime Minister for his ideas and for his desire to end the conflict peacefully and as quickly as possible,’ Putin added. pic.twitter.com/o7BvzJ5EP7
At the earlier Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Modi told Putin, “We need to move from endless war to an end to the war.”
Moscow, too, has welcomed New Delhi’s efforts at peace. Ahead of the BRICS Summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia appreciates Indian initiatives to help end the conflict.
In an August interview with Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun, Modi said both Putin and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had shared their perspectives on the conflict with him. Putin said last week that proposals for a settlement remained on the table, although Moscow would have to assess them against its own interests.
Meanwhile, Washington has proposed a trilateral meeting with Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates, Zelensky said last week. The proposed talks would take place at a technical level, but a date has yet to be agreed. The Kremlin said such a meeting could take place soon.

Anthropic's Dario Amodei: AI's most visible CEO and enigma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:12:55 UTC
17:12:55 KST

The surge in artificial intelligence and the heated debate around its risks have made Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei the most visible tech leader — though the 43-year-old remains an enigma.
“I think he is one of the great legends in tech and business,” says Alex Karp, CEO of data-analytics specialist Palantir.
The San Francisco native built in just five years a company that could be valued at $2 trillion when it goes public this fall.
“There’s obviously Dario, there’s Sam Altman, there’s still your Jamie Dimons and your Bernard Arnaults of the traditional economy,” says Stephen Henriques, a senior fellow at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.
“He’s probably one of the most well recognized CEOs.”
With unruly hair, round glasses, an affable demeanor and a taste for V-neck sweaters, Amodei is worlds away from the corporate executive archetype — and seems to be motivated by something his peers are not.
This both fascinates and irritates venture capital barons and President Donald Trump’s inner circle, who struggle to decode his approach and bristle at what they view as catastrophist warnings about AI’s dangers to humanity.
Even more perplexing was his decision in March to confront the Pentagon over certain military and security uses of his AI, at the risk of losing everything.
Some see a humanist concerned about AI’s impact on society, able to attract the world’s best researchers to history-changing projects.
Others describe a skilled operator willing to exploit collective fears about technology to serve Anthropic’s interests.
“He was very idealistic...in a technical or scientific sense,” recalls Michael Berry, an associate professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute who advised Amodei’s doctoral work in the late 2000s.
“He wanted to try to tackle big problems with big impact.”
A physicist by training, Amodei turned to biology for his doctorate. He was interested, Berry says, in “developing skills that would maybe at a later point allow him to cure various diseases.”
But not everyone remembers him that way.
“I never saw someone engaged in a strong moral or ethical quest,” says Olivier Marre, who worked with Amodei at Princeton on a retinal analysis device.
“Dario was ambitious, eager to succeed and be recognized for it, but not excessively or abnormally,” says Marre, now a research director at France’s INSERM. “He wasn’t a megalomaniac who crushed others.”
After Princeton, the keen swimmer took a postdoc at Stanford focused on protein analysis.
The period coincided with major advances in AI, particularly future Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton’s work showing that bigger models perform better.
“The pivotal moment for me comes when he became interested in both AI and Effective Altruism, which determined his trajectory,” says a witness who spoke on condition of anonymity.
“Before that,” the person says, “I frankly think he could have gone into less original things, or at least things with less spotlight.”
Amodei is considered a leading figure in the effective altruism and rationalism movements, which aim in part to reduce AI’s risks.
Anthropic told AFP that Amodei has repeatedly said he does not identify as part of the EA community, and that the company is focused on solving problems rather than driven by any particular movement or ideology.
He left Baidu for Google, and later left OpenAI as well over strategy, believing AI safety there had been sidelined.
Last weekend, a “Saturday Night Live” sketch cast him as a tortured figure, barely masking his dread of AI.
“You’re seeing a lot of an internal battle on what he thinks of AI, which is encouraging,” says Henriques. “Are there other marketing strategies embedded in that? Maybe.”

G7 to work in 'coordinated manner' to 'bring down prices of petroleum products,' Macron says

→ make production more flexible to produce at the maximum capacity of our refineries,
→ release our strategic reserves up to 100 million barrels, within 4 months, with our partners, under the coordination of the International Energy Agency,

G7 to release 100m barrels of diesel, coordinate maintenance schedule to stabilise energy supplies
Here is the G7’s statement in full, as released by the Élysée Palace.
I used bold to highlight the key bits for you.
“Today, We, the Leaders of the G7, convened a virtual meeting to address the deepening challenges to our energy security. Facing unprecedented volatility in oil markets - with surging prices threatening economic stability and the well-being of our citizens - we have agreed on decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks, and strengthen the long-term resilience of global energy systems.
We will coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible. We also encourage engagement with countries holding significant refining capacities to boost global production of refined products, particularly diesel, in light of ongoing market pressures in this segment.
The G7 requests the IEA to monitor the immediate and full implementation of the March 2026 commitments. In this regard, taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels (MB) to begin immediately over 4 months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners. We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary.
We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions.
We invite the IEA to monitor the impact of these measures on energy security and market stability and to monitor implementation of commitments. A follow-up report should be delivered before 20 days, include actionable recommendations to enhance future responses, including stocks replenishment.
We condemn Iran’s continued attacks against its regional neighbours and its disruption of international trade, energy security and the global economy. We call for the immediate and full restoration of navigational rights and principles in the Strait of Hormuz and express our determination to redouble our collective efforts to that end. We commend the United States for its efforts to ensure the free flow of commerce through the strait of Hormuz.
We will maintain sanctions against Russia while working with the IEA and global partners to prevent further spillovers into fuel, gas, and other commodity markets.
Our citizens’ concerns about energy prices remain a top priority. We will monitor developments closely and stand ready to adjust measures as needed. Today’s agreements mark a step toward a more secure, transparent, and resilient energy future.”

The Mediapart website on Monday published the messages, dating back to 2013, in which Bardella – then a 17-year-old activist in Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) – allegedly wrote comments including “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so” and “all the banks are owned by Jews”.

It said they were provided by two sources close to Bardella, had been authenticated with Meta, Facebook’s parent company, and the data extraction had been certified by a bailiff.
“Extracting the conversation allows us to date it, to confirm that this conversation has not been subsequently modified, and to confirm that the person involved in the conversation is listed by Meta/Facebook under the name Jordan Bardella.”
It added that an analysis of the content also “possible to verify that it is indeed the real Jordan Bardella”: biographical details in the conversation included mention of a mother born in Italy, a 2013 interview Bardella gave to Le Parisien newspaper, and his failure to pass the entrance examination for the prestigious Sciences Po university.

The evidence was “therefore not evidence at all, and will not hold up for a second in court”, he said on social media.
“The so-called ‘investigation’ is already collapsing. The French people will be the judge of this blatant fabrication.”

The French justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, told French radio on Friday there was “little doubt” Bardella had made the comments.
“Do we want a prime minister who is not only antisemitic, but also lies to the French people in the face of overwhelming evidence? … His strategy raises serious doubts about his ability to hold political office,” he said.
The French Socialist party’s leader, Olivier Faure, said Bardella was “lying. So we have a two-pronged issue here: his antisemitism and lying in politics. Neither is forgivable.”
Faure added: “He could have had another defence – he could have said: ‘I was young, I’ve changed since then.’ That’s not what he’s saying.”

Ukraine submitted law on national minorities, Hungary approved it: more achieved than under the Orbán government in 10 years
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

11:09:03 EEST

Ukraine submitted law on national minorities, Hungary approved it: more achieved than under the Orbán government in 10 years
Kyiv • UNN
Hungary welcomed the submission to the Verkhovna Rada of a bill on the educational rights of national minorities. The document expands the use of EU and Indigenous peoples’ languages.
Hungary welcomed the submission to the Verkhovna Rada of a bill on the educational rights of national minorities and expects it to be adopted as early as October. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban said this on October 2 on social media, UNN writes.
Details
"Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov personally informed me that a bill on the educational rights of national minorities would be submitted to the Ukrainian parliament. We welcome this step, which was preceded by bilateral Hungarian-Ukrainian professional consultations and consultations with representatives of the Hungarian community of Zakarpattia over the past few weeks," Orban wrote.
She noted that the adoption of the bill "could strengthen the legal guarantees of education in the Hungarian native language and the network of educational institutions."
"The Ukrainian parliament is expected to make a decision on the bill in October," Orban noted.
According to her, Hungary "remains interested in dialogue and tangible results in the everyday life of the Hungarian community of Zakarpattia."
"We are pleased that in a few months we have achieved greater and more tangible results in strengthening the rights of the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia than the Orban government achieved in 10 years," the Hungarian foreign minister emphasized.
Bill on national minorities already in parliament — what it provides for
The draft law on amendments to certain laws of Ukraine concerning ensuring the educational rights of the indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to national minorities (communities) of Ukraine was registered in parliament under No. 16119 on October 1, 2026.
As stated in the explanatory note, the bill provides for clarification of legislative provisions concerning the use of the languages of national minorities (communities) of Ukraine that are official languages of the European Union, and the languages of the indigenous peoples of Ukraine in the educational process alongside the state language. In particular, it is proposed to allow the relevant languages to be used not only directly in the educational process, but also in other forms of communication between education seekers and other participants in the educational process on the premises and grounds of an educational institution.
In order to create appropriate conditions for the functioning of educational institutions where instruction is provided in the languages of national minorities (communities) of Ukraine and the indigenous peoples of Ukraine, the bill provides for the possibility of granting general secondary education institutions an appropriate status. Such status makes it possible to take into account the linguistic, cultural, and educational needs of education seekers and their families.
Certain provisions of the bill are aimed at ensuring the possibility of taking into account the cultural and linguistic identity of the relevant communities in educational programs, in particular by providing for the study of national history, the preservation of material and spiritual culture, national traditions, symbols and customs.
The draft law also provides for improving guarantees of access to education in the event of the reorganization or liquidation of a general secondary education institution with the status of a general secondary education institution of a national minority (community) of Ukraine or a general secondary education institution of an indigenous people of Ukraine. In particular, upon the application of a student's parents, the possibility of continuing to obtain education at the relevant level in another educational institution with the corresponding status, where instruction is provided in the language of the relevant national minority (community) of Ukraine or indigenous people of Ukraine, is to be guaranteed.

Türkiye’s passenger car and light commercial vehicle market contracted 24.3 percent year-on-year in September to 83,469 units, according to data from the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD).
Passenger car sales fell 27.8 percent year-on-year to 63,736 units in September, while the light commercial vehicle market declined 10.42 percent to 19,733 units.
Compared with the five-year average for September, the passenger car market was down 1.9 percent, while the combined passenger car and light commercial vehicle market rose 0.8 percent.
In the January-September period, Türkiye’s total passenger car and light commercial vehicle market decreased 13.39 percent year-on-year to 803,465 units.
Passenger car sales during the first nine months fell 15.45 percent year-on-year to 627,977 units, while light commercial vehicle sales declined 5.12 percent to 175,488 units.
Electric vehicle (EV) sales rose 17.1 percent year-on-year to 15,128 units in September, accounting for 23.7 percent of total vehicle sales.
In the January-September period, EV sales fell 9.5 percent year-on-year to 121,079 units.
Domestic EV maker Togg sold 37,426 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, while Tesla delivered 6,093 units over the same period.

DARPA wants AI built into running its biotech research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:08:25 UTC
17:08:25 KST

- DARPA awarded Systems Planning and Analysis a $10.9 million task order to support management of its new and ongoing biotechnology programs through October 2031.
- The order calls for AI-enabled support, drew three offers, and obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at award.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s research arm that funds high-risk military technology, has hired Systems Planning and Analysis to help manage its biotechnology programs, and it wants artificial intelligence built into how that work is done.
The Alexandria, Virginia-based company received a $10.9 million task order for operational and program support services, the U.S. Department of War said. The order covers technical, administrative, programmatic and financial management of new and ongoing biotechnology programs, carried out in what the notice calls an “AI-augmented, -integrated, and -enabled manner.”
The notice does not explain what that means in practice. It does not say which tasks AI tools would handle, which tools would be used, or whether DARPA requires specific software.
Work will take place in Arlington, Virginia, where DARPA has its headquarters, and is expected to run through October 2031. DARPA obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award. The order was competed, and three companies submitted offers.
The deal is a cost-plus-fixed-fee and award-fee order. SPA will be reimbursed for its costs and paid a fixed fee, plus an additional fee that depends on how DARPA rates its performance.
DARPA has no labs of its own. Its program managers fund outside teams at universities, laboratories and companies, and lean on support contractors for engineering, science, financial management, administrative and acquisition work. That support role is what SPA will fill for the biotechnology portfolio.
The notice does not name the DARPA office involved. The agency’s biotechnology research is run by its Biological Technologies Office, whose most recent office-wide solicitation, issued in October 2025, sought proposals in AI and machine learning for biology, combat casualty care, human performance under extreme stress, and bio-inspired materials and sensors. That solicitation stopped accepting proposals on Sept. 30.
SPA has done this kind of work for DARPA before. In 2023, it was one of six companies, along with Booz Allen Hamilton, ManTech, Amentum, ECS and Strategic Analysis, selected for DARPA’s Technical and Analytical Support Services II contract, a five-year vehicle with a combined $1.25 billion ceiling covering advisory work for all of the agency’s technical and support offices. DARPA received 12 offers for that contract.
Earlier this year, SPA won a five-year, $151.4 million contract to provide scientific, engineering and technical assistance to DARPA’s Information Innovation Office, which runs the agency’s AI and cyber programs. The company said at the time that it had supported DARPA for more than 17 years.
Founded in 1972, SPA employs nearly 3,000 people and is owned by private equity firm Arlington Capital Partners. Much of its work is analysis and engineering for the U.S. Navy, including the Strategic Systems Programs office that manages the service’s submarine-launched ballistic missiles.

Türkiye’s broadband Internet subscribers surpass 100 Million
Unknown

2026-10-02
08:08:12 UTC
17:08:12 KST

The number of broadband internet subscribers in Türkiye exceeded 100 million for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, according to data from the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) quarterly market report.
The total subscriber base increased by 11.3 million over the past five years.
Broadband subscriptions, including both mobile and fixed-line connections, reached 100.8 million in the second quarter, consisting of 79.7 million mobile subscribers and 21.2 million fixed subscribers.
The total number of broadband subscribers rose steadily from 89.5 million in the second quarter of 2022 to 93.1 million in 2023, 95.5 million in 2024, 97.4 million in 2025, and 100.8 million this year.
Fiber internet subscriptions also recorded strong growth during the period. The number of fiber subscribers increased from 5.2 million in the second quarter of 2022 to 10.7 million in the second quarter of 2026, surpassing the 10 million mark for the first time.
The fiber subscriber base expanded by more than 5.4 million over the last five years, reflecting continued growth in high-speed internet adoption across the country.

17:07:10 KST

The United States Senate unanimously passed a bipartisan resolution honoring the American citizens killed by Hamas on October 7, 2023, on Wednesday.
The resolution, S.Res.938, lists out 40 of the 46 Americans killed on October 7, as well as the seven hostages who were successfully freed alive from Hamas captivity.
In passing the resolution, the Senate resolved to honor and mourn the victims; express condolences to the victims' families; condemn Hamas and its affiliates; commend the US government for its role in freeing some of the hostages; urge the government to continue working to free US citizens held hostage across the world; and supports continued engagement by the US government with October 7 victims and their families.
The resolution also directs the Senate to dispatch a copy of the resolution to the families of American October 7 victims.
US has duty to secure justice for its people, senator says
Florida Sen. Rick Scott, who cosponsored the resolution along with Jewish Nevada Sen. Jacky Rosen, celebrated its passing in the Senate.
“Three years ago, the world watched in horror as Hamas terrorists massacred innocent civilians, including American citizens," the Republican senator said. "Families were torn apart, communities were decimated, and innocents, including babies and young children, were barbarically murdered. Americans were among the victims. There is no moral gray area here; Hamas is evil. Our country must protect our people and has a duty to secure justice for them. I was proud to work with Senator Rosen to honor the Americans whose lives were unjustly taken from them and the hostages who will spend the rest of their lives scarred by that tragic day.”
Rosen also responded to the resolutions' passing, saying that "It is our responsibility to make sure the world never forgets the unspeakable violence carried out by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023 – the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust."
The Democratic senator added that she introduced the bipartisan resolution "to honor the Americans who were killed on that day and those taken hostage by Hamas. It also honors the hostages’ families, who demonstrated remarkable courage during a time of intense grief and anxiety by being steadfast and fierce advocates for the return of their loved ones. Today, nearly three years after the horror of October 7, we mark this tragic date and reaffirm our commitment to supporting the American victims and their families and all those held hostage around the world.”

The aircraft made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain. Passengers subdued the attacker, and additional pilots traveling aboard the aircraft helped bring it down safely.
“He has no other nationality,” a source said.
The sources also said the bilateral aviation agreement between Israel and the United Arab Emirates did not stipulate that pilots operating flights between the two countries must be nationals of countries maintaining diplomatic relations with Israel.
That account adds a new dimension to the dispute over how the Omani co-pilot was permitted to operate the flight. Questions over the conditions for flying to Israel
A Transportation Ministry source previously told the Post that flydubai’s agreement to operate in Israel required pilots to be nationals of countries that had normalized relations with Israel.
“This is a clear breach of the agreement,” the ministry source said at the time, calling for the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to investigate.
The sources’ account on Friday concerned the bilateral aviation agreement. It did not address whether a separate operating or security arrangement imposed additional requirements on flydubai. Their description therefore does not, on its own, resolve whether the co-pilot’s assignment violated the conditions governing the airline’s flights to Israel.
The sources provided no further information about the suspect’s motives or possible connections to others.

In a separate interview published by the Post on Thursday, an Israeli passenger identified as Tal described an interval during the confrontation when the cockpit was empty, and the aircraft was descending. The precise sequence inside the cockpit and the duration of that interval have not been independently established by the Post.

Key bill to appease Hungary, advance EU membership lands in Ukraine's parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:06:17 UTC
17:06:17 KST

The parliament on Oct. 1 formally registered a draft law that will expand the provision of education for national minorities in Ukraine, paving the way for a vote that could help unblock Kyiv's EU bid.
The bill, which is expected to be voted on Oct. 12, has been a key demand of the Hungarian government to lift its veto on Ukraine's EU accession process.
"Everyone has the right to receive education in their mother tongue, and we expect these rights to be fully respected and guaranteed in practice," wrote Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar in a social media post.
"I would like to thank all the experts — Hungarian and Ukrainian — for their constructive, forward-looking, and insightful work in the past weeks," said Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban.
The law would give Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking community and other EU-language national minorities more room to use their language in education. Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Schools where more than 50% of pupils study in the relevant minority language may be granted a special status, and the head or deputy head of such a school must be proficient in the minority language.
The bill is also being worded so as not to open the door to campaigns promoting the Russian language.
The draft bill repeatedly refers to "the language of a national minority of Ukraine, which is an official language of the European Union." Hungarian is one of the EU's 24 official languages, whereas Russian is not.
Ukraine hopes that the passage of the law could help restart its stalled EU accession bid.
In Brussels, EU officials aim to open all six enlargement clusters – to-do lists of reforms that Ukraine must complete to be fully aligned with the bloc – by the end of 2026.
The European Commission has said for over a year that Ukraine is technically ready to open all six, but politically motivated objections have meant that only two have been opened so far.
The law's passage could help open clusters two and three — lists of reforms covering the breadth of Ukraine's economy.
However, clusters four and five, which are more sector-specific, are still expected to raise concerns among countries like Poland, which are worried about Ukraine's competitiveness in the agricultural and trucking sectors.
Formal decisions to advance EU membership talks with a candidate country usually occur on the sidelines of a meeting of EU European affairs ministers, known as the General Affairs Council (GAC).
The next GAC is scheduled for Oct. 13.

Bill on national minority education rights registered in Rada to lift Hungary's veto on opening negotiation clusters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:03:40 EEST
17:03:40 KST

Members of the Verkhovna Rada have registered a bill on education for national minorities aimed at unblocking the opening of two negotiation clusters regarding Ukraine's accession to the European Union by lifting Hungary's veto.
"We have found a solution that simultaneously protects the Ukrainian language, grants clear rights to national minorities and indigenous peoples, and removes one of the obstacles to Ukraine's European integration, specifically, it will help us unblock the opening of two negotiation clusters by lifting Hungary's veto," wrote Serhiy Babak (Servant of the People faction), head of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation, on his Telegram channel.
Specifically, the measure in question is Bill No. 16119, "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the right to education for indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to national minorities (communities) of Ukraine."
Babak emphasized that the Ukrainian language remains the language of the educational process, and the bill neither diminishes its status nor reintroduces the Russian language into the education system.
"It is about something else. We need to regulate the right to education for Ukraine's indigenous peoples and national minorities whose languages are official languages of the European Union, while simultaneously fulfilling a crucial part of our European integration commitments," he added.
According to him, the bill is intended to create the necessary conditions for further unblocking the negotiation process, particularly regarding the next two clusters.
"At the outset, our negotiating position was far from simple. The groundwork and agreements established by those previously responsible for this process had effectively led the discussion into a dead end. Furthermore, the version of the bill they had agreed to would not have garnered sufficient support even within the relevant committee, let alone on the floor of the Verkhovna Rada. Yet, politics is the art of reaching agreements while upholding one's state's position," the MP wrote.
The committee chair noted that the bill more clearly defines how the languages of Ukraine's indigenous peoples and national minorities, specifically those that are official EU languages, may be used alongside the state language.
"For instance, if an educational institution has a class where children are taught in Hungarian, they will be able to use the language of an EU country (alongside Ukrainian) not only during instruction but also when communicating with teachers and other participants in the educational process. Ukrainian remains the state language of instruction, and these changes apply exclusively to the languages of European Union countries," he wrote.
The bill also introduces the concept of a general secondary education institution with the status of a national minority (or community) institution; to qualify for this status, an institution must have more than 50% of its students (specifically, 50% plus one) studying in the language of that national minority (or community).
"According to Ministry of Education and Science estimates, this potentially affects 149 educational institutions—about 1.2% of all general secondary education institutions in Ukraine. In other words, we are talking about a very specific and rather limited group of institutions, and certainly not a change to the overall language model of education in Ukraine," Babak emphasized.
Furthermore, according to the draft document, parents will be able to initiate an expansion of the list of subjects taught in Ukrainian. In other words, if a child is studying in a class or group where the language of instruction is that of an indigenous people or a national minority, provided that language is an official EU language, the number of subjects taught in Ukrainian may be increased.
Among other things, the requirement regarding language certification is changing for the heads of certain private educational institutions.
"This provision applies to a very narrow group of heads of private educational institutions (specifically, those serving as heads at the time the law enters into force) that have classes or groups where the educational process is conducted in the language of an indigenous people or a national minority that is an official EU language. They will not be required to provide a state certificate confirming their Ukrainian language proficiency for as long as they remain in their position," the message reads.
According to the Ministry of Education, this affects the heads of only 29 institutions across Ukraine.
"That is why I would very much dislike seeing the discussion around this bill reduced to a simplistic 'Ukrainian language versus minority languages' confrontation. We have actually found a solution that ensures the rights of national minorities without compromising the position of the Ukrainian language. We are fulfilling our obligations to the citizens of Ukraine and continuing our progress toward European Union membership," Babak stated.
The bill's authors include Ruslan Stefanchuk, Oleksandr Kornienko, Olena Kondratiuk, Serhiy Babak, Mykyta Poturayev, Oleksandr Danutsa, Yevhenia Kravchuk, Serhiy Kalchenko, Andriy Klochko, Oleksandr Horobets, Dmytro Liubota, Mykola Davydiuk, Vadym Halaichuk, and Maria Mezentseva-Fedorenko.
As reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha expressed hope for the early convening of a special session of the Verkhovna Rada to consider a package of documents on European integration and a bill on national minorities.

Russia tries to freeze Ukraine as it suffers record casualties and retreats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:03:02 UTC
17:03:02 KST

Russia tries to freeze Ukraine as it suffers record casualties and retreats
Moscow has suffered further losses of occupied territory, but is using new drones to beat Ukraine’s defences ahead of winter.
Russia suffered its highest losses of 2026 in September, when 46,230 of its soldiers were killed or wounded, according to the Ukrainian military.
The new record comes after Russian casualties of about 40,000 a month since June, and is close to the goal Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set in January of 50,000 Russian casualties a month. Russia reportedly lost 2,090 troops on September 28 – its highest 24-hour casualty rate of the war.
Al Jazeera cannot verify casualty claims from either side. Ukraine says it has video of each casualty, as more than 90 percent of them are caused by first-person view (FPV) drones.
But despite setbacks, Russia has been trying to seize the remaining areas of Ukraine’s eastern regions of Luhansk and Donetsk that it doesn’t control — which is where casualties have been heaviest.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has inflicted particularly heavy losses in the area around Lyman, where the third phase of a counteroffensive called Operation Vivaldi has reclaimed 176sq km (68sq miles) of territory in recent weeks.
Corps commander Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky said it succeeded by feigning an attack from the west, and “forced it [the Russian army] to senselessly burn through its reserves in counterattacks precisely in that direction”. Then it attacked from the north.
Among its tactics was the use of remotely operated Russian armoured personnel carriers filled with explosives that smashed into Russian defences.
A Ukrainian commander on the Lyman front described how Vivaldi’s first phase eliminated a vanguard of Russian soldiers. Ukrainian drone operators have also been busy disrupting Russian ammunition and fuel supplies, starving the front.
Russia denied the Ukrainian counteroffensive’s gains, posting videos as purported evidence.
Russia has frequently claimed to hold positions and gain territory. But assessments by the Institute for the Study of War and DeepState, organisations that track territorial gains using open source, geolocated footage, rarely reflect Russian claims on their maps.
The ISW has estimated Russia’s net gains this year at 148sq km (57sq miles), nowhere near the 5,300sq km that Russia claims.
Russia pounds Kyiv
Still, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities during the past week, striking energy infrastructure but also residential buildings, kindergartens, schools, office buildings and other nonmilitary targets.
Several people were killed on September 28, when a drone destroyed part of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv.
Kyiv experienced power outages on September 30, when Russian drones struck a thermal power plant in the Kyiv region. At least five people were killed across the country.
“Since the summer, there has not been a single day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. However, such a massive and combined attack has not occurred since the end of the last heating season,” wrote Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi on social media.
Zelenskyy has warned for weeks that Russia intends to strike Ukraine’s energy sector hard to cause suffering this winter.
On September 30, Russia also tested a drone with a cumulative cutting warhead “specifically designed to destroy high-voltage pylons,” said Ukraine’s defence ministry electronics adviser Serhii Beskrestnov. “I believe the enemy’s plan is to attack important high-voltage power lines.”
Russia has also targeted data centres during September, in an apparent effort to disrupt connectivity and digital commerce.
Ukraine has been suffering from a shortage of interceptors with which to stop ballistic missiles, and several got through on September 30, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine believes it can manufacture interceptors faster and more cheaply than its allies if the technology is shared.
Zelenskyy had persuaded US President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to manufacture interceptors for the Patriot system under licence at the NATO summit last July, but Trump later retracted the offer.
Jet-powered drones are a recent challenge, too. Ukraine had mastered the art of shooting down propeller-powered ones, eliminating well over 90 percent. During the week ending October 1, however, they downed only 81 percent of the 1,933 long-range aerial drones Russia launched because many of them were jet-powered.
“Ukraine’s interception rate for jet-powered “shaheds” is now 55 percent,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Worse may be to come. Beskrestnov said Russia was working on a system of radio beacons to better guide drones.
“This system will allow them to navigate deep within our territory, at a distance of up to 100 km. This essentially means the ability to accurately attack a vast portion of Ukraine,” he wrote.
Zelenskyy said Russia planned to spend $12bn on jet-powered drones and loitering munitions next year.
Ukraine strikes back
Ukraine, too, has continued deep strikes against Russian refineries to starve its war machine of fuel and disrupt its economy.
Ukrainian drones struck the Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries on September 25, and the Ilsky refinery the following day. Two days later, they struck four oil deposits in the Krasnodar Krai region.
Ukraine also struck defence industries. On September 25, it struck the NPP Zavod Iskra factory, which makes electronic components for the Kh-59 cruise missiles Russia flies into Ukraine, and the Pantsir-S air defence system. It also struck the Efremovsky Synthetic Rubber Plant, which makes solid rocket fuel for the Iskander-M ballistic missile.
The next day, Ukraine hit the foundry and five buildings of the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, which makes optics for artillery, missile and antitank weapons.
Cost overruns
Both Russia and Ukraine have outspent their defence budgets for the year.
Ukraine said it was looking for an additional $27bn, in meetings with the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund.
“Part of these resources is needed immediately for advance payments for supplies that are expected to arrive in the first quarter of 2027,” said Prime Minister Koretskyi.
Some of the money would come “by reallocating funds”, he said, but “we are also counting on support from the EU”.
It was a similar story in Russia, which has spent 30 percent more on its war in the first half of the year than the same period last year, according to the Ukraine Foreign Intelligence Service.
Reuters cited leaked Russian government documents indicating that Russia plans to raise its defence spending by another 27 percent next year. It put the estimated budget at $204bn for 2027.
Moscow planned to pay for the increase through extra borrowing and budget cuts to nonmilitary expenditures.

One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:00:14 UTC
17:00:14 KST

A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her.
Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.
Agbani saw first-hand the toll on Nigerians who protested against the damage inflicted in the delta by big oil companies.
Her mother, Theresa Terabiewaa Agbani, was an activist and, when Agbani was in college, they were devastated by the state’s execution of Ogoni activist and playwright Ken Saro-Wiwa, who, along with eight other environmental campaigners, was hanged in 1995.
“The execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and the other Ogoni land defenders decades ago opened my eyes to what really lay behind the destruction of my home town,” she says.
Agbani has adopted a different kind of activism – planting trees. In 2003, soon after the death of her mother, she established the Lokiaka Community Development Centre, to support female Ogoni farmers in caring for the environment and helping to restore the mangroves, devastated by more than five decades of oil pollution.
Her aim isn’t just to put trees back in the ground but to heal the wetlands, restore livelihoods and peace, and rebuild the sense of ownership Ogoni communities lost along with their mangroves.
In the swamp flats at Teenama, Joy Lebewi is ankle-deep in mud, holding a sapling in one hand. Trained at Agbani’s centre, Lebewi works alongside a dozen other women, all planting while keeping an eye out for crabs and periwinkles worth collecting. In the wetland of Teenama they have planted more than 150,000 mangrove saplings.
“We want to space the mangroves right,” says Lebewi, her brow furrowed with concentration. “This is our forest.” She knows that restoring a forest is about more than putting a bunch of seedlings into the ground. When the women started restoring mangroves in 2018, they planted them too close together, and the trees’ canopies crowded each other out. Now, they use a stick – 2 metres long, with one end pressed into the swampy ground to mark where the next seedling will be planted. It is a simple tool in a landscape of widespread losses, but each mark is a small act of reconstruction.
Teenama sits between the Kwawa and Kpean oil settlements in the Yorla oilfields of Ogoniland, a region ravaged by decades of oil production and spills.
The ecological damage has been felt across the region – people who relied on mangrove-lined creeks to fish and gather shellfish have lost a valuable food source and income.
In Bodo, where Shell was ordered to pay £55m in compensation to local people after two big oil spills in 2008 and 2009, Dr Ferdinand Giadom is deputy project director of the Bodo Mediation Initiative, a stakeholder group overseeing oil cleanups around the region.
About 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of mangroves were directly destroyed in the 2008 Ogoniland spill and Giadom estimates that more than 500,000 barrels of crude oil have been spilt into the environment in under 20 years, an impact felt across generations.
“Two decades have been lost,” Giadom says. “Livelihoods over that span of time have been lost.”
The wetlands are also being encroached on by the nipa palm, also called mangrove palm, an invasive species from south-east Asia that has spread through disturbed areas of the Niger delta. Thick clusters of nipa crowd out native species and make it difficult for local people to access the wetlands.
Clearing nipa is demanding work. In Teenama, men from surrounding communities are clearing the land to prepare it for the women who will plant the native mangrove saplings. The mangrove ecosystem in the Niger delta region is the largest in Africa and the third-largest globally, covering about 1m hectares.
These forests provide habitat for fish, shrimps and molluscs and act as nurseries for other aquatic life. They help protect coastlines, store carbon and support communities whose food and incomes depend on the wetlands.
“Millions of people’s livelihoods depend on healthy mangroves,” says Oluwakemi Odufuye, a coastal ecologist at the Nigerian Institute of Oceanography and Marine Research.
For Agbani, that connection between environmental destruction and human lives is deeply personal. She watched pollution alter her childhood landscape, and saw women losing access to vital forests and waterways.
Inspired by her mother’s activism and the risks faced by Ogoni activists such as Saro-Wiwa, she chose her path in restoration. Her Lokiaka Community Development Centre merges environmental justice, gender inclusion and biodiversity.
Instead of classrooms, women are taken into swamp forests, supervised by experienced restorers.
Her goal is to empower women in the Niger delta to restore their wetlands independently. She has trained more than 400 women from various communities, many of whom have replicated the training locally.
Since 2018, Lokiaka’s teams have restored 3m mangroves and reclaimed 190 hectares of swamp forest in Ogoniland.
For Agbani, the return of fish and crabs demonstrates progress. “Life is returning,” she says.
Erabanabari Kobah, an environmental scientist and campaigner from Ogoniland, says one measure of success is what happens to a forest over time, not just how many trees are planted. “Planting in unsuitable areas won’t ensure long-term success,” he says.
For the planters, that means understanding how the forest behaves – where the water moves, where the mangroves can survive, how the forest can eventually support marine life again.
Collins Lebeteh, an environmentalist who works in community-led conservation, says a different way of measuring success is needed.
“What is really important is who is doing the planting. Many women who rely on and are affected by the degraded environment are often left out of decisions around the restoration of ecosystems,” he says.
Agbani wants to change that. Her organisation also works with local fishers, training them in species identification and managing mangrove buds.
Her hope is for restoration to become a process communities own and control, rather than another “top down” intervention.
Back in Teenama, Lebewi pushes her spacing stick into the mud again. It is a mark almost invisible in the vastness of the wetland but here another sapling will be planted – and spread its roots.

A small Singaporean research team has beaten scientists in China and the United States to build the world’s most accurate atomic clock.
The clock, built with a single ion of a rare earth metal element known as lutetium, is so precise that it would lose one second every 260 billion years – nearly 20 times the age of our universe.

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Korea claimed its second consecutive League of Legends title after beating Chinese Taipei 3-0 in the final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday.
Chinese Taipei held solid leads in the first two games and built a gold advantage of more than 5,000 in the second, but South Korea fought back in both to take a 2-0 lead in the series.
In the third game, the defending champion dominated and closed out the contest in under 30 minutes to complete the sweep.
The Aichi Sky Expo Hall was packed with spectators throughout the final. South Korea's Lee "Faker" Sang-hyeok, widely regarded as the greatest League of Legends player of all time, did not feature in the match and remained on the bench.
A total of eight teams competed in the tournament under the "Hard Fearless Draft" rule, under which each champion could be selected only once per series. The competition consisted of a single-round-robin group stage followed by a single-elimination knockout stage.
At the conclusion of all 11 esports events at the Asian Games, China topped the esports medal table with three golds, while South Korea and host Japan each won one gold medal.
Esports became an official medal sport at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, following its debut as a demonstration event at Jakarta 2018. ■

As Write for Rights turns 25, here are 7 times it helped to deliver justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

This year marks the 25th anniversary of Amnesty International’s global Write for Rights campaign, which has supported more than 200 people and groups.
That’s 25 years of people taking action against injustice, writing letters and signing petitions in support of people whose human rights have been denied. Some have been imprisoned for peacefully expressing their views. Others have been targeted because of who they are or who they love. Some have been criminalized simply because they were in the wrong place at the wrong time.
More than 50 million actions have been taken – in the form of letters, emails, cards, petition signatures, social media posts and more – since Write for Rights started in 2001. Amnesty’s brilliant supporters have written letters both to those whose rights are being violated, and the person in authority who can make change happen.
People have taken action because they believe hope and humanity can win over fear.
As a result, over 100 people featured in our Write for Rights campaign have seen a positive outcome in their situation. People unlawfully detained have been released, families have been reunited and justice achieved. Just as important – individuals have been reminded that they have not been forgotten.
Here are the stories of a few of them, whose lives have changed – and even been saved – thanks to the support of people like you…
Germain Rukuki – Burundi
On 30 June 2021, Burundian human rights defender Germain Rukuki was released from prison four years into a 32-year sentence. He had been found guilty of a number of sham charges relating to his human rights work. He was jailed before getting a chance to hold his youngest child, born just weeks after he was arrested in July 2017.
Through Write for Rights 2020, hundreds of thousands of people around the world demanded Germain’s release.
“I am so grateful for the support I received from human rights organizations during my arbitrary detention and since my release from prison. Being part of Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign was incredible and the waves of messages and letters from its supporters around the world gave me strength and courage and reinforced my commitment to defending human rights.”
Yves Makwambala and Fred Bauma – Democratic Republic of Congo
Youth activists Yves Makwambala and Fred Bauma were released at the end of August 2016 in the Democratic Republic of Congo. An amazing 170,000 people took action for the pair as part of Write for Rights 2015. “Every letter, every visit, every word has strengthened us and reinforced our determination in this long but just struggle for freedom and democracy,” said Yves.
Seán Binder – Greece
In January 2026, human rights defender Seán Binder and 23 others connected to a search and rescue NGO were acquitted of all charges in Greece. After years on trial, Seán no longer faces the possibility of a 20-year prison sentence for helping refugees.
His humanitarian work saved lives, yet like many others across Greece, Seán was criminalized for helping people in need. Amnesty International had been campaigning for the charges against him to be dropped since 2018. In 2019, Seán became a Write for Rights case, and hundreds of thousands of people around the world took action in support of him. They wrote letters, sent messages and demanded justice.
Eight years after Amnesty first called for the charges to be dropped, Seán was finally acquitted.
“It is a huge relief that I will not spend the next 20 years in a prison cell,” Seán said. “But at the same time, it is troubling that this should ever have been a possibility.”
Seán’s story is a powerful reminder of what collective action can achieve.
Moses Akatugba – Nigeria
Moses Akatugba was a 16-year-old student when he was arrested in 2005 by police in southern Nigeria, on suspicion of armed robbery and stealing three telephones. He was tortured by police during their interrogations, beaten and suspended upside down from a ceiling fan for hours. His nails were pulled out with pliers to coerce him into signing a “confession” – the only basis for his death sentence eight years later.
After 10 years in detention and 800,000 letters from people all over the world through Write for Rights 2014, Moses was granted pardon by the governor of the Niger Delta State on 28 May 2015. Thanks to this outpouring of solidarity he can now tell his story.
“I am overwhelmed. I thank Amnesty International and their activists for the great support that made me a conqueror in this situation. Amnesty International members and activist are my heroes.”
Rita Mahato – Nepal
In 2009, human rights defender Rita Mahato was threatened with death, rape and kidnapping for helping women in Nepal who had suffered acts of violence. She was a health adviser at the Women’s Rehabilitation Centre (WOREC), a leading NGO in Nepal, yet police failed to provide Rita with protection or to investigate the threats. After Amnesty took up her case for Write for Rights 2009, schools, campuses and other institutions around the world started sending letters, postcards and other materials in support of her. The publicity and posters became so widespread that the police and local authorities began calling Rita to provide support, making her feel less alone. While the harassment has ended, Rita still stands up for what she believes in.
“Even today, I continue to work for human rights and women’s rights, and I will continue to do so. “Working for human rights is not easy. Understanding the importance and responsibility of human rights work, and through collaboration and collective efforts, I will continue to raise the voices of those who are unheard, with courage, inspiration and determination. Things have become easier for me because I know that I am not alone.”
Aleksandra (Sacha) Skochilenko – Russia
Russian artist Aleksandra “Sacha” Skochilenko was arrested for protesting Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In March 2022, she replaced price tags at a supermarket with paper labels that contained information censored by Russian state-run media. She was charged with “dissemination of knowingly false information about Russian Armed Forces” and sentenced to seven years in December 2023. In 2024, thanks in part to international pressure from Write for Rights 2022, Sacha was finally released as part of a huge prisoner swap, involving Russia and Belarus, who agreed to a swap with the United States, Germany, Norway, Poland, and Slovenia. Sacha now lives in exile in Germany.
“Thank you for all the support that you gave me back there when I was in prison, because it helped me to survive. Helped me to believe in some miracles. Because of your support I’m here.”

The Architecture of Water: ArchDaily's October Editorial Focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Water is life. Animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria all depend on it: water structures their cells, carries their nutrients, and hosts the chemistry that keeps them alive. Even the rare exceptions confirm the rule. Some seeds and spores can lose nearly all their water and enter a dormancy so deep that their metabolism almost stops, yet it is water that brings them back. In the most literal sense, water connects us.
But it also divides us. Every year, thousands of people leave North Africa in overcrowded boats bound for Lampedusa, seeking better living conditions in Europe; more than 30,000 have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean since 2014. Water draws borders and controls flows. Before the war on Iran began in February 2026, the Strait of Hormuz carried around 25% of the world's seaborne crude oil, with effects felt in fuel prices far from the Gulf. Water also sits at the center of the environmental debate, where its excess can be as lethal as its absence. Severe floods increasingly strike countries that have contributed least to global emissions, while the largest polluters remain better equipped to resist. If water is life, it can also mean death. Ultimately, water is political.
This tension is the starting point for ArchDaily's October Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Humans have always gravitated toward water, from the river valleys where agriculture began to the coastlines that now concentrate many of the world's largest cities. As seas rise and floods and erosion intensify, the idea of "controlling" water looks increasingly fragile, and building at its edge raises questions of necessity, freedom, and responsibility. Should buildable land be expanded through reclamation, and at what cost to fragile ecosystems? Where does ownership end and stewardship begin? And who gets to claim land on or around water?
Throughout the month, the coverage moves across scales and geographies. It digs into the ground itself, examining how soil, drainage, and access to water have always been matters of power. It revisits historic water structures, long preserved as monuments, and asks whether they could work as infrastructure once again. Along the coasts, it looks at mangrove forests as living barriers that rival concrete seawalls, and at the bayous, where design is learning to negotiate with shifting land and rising water.
In cities, the coverage follows Southeast Asian canals being reclaimed as ecological and public networks rather than treated as drains, and Latin American plazas and parks designed to flood. Where water is scarce, it explores technologies that draw it from the air, weighing their promise against their limits. Together, these stories point toward a Blue Economy grounded in regeneration rather than exploitation.
Can architecture accept a degree of uncertainty, designing for water that rises, recedes, and returns? Who decides where water ends and land begins? And what would it mean to treat water not as a resource to be controlled, but as a common to be shared?
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Whale stranding leaves at least 12 dead on New Zealand beach
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:59:57 CST
16:59:57 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- At least 12 pygmy killer whales have died after becoming stranded on New Zealand's Ninety Mile Beach, with conservation officials, Maori tribes and volunteers continuing efforts to rescue surviving whales.
Between 12 and 15 whales had died so far, while an unknown number had been refloated from the beach in New Zealand's Far North, an official from the Department of Conservation told Radio New Zealand (RNZ) on Friday.
The department was alerted to the stranding at about 7:00 p.m. on Thursday local time. Staff went to the site but withdrew as an incoming tide and fading light made conditions unsafe, RNZ reported.
Rescue efforts continued on Friday in challenging conditions, with the department working with Far North Maori tribes. Dead whales were being moved for burial, according to the report.
Pygmy killer whales, a species of oceanic dolphin which can grow up to 2.6 meters long, had stranded on Ninety Mile Beach before. About 12 stranded in 2018, with eight transported to calmer waters on the opposite coast. Only one survived the subsequent refloating attempt, the report said. ■

Top 10 Comedies for the Weekend: Films That Will Help You Relax and Have a Laugh
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:59:20 EEST
16:59:20 KST

Top 10 Comedies for the Weekend: Films That Will Help You Relax and Have a Laugh
Kyiv • UNN
A selection of ten comedies for relaxation and laughter — from "The Hangover" to "Yes Man."
If over the weekend you feel like putting serious matters aside, getting comfortable on the couch, and simply having a laugh, then it is time to choose a good comedy. UNN has compiled a top 10 list of films featuring hilarious characters and incredible adventures that certainly cannot be called ordinary.
A Million Ways to Die in the West
The Wild West is not the best place for someone who dislikes conflict. That is exactly the situation farmer Albert finds himself in: instead of accepting a challenge to a duel, he backs down and loses his beloved Louise. The girl quickly finds a replacement for him—the local womanizer Foy—but Albert’s life changes after he meets Anna, the wife of notorious outlaw Clinch Leatherwood. She helps him believe in his own strength, and together they spend time shooting, having fun, and learning the local rules of survival. There is only one problem: Anna’s husband soon arrives in town with his gang. And clearly not for a friendly conversation.
The Miser
François Gautier is a talented violinist, but his greatest talent, it seems, has nothing to do with music. He knows how to economize on literally everything. For him, spending money is almost a personal tragedy, and any bill can ruin his mood. However, one day the man’s ordinary life begins to fall apart. He will have to reconsider his attitude toward money, relationships, and the people around him—especially after an already-grown daughter unexpectedly appears in his life.
We're the Millers
David sells drugs and is quite happy with his not entirely law-abiding life until one unpleasant situation causes him to lose both his merchandise and his money. His boss offers him a chance to make things right. He has to transport a large shipment of drugs from Mexico to the United States, so David comes up with what he considers a brilliant plan: create a fake family. A stripper named Rose, a teenager named Kenny, and a rebellious young woman join him. The four set off under the guise of an ordinary American family. All they have to do is avoid giving themselves away—and avoid falling out with one another before crossing the border.
Dirty Grandpa
After his wife’s death, Jack moves in with his daughter’s family. It seems like a wonderful opportunity for him not to be alone, but his grandson is not at all thrilled about sharing his room with his grandfather. At first, the relatives try to reach a peaceful agreement, but the struggle for personal space quickly reaches a new level. Instead of a quiet family life, the house turns into a real battlefield, where everyone is ready to go all the way.
The Hangover
Four friends travel to Las Vegas to throw the groom an unforgettable bachelor party before his wedding. It truly does become unforgettable, but not at all in the way they planned. In the morning, the men wake up amid complete chaos, with a tiger and a small child in their hotel room, while the groom has disappeared. The worst part is that no one remembers what happened during the night, so the friends now have to piece together the events of the previous evening to find their missing friend and return in time for the wedding, which is about to begin.
Serial (Bad) Weddings
Monsieur and Madame Verneuil raised four daughters and dreamed of a peaceful family life, but their older daughters’ choice of husbands became a real test for the parents: their sons-in-law have different cultural and religious backgrounds. When the family had almost come to terms with the situation, the youngest daughter announced her own choice, once again shocking her parents. The two families are about to meet and prepare for a wedding that has every chance of turning into family chaos.
DZIDZIO: The First Time
Mykhailo Khoma's character misses his flight to Portugal, where his mother lives. This failure comes at a high price: his furious mother throws her son out of his Kyiv apartment and sends him to his native village. There, the protagonist meets old friends, gets to know new people, and unexpectedly finds love. At the same time, he has to help local talents prepare for a performance at a church festival. And although the film's title may hint at an entirely different story, it is actually a romantic comedy about growing up, friendship, and the search for one's own happiness.
Norbit
Norbit has lived under the pressure of Rasputia since childhood—a large woman with a very difficult personality who has essentially decided what his life should be like. Everything changes when Kate, the girl Norbit truly loves, returns to town. Now the protagonist must not only find the courage to fight for his love, but also figure out how to break free from Rasputia's influence. The task is, to put it mildly, not easy. Especially when the person you want to escape from has entirely different plans.
Spy
Susan Cooper works as a CIA analyst and is used to staying in the shadows. She coordinates the work of field agents and dreams of one day taking their place, but when the agency's covert network is threatened, Susan unexpectedly gets the chance to go on a real mission. The reason is simple: the enemies do not know what she looks like, so the woman who used to observe dangerous missions through a headset now finds herself in the middle of a spy adventure. And it quickly becomes clear that theory and practice are two completely different things. The film also features a funny episode with Verka Serduchka, which adds even more color to this already absurd spy story.
Always Say "Yes"
Carl Allen is used to turning down everything new: meetings with friends, spontaneous trips, unusual offers, and even the chance to change his own life. After attending an unusual seminar, he decides to test a simple rule on himself: never say "no" again and agree to any opportunities that come his way. At first, this change brings Carl a genuine burst of positive emotions. He meets new people, gets into amusing situations, and finally begins living a much more active life. However, the protagonist gradually realizes that constantly saying "yes" is not so easy either. The comedy starring Jim Carrey combines absurd humor with a story about how it is sometimes worth stepping outside one's comfort zone, while also remembering to think things through.

Breadcrumb
Yemen carried out 20 strikes on Houthi targets in Taiz province, spokesperson says
The military spokesperson for Yemen's internationally recognised and Saudi-backed government said on Friday that warplanes carried out 20 strikes over the past three hours targeting Houthi movements, personnel, vehicles and military equipment in Taiz province.
The strikes come amid the most serious conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022.
Unchallenged occupation of southwestern Yemen's Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north, a tighter grip on the Red Sea coast and easier access to the south and the southern port city of Aden, seat of the government.
The renewed conflict has already displaced tens of thousands of people and could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia said on Thursday the Houthis attacked a power distribution station in Medina that supplies electricity to the Prophet's Mosque.
A Houthi military source, quoted by the Houthi-linked Saba news agency, denied the claim and said it was intended to cover up what he described as Saudi Arabia's failure to substantiate an earlier accusation that the Houthis had targeted the Muslim holy city of Mecca.
Saudi Arabia said two weeks ago it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered restricted airspace over the city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca or any other Islamic holy site.
Fighting was widespread across Taiz and authorities had ordered the closure of all roads leading into the province, designating them military operational areas, six military sources told Reuters.
Around 19 roads were affected by the closures, including the main route running from southern Sanaa to Taiz, the sources said.

Uzbekistan wins home gold at record-breaking Chess Olympiad in Samarkand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:58:34 UTC
16:58:34 KST

Almost 400 teams from more than 190 countries competed over 11 rounds. Germany took bronze, while Hungary, France and Spain also finished in the top 10, alongside Azerbaijan and Armenia.
The biggest Chess Olympiad in history brought almost 400 teams from around the world to Samarkand, where host nation Uzbekistan won gold in the Open competition after defeating Ukraine in the final round.
Uzbekistan won its first Chess Olympiad title in India's Chennai in 2022 and followed it with bronze in Budapest two years later.
“This is our second Olympiad victory. Winning it at home feels different,” Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov said. “I think we played the tournament at the highest level.”
Sindarov’s next major test will come later this year. After winning the Candidates Tournament, he will challenge India’s Gukesh Dommaraju for the world title in Geneva from 22 November to 12 December.
Both players will be 20 when the match begins, making it the youngest World Championship contest in chess history.
How the Chess Olympiad works
Organised by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), the Chess Olympiad is the leading international team competition in chess.
Unlike most major chess tournaments, players compete for their countries rather than only for themselves.
Four players from one national team face four from another at the same time, with their individual results combined to determine the result between the two countries.
Teams compete over 11 rounds, facing different opponents as the tournament progresses.
Uzbekistan finished the competition with 20 of 22 possible match points, winning 10 of its 11 matches. Among the teams it defeated were defending champions India, China and the top-seeded US. Its only loss came against eventual bronze medallists Germany.
Uzbekistan claims second Open title
Nodirbek Abdusattorov was another key member of the winning team. Playing on Uzbekistan’s first board, meaning he generally faced the strongest player from each opposing team, he completed the Chess Olympiad without losing a game and received an individual gold medal for his performance.
“I think we can now confidently say that Uzbekistan is unrivalled in the world of chess,” Abdusattorov said after the victory.
India finished with silver, while Germany took bronze.
For Germany, the result marked its first Open team medal at a Chess Olympiad since 2000, when it won silver in Istanbul.
“I think it’s by far the best Olympiad we’ve had in recent years, at least as long as I’ve been playing,” German grandmaster Vincent Keymer told Euronews.
Several European countries also finished near the top, with Hungary, France and Spain all placing inside the top 10, alongside Azerbaijan and Armenia.
In the women’s competition, China won gold, Kazakhstan finished second and defending champions India took bronze.
Indian grandmaster Koneru Humpy was part of the bronze-medal-winning team.
“There is a lot of attention from all the spectators and followers, and this is one of the widely followed tournaments from all over the world,” Humpy told Euronews.
The biggest Olympiad yet
The final field included 205 teams in the Open and 189 in the Women’s competition.
For almost two weeks, hundreds of games were played simultaneously in the same competition hall, bringing national teams from around the world together in Samarkand.
The tournament also coincided with a change at the top of international chess. Timur Turlov, then president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, was elected president of FIDE during the federation’s General Assembly in Samarkand. At 38, he became the youngest person ever elected to the post.
“The interest in the game is definitely rising year over year,” Turlov told Euronews. “It’s not just a professional sport. It’s a sport which is getting more and more popular almost everywhere.”
At the end of the tournament, the Olympiad flag was handed to representatives of the United Arab Emirates.
Abu Dhabi will host the 47th Chess Olympiad in 2028.

Europe’s LNG imports hit four-month high in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:56:23 UTC
16:56:23 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Europe imported the largest volume of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in four months in September amid the need to accelerate the replenishment of gas inventories ahead of winter, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
In September, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system totaled around 10.6 bln cubic meters, up 15% from August but down 6% compared with September 2025.
In January-September 2026, LNG flows from terminals into Europe’s gas transmission system slowed to around 101 bln cubic meters, 3% less than in the same period of 2025.
LNG accounted for the largest share of Europe’s gas supplies in January-September at 42.2%, according to data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG) as of September 29. Supplies from the North Sea, primarily Norwegian gas, ranked second with a 38.7% share, followed by gas supplies from North Africa at 9.6% and supplies from the east at 6%, including Russian gas, gas supplies from Ukraine, and withdrawals by European companies of their own gas from Ukrainian storage facilities.
Gas supplies from Azerbaijan accounted for 3.5%.
