Evacuated in an incubator, now back in Gaza getting to know mama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:08:11 UTC
14:08:11 KST

Evacuated in an incubator, now back in Gaza getting to know mama
CAIRO/GAZA, Oct 2 - Bissan was born because of an airstrike.
Two weeks into the war in Gaza in October 2023, an Israeli attack ripped through her family's home in Beit Lahiya near the Israeli border, killing a sister she never got to meet. The blast seriously injured her pregnant mother, who was forced to deliver Bissan six weeks early to save both their lives.
Weeks later, the baby was driven out to Egypt in an ambulance while still in an incubator, one of a group of 29 preterm infants evacuated from a neonatal hospital ward as Israel's invading forces drew close.
Seven of those babies died in Egypt, but Bissan survived. While she grew in Egyptian hospitals and a care home, her mother, Sundus al-Kurd, never lost hope that they would be reunited. Back in Gaza, as the war raged on, Sundus made video calls to speak to the baby whenever she had internet access.
In March this year, with a ceasefire ostensibly in place, Bissan was returned to Gaza to be reunited with her family in a mission assisted by the UN, along with 10 other children from the same group evacuated as preterm babies.
When they were finally reunited, Bissan didn't recognise her mother, Sundus said. The girl, now 2-1/2, would say "mama" to any woman who showed her kindness.
Reuters documented their reunion and visited with them and several of the other children in the months that followed as they built bonds with their mothers and fathers. Here are their stories.
GETTING USED TO EXPLOSIONS
Returning to Gaza as a toddler meant learning to live in a war zone, where Israeli airstrikes have continued despite the ceasefire agreed a year ago between Israel and Hamas.
When Bissan first heard the booms, she would freeze in a state of fear for several minutes, Sundus said. She still begins to panic if a balloon pops near her.
"Her life changed. Her life became sleeping and waking up to the sound of explosions, to the sound of the numerous attacks and missiles," said her mother.
On a sunny morning soon after their reunion, her mother took her to a small zoo in central Gaza. Bissan, who wears pink-framed glasses, gazed in awe as a blue parrot latched onto her mother's arm.
'HE WAS SUPPOSED TO CALL ME DAD'
Of the 11 preterm babies evacuated to Egypt in November 2023 and returned to Gaza this year, not all were able to meet their mothers. For baby Ibrahim it was already too late.
His mother, Israa Badr, fell into a deep state of depression after her son, born during her eighth month of pregnancy, was evacuated to Egypt. She died the following month. Her husband Jabri Badr said doctors "told us she died of sorrow, of sadness."
"Ever since he was in her womb, she thought about him, dreamed of holding him, playing with him, and feeling what it was like to be a mother," he said.
Ibrahim is now reunited with his father in Gaza, but Badr said they have struggled to connect.
"He was supposed to call me dad. Today he doesn't even say dad, or anything. I tell him to come, and he ignores me."
Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental health expert, said that after two years apart it was natural that it would take time for parents to connect with their children.
MOTHER'S MILK, AND HER EMBRACE
Bissan, Ibrahim and the others "were deprived not only of their mother's milk but also of her embrace and the emotional development that comes with it," Abu Mashayikh said.
Rebuilding the bond takes time. Some days, Bissan and Sundus walk down to Gaza's Mediterranean shore. On a recent afternoon, they held hands as they walked where the sand meets the sea. Bissan flashed a big smile as she gazed out to the horizon.
The evenings are more difficult, but still bring them closer together, Sundus said.
When explosions ring out in the middle of the night, Bissan wakes up and seeks out her mother's care.
"Bissan has begun to understand who mama really is, who her mother really is," Sundus said. "I am the only person present in her life. I am the one who feeds her, changes her clothes, combs her hair, and plays with her." REUTERS

Latvijas Banka grants crypto-asset and payment licences to three companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:06:01 UTC
14:06:01 KST

Latvijas Banka’s Supervision Committee granted four licences to three companies on 30 September: Noah LV SIA received authorisation to provide both crypto-asset and payment services, Neverless SIA obtained a payment institution licence, and Atrya Technologies SIA was authorised to provide crypto-asset services.
Noah LV SIA’s crypto-asset licence covers custody and administration of crypto-assets on behalf of clients, exchanging crypto-assets for funds, executing client orders and providing crypto-asset transfer services. Its payment institution licence authorises the execution of payment transactions, including credit transfers and standing orders.
Neverless SIA also received authorisation to execute credit transfers and standing orders. The company already holds a crypto-asset services licence from Latvijas Banka, which it obtained in May 2026.
Meanwhile, Atrya Technologies SIA’s licence allows it to provide custody and administration of crypto-assets on behalf of clients and to exchange crypto-assets for other crypto-assets.
The latest approvals bring the number of companies authorised by Latvijas Banka under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) to 12, while 13 companies in Latvia hold payment institution licences. Crypto-asset service providers authorised under MiCA in one EU member state may offer their services across the bloc through the cross-border notification mechanism.
The list of authorised crypto-asset service providers is available in Latvijas Banka’s financial market participant register, while the European Securities and Markets Authority maintains an EU-wide register.
Latvijas Banka encourages businesses preparing licence applications to consult its licensing guides, which explain the requirements, supporting documents and application review deadlines. Crypto-asset businesses can also use the central bank’s guidance on classifying assets under MiCA and determining whether they fall within its scope or are governed by other legislation.
Companies can request pre-licensing consultations to discuss the applicable legal framework and obtain an initial assessment of their compliance with regulatory requirements. According to Latvijas Banka, this early cooperation helps businesses prepare stronger applications and supports a smoother licensing process.

How many birds are killed by offshore wind turbines? Scientists use thermal cameras to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:02:08 UTC
14:02:08 KST

A year-long study has observed millions of birds migrating across the North Sea to measure the threat of offshore wind farms.
Europe leads the world in offshore wind energy, with more than 30 gigawatts (GW) of installed capacity across the continent – enough to power more than 26 million homes annually.
Earlier this year, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK committed to deliver 100GW of joint offshore wind projects across shared North Sea waters by 2050.
The €9.5 billion plan, known as the Hamburg Declaration, aims to turn the North Sea into the world’s “largest clean energy reservoir” and mobilise €1 trillion of capital in Europe.
But is our path to a fossil fuel-free future jeopardising birds that are already plummeting in number due to human-caused climate change?
Are offshore wind turbines a threat to birds?
Most studies into bird collisions with turbines tend to focus on wind farms located on land. But every year, millions of songbirds cross the North Sea during spring and autumn migration, mostly at night.
Capturing collisions at sea can be difficult, due to a lack of light and the remote location.
However, a new year-long pilot study has allowed researchers to detect these small birds and bats during hours of darkness, as well as larger birds during daylight hours, using a combination of thermal cameras and artificial intelligence (AI).
The study, initiated by the energy company Vattenfall, was carried out at the Hollandse Kust Zuid offshore wind farm in collaboration with Wildlife Imaging Systems (WIS) and Wageningen University & Research (WUR).
WIS installed 16 thermal cameras on an offshore wind turbine, covering all angles and operating 24 hours a day. Combined with AI, the system detected and interpreted bird movements day and night, including in poor visibility such as fog or rain.
“Safeguarding biodiversity is an important part of the energy transition,” says Karen Krijgsveld, a bird ecology researcher at Wageningen University & Research.
“On land, we already know quite a lot about when and why birds collide with turbines, and which species are most at risk. As offshore wind energy continues to expand, we need to develop that same understanding at sea.”
Over almost a year of monitoring, covering both a spring and an autumn migration season, 22 possible bird collisions were identified – two of which were confirmed and one considered highly probable.
“Until now, estimates of offshore bird collisions were mainly based on theoretical models,” says Jesper Kyed Larsen, a bioscience expert at Vattenfall.
“At sea, it’s extremely difficult to verify fatalities because there are no remains to recover. This study demonstrates how we can get the empirical data needed to improve collision estimates and secure efficient mitigation measures.”
The study does not claim that collisions are rare or that these initial results from one turbine can be applied everywhere. The primary aim was to test the technology’s performance under real offshore conditions.
But a previous study by the German Offshore Wind Energy Association (BWO) also yielded similar results.
Researchers analysed more than four million bird movements over one and a half years, using radar and AI-based cameras. They found that more than 99.8 per cent of migratory birds reliably avoided the wind turbines.
Vattenfall previously conducted another study on an offshore wind farm near Aberdeen, Scotland. Over a period of 19 months – from June 2023 to December 2024 – video recordings of a wind turbine were made with the help of AI-supported analyses.
A total of 2,007 bird flight paths near the monitored turbine were examined and no collisions were found.
How can Europe protect its endangered birds?
Despite all three studies suggesting a minimal impact of offshore wind farms on birds, conservationists warn that measures must still be put in place to help protect endangered species.
Of the 26 seabirds that breed on the UK’s coastlines and islands, 10 are already on the endangered list.
Back in 2020, the land-based Smola wind farm in Norway, which consists of 68 turbines, painted one blade on each turbine black to make them stand out to birds. They found the initiative reduced avian fatalities by a staggering 70 per cent, from 11 recorded bird carcasses before painting to six afterwards.
Some critics argue that making wind farms more visible could impact birds’ migration patterns, forcing them to fly longer routes around a turbine. This means they will use up more energy, and it will take them longer to get back to their chicks.
Other measures include placing turbines far away from sensitive habitats and avoiding migration paths in the first place. Thermal cameras and radar can also be used to further investigate the risk these turbines pose to our flying friends.

National e-calculation math competition returns for 3rd year on October 8
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:02:00 UTC
14:02:00 KST

National e-calculation math competition returns for 3rd year on October 8
Estonia's annual nationwide online math competition, e-rehkendus (e-calculation), takes place for the third time next Wednesday.
Organized by Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) in conjunction with public broadcaster ERR and major bank SEB, the contest asks participants to solve 12 school math problems, with €1,234 in prize money up for grabs, as well as other prizes.
Twelve math problems covering the school curriculum from grades 1 to 12, though adults are eligible to take part too. The questions will be available on the site: erehkendus.err.ee. The winner will be the first person to correctly solve all 12 problems by 1 p.m. Since the questions go live at 10 a.m. on the same day, time will be of the essence.
This year's theme is anxiety about math —the fear or tension associated with learning or solving math problems, which in a vicious cycle can make it harder to concentrate and lead to worse results. e-rehkendus' creators say it offers a playful, low-pressure environment to help ease it.
Organizers also note that adults' attitudes matter too: Research shows that teachers' and parents' own math anxiety is easily passed on to children.
"Mathematical thinking is the foundation for those choices, and e-rehkendus helps highlight its importance in a playful and inclusive way," said SEB board chairman Allan Parik, commenting on the bank's third year supporting the initiative.
Prizes include, for the best high school student, a place on a freely chosen bachelor's program at TalTech without the usual entrance exams; a micro-degree program for the winning adult, and awards for the best primary school pupil, student, teacher, lecturer or researcher. Special and lottery prizes are provided by Tele2, Piletilevi, Enefit, the Energy Discovery Centre, Prisma, Domino's Pizza and Raw Edge drinks, as well as by the organizers, TalTech, ERR and SEB.
Last year's competition attracted nearly 30,000 people, while the high schools with the highest turnouts were the Nõo Reaalgümnaasium, Gustav Adolfi Gümnaasium and Narva Gümnaasium. Cellphone network provider Tele2 and electronics firm Scanfil performed well among companies.
The e-rehkendus competition takes place on Wednesday, October 8, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., and is open to all.
The main prize, the €1,234 donated by SEB, will be divided up equally by all those who solved all 12 problems correctly.
Results solved with the help of artificial intelligence will not be admissible.
The problems were created by members of the Estonian Mathematical Society's (Eesti Matemaatika Selts) School Mathematics Association (Koolimatemaatika Ühendus).

How India's classrooms are coping in the age  of instant gratification &amp; low attention spans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:01:56 UTC
14:01:56 KST

Classrooms in parts of India are grappling with an underlying problem that no curriculum revision can easily fix. Students raised on on-demand food delivery, constant social media reels and instant AI answers are finding it harder to sustain attention, tolerate boredom, or work toward rewards that don't arrive at once.Teachers, as a result, are increasingly engaging a generation that is much less attentive than before. A recent nationwide survey by the National Council of CBSE Schools found that almost 70% of teachers across the country have observed a sharp decline in their students' focus and classroom attention.The survey, which covered around 6.3 lakh respondents -- teachers, under 18 students and their parents -- also found that 74% of students spend more than two hours a day on screen for non-academic purposes. And teachers reported rising anxiety, irritability and reduced face-to-face interaction among children.Parmeshwar Dattarao Bhurke, a teacher, says the trend is evident in everyday classroom experiences. "Many children no longer have the focus needed to sit through an hour-long lesson or read a passage without their minds wandering," he said. This has prompted many teachers to experiment with newer learning methods, he added.
"Earlier, one student could read a chapter aloud while the rest of the class listened. That no longer works... The idea now is to keep their minds actively engaged through the session."Priya, another middle school teacher, says she has noticed a decline in students' retention levels. "Even when children appear to be listening, their minds are elsewhere. They are also less willing to struggle through any difficult task. This affects their performance in school as well as their behaviour, as they become averse to any kind of challenges or discomfort."For 15-year-old student Chinmayee Sonna, the shift is visible in the way her classmates now study. "Instead of sitting with textbooks or working through ideas, many of my classmates look for the easier option, whether that is AI-generated summaries or explainer videos. They are able to retain less through this method but it helps revise quickly and saves time," she said.Psychologists say such habits reflect a behavioural shift driven by constant access to instant rewards. "They trigger dopamine, giving us a brief rush of joy that reinforces the behaviour and makes us want to repeat it. This is different from the real-life feats, where satisfaction comes only after much effort and patience," Rashi Bhatnagar, a psychologist, said.It is these consequences that extend into the classroom. "When rewards come with almost no effort, the brain begins to prefer them. Like an unused muscle, our ability to wait, tolerate boredom and sustain attention gradually weakens, leaving us restless when tasks demand patience," Bhatnagar said.This is why there is a downside to schools trying to make every lesson entertaining, she adds. "Education cannot always provide instant pleasure if it is to encourage deep thinking. Schools need to consciously create opportunities for children to reflect and generate new ideas."The habit of expecting immediate outcomes also affects resilience. "Because children have not developed the ability to wait for results, many give up too quickly. We need to teach them not to quit at the first sign of difficulty," Bhatnagar said.Psychiatrist Nisha Singla, talking about the digital ecosystem, says it is deliberately designed to reinforce instant gratification. "Social media apps, notifications and quick commerce applications are addictive and the brain begins to crave them. Reading or learning something new also gives us a sense of achievement, but the reward is delayed. That is where all the difference lies."Rebuilding patience, she says, begins with allowing children to slow down. "We need to let them get bored... There is a tendency to fill every moment of their day with something or the other, but boredom is equally important. Parents and schools should consciously encourage delayed gratification."
Another challenge to consider in adapting classrooms is large class sizes and poor teacher-student ratios. "This leaves little room for us to nurture each child's curiosity and individual learning needs. At the same time, schools remain under pressure to deliver high marks and pass percentages, leaving us focused on examination outcomes rather than redesigning learning around children's changing needs," Priya said.As educators wait for the national mental health and well-being policy for schools, they say it should help students find meaning in a learning process whose greatest rewards cannot be a sprint and a quick fix.
A Dehradun-based journalist focused on human-interest stories that link local issues to wider national conversations. She covers developments across genres, with a special interest in civic issues, education, and the environment.

Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?
Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year
Gambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget.
The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes.
But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder of Paddy Power who has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”.
So who’s right? It’s complicated …
What does the industry say?
Bookies might be best known for bets on horses or football but they make big money from slot machines. The Betting and Gaming Council, an industry lobby group, commissioned a report from the accounting firm EY that estimated a duty rise to 40% could close up to 1,470 betting shops (nearly a third of the total 5,617), resulting in 15,900 job losses and a net loss to the exchequer of about £120m. Horse racing, which receives a levy from bookies’ profits, would also take a hit.
Done said he alone would be forced to close about 495 betting shops, nearly half of Betfred’s estate, with the loss of 2,475 jobs and £67m in taxes.
Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has written to Burnham saying it would have to make job cuts across its nationwide estate of 2,300 shops, were the policy to go ahead. Casinos and bingo halls are in the firing line too. Rank Group, which owns Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos, cautioned that a third of its venues could close, affecting 2,000 staff.
Are they crying wolf?
When dealing with bookmakers, it is wise to be sceptical.
Back in 2019, Betfred had about 1,620 shops. Since then, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to tougher regulation or taxes. While most of the policies it objected to have come to pass, the number of shops has decreased by only about 330. Some of that is down to a broader shift to the web that has led to soaring online gambling revenues.
In one Betfred TV ad, Done encourages punters to “come and see me”. In your neighbourhood bookies? No, at Betfred.com. Meanwhile, the Done family has taken out tens of millions of pounds in dividends, including £50m in 2022 alone.
What it failed to mention is that it has been increasing its use of AI within the business since well before the tax rise. Some staff at Bet365’s Stoke HQ are understood to feel that government policy is a convenient smokescreen for good old-fashioned corporate cost-cutting.
A spokesperson said Bet365 was responding to a “highly competitive trading environment, plus increased regulatory and tax-related costs”.
So it’s all a bluff?
Well, no. The UK’s biggest gambling companies, including Betfred, Entain, Flutter and more, have all announced cuts since Reeves’s duty rise. It is impossible to say how much of this retrenchment might have happened anyway, given economic worries and structural shifts within the sector. However, it makes sense that any further increase in costs, in the form of higher taxes on slot machines, will negatively affect the gambling sector.
Simon Thomas, the chief executive of the Hippodrome Casino in London, says that fear of the tax is already hurting investment.
“We have a £6m rooftop expansion plan with full planning permission, ready to go. With MGD up in the air, we’ve had to shelve it,” he said, adding that if MGD goes up to 40%, a third of bingo halls and a third of casinos could close.
Does the government want a smaller gambling sector?
Burnham has already moved to limit the opening of new gambling premises. He has voiced particular concerns about 24-hour adult gaming centres (AGCs), high street venues packed with the sort of machines that would be more heavily taxed by an MGD increase. The rise of these “slot farms” is understood to be the main driver for any such move.
But there are question marks over whether AGCs would actually take the hit. They already have much lower overheads and looser regulation than casinos and bingo halls, which have experienced negligible growth. Last year, AGCs managed to increase their takings from £528m to £613m by packing more machines into larger venues.
So if slot machines taxes go up, in theory AGCs are best placed to survive the impact. The AGC operator Merkur has already offered to buy some of the 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale, indicating it is unruffled by the prospect of a tax rise. If others follow suit, just as bookies retrench, an MGD rise could simply lead to bookies being replaced by 24-hour slot farms.
As Treasury officials weigh up duty rises, they will have to consider the law of unintended consequences.

After rape allegations at Cornell University, why are women again being urged to talk to their sons? Why not men? | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

There were seven men in all, and it lasted almost seven hours.
What followed, according to the woman at the heart of the Cornell University case that has gripped student campuses around the world, was less a sexual encounter than a grim pack-bonding exercise fuelled by booze and ketamine, in which she was passed around like a blow-up doll.
Twenty years old and drunk at a college frat house party, she had reportedly agreed to a threesome with a student she liked, though her lawyer maintains she wasn’t sober enough to consent. But it is what allegedly followed – including a crude invitation sent to a group chat of more than 50 of the men’s friends, advertising “free pussy” upstairs if they wanted to join in – that really makes the blood boil. Could so many men really see nothing here to challenge?
One reportedly texted back “Shop still open?” in the early hours of the morning. By that stage, she was concluding that “there was no way for her to escape” a room full of predatory men, according to the lawsuit filed by the alleged victim against both the students she accuses of pressuring her into taking drugs and raping her in the autumn of 2024, and Cornell University which, she argues, failed to protect her. (All deny wrongdoing.) Though two of the seven were reportedly expelled after she went to campus police, none were arrested; five were free to continue their education after variously writing essays about what they’d done, serving short suspensions and attending workshops. It was the alleged victim who lost her future, dropping out of university and struggling with her mental health to the point that her lawyer says she is “barely hanging on”.
Her story, emerging just as this year’s freshers were settling into halls in Britain, has left young women understandably incandescent with rage but touched a deep nerve with older ones too.
All over social media, mothers are posting and swapping advice on how to raise sons who don’t just refrain from rape but who would, if they ever got such a message, realise something was wrong and be brave enough to intervene. Some of that advice is excellent, and I completely understand the urge to do something – anything – rather than let another generation of young women go through the same wringer. Bringing up our own boys to do better feels like the one practical step any mother can take. Yet it makes me angry, all the same; angry and exhausted.
How has rape prevention become yet another thing on mothers’ to-do lists? Where are all the men – the celebrity dads, the sports coaches and the role models, the male politicians who are usually only too keen to talk about sexual assault if the perpetrators are immigrants – with ideas for countering the warped, pornified messages boys receive? I understand why good men might be wary of speaking over women. But this is a job for all parents, not just half of them.
The University of Bath this week announced an investigation into claims that members of a student sports club had supposedly been overheard talking about spiking freshers’ drinks. Even if it was just a tasteless joke, it’s not funny: the Office for Students found that one in seven British students finishing university reported suffering sexual violence, with men as well as women becoming victims. Though freshers at many universities are now routinely made to sit through mandatory lessons on sexual consent and healthy relationships, those can’t unpick in an hour everything they’ve absorbed over the previous 18 years, including sometimes in their own homes.
It’s hard to talk about this without alienating what is still a majority of teenage boys who don’t want to hurt anyone, feel vulnerable themselves at times, and need help resisting aggressive peer pressure. That’s precisely why they need to hear about consent from grown men who understand exactly what it was like to be 14, horny and confused. Yet in too many homes it’s mothers who end up shouldering the burden of conversations about consent, perhaps in part because they start not with an awkward lecture on the eve of university drop-off but way back in the nursery years. (You don’t talk to a three-year-old about sex, obviously. But you can teach them to respect other people’s feelings, to stop the game if it’s obvious someone isn’t enjoying it and not to take what they want by force. Consent is above all a social skill.)
If fathers don’t know how to raise these subjects – well, mothers are equally mortified, but we muddle through because we don’t want our sons to be a danger to other people’s daughters or themselves. It’s what male role models do, however, that perhaps matters most. Boys learn by watching how the men they look up to treat their partners, female colleagues, women on the street. They notice how you react to sexual assault allegations made against a favourite celebrity, or indeed wannabe president. As always with parenting, sometimes you try your best and it’s not enough. But that does not make trying optional.
I suspect there are more than enough men out there eager to do the right thing, even if some aren’t sure what that is. At the Labour party conference in Liverpool this week, a fringe meeting hosted by More in Common aimed at building bridges between women and men on tackling male violence was so packed there was a crowd of both men and women outside the door, straining to hear the speakers from a noisy corridor.
There’s something uplifting too about the social media campaign launched this autumn by the gen-Z anti-rape movement Enough, roping in male student rugby players to preach the message on campus that this isn’t just a women’s issue. Though Enough has been criticised in the past by survivor organisations for promoting self-swab kits for rape victims, it’s right that culture for boys is formed among their peers.
Across the Atlantic, it is now for the courts to decide whether what happened at Cornell meets New York’s bar for prosecution, with the local district attorney – who decided in 2024 not to press charges – reopening an investigation into what he now calls allegations of “heinous and despicable acts”. But it’s already clear that lives were ruined that night; that it was a tragedy, and a preventable one. Precisely the kind, in other words, that parenting exists to stop.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Increased air pollution linked to more night-time coughing, UK-led study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

New research has found that increased air pollution is associated with more night-time coughing, leading to disturbed sleep.
Most air pollution research looks at symptoms that are severe enough for people to seek medical help, but day-to-day symptoms can be overlooked. Prof Cecilia Mascolo, who led the study from the University of Cambridge, said: “I come from an area in Italy with very high pollution and I am very aware of its not-talked-about effects.”
Many more of us are using apps to monitor our sleep patterns. A recent survey of 18- to 30-year-olds in the UK found that 37% used sleep apps, while data from 2025 suggested that more than 40% of UK adults used tech to track their sleep.
The researchers looked at data from a commonly used sleep app. For 18 months they collected anonymised data from 32 cities in 12 countries, an average of 98,000 people a night.
As well as tracking sleep, the app also counted how many times people coughed. About half of the people coughed during the night, with 1% coughing more than 10 times. The greatest frequency of coughing was recorded in Milan and around Monza, both cities in north Italy’s Po Valley, one of the most polluted areas in western Europe.
A look at the data for Los Angeles and London shows that people cough more in cold weather and there are more coughs recorded when flu is circulating.
Mascolo said: “The hardest part was understanding if what we were seeing in the cough peaks was really affected by pollution or rather by viruses/flu trends as well as weather.”
Dr Tong Xia, part of the research team and now at Tsinghua University, added: “I thought that adding in the confounding factor of flu season would make the link in the data disappear, but it didn’t.”
High daily particle pollution was consistently associated with increased night-time coughing, but effects could also be seen at lower concentrations, well below the World Health Organization’s (WHO) air pollution guidelines.
Mascolo said: “Even in cities with relatively low levels of air pollution, such as Melbourne and Sydney, we observed positive associations between particle pollution and increased coughing.
“The LA wildfires were the clearest and most severe pollution spike in our study window.” Night-time coughing increased by 13 % during the wildfire smoke, and some people experienced effects that were delayed by several days.
Mascolo and Tong also found increased coughing in the London data around the time of Guy Fawkes fireworks and bonfires: “During the first week of November 2025, when influenza activity remained low, days with PM2.5 [particulate matter of less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter] concentrations exceeding the WHO guideline became more frequent, accompanied by a noticeably higher cough rate than previous months.
“Emission sources, such as firework displays, may have contributed to episodic air pollution and subsequent airway irritation, although source-specific data are needed to substantiate this.”
Rather than stopping action on air pollution once legal limits are met, we should be continuing to reduce air pollution.
Mascolo added: “These findings underscore the global health relevance of air pollution and suggest that the potential chronic health effects of long-term exposure to low concentrations of particle pollution warrant attention, even in comparatively less polluted cities.”

Helen Goh’s recipe for flourless walnut, date and espresso cake | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

There’s enough dark chocolate in this gluten-free cake to put it firmly in chocolate cake territory, but the hero flavour comes from the sweet, creamy nuttiness of walnuts, so it’s important to use very fresh ones, because stale walnuts can quickly turn bitter. The dates bring a deep, caramel richness, while the espresso pulls everything back from being overly sweet. Despite all that richness, the cake is wonderfully light in texture. Serve with creme fraiche and perhaps some poached pears, if you want to turn it into a full-blown dessert.
Flourless walnut, date and espresso cake
Prep 10 min
 Cook 1 hr 30 min, plus cooling
 Serves 8-10
150g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
150g pitted dates
  120ml just-brewed espresso 
  200g shelled walnuts
  1 tbsp cocoa powder, plus extra for dusting
1 tsp ground cinnamon
  ¾ tsp baking powder
  ½ tsp fine sea salt
  100g dark chocolate, broken into rough pieces
  5 large eggs, separated
75g light brown sugar
  1 tsp vanilla extract
  75g caster sugar
Grease a 20cm cake tin with a removable base, then line it with baking paper. Put the dates in a small bowl, pour over the hot espresso and leave to soften.
Meanwhile, put the nuts in a food processor and process until finely ground, taking care not to overprocess or they will become oily. Tip into a medium bowl, add the cocoa powder, cinnamon, baking powder and salt, and stir to combine.
Without washing the food processor, tip in the soaked date and coffee mix, then process to a smooth puree.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the butter and chocolate in a heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of barely simmering water, making sure the base of the bowl doesn’t touch the water. Stir until melted and smooth, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.
Meanwhile, put the egg yolks and brown sugar in the bowl of an electric mixer and beat on medium-high for about three minutes, until thick and pale. Turn down the speed to low, then gradually work in the melted chocolate and butter, followed by the date puree and vanilla. Fold in the walnut mix until combined, then scrape the batter into a large bowl.
Thoroughly clean and dry the mixer bowl and whisk attachment. Whisk the egg whites until foamy, then gradually add the caster sugar and continue whisking until they form medium peaks. Fold one-third of the meringue into the batter to loosen it, then gently fold in the rest.
Pour the batter into the lined tin, then bake for 55-60 minutes, until the edges are set but the centre still has a slight wobble – a skewer inserted into the centre should emerge with a few moist streaks, rather than be completely clean. Leave the cake to cool completely in its tin, then unclip and transfer to a serving plate. Dust with cocoa powder, then slice and serve.

Staff fears grow that BBC will shut its Three and Scotland channels next week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

The BBC has started a redundancy process in its TV and streaming division, heightening staff fears that Matt Brittin will announce the closure of the poorly performing BBC Three and BBC Scotland channels next week.
The corporation’s director general, who has repeatedly said that linear TV and radio services may have to shut as audiences move online, is expected to inform staff on Wednesday of the latest stage of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.
This week, Dan McGolpin, the director of the BBC iPlayer and Channels division, which includes all the corporation’s TV stations, called for expressions of interest across the department in taking voluntary redundancy.
In an email he said the plan to “mitigate the number of [enforced] redundancies” included sounding out staff interest about job-sharing arrangements, a reduction in hours, and “relocating to another BBC base across the UK”.
The move has fuelled speculation that the BBC is about to take the two channels online-only, according to sources, as Brittin focuses on cutting back on TV and radio services and content that delivers the least value for money.
“It is no secret that BBC Scotland and BBC Three are very expensive on a cost-per-viewer basis – a key metric being looked at – and they clearly haven’t achieved what was hoped,” said one insider.
It would be the second time BBC Three has been taken off linear broadcast. The youth-focused channel – which launched in 2003 and generated hits including Gavin and Stacey, Fleabag, Killing Eve and the lockdown hit Normal People – moved online-only in 2016 to save costs.
Since making a comeback to linear TV in 2022, it has struggled as audiences increasingly drift to streaming TV and video platforms such as YouTube. BBC Three recently announced it was canning the high-profile RuPaul’s Drag Race UK owing to financial pressures.
On Tuesday, the channel’s highest-rating show was Stacey Dooley Sleeps Over, which was broadcast in a primetime 9pm slot but only managed an average audience of 74,000.
Typically about 4% of the UK population watch the channel live in a week. Its cost per user hour was 26p in 2023-24 and 18p in 2024-25, the last year the BBC broke out statistics for individual services. This compares with 10p for BBC One that year, 9p for BBC Two and 6p for BBC Four.
BBC Three’s budget was doubled to about £80m when it returned to linear TV, rising to £90m in 2023-24, but it was cut to £66m in 2024-25.
A similar online-only fate is looming for the BBC Scotland television channel, which was launched in 2019 as a dedicated outlet for Scottish programming, separate to the Gaelic-language BBC Alba.
According to the BBC’s latest annual report to 31 March just 12% of people in Scotland watch the channel live. That compares with 54% of the adult population consuming BBC Scotland content each week across BBC TV/iPlayer, BBC Radio and BBC Online.
The BBC Scotland TV channel had a budget of £42m in 2024-25, while its cost per user hour was 13p.
“If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services,” Brittin told BBC One’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme. “When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.”
In June, the BBC announced plans to cut 60 jobs in Scotland, to save £10m. The BBC Scotland channel has received about £250m in funding since its launch but has failed to attract large audiences. Its flagship news magazine programme, The Nine, was scrapped two years ago after some episodes drew as few as 1,700 viewers.
One source believes that completely shutting the TV channel would be too politically difficult for the BBC, and that an online-only future would be a cost-effective and acceptable solution.
Brittin has also suggested radio services could be axed, having already announced that between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.
The corporation has already made a number of cost-saving announcements, including permanently reducing the presenter roster on Radio 4’s Today after the departure of Amol Rajan. It also axed the evening news programme The World Tonight after more than 50 years.
In 2010, Mark Thompson, then director general, proposed shutting the Asian Network and 6 Music. Ultimately both survived following a backlash, although the Asian Network was relocated to Birmingham last year and had its dedicated news bulletins replaced by Newsbeat two years ago.
Cost per user hour, the Asian Network, Radio 1Xtra and Radio 3 are the most expensive of the BBC’s stations.
The BBC said it did not comment on speculation.

Four hidden trails with medieval roots in the Eastern Alps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

Celtic tribes, Roman soldiers and medieval knights paved the way in the forests of the Eastern Alps. These trails are still there and can be discovered by history lovers during a sunny autumn weekend.
If you like active weekends with hiking and learning, one of the best places to go in Central Europe are the eastern slopes of the Alps.
The lower peaks of the mountains are in Austria, but the foot of the slopes reach Hungary.
It's not only the forests and the mountains which connect the two countries, but also the past, with the mountain bike trails and hiking routes passing through hundreds of years of history.
Velem, Hungary: A small village with rich past
Driving to the village of Velem you can see the white chapel of Saint Vid (or Vitus) from tens of kilometres away.
At an altitude of 589 metres, the chapel is located deep in the forest of the Kőszeg Mountains range, at the end of a moderate hiking trail. It was built in the early 18th century on the ruins of an ancient town.
Celts inhabited the area approximately 2,000 years ago, then the Romans built a watchtower to defend the aqueduct system supplying water to the ancient city of Savaria. If you walk in the forest, the man-made Celtic terraces can still be seen.
The other popular hiking trail from Velem leads to Geschriebenstein, the region's highest peak which is right on the border of Hungary and Austria.
Hiking from Velem is a bit adventurous, but from Austria it is an easy walk.
The third hiking route is the "Springs Trail" (Források útja) that showcases both popular and lesser-known springs in the Kőszeg Mountains. It is 14 kilometres long and features 11 stations.
Kőszeg: The small Hungarian town that prevented the advance of the Ottoman army in 1532
Only a few kilometres from the Austrian border lies Kőszeg, one of the most charming small towns of Hungary. Kőszeg is most famous for Jurisics Castle, a medieval Gothic castle that was in the centre of the siege of Kőszeg in 1532.
The captain of the castle had approximately 50 soldiers joined by 700 Hungarian locals who faced the Ottoman army which wanted to reach Vienna. How did the defenders of the town prevented the advance of the mighty army? The real story remains a mystery but some say the heavy August rains had their say.
Hiking across the mountain from Velem to Kőszeg is a day-long programme, but really worth it. You can pass cold water springs, see the chapel of Saint Vid and visit the Styrian houses used by foresters in the 1800s.
Lockenhaus: Do modern knights ride bicycles?
Lockenhaus knight's castle, once home of the mysterious Templars, is embedded in the beautiful landscape of Austria's Geschriebenstein Nature Park.
The surrounding forest is criss-crossed by mountain bike trails rated from light to extremely hard.
From the nearby town of Rechnitz, the Burgenland Trails shuttle bus helps cyclists take their bikes up to the designated stops. Minibuses equipped for bike transport operate on a regular schedule on weekends and public holidays.
From Geschriebenstein, the highest peak of the region, bikers can reach Lockenhaus, Rechnitz Badesee or Hungary as well.
The bicycle trails are separated from the walking routes, so hikers and bikers do not get in each other's way.
The 13th century castle of Lockenhaus has a remarkable Geoffroy's bat colony that visitors can observe from April to July.
Other feathered castle inhabitants include the majestic kestrels and lightning-fast swifts. And if you are lucky, you can also observe a beaver family by the lake near the castle.
Stadtschlaining: An Austrian town that kept its medieval look
Another 13th century medieval castle in Austria, near the Hungarian border, is Burg Schlaining. Located on the outskirts of Stadtschlaining, it is only 22 kilometres from Lockenhaus on the R1 Jubiläumsradweg bicycle road.
With its medieval centre, Stadtschlaining is situated in a beautiful hilly countryside, and therefore offers possibilities for recreation like walking and bike rides. At the end of the tour, visitors can enjoy the atmosphere of the castle gardens for free.
Stadtschlaining is also the starting point for excursions into the idyllic “weinstrasse” (wine route) of the Südburgenland. Here you can discover charming vineyards with “heuriger” wine taverns and farms which produce cider.

UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland

UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland
The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
- 
    Hundreds of British personnel train with allies from the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to counter rising Russian threat in Exercise Lion Protector 26.
- 
    Training takes place across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea, with Royal Marines conducting the first exercise in the Faroe Islands since the Second World War.
- 
    Comes as the Defence Secretary meets JEF counterparts in Iceland, with Canada and Ukraine also in attendance.
The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
Allies from the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which is led by the UK, have conducted Exercise Lion Protector 26, which saw forces train across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea to protect critical national infrastructure, strengthen joint command and control, and counter emerging threats.
From the data cables that connect the UK to the world, to the energy infrastructure that powers homes and businesses, the North Atlantic and High North are vital to our national security.
It comes as the Defence Secretary today meets with his JEF counterparts at a summit in Keflavik, Iceland, where ministers will progress discussions on Canada’s application for membership of the JEF Framework.
Ministers will also discuss deepening cooperation on countering hybrid threats, furthering industrial collaboration, and support to Ukraine through the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership. As Canada and Ukraine continue to cooperate closely with JEF, Canadian and Ukrainian ministers will also be in attendance.
Part of Exercise Lion Protector 26 saw Royal Marines from the UK’s Special Operations Maritime Task Group conduct the first exercise since the Second World War on the Faroe Islands, alongside Danish forces.
Marines and their Danish allies carried out maritime interdictions, amphibious landings, and vertical ascent training on the Faroes, which was the location of a key Royal Marines deployment during the Second World War.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence.
From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats.
I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.
Lion Protector launched in August with a rehearsal of a multi-national maritime escort operation stretching the length of the Baltic Sea. Warships and aircraft from Denmark, Latvia, Sweden and the UK escorted a Danish vessel carrying military equipment to Latvia, testing the JEF’s ability to coordinate rapidly across sea, land, air, cyber and space.
The UK’s Standing Joint Force Headquarters coordinated activity across the High North and Baltic Sea region, deploying north of the Arctic Circle in Norway to test its ability to command allied forces at speed and range.
JEF is a UK-led coalition of ten like-minded nations comprising high readiness forces configured to respond rapidly to crises in support of NATO security. JEF brings together the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden to secure the Baltic Sea, North Atlantic, Arctic and High North for NATO.
Today’s summit builds on the JEF Leaders’ Summit in Helsinki in March where leaders agreed to reinforce steadfast support to Ukraine through ambitious delivery of the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership.
It also builds on the Prime Minister’s discussions with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Støre this week about the hybrid threat Russia poses.
Exercise Lion Protector 26 comes ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference, both taking place in Oslo in November.

Speed up EU health security prep, says NATO chief medic

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
SNEAK PEEK
— Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure.
— Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension.
Advertisement
— Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein,with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight.
Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter. This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe.
GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein.
Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference.
Advertisement
Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.”
Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.”
Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.”
Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care.
Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here.

INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health.

On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting.
We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said.
Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.”

FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure.
Recap: France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”
Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response.
Advertisement
Austria is on board: “As Europe… if we do not now see the need to act more [uniformly] and more together, I don't know when we should see it,” said Stefan Eichwalder, director of the health systems division at the Austrian health and social affairs ministry.
It doesn’t mean not doing anything: “It would be dangerous not to act now, but then I think we need to find ways of working together,” he said. Eichwalder added that it was important that national deals — with industry or the U.S. — do “not weaken the position of the EU, and in the end, the position of any member state within the EU.”
The bottom line: Countries should work together “no matter how difficult it is,” he said. “I don't see a solution for Europe to go 27 different different routes.”
Think this through: Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform, said countries should be asking themselves this question: If we were to accept paying higher prices, what can we get in return? “From a first reading of this agreement, France is committing to pay higher prices in return for what exactly? And what are companies committing to delivering in exchange for these higher prices?”
The bigger picture: “Many narratives are going around. Narratives that are used by different sectors to serve specific interests,” Natsis said. “And in this case, this narrative is used to ask and demand higher prices. But again, the question is: if we were to pay these higher prices in Europe… what happens to the other countries? Because if France signs an agreement, if Germany signs an agreement, what about the rest of us?”
Pushing back: Richard Bergström, vice president of European affairs at health data firm IQVIA and former chief of pharma lobby EFPIA, pushed back. “If you read the French deal… there’s a lot of wins for the governments as well,” he told panelists from the audience. “There are requirements on clinical trials, requirements on manufacturing in Europe, and most importantly, there is a gain at the end of life cycle.” It’s a “quite balanced deal,” he added.
Advertisement
OVER IN BRITAIN: The U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal — which is hailed by the Trump administration and industry as a blueprint for other European countries — is running up against some challenges, our colleague Caroline Hug writes in. Four pilots rolled out to try to meet U.S. demands to double medicines spending as a percentage of GDP by 2028 are currently falling short. Britain’s new Science Minister Chris McDonald has signaled the government is willing to try new ideas.
Pilots ongoing: The government — with industry and the U.S. administration — launched the pilots running through September 2027, and the results will inform the next drug-pricing scheme.
The line: “What’s really important here is that we start with what is the objective we want to achieve, rather than the means by which we want to achieve it,” McDonald told Morning Trade U.K. during a fringe event Tuesday at the Labour Party Conference. “I don’t mind trying things, and then if they don’t work, then learning from that and moving on and trying some other things.”
New blood: McDonald replaces former Science Minister Patrick Vallance, who played a key role in the U.K.-U.S. pharma negotiations. One pharma industry figure told MTUK that McDonald “brings rare commercial instinct to the policy debate.”
Deal mode: “It was quite hard to reach an agreement across the entirety of the industry [on pilots],” said Shaun Grady, AstraZeneca U.K. chairman, pointing to varying demands of some pharma companies versus big pharmas like GSK and AstraZeneca which “invest very significantly in the U.K.” He added that conversations are “now moving much more into a bilateral phase where each company will engage with the government.”
BIOTECH ACT
APPROVED: Parliament’s environment committee has confirmed its position on the Biotech Act, with 53 in favor of adopting the opinion led by Nicolás Gonzalez Casares and 11 against. It supported keeping a 12-month extension of patents under certain conditions. Parliament’s legal committee also voted to keep the one-year extension in its opinion.
Advertisement
Coming to the table: The co-leads on the Biotech Act — Vytenis Andriukaitis (S&D) in the health committee and Wouter Beke (EPP) in the industry committee — will meet in Strasbourg next week to try and find a compromise on the patent extensions they can bring back to shadow rapporteurs.
Making progress: Andriukaitis told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of Gastein that political groups will likely have “more compromised solutions” on supplementary protection certificates, cross-border clinical trials and financing for the law by the end of October.” Read more about what he said here.
Feedback: Shadow rapporteurs on the Biotech Act on Thursday submitted their feedback to the co-rapporteurs following a roundtable between MEPs, Commission officials and industry on Tuesday.
Remember: Some MEPs weren’t happy at being offered a roundtable in lieu of an independent assessment on the supplementary protection certificate extension (SPCs) while some NGOs were also upset they didn’t get a seat at the table. Catch up on the controversy here.
UCPM
COMMITTEES BOOST PREPAREDNESS, CIVIL PROTECTION FUND: Lawmakers in the health and environment committee adopted their position on the EU’s next civil protection mechanism (UCPM), which now includes health emergency preparedness and response.
Details: The compromise text boosts the budget of the mechanism from €10 billion to €12.42 billion, earmarking 40% of the funding for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility. The position was approved with 61 votes in favor, nine against and nine abstentions. It will now need to be put to a vote in Parliament.
Advertisement
Sneaky global health reference: The adopted text includes several references to strengthening global health infrastructure. For example, it says that “strengthening cooperation … as well as the global health infrastructure and the World Health Organisation is essential to enhance the global ability to act.”
WHAT WE’RE READING
There have been four more deaths from the West Nile virus in the Netherlands, the NL Times reports.
**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act can be an important step towards Europe’s life sciences future. Done well, it can make clinical research faster, attract more investment to Europe, help biotech companies scale, and ensure Europe is the place where the next generation of medicines is developed. However, it cannot deliver the change that Europe urgently requires in isolation. Access shapes where capital flows right from the start. When market access is slow or fragmented, investors notice and capital follows opportunity elsewhere. Reversing Europe’s decline in research and development investment would require sustained structural reform, stronger action at the Member-State level, and a rethink of how healthcare systems invest in innovation. Europe has both scientific excellence and talent. Now it must create the right conditions for companies to choose Europe as a place to research, develop and deliver new medicines to patients. If we get it right, the reward is higher growth, greater resilience, and better health. The choice is ours. Read more.**

LRT English Newsletter: Seeing red
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – October 2, 2026.
Western media has practically taken over from the Baltics and Eastern Europe in calling out the Russia threat on a near-daily basis. Contrastingly, it is the Baltic officials who are calling for calm nerves.
But let’s go over the role-reversal from the beginning.
For weeks, European intelligence agencies and some Western leaders said Moscow could attack the Baltic states, with prognoses ranging from increased (and, by now, routine) disinformation plays to a boots-on-the-ground attack. These warnings came amid the eerie and unannounced CIA chief visit to Moscow, as well as reported warnings from Washington issued to the Baltic governments about a potential Russian attack.
Western media has therefore been filled with headlines prophesying the impending doom. Playing to the same tune, Moscow has issued (another) nuclear threat, this time focusing on Kaliningrad.
This, along with the rest of the media-political noise, is part of an ongoing campaign to disorient societies, Baltic leaders keep stressing. Intelligence reports also do not indicate anything major happening anytime soon, they say, but there is a threat of sabotage and intelligence operations which have only intensified.
Some analysts and officials are worried about what would happen if Russia launched a few dozen “stray” drones, or something along the lines, but Vilnius-bound Russian tanks are far from likely. In an interview with LRT, Britain’s top navy general also said that he was only worried about Russia doing “something stupid” that would fall under NATO’s collective defence threshold.
Some constructive statements did surface over the past week, including during Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius’ presser with the NATO secretary general, where the latter stressed that NATO isn’t idly sitting by. The words of Lithuania’s PM were later taken out of context, when a Kremlin aide welcomed that the threat from Russia was being toned down by a Lithuanian prime minister himself.
Adding to the chaotic information bubble, the Baltic states – along with France and the United Kingdom – were not invited by Washington to a NATO meeting. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda dismissed it as "artificial hype".
BANS AND SANCTIONS
Lithuania’s government approved a bill that will see additional bans on Belarusian and Russian nationals. If passed by the parliament, they will be banned from buying property near strategic sites. Additionally, people who have performed in occupied or annexed Ukraine will also be banned from performing, or taking part in other public cultural and sports activities. Some things remain unclear, for example, how the idea to have them sign a public statement against the Kremlin would actually play out. In related news, Lithuania has imposed sanctions on Kremlin-linked billionaires that escaped EU-level sanctions.
ECONOMY UPDATES
– The budget deficit is likely to exceed 3 percent next year.
– Lithuania’s historical Snaigė fridge manufacturer is going belly up.
– Lithuania will try to stick to the 2030 Rail Baltica deadline.
– The construction of a Leopard 2 tank plant has begun in Kaunas.
LANGUAGE CHANGES
Some interesting statistics popped up this week since Lithuania intensified efforts to reduce Russian language in schools. Since 2022, the number of Lithuanian school students studying Russian as a second foreign language has fallen by more than 40 percent. There is now also a growing number of kids learning German, French, or Spanish.
FINALLY?
The Catholic Church in Lithuania has decided to investigate the scale of abuse against minors since the country's independence. This landmark decision follows years of successive scandals, in which the priests involved would often face little to no consequences. Observers are naturally calling for the enquiry to be as independent as possible. 
EDITOR’S PICKS:
– US and Lithuanian intelligence services allegedly warned two Russian dissidents of an urgent threat to their lives.
– The Justice Minister has taken another L in trying to block same-sex marriages.
– Shaq was in Lithuania to watch a game and do some promo.
– And young farmers showed off their tractor-driving skills.

How Switzerland lost 20 percent of its ice in five years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:59:58 UTC
13:59:58 KST

How Switzerland lost 20 percent of its ice in five years
Swiss glaciers have lost more than 5 percent of their ice, threatening the country’s alpine economy.
Switzerland’s glaciers are rapidly receding due to a combination of winters with too little snow and record-high temperatures across Europe this summer, scientists say. In all, one of the world’s top ski destinations has lost nearly one-fifth of its glacial ice in just five years.
In a report (PDF) published by the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (GLAMOS) and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation of the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT) on Thursday, researchers said Swiss glaciers lost 5.5 percent of their ice volume over the hydrologic year ending September 30, 2026, and nearly 20 percent since 2021.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Are Europe’s extreme summers the new normal? What the science says
- list 2 of 3Why Nepal is demanding climate justice and compensation after deadly floods
- list 3 of 3India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
Why is Switzerland, famed for its Alpine terrain and winter sports, losing its glaciers and what does this mean for the country?
Here’s what we know.
What have scientists discovered?
In September, a GLAMOS team visited 23 glaciers in Switzerland to record end-of-summer measurements of ice melt and snow accumulation.
Visiting one glacier named Scex Rouge in the Western Swiss Alps in early September, GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, one of the report’s researchers, told the Reuters news agency that a measuring pole, about four metres (13 feet) high, was drilled into the ice in July to provide the team with a point of reference.
“Now when we have come back here, we saw the pole was out by three metres [10ft]. So just in August and September of this year, even excluding the heatwaves of June and July, we have lost three metres of ice at an elevation of almost 3,000 metres [9,843ft],” he explained.
“This clearly indicates these conditions that we had this summer, they are just inconsistent with the survival of these small glaciers in the Alps,” he added.
Why are glaciers in Switzerland losing ice?
According to the report, the total mean thickness of individual glaciers in Switzerland has fallen by between 2.5 and four metres in 2026. At glacier tongues – narrow glacial extensions of a glacier which project from land into a body of water – it had decreased by as much as 10 metres in some places over the summer.
“We can clearly attribute the massive ice loss to the warming, and thus anthropogenic [caused by humans] climate change. The summer has been the hottest on record in Switzerland. In addition, there was little snow in winter, and therefore the glaciers were poorly protected when the heat started,” GLAMOS chief Huss told Al Jazeera.
He noted that while their measurements have indicated that the melting has affected all glaciers in Switzerland equally, the effects were most visible on smaller glaciers.
“Those shrink very quickly and sometimes even completely disappeared. Also, large glaciers lost an enormous quantity of ice, but they remain impressive,” he added.
The report’s scientists warned that the glaciers also lost a total of about 2.2 trillion litres of water (581 billion gallons) between July and September alone.
“This is more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of all Swiss households,” the report’s researchers said and warned this could impact the country’s future water supply.
What does this mean for Switzerland?
Switzerland is a country known for winter sports and Alpine tourism, which depends on the glaciers. About 4 percent of the country’s entire workforce is employed in the tourism sector.
“This affects tourism and also how we perceive the mountains – they are no longer white but increasingly grey and black,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the water provided by glaciers is also important for the economy. “It is used to fill up hydropower lakes that produce clean energy, and supplies the biggest streams of Europe,” he said.
“We’re not yet seeing the full consequences as glaciers are still around and they contribute water when we need it. But this potential is soon being lost,” he added.
Harry Zekollari, a glaciologist and associate research professor at the Department of Water and Climate at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, shared a similar view.
He stressed that glaciers are important natural water suppliers, as they provide water when people need it most – in summer, when it is hot and dry.
“With climate change, glaciers initially provide more water during summer as they rapidly melt. However, as glaciers become smaller, there is less ice to be melted, and as such the water supply in summer decreases. This peak in water supply has now been passed for glaciers in the European Alps, meaning that we expect glaciers to provide less and less water in the coming years,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Glacier changes can also cause natural hazards, and since most of the ice lost turns into water that reaches the oceans, the consequences of glacier loss [in Switzerland and elsewhere] will be felt for coastlines all around the globe,” he added.
Is there a solution?
Yes. According to Zekollari, in order to save as much glacier ice as possible in Switzerland, the world needs to stabilise rising temperatures as soon as possible.
“Projections for the European Alps and Swiss glaciers show that if we are able to rapidly stop emissions, we may still be able to save about one-third of their ice mass. However, in a case with strong warming, these glaciers are projected to lose more than 90 percent of their volume by 2100,” he said.
He noted that the situation is less grim globally as some glaciers in other regions are more persistent.
“However, even globally, future emissions play a big role and will decide whether we lose about 25 percent of glacier mass by 2100 – that’s the good case, with limited warming – or rather 50 percent – the bad case, with more warming,” he said.
“The losses in the longer term – past 2100 – are even larger due to the long response of glaciers, but also here it is the future warming that decides how much remains. Every 0.1 degree Celsius warming matters.”

Amy Shark to lead NRL grand final musical tribute to Jai Arrow

An all-star ensemble of Australian musicians is set to take part in this weekend's NRL grand final pre-game entertainment.
Pop sensation Amy Shark is leading the performance, alongside members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, electronic duo Peking Duk, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.
The all-Australian supergroup will soundtrack an on-ground tribute to South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow, who told ABC earlier this week he knew "nothing" about plans for him to take a lap of honour around Stadium Australia on Sunday.
The ABC understands that Shark, who performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and company will perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.
Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.
The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred on the NRL's insistence that she perform her 2019 mega-hit Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.
Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment — running close to $1 million — could be put to better use.
"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend $1 million on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.
"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league."
V'landys also said the league would be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, following the Rabbitohs player's departure from the NRL earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.
The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year, and previous acts such as Billy Idol and Tina Turner.
"Our game sells itself," said V'landys.
"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung warned Friday that Seoul will take “additional measures” if Ukraine refuses to acknowledge a confidentiality agreement concerning the transfer of two North Korean soldiers to South Korea and does not apologize for saying that no such agreement existed.
“If you (Ukraine) continue to refuse to acknowledge the facts and apologize publicly, we will take additional measures. As this is a matter concerning the honor of the Republic of Korea's people and nation, we cannot overlook it,” Lee said in a statement on the US social media platform X.
Diplomatic tensions have escalated between the two countries after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during his address last week to the UN General Assembly disclosed that two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia were transferred to South Korea.  
The soldiers were captured in Russia’s Kursk region in early 2025 after being deployed to support Russian forces against Ukrainian troops. 
South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned the Ukrainian ambassador Monday to express strong concern about the denial and demanded an apology from Kyiv.
Seoul said it was Ukraine that violated a mutual confidentiality agreement aimed at keeping the transfer confidential in order to protect the soldiers, saying Kyiv was the first to request secrecy over the matter. 
“In response to a demand to acknowledge the agreement and apologize, it has instead mentioned (the possibility of) an imminent inter-Korean military conflict," Lee said, accusing Ukraine of attempting to bring "war on the Korean Peninsula" and expressing "serious regret,” according to Yonhap News Agency.
An unnamed senior South Korean government official told reporters Friday that Seoul and Kyiv had agreed to a confidential clause on the transfer of the two prisoners of war (POWs) and said the foreign ministers of the two nations have been discussing "how Kyiv should respond to South Korea's demand for an apology over the disclosure of the transfer."

A Himalayan avalanche killed at least 15 expedition workers, as rescuers continued efforts to recover bodies from a mountain camp in central Nepal.
Rescuers recovered eight more bodies on Thursday from the area of the avalanche that swept through the base camp of the 7,126-metre (23,345-foot) Himlung peak early on Sunday, in one of the worst mountain disasters in recent years.
