Nepali workers were pitching tents and fixing ropes for later expeditions on the mountain located near the Chinese border.
Rescuers have so far recovered 15 bodies from the site, said Tul Singh Gurung, president of Nepal National Mountain Guide Association.
“The bodies that were recovered today are expected to be brought by a helicopter to Kathmandu,” Gurung told Reuters.
He said chances of finding the one missing worker were slim and the rescue operation is likely to wind up. The foreign climbers had not reached the site at the time of the avalanche.
A team of eleven rescuers, including experienced guides, were at the site, digging through more than four metres (14 feet) of snow which had buried tents at the base camp.
The bodies of two mountain guides were recovered on Sunday, and those of two kitchen staff were pulled out on Monday, followed by another three bodies on Tuesday.
Nepal’s worst mountaineering disasters in recent years occurred in 2014, when an avalanche killed 16 people on Everest, and in 2015, when an earthquake killed 18 people, also on Everest.
Authorities are still searching for bodies from devastating floods sparked by a mountain glacial collapse on 26 August that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.
Heavy rain since Thursday has triggered more floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the national disaster agency.
Home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, Nepal’s economy relies heavily on mountaineering and trekking tourism.
Himlung, where Sunday’s avalanche occurred, is a popular destination for mountaineers looking to begin climbing 7,000-metre peaks.

New ICE guidance sets tighter rules for vehicles stops, bans officers from high-speed chases, memo reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:47:29 UTC
13:47:29 KST

The new guidance comes as the Trump administration faces mounting criticism over a string of deadly incidents involving ICE officers. The agency downplayed the new measures, insisting they’re mere reminders and that current protocols will continue.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several people were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division warned they are not authorised to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances.
Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
US President Donald Trump's administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops.
But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency's rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
In a statement, ICE downplayed the significance of the memo, which said the new guidance was intended to replace and amend prior directives issued earlier this year, last year and in 2018.
“Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers,” the statement said. “Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.”
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated.
All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must also wear and activate their body cameras under the new guidance. In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops.
Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance however says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training.
Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop, before eventually catching up to him and shooting him, without a body camera in sight.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez's vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

Japan and Australia: Toward a More Autonomous and Resilient Partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

The security environment in the Indo-Pacific is undergoing a profound transformation. Cooperation among revisionist powers, including China, Russia, and North Korea, is deepening, while the strategic priorities of the United States — the country that has long underpinned the regional order — are also changing. At the same time, technological advances in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, unmanned platforms, quantum technologies, and cyber capabilities are fundamentally changing the character of warfare and the sources of military advantage.
Against this backdrop, Japan and Australia have deepened their comprehensive security partnership across military and economic domains. What matters increasingly is their ability to build both strategic autonomy and strategic resilience.
Strategic autonomy does not mean “independence” from the United States. Rather, it means reducing excessive dependence on any single major power and preserving greater room for strategic choice and freedom of action. Strategic resilience, meanwhile, refers to the ability to withstand and recover from strategic shocks, whether they take the form of military conflict, economic coercion, supply-chain disruption, or energy crises. Together, these two concepts provide a useful framework for thinking about the current state and future direction of Japan–Australia cooperation.
For much of the post-Cold War period, both Japan and Australia benefited from what might be called “dual dependence.” In security terms, both relied heavily on the United States, while economically they developed increasingly deep interdependence with China. This arrangement allowed them to enjoy security at relatively low defense costs while benefiting substantially from China’s economic growth.
As U.S.–China rivalry and broader great-power competition intensify, however, this model is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet neither replacing dependence on the United States with dependence on China, nor pursuing economic decoupling from China, is a viable option for either country. Rather, the goal is to diversify dependence itself — to expand the range of partners and capabilities available so that neither country becomes excessively vulnerable to the decisions of any single major power.
This is the direction the Japan–Australia relationship has taken over the past few years. While maintaining their respective alliances with the United States, Japan and Australia have strengthened their own capabilities and built a more autonomous bilateral security relationship — one that goes beyond simply “supplementing” the U.S. military presence in the region.
The cooperation surrounding the Australian Navy’s acquisition of Japanese-designed Mogami-class frigates is a good example. Its significance extends well beyond the transfer of a particular platform. Developed into sustained cooperation across joint development, production, maintenance, and future technologies, it could strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries — enhancing their ability not just to acquire military capabilities but to produce, maintain, and sustain them over time.
Australia’s strategic depth is equally important. Japan is geographically located on the front line of the First Island Chain, whereas Australia can provide vast training areas as well as logistics, maintenance, and rear-area support. By developing these arrangements during peacetime, the two countries can build the capacity to sustain military operations over a prolonged period in the event of a crisis or conflict. This will also become increasingly important as the operational horizon of the Japan Self-Defense Forces expands beyond the First Island Chain toward the wider Pacific.
The same logic applies to economic security. Building more diversified supply chains for energy, critical minerals, critical technologies, and other strategic goods can enhance the autonomy and resilience of both Japan and Australia. Importantly, however, such efforts are not limited to the bilateral relationship.
One example is a regional initiative such as “POWERR Asia.” Through mechanisms for energy stockpiling, sharing, and emergency supply arrangements, Japan and Australia could help strengthen energy resilience across the wider Indo-Pacific. The objective would be to create regional networks capable of absorbing shocks rather than leaving individual countries vulnerable to sudden disruptions or external pressure.
A similar logic should guide engagement with Pacific Island countries. Assistance to these countries should not be viewed solely through the prism of strategic competition with China; instead, Japan and Australia have focused on strengthening resilience in areas such as infrastructure, energy, communications, and economic security. The aim should be to create an environment in which smaller states are not forced to “choose” between the United States and China simply because they lack viable alternatives.
Ultimately, this strategy is neither about achieving “independence” from the United States nor about “containing” China. The U.S. military presence will remain indispensable to regional stability, while economic and diplomatic relations with China will continue to matter greatly. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate dependence, which is neither possible nor desirable, but to diversify it in ways that preserve greater freedom of action.
This logic should eventually be extended to the region as a whole. By building networks through which regional countries complement one another’s capabilities across defense, energy, technology, infrastructure, and economic security, the Indo-Pacific can become more resilient to strategic shocks and less vulnerable to sudden changes in the policies or preferences of major powers.
The ultimate purpose of Japan–Australia cooperation, therefore, extends beyond conventional alliance management or burden-sharing with the United States. It should contribute to building a region in which countries of the Indo-Pacific possess greater agency and a greater capacity to sustain stability and order.
In this sense, Japan–Australia cooperation should evolve from a partnership designed primarily to adapt to an order dominated by great powers into one that enables regional countries to play a greater role in shaping the regional order themselves.

Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:41:46 UTC
13:41:46 KST

Russian forces repeatedly struck Kyiv’s Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge from Thursday morning into the early hours of Friday, bringing Moscow’s expanding drone campaign directly onto one of the capital’s most important transport arteries across the Dnipro.
The attacks began with two drone impacts near a bridge support Thursday morning. A third drone later struck the roadway in the evening. On Oct. 2, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported emergency crews headed back to the crossing.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Oct. 1 attack marked the first time Russian drones had struck a major Kyiv bridge since the beginning of the full-scale war – a notable expansion of a campaign increasingly focused on infrastructure essential to keeping Ukrainian cities functioning.
The Southern Bridge links Kyiv’s eastern and western banks across the Dnipro and carries both road traffic and the Green Line of the city’s metro.
During the first attack, a metro train was actually crossing the bridge.
At around 11:30 a.m., the blast wave forced dust through the train’s ventilation system and into passenger carriages. No passengers or crew were injured, the windows remained intact, and the train was later taken to a depot for inspection.
For several hours Thursday, Kyiv authorities were forced to repeatedly halt, reroute and restore road and metro traffic as specialists inspected the crossing.
By Thursday night, what had begun as an unusual morning strike had developed into a sustained sequence of attacks on the same piece of infrastructure.
Russian Attack Kills 1 in Kyiv High-Rise, Shuts Down Bridges Across the Capital
A bridge under repeated attack
Klitschko initially reported two drone strikes near the bridge’s support structure, prompting authorities to suspend traffic while engineers inspected the crossing.
A preliminary assessment found no critical structural damage, and some service resumed.
Hours later, another Russian drone struck the roadway.
After midnight, Klitschko reported yet another hit, sending emergency crews back to the scene.
The overnight attack also caused damage elsewhere in Kyiv. In Holosiivskyi district, debris damaged a non-residential building and several cars, while a 25-story residential building was damaged in Darnytskyi district.
Why the bridge – and why now?
The Southern Bridge is one of Kyiv’s principal crossings over the Dnipro and an important link between the city’s left and right banks.
The bridge’s dual role as a road and rail artery means even limited damage can disrupt multiple forms of transport at once.
That makes repeated attacks on the crossing particularly consequential for a city whose population relies heavily on public transport during wartime.
The morning strike demonstrated the vulnerability in unusually vivid fashion: a Russian drone hit the bridge while a metro train was physically crossing it.
The blast did not derail the train or injure passengers, but the shock wave was strong enough to force dust through the ventilation system and into the carriage.
By nightfall, damage to the bridge and metro infrastructure had forced authorities to halt traffic entirely.
Kyiv says it obtained Russia’s winter strike plans
The bridge strikes also come only days after Ukraine revealed that it had obtained detailed Russian documents outlining planned winter attacks against critical infrastructure.
First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Ukrainian intelligence obtained two extensive Russian documents detailing potential strikes on electricity generation, heating, water supply, sewage systems and other energy infrastructure.
The documents reportedly include tables calculating the types and quantities of weapons required to destroy individual facilities – from ballistic missiles to conventional and jet-powered drones.
The plans also cover electricity interconnectors used to import power from Europe.
Kyiv Post reported that Ukraine had already constructed more than 200 protective structures around priority infrastructure sites and was positioning repair equipment in preparation for further Russian attacks.
A school struck hours earlier
The bridge was not the only major Kyiv target hit Thursday.
Earlier that morning, a Russian Geran-4 attack drone slammed into School No. 12 in the Solomianskyi district while more than 100 children and over 60 teachers were inside.
The children and staff were already in the school’s shelter when the drone struck.
The attack caused a fire, partially destroyed a wall and damaged windows and doors. No one was injured.
Investigators later discovered just how close the school had come to a far worse outcome.
Kyiv police said the Geran-4 struck the stairwell wall between the second and third floors. Its warhead – weighing about 50 kilograms – penetrated the floor structure and fell onto the stairs without detonating.
Bomb-disposal specialists removed the unexploded munition and transported it for destruction.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 334 educational institutions in Kyiv have been damaged, including 165 schools and 134 kindergartens, according to the Ukrainian presidency.
FP-7 debut on the same day
The strikes coincided with another major development in Ukraine’s expanding domestic weapons program.
On Thursday, president Zelensky announced the first combat use of Ukraine’s domestically produced FP-7 tactical ballistic missile.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next – production,” he wrote.
Ukraine did not disclose where the missile was used or what target it struck.
The FP-7 was developed by Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and has a reported range of roughly 200-250 kilometers (124-155 miles), depending on the source.
Its first combat use represents an important milestone in Kyiv’s effort to build an indigenous ballistic-strike capability after years of relying heavily on Western-supplied long-range weapons.
The timing inevitably places the two developments side by side – Ukraine publicly unveiling the FP-7’s first combat use while Russia escalated drone attacks against the capital.
From schools to bridges
What is clear is the breadth of targets hit across Kyiv in a remarkably compressed period.
Within roughly a day, Russian drones struck a school filled with children and teachers, repeatedly hit one of Kyiv’s major Dnipro crossings, damaged residential property and sent debris into other parts of the city.
The operational consequences were immediate – halted metro service, suspended surface transport, emergency inspections and rerouted commuters.
At School No. 12, the consequences could have been far worse.
The 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead lying unexploded inside the building became a physical measure of just how narrowly Kyiv avoided another mass-casualty attack.
The pattern is familiar: when Russia struggles to achieve its aims on the battlefield, it intensifies attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure. Today, the targets were people traveling home – and children studying at school.

Ukraine, South Korea clash over transfer of 2 North Korean prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:40:00 UTC
13:40:00 KST

Ukraine, South Korea clash over North Korean prisoner swap
October 2, 2026
Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sparked a diplomatic dust-up with South Korea.
In his speech, Zelenskyy mentioned that Ukraine had recently "sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea" — men who had been captured by Ukrainian forces during fighting in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025. Both had expressed a wish to resettle in South Korea, he said.
The reaction from Seoul was swift: South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador to Seoul, Andrii Vieshkin, and demanded an explanation for what it described as Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the prisoners' transfer, despite a prior agreement to keep the matter confidential, along with an official apology.
Responding to Zelenskyy's speech, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war was a sensitive topic with wide-ranging consequences for diplomacy and national security on the Korean Peninsula.
Did Kyiv and Seoul have a secret agreement?
Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's spokesperson, wrote on Facebook that no such confidentiality agreement existed between the two countries, adding that it was wrong to keep secret where such prisoners were being transferred.
Soon after, South Korean presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan called Lytvyn's denials false, according to news agency Reuters. Kim said Ukraine had asked for confidentiality — allegedly over concerns there might be criticism at home if the North Korean prisoners weren't swapped for Ukrainian prisoners being held in Russia.
Seoul had agreed to the secrecy for diplomatic reasons, he added, but also to protect the prisoners and their families who were still living in North Korea.
Missed opportunity to 'improve bilateral relations'
Nataliya Butyrska, an Asia-Pacific expert at the New Europe Center in Kyiv, told DW that Ukraine and South Korea lacked a continuous, trust-based dialogue, especially under the current government in Seoul.
"We should actually be natural partners — we should be standing shoulder to shoulder, with North Korea fighting against Ukraine," she said. "But that's not the case, due to a lack of trust."
The prisoner transfer has been a hotly debated topic in South Korean media in the last week — not least because, according to South Korea's constitution, North Koreans are considered citizens of South Korea. It's also been instrumentalized by opposition lawmakers, while President Lee, aiming to ease tensions with the North, has taken a more measured approach.
"The prisoners could have been used by Ukraine to improve bilateral relations between Kyiv and Seoul," said Butyrska, adding that no one in South Korea was now thinking of thanking Ukraine for transferring the prisoners.
Butyrska pointed out that Russia, which usually doesn't express any interest in foreign prisoners, had actually demanded the return of these two North Koreans. "There was even a period of six months when the Russians refused to release any Ukrainian prisoners of war," she said. "They were not prepared to undertake any swap, because they wanted the North Koreans."
Is Ukraine being held hostage by South Korea's domestic politics?
For some observers, the diplomatic crisis can be linked back to domestic conflicts in South Korea. The opposition wants to know why the president agreed to keep the prisoner transfer secret, and have accused Lee of trying to gain favor with the North.
"President Lee Jae Myung was surprised by the incident, and now wants to shift the blame in part on Ukraine," said Mykola Polishchuk, a Korea expert based in Ukraine. He believes the transfer would have become public knowledge sooner or later, and that Seoul knew that Kyiv was going to comment on it. Reports that Ukraine had asked for secrecy were, he added, a way for a frantic politicians in Seoul to come up with an explanation.
"Ukraine has ended up mired in a scandal which it neither wanted nor planned for," said Polishchuk.
"South Korea has been pursuing the transfer of the prisoners for a long time. And now everybody seems to be happy that those Korean prisoners are in custody," said Shim Sangmin from the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul. "But what really complicates the matter is the fact that the South Korean government is trying to make new ways to reconcile with the North Korean regime." He said Seoul was now worried that this transfer of North Korean prisoners could hamper efforts to reestablish communication between the North and the South.
In his view, the Lee government is "more open to the idea of reestablishing ties" with Russia, rather than continuing to cooperate with Ukraine. "That's possibly one of the reasons why this government is skeptical about containing military cooperation with Ukrainian military forces, even though there would be a definite military advantage for South Korean military forces," he added.
Ukraine shouldn't expect military support from South Korea
Butyrska said the latest developments indicate a likely further cooling of ties between Kyiv and Seoul.
"The South Korean government wasn't particularly friendly toward us to begin with, and will now likely keep its distance," she said, adding that it would have been better for Kyiv to have stayed quiet.
In return for a gesture of goodwill and "quiet diplomacy," she added, Ukraine might have seen support from South Korea in another form — technology, for example, especially via third countries. While South Korea isn't directly selling weapons to Ukraine, it does deliver to Poland, Finland, the Czech Republic and Romania, and it's pursuing further integration with the European military equipment supply chain.
For Polishchuk, any cooperation on military technology between Ukraine and South Korea is out of the question, now and in the future. He believes trade and humanitarian help would continue, however. South Korea, he said, is highly unlikely to side with Russia, especially given Seoul's many obligations toward the United States.

Quote from Bocharov: "A fire has broken out in a high-rise residential building on Udmurtskaya Street in the Krasnoarmeysky district of Volgograd following a large-scale terrorist attack by UAVs carried out by the criminal Kyiv regime against industrial infrastructure facilities in Volgograd Oblast overnight. One person has been hospitalised and the fire has been contained. Emergency services are working at the scene, and efforts to deal with the aftermath are ongoing."
For reference: The Volgograd oil refinery is part of Lukoil and is one of Russia's largest oil refining facilities. It produces petrol, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen.
Kaustik is a chemical plant in southern Volgograd. According to Astra, it produces dual-use products that are important to Russia's defence industry.

Russian airstrikes choke bridges across Dnipro River in Kyiv
KYIV, Oct 2 - Russian airstrikes forced the closure on Friday of two bridges over the Dnipro River that link the two sides of the Ukrainian capital, as Moscow steps up its bombardment of infrastructure before winter.
Long traffic jams formed in the morning and video footage posted online showed residents walking across a bridge that had been closed for cars and metro trains after it was struck multiple times on Thursday.
Russian drones on Thursday had smashed into the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro and also hit a school, although pupils were unhurt as they were in a shelter at the time, officials said.
Traffic across the Southern Bridge and part of the Paton Bridge, both of which are important arteries for residents of the southern part of Kyiv, was temporarily halted on Friday morning. Traffic on another bridge was also partially suspended.
Movement across the bridges was restored by around midday, Reuters witnesses said. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said he held a city security council meeting on Friday to assess the risks, describing the situation in the city as "very dramatic".
According to city authorities, more than a third of the capital's 3 million residents lived on the east, or "left", bank before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but only 18% of jobs were located there.
The vast majority of Kyiv residents work on the western, or "right", bank where most government institutions and companies are located.
Separately on Friday, a Russian drone strike killed one person and injured two others in the capital after a fire broke out on the upper floors of an apartment building, officials said.
In the northeastern city of Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest, two people were killed and 28 wounded in a guided-bomb strike, according to the regional governor.
NEW ORDERS FROM PUTIN
A senior Ukrainian official said the strikes on the bridges and other sensitive infrastructure - including data centres and power installations - appeared to be linked to an order by President Vladimir Putin last month to scrap constraints on Russia's air campaign.
The order was first reported by the Financial Times.
Andriy Shevchishin, an economic analyst, said on Facebook that about 500,000 people commute from the left to the right bank each day.
Residents of the left bank have also borne some of the worst power and heating outages every winter during the war as a result of Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. One district there, Troyeshchyna, was left without heating for over a week last winter in sub-zero temperatures.
Memories of last winter, the worst of the war, are prominent in residents' minds after Russia launched what was seen in Ukraine as the first salvo of an expected winter bombing campaign against power facilities supplying the capital.
The Southern bridge, which was hit by a drone on Thursday, is also crucial for those commuting from towns and villages east of Kyiv.
Since the end of summer, Russia has been launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered drones a day at Ukraine, whose defences have struggled against the new threat.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram that its drones had hit a Kyiv bridge over the Dnipro, a power station in the surrounding region, the southwestern port of Izmail and a cargo vessel. All targets were used for military purposes, it said.
In Russia, Ukrainian drones targeted the Lukoil refinery in Volgograd and another oil facility in Samara region, Ukraine's military said.
Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries in Russia, one of the world's leading oil producers, have cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said. Long lines have formed at Russian petrol stations.
UKRAINE SEEKS INTERCEPTOR MISSILES, AMMUNITION FOR JETS
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told reporters on Thursday that Poland, Belgium and Spain had agreed to supply 20mm rounds for cannons on Ukraine's F-16 jet fighters, one of its most effective tools for the fight against the new, faster drones.
He said Kyiv was anticipating a possible agreement on the supply of "several million" rounds of this ammunition in the near future, but did not specify from whom.
Sybiha also said Ukraine needed at least 300 Patriot interceptor missiles - the only weapon it can reliably use to bring down Russia's ballistic missiles - to have a minimum level of protection for the winter period.
Moscow is thought to be making 120 to 140 ballistic missiles each month, he said, with 600 already in its stocks. REUTERS

Turkey's stock market scandal affects nearly half a million investors. Police have made several arrests and an AKP politician has resigned.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:32:00 UTC
13:32:00 KST

Turkey's stock market scandal hits half a million investors
October 2, 2026
Investors in Turkey want one thing above all else: for their money to retain its value. Given inflation of around 30%, that is not exactly easy. As a result, many people are buying gold, foreign currency or stocks and increasingly, mutual fund shares that promise high returns.
But the stock market has become a trap for around half a million Turkish investors. In mid-September, the benchmark BIST 100 index plummeted by 6% in a single day and lost about 12% within just a few trading days.
This sharp drop in stock prices was triggered by a major market manipulation scandal. Approximately 455,000 investors have been affected, more than 45 people have been arrested and a high-ranking politician from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has resigned.
What happened?
Everything started when some investment fund providers had trouble making timely repayments to investors. Among those affected were funds managed by the companies Pusula Portfoy and Tera. Two Tera funds alone held assets totaling around €6.5 billion ($6.37 billion).
In response, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) intervened and shut down the funds of seven asset managers, including Tera, Pusula and Atlas. According to the state-run news agency Anadolu, a total of 131 funds are set to be liquidated.
The Istanbul Public Prosecutor's Office is now investigating charges of fraud, violations of the capital markets law and the formation of a criminal organization, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.
The suspicion: The fund companies are alleged to have artificially inflated the value of their funds, while in reality their funds contained worthless "junk stocks."
Among the 45 people arrested so far are executives from investment firms. In addition, the assets of 42 individuals and 46 legal entities have been frozen, according to Gurlek on X.
The Istanbul Stock Exchange has also taken action: it excluded 27 stocks from the BIST 100 benchmark index as of October 1.
Will investors get their money back?
The funds are being liquidated: Their assets will be sold and the proceeds distributed to investors in proportion to their fund shares. The deadline for this has been extended from three to six months. According to Aysel Gundogdu, an independent financial advisor in Istanbul, this is intended to reduce selling pressure so that stocks are not sold at fire-sale prices. However, this does not mean that the liquidation of each fund will take six months. Depending on market conditions, it may be completed more quickly.
Only, there is no guarantee. An investment fund is not a savings account and any loss in value affects the investor. Gundogdu expects that money market funds will largely be redeemed. With hedge funds and equity funds holding "junk stocks" that are virtually untradeable, however, the situation could prove more difficult.
It is important to distinguish between market losses and damages resulting from potential irregularities.
Economist and columnist Guldem Atabay emphasized that a distinction must be made between price losses and manipulation: Investors bear the market risk, but they do not have to accept false information, artificially inflated prices, or a lack of oversight.
Are the fund company and managers liable for the damages?
If funds are closed or liquidated, the shares and other securities in the portfolio can be sold. The question is how much they are worth and how easily they can be sold.
Financial expert Gundogdu believes that the fund's assets will not cover investors' claims. Furthermore, she says there have been structural failures. "The crisis is far greater than a simple liquidity crisis. There are flaws in management and oversight."
She therefore considers it possible that the assets of the fund founders and managers could also be tapped to make up for the shortfall.
Economist Atabay calls for those responsible to be identified and for the damages to be recovered from them. Following the liquidation of the funds, it must be clarified who is responsible for any legal violations. "Liquidation is no substitute for accountability," Atabay said.
What are the political costs of the crisis?
The crisis has already led to the resignation of a high-ranking female politician in the ruling AKP party. Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, deputy party chair and former minister of family affairs, asked Turkish President and AKP leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan to "relieve her of all her posts." This has been a phrase frequently used within the AKP for years when someone is forced to resign.
She was facing allegations regarding stock transactions by her and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, in connection with the fund crisis. Political responsibility, she wrote on social media, goes beyond legal responsibility. She said her position should not hinder the investigation.
The opposition now intends to bring the issue before Parliament. Selcuk Ozdag, deputy leader of the Yeni Yol parliamentary group, announced that as soon as Parliament reconvenes, he will submit a motion for a parliamentary investigation. The investigation is intended to determine whether politicians are involved in the manipulation scandal.
This article was originally published in German.

CANBERRA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Australia's online safety regulator has called for online gaming service providers, including Roblox and Fortnite, to strengthen protections against child sexual exploitation.
Julie Inman Grant, Australia's eSafety commissioner, on Friday released a report showing significant differences in the child safety measures taken by game service providers.
The report found that the providers behind Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam have inconsistent approaches to preventing high-risk games from being accessed by children, warning that such games can create environments for child sexual exploitation or activity that promotes crime or violence.
"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," Inman Grant said.
"Service providers should leverage systems that actually detect and disrupt serious harms before children are exposed to them."
According to the report, the providers of both Fortnite and Minecraft offer protections for child accounts, but generally rely on age information declared by users, allowing users who stated they were adults to access higher-risk features without additional age checks.
It said that Valve, the provider of the game distribution platform Steam, failed to use tools to proactively detect harms on messaging service Steam Chat.
Roblox and Valve reported using only internal datasets to train language detection systems, with neither regularly retraining those models.
Inman Grant said that it is critical for game service providers to adopt meaningful and continuing safety measures to protect young players. ■

New Zealand temperature up 1.36 degrees Celsius over 117 years: statistics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:53 CST
13:29:53 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's average annual temperature increased by 1.36 degrees Celsius over the 117 years to 2025, while rainfall patterns shifted across the country, official data showed on Friday.
The country's average annual temperature has been recorded since 1909, with 2022 being the warmest year on record at an average of 13.76 degrees Celsius. The year 2012 was the last with an average temperature below the 1991-2020 baseline of 12.74 degrees Celsius, Stats NZ reported.
Data from New Zealand's 30 climate stations showed average annual temperatures increased across the country, with temperatures rising fastest in winter and slowest in spring, Stats NZ environment statistics spokesperson Tehseen Islam said in a statement.
Rainfall patterns were more complex. From 1960 to 2025, nine climate stations recorded an increase in average annual rainfall, and six recorded a decrease, Stats NZ said, adding the South Island was generally getting wetter, while rainfall trends varied across the North Island.
Islam said changing rainfall, particularly increased spring rainfall, could affect farmers, fisheries and hydroelectricity generation.
Extreme rainfall also accounted for an increasing share of annual rainfall at 11 of the 30 stations, while three recorded a decrease between 1960 and 2025, according to Stats NZ.
Separately, carbon dioxide concentrations in New Zealand's atmosphere reached 423.1 parts per million in December 2025, up 5.5 percent from December 2016, with methane and nitrous oxide concentrations also showing increasing trends, the department said. ■

Interview: A more stable U.S.-China relationship matters for the world, says U.S. expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:13 CST
13:29:13 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- A more stable U.S.-China relationship has effects well beyond the bilateral relationship because the two countries are deeply connected to the global economy and play major roles in international institutions and global governance, a renowned U.S. expert on China affairs has said.
In a written interview with Xinhua, Denis Simon, former senior adviser for China affairs to the president of Duke University, noted that Chinese President Xi Jinping said during the recent state visit to the United States that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world.
"I read this as an attempt to frame the relationship in terms of mutual national interests rather than as a zero-sum contest. Both China and the United States have their own national ambitions and domestic priorities, but those objectives do not necessarily require the other country to fail," said Simon, who also served as executive vice chancellor of Duke Kunshan University in 2015-2020.
"Rather than asking either side to abandon its own national goals, the message is that China's development and America's prosperity can coexist and, under the right conditions, reinforce one another," he said.
Regarding the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences and promises of peace, Simon described the formulation as "an effort to provide a practical framework for managing a relationship in which competition is unavoidable but conflict is not inevitable."
"The key phrase for me is 'competition within bounds.' It recognizes that China and the United States will compete in areas such as technology, trade and strategic influence. The objective is not necessarily to eliminate that competition, but to establish boundaries so that competition does not become confrontation," he said.
Simon said "manageable differences" acknowledges that some disagreements may be very difficult to resolve in the foreseeable future. A stable relationship, therefore, cannot depend on resolving every difference.
"It needs mechanisms that allow the two sides to disagree without allowing individual disputes to destabilize the entire relationship," he said. "If implemented consistently, the framework could shift the emphasis from trying to eliminate competition toward making competition predictable and manageable, while expanding cooperation wherever interests genuinely overlap."
Simon identified economic and trade issues as an obvious area where concrete progress could have immediate effects, while noting that technology and supply-chain questions are more difficult "because they involve both economic and national-security considerations."
"But precisely for that reason, they require sustained dialogue and clearer communication," he said, adding that beyond bilateral issues, cooperation on climate, energy, public health and other transnational challenges could demonstrate that competition does not have to prevent practical collaboration. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Top US diplomat Marco Rubio signed off on the waiver but argued that Washington’s concerns over its Middle Eastern ally’s human rights record will remain a point of discussion in full bilateral discussions.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has waived a restriction on $320 million (€284.4 million) in military aid to Egypt that had been previously withheld over human rights concerns, citing Cairo’s help in dealing with Iran since the conflict began earlier this year.
The US State Department said on Thursday that Rubio had signed off on the waiver “in the interest of US national security.”
"The Secretary’s determination reflects the importance of Egypt to US national security interests, and the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States,” the department said.
In a letter sent to lawmakers, Rubio cited, in particular, Egypt’s “helpful role” in the war with Iran. Egypt has been a key mediator between the US and Iran in the efforts to wind down the more than seven-month-long conflict.
The State Department maintained that the Trump administration would continue to raise human rights matters as part of its dialogue with Egypt “on the full range of issues in our bilateral relationship.”
“The waiver determination recognises the importance of maintaining security cooperation with Egypt at a time of significant regional security challenges,” the department said.
The $320 million is part of an annual US contribution of $1.3 billion (€1.16 billion) in economic and military assistance to Egypt. More specifically, it is for foreign military financing, which provides money for recipient nations to purchase US-produced weaponry.
Congress inserted the requirement over concerns about Egypt’s human rights record, which many experts regard as problematic. The State Department itself in recent years has pointed to credible reports of torture, arbitrary arrest, child labour and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
But granting a waiver to Egypt has become routine for both Republican and Democratic administrations. The Biden administration, for example, last issued a waiver in September 2024, citing Egypt’s assistance in US efforts to bring an end to the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.

Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.

Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.
September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Low wind and limited sunshine combined with high gas prices pushed Denmark’s raw electricity prices to their highest monthly level in nearly four years, according to energy company OK.
The average raw electricity price in September was 1.07 DKK per kilowatt-hour east of the Great Belt and 1.05 DKK west of it. VAT, taxes and tariffs are added to those prices.
By comparison, prices averaged 0.62 DKK east of the Great Belt and 0.54 DKK west of it in September last year.
“Unfortunately, there has not been enough wind and sun to push prices down in September,” said Troels Skipper, commercial manager at OK.
He said high gas prices caused by geopolitical unrest had influenced electricity prices for much of the month.
Despite the increase, OK said Danish consumers’ bills will not be higher than last year because the electricity tax has been reduced to the EU’s minimum rate in 2026 and will remain there next year.
Prices also varied significantly during September. On September 14, electricity cost more than 5 DKK per kilowatt-hour for short periods, while several weekend days had hours when prices were around zero.
Skipper encouraged consumers to follow electricity prices and adjust their consumption when possible.
“This will also be important over the winter, where we will see more large fluctuations in the electricity price. But the fluctuations thus also provide an opportunity to lower one’s electricity bill,” he said.
The average electricity price has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour during four weeks so far in 2026, including two weeks in September.

The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

Gender pay gap in Denmark narrows for first time in three years
The pay gap between men and women in Denmark narrowed last year for the first time in three years, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
In 2025, women earned on average 12.3 percent less than men, compared with 12.9 percent in 2024.
Statistics Denmark has tracked the pay gap since 2004, when the difference was 16 percent. It fell to 11.9 percent in 2020, but then widened again in 2023 and 2024 before declining last year.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension company Danica, said the development also matters for retirement savings.
“Salary is the factor that matters most for the size of pension savings,” he said. “Therefore, the development in pay gaps is also one of the most important things to keep an eye on if you want less economic inequality between men and women as retirees.”
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension company Sampension, also called the decrease positive, while stressing that women still earn “significantly less than men.”
She said women’s growing educational advantage over men could support higher wages over time. She also pointed to rules on earmarked parental leave, which have led more men to take leave, as another factor that could improve women’s finances.
“After a few years with bumps in the road, the development once again went in the right direction last year,” Dalsgaard said.
German military drone makes first test flight of its kind over Denmark
A German military surveillance drone is flying over Jutland on Tuesday in what the Danish Defence says is the first test flight in Danish airspace involving an unmanned military aircraft of its size.
The German Heron TP weighs more than five tons, is 13 meters long and has a wingspan of 26 meters. It is flying at an altitude of about seven kilometers, sharing airspace with manned aircraft.
The drone belongs to the German air force, the Luftwaffe, and is being remotely controlled by a pilot at a military base in Schleswig, Germany.
The roughly two-hour flight begins at the Danish-German border in South Jutland, continues over eastern Jutland to Aalborg and then returns to Germany over western Jutland.
During the flight, the German pilot remains in contact with Naviair, which manages air traffic in Danish airspace. Denmark’s Civil Aviation and Railway Authority has approved the safety procedures for flying the drone beyond visual range, including procedures for a possible loss of control or radio connection.
The test is part of preparations for the Danish air force to receive its own General Atomics MQ-9B unmanned aircraft in 2028. They will operate from Aalborg Air Base under Squadron 729 and will be used, among other tasks, for patrol and surveillance over Greenland and the North Atlantic.
Brigade Commander Hans Peter Andersen called the flight “yet another important step toward receiving our own unmanned aircraft in the coming years.”

Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:22:13 UTC
13:22:13 KST

Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”
Lidl to invest more than 100 million DKK renovating all Danish stores
Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.
The German-owned supermarket chain said the redesign would improve the use of space, create a consistent appearance and make shopping easier.
Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.
Lidl has tested the concept through renovations at several locations. The first store to open after the official introduction of the concept began operating in Holbæk on September 27.
More renovated stores are expected to open in the coming months.
“The goal is to have all stores in Lidl Denmark renovated within the next few years,” said Mads T. Nielsen, Lidl’s development, property and sales director.
He said customers had responded positively to the test stores and newly built locations using the same design.
Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.
Suspected female wolf pup killed in traffic near Karup and sent for examination
A suspected female wolf pup has been killed in traffic on Hessellundvej near Karup, Danish authorities said Friday.
The Agency for Green Land Restructuring and Water Environment confirmed the incident to regional broadcaster TV Midtvest.
The Danish Nature Agency, which manages state-owned natural areas and wildlife matters, collected the animal Friday morning.
Officials believe it is a wolf and likely a female pup. The animal will be examined at the University of Copenhagen, though the specific purpose of the examination has not been disclosed.
Authorities could not provide further details about the collision Friday afternoon, including whether the driver involved contacted them.
Other wolves killed in traffic have previously been found and examined in Denmark.
Five dead wolves were examined in January, including three that had been struck by vehicles. The results were sent to the Natural History Museum Aarhus, which monitors Denmark’s wolf population and collects documentation.
“Through the autopsies, we gain an important understanding of the wolves’ health and way of life,” research director Kent Olsen said in January.
The examinations can include DNA testing and provide information used for research and wildlife management.
Wolves returned to Denmark in 2012 after being absent from the country for about 200 years.
The wolf is a protected species in Denmark and the country’s only apex predator.
Old systems and extensive personal data make universities vulnerable to hackers, expert says
Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.
DTU has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many users were affected.

Denmark to see sunshine Saturday before clouds and rain return Sunday
Denmark will have periods of rain and sunshine this weekend, with Saturday expected to bring the best weather, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the country’s national weather service.
Friday began cloudy as a slow-moving front brought scattered rain across central Denmark.
Conditions were expected to clear gradually, with sunshine reaching Jutland first, followed by Funen and parts of Zealand during the afternoon.
Some areas of Zealand could remain cloudy because of the front’s slow movement. Friday’s temperatures were expected to reach 15 to 18 degrees Celsius.
Saturday will begin with fog and haze in many places before clearing to sunshine across most of the country.
“The weekend starts foggy and hazy in many places, but it will clear up so that most will get sun,” meteorologist Mette Wagner said.
Temperatures could reach 19 degrees, making Saturday suitable for outdoor activities.
A second weather front is expected to enter northwestern Denmark during Saturday afternoon, bringing scattered rain.
The front will move slowly southeast Saturday evening and overnight.
Sunday will be cloudier, with rain in some places. The rainfall is not expected to be heavy, and breaks in the clouds may occur during the day.
Temperatures will fall slightly Sunday, reaching between 14 and 16 degrees.
Copenhagen Airport records busiest September with 3.2 million passengers
Copenhagen Airport handled 3.2 million passengers in September, its highest total for that month.
The number was four percent higher than in September 2025, the airport said Friday.
“The peak season no longer ends with the summer vacation,” commercial director Peter Krogsgaard said. “In September, we had almost as many travelers as in the summer months.”
About 270,000 passengers traveled between Copenhagen and Norway, making it the largest country market.
Spain followed with 255,000 passengers, while routes to and from the United Kingdom carried 245,000.
London, Stockholm, Oslo, Amsterdam and Paris were the five most popular destinations.
Demand also increased for direct routes between Copenhagen and the United States.
Those flights carried 140,000 passengers, an increase of eight percent from September 2025.
Krogsgaard said both direct traffic and the number of American visitors to Denmark had increased.
Copenhagen Airport is Denmark’s only airport offering direct flights to and from the United States. Some American passengers visit Denmark, while others continue to destinations elsewhere in Europe.
The airport expects about 1.1 million passengers during Denmark’s October school holiday. More than 115,000 travelers are expected on the busiest days.
Spain, Italy and France are the most popular southern European destinations, with about 220,000 passengers expected around the holiday period.
Petrol-only cars fall below half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet
Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.
Petrol-only cars make up 49.98 percent of registered passenger cars, down from 65 percent at the end of 2020.
The category does not include hybrid or plug-in hybrid vehicles because they use more than one source of power.
Over the same period, electric cars have increased their share of the Danish fleet. They now account for 24.3 percent of passenger cars.
Mobility Denmark, the main association representing Denmark’s automotive industry, said the figures showed how quickly the country’s vehicle fleet was changing.
“Pure petrol cars have for decades been completely dominant on Danish roads. Now they make up less than half of the passenger car fleet,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
“That says something about how strongly electric cars have moved in a few years,” he added.
