'He has good ideas': Putin lauds PM Modi's peace push to end Russia-Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:02:48 UTC
11:02:48 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday lauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to seek an end to the Ukraine conflict, saying that he has “good ideas” for achieving a peaceful resolution.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.
Asked about the issue at the Valdai Club forum, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been actively working to find mutually acceptable solutions to the Ukraine conflict.
"He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict. I think it's my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas," Putin said.
Putin thanked PM Modi for his efforts and continued support for resolving the Ukraine conflict through dialogue.
"We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible," he added.
Prime Minister Modi and Putin last met in September on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they discussed strengthening trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, along with cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.
PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
"India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. In line with this, both the leaders spoke to me to share their perspectives on the developments related to the conflict. I reiterated India's principled and consistent stand and encouraged dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict," the Prime Minister said during an interview with Japanese news outlet 'The Yomiuri Shimbun' while on a visit to the country in August.
Responding to a question on India’s role in peace efforts between the two countries, Prime Minister Modi said, "I have already indicated India's willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict. I believe, by virtue of our good relations with both sides, including key stakeholders, we can strengthen efforts dedicated to the restoration of an early and lasting peace in Ukraine."
This comes as Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons” at its disposal.
He also accused Western countries, particularly in Europe, of escalating tensions by discussing preparations for a possible war with Moscow, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea and seizing Russian vessels.
European leaders and intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could be capable of launching an attack on another country within the next few years, particularly if it emerges victorious from the war in Ukraine.

Conservative ex-mayor Andy Street out of the running for top railways job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

Conservative ex-mayor Andy Street out of the running for top railways job
Labour ministers have now spent more than eight months seeking a chair for Britain’s nationalized railway network — as people who have worked with Street believe he could return to frontline politics
LONDON — Conservative former mayor Andy Street will not be appointed to oversee Britain’s nationalized railways after a recruitment process that has now lasted more than eight months.
POLITICO reported in June that Street was seen as a leading candidate for the first chair of Great British Railways, which will oversee rail infrastructure and services as part of Labour’s reversal of the Conservative rail privatization three decades ago.
He was interviewed for the role but Labour ministers will not hand it to him, according to two people with knowledge of the decision, both of whom were granted anonymity to speak frankly. One suggested the decision was mutual.
Advertisement
Both of the people said a key reason was that Street still appeared to harbor a desire to return to frontline politics. One of the people, a government official, said he had been “unable to subdue his political ambitions.” Street was the Conservative mayor of the West Midlands for seven years until Labour narrowly defeated him in 2024.
Street declined to comment on the Great British Railways recruitment process, and told POLITICO that supposition about his political intentions was “speculation” and “conjecture.”
‘Political ambitions’
Recruitment began in January for the role of chair, which will pay £200,000 to £300,000 a year for 10 days of work a month. Great British Railways is due to be up and running in 2027, with passenger services transferred to public ownership by the end of that year as private rail operators’ contracts expire.
The Department for Transport declined to comment on whether a decision was imminent or the process of finding a chair had slowed. A government official said a “fair, open and merit-based process” was underway.
Street has history with Britain’s railways. He narrowly decided not to quit the Conservatives in 2023 when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak scrapped a leg of the planned High Speed 2 rail line from Birmingham to Manchester.
Supporters describe him as a figure who reached across political lines and was respected for his nine-year stint as managing director of department store John Lewis.
Advertisement
The job of West Midlands mayor — who holds one of the largest single electoral mandates of any British politician — will come up for election again in 2028.
Street has continued to make appearances around the region, including visiting the scene of wildfires outside Birmingham over summer. He also has a busy schedule at the Conservative Party Conference this weekend in the same city, including with the center-right policy network Prosper which he co-founded with former Scottish Conservatives Leader Ruth Davidson.
Prominent Conservatives from the center-right flank have, however, been blocked from the party’s list of candidates for the next general election, expected by 2029. Party Leader Kemi Badenoch has insisted that future candidates must agree to abandoning net zero carbon policies and to withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights.
A person who has worked with Street said he was “building up a campaign and keeping key relationships alive,” and that any move by the party to block him from running on a Conservative ticket if he chose to would be “a ridiculous act of self-harm.”
Street said it would be wrong to draw any conclusions about his future ambitions in frontline politics. “This is pure political speculation with two and two making five,” he said. “It is true that I will be active at conference as co-chair of ProsperUK making the case for moderate Conservatism, and demonstrating the support our movement has.
“It is also true that I remain deeply committed to the West Midlands. It is my home and I will continue to dedicate time and energy to its future. But the idea that these two facts are part of a wider plan is just conjecture.”

====================================================================================================

Burnham wants to change British elections. Voters think they’re fine already.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham has his work cut out to convince voters the U.K. should change the way it elects MPs, according to a new POLITICO Poll.
This week the prime minister vowed to come up with proposals to ditch the first-past-the-post voting system, which has been used in British general elections since 1884, to provide more political stability and a system that is fairer to all voters.
But a survey by pollsters Public First, conducted before Burnham’s announcement, found that 57% of respondents regard first-past-the-post as a “mostly” or “completely” fair way to decide elections. (A majority of voters across parties feel this way.)
Advertisement
At the same time, the survey revealed potential openness to a system of proportional representation, in which the number of parliamentary seats each party wins is more closely linked to the total number of votes it receives across the country.
“Most people don’t spend much time thinking about how we elect MPs and, broadly, people think the current system is fair,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Burnham will need to make a convincing case to voters about why changing the electoral system is necessary, if he is to gain support for his plans.”
Under first-past-the-post, whichever candidate wins the most votes in their constituency is elected to represent that seat, even if they fall far short of a majority of local voters. Nationally, that can result in a party taking power with relatively low popular support.
Labour won the last election in 2024 by a landslide, taking 63% of seats in Parliament with just 34% of the vote — the most disproportionate result in British history.
Since then, some polling projections have suggested Nigel Farage’s populist-right Reform UK party was on track to win a majority with around 30% of votes under the first-past-the-post system.
In a speech to Labour members in Liverpool, Burnham said recent turbulence in British politics — he’s the country’s seventh prime minister in 10 years — meant a new system was needed. “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No. 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote,” he said.
Advertisement
How to choose
Many voting systems could replace first-past-the-post, some based on a form of proportional representation (PR). Public First’s analysis found that support for moving to PR varied depending on which party was proposing it.
When Labour voters were shown a Labour proposal to move to PR, 54% supported the idea, whereas when they were shown an identical proposal branded as coming from Reform UK, only 36% supported it. The same broad pattern was true of Reform voters.
A man walks past a fallen placard as he exits a polling station after casting his vote in the local elections on May 7, 2026 in Surbiton, England. | Carl Court/Getty Images
Overall, 41% of U.K. adults responding to the poll said they would “somewhat” support or “strongly support” a Labour proposal to move toward PR. Another 26% would neither support nor oppose it, and 22% somewhat opposed or strongly opposed the idea.
“While they lean toward supporting reform, many voters judge it by who is proposing it,” said Wride. “With trust in politicians so low, if electoral reform looks like just one party’s project, it risks being seen as political game-playing.”
Burnham’s pledge on electoral reform could boost his chances of staying in power, but much could change ahead of the next election, which could take place as late as 2029. Polls currently predict a hung parliament with Labour falling short of a majority, but the Liberal Democrats have long campaigned for electoral reform and would be Labour’s most likely coalition partners.
Farage has also spoken in favor of replacing first-past-the-post with an alternative voting system, but has recently said less on the topic. This week, the party’s deputy leader Richard Tice said it was “no time” to be discussing electoral reform.
Advertisement
One person familiar with the thinking in Burnham’s team said they expected the government preference would be for the same “supplementary vote” system used in Greater Manchester mayoral elections. It allows voters to pick a second preference — with those votes being counted if the lead candidate doesn’t win at least 50% of first preference votes.
Separately, a government official said a “constituency link” in any new voting system would be “critical” for Burnham.
“I found it better being elected under a different system as mayor of Greater Manchester where people had one or two — they could put that on the ballot paper,” Burnham told the BBC this week. “Because you had a reason to stop on every doorstep and chat to people who might not always support your party and try and get their second preference. It just led to a better politics.”
Sam Blewett and Emilio Casalicchio contributed reporting. Public First surveyed 2,028 U.K. adults online Sept. 13-15, 2026.

'Killed' in Kashmir, alive in Rawalpindi — Pakistan shows ex-soldier India claims it killed as rebel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:00:19 UTC
11:00:19 KST

Pakistan's military has disputed India's claim that its military had killed a senior rebel commander in India-administered Kashmir, presenting a man to the media whom India and its news channels had identified as the slain fighter, raising questions over who exactly was killed in the alleged gun battle.
Pakistani Army spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry dismissed the Indian account as fabricated during a televised news conference on Thursday.
The man, whom Chaudhry identified as Mohammad Asif, said he was a former Pakistani soldier who retired in 2023.
It came a day after India's Ministry of Home Affairs said Indian troops had killed a senior Lashkar-e-Taiba commander identified as Musa, also known as Asif Fauji, in an intelligence-led operation in India-administered Kashmir.
The Indian ministry described Wednesday's killing as a major blow to the rebel group, saying he was the last surviving member of a four-man group of commanders responsible for several major attacks in the disputed region since 2022.
"So, here is that superman. You can see this superman. Please, come, my brother. Tell us about these achievements of yours, what all you have been doing," Chaudhry quipped as reporters laughed during the news briefing.
Asif told media that his friends contacted him after seeing Indian media reports of his killing in Kashmir gun battle. "To their concerns, I responded that I was here, alive and healthy," he said.
Asif said he came forward to clarify his identity and expressed surprise that Indian media outlets had displayed what he described as his national identity card while reporting his killing.
"I saw Indian news broadcasts showing my photograph and personal military record, claiming that I had been martyred in Kashmir," the ex-soldier said.
"I was utterly astonished. I was sitting at home, yet they were claiming to have killed me in Kashmir," he added. "By the grace of God, I am alive and present before you."
'No self-respecting nation does this'
Chaudhry said India was fabricating allegations and staging operations to blame Pakistan for rebel violence. "It is a very shameful and embarrassing thing. No self-respecting nation does this," he said.
Chaudhry also accused India of jailing Muslim Kashmiris, saying: "They take them out, kill them, and stage that as a false flag operation, portraying it as a terrorist act."
"This time they went ahead; they said this is not very spicy, let’s take an army soldier of Pakistan and portray him as one that we have killed," he added.
Asked whether the development could trigger another armed conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbours, Sharif said Pakistan’s military was prepared and warned of "very harsh" retaliation.
"If they want to do anything, most welcome," he said. "But let it be clear that this time we will not leave them so easily. This time the cost that Pakistan would inflict on their strategic folly will be very, very severe," Sharif warned.
Pakistan and India have a history of strained relations and have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.
The disputed Himalayan region is divided between the two countries, which both claim it in full.
India has deployed over 500,000 troops in the region since 1989 when the popular armed revolt broke against New Delhi's rule.
Most Kashmiris support rebel demands that their territory be united either under Pakistani rule or as an independent country in a UN-sponsored right to self-determination vote.
Between 70,000 to 100,000 people, mostly civilians, have been killed in the armed revolt against India's rule.

A classic coming-of-age novel spurred this writer to 'blow up' her life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Grace Chapple exposes political heart of A Room with a View in new play
When Grace Chapple visited Florence, Italy, in 2022, she was listening to the audiobook of A Room with a View.
Travelling solo for the first time, aged 27, she found herself in the Uffizi Gallery — where Botticelli's The Birth of Venus hangs — feeling unsure what to do with her life.
"I was thinking, 'Do I even know who I am?'" Chapple says.
"You know that first time you're forced to confront yourself alone and how you interact with the world?"
As she wandered the city, a little hungover, so too did the protagonist of the novel: Lucy Honeychurch.
In English author EM Forster's 1908 novel A Room with a View, Lucy visits Italy, chaperoned by her spinster cousin Charlotte Bartlett.
There, she meets the charismatic but strange George Emerson and is wooed by another suitor, the wealthy but condescending Cecil Vyse.
It's the set-up for a love triangle, but Forster's novel was more than a romance; it's Lucy's coming-of-age story, which also pokes fun at turn-of-the-century English society.
That complexity spurred Chapple to adapt it for Sydney's Belvoir St Theatre, where it opens this month before travelling to Melbourne Theatre Company.
"The novel hit me hard," she says. "It found me at the moment in my life where I really needed it."
Listening to A Room with a View in Florence did more than inspire Chapple creatively. It encouraged her to "blow up" her life.
Returning to Sydney, where she had moved from Perth to study playwriting at the National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA), Chapple broke up with her long-term boyfriend.
"When you're stuck on train tracks in life, you need something huge to shake you out of it," Chapple says.
Finding inspiration at home
That year, Chapple's debut play, Never Closer, set during the Troubles, premiered as part of Belvoir's independent 25A program. Two years later, it opened on the theatre's main stage.
A new production from indie company Patalog Theatre will return to Melbourne this month, after earning rave reviews in May.
Never Closer is the story of five schoolfriends reuniting for Christmas Eve at Deidre's house in Northern Ireland in 1987.
Seeing each other a decade after they finished school, with many of them leaving Northern Ireland to work and study, unresolved tensions rise to the surface, especially after Niamh brings home her English fiancé Harry.
It was the play Chapple wrote while studying at NIDA.
She recalls being asked when she applied: "If you had a year left to live, what would you write about?"
She doesn't know why she burst into tears: "I just said, 'My mum'."
Chapple's mum grew up in Northern Ireland and moved to London at 17 to study medicine, where she met Chapple's dad, an Englishman.
"That became the base of the play," Chapple explains.
"But it was mixed in with the fact I had just left home for the first time and was dealing with all these weird feelings about leaving behind my friends and my home and not knowing if there would be a home to go back to.
"It made me think about my mum and how she never went back."
Beneath the period romance
After members of the Belvoir team saw Never Closer during its 25A season, they wanted to know what Chapple was going to do next.
"They were keen to invest in me as an artist," she says.
"They said, 'What else do you have? Is there anything you want to adapt you might be able to turn around quicker than an original?'"
When she listened to A Room with a View earlier that year, Chapple had been struck by its theatricality.
"[Forster] writes in scenes and it's all about relationships," she explains. "The action hinges around conversations."
With buy-in from Never Closer director Hannah Goodwin, Chapple pitched the adaptation to Belvoir artistic director Eamon Flack.
"At first glance it feels like a quite conventional period romance … but the romance is really a vehicle for talking about more exciting political and transgressive topics than we're used to getting out of your Jane Austens," she explains.
Chapple says A Room with a View resonates with a modern audience because Lucy is, like all young people, "learning to think for yourself in a world that is really trying to tell you how to think".
"It's about how dangerous it can be to a dominant culture when people start to break away and carve their own paths.
"It's a journey everyone has to go on of figuring out how to live honestly in this world and be true to the person you are and how much that can cost."
A show about the housing crisis
That question of cost is something Chapple is thinking about with her next project, her second original play, The Landlord, which will feature in Belvoir's 2027 season.
It reunites the writer with Goodwin and Never Closer star Ariadne Sgouros (High Country) and breaks down intergenerational inequality in a story set across two Surry Hill terraces. Both are owned by 65-year-old John — but only one is falling apart.
Chapple started writing The Landlord in 2024, when she was on a research trip to Cambridge University to pore over its archive of Forster's manuscripts and diaries for her A Room with a View.
"[The Landlord] is born out of just all the dehumanising experiences that come from being a renter," she says.
It's a subject many millennial artists are grappling with in their work.
"Every conversation I've had since I moved to Sydney works its way back to the housing crisis eventually," Chapple says.
"Like, someone's got a shitty rental situation or they're getting kicked out or they're paying too much or they're trying to buy and can't."
While it's the subject on everyone's lips, not everyone has Chapple's expertise.
She's approaching the subject armed with a degree in economics.
"I was taught the narratives that are constructed around capitalism that protect it and make it seem like this perfect, inevitable thing," she says.
"I liked the idea of unpicking the narratives I was taught, but for people who didn't study it."
A Room with a View is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from October 3 - November 1 and Melbourne Theatre Company from November 14 - December 19.
Never Closer is at fortyfivedownstairs, Melbourne, from October 15 - November 1.
The Landlord is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from September 25 - October 24, 2027.

Europe war-games life after Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The EU can’t pretend Friedrich Merz isn’t in trouble any longer.
After a string of humiliating election losses where the far right has made historic gains and an internal fight with his own coalition over social care policy, EU partners are starting to plan for the prospect that the German chancellor could be ousted — or at least distracted — in the crucial coming months, according to five diplomats and officials who spoke to POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive talks.
Two European governments have even held internal sessions to game out what the end of Merz’s chancellorship would mean for EU policymaking, two of those familiar with the discussions said.
Advertisement
It’s not a prospect they take lightly. Merz leads the EU’s largest economy and is the chief negotiator for wealthy countries seeking to rein in spending in the bloc’s proposed €2 trillion seven-year budget. He is also a driving force behind EU efforts to save heavy industry.
“Any debate about the German chancellor weakens Germany’s role in the EU and in the world,” said Wilhelm Gebhard, a member of the Bundestag and an official in Merz’s governing CDU party.
With France facing its own far-right surge and a presidential election next year that could hand power to euroskeptic Marine Le Pen, few in Brussels relish the prospect of Germany, historically the EU’s other major player, turning inwards or derailing important negotiations.
The contingency planning, which has seen officials and diplomats brainstorm the situation, comes after months of mixed signals from Berlin on EU policy, including car emissions and a proposed social media ban for children. Even if Merz stays in office, the political turmoil is already complicating Berlin’s work on the EU’s biggest files.
The worst-case scenario for Brussels would be a leaderless Germany, or one with a far-right government. But that is seen as virtually impossible in the short term, with none of the mainstream players seeking new elections while the far-right Alternative for Germany party are leading in the polls.
“All coalition partners know that they have a great deal to lose from early elections,” said Hannah Neumann, an opposition Green MEP who sits on the European Parliament’s security and foreign affairs committees. “My expectation, therefore, is that they will stay together and muddle through.”
Advertisement
While Merz himself could be forced to resign in the face of his growing unpopularity, he would be replaced straight away by a successor from either his center-right CDU party or his center-left coalition partner, the SPD. That should give Brussels confidence “someone will always be in charge,” said one of the diplomats.
Those who know him insist Merz won’t be distracted when it comes to EU affairs.
“Other politicians might say ‘OK, I focus less on EU politics.’ For him it’s just the opposite: It’s an additional incentive to show leadership in Europe,” said a person familiar with the chancellor’s thinking.
In the immediate term, Merz’s political weakness at home could make finding compromise on the bloc’s next seven-year budget harder by pushing the chancellor to double down on Berlin’s hardline stance in search of a win, a further two diplomats warned.
As the leading voice for countries seeking a smaller EU budget, which leaders hope to agree by year-end, Merz has called for cuts of “hundreds of billions of euros.” Germany, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands are pressing for overall reductions, while net recipients such as Poland and Romania want to protect their share.
Advertisement
Nobody who could replace him as chancellor “would be able to be more flexible than Merz is,” said one of the diplomats, but “the risk is he has to show his self-perceived leadership in Brussels in the hope it will help his standing in Germany.”
An envoy from another country said “domestically he is weak [which means] he can’t compromise” and needs to be seen to score a win by slashing the budget as far as possible.
But Merz’s allies say his fight on the world stage is only worthwhile if his coalition partners play along behind the curtain.
“Strength comes not just from grand appearances in Brussels, but above all from stability, reliability and the ability to push through decisions at home. That is precisely what is lacking at the moment,” said CDU Bundestag member Fabian Gramling. “Germany’s influence in Europe also depends on how united and capable of action the federal government appears at home.”
Friedrich Merz is pictured during a meeting with soldiers in Münster, Germany on Oct. 1, 2026. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images
Infighting and indecision
The fractious relationship between the CDU and the SPD has already been undercutting Berlin’s stance on issues of critical national importance.
Throughout 2025, as Brussels renegotiated a planned phaseout of combustion engine cars, in the face of fierce lobbying from Germany’s influential automotive sector, German officials and diplomats were unable to articulate a clear position, with center-right ministers wanting to scrap the green policy and their center-left counterparts pushing to preserve it.
Advertisement
Ultimately Merz’s fellow German conservatives in Brussels — Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European People’s Party chief Manfred Weber — stepped in to kill the proposal at the eleventh hour.
Another key policy area where the coalition struggled to agree a position was on whether children should be banned from social media, a flagship EU-wide proposal from von der Leyen. While Merz personally backed the idea at the start of the year, he and his political allies spent more than six months struggling to land on a specific age limit to lobby for when von der Leyen was consulting with partners, according to officials and diplomats involved in the talks.
Even before the latest crisis, Merz’s domestic troubles were spilling into Brussels at the highest level. Last year, he surprised fellow EU leaders by demanding that a summit scheduled to cover geopolitics and other policy files should instead focus on saving European heavy industry from competition with the U.S. and China.
Germany lost around 124,100 industrial jobs last year, according to an analysis by EY, with the government concerned deindustrialization is helping drive support for Merz’s far-right and far-left rivals. Other capitals share his concerns, but Merz has insisted industry should top the agenda at future summits.
But even inside the chancellor’s own CDU, he has struggled to achieve consensus on what to do about it. As the Commission plans a push against unfair Chinese trade practices, Merz’s fellow party member and foreign minister Katherina Reiche is seen as more protective over the relationship with Beijing, and the German industrial giants like Volkswagen and BASF that trade with it.
In a speech on Thursday commemorating 36 years of German reunification — the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of communist East Germany —the country’s ambassador to the EU, Thomas Ossowski, told fellow envoys and officials that “whenever we celebrate German unity, we celebrate European unity. And we need this unity [now] more than ever.”
Gabriel Gavin reported from Brussels. Frida Preuß reported from Berlin.Jordyn Dahl, Eliza Gkritsiand Carlo Martuscelli contributed to this report.

2 new islands appear near Indonesia’s Anak Krakatoa volcano after eruption
The island-like mounds are likely the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s 1883 eruption
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Two new islands have appeared off Anak Krakatoa, potentially the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s catastrophic 1883 eruption.
The formations, discovered following a 25-hour eruption in early September, sit hundreds of metres off opposite sides of Anak Krakatoa – one to the northwest and the other to the southeast – almost on a straight line through the volcano’s crater, according to Indonesia’s Geological Agency.
The agency places one about 760 metres (0.5 miles) off Anak Krakatoa’s northwest coast and the other some 495 metres to the southeast. It has not verified their dimensions or elevation above sea level.
The agency’s preliminary interpretation is that relatively fluid magma released during the continuous eruption reached the surface via an elongated northwest-southeast opening, with erupted material forming two island-like mounds offshore.

CCTV Captures Russian Drone Slamming Into Kyiv School With 104 Children Inside – Warhead Fails to Detonate

A terrifying CCTV video from Kyiv on Thursday captured the moment a Russian drone slammed into a school where more than 100 children had begun their day – another chilling reminder of how Russia’s expanding aerial war is reaching into the places Ukrainian children are supposed to be safest.
At around 9 a.m., a Russian drone struck School No. 12 in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district, smashing through the building, shattering windows and partially destroying a wall and staircase.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside were 104 children and 60 members of staff.
They survived because classes had already moved into the school’s underground shelter after an air raid alert sounded.
But there was another extraordinary stroke of fortune: the Russian drone’s warhead failed to detonate.
The explosive payload was found inside the damaged school after the strike. Had it functioned as designed, the consequences inside a building holding 164 children and staff could have been dramatically more devastating.
Two things stood between the children and a potential catastrophe: Ukraine’s decision to send them underground and the failure of the weapon that struck their school to explode.
No children or teachers were injured.
The 21-second CCTV recording captures the sudden violence of the impact, followed by debris and smoke engulfing part of the school.
“They spare no one,” headteacher Valentyna Chorna said as she surveyed the damage.
Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
“Children are our future, the future of our nation. In order to destroy a nation, of course, they need to destroy children.”
A Relentless Pattern
Thursday’s near-disaster comes amid an intensifying wave of Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with schools, homes and other civilian facilities repeatedly caught in the strikes.
The danger is growing as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones that are more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
That makes the strike on School No. 12 particularly chilling.
This was not simply debris falling from an interception high above the capital. A Russian attack drone crashed directly into the building carrying an explosive warhead.
The weapon failed to complete the destruction it was capable of causing.
The strike came amid a broader pattern of attacks affecting Ukrainian children and educational facilities.
Human Rights Watch reported in September that 314 educational facilities in Kyiv alone had been damaged since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, including at least 107 during 2026.
Across Ukraine, the scale is far greater. UNICEF told the UN Security Council earlier this year that more than 1,780 educational facilities had been verified as damaged or destroyed since 2022, disrupting education for children already entering another year of wartime schooling.
Recent Russian attacks have repeatedly reached places where children live, study and shelter.
On Sept. 29, Russian forces struck Sumy with four glide bombs, hitting a school while pupils were sheltering inside. Children were among those injured, while civilians were killed elsewhere in the city.
A day earlier in Kharkiv, a Russian glide bomb struck a residential area, injuring dozens of people, including children.
For Ukrainian families, everyday routines – walking to school, sitting in class or sleeping at home – continue to unfold under the threat of another missile or drone alert.
Schools under the laws of war
Under international humanitarian law, schools are civilian objects unless and for such time as they are being used for military purposes.
Parties to a conflict are required to distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives and to take feasible precautions to avoid harm to civilians.
Intentionally directing an attack against a school that remains a civilian object can constitute a war crime.
But the repeated destruction and damage inflicted on educational facilities across Ukraine has left children learning under conditions that would have been unimaginable before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has responded by expanding underground classrooms, school shelters and remote education.
At School No. 12 on Thursday, those precautions proved decisive.
More than 100 children were underground when the Russian drone tore into the floors above them.
Had they still been sitting in ordinary classrooms – or had the drone’s warhead detonated as designed — the outcome could have been catastrophic.
Zelensky visits Kyiv school after Russian Shahed strike
President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the school, where he met with the principal and teachers following the morning Russian Shahed strike.
“Most importantly, everyone is alive,” he wrote on X, thanking the school staff for their “clear and coordinated actions,” which he said saved lives.
“Striking schools and kindergartens is a deliberate Russian tactic aimed at making ordinary life a target,” Zelensky wrote.
“And we are working nonstop to strengthen our air defense and increase the production of Ukrainian interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds – in order to protect our cities and communities from such strikes.”

IN BRIEF: Putin speaks on Russia’s economic sustainability, Europe’s aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:50:02 UTC
10:50:02 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Despite the existing problems, Russia continues to develop, and its economy remains healthy and sustainable, Russian President Vladimir Putin told the plenary session of the 23rd Valdai International Discussion Club.
He also said that Russia’s offensive in the special military operation zone is gaining momentum, and that Europe’s aggressive attitude towards Russia is aimed at diverting attention from domestic economic failures.
Below are the Russian leader’s key remarks.
Russia’s sustainability and way to future
Russia is ready to forge its path to the future with realistic assessment of risks, opportunities and necessary goals, "and, of course, it is ready to engage in such efforts jointly with other countries and peoples."
"We do have some difficulties, but we are resolving them. Macroeconomic indices show that our economy is healthy, and that our financial system and economic institutions are working in a sustainable manner."
Russia’s economy has certain problems and issues that need to be solved, but "who does not?" "Look at any other region of the world. Everyone has its own problems."
Russia had inflation problems: "We jump-started the economy, we overheated it. And we made a deliberate choice to cool it down. We did it deliberately, being perfectly aware that if the Central Bank raises the key rate, investment will decline. It was obvious to everyone, and it did lead to such consequences. What matters now is to make sure that we don’t overcool the economy."
This year, inflation nearly halved compared to 2025. "This year’s budget deficit is around three percent. I’m sure that next year it will be two."
Situation in special operation zone
The situation in the special operation zone is gaining momentum, with over 1,300 square kilometers of territory taken under Russia’s control in September alone. "This is 2.5 times higher than in the previous months."
The government of Ukraine and the European Union claim they will be able to hold the remaining 11% of Donbass’s territory over the next year and a half or two. "We believe that it will happen way sooner, given the pace of our advance, which, as I have just mentioned, is accelerating."
For Russia, the situation around Ukraine is not a question of land, it’s a question of people. "It’s not about a piece of territory, it’s about people. The point is that we need to create conditions not for a temporary truce, but for a lasting peace. And we need security guarantees for that."
It is necessary to strive for peace agreements on Ukraine: "If they [Western countries and Ukraine] agree to terms that Russia also finds acceptable, it will be better to put an end to these sad events and avoid additional casualties on both sides."
Russia is ready to launch and complete negotiations on Ukraine as promptly as possible, but, "naturally, on conditions that the Russian Federation and its people find acceptable."
"However, it appears that the other side simply does not want to end the hostilities."
Russia’s response
Kiev troops started to strike Russian cargo ships in the Black Sea, and Russia had to respond: "Well, we gave our answer. And now they are asking us to stop via all channels. But they [the Kiev government] were the ones to start this."
"They started attacking our refineries, openly declaring that their objective is to harm our economy. They attained their goal to a certain extent because, according to our estimates, we lost about 1% of our GDP. They deliberately started striking civilian targets. Well, they got a tit-for-tat response."
The Russian armed forces started delivering strikes on sites that are crucial for the Ukrainian economy: "Now, by their own admission, they effectively have no metallurgical industry left."
Europe’s aggression
At this point Europe’s leading countries "are much more hostile towards Russia than the United States."
While the United States "is seeking to end the conflict," many European countries, "have now perhaps become the ‘instigators’ of aggressive attitude toward Russia, creating additional crises between Russia and Europe." They are "driven by the unfavorable situation in their own economies, and, consequently, by the unfavorable situation for the ruling elites, combined with shifting political moods."
European politicians want "to justify the need of preparations for war, and to mobilize as many supporters around themselves as possible in order to remain in power." "The logic is very simple, and I’m sure that this constitutes a significant portion of the reasoning behind Europe’s behavior towards the Russian Federation."
"We are not threatening anyone, and we have no intention of attacking anyone, neither in 2029, nor in 2030, nor in 2050. However, if we face aggression, we will be forced to respond. European citizens should clearly understand this and distinguish between our position and the stance taken by certain political leaders in their countries."
The continuous stoking of rhetoric by many European countries is driven by the serious worsening of their domestic economic and political situation. "Look at what is happening in the economy, look what is happening in the social sphere and the quality of life in major European countries. In this situation, they have to shift the focus of their citizens’ attention from domestic issues to outside problems."
"We have no preconditions for resuming and restoring relations with Europe in general or with particular countries."
EU countries "will collapse on their own" because they continue to make mistakes that negatively impact their own economies. "But this is none of our business. We are not interfering."
Weapons as competitive advantage
Russia understands that in case of a direct attack by NATO, it will have to face "an adversary more than twice our size in terms of numbers." "They have huge economic potential, huge military potential. Indeed, our forces and assets would not be that extensive to counter such a threat. And we will have to use our competitive advantages in this struggle."
One of Russia’s main competitive advantages are its strike capabilities. "Yes, of course, France and the United Kingdom are nuclear powers. We understand that, and we are fully aware of that. However, no one else possesses the strike capabilities that Russia has today. And this is our competitive advantage."
"We are not threatening anyone. We simply make it clear that our tools to defend ourselves are not that numerous."
Russia has advanced new weapons systems: "We have new, modern capabilities, including entirely new missile defense penetration systems, advanced medium-range weapons, and state-of-the-art systems that other nations do not possess yet."
"All nuclear powers are highly technologically advanced countries. They will have it at some point in the future. But now they don’t, only we do."
While building new facilities, Russia is taking modern methods of warfare into account: "I assure you, we are currently considering this, and, when we build new enterprises in this sector, we are taking modern methods of warfare into account and do everything possible to ensure they are located in the safest areas possible." "Construction is under way."
Relations with US
Factors marring and damaging Russia-US relations have developed over decades: "We would very much like to see these divisive factors to become a thing of the past, allowing new prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation to emerge."
Russia has proposed and continues to propose to the United States to resume dialogue on strategic arms limitations: "We don not mind resuming this dialogue; we have never been against it. We have offered it, and we are offering it now. There is no answer. Well, if there is no answer, then so be it."
It was Washington that withdrew from agreements curbing the arms race and the proliferation of nuclear weapons: "We were not the ones to walk out of these treaties. The United States did it, under this or that pretext."
"I have quite good, long-standing relations with President (of the US Donald - TASS) Trump. I’m thankful for his efforts to resolve the Ukrainian crisis, and, as I’ve said many times, he is doing it in good faith. And I’m thankful for that, too."
Partnership with China
Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping understand each other without words or interpreters: "You know, what is interesting. It only took one word from him or me, and without interpreters - and without knowing each other's languages - we understood each other instantly."
China never seeks to resolve emerging problems and issues through pressure or military force. This is alien to its philosophy, which is fundamentally rooted in pursuing solutions through peaceful means. For its part, Russia recognizes Beijing's approach, shares this perspective, and notes the strong outcomes generated by the joint efforts of Moscow and Beijing.
"Can China play any role [in promoting peace] at this point? Of course it can. And, first of all, this stems from its growing economic and military potential, from its readiness to expand the zone of free cooperation, and this is what Chinese President Xi Jinping’s initiative ‘One belt, One Road’ is aimed at."
"Together with China, we are developing this initiative, aligning it with Russia's respective projects, including the Greater Eurasian Partnership. We are working jointly, and this is yielding strong, positive results."
Moscow and Beijing will undoubtedly establish a joint framework to actively utilize the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to serve the interests of Russia and China.
Indian premier and peace initiatives
The diversity and unity of Indian culture are highly admirable: "There is something about Indian culture that possesses such uniqueness - a distinctiveness and unity at the same time - that it undoubtedly serves as an exemplary model. This, of course, deserves to be an example."
At every meeting, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi raises the question of resolving the conflict in Ukraine: "He comes up with very good ideas, aimed at searching for mutually acceptable - specifically mutually acceptable - solutions."
The head of the Indian government has a neutral stance, which is nevertheless aimed at bringing the conflict to an end: "By the way, we are grateful to the Indian premier for his desire to resolve this conflict peacefully, and as quickly as possible."
Multipolarity and BRICS
The world should be multipolar; it cannot be bipolar: "It should take into account the interests of all participants of international relations. And, as we have said many times, there is the cornerstone, basic principle: the security of one nation cannot be achieved at the expense of the security of others. This is one of the cornerstones that we believe should form the foundation of the future world order."
"We cannot say exactly how this world will look like. <...> But we need to strive to jointly determine <…> the pillars of the future world order. And this needs to be done without any preconditions."
"An organization such as BRICS may certainly become the prototype for building the future world order."
At this point, BRICS represents nearly half of the planet’s entire population, and its share in the global economy is constantly growing. "This is happening every year, and we can see it in the statistics. And, most importantly, the principles of BRICS' formation and functioning stipulate that everyone is equal. There is no domination of any kind there, and this is what makes it so attractive."
So far, it is hard to say what role BRICS will play in the new architecture of international relations, but it can already be said with certainty that it is "a useful mechanism."

Significant rainfall is expected to continue across much of a state that's already been battered by storms and flash flooding.
Melbourne recorded one of its wettest October days in several years after the city received up to 25mm of rain within an hour on Thursday afternoon, with other areas of Victoria also hard hit.
More than 200 calls for help were made to the SES, including six water rescues, after parts of Melbourne were hit by the flash flooding.
The city was plunged into darkness about 3pm as the system moved through, with Melbourne Olympic Park recording 47.8mm of rain since 9am on Thursday.

The busiest units included Barwon South West and metro Melbourne areas, although attention will now move to north-eastern suburbs along with Gippsland.

02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Hundreds of people rallied in Milan on Thursday against a controversial antisemitism bill under consideration in Italy’s parliament, with Jewish groups joining calls to reject the legislation.
The bill, known as DDL 1004, was introduced by the far-right League party, a junior partner in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing coalition government.
It would use criteria adopted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) to define antisemitism. After passing the Senate in March, it is now before the Chamber of Deputies for final approval.
Demonstrators gathered outside the renowned La Scala Opera House, waving Palestinian flags, ringing bells and blowing whistles.
They held signs saying “No to the antisemitism bill,” “Criticizing Israel is not antisemitism” and “Protest is a right” while chanting “Free Palestine.” Some unfurled a large banner saying “One voice. No to Bill 1004.”
Speakers at the rally described the bill as dangerous, arguing that it equates criticism of Israel with racial hatred and could silence those criticizing the occupation and discrimination imposed on Palestinians.
Giulia, a member of the Jewish Anti-Racist Laboratory, told Anadolu that her group and other Jewish organizations oppose the bill, noting that Italy already has legislation against hate crimes, racism, discrimination and fascist propaganda under the 1993 Mancino law.
“We do not need a specific law based on the IHRA definition that treats criticism of Israel as antisemitism. We believe this law will increase antisemitism rather than prevent it, because it will silence dissent and solidarity with Palestine,” she said.
“We Jews can play a role by saying that this kind of legislation makes us feel less safe and leads us to believe that antisemitism will increase,” she added.
Bulgarian-born Italian Jewish artist Moni Ovadia also voiced strong opposition.
“This legislation persecutes Jews as well as people who are just and free. I will only say this: If Albert Einstein and Sigmund Freud were alive today, they would be convicted under this law. So would (German-American historian and philosopher) Hannah Arendt,” he said.
Another protest against the bill is scheduled to take place outside the Chamber of Deputies in Rome on Friday.

While Congo reported following 79% of listed contacts on Sept 29, Africa CDC estimates responders are reaching only about 23% of the number of contacts expected from known cases. Congo was monitoring more than 30,000 identified contacts that day.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:44:04 UTC
10:44:04 KST

Spanish fashion retailer Zara removed a children’s Halloween costume from its website on Wednesday after social media users noted that the gray-and-blue striped outfit resembled prison garb worn by inmates in Nazi concentration camps.
Zara described the ensemble as “Kids costume featuring vertical stripes with decorative topstitching, a lapel flower and a distressed effect. Includes a cardigan and shorts. Gray / Blue.”
The post was visible via a Google search that continued to display an indexed version of the Zara product page after the listing itself had been removed.
The costume resembles the suit worn by Michael Keaton’s title character in the 1988 horror-comedy “Beetlejuice” and its 2024 sequel, “Beetlejuice Beetlejuice.” Even so, social media users said the vertical stripes and shiny crisscrosses, which some media outlets described as “fake stitched scars,” resembled concentration camp uniforms and the barbed wire visible in many World War II photos.
Priced at $59.90 in the US, according to another indexed version of the listing, the costume drew criticism online in Europe on Tuesday. It gained wider attention Wednesday after Israeli journalist Dov Gil-Har, activist Hen Mazzig and others shared images of it on X/Twitter.
The listing was no longer accessible by Wednesday afternoon. It was unclear exactly when Zara removed it. No reason was given for its removal, and Zara has not made any public statements regarding the controversy, nor has it responded to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency’s request for comment.
One Instagram commenter wrote “@zara how many levels of approval did this go though (sic)? Who is working for you?” A Facebook user said “It’s supposed to be a groom costume. It does somewhat resemble a (sic) Auschwitz uniform. With all the anti-semitism on the rise I am not surprised.” Another Instagram user asked, “What were they claiming it was meant to be?”
Not Zara's first time facing controversies surrounding Holocaust imagery
Zara has in the past faced similar controversies over clothing that evoked Nazi or Holocaust imagery. In 2007, it withdrew a handbag from its stores after a customer discovered a swastika embroidered on it; Inditex, Zara’s parent company, said the symbol had not appeared on the design Zara had approved.
In 2014 Zara apologized for selling a blue-and-white-striped shirt with six-pointed yellow-star badges on the chest. The Zara Israel website identified it as a “striped sheriff t-shirt” and the word sheriff was cut out in small letters on the star. The likeness to concentration camp uniforms and the yellow Star of David badges Jews were forced to wear under Nazi rule led Zara to stop selling the shirts and destroy the remaining inventory.
Incident underscores need for Holocaust education
When reached for comment, the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany, which represents Holocaust survivors in compensation negotiations, said the repeated incidents underscore the need for Holocaust education.
“This is not the first time this has happened and it once again makes abundantly clear: The glaring absence of Holocaust knowledge is pervasive,” Gideon Taylor, Claims Conference president, wrote in an email to JTA. “It shouldn’t take the risk of a Shoah survivor opening their door and seeing children that look like they are in concentration camp uniforms for us to see where we have to do better. This should serve as a message to us all of why Holocaust education is so important.”

Ellaboudy had also purchased parts used for the construction of drones and remotely operated aerial systems.
According to the criminal complaint, in December 2024, Ellaboudy took sick leave, claiming he'd been exposed to highly concentrated nitric acid, a common chemical used in the construction of explosive materials.
In 2025, Ellaboudy traveled from Richland, Washington, to Oman using an official passport from his time employed by the US Army Corps of Engineers. He then used the passport to cross into Yemen, intending to travel to Sanaa, Yemen's capital, which is under control of the Houthis.
When he returned to the US, Ellaboudy told US Customs and Border Protection Officers that he'd been traveling on official government business.
Ellaboudy's DOE supervisor stated that Ellaboudy had no such authorized official government travel to that region.
Ellaboudy provided expert assistance to FBI source claiming to work for Houthis
During the investigation, Ellaboudy began communicating with an FBI confidential human source (CHS) who stated he was working for a Houthi "Colonel" to acquire communications equipment to send to Yemen for use in a mobile communications center.
Ellaboudy provided expert advice and assistance based upon his background in electrical engineering by assisting the CHS in testing and modifying solar power generators and communication equipment.
Ellaboudy also provided guidance on the power and communication systems, provided schematics and diagrams for the setup, and conducted research on other equipment that could be acquired to better the equipment.
If convicted, Ellaboudy faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

California has outlawed child marriage, joining 17 other US states where the taboo practice is also banned.

I will keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states.”
Unchained at Last, the advocacy group that pushed for the legislation, says 9,000 children are married in California every year.

Jewish groups hail California law making it the first state to list ‘Jewish’ as an ethnicity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:43:11 UTC
10:43:11 KST

California is now the first state in the nation to deem “Jewish” an ethnic and racial identity, rather than just a religious affiliation.
Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom on Wednesday signed SB 1387, a bill that expands California’s legal definition of ethnicity “to include Jewish identity” in demographic data collection. As of Jan. 1, 2029, forms distributed by public entities like schools and prisons will need to include a “Jewish” category when asking for voluntary disclosures of ethnicity or race.
David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, a group that lobbies on behalf of a number of Jewish organizations in the state, described the signing in a statement as “a historic step for the Jewish community.”
“Under the shadow of Nazi race theory, American Jewish leaders asked the government to count us only as a religion,” he said, noting that this approach “didn’t work” and led to exclusion from data that shapes policy.
“Now hate crime, health, poverty, and education data will reflect who Jewish Californians actually are so we can ensure the best support for our community,” Bocarsly added. “Most importantly, it allows us to be seen as the diverse, complex people we are.”
The legislation was a priority among many Jewish groups across the Gold Rush state, who believe that Jewish peoplehood should be connected to more than just religion — and that the law should reflect this relationship.
Newsom expresses reservations over law
Newsom, however, expressed some reservations in signing the bill into law.
“I strongly support this bill’s goal: accurate data leads to better understanding to inform policy,” Newsom, who is considering a presidential run in 2028, wrote in a signing statement. But he said he was concerned that the bill’s strictures would make it hard for state agencies to comply with the new law and with federal laws, and recommended revisiting the bill.
In addition to signing SB 1387 on Wednesday — the final day on which he could approve or veto bills in this year’s legislative session — Newsom also authorized AB 395, which will prohibit public meetings and graduations from being scheduled on major cultural and religious holidays.
“Californians of all faiths and backgrounds should be able to fully participate in public life,” the bill’s author, Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, said in a statement.
“For too long members of our religious communities have been forced to choose between observing their faith and participating in important public events and academic milestones,” added Gabriel, who chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.
Newsom approves seveal bills relevant to Jewish community
Also on Wednesday, Newsom approved AB 1763, which will include religious holiday observance as a type of excused absence in schools without requiring a written request from a parent or guardian.
Newsom signed other bills relevant to the Jewish community in the past few days, including AB 2664, which will establish 100-foot protective zones around entrances to houses of worship.
Another new law is AB 1836, which will close a gap in California’s nonprofit security grant structure by extending funds to off-site religious events like Hanukkah menorah lightings. The governor also approved AB 1853, enacting a ban on including misleading or threatening information, like hate speech, in California voter guides.

Hurricane Rachel strengthened into a Category 2 cyclone off Mexico's Pacific coast Thursday, prompting authorities to warn of heavy rain, strong winds and high waves across several western states.
Rachel was located about 370 kilometers (230 miles) south of the southern tip of Baja California, moving west-northwest at 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) per hour, with maximum sustained winds of 165 kilometers (103 miles) per hour, according to the US National Hurricane Center.
Mexico's National Civil Protection Coordination said Rachel was expected to reinforce very heavy rainfall in Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Nayarit and Jalisco, coastal states along western and northwestern Mexico.
The agency also warned of heavy to very heavy rainfall in central and southern Mexico as well as the Yucatan Peninsula in southeastern Mexico and other southeastern parts of the country.
In northern Mexico, intense rainfall with thunderstorms and possible hail was forecast in Coahuila, Nuevo Leon, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosi, Durango and Zacatecas, while strong winds could also lead to possible tornadoes in northern Coahuila, according to the agency.
Rachel's strengthening came as Mexico was still dealing with the effects of Hurricane Polo, which made landfall in Baja California Sur earlier this week before crossing into mainland Mexico.
Polo brought heavy rain, strong winds and flooding to parts of Mexico, while its remnants also contributed to heavy rainfall in the southwestern US.
The US National Hurricane Center said Rachel was expected to move along the Mexican coastline before turning west and moving farther into the Pacific.
Despite remaining offshore, Rachel was expected to produce dangerous surf and heavy rainfall along parts of the Mexican Pacific coast.
Authorities urged residents in affected areas to monitor weather updates and take precautions against flooding, landslides and strong winds.
Rachel became the 20th named storm and 10th hurricane of the Central and Eastern Pacific hurricane season, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Officials urged residents to remain alert, as conditions could change rapidly.

Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings
In a series of campaign-style rallies, Trump seeks to boost Republican odds despite opposition to the Iran war and rising fuel costs.
United States President Donald Trump has kicked off a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections that could see his Republican Party hurt by his handling of the war on Iran and the economy.
On Thursday, Trump travelled from Washington, DC, for back-to-back rallies in Texas and Oklahoma.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Most Americans say US-Israel war on Iran not worth fighting: Poll
- list 2 of 3US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns
- list 3 of 3Despite praise and White House visits, Trump avoids endorsing Netanyahu
At his first stop in Denton, Texas, Trump sought to shift the narrative around his drooping approval ratings, offering a personal assessment of his administration’s performance.
“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at the Peterbilt Motors Company, a truck manufacturer.
The president also blamed unfair media coverage for his growing unpopularity, arguing that his pre-election rally blitz was necessary to set the record straight.
“We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion and an extremely great job of running the country,” Trump said.
But Trump’s poll numbers have raised concerns about Republican prospects ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
Trump himself is not on the ballot, but Republican candidates across the country are seeking to defend the right-wing party’s majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.
The economy and Trump’s war on Iran are expected to weigh heavily on the election outcome.
On Thursday, The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research released new poll results showing that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of the war, which has driven up the price of fuel.
About half of survey respondents also said they were worried they would not be able to afford food and petrol. Only 26 percent approved of Trump’s handling of the economy.
Taking centre stage
Still, despite record low approval ratings, Trump has positioned himself as key to the Republican midterm strategy.
At a first-of-its-kind Republican midterm convention in September, Trump encouraged voters to consider his record while at the ballot box. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said.
During Thursday’s tour, he touted the impact of his tariff campaign, which he credited with creating thousands of manufacturing jobs.
“For decades, you were heartlessly betrayed by politicians, lousy politicians, who let foreign trade cheaters plunder your wages, loot your factories, close up your jobs,” Trump told Peterbilt workers. “They’d still be doing it if I wasn’t here, believe me.”
Trump’s tariffs, however, have been highly controversial, prompting a series of court challenges. Critics have argued that the sweeping import taxes surpass the president’s constitutional powers.
Trump also used his stump speech to ease concerns about the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28. Both sides have declared victory, though a ceasefire remains elusive.
“Just as I promised, I’m ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended. I will tell you the energy prices are going to be rapidly, rapidly coming down,” Trump said.
“We’ll win very easily right now,” he added. “I believe right after the election we’ll win, but maybe before the election.”
The war, however, resulted in Iran stopping commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global fuel trade.
The price of diesel — the fuel the trucks built at the plant use — soared to record highs of more than $6 per gallon (3.8 litres) last week. Petrol prices have similarly skyrocketed.
Hurting or helping his fellow Republicans?
Trump, however, has acknowledged that the stakes are high for his presidency in the upcoming midterms.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, as are 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.
Losing Republican control of either chamber could create roadblocks for Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.
But Trump has also expressed concern that he could be impeached for a third time, after two prior impeachments during his first presidency.
At Thursday’s second stop, in Durant, Oklahoma, the Republican leader repeated that fear. “Pretend I’m running, please,” he told the crowd. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”
Many of the places Trump is scheduled to visit this month are perceived as reliably Republican voting districts. Following his stops in Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump will be heading to Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska in the coming days.
Still, some elections that ordinarily would be considered shoo-ins for Republicans have grown more competitive in recent months.
In Texas, for instance, no Democrat has won a statewide race since the 1990s. But this year, Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is struggling to win a Senate contest against Democrat James Talarico.
During both of Thursday’s stops, Trump sought to bolster Paxton’s prospects. At the Peterbilt factory, for instance, he called Paxton “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”.
“We gotta get this guy elected,” Trump said, before pivoting to criticisms of Talarico, whom Republicans have sought to paint as out of touch with Texas’s large beef industry.
“He’s a vegan,” Trump said of Talarico, repeating an unsubstantiated rumour. “And vegans don’t do well in Texas.”
But leaked audio appeared to show Paxton lamenting the negative impact Trump had by holding the Republican midterm convention in Texas last month.
“It dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped,” Paxton reportedly said.
Trump touts social conservatism
Trump has nevertheless used his pre-election tour to highlight social issues he feels will help rally voters to the Republican cause.
On Thursday, he returned to familiar subjects like immigration and transgender rights, which he depicted as a part of the Democrats’ “radical” agenda.
“They want women in men’s sports. They want open borders. They want transgender mutilation for your children,” Trump said. “What the hell are you thinking about, you liberals?”
The president also used his Texas appearance to push back against critics of data centres, despite bipartisan concern.
Critics worry that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has fuelled the proliferation of data centres, which require large amounts of electricity and water to process mass data quantities.
While Trump has dismissed fears about AI as largely unfounded, a poll last month found 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the technology’s environmental impacts.
Even fellow Republicans in Texas are responding to public pressure about the growing number of data centres, more than 300 of which are operational, with hundreds more in progress.
In August, Governor Greg Abbott called for an audit of all data centres to map their water and electricity usage, and the following month, Paxton in his role as state attorney general launched an investigation into whether they were complying with water reporting requirements.
Trump nevertheless used his Texas rally to tout the expansion of such enterprises.
“It’s a huge thing. It’s bigger than the industrial revolution,” he said, dismissing the concerns as part of a “scam”. He then explained he had urged AI companies to “take care of the people”.
“They’re making a fortune for the communities,” he added.

Ukraine prepares sanctions on 20-plus Russian oligarchs in response to EU delistings
Ukraine is planning to sanction more than 20 Russian oligarchs in response to the European Union's decision to remove billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Oct. 1.
The list has already been approved by President Volodymyr Zelensky and is being formalized, Sybiha told journalists, describing the move as an "asymmetric response" to the EU decision.
"We fought until the last moment, both publicly and privately, to prevent this from happening," Sybiha said. "You removed two oligarchs, and we will add twenty."
According to Sybiha, Canada has already confirmed to Kyiv that it does not plan to lift its own sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman. Ukraine is also working with the U.K., Japan, Australia, and other partners to ensure the two oligarchs remain sanctioned by other countries.
The EU had removed the two oligarchs from its sanctions list on Sept. 22 as part of a compromise to extend the bloc's broader individual sanctions regime for 36 months. The measures had previously been renewed every six months, requiring recurring unanimous agreement among EU member states.
The longer extension reduces the frequency of politically challenging renewal negotiations, during which in the past individual member states have exerted pressure for specific names to be removed from the list.
France had pushed for Usmanov's removal, while Slovakia was also involved in negotiations, and Latvia agreed to allow the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman in order to prevent the sanctions regime from lapsing completely.
Usmanov, who controls mining and steel giant Metalloinvest, and Fridman, founder of the Alfa Group conglomerate, are among Russia's wealthiest businessmen. Both were sanctioned by the EU following Russia's full-scale invasion over their alleged ties to the Kremlin.

November interest rate rise a 'live' possibility, CBA chief says

Commonwealth Bank boss says Reserve Bank rate hikes probably finished
In short:
The CBA chief executive says he believes the RBA is done hiking interest rates but a lot will depend on the next round of quarterly inflation data.
Matt Comyn says house prices will bounce back once interest rates drop and reducing regulation will improve the nation's productivity.
What's next?
The next round of inflation data is released at the end of October and the RBA meets on November 3.
The chief executive of Australia's largest bank, Matt Comyn, says CBA believes the Reserve Bank has finished hiking interest rates for now, but the board's November meeting is "live" and another rise remains a possibility.
Speaking with the ABC's Alan Kohler, the Commonwealth Bank chief executive said the next movement of the RBA would depend on the quarterly inflation data released at the end of the month.
"We believe that's the last [rate rise], but certainly I think the last meeting of this calendar year is live," he said.
"We see and feel … the impact of higher rates. We feel that customers obviously are feeling the increasing burden from higher rates.
Mr Comyn said the September hike was needed due to rising inflationary pressures from global forces such as the Middle East conflict and fuel price rises.
Loading...
He said cost-of-living pressures were affecting different cohorts of CBA customers in different ways.
"We're seeing … where people are exposed particularly to higher borrowing costs and higher mortgages, a reduction in spending in some instances, [a] reduction in terms of savings," he said.
"I think households are feeling the pressure. We saw an increase in, for example, the proportion of customers that are requiring financial assistance or struggling to meet repayments.
"There are some subsectors, let's say in business, which are starting to feel the pressure of less consumer and household demand and expenditure."
Comyn says housing will bounce back
But there have been pockets of hope, with the bank seeing a 13 per cent growth in business lending across the 2026 financial year.
Doubtful debts were also still low and "well below where you would expect the average to be", mostly because unemployment was still low, he said.
Housing is also an area of optimism, with Mr Comyn predicting Australia's tanking property prices will bounce back.
He recalled that when interest rates last peaked in 2023, house prices fell nationally by 8.2 per cent, and compared it to current predictions of an estimated 10 per cent drop.
"I seem to remember considerably less focus on house prices during that time. But yes, I do think house prices will weaken over the course of this year," he said.
Consequently, he said, if interest rates reduced through next year as expected, property prices would pick up again in line with rising demand that was also bolstered by a "structural undersupply of housing".
"Housing is a very important asset in Australia. I think it's 57 per cent of household wealth in the country," he said.
"The biggest issue over the long term is our inability to grow productivity in terms of the production of housing."
Reduce regulation to grow the pie
Mr Comyn added his voice to calls for Australia to boost its productivity, saying a rate of 3 per cent compared to 2 per cent made "a really big difference".
"Productivity is what enables you to earn on an ongoing basis the income to be able to support improvement in in living standards," he said.
He said this was achieved through housing, low-cost energy, skills, migration and technological advancements including AI.
"We need to make it easier for small businesses or new businesses to be created that are successful and productive. And I think that's very hard in the current context," he said.
"Where I would be focusing on most is all on the supply-side reform. How do we reduce layers of approvals? How do we reduce layers of, in some areas, regulation? How do we accelerate a number of those processes.
"It's much easier to distribute a growing pie than one that isn't."
The federation is a bad business
Mr Comyn said fragmentation across both the Commonwealth and the states was particularly problematic in the context of regulation.
"It's the same inside a company; you're often adding an extra control, an extra process," he said.
"It's much harder to actually look at the totality and work out whether there's complete coherence, if there's anything there that's waste.
"If the federation was a company, I don't think you'd invest in it."
Mr Comyn said there were examples where the states were working very constructively with the Commonwealth but said there needed to be "real urgency across a number of these topics".
The banking boss said worried about the federal government running deficits "particularly at this point in time".
"Typically over a decade, there's times when the economic conditions are better and you should be able to run a surplus," he said.
"You're then creating fiscal capacity and degrees of freedom for some form of exogenous shock
"We're seeing a big increase in fiscal deficits around the world. I think this is reducing degrees of freedom.
"This puts a lot of pressure on future generations in particular."
More volatility the new norm
Like RBA governor Michele Bullock, Mr Comyn said he had also noticed frequent and potentially larger volatility.
"So for these shocks, we have a number of structural challenges as well, including demographics, how we actually deliver the services that Australians expect today and reasonably demand for the future," he said.
Mr Comyn also weighed in on defence spending, saying he supported raising how much the country allocated.
"There's no question we're in a different geopolitical and national security environment,"
"We've got to be able to pay for that. Obviously, we need to spend that well. But I find it challenging looking at all of the budget papers and documents and trying to work out how to chart that course. And those trade-offs are not easy to achieve now."
