7 needles, 2 lethal doses and a doctor tied to prior botch: how Christa Pike’s execution failed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:34:37 UTC
10:34:37 KST

Christa Pike remains in critical condition and is receiving life-saving treatment after surviving Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, as her lawyers revealed new details of a procedure they described as “cruel” and “torture.”
“Christa is alive. We do not have a clear picture of her prognosis or a meaningful update on her condition,” attorney Randy Spivey said. He said execution staff inserted at least seven needles while trying to establish intravenous access, and that one was bent when removed from her arm. Pike is now suffering from blistering and a burning sensation around the injection sites. Her lawyers are urging Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence and prevent the state from attempting to execute her again. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted further executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year.
Spivey said Pike, 50, actively tried to help the execution team find a usable vein. “She wasn’t just cooperative,” he said, recalling that she repeatedly told staff: “Please try higher, near my shoulder. Try here, I think it will be OK.” Even after receiving the first dose of pentobarbital, intended to kill her, Pike remained conscious, sang and spoke to people in the witness room. Her attorneys said they had warned before the execution that a blood disorder and problems accessing her veins could make lethal injection prolonged and painful.
The execution began Wednesday evening at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike, sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was strapped to a gurney and said in her final statement that she was at peace and “ready to be free.” But after the drugs began flowing, she remained awake and at one point asked whether her arm was “supposed to feel like this.” A witness said she complained that a vein felt as though it was “going to explode.”
Prison officials administered the initial dose of pentobarbital and then the backup dose required under Tennessee’s protocol when the first fails to cause death. Neither killed her. Nearly half an hour after the second dose, Pike could still be heard snoring behind the closed curtain. The microphone was eventually switched off, witnesses were removed and Pike was taken by ambulance to a hospital. Her lawyers filed emergency court motions while the procedure was still underway, arguing that she was suffering “unnecessary agony.”
Spivey also described confusion over whether Pike was receiving emergency medical treatment after the execution failed. For about 40 minutes after the first dose, he said, communication with her was difficult and he did not know whether medical professionals had begun treating her. He said he received his first confirmation that an ambulance was coming only at about 8:50 p.m.
Same doctor, second failed execution
The case has drawn additional scrutiny because Dr. Mark Fowler, who oversaw Pike’s execution procedure, had also been involved in Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Tony Carruthers in May. In that case, staff established one intravenous line but were unable to place the backup line required by protocol despite trying for more than an hour. The execution was called off before lethal drugs were administered, and Carruthers was granted a one-year reprieve.
Carruthers’ sister later filed a complaint alleging he suffered severe pain during the attempts and subsequently had a stroke that left him partially paralyzed. The claimed connection between the procedure and his stroke has not been officially established. Fowler has previously said his role in executions does not involve carrying them out, except for pronouncing death.
Tennessee’s Department of Correction has maintained that staff followed the state’s approved execution protocol. But that protocol provides for a second dose if the first fails to kill the prisoner and does not set out an additional step if the backup dose also fails. In Pike’s case, officials effectively reached the end of the protocol while she was still alive.
Death Penalty Information Center executive director Robin Maher said other prisoners have survived execution attempts after officials failed to establish intravenous access, but Pike’s case was different because she actually received the drugs intended to kill her and survived long enough to be hospitalized. The case has been described as unprecedented in the modern era of U.S. lethal injection. 
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted in the killing of Slemmer in Knoxville. Pike has never denied her role in the murder, but her lawyers have argued that insufficient weight was given at sentencing to her age, mental health and severe childhood abuse. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Pike had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. A federal appeals court initially halted the execution shortly before it was due to begin, but the U.S. Supreme Court later allowed the state to proceed.
There is now no new execution date. Pike’s lawyers say the state has already attempted to carry out her sentence and left her critically ill, and they are demanding that her punishment be commuted. Attorney Stephen Ferrell said they hope she recovers sufficiently to participate in decisions about what happens next: “We want to think through things, make sure Christa recovers, and make sure she has a part in what she wants to do.”

Man charged by US with illegally shipping Nvidia chips to China

AI generated
Federal prosecutors arrested a California man on Oct 1 on charges of smuggling computer servers containing US$300 million (S$384.5 million) worth of Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China in violation of US export controls.
The authorities said that Greg Lui, the owner of privately held Earthmade Computer, worked with other unidentified co-conspirators from 2023 to 2024 to ship servers containing the restricted chips to buyers in China without the required US licences.
The charges against Lui mark the latest in a series of federal prosecutions of individuals accused of violating export controls aimed at keeping advanced US-made chips out of Chinese hands over national security concerns.
In March, the authorities charged a co-founder of Super Micro Computer with illegally diverting billions of dollars in Nvidia chips to China. He pleaded not guilty.
Lui, 38, was expected to be arraigned later in the day, the Justice Department said in a statement. He faces one count each of conspiracy to violate US export controls, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering, the agency said.
Prosecutors argued in a court filing that Lui should be detained without bail because of a “serious risk” he would flee if released.
“This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than US$300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli in Los Angeles. “We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”
The Justice Department said that Lui and others exported the equipment initially to Malaysia and Singapore, jurisdictions that do not require licences for the purchases of advanced AI chips from US companies. The servers were then shipped to the final buyers in China, according to the agency.
Lui arranged for the sales of the servers knowing that the chips they contained were subject to US export curbs, the prosecutors alleged.
As part of the scheme, the authorities said, Lui and his co-conspirators provided false documentation to US manufacturers that misrepresented the final destination of the products.
In one purchase order, Lui obtained 27 servers from an unidentified US manufacturer containing Nvidia H100 GPUs for approximately $7.6 million, prosecutors said.
The charges were announced jointly by federal prosecutors, the FBI and the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees US export-control programmes.
If convicted of all the charges, Lui could face more than 20 years in prison, the Justice Department said.
The court docket did not provide information on lawyer representation for Lui.
Nvidia representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment. BLOOMBERG

G20 trade ministers deadlocked over industrial overcapacity, says US trade chief

G20 trade ministers deadlocked over industrial overcapacity, says US trade chief
G20 trade ministers failed to agree on tackling excess industrial capacity and eliminating forced labour from supply chains, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Thursday. Speaking during talks in Milwaukee, Greer highlighted overcapacity, a criticism often directed at China, which rejects it. The United States holds this year's rotating presidency.
Group of 20 (G20) trade ministers are at an impasse on countering excess industrial capacity, top US trade official Jamieson Greer said Thursday, an accusation often levied at China which rejects the criticism.
His comments came as trade ministers from the G20's major economies met for a second day in the Midwestern US city of Milwaukee. The United States holds the G20's rotating presidency this year.
Ministers failed to find agreement across the grouping on overcapacity, seen as driving down prices unfairly, and on eliminating forced labor in supply chains, Greer said.
"Nearly all countries agreed that this is an issue that requires action," Greer told a press conference, referring to excess capacity. He did not respond to questions on whether this was due to China's objection.
"And nearly all countries agreed that our current system of trade remedies or responses is inadequate to solve this problem," he said. He added that this justified unilateral US action.
There are US investigations into 16 economies on overcapacity, targeting China, the European Union, Japan, India and others.
Greer warned that countries which overproduce risk "creating an economy that rests on a house of cards."
Trump also recently slapped tariffs on 60 trading partners over alleged forced labor concerns – another issue the G20 failed to reach agreement on.
Read moreTrump’s tariffs loom over talks as G20 meets in US
'Not acceptable'
But G20 countries did find consensus against "the weaponisation of food through coercive trade actions," Greer said.
Temperatures rose over the issue at the two-day gathering as European officials criticised Russia's attacks impacting Ukraine's grain exports.
Moscow and Kyiv have been locked in war since Russia's 2022 invasion of its neighbour.
Russian and Ukrainian strikes targeting Black Sea ports have been wrecking and idling agricultural export capacity more quickly than trade flows can recover.
France's Minister Delegate for Foreign Trade and Economic Attractiveness, Nicolas Forissier, told AFP on Thursday that European officials including himself, alongside German and British representatives to the G20 criticised Russia over the matter.
"We have to say what we think, especially on the weaponisation of food," he said.
He added that European leaders' comments against "the aggression of Russia in Ukraine" on food exports merely constitute "the truth".
This did not mean the mood at G20 talks were bad, Forissier said: "On the contrary, I think the discussions are quite constructive."
"There is a consensus on the fact that it's not acceptable to weaponise food and agriculture," he added.
Russia is represented at the gathering this week by minister for economic development Maxim Reshetnikov.
He criticised European leaders Wednesday for speaking in political slogans, state-controlled network Russia Today reported.
Read moreVenezuela to join G20 energy talks in Texas at US invitation
Widening trade ties
Trade ministers from several G20 economies are also seeking to widen trade talks beyond their US host this week.
Canada for example is seeking bilateral trade deals with India, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and with the European Union on digital trade, Ottawa's minister for international trade Maninder Sidhu told reporters Thursday.
He said Canada and India look forward to concluding negotiations "in the coming months."
Sidhu also met Greer on the G20 sidelines, telling AFP that both sides discussed further Canada-US cooperation among other issues.
Countries are seeking cooperation with Washington to lower tariffs.
A Mexican official said Thursday that the country is making "steady progress" towards a US tariff deal.
"We would expect to have some reductions in steel and cars and aluminum," the official added, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Mexico is not looking to rush negotiations, the official said when asked if a deal would be struck before key US midterm elections.

US sends third aircraft carrier to Middle East amid stalemate in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:17:37 UTC
10:17:37 KST

The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as President Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The deployment, which includes a specialist amphibious attack group, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as midterm elections in the US loom large.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation remains a viable option – despite his initial promises that the war would last a matter of weeks.
The group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines. It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, with its two amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to a US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
It is possible the Washington could move to seas off Japan, once the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group arrives.
In a Time magazine interview published on Thursday, Trump raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough”.
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican party chances in November, Trump at first responded: “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide”.
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
In her statement, Hochul said the decision by Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, not to prosecute the 2024 case, and the questions raised in recent days over the Cornell police department’s investigation of the allegations, have “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time”.
Hochul said James would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
The former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024 filed a lawsuit in September, in a case that has sparked national outrage, roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
Van Houten declined at the time of the alleged assault to bring criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe.
He has maintained that the woman’s first account to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he had never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser.
She is suing seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity and others.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client had not touched the woman or engaged in any drug use.
Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell, a private university, agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

Drumcree talks break up without agreement on fifth day of standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:07:09 UTC
10:07:09 KST

Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.
Speaking on Thursday night after the latest talks with the Orange Order and residents of Garvaghy Road broke up, Bryant said: “I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven’t come to a settled agreement, and it’s a shame, but my door remains open.”
Last Friday’s Parades Commission decision to grant the Orange Order the right to hold a procession down the nationalist Garvaghy Road plunged Northern Ireland into one of its most perilous periods since the 1998 peace deal.
A legal appeal by the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition originally scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Monday to facilitate any further talks.
“Obviously we’ll have to see how that plays out,” Bryant said, indicating he would not be intervening unilaterally. “I would say that the law, in the end, is the law.”
Five days of talks ended in deadlock, he said, outlining the compromises on the table for the first time. “We’ve discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn’t exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we’ve not managed to come to agreement on any of all that.”
Earlier in the week, reports suggested one option was a “one and done” parade involving just a dozen people without insignia in October. This would have been on condition the Orange Order would never apply for permit for that parade route again.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said “the reality is” there was “no such thing as half a march”. “There’s a march or there’s not a march – simply that,” he said.
Jamie Bryson, a legal adviser to the Orange Order, who earlier this week said he would “not surrender” said he would accept Monday’s ruling.
“The challenge that we would put down to the Garvaghy Road residents – they’re going to the court of appeal on Monday – if the court of appeal upholds this determination, commit to accepting the law and walk away, and we’ll do the same,” he said. “Abide by the law, and if the court of appeal upholds the determination, get off the road, stop breaking the law and allow the parade to go ahead. If we lose, we’ll accept that.”
The dispute began last week after the march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness” and by the taoiseach as “incomprehensible and wrong”.
The dispute, which threatened to collapse Stormont and has returned Northern Ireland to bleak days of the past, has also revived the interest of key US Democrats. Richie Neal, the US representative for Massachussetts’ 1st congressional district, described the parade as “needlessly provocative”.
The Congressional Friends of Ireland Caucus, which Neal sits on, wrote to Bryant urging him to use his powers to reverse the Parades Commission decision.
“Over the last three decades, the progress made on the island of Ireland has been nothing short of extraordinary. Twenty-eight years have passed since the signing of the Good Friday agreement, and a generation has grown without a single memory of the Troubles,” the lawmakers wrote.
“Without decisive action, we risk reopening one of the most painful chapters of Northern Ireland’s history and undermining nearly three decades of peace, stability and reconciliation made possible by the Good Friday agreement.”
The Northern Ireland Policing Board has been told that the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) operation around the parading dispute has topped £3m.

LFI spokesman Manuel Bompard urged the government “not to descend into conspiracy theories or treat high school students like children.”
“This spontaneous movement was born out of frustration with utterly unacceptable educational conditions,” Bompard told AFP.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI’s candidate in next year’s presidential election, called on students to use only nonviolent methods.
The students are demanding more funding for public education, less overloaded timetables and smaller classes. Christelle Kauffmann, deputy secretary general of the SNPDEN-Unsa school administrators’ union, said principals lacked the resources to reduce class sizes.
Speaking to BFM TV, she condemned attacks on school principals, several of whom had been injured during the protests.
Several schools were damaged and vandalized, including Lycee Diderot in Paris, where the facade was blackened by a large fire involving garbage bins and scooters, and Lycee Nelson-Mandela in Nantes, where a deliberately set fire damaged the building.

Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor

Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor
A Weibo hashtag about ancient cinnabar sites has reignited debate over the ‘rivers and seas’ in Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.
The claims, which sent related hashtags trending on social media late last month, centred on three sites in Xunyang where archaeologists last year found evidence of cinnabar mining, processing and transport during the pre-Qin and Qin-Han periods.
The underground burial complex, at the northern foot of Lishan Mountain, has never been opened, but one of the most enduring accounts of what lies beneath comes from Sima Qian, the early Han dynasty (206BC-AD220) historian who described a vast subterranean realm, elaborate in its design and ambition, that mirrored the heavens above and the Earth below.
In his masterwork, the Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, Sima Qian wrote that mercury was used to recreate the “rivers and seas” inside the tomb, with a mechanism designed to keep the metal flowing.

Riot police in Chile clashed with student protesters in central Santiago on Thursday following demonstrations against expected cuts to public education funding under President Jose Antonio Kast’s proposed 2027 budget.
The mobilizations, organized by major student unions, brought thousands onto the streets just one day after Kast presented his administration's initial budget proposal.
The conservative leader, who took office in March on an austerity platform, pledged Wednesday to protect free higher education for more than 600,000 students, backing down from earlier discussions to restrict the program. But student leaders argue that broader funding for the sector remains severely at risk.
Demonstrators gathered at Plaza Italia before marching down La Alameda toward the La Moneda presidential palace. About 800 meters into the route, the Chilean national police blocked the march, firing water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowd. Some protesters responded by hurling stones, bottles and wooden sticks.
In a press briefing following the unrest, the Undersecretary of the Interior confirmed that at least 17 people had been arrested.
Tensions flared near the main campus of the Pontifical Catholic University (UC) when a small group of masked protesters attacked a counter-demonstration held by pro-government student groups.
The conservative groups were displaying a banner saying "We do not want a paralyzed Chile; we want a Chile that prospers."
Hours later, before the press, President Kast swiftly condemned the violence directed at students aligned with his political movement.
While the government has not yet released the full text of the 2027 fiscal package, leaked details reported by local media reveal significant rollbacks in the Ministry of Education's draft, including reductions in direct funding for state universities.
As street dynamics heat up, student organizations signaled that further mobilizations will follow once the full budget bill enters Congress for debate.

EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:54:00 UTC
09:54:00 KST

EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
October 2, 2026
The interior ministers of European Union countries met in Luxembourg on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen border controls and curb undocumented migration into the 27-member bloc.
Following the talks, they approved a new regulation to boost deportations of irregular migrants.
It will allow member states to establish so-called return hubs outside the EU for migrants who are legally required to leave the bloc but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
Countries including Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy and set up such migrant centers.
What did the ministers say?
"When it comes to return hubs," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters, "it's progressing very well."
"We are moving in the right direction," he said without providing further details.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said there were "preliminary" talks on return hubs but declined to say which countries were involved.
More work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits, he said.
"These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term," Dobrindt noted, adding that he was nevertheless hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said a technical mission already visited a potential host country in early September.
Supporters of the policy say return hubs could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
But critics question their legality and argue that they violate migrants' fundamental rights.
Suspending asylum process in emergencies?
On Thursday, Greece even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations. The right to seek asylum is guaranteed by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
Athens argued that current rules are inadequate to handle mass arrivals as in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.
The Spanish government estimates over 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most of them have since returned, some 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some EU capitals for a tougher approach. The Spanish government has said only minors and small groups of the people who entered Ceuta were brought to mainland Spain.
Greece's proposal appeared to draw support from some member states.
"We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure," said Dutch Migration Minister van den Brink. "In situations like Ceuta, it should be treated as a border management issue rather than an asylum issue."
Asked whether he saw a suspension of asylum as possible under the new emergency law, Magnus Brunner, EU commissioner for migration, said: "Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times," while stressing that "we will always comply with fundamental rights and values."
Plans to curtail irregular migration
The interior ministers' talks come as undocumented migration remains high on the EU's political agenda, with far-right parties increasingly gaining support across the bloc.
The situation has pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this month that the Commission will propose an emergency tool for countries to better deal with mass migration movements.
But details are still being worked out.
There are also plans to strengthen the EU's border agency, Frontex, with many stressing the need for the organization to have a rapid intervention force that could intervene in border crises.

Russia’s Navy Shows Its Reach Around Japan’s Southwestern Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:54:00 UTC
09:54:00 KST

President Vladimir Putin’s mid-August visit to the Kuril Islands, his first as Russia’s leader, inflamed a decades-old territorial dispute with Japan and drew worldwide attention to the two countries’ border in the northern Pacific. But over the past several years, Russian forces have been increasingly active far to the south, around Japan’s southwestern-most islands, in a demonstration of the Russian military’s reach and its willingness to challenge its rivals on its own and alongside China.
The dispute centers on the southernmost islands in the Kuril chain, which Japan calls its Northern Territories and says the Soviets seized illegally after Tokyo’s surrender at the end of World War II. Thousands of former Japanese residents of the islands are still alive, and resolving the dispute is a high priority for Japanese leaders. Russia’s activity on the islands, especially its military buildup, is therefore a sensitive issue for Tokyo.
Putin’s visit to the island Russia calls Iturup and Japan calls Etorofu on August 13 struck a chord with Tokyo not only for its location but also for its timing. Putin first traveled to Sakhalin Island – his first visit there in 13 years – to observe drills by Russia’s Pacific Fleet, part of a month-long series of exercises in the area that Japan protested. His visit also came days after the anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and days before the anniversary of Japan’s World War II surrender announcement.
Putin’s Kuril visit coincided with another Russian movement much farther south. The same day, Japan’s Defense Ministry reported that it had observed a Russian navy Improved Kilo-class submarine and a search-and-rescue vessel sailing north between the two Japanese islands closest to Taiwan, Yonaguni and Iriomote. That was one of at least 14 transits by Russian vessels around Yonaguni so far in 2026, a considerable increase over recent years.
A review of releases by the Japanese military’s Joint Staff from the past five years shows no such transits in 2021 and just two in 2022, both between Yonaguni and Iriomote. 2023 saw another two transits between Yonaguni and Iriomote, followed by a jump to six transits – five between Yonaguni and Iriomote and one between Yonaguni and Taiwan – in 2024. After a dip to four Yonaguni-Iriomote transits in 2025, there have been 11 transits between those islands and three between Yonaguni and Taiwan so far this year, the most recent on September 25.
Activity around Japan’s Southwest Islands is a growing concern for Tokyo. China has increased its military operations there since the early 2010s, training to sail and fly around and through that island chain. Chinese activity near Yonaguni and its neighboring islands, known as the Sakishima Islands, has also picked up in recent years, a sign of Beijing’s interest in familiarizing its forces with the area around Taiwan. In late 2024, a Chinese aircraft carrier sailed between Yonaguni and Iriomote for the first time, drawing a formal protest from Tokyo. In response, Japan has increased its military presence on the islands, opening bases for radars, electronic-warfare units, and surface-to-air and anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni and Ishigaki, which is just east of Iriomote.
Some Russian transits around Yonaguni appear to be part of routine voyages to and from the Pacific Fleet’s bases near Vladivostok. There may be a practical reason to use that route. “For ships coming south from Vladivostok through the East China Sea, the passage between Yonaguni and Iriomote provides a convenient way into the Philippine Sea without going farther northeast through the Miyako Strait,” Thomas Shugart, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security and a retired U.S. Navy officer, said in an email. Shugart said Russia’s navy may also have a political reason to avoid the more direct route to the South China Sea through the Taiwan Strait: “Given Beijing’s sensitivity to foreign naval transits of the Strait, routine Russian use could invite the observation that even the Russians treat it as an international waterway.”
But the behavior of other Russian vessels around Yonaguni appears more likely to be “deliberate signaling toward Japan,” Shugart said. In some cases, Russian vessels have loitered in the area, perhaps to monitor Japanese activity and response measures. In its annual “Defense of Japan” report, Japan’s Defense Ministry singled out an unusual operation in January this year, in which a Russian Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship was seen “navigating for an extended period” around the Sakishima Islands and Okinawa. Joint Staff releases showed that over the course of 12 days the vessel sailed south between Taiwan and Yonaguni and circled the Sakishima Islands before crossing the Miyako Strait and lingering southeast of Okinawa for three days. “Notably, this marked the first confirmed instance of such a vessel circumnavigating the Sakishima Islands,” the report said.
The ministry’s report linked recent activity around the Sakishima Islands with a years-long uptick in Russian operations around Japan, “including exercises and training likely intended to verify the results of military reforms” and operations farther afield that are likely meant to keep the U.S., Japan, and others “in check.”
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, its navy “has been continuously involved in active deterrent operations against the United States and its Western allies,” Alexey Muraviev, a professor at Edith Cowan University in Australia who studies Russian military strategy, said in an interview late last year. Regular deployments to Southeast Asia, where Moscow has sought to bolster its military ties, are a part of those operations, Muraviev said, but they also reflect continued concerns about the US and its allies, especially Japan. “Russia clearly sees Japan as a military risk – partially because of its alignment with the United States through security and defense ties, partially because of [the] unresolved territorial dispute,” Muraviev said.
Russia’s activity around Japan also shows its deepening military ties with China, which has become a more important partner amid Moscow’s international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine. Over the past several years, Sino-Russian bomber and naval patrols have incorporated a wider range of ships and aircraft, including diesel-electric submarines and nuclear-capable bombers, and traveled farther, sometimes circling the Japanese archipelago. During their most recent naval patrol, in July, their ships transited east through the Miyako Strait, headed north along Japan’s east coast, and then sailed west through the Vries Strait, which separates the Kuril Islands that Japan claims from the rest of the chain. The route demonstrated the two navies’ increasing ability to operate through “strategic waterways,” Chinese experts told state media.
Russia has also echoed China’s criticism of what it calls Japan’s “militarism,” a line of attack that Beijing started pushing late last year, likely in an attempt to stoke backlash to Japan’s growing military investments and regional security role. Russian officials returned to that talking point in the weeks following Putin’s visit to the Kuril Islands, lashing out at Japan for hosting a military exercise with the U.S. around Hokkaido, the Japanese main island closest to the Kurils, and objecting to its proximity to Russian territory. “The Japanese side was firmly informed that provocative military activity near our country’s far eastern borders is categorically unacceptable,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on September 1.

SpaceX flight led by first Black female commander sets US speed record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:50:49 UTC
09:50:49 KST

Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a US speed record, and that created further history with the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for Nasa after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but skies cleared enough to allow a safe liftoff from Cape Canaveral at 11.10am (1510 GMT).
Seven hours and 55 minutes later, the SpaceX Dragon “Grace” capsule docked at an ISS port, setting a record for the fastest trip by a US spacecraft to the outpost.
In a live broadcast on Nasa TV, the capsule appeared to glide gently toward a stationary ISS as both hurtled through space at about 17,500mph (28,100 km/h).
The new arrivals – Americans Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Joshua Kutryk, and Russian Sergey Teteryatnikov – floated into the space station through a pressurized vestibule and addressed colleagues on Earth late on Thursday.
“We are so excited to be here. This is truly a special place,” Watkins said on the Nasa livestream. “It’s amazing and kind of ironic to think that it’s such a short trip to get here because the journey to get here has been long.”
Canadian Kutryk, whose wife will give birth while he’s away, said it “feels really good” to represent his country in space, adding he was “looking forward to a good mission after some sleep. That’s what I’m gonna go do next.”
The duration of the journey depends greatly on the distance between the ISS and the spacecraft at the time of launch. It took more than 30 hours for the last crew that launched from American soil to reach the station.
With the late-morning launch, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with Nasa’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station after a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed after liftoff.
Although their stay at the ISS will last six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk’s company, but any American entity, including Nasa.
Aside from Watkins, the other astronauts are newcomers to space: Delaney is a retired marine; Kutryk is a colonel in the Royal Canadian air force; and Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for Nasa, not counting 2020’s test flight. The Crew-13 designation in their mission patch pays homage to Apollo 13, the harrowing 1970 moonshot that ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
References to the number 13 abounded on Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13”. They also carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck.
“We figured it wouldn’t hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don’t need it,” Watkins said from orbit, noting they were “four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth”.
Heather Kutryk will give birth while her husband is orbiting Earth, making him the fourth man to become a father while doing so. Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November.
“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” Nasa manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency would do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family. The Canadian Space Agency also promised to support the family.
In 2004, Nasa provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehböck. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.
Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the national reconnaissance office. All this comes the same week the company’s massive Starship reached orbit for the first time.

Five ways the US and China clash over AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:50:00 UTC
09:50:00 KST

Five ways the US and China clash over AI
- The US and China clash over AI on issues of chip smuggling, remote access, and accusations of unauthorised copying of AI models, complicating export controls and cooperation.
- Both nations face catastrophic AI risks, with industry leaders calling for regulation and safety measures, but political mistrust hinders joint frameworks to manage AI threats.
- AI humanoids and military AI development fuel competition, with the US restricting Chinese imports and exports to curb China's technological and defence advances amid supply chain dominance concerns.
AI generated
Both the US and China see AI as the new focal point of their economic rivalry. US President Donald Trump declared on Sept 13 that “whoever wins AI, wins”.
The question is whether the two nations can put aside their disagreements and cooperate in building a safe and sustainable AI environment. For now, neither trusts the other’s motives, and neither wants to slow down.
Here are the biggest flashpoints in the US-China AI race.
Chip smuggling and remote access
The US has restricted exports of the most powerful AI chips to China since 2022 on national security grounds. There is a growing awareness that these measures have not been working as well as planned.
Prosecutors in the US have pursued several major investigations into suspected smuggling of advanced AI chips made by Nvidia to customers in China.
In the highest-profile case to date, the Justice Department earlier in 2026 charged a co-founder of Super Micro Computer, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, with helping send US-assembled servers containing Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips to Chinese customers in violation of the US export curbs. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, and Nvidia has said it has strict compliance procedures.
When Chinese lab Moonshot AI released a large language model, Kimi K3, that almost matched the performance of leading US rivals, a White House official accused the company of illegally obtaining Nvidia chips and accessing them remotely through Thailand. China’s government has pushed back on the allegations, while Moonshot has not responded to them.
US lawmakers have also claimed that Chinese AI firms are exploiting a loophole in export curbs by renting computing power located in other countries.
A bipartisan bill, currently pending in Congress, aims to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia chips via cloud computing. The Commerce Department is also scrutinising ways to possibly use its export control authority to crack down on the practice.
Distillation
The US government has accused half a dozen Chinese companies including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Z.AI and Alibaba Group Holding’s AI unit of using “industrial scale” distillation to reproduce the capabilities of leading US AI models.
Distillation is a widely used technique whereby a smaller model is created by copying the reasoning and behaviour of a much larger, more complex and capable model as a shortcut to avoid costly, time-consuming training. The issue arises when that is done without permission. China’s government has said the accusations are unfounded.
Finding a compromise on the issue will be a challenge as the two nations would need to concur on what activities amount to improper distillation and agree to mechanisms for gathering evidence and confirming any unauthorised model extraction.
Catastrophic risk
In 2026, AI “agents” have emerged that are capable of completing complex tasks independently, and AI systems have begun to improve themselves with minimal human intervention. This has sparked a wave of concern across the industry that AI is becoming so smart that humans will no longer be able to control it.
Leading industry figures are warning that, without new guardrails, AI could do untold damage to the digital ecosystem, and even threaten mankind.
Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei warned that AI posed an existential threat in a 3,800-word essay earlier in October that intensified the safety debate. Amodei vowed to slow the company’s development of cutting-edge models in order to better understand the risks they pose, and US competitors including OpenAI pledged to implement similar measures.
The Anthropic chief also called for more government regulation of AI and indicated that Washington would need to coordinate an international push on AI safety amid concerns that, even if US firms shift to a more cautious pace of development, Silicon Valley’s rivals in China might not.
Amodei’s message prompted a sharp pushback from Trump, who rejected the Anthropic chief executive’s calls for new guardrails on AI and dismissed the existential warnings as “a hoax”.
The authorities in Beijing also reacted sharply to Amodei’s missive, calling it “fearmongering” and accusing US AI labs of “malicious competition”.
Amodei has long antagonised the government in Beijing with his support for tighter US export controls to deny Chinese AI firms access to crucial equipment such as chips. He reiterated that call in his latest essay. At the same time, China has expressed its own safety-related concerns, including that Anthropic’s Mythos model’s cyber capabilities could be used as a weapon against Chinese interests.
Significant trust building would be required for the two nations to craft a framework that would potentially slow the breakneck race to dominate cutting-edge AI. They would need to agree on what an unsafe AI system looks like, or what should be done when its capabilities go beyond controllable limits.
For now, damage mitigation could be one area of potential cooperation. The US and China might work together to keep powerful AI models beyond the reach of cyber criminals and terrorists who might use them to attack sensitive infrastructure or design new bio-weapons.
Some security specialists have urged the US and Chinese governments to prepare for the possibility that a rogue AI agent might infiltrate a nation’s nuclear command system, or set off a cyberattack on a country that is misread by the target government as a deliberate attack.
One suggestion is that a hotline be established for one government to warn the other of an AI-triggered attack.
During a summit in Washington in late September between Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the two sides agreed to create a bilateral dialogue to exchange views on the “risks and benefits” of AI, according to the White House.
AI humanoids
A race is underway to make commercially viable humanoid robots by endowing them with AI so they can better navigate the physical world. US firms have made many of the biggest advances in robotics, but Chinese companies are now driving ahead in pushing the widespread commercial use of humanoid robots. China wants greater access to Western markets for these products.
Instead, the US has restricted imports of Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots on the grounds of national security. And in January 2027, procurement rules are due to kick in that would prohibit US defence contractors from sourcing a range of materials that were mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China, in a bid to spur more production of those materials in other countries.
China was able to use its dominant role in the supply of minerals that are critical to several US industries as leverage in its tariff showdown with the Trump administration last year. China controls roughly 80% of several critical layers of the hardware supply chain including rare-earth magnets and the actuator assemblies required to build humanoids at scale, according to experts including those at the International Energy Agency and Jamestown Foundation.
Elon Musk’s robot project, Tesla Optimus humanoids, has already been affected by Chinese export restrictions on magnets. If a compromise is eventually struck, the two sides would need to agree on safety standards for robots working in close proximity to humans before bilateral trade in humanoids can take off.
Military AI
US technology export controls are aimed partly at stopping the People’s Liberation Army from accessing the most advanced US AI chips that might give it an advantage on the battlefield.
Beijing’s military programmes are ultra-secretive, but the priority is clear. At least seven university labs that support the nation’s armed forces have been trying to obtain advanced chips from Nvidia.
Two of the institutions that have expressed interest – Beihang University and Northwestern Polytechnical University – rank among China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense”, an elite group dedicated to aiding the PLA. BLOOMBERG

F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:49:28 UTC
09:49:28 KST

Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East.
Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities
Another pilot currently stationed in Europe received a DFC for a mission in the Middle East, but the Air Force did not say when or where the actions that earned that pilot the award occurred.
The six Airmen from Langley were decorated for their actions escorting B-2 Spirit stealth bombers that struck the Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites in Iran. The strike package also included F-16 Fighting Falcons and F-35 Lightning II fighters, and pilots from those units received DFCs earlier this year; tanker crews from multiple units have also received the award for supporting the mission. No individual awards have yet been announced for the B-2 aviators who participated in Midnight Hammer.
The DFC recognizes acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement in the air and is the military’s fourth-highest award for heroism.
Four of the pilots came from the Active-Duty 94th Fighter Squadron, part of the 1st Fighter Wing at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va., and two pilots came from the associated Virginia Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Squadron, part of the 192nd Wing.
The medals were presented Aug. 31 by the head of Air Combat Command, Gen. Adrian L. Spain, in a ceremony at the Virginia base.
The F-22s were among an armada of fighters that escorted the seven B-2s that dropped 14 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weapons on Iran’s nuclear facilities. Around 125 U.S. aircraft of all types were involved in the mission, which came after a nearly two-week Israeli air campaign against Iran. The stealthy F-22s serve as the Air Force’s premier air-to-air fighters and can use their capabilities to penetrate defended airspace.
“Their job was to provide air superiority,” Spain said, according to an account of his remarks provided by the 1st Fighter Wing. “The bombers and the rest of the support package relied on these Raptor pilots to clear the skies, shield them from surface threats, and ensure a safe route through heavily contested airspace.”
Officials from Air Combat Command and the 1st Fighter Wing declined to provide further details on the mission that earned the pilots their decorations or medal citations, or to publicly disclose pilots’ identities, citing operational security concerns.
“We haven’t awarded many of these in the last few decades, as it’s intended to recognize true heroism and highly exceptional accomplishment in flight, which means that it should be rare, and it is,” said Spain.
Iran’s air force was largely destroyed during the 2026 air campaign against the country, Operation Epic Fury. But even during Midnight Hammer, Iran posed a limited air-to-air threat, with most of its capability consisting of aircraft purchased before the Iranian revolution in 1979. Before the Shah was overthrown and a theocratic government took over, Iran was the largest purchaser of American arms. Iran also has Soviet-designed fighters.
Still, Iran showed the ability to generate some airpower, launching aircraft to attack Gulf countries after Israel and Iran began their air campaign on Feb. 28 of this year, and was able to strike a base in Kuwait used by the U.S. with one of its aging fighter jets.
F-22s from Langley deployed to support Operation Epic Fury and follow-on actions against Iran earlier this year but have since returned.
“It was your support that enabled their excellence—from the maintainers, the operations team, the intel professionals, and the logistics involved,” Spain said. “Let there be no doubt heroism like this is earned by the entire formation. These pilots were the leading edge that day, but the foundation of their success was laid by the hard work of the entire organization in the days prior and every day since. And that’s what Air Force readiness looks like.”
The seventh F-22 pilot received their decoration Sept. 22 from U.S. Air Forces in Europe commander Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds for leading a strike package during a mission in the Middle East that operated in contested airspace, according to a release from the command. U.S. officials did not immediately say whether the mission was part of Operation Epic Fury, Operation Midnight Hammer, or Operation Rough Rider, the 2025 campaign against the Houthis in Yemen.
The pilot faced “challenging conditions including enemy threats” and “directed the aircraft formation, making critical decisions with limited time and little margin for error,” according to USAFE.
The command, like ACC, withheld the Airman’s identity.
“For more than an hour, [the pilot] remained focused on protecting teammates” and “acted decisively to protect the larger force, and ensured the formation could safely return,” Hinds said. “Their actions helped give the strike package the time and freedom needed to accomplish its mission.”

Google faces US$3.2 billion damage claims on ad-tech monopoly

Google faces US$3.2 billion damage claims on ad-tech monopoly
- A New York federal judge ruled that USA Today, Daily Mail, and a class of publishers can seek over US$3.2 billion in damages from Google for monopolising ad-tech markets.
- The ruling allows jury trials to proceed on how Google's AdX exchange harmed major publishers, with specific damages amounts set for the class and individual plaintiffs.
- Google plans to defend the claims in court, while the US Justice Department has separately sued Google for illegally monopolising ad technology markets in 2023.
AI generated
USA Today, Daily Mail General and Trust, and a class of large publishers can seek more than US$3.2 billion (S$4.1 billion) in damages for harm caused by monopolisation of advertising technology markets by Alphabet’s Google, a New York federal judge ruled.
In an opinion late on Sept 30, US District Judge P. Kevin Castel in Manhattan said he will allow jury trials to move forward on how Google’s conduct related to its AdX advertising exchange harmed major publishers.
A class of about 5,000 publishers can pursue about US$1.7 billion in damages from Google, he ruled, rejecting a bid by the company to contest the damage calculations.
USA Today and Daily Mail, which each sued separately, will be allowed to seek about US$900 million and US$600 million, respectively, he found.
In a statement, Google said the ruling also dismissed claims by some publishers who used a different ad-buying tool and that it will “defend the rest in court”.
“The ruling allows USA Today to pursue its US$1 billion in worldwide damages (before trebling under the antitrust laws), a significant victory that streamlines our path to recovery,” Polly Grunfeld Sack, the company’s chief legal counsel, said in a statement to Bloomberg.
“We are pleased with this result and look forward to proving our claims at trial.”
Philip Korologos, a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, the law firm representing the publishers, said the firm looks forward to presenting the claims at trial, where the class will seek to recover damages.
The US Justice Department and a group of states sued Google in 2023, accusing the company of illegally monopolising several areas of the advertising technology used to buy, sell and serve the online display ads that appear on many websites.
A federal judge in Virginia found that the company illegally monopolised two advertising technology markets and ruled in September that Google must make its ad tech tools work with those operated by rivals, but declined to order a breakup of the business.
The lawsuits pending in New York seek damages related to the same conduct. Castel has not yet scheduled a trial date.
USA Today and Daily Mail did not immediately respond to requests for comment. BLOOMBERG

‘A Tower of Jelly’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:39:00 UTC
09:39:00 KST

“What is the use of a fire brigade which vanishes from the scene as soon as the first smoke and flames appear?” asked Abba Eban, addressing an emergency session of the United Nations General Assembly soon after the 1967 Arab-Israeli War had ended.
In a fiery speech, the foreign minister of Israel lashed out at the U.N. for pulling peacekeeping troops out of the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip. The “disastrously swift” withdrawal, Eban argued, had endangered the “national survival” of the Jewish state.
Israel’s Six-Day War was nevertheless a spectacular military success. The Israel Defense Forces neutralized three Arab armies (Egypt, Jordan, and Syria) within a week and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.
In his latest book, “Peacemaker,” historian Thant Myint-U offers new insights on the U.N.’s role in the events leading up to the six-day conflict.
The book’s title refers to U Thant, the author’s grandfather. As U.N. secretary-general, the Burmese diplomat was the chief “firefighter” charged with deploying peacekeeping troops to conflict zones. The “most successful peacekeeping operation” was UNEF (United Nations Emergency Force), which had maintained a fragile peace along the border between Egypt and Israel for more than a decade.
When the Egyptian military sent the U.N. an informal communication in mid-May requesting a withdrawal of peacekeeping troops, Thant faced a dilemma. Denying Cairo’s request would violate Egypt’s sovereignty, but removing the forces might jeopardize the U.N.’s conflict-prevention mission. The Secretary-General acquiesced after receiving an official letter from the foreign minister. However, as Thant was negotiating UNEF’s exit, Israeli jets strafed a convoy in the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip, killing three soldiers.
Thant faced “a deluge of criticism” for the troop withdrawal and for his inability to counter “Egyptian bluster.” Former British Prime Minister Alec Douglas-Home called the Secretary-General’s visit to Egypt in late May a “dreadful mistake.” When Thant landed in Cairo, President Gamal Abdel Nasser was already in war mode, having closed the Straits of Tiran, a vital shipping route for Israel. A Western diplomat quoted in The Wall Street Journal called the U.N. chief “a tower of jelly.”
Gideon Rafael, the Israeli ambassador to the U.N., defended his friend in the Hebrew-language newspaper Maariv, saying, “U Thant is not responsible for the situation in the Middle East.”
In a chapter titled “Gaza and the Sinai,” the author highlights an intriguing detail on how misinformation played a role in the lead-up to the war. Nasser’s actions were influenced by false intelligence reports relayed by Moscow and Damascus about a buildup of Israeli forces along the Syrian border. Arab leaders did little to verify the claims, even as U.N. observers cast doubt on the report’s veracity.
“The Syrians could have looked from the Golan Heights (which they controlled) down into Israel and seen that there were no troop concentrations, as alleged, but they were happy to pass on to Cairo the misinformation as it confirmed their longstanding claim of an imminent threat,” commented the author.
In 1959, U Thant was the frontrunner for the top U.N. job as the only candidate acceptable to both Israel and the Arab states. Golda Meir, then Israel’s foreign minister, indicated that Thant was Tel Aviv’s sole choice for the position. However, the first Asian secretary-general of the U.N. did not have a “feel for the passions surrounding the conflict” once war broke out in the Middle East.
His low-key style worked when both parties were motivated to defuse a confrontation. During the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the U.N. Secretary-General helped create “an opening for diplomacy.” U Thant “injected himself into the very heart of the simmering crisis,” the author wrote, giving the Soviet Union and the U.S. a face-saving option to back away from a nuclear showdown. In 1965, the veteran diplomat was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for his mediation efforts.
The goodwill earned during his first term had evaporated by the late 1960s. In certain circles, Thant was considered “Israel’s nemesis,” and his relationship with Washington deteriorated. The secretary-general was a critic of the Vietnam War and spoke out against the Johnson Administration’s bombing campaign in Southeast Asia.
“Thant retired, then virtually disappeared,” wrote his grandson, almost as if he was “airbrushed from history.”
The former Secretary-General spent his final years in a colonial-style house outside New York City with “a meditation room, a glass-enclosed annex with images of the Buddha and views of the Westchester countryside.”

UK-Mauritius Chagos sovereignty deal stalls amid fears of further delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:29:57 UTC
09:29:57 KST

UK-Mauritius Chagos sovereignty deal stalls amid fears of further delays
Renewed talks over the stalled agreement have revived hope of resettlement, but ageing Chagossians fear time is running.
Pointe aux Sables, Mauritius – “At one funeral, we scattered sand from Chagos into an elder’s tomb to honour his unfulfilled wish to breathe his last in his homeland,” says Olivier Bancoult of the Chagos Refugees Group.
For elderly Chagossians displaced from their Indian Ocean homeland decades ago, delays to a treaty allowing their return are raising fears that they may never see the islands again.
The agreement, signed by Britain and Mauritius in May 2025, would allow resettlement on islands other than Diego Garcia, which would remain a military base. But it has yet to enter into force amid opposition from US President Donald Trump.
“We remain unshaken by Trump’s interference in the Chagos deal,” Bancoult says.
“The 2019 ICJ advisory opinion in favour of the archipelago’s return to Mauritius has restored our dignity and faith in our rights as native Chagossians.”
The Chagos archipelago, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, was separated from Mauritius by Britain in 1965, three years before Mauritius gained independence. Britain later established a military base with the US on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the group.
Between 1968 and 1973, Britain removed an estimated 1,400 to 1,700 Chagossians from the islands. Many were resettled in Mauritius and the Seychelles, with others later moving to the United Kingdom. British authorities also made it illegal to remain on or return to the islands without permission.
“If Trump wants to meddle in this matter, well, let him,” Bancoult says. “We’ve had the 2019 ICJ [International Court of Justice] advisory opinion, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea’s 2021 judgement, and the 2025 UK-Mauritius treaty providing for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the archipelago. International law is squarely on our side.”
Signed on May 22, 2025, the treaty provides for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, while allowing the UK to exercise rights over the Diego Garcia military base for an initial 99-year period. It also allows Mauritius to arrange for the resettlement of Chagossians on islands other than Diego Garcia. The treaty has not yet entered into force.
In April, the UK government told Parliament that the legislation needed to implement the agreement could not complete its passage during the 2024–26 parliamentary session. The session ended on April 29, meaning the bill made no further progress.
In January, Trump criticised the agreement, calling it an “act of great stupidity ” and questioning whether it adequately protected the Diego Garcia military base.
The issue returned to the diplomatic agenda in September. On September 21, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK would work with Mauritius and the US on a way forward that secures the operation of Diego Garcia and protects UK national security.
On September 26, Mauritian Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam travelled to the UK for talks with British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell and other officials on the Chagos issue. He remains in London, with the Mauritian government saying the discussions would cover recent developments concerning the archipelago.
For Bancoult, the central question is whether elderly Chagossians will live long enough to see the treaty’s promises fulfilled.
“Chagossians born on the archipelago are now aged between 58 and 100. We are growing old, and we have lost several Chagossian elders this year alone,” he says.
For younger Chagossians, the consequences are also cultural.
Chrisyl Wong-Hang-Sun, a PhD researcher in anthropology at the University of Edinburgh, says years of displacement and migration are making it harder to preserve Chagossian culture.
“During my fieldwork, many diaspora members expressed concerns over cultural loss, such as words in Chagossian Creole and recipes that are difficult to recreate abroad,” she says. “Descendants of Chagossians, myself included, long to know the islands of their relatives and ancestors.”
The dispute has also exposed political differences among Chagossians.
“The actions of both the British and Mauritian governments have resulted in very nuanced and differing political opinions among Chagossians across the UK, Mauritius and the Seychelles,” Wong-Hang-Sun says.
The Chagos Refugees Group is at odds with UK-based second-generation Chagossian Misley Mandarin and his supporters, who favour resettlement under British rather than Mauritian sovereignty and have received backing from Reform UK.
Wong-Hang-Sun says those differences should be recognised as negotiations continue.
Both governments, she says, need to “find ways to prioritise and engage with the Chagossian diaspora as a whole”.
Mauritius keeps talks largely private
Mauritius has disclosed little publicly about the substance of the latest talks on Chagos.
At the United Nations General Assembly in September, Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful reiterated Mauritius’ position that its sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago was “non-negotiable”. He also described the 2025 agreement as a vindication of international law and said Mauritius was committed to diplomacy and dialogue over the issue.
Beyond official statements and communiques, the Mauritian government has provided few details about the substance of the current discussions.
International relations consultant Bruno Donat, who has previously worked at the UN, says Mauritius should focus on sustained engagement with diplomatic partners, including the African Union, small island states, the Commonwealth Secretariat and sympathetic voices in the US Congress.
“Being in New York corridors for a photo” is not the priority, Donat says. Sustained engagement, he argues, can build pressure on Washington and prevent the issue from remaining unresolved indefinitely.
The Chagos Refugees Group has pursued a similar approach. In June, two months after the treaty stalled, its members travelled to the UK to lobby representatives of British political parties, with the exception of Reform UK.
The unresolved question of Diego Garcia
But Diego Garcia remains the most contentious part of the agreement.
Lalit, a Mauritian political organisation that has campaigned for decades for the closure of the base, opposes its continued military use. Lindsey Collen of Lalit says the treaty, as it stood in April, would have kept the base open and brought Mauritius into a closer relationship with the US military presence on the island.
“In addition to the moral responsibility, we have the knowledge that we might become a target for self-defence if our land is used this way,” she says.
Collen is also concerned about a new partnership between the Mauritius Police Force and the New Mexico National Guard, as well as what she describes as the “enormous military-looking buildings” of the new US embassy in Mauritius.
Donat argues that the treaty could instead give Mauritius greater leverage over how Diego Garcia is used.
“Mauritius has publicly stated that the strikes launched from Diego Garcia against Iran breached international law,” he says. “That is not the position of a government staying silent to protect a lease payment.”
For Bancoult, those wider strategic questions are secondary to the need to ensure that elderly Chagossians have the chance to return to their homeland during their lifetimes.
“We are opposed to war, ethically, but we are also running out of time.”
The Chagos Refugees Group hopes to soon celebrate the 101st birthday of one of its members.
“God willing, he’ll stay with us for more years,” Bancoult says.

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft carrying four astronauts for NASA's Crew-13 mission docked with the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday, after a nearly eight-hour journey from launch to the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft lifted off at 11:10 a.m. Eastern Time (1610 GMT) aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It autonomously docked with the ISS at 7:05 p.m. Eastern Time (0005 GMT).
The crew comprises NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
The mission, codenamed Crew-13, marks the 13th crew rotation mission to the ISS conducted by a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft under NASA's Commercial Crew Program.
The crew will spend several months aboard the space station conducting scientific research and technology demonstrations to support future human exploration of the Moon and Mars, as well as studies with potential benefits for people on Earth, according to NASA. ■
