'Right to access to justice equal for all': SC frowns at out-of-turn hearings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:28:38 UTC
06:28:38 KST

'When we grant early hearing to one litigant who has the resources to approach the SC, we do injustice to millions of litigants who are waiting for a hearing on their petitions,' the bench said.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday said a bus conductor's right to access to justice is equal to that of a top bureaucrat, and granting out-of-turn hearing to a litigant having the wherewithal to approach the SC would violate the right to speedy justice of millions languishing in the queue.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to entertain a plea for expeditious hearing of a petition by an additional district judge challenging his dismissal from service for corruption in 2022. His petition has been pending in Allahabad HC since 2022.
Sacked for taking bribe, can’t allow early hearing: SC
"When we grant early hearing to one litigant who has the resources to approach the SC, we do injustice to millions of litigants who are waiting for a hearing on their petitions," the bench said.In his plea for a direction to HC for expeditious disposal of his plea, the judge said he has suffered a lot in the last four years and that since his retirement is due on Nov 30, he would like to leave service with dignity.Referring to the pendency of more than 12 lakh cases in Allahabad HC, the bench told the counsel: "You are making a submission which is against the equal right to access to justice of every litigant, be it a bus conductor or a principal secretary.
We will not request HC to grant out-of-turn hearing unless we are convinced about egregious circumstances in the case that warrant urgent hearing."The petitioner is one of the three additional district judges - Ashok Kumar Singh, Himanshu Bhatnagar and Rakesh Kumar Nain - who were dismissed from service on corruption charges through a full court resolution passed by Allahabad HC in May 2022.
He complained that "no show-cause notice was ever issued to the petitioner and no opportunity was ever afforded to give any representation against the major penalty so imposed upon the petitioner, therefore, the resolution dated May 12, 2022, and the order dated May 17, 2022, by which the services of the petitioner were terminated, was passed in violation of principles of natural justice".The bench said that as the petitioner has been dismissed from service on charges of acceptance of bribe, it is not a fit case for requesting the HC to grant an out-of-turn hearing.The petitioner, who joined judicial service in Aug 1999 and was promoted as additional district judge in 2013, was accused of taking a Rs 6 lakh bribe to acquit a person in 2015. The inquiry and disciplinary proceedings were concluded in 2022, following which his services were terminated.

Spanish housing decree imperilled by opposition of Junts party
MADRID, Oct 1 - Chances that Spain's Congress would pass a decree aimed at curbing the housing crisis grew dimmer on Thursday after Catalan kingmaker party Junts raised last-minute issues and requested the government devise a new proposal on the eve of a scheduled vote.
Junts, a separatist centre-right party with seven MPs, argued that the proposed measures would make matters worse by reducing housing supply. These include a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year rent freeze extension for existing leases, and tighter rules for short-term rentals.
"Many of the measures included will produce the opposite effect of what is intended: they will reduce the supply of rental housing, drive up prices, and make it even harder for people with limited financial means to access housing," Junts said in a statement.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's minority leftist government has only 147 seats in the 350-seat chamber and relies on the support of a patchwork of smaller parties to pass legislation.
Opposition parties have already signalled that they will not support the decree, one of two crafted by Spain's Socialist government after protests sparked by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week.
Thousands of mostly young activists camped out in Madrid's main square and other Spanish cities to protest the eviction and call for major reforms.
A second decree, which would permit automatic and indefinite renewal of rental contracts, was already expected not to pass, failing to secure the minimum support required from Spain's fractured Congress.
"I already thought the measures were insufficient and only temporary, but vetoing them is selfish and abandoning the people," Aidan, a 26-year-old wildfire firefighter, said of Junts' decision not to back the measures. "We'll keep up the encampment," he added. REUTERS

“The ink was barely dry on NAB’s last fixed-rate hike announcement and it’s already served up another one," said Canstar data insights director, Sally Tindall.

CBA, Westpac and ANZ have also hiked their fixed rates last few weeks - CBA hiking by up to 0.48 percentage points while Westpac hiked by up to 0.45.
The lowest fixed rate you can get from one of the big four bank is now 6.49% at ANZ for either a 1 or 2-year term.
In a statement to the ABC, NAB said: “Fixed home loan rates are influenced by a range of factors, including wholesale funding costs and market conditions. Like other lenders, NAB regularly reviews its pricing and adjusts rates when required.”

An ASX-listed international money transfer provider has been hacked and some of its client data may have been accessed.
OFX Group released a statement to the ASX on Friday which revealed the firm was investigating a cybersecurity incident that involved "unauthorised access to data, including data related to some clients".
The international payment provider said it had not identified any cases where client accounts or funds had been compromised, and did not believe any clients had suffered financial loss as a result of the hack.
Hackers had accessed identity documents but did not seem to have made copies, according to the firm.
And of the information they did obtain, it couldn't be used to make payments on OFX's platform, the business also said.
They warned that some non-clients' data had also been breached, such as job applicants.
OFX said its security teams "responded immediately" once they learned of the breach and that their investigations are continuing "as a matter of urgency" and the relevant authorities have been notified.

USD at 17-month high
The US dollar is heading for its third straight week of gains as a bond market rout pushes borrowing costs to multi-decade peaks.
Yields on benchmark US 10-year Treasuries hit 5.344 per cent yesterday, their highest since 2002, ahead of a US jobs report that could influence the near-term policy outlook.
The dollar index, which measures the US currency against six rivals, was at 102.08, set for a 1 per cent gain this week, its third consecutive weekly gain, a run it last had in May 2025.
Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, says investors are confronting the uncomfortable mix of sticky inflation, heavy government borrowing and large bond supply.
"The fact that long-end yields are pushing higher even as expectations for an immediate Fed hike have eased suggests this is increasingly about the term premium and fiscal risk, not just the next Fed decision," she said.
Data on Wednesday showed US consumer prices rose less than expected in August, along with downward revisions to July's figure, leading traders to rein in wagers of a rate hike from the Federal Reserve later this month.
Two of the Fed’s top policymakers this week staked out an unusually clear case for taking in more data before deciding about another hike.
That has sharpened the focus on the US payroll report due later in the day, with data likely to show that job growth slowed in September, and that the unemployment rate is forecast to have been 4.1 per cent for a third straight month.
"With the Fed now myopically focused on inflation and price pressures, a hot wages print could prove particularly influential for US rates, Treasuries and the USD," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.
Brent crude futures were back above $100 per barrel as traders kept an eye on the stalled talks between the US and Iran to end the conflict in the Middle East.
Sterling was at $1.3187 while the Australian dollar was 0.18 per cent softer at $0.6918, as both hovered around their three-month lows.

The KPMG audits scandal that rocked the corporate world
ANZ cutting ties with its long-time auditor KPMG after nearly 60 years working together is just the latest consequence the firm has faced since its dirty laundry was aired earlier this year.
In March, Senator Deborah O'Neill exposed in a speech to parliament allegations from a whistleblower that KPMG had used confidential client data to win corporate audit contracts for two years.
The whistleblower alleged that for two years, KPMG had batted away accusations that information obtained during an audit of Lendlease accounts was used to win work elsewhere.
It was also alleged the auditors had been expressly forbidden by the company to access the confidential board documents.
In the six months since, KPMG has been in almost constant upheaval.
Some of the allegations were substantiated and chief executive Andrew Yates and audit boss Julian McPherson left the firm.
KPMG was also referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission.
The firm apologised and admitted its internal investigations were conducted without the "necessary rigour required".
KPMG agreed to a three-month freeze on new Commonwealth government contract bids that ran until September 30.
This prompted KPMG to lay off about 5% of its staff, which was about 400 people.
The firm's revenue fell from $2.28 billion the previous year to $2.26 billion in the 2026 financial year, and KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams expected more revenue falls.
Lendlease unsurprisingly cut ties with the big four accounting firm.
In August, so did Macquarie Bank.
The ABC has contacted KPMG for comment in the wake of ANZ ending their business relationship. A call was returned by veteran crisis communicator David Luff, who said the firm declined to comment.
You can read more on the context of this scandal-plagued firm from a piece my colleague Ian Verrender wrote a few months ago.

Sudan's ousted president Bashir sent to Khartoum for treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:18:22 UTC
06:18:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan's ousted president Bashir sent to Khartoum for treatment, lawyer says
Ousted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has been transferred to a military-run hospital in Khartoum for medical treatment and requires further care outside the country, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Bashir, 82, was toppled by the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2019, following a months-long popular uprising.
The RSF and army later fell out over plans to integrate their forces during a planned transition to civilian rule and have been fighting a civil war that has laid waste to much of the country over the past three-and-a-half years.
Bashir had been moved from prison to hospital prior to the outbreak of war, and later transferred to the town of Merowe in northern Sudan, where he had been put under military guard.
Bashir was sent to Khartoum for medical tests and he had symptoms that required diagnosis and treatment outside Sudan, his lawyer, Mohamed Alhassan Alameen, told Reuters.
In a statement on Wednesday, Bashir's family said his need for medical treatment outside Sudan "has become critical and urgent, and cannot be delayed any longer", but they had not received official permission to send him abroad.
It was unclear precisely what condition Bashir was suffering. Sudan's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several prominent Sudanese Islamist figures also called for his transfer out of the country on social media.
Any such move would likely cause discord within Sudan and could draw international condemnation since Bashir is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges including genocide and also has open cases against him in Sudan.
During Bashir's three decades in power, Sudan was listed by the US as a state sponsor of terrorism and was subject to wide-ranging sanctions. Protesters during the popular uprising accused him and his Islamist National Congress Party of widespread corruption and repression.
After his ouster, Bashir was tried on various charges and convicted of corruption and illicit financing, for which he was serving prison time at the start of the war.

Trump could target three Fed governors. Removing them may be harder than it looks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:14:49 UTC
06:14:49 KST

President Donald Trump has new ammunition he can use in his campaign against his perceived opponents at the Federal Reserve, although a watchdog report released Wednesday found no basis for criminal charges stemming from the Fed's costly renovations to its headquarters.
Combined with separate disputes involving governors Lisa Cook and Michael Barr, Trump's decision to pin the headquarters spending issues on former Chair Jerome Powell means the president could potentially seek the removal of as many as three of the Fed's seven board members. But recent court rulings suggest any attempt would face significant legal hurdles.
Any legal maneuvers could take months to play out and may have the effect of persuading his targets to postpone any plans to leave the Fed, as Powell has already done. Trump's ability to force the Fed off its recent decision to raise interest rates appears limited, despite the institutional damage he could do if he took further legal action.
Trump appears to be weighing his options for how to proceed. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest-rate decision on Oct. 28, only days before the Nov. 3 midterm election. The administration faces a deadline in the Cook case shortly after the election.
If the administration does move against any of the three governors, it may backfire for Trump, said Scott Alvarez, a former Fed general counsel.
"All have an incentive to litigate and stay," Alvarez said.
"The Supreme Court said that Lisa Cook can stay while the litigation goes on. If they all stay while he goes on, then all he's done is hurt his own agenda," Alvarez said of Trump.
Trump fumed in the wake of Wednesday's report from the Fed's inspector general. "Powell is a disaster," the president said Wednesday when asked by reporters about the findings. Powell "should not be sitting on the Federal Reserve Board."
Trump appointed Powell during his first term, then quickly soured on him.
Trump asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to review the IG report. A spokesman for Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia said her office was also reviewing the report.
The Department of Justice didn't respond to emailed questions about its plans and how Blanche's review might differ from Pirro's. Pirro previously oversaw a criminal investigation into Powell. A judge quashed her subpoenas in the matter, saying their "dominant (if not sole) purpose is to harass and pressure Powell."
The Fed declined to comment on Trump's remarks about Powell.
The long-awaited IG report found a raft of managerial problems had allowed construction costs to jump by about a billion dollars as the Fed renovated its Washington office space. But the report found no evidence of administrative misconduct and saw nothing meriting a criminal referral to prosecutors.
"I personally don't think the renovation report would be enough for a court to remove Jay for cause," Alvarez said. "It exonerates him on the criminal side, but it also says they didn't identify any administrative misconduct."
The report details how bureaucratic disorganization left the Fed vulnerable to overspending on a project to renovate and connect a pair of historical federal buildings in Washington. The IG's office faults the Fed for failing to enforce a guaranteed maximum price for the project, among other issues.
But the backward-looking report can't directly prove the Fed would have saved money had it operated better. It acknowledges in a footnote that better management "does not necessarily mean the project's overall cost will be lower."
Nor does the report pin the cost overruns on Powell or any individual governor, instead describing failures in project management, contracting and the board's governance and oversight systems. The IG's office notes that the board delegated responsibility to the staff, as it would have expected for a construction project at a large organization.
Powell can stay on the Fed as a governor through January 2028. He said in March he would remain until the legal threat was "well and truly over, with transparency and finality."
The Supreme Court in June blocked Trump's attempt to remove Cook over allegations that she had lied on a mortgage application. The court said she was owed notice of the allegations and a chance to respond, and issued guidance for what a later finding of cause might entail.
As of August, Cook has received the notice and opportunity to respond, removing one obstacle to her potential removal. The administration would still need to show courts it has met the threshold for cause, which would likely require another Supreme Court review.
The White House hasn't publicly addressed the issue since Cook's response, though in an interview published by Time on Thursday Trump complained about Cook. The White House declined to comment on how the president might respond further to the IG report's findings.
Newly confirmed Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is "controlled to a certain extent" by the board, Trump said. "We have Lisa on there," he said.
For now, the Cook case is pending before U.S. District Court Judge Jia Cobb. She has asked the parties for a joint status report by Nov. 6 on how the litigation should proceed.
Meanwhile, an outside investigation into the Fed's handling of the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank is ongoing. A preliminary report by the investigative firm Starling Advisory Group faulted the Fed's bank supervisors, whom it said should have known about the risks to the bank as much as a year ahead of its failure.
The preliminary review doesn't assign responsibility to Barr personally. But the White House heaped the blame for the episode at Barr's feet, while stopping short of calling for his firing.
There may not be evidence enough in that report to justify his removal to a skeptical judiciary.
But some in the Fed believe Trump has already proved the administration is willing to act on thin evidence.
Powell issued an extraordinary statement in January after subpoenas for evidence involving the renovation.
"This new threat is not about my testimony last June or about the renovation of the Federal Reserve buildings," Powell said. "Those are pretexts."

Finland’s prime minister says ‘foreign forces’ could be behind a string of intrusions at lawmakers’ homes
Several Finnish lawmakers have said someone entered their homes while they were away, Yle reported.
The incidents took place over the past year. Nothing was stolen during the suspected intrusions, but lawmakers reported noticeable signs that someone had been there — for example, doors left open or lights turned on. Parliament Speaker Jussi Halla-aho said this may have been deliberate.
The exact number of lawmakers affected has not been reported, but Yle puts it at “fewer than 20.” Halla-aho said they did not belong to the same party or share any other common characteristics.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said foreign actors could be behind the incidents. “If someone is trying to destabilize Finland, undermine our sense of security, or weaken our support for Ukraine, for example, it has the opposite effect,” he said.
Orpo also said Russia had previously tried to interfere in European elections. Finland’s next parliamentary election will be held in April 2027.

Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, according to the outlet, describing the weapons as a new category between attack drones and missiles.
Defence Blog noted that the company provided no prices, production numbers or performance figures. It added that the figures and Rostec's claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
Rostec argued that a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle, though not every such drone qualifies as one. Its statement, as quoted by Defence Blog, claimed that “in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased.”
The report described Rostec's assertion that the drones combine the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles at a significantly lower price. Rostec also expects the gap between the two kinds of weapons to keep narrowing as drone production matures.
The company anticipates that the drones will become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023, the outlet wrote.
Rostec told the state news agency TASS that the S-71M and S-71K are designed for launch from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Defence Blog stated. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57's internal weapons bay, allowing the jet to carry them without compromising its radar-evading shape.
Russia's arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September, the report noted.
Ukrainian military intelligence has examined debris from both, Militarnyi reported, as cited by Defence Blog. According to those findings, the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance.
The S-71M, called Monokhrom, reportedly contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small US-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board. The outlet cautioned that some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec also told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets, a claim that Defence Blog did not independently verify. The company stated that the weapon can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones. Based on the outlet's reading, this suggests Rostec is targeting the Dan-T at export buyers.
Defence Blog described conflicting accounts of the weapon's origin. Some analysts present it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt. Ukrainian experts, by contrast, have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T's range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, per the Defence Blog account. The outlet cited Ukrainian intelligence officials, who noted that Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025, the report explained. It is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region.
Ukraine's military intelligence found a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly US-made electronics inside the weapon, Euronews reported, as relayed by Defence Blog.
The outlet emphasized that cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build. That logic mirrors Russia's mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Defence Blog added that Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons. That family includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group's KUB loitering munitions.
The pitch comes as jet-powered munitions already make up a growing share of Russian salvos.
During the large-scale attack on August 21–22, Russia launched 217 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and decoys, of which more than 50 were jet-powered.
Ukrainian defenses destroyed or suppressed 191 aerial targets that night, among them six Banderol munitions. Several Banderol weapons strayed into Belarus, with at least one reportedly flying around 75 miles into Belarusian territory before running out of fuel and crashing in a field.

Putin warns Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in arsenal if any of its territory is attacked

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal.
In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.

U.S. designates Russia-linked sanctions-evasion payment network A7 a ‘significant transnational criminal organization’

U.S. designates Russia-linked sanctions-evasion payment network A7 a ‘significant transnational criminal organization’
The U.S. Treasury Department has designated A7, a Russia-linked payment network created to evade sanctions, a “significant transnational criminal organization.”
The designation will make it possible to bar U.S. financial institutions from making any transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents,” foreign shell companies through which the network processes payments for clients in Russia.
The restrictions on A7 were formally imposed as part of sanctions targeting Iran. The Treasury Department said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and central bank used the network’s services.
Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor launched A7 in 2024, with Russia’s Promsvyazbank also taking part. The network consists of hundreds of companies in third countries that process payments for clients in Russia. By Promsvyazbank’s own estimate, A7 processed 7.5 billion rubles in payments in the first half of 2025.
The Russian company A7 itself and A7A5, the ruble-denominated stablecoin it created, have been under U.S. sanctions since August 2025.

Meat industry says it's focused on US trade review, following minister's super proposal
The trade minister has received a rather lukewarm response to his latest proposal to shield Australian farmers from a new round of Trump administration tariffs.
In Wisconsin for a G20 meeting, Don Farrell suggested Australia's wealthy super funds might invest in the US lamb industry, to ultimately help boost sales in America.
Australian lamb is currently subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, which could rise even higher depending on the outcome of a US trade review that's underway.
Asked for his response to Farrell's plan, Australian Meat Industry Council CEO Tim Ryan said the sector was squarely focused on the trade review.
"AMIC maintains that imported lamb is not a cause of injury to the US sheep industry," he said in a statement to the ABC.
"Australian businesses and exporters have already made significant investments in the US lamb supply chain and in developing demand — which ultimately benefits the US industry.
"The Australian and US sheep industry have a history of collaboration across a range of forums for mutual benefit."
Earlier, the superannuation sector pushed back strongly against any moves by the government to dictate how and where it invests its members' money.
Roblox responds to eSafety's call for more action on child safety
Roblox has responded to the eSafety commission's call for large gaming companies to "lift their game" on child safety.
The commission found big differences in how Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam deal with serious harms including grooming, child exploitation, and violent extremist content.
It identified gaps in harmful-content detection, repeat-offender prevention, and information-sharing initiatives.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Roblox says the company prioritises the safety of children.
"We have invested heavily in what eSafety acknowledges is one of the gaming industry's largest Trust & Safety teams, and continue to strengthen our multi-layered safeguards, including advanced detection technologies and mandatory age checks to access chat that no other large online platform has adopted at the scale we have," the spokesperson says.
ATO faces growing calls to reverse credit card payment ban for tax bills
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) is facing mounting calls to reverse its decision to ban credit card payments for tax bills from the end of November.
The ATO announced the surprise move yesterday in response to the Reserve Bank (RBA) outlawing card surcharges, which cost Australians about $1.6 billion a year.
But small businesses are crying foul, arguing they have no option but to absorb the surcharges (or merchants' fees).
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson agrees and has called on the ATO to reverse its decision and allow credit card payments.
"Businesses are expected to absorb these fees, while the ATO avoids them by withdrawing credit card payments," Hanson said in a statement.
"Credit helps businesses manage cashflow and meet tax obligations on time. Removing this option will drive businesses to the wall when they are already doing it tough."
The ATO says the vast majority of Australians do not pay their tax bills using credit cards, and says it would not be appropriate for a government agency to transfer the cost of credit card merchant fees to the community.
Government extends lower fuel quality standards amid Middle East war
Energy Minister Chris Bowen has confirmed the federal government has extended the lower quality standards for fuel as the Middle East war continues.
In March, Labor decided to lower fuel standards to allow more fuel supply into the domestic market in response to higher oil prices.
It allowed high-sulphur fuel, which was restricted a few years ago, to be blended into the Australian fuel supply.
The energy minister says the government intends to keep the lower fuel standards in place until January 2027.
Bowen says it won't affect Australia's emissions.
"It's about sulphur levels and the flashpoint for diesel, so it has no impact on emissions," Bowen says.
"It's about the temperature at which it ignites. It's got no reference to emissions whatsoever."
Opposition leader criticises end of surcharge payments
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has criticised a decision to ban businesses from charging surcharges to cover the cost of bank fees.
From yesterday, businesses were banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has also announced it will stop accepting credit card payments from November 30 because of the surcharge ban.
"This prime minister pretending that somehow there's going to be a discount on his behalf. Well, actually, what's going to happen is everyone will pay more," Taylor says.

Taylor lashes Farrell's super proposal for US lamb as 'harebrained'
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has lashed Trade Minister Don Farrell's idea to use super funds to invest in the US lamb industry as "hai
Farrell has asked the Trump administration to consider sparing Australian sheep farmers from further tariff pain in exchange for Australian investment in the US lamb industry.
The Super Members Council has labelled the comments "ill-informed" and says super funds will only invest in areas that yield the strongest returns for members.
Taylor says the trade minister needs to explain why the government wants to use Australians' money to invest in the US lamb sector.
"Superannuation is Australia's money and not the government's money," Taylor says.
"Now the government wants to go and buy American sheep. They need to explain that to the Australian people. But I can tell you that they shouldn't be using Australia's money to do it. So, I don't know where this idea came from.
"We want access to markets. This is critically important. But a harebrained scheme like this? Seriously?"

Super sector labels minister's idea to invest in US lamb as 'ill-informed'
Australia's superannuation industry has pushed back against Trade Minister Don Farrell's idea to use members' funds to invest in the US lamb industry.
Farrell has asked the Trump administration to consider sparing Australian sheep farmers from further tariff pain in exchange for Australian investment in the US lamb industry.
But Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert says super funds will only invest in areas that yield the strongest possible investment returns for members.
"Comments like this are ill-informed. Super funds invest completely independently of governments for very good reason — they invest only in the interests of their members," Schubert says.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty says the industry will assess any opportunity on its merits.
"The idea reported today has not been raised with the superannuation sector. We would welcome a discussion with the government and are always on the lookout for how funds can bring good financial returns home to Australian savers," Delahunty says.
Analysis: Albanese leaves grim domestic scene as he flies to the Pacific
Having a Pre-COP meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu is one of those initiatives that probably seemed like a good idea at the time.
No doubt it still has resonance as part of Australia's wider diplomacy in the Pacific, in the battle to limit China's influence. But when Anthony Albanese, still coming down from his New York high, steps onto his plane on Monday bound for Pre-COP, it could feel more like a chore than an opportunity.
Even COP itself, to be held in Turkey from November 9 to 20 and also on Albanese's itinerary, is not expected to break much ground.
Big issues have their high time, seizing public and media attention for brief or long periods. When Labor announced in 2021 that it would bid to host COP (the United Nations' annual climate meeting), climate change was still front and centre. But now — as we (with Pacific countries) are co-hosts with Turkey — global warming has slipped down the public's agenda.
This doesn't mean that, objectively, climate change is any less important. It means other issues have supplanted it on the public's and the media's radar.

Minister confirms Ukraine has knocked back Australia's Tiger helicopters
The federal government has confirmed Ukraine has decided not to accept Australia's Tiger helicopters for defence against Russia's invasion.
Ukrainian media reports Kyiv believes the helicopters' maintenance requirements would outweigh the benefit of receiving the aircraft.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Ukraine's President, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week.
When asked if Australia is considering gifting Ukraine drones, cyber capabilities and missiles, Industry Minister Tim Ayres says he won't go into details.
But he points out that drone technology has been "critical" to Ukraine's defence.
"The decision from Ukraine not to take that technology from Australia is a decision for them. It is, as I understand it, based on their technical requirements and the way that it integrates with the rest of their systems," Ayres says.
"We will continue to find ways of supporting Ukraine, but I can't provide additional technical details or security details of the nature of that ongoing contribution."
Minns takes another swipe at federal Labor over spending
The NSW Premier Chris Minns has taken another veiled swipe at the federal government over its spending.
On Wednesday, the NSW Labor premier took a jab at the federal government over its spending, saying his state had been careful with public money.
He also declined to defend federal Labor's fiscal approach.
On the Future Women Leadership Series podcast, Minns warned that if the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates again, it risked tipping the economy into a recession.
He also doubled down on his comments, saying governments had a role to play in reducing spending, and that NSW felt the effects of interest rates more than other states.
"Interest rate rises in our economy are felt harder than anywhere else in the country, so NSW mortgage holders have to do the heavy lifting for demand in Western Australia or South Australia," Minns said.
"Government has got a role to play here too. We have worked really hard on being a commonsense, sensible government when it comes to public finances and we've got the lowest spending growth of any jurisdiction in the country."
Farrell suggests superannuation investment in US lamb industry to avoid more tariffs
Trade Minister Don Farrell has asked the Trump administration to consider sparing Australian sheep farmers from further tariff pain in exchange for Australian investment in the US lamb industry.
Farrell floated the idea, which could see Australians' superannuation savings invested in the American sector, during this week's G20 trade meetings in Milwaukee.
The proposal aims to get ahead of a US trade investigation into lamb imports, which could result in new tariffs.
Australian lamb exports to the US are already subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, along with many other Australian products.
But American sheep producers, backed by dozens of Republican members of Congress, have been lobbying for tariffs specifically on sheep meat and wool from Australia and New Zealand.
Farrell's office has confirmed he discussed a possible lamb-industry "support package" with trade representative Jamieson Greer during the G20 event. Greer is a key architect of Donald Trump's tariff policies.

Shoebridge responds to Labor MP's Jewish 'prejudice' accusations
Greens leader David Shoebridge has responded to accusations from a Labor MP that he displayed "prejudice".
When asked at a press conference how he would repair the party's relationship with the Jewish community, Shoebridge said he had strong connections with Jewish Australians who were "fighting genocide", referring to the crisis in Gaza.
But Labor MP Josh Burns says Shoebridge's answer to the question is "shocking" and that people shouldn't be placed into categories based on their views.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Shoebridge has described Burns's position as "extraordinary".
"What I've said is there are so many progressive Jews who join with us in being horrified at the genocide that they're seeing in Gaza, horrified at what's happened in the name of the State of Israel," Shoebridge said.
"And the fact that when we say that there's this large part of the Jewish community who join with so many Australians in speaking out against the genocide, the fact that that is spun and twisted to suggest that's somehow divisive."
eSafety to act if gaming companies don't comply with child protection requirements
The eSafety commissioner says her agency is prepared to take action if big gaming companies fail to comply with age-assurance requirements.
The online safety watchdog has identified gaps in Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam's protections for children.
Those gaps include harmful-content detection, repeat-offender prevention, and information-sharing initiatives.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, commissioner Julie Inman Grant says the warning applies to Steam and Valve.
"We've told them what their requirements are, and they're looking at the other privacy preserving age-assurance tools that they may be able to offer," Inman Grant says.
"We'll have to see what they actually deliver in the coming months. And we can always take formal enforcement action if they don't comply."
Labor targets migration lawyers and agents over 'futile' visa cases
Migration lawyers and agents who help people pursue baseless visa claims will be targeted under a federal government crackdown on those who profit from attempts to "game" the system.
Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney on Friday to condemn professionals who sell "false hope" to clients with little prospect of remaining in Australia and flag plans to restrict their activity.
Hill will also unveil more details of Labor's broader migration overhaul announced last month, including that new restrictions on international students will take effect from today.
Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) was 292,100 in the year to March, with the government pledging to reduce the rate to 225,000 by next financial year.

Malinauskas defends federal government spending after NSW premier's comments
SA Premier Peter Malinauskas has pushed back on the suggestion the federal government isn't doing enough to rein in spending.
On Wednesday, NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns took a swipe at the federal government over its spending, saying his state has been careful with public money.
He also declined to defend federal Labor's fiscal approach.
But Malinauskas has defended the federal government on ABC Radio National Breakfast, saying states "aren't immune from scrutiny".
"All too often the critique is made in the absence of any thoughtful suggestion about what should be cut. I mean, is it the Commonwealth government investment in Medicare or education services? I mean, I don't think that would be particularly good for the country," Malinauskas says.
Ayres says government's focus with Bell Bay $200m bailout was securing jobs
Industry Minister Tim Ayres has evaded questions about why taxpayers won't see much return from the Bell Bay aluminium bailout.
The Australian and Tasmanian governments yesterday announced a $200 million package for the Bell Bay aluminium smelter in Tasmania.
The package was delayed because the smelter's owner, Rio Tinto, had been locked in protracted negotiations with the state-owned power company Hydro Tasmania over a new power deal.
Ayres has sidestepped questions about why the power deal was only for five years, when other comparable power agreements are for 10 years.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Ayres says the government's focus was about securing jobs in northern Tasmania.
"The overwhelming objective here is to secure these 550 jobs, 1,000 indirect jobs, in what is a part of Australia where these blue-collar jobs are really not just really important here but there's this capability here that can make Australia's economy stronger," Ayres says.
Hume calls on ATO to reverse credit card payment ban
Deputy Liberal Leader Jane Hume has urged the government to reverse the tax office's decision to stop accepting credit card payments.
From yesterday, businesses were banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has also announced it will stop accepting credit card payments from November 30 because of the surcharge ban.
Some businesses have increased prices after the ban to cover bank and card fees.
Speaking to Channel Seven, Hume says customers will ultimately have to pay more.
"The Coalition is calling on the government to reverse this change that the ATO is imposing on small businesses, because, quite frankly, it's been very clear that this government doesn't understand small business and it's imposing unnecessary costs on them," Hume says.
Appearing on the same panel, Wentworth MP Allegra Spender says she'll write to the ATO to ask it to reverse the ban on accepting credit card payments.
Cutting corporate tax rate could help lift productivity, Productivity Commission says
The Productivity Commission says its proposal to cut the company tax rate would help with Australia's productivity challenge.
The commission has previously called for a 20 per cent tax rate on profits for companies with revenue of up to $1 billion, but it was never adopted in May's federal budget.
On Tuesday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said productivity was "doing nothing", and that stronger productivity would allow more to be produced without adding to inflation.
Angela Jackson, from the Productivity Commission, says cutting corporate tax rates is one of the easiest ways to lift productivity.
"We want to ensure that all the settings are encouraging business investment," Jackson says.
"We did look at the real drop-off that we've seen since the GFC [Global Financial Crisis] in business investment and what we could do to lift that. Company tax reform is one of the sort of the easiest ways, if you like, pathways to doing that."
Leeser calls on PM, minister to visit WA over child protection concerns
Shadow Indigenous Australians Minister Julian Leeser has called for federal agencies to get involved in the case of unsupervised children in WA in state care.
Up to 15 Aboriginal children, some as young as five, were living unsupervised in a state-owned home in South Hedland.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Leeser says services across the state and federal government have failed to coordinate.
He says there has been a failure of welfare checks, and has called on the PM and the federal Indigenous Australians minister to visit the area.
"The state government now has set up a coordination committee. It doesn't include the federal agencies. I'd like to see the federal agencies involved as well. And I'd like to see the federal minister and the prime minister visit there too," Leeser says.

US is moving around 9,000 troops aboard ships to Middle East as Trump weighs new attacks on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:00:09 UTC
06:00:09 KST

The US military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a US official has said. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
Trump also said on Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
The group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the US official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines and hundreds of aircraft.
The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
The Washington is typically deployed to Pacific Ocean but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Republican Party chances in midterms
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published on Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is "possible" that he will ramp up attacking Iran after the November 3 elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go further in detailing his strategy.
"I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?" Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted on Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because "things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today."
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to "open up" the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was "not good enough."
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, "It’s possible." But then he added, "It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon."
The president said "100% of the people" oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities "including worldwide."
"So, when you say it that way, It would help," Trump added. "If you don’t say that, it could hurt."

18th-century mansion on fire in downtown St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:58:48 UTC
05:58:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. A mansion built in the 18th century is on fire in downtown St. Petersburg, the press service of the Russian Emergencies Ministry told TASS.
"We received a report of an open fire in the four-story building," the ministry said, noting that the mansion, designed by architect Ferdinand Miller and also known as the Bremmer House, was on fire.
The Emergencies Ministry later specified that the area affected by the fire is 2,000 square meters. The fire has been classified as a third-alarm fire (out of a possible five), the press service noted.
According to its statement, 125 employees and 25 pieces of equipment were extinguishing the fire, which has started to engulf a nearby building.
Constructed in 1872 in the eclectic style according to a design by Ferdinand Miller, an academician of architecture, the Bremmer House has been a landmark of St. Petersburg’s social and cultural life for decades. Its ongoing renovation was supposed to be finished by the end of 2027.

Inferno devours historic St. Petersburg landmark (VIDEO)
A massive fire has broken out in a historic apartment block located in St. Petersburg’s city center. Known as the Miller House, the building stands just across the street from the iconic Saint Isaac’s Cathedral.
The blaze that stated on Thursday evening quickly spread through the massive three-storey house. Videos from the scene that surfaced on social media show almost the entire building engulfed in flames, with sprouts of fire coming out of its windows and plumes of thick black smoke rising high into the night sky.
Built in the late 18th century, the Miller House got its name after its late 19th century owner, Colonel Karl Miller. It was known for its ornate interiors of historical and artistic value, including stucco decoration, fireplaces, tilework, and natural wood elements.
Nationalized after the Revolution in 1917, the house served as an apartment block until the 2010s when it was designated as in need of renovation. In 2021, it was added to the regional list of cultural heritage sites.
The repairs and renovation works began this past spring, with the building owners planning to turn it into a luxury apartment block.
According to the emergency services, the blaze engulfed an area of 2,000 square meters. Nearly 40 fire engines and 165 firefighters were deployed to the scene. At some point, the blaze spread to the neighboring residential building, prompting an emergency evacuation.
The regional emergency services announced at around 2am local time that the fire had largely been extinguished.
The fire allegedly caused a roof and floor decks collapse, local media reported, citing eyewitnesses. The witnesses also claimed that the fire spread through the entire building in mere minutes. Police have been deployed to the scene, with the reasons for the incident still being investigated.
The renovation works were “proceeding at full speed,” the company that owns the building told the local media. According to the company’s press service, the work was focused on reinforcing the floor structures, while no construction workers were present at the site when the fire started. “We are looking into the situation and are in constant communication with all relevant authorities,” TAS added. The work was expected to be finished by late 2027.

How Vyacheslav Volodin secured a record third term as speaker of Russia’s State Duma — and why Putin keeps him there
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:55:34 UTC
05:55:34 KST

How Vyacheslav Volodin secured a record third term as speaker of Russia’s State Duma — and why Putin keeps him there
Newly elected State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin opened the new parliament’s first session with some advice for lawmakers:
History shows that our country cannot be defeated from the outside. All our problems come from within: conflict, betrayal by the elites, weak leadership. So we need to learn from this. We must not lose our country.
Volodin became speaker of parliament’s lower house for the third time, breaking Boris Gryzlov’s record. Gryzlov served twice, during the fourth and fifth parliamentary terms.
In 2021, ahead of elections to the eighth State Duma, United Russia leader Dmitry Medvedev expressed interest in becoming speaker. But Vladimir Putin did not approve putting him at the top of the party’s candidate list.
The same thing happened in 2026. Kremlin-friendly media reported that Medvedev might head the top three or top five candidates on the party’s list. Meduza’s sources said Medvedev himself was lobbying for this arrangement, but Putin had not approved it.
Medvedev was again left off the party’s national candidate list, closing off his path to the speakership. The main beneficiaries of the former president’s exclusion were Volodin and the Kremlin’s domestic policy team, which feared that Medvedev’s involvement in the campaign could further depress United Russia’s already low approval ratings.
Volodin began his political career in the Saratov region. In 1990, the 26-year-old, who held a doctorate in agricultural sciences, won a seat on Saratov’s city council as an independent, defeating a candidate from the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
After the Soviet Union collapsed, Volodin effectively worked as a political consultant, helping Yury Kitov, a member of the Russian republic’s Supreme Soviet, become mayor of Saratov. He persuaded city council members to approve Kitov’s candidacy, even though the regional administration backed someone else.
Once Kitov took office, Volodin became his deputy and chief of staff at city hall. He soon became deputy governor of the Saratov region, then led by one of Russia’s most colorful governors, Dmitry Ayatskov.
By the late 1990s, Ayatskov had grown suspicious of his young, ambitious deputy, whose responsibilities included finances, social policy, and infrastructure. Their conflict prompted Volodin to leave for Moscow, where he began building Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov’s political movement, Fatherland.
In 1999, Fatherland formed a bloc with All Russia, a movement of powerful regional governors, and secured the support of former Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov. As a result, the Fatherland–All Russia bloc was seen as a likely winner of the State Duma elections.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin was promoting the Unity bloc and the Union of Right Forces, whose main opponent was Fatherland–All Russia. Putin, then prime minister, openly backed Unity.
The Communists won the largest share of the vote (24.3%), Unity came second (23.32%), and Fatherland finished only third (13.33%). But Volodin won a seat in parliament, where he was appointed deputy leader of the Luzhkov–Primakov bloc’s parliamentary faction and later became its leader.
In 2001, Fatherland became Unity’s ally, and two years later they merged into a single party. “Our three organizations supported the president. His last name is Putin,” Volodin told Kommersant at the time.
Volodin rose quickly through United Russia’s ranks. In 2005, he was appointed secretary of its General Council, a key governing body. “There were no other candidates,” a party source told Kommersant at the time. “He [Volodin] has an appetite for this work and the political experience the job requires.” Another source told the newspaper that Vladislav Surkov, then head of the presidential administration’s domestic policy team, was entirely happy with Volodin as a candidate. Volodin owed his appointment to Surkov.
Volodin quickly imposed his own bureaucratic order on the party. A Saratov political consultant who has known him for years told Meduza on condition of anonymity that even before his appointment to the General Council, Volodin wanted to make United Russia’s branch in his home region a model for the rest:
Everything that later became standard practice in United Russia [nationwide] was tried out in Saratov. For example, they started collecting campaign money from businesspeople — developers, retailers — through a centralized system. “Want your own lawmakers? You need to pay.” They set up centralized propaganda on local TV. I’d worked in other regions, and United Russia didn’t have anything like that there. We felt we were ahead of the curve.
A political consultant who worked with the party’s national leadership told Meduza how closely Volodin managed party affairs once he became General Council secretary:
If the party had a crisis, a scandal, or a conflict somewhere in the regions, he could fly out there the next day. By the time he arrived, he already knew everything about the region. He tried to put his own people in place wherever he could. He worked closely with the authorities in regions that had set up systems for rigging elections, [because] he wanted to spread those practices elsewhere, too.
Volodin was one of the main organizers of United Russia’s 2007 State Duma election campaign. Putin headed its candidate list that year — the only time he has done so in the party’s history.
During that campaign, the president got to know Volodin better and “took note of the party manager,” according to a source who worked with the presidential administration’s domestic policy team at the time and another who worked in the federal government. In 2010, Putin, by then prime minister, “brought” Volodin “back” into the executive branch, offering him the job of government chief of staff.
That made the politician from Saratov Putin’s chief political strategist. Ahead of the 2011 State Duma elections, United Russia’s ratings were low, and Volodin proposed that the prime minister and party leader mask the party’s role in the campaign so its stale image would not put off Russian voters. The idea was to create a pro-Putin movement that would ostensibly run the campaign, with United Russia nominating candidates for the movement. Putin liked the proposal.
The new movement was named the All-Russia People’s Front. Putin himself was its formal leader, but in practice Volodin, who had devised it, ran it.
Soon after the 2011 State Duma elections, Volodin, then a deputy prime minister, became head of the Kremlin’s domestic policy team, which ran Putin’s campaign to return to the presidency. Under the team’s direction, the State Duma passed repressive laws and later earned the nickname “the mad printer.”
After the annexation of Crimea, Volodin made perhaps his best-known declaration: “No Putin — no Russia.” Speaking at the 2014 Valdai forum, he used those words to describe the mood among Russians. A source in the speaker’s circle believes that as far back as the 2000s, Volodin “realized that [to advance his career] he needed to work for one person — the head of state”:
He doesn’t belong to any influential group, though he may, for example, have good relations with certain security and law enforcement officials. But they don’t have a shared history or any joint dealings. If you belong to a group and lose your post in the broader power structure, your patrons will find you a place within the clan. They won’t abandon you. Volodin doesn’t have that option, so he constantly makes a show of pledging allegiance to the president.
But even this extreme loyalty did not help Volodin keep his job as deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for domestic politics in 2016. Both the source in the speaker’s circle and a source close to the current domestic policy team say he wanted to stay in the Kremlin.
That was when Volodin became State Duma speaker. One account attributes his move to parliament to election turnout falling short of the president’s expectations: in 2016, it did not reach 50%. Another holds that the president was deliberately moving officials who had grown more powerful to different jobs, “taking them out of their comfort zone,” as one Meduza source close to the presidential administration put it.
In parliament, Volodin made a show of enforcing discipline while continuing to make pro-Putin statements. He repeatedly said lawmakers should support the president, and after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he became one of the most prominent officials voicing ultrapatriotic views. Russians who had emigrated became one of the speaker’s favorite targets: he repeatedly called them “traitors” and demanded that they be punished.
“Volodin often goes too far. He knows why he does it — to make his loyalty more visible. But he also knows where to draw the line and doesn’t turn into Medvedev,” said the source in the speaker’s circle. On his Telegram channel, the former president regularly insults the leaders of Ukraine and European countries and threatens to use nuclear weapons.
According to the same source, this loyalty is the main reason Volodin remains close to the president. The speaker shows it in different ways, the source said, for example by telling Putin about proposals that influential players bring to the Duma:
Often these are things that are nowhere near important enough to bring to the president — some perks buried in clauses of bills. But the speaker is showing that he’s keeping an eye on things. All he has to offer is this show of loyalty. You couldn’t say he’s interesting to talk to, for example.
The source believes Volodin retained the speakership because of his loyalty and because he keeps an equal distance from all influential groups: “That way, Putin preserved the balance.”
Once it became known that Medvedev had been left off the candidate lists, Volodin began attending meetings about committee assignments and “drawing up a legislative agenda” even before the elections, the same source said: “Who else on the lists could [be] both a public figure and a political operator?”
Another political consultant who works with the presidential administration said Volodin kept his post because of “his good relations with [Putin aide Nikolai] Patrushev and the fact that Putin has long preferred to keep people in their posts when he is happy with their work.”
A political consultant who worked with Volodin’s domestic policy team praised his “instinct for bureaucratic maneuvering” and called him a “bureaucratic animal”: “He can orchestrate intrigues and elaborate schemes, and the people involved often have no idea they’ve been drawn into anything.”
The same consultant said the speaker has no real friends. He sees the people around him as “temporary allies” or “tools for achieving his goals.”
The source gave the example of former State Duma Deputy Speaker Sergey Neverov, a longtime Volodin ally. In April 2023, Neverov proposed inviting Yevgeny Prigozhin, founder of the Wagner private military company, to the Duma. Prigozhin was sharply critical of the Defense Ministry’s leadership. In June that year, he and his private military company staged a mutiny and marched toward Moscow. Afterward, Volodin made a show of cutting ties with Neverov. A year later, Neverov lost his post as deputy speaker, and this year he failed to win a seat in the new Duma.
But the political consultant who worked with Volodin’s domestic policy team cautioned against confusing a “bureaucratic animal” with a “political animal”:
As a politician, he’s still stuck in the 1990s, in the backwaters of the Saratov region. Of course, compared with today’s party leaders — [Liberal Democratic Party leader Leonid] Slutsky and [New People leader Alexey] Nechayev — he’s a god and Michael Jackson rolled into one. But overall, he’s a pretty crude, provincial politician. Maybe that suits the higher-ups.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this while speaking with journalists, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.

Bolivia detains attorney general, government ministry says

Bolivia detains attorney general, government ministry says
Oct 1 - Bolivia's Attorney General Roger Mariaca has been arrested two days after the United States revoked his visa and accused him of accepting bribes to facilitate drug trafficking, the country's Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo said on Thursday.
Mariaca was arrested along with 13 other people on Wednesday as part of an operation targeting what authorities described as a “criminal organization” embedded within the judiciary and the Public Prosecutor’s Office, Oviedo told a press conference.
The operation followed the circulation of a video and audio recordings attributed to suspected Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastian Marset.
"A criminal organization embedded in the justice system and in the administration of a very important institution in our country, the Public Ministry, has been dismantled," Oviedo said. He alleged that the network, led by Mariaca, worked to protect and facilitate drug trafficking activities in Bolivia.
Marset was captured in Bolivia in March and later transferred to the US, where he awaits trial.
Authorities launched the operation after the release of material in which Marset allegedly referred to Mariaca as a "friend" and claimed he had paid $500,000 to remain in Bolivia and continue his operations.
The arrests come at a time of improving relations between La Paz and Washington after years of strained ties. President Rodrigo Paz, who took office in November 2025, has pledged to rebuild relations with the US, as his government seeks to secure a $1.9 billion IMF program approved by Bolivia's congress last month.
On Monday, the US State Department accused Mariaca of taking bribes "to facilitate drug trafficking and help violent criminals evade justice." Mariaca denied the accusations, calling the US decision political interference linked to investigations he had overseen.
Local media said Mariaca was detained at Viru Viru International Airport in Santa Cruz. During a live broadcast on the Attorney General's Office's social media accounts, an official denounced what he described as an "abduction."
Nearly 20 people from Bolivia, Colombia and Ecuador were blacklisted by Washington this week for corruption, links to drug trafficking or plotting against their governments. The United States revoked the visas of 12 Bolivian officials. REUTERS

Boeing engineers and technical workers approve new contract, avoiding strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:52:52 UTC
05:52:52 KST

Boeing engineers and technical workers approved a sweetened four-year contract with immediate 10% raises, avoiding a potential strike at the aerospace giant as it seeks federal approval for new aircraft and to increase aircraft production.
"We secured many victories that some thought were completely out of reach when this negotiation cycle started," said the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace, which represents about 13,000 Boeing engineers and 4,000 technical workers.
Boeing increased its offer in mid-September after the workers rejected an earlier proposal. In addition to the 10% ratification wage increase, the four-year contract includes annual raises of 4%, with an increase of up to 6% based on merit.
The professional unit, which includes engineers, voted 67.62% in favor of the new contract, and the tech unit approved the contract with 53.48% in favor, the union said.
The work groups, which make up Boeing's largest white-collar union, overwhelmingly rejected an earlier offer with 3% annual raises.
Boeing said in a statement that it was "pleased with the outcome of the vote."
The approval lets Boeing avoid a strike just as it's trying to stabilize and increase production of its fast-selling jets and win federal approval for the 737 Max 10 and 777X, which are years behind schedule.
The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it's assessing whether a software issue on the 737 Max 10, which could affect landing procedures in certain scenarios, poses a safety of flight issue.
A machinist strike two years ago halted production until the two sides reached a deal.

Spanish king to visit Ceuta and Melilla, testing Morocco ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:50:22 UTC
05:50:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Spanish king to visit disputed enclaves, testing Morocco ties after border crisis
Spain's King Felipe will visit the disputed North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla this month, sources in the royal household said on Thursday, a move that could further strain tense relations between Madrid and Rabat following a border crisis this summer.
The trip by Felipe and Queen Letizia on 13 and 14 October will be his first to the enclaves during his 12-year reign. It comes just over two months after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta from Morocco in late July.
The Moroccan government has historically opposed Spanish royal visits to the two cities, over which it claims sovereignty and which it regards as occupied by Spain.
Madrid considers the strategic outposts an integral part of its territory. Ceuta and Melilla have been part of Spain since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively.
Felipe, Spain's ceremonial head of state, has mostly refrained from commenting publicly on the Ceuta crisis since it began, first mentioning the enclave two weeks ago to praise civil protection workers there.
But at an official dinner for French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday during his state visit to Spain, Felipe said European countries should have shown more solidarity with Madrid, calling the situation in Ceuta "unacceptable.".
Morocco's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the planned visit.
Political debate in Spain since the border surge has largely centred around Morocco's precise role in the crisis. Opposition parties have accused Moroccan officials of complicity or inaction and accused Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of being too soft on Rabat.
After initially praising Morocco for its cooperation in repatriating the migrants and repeatedly denying that Rabat had orchestrated the crisis, Sanchez told CNN in an interview last week that Morocco's border controls had failed during the rush.
Morocco has denied any laxness, blaming the crossing on social media disinformation, human traffickers, and the misinterpretation of a Spanish court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea.

Most Americans say US-Israel war on Iran not worth fighting: Poll
Nearly 70 percent of Americans say the US-Israeli war is not worth fighting, marking a significant spike since July.
Approximately 70 percent of US adults in a new nationwide poll say the US-Israeli war has not been worth fighting, a five-point spike since July.
“Seventy-one percent of adults disapprove of how Trump is handling Iran and 69 percent say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting,” said the survey released on Thursday by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

The poll, which surveyed more than 2,000 adults in the US, also suggested that Americans are deeply frustrated with US President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with only 17 percent of US adults polled approving of his handling of the cost of living. Just 26 percent approved of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.
Public angst over fuel costs has surged, with about half of respondents now deeply concerned about being able to fill their tanks —up from 39 percent in July. Roughly half of respondents are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.
The data comes as Trump kickstarts his midterm campaign trail in an all-in effort to galvanise the Republican base, stumping first in Texas and Oklahoma amid widespread voter anxiety surrounding the war on Iran’s mounting economic fallout.
The poll also indicated that, despite their frustration, two-thirds of Republicans surveyed said that higher than usual prices are due to factors outside of Trump’s control, with about one-third saying it was directly related to Trump’s policies.
The sombre numbers suggest the president remains deeply unpopular nationally, with some Republicans also faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.
‘Pollsters are corrupt’
Overall, more than half of adult respondents said the national economy and the country as a whole are worse off since President Trump took office again in 2025.
In an interview with TIME magazine, published on Thursday, Trump was asked if the deeply unwanted war would threaten his party’s chances in November, to which he initially responded, “It’s possible,” before adding that “it should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
Confronted with sliding poll numbers, Trump said that the “pollsters are corrupt” and that the bad polls “are fake”, adding that he would beat anybody running today “by 20 points”.

OIC, Arab states condemn drone attack on Saudi Arabia's Medina power station
Unknown

2026-10-01

Lina Altawell
01 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and several Arab countries on Thursday condemned a drone attack on a power station in Medina, Saudi Arabia, that the Saudi-led coalition attributed to the Houthis.
The statements from the organization, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain followed a Saudi announcement that the Taiba electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque, had been targeted.
OIC
The organization's General Secretariat said it "strongly condemned and denounced" the attack.
It described the targeting of vital infrastructure and facilities in Medina as "a dangerous escalation and a blatant violation of the sanctity of holy sites," as well as international and humanitarian laws and norms.
The organization affirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia in measures taken to protect its territory, security and stability, defend Islamic holy sites and safeguard citizens and residents.
UAE
The UAE Foreign Ministry said the drone attack constituted "a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia and a threat to its security and stability."
It reiterated Abu Dhabi's full solidarity with the kingdom and support for measures aimed at safeguarding its security and stability.
Jordan
Jordan also condemned the attack, saying it represented a "blatant violation" of Saudi sovereignty and threatened the kingdom's security, stability and territorial integrity.
It also described the attack as a violation of international law and the UN Charter.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Fuad Majali affirmed Jordan's "absolute solidarity" with Saudi Arabia and its support for measures taken to protect the kingdom, its institutions, citizens and residents.
Kuwait
Kuwait said the targeting of an electrical facility serving the Prophet's Mosque was part of what it described as repeated hostile attacks against civilian infrastructure.
"Such attacks constituted a violation of Saudi sovereignty, international law and international humanitarian law, while also provoking the feelings of Muslims worldwide and threatening the sanctity of Islamic holy sites," the Foreign Ministry said.
Kuwait reaffirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying the kingdom's security was inseparable from the security of Kuwait and other Gulf Cooperation Council states.
Bahrain
Bahrain condemned "continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia."
Manama said it supports Saudi Arabia in measures taken to defend its sovereignty and security under its right to self-defense.
Bahrain also called on the UN Security Council to take a firm position against repeated Houthi attacks and ensure the implementation of relevant resolutions, including Resolution 2216 of 2015 and Resolution 2817 of 2026.
Earlier Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said a drone attack it attributed to the Houthis had targeted the electricity distribution station in Medina.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said the attack occurred early Tuesday, Sept. 29, and caused one transformer to go out of service without affecting the electricity grid.
Al-Maliki said investigation findings, operational data and examination of debris from the drone "proved the Houthi militia's involvement in planning and carrying out this act."
He accused the group of targeting civilian facilities providing electricity services to the Prophet's Mosque, describing the attack as part of what he called repeated attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the coalition's statement as of 1845GMT.
On Sept. 15, the coalition said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone it attributed to the Houthis south of Mecca before it entered the city's restricted airspace.
