Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:47:58 UTC
04:47:58 KST

Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law
New York law treats intoxicated victims differently depending on whether they willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.
New York lawmakers are renewing a push to change the state’s sexual assault laws after prosecutors in the United States said the current rules made it difficult to bring charges for an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house.
At issue is whether someone who willingly becomes intoxicated can be considered mentally incapacitated and therefore unable to consent to sex.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Epstein files: The arrests and the resignations
- list 2 of 4Alleged rape on campus sparks violent protest at Indian university
- list 3 of 4Indian university suspends classes amid violent protests over alleged rape
- list 4 of 4Why has a Cornell rape investigation been reopened?
Under current New York law, only someone who was drugged or given alcohol without their knowledge can be considered “mentally incapacitated” because of intoxication and unable to consent. The same does not apply to someone who willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.
State Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz and State Senator Nathalia Fernandez are sponsoring bills in their respective chambers that would change that.
In the state Senate, the bill is known as S10632, and in the New York Assembly, it is filed as Assembly Bill A101.
In a post on the social media platform X, Dinowitz said the proposed law would allow prosecutors to focus on whether someone was capable of consenting, rather than how they became intoxicated, and whether the accused “knew or should have known” that the person was unable to consent.
He said people who voluntarily drink or take drugs currently face significant barriers in sexual assault cases, particularly if they remain partly conscious or responsive during an alleged assault.
“The fact that someone made the choice to consume alcohol or another intoxicating substance should never be used to undermine their experience or shift responsibility onto the survivor when they’ve been sexually assaulted,” Dinowitz wrote.
The years-long reform effort has gained new momentum after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said the existing law was one reason his office initially declined to pursue charges against several Cornell students accused of sexually assaulting a woman on October 19, 2024.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe, was 20 at the time. She has since filed a civil lawsuit against seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as Cornell University and several other defendants.
The lawsuit alleges fraternity members gave her alcohol and ketamine and sexually assaulted her after she became incapacitated.
Doe also reported her allegations to campus police in November 2024.
In a statement explaining why his office did not pursue charges afterwards, Van Houten said Doe never claimed at the time that she had been involuntarily intoxicated, physically forced or unconscious. He also said she did not clearly express that she did not consent.
Any of those circumstances could have provided grounds for prosecutors to pursue rape charges under New York law, according to the district attorney.
“On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual,” Van Houten wrote.
“In this case, multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe’s statement and correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime.”
Since the lawsuit was filed, Van Houten’s office has faced intense scrutiny. It said on Monday that it will reopen the investigation and bring the case before a grand jury, which will consider whether there is enough evidence to indict anyone.
Van Houten also told CBS News on Wednesday that he had not seen a transcript of a campus police interview conducted three weeks after the alleged assault in which the woman said: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
Cornell has defended its handling of the case, saying it investigated the allegations and disciplined the accused students, with penalties ranging from suspension to expulsion.
On Wednesday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the university had agreed to her request to bring in an outside law firm to conduct a new investigation into its handling of the case.
Previous efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws have foundered in the state legislature. Senate bill S10632 has passed its chamber but has never received a vote on the Assembly floor.
“Rape is the only crime that I’m aware of where, if the victim was drunk, they may not get justice,” Dinowitz, the assembly member, said in an interview with Reuters. “There shouldn’t be any difference in terms of the survivors of sexual assault between the people who are voluntarily intoxicated and who are involuntarily intoxicated.”
New York is one of 19 states where a person can be considered mentally incapacitated because of intoxication only if they did not willingly become intoxicated, according to Elizabeth Jeglic, a professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice who studies sexual abuse.
“It doesn’t make sense,” Jeglic said. “If you’re incapacitated, you’re incapacitated, regardless of whether you consumed it yourself or somebody else gave it to you without your consent.”

The card surcharge ban is in force. Now Australians are questioning new fees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:45:46 UTC
04:45:46 KST

In brief
- Consumers have raised concerns about whether new fees will effectively take the place of card surcharges.
- Following an RBA review, businesses can no longer charge customers a surcharge for paying by card.
It took just hours for fresh frustrations to emerge after Australia's card surcharge ban came into effect on Thursday.
Consumers on social media questioned new charges appearing at checkouts online, including some described as "platform" or service fees.
Some said they had encountered the charges in transactions made after new rules came into force preventing businesses from imposing surcharges on credit and debit card payments, prompting questions about whether other fees were effectively taking their place.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) told SBS News it was "aware of concerns about businesses introducing fees described as platform, booking or service fees" since the card surcharge ban took effect.
But the regulator said such fees are not necessarily prohibited.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Whether a charge is a genuine fee for a particular service or amounts to a "card payment surcharge by another name" depends on what it covers and how it operates, an ACCC spokesperson said.
The new rules do not prevent businesses from charging genuine fees for services such as ordering or booking platforms.
However, under Australian Consumer Law, businesses cannot mislead customers about their prices, including the nature or reason for an additional fee or whether it is optional.
Businesses must also display the total minimum price of a product as a single figure, including mandatory fees that can be calculated in advance.
The card surcharge ban followed a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.
"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.
In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, consumers should expect to pay $100 at the checkout with either cash or a card.
'Teething issues'
Australian Payments Network chief strategy officer Rajat Jain said a "change of this scale is not immune to some teething issues".
Card networks like Visa and Mastercard, as well as payment service providers, are responsible for administering and enforcing the no-surcharge rules.
Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but they're no longer permitted to add them as an extra fee.
Businesses may choose to reflect those costs in their overall pricing.
"Shoppers shouldn't assume today’s surcharge ban means they'll now start paying less," said Sally Tindall, data insights director of financial comparison site Canstar.
"Businesses still have to pay to accept card payments, so some may choose to build those costs into their prices instead."
For some business owners, the changes have prompted difficult decisions.
David Bitton, owner of the Bitton Rose Bay cafe in Sydney, said more than 90 per cent of his sales are made via card.
With surcharges no longer an option, he estimated the change could cost his business as much as $40,000.
"So I've got to be clever and strategise how I'm gonna pass on that cost, without upsetting people basically," he told SBS News.
Rather than raising menu prices, Bitton said he's increasing his weekend surcharge fee from 10 to 12 per cent.
The RBA says the changes only apply to surcharges specifically added for customers paying by card; booking fees, service fees and hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays are permitted.
Concerned about a fee you've been charged?
Consumers who believe they are still being charged a fee specifically because they paid by card should first seek clarification from the business and ask for the surcharge to be refunded, the ACCC said.
Concerns about ongoing card surcharges can also be raised with the relevant card network or payment service provider.
Jain from the Australian Payments Network said businesses that continue to impose prohibited card surcharges may be directed by their bank or payment provider to remove them and could face penalties.
Meanwhile, concerns about misleading fees or pricing — including a failure to display the total minimum price as a single figure — can be reported to the ACCC or the relevant state or territory consumer protection agency.
The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.
American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.
The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.
The change applies to both online and in-store transactions.
— With reporting by Cameron Carr and Jasmine Kassis

Clocks forward or back? Daylight saving is almost here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:45:23 UTC
04:45:23 KST

in brief
- NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory observe daylight saving.
- During daylight saving, Australia operates across five time zones rather than its usual three.
Daylight saving begins this weekend in several parts of the country, bringing more sunlight into the afternoon and evening.
But the annual clock change also means losing an hour of sleep overnight, and it can take some people a little while to adjust.
Here's what to know.
When does daylight saving start in Australia in 2026?
Daylight saving begins on Sunday 4 October 2026.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In NSW, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT, clocks move forward by one hour at 2am, jumping to 3am.
In South Australia, clocks also move forward by an hour, changing from 2am Australian Central Standard Time to 3am Australian Central Daylight Time.
Daylight saving will continue until Sunday 4 April 2027, when clocks move back by one hour.
Do clocks go forward or back for daylight saving?
Forward.
An easy way to remember the change is "spring forward".
At 2am on Sunday, clocks in the daylight-saving states and territories will jump straight to 3am.
That means one hour effectively disappears from the night.
The benefit comes later in the day. Sunrise and sunset will appear an hour later on the clock, giving people more daylight after work and school.
The downside is that mornings will become darker, particularly for early risers.
Which Australian states and territories observe daylight saving?
Daylight saving isn't observed across the whole country.
NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory observe daylight saving.
Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory do not.
There are also some local variations. Broken Hill in western NSW follows South Australia's time zone and observes daylight saving, while Lord Howe Island moves its clocks forward by 30 minutes rather than a full hour.
During daylight saving, Australia therefore operates across five time zones rather than its usual three.
Can daylight saving affect your sleep?
Losing an hour might not sound like much, but changing the clock can temporarily disrupt the body's internal sleep-wake cycle.
The Sleep Health Foundation says the spring transition can be harder to adapt to than the autumn change, when you gain an hour.
Most people adjust without much difficulty, although some may feel more tired or sleepy while their bodies adapt to the new schedule.
Professor Ben Bullock of Swinburne University told SBS News how the change can have "significant effects" on physical and mental health.
"There is evidence to show that if you adjust light levels and light timing, it can affect people's circadian rhythms, their underlying biological rhythms," he said.
"And if you're vulnerable to the effects of sleep, it can have quite significant effects on your physical and mental health as well."
How to prepare for the daylight saving time change
A little preparation can make the adjustment easier.
The Sleep Health Foundation recommends gradually bringing bedtime forward by around 15 to 20 minutes for three or four nights before the clocks change.
It also suggests:
- Getting natural light in the morning can also help reset the body's internal clock.
- Getting enough sleep in the days leading up to the change.
- Keeping your bedtime and wake-up time consistent.
- Spending time outside during daylight, particularly in the morning.
- Exercising during the day.
- Avoiding caffeine later in the day or evening.
- Making your bedroom dark, quiet and comfortable at night.
Don't forget about clocks and appliances that don't automatically update.
Most smartphones, computers, and internet-connected devices should adjust automatically, but watches, clocks, ovens, and other household appliances may need to be set manually.

U.S. Energy Secretary is "quite confident" that Europe will release its diesel fuel reserves
Kyiv • UNN
The Trump administration urged Germany and France to use their diesel fuel reserves to curb global prices. Chris Wright expects positive news.
On Thursday, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News that he was completely confident in Europe’s ability to help curb the sharp rise in global fuel prices by using emergency diesel fuel reserves, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"I think positive news is ahead for us," Wright said.
According to three people familiar with the discussions, the Trump administration urged Germany and France to use emergency diesel fuel reserves to curb rising global prices, warning that the United States could ban diesel fuel exports if they refused.
"Europe can also help in this situation, and I am completely confident that it will. Now is the right time for a coordinated release of diesel fuel reserves, as we are approaching the harvest season and the heating season. It is time to put more diesel fuel on the market, and such reserves are available. I think positive news is ahead for us," Wright said.
Context
At the end of September, the European Commission said that the supply of oil and petroleum products in the EU remained stable for the time being, but diesel and jet fuel prices remained high due to a shortage on the global market. European refineries are operating near full capacity, while emergency reserves remain available in case of supply disruptions. The situation is also being affected by Europe’s dependence on imports of U.S. diesel following the abandonment of Russian petroleum products, as well as supply disruptions from the Middle East.
It should be noted that the largest reserves among EU countries are concentrated in France and Germany. According to Reuters estimates, together they control about 35% of the bloc’s relevant reserves.
Reminder

PNG's NRL franchise faces trademark fight over Chiefs name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:43:05 UTC
04:43:05 KST

Papua New Guinea's NRL franchise has been told its brand is too similar to the Super Rugby club, The Chiefs.
IP Australia, which administers trademarks, has declared there is a "real and tangible danger" of brand confusion.
What's next?
The PNG Chiefs are due to launch their brand on October 21.
With just weeks to go before unveiling its logo, Papua New Guinea's NRL franchise is yet to securerights over its name — the Chiefs.
IP Australia,the government agency that administers rights to trademarks, is yet to be persuaded that the PNG club's brand is clearly distinct from that of the Super Rugby Chiefs, who play out of Hamilton in New Zealand.
So far, the NRL has received three adverse reports in response to the PNG club's trademark applications, with IP Australiadeclaring there is a "real and tangible danger" of brand confusion.
An adverse report from IP Australia is a formal notice identifying issues with a trademark application that need addressing before it can be accepted.
If the issues are not resolved within the prescribed period, the application can lapse.
The PNG Chiefs are due to launch their brand on October 21, backed by major sponsors Coca-Cola and Bank South Pacific, which has signed the NRL's biggest sponsorship deal worth $15 million.
They are due to debut in the NRL in 2028, with the help of a $600 million Australian government funding package.
University of Technology Sydney intellectual property law specialist Sarah Hook said she was surprised lawyers did not advise against using "Chiefs" at the start of the process.
"I would have thought they would have said they need something a bit more distinctive," Dr Hook said.
"If they do launch [the name and logo], it's going to be difficult to go back and rebrand if this does end up in Federal Court."
Sydney Law School associate professor Fady Aoun said receiving three adverse reports from IP Australia was unusual.
"If the PNG Chiefs are to proceed [with that name], it does come with some risk and potential embarrassment if later, they're denied registration rights," he said.
'People will be asking which one'
In New Zealand, chief executive of Super Rugby franchise The Chiefs, Simon Graafhuis, said three decades of brand building would be at stake for his club if the PNG franchise dug its heels in and pushed forward with the name.
He said he hoped a deal could be reached with the PNG club before its launch to avoid potential confusion.
"If you have a trademark, you've virtually got an obligation to defend it, and the best time to do that is before any damage is done," he said.
While it is uncertain how the PNG's trademark application will play out in Australia, the Super Rugby side believes its standing in its home country is watertight.
Mr Graafhuis said his club's brand had legal protection that would make it problematic for a team of the same name to play on New Zealand soil.
He said if the PNG side stuck to "Chiefs", the team may be forced to take to the field in jumpers that do not carry their logo when they play NRL club the New ZealandWarriors in Auckland.
"You talk about the Chiefs and people will be asking which one,"
Mr Graafhuis said.
"We've spent 30 years developing a brand and a reputation, and our sponsors leverage off that, so any risk of confusion [means] there's a very real chance of costing us commercially."
Dr Aoun said he would not be surprised if some sort of co-existence agreement was "nutted out" between the New Zealand and PNG franchises.
New Zealand Rugby meanwhile penned a letter to the NRL last month, saying the Chiefs was not an acceptable name for the incoming team and asked league officials to reconsider it.
The ABC approached New Zealand Rugby and the NRL for comment.
Brand confusion could spread beyond NZ, expert says
But the New Zealand club might not be the only brand to take issue with PNG's chosen name.
In addition to the clash with the Super Rugby Chiefs, IP Australia also identified seven other companies and businesses across Australia, Hong Kong and the United States that could potentially object to the PNG Chiefs' trademark applications.
Dr Hook said the global nature of sports merchandising meant the potential for brand confusion was not confined to a single market.
"We're not talking about a product that's sold in one place or another," she said.
"We're talking about brand merchandising that lots of people around the world might be interested in."
The PNG club's chief executive Lorna McPherson appears confident it will secure rights to the Chiefs name, telling the ABC that "the NRL are dealing with it and the planned launch is set for October 21".
Dr Hook said that was likely wishful thinking, adding that it was risky for the PNG club to push forward with its trademark application unresolved.
"Even if they were to settle with every single company, that doesn't mean IP Australia will register it if it's still similar to other trademarks," she said.

Suspect in flydubai attack handed over to UAE, Saudi authorities say

The co-pilot who allegedly stabbed the captain of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, sending the aircraft into a nosedive, has been transferred to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) along with the captain, Saudi Arabia said Thursday.
Both men left the kingdom for Abu Dhabi after their health conditions improved and medical staff cleared them to travel, the Saudi Interior Ministry said in a statement. They were accompanied by an Emirati security team.
The flight operated by Emirates-based carrier flydubai was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when violence erupted in the cockpit.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot stabbed the captain and tried to crash the plane, which was carrying 174 passengers, almost all of them Israeli nationals.
The captain, an Indian national, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot, Netanyahu said. An off-duty flydubai crew took control of the aircraft and made an emergency landing in the Saudi city of Tabuk.
Saudi Arabia said preliminary investigations by its authorities indicated that the co-pilot, an Omani citizen, had assaulted the captain during the flight, with both pilots sustaining injuries.
The UAE government said its own investigation team had begun looking into the attack and "whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose," noting that Emirati authorities have jurisdiction because the plane is registered there and UAE law applies to crimes committed on board.
Someone in the cockpit sent out two four-digit codes to discreetly signal distress while the plane flew erratically near the Jordanian border with Saudi Arabia, according to Flightradar24.com. The first code was "7700," the universal "squawk" signal for an emergency, then "7500," which indicates unlawful interference, including a possible hijacking.
The codes are used by pilots when speaking over the radio may not be possible or wise.
Flydubai said Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members "who diverted and landed the aircraft safely." A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
In the chaos that began about two and a half hours after takeoff, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk, according to Flightradar24. The site identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.
Flydubai said crew members helped secure the plane but released no details about them.

Microsoft executive Ryan Roslansky, who led the software company's LinkedIn subsidiary for six years, will leave at the end of 2026. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, announced the departure in a Thursday memo.
"Ryan leaves the organization in a strong position," Nadella wrote in his message to employees.
Alongside other technology heavyweights, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft has been trying to evolve and make use of the rise of generative artificial intelligence. Gaming head Phil Spencer and Office leader Rajesh Jha both left this year, and Charlie Bell, the company's head of security, became an individual contributor.
Roslansky joined LinkedIn as product chief in 2009, when it was still a privately held company. Previously, he had held management roles at Yahoo and Glam Media. Microsoft acquired LinkedIn for $27 billion in 2016. In 2020, Roslansky replaced Jeff Weiner as LinkedIn CEO. During Roslansky's tenure, LinkedIn's membership expanded from 700 million to 1.3 billion.
In 2025, Roslansky took on additional responsibility in Microsoft's Office productivity software group. Earlier this year, Nadella named Roslansky and two other executives as leaders of the Microsoft 365 applications and the Copilot artificial intelligence platform, and Dan Shapero, LinkedIn's chief operating officer, became the professional social network's CEO.
Nadella noted Roslansky's contributions to the unified Copilot app, which Microsoft announced last week.
"With Copilot, we are executing rapidly against our vision to build a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task, with Office fully embedded in Copilot and vice versa! Over the past year, Ryan's team has done critical work bringing together the product, engineering, and design foundations that have made this next phase possible."
In July, Microsoft disclosed that LinkedIn revenue growth for the June fiscal year sped up to 11% from less than 9% a year earlier. Weeks earlier, Reid Hoffman, a LinkedIn co-founder, had announced plans to leave Microsoft's board, which he joined in 2017.
Roslansky told workers in a memo that he was Weiner's first hire at LinkedIn, and he's been inspired by the progress in Office around AI.
"I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day," Roslansky wrote. "But my life and my family's life are here in the Bay Area."

Google’s Project Suncatcher has officially launched to space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:31:10 UTC
04:31:10 KST

Google’s first step toward putting data centers in space is officially underway. On October 1, at approximately 2:32 P.M. EDT, a SpaceX rocket launched an experimental satellite carrying artificial intelligence chips into low-Earth orbit.
The satellite, Project Suncatcher, is loaded with Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), chips that the company uses to train and run its AI models. The mission’s goal is to evaluate how the chips fare during the launch, as well as in the hostile space environment.
The trial TPUs have already been put through their paces on land, with some of the chips subjected to simulated solar radiation and cosmic rays at a proton beam facility at University of California, Davis. In a blog post, Google said that the chips held up “remarkably well” and that the data indicate they could handle more ionizing radiation than what they could be expected to encounter over five years in space.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Along with the chips, Project Suncatcher will also test a new cooling system. Because there is no airflow in space, Google’s engineers developed a novel method of dispersing the intense heat generated by TPUs as they perform AI-related functions.
Orbital data centers are many AI companies’ answer to the increasingly resource-heavy terrestrial infrastructure required to power AI models—not to mention the fact that ground-based data centers are increasingly politically unpopular. At the same time, these satellite data centers could feasibly harness the nearly unlimited, clean solar energy that an orbital location affords. Aside from Google, OpenAI and xAI are also pushing this idea as a means to solve their Earth-bound problems.
Even so, experts caution that there are numerous engineering and cost efficiency challenges that need to be addressed before these plans could be realized. Astronomers have also criticized the plans, saying orbital data centers could contribute to the growing problem of light pollution that’s making observing the night sky increasingly difficult.
Google plans to launch two experimental satellites in 2027 to help test how its potential data centers might communicate with one another via lasers.

Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving Tennessee execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:31:00 UTC
04:31:00 KST

Christa Pike was in critical condition Thursday and receiving "life-saving care" at a hospital, her lawyers said, a day after a failed attempt to execute her in what U.S. state of Tennessee's governor called a "deeply disturbing" outcome.
Pike, who was sentenced to death in a 1995 murder, was taken to a hospital Wednesday night after she received a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners but survived.
"We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. "What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care."
The failed execution, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Republican Gov. Bill Lee to order a review and to indefinitely postpone Pike's execution and Tennessee's lone other one scheduled for this year. It also reignited the debate over the state's execution procedures, including its single-drug lethal injections.
Spivey called the process cruel and torturous, saying he was "haunted" by what he saw after the execution team struggled to find a vein for the lethal drugs. He said he counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
During the struggle to locate a vein, Pike even suggested where they might find a spot, he said.
"Please try here, please try here," Spivey recalled her saying. "She told them over and over, please try higher on my shoulder."
The state tried to execute Pike by lethal injection, but neither the initial nor backup dose of pentobarbital killed her, and she was still snoring when the execution chamber's microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt. She was later taken to a hospital for treatment.
At one point during the execution attempt, she asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way, though it's unclear if it was after the first dose entered her body, as officials don't share that information. Later, more than an hour after the process began and nearly 30 minutes after a backup dose of pentobarbital was administered, she could be heard snoring loudly.
Another of Pike's attorneys, Steve Ferrell, said she feared there would be complications with the lethal injection because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. "Throughout her life, she's explained to us that she had trouble having blood drawn," he said.
It was quite possible, Ferrell said, that the IV line didn't enter her vein properly and that the drug was filling her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.
Her lawyers called for her death sentence to be commuted, saying what she went through Wednesday amounted to torture.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to watch the execution, told NBC News "it was a mess."
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, called the failed execution unprecedented.
"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," she told The New York Times.
U.N. rights chief Volker Türk on Thursday urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," his office said on X.
"The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved."
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for a murder she committed at age 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court stopped the lethal injection an hour before it was scheduled to begin, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee was unable to complete an execution. In the other case, officials couldn't find a suitable vein for an IV line, so the drugs weren't administered.
The governor said it appeared prison staff followed procedure, but he described what transpired as "deeply disturbing."
"There are very few answers this morning. It's very early," Lee told reporters Thursday. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered."
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The drug has been used in executions in multiple states and by the federal government, but there have been concerns raised about the potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering."
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office."
Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to a single drug, pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly.
Maher of the Death Penalty Information Center said what Pike experienced is "singular and unparalleled" in that she survived long enough to be moved to a hospital.
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Executions in the U.S. have fallen sharply since the beginning of this century amid growing public opposition and concerns about the costs and the drugs used. But the number of executions nearly doubled last year behind a record increase in Florida.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.
Strapped to a gurney in the execution chamber, Pike described herself as at peace.
When asked if she had any last words, Pike said several things, including, "I'm at peace. I'm ready to be free.... This is a happy day."
But she remained awake, and at one point complained about the feeling in her arm. The chamber's curtains were closed briefly, suggesting it had been five minutes since the first dose was administered. But they were reopened three minutes later.
An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
Last May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried for over an hour but failed to find a suitable vein for a secondary IV line.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer's body.
Pike's boyfriend wasn't eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of the killing and received a sentence of life in prison. He was denied parole last year.
Pike didn't dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that Pike's age at the time of the murder, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.
"It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," she once said.

Several of the exposed journalist-operatives were particularly well known in the West and worked as a journalist for Western news organizations, such as AP and CNN

Wael Fanuna is more recognisable to Arabic speakers. He was the general manager ofAl-Quds TV, one of the main channels in Gaza. Police investigating accused paedophile's links to celebrated charity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

AFP and Cambodian police probe accused paedophile Mark Dennis's links to Cambodian charity
In short:
Mark Dennis was arrested in January as he returned from Cambodia where he had visited a property at Sunrise Cambodia.
He was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material but was found dead before entering a plea.
ABC Investigations and Background Briefing can reveal Australian and Cambodian police are investigating the former Sunrise chairman and his connections.
Australian and Cambodian police are jointly investigating accused paedophile Mark Dennis's network and links to celebrated charity Sunrise Cambodia, following his death after being charged with possessing child abuse material.
Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse.
ABC Investigations and Background Briefing can reveal the Australian Federal Police and Cambodian National Police have an active child protection investigation into people connected with Mr Dennis.
Mr Dennis was chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia from 2018 to 2020.
He claims to have visited children in the orphanage in Kandal once or twice yearly since 2008.
A spokesperson for Sunrise said it was not aware of any current investigation, and that it had been advised by police that no current or former child in Sunrise's care had been identified in connection with Mr Dennis's arrest.
Mr Dennis was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material after he was arrested at Sydney Airport in January while returning from a trip to Cambodia, where he had visited Sunrise Cambodia in Kandal.
During Mr Dennis's bail hearing the following day, Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch said police found a Dropbox account connected to at least 12 devices.
The prosecutor also alleged Mr Dennis was chatting online with at least two individuals to whom he allegedly expressed sexual interest in children under the age of 18.
Mr Kisch described the offending as "serious" and said Mr Dennis had expressed a "desire to rape" a 16-year-old and possessed an image of a boy aged between six and 10 years old.
Mr Dennis was released from custody on strict conditions, including that he not use the internet or contact anyone under 16, but was found dead in his house under non-suspicious circumstances before entering a plea or the case being tried.
Cambodian National Police head of Transnational Crime Tream, Major General Chhuo Chanthan, exclusively told the ABC in June the cross-border investigation was ongoing as authorities worked together to probe Mr Dennis's network.
"Even though he has died, the investigation is not finished since the people who are involved with him in Cambodia are still alive," Major General Chanthan said.
The Cambodia Ministry of Interior told the ABC in August that the case concerning Mr Dennis was "ongoing and confidential" and that further details could not be provided.
Two weeks after Mr Dennis's death, the AFP's child protection team retained an officer to work full time on the investigation, codenamed Operation Queenstown, which an officer said involved a "substantial amount of material", according to emails seen by the ABC.
Documents from the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, obtained by the ABC under Freedom of Information laws, reveal Mr Dennis denied in an interview with police the allegation he possessed child abuse material, but never entered a formal plea.
A fact sheet among the documents revealed Mr Dennis was charged with using a carriage service to transmit child abuse material by sending Whatsapp messages to two accounts between February 2023 and June 2025, including one account with an Australian number and username "Kanje".
But parts of the fact sheet related to these two accounts were redacted, citing the "current or pending investigation" and "communication the subject of which is under investigation by the Cambodian authorities".
Loading...
An AFP spokesperson said investigations involving alleged offending in foreign countries were "inherently complex" and the organisation worked with international law enforcement partners to "investigate allegations of serious criminal offending".
"As the matter remains ongoing, no further comment is appropriate at this time," the spokesperson said.
The AFP also said "investigators would greatly appreciate" if people with information relevant to Operation Queenstown reported it via its crime portal.
Sunrise was founded by celebrity philanthropist Geraldine Cox in 1993 when she was given land by Cambodia's former prime minister, Hun Sen, and has since supported many disadvantaged children.
There is no suggestion that Ms Cox is personally under investigation or suspected of any wrongdoing.
Sunrise country director Tracey Shelton, who formerly worked as a journalist at the ABC and was appointed ACF director in 2021, said there had been no adverse reports about Mr Dennis during his time as a visitor, donor and director.
Ms Shelton said Mr Dennis had a reputation as a "huge barrister in Sydney, well respected" but stressed Sunrise Cambodia had very strict child protection policies that apply to everyone. She said management had contacted some of the children Mr Dennis sponsored after he was arrested.
The Australian Cambodia Foundation remains responsible for managing bequests to Sunrise Cambodia, according to Sunrise treasurer Hugh Darwell, but Brisbane-based non-government organisation Global Development Group (GDG) is now largely responsible for managing donations from Australia and around the world.
A spokesperson for GDG said it had not been contacted by Operation Queenstown but was alerted to Mr Dennis's arrest at the time, which triggered a review of Sunrise's operations.
"Our aim was to ensure that Sunrise Cambodia had responded appropriately to the news regarding Mark Dennis and that they were following their safeguarding policies and procedures.
"Following our review, we have decided to continue our support for Sunrise Cambodia."
The spokesperson said "all charities should continuously assess and strengthen their safeguarding approach" and "any further information that comes to light will be carefully reviewed and responded to appropriately".
Sunrise has not published a statement on its website about Mr Dennis's alleged offending. Another charity he also donated to, Cambodian Children's Fund, publicly cut ties immediately after charges were laid.
Responding to questions from the ABC this week, Sunrise Cambodia treasurer Hugh Darwell said that after Mr Dennis's arrest, the charity made enquiries to local police and authorities regarding Sunrise children.
"After a period in which they carried out investigations, they advised us that no child in Sunrise's care has been identified in connection with Mr Dennis's arrest," he said.

====================================================================================================

The President of the Government of Spain calls for order based on "the values of advancement and progress"
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:25:00 CEST
04:25:00 KST

8th edition of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum'
The President of the Government of Spain calls for order based on "the values of advancement and progress"
President's News - 2026.10.1
La Toja Island, Pontevedra
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during his speech at the inauguration of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum' (Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has called for order to be based on "the values of advancement and progress", to prevent "others from deciding for us simply because they have more power", whilst pushing ahead with regulation to address the "collapse" of the international order and the multilateral system, economic and trade uncertainty, the climate emergency, and to ensure the responsible deployment of artificial intelligence.
He made this point during his opening address at the 8th edition of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum', held under the theme 'A world in disarray' in Illa da Toxa (Pontevedra) and presided over by His Majesty the King. The forum was attended by the Minister for Finance, Arcadi España, and former Presidents of the Government of Spain Felipe González and Mariano Rajoy, with the President of the Xunta de Galicia, Alfonso Rueda, also taking part.
Pedro Sánchez pointed out that "chaos is not neutral", because "when international law loses its force, the winner is whoever has the most weapons; when markets abandon the rules, the winner is whoever has the most power to impose their conditions; when labour rights are weakened, the winner is whoever holds the stronger hand in negotiations; and when technology advances without limits, the winner is whoever controls the algorithms". The fact is that "disorder has its beneficiaries, and they are almost never those who need protection the most". For this reason he called for order - "a word mistakenly associated for far too long with conservative thinking" - based on "the values of advancement and progress".
In this regard, he explained that "order consists of establishing rules and preventing others from deciding for us simply because they have more power, and in updating those rules in keeping with the spirit of the times", something achieved through "labour rights, the welfare state and market regulation", which, in his view, is "the very essence of democracy".
International order and the multilateral system
Group photograph of the inauguration of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum', presided over by H.M. the King. | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
With this, he said, we must "look to the world that lies ahead and the one we are in" in order to make progress in four areas, such as tackling the "collapse of the international order and the multilateral system", citing the war in Ukraine, the "genocide" in Gaza and the armed conflicts that "claimed more than 150,000 lives worldwide last year alone", seven times more than in 2002, with 117 million people forcibly displaced - three times as many as at the start of this century. "Many because of conflicts, others simply fleeing poverty. The tragedy of irregular migration reminds us of this, and what happened in Ceuta this summer is proof of it," he added, arguing that "no wall or barrier, however high or insurmountable it may be, will be able to contain people's desperation to have a better life".
The head of the Executive stated that the United Nations system is "absolutely essential" and "the best tool we have ever had - and will probably ever have - for tackling global challenges and preventing present and future conflicts", as he argued last week at the UN General Assembly, although it requires "far-reaching reform to reflect today's world", with a "more representative Security Council, more agile and effective organisations, and an international justice system capable of ensuring that crime has consequences and that there is no impunity". "A rule that only the weak must obey is not a rule; it is another form of power", he argued, in defence of multilateralism. "Today we are paying the price for unjust, utterly unjustified and illegal wars which Spain has firmly opposed: Putin's war in Ukraine; Netanyahu's war, with his genocide in Gaza and occupation of Palestinian territory; and the immense mistake of the war in Iran", he lamented.
Economy and trade
Another area in which global turmoil is at play, as cited by Sánchez, is that of the economy and trade, where he emphasised that, in the face of "years of uncertainty and upheaval", Spain "continues to grow and is demonstrating quite commendable resilience", with growth of around 2.6 per cent this year - almost triple the forecast for the euro area - where Spain accounts for 85 per cent of salaried employment, with over 22.5 million national insurance contributors, whilst the proportion of temporary contracts has fallen to 12.3 per cent. "These figures illustrate a model of success in very adverse conditions, but they do not allow us to turn a blind eye to the serious difficulties that still persist", he pointed out, particularly in terms of ensuring access to housing and tackling the housing crisis.
The President of the Government of Spain called on the Lower House of Parliament and the parliamentary groups to show "broad-mindedness" in order to ratify the decrees at this Friday's sitting, following the agreement - "the result of dialogue with the parliamentary groups" - reached on Tuesday. "I ask that we set aside ideology and party politics and focus on an issue that is purely a matter of humanity", he added. However, he referred to other challenges, such as the rise in fuel prices and its impact on the cost of living, with inflation standing at 4.9 per cent in September, due to the impact of energy prices, particularly fuel and gas. "To tackle this 'cost of turmoil', the Government has approved extending protection for families and businesses against the price rises caused by the war in Iran, the pandemic and the invasion of Ukraine, and we will do so again in the face of each and every crisis." With the third Royal Decree-law, a total of more than 12 billion euros is being mobilised, which prevents half of the price rise that would otherwise have occurred, he noted.
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, talks with King Felipe VI at the opening ceremony of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum' | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
He also criticised the use of tariffs as a "tool of coercion", despite the fact that "in a trade war, there are never any winners, only losers". In response, Spain has advocated a rules-based multilateral trading system, managed by the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which "favours the countries most in need". Within the current framework of trade negotiations between the EU and China, he made it clear that "trade and investment that bring jobs and technology are welcome, but it is imperative to rebalance this relationship between Europe and China, with 'balance and common sense', alongside 'clear and predictable rules'".
Climate emergency
Similarly, the President of the Government of Spain referred to the climate emergency as one of the areas in which it is urgent to reverse the global crisis so as not to take a step backwards, as "climate change kills and impoverishes us", bearing in mind that "Europe is not prepared for the climate emergency; it is warming at twice the global average rate, and its dependence on fossil fuels - exacerbated by wars - makes it doubly vulnerable". In fact, since the start of the war in Iran, Europe has paid an extra 100 billion euros for the fossil fuels it imports - over 3 billion more each week - a figure equivalent to a quarter of all direct grants from the 'Next Generation' funds.
"What Europe built to emerge from the pandemic has been snatched away from us by the chaos of war", he emphasised, which is why Spain advocates "relying less and less on decisions made by others on our behalf" and is therefore promoting renewable energy, which already accounts for nearly 60 per cent of electricity generation. "Sun, water and wind rather than the Strait of Hormuz", he added, particularly given that extreme temperatures in Europe could reduce European GDP by more than 1 per cent and, between 2021 and 2024, the cumulative losses associated with disasters and extreme weather events are estimated at over 200 billion euros for European countries. Consequently, he argued that adaptation and resilience policy should be "the second major pillar of European climate policy, alongside decarbonisation" and that future budgets should include a substantial allocation of resources for adaptation to the climate emergency. In short, "we need the order of reason and science, which are currently being challenged by the chaos leading to the disaster of the climate emergency".
Responsible deployment of artificial intelligence
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, greets the former President of the Portuguese Republic, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, who was awarded a prize at the opening ceremony of the La Toja Forum | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
The head of the Executive also called for order to ensure a 'responsible' roll-out of artificial intelligence, with rules that anticipate potential issues and the 'capacity to govern it'. "Yesterday we saw a photo which I personally found clearly inadequate. The US President telling the techno-oligarchs that they must regulate themselves. I believe it is a mistake to put the fox in charge of the hen house. This is not about voluntary agreements between tech oligarchs and self-regulation", but rather about "legal obligations, public scrutiny, social control, government oversight and the assumption of responsibility, including criminal liability", he emphasised. In this vein, he recalled that Spain was the first country to establish an Artificial Intelligence Supervisory Agency and has just presented the AI 360 Plan, a national roadmap focused on responsible deployment to capitalise on all opportunities. Drawing on this "moral authority to champion AI with a humanist ethos", he called for "robust regulatory frameworks" at national, European and multilateral levels to guarantee safety and the protection of human rights.
He also stated that "progress has never meant abandoning the rules; it has meant establishing rules that are equal to the challenges facing each society at any given time". "The powers we are trying to govern have taken on a global scale; there has never been a level of inequality in the history of humanity like the one we are seeing right now", he warned, and therefore argued that, "in the face of the forces of disorder, Spain advocates a Europe with a greater capacity for action", with a "far more ambitious" European budget to address the funding of European public goods (security, defence, the climate emergency, science, the CAP and the social pillar). "Who stands to gain from a world in disarray? The answer is clear: those who know that, when the rules disappear, they can impose their own", he warned, emphasising the need for "fair rules".

Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:23:01 UTC
04:23:01 KST

- Category
- World
Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace
Poland has introduced simplified rules allowing its military to identify and shoot down foreign objects in its airspace without visual confirmation, Gazeta Prawna reported on September 30.
The new procedures took effect on October 1 as Poland adapts its air defense rules to repeated risks from Russian drone and missile attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed that the military had completed preparations for the change.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
UNITED24 Media recently documented a sharp rise in Russian drone and missile incursions near NATO’s eastern flank, with 2026 recording almost as many confirmed and likely Russian-origin incidents as 2024 and 2025 combined. Poland has responded by strengthening air defenses and revising procedures for dealing with unidentified aerial threats.
Under the previous peacetime rules, Polish fighter pilots generally had to approach an unidentified object closely enough to identify it visually before engaging it. Gazeta Prawna noted that the requirement is being replaced by so-called positive identification.
Pilots or commanders will now be able to authorize an interception using information from radars and other surveillance systems, as well as data provided by Ukraine during Russian aerial attacks.
Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Operational Commander General Ireneusz Nowak had reported that the new procedures were fully prepared and being implemented.
“October 1 is always a good moment not only to begin the academic year, but also to introduce new procedures,” Kosiniak-Kamysz stated.
The changes do not require amendments to Polish law and are being implemented at the military level, Gazeta Prawna wrote. The defense minister described the new rules as clear procedures that pilots and other personnel involved in air defense would be expected to follow.
Under existing Polish law, the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces remains responsible for protecting national airspace through the Air Operations Center. The commander can order an intruding object to be shot down or delegate that authority to fighter pilots.
Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk earlier explained that the previous visual-identification requirement was designed to reduce the risk of mistakenly shooting down civilian aircraft during peacetime. Poland’s current security environment, however, required different procedures.
“Until now, we did not use this type of capability because it is usually reserved for a state of war or martial law,” Tomczyk stated.
“Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day, so we have to introduce these changes for both our pilots and the security of the state,” he continued.
Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft and activated air defenses during large Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly when drones and missiles approach its eastern border. The revised rules are intended to give Polish forces more time to respond when unidentified aerial objects enter national airspace.
Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn crossing on Ukraine’s border with Poland, with the blast wave damaging the checkpoint area. Poland scrambled fighter jets and placed air defense and radar units on heightened readiness as the drone approached the border.

Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:19:00 BST
04:19:00 KST

Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
- Published
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.
Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.
Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.
The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.
The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".
Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.
In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.
While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.
The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.
At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.
On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.
Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.
He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.
"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.
While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.
Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.
LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.
Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."
The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.
While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.
Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

Kyiv • UNN
The EU has refused to provide Ukraine with part of the loan ahead of schedule due to doubts about the deficit assessment and demands for reforms.
The European Union has currently rejected Ukraine’s request to accelerate the disbursement of loan funds to cover an unforeseen deficit in financing military needs for the current year. Bloomberg reports this, citing people familiar with the situation, according to UNN.
The publication notes that the decision followed Kyiv’s unexpected announcement in the summer of an additional funding shortfall of €27 billion ($30.4 billion) due to rising war-related expenditures.
Ukraine appealed to Brussels to accelerate the provision of a €90 billion loan intended to meet the country’s needs through the end of 2027.
The EU has become Kyiv’s largest donor since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, playing a key role in supporting Ukraine ahead of the fifth winter of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
During a tense meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU still had €37 billion available for budget support in 2026. However, she linked this to Kyiv’s progress in implementing key reforms aimed at combating the shadow economy, increasing tax revenues, and bringing legislation closer to EU standards—processes that are currently being stalled in parliament.
"We have identified resources to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and defense needs for 2026," the European Commission and Ukraine said in a joint statement released on Thursday. "We also confirmed the steps necessary to ensure the timely provision of these funds," the parties said, signaling that the EU continues to insist on progress in reforms.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive body, declined to comment further.
According to people who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of the negotiations, the EU questioned some of the figures provided by Ukraine and said that disbursing the loan funds early would only create a new problem for 2027.
It was also suggested that additional funding should be provided by other partners, including Canada, Norway, and Japan. The EU loan was intended to cover only two-thirds of Ukraine’s needs, with the remainder to be provided by partners. According to the statement, €45 billion of the loan earmarked for 2027 will be disbursed "promptly," but not before the beginning of next year; at the same time, work will begin on "identifying additional budgetary and defense needs."
Separately, on Thursday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on the social media platform X that Ukraine and its partners would henceforth "coordinate this work and align their actions every month, ensuring continuous coordination."
This week, the International Monetary Fund estimated that Kyiv would face a funding shortfall of between $30 billion and $35 billion next year, while in 2028 and 2029 the figure would be $17 billion and $2 billion, respectively (according to people familiar with the situation). These figures may change.
IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said on Thursday that the Washington-based Fund was holding active discussions with Ukraine and international partners regarding the potential size of the financing shortfall.
She said the IMF was working with Kyiv to combine the second and third reviews of the $8.1 billion financing program and planned to submit them to the Executive Board by December. Implementation of this plan depends on "obtaining sufficient and credible financing assurances" to cover the shortfall, Kozack said.

Turkish Super Lig club Trabzonspor hosted Irish side Drogheda United in a friendly, bringing together the sister clubs as Türkiye and Ireland mark 75 years of diplomatic relations.
Thursday’s match at Papara Park marked Drogheda United's first appearance in Türkiye and came as the two countries celebrate longstanding historical and cultural ties.
Before kickoff, players from both teams posed together for a group photo, highlighting the friendship between the clubs.
The first half ended goalless, with Drogheda goalkeeper Fynn Talley making saves from Ahmet Cemil Guren and Metehan Mimaroglu as Trabzonspor sought the opener.
Trabzonspor came close to taking the lead in the 72nd minute when Paul Onuachu dribbled past the goalkeeper and shot from a difficult angle, but Drogheda's defence cleared the ball off the goal line.
Drogheda broke the deadlock in the 86th minute when Shane Farrell sent a free kick into the box and Edwin Agbaje finished from close range with one touch.
Trabzonspor fans applauded the opposing team after the goal, further highlighting the friendly atmosphere surrounding the encounter.
Drogheda United won the match 1-0.
Football friendship rooted in history
Trabzonspor and Drogheda United became sister clubs in 2010, formalising a relationship built around sporting and historical ties.
Trabzonspor said the partnership was inspired in part by similarities between the clubs' crests and the historical connection between Ireland and the Ottoman Empire.
The clubs share similar burgundy-and-blue colours, while Drogheda's coat of arms features a star and crescent, elements also used in Drogheda United's crest.
According to Drogheda United, links between supporters developed earlier, while Trabzonspor fans provided financial support to the Irish club during a period of difficulty in 2008-09.
Both clubs point to humanitarian aid provided by the Ottoman Empire to Ireland during the Great Famine in 1847 as part of the historical foundation of their relationship.
A planned friendly between the clubs in Dublin on March 21, 2013, was cancelled because of heavy rain, making Thursday's encounter their first meeting on the field.
The match comes as Türkiye and Ireland mark 75 years of diplomatic relations, which were established in 1951.

Howard-era minister voted to outlaw offshore casinos, then co-founded one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:07:46 UTC
04:07:46 KST

Former National Party minister De-Anne Kelly revealed as co-founder of offshore casino
In short:
A German activist has released documents from inside a Caribbean gambling regulator.
The leak revealed De-Anne Kelly's past involvement with LuckyBet casino.
Ms Kelly had argued in support of the Interactive Gambling Act decades before LuckyBet was warned about allegedly contravening it.
Howard-era minister De-Anne Kelly has been revealed as a co-founder and former part-owner of LuckyBet, an online casino registered in the Caribbean.
LuckyBet was formally warned by the communications regulator for allegedly contravening an Australian gambling law in September last year, after Ms Kelly had ceased to hold a stake in the company.
Decades earlier, Ms Kelly had voted to pass the Interactive Gambling Act (IGA).
The IGA banned certain forms of online gambling offered to Australian customers, including digital slots and the placing of bets after sports matches have started.
Ms Kelly argued in support of the bill, saying it was needed because gambling websites were "exploiting the vulnerable and susceptible in our society".
Loading...
The revelations come from newly leaked internal documents from the Curaçao Gaming Authority, the small Caribbean island's gambling regulator, which were released online last week by German activist Lilith Wittmann.
The ABC has sought to verify their contents through public sources where possible.
The files show that the former minister was both a major shareholder and the chief compliance officer of LuckyBet when it first applied for a gambling licence in March 2024, which the Curaçao regulator's staff noted was a "conflict".
Ms Kelly's son, Ian Parke, was listed as the company's director and the other major shareholder.
Documents later filed with the Curaçao regulator indicate that the Australian company, LBC Enterprises Australia Pty Ltd, through which Ms Kelly and other shareholders held a stake in LuckyBet, was removed as a shareholder on March 6, 2025.
The change left a company controlled by Mr Parke as the sole shareholder.
The Curaçao regulator revoked the casino's licence at the end of 2025. However, the LuckyBet website is still live.
Ms Kelly and Mr Parke did not respond to requests for comment.
Regulator unaware of Australian ownership at time of alleged breach
Since the IGA was passed in 2001, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has been charged with investigating unlicensed online casinos that accept Australian customers.
On August 7, 2025, the ACMA received a complaint about LuckyBet.
Seven days on, the regulator launched its investigation. It later found LuckyBet was unlicensed in Australia and provided "a prohibited" service to customers in Australia, according to the published warning.
The Australian regulator did not have the leaked documents at the time.
"Information available during the investigation indicated that [LuckyBet]'s owners and directors were registered in Curaçao," a spokesperson from the Australian Communications and Media Authority told the ABC.
"We will assess the new information about a possible Australian ownership connection and determine whether any further action is warranted."
Minister's founding role declared to Caribbean regulator
A National Party MP, Ms Kelly was the federal member for Dawson from 1996 to 2007, and served as the minister for veterans' affairs for 15 months.
She was listed as a major shareholder and the chief compliance officer of LuckyBet in an early business plan, dated March 2023, submitted to the Curaçao gambling regulator.
The Australian company that originally owned LuckyBet listed Ms Kelly's investment firm, Calliope Investments, as a shareholder along with more than a dozen other individuals and companies.
The former minister was serving as a member of Australia's Administrative Appeals Tribunal when LuckyBet applied for its gambling licence with the Curaçao regulator in March 2024.
She left that role before the licence was approved and the casino commenced operation.
While Ms Kelly's involvement was not announced in the press, her son was open about his role at LuckyBet.
Mr Parke was quoted in a press release announcing the sale of LuckyBet to Apple iSports in June 2025. "This partnership represents a major step forward for LuckyBet and the broader LBC ecosystem," he said.
Apple iSports later filed a notice with the US securities exchange saying this deal had fallen through.
Activist says 'public interest' drove her actions
Ms Wittmann, a Berlin-based activist and freelance journalist, says she tried "all conventional methods" to determine who owned several Curaçao-based casinos that were allegedly illegally targeting German citizens.
LuckyBet was not one of the casinos she was investigating.
Ms Wittmann says she monitored the Curaçao gambling regulator's activities and downloaded "every single regulatory document stored in the system".
She says this was in the "public interest".
Ms Witmann worked with investigative journalists in Europe, including Dutch outlet Follow The Money, to interrogate the leaked files. She later released the entire dataset on a public website.
The Curaçao Gaming Authority says it is investigating a breach of its systems and "will take any further action that may be warranted based on the findings".
