Ukraine's interceptor tech outpaced by Russia’s jet-powered Geran-5 drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:16:41 UTC
03:16:41 KST

Ukraine's interceptor tech outpaced by Russia’s jet-powered Geran-5 drones
Rescuers work at a school damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Tetiana Dzhafarova / AFP via Getty Images)
The jet-black Russian munition slammed into the Presidium building of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences, an iconic Tsarist-era structure right in the center of Kyiv, setting the building on fire. Survivors climbed out of the windows and clambered onto the building's ledges, fleeing the flames and choking black smoke. Two people were killed in the attack. Around an hour later, an identical munition struck a private medical clinic a few blocks away.
The Geran-5 jet-powered drone is Russia's latest attempt to destroy civilian life in Kyiv and force Ukraine to capitulate, as Russian offensives stall and Moscow's forces lose ground on the battlefield. Small, and with a tubular fuselage reminiscent of a missile rather than a drone, the Geran-5 flies higher, faster, and is significantly more difficult to shoot down.
"The Geran-5 is a significantly more difficult target to intercept than the Geran-4, or any of the previous generation of Russian drones," a senior engineer working for a defense contractor told the Kyiv Independent, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the work's sensitive nature. "We have multiple teams attacking the problem from 4-5 different angles at the same time," he said.
"The Geran-5 flies 150km/h faster than the Geran-4, so the goal is to intercept from the front rather than the rear - a much harder problem to solve," the engineer said.
Launched at the city in waves, Russia's jet drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Planning everyday activities with any degree of certainty has become increasingly difficult through the disruptive effect of constant air raids. When an air alert is sounded, shopping malls, bridges, gas stations, restaurants, and government buildings close. Constant explosions wrack the nerves of Kyiv's residents as the sense of danger in districts once considered safe becomes nearly palpable.
Russia is attempting to “destroy pretty much the entire economy," economy minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian, claiming that air raid alerts cost the Ukrainian economy $45 million for each hour businesses stop their operations. The past week saw air raids of over 20 combined hours in a single day.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russia is rapidly scaling the number of jet-powered drones it uses in raids on Kyiv. "Sometimes, two-thirds of all drones launched during the day are jet-powered," Colonel Yurii Ihnat, head of the Air Force Command's Communications Department, told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian intelligence estimates that Russia can currently produce 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 models per month, a figure Moscow seeks to rapidly increase. Like many of Russia's other high-end munitions, both the Geran-4 and Geran-5 include many Western components, according to the Ukrainian government and independent analysis of crashed models.
Only 57% of jet-powered drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, President Zelensky acknowledged in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
The methods Ukraine pioneered and perfected for dealing with Russia's older, piston-powered drones, such as mobile anti-aircraft teams and interceptor drones, are no longer sufficient.
read also
A new generation of Russian drones
The older jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 have a delta-winged aerodynamic form similar to Russia's older, Iranian-derived, piston-engined Geran-1 and Geran-2 drones. The Geran-5's form is far closer to a traditional cruise missile, giving it a significantly higher maximum speed.
"The Geran-5 much more resembles a low-cost cruise missile than a long-range drone like the original Shahed derivatives," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
A low-cost cruise missile is a type of munition that occupies a middle ground between Russia's cheap piston-engined long-range drones, and its expensive, highly sophisticated cruise and ballistic missiles, Hoffmann explained.
As such, Russia's Geran-5 drones are more expensive than older piston-engined models, with the Chinese-imported turbojet engine alone costing $40,000. The drone's overall price is estimated at around $115,000, compared to older piston-engined models, estimated at as little as $30,000.
"The biggest weakness probably is that Russia is not yet able to mass produce the engine on its own and relies on Chinese imports," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent.
Yet, the cost of the Geran-5 is just a fraction of a traditional cruise missile’s cost, allowing Russia to produce and launch them en masse. At the same time, the Geran-5 is less destructive than a traditional cruise missile.
The drone carries a warhead of about 90 kg, Ukrainian military intelligence estimates, compared to the 480 kg warhead carried by the ground-launched 9M728 Iskander-K, which costs around $1.5 million per missile, or the air-launched Kh-101 cruise missile, which can carry a warhead of up to 800 kg, and costs around $2 million per missile.
read also
An airborne arms race
Commenting on the recent waves of Russian jet-powered drone strikes, Serhiy Sternenko, drone warfare adviser to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, said "there is currently no mass produced effective product among interceptors."
"There are prototypes that showed different results, but to bring the prototype to a large series requires a lot of effort, and sometimes it is even impossible due to limited access to certain components," Sternenko said.
Successfully demonstrated prototypes include the STING S interceptor, manufactured by Wild Hornets and the P1-SUN Jetkiller, manufactured by SkyFall, which are confirmed to have shot down a small number of Geran-5 drones.
Another promising prototype is manufactured by Quantum WIY Industries, the Ukrainian subsidiary of German defense concern Quantum Systems. Video released by Quantum Systems shows one of the company's "SPYS" drones successfully intercept a Geran-5 over Ukraine.
The "SPYS" drone is a propeller-powered interceptor, whose special motors allow the drone to 'sprint' to 600kph for short periods of time, a company representative told Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. It trades this increased speed for decreased flight endurance to intercept the much faster Geran-5.
"It's not only us who are working on such solutions," Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that many other companies also work on improved interceptor drones.
"I think that in the next upcoming weeks, we can hopefully see the results from these companies," Kruck added. "So I would say that maybe in four to eight weeks, we should see we are more controlling the air again".
Besides the upgraded propeller-powered interceptors, Ukraine is also developing a new generation of jet-powered interceptor drones. The first model, the Alexa Spatium, entered service on Aug. 21, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.
Ukraine's internal security service, the SBU, has been developing a different, delta-winged jet-powered interceptor, Zelensky announced on Sept. 19, sharing video of the interceptor successfully downing a Geran-5.
Quantum Systems is also developing a jet-powered interceptor. "We have invented a jet, a counter-UAS element, which we call SPICE, which is able to counter these jet Shahed drones," Kruck told the Kyiv Independent.
"The jet-powered interceptor design is still maturing, but Ukraine will get there," Hoffmann said. "The main problem is that Ukraine will be much more reliant on American and European partners, Taiwan, and China for jet engine imports, as it is not producing these engines itself. So scaling production will require steady and growing supply from abroad, or establishing licensed production facilities to mass produce engines in Ukraine."

U.S. Army opens permanent anti-drone test lanes in Arizona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:14:50 UTC
03:14:50 KST

- Yuma Proving Ground hosted Joint Interagency Task Force 401's Falcon Peak 26.2 counter-drone exercise through most of September, testing systems from multiple vendors.
- The event set up permanent counter-drone test lanes at Yuma and used Anduril's Lattice software as the baseline for evaluating systems.
The U.S. Army has set up permanent test lanes for counter-drone weapons at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, where it spent most of September putting systems from multiple companies through scenarios modeled on drone incursions along the U.S. southern border.
The work was part of Falcon Peak 26.2, an operational experiment run by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Pentagon office set up in August 2025 to coordinate counter-drone efforts across the military and other agencies. The exercise supported U.S. Northern Command and Joint Task Force Southern Border, and was the first Falcon Peak event to simulate drone incursions in the desert conditions found along the border.
Yuma now has three permanent lanes, one each for sensors that detect drones, electronic systems that jam or take them over, and kinetic weapons that shoot them down. The Army says vendors ran their systems through multiple realistic scenarios in each, and that the lanes will stay in place for ongoing testing involving the Department of War, military units, industry and defense partners. The Army has not said which companies took part or how their systems performed, though Allen Control Systems’ Bullfrog robotic gun turret was photographed firing at drone targets during Falcon Peak on Sept. 9.
“The range is standardizing the spec sheet for each of these three lanes. The goal is to have set standards of measurement so we all have a baseline to start with,” said Hi-Sing Silen, the task force’s test integrator.
Falcon Peak 26.2 was also the first test event to use Lattice, Anduril’s autonomous command-and-control software, as the baseline for evaluating how well commercial counter-drone systems pass targets from sensors to weapons. In practice, that means vendors’ radars, cameras and weapons were measured on how well they plugged into a common software system that tracks drones and assigns them to the right weapon.
“YPG is the first deployment of Lattice for test and evaluation purposes. There are a lot of lessons learned, especially from a test and evaluation perspective,” said David Bates, a capability integrator in Yuma Proving Ground’s Air Combat Systems Directorate.
Since the task force was created, the Yuma Test Center has served as its primary dedicated range for testing and training against small drones. Bates said Yuma is meant as a model that could be copied at other Department of War test sites, with changes depending on each site’s capabilities and location.
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle visited the range near the end of the exercise.
“We can’t assume that we are only going to face these threats overseas,” Telle said in a social media video recorded at Yuma’s Castle Dome Heliport.
The task force is in the middle of a large buying push. On Sept. 28, the U.S. Army awarded counter-drone contracts with a combined ceiling of $4.15 billion to 10 companies, including Allen Control Systems, to support Domestic Shield, its effort to protect U.S. bases and infrastructure from small drones.
“It really all comes down to fundamentals. We want simple, reliable systems that work every time,” said Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross, the task force’s director.

LONDON - British counter-terrorism police investigating a suspected plot involving an air base used by the US to target Iran said on Oct 1 they had arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
In an incident which triggered a huge police response, raised alarm among Western allies, and remains largely unexplained, five British men in their 20s were arrested on Sept 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offences near RAF Fairford in western England.
The men were later released without charge on police bail. But counter-terrorism police said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved in the incident and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Sept 30 it might have had an Iranian link.
Iran has said accusations it was involved were baseless and on Oct 1 summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue.
In the latest development, police said they had arrested the 27-year-old dual national in London while a second British man, 26, had also been questioned under caution and searches carried out at two properties.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Britain’s senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
Police launched a massive operation in the early hours of Sept 27 “due to a range of information” including an alert from a local farmer who became suspicious of the men who she had seen near the base in three vans.
However, the Times newspaper reported that one of the men had also called emergency services shortly before being arrested.
Detectives have confirmed that although petrol was found in the vans used by the men, no improvised explosive device was present.
Burnham said Britain was working closely with the US, whose bombers have in recent months used Fairford to launch missions against Iran, although US President Donald Trump said he would not have released the men, who police said were only freed under stringent conditions.
Trump previously said those involved had planned “big damage”, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the “hands of a foreign actor” in the incident. REUTERS

Putin Raises Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad, Says Russia Monitors Arms Factories in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:11:03 UTC
03:11:03 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that a direct attack on Russia or Kaliningrad exclave would immediately raise the question of using all of Moscow’s weapons, including nuclear, days after Russia previously threatened NATO over the exclave.
Speaking during the annual Valdai Discussion Club forum, Putin also said Russia was monitoring European factories that are producing weapons for Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If it comes to a direct attack on Russia, on Kaliningrad, the question of using all the weapons we have will immediately arise,” Putin said, according to translated excerpts published by Clash Report.
“No one currently has weapons like those possessed by Russia,” he claimed.
Insisting that Moscow will not attack Europe
Putin reiterated that Moscow has no initiative to attack Europe, even as Russian drone incursions, airspace violations and sabotage campaigns increase across the EU.
His claims came a week after a Russian military helicopter violated Polish airspace and two days after Estonia concluded that Russian intelligence ordered an arson attack on a defense company supplying Ukraine.
“We don’t intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, or 2050, but if we are attacked, we will have to respond,” he said, adding that “citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that.”
Yet, the First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on CIS Affairs, Viktor Vodolatsky, called for mandatory military training to begin in fifth grade, arguing that Russia must prepare its youth for a possible war with NATO and the EU by 2030.
‘A Deliberate Tactic’: Zelensky Condemns Russian Drone Strike on Kyiv School
From Sept. 1, Russia has already expanded military training for children, including in occupied Ukrainian territories, and raised the share of mandatory instruction to 50% of school time.
During the same address, he said that arms production for Ukraine remains a threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin is monitoring them closely.
“I am not saying that we are going to strike enterprises in the countries supplying weapons to Ukraine, but this is a threat,” Putin said.
In August, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as an attack from NATO itself, particularly because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
Speaking about nuclear weapons, Putin cited a principle associated with Russian writer Anton Chekhov; “If a gun is hanging on the stage, sooner or later it must go off,” he said, repeating the Kremlin’s long-standing claims that the war “was started against us.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has so far rejected every proposal for a direct meeting or a possible ceasefire.
Why Kaliningrad matters
Putin’s assurances contrast with a series of direct threats from Moscow against NATO and its members in recent weeks.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium said it had delivered a position to NATO’s International Secretariat and Belgium’s Foreign Ministry warning that Moscow was ready to deploy its entire arsenal if alliance members tried to isolate Kaliningrad.
The embassy accused NATO of an “aggressive policy” without specifying which actions prompted the warning.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance had responded to Moscow’s informal diplomatic document by reiterating that NATO is an exclusively defensive alliance, simultaneously condemning Moscow’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
The exclave Russia seeks to “protect” is wedged between Lithuania and Poland, both NATO members, and is connected to Russia only by sea. However, it is Russia’s only ice-free Baltic port, which may be particularly important due to Western sanctions imposed on Russia and its shadow fleet vessels.
Kaliningrad also hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet and has Iskander missiles with a range of about 500 kilometers (about 311 miles).
The Suwałki Gap, a roughly 65-kilometer (40 miles) stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border separating Kaliningrad from Belarus remains a big concern for NATO. Should a conflict emerge, Russian forces could try to seize the corridor and cut the Baltic states off from allied reinforcements.
Further threats aimed at NATO and the Baltics
Earlier on Thursday, Russia has also accused the alliance of a reckless course carrying a high risk of direct armed conflict and threatened to strike “decision-making centers” in member countries.
On Sept. 11, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would “disappear from the map” if it lifted its ban on nuclear weapons, claiming NATO would not invoke Article 5 to defend the country as that would mean a “global catastrophe.”
Two weeks later, Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states, the same grievance the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The string of latest threats has raised fears that the Kremlin may be seeking a justification for a direct attack on the Baltic states.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Russia could directly attack another European country, including through a limited ground incursion.
Speaking during a summit in Brussels on Wednesday, Sept. 30, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned Moscow’s rhetoric. NATO’s combined strength exceeds Russia’s, he said, adding that he does not take the nuclear threats seriously.

Ukraine war latest: Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:07:46 UTC
03:07:46 KST

Key developments on Oct. 1:
- Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
- Russian drones strike Kyiv school, key bridge linking eastern, western banks of city
- Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
- Ukrainian pilot dies after MiG-29 fighter shot down by Russian missile
- 'Returning Russia's sick war to where it came from' — Ukraine marks Defenders Day
Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1.
The September figure surpassed previous summer highs of 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August. According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
"This dynamic demonstrates the complete inability of the occupying forces' military leadership to achieve its objectives, as well as the growing accuracy and effectiveness of Ukrainian units' strikes," the General Staff said on Telegram.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The September figure brings Russia's estimated monthly losses closer to that target than at any previous point this year.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
December 2025 marked the first month in which Russian personnel losses exceeded the number of troops Moscow managed to recruit, according to the General Staff. Since then, the manpower balance has remained an increasingly important issue as the Kremlin seeks to sustain the war without announcing a new wave of mobilization.

Russia strikes Kyiv bridge for first time
Two Russian drones struck near the supports of Kyiv's Southern Bridge on Oct. 1, disrupting a key metro link between the city's eastern and western banks, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
This is the first time Russian drones have struck one of the capital's bridges.
The attack took place at around 11:30 a.m. local time, as cars and a metro train continued to cross the bridge. Videos began appearing on social media around the same time, showing a fire on the bridge and a column of smoke rising above it.
Following the strikes, traffic across the bridge was halted as emergency services inspected the site and assessed the damage, the mayor said.
As the train was passing through the area, dust entered the carriage through the ventilation system following the blast wave. Neither passengers nor the driver were injured, and the train's windows and carriage were undamaged. The train was sent to a depot for further inspection, the Kyiv City State Administration said.
Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
A Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv on Sept. 30, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine's State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said on Telegram on Oct. 1.
The strike, which occurred at around 6:18 p.m. local time, sparked a fire that was quickly extinguished. No one was injured in the attack, according to the statement.
The VVR-M research reactor itself and systems important for its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator. Radiation levels remained within the normal background range of 0.16-0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022, when its core was fully unloaded to reduce radiation risks following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. It is currently used only for maintenance of safety-related systems.
The institute is part of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences and conducts research in nuclear physics, atomic energy, and radioecology.
"The drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research was an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes," the regulator said.

A Ukrainian pilot has died after his MiG-29 fighter jet was shot down by a Russian missile whilst performing a combat mission in eastern Ukraine, the country's Air Force said on Oct. 1.

"We express our sincere condolences to Marat’s family and friends, he defended Ukraine until his last breath," the Air Force said.

Early-life sugar restriction tied to better mental health in adulthood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:00:50 UTC
03:00:50 KST

A recent study suggests that people exposed to post-war sugar rationing from conception through their second birthday had a lower risk of being diagnosed with anxiety and depression in adulthood. These findings provide evidence that early-life nutritional environments can have long-lasting effects on mental health. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
The research, led by Hana F. Navratilova and Nophar Geifman, who conducted the work at the University of Surrey, focused on a critical developmental window known as the first 1,000 days of life. Spanning from conception to a child’s second birthday, this is a period of rapid physical and brain growth. Nutrition during this specific time is thought to set the foundation for lifelong health and disease vulnerability.
To study the long-term effects of sugar intake during this period, scientists turned to a unique historical event. During and after World War II, the United Kingdom implemented strict food rationing, which included severe limits on sugar. Sugar rationing abruptly ended in September 1953, creating a natural experiment. People born in the years before this date spent some or all of their first 1,000 days under rationing, while those conceived afterward grew up with abundant access to sugar.
Previous research has used the end of post-war British sugar rationing to show that restricting sugar during the first 1,000 days of life was linked to a lower risk of dementia in older age, as detailed in a 2026 study. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that this same early-life restriction was associated with a lower risk of asthma and lung conditions in adulthood.
“We have been working on the effects of diet on health using the UK Biobank study that has data from over 500,000 volunteers for some time now, and in particular the effects of diet on mental health,” Nophar Geifman, a professor of health and biomedical informatics at the School of Health Sciences at the University of Surrey, told PsyPost. “We then came across the study from Gracner and colleagues, published in the leading scientific journal Science, that stated sugar rationing in utero and in early life (first 1000 days) was associated with decreased risk of diabetes and hypertension.”
“This is absolutely plausible, because fetal and infant nutrition is known to influence later metabolic disease risk,” added Geifman, who is also the Director of Informatics for the Veterinary Health Innovation Engine. “But what about mental health? We had access to all the data and a developed toolkit to ask the question and so Dr. Hana Navratilova, our colleague (who was a PhD candidate at the time), put in the hard miles to find the answer.”
Building on this research progression, Navratilova and colleagues tested whether this same early-life nutritional environment was associated with a lower risk of psychiatric conditions, specifically anxiety and depression. They also sought to look at brain structures and dietary preferences to understand how these associations might arise as a person ages.
The scientists analyzed data from 46,448 participants in the UK Biobank, a large-scale biomedical database. These individuals were born between October 1951 and March 1956. The team divided the participants into different groups based on how many days of their early life coincided with the strict sugar rationing period.
For example, the longest-exposed group experienced rationing for about 1,000 days, starting in the womb and continuing up to 24 months of age. Other groups experienced shorter rationing windows, ranging from about 817 days down to 270 days. The primary comparison group consisted of participants conceived well after all food rationing ended in the United Kingdom, meaning they grew up with no restrictions on sugar.
The team tracked medical diagnoses of anxiety and depression using the participants’ linked health records. They also gathered questionnaire data from a subset of participants to gauge their preference for sweet foods and their actual daily sugar intake.
During an average follow-up of about 15.7 years, 2,776 participants were diagnosed with anxiety and 3,147 with depression overall. The results indicate a protective association between prolonged early-life sugar rationing and adult mental health. Participants exposed to the longest period of rationing had a 33% lower relative hazard of being diagnosed with anxiety in adulthood compared to the non-rationed group. In unadjusted terms, 5.79% of the longest-exposed group was diagnosed with anxiety during follow-up, compared with 6.28% in the non-rationed group.
“The size of the UK Biobank volunteer population means we can find a lot of people who experienced sugar rationing in early life,” Geifman explained. “That means our study is statistically quite powerful. Technically this means the so-called Hazard Ratio of sugar intake in the first 1000 days of life links very well to anxiety in later life.”
“This is subjectively pretty amazing, but also, it is a statistically sound conclusion,” Geifman added. “We set out to this work open-minded and as objectively as possible, but the significance of the link to anxiety was highly intriguing.”
Similar patterns emerged for depression. The 1,000-day rationing group had a 29% lower relative hazard of being diagnosed with depression. In unadjusted terms, 6.69% of this group received a diagnosis, compared with 7.23% in the highest-risk group, those conceived just after sugar rationing ended. Groups rationed for about 635 and 817 days also had lower risks for both conditions, while those rationed only in the womb or up to six months of age did not differ from the non-rationed group. This suggests that a longer period of early-life restriction may be needed for the association to appear.
The associations ran in the same direction for both men and women, though they appeared stronger in women. To verify their findings, the researchers checked for links to two conditions not expected to be affected by early sugar intake, type 1 diabetes and PTSD, and found none. They also found no association in a small group of participants born in Ireland, where sugar rationing ended in December 1951, though the authors note this check was too small to be conclusive.
Interestingly, the study found no major differences in the amount of sugar the participants consumed as adults. However, those exposed to the longest period of rationing did report a slightly lower preference for sweet foods, scoring an average of 5.82 out of 9, compared to 6.04 in the non-rationed group.
When the researchers adjusted their mathematical models to account for the participants’ adult sugar intake, the lower risk of anxiety remained, though the authors note this check relied on limited dietary data from a subset of participants. In contrast, the lower risk of depression weakened and became statistically non-significant. This shift suggests that an individual’s diet in adulthood might play a larger role in mediating their depression risk, whereas anxiety risk appears more deeply tied to early-life factors.
“We think that people who look at this study will hopefully recognize that wellness and mental health (especially anxiety) in later life can be influenced by diet in the first 1000 days of life,” Geifman said. “However, that isn’t to say that those first 1000 days are fatalistic, and current food choice of course can shape one’s health.”
Brain imaging analyses also pointed to structural differences linked to early diet. Analyzing brain scans from 5,990 participants, the researchers noted variations in the grey matter volume of certain brain regions. Grey matter is the tissue in the brain and spinal cord composed mostly of nerve cell bodies, which plays a major role in processing information.
While grey matter volume differed across the rationing groups in 80 of 139 measured regions, only 11 of these regions differed between most of the rationed groups and a never-rationed group conceived just after sugar rationing ended. These differences were particularly noted in the brainstem, which sits at the base of the brain and controls basic life functions, and the cerebellum, a structure at the back of the brain involved in movement and some cognitive processes.
The variation in these areas suggests that early-life sugar restriction might subtly influence how the nervous system develops. However, exploratory models did not support brain structure as a pathway linking rationing to lower anxiety.
The findings align with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which also linked higher sugar intake to greater odds of anxiety and depression. Similar patterns have been noted in a 2017 study linking sugar intake to later mood disorders, and in a 2024 study by the same Surrey team linking a preference for sweet foods to depression. However, a measurement caveat is needed when comparing these results. The previous studies primarily evaluated adult sugar intake or preferences alongside self-reported symptoms, whereas the new study focused on early-life sugar rationing and formal medical diagnoses decades later.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the new findings. The research relies on an observational, natural experiment, meaning it cannot confirm that sugar restriction directly caused the lower rates of anxiety and depression.
“This study is all about probabilities and potential risk,” Geifman told PsyPost. “Early-life sugar restriction was only associated with altered anxiety risk decades later, there is no attempt on our part to imply causality, i.e. that one leads to the other in all cases of high sugar intake in the first 1000 days of life.”
Other unmeasured historical factors, such as maternal stress during the post-war period or shifts in healthcare policies, might have influenced the outcomes. Rationing also changed families’ whole diets, not just sugar, meaning broader nutritional shifts could have played a role. Additionally, the medical records used to track anxiety and depression largely capture diagnoses made later in life. Mental health conditions were historically under-diagnosed, and many participants might have experienced symptoms in young adulthood that were never officially recorded in their health files.
Future research might explore the specific biological pathways involved in these associations. Scientists could investigate whether genetic predispositions interact with early-life nutrition to shape mental health, or look closer at inflammatory markers in the body to understand exactly how diet translates to psychological resilience.
“We will continue with follow-up studies when more data on primary health care is available from UK Biobank, and for example, when proteomic data is available for all participants and we can explore associations with biomarkers,” Geifman added.
Geifman also thanked the study’s participants. “Just to thank all of the UK Biobank volunteers, your selfless actions are making a difference to human health,” Geifman concluded.
The study, “Dietary sugar exposure in early life and risk of adult mental health disorders: UK Biobank cohort study,” was authored by Hana F. Navratilova, Anthony D. Whetton, and Nophar Geifman.

US sanctions target Iran’s auto, rail sectors, after blockade chokes shipping lanes

US sanctions target Iran’s auto, rail sectors, after blockade chokes shipping lanes
- The US imposed sanctions on Iran's automotive and rail sectors, targeting major companies like IKCO and SAIPA to cut Tehran's economic resources.
- These sanctions are part of "Operation Economic Outcast," aiming to stop Iran's funding for war, missile development, and cyberattacks.
- The move follows a US blockade on Iranian oil via the Strait of Hormuz, aiming to disrupt Iran's alternative transport methods for goods and fuel.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration imposed sanctions on Iran’s rail and auto sectors and their foreign suppliers, the Treasury Department said on Oct 1, widening its wartime economic campaign to isolate Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department’s “Operation Economic Outcast”, which aims to cut Tehran’s funding for the war, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
The move extends US economic pressure on Iran from sea to land, targeting sectors Tehran has leaned on since a naval blockade cut off its oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
But the expanding sanctions risk inflicting severe costs on ordinary Iranians, one analyst said.
The US blockade of Iranian ports has forced Tehran to rely more on road transport and rail for moving petroleum, fertiliser, chemicals and other goods.
The Oct 1 sanctions target those alternatives, according to the Treasury Department.
The sanctions designate Iran Khodro Company, or IKCO, and SAIPA Iranian Automobile Manufacturing Company, or SAIPA.
The Treasury Department said the two companies represent more than 90% of Iran’s domestic auto market.
It also designated the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company, which provides passenger and freight services, the Raja Passenger Trains Company and Sherkat-E Rah Ahan-E Khamle-O-Naghle, also known as the Railway Transportation Company, which it said is a top private freight line.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action “directly targets Iran’s enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime’s revenue once and for all”.
The Oct 1 sanctions also target foreign firms in Indonesia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey that supply Iran’s auto industry.
“The blockade squeezed Iran at sea, sanctions increasingly isolate it by air, and now Washington is constricting its economic arteries on land,” said Brett Erickson, a sanctions expert and managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
“You cannot choke an economy like this without choking the livelihoods of the people who depend on it.” REUTERS

Attack at Mexico secondary school kills vice principal, injures three

Mexico school attack leaves vice-principal dead, three people injured
- An attack at a secondary school in Torreon, Mexico, by two 18-year-old former students left the vice-principal dead and three others injured.
- The suspects used machetes and rudimentary explosives and were detained by local neighbours until authorities arrived.
- School attacks are rare in Mexico but have occurred in recent years, often involving young attackers and resulting in fatalities and injuries.
AI generated
MEXICO CITY - An attack at a secondary school in Mexico's northern Coahuila state left a vice-principal dead and three people injured on Oct 1, local authorities said, in a rare case of school violence in the country.
The attack was allegedly carried out by two 18-year-old brothers who have both been detained, State Prosecutor Federico Fernandez said, and took place at Secondary School No. 13 in the La Union area of the city of Torreon.
The suspects were former students, according to a state government official.
According to reports in local media, the two alleged attackers entered the school armed with machetes and rudimentary explosive devices.
The two alleged attackers were apprehended by local neighbours who entered the school upon hearing detonations, and held the suspects until authorities arrived at the scene, a neighbourhood resident told local media.
"Preliminary investigations indicate that two people, who are the probable perpetrators, attacked administrative staff. A woman, the school's vice principal, lost her life," Fernandez told reporters.
He described the incident as a "brutal attack".
The federal Security Cabinet said the three people injured were receiving medical attention.
Attacks on schools are unusual in Mexico, where most violence is tied to organised crime, but there have been several high-profile cases in recent years.
In March this year, a 15-year-old was arrested after reportedly shooting and killing two female staff members at a private school in Mexico's western state of Michoacan.
An attack also took place at a private school in Torreon in January 2020, when an 11-year-old boy shot a teacher dead and wounded five classmates before taking his own life, officials said at the time.
In 2017, a 15-year-old student in the northern city of Monterrey shot and wounded a teacher and three classmates at a private school before turning the gun on himself. The teacher died in hospital two months later. REUTERS

Latvians head to the polls with Russia on their minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:57:00 UTC
02:57:00 KST

Latvians head to the polls with Russia on their minds
October 1, 2026
Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3.
Security fears ahead of elections
Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded.
In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet.
On top of that there are hybrid threats, including migrant flows that Latvia and its neighbors say are being encouraged by Russia's ally Belarus to pressure the EU and test border security. Intelligence officials of several European countries, including Latvia and the Czech Republic have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO in the upcoming "months, not years."
"There are concerns in the West and also here in the Baltic states that Russia might be trying some further actions here in the Baltics," says Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. "If you want to test NATO, there is no better place than the Baltic states."
Near-unanimous agreement on defense
Latvia elects its 100-seat parliament, Saeima, through proportional representation, meaning coalition governments are the norm. Polls currently put the centrist United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ahead, followed by the populist alliance Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and Latvia First led by Ainars Slesers. The center-left Progressives and the conservative National Alliance are also expected to enter parliament.
Most of these Latvian parties view Russia as a security challenge.
"The biggest threat is our neighbors, Russia and Belarus," says Agnese Kupca of the United List. "Our partners in the EU should understand: it is not only our border with Russia, but also EU and NATO border with aggressor."
Latvia is one of the few NATO members that have committed by law to spending 5% of GDP on defense, and analysts say the country's foreign policy orientation is unlikely to change regardless of which coalition emerges after the vote as there is nearly unanimous consensus on the importance of NATO. Which is backed by their voters: according to Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Security Radar 2025 Latvians generally have a positive view of NATO.
Economic concerns among voters
But while security policy enjoys broad agreement, the economic consequences of Latvia distancing itself from Russia remain contentious.
Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was among Latvia's most important trading partners. Since 2022, Latvia has reduced imports from Russia and Belarus by more than 90% and introduced some of the toughest restrictions in the EU on goods from the two countries. Latvia's economy has adapted, but businesses with strong pre-war links to Russia were among the hardest hit.
"This closeness to the theater of war has strongly influenced the investment climate," says political analyst Filips Rajevskis. "So the big question is how to increase the investments and grow the economy."
Many Latvians reject any economic cooperation with Russia on security grounds. Sixty percent said they want Latvia to reduce dependence on Russia, according to FES Security Radar 2025. "In the current situation, it's absolute nonsense. We can't watch what's happening and still be friends with Russia," one passerby in Riga told DW.
Not breaking up with Russia completely?
At the same time 20% of Latvians, according to FES, favor closer ties with Russia. Calls for a more pragmatic approach towards its eastern neighbor are not uncommon in the political debates.
Julija Stepanenko, leader of Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, has repeatedly argued against completely severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus.
Earlier this year, it emerged that Stepanenko has received gifts worth roughly €400,000 ($470,000) from her father, a Russia-based businessman whose company manufactures construction materials, including anti-tank fortifications known as "dragon's teeth." But despite that, her party remains in second place in the polls.
When DW met Lyubov Shvetsova, one of Sovereign Power/Union of New Latvians party candidates at a campaign stand just outside the center of Riga, she rejected accusations that the party is pro-Russian.
"Our approach is pragmatism oriented toward the interests of Latvian business," she said.
Economic pragmatism
Another advocate of a more pragmatic economic approach is Ainars Slesers, former businessman and leader of Latvia First.
During an interview on Latvian public television earlier in September, Slesers argued that transit of goods with Russia should continue as long as it is not prohibited by EU sanctions.
His party has focused heavily on economic issues, arguing that Latvia should prioritize growth and investment over what it sees as excessive self-imposed restrictions. And this approach has found support: more than 9% are ready to vote for Latvia First, which is in third place in the polls.
However, discussions about fully restoring trade with Russia are premature, party member Edmunds Zivtins told DW. "As long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing, we cannot talk about it," he said.
Language and identity dividing Latvia
Analysts say such parties may attract some voters who feel alienated by Latvia's increasingly restrictive approach toward Russia.
The appeal is not necessarily driven by support for the Kremlin. Rather, it often comes from parts of the country's Russian-speaking minority who feel overlooked by mainstream parties and uneasy about policies such as the phase-out of Russian-language school education and the reduced role of Russian in public life.
About one-third of Latvia's population speaks Russian at home.
However, the outcome of these elections is hard to predict. Filips Rajevskis says many voters are hiding not only their party preference, but even their decision to go to vote ahead of elections.
As Latvians head to the polls, Moscow is shaping the campaign in ways both direct and indirect: as a security threat driving support for NATO and defense spending, and as an economic and cultural question that continues to divide parts of the electorate.

Unexploded drone warhead removed from school in Kyiv
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv police said this on Facebook.
"A Geran-4 unmanned aerial vehicle struck the wall of a stairwell between the second and third floors of an educational institution in the Solomianskyi district. The students and school administration were in a shelter," the statement said.
During an inspection of the scene, law enforcement officers determined that the warhead, weighing approximately 50 kilograms, had pierced the floor structure between the levels and fallen onto the stairs.
According to specialists, had it detonated, the explosion could have caused the collapse of all four floors of the building. Bomb disposal experts removed the munition and transported it to a training ground for subsequent disposal.
As Ukrinform reported, a Russian drone struck a school building in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district on the morning of October 1, causing a fire.

Algeria: Upper house of parliament must reject regressive legislation expanding the death penalty after 30 years without executions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:52:22 UTC
02:52:22 KST

Responding to the lower house of the Algerian Parliament adopting today legal amendments that expand the scope of the death penalty after more than three decades without any executions, Amnesty International’s Diana Eltahawy, Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said:
“Today’s decision by the Algerian People’s National Assembly to approve these regressive amendments to the Penal Code is a devastating blow for human rights and is at odds with Algeria’s international human rights obligations.
“The lower house parliamentary vote took place just one month after devastating wildfires erupted across north-eastern Algeria between 26 and 30 August. Within days, Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the Minister of Justice to amend the country’s Penal Code to ‘reintroduce’ the death penalty for arson, warning that anyone who exhausted their right of appeal would face execution. The Minister of Justice also warned the press that the death penalty would be applied.
“The amendments, which were rushed through parliament in a process devoid of meaningful consultations with relevant stakeholders, including human rights NGOs and lawyers, introduced the death penalty for broadly worded actions such as inciting, encouraging or facilitating arson, including on social media, as well as the abduction, torture and sexual assault of children.
“It is deeply alarming that the Algerian authorities are moving so quickly to follow through on their plans to expand the scope of the death penalty. This dangerous step backwards, coupled with threats to resume executions for the first time in more than 30 years, contradicts Algeria’s consistent support to UN General Assembly resolutions calling for a moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty and runs contrary to the global trend towards its abolition.
“Algerian lawmakers must reject the amendments to the Penal Code in the upcoming vote in the Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, and halt all plans to expand Algeria’s use of the death penalty.
“While the devastating wildfires demand thorough investigations and accountability, the tragic loss of life they caused must not be used to justify further loss of life. The death penalty is the ultimate cruel, inhuman, and degrading punishment and an assault on the right to life. Instead of broadening its application, Algeria’s authorities should establish an official moratorium on executions as a first step towards full abolition of the death penalty.
“Algeria’s response to the wildfires must ensure respect for the right to effective remedy, including providing guarantees of non-repetition. While authorities have announced compensation for victims and plans to provide more resources for firefighters, they have yet to disclose comprehensive casualty figures for the fires and officials have focused on highlighting the responsibility of alleged arsonists and foreign entities before judicial investigations concluded. Genuine accountability must involve a thorough investigation into all factors that contributed to loss of life, including any failures by public officials in prevention or in emergency response procedures.”
Background
Under the current Algerian law, arson carries penalties ranging from three years to life imprisonment and the death penalty if it causes death. Although Algeria has not carried out executions since 1993, courts continue to impose death sentences most commonly for murder and have in some instances resorted to the death penalty in politically motivated trials. In July 2025, authorities already broadened the scope of the death penalty to include several drug-related offences.
Algeria is party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which restricts the use of the death penalty to the “most serious crimes” involving intentional killing while setting abolition as a goal in countries that still retain this cruel punishment. State parties to the ICCPR should not expand the scope the death penalty nor increase its application.
Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all cases, without exception regardless of the nature or circumstances of the crime; guilt, innocence or other characteristics of the individual; or the method used by the state to carry out the execution.

Forterra reveals lessons from 1,400 Lancer missions in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:50:56 UTC
02:50:56 KST

- Forterra says combat use of its Lancer autonomous ground vehicles in Ukraine led to Starlink integration and remote AutoDrive updates for terrain and traction.
- The company confirmed some Lancers were lost to Russian drones and said Ukrainian troops teleoperate the vehicles when reacting to immediate threats.
Forterra says well over a thousand missions in Ukraine have shaped how it builds autonomous ground vehicles, from coping with jamming and mud to keeping them running under constant threat from Russian drones.
The company develops autonomy systems for military vehicles. Its Lancer is a Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicle fitted with Forterra’s AutoDrive self-driving software and Vektor communications system. Forterra delivered more than a hundred Lancers to Ukrainian forces under a U.S. government program, a deployment it first disclosed in July. Ukrainian troops use them for supply runs, casualty evacuation and other frontline tasks.
In written answers to questions from The Defence Blog, Forterra said running more than 100 vehicles in combat has taught it more about durability, supply chains and field maintenance than any test range could.
The company’s full answers appear below, unedited.
Q: Forterra has now accumulated experience from more than 1,400 Lancer missions in Ukraine. Looking beyond the mission count itself, what have been the most important lessons from operating autonomous ground vehicles in an active, contested battlefield?
A: A few things stand out for us at Forterra. Electronic warfare changes constantly. A solution that works one month may not work the next, so the system has to be updated quickly. That requires trust and good operational communication with the unit executing missions. We’ve built our comms and autonomy stack in a way that can be updated and adapted remotely, and often in near real time. So being able to iterate rapidly from a remote location is just as important as the hardware itself.
Terrain has been another major lesson. It is difficult to reproduce the combination of mud, poor traction, improvised routes, and recovery challenges in testing. In Ukraine, the best results have come from combining autonomy with human judgment. That experience is shaping how we design the next generation.
We’ve also learned that just because a vehicle can operate fully autonomously, there are times soldiers want to be in control. The troops in Ukraine choose to teleoperate the Lancers when reacting to an immediate threat. Our Lancers were designed to assist and support the troops in the best way they see fit, and when it comes to contested environments such as the ones they’re facing in Ukraine, autonomy combined with human judgment will like result in the greatest success, and it’s shaping how we design the next generation of the system.
And ultimately, reliability at scale matters more than any single capability. Keeping over a hundred vehicles running, maintained, and mission-ready for as long as we have, under combat conditions, has taught us more about durability, supply chains, and field maintenance than any test range ever could.
Q: What did Ukrainian operators teach Forterra about the system that the company could not have learned through testing in the United States? Were there assumptions made during development that had to be reconsidered once Lancer entered combat operations?
A: Testing can reproduce rough terrain, jamming, or a mechanical failure. It cannot fully reproduce the urgency, pressure, and improvisation involved in making those decisions under fire.
Operators constantly find practical fixes in the field. Operators would add armor plating or reflective tape with whatever they had on hand, faster than we could respond to one of their requests, and we’ve had to build our process to absorb that kind of frontline fix. This is something the US misses in each of its programmatic efforts. It underutilizes operational assessments where this ingenuity emerges and presses the government and industry teams forward with new solutions.
Trust in autonomy is earned incrementally. Soldiers wanted to retain control in certain situations and that has reshaped how we think about the balance between autonomous and remotely piloted modes. Ukraine’s electronic warfare environment also pushed us to accelerate work on resilient communications and made clear that maintainability has to be a core design requirement.
Q: Ukraine presents an unusually difficult environment for autonomous systems, with electronic warfare, disrupted communications, GNSS interference, drones, mines and rapidly changing front lines. Which of these challenges has been the hardest for Lancer and its autonomy stack to deal with?
A: The pervasive drone threat has been a challenge. There is a lot of surveillance and the coordination of these vehicles under near persistent observation means human judgment for when to move and when to pause is critical.
So, on a go forward basis looking at how this context of the battlefield, in a comms restricted environment, gets to operators and assets is critical. The information exists, the automated behaviors are in work.
Q: Forterra has acknowledged that some Lancer vehicles have been lost to Russian drones. What have those losses taught you about survivability, signature management, redundancy and the way unmanned ground vehicles should be designed for a battlefield saturated with UAVs?
A: We have lost Lancers. They demonstrate the value of using unmanned systems for missions that would otherwise resulted in a loss of life. Some of these assets have been resurrected and repaired. The thoughts around sustainment and reconstitution on the edge are important.
I think there is room for automated defensive measures which have proved to be effective. This seems like a natural next step.
Q: Has combat experience in Ukraine already resulted in hardware or software changes to Lancer, AutoDrive or Vektor? Can you give examples of improvements that originated directly from feedback from Ukrainian units?
A: Yes. This program has been able to move fast because we’ve treated frontline feedback as a direct input to engineering. Integrating Starlink into our comms architecture was a direct response to the environment. It gave operators another way to maintain connectivity to assets executing missions.
Another example is with our mobility capability AutoDrive. We’ve been able to push updates to AutoDrive around terrain handling, traction, and recovery behavior based directly on where and how vehicles were getting stuck in the field.
More broadly, the feedback we get and our ability to push these updates remotely in response has been one of the biggest benefits of this deployment.
Q: How quickly does that feedback loop work in practice? When Ukrainian operators identify a problem or new requirement, how does that information move from the battlefield back to Forterra and eventually into a software update, design modification or production change?
A: We have deliberately kept the feedback loop short. We treat the front line as a live input to engineering, not a lagging indicator. Operators flag an issue directly through the units and program touchpoints we have in place, and it gets to our engineering team almost immediately. For software, that often means a fix or update pushed remotely within days. For hardware or production changes, it is much faster than typical defense programs.
Q: Ukraine has become an operational environment for unmanned technologies on a scale and with a technological intensity that is difficult to reproduce elsewhere. From an engineering perspective, how has exposure to this environment changed Forterra’s understanding of what future ground autonomy needs to look like?
The biggest shift has been recognizing that autonomy is not a standalone capability. A vehicle can be great at driving itself and still fail the mission if it can’t handle jamming, can’t be fixed in the field, or can’t be updated fast enough to keep pace with new threats.
We believe that “good autonomy” is less about maximizing autonomous capability for its own sake, and more about knowing where autonomy helps and where human control still matters. Ukraine has made that split much clearer than any test range could.
It’s also changed our sense of pace. Traditional defense development cycles measure in years but this engagement demands fixes in days. Any future ground autonomy platform has to be built for that kind of iteration from day one. Future systems need to be designed as complete operational systems – from autonomy and communications to logistics, maintenance, human controls, and rapid updates.
Q: If Forterra were starting the Lancer program again today with everything the company has learned from Ukraine, what would you design differently from the beginning?
A: The core architecture has held up: a proven commercial platform with modular autonomy and communications. If we were starting again, I’d prioritize field maintenance and local supply chains, recovery, communications resilience, and operator control even earlier in the design process.

Glacier in Gran Paradiso Park at risk of disappearing by 2040
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:48:18 CEST
02:48:18 KST

The iconic glacier in Italy's
northern Gran Paradiso Park is at risk of disappearing by 2040
amid the climate crisis, the Italian Meteorological Society said
Thursday.
                                    
                                       
				 "At the current rate of mass loss, it is likely that the
Ciardoney glacier will not survive until 2040," was the
conclusion reached by the Italian Meteorological Society in a
report following end-of-summer measurements taken on September
21 at the Ciardoney glacier in the Soana Valley, on the Piedmont
side of the Gran Paradiso National Park.
                                    
                                       
				The data were collected in collaboration with Iren Energia, Gran
Paradiso National Park, the University of Turin, Sapienza
University of Rome, Arpa Piemonte, and the Altra Quota
association, as part of observation campaigns led by the Italian
Glaciological Committee Foundation.
                                    
                                       
				"A lack of spring snow and, above all, the extreme and prolonged
summer heat have caused massive losses of glacial mass," the
report—released via social media—continued.
                                    
                                       
				"Over three years, 2.2 million cubic meters of ice have been
lost, representing a volume of water runoff sufficient to fill,
on average, about 250 Olympic-sized swimming pools per year."

Conflict escalation never one-sided — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:47:32 UTC
02:47:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Conflict escalation is never one-sided, and the moment when nothing can be changed may arrive very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club.
"The scale and, more importantly, the pace of the changes taking place in the world are unprecedented. We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed may arrive very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. It may simply turn out that the logic of increasingly harsh mutual responses leads to a fatal point of no return," Putin noted.
"Today, when various global conflicts are described and forecast, the word 'escalation' is often heard," he continued. "The reluctance to turn to genuine diplomacy grounded in reality and taking into account the interests of all parties leads to inflaming the situation, raising the stakes, often bluffing and crossing red lines in the hope of suppressing and intimidating an opponent and bending them to one’s will. Escalating hostilities and imposing sanctions are not new practices. This approach has been used in many conflicts, and escalation is never one-sided. Provocative steps by one side prompt a response from the other. The spiral thus tightens further, while the destructive consequences grow."

Türkiye-Ukraine free trade pact takes effect, aims for $10B in bilateral business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:46:51 UTC
02:46:51 KST

The free trade agreement between Türkiye and Ukraine came into force to establish a predictable framework and boost the bilateral trade volume to $10 billion in the short term.
The Turkish trade ministry announced on Thursday via the Turkish social media platform NSosyal that the Türkiye-Ukraine Free Trade Agreement entered into force on October 1, 2026.
Türkiye and Ukraine aim to develop commercial relations within a more predictable framework.
Customs duty regulations regarding the trade of goods will take effect on January 1 2027.
The agreement aims to contribute to maintaining trade between the two countries under more predictable rules in current conditions.
The deal, signed on February 3 2022, creates a framework to develop commercial relations in line with the joint goal of reaching a bilateral trade volume of $10 billion in the short term.
The agreement, prepared by considering the sensitive sectors of the parties, includes regulations on services, investments, electronic commerce, trade facilitation, and customs cooperation, in addition to the trade of goods.
Regulations for conducting quota-free bilateral and transit transportation between Türkiye and Ukraine aim to support commercial flows.
As Ukraine's economic integration with the EU advances, the agreement offers a framework to maintain preferential trade opportunities for Turkish and Ukrainian businesses while providing a competitive advantage against third-country suppliers.

The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police "under caution," which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions.
On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation "is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles - including possible foreign state involvement," she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.
Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets, but the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under "the strongest grip and the closest control," and British officials had been "talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done."

Government holds crisis meeting

In the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, crowds gathered in front of police lines, with one student holding a sign reading: “Can we explain ourselves without being tear-gassed?”
Students have accused police of using heavy-handed tactics, including tear gas. The government has condemned violence during some protests while acknowledging concerns over conditions in high schools.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said troublemakers were moving between schools to incite violence.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said he would meet staff unions, parent groups and student associations on Friday. He also called on schools to switch to remote classes if protesters blocked access.

Luca Sabbatucci is the new Italian ambassador to Bern

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announces that Luca Sabbatucci has taken up his post today as Italy’s Ambassador to Bern. He was born in Rome on March 5, 1963. He graduated with honors in Political Science with a concentration in international relations from La Sapienza University of Rome in 1988 and completed his military service in the Carabinieri.
                                    
                                       
				   He joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 1990; during the early years of his career, he served in the Diplomatic Protocol Office and the Minister’s Office. In 1992, he was assigned to the embassy in Seoul, where he remained until 1996, when he was appointed Consul in Athens. In April 2000, he returned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as Chief of Staff of the Directorate General for Human Resources. From 2004 to 2008, he served in Ankara as Deputy Chief of Mission. In 2008, he returned to the Ministry and once again oversaw the management of human and financial resources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, first as Deputy Director General and later as Director General for Resources and Innovation. In this role, he completed the process of reorienting Italy’s diplomatic and consular network launched by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, supported reforms aimed at increasing the emphasis on merit in human resources management policies, and promoted the adoption of innovative work methods to ensure their effective implementation. 
   In January 2019, he was appointed Director General for Global Affairs. In this capacity, he was responsible for a wide range of issues, both bilateral and multilateral: from relations with Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Latin America, to Italy’s membership in the G7, the G20, the OECD, the IEA, and other global forums on energy, climate, the economy, and finance.
                                    
                                       
				   In 2022, he served as Chief of Staff to the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, a position he retained following a change in government. On November 15, 2022, in Paris, he served as Permanent Representative to International Organizations, where, among other duties, he chaired the OECD’s External Relations Committee. Since October 1, 2026, he has been Italy’s ambassador to Switzerland.

Ukraine deploys FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for first time, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:33:19 UTC
02:33:19 KST

Ukraine deploys FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for first time, Zelensky says
- Ukraine has deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, as confirmed by President Zelensky on October 1.
- The FP-7 is a short-range missile with about 200km range, developed to enhance Ukraine's defence against Russian missile strikes.
- Ukraine aims to integrate the FP-7 into the European Freyja missile defence system, with a prototype expected by mid-2027.
AI generated
KYIV - Ukraine deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 1.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile FP-7. First combat use,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
“Thank you for the result. Next - production.”
He did not say where the FP-7 had been used in combat or against what target.
Russia frequently uses ballistic missiles in strikes on Ukrainian targets, and Ukraine has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element in ensuring its defence needs after four and a half years of conflict with Moscow.
The need for effective interception of ballistic missiles has intensified as Kyiv prepares for an expected sustained Russian assault in the coming winter. Ukraine’s missile production is well behind that of Russia.
Zelensky praised the test results of tactical ballistic missiles earlier in 2026, saying they showed good potential for their use by the military.
Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km.
The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme Freyja launched in 2026.
Military analysts have likened the FP-7 to the US Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACMS, some of which have already been transferred to Ukraine. But the FP-7, which has undergone accelerated development to counter the Russian threat, is considerably cheaper.
Fire Point is also developing a FP-9 missile with a range of up to 850km, which company officials say should be ready by the end of 2026.
Analysts suggest that deployment of both missiles would enable Ukraine to strike Russian missile launch and production sites and apply pressure on Moscow’s war infrastructure.
Ukraine and key Western allies announced an air defence coalition in July to proceed with the Freyja project that aims to jointly develop a cheaper alternative to the US Patriot system.
Ukraine wants a prototype for the Freyja European anti-ballistic system to be ready in the first half of 2027, Davyd Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council said in July. REUTERS

Failed Christa Pike execution ‘a tragedy’, says Tennessee governor, as inmate survives two lethal injections
- Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called the failed execution of Christa Pike a tragedy and ordered a suspension of executions with a third-party review after she survived two lethal injections.
- Pike, sentenced for a 1995 murder committed as a teenager, endured "unnecessary agony" during the botched execution using a new one-drug protocol, highlighting issues with lethal injections.
- The incident sparked criticism from the UN and renewed debate on the death penalty, as most countries have abolished it due to its cruel and inhumane nature.
AI generated
NASHVILLE - Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called the failed execution of Christa Pike a tragedy on Oct 1, hours after she survived two lethal injection attempts at a Nashville prison and was taken to a hospital.
“There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen,” Lee, a Republican, told reporters.
“It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better, and we’re going to make sure that happens.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in the 1990s after a jury convicted her of a murder she carried out as a teenager.
Her botched execution on Sept 30 at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, the second this year in Tennessee, highlights the difficulties US states face in carrying out lethal injections.
Tennessee switched to a one-drug lethal injection protocol using pentobarbital, a powerful barbiturate, in 2024. Prison officials injected two syringes into Pike, her lawyers said in a late-night court filing, causing her “unnecessary agony” but not killing her.
The Tennessee Department of Corrections said the execution was halted, and she was taken away in an ambulance, but her condition was unclear on Oct 1.
She would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
Lee told reporters that it was unclear what went wrong. He said he had no update on Pike’s condition and had not spoken with her family.
After the botched execution, he ordered a suspension of scheduled executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year and a third-party review of the Sept 30 failed attempt.
Most countries in the world have abolished the death penalty, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said Pike’s case showed that the US should follow suit.
“The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel,” Turk said, in a statement on X.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and a third companion lured Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted of first-degree murder.
Pike’s lawyers and supporters tried unsuccessfully to halt Pike’s execution by pointing to her young age at the time of the crime, her history of childhood sexual abuse and untreated mental illness.
The US Supreme Court threw out an 11th-hour stay on Sept 30 issued by a lower court.
Tennessee halted the execution of convicted murderer Tony Carruthers in May after prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines to administer the lethal drugs. REUTERS
