Flydubai heroes say attacker begged ‘Kill me’ after passengers overpowered him in cockpit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:23:40 UTC
00:23:40 KST

Yaniv Hayun, the Israeli plumber who helped stabilize the Flydubai aircraft after passengers stormed the cockpit, is still struggling to process the midair drama and his unexpected place among its heroes.
“We should celebrate a birthday on this day,” he said Thursday at his home in Ness Ziona after learning that he would receive the city’s Hero Award for his actions. “All the passengers said, ‘We were born again.’”
New footage shows the stabbed Indian pilot receiving treatment, while the attacking pilot is seen restrained:
Later Thursday, Hayun met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the second time. Netanyahu hosted several of the flight’s other rescuers at his office, including Dr. Shota Musaev, who treated the wounded Indian captain, Musaev’s wife Sigalit and Or Pradilov. “The whole world is seeing Israeli heroism,” Netanyahu told them.
He announced that the four would light a torch honoring civilian heroism at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony, which is still about six months away. The composition of Israel’s government, and who will lead it by then, remains uncertain.
Netanyahu said the passengers had acted “with supreme courage, resourcefulness and faith” to prevent a major disaster and save many lives. “I tell the citizens of Israel to learn from you, keep your eyes open and remain vigilant,” he said. “We are in a very sensitive period. Our enemies intend to harm us.”
During the meeting, the passengers offered new details about the moments after they subdued the Omani co-pilot. “We tied the stabbing pilot up with the headphone cord,” they told Netanyahu. “He said, ‘Kill me.’ That means he had failed in his mission and preferred to die.”
‘There was blood everywhere’
Musaev, who treated Capt. Smit Machchhar after he was stabbed during the cockpit struggle, described the scene he encountered. “I saw the terrorist was injured. On the floor, I saw a lot of blood,” he said. “It was the pilot’s blood. We don’t know, maybe he was injured too, the terrorist, but not like the pilot. Everything was cut, his hands, his head, everything. Really deep wounds.”
Musaev said his attention then turned to stopping the bleeding. “I was constantly checking his pulse and seeing what condition he was in,” he said.
The passengers said the most dramatic moments lasted only seconds. “In the end, I came up with the idea of tying him up with the headphone cord, and we tied him because we had no other option,” Musaev said. “Only afterward did they bring us zip ties. The only thing in my head was somehow tying him down so he couldn’t start going wild again.”
Earlier Thursday, Ness Ziona Mayor Shmuel Boxer visited Hayun at home and told him he would receive the city’s Hero Award. Hayun, visibly uncomfortable with the attention, responded: “That will be too much.”
“Why is it too much?” Boxer replied. “You saved dozens of lives. You saved three families from Ness Ziona who were on that plane, and the entire country is thanking you.”
Among previous recipients of the city honor is retired Brig. Gen. Avigdor Kahalani, one of Israel’s best-known heroes of the 1973 Yom Kippur War and one of the few soldiers to receive both the Medal of Valor and the Medal of Distinguished Service.
Hayun said he was not sure what he had done could be called courage. “In moments like that, you operate automatically,” he said.
Boxer said that when he first heard what had happened, he wondered about Hayun’s military background. “Those are actions that come with experience and background,” he said. “To function like that isn’t natural. It’s inconceivable.”
Hayun’s wife, Meital, said people kept asking what her husband did for a living. “I told them, ‘He unclogs sewers,’” she said.
The couple recalled the moments when they felt the aircraft suddenly descending. “At first we thought it was turbulence,” they said. “The plane shook a little at first. Something crazy.”
“This isn’t a joke. It’s a historic event,” Hayun added. “When you think about it, it’s unbelievable.”
He returned to the same thought that had stayed with him since the flight landed safely. “This should be the passengers’ birthday,” he said. “We were all born again.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, was among the Israelis who overpowered the Omani co-pilot alongside Tzvika Mans and Assaf Reguan.
He also responded Thursday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks about his role in the incident. Trump had described Hayun as an Israeli plumber with virtually no aviation experience who recognized what was happening and acted.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with filthy pipes, and he was right. It didn’t offend me.”
Hayun said all he wanted now was to return to his normal life. “In my wildest dreams, I never thought Trump would talk about me and refer to what I did,” he said. “I actually like his humor. The way he described it was funny.”
“I’m no Bruce Lee,” he added. “But I managed to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis, pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Netanyahu admits Flydubai security ‘loophole’
Separately, Netanyahu acknowledged in a Fox News interview that the incident had exposed a loophole in the security procedures governing pilots operating flights to Israel.
“The first thing is you want a background check on pilots,” Netanyahu said. “Even if you have metal detectors, they’re usually for the passengers, and it’s quite possible that pilots just don’t go through that. So obviously, that’s a loophole that has to be corrected.”
Netanyahu also said the Omani co-pilot had undergone radicalization. “We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” he said.
Meanwhile, Indian media reported that Machchhar, the Indian captain attacked in the cockpit, apparently with an emergency axe, had been transferred from Saudi Arabia to Dubai for further medical treatment.
The government of Gujarat announced that it would honor Machchhar for his actions. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised his “unwavering courage,” saying the captain’s actions helped save the lives of the passengers.

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:23:32 UTC
00:23:32 KST

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
- SpaceX launched its 13th long-duration astronaut crew to the International Space Station, carrying two US astronauts, one Canadian, and one Russian for a mission on human health in orbit.
- The Falcon 9 rocket successfully delivered the Crew Dragon capsule into orbit, with a reusable booster returning safely to Earth after launch from Cape Canaveral.
- Crew 13 will conduct biomedical studies on microgravity's effects and join seven ISS occupants, continuing research aboard the US-Russian-led space station operating since 1998 and planned until 2030.
AI generated
CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida - A SpaceX rocket lifted off from Florida on Oct 1 with a crew of two US astronauts, a Canadian astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut headed to the International Space Station (ISS) for a science mission devoted to human health and performance in orbit.
The two-stage Falcon 9 rocket, topped with an autonomously operated Crew Dragon capsule carrying the four-member crew, was launched from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, along Florida’s Atlantic Coast.
A live webcast showed the 25-storey-tall rocket thundering off the launch pad as its nine Merlin engines roared to life in billowing, incandescent plumes of vapour.
Falcon 9’s reusable lower-stage booster separated from the rest of the vehicle within three minutes of launch and flew itself back to Earth for a return landing.
The rocket’s upper stage climbed higher and released into orbit the Crew Dragon carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
“Dragon separation confirmed. Jessica, Luke, Josh, Sergey, welcome to orbit,” SpaceX mission control in Hawthorne, California, told the crew.
The capsule is thrusting itself along an eight-hour orbital voyage to the space station and is set to dock with the orbiting laboratory platform some 400km above Earth around 7pm EDT (7am on Oct 2 in Singapore).
The mission marks the 13th long-duration space station team that NASA has flown aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle since the rocket venture founded in 2002 by Elon Musk began sending US astronauts to orbit in May 2020. The company went public in a record-breaking IPO in July.
The launch also comes days after SpaceX launched its next-generation Starship spacecraft on its first trip to orbit and first commercial satellite deployment, marking the vehicle’s 14th uncrewed test flight since 2023.
Crew 13 is led by geologist-turned-astronaut Watkins, 38, making her second voyage to space and becoming the first NASA astronaut to fly twice aboard a Crew Dragon.
Seated beside her in the pilot’s chair is Delaney, 47, a former test pilot and fighter pilot making his debut in space.
Rounding out Crew 13 are two other spaceflight rookies ranked as mission specialists - Kutryk, 44, a former test and fighter pilot, and Teteryatnikov, 37, an engineer who specialised in the operation of submarines.
The four crewmates are to be welcomed aboard the space station by seven current occupants of the orbital outpost, including the four members of Crew 12 who are due to fly back to Earth as soon as their seven-month-plus mission comes to an end.
The latest arrivals are expected to focus their attention on a series of biomedical and human performance studies, including research on how microgravity affects blood circulation and clotting, and gathering health data to inform future space missions.
The ISS, which spans the length of a football field and ranks as the largest human-made object in space, has been continuously operated by a US-Russian-led consortium that includes Canada, Japan and 11 European countries.
The first hardware for the outpost was launched more than a quarter-century ago. NASA has said it is committed to keeping the space station operating through 2030. REUTERS

“Dragon separation confirmed. Jessica, Luke, Josh, Sergey, welcome to orbit,” SpaceX mission control in Hawthorne, California, told the crew.
The capsule is thrusting itself along an eight-hour orbital voyage to the space station and is set to dock with the orbiting laboratory platform some 400km above Earth around 7pm EDT (7am on Oct 2 in Singapore).
The mission marks the 13th long-duration space station team that NASA has flown aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle since the rocket venture founded in 2002 by Elon Musk began sending US astronauts to orbit in May 2020. The company went public in a record-breaking IPO in July.
The launch also comes days after SpaceX launched its next-generation Starship spacecraft on its first trip to orbit and first commercial satellite deployment, marking the vehicle’s 14th uncrewed test flight since 2023.
Crew 13 is led by geologist-turned-astronaut Watkins, 38, making her second voyage to space and becoming the first NASA astronaut to fly twice aboard a Crew Dragon.
Seated beside her in the pilot’s chair is Delaney, 47, a former test pilot and fighter pilot making his debut in space.
Rounding out Crew 13 are two other spaceflight rookies ranked as mission specialists - Kutryk, 44, a former test and fighter pilot, and Teteryatnikov, 37, an engineer who specialised in the operation of submarines.
The four crewmates are to be welcomed aboard the space station by seven current occupants of the orbital outpost, including the four members of Crew 12 who are due to fly back to Earth as soon as their seven-month-plus mission comes to an end.
The latest arrivals are expected to focus their attention on a series of biomedical and human performance studies, including research on how microgravity affects blood circulation and clotting, and gathering health data to inform future space missions.
The ISS, which spans the length of a football field and ranks as the largest human-made object in space, has been continuously operated by a US-Russian-led consortium that includes Canada, Japan and 11 European countries.
The first hardware for the outpost was launched more than a quarter-century ago. NASA has said it is committed to keeping the space station operating through 2030. REUTERS

IMF aims to bring combined second and third EFF reviews for Ukraine to Executive Board by December
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:22:08 EEST
00:22:08 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) continues constructive engagement and discussions with the Ukrainian authorities and its donors on the provision of further financing and aims to bring the combined second and third reviews of Ukraine's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program to the Executive Board for consideration by December this year.
"The staff is working to bring the issue of the combined second and third reviews of the program to the Executive Board for consideration by December," IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said at a briefing on Thursday.
She recalled that the IMF completed the first review of the four-year program approved at the end of February this year in July. Its mission then visited Ukraine, concluding its visit on September 2. More recently, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva held a bilateral meeting with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and with Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko in Dublin during an ECOFIN meeting.
"Bringing this issue to the Board for consideration depends on receiving sufficient and reliable financing assurances to cover the projected financing gap on terms consistent with ensuring Ukraine's debt sustainability," Kozack said.
Regarding the potential size of the financing gap, she again referred to active discussions with the Ukrainian authorities and their international partners, but was unable to provide specific figures.
"The aim of these discussions is to confirm Ukraine's financing needs and obtain the financing assurances needed to complete the program reviews in a timely manner. Regarding the period after 2026, the specific size of the financing gap will depend, and this is very important, on the course of the war, implementation of reforms by the authorities, the economic situation and continued support from Ukraine's international partners," the IMF spokesperson stressed.
Marchenko said last week that an IMF mission to review the EFF program is expected in November, and that by then it would be desirable to obtain confirmation of all sources of the $52.6 billion in external financing for the state budget in 2027. He recalled that about $32.6 billion of this amount still requires additional confirmation.
According to Marchenko, Kyiv expects the European Union to fulfill its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's external financing needs next year as well, which would mean an increase of about $17.5 billion in confirmed financing. As for the remaining approximately $15 billion, the minister said there are a number of potential sources of financing, including bilateral financing and guarantees, as well as programs with international financial institutions.
He also said work is underway on the possibility of increasing financing through frozen Russian assets, for example by transferring them from Belgian jurisdiction to EU jurisdiction and placing them in higher-yielding instruments, although no ready-made solutions are currently available.
Marchenko stressed the critical importance of Ukraine fulfilling its commitments both for reaching an agreement on new financing and for receiving financing already agreed. He said the domestic political agenda in EU countries and the results of elections in partner countries that have already taken place or are expected to take place have a serious impact on the course of negotiations. At the same time, the minister said the government is determined to fulfill all its commitments and hopes to receive support from the Verkhovna Rada.
As reported, in February 2026 the IMF Executive Board approved a new four-year EFF program for Ukraine worth $8.1 billion for 2026-2029. In July, the Fund completed the first review of the program and disbursed a second tranche of about $690 million, bringing total financing received under the new program to $2.2 billion.
At the same time, deadlines for implementing some of the program's structural benchmarks were missed. Following the first review, the updated EFF program was supplemented with eight structural benchmarks, seven of them fiscal.
Under the second review, Ukraine was scheduled to receive SDR 0.50 billion (about $0.7 billion), while the third review, scheduled under the program for the end of the year, was to provide SDR 0.70 billion (about $0.95 billion).

Ukrainian Сompany SkyFall Presents Thor Hammer Strike Drone in Two Versions—With Ranges of 350 and 600 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:21:05 UTC
00:21:05 KST

Ukrainian defense company SkyFall has unveiled its new Thor Hammer middle-strike drone in two versions.
The company shared details about the new strike UAV’s specifications with Militarnyi.
Currently, the Thor Hammer is available in two main variants—with ranges of up to 350 and up to 600 km.
The drone is already being used on the front lines. It can carry a 40–50 kg payload and reach speeds of up to 180 km/h. Depending on the configuration, the cost of a single unit ranges from 25,000 to 30,000 dollars.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that SkyFall had already tested a new middle-strike class attack drone on the front lines. At that time, its name had not yet been disclosed.
The Thor Hammer has a wingspan of 3.5 meters, a length of 3 meters, and a maximum flight altitude of 4,000 meters. The drone can be equipped with a daytime or thermal imaging camera, and the system’s deployment time is approximately 18 minutes.
To engage targets, the system is designed to use fragmentation, high-explosive fragmentation, and other types of warheads. Launch is carried out via a catapult or a rocket booster.
This configuration allows the Thor Hammer to be deployed from both fixed positions and mobile launchers mounted on trucks or other vehicles. This makes it possible to quickly change position after launch.
Depending on the mission, the drone can be equipped with Starlink or other secure communication channels. The navigation system combines satellite, inertial, and backup positioning, which is designed to ensure continued flight even under active electronic warfare conditions.
Thor Hammer autonomously follows a predetermined route and transmits video in real time. As it approaches the target, the system alerts the operator, who makes the final decision on engagement.
After target confirmation, the drone uses artificial intelligence and computer vision algorithms to automatically adjust its flight path. According to SkyFall, guidance can continue even after complete loss of radio or video communication.
The Thor Hammer’s key electronics are developed in-house by SkyFall. At the same time, the company’s R&D team is working on developing its own engines for middle-strike-class drones.
The drone is also integrated with SkyFall’s remote control system, which allows it to be operated from a remote location. The company provides mass production of the systems, proprietary software, training for operators and technical specialists, as well as round-the-clock service support.
By the end of the year, SkyFall plans to increase production capacity to 5,000 Thor Hammer drones per month. At the same time, the company is working on a new variant with a flight range of over 1,000 km.
SkyFall is also developing P1-SUN interceptor drones. In September, one of them destroyed a Russian Geran-5 jet drone during combat operations.

Greece: Human rights defenders Tommy Olsen and Panayote Dimitras on trial for their work supporting refugees and migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Ahead of the trial of human rights defenders Tommy Olsen and Panayote Dimitras on 6 October in Rhodes on charges relating to their work in support of refugees and migrants Dinushika Dissanayake, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe said:
“The criminal charges against Panayote Dimitras and Tommy Olsen are a gross misuse of anti-smuggling legislation and are not backed by evidence. Both are being targeted for their work documenting serious human rights violations against migrants and refugees.
“The Greek authorities have a long-standing record of going after human rights defenders and criminalizing human rights work, but this is a new low. For the first time, human rights workers are being referred to trial for helping people access asylum procedures. Construing this as ‘smuggling’ is not only a distortion of international and domestic law but a dangerous vilification of NGOs’ valuable work.”
In July 2021, Dimitras and Olsen were supporting people seeking asylum on the island of Kos including helping them to access the asylum procedure. They also documented and reported cases of pushbacks by the Greek authorities – the illegal and often violent practice of summarily returning people across borders, a practice that Greece has been found guilty of by the European Court of Human Rights.
The authorities accuse Dimitras and Olsen of establishing and participating in a criminal organization and jointly facilitating the “unlawful entry” and “unlawful stay” of third country nationals in Greece. Based on information available to Amnesty International, there is no indication that Dimitras’ and Olsen’s work went beyond the legitimate activities of assisting people in legally exercising their human rights and documenting the situation.
If convicted they face up to 20 years in prison.
Tommy Olsen said: “When human rights defenders face criminal prosecution for documenting what happens at Europe’s borders, while pushbacks and other serious human rights violations continue with impunity, it sends a powerful message to everyone doing this work: stay silent, or risk becoming the accused yourself.”
Panayote Dimitras said: “This prosecution had the sole aim to harass us and severely limit our work documenting human rights violations at Greece’s borders. It has left me stigmatized and has prevented me from travelling abroad to continue our human rights advocacy at an international level for more than three years.”
“The charges brought against Olsen and Dimitras send an alarming message that supporting people in need of protection to exercise their rights can be misconstrued as complicity in smuggling. This doesn’t just harm refugees and migrants who have undertaken dangerous journeys at sea, as it discourages the provision of assistance, but has a chilling effect on civil society a whole,” said Dinushika Dissanayake from Amnesty International.
Background
Tommy Olsen is a Norwegian human rights worker who founded the NGO Aegean Boat Report in 2017 to monitor arrivals to the Greek islands and document rights violations. Panayote Dimitras is the legal administrator and representative of the NGO Greek Helsinki Monitor, an organization that documents racist violence and racist speech including pushbacks of asylum seekers by Greek law enforcement officers at borders.
Since 2023, the Greek authorities have imposed extremely onerous pretrial measures on Dimitras, including a ban on leaving the country, a duty to regularly report to the police station, and a bail payment of €10,000.
Tommy Olsen is currently living in Norway. Earlier in the year, Norway’s authorities rejected an extradition request from Greece, finding that the actions for which Olsen had been prosecuted in Greece are not illegal in Norway and represented a real risk for Olsen’s right to freedom of expression.
Amnesty International has repeatedly highlighted shortcomings in Greek anti-smuggling laws, noting that the legislation is based on broad and vague language, and does not adequately protect human rights defenders and humanitarian actors from criminal prosecution.

- Amnesty International: Europe: Punishing compassion: Solidarity on trial in Fortress Europe

US jobless claims fall to lowest since mid-July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US jobless claims fall to lowest since mid-July
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices
The number of people applying for US unemployment benefits dipped last week to the lowest level since mid-July as lay-offs remain low and most American workers enjoy job security.
The Labor Department said on Thursday that initial jobless claims ticked down to 197,000 from a revised 198,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped by 2,500 to 200,000.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for lay-offs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have mostly stayed below 220,000 – historically low.
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began February 28.

Why Are Modi Government Critics Now Targeting India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

“You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
“Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office.
Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago.
Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust.
The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders.
Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.
The opposition’s challenge to the law has not made much progress in the Supreme Court yet, with a five-judge constitutional bench expected to start hearing it.
The Indian Express report dropped like a political bombshell. Opposition parties jumped in to claim that the report vindicates what they have been alleging for a long time: that the BJP government is using Chief Election Commissioner Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP, starting with the voter roll.
Trying to downplay the internal rift, the commission’s reply was measured: differences are normal in any institution. Despite the concerns raised at different stages, the final decisions were unanimous, the commission said.
Its defense has not calmed the room. The Indian Express disclosures landed amid the highly contested overhaul of the voter roll, the Special Intensive Revision, which has removed millions of names from the electoral rolls. Several opposition leaders and civil society personalities, including Rahul Gandhi of the Congress, India’s main opposition party, have alleged that the electoral roll revision process is being used to steal votes.
A dispute inside a constitutional body has thus become evidence, for opponents, not only of a wider institutional failure, but also of “sabotage” of an institution that is most critical for the smooth functioning of an electoral democracy.
The CJP, a youth movement that spearheaded the July agitation, moved quickly. “Gyanesh, it’s done bro,” CJP leader Abhijit Dipke wrote on social media the day the Indian Express report was published. The CJP gave Kumar 48 hours to quit. In the national capital of New Delhi, the Jantar Mantar premises, the site of the June-July protests, were heavily barricaded on September 25 as organizations and activists, mostly leftists, marched. Several protesters were detained.
Opposition parties echoed the demand for Kumar’s resignation, accusing him of sidelining his fellow commissioners. Kumar, as expected, did not oblige.
Therefore, protests are expected in different parts of the country over the coming days, some led by the CJP, some by opposition parties. Over the past few days, Congress workers demonstrated in different states, with a rally outside the Election Commission’s office in the national capital.
The tension can perhaps be sensed from the fact that after some Congress workers defaced the gates and walls of Kumar’s residence in the BJP-ruled north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, police booked them under charges of attempt to murder.
While Kumar is the visible immediate target, the movement’s demands go further than one man’s exit. The CJP and opposition parties also want the entire SIR exercise to be scrapped. Gandhi asked people not to forget that it was Modi who appointed Kumar, which means the prime minister cannot escape responsibility for Kumar’s deeds and misdeeds.
BJP supporters argue that cleaning the rolls is a legitimate duty of the government. Some BJP leaders have even demanded that Kumar be awarded some of India’s highest civilian awards for his service in electoral reforms.
As a target, Kumar is much tougher to unseat than Pradhan. A minister serves at the government’s pleasure, and a prime minister can sacrifice one minister to defuse a larger crisis. A chief election commissioner’s position is designed to be harder to dislodge, because the office’s independence depends on that insulation. Article 324(5) gives the CEC the same removal protection as a Supreme Court judge.
That means a parliamentary motion on the grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity must be passed by special majorities in both houses of parliament. No such move has ever succeeded. Earlier this year, the chairpersons of both the upper and lower houses of Parliament rejected the opposition’s notice for Kumar’s removal.
Understandably, the Modi government would likely wait for the proceedings at the apex court, even as the ruling party is expected to garner public sympathy for Kumar and his “bold actions.”
The CJP and different student organizations and youth forces, on the other hand, seem to believe in the power of the street protests. To what extent the CJP, the student organizations, and opposition political parties manage to build sustained pressure through street protests remains to be seen. October being a month when festivals will be celebrated in most parts of the country, it would not be easy for them to maintain the momentum.

Civil Protection Unit in Ottawa: Solidarity and Cooperation Between Italy and Canada
Italy

00:07:27 KST

In recent days, the Civil Protection Operational Unit (NOPC) carried out a new, delicate international mission in Ottawa, ensuring the transport to Italy of hematopoietic stem cells from a compatible donor identified in Canada, intended for an Italian patient suffering from acute myeloid leukemia and awaiting a transplant at a specialized center in northern Italy. 
     A special container provided by the Rotary Club of Bergamo was used to transport the cells, a testament to the network of solidarity that actively supports these delicate missions. The mission to the Canadian capital by NOPC volunteer Dr. Sabrina Foti coincided with a visit to Ottawa by Minister for Persons with Disabilities Alessandra Locatelli. During a meeting held at the residence of Ambassador Alessandro Cattaneo, Locatelli thanked the NOPC for its important work, emphasizing that it is an Italian organization founded on solidarity, volunteerism, and the ability to build concrete connections between people and healthcare systems—even thousands of kilometers apart.
                                    
                                       
				     Thanks to the work of approximately 140 volunteers, the Unit has so far assisted 16,348 people in receiving transplants, carrying out 1,061 missions in 2026 alone. Canada represents an increasingly important hub in this international network. In 2025, the Unit carried out organ retrievals in Calgary, Ottawa, Quebec City, and Toronto, while in 2026, transports have already been conducted from Toronto, Ottawa, and Vancouver. The recent mission in Ottawa is thus yet another example of the deep human bonds that unite Italy and Canada and of how international cooperation can translate into a concrete gesture of solidarity and hope.

What we're learning about the FlyDubai co-pilot who allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to crash the plane
One day after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his identity and motive continued to swirl Thursday.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
There were 174 people aboard the plane. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday.
Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot?
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Co-pilot's motive unknown

Airborne T-7 Links Up with Simulators in Air Force First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:05:14 UTC
00:05:14 KST

Three T-7A Red Hawks flew together at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas, on Sept. 16—but only one was a real aircraft in the air. The other two jets were virtual, controlled from simulators on the ground. All three shared a single, common operating picture.
The demo marked the first time Air Education and Training Command has demonstrated live, virtual, and constructive simulation with its future jet trainer, the T-7 from Boeing. The demo inserted physical and digital assets into one synthetic environment, in which all three could communicate and work together.
“Think of it as a gaming area,” said Steven “Stein” Dobrinski, a Boeing flight simulator design engineer, in a January interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “If I’ve got everything programmed and I’m in the data link, now I’m able to have all the entities, the sims and the airplanes, that are all talking to each other in the same gaming area.”
Using LVC, the simulators and jets can fly as if equipped with missiles, bombs, or pods attached, and when employed by a pilot, others will “see” the effects play out on their displays. The simulators can also “inject” adversary aircraft or threats into a scenario, with threats appearing on everyone’s displays.
The Sept. 16 flight aimed to test and validate the “foundational digital architecture” for LVC to work with the T-7, according to a release from AETC.
The real T-7A was crewed by Col. Michael Trott and Lt. Col. Phillip Bourquin of the 99th Flying Training Squadron, while the simulators were controlled by civilian instructors with the 12th Training Squadron: Robb Erickson, a retired Air Force colonel, and Ryan Sparkman, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel.
“Through secure, high-bandwidth tactical data links, ground-based flight simulators communicated directly with the airborne T-7A maneuvering across local military training airspace,” according to the release.
Boeing and the Air Force refer to the T-7 simulator as the Ground-Based Training System and see it as integral with the new trainer aircraft. The ability to pair simulators with real planes and inject virtual opponents into a scenario opens up a whole range of trainin capability that legacy T-38 Talon trainers could not support.
Officials envision future fighter pilots collaborating with manned and unmanned systems, along with automation, to manage enormous information streams, as they face off against high-level threats that will be difficult if not impossible to simulate in the physical world.
The most advanced versions of the T-7 GBTS simulator resemble an egg shell, with a 360-degree field of view, cockpit controls that mirror the real T-7 exactly, a seat that moves based on users’ inputs, and even an associated G-suit.
Trott, commander of the 99th and one of the first Airmen to be qualified as an instructor pilot on the T-7, praised the simulator to Air & Space Forces Magazine, calling it far more realistic than existing systems for the T-38 and F-15E, both of which he has used in the past.
The Sept. 16 flight is not the first time the T-7’s LVC capabilities have been tested—Dobrinski told Air & Space Forces Magazine in January that Boeing tried it out in a series of test flights last year. As one of the jets flew to Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., for climate testing, Boeing officials paired it with a simulator in St. Louis and inserted constructive entities.
“It worked like a champ on the way out,” Dobrinski said. “When it came back, we intercepted it again, and I was in one of [the simulators]. We had a four-ship, so we had four pilots in the sims, and we rejoined on the live aircraft and flew with them until they got sick of us, because we were talking on the radio. And we locked them with the radars, and that worked really, really well.”
More test flights followed, expanding up to a six-ship flight, Dobrinski said.
Training officials say live, virtual and constructive training is the future, not only for the T-7 but for other new aircraft, as well. The F-35 is starting to add elements of LVC through its highly advanced Joint Simulation Environment and new F-35 Emulated Non-Operational Flight Program Interoperability Experience, or FENIX, simulators. Air Force aviators used FENIX during Exercise Valiant Shield this summer to connect crews across the Pacific, according to a service release.

CX2 turns FPV drones into hunters of enemy drone pilots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:59:04 UTC
23:59:04 KST

- CX2 launched Vadris SDR, a software-defined version of its FPV-mounted RF direction-finding payload that adds TBS Crossfire and DJI OcuSync detection.
- The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have been fielded to the U.S. Department of War.
U.S.-based defense technology firm CX2 has released a new version of Vadris, a small radio sensor that rides on an FPV drone and steers it toward the source of an enemy drone’s control signal, now able to pick up several of the most common drone control systems instead of just one.
CX2 announced Vadris SDR on Oct. 1. The original Vadris was built to detect ExpressLRS, an open-source radio control link widely used on first-person-view drones by hobbyists, commercial users and militaries. The new software-defined radio version adds TBS Crossfire and DJI’s OcuSync, two other widely used control links, and CX2 says it can add more through software updates as new links appear, without fitting new hardware each time.
Vadris is mounted directly on an FPV drone. It detects radio activity, works out the direction it is coming from, and overlays directional cues on the operator’s video feed, letting the pilot fly toward the transmitter. CX2 describes the goal as “Hunt the Archer, Not the Arrow,” meaning the system goes after the ground station or pilot controlling an enemy drone, rather than chasing the drone itself.
“Drones speak different languages. If you want to hunt drones, you need sensors that can speak all of those languages. Vadris does that. Moving ahead, Vadris can speak any language for counter-UAS,” said Porter Smith, CEO of CX2.
The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have already been fielded to the U.S. Department of War. It did not say which units have them, how they have been used, or whether any customer has ordered the new SDR version. It also did not give prices, detection ranges or a delivery date.
The pitch rests on cost. Attaching a cheap sensor to an expendable FPV drone gives small units their own way to find and strike enemy drone teams, a task that otherwise requires larger, dedicated electronic warfare equipment. CX2 calls Vadris a low-cost, attritable payload, meaning the military can afford to lose it.
The update targets a problem seen on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides change drone radios, frequencies and control links quickly to stay ahead of jamming and detection. A sensor tuned to a single protocol can become far less useful once the other side switches. Radio-based hunting also has a clear limit: drones guided over fiber-optic cable, now common on the front in Ukraine, give off no control signal for a sensor like Vadris to follow.

New Sarcophagus Ready for Tsar Samuil as Bulgaria Prepares to Welcome His Remains on October 3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:58:33 UTC
23:58:33 KST

A specially commissioned marble sarcophagus for the remains of Bulgarian Tsar Samuil will be decorated with symbols associated with the medieval ruler, including lions, a palace, a Christian monogram and an icon of Archangel Michael.
The sarcophagus is being made at a marble workshop in Velingrad and is expected to be completed and installed by Friday evening. Nadежda Klyuchkova, who is directly involved in its production, said she was selected for the project by the Sofia Metropolitanate and the Ministry of Culture.
The marble will feature two lions alongside a fortress, two peacocks with Samuil’s palace, an icon of Archangel Michael and a Christogram. The design also includes a coat of arms taken from the shroud in which the Bulgarian ruler was buried, as well as a cross that Samuil had placed on the monument to his father.
The name of Tsar Samuil will also be inscribed on the marble.
Klyuchkova described her involvement in the project as a great honour.
Samuil’s Remains to Be Laid to Rest at St. Sofia
The sarcophagus will be placed in the southern part of the transept of the Basilica of St. Sofia – Holy Wisdom in central Sofia, according to Father Kiril Didov, chairman of the church board at the historic basilica.
He said the coffin containing Samuil’s remains will be placed inside the sarcophagus following the official ceremony on October 3.
A procession will set off from Battenberg Square in front of the National Gallery and the former royal palace and will proceed to St. Sofia Basilica. A memorial service for Tsar Samuil is expected to be led by Bulgarian Patriarch and Sofia Metropolitan Daniil.
After the service, the coffin will be placed in the sarcophagus, allowing members of the public to pay their respects to the medieval ruler. The remains will remain accessible to visitors wishing to honour Samuil in the future.
Father Didov said it was possible that Samuil had embraced Christianity or even been baptised at St. Sofia, although he stressed that this remains a historical supposition. He pointed to Samuil’s construction of the Basilica of St. Achilleios and the transfer of the relics of St. Achilleios of Larissa there as evidence of the ruler’s Christian faith.
Historic Agreement Between Bulgaria and Greece
The return of Tsar Samuil’s remains to Bulgaria follows a memorandum of understanding signed on September 29 in Athens by the Bulgarian and Greek culture ministers, Evтим Miloshev and Lina Mendoni.
The agreement provides for the reciprocal transfer of historically significant relics between the two countries. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described it as a historic agreement resulting from intensive negotiations between Bulgaria and Greece.
Under the arrangement, Greece will return to Bulgaria the remains discovered in 1965 at the Basilica of St. Achilleios by Professor Nikolaos Moutsopoulos and identified as belonging to Tsar Samuil, who ruled Bulgaria from 997 to 1014. The transfer also includes other anthropological material found in the four sarcophagi at the basilica.
The remains have been kept in the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki in recent years.
In return, Greece is to receive 48 ecclesiastical artefacts originating from the Monastery of Panagia Ikosifinissa, the Monastery of St. John the Baptist near Serres and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita. The items were brought to Sofia in 1917 during the First World War and have since been displayed or stored at Bulgaria’s National Historical Museum.
Greek authorities described the agreement as historically significant.
Free Train Travel for the October 3 Ceremony
The Ministry of Transport and Communications and BDZ Passenger Services will provide free round-trip train travel to Sofia for people wishing to attend the official ceremony welcoming Tsar Samuil’s remains on October 3.
Special trains will operate from several regions of Bulgaria, allowing passengers to reach Sofia before the ceremony begins at 12:30 p.m. and return home the same day. Passengers will only pay a €0.51 seat reservation fee in each direction.
Free travel will be available on designated trains from Burgas, Plovdiv, Gorna Oryahovitsa, Petrich and Vidin, with return services departing Sofia later that afternoon.
Tickets can be issued at railway stations across the country for travel on the designated services to stations and stops in Sofia, including Sofia Central Railway Station, Poduyane, Iskar, Zaharna Fabrika, Gorna Banya, Sofia-North, Iskarsko Shose and Gorna Banya station.
Online ticket sales for the designated trains will be temporarily suspended from October 1 through October 3 to facilitate the organisation of the free travel scheme. Tickets under the regular tariff for other destinations along the trains’ routes will continue to be available at railway ticket offices.
Prime Minister Radev has invited citizens to gather at Battenberg Square at 12:30 p.m. on October 3 to welcome the remains of Tsar Samuil before accompanying them in procession to St. Sofia Basilica.
The return of Samuil’s remains marks the culmination of decades of discussions between Bulgaria and Greece and is being carried out under the framework of the countries’ cooperation within the European Union.

EU Finalizes Stricter Rules on Returning Illegal Migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:56:22 UTC
23:56:22 KST

The Council of the European Union has granted final approval to a new regulation governing the return of third-country nationals with no legal right to remain in the bloc. The legislation significantly tightens deportation procedures and aims to address ongoing enforcement gaps across the EU. According to Council data, roughly two-thirds of individuals ordered to leave the Union currently fail to do so and remain illegally.
The new rules complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum, replacing the previous Returns Directive. The regulation enters into force in the coming days following its publication in the Official Journal of the EU, with certain provisions (such as offshore return hubs) taking immediate effect while others carry a one-year transition window.
Key Provisions of the Regulation
- 
Mandatory Cooperation & Penalties: Migrants subject to return orders are legally obligated to fully cooperate with authorities to establish their identity. Refusal to comply will trigger penalties, including the reduction or forfeiture of social benefits, loss of financial incentives for voluntary return, monetary fines, or criminal prosecution under national law.
- 
European Return Order: A standardized European document template will capture all details of a return decision, facilitating mutual recognition of deportation orders across member states. Mutual recognition will remain voluntary for the first three years, after which the European Commission may propose making it mandatory.
- 
Heightened Security Measures: For individuals deemed a threat to public order or national security, member states may now issue indefinite Schengen entry bans and extend detention periods beyond 24 months.
- 
Offshore Return Hubs: Member states are authorized to transfer individuals awaiting deportation to transit centers established in non-EU countries. Such bilateral agreements can only be concluded with third countries that strictly adhere to international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement. Unaccompanied minors are explicitly excluded from this policy.

Authorities in five European countries carried out coordinated searches on Wednesday as part of an investigation into a suspected far-right criminal organization accused of producing and selling sound recordings containing music that incited hatred and spread National Socialist, antisemitic, racist and dehumanizing ideology.
The Rostock Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania State Office of Criminal Investigation said four suspects, aged 55, 52, 48 and 43, are being investigated for alleged membership in a criminal organization. One of them is also suspected of acting as its ringleader. The searches were carried out under warrants issued by an investigating judge at the Rostock Local Court.
Investigators suspect the four formed a permanent association no later than 2020 and worked together in an organized division of labor to produce and sell recordings containing hate-inciting music.
German authorities searched premises of the four suspects in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Schleswig-Holstein and Bavaria. Searches were also carried out at the homes of eight additional suspects in six German states who are being investigated for alleged incitement to hatred in connection with recordings produced by the organization.
At a search in Reddelich, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, officers removed numerous boxes from a house, and vinyl records appeared to be visible through an opening in at least one of them, according to dpa.
Investigators also searched properties of 10 people who authorities said were not suspected of a crime but were closely associated with the suspects. More than 394 police officers took part in the operation, including a special police unit during some of the searches in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The operation extended beyond Germany to Warsaw, Poland; Soinaste, Estonia; Čelákovice, Czech Republic; and Italy, with the international measures coordinated through Eurojust. The EU judicial cooperation agency said prosecutors and police from all five countries participated in the joint action. Eurojust also set up a coordination center to allow authorities to exchange information in real time and coordinate the execution of judicial and investigative measures.
In Poland, the authorities involved were the Circuit Prosecutor’s Office Warsaw and the Investigation and Detection Department of the Warsaw Police Headquarters. Estonia was represented by the Office of the Prosecutor General and the Police and Border Guard Board. Czech and Italian prosecutors and law enforcement agencies also participated.
Eurojust said the searches were intended to clarify and gather evidence concerning the existing suspicions. German authorities said no arrests were planned as part of the operation.
Neither the German authorities nor Eurojust identified the suspects, the organization, any record label or musical group allegedly involved. The official statements also did not name specific songs or albums under investigation. The investigation is ongoing, and German authorities stressed that the suspects are presumed innocent.

China’s Stake in the Russian Duma Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:47:00 UTC
23:47:00 KST

What did observers in China think about the Russian State Duma election on September 20? While retaining a veneer of democratic procedure, Vladimir Putin has steadily eliminated potential rivals and term limits, much like Xi Jinping has done. In past Russian election cycles, Chinese officials and experts by large have emphasized the importance of outcomes reinforcing political stability in Russia.
In terms of the latest election, most Western commentary criticized the unfair process preventing Putin’s primary opposing party, Yabloko, from running. Yabloko – which means apple in Russian but actually is an acronym for the last names of its three founders – is the only pro-democracy and anti-war party in Russia. By contrast, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun congratulated Russia for the “smooth conclusion” of the process and hailed the elections for representing “the will of the Russian people.”
Chinese media commentary did note that Yabloko was prohibited from participating in the election as a party, although some Yabloko candidates were still running in single-member districts (and all lost). Given the lack of real electoral competition, a Hong Kong media outlet, China Review News Agency, pointed out that the 59 percent turnout (7.6 percentage points higher than the previous Duma election in 2021) reflected “the state’s mobilization capabilities,” not increased political participation.
Putin’s televised address in the lead-up to the election framed it as an opportunity for Russians to express their support for the war in Ukraine and as “a collective response to those who seek to weaken Russia,” Chinese commentary reported. More than 200 Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine ran for the Duma and election commission chair Ella Pamfilova reported that 46 of them won seats – 41 of whom belonged to United Russia, the ruling party that has dominated the Russian political landscape throughout Putin’s leadership.
With the elections held against a background of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian soil and rising prices, Ma Bin, deputy director of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Fudan University, called the Duma election a major test and demonstration of Russian political stability. Chinese military analyst Shi Hong agreed that United Russia’s overwhelming victory demonstrated that for Russia “stability was paramount” and would support continuity in Russia’s military strategy and appropriations. Zhang Yanjun, a research fellow at the Institute of International Studies in Shanghai, predicted that the results of the election (held for the first time on occupied Ukrainian territory) would make Putin more intent on demonstrating strategic resolve and less likely to make concessions on Ukraine.
Since the failed coup attempt by the (since deceased) Wagner Group chairman, Yevgeny Prigozhin, in 2023, Chinese officials have made some efforts to reach out to officials beyond Putin’s inner circle. Wu Dahui, deputy director of the Russian Research Institute at Tsinghua University, emphasized that the Sino-Russian partnership has become institutionalized in a dense network of 60,000 channels at all levels of society, which he likened to the “blood vessels” sustaining the partnership.
Nevertheless, recently Chinese and Russian officials have emphasized the importance of top leader ties for their partnership. Following their most recent summit in May 2026, a Chinese diplomat hailed the relationship between Xi and Putin as “the fundamental guarantee” of the partnership. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov credited the “diplomacy of leaders” for codifying progress in the partnership in concrete agreements.
With the Russian ruling party, United Russia, capturing the majority of seats in the latest election (349 out of 450), Guo added that China would continue to work with Russia to implement “the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.”
A 2019 article by Professor Wang Zhihua in the Rule of Law Forum of the Shanghai University of Political Science and Law about the role of the Duma in the Russian political system noted that in the Russian system the president has “absolute power” and constitutionally outlined checks and balances are “merely nominal, resulting in a unique presidential system with Russian characteristics.” Wang concluded that “In short, in Russia’s political system, the president has too much power, the parliament has less power, and the judiciary is also weak.”
In Wang’s view, the configuration of the Russian political system based on a strong president with personal charisma may be expedient in the short term for the country’s revival and rise. However, he cautioned that the expansion of presidential power may ultimately lead to a crisis and undermine the long-term development of legally based governance.
Such conclusions could easily be applied to China and it is not surprising that this article, which I obtained on September 11, 2026, is no longer accessible on the CNKI database of academic articles and or on the Baidu search engine.
Chinese scholars’ assessments of Russian political developments also contribute to our understanding of Chinese views about the long-term viability of the Sino-Russian partnership. An analysis of the Duma election by a Chinese military blogger emphasized the importance of Putin’s continued hold on power and his ability to restrain hardline factions from even more escalatory actions in Ukraine. The blogger wrote: “For China, while the specific choice of Russian leader is important, Russia’s ability to maintain stability and policy continuity is even more crucial. This is why Sino-Russian relations have been continuously strengthening institutional ties in recent years.”
The results of the Russian Duma election startled no one in Beijing, but Chinese observers followed them closely. The topic is a controversial one in China due to the obvious parallels between the Russian and Chinese political systems and the stake the Chinese leadership has in the stability of their neighbor.

A Russian drone struck the grounds of Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine reported that the attack occurred on September 30.
The attack caused a fire, which has been extinguished. There were no casualties. An investigation and assessment of the damage are underway. The VVR-M research nuclear reactor is located on the institute’s grounds.
“The reactor itself and the safety-critical systems were not damaged. No changes in the radiation background have been recorded; its levels remain within the natural background range (0.16–0.20 μSv/h) and have not changed,” the statement reads.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine noted that to reduce radiation risks, the reactor has been shut down since February 2022, with the core fully unloaded.
Its operation is limited to routine maintenance of safety-critical systems.
Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine is a leading research institution in the fields of nuclear physics, nuclear energy, and radioecology. The VVR-M nuclear reactor is used as a neutron source for fundamental and applied research in nuclear physics.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine described the UAV strike on the territory of Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research as “an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that serves exclusively scientific and research purposes, and represents yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety, as well as a war crime.”
This is not the first Russian attack on critical facilities. Last year, a Russian strike drone carrying a high-explosive warhead struck the shelter of the number 4 reactor unit at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.

System sprang into action within seconds: Behind the scenes of the Flydubai terror drama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:37:43 UTC
23:37:43 KST

A single distress signal sent from the cockpit of a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was enough to send Israel’s security establishment into one of its most tense and complex operations in recent memory.
The activation of various security bodies follows an orderly, almost automatic mechanism linking events aboard the aircraft directly and immediately to IDF command centers, putting the system on maximum alert within seconds.
At first, there was genuine concern that an aircraft bound for Israel had been hijacked. Even before the full picture became clear, the first contingency plan was activated — the protocol for a suspected hijacking. The plan’s code name is barred from publication.
Two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the aircraft, escort it and isolate the surrounding airspace. At the same time, Home Front Command units were placed on alert and General Staff negotiation teams were put on full readiness in case the plane landed in Israel.
Within minutes, however, the situation changed dramatically.
The “hijacked” plane made a sharp U-turn and moved away from Israel’s borders, heading back toward Saudi Arabia. Initial reports sent to the operations command center indicated that a violent confrontation had erupted inside the cockpit between the captain and the co-pilot — a fierce struggle during which passengers and crew members managed, with considerable resourcefulness, to overpower the attacker.
As the aircraft headed for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s course of action shifted completely.
At that stage, a second contingency plan was activated — a readiness order for a complex hostage-rescue operation in a foreign country. The code name of that plan is also barred from publication.
Once the alert was received that the aircraft was expected to land in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s security forces raised their readiness further. Air Force transport aircraft, including three Hercules planes, were prepared for immediate takeoff, and additional steps were taken as part of hostage-rescue procedures.
Shortly afterward, the IDF Operations Directorate and the broader security establishment concluded that the aircraft was landing in Saudi Arabia without having been hijacked and that its passengers were not being held hostage.
A senior military official said the options were examined with great caution, and three main alternatives were prepared for bringing the Israeli citizens home.
The first was a direct military evacuation using three Air Force Hercules aircraft that were standing by as part of the hostage-rescue order. The second was dispatching a designated civilian aircraft carrying military rescue teams. The third was relying on a civilian Flydubai flight.
In the end, after detailed assessments and complex coordination behind the scenes, officials decided to use what they considered the fastest and safest option for the passengers: evacuation aboard a civilian flight.
Security officials said the main consideration for decision-makers was to avoid unnecessary diplomatic friction on Saudi soil.
At the same time, security officials stressed that all physical and operational systems were fully prepared to carry out any of the other options, including a direct military landing, if difficulties or security risks had emerged.
Senior Israeli security officials said the Saudi government’s conduct during the tense hours was very positive.
“Behind the scenes, there was a great deal of willingness on the Saudi side,” senior Israeli officials said, “and in the end, they took very significant action from our perspective.”
Although military officials have avoided describing the incident as a diplomatic breakthrough and have left such interpretation to the political leadership, the ongoing and positive coordination in such a sensitive setting demonstrated the ability of the two sides to work together in real time.
The IDF said afterward that the operational orders and automatic mechanisms designed to protect Israeli airspace functioned adequately. The General Staff is expected to carry out a routine lessons-learned process in the coming days to further improve the system, with an emphasis on responding appropriately to rapidly developing and changing events.
Still, much remains unclear about the investigation, and difficult questions remain for Israeli security mechanisms that work with international airlines.
Officials will have to determine how an Omani pilot came to be flying Israeli passengers and entering Israeli airspace, and how the relevant security authorities were unaware of his recruitment by an airline that operates extensively in Israel, particularly in recent years.
Another question is whether he was part of a terrorist infrastructure or cell capable of deploying attackers in similar scenarios against Israelis abroad.
The investigation into the apparent security gap comes against the backdrop of the Shin Bet having barred Israeli airlines for months from landing in Dubai because of security concerns. However, the scenarios officials had considered were not similar to what ultimately unfolded aboard the Flydubai flight.
The expectation is that, following the unusual incident, changes will be made primarily behind the scenes in the relationship between the airline, similar carriers and Israeli security bodies.
The screening, questioning and vetting mechanisms relating to pilots carrying Israelis to Israel and other destinations are expected to undergo significant review and overhaul.

This is the story of only Turkish village that dislikes smoking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:32:47 UTC
23:32:47 KST

Whether you're in a crowded alley in Istanbul or near a beach resort in Antalya, you’ll likely come across a Tekel shop. These roadside stores, mostly with blue-painted exteriors, are remnants of the State Tobacco Monopoly (Tekel). That’s where you go to buy cigarettes.
Tekel was created in the mid-1920s as the young Turkish state took control of the lucrative tobacco business from foreign companies, which had captured the market in the final years of the Ottoman Empire.
Türkiye was already a tobacco producer. Even the image of the camel that became synonymous with the Camel brand has Turkish roots. RJR, the American behemoth that made Camels, used a blend of Turkish tobacco in its cigarettes. So someone in the company’s marketing department thought it fit to emboss a camel as a logo — even though Türkiye is not known for these humpy-backed mammals.
It was a pivotal moment for the Turkish cigarette industry.
But right around that time in Tazlar, a tiny village in the Sinanpasa district of Türkiye’s western province of Afyonkarahisar, another revolution was taking place.
Led by a village elder, Ahmet Aga, the villagers took a vow not to smoke and set an example for future generations.
That decision permanently transformed Tazlar Village into a smoke-free sanctuary nearly a century before modern public health legislation existed.
It has been almost a hundred years, and the village, with its population of roughly 2,000 people, still boasts a reputation as a place where the sight of smokers is almost nonexistent.
Tazlar’s story is all the more relevant now as the Turkish government is pushing hard to curb smoking. Ankara is considering a law that will impose a lifetime ban on smoking for people born after January 2015.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is known for his strong opposition to smoking. He reportedly told the Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to quit, which she did earlier this year.
Multiple studies show Turks rank among the highest consumers of cigarettes. But that’s not a problem in Tazlar.
How did it all start
History has mostly forgotten Ahmet Aga, and the Tazlar residents can recall only what they were told by their parents. But as the story goes, Aga was driven by a desire to protect both the physical health and the limited financial resources of his people. In 1928, when the villagers took a collective oath against tobacco, Aga was able to capitalise on a moment when only a handful of villagers smoked, and he successfully persuaded them to quit.
“We grew up without people smoking around us,” says 66-year-old Mehmet Aydogmus, who serves as village preacher and is also an accountant. “In a sense, not smoking was not a decision we made later in life. It became directly part of our lives and our culture.”
That distinction is central to understanding Tazlar’s experience.
Rather than relying solely on individual decisions, the village appears to have developed a collective culture in which smoking never became normalised.
Aydogmus says the principle was not presented to children as a rule imposed from above. Instead, it was something they absorbed by watching their parents, grandparents and neighbours.
“When I was a child, seeing someone smoking in the village was not something we were accustomed to,” Aydogmus recalls.
Tazlar is a village of red-bricked houses, surrounded by fields of yellow tomatoes and sugar beets. Villagers here follow a set routine. They wake up early and go to bed after sunset. Here, everyone knows each other.
The villagers’ opposition to smoking is rooted partly in health concerns, but Aydogmus says the tradition cannot be explained by health alone.
“Our elders would constantly tell us about the damage smoking causes to human health,” he says. “But they would not stop at saying that it was harmful to health.”
They also spoke about the effects of harmful habits on families, communities and individual willpower.
“We gradually learned this,” he says. “Even when we were children and did not fully understand what it meant, we knew from the attitude of our elders that this was an important issue for us.”
The village’s approach combined family responsibility, religious values and communal solidarity, says Aydogmus.
Families looked after their children. Older people warned younger generations. Neighbours knew one another. And behaviour was understood not only as an individual matter but also as something that could affect the wider family and community.
If a child begins to develop what the family considers a harmful habit, relatives and neighbours do not necessarily remain passive.
“If a young person makes a mistake somewhere, people do not say, ‘It has nothing to do with me,’” Aydogmus says. “People know one another in the village. Everyone knows whose child and whose grandchild someone is.”
But how do you preserve a culture if there are no young people to follow in your footsteps?
Dispersing like smoke
Murat Karasogut, 29, who grew up in Tazlar, always gets a cultural shock when he travels to other parts of the country.
“When we see someone smoking outside, sometimes we think, ‘We do not have something like this in our village.’”
In Tazlar, he says, not smoking became the expected norm. Young people did not necessarily need to be repeatedly told to reject smoking because cigarettes were already outside the village’s everyday culture.
“Not smoking is something that is customary in our village, so young people adopt it more easily,” he says.
That difference, he believes, remains significant even as young people encounter cigarettes more frequently elsewhere.
But more and more young people from Tazlar are moving to cities, raising concerns that the steadfast opposition to smoking might fade over time.
More than two-thirds of the village’s young people now live in cities such as Istanbul and Bursa, lured by better education and employment prospects.
For both Aydogmus and Karasogut, the future of Tazlar’s tradition ultimately depends on whether younger generations choose to carry it forward.
Karasogut believes young people have a particular responsibility.
“We do not want to remain in the past,” Aydogmus says. “But we do not want to lose our past either.”

According to figures released last month, 227 Indian nationals have been recruited into the Russian army since the beginning of the war in 2022.
Of them, 139 had been discharged from service, while 51 people died.
“This is an issue that we are in constant discussions with the Russian side,” Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri told reporters in New Delhi last month.
In July this year, the Indian parliament was informed that there were 127 Indian nationals in the Russian armed forces, out of whom the services of 98 individuals were discontinued.

EU to Add €2 Processing Fee for Online Imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

EU to Add €2 Processing Fee for Online Imports
A new €2 processing fee will be imposed from November 1 on goods bought online and imported into the European Union from non-EU countries, according to a European Commission document.
The measure forms part of a broad overhaul of EU customs rules and is aimed at the large volume of small parcels arriving each day from countries outside the bloc, including China and the United States.
The new charge was already envisaged under the EU's new Customs Code, but the European Commission document now sets its amount at €2.
Consumers will not be responsible for paying the fee directly. Instead, the customs rules place the obligation on the economic operator handling the import, which in online commerce generally means the platform, seller or their representative. National customs authorities will collect the payments.
Major e-commerce platforms are among the companies expected to be affected, as they handle large numbers of low-cost products entering the EU from non-EU countries.
The fee is being introduced as customs administrations face growing expenses from processing the shipments. The money is intended to cover tasks including checking the information submitted, carrying out risk analysis, maintaining the required infrastructure, and performing documentary and physical inspections of goods.
EU customs authorities handled about 6 billion shipments from online retailers in 2025, with approximately 90% of them coming from China.
The €2 processing charge is separate from the customs duty that already applies to low-value online purchases imported from outside the EU.
On July 1, 2026, the EU ended the previous customs duty exemption for goods worth less than €150 and introduced a temporary €3 charge for different categories of products contained in small shipments. That system is scheduled to continue until the permanent arrangement takes effect in 2028.
The €2 fee that begins in November will therefore be an additional customs processing charge rather than a replacement for the existing customs duty.
The new rules are intended to limit the growing volume of direct online deliveries from outside the EU while also increasing checks on goods that may be dangerous or do not comply with European standards.
