As University of Tokyo Gets Its First Female President, How Far Is Japan From Gender Equality?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:26:00 UTC
23:26:00 KST

On September 28, 2026, Fujigaki Yuko was selected as the next president of the University of Tokyo. Following formal appointment by the minister of education, culture, sports, science, and technology, she will take office on April 1, 2027, for a six-year term.
As the university marks its 150th anniversary, Fujigaki will become the first woman to lead it. Yet at the institution she is about to head, only about one in five undergraduates is a woman.
Fujigaki is not Japan’s first female university president. In 1997, Niwa Masako became president of Nara Women’s University, the first woman to head a national university in Japan, and in 2001, Honda Masuko became the first female president of Ochanomizu University. Coeducational national universities also have earlier precedents: Ikehata Setsuho became the first female president of Tokyo University of Foreign Studies in 2001, and Kina Ikue became the first female president of the University of the Ryukyus in 2025.
Even so, the appointment of a woman to lead the University of Tokyo, often seen as Japan’s most prominent university and an institution with considerable social influence, carries particular symbolic weight.
The Selection Process
Fujigaki, 64, is a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, specializing in science and technology studies and scientometrics. She earned her bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees at the same university, completing her doctorate in 1990. Apart from nearly four years as a senior researcher at the government’s National Institute of Science and Technology Policy, she has spent her career at the university, becoming a professor in 2010. Starting in 2021, she served for five years as an executive vice president, overseeing areas including admissions, student support, and research ethics.
Her selection has nevertheless generated controversy both inside and outside the university. Most notably, Fujigaki did not receive the most votes in the university’s opinion vote. On September 28, eligible faculty and administrative staff took part in two rounds of voting, with the top three candidates in the first round advancing to the second. The vote was intended only as one source of information for the selection process and did not directly determine the final choice.
In the first round, Someya Takao, a professor at the Graduate School of Engineering, received 818 votes, or 38.0 percent of the 2,155 ballots cast, including blank ballots. Fujigaki received 400 votes, or 18.6 percent. In the second round, Someya received 1,107 votes, or 51.0 percent of the 2,169 ballots cast, while Fujigaki received 553, or 25.5 percent. Fujigaki therefore finished second in both rounds, with less than half as many votes as Someya. According to The Todai Shimbun, this appears to be the first time under the university’s established presidential selection system that a candidate who did not finish first in the opinion vote was ultimately chosen.
The final decision rested with the University President Screening & Inspection Committee. Half of its 16 members are chosen by the university’s Education and Research Council and include senior officials such as graduate school deans; the other half are external members of the university’s Administrative Council, with backgrounds in business, media, and other fields. Kuniya Hiroko, who chairs the committee, is a trustee of Tokyo University of the Arts and anchored NHK’s current affairs program “Close-up Gendai” for many years. The committee considers candidates’ policy statements, interviews, the opinion vote, and other materials before making its final decision.
Selecting the second-place candidate therefore did not violate the university’s procedures. But the committee’s authority to make the final decision does not eliminate the need to explain the gap between the vote and the eventual outcome. When one candidate receives majority support from participating faculty and staff but another is selected as president, members of the university can reasonably ask how much weight was given to the various criteria, what strengths outweighed the vote, and ultimately how much significance the university still attaches to its long-standing internal ballot.
In its statement, the committee said that through her experience as an executive vice president, Fujigaki had become keenly aware of the university’s role as a symbol of academia, and that she had the strong will and ability to restore trust in academia, drawing on her skill in communicating science and technology to the public. It also said that, drawing on her extensive international experience, Fujigaki had the ability to make the university more open by integrating the arts and sciences and strengthening communication within and beyond the university.
The committee’s reference to “restoring trust” has a clear context. In November 2025 and January 2026, an associate professor and a professor at the University of Tokyo Medical School Hospital were arrested on suspicion of bribery. The associate professor was accused of favoring a medical device company in procurement decisions and receiving roughly 700,000 yen (around $4,400) through a donation arrangement. The professor was accused of repeatedly accepting expensive entertainment, including at upscale clubs, from the head of an organization that had partnered with the university on a collaborative program. The university apologized, and the hospital director subsequently resigned.
At the same time, the University of Tokyo’s application to be designated a University for International Research Excellence, a status that would give it access to grants from the government’s University Fund, has remained under continued review since December 2025. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science, and Technology said the university still needed to clarify how it allocates resources and strengthen its institution-wide governance. Restoring trust and advancing governance reform are therefore important challenges for the next president.
The Controversy
Kuniya also said at the press conference that gender had not been a subject of discussion during the committee’s deliberations.
It is important to distinguish questions about the transparency of the process from arguments about Fujigaki’s gender. Questioning how the selection was made does not amount to opposition to female leadership. Nor, in the absence of evidence, should the outcome simply be attributed to a preference for appointing a woman. Supporting more women in leadership and asking a university to explain a major personnel decision are not contradictory positions.
At the same time, debates of this kind can reflect the unusually demanding standards sometimes applied to female leaders, making it important to remain alert to gender-based double standards.
Some critics have also compared Fujigaki’s academic record unfavorably with Someya’s. Japanese internet personality Nishimura Hiroyuki, for example, amplified claims on X that Someya’s papers had received roughly 70 times as many citations as Fujigaki’s.
Someya is an engineer specializing in flexible electronics. His best-known work includes ultrathin electronic devices that can be attached directly to the skin. He has received numerous academic honors, including the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Prize in 2008, the Leo Esaki Prize in 2019, and the Fujiwara Prize in 2024, and has repeatedly appeared on Clarivate’s list of Highly Cited Researchers. Fujigaki, by contrast, mainly uses approaches from the humanities and social sciences to examine the relationship between science, technology, and society.
Publication practices, research team size, language of publication, and citation patterns differ greatly across disciplines. Simply comparing total citation counts or numbers of awards therefore offers only a limited basis for judging the academic achievements of two scholars in different fields.
More importantly, a university president is responsible not only for research but also for educational and research administration, organizational coordination, resource allocation, and public communication. Academic achievement is only one part of the selection criteria.
Japan’s Remaining Gender Gap
There is a broader context to the debate. Even as the University of Tokyo prepares to install its first female president, the gender imbalance among its students remains pronounced. As of May 1, 2026, the university had 14,098 undergraduate students, of whom 3,023 were women – just 21.4 percent.
Across Japan, more than half of women now go on to university, but the overall figure conceals substantial inequalities between fields of study and stages of education. In 2025, 56.5 percent of women and 60.7 percent of men advanced to undergraduate programs, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. The gap becomes much wider at the graduate level: only 6.9 percent of female university graduates went directly on to graduate school, compared with 16.0 percent of men.
Differences by field are equally striking. In 2025, women accounted for 29.4 percent of undergraduates in science and just 17.9 percent in engineering. At the master’s level, their shares fell further, to 24.0 percent and 15.9 percent, respectively. The fact that more women are entering higher education does not mean that they participate equally across academic disciplines.
Women remain underrepresented at senior levels after entering academia as well. In 2025, women accounted for 28.2 percent of full-time faculty at Japanese universities and graduate schools, but only 20.1 percent of presidents, vice presidents, and professors. In 2024, just four of the 86 presidents of Japan’s national universities were women, or 4.7 percent, compared with 14.9 percent at public universities and 15.1 percent at private universities.
The same pattern is evident in corporate management. In 2025, women made up 16.1 percent of section managers and 9.3 percent of department managers at companies with at least 100 regular employees. As of October 2025, women headed only 8.6 percent of Japanese companies. Although this was a record high, the figure remained below one in ten.
Politics shows a similar imbalance. Takaichi Sanae became Japan’s first female prime minister in October 2025. Yet after Takaichi’s September 2026 Cabinet reshuffle, only three of the 19 Cabinet members, including the prime minister herself, were women. As of February 2026, women accounted for 30.0 percent of members of the House of Councillors but only 14.6 percent of members of the House of Representatives. These gaps show that women’s expanding access to higher education has not yet translated fully into representation in leadership and decision-making positions.
The appointment of the University of Tokyo’s first female president is symbolically important, but substantive progress will depend on what universities do to support women at different stages of their education and careers. That means encouraging women to continue into graduate education, supporting their participation in science and engineering, and creating classrooms in which they feel comfortable expressing their views and taking part in discussion.
For researchers, it means reducing gender discrimination in the workplace, ensuring fair and transparent recruitment and promotion, and making it easier to combine research careers with caregiving responsibilities. Together, these measures can give women greater opportunities to develop their abilities and participate in decision-making, not only in academia but also in business and society more broadly.

A Russian motorcyclist with alleged links to a senior Russian military intelligence official has been identified as the suspected mastermind behind an attempted sabotage attack at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle airport, according to a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag.
The investigation identified Oleg Levushkin as the suspected planner of an operation in which a drone carrying a tin packed with explosives struck the wing of a Ukrainian airliner at Leipzig-Halle airport.
The incident, which occurred in September, could have triggered an explosion and caused severe structural damage to the airport, according to the report.
Classified intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania and Poland, along with interviews with senior Western intelligence officials, reportedly indicate that Levushkin and a “disposable agent” traveled to Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect Levushkin planned the attack and subsequently instructed Andrei Karshakou, a Belarusian proxy agent, to execute it.
Evidence examined by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag reportedly showed similarities between the Leipzig incident and a separate foiled Russian sabotage plot involving drones and explosives targeting locations in Poland, Lithuania and Germany.
The explosive device recovered in Leipzig was said to closely resemble devices used in other alleged Russian sabotage operations across Europe.
Levushkin, a Russian passport holder with an interest in motorcycles, has reportedly maintained contact for years with Denis Smolyaninov, who has been described as an alleged chief planner of Russian bomb attacks across Europe.
Smolyaninov was sanctioned by the UK Foreign Office last year.
A December 2025 report by Lithuanian intelligence, reviewed by The Telegraph, said Smolyaninov led the Ukraine department at Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU.
The report said he specialized in psychological operations and was associated with covert sabotage campaigns in Europe using Telegram.
According to information provided to German newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung by the Dossier Centre, Levushkin and Smolyaninov met in 2007 after Smolyaninov mediated a financial dispute involving Levushkin's business.
The Leipzig incident has also been linked to GRU unit 29155, which German intelligence officials reportedly regard as a key force behind Kremlin-ordered operations.
German security authorities believe Russia is seeking to make Europeans view their support for Ukraine as risky, potentially affecting public debate and support for Kyiv.
Germany is increasingly an “operational theatre” for Russian intelligence services, according to a senior German intelligence official.
“What used to be isolated cases, we are now seeing on a broad scale,” they said.
The Lithuanian intelligence files reportedly also identified links between the Leipzig incident and a wider network of alleged sabotage plots across Europe, which investigators attributed to a hard-line GRU unit.

The latest demonstrations followed incidents on Thursday that prompted numerous secondary schools in Liege to close as a precaution.
The movement in Belgium came as French high school students have been blocking access to and staging protests outside their schools for several days, demanding better learning conditions.

Prosecutors' request to revoke bid to shelve Ustica probe granted
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:01:05 CEST
23:01:05 KST

A Rome preliminary investigations
judge (GIP) on Friday granted a request from prosecutors' in the
capital to revoke their petition to shelve a new investigation
into the 1980 Ustica air disaster, in which 81 people were
killed, after the French authorities said they were willing to
transfer to Italy all their documentation related to it.
                                    
                                       
				"The French authorities' willingness to cooperate opens a new
line of inquiry and new prospects," Chief Prosecutor Francesco
Lo Voi told the GIP on Wednesday.
                                    
                                       
				The material reportedly includes French defence ministry
documents covering a long period extending into the 1990s that
were the subject of past letters rogatory issued by the Rome
Public Prosecutor's Office.
                                    
                                       
				The French authorities have also reportedly expressed their
willingness to accommodate any additional requests from Italy
regarding the case.
                                    
                                       
				The mysterious air disaster known in Italy as the 'Ustica
Massacre' (Strage di Ustica) of June 27 1980 has been the
subject of numerous investigations, legal actions and
accusations, including claims of conspiracy.
                                    
                                       
				Hypotheses on the causes of what has been one of Italy's
enduring mysteries have included a terrorist bombing and a
missile strike during a military aerial dogfight, with a Libyan
plane possibly being the intended target.
                                    
                                       
				Rome's State attorneys have been unable to identify the
nationality of the aircraft that allegedly caused the crash of
the Bologna-Palermo flight operated by the now-defunct Itavia
airline.
                                    
                                       
				In 2013 the Court of Cassation found that a missile fired from
an unknown source was the definite cause of the disaster, and
said that "cover-ups" in investigations into Itavia Flight 870
must now be considered "definitively ascertained".
                                    
                                       
				Ten years later, ex-premier Giuliano Amato said in 2023 that a
French missile was behind the mysterious crash.
                                    
                                       
				Amato said at the time that the DC9 was hit in an attempt to
assassinate late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
                                    
                                       
				Daria Bonfietti, chair of the Ustica victims' families group,
welcomed Wednesday's decision and said now was the time for
facts, with the delivery of documents from France.
                                    
                                       
				"We welcome the decision to continue the investigation. For the
victims' families, this is a significant step after 46 years of
waiting and hard work. Now, we need concrete results. France's
willingness to cooperate must translate into the actual handover
of documentation, and it will be up to the judiciary to
determine the investigative value of those papers. That is where
the true measure of the step forward announced today lies," said
Bonfietti, President of the Association of Relatives of the
Victims of the Ustica Massacre.
                                    
                                       
				The Association, Bonfietti noted, "has kept this quest alive for
nearly half a century with unwavering determination. The
Municipality of Bologna has stood by us and will continue to do
so, including through the Museum for the Memory of Ustica.
                                    
                                       
				"I thank the institutions that helped make this new development
possible. Now we await the chance to read the documents, hoping
they will shed light on the truth that is still missing."

ROMA,
02 October 2026, 15:26

- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The “2026 Jirisan International Environmental Biennale” will feature an independent national pavilion dedicated to Italy. This marks the first national pavilion within a biennale organized by a private entity in South Korea and the largest national pavilion ever created.
The project, supported by the Magma cultural association in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Seoul and the Italian Embassy, offers a reflection on the role of art in the era of the climate crisis.
The Italian Pavilion will cover approximately 330 square meters and will host the exhibition “Diario Italiano: Revelations and Shadows,” curated by Maria Mancini, director of Mxm Arte. The exhibition will feature 45 works by 20 Italian artists.

Lidl to invest more than 100 million DKK renovating all Danish stores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:07:04 UTC
23:07:04 KST

Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.
The German-owned supermarket chain said the redesign would improve the use of space, create a consistent appearance and make shopping easier.
Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.
Lidl has tested the concept through renovations at several locations. The first store to open after the official introduction of the concept began operating in Holbæk on September 27.
More renovated stores are expected to open in the coming months.
“The goal is to have all stores in Lidl Denmark renovated within the next few years,” said Mads T. Nielsen, Lidl’s development, property and sales director.
He said customers had responded positively to the test stores and newly built locations using the same design.
Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.

Suspected female wolf pup killed in traffic near Karup and sent for examination
A suspected female wolf pup has been killed in traffic on Hessellundvej near Karup, Danish authorities said Friday.
The Agency for Green Land Restructuring and Water Environment confirmed the incident to regional broadcaster TV Midtvest.
The Danish Nature Agency, which manages state-owned natural areas and wildlife matters, collected the animal Friday morning.
Officials believe it is a wolf and likely a female pup. The animal will be examined at the University of Copenhagen, though the specific purpose of the examination has not been disclosed.
Authorities could not provide further details about the collision Friday afternoon, including whether the driver involved contacted them.
Other wolves killed in traffic have previously been found and examined in Denmark.
Five dead wolves were examined in January, including three that had been struck by vehicles. The results were sent to the Natural History Museum Aarhus, which monitors Denmark’s wolf population and collects documentation.
“Through the autopsies, we gain an important understanding of the wolves’ health and way of life,” research director Kent Olsen said in January.
The examinations can include DNA testing and provide information used for research and wildlife management.
Wolves returned to Denmark in 2012 after being absent from the country for about 200 years.
The wolf is a protected species in Denmark and the country’s only apex predator.
Old systems and extensive personal data make universities vulnerable to hackers, expert says
Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.
DTU has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many users were affected.
Copenhagen parties seek investigation into possible police report over Sikandar Siddique’s residence case

The parties want possible forgery and false testimony investigated. They also seek an assessment of whether Siddique should repay his council pay or face a fine under Denmark’s residence registration law.
Siddique denied wrongdoing and called the proposal “theater to get attention.”

Denmark to see sunshine Saturday before clouds and rain return Sunday
Denmark will have periods of rain and sunshine this weekend, with Saturday expected to bring the best weather, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the country’s national weather service.
Friday began cloudy as a slow-moving front brought scattered rain across central Denmark.
Conditions were expected to clear gradually, with sunshine reaching Jutland first, followed by Funen and parts of Zealand during the afternoon.
Some areas of Zealand could remain cloudy because of the front’s slow movement. Friday’s temperatures were expected to reach 15 to 18 degrees Celsius.

Sunday will be cloudier, with rain in some places. The rainfall is not expected to be heavy, and breaks in the clouds may occur during the day.

Copenhagen Airport records busiest September with 3.2 million passengers
Copenhagen Airport handled 3.2 million passengers in September, its highest total for that month.
The number was four percent higher than in September 2025, the airport said Friday.
“The peak season no longer ends with the summer vacation,” commercial director Peter Krogsgaard said. “In September, we had almost as many travelers as in the summer months.”
About 270,000 passengers traveled between Copenhagen and Norway, making it the largest country market.
Spain followed with 255,000 passengers, while routes to and from the United Kingdom carried 245,000.
London, Stockholm, Oslo, Amsterdam and Paris were the five most popular destinations.
Demand also increased for direct routes between Copenhagen and the United States.
Those flights carried 140,000 passengers, an increase of eight percent from September 2025.
Krogsgaard said both direct traffic and the number of American visitors to Denmark had increased.
Copenhagen Airport is Denmark’s only airport offering direct flights to and from the United States. Some American passengers visit Denmark, while others continue to destinations elsewhere in Europe.
The airport expects about 1.1 million passengers during Denmark’s October school holiday. More than 115,000 travelers are expected on the busiest days.
Spain, Italy and France are the most popular southern European destinations, with about 220,000 passengers expected around the holiday period.
Petrol-only cars fall below half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet
Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.
Petrol-only cars make up 49.98 percent of registered passenger cars, down from 65 percent at the end of 2020.
The category does not include hybrid or plug-in hybrid vehicles because they use more than one source of power.
Over the same period, electric cars have increased their share of the Danish fleet. They now account for 24.3 percent of passenger cars.
Mobility Denmark, the main association representing Denmark’s automotive industry, said the figures showed how quickly the country’s vehicle fleet was changing.
“Pure petrol cars have for decades been completely dominant on Danish roads. Now they make up less than half of the passenger car fleet,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
“That says something about how strongly electric cars have moved in a few years,” he added.
Lego Foundation invests 200 million DKK to strengthen Danish teacher training
The Lego Foundation will invest 200 million DKK over five years in efforts to attract and retain more teachers and educators in Denmark.
The funding expands a partnership with Danske Professionshøjskoler, the association representing Denmark’s six university colleges.
The colleges will develop an action plan explaining how the money will be used to increase enrollment in teacher and educator training programs and help graduates remain in those professions.
“It is not a task for the Lego Foundation to define the concrete efforts,” foundation CEO Sidsel Marie Kristensen said. “They know much better than us what it takes to solve it.”
The initiative builds on cooperation that began in 2018.
The foundation cited shortages of qualified teachers and educators, falling academic performance in public schools and an increasing number of children excluded from school communities.
“Skilled teachers and educators are completely crucial for children’s well-being and learning,” Kristensen said.
A recent study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found that teacher shortages remain a problem in Denmark.
The latest PISA study also showed historically weak results among Danish 15-year-old students.
The foundation’s total support for Danske Professionshøjskoler has now reached 565 million DKK since 2018.
The Lego Foundation is a Danish commercial foundation that owns 25 percent of the Lego Group.
Danish justice minister wants prosecutors barred from wearing religious and political symbols in court
Danish prosecutors should follow the same rules as judges and be barred from wearing visible religious or political symbols during court hearings, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said.
“Neither Muslim nor other visible religious symbols must be allowed to weaken the public’s confidence that what takes place in Danish courtrooms is objective,” Wammen of the Social Democrats told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Since 2009, Denmark’s Administration of Justice Act has prohibited judges and lay judges from wearing religious or political symbols during hearings. The rule does not currently apply to prosecutors.
The debate began after Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor with the State Prosecutor in Viborg, wrote on LinkedIn that she was proud to be Denmark’s first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.
Dennis Flydtkjær, immigration spokesperson for the Denmark Democrats, said wearing a headscarf did not necessarily make a prosecutor biased. However, he said there should be no doubt about objectivity in court.
The Danish People’s Party has also criticized the different rules for judges and prosecutors.
The Association of Public Prosecutors said it did not understand the attention directed at Sediqi and supported her unconditionally.
The association said she had followed all current rules.
Denmark’s prosecution service confirmed that it has no internal rule preventing employees from wearing a hijab at work.
Sediqi has not commented.
Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.

Conservative People’s Party leader Mona Juul receives 25,000 DKK a month, while Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh and Denmark Democrats leader Inger Støjberg each receive 40,000 DKK a month.
Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

Train services between Zealand and Jutland are expected to return to normal Tuesday morning after Banedanmark repaired a fallen overhead wire near Sorø.

Gender pay gap in Denmark narrows for first time in three years
The pay gap between men and women in Denmark narrowed last year for the first time in three years, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
In 2025, women earned on average 12.3 percent less than men, compared with 12.9 percent in 2024.
Statistics Denmark has tracked the pay gap since 2004, when the difference was 16 percent. It fell to 11.9 percent in 2020, but then widened again in 2023 and 2024 before declining last year.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension company Danica, said the development also matters for retirement savings.
“Salary is the factor that matters most for the size of pension savings,” he said. “Therefore, the development in pay gaps is also one of the most important things to keep an eye on if you want less economic inequality between men and women as retirees.”
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension company Sampension, also called the decrease positive, while stressing that women still earn “significantly less than men.”
She said women’s growing educational advantage over men could support higher wages over time. She also pointed to rules on earmarked parental leave, which have led more men to take leave, as another factor that could improve women’s finances.
“After a few years with bumps in the road, the development once again went in the right direction last year,” Dalsgaard said.
German military drone makes first test flight of its kind over Denmark
A German military surveillance drone is flying over Jutland on Tuesday in what the Danish Defence says is the first test flight in Danish airspace involving an unmanned military aircraft of its size.
The German Heron TP weighs more than five tons, is 13 meters long and has a wingspan of 26 meters. It is flying at an altitude of about seven kilometers, sharing airspace with manned aircraft.
The drone belongs to the German air force, the Luftwaffe, and is being remotely controlled by a pilot at a military base in Schleswig, Germany.
The roughly two-hour flight begins at the Danish-German border in South Jutland, continues over eastern Jutland to Aalborg and then returns to Germany over western Jutland.
During the flight, the German pilot remains in contact with Naviair, which manages air traffic in Danish airspace. Denmark’s Civil Aviation and Railway Authority has approved the safety procedures for flying the drone beyond visual range, including procedures for a possible loss of control or radio connection.
The test is part of preparations for the Danish air force to receive its own General Atomics MQ-9B unmanned aircraft in 2028. They will operate from Aalborg Air Base under Squadron 729 and will be used, among other tasks, for patrol and surveillance over Greenland and the North Atlantic.
Brigade Commander Hans Peter Andersen called the flight “yet another important step toward receiving our own unmanned aircraft in the coming years.”
A majority in the Climate, Environment and Technology Committee at Copenhagen Municipality approved a new plan Monday afternoon.
According to it, the city has moved a step closer to introducing a zero-emission zone in part of Vesterbro, where petrol and diesel vehicles would generally not be allowed to drive.
“It is really good that Copenhagen is now getting its first zero-emission zone. It is good for the climate and for reducing local air pollution,” Kristine Ammitzbøll-Bille of De Radikale, the Danish Social Liberal Party, told TV 2 Kosmopol.
The proposal was originally larger but was changed after 768 consultation responses from residents, businesses and interest groups.
Around 80 percent of the responses were either critical or reserved about the plan.
The revised version exempts all of Vesterbrogade, the area around Copenhagen Central Station, Skelbækgade and part of Halmtorvet.
Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.

Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.
DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ organization, criticized the government’s plan.
Thomas Sørensen, director of DI’s automotive branch, called it an “own goal to let taxes on electric cars rise from the new year.”
According to FDM, Denmark’s main association for car owners, a VW ID.4 Style could cost around DKK 10,300 more in tax, while a Tesla Model Y Long Range with all-wheel drive could face an increase of nearly DKK 28,000.
Mobility Denmark, an industry association representing the automotive sector, also criticized the proposal.
“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

Suspected female wolf pup killed in traffic near Karup and sent for examination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:06:58 UTC
23:06:58 KST

A suspected female wolf pup has been killed in traffic on Hessellundvej near Karup, Danish authorities said Friday.
The Agency for Green Land Restructuring and Water Environment confirmed the incident to regional broadcaster TV Midtvest.
The Danish Nature Agency, which manages state-owned natural areas and wildlife matters, collected the animal Friday morning.
Officials believe it is a wolf and likely a female pup. The animal will be examined at the University of Copenhagen, though the specific purpose of the examination has not been disclosed.
Authorities could not provide further details about the collision Friday afternoon, including whether the driver involved contacted them.
Other wolves killed in traffic have previously been found and examined in Denmark.
Five dead wolves were examined in January, including three that had been struck by vehicles. The results were sent to the Natural History Museum Aarhus, which monitors Denmark’s wolf population and collects documentation.
“Through the autopsies, we gain an important understanding of the wolves’ health and way of life,” research director Kent Olsen said in January.
The examinations can include DNA testing and provide information used for research and wildlife management.
Wolves returned to Denmark in 2012 after being absent from the country for about 200 years.
The wolf is a protected species in Denmark and the country’s only apex predator.
Lidl to invest more than 100 million DKK renovating all Danish stores
Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.
The German-owned supermarket chain said the redesign would improve the use of space, create a consistent appearance and make shopping easier.
Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.
Lidl has tested the concept through renovations at several locations. The first store to open after the official introduction of the concept began operating in Holbæk on September 27.
More renovated stores are expected to open in the coming months.
“The goal is to have all stores in Lidl Denmark renovated within the next few years,” said Mads T. Nielsen, Lidl’s development, property and sales director.
He said customers had responded positively to the test stores and newly built locations using the same design.
Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.

Old systems and extensive personal data make universities vulnerable to hackers, expert says
Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.
DTU has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many users were affected.

Denmark will have periods of rain and sunshine this weekend, with Saturday expected to bring the best weather, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the country’s national weather service.
Friday began cloudy as a slow-moving front brought scattered rain across central Denmark.
Conditions were expected to clear gradually, with sunshine reaching Jutland first, followed by Funen and parts of Zealand during the afternoon.

Copenhagen Airport records busiest September with 3.2 million passengers
Copenhagen Airport handled 3.2 million passengers in September, its highest total for that month.
The number was four percent higher than in September 2025, the airport said Friday.
“The peak season no longer ends with the summer vacation,” commercial director Peter Krogsgaard said. “In September, we had almost as many travelers as in the summer months.”
About 270,000 passengers traveled between Copenhagen and Norway, making it the largest country market.
Spain followed with 255,000 passengers, while routes to and from the United Kingdom carried 245,000.
London, Stockholm, Oslo, Amsterdam and Paris were the five most popular destinations.
Demand also increased for direct routes between Copenhagen and the United States.
Those flights carried 140,000 passengers, an increase of eight percent from September 2025.
Krogsgaard said both direct traffic and the number of American visitors to Denmark had increased.
Copenhagen Airport is Denmark’s only airport offering direct flights to and from the United States. Some American passengers visit Denmark, while others continue to destinations elsewhere in Europe.
The airport expects about 1.1 million passengers during Denmark’s October school holiday. More than 115,000 travelers are expected on the busiest days.
Spain, Italy and France are the most popular southern European destinations, with about 220,000 passengers expected around the holiday period.
Petrol-only cars fall below half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet
Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.
Petrol-only cars make up 49.98 percent of registered passenger cars, down from 65 percent at the end of 2020.
The category does not include hybrid or plug-in hybrid vehicles because they use more than one source of power.
Over the same period, electric cars have increased their share of the Danish fleet. They now account for 24.3 percent of passenger cars.
Mobility Denmark, the main association representing Denmark’s automotive industry, said the figures showed how quickly the country’s vehicle fleet was changing.
“Pure petrol cars have for decades been completely dominant on Danish roads. Now they make up less than half of the passenger car fleet,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
“That says something about how strongly electric cars have moved in a few years,” he added.

Danish justice minister wants prosecutors barred from wearing religious and political symbols in court
Danish prosecutors should follow the same rules as judges and be barred from wearing visible religious or political symbols during court hearings, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said.
“Neither Muslim nor other visible religious symbols must be allowed to weaken the public’s confidence that what takes place in Danish courtrooms is objective,” Wammen of the Social Democrats told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Since 2009, Denmark’s Administration of Justice Act has prohibited judges and lay judges from wearing religious or political symbols during hearings. The rule does not currently apply to prosecutors.
The debate began after Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor with the State Prosecutor in Viborg, wrote on LinkedIn that she was proud to be Denmark’s first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.
Dennis Flydtkjær, immigration spokesperson for the Denmark Democrats, said wearing a headscarf did not necessarily make a prosecutor biased. However, he said there should be no doubt about objectivity in court.
The Danish People’s Party has also criticized the different rules for judges and prosecutors.
The Association of Public Prosecutors said it did not understand the attention directed at Sediqi and supported her unconditionally.
The association said she had followed all current rules.
Denmark’s prosecution service confirmed that it has no internal rule preventing employees from wearing a hijab at work.
Sediqi has not commented.
Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.
September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Low wind and limited sunshine combined with high gas prices pushed Denmark’s raw electricity prices to their highest monthly level in nearly four years, according to energy company OK.
The average raw electricity price in September was 1.07 DKK per kilowatt-hour east of the Great Belt and 1.05 DKK west of it. VAT, taxes and tariffs are added to those prices.
By comparison, prices averaged 0.62 DKK east of the Great Belt and 0.54 DKK west of it in September last year.
