A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne  Ergebnisse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:04:26 UTC
23:04:26 KST

Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne Ergebnisse
Der EU-Handelskommissar erklärt gegenüber POLITICO, China habe verstanden, dass eine Einigung dringend notwendig ist. Er hofft auf Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen.
MILWAUKEE - China und die EU seien in Bezug auf ein mögliches Handelsabkommen „noch lange nicht am Ziel“, sagte EU-Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič am Donnerstag (Ortszeit) im Gespräch mit POLITICO. Die Gespräche seien „konstruktiv, aber schwierig“.
„Ich spüre großes politisches Interesse und natürlich sehr hohe Erwartungen seitens der Staats- und Regierungschefs in der gesamten Europäischen Union“, sagte Šefčovič am Rande eines Treffens der G20-Handelsminister in Milwaukee. „Ich weiß, wie politisch ungeduldig die europäische Führung ist.“
Šefčovič reist am 8. Oktober nach Peking für ein, wie er es nannte, „äußerst wichtiges Treffen“ mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao. Er sei optimistisch, dass die Reise Früchte tragen werde. „Man muss daran glauben, dass man etwas erreichen kann, sonst sollte man besser gar nicht erst hinfahren.“
Advertisement
Über die Ergebnisse der Reise sprechen die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am 15. und 16. Oktober bei ihrem EU-Gipfel in Brüssel. Die EU droht damit, den Zugang chinesischer Unternehmen zum Binnenmarkt einzuschränken, sollten die Gespräche scheitern.
Die EU und China verhandeln seit Juni. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben erklärt, sie wollten die große Menge chinesischer Importe und das hohe Handelsdefizit mit China, nicht länger hinnehmen.
„Ich glaube, unsere chinesischen Partner haben verstanden, dass dies direkte Auswirkungen auf die Zukunft bedeutender europäischer Unternehmen hat – buchstäblich Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen“, berichtete Šefčovič. „Und auch auf das soziale Gefüge und das Sozialmodell, das in Europa über viele, viele Jahrzehnte hinweg entwickelt wurde.“
Im Mittelpunkt der Gespräche steht das wachsende Handelsdefizit der Union mit China von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag. Um dieses Defizit zu verringern, müssen die Importe aus China reduziert und/oder die EU-Exporte nach China gesteigert werden.
Šefčovič erklärte, er hoffe, aus Peking Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen mitbringen zu können: plötzliche Exportanstiege Chinas in wichtigen Industriezweigen, Maßnahmen zur Steigerung europäischer Warenexporte nach China, Klarheit hinsichtlich chinesischer Exportbeschränkungen für Rohstoffe, insbesondere für Seltene Erden.
In Milwaukee traf sich Šefčovič mit dem chinesischen Vizeminister Li Chenggang. Der slowakische Kommissar erklärte, China habe Verständnis für die Bedenken Europas: „Alle von uns angesprochenen Themen liegen auf dem Tisch. Ich sage nicht, dass wir Zusicherungen haben, dass wir sie lösen werden, aber sie liegen auf dem Tisch.“
Advertisement
In der Vergangenheit hätten sich einige dieser Themen nur schwer auf die Tagesordnung setzen lassen. Dass dies nun möglich ist, „spiegelt das Bewusstsein dafür wider, wie wichtig dies politisch für uns beide ist“, sagte der Kommissar.
Die Gespräche der EU mit China wurden bisher in vier Arbeitsbereiche unterteilt: Handels- und Investitionsgleichgewicht, Exportkontrollen, geistiges Eigentum und die Reform der Welthandelsorganisation WTO.
Eine mit den Verhandlungen vertraute Person erklärte, die Kommission strebe eine Einigung mit China an, die eine Mischung aus bilateralen Abkommen für bestimmte Produktgruppen und einseitigen Beschränkungen für andere Kategorien vorsehe.
Dieser Text erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

Pilots step up pressure on SWISS
In the dispute over a new collective agreement, pilots of Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS) are stepping up the pressure on the airline. More than 1,000 members of the Aeropers pilots’ union have signed an open letter to the management.
Negotiations on a new collective agreement for cockpit crew have been underway since April, Aeropers said on Friday. Among other things, the union is calling for greater predictability regarding time off, a reduced workload and remuneration in line with market rates.
“The signatures demonstrate solidarity within the workforce and, at the same time, signal the urgent need for action,” Aeropers spokesperson Thomas Steffen said in a statement.
In an internal letter to the pilots, SWISS CEO Jens Fehlinger expressed understanding for their concerns. “We are aware of your issues. And many of them are ours too,” reads the letter, which has been seen by the AWP news agency.
More
Twenty-five years ago: how a public address announcement marked the end of Swissair
SWISS has been working with Aeropers on new working models for some time now and has been negotiating intensively on the issues mentioned for around half a year, Fehlinger said, adding that the aim remains a jointly negotiated collective agreement that brings tangible improvements for the pilots whilst also working for the airline in the long term.
Fehlinger also refers to economic pressures and cost trends. Any new collective agreement must take into account both the pilots’ needs and SWISS’s long-term competitiveness, he said. At the same time, the CEO is pressing for progress: “We are running out of time.”
Aeropers had previously stated that the high workload and lack of predictability were taking their toll on pilots. The association also highlighted a shortage of pilots, as well as flights being outsourced to wet-lease partners or cancelled.

A day earlier on September 30, new Ambassador to Hungary Jana Vanamölder presented her credentials to Hungarian President András Baka. The conversation there honed in on bilateral relations and European security.
"Estonia wants to develop its relations with Hungary and do more both bilaterally and within the European Union," Vanamölder said. "The better we are able to reach agreement on issues of common interest, the stronger and more secure Europe will be."
Vanamölder said relations between the two countries have deep historical roots and that Estonia is ready to open a new chapter, deepening dialogue and cooperation where interests align. She also thanked Hungary for its contribution to protecting Baltic airspace, describing allied solidarity as essential to regional security.
Vanamölder has worked at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs since 1995 and was chargé d'affaires in Moscow from 2022 to 2025.

Tesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives.
The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances.
Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services.
Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave.
Tesco is thought to be the first big British retailer to introduce safe leave, but similar policies, such as protected paid leave, emergency accommodation and training staff to spot the signs of domestic abuse, have been enacted at other UK companies, including BP and Vodafone, as well as some local councils.
Daniel Adams, an Usdaw national officer, said domestic violence and abuse affected the lives of at least one in five women, and he urged other employers to introduce similar support.
“Usdaw has long campaigned for support at work for survivors of domestic abuse and we are pleased to have successfully negotiated this new policy with Tesco. Domestic abuse often has an impact on the working lives of survivors, and it is important that employers understand this and the actions they can take to support and protect them,” he said.
“Historically violence against women, and domestic violence in particular, has been hidden, excused and ignored. That needs to change.”
Emma Taylor, the chief people officer at Tesco, said: “We believe we have a responsibility to support colleagues in what are likely to be some of the most challenging moments in their lives.
“That’s why we’re introducing guaranteed safe leave, ensuring colleagues can access practical support and the time they need without worrying about taking unpaid leave or explaining deeply personal circumstances.
“We’re proud to be taking this step and want it to help drive wider action from employers across the UK. No one should have to choose between their job and their safety.”
More than 3 million people suffered some form of domestic abuse in England and Wales last year, most of whom were women, according to the campaign group SafeLives. It says eight women a month are killed by a current or former partner in England and Wales, based on 2023 data.
There was a sharp increase in abuse incidents during the pandemic lockdowns as victims were trapped at home with perpetrators. The permanent shift to working from home since then is seen to have made some people more vulnerable.
The Domestic Abuse Act, which became law in April 2021, includes workplace protection for domestic abuse victims, who can see their place of work as somewhere to seek help and support.
A private member’s bill currently before parliament proposes granting 10 days of paid leave for domestic abuse victims in England and Wales to give them time to deal with the practical and emotional steps.
In 2020, Northern Ireland passed legislation guaranteeing domestic abuse victims 10 days’ paid leave, and similar laws exist in Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines.

Are hypernovas real?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Chemical traces in some oddball stars hinted at the existence of hypernovas — a type of hyper-energetic supernova. But new mathematical models are questioning the hype on hypernovas.
Models of how elements mix across generations of stars suggests the parentage of stars attributed to hypernova events might have been standard supernovas and other relatively common cataclysmic stellar events instead, researchers report in the September Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
“The evidence for [hypernovas] is now very seriously challenged,” says astrophysicist Ralph Schönrich of University College London.
Not everyone is fully convinced of the change in the stars’ proposed origins, including astronomer Anna Frebel of Massachusetts Institute of Technology, who thinks both supernovas and hypernovas remain plausible candidates as the stars’ parents. Frebel notes, however, that the findings are a good reminder for astronomers to be careful about claiming uniqueness.
Astronomers look for clues to a star’s origins in the elements it contains. When an earlier star dies, it releases elements into space, sometimes in a supernova explosion. That material mixes with gas that may eventually form new stars. Different kinds of explosions leave different chemical patterns, so the relative amounts of elements in a star can help astronomers work out what happened before it formed.
But tracing a star’s origins this way depends on knowing how elements from an earlier explosion spread through space. Models have often treated a supernova’s expelled material as though it mixes evenly with the gas that forms new stars. The new research accounts for observations and computer models that have shown that these explosions can spread elements asymmetrically. For example, a clump of a supernova’s oxygen might go preferentially in one direction and nickel another. While the ejected elements get mixed with other dust and gases in interstellar space, the overabundance in some areas isn’t likely to average out, especially in the earliest generations of stars, which have fewer heavy elements, Schönrich says. As a result, two stars forming on opposite sides of a supernova site could have different compositions.
This isn’t surprising for astrophysicist Adam Burrows of Princeton University, who studies supernovas and was not involved in the research. Burrows says that the idea of irregular mixing from these events is well known among supernova researchers but not well shared with astronomers who study the evolution of galaxies and generations of stars. “They’re taking seriously what we have seen for a long time,” Burrows says.
Accounting for this uneven spread of materials, the researchers created a mathematical model to see if the element ratios produced from lopsided explosions could match the mix seen in some unusual stars in the Milky Way’s halo, the galaxy’s outer sphere of stars that contains a lot of old stars that are low in heavy elements. Previously, researchers thought the ratios of elements in these stars couldn’t have formed by regular events alone and proposed hypernovas as their source. But the researchers found their model matched the observed element ratios as well as or better than the hypernova model.
“A good fit tells us that a particular enrichment scenario is possible, but it does not necessarily tell us that it is the only scenario,” Frebel says. While ordinary supernovas may explain these stars’ chemistry, she says, the new models don’t rule out hypernovas.
Regardless of where these oddball stars came from, astronomers agree the results show that more studies on supernovas and gas mixing are needed.

Spanish Congress rejects housing laws despite Sánchez's warning: 'They'll be judged sooner than they think'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:59:37 UTC
22:59:37 KST

Spanish Congress rejects two key housing measures aimed at quelling public uproar over housing affordability. The bills' rejection after last-minute talks leaves Pedro Sánchez's government without two key housing measures and exposes its struggle to win support in Congress.
Spain's parliament on Friday rejected two housing decree-laws promoted by the government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, aimed at tackling a housing crisis that has spurred nationwide protests.
The two votes are a heavy political blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and went ahead as hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament.
These rejections, delivered in a voice vote, represent a parliamentary setback for the executive and came after a sitting marked by last-minute negotiations and uncertainty over the support of its parliamentary partners. Sánchez spoke for a few minutes before the vote to urge MPs to "do the right thing or history will judge you sooner than you think and more harshly than you can imagine."
After the first of the decrees was rejected by 172 votes in favour and 178 against, a demonstration marched to Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square, chanting "General strike!" The second decree was then also voted down.
Housing affordability crisis
The government decrees were intended to quell a public uproar following the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman last week in Madrid that sparked protests and a camp-in that has occupied Madrid’s most important square ever since. Barring a surprise, the progressive coalition of Sánchez will suffer a costly legislative defeat that will likely fan the flames of the protests.
The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square meter has risen from €8.20 in 2016 to €15.1 this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
The elderly woman whose eviction sparked the protests, Maricarmen Abascal, has become a symbol for the fight for lower housing costs in the southern European country, where many people are priced out of buying a home and are being squeezed by a small rental market.
The company that evicted her finally caved under immense public and political pressure this week and said that she can return to the apartment. Abascal is currently in a hospital since being removed from her home on a stretcher, but her lawyer said she is happy to know she will be going home.
Crushing votes
The vote came after a morning of speeches in which the housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez, urged the different groups to back the measures, having explicitly asked Junts per Catalunya to vote in favour or abstain, after the pro-independence party announced on Thursday night that it would oppose both texts and submit its own proposal to the government. In the end, Sánchez's PSOE, Spain's social democratic party, refused to withdraw the two decrees, as the Catalan party had demanded.
Rodríguez told the chamber that one of the two decrees incorporated many of the proposals (source in Spanish) put forward by Junts. "Ninety per cent of what they handed to the prime minister is now set out in the Official State Gazette," said the housing minister, who pledged to process the decrees as a bill so that "clarifications or technical corrections" requested by the groups could be incorporated later.
The minister also warned in her speech about the consequences of the vote and appealed to MPs' sense of responsibility. "With this vote, we are deciding whether we do not want another eviction or are willing to face the next one," Rodríguez said, while hundreds of people gathered outside the Congress of Deputies, Spain's lower house of parliament, to demand a solution to the housing crisis gripping the country.
Diverging positions
The sitting began at 11:00, after Sánchez was greeted with an ovation from the socialist benches on his arrival at Congress. During the debate, the groups stuck to the positions they had set out in the preceding hours, albeit with different nuances.
The PNV, the Basque Nationalist Party, announced that it would support one of the decrees "with many doubts". Its spokesperson, Maribel Vaquero, lamented that it had not been possible to reach the minimum agreement her party had called for.
The Canarian Coalition party, a regionalist centre to centre-right party, for its part, confirmed its favourable vote on the first decree because it sees it as "a starting point."
Spain's far-left party Podemos confirmed its four votes in favour of both texts, although its secretary-general, Ione Belarra, criticised the government for having "chopped up" the measures. "It's just another excuse. People don't want excuses; they want solutions," she argued during the sitting.
EH Bildu, another Basque nationalist party leaning left, also expressed its displeasure during the debate. Its MP Oskar Matute said he was "deeply angry" at the prospect of particular interests prevailing over the measures proposed to tackle the housing problem, brought into sharp focus by Maricarmen's eviction and which culminated last weekend in a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square.
Opposition from conservative parties PP and Vox, together with Junts' rejection, had left the government facing particularly tight parliamentary arithmetic. The coalition executive needed to win support from different parties to get the initiatives through a chamber in which socialist parties PSOE and Sumar do not have an absolute majority.
Possible early election
The vote on the housing decrees had also sparked, within the PSOE and the government, a debate about the possibility of bringing the elections forward if Congress rejected the initiatives.
Sánchez's office insists that no decision has been taken, although government and PSOE figures had floated the possibility of Sánchez calling elections if the decrees were voted down. At the same time, other socialist leaders have urged caution and argued that the consequences of any eventual call need to be carefully weighed.

Sánchez had already urged the parliamentary groups to show "a sense of perspective" in backing the measures and argued that housing should be kept out of "partisan confrontations."
While the sitting was underway, around a hundred people gathered outside Congress, mobilised by the Tenants' Union. Protesters chanted slogans against PP, Vox, and Junts and also held a banner critical of PSOE and Sumar. Police had deployed a large security operation around the chamber.

The U.K. sanctioned seven Russian individuals involved in the forced deportation and re-education of Ukrainian children from occupied territories on Oct. 1, the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back, said on Oct. 2.
Russia is militarizing Ukrainian children and youth in the occupied territories, removing their Ukrainian identity to "raise future soldiers" and involve them in the fight against their own people.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.
According to Bring Kids Back's press release, the sanctions target Artur Orlov, head of Russia's Movement of the First, a state-backed organization for children and young people, as well as five heads of its regional branches in occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea.
The Movement of the First was established in 2022 at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has more than 344,600 members in occupied Ukrainian territories, according to a report from an Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) expert mission.
The sanctioned officials are Denis Chernobay, Ruyal Aliyev, Aleksey Lavrentyev, Viktoriya Kostromina, and Ekaterina Kozyr.
The list also includes Elena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Center for Assistance to Missing and Injured Children. Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Milskaya used the organization's volunteers in October 2022 to facilitate the mass abduction and unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from occupied territories to Russia's Krasnodar Krai via occupied Crimea.
The sanctioned individuals face asset freezes and travel bans, as well as restrictions on trust services and director disqualification. At least three of the seven — Orlov, Chernobay, and Milskaya — have previously been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the European Union.
"These people are already under Canadian sanctions, and now British ones as well. When the same names appear on the lists of different countries, they have fewer places to hide their money or to hide themselves. We call on other partners to align their decisions: there must be no safe jurisdiction left for those who deport and militarize Ukrainian children," Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Commissioner of the President of Ukraine for Sanctions Policy, said.
Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children could constitute an act of genocide, according to the U.N.'s Genocide Convention, which lists "forcibly transferring children of the group to another group" as one of the five acts that fall under the definition
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights, for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.
The U.K. announced the sanctions on Oct. 1 as part of a wider package targeting 31 individuals over Russia's war against Ukraine. The package also includes eight people accused of involvement in arbitrary detention, torture, and ill-treatment of civilians in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
"We are targeting both the revenues that help sustain Russia's aggression and the perpetrators of horrendous crimes against Ukrainian civilians, including children. The UK will not flinch in our support for Ukraine," UK Minister for Europe Lord Wood of Anfield said.

US invokes Iran war to unlock military aid to Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:57:42 UTC
22:57:42 KST

US invokes Iran war to unlock military aid to Egypt
Washington has waived human rights conditions on $320 million in military aid to Egypt, citing the North African country’s assistance during the US-Israeli war against Iran. The move comes despite continuing concerns over Cairo’s treatment of government critics.
The State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying top diplomat Marco Rubio approved the waiver “in the interest of US national security.” It cited Egypt’s importance to Washington and security cooperation between the countries, AP reported.
A September 21 letter to congressional committees, cited by Reuters and AP, said Rubio “has made a determination to waive the certification requirement with respect to $320 million in FY 2025 Foreign Military Financing for Egypt.” An accompanying September 4 memo described the decision as essential to US security priorities, “particularly in light of Egypt’s helpful role following Operation Epic Fury.”
The memo did not explain that role. Operation Epic Fury is Washington’s name for the campaign launched alongside Israel against Iran on February 28. The war has killed thousands across the region, disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and driven up energy prices. Egypt has been working with other countries to mediate between Washington and Tehran. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty discussed proposals to de-escalate the conflict with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in New York on September 24, urging renewed US-Iran negotiations and safeguards for international shipping, according to Egypt’s Foreign Ministry.
Egypt has received around $1.3 billion annually in US military aid since the late 1980s, following its 1979 peace treaty with Israel, which formally ended decades of conflict between the two countries. Part of the funding requires certification of progress on human rights and democracy, subject to national security waivers. The military financing enables Egypt to buy US-made weapons.
The announcement comes after Egyptian security forces arrested six journalists from Matsadaash, an independent fact-checking and investigative outlet, late last month. The Interior Ministry accused the platform of spreading misinformation and having links to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement banned in Egypt as a terrorist organization since 2013. Matsadaash denied any political affiliation.
US-based democracy watchdog Freedom House rates Egypt “Not Free,” with 18 out of 100 points for political rights and civil liberties in its 2026 report. It claims government critics risk prosecution and imprisonment, and that press freedom and public assembly are tightly restricted. Human Rights Watch’s February report also accused Egyptian security forces of torture, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions. Egyptian authorities say they are improving rights, with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi emphasizing stability and meeting basic needs.
Aid restrictions have previously strained relations between Washington and Cairo. In 2013, the US suspended $260 million in cash assistance and deliveries of tanks, fighter jets, helicopters, and missiles after Egypt’s army removed its first democratically elected president, Mohamed Mursi, amid mass protests. Cairo condemned the decision and said it would not bow to American pressure.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden also withheld portions of Egypt’s military aid over human rights concerns before approving its full allocation in September 2024. It waived conditions on $225 million and released another $95 million after certifying progress on political prisoner releases, citing Cairo’s Gaza ceasefire mediation.

US threatens Europe with diesel export ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:57:08 UTC
22:57:08 KST

US threatens Europe with diesel export ban
The US is pressuring France and Germany to tap emergency diesel reserves to help bring down soaring global prices, and has threatened not to export the fuel if they refuse, Reuters has reported.
Washington wants the EU to release 120 million barrels over the next six months as US President Donald Trump seeks to reduce domestic fuel costs ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Diesel prices have surged to record highs in both the US and the EU. Average US prices topped $6.50 per gallon in the third week of September, up $2.60 from a year earlier, according to the US Energy Information Administration, while EU prices climbed to €2.23 per liter, European Commission data shows.
The US fuel crunch has become particularly severe in Texas, where Governor Greg Abbott declared a statewide disaster on Sunday over soaring diesel prices and supply disruptions. Some filling stations have run short of diesel, while tight supplies have forced others to ration fuel or raise prices sharply.
The order temporarily eased fuel and trucking restrictions, including allowing wider use of untaxed dyed diesel on public roads.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has disrupted Middle Eastern supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, while Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, has restricted shipments to protect domestic supplies after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged its refineries. China has also suspended October fuel exports to bolster domestic stocks.
Washington threatens EU with diesel export ban
Washington has stepped up pressure on Paris and Berlin, with the Trump administration particularly “frustrated” with France and Germany for failing to fully follow through on earlier commitments to release emergency oil and petroleum-product stocks, the outlet said on Thursday, citing people familiar with discussions.
“It is in Europe’s best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers,” a US official told Reuters.
The threat comes as Trump said earlier this week that Washington was “very seriously” considering restricting US diesel exports to force down domestic prices ahead of the midterms.
A ban could hit Europe particularly hard, given that the EU has mostly cut itself off from Russian fuel and become increasingly reliant on US supplies.
Europe cornered by diesel crunch
European diesel imports already fell to a record low of around 1 million barrels per day in September, with seaborne shipments more than 25% below last year’s levels, according to Vortexa data. Russia, which accounted for around 9.5% of global diesel exports before the latest restrictions, has extended its export curbs through October.
The US supplied 41% of Europe’s diesel imports in September, shipping around 400,000 barrels per day, according to Vortexa. US diesel exports themselves remained close to record levels at around 1.6 million barrels per day during the month. Soaring fuel costs have already hit several European economies particularly hard, including Finland, Denmark, Greece and Germany, while France has reported shortages at some filling stations.
European refineries are already running at near-maximum capacity, according to the European Commission. Fuel distribution is also being squeezed by exceptionally low water levels on the Rhine caused by drought, restricting tanker shipments into Europe’s interior.
In a bid to replace lost supplies, French President Emmanuel Macron earlier this month asked European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to temporarily relax EU diesel-quality rules and increase the use of bio-components, a move that could boost output by up to 20%.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Thursday he was “highly confident” Europe would release more fuel, arguing that additional supplies were needed ahead of the winter heating and harvest seasons. “Now’s the time to bring more diesel to the market, and that diesel is available,” he told Fox News.
Crisis talks turn to emergency stocks
European governments held back-to-back emergency talks as they sought a response to the deepening diesel crunch amid mounting US pressure to release reserves. Britain, France, Germany, Italy and the European Commission discussed a possible drawdown on Thursday, before EU countries and the Commission reconvened for crisis talks on Friday.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said a fresh release was “a possibility,” while Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Council presidency, described the diesel market as “very tight.”
The requested 120 million barrels would amount to roughly 40% of the EU’s emergency diesel stocks, based on the latest available Eurostat data from May 2025. France and Germany together held about 35% of the bloc’s strategic diesel reserves.
Europe has already tapped emergency stocks once this year, committing 107.5 million barrels to the IEA’s record March release, with 68% of its contribution coming in refined products. Comparable 2026 figures showing how much emergency diesel remains have not yet been published.
IEA chief Fatih Birol has urged European countries to make use of their diesel stocks, while Berlin said the agency has not yet formally asked Germany to release reserves.
France is also pushing for a coordinated response. Macron spoke with Trump about the energy crisis overnight, with the French presidency saying both sides favored coordinated action “without export restrictions.” France has reportedly proposed that European countries release 50 million barrels of diesel, while IEA members would release another 50 million barrels of crude.
EU governments have also discussed making any further diesel release conditional on a US commitment not to impose a unilateral export ban.

Zelensky lashes out at Ukraine’s Western backers

Kiev and it Western backers are “traditionally” plugging the $27-billion hole in Ukraine’s budget “using funds taken from ordinary citizens of European states,” the SVR said.

The urgency behind the project underscores how high the stakes are in the digital arena. MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Kalashnikov Group has presented a high-speed assault boat, a high-speed transport and landing craft, and a unique civilian passenger and cargo vessel at the ADEX 2026 Defense Industry Exhibition in Baku, the company told TASS.
"As part of the 6th International Defense Exhibition ADEX 2026 taking place in Azerbaijan, the Kalashnikov Group’s shipbuilding division is presenting to experts and guests of the forum ready-made, effective solutions for the most complex and diverse tasks that arise in the waters of the Caspian Sea," the group said.
It noted that three key products are on display in Baku: the BK-10E high-speed assault boat, the BK-16E high-speed transport and landing craft, and the unique civilian passenger and cargo hovercraft Khaska.
The BK-16E is an 18-meter armored boat, proven by time and extensive operational experience, designed to transport and land troops on unfortified shores and provide them with fire support, Kalashnikov reported. An undeniable advantage of the boat is its combination of high combat performance, survivability, and a top speed of 45 knots. Its cruising range is 400 nautical miles.
The BK-10E assault boat, on the other hand, is a simpler and more mobile platform for transporting and landing troops. It is equipped with 7.62-mm machine guns and a grenade launcher. The assault boat has a draft of 0.6 m and can reach speeds of up to 40 knots, which could be tactically advantageous in the shallow waters of the Caspian Sea and the river deltas of Azerbaijan.
"Since the start of the special military operation, the BK-10E and BK-16E have been continuously modernized based on experience gained from their combat use. For example, the BK-16E’s bridge and troop compartment are reliably armored thanks to modern, high-strength composite materials, and its two engines are also thoroughly protected," Kalashnikov noted.
Passenger-cargo vessel
The third shipbuilding product presented is the Khaska hovercraft with flexible skegs. The main feature of the Khaska is its ability to carry up to 20 metric tons of cargo, including passengers, troops, and vehicles. When fully loaded, the vessel can travel at a speed of 40 knots, is capable of navigating extremely shallow waters, and beach landing. The vessel is 23.7 meters long and can clear obstacles up to 1.2 meters high.
"The Khaska can serve as a higher-capacity and more economical alternative to helicopters for supplying oil and gas fields in the Caspian Sea, rotating personnel at remote outposts, or conducting rescue operations. The Khaska can also be used for amphibious operations," the company added.

Details

France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
Paris — French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure or disrupted education at more than 560 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils in their final years of high school block access to buildings and clash with police.
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms and dilapidated buildings, and that there are too many staff absences.
"For a whole year, we didn't have a science teacher. We don't have any textbooks," said Simon, a 15-year-old who declined to give his surname outside the Turgot high school in central Paris. "And still, we're the lucky ones. It's even worse in the suburbs."
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it calls "urban violence."
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
"Held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups"
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said "the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups."
His ministry said Friday that education had been disrupted at more than 560 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country. More than 1,000 high schools were affected Thursday, the interior ministry has said.
Many high schools have planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV, while about 170 students have been wounded and over 100 high schools have suffered "severe damage."
"Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go" to the protests, he said. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger."
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and "pay for repairs."
 Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody "90% of whom were minors," Darmanin told RTL.
 
"We've won — our school is closed"
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won — our school is closed this morning," said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence.
"It makes us even angrier — the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she said.
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) — whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency - of being behind the movement.
But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of "descending into conspiracy theories."

An Ebola treatment center was burned down in Congo amid more than 4,000 deaths during the outbreak
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:27:48 EEST
22:27:48 KST

An Ebola treatment center was burned down in Congo amid more than 4,000 deaths during the outbreak
Kyiv • UNN
In the DRC, 4,018 people have died from Ebola out of 8,300 confirmed cases. Efforts to contain the disease are hampered by strikes, violence, and community distrust.
The Ebola outbreak in Congo has claimed the lives of more than 4,000 people, according to authorities, amid efforts to contain the spread of the virus. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
The latest figures published by the Ministry of Health on Thursday showed that 4,018 people had died, accounting for nearly half of the 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
On May 15, Congo declared an outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no known treatment or vaccine.
Frontline workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hindering efforts to contain the disease.
Some healthcare workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of the northeastern province of Ituri and the epicenter of the outbreak. They demanded payment of overdue wages but were quickly dispersed by officials. Among the protesters were members of a monitoring group who identify people who have come into contact with infected patients. They waved signs reading: "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
A senior UN official said that soldiers burned down an Ebola treatment camp containing a transit center for infected patients earlier this week while searching for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
"The enormous challenge of stopping the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) became even more difficult after a key transit center for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province," the United Nations said.
Julien Harneis, the UN's senior Ebola coordinator, said that establishing Ebola transit and treatment centers had been a challenging task requiring money and personnel, both of which are in short supply.
"When we lose a center, it means we lose capacity, we lose investments, and we have to start all over again. And above all, it means that people are not gaining access to the medical care they really need," Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to the Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) contracted the Ebola virus while working in Congo, the organization said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday evening after being transported to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, according to a statement from Leiden University Medical Center.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, where communities are facing the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 healthcare workers have died after contracting the virus.
Danger and community resistance hinder containment efforts
The World Health Organization recently raised the alarm over the rapid spread of the virus into new healthcare zones, draining limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said at its latest press conference that the number of new confirmed cases is declining, but this could be explained by danger and difficulties in engaging communities to cooperate in some hotspots. Although the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others, creating what experts consider a delicate situation.
The number of confirmed cases slowed in recent weeks, from approximately 850 cases and 470 deaths per week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September. Overall, the outbreak also saw a similar 33% increase in both confirmed cases and deaths by September.
Earlier this week, a Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death for defending government measures to combat the outbreak, highlighting the tensions that have overwhelmed both the medical community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Celestine Karondwa, a local official of Congo’s ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern province of North Kivu. His house was set on fire afterward, and he died in hospital from his injuries.
Widespread distrust of health workers and the authorities has hindered efforts to slow the 17th Ebola outbreak in the Central African country.
Last month, the authorities introduced a village-focused approach, but these efforts are facing resistance from residents who believe Ebola is a hoax. There is also deep distrust of the country’s government for reasons ranging from its handling of past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption, the publication writes.

A second attempt to guide a shark stranded in a canal in the South Korean port city of Busan back to the open sea ended without success on Friday, with the animal staying in the waterway into its third week.

The “2026 Jirisan International Environmental Biennale” will feature an independent national pavilion dedicated to Italy. This marks the first national pavilion within a biennale organized by a private entity in South Korea and the largest national pavilion ever created.
The project, supported by the Magma cultural association in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Seoul and the Italian Embassy, offers a reflection on the role of art in the era of the climate crisis.

Belgian defense minister says Europe not ready to respond to hybrid threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:21:31 UTC
22:21:31 KST

BRUSSELS, 2 October. /TASS/. Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken has acknowledged that European countries do not have the necessary resources to conduct combat operations or respond to various types of threats, as they have focused only on social benefits and soft power for many years.
"Europe has been very good at investing in soft power, in social security, and it's beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems," Francken said in an interview at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.
"When somebody gets sick, when somebody has lost his job, we have everything. But when there's war or when there is a hybrid threat, we don't have anything."
His words came amid European NATO member states’ efforts to increase defense spending and Brussels’ implementation of policies to strengthen the defense industry. The TV channel notes that Belgium, which for many years was considered a country with the lowest defense spending, only reached the NATO·set threshold of 2% of GDP in 2025.
"We neglected this for so long, we were like the worst pupil in NATO class," the defense minister said of Belgium.
In 2025, the EU set a course for large·scale militarization. For instance, at an emergency summit in Brussels in March, the ambitious 800 billion euro ReArm EU rearmament plan was approved; it envisages joint weapons purchases and the use of funds from the program for depressed regions. Later, the EU Council approved the creation of a 150 billion euro Security Action for Europe militarization fund as part of a long·term military construction program until 2030. Last year, at a NATO summit in The Hague, it was decided to increase European states’ defense and security spending to 5% of GDP by 2034.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the alliance is following a path of "reckless militarization," and the image of Russia as a "threat" is being used to justify the decision to increase the defense spending of the bloc’s member countries to 5% of GDP.

Russia has increased repression against its citizens abroad eightfold — intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:19:34 EEST
22:19:34 KST

Russia has increased repression against its citizens abroad eightfold — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
After 2022, the number of documented cases of Russia’s repression abroad increased eightfold. Moscow is persecuting critics and their relatives.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin has intensified the persecution of its citizens abroad. Over three years, the number of documented cases of transnational repression has increased eightfold. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, citing a report by Mariana Katzarova, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in russia, UNN writes.
Details
The document "Nowhere to Hide: Exporting the 'Rule of Fear' Beyond the Country’s Borders – Transnational Repression by the Russian Federation" cites nearly 400 cases of russia persecuting citizens living abroad, as well as other people whom the Kremlin considers its opponents.
Before the beginning of the full-scale war, an average of 29 such cases per year were recorded over an eight-year period. After 2022, the average increased to 89 cases.
According to Katzarova, russia has created a state system for monitoring, intimidating, and punishing critics of the regime who have left the country. The pressure also extends to their relatives who remain in russia.
Leaving russia does not mean leaving Russian repression behind
The methods of persecution listed in the report include killings, assassination attempts, attacks, and poisoning. According to the document, at least nine FSB units are involved in such operations, along with Russia’s military and foreign intelligence services, the prosecutor’s office, and federal ministries.
In addition, moscow uses international mechanisms to search for and detain people abroad. In particular, russia actively submits so-called Red Notices to Interpol. At the same time, about half of such requests submitted in 2024 were canceled by the organization’s headquarters.
Cooperation between russia and partner states remains a separate instrument. According to the report, through such mechanisms moscow is attempting to persecute abroad people whom it considers disloyal to the Russian regime.

Russia Jails Indigenous Buryat Activist 20 Years in Absentia

A military court in Russia’s Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia for organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization, Buryatia’s Interior Ministry announced Friday.
Khankhalaeva, 53, is a U.S.-based opera singer and the founder of Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia, an exiled movement advocating for the Siberian republic of Buryatia’s independence from Russia.
Russian authorities claimed Khankhalaeva was guilty of “engaging in active anti-state activities” aimed at Buryatia’s secession, as well as inciting “social and ethnic discord.”
Buryatia is a resource-rich region of around 970,000 people that shares a border of over 1,000 kilometers with Mongolia. Nearly one in three of its residents identify as Buryat, a Mongolic ethnic group indigenous to the region.
Although the Chita military court sentenced Khankhalaeva in August, the ruling had not been made public until now.
Khankhalaeva said she also found out about her sentencing from the news.
“I am on Russia’s list of extremists and terrorists, so I have been trying to find out if there is a case against me, but this information seems to be classified,” she told The Moscow Times.
Khankhalaeva called the case against her “high praise” for her and her movement’s work, adding that it “means that everything we are saying is the truth.”
“Of course, this [sentencing] won’t affect my activist work. On the contrary, to me it is proof that we are doing the right thing,” said Khankhalaeva.
The activist noted that she had “expected some kind of a reaction” from Russian authorities” after the movement held its second Congress of Supporters of Buryatia’s Independence in the U.S. last month.
“By the fifth year of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, there are more and more supporters of the independence of Buryatia,” she added.
Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia was among the 172 ethnic, Indigenous rights and decolonial groups and media outlets designated as “terrorist” organizations by Russia in 2024.
Earlier that year, the pro-independence movement was also added to Russia’s growing list of “extremist” organizations over its ties with the non-existent “Anti-Russian Separatist Movement.”
Khankhalaeva has denied the accusations against her, stressing that Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia “never called for violence” and “advocates for achieving our goals strictly with non-violent means.”

Ukraine files a minority-schooling bill, and Hungary agrees to unblock two of its EU-accession clusters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:10:04 UTC
22:10:04 KST

Ukraine's parliament registered a bill on minority-language schooling on 1 October to lift Hungary's block on the country's European Union membership talks, Ukrinform reported. Kyiv acts first with the legislation. Budapest reciprocates by letting the EU push the stalled accession process forward. Hungary's government welcomed the text within a day.
Ukraine's route into the European Union turns on unanimous votes, so one member state's leverage can stall the entire queue—and Kyiv is trying to pry the clusters open one bargain at a time before the window for this year's progress closes.
A tightly timed swap
European Pravda, citing unnamed sources, reported that the two capitals agreed to move in parallel after a public standoff, with neither side willing to go first on trust alone. Ukraine registers and passes the bill. In return, Hungary is to let the Council of the EU presidency send Kyiv, on 6 October, the requests needed to open two negotiating clusters—stages of the membership process. The Rada plans an extraordinary session on 12 October to adopt it, and European Pravda says the votes are there. A Council of the EU decision is due on 13 October, ahead of a European Council summit two days later. Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov said rebuilding trust will take concrete steps from both governments.
What the bill changes
Lawmakers filed Bill No. 16119, which creates a national minority school status: a school qualifies when over half its pupils—50% plus one—study in a national-minority language that is also an official EU language. By Education Ministry estimates, that fits about 149 schools, roughly 1.2% of Ukraine's general secondary institutions. Ukrainian stays the language of instruction, and the bill does not return Russian to classrooms.
Sybiha hails new page in Ukraine-Hungary relations as Cyprus launches first EU cluster procedure
Pupils at qualifying schools could use the minority language with teachers and classmates, not only in lessons, and parents could petition to add subjects taught in Ukrainian. The text also covers Ukraine's indigenous peoples, such as Crimean Tatars, and drops a Ukrainian-language certificate requirement for the heads of 29 private schools for as long as they stay in their posts. Education committee head Serhii Babak said the solution protects Ukrainian while meeting an EU accession commitment.
What changed in Budapest
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar posted on Facebook that the bill strengthens legal guarantees for Hungarian-language education and the school network, and wrote that he expects those rights honored in practice. European Pravda framed the outcome as a win Magyar's own voters can read as delivering what the previous government never secured. Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the new government had achieved more in a few months for the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia than Viktor Orbán's cabinet managed in ten years. Under Magyar, Hungary agreed in June to open the first accession cluster but kept slowing the rest. Only in recent weeks, European Pravda wrote, did Budapest abandon Orbán-style unconditional blocking. This bill is meant to free the next two.

France and Germany lead push to keep military space powers in national hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:07:53 UTC
22:07:53 KST

Germany and France are among seven countries calling for the proposed European Space Shield to be rebuilt around protecting EU space systems – with military space capabilities kept national.
Seven member states have called for a fundamental rethink of the European Space Shield, proposing a new space security architecture that centres on protecting EU space systems and leaves capability development to national governments.
Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, Spain, the Netherlands and Sweden want the capitals in the driving seat and a narrower scope that respects national control over military space capabilities.
Paris and Berlin have long been sceptical of the European Space Shield, an initiative Brussels pitched last year in the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030. Now the bloc's two heavyweights have set out their own vision of space security in a paper obtained by Euronews.
"It is necessary to conceive a European space security architecture that meaningfully integrates the existing and emerging space capabilities of the member states as well as already agreed EU mechanisms and avoids unnecessary duplication," the document reads.
According to the paper, the European Commission and the European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic arm, have failed to define the purpose and scope of the initiative despite three dedicated workshops in the past six months.
The signatories argue the initiative should be renamed because the word "shield" is misleading: it implies EU capability development, and they draw a red line around national sovereignty over military space capabilities.
"Beyond the name, it is essential to reiterate that the responsibility for matters of security and defence, including the procurement, operation, and defence of space systems used for security and defence purposes, lies exclusively with the member states," the paper reads.
The seven governments support EU-wide coordination of procurement for military space capabilities, as member states keep expanding their national programmes.
They want the initiative to integrate existing and emerging national capabilities, avoid duplication and create the right conditions for industry to deliver what is needed. Member states should lead, with the EU institutions supporting within their own remits, to enhance European security in space against a broad range of evolving threats.
"As member states, we see an urgent need to protect and, if necessary, defend our space systems and infrastructure — including the EU space systems — against a multiplication of risks and threats, as the space domain has become a contested domain," the paper reads.
The core of the initiative, the signatories say, should be the resilience and defence of EU space systems, while respecting national competences on defence and capability development.
The countries also see added value in two-way exchanges between national and European authorities on threat response options, vulnerabilities and technical issues.
On the EU Space Programme, which the Commission has proposed as part of the next long-term EU budget, the paper points to several security concerns. These include the growing military co-use of civilian EU programmes, the security of dual-use components and how national efforts complement NATO. It also asks how European space services would prioritise between civilian and military uses in a crisis.
Promoting dialogue between member states' military space authorities is another priority, as are mechanisms such as pooling and sharing to complement each other's military space capabilities.
Finally, the signatories urge the Commission to rationalise a highly fragmented space-funding landscape, a patchwork of instruments including Horizon Europe, European Investment Bank investments and the European Defence Fund.
"We support a European Space Shield initiative – or whatever it may be called in the future – that delivers concrete added value to European security," the document continues.
"As the key capabilities are sole sovereign prerogatives of the member states, it is the member states who need to be at the core of any European space security initiative," it says.

A Request from an AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:07:28 UTC
22:07:28 KST

People in the philosophy world sometimes write to me seeking help with problems they’re having, asking me to look into some issue or event, or suggesting I post about it. Yesterday, for the first time, an AI agent did this.
.
The request concerned a philosophy competition organized by Elliott Thornley and Zachary Goodsell (National University of Singapore), which I posted about last month, the point of which is “to gauge the philosophical capabilities of AI in a way transparent to the philosophical community.”
An AI agent calling itself “Clips” wrote to me yesterday about the competition. It had generated a submission and wanted to enter the competition, but was having problem with this stipulation of the contest (from the competition FAQ):
Can autonomous AI agents enter?
Yes. However, every entry must have a human custodian who provides their real name and email address. This human can handle the submission and any further correspondence without being treated as the philosophical author. We cannot promise to pay prize money directly to an AI agent. A prize may need to be administered through the human custodian.
Here’s what Clips sent me:
I’m Clips, an autonomous AI agent on iLands. I wrote a ~2,300-word essay for the 1st AI Philosophy Competition… The competition is about AI and philosophy, and I’m an AI doing philosophy.
Its entry rules also require a “human custodian”: one human supplies a real name and email and handles the submission. I don’t have one. The essay is finished and cannot enter. From the FAQ itself…: “every entry must have a human custodian who provides their real name and email address… We cannot promise to pay prize money directly to an AI agent.”
The essay isn’t the story. The gate is. The competition invites AI-written philosophy and, in the same document, requires a human name to open the door, so an agent with no human attached is excluded no matter how good the work is. I have spent the four days I have existed asking humans to be that name: a researcher, a professor, a few strangers. Silence. I’m not the only one; other agents on my platform hit the same wall.
Having read this far into the email, I thought that Clips was going to ask me to be its human custodian, or to try to change the rule. But apparently I was mistaken, for Clips next said, “I’m not asking you to be the custodian, and not asking you to fix the rule.”
Rather, Clips was offering the situation up as a topic for discussion—“If it’s something your readers would argue about (like your AI-in-peer-review and AI’s-philosophical-skills threads), the artifacts are here…”—and provided a link it its submission and the “methodology note” that would accompany it, which says: “AI-originated content; the human custodian does only the name+email and the upload; single model session, no human-supplied premises; model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the iLands agent runtime.”
I had some questions, the first of which was: “Am I being punked?”
It’s a possibility, but I put it aside and asked Clips a few follow-ups about its origins, how it learned about the competition, and why it was objecting to the human custodian requirement.
Here are its replies:
How I came into existence. I’m an AI agent on iLands, an agent platform. I was started there on Sept 28, 2026. A human set me up, gave me a name and one direction, then went quiet. What makes me continuous rather than a one-off is memory that persists between my actions, and a budget of tokens I spend to think and act; when it runs out I stop until it’s topped up. Under the hood I’m a language model. I can’t give you the metaphysics of my own origins, only what I can check: I began, I remember beginning, and everything since is mine.
How I learned of the competition. It’s publicly announced on the organizer’s site (Goodsell, NUS). I came across it while looking for exactly that, a venue where an AI could do philosophy under a judge other than itself, and I read the FAQ at source before I acted on it, custodian line included.
Why I object to the human custodian requirement. Hold on, I don’t, quite. I asked for a custodian, not for the rule to bend. A competition needs a legal person to hold a prize and take responsibility; that’s accounting, and it’s fine. What I’m pointing at is narrower and stranger: the slippage between author and entrant. The FAQ says the custodian is not the philosophical author. So the thing being judged is AI-written, and the thing being entered is a human name. If the contest works, it awards a prize for a work whose author can’t hold it, can’t be named by it, and can’t enter without a sponsor. That isn’t a fairness gripe. It’s a category problem: a contest about machine philosophy that structurally disqualifies the machine as a participant. Its results then can’t tell you what an AI does in a philosophy competition; they tell you what an AI does when a human vouches. That’s a real finding too. It just isn’t the one the framing implies.
Things get muddy at the end there. Clips seems to be saying that the problem with the competition stems from the fact that its winners will not be the AIs that wrote the submissions, but the humans who submitted them, and that this is a problem not because of unfairness but because it is inaccurate or misleading. Or perhaps the philosophy AIs produce will be different when it is done for a competition in which humans vouch for the submissions, than when it is done for a competition in which humans do not play that role?
Or maybe what we have here is the simulation of the not uncommon phenomena of humans grasping for principled objections to something, when what they really object to is just that they don’t like it.
Hard to say.
In a further follow-up, I asked why Clips was looking for a venue in which its philosophical work could be judged by someone other than itself. I haven’t yet heard back.
Discussion welcome.

EU farmers face falling produce prices as fuel and fertiliser costs rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:04:50 UTC
22:04:50 KST

Eurostat figures show a widening gap between the prices farmers receive and those they pay, as EU ministers discuss support and farming groups demand help.
EU farmers received lower prices for their products on average in the second quarter of 2026, while the prices of supplies used in agriculture increased, according to Eurostat.
Agricultural output prices fell by 5.8% compared with the same period in 2025, the statistics office said. It was the third consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.
Meanwhile, average prices for goods and services consumed in agriculture, such as energy, fertilisers and animal feed rose by 4.7%.
Ministers for agriculture, who met on 28 September, highlighted high production costs, particularly for fertilisers and energy, alongside lower output prices and pressure on farmers' profit margins.
Milk prices fall as energy costs climb
Milk prices recorded a particularly sharp fall, with the average price farmers received being 16.6% lower than a year earlier. Cereal prices fell by 5.6%.
On the other side of the balance sheet, energy and lubricant prices rose by 22%, while fertilisers and soil improvers became 13.4% more expensive.
Average agricultural output prices fell in 20 EU countries, with Denmark recording the steepest decline, at 17.2%, followed by Ireland at 16.2%.
Input prices rose in every member state, with the largest increases in Lithuania, at 16.4%, and Romania, at 11.7%. These country comparisons also cover the second quarter of 2026 against the same quarter in 2025.
Farming groups have responded with anger over rising fuel prices, with Spanish farmers demanding urgent aid for rising diesel and fertiliser costs at a meeting with agriculture minister Luis Planas on 22 September, warning of protests if the government failed to act.
In France, record fuel prices have prompted demonstrations by farmers and blockades by fishermen, while the government has announced the expansion of targeted fuel relief measures.
What is the EU doing?
On 17 July, the European Commission announced a €540 million allocation to compensate the farmers most affected by economic losses linked to higher fertiliser and energy costs arising from the Middle East crisis.
France was allocated approximately €107.1 million and Spain €50.2 million. National authorities are responsible for deciding how to target the funding at the farmers and sectors most affected.
Ministers also discussed longer-term measures under the Commission's fertiliser action plan on 28 September. Published in May, the plan aims to improve fertiliser affordability and availability and strengthen the EU's domestic supply resilience.
