From Nazi founders to Netanyahu friends: Israel's new far-right allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:04:35 UTC
22:04:35 KST

Farid Hafez is a senior research fellow at The Bridge Initiative – a multi-year research project on Islamophobia at Georgetown University in Washington, DC – and assistant teaching professor of international relations at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia.
When Austria's Freedom Party (FPO) entered a government coalition in 2000, it became the first far-right party in the European Union to do so. Its notorious leader, the rhetorically gifted lawyer Jorg Haider, was denied entry to Israel, and an official boycott of the party has been in place ever since. The rationale was the FPO's history: in the words of political scientist Anton Pelinka, "it was a party founded by former Nazis for former Nazis.” Haider and other high-ranking members also used antisemitic language throughout their careers. In 2000, Israel even recalled its ambassador from Vienna over the party's participation in government.
From pariahs to partners
Much has changed since. Alongside many other radical right parties in Europe, the FPO has worked to normalize its relationship with Israel. As these nationalist movements win more votes and enter coalitions from Italy to Sweden and from Germany to the Netherlands, they have tried to present themselves as trustworthy allies of Israel, both to shed their antisemitic baggage and to establish themselves as credible partners on the international stage.
In 2010, a delegation of hard-right functionaries visited Israel and the West Bank to build ties with Israeli politicians. They were welcomed by fringe extremist figures but still shut out of the corridors of power. When the FPO again entered a coalition with the Conservatives in 2017-18, Israeli politicians including lawmaker Yehuda Glick and former member of the Knesset Michael Kleiner advocated regular contact with the party, but many pushed back. Israel’s official line was to work with the civil servants of FPO-led ministries while limiting contact with the ministers themselves.
Today the FPO is arguably Austria's most successful party and leads in the polls, though it is no longer in government. Yet after FPO leader Herbert Kickl's mid-September speech in Strasbourg on "Islamism, Antisemitism: Threats to Europe’s Freedom," his remarks on Israel and antisemitism drew a wave of warmth from the highest levels of the Israeli government.
In 2010, Kickl's party colleague Andreas Molzer, a long-time right-wing populist politician, still evaded any discussion of Austria's Nazi past and the murder of millions of Jews. This time, for the first time, the party leader said the FPO must confront its history. He also affirmed Israel's "right to exist" and endorsed the contested International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism. He recognized the Jewish people's historic connection to "Judea and Samaria" (the West Bank), a stance that effectively denies Palestinian statehood, and pledged to move Austria’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem if he became chancellor.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called Kickl's remarks an "important and positive development," signaling that Israel is prepared to open a substantive dialogue with the FPO despite its past. The Israeli Embassy's official X account reposted Sa'ar's statement in German and called the speech "significant," even though Austria's Jewish community has not welcomed the FPO's shift. Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli described the Strasbourg gathering as a "historic turning point." The governing Likud, which has already joined the European far-right bloc as an observer member of Patriots for Europe, took part directly. Likud's political director Ariel Bulshtein, Knesset member Ariel Kellner, and two rabbis thanked Kickl and FPO Member of the European Parliament Harald Vilimsky by name and called the FPO "friends of Israel and the Jewish people."
4 factors behind Israel's strategic pivot
Why is the Israeli government changing its stance? Several factors are at play.
First, the radical right keeps growing across Europe. The AfD recently won two state elections in eastern Germany. Right-wing parties have led governments in Italy and, until recently, the Netherlands, and they poll at or near the top in Austria, the UK, and Sweden. It makes sense for Israel to move closer to forces that may shape Europe's future.
Second, over the past 15 years, the European hard-right has recast itself as anti-Muslim, distanced itself from its antisemitic past, and reinvented itself as the defender of a "Judeo-Christian" Europe. This has allowed it to side with Israel against the supposed threat of "Islam."
Third, the growing normalization of the far-right within Israel itself has helped. Vilimsky was recently received in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office in Jerusalem, which many saw as a historic turning point. Likud's observer status in Patriots for Europe has also increased the political cost for other potential partners in Europe.
Fourth, and probably most important, as Sa'ar's move shows, diplomacy has become a more critical battlefield for Israel than the military one, especially after the genocide in Gaza and Israel's growing isolation on the world stage. Winning over the growing ranks of far-right voters can only help improve Israel's image.
What remains to be seen is how this will translate into an official diplomatic shift. As of last year, the boycott of the FPO was still on the books, but a new assessment appears to be on the horizon. It would be a huge win for the far-right, not only in Austria.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

The olive harvest begins in early October and continues through the end of November, making it one of the most important agricultural and economic seasons for Palestinian towns and villages.
With the start of the season, attacks by occupiers and Israeli restrictions on farmers’ access to their land have intensified, including beatings, blocking access to fields, theft of crops and the uprooting or damaging of trees.

Of these, 1,404 were carried out by the Israeli army and 647 by occupiers, according to the commission.
Ramallah and Al-Bireh recorded the highest number with 506 attacks, followed by Nablus with 342, Hebron with 272, Jenin with 202, Bethlehem with 187, Tulkarem with 152 and Jerusalem with 149.
The attacks included assaults on Palestinians, damage to property and crops, restrictions on access to land, and the demolition of homes and agricultural structures.

Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in illegal settlements and outposts across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.

Can releasing more of Europe’s emergency reserves bring diesel prices down?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:59:32 UTC
21:59:32 KST

The EU says it is ready for collective action with the IEA on a fresh emergency release. Analysts say releasing diesel reserves could lower pump prices within days, but would offer only short-term relief.
Historically high diesel prices in the EU and growing concerns about a potential US diesel export ban have prompted calls for action in the bloc.
European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said on Friday that the bloc was ready to work with the International Energy Agency on the possible release of fuel reserves to bring down energy prices.
On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency confirmed that it could consider releasing more emergency oil stocks if supply disruptions worsen.
At the time of writing, the size of a potential release has not been confirmed, although France suggested releasing 50 million barrels of diesel — approximately 6.7 million tonnes — alongside 50 million barrels of crude oil from the International Energy Agency’s emergency stocks on Friday morning, according to EU diplomats.
George Shaw, senior insight analyst for distillate markets at Kpler, sees the proposed 50-million-barrel diesel release as substantial.
According to Kpler, the EU and UK imported 24.25 million barrels of diesel from outside the region in September, meaning the proposed release would amount to roughly twice that monthly volume.
Analysts agree that the impact on prices would depend on both the volume released and how quickly it reaches the market.
Alan Gelder, senior vice-president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, said: "A major release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by US$20–30/bbl, which equates to about €0.10–0.15 per litre at the pump," adding that motorists could see prices fall within a few days. Shaw said significant market price changes typically take one to two weeks to reach the pump.
However, this is a short-term remedy, Gelder added. "Any further release only buys time, as global diesel supply is still below global diesel demand, so we continue to draw on inventories and are vulnerable to the export policies of others (such as the US)," Gelder said.
The chart below shows overall emergency oil stocks by country, including diesel reserves.
Diesel supply in Europe has been severely affected, partly because Russian refineries are not fully operational following drone strikes. This is compounded by reduced exports of refined products from the Middle East and lower exports from Asia in response to the US-Iran conflict, which is restricting crude exports from the Middle East.
On the size of European countries’ strategic reserves, Gelder said that "major countries have 70 to 100 days of cover", adding that the requirement is to hold stocks equivalent to approximately 60 days of inland consumption or 90 days of imports, whichever is greater. "We hence have at least two months of cover if there is no supply and European refineries continue to operate."
Petrol and diesel have remained particularly expensive in Europe not only because of rising international crude oil prices but also because of the soaring cost and limited availability of refining capacity.
European refineries have been running close to full capacity, and there is little room to increase production.
According to Gelder, refinery capacity in use across European OECD members "is at over 80% (measured by crude intake against nameplate capacity), processing about 11 million b/d of crude," meaning that production is close to maximum levels.
These constraints leave Europe reliant on diesel imports. Releasing refined products from EU countries’ strategic reserves could therefore be the fastest way to affect prices.
However, replenishing those reserves would take time. “Releasing strategic stocks would mean that you are eroding an important buffer,” Shaw said, warning that the duration of the crisis remained uncertain. He said rebuilding stocks would depend on increased production and exports from the Middle East.
The EU has been under pressure from the United States to release some of its strategic oil reserves “immediately” to help lower global diesel prices.
On Friday, Brussels criticised the threatened US ban on diesel exports, warning that it would undermine trust in Washington as a reliable partner. "We fully reject any ban on diesel."
A fresh release would follow the agreement reached by IEA member countries in March to make 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available to the market, with each country following its own release timetable.
Shaw said Middle Eastern diesel exports in September were still more than 50% below their level a year earlier.
According to Gelder, "for diesel prices to fall sustainably, the global refining system needs to ease, which requires a resolution of the US-Iran conflict to enable higher production from Middle East exporting countries, along with greater exports from other suppliers, such as Russia".
Pressure on diesel supplies could also ease if high energy prices and high government bond yields trigger a global economic slowdown, reducing demand for the fuel.

Casa de México in Madrid unveils 2026 Day of the Dead altar inspired by Michoacán and Agustín Lara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:57:54 UTC
21:57:54 KST

Casa de México in Madrid unveils "Viva la vida!", its 2026 Day of the Dead altar honouring Agustín Lara, inspired by Michoacán and the monarch butterfly, with a musical tour. Free entry from 2 October to 8 November.
The Casa de México in Spain Foundation is unveiling the ninth edition of its Day of the Dead altar, the institution's most visited exhibition of the year. Under the title "Viva la vida!", the 2026 installation has been designed by Mexican artist Beatriz Redo and pays homage to composer Agustín Lara, with a set design inspired by the cemeteries and mountains of Michoacán.
The set recreates a mountain cemetery in Michoacán on the night of Day of the Dead, when, according to tradition, families gather to symbolically reunite with their deceased loved ones.
Beatriz Redo, the designer of this year's installation, explains that she wanted to pay tribute to the monarch butterfly, one of the region's great symbols: "Michoacán is an area of Mexico that receives the migration of the monarch butterfly, a massive migration that comes from Canada and coincides with the days at the end of October and the beginning of November. Tradition also links it to Day of the Dead," she notes.
Among the Purépecha and Mazahua communities of Michoacán, the arrival of these insects in the region's forests is interpreted as the return of the souls of the departed.
Agustín Lara, the musical protagonist of the tour and a great lover of Madrid
The altar is dedicated to Mexican singer and composer Agustín Lara (1897–1970), who was married to film star María Félix. Lara, known as 'El Flaco de Oro', was a prolific composer and author of classics such as 'Granada', 'Solamente una vez', 'María Bonita' and the emblematic chotis 'Madrid', which reflects his close relationship with Spain.
The artist is depicted at the top of the altar as a papier-mâché skull next to his piano, created by artisans Raimundo Amezcua and Marta Linares. New this edition, the entire tour will be accompanied by his most emblematic songs, something unprecedented in this exhibition and which will guide visitors on a visual and sonic journey through one of the most colourful traditions in the world.
Papel picado, a tradition rich in symbolism, and an altar for pets
One of the most representative craft elements on the tour is papel picado, a traditional technique created with hammer and chisel that is also used for patron-saint festivities and birthday parties.
Its role on Day of the Dead goes beyond decoration: "When it is hung up and begins to move, it represents the moment when the souls arrive at the altar to consume everything we have placed in the offering for the deceased," explains Citlali Pérez from Casa de México's Communications Department.
In addition to the main altar, the experience includes a tour with pieces of Mexican folk art and other complementary altars. New for 2026, an altar dedicated to pets has been added to remember the animals that bring so much companionship and happiness to households. On the second floor, visitors can also leave a message for their deceased loved ones; once Casa de México removes the exhibition, these messages are burned in a ceremony.
Beyond Casa de México: altars in Madrid and Santander
The foundation is extending the celebration beyond its headquarters on Calle Alberto Aguilera. In collaboration with Madrid City Council, three other altars will be open to visitors from 23 October to 2 November at:
- CentroCentro, designed by Guillermo González
- La Montaña de los Gatos, in El Retiro park, designed by Fer Ferez
- Arganzuela Greenhouse, designed by the studio Señoritos Creativos
The newly opened Faro Santander cultural centre will also host an altar designed by set designer Cristina Faesler, in collaboration with Casa de México.
A heritage recognised by Unesco
The Day of the Dead celebration in Mexico was declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by Unesco on 7 November 2003.
Of pre-Hispanic origin, the tradition understands death as the beginning of a journey to Mictlán and sees the altar not as a reason for sorrow, but as a celebration of memory and the bond between generations, through photographs, candles, cempasúchil flowers and objects that were meaningful to the deceased.
Dates, opening hours and free entry to the 2026 Day of the Dead altar
The altar can be visited from 2 October to 8 November, Monday to Sunday, including the public holidays on 12 October and 2 November. Admission is free.
Monday: 10:00 – 18:45
Tuesday to Friday: 10:00 – 13:45
Saturday and Sunday: 10:00 – 12:30
Guided visit (around 20 minutes, covering the building's three floors): Tuesday to Friday from 14:00 to 20:30, Saturdays from 13:00 to 20:30 and Sundays from 13:00 to 18:30.
Access without a booking is via a queue and is subject to capacity; for the guided visit with booking, you must subscribe to Casa de México's newsletter at casademexico.es.

As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.
“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”
“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June.
“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.
The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.
Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.
The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.
Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.
Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.
“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”
On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”
Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.
Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”
He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”

The US plans to increase the number of unmanned &quot;canoes&quot; for border protection — what Ukraine&apos;s experience has to do with it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:56:57 EEST
21:56:57 KST

The US plans to increase the number of unmanned "canoes" for border protection — what Ukraine's experience has to do with it
Kyiv • UNN
Autonomous Lightfish boats help detect trespassers and contraband on the Rio Grande. The Pentagon is considering deploying them in the Gulf.
The Pentagon may expand its use of autonomous surveillance boats on the Rio Grande River and in the Gulf of Mexico after the canoe-sized vessels helped authorities detect and prevent instances of illegal border crossings and drug smuggling as part of a pilot program launched in January. A U.S. government official said this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The publication notes that these unmanned surface vessels, created by San Diego-based startup Seasats, patrol the river for extended periods without a crew. They are part of a broader initiative by the military and law enforcement agencies to use relatively inexpensive autonomous systems for surveillance and security missions.
The use of these vessels along the border also demonstrates how a new generation of venture-backed defense startups is gaining the opportunity to win contracts previously handled primarily by traditional contractors. The Pentagon is seeking faster and cheaper ways to deploy cutting-edge technologies capable of operating around the clock.
Defense officials are considering broader use of these solar-powered boats to monitor remote sections of the Rio Grande. In addition to Seasats, similar maritime drones are supplied by Saronic, Saildrone, and Splash.
Military officials plan to increase the number of robotic vessels—10 are currently being tested—by another 50 units. This is intended to reduce the workload of Coast Guard boats and manned aircraft patrolling the border with Mexico as part of President Donald Trump's administration's efforts to combat illegal immigration.
Maritime drones are "cost-effective solutions for intercepting violators and maintaining a presence in areas where drug traffickers are now moving," said M. Roosevelt Ditlevson, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Hemispheric Affairs.
In recent years, small drones and other unmanned platforms have become widespread in the U.S. military after repeatedly proving their effectiveness during the war in Ukraine.
In addition
According to media reports, Lightfish— a low-profile autonomous vessel made by Seasats—is approximately 3.3 meters (11 feet) long and weighs 154 kilograms (340 pounds). It costs approximately $240,000 and can be launched from a boat ramp or from the bed of a pickup truck. The drone is capable of operating for months, even in challenging maritime conditions. These vessels are equipped with various sensors—including electro-optical, infrared, and hydroacoustic (sonar) systems—that transmit tracking data in real time directly to military software networks, such as Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System and Anduril Industries' Fortress platform, alerting Customs and Border Protection and Coast Guard units.
The Pentagon said that, on average each month, Lightfish drones help detect 452 violations, carry out 350 apprehensions, and prompt 100 turnarounds (when a group of people abandons an attempt to cross the border after realizing that they have been detected).
"They see that the vessel is waiting for them and realize that they have effectively been exposed," Ditlevson said.
The drone manufacturer attracted global attention in July, when Reuters reported that the commercial Lightfish vessel, operating in the Philippines' exclusive economic zone, came close enough to a People's Liberation Army Navy destroyer equipped with guided missiles. This made it possible to record detailed close-range video and demonstrate how inexpensive autonomous vessels can monitor military assets worth billions of dollars.
According to Ditlevson, if the project continues to succeed, the number of Lightfish vessel orders could increase by 50 units; their use in the Gulf of Mexico to create a radar barrier between Texas and Key West is also being considered. At the same time, he noted that the expansion of their application would take place gradually, alongside the testing of various technologies.
"We are not tied to a specific manufacturer. We need the best technology," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Seasats CEO Mike Flanigan said that unmanned systems provide continuous monitoring that traditional means, which require large amounts of fuel, cannot match.
"An aircraft or ship can cover vast distances quickly, but if you wanted, say, to keep a Boeing 737 over a certain area of the ocean for an entire day, that would simply be impossible," Flanigan explained. "Our vessel does not cover such a large area in a short time, but it can remain in a designated area for months, which is a key advantage for security and monitoring missions."
As intensified border controls and targeted military operations have closed off a number of drug-smuggling routes, cartels are increasingly shifting their activities to coastal waters and areas near the shore. The expanded use of these unmanned vessels in the Gulf of Mexico precedes their testing in more challenging conditions in the Pacific Ocean, near San Diego.

The United Nations reported on Friday that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, capital city of Ituri Province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.
The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.
“The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province,” the UN said.
People’s mistrust and anger towards health workers and authorities have also contributed to the obstacles the government faces in its efforts to contain the outbreak.
A senior member of DRC’s governing Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party was beaten to death days ago after taking part in a radio programme to raise awareness about the epidemic.
The attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a local official with UDPS, took place last Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterwards, and he died at hospital from his injuries.
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “far from over” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
Caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, the current epidemic became the largest and deadliest in the DRC after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
Several treatments and vaccines are being trialled against Bundibugyo, but currently, there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the Ebola epidemic so far. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, although that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.

Swiss president Guy Parmelin to quit government
- Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced he will quit the government at the end of 2026 after 11 years of service, citing weariness and the need for new energy.
- Parmelin played a key role in negotiating a tariff reduction with the US, lowering duties on Swiss goods from 39% to 15% and securing a US$200 billion Swiss investment pledge.
- He has served as defence and economy minister, was president in 2021, and his successor from the Swiss People’s Party will be chosen by Parliament in December 2026.
AI generated
GENEVA – Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced on Oct 2 that he will quit the government at the end of 2026, in a sudden move after more than a decade of ministerial service.
Switzerland’s presidency rotates annually among the seven members of the government, called the Federal Council, of which Parmelin, 66, was the longest-serving minister.
Parmelin told a press conference in Bern that he had informed ministerial colleagues of his decision to step down on Dec 31.
“By then, it will have been 11 years since I was elected to this role, and the time has come for me to make way for new energy in these times of great uncertainty,” he said, admitting to feeling “a certain weariness”, while insisting he was not stepping down for medical reasons.
Tariff tussle with Trump
A pragmatist, Parmelin seemed to make more headway with US President Donald Trump than his predecessor Karin Keller-Sutter.
Trump shocked Switzerland in Aug 2025 when he announced 39% duties on imports of Swiss goods, among the highest in his global tariff blitz.
Parmelin, the economy minister, went to Washington three times in a bid to reduce the rate.
Eventually, Switzerland and the United States announced a declaration of intent to cut tariffs to 15%, with the Swiss vowing to invest US$200 billion (S$256 billion) in the United States.
A wine-grower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People’s Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Parmelin was previously president in 2021 and took centre stage as Switzerland hosted a summit in Geneva between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Joe Biden.
The president of the Swiss Confederation is first among equals on the Federal Council, chairs its meetings and typically represents the country in major domestic and international matters.
The position goes to whoever has had the longest run on the council without being president.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will become president in 2027.
Parmelin joined the Federal Council in 2016 as defence minister and has held the economy brief since 2019.
The Federal Council seven seats are shared 2-2-2-1 among the four main political parties under a decades-old tacit agreement known as “the magic formula”.
Parmelin’s successor will come from the SVP. Candidates have until Oct 23 to come forward, and Parliament will choose on Dec 9.
Parmelin will visit India for a three-day state visit from Oct 5. AFP

Fentanyl is increasingly displacing heroin on the drug market in the Bulgarian capital, Nikolay Shopov of the Narcotics Sector at the Sofia Directorate of the Ministry of Interior told our reporter Nikolay Hristov.
“We can now say that heroin is no longer available on the streets of Sofia, or is extremely rare, with the entire market having been taken over by fentanyl,” Shopov said. 
According to him, fentanyl entered the capital four to five years ago, but its presence has become increasingly noticeable over the past one to two years. Shopov also said that a single dose of fentanyl in Sofia costs around €10, while the price per gram ranges from €70 to €100.

Bulgaria has received approval from the European Commission for a state aid scheme entitled “Support for farmers engaged in primary agricultural production in connection with the crisis in the Middle East”, known as the “Iran aid”, the Ministry of Agriculture said. The measure was developed under the Temporary Crisis Framework for State Aid in response to the crisis in the Middle East and was submitted by Bulgaria for notification on 1 September 2026.
The scheme has a budget of €170 million and will provide grant support to cover part of the increased costs of gasoil and fertilisers resulting from the crisis in the Middle East. The maximum amount of aid is €50,000 per undertaking. Payments are to be completed by the end of this year.

France's Le Pen pledges to hardwire deficit cuts with 'golden rule'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:43:14 UTC
21:43:14 KST

France's Le Pen pledges to hardwire deficit cuts with 'golden rule'
PARIS, Oct 2 - French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen set out on Friday plans for a binding budget rule she said would put France's public finances back on track, seeking to ease investor concerns about her fiscal credibility.
Le Pen leads the polls for both rounds of the April 18-May 2 election, but investors have cut exposure to French assets, doubting that whoever wins the presidency next year can bring the deficit under control.
The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over their German equivalent rose above 150 basis points on Friday, its highest since late 2011, after the government's budget bill for 2027 offered little relief.
Writing in French newspaper L'Opinion, Le Pen said a "golden rule" she has proposed would be put to referendum, binding lawmakers in annual budget legislation, with exceptions tightly limited, similar to the way Germany's debt brake works.
The rule would require the deficit to fall by at least half a percentage point of economic output each year, which she said would cut it from 5.4% this year to 2.9% in 2032, the end of the next presidential term.
It would keep falling and stay near balance until debt - currently at 119% of GDP - reaches 60%, she said.
She did not spell out when the referendum might happen or how the government would achieve that level of cuts.
But Le Pen called the figures she had outlined a minimum and said that her fiscal programme, to be outlined on Tuesday, would cut spending even faster.
She reiterated a pledge to carry out €125 billion ($140.35 billion) in savings over five years, which she said would be net of tax cuts. Neither growth nor tax rises could repair the finances, she said.
Lawmakers could allow a larger deficit only with a three-fifths majority, she said. A second consecutive exception would require a referendum.
The High Council of Public Finances would validate the assumptions behind the annual deficit ceiling, and the Constitutional Council would reject "insincere" budgets, she added. REUTERS

School protests send shivers down French government's spine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:43:02 BST
21:43:02 KST

School protests send shivers down French government's spine
- Published
It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.
Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth.
Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.
Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.
For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.
Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".
A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.
On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in.
Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros.
According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said.
In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth.
The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past.
The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings.
On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight.
This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!"
Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question.
But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed.
But that is the lesser of the worries.
The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming.
For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate."
An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI."
It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".
In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.
The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".
But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing.
Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.
But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.
Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.
If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

US Navy to buy 30 medium drone warships from three firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:30:56 BST
21:30:56 KST

The US Navy plans to buy 30 Medium Unmanned Surface Vessels (MUSVs) from Galliano Marine Services, HII and Saronic Technologies after completing the first phase of at-sea testing, with the first vessels due for delivery before the end of fiscal year 2027, according to the service.
Each of the three companies has been awarded a production Other Transaction Authority agreement covering 10 vessels, at an average procurement cost of $40 million per boat. Across the three agreements, that amounts to roughly $1.2 billion. Three other firms that took part in the prototype phase, Leidos, PAC MAR and Sea Machines, were judged to have completed the work set out in their prototype agreements and will each receive a $15 million award under the terms previously agreed.
All six companies will be accepted onto the Maritime Marketplace hosted by Drones.mil, the Navy said, making them eligible for follow-on production agreements from acquisition authorities across the Department of War. On 23 September the service also released a Phase II Integration and Testing Call for Solutions, which it says is intended to widen the pool of offerings and meet future MUSV mission sets.
According to the Navy, Phase I testing assessed the vessels’ ability to perceive and understand the surrounding maritime environment, their autonomous navigation in line with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, and their capacity to carry out long-duration missions.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in the release: “Our warfighters don’t have time to wait on bureaucracy while our adversaries pace forward.” He added: “Our message to the defense industrial base is simple: build fast, deliver on time, and match the urgency of the threat. This MUSV award is a prime example of how we are streamlining acquisitions to ensure our Sailors and Marines have the capabilities they need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The Navy’s interest in medium-sized uncrewed surface vessels dates back several years, with earlier efforts including DARPA’s Sea Hunter, the Overlord programme and a 2020 MUSV prototype contract awarded to L3Harris. The three production awardees take different approaches. HII has developed its ROMULUS family of autonomous vessels, Saronic has expanded from small autonomous boats towards larger designs, and Galliano Marine Services comes from the Gulf Coast offshore vessel sector.
The Chief of Naval Operations was quoted in the release as describing MUSVs as part of the hedge strategy set out in the service’s Fighting Instructions. “They give commanders a Tailored Offset — additional capacity and capability that can be rapidly adapted to the threat, distributed across the battlespace, and placed at risk without placing Sailors at unnecessary risk,” the CNO said. “Just as importantly, MUSVs give us a platform for rapidly integrating new sensors, weapons, and other mission payloads as technology and operational requirements change. This is about moving beyond experimentation and putting reliable, combat-relevant capability into the hands of our Sailors at the speed the Fleet requires.”
Fielding will be led by the Direct Reporting Program Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems, working alongside the Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center, which is responsible for developing tactics, training and operational experience for the vessels. Under the Navy’s Containerized Capability Campaign, the service intends to use modular payloads so commanders can fit sensors, weapons and other mission equipment to the boats according to the task at hand.

VILNIUS - Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas urged the European Union to cooperate more closely with third countries on the return of illegal migrants.
"In the area of returns, we must move from discussions to results. If a decision is made that a person has no right to stay in the European Union, states must have realistic opportunities to implement it. The council also stressed that the response to drug crime and related violence and intimidation must include not only law enforcement measures but also stronger prevention and assistance to victims.
Katelynas also drew attention to hybrid threats posed by Russia, cyberattacks, disinformation and the malicious use of drones, calling for stronger mutual information exchange and greater investment in preparedness for such threats.
Lithuania promises to raise these issues during its presidency of the European Union Council in the first half of 2027.

Survey: People lack faith in an adequate state pension  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:05 UTC
21:29:05 KST

TALLINN - As many as 74 percent of people in Estonia do not believe they will receive a state pension sufficient for a normal standard of living, a Norstat survey commissioned by LHV reveals.
Furthermore, for half of Estonia's residents, an adequate retirement income would be twice the current average pension.
Faith in receiving a state pension that allows for a normal standard of living is lowest among those aged 30-39. A striking 81 percent of people in this age group do not consider it likely. The corresponding figure is 68 percent for the 18-29 age group, 77 percent for those aged 40-49, 70 percent for the 50-59 age group, and 71 percent for those aged 60-75.
According to Vahur Vallistu, chairman of the management board of LHV Asset Management, the results reflect higher expectations for quality of life throughout the entire lifespan than before. "An increasing number of people in Estonia know that relying solely on the state pension is likely not the best strategy. A financial buffer for a dignified old age is built over a long period, and smart savers first take advantage of the tax-benefited opportunities of the second and third pillars," he said.
Vallistu added that it is also worth considering increasing personal contributions to the second pillar to four or six percent of one's gross salary to maximize the results of decades-long saving. If possible, one should also consider making regular contributions to the third pillar. "It is consistent and automated investment solutions that most effectively support the growth of wealth in the long term," Vallistu is convinced.
The survey revealed that 48 percent of people in Estonia consider a pension of over 1,500 euros per month necessary for a normal standard of living. A pension in the range of 1,001-1,500 euros is considered as such by 42 percent of respondents. The actual average pension in Estonia is currently 860 euros.
In Vallistu's view, these numbers clearly illustrate the gap between people's expectations and reality. The income of Estonian residents experiences one of the largest drops in the European Union after retirement. While the average pension in the EU constitutes nearly 70 percent of a person's previous income, in Estonia it is about 40 percent.
Vallistu pointed out that, primarily due to the demographic situation, the gap between the average salary and the state pension will only widen. Therefore, it is important to save additionally to the first, or state, pension pillar. "Saving in the second pillar, increasing personal contributions, and investing in the third pillar form a good foundation that allows one to face the future with more confidence," he said.
To start receiving more money in the second pillar monthly as early as next year, an application to increase contributions must be submitted before November 30. To date, more than 123,000 second-pillar savers have already submitted the relevant application. For contributions made to the third pillar by the end of December, a tax refund can be received next year on an amount up to 15 percent of a person's gross income, but not more than 6,000 euros in one year.
The survey was conducted this September by the research firm Norstat. Across Estonia, 1,000 people aged 18-74 were surveyed.

Shortage of refined oil products has reached a critical level  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:05 UTC
21:29:05 KST

TALLINN - Supply disruptions and government interventions to regulate fuel prices are causing sharp fluctuations in gasoline and diesel prices across Europe at a time when the shortage of refined oil products has reached a critical level.
Supply crises in the Middle East and Russia, along with disruptions in refinery operations, have led to a situation in the European fuel market where the market is unstable and fuel stocks are at historically low levels.
The conflict between the US and Iran continues to disrupt refinery operations in the Persian Gulf region, significantly limiting the availability of refined oil products. Russia's decision to extend its diesel export ban has further strained Europe's security of supply. The result is a scarcity of refined oil products at a time when refining margins are at historically high levels.
"Global diesel flow remains 1.3-1.4 million barrels per day lower than a year ago, which has left Europe with a minimal buffer before the autumn refinery maintenance season. It remains to be seen in the near future whether and to what extent the regular autumn maintenance of the plants will be postponed until spring to keep production running in this tense situation," commented Indrek Sassi, head of motor fuel pricing at Circle K.
The production capacity of European oil refineries remains exceptionally high this autumn. TotalEnergies' European plants are operating at full capacity and, according to CEO Patrick Pouyanne, have become a "gold mine." Due to high profit margins, the company postponed maintenance at its Gonfreville plant in northern France until the spring.
To regulate high fuel prices, several European countries have introduced special measures to limit retail prices and ease budgetary pressure. From October 1 until the end of the year, Germany lowered the energy tax on road transport fuels by 14.04 cents per liter and plans to introduce a fuel price cap by January 1, 2027, at the latest.
The Czech Republic will lower the excise duty on diesel fuel from October 1 to 31, limit retail prices for motor fuels, and plans to impose a temporary windfall tax on its only refining company, Orlen Unipetrol.
Italy has introduced price caps through major retailers Eni and IP. For 30 days starting September 28, Eni set the maximum price for diesel at 2.19 euros per liter and for gasoline at 1.99 euros per liter. Since March, the Italian government has approved 15 separate aid packages, costing the state over 2.3 billion euros. Among Estonia's neighboring countries, Latvia has lowered its fuel excise duty to the minimum level allowed by the European Union.
"Last week, the Estonian Association of Transportation Fuels, together with other professional associations, sent a joint appeal to the government to follow the practice of other European Union countries and temporarily reduce the tax burden on fuels. This is to alleviate the energy crisis and prevent a situation where high fuel prices severely impact both households and businesses," said Sassi.
Additional supply restrictions also pose a significant risk to motor fuel prices. U.S. President Donald Trump is still considering a ban on diesel exports to lower domestic prices. According to Goldman Sachs, a complete U.S. ban on diesel exports would raise European diesel prices by three dollars per barrel, or just under 2 percent. Yesterday, Reuters reported that China has halted fuel exports and canceled previously agreed gasoline and jet fuel deliveries for October. In this situation, releasing Europe's strategic reserves could help mitigate the price increases.
"It is expected that European Union leaders will meet on October 15 to discuss the use of emergency reserves, but it must be kept in mind that Europe's gasoline stocks are critically low compared to its diesel stocks," Sassi noted.
According to the European Commission, fuel stocks in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region are below the five-year average but have remained stable in recent weeks.

Eamets: Autumn will not bring relief from inflation  - The Baltic Times
Unknown

TALLINN - Raul Eamets, chief economist at Bigbank, stated that inflation accelerated in September and predicts that the autumn will bring no relief.
"This summer, we were getting used to an inflation rate of two percent or less year-on-year, a level the European Central Bank considers reasonable," Eamets said. "However, on Friday, Statistics Estonia released its flash estimate of the harmonised index of consumer prices for September, which showed a year-on-year price increase of 3 percent - double the rate seen in August."
"Looking ahead to the autumn, it's clear we cannot expect a slowdown in price growth. The main reasons are the ongoing oil and gas crisis and the uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. This is compounded by the actions of the Houthis in Yemen, who have successfully blocked shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb strait - a key maritime gateway connecting the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea to the Suez Canal," Eamets explained.
"Today, most cargo ships are sailing around Africa for fear of Houthi attacks. Nearly a quarter of the world's maritime transport passes through these straits, and blocking them increases the cost not only of oil and gas but of all goods transported by sea from Asia to Europe," Eamets said.
"Rising energy prices continue to have the greatest impact on inflation. As autumn progresses, demand for heating and electricity will grow, pushing energy prices even higher. This will be particularly painful for local governments and private consumers who rely on natural gas, as gas prices are already very high and are set to rise further with increasing demand across Europe. Alternative fuels such as wood pellets and firewood have also become more expensive due to increased demand. The rising price of diesel will, sooner or later, translate into higher consumer prices through increased transportation costs. Therefore, we should expect inflation to accelerate this autumn," Eamets added.

ZAGREB, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Croatia's inflation accelerated to 4.7 percent year-on-year in September, mainly driven by energy price hikes, the Croatian Bureau of Statistics said on Friday.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.9 percent, up from 0.3 percent in August. Energy prices were the main driver of inflation, rising 20.5 percent year-on-year amid supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Prices of services increased 7.6 percent, while prices of food, beverages and tobacco edged up 0.2 percent.
According to Eurostat, Croatia's annual inflation stood at 4.3 percent in September, up from 3.7 percent in August. Meanwhile, inflation in the euro area as a whole accelerated to 3.8 percent in September from 3.2 percent in August.
Croatia's inflation has been among the highest in the euro area in recent years, but the gap has narrowed in the last few months. Finance Minister Tomislav Coric said earlier that the government expects inflation to match the euro area average in the first quarter of 2027. ■

BISHKEK, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Kyrgyzstan's first national satellite was launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the United States, on Oct. 1 local time, according to a statement published by the official website of the president of Kyrgyzstan on Friday.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov attended the satellite's launch ceremony during a working visit to the United States. The satellite was launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket operated by the U.S. company SpaceX, the statement said.
The satellite was launched into orbit as part of a group of spacecraft carried by a single launch vehicle. The satellite will be controlled from a center in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, it said.
Data obtained from the satellite will enable the monitoring of agricultural land, glaciers, water bodies, forests and pastures, as well as changes in natural ecosystems, the statement said.
Satellite technologies will be particularly important for the monitoring and early detection of natural hazards, it added, noting that the data obtained will enable the faster detection of signs of droughts, floods, landslides, mudflows and forest fires, creating additional opportunities for timely response and mitigation of potential damage.
In the future, satellite data will be integrated into the country's government digital systems and used to create spatial maps and analytical models. This will enable the use of objective data in government decision-making, investment planning and monitoring the implementation of state programs, the statement said. ■

America moves guided missile destroyer to Europe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:15:33 BST
21:15:33 KST

The U.S. Navy destroyer USS John Basilone (DDG-122) will move its homeport from Naval Station Mayport, Florida, to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain this autumn, according to U.S. Fleet Forces Command.
The Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer is described by the U.S. Navy as capable of ballistic missile defence, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction operations and integrated air and missile defence. Built by General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine, the ship was commissioned in November 2024, making it one of the newest destroyers in the fleet to be forward deployed to Europe.
At Rota, John Basilone will join the U.S. Navy’s Forward Deployed Naval Forces-Europe, a group of destroyers permanently based in Spain and operating under U.S. Sixth Fleet. The arrangement began in 2014 and 2015 when four destroyers, USS Donald Cook, USS Ross, USS Porter and USS Carney, moved to the Andalusian base as part of the U.S. contribution to NATO ballistic missile defence under the European Phased Adaptive Approach. Their Aegis combat systems and Standard Missile interceptors were intended to provide sea-based protection for Europe against ballistic missile threats from the Middle East.
In June 2022, during the NATO summit in Madrid, Washington and Madrid agreed to increase the number of U.S. destroyers based at Rota from four to six. The expansion has been accompanied by a gradual rotation of ships, with older destroyers returning to the United States and newer hulls taking their place. Ships based at Rota spend more time on station in the Mediterranean, the Black Sea region before 2022, the Baltic and the High North than destroyers deploying from the U.S. East Coast, as they avoid the lengthy Atlantic transit at either end of each patrol.
Naval Station Rota is a Spanish naval base at which U.S. forces operate under a bilateral defence agreement between the two countries. Located near the Strait of Gibraltar, it gives ships quick access to both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and also supports U.S. Navy logistics and maritime patrol aircraft.
The ship’s namesake, Gunnery Sgt. John Basilone, received the Medal of Honor for his actions defending Henderson Field on Guadalcanal in October 1942, when his machine gun section held off repeated Japanese assaults. After returning to the United States to promote war bond sales, he requested a return to combat and was killed on the first day of the landings at Iwo Jima in February 1945. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions there, making him one of the most highly decorated Marines in U.S. history, the U.S. Navy noted. A Gearing-class destroyer, USS Basilone, previously carried his name and served from 1949 to 1977.
U.S. Fleet Forces Command, which announced the move, is responsible for manning, training and equipping more than 125 ships and 1,000 aircraft and supplying combat-ready forces to numbered fleets and combatant commanders around the world.

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board reviews payment schedule

2026-10-02

21:15:32 KST

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, held its second meeting on Oct. 2 to discuss the payment schedule for fund accounts and a draft amendment to the Capital Markets Law.
On Sept. 30, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation.
According to a statement issued after the meeting, the Coordination Board reviewed the work being carried out by relevant institutions on the calculation methodology for net investment amounts under the SPK’s Sept. 30 decisions.
The board also assessed secondary regulations and the payment timetable related to the SPK’s decision on payments.
In addition, the board discussed a draft law amending the Capital Markets Law, which has been under preparation for some time. The statement said instructions had been conveyed to relevant institutions and organizations to finalize the draft.
“The necessary efforts regarding the resolution of problems that have emerged in a specific and limited segment of the fund market will continue swiftly and effectively within the framework of capital markets regulations, with due regard for fairness and justice,” the statement said.
The SPK said on Oct. 30 that payments will be made to investors whose account reconciliations have been completed and will be treated as advances against final liquidation proceeds.
The payments will be calculated based on each investor’s net investment amount determined by the Central Securities Depository (MKK). Investors with net investments below 1 million liras will receive the full amount, while payments for investors with net investments of 1 million liras or more will be capped at 1 million liras.
The liquidation process will begin with money market funds, while other funds will be liquidated according to investor numbers.
According to the SPK, 131 investment funds designated for liquidation hold approximately 826 billion liras in assets across 455,758 investors.
On Oct. 1, Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said in a social media post that stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and the measures being taken would limit the impact of recent developments on the financial system and the real economy.
The measures would also give Türkiye’s capital markets a stronger, healthier and more resilient structure, he said.
Meanwhile, speaking online at S&P Global Ratings’ 6th Annual Global Emerging Markets Conference on Oct. 1, Şimşek said authorities had moved swiftly.
“We acted very quickly. We “quarantined” the troubled portfolio management companies and the relevant funds,” he said.
Şimşek said the main objective was to prevent the problem from spreading to the rest of the financial system.
“Our aim here was to stop the contagion from spreading to the rest of the system, and I believe we have been largely successful in doing so,” he said.
“There has, of course, been a limited impact, but we are not talking about a systemic problem. We will continue to deepen the capital markets,” Şimşek added.

The European Commission on Friday rejected any potential US ban on diesel exports, saying such a measure would benefit no one and could undercut the European Union's trust in the US as a "reliable partner."
"We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters in Brussels.
Itkonen said the EU is ready to act collectively through the International Energy Agency (IEA), which she said was responsible for organizing any possible release of oil stocks.
She stressed that the bloc's role is to coordinate member states' positions within the IEA, rather than independently decide on a stock release.
Her comments came after US President Donald Trump said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as his administration considers restricting US diesel exports amid pressure on global refined-fuel supplies.
Itkonen said member states had coordinated their positions at an Energy Union Task Force meeting on Friday and that discussions are continuing with international partners.
She said the EU would remain united in whatever further steps are taken, while declining to specify whether the bloc is considering "retaliatory" measures against Washington.
"We take one step at the time," Itkonen said.
She added the EU currently sees no immediate security-of-supply problem, with oil supplies stable for the time being, but warned that high energy prices are creating an affordability crisis for households and industry.
Paula Pinho, another spokesperson, said France, which holds the G7 presidency this year, intends to convene a video conference of G7 leaders "as soon as possible" to coordinate measures aimed at easing energy price pressures and guaranteeing supplies of crude oil and refined products.
She said EU coordination groups had been closely monitoring energy markets for months and that gas prices in Europe had risen by 140% since the end of February, when the US and Iran launched their war on Iran, while diesel prices had doubled.

The African Union must convene an emergency session on the situation in northern Ethiopia as the latest armed conflict which broke out in the Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions on 21 September expands, Amnesty International said today.
Since the outbreak of fresh fighting, the organization has continued to receive credible reports of destruction of civilian objects through shelling and air strikes, intensified forced conscription, and other acts that may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law.
“The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
“The starting point is for the Peace and Security Council to urgently convene an emergency session on the situation in Ethiopia. This is especially critical as fears of regionalisation of the conflict are on the rise”.
The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late.
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The fighting between Tigrayan forces and their allies on one side, including Amhara Fano forces, and the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and its allies, on the other, has significantly intensified across southern Tigray and the Northern Amhara and Western Afar regions since it began a week ago. In addition to the extensive use of heavy weaponry, the renewed hostilities have involved intensified aerial attacks across Tigray including in the town of Axum and the regional capital Mekelle.
Amnesty International is particularly alarmed by reports that civilian infrastructure, including several schools, has been damaged or targeted during aerial attacks. Fighting involving heavy weapons in and around the towns of Maychew and Alamata has reportedly resulted in civilian casualties and further endangered critical civilian infrastructure.
The disruption of communication services across Tigray, and parts of Afar and Amhara regions combined with increasing restrictions on civic space by the Ethiopian government, raises serious concerns that grave human rights violations could occur under the cover of darkness, hidden from independent monitoring.
“Disrupting communications in conflict-affected areas is a well-documented pattern in Ethiopia’s armed conflicts. Such restrictions have frequently concealed atrocities and isolated civilians from the outside world. We call on all relevant authorities to immediately restore access to communications services and ensure civilians are not cut off from life-saving information and assistance at this critical time,” said Tigere Chagutah.
The current outbreak of conflict in Tigray and the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions comes on the backdrop of six years of persistent armed conflict across Ethiopia, including in the Oromia region. These armed conflicts have devastated communities across the country with most of the armed actors involved in the fighting linked to serious violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. Yet, despite the scale and gravity of these abuses, meaningful and independent accountability remains largely absent.

They must take urgent measures to protect civilians from harm, renew efforts to restore independent investigations into serious violations committed by all parties to Ethiopia’s conflicts, and ensure unhindered access for journalists, humanitarian organizations, and human rights monitors,” said Tigere Chagutah.
Background
The Peace and Security Council (PSC) is AU’s standing decision-making body for the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in Africa. During the 2020-2022 armed conflict in Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions, the PSC held its first session on the situation in Ethiopia in November 2021, one year after the conflict began.
The conflict was described by the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE) as ‘one of the deadliest conflicts of the twenty-first century.’ Reports indicate that hundreds of thousands of people died, millions were displaced, and thousands of women and girls were subjected to conflict-related sexual violence and other grave violations.
The conflict was marked by an unprecedented communications blackout as civilians in Tigray were largely cut off from telephone services, internet access, and other forms of communication for more than a year.
Although hostilities formally ended in November 2022, the consequences of the conflict continue to be felt. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people remain unable to return home. Victims of serious violations continue to await truth, justice, and reparations.

The specially designed structures, built using a hybrid construction system, will serve as rest areas for participants attending the COP31 summit in the Mediterranean resort city.

Cankaya said the units produced for COP31 feature a hybrid design developed specifically for the event.
He said Karmod reinforced the wall panels with steel frames beyond its standard specifications to improve the buildings’ structural performance.
“The buildings have been upgraded to the highest level in terms of insulation. On-site installation of the seven blocks is nearly complete, with each block covering 300 square meters. The container buildings, which will serve as lounges for international participants during the summit, include amenities such as accessible restrooms. All of the buildings were produced as demountable structures and will be reused at different locations after the summit,” Cankaya said.
