Inside Washington's tougher position on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:16:59 UTC
20:16:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside Washington's tougher position during the latest talks with Iran
Just a few weeks ago, the administration of US President Donald Trump was prepared to reach a deal with Iran that would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz. But, today, it is rejecting in the current negotiations with Iran what it had been prepared to accept less than three months ago.
On 26 September, Trump publicly rejected a ceasefire proposal from Iran that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for lifting the US naval blockade, ending sanctions on oil exports and resuming nuclear negotiations. He said Iran was losing badly and wanted to reach a deal.
So what changed for the Trump administration?
The United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports on 13 April, before Trump announced on 19 August the start of what he described as the "most crushing economic operation ever"; part of a broad campaign of economic warfare and isolation against Iran, which included sanctions on banks, companies and importers, a ban on Iranian aviation, coordination with foreign countries and threats of sanctions against countries cooperating with Tehran.
Trump and his team believe the United States can achieve more by waiting and tightening the military naval blockade and economic sanctions.
His administration and Treasury Department officials estimate that the amount of Iranian oil available at sea will run out by the end of next week, which will increase Tehran's hardship and may push it to make further concessions.
The US president said earlier this week that he does not know "whether the Iranians will surrender now, but they will surrender".
On Sunday, 27 September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in comments to Fox News that the blockade on Iran was succeeding and that the remaining Iranian oil at sea amounted to no more than an additional 15 million barrels and expected the final shipments to reach China within the next two weeks, adding that "after that, it will have nothing left to bargain with".
Iran already acknowledges that the new sanctions are highly effective, although it has stressed that surrender is impossible.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in comments to Fox News on Sunday, on the sidelines of his attendance at United Nations meetings, "One of the problems we face is that our money is being held in China."
"We cannot even recover our money from countries to which we exported goods," he added.
No shipment of Iranian crude oil has passed outside the US-imposed blockade area since 14 July, according to data from tracking companies.
The figures cited by the US Treasury secretary also match shipping-tracking data.
Data from Kpler, according to what was published by The Wall Street Journal, showed that the amount of Iranian crude oil aboard tankers at sea outside the blockade area stood at 29 million barrels on 1 September, compared with 90 million barrels in mid-July.
It is expected the supply to run out by mid-October and the flow of payments to stop by mid-March next year.
President Trump argues that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to pre-war levels and has again called for Tehran's surrender.
However, Kpler data published by Reuters indicate that total volumes leaving through the strait amounted to about 9.7 million barrels out of a total of about 16.3 million barrels of oil exported by major Middle Eastern oil producers during September, compared with 19.5 million barrels in February.
The remaining volume is being transported through alternative routes.
Paulo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University, told The New Arab that the reason for the notable change and tougher US position is that Washington has found a pressure point that is actually affecting Iran.
"As the blockade continues and its actual effects on the Iranian economy begin to emerge, Washington is no longer prepared to accept what it had previously agreed to," he said.
He further explained that the US realised that the economic blockade and sanctions were actually working, and that they were the strongest pressure tool, with Iran suffering the most, in turn led them to see any negotiations to lift the blockade in return for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of initial talks as "unacceptable at the present time".
Schirach added that months ago, Washington could have accepted a deal that would have reopened the strait to end the war and the impasse that had led to Iran controlling it.
He also noted that the factor of time is now in the US' favour, saying that "the current stalemate serves the pressure on Iran", and that the US blockade is working effectively despite Iranian claims that the domestic situation remains stable.
"The blockade prevents the movement of goods through Iranian ports and prevents Tehran from selling oil as usual, despite the existence of land routes and railways with China," he said.
He pointed to another variable, namely that Washington believes it has, to some extent, secured "the use of the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool".
"The United States has succeeded in escorting oil tankers through the strait so that traffic has become more than 75% of what it was before the war," he added.
Schirach also noted that "global markets have begun to adapt and no longer see the situation as an existential threat, unlike what Tehran had sought by using the strait as a tool to impose its conditions".
He estimated that the chances of reaching an agreement at the current time appear extremely slim, given the wide gap between the two sides' positions.
He pointed out that Washington's current goal is the complete halt of Iran's nuclear programme, while Tehran refuses to completely give up enriched uranium.
Iranian demands go far beyond what Washington can accept, such as the release of frozen assets and the closure of military bases, which he described as "ridiculous".
Although the Iranians have extensive experience in dealing with sanctions and pressure, they have not faced a crisis like the current one or such a large and highly complex and interconnected set of sanctions, according to the US researcher.
He argued that the continuation of the blockade for several more months could put the regime before a genuine survival crisis, and they may rely on land routes through the Caucasus, but this will not compensate for the losses.
Schirach also noted that the United States has "a lack of patience in dealing with long-term conflicts, especially as the current situation affects public opinion and citizens, which could save Tehran before its economy completely collapses".
President Trump shared on his platform on Monday an analysis written by Alexander Stahl, an investor and energy analyst, arguing that Iran had lost the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool and that oil levels had returned to pre-war levels.
However, Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International Studies who specialises in Iranian political economy and the effects of sanctions, wrote on X, pointing to several factors that go beyond the issue of control over the strait alone.
"Yes, Iran may no longer be able to disrupt the flow of energy as effectively as it did during the first phase of the war, but it still retains a significant ability to destroy assets (in the Middle East), including production, refining and distribution infrastructure," he said.
He added that saying Iran had lost control overlooks the fact that it can still escalate and target these facilities if it believes it needs to send a message that it can inflict damage that forces Trump to accept the diplomatic options on the table.
He cited the 2019 attacks on Aramco facilities in Abqaiq and Khurais.
He noted that Trump's unpredictable and volatile approach and his strong insistence on victory in the war could push Iran towards escalation.
He also said that the strait is not the main source of Iranian leverage in this war, but rather Iranian attacks on infrastructure, countries and US bases.
He added that this is being downplayed because acknowledging it would mean recognising the United States' inability to neutralise Iran's capabilities.
He warned that Iran could resort to a "scorched earth" policy if the current situation continues for a long period.
He said, "The US Navy can certainly escort ships at great cost and ensure the continued flow of oil, but the deeper problem remains unresolved, which is the failure of US security guarantees across the Gulf region, and this gives Iran leverage in negotiations."

EU ‘fully rejects’ US threat to ban diesel exports unless bloc releases more fuel stocks
The European Union on Friday pushed back against a US threat to ban any diesel exports unless the 27-member bloc releases more of its fuel stocks, “fully” rejecting the move, an EU official said. French President Emmanuel Macron will chair a video call with his G7 counterparts Friday to discuss possible measures on global fuel markets.
The EU pushed back hard Friday against US threats to impose a diesel export ban, as Washington pressures Europe to tap its strategic reserves in a bid to bring down fuel prices.
The United States’ war in Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite US President Donald Trump at home with high fuel costs, a key issue in the run-up to midterm congressional elections next month.
“We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner,” European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said.
Read moreEuropean drivers choke on rising diesel prices due to Iran conflict
The 27-nation bloc was ready to work with the International Energy Agency on the possible release of fuel reserves to contain prices, she added, following crisis talks between member states and commission to forge a unified response.
Earlier Friday, French leader Emmanuel Macron spoke to Trump and urged G7 nations to work together on the matter – while also speaking out against any export ban.
“The president stressed that G7 countries had a common interest in acting in a coordinated way, without export restrictions,” Macron’s office said after his exchange with the US leader.
Macron will chair a video call with his counterparts from the G7 from 2.30pm local time (12.30pm GMT) to discuss possible measures on the world markets for crude and refined products, the Élysée Palace said in a statement.

“Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” Bessent posted on social media.
“American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage,” he wrote.
Earlier this week, the Executive Director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), Fatih Birol, said European nations were yet to release part of the stocks they had agreed to in an earlier bid to ease prices in March.
“A big chunk of the stocks have been released, but still some remain, both in terms of crude oil and products,” Birol told reporters Tuesday after a meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin.
‘Dramatic consequences’
The 32 members of the IEA agreed last March to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves, their largest release ever.
About a third was yet to come to market, Birol said, adding that further releases were possible with 80 percent of overall IEA stocks “still in our pocket”.
Diesel prices in the United States and Europe have hit record highs due to the US-Iran war, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure also blamed for pushing up prices.
The issue has emerged as a major drag for Trump’s Republican Party in the coming midterm elections, in which it risks losing control of Congress.
Trump on Wednesday floated the possibility of banning US exports of diesel, which is used in trucks and other hauling vehicles – an alarming prospect for the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports.
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers gathering in Milwaukee that the ban would have “dramatic consequences for our economic performance.”
Reports said the Trump administration wants France and Germany in particular to tap their stockpiles of diesel to try to curb prices.
“It is in Europe’s best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers,” a US official told AFP.
At the G20 trade talks, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer struck a conciliatory tone, saying there was an “eagerness on both sides to work together” on the diesel issue.
Average US diesel prices have surged more than 70 percent to $6.39 a gallon since the start of the Iran war, according to the American Automobile Association.

Father of Navy officer who was threatened by FSB rescued from occupied territory
The Angels, a special reconnaissance detachment, have evacuated the father and aunt of a Ukrainian marine officer from the occupied territories.
Source: Ukrainian Navy press service
Quote from the Navy: "Relatives of the Ukrainian defence forces' military personnel who remained in the temporarily occupied territories may face pressure from the Russian secret services. The occupiers use them as an instrument of blackmail, threatening them, illegally detaining them, and trying to force Ukrainian defenders to cooperate.
This is exactly what happened to the father and aunt of a marine officer of the Ukrainian Navy. Representatives of the Russian FSB [Federal Security Service - ed.] detained them and tried to use them as leverage against the Ukrainian serviceman.
However, fighters of the Angels, a special reconnaissance detachment of the Navy, intervened in the enemy's plans."
Details: The video states that in June this year, the Ukrainian marine officer received a call from his father's number, but a representative of the Russian secret services spoke to him. The unit commander reported this to his superiors.
The Navy emphasised that the evacuation operation from the temporarily occupied territory was complex and multi-stage. Thanks to the cooperation between the Angels and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Navy officer's relatives were successfully returned home.
According to the officer's father, the occupiers beat and tortured him after detaining him.
Quote from the Navy: "Russia may try to use relatives as hostages, threaten families, and blackmail Ukrainian soldiers. But there is one thing the enemy cannot change: Ukraine does not abandon its own."

British forces land on Danish territory near Arctic circle
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:52 BST
20:12:52 KST

Royal Marines have deployed to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the Second World War, training with Danish and Faroese forces around the strategically important Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap, according to the Royal Navy.
The deployment formed part of Exercise Lion Protector 2026, a Joint Expeditionary Force activity intended to test how quickly participating nations can respond to events across the High North and the approaches linking the North Atlantic with the Baltic Sea.
Commandos from the UK Commando Force deployed as part of the Allied Reaction Force Special Operations Maritime Task Group, or SOMTG, working with Danish forces and maritime agencies from the Faroe Islands.
Training included maritime interdiction operations, with personnel practising the boarding, inspection and seizure of vessels, as well as small boat operations and coastal landings on steep and difficult terrain.
The Faroe Islands sit between Iceland and Scotland in the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap, an important maritime route connecting the North Atlantic and Arctic. The area has long been closely watched by NATO because Russian naval vessels operating from bases in the north use routes through the wider region to reach the Atlantic.
According to a Royal Navy news update, First Sea Lord and Commandant General Royal Marines General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said: “Defending the Atlantic is fundamental to our economy, national security and way of life. In troubling times, we cannot be complacent.
“The return of the Royal Marines to the Faroe Islands should send an unequivocal message: the UK, alongside Denmark and our other allies in the Joint Expeditionary Force, stand ready to protect the waters, islands and vital routes that keep our nations secure.”
The exercise is the principal 2026 deployment for the UK Commando Force’s Allied Reaction Force Special Operations Maritime Task Group. The formation is designed to provide NATO with forces able to deploy at short notice for missions including recapturing vessels or offshore infrastructure and conducting reconnaissance or raids along coastlines ahead of larger amphibious operations.
The task group includes specialist personnel from across the Royal Navy and UK Commando Force, including boarding teams, pilots, engineers and small boat crews.
During Lion Protector, personnel practised approaching target vessels, using boarding ladders and climbing aboard before carrying out searches and simulated seizures.
Training later moved ashore across the Faroes’ 18-island archipelago, where Royal Marines operated around steep volcanic terrain, established observation posts above maritime routes and conducted cliff ascents. The deployment also has a historical connection. Royal Marines last operated in the Faroe Islands during the Second World War after Germany invaded Denmark in April 1940.
Britain subsequently launched Operation Valentine, with Royal Navy destroyers sent to Tórshavn before around 250 Royal Marines landed from HMS Suffolk. British forces remained on the islands until 1945, when control was returned to Denmark. The Joint Expeditionary Force brings together the United Kingdom, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, with its activities focused primarily on Northern Europe, the North Atlantic, Baltic Sea and High North.
Exercise Lion Protector ran between August and October and was designed to rehearse military response options across the High North and through the Danish Straits into the Baltic Sea. The Royal Navy said the activity was intended to improve the ability of JEF forces to deploy and operate together across the region.
The training takes place ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and International Sea Power Conference aboard HMS Prince of Wales later this autumn, which will bring together defence leaders, industry representatives and policymakers to discuss Euro-Atlantic security.

Taiwan's Msscorps sees revenue hit records on chip analysis demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:12:35 UTC
20:12:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Semiconductor analysis firm Msscorps Co. posted multiple revenue records in September, with monthly, quarterly, and nine-month figures all reaching new highs.
Revenue reached NT$265 million (US$8.3 million) for the month, up 36.71% from the same period a year earlier. This marked the company's third straight monthly record, according to CTEE.
Third-quarter revenue totaled NT$759 million, rising 31.63% year-over-year. Revenue for the first nine months reached NT$1.97 billion, up 24.38% from the previous year.
The growth came as Msscorps saw continued interest in advanced process materials analysis and services related to AI chips. The company primarily provides semiconductor materials analysis and failure analysis services, according to Business Next.
Its work includes examining chip samples with advanced equipment to study their internal structures, layer thicknesses, and material composition. Such analysis is used to verify that chip structures meet design specifications when new materials are introduced into manufacturing processes. It can also help identify the source of problems when a chip shows abnormal performance.
Msscorps is also seeing growth from newer applications. As data center network speeds advance from 800G to 1.6T and technologies such as silicon photonics move closer to commercial use, chipmakers need more detailed analysis to develop, test, and manufacture components.
Overseas operations also contributed to growth this year. Msscorps' US and Japan sites took on more projects and improved operational efficiency, with both moving toward profitability as they benefit from greater scale.
The company has also expanded cooperation with major international AI customers and completed three dedicated facilities. Discussions are underway on three additional facilities, which are expected to begin operations progressively in the fourth quarter.

Brazil's election: Lula or Bolsonaro Jr?

Brazil's election: Lula or Bolsonaro Jr?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
PRESS REVIEW – Friday, October 2: We look at reactions in the French papers after high school blockades turned violent across France. We also look ahead to Brazil's two-round presidential election, which begins this weekend. The electoral campaign culminated with the cancellation of a presidential debate after both President Lula and his rival Flavio Bolsonaro pulled out. Finally, this year's Comedy Wildlife Awards finalists do not disappoint.
There's lots of focus on this week's high school protests in France that turned violent on Thursday. Le Parisien evokes the anger of pupils and talks of a "situation that escalated", with more than 2,000 arrests.
Many of the papers point their finger at the far-left France Unbowed party, whose members have publicly supported the high schoolers. Le Figaro, the right-wing daily, calls them "the proxies" of the protesters and says that behind the demonstrators lurks the "shadow of the France Unbowed party". La Croix is more tempered in its coverage, reminding us that the violence of the protests is still marginal. Libération, the left-wing paper, is one of the few dailies that actually looks at what high schoolers are demanding: more funding for schools, better school facilities and adequate numbers of teachers and personnel. It offers some examples of how bad the situation is for some schools: one maths teacher was absent for three months and in one school, only one toilet was available for 1,200 pupils. Communist paper L'Humanité denounces the police action against protesters on Thursday. Its headline reads "Take your police away first" – a play on words of the word "bac", which also means high-school leaving diploma.
L'Humanité is also focusing on Brazil on its front page. Brazilians head to the voting booths this Sunday for the first round of presidential elections and the election is garnering a lot of attention in the papers there. The election pits incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Jornal do Brasil is focusing on polls that predict Lula will win the first round, but it could be neck and neck for the run-off on October 25. The paper also reports that international observers have arrived in Brazil to observe the correct undertaking of the electoral process.
It has been a bitter electoral campaign, culminating on Thursday with the cancellation of the final presidential debate, set to be hosted by O Globo, after both Lula and Bolsonaro refused to attend. In its editorial, Brazilian daily O Globo explains why it cancelled the debate. The Superior Electoral court authorities refused to leave an empty chair for absent candidates to allow the other candidates to direct questions at them in absentia. As O Globo explains, this is a deep-seated tradition in campaign debates and part of the democratic process. The other grievance was the inclusion of certain candidate from Lula's party who did not meet the requirements necessary to participate in the debates. O Globo says that faced with political interference and violations of the constitution and press freedom, it had no option but to cancel the presidential debate. A columnist for another daily, Folha da Sao Paolo, says the Supreme Electoral Court's meddling with the debate "with such brazenness would have been unthinkable not long ago, something associated with banana republics. Not anymore."
Finally, this year's Comedy Wildlife Awards finalists have been announced and they do not disappoint! We look at some of those in the running for Nikon's Comedy Wildlife Awards, which will be announced in December. They include an orangutan flipping the bird, a pair of elephant seals necking each other and a macaque learning the hard way that you shouldn't ram into a tree at full speed!
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

Polanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:04:06 UTC
20:04:06 KST

Zack Polanski has said his authority as leader of the Green party of England and Wales does not depend on winning next week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection, amid suggestions the party’s popularity may have peaked.
Polanski, who is trying to take Keir Starmer’s former seat from Labour, described the contest as “probably 50/50 right now” and “really on a knife edge”.
Asked in an interview with the Guardian how much his position as leader depended on victory, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”
He added that the election had ramifications for politics nationally but “not for my leadership”.
“I’ll be completely honest, it won’t surprise you to know that I want to win the seat,” Polanski said. “I think the seat is winnable, and I think it’s probably 50-50 right now. It’s really, really on a knife edge.”
Senior Green party figures privately fear defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.
Attempts to concentrate resources on the byelection have caused internal friction, with the Guardian revealing last month that Polanski wanted the Greens’ annual conference postponed so the party could focus on the contest. That proposal was rejected by its executive.
Polanski, who has never been an MP, maintained there were “still advantages to being a leader outside Westminster”, while also arguing that entering parliament would offer another way of putting pressure on the Labour government.
The byelection has become an early test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can reclaim progressive voters who have moved towards the Greens, and the result may inform the government’s decisions over expanding North Sea oil and gas drilling.
“I see this election as high stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.”
The Guardian has reported the Jackdaw decision is likely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs.
Both projects already hold licences granted under the Conservatives, meaning approval by Labour would not amount to issuing new exploration licences.
Asked whether Burnham’s surge could win back younger and progressive voters from the Greens, Polanski said there were two possibilities. One was that Burnham “means what he’s saying right now” and would actually “implement action today and not tomorrow, and not after the next general election”. In this case, Polanski said, the country would improve as a result of pressure from the Greens and others.
The other, which Polanski called “the more likely scenario”, was that “what we’re getting is talk”. He said Burnham was “promising things after the next general election, but soon we’re going to have a budget that he’s already warning is going to be a difficult budget”.
In this case, he said, “more and more people will start to question why would you vote for the Labour party or get involved with the Labour party when the Green party has been growing for over a year now”.
He added: “You don’t have to accept the half-fat version. You can join the Green party and actually make sure we have the country that Andy Burnham’s talking about, but not taking the action on.”
Arguing that Labour’s climate policy had a gap between rhetoric and actions, Polanski asked: “Does Andy Burnham just not care about the climate crisis? It just feels like such a glaring gap in everything that he’s talked about, not just because of Rosebank and Jackdaw, but in the need to invest in renewables, the need for a clean green revolution, the need for new jobs, and it just feels like this vision is just not there.”
He added: “When are we going to see difficult choices for the super rich and the very, very wealthy? Instead, he’s talking about difficult choices for pensioners. So already, the action is not meeting his ‘hope’ rhetoric, and I think people are already starting to ask questions.”
Referring to arrests of Palestine Action supporters outside the Labour party conference, Polanski said: “Those people on the doorstep, they can see that Ed Miliband stood on stage and told many of us that we were right on Palestine, but just behind him, outside the conference hall, pensioners were still being dragged off, being arrested for holding signs up saying ‘I support Palestine Action’.”
Polanski is facing a separate test of his leadership at the Green party’s annual conference, where members are due to debate a deeply contentious motion declaring “Zionism is racism”.
Asked about criticism from senior Greens who believe he has failed to provide leadership over the issue, he said: “Leadership is about priorities, and this motion isn’t my priority. My priority is the cost of living. My priority is nationalising Thames Water. My priority is ending the genocide that’s happening in Gaza and freeing Palestine.”
Some Jewish Greens have raised concerns about what the motion could mean for their place within the party.
Asked whether he could guarantee that a Jewish member would not face disciplinary action simply for attending a synagogue that identified as Zionist, Polanski said: “I can guarantee that this motion has absolutely nothing to do with disciplinary action against anyone.”

Russia Stops Cyprus-Flagged Cargo Ship Heading to Estonia in Gulf of Finland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:03:52 UTC
20:03:52 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Stops Cyprus-Flagged Cargo Ship Heading to Estonia in Gulf of Finland
Russian border guards detained a Cyprus-flagged cargo vessel bound for the Estonian port of Sillamäe while it was passing through Russian territorial waters in the Gulf of Finland, ERR reported.
The vessel, Vasterbotten, was traveling through an area of Russian territorial waters where ships are permitted to transit under an agreement between Estonia, Finland, and Russia. Estonia’s Police and Border Guard Board confirmed that the vessel had been detained.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to vessel-tracking data cited by ERR, Westerbotten appeared to have entered Russian territorial waters before it was stopped. The ship was later allowed to resume its voyage, departing at around 5 p.m. and continuing toward Sillamäe.
The route through Russian waters is covered by an agreement between the three countries because it provides a safer passage for larger vessels than navigating shallower waters on the Estonian side.
Are Piel, head of the Vessel Traffic Management Department at the Estonian Transport Administration, said that while the incident was unwelcome, inspections of vessels within a country’s territorial waters were not unusual.
“Every country has the right to inspect vessels in its territorial sea, and apparently the Russian administration considered it necessary to inspect this vessel as it passed through their territorial sea,” Piel said.
He added that all vessels have the right to innocent passage through another country’s territorial sea, but stressed that this does not prevent the coastal state from inspecting them.
The Estonian Transport Administration said it had received no explanation from Russia regarding the reason for the vessel’s detention.
The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of Russian maritime activities in the region. Russia is working to expand a new “shadow fleet” of tankers in an effort to bypass British sanctions and preserve revenues from energy exports, The Telegraph reported on October 1, citing the UK Foreign Office.
The reported expansion involves a network of civilian vessels used to transport Russian fuel and generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war against Ukraine. The fleet reportedly includes at least two newly built tankers designed to carry liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Arctic waters.

Many G20 countries see need to consolidate, reach consensus — minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:00:49 UTC
20:00:49 KST

MILWAUKEE /Wisconsin/, October 2. /TASS/. Many Group of Twenty (G20) countries believe it is necessary to consolidate around the most pressing issues and seek consensus, Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov told reporters on Thursday following the G20 meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
"Many expressed the view that it would be wrong to abandon the G20’s standard working format, under which all decisions are made by consensus among all countries, in favor of an approach where certain countries simply sign on to a particular position. The task is not to divide the world into camps - it is already doing that on its own. The G20’s task has always been to bring countries together, consolidate around the most pressing issues, and reach agreement," Reshetnikov noted.
He stressed that the G20 has strong potential to resolve issues constructively. "We need to focus on that rather than go our separate ways, form yet more blocs, and gather groups of countries to sign various statements. We need to concentrate on what unites us. Ultimately, global trade is what makes every nation richer," the minister emphasized.
The ministerial meeting in Milwaukee, which Reshetnikov attended, focused on international economic development and trade. It was held from September 30 to October 1. The United States holds the G20 presidency this year. The G20 events in the US will culminate in a summit to be held on December 14-15 near Miami, Florida.

Harri Tiido: On the closed nature of Russian thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:50:00 UTC
19:50:00 KST

Harri Tiido: On the closed nature of Russian thinking
In Harri Tiido's commentary series, this time, with the help of Andrei Kolesnikov, Russian people and the thinking that leads them are under observation. Kolesnikov thinks that in the war in Ukraine peace is possible only if Putin decides that the empire has been restored and the world has once again been divided between great powers.
The basis of the discussion is the book in English by Russian journalist and political observer Andrei Kolesnikov "The Closing of the Russian Mind: How Putin's Ideology Took the Nation Hostage", 2026.
I have used Kolesnikov's writings before as well, he appears in the West, he is a former analyst at the Carnegie Endowment's Moscow Center and currently a contributor to Novaya Gazeta. What is interesting in Kolesnikov's case is that he continues to publish his thoughts while living in Russia. He himself notes in the book that there are few like him, but they do not feel at all isolated, they organize discussion circles in someone's apartment or in a café and continue living their lives.
The idea for the book is said to have been born while sitting with his family in a café in Paris. So he can travel freely. All this seems surprising, considering that the current Russian authorities send people behind bars for years already for some old post. So far Kolesnikov has earned from the authorities only the title of foreign agent, but this does not prevent the publication of writings critical of Vladimir Putin's regime.
It leaves the impression that he is kept precisely as an example of the existence of media freedom in Russia, but one cannot reproach a person for having been very lucky. Also in Soviet times there were, among the intelligentsia, those who could go abroad and thereby demonstrate the regime's liberalism.
But now to the book, in which Kolesnikov calls Putin's regime a personalistic autocracy, but the term is perhaps not important, more weighty is the description of the regime, and that is in many ways familiar. By the way, the main value of the book is precisely its publication in English. For people who constantly follow Russia there may not be very much new in it, but for a Western reader it should be useful reading. I do not agree with everything, but that is another matter.
Kolesnikov affirms that, according to Putin's guiding thought, Russia has its own, special path, and Russian citizens must submit to his rules as he steers the country toward this unique destiny. For Putin, the symbol of Russian identity is territory, which, similarly to Stalin, is one of his fixed values.
With Stalin's era as well as with earlier tsarist Russia, Putin's regime has much in common. As through the centuries, so in Russia even now a simple logic applies, that for the sake of the size of the state one may sacrifice hundreds of thousands and, if necessary, also millions of human lives. According to this ideology, human life is worth nothing, and for a higher goal it can always be given up.
In some respects, the model Putin is building resembles the Soviet state, but internally it is completely different. The Soviet legacy is a hierarchical administrative system, state-centeredness and the sacralization of the state. The nomenklatura is also in place, as is the corporativeness of the system.
Putin thinks more in terms of imperial Russia; the Soviet state is for him only one form of expression of the Russian idea or imperial dream. After the start of the war in Ukraine, Putin tried to fill the void of uncertainty that had arisen in mass consciousness with a new ideology, which was put together from old Russian and Soviet ideological currents. Putin's regime has developed from controlled democracy through authoritarianism into neo-totalitarian or hybrid-totalitarian, combining the silence of the majority and the making of the people complicit in the regime's crimes.
One of the most important observations of the book is how learned indifference and passive conformism became the main behavioral pattern of the average Russian. On the ideology market there is only one product that is allowed by the authorities, and it becomes a kind of mass commodity, because everyone carries it. It is the mainstream, but one could say that it is also the fashion in today's Russia.
Since Russia did not manage to catch up with the West in modernization, it was decided to embark on de-modernization, that is, moving back in history. In seeking the future in the past, Putinism has lost its goal. The only future aim is the struggle with the West, although it is not possible to formulate victory in this.
In Kolesnikov's opinion, the primary condition for normalizing the state is the abandonment of the Russian imperial idea and also of the neo-totalitarian model of a parasitic oil state. But normalization must be preceded by a thorough moral and ideological rethinking of the place of the Russian people. Kolesnikov calls this the reopening of Russian consciousness, although it would probably be more correct to say simply opening, since this consciousness has never been open.
Kolesnikov also thinks that in the war in Ukraine peace is possible only if Putin decides that the empire has been restored and the world has once again been divided between great powers, and he adds that it is unlikely that Putin would then strive further west. In my opinion, one cannot be at all sure of that…
As for the Russian person, he is used to living in conditions of brutal armed conflict. A large part has accepted that in the current circumstances one must live for a long time yet, and therefore it is necessary to adapt. The majority of the population may not identify themselves with the regime, but they rally around the Kremlin, which in their eyes fights against the West that is trying to destroy the state. In this sense, the processing of mass consciousness in Russia has been successful.
Putin's regime is kept afloat precisely by the population's indifference, opportunism and readiness to adapt. It is indeed possible to live in an Orwellian dystopia, especially if the market economy with goods and services still functions. The situation could perhaps be shaken only by the declaration of general mobilization.
All of Russia's attempts at reform so far have run into the sand because of political compromises, lack of political will and inability to overcome ideological stereotypes, and behind this has been the leaders' and the elite's fear of losing power.
At the end of the last century there was an attempt, but it ran into the sand. Socially, the biggest problem at that time was that the market economy in Russia produced, in Western terms, a standard consumer type, but it did not produce a citizen. That is, the market economy produced consumers, yet the state remained without citizens. The consumer did not see a connection between the free market and political democracy. And does not see it to this day. Without democracy, modernization unfortunately does not take place, especially in an empire.
It is said that in Russia one must live for a long time to see the restoration of freedom. And if you live even longer, then you may also get to see the arrival of a new, successive despotism.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Once every four years, every eligible Latvian citizen has an opportunity to influence the country’s political direction, prosperity and who will be at the helm of the state. All it takes is making a choice and going to vote. Why is this so important, and what happens to votes cast for political forces that fail to cross the 5% threshold? BNN discusses these questions with political scientist Filips Rajevskis, co-founder of the company Mediju tilts.
“This is not just about saying ‘don’t stay at home’. It is very important for people to turn out for the election, especially Riga residents voting in Riga,” the political scientist says.
“Riga is a very strong constituency for parties supported by Russian-speaking voters, and we know very well that there are parties here that have always benefited precisely from Latvian voters being less active. Riga is a very large electoral district with 38 seats. So, if people are concerned about what the composition of parliament will look like, they need to come out and vote, increase participation and cast their ballot for the political force they themselves have chosen.”
Rajevskis also points out that if Riga residents care specifically about the result in the Riga electoral district, they should not leave the capital to vote in rural areas.
“That is a vote that would otherwise be lost from the Riga constituency.
Asked what incentive there is for political forces that realise they are unlikely to cross the 5% threshold but still enter the pre-election battle, Filips Rajevskis explains that parties receiving more than 2% of the vote also receive state funding, which is extremely important for a party’s future.
Votes cast for parties that do not cross the threshold are subsequently redistributed among the parties that are elected.
“If there are parties below the 5% threshold, voters themselves have to decide what they want to achieve with their vote. If you vote for a party that crosses the threshold, then it is clear that your vote will translate into parliamentary representation.”
Filips Rajevskis stresses: 
“Everyone should go and vote. Don’t leave it until the last moment.”
During the week of Latvia’s 15th Saeima election, voters can still deposit their ballots for safekeeping on Friday, the 2nd of October, from 12:00 to 15:00 at any of the 933 polling stations across Latvia.
On election day, the 3rd of October, polling stations throughout Latvia will be open from 08:00 to 20:00.
Voters must bring a valid Latvian citizen’s passport or eID card. Polling station addresses and accessibility information are available on the Central Election Commission’s website.

US-India trade deal not imminent – top official
The US and India are not on the cusp of a trade deal despite negotiations nearing completion, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Thursday following talks with Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal in Milwaukee.
The two sides have identified the remaining sticking points and are working to resolve them, Greer told reporters after the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting. “I don’t think there is something imminent,” he said, adding, “We’re in the short strokes” and that negotiations were approaching their final stages. He did not specify which issues remained unresolved.
Greer described his meeting with Goyal as constructive and said officials from both countries were continuing discussions. The Indian minister said the talks focused on concluding an interim agreement under the broader India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA).
The meeting came on the heels of a phone call between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump on Wednesday. The leaders reviewed cooperation in trade, defense, energy, and critical technologies. Greer called their conversation “very constructive” and said the two leaders could speak again soon to assess progress.
India and the US agreed on a framework for an interim trade agreement in February, but subsequent changes in Washington’s tariff policies have prolonged negotiations. The framework envisaged lower Indian tariffs on US industrial and selected agricultural products, alongside tariff relief for certain Indian exports.
Goyal said last week that the pact was almost “done and dusted,” but its implementation depended on India securing competitive tariff treatment relative to rival exporters.
The negotiations are also taking place amid renewed US tariff pressure over India’s Russian oil purchases. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act last month, authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
New Delhi has warned that such measures could affect bilateral relations and international energy markets. Greer did not identify Russian oil as one of the remaining obstacles to the trade agreement.

====================================================================================================

Fact check: What's going on with Spain's 'Maricarmen' housing protests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:30:25 UTC
19:30:25 KST

Spanish protests against the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen have led to misleading claims about Spain's housing activists and the wider rental crisis.
Thousands of people are protesting across Spain after authorities evicted Maricarmen Abascal from her home in Madrid.
Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, had been living there for over 70 years. Images of police forcibly removing her from the flat on a stretcher have now turned the legal dispute into a symbolic fight for housing activists.
The protesters marched through Madrid, camped out in Puerta del Sol, and organised demonstrations in other Spanish cities.
They are using Maricarmen's case to protest the wider housing crisis: rising rents and a shortage of affordable homes, which are fuelling fears that tenants can no longer afford to stay in major cities.
The situation has become a very politicised debate, fuelling several false, misleading, and selectively edited claims.
A legal decision
One of the most prominent claims circulating online is that Maricarmen’s eviction was "illegal". This is false: courts authorised the eviction after a years-long dispute over a protected rental contract dating back to the 1950s. It was carried out under a valid court order, despite the backlash it received.
Maricarmen's father originally held the lease, which later passed to her mother and then to Maricarmen herself. The courts ruled that this second transfer could continue for only two years unless Maricarmen had a recognised disability above 65%; authorities recognised hers at 50%.
Spain's Supreme Court upheld the owner’s position, which meant the old, protected tenancy had legally expired and the company could recover the flat. The eviction was therefore lawful.
The goal of the protests
So, contrary to what some misleading headlines imply, protesters are not arguing whether the eviction was lawful, but whether it was fair.
This is partly because, under Francisco Franco’s dictatorship laws, married women could not legally sign financial contracts or property leases independently.
Maricarmen's mother could inherit the lease only by subrogation upon her husband's death. Had she been a co-owner or co-signer from the start, Maricarmen's inheritance of the lease would have counted as the first subrogation, legally protecting her right to stay in the home for life.
Protesters also point out that Maricarmen is 87, has lived in the property for more than seven decades, and continued paying her protected rent.
After the old tenancy ended, property management company Urbagestión proposed a rent of around €1,650 a month, far above the roughly €440 to €500 she had previously paid. This is higher than her monthly pension of around €1,350, therefore forcing a vulnerable long-term tenant out because she cannot afford the new rent.
Protesters are asking for stronger protections against evictions of vulnerable tenants, longer or automatically renewed rental contracts, and tighter limits on rent increases.
Some groups also want tougher rules on speculative housing practices and greater public intervention in the rental market. They are now pressing parliament to approve new protections for vulnerable tenants and longer lease terms.
Other false and misleading claims
Another disputed claim going around online is that the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Spain's main union for tenants, prevented Maricarmen from reaching an agreement with the owner before the eviction.
Urbagestión says the union made it hard to contact Maricarmen directly, while Maricarmen’s lawyer says the opposite: that the company had refused repeated attempts to negotiate.
Urbagestión has also accused people involved in the dispute of coercion, extortion and hacking phones and email accounts. However, the company did not provide evidence for these claims in reporting reviewed by fact-checkers like Spain's Maldita.es.
Another misleading assertion comes from a shortened video of Maricarmen herself. In the clip, she appears to blame left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez specifically for her situation, but the full interview adds more names: she also criticises Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida (both members of the right-wing Popular Party) and Urbagestión itself. The clip therefore uses a genuine quote but removes the wider context of her answer.
A separate false claim involved two protesters called "Irene and Pablo" who spoke to elDiario.es at a protest camp at the Puerta del Sol square in Madrid. Some social-media users suggested they were Pablo Iglesias, former leader of far-left party Podemos, and MEP Irene Montero, from the same party.
However, a quick look at the article itself shows us that they are actually a different 28-year-old woman and 37-year-old man, with no indication that they were the politicians in question.
The next steps
Maricarmen has now accepted an agreement that will allow her to return to the apartment once she leaves hospital. Under the new arrangement, she will pay roughly the same as her previous rent, around €500 a month, capped at 30% of her income. The agreement creates a new tenancy; it does not overturn the court ruling that ended her old, protected lease.
Meanwhile, Spain's government has proposed measures that would extend some eviction protections and lengthen rental contracts, but parliament still needs to approve them. Protesters are therefore continuing their campaign and pushing politicians to adopt those measures while demanding broader reforms to Spain's housing system.

The participants can also focus on ways to make health services more intelligent, enhance the quality of healthcare, develop digital tools, and develop innovative ideas to address challenges faced by the healthcare system.
Opportunities, challenges of digital health in Iran
Modern communication technologies have fundamentally changed people’s lifestyles, social interactions, and access to information, with the health sector going through digital transformation, being no exception.
The emergence of tools such as health applications, telemedicine, electronic health records, and online health platforms has made digital health an important part of the health system. Digital health provides advantages, but it also brings challenges.
Digital health refers to the use of information and communication technologies to promote health, improve access to health services, and enhance the quality of health care. Bridging the distance between the patient and the service provider, digital health makes it easier for different groups in society to receive health services.
It plays a pivotal role in raising public awareness, preventing diseases, and improving health-oriented behaviours.
Despite these benefits, digital health faces some challenges. The most important one is the digital gap, which refers to inequality in accessing and using communication technologies. The gap can be caused by different reasons such as income, place of residence, age, and literacy level.
Researchers at Tehran’s Allameh Tabatabaei University have studied digital health in the country to identify its strengths, shortages, opportunities, and threats, ISNA reported.
 
 The research findings show that digital health in Iran has significant strengths, including national healthcare platforms, the growing use of artificial intelligence tools in healthcare services, and online healthcare services.
Meanwhile, a lack of a comprehensive legal framework for health data protection, integration among digital platforms, digital literacy, and communication infrastructure, as well as structural resistance to technological change, are among the main weaknesses, which highlights that digital health needs both new technologies and reforms in structures and laws.
To realize the healthcare system transformation goal, the health ministry has developed eight projects with a focus on smart e-health using artificial intelligence.
The projects include improving health literacy and self-care, designing a smart referral system, launching a national health observatory, changing health data into operational knowledge, managing the healthcare supply chain of subsidized medicines using AI, establishing a diagnosis-related groups (DRG) payment system, designing a productive smart hospital, and integrating online insurance processes.

Your Driverless Cab Is Spying on You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

One afternoon this past summer, a self-driving Waymo pulled into a parking lot in San Mateo County, California, and stayed there until the police arrived. Local cops had gotten a 911 call from Waymo staffers—humans, it should be said—who were viewing the car’s passengers through cameras installed inside the vehicle. It looked like two teens were shooting a black handgun out the window of the vehicle, playing with it and drinking between shots, a police report said.
The story has a happy(ish) ending: The gun was shooting water-filled Orbeez, not bullets. But the incident drew attention to Waymo’s surveillance system. The cars are equipped with automated tech that can flag the presence of a firearm inside, the company said.
The outsides of self-driving cars are studded with cameras, which help them “see” the world around them. (Most also use other sensors, including radar and lidar.) Less appreciated are the cameras inside the vehicles, which companies say are essential to keeping riders safe and enforcing their rules. Earlier this year, Waymo said it used its cabin cameras to do both after some California passengers, many in their twenties or older, reported that Waymo employees suddenly took over the vehicles’ intercoms mid-ride to make sure they were old enough to ride on their own. (One 35-year-old told WIRED he thought his backpack sent up red flags.)
Still, robotaxi privacy policies can be broad. They suggest that footage captured inside vehicles can be used for many innocuous and commonsense reasons—to check cleanliness between rides, to detect lost items—but also to improve their products or services. These catch-all terms could cover many uses. Experts say that in the US, few clear rules govern this sort of surveillance, especially because riders often must agree to lengthy “terms of service” printed in minute fonts before they use ride-hailing apps. That leaves riders to trust that the companies are handling their information responsibly.
“We are being essentially abandoned by our lawmakers when it comes to consumer privacy and what companies can do with information after they’ve collected it,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he works on surveillance and policing issues. His advice? “Just because you’re alone in the car doesn’t mean you’re alone in the car. You should behave as if there’s a jumpy person in the front seat.”
In general, robotaxi companies including Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla say that human staff view interior cameras only when needed. All say personal data, including recordings, may be sent to law enforcement or regulators. (A Waymo support page says that government agencies seeking data “are directed to follow valid legal processes in making such request.”)
But that doesn’t mean the interior cameras aren’t on and working. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina says the company uses “automated technology to support our teams in identifying potential violations.” A 2025 patent held by Waymo describes a system in which vehicles’ interior camera systems conduct automated "predetermined ride checklists” before, during, and after rides. (Ilina did not say whether that system is in use.)
Zoox’s website says its interior cameras “record the entirety of your ride.” This sort of personal data can be used to help operate rides, but also to develop and improve Zoox’s product. The company—owned by Amazon—says it might record conversations between riders and its support employees, but that it doesn’t save recordings. Zoox spokesperson
Whitney Jencks said the company had nothing more specific to share about its privacy policies.
Online documents for Tesla’s Robotaxi service say a green indicator shows up on the vehicle’s central touchscreen when the camera is activated. Riders can opt in to sharing in-cabin video and audio with the company through a toggle menu in the “data and privacy” section of its app. The documents also say riders in the company’s “early access” program automatically opt in to data sharing. The company didn’t respond to questions for this story, including whether that early access program has technically concluded. The company opened its Robotaxi app to the public in a handful of Texas and Florida cities in early September.
Cameras inside robotaxis make plenty of sense. “You need some kind of check on what people do in a car with no driver,” says Justin Brookman, who directs technology policy at Consumer Reports. “People are going to have sex in Waymos if there are no cameras.” (Media reports suggest that the cameras don’t always stop them.)
But the law hasn’t yet fully contemplated what companies should be able to see, save, and use. “These vehicles are relatively new, so there are no expectations around what’s appropriate,” Brookman says. “There should be some check in place.”
Auto companies don’t have the best record on data privacy.
In 2023, Reuters reported that groups of Tesla employees had, over several years, shared sensitive videos and images captured by owners’ cars. Shared recordings reportedly included a video of a man approaching a car while naked, and a violent collision between a car and a child on a bike. Tesla boasts that its years-deep repository of data from personal vehicles gives it an edge in developing autonomous vehicle software, and its privacy policy says camera recordings are kept anonymous. But former employees told Reuters that the system easily revealed where the images were recorded, which could have allowed them to link recordings to specific owners’ garages or driveways.
Earlier this year, General Motors paid California motorists nearly $13 million in penalties after the company was found to have sold driving data to brokers and eventually insurers without their consent.
“My big concern is that automakers love to collect data,” Guariglia says. “With autonomous vehicles, there’s even more data to collect. And the more data they collect, the more they’re going to find reasons to sell it.”
In the meantime, his privacy-related advice? Behave.

More than 350,000 public administration workers are covered by the strikes called by three CGTP-affiliated unions for this Friday in Portugal. The biggest effects are being felt in education, with dozens of schools closing their doors due to a lack of staff.
"We have schools closed from the north to the south of the country, in the Azores and Madeira as well," explained Sebastião Santana, speaking to TVI. Outside the Francisco Arruda School in Lisbon, which kept its gates shut this morning, the coordinator of the Common Front highlighted the "strong turnout" for the protest.
The union leader was speaking at the Francisco Arruda School in Lisbon, which did not open because of the 24-hour stoppage.
The protest was called by the National Federation of Public and Social Service Workers' Unions (FNSTFPS), the National Union of Local and Regional Administration Workers, Public Companies, Concessionaires and Related Entities (STAL) and the Lisbon Municipal Workers' Union (STML), covering operational assistants, technical assistants and senior technicians.
As well as school closures, the strike may also cause disruptions to social security services, registry and notary offices, the justice system and rubbish collection.
The walkout may also have some impact on local health units and other bodies under the Ministry of Health.
Dozens of people have gathered in Lisbon for a march between Praça da Figueira and the Ministry of Finance.
The unions are calling for the immediate upgrading of these professionals' career structures.
EasyJet: union reports strong support and hundreds of flights cancelled
easyJet cabin crew launched a five-day protest action on Friday, with the strike continuing until Tuesday. The National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel (SNPVAC) reports strong participation and expects 80% of flights to be cancelled during the five days of stoppage.
Speaking to the Lusa news agency, SNPVAC president Ricardo Penarroias said that 443 flights have already been cancelled for the coming days at Lisbon, Porto and Faro airports.
Also speaking to Lusa, an official easyJet source said it expects to operate around 55% of its schedule during the strike period, through minimum services and flights operated from other European bases.
"The company will carry out the minimum services, which are compulsory, and the other flights it has not cancelled (...) are flights it will operate illegally," said the union president.
The workers' demands include more stable rosters, pay progression based on seniority and the conditions proposed as part of the negotiations for the company agreement.
A second stoppage has been scheduled for 19 to 23 December.

Tories warn Burnham’s EU ‘pandering’ will shred post-Brexit trade deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:28:42 UTC
19:28:42 KST

Tories warn Burnham’s EU ‘pandering’ will shred post-Brexit trade deals
Three former ministers tell POLITICO of “grave consequences” if the U.K. moves closer to the EU under prime minister’s bid for a revamped relationship.
LONDON — The architects of Britain's first post-Brexit trade deals have warned that the country's independent trade policy is under threat after Andy Burnham pledged a major review of its relationship with the EU.
Their intervention marks the latest salvo in a political fightback against Burnham's EU policy as the Conservative Party conference gets underway in Birmingham this weekend.
Burnham this week vowed to discuss a revamped relationship with Europe, including rejoining the EU's customs union, moving closer the bloc's single market — or even pushing to outright rejoin the bloc. It marks a fundamental shift from a Labour Party that has previously ruled out all three.
Advertisement
Customs union membership — a popular option among some members of Burnham’s Cabinet — would ease trade between the U.K. and its largest trading partner, but require Britain to sacrifice the trade deals it has struck since leaving the bloc six years ago.
Greg Hands, who served as trade minister four times between 2016 to 2024 under Conservative governments, said that all options presented “grave consequences for Britain's independent trade policy.”
“Depending exactly on what is agreed, it is likely to invalidate or make very difficult most — if not all — of those existing trade agreements, or many of those existing trade agreements,” he said.
Since Brexit, the U.K. has negotiated free trade deals with nations including Australia, New Zealand, Japan and — more recently — the Asia Pacific trading bloc CPTPP, India, the Gulf states, as well as upgraded deals with South Korea and Switzerland.
Although the U.K. could technically copy-and paste EU versions of trade deals, Hands warned that the terms might not be so favorable, highlighting that the U.K.-Japan deal he had helped to negotiate “has got much more liberal rules on data” than the EU equivalent.
As a non-EU member, the U.K. would also surrender its ability to negotiate the terms of any new trade deals, Hands argued. “Why would the EU prioritize the U.K., which is not a paying member of the EU, over paying full members of the EU when it does trade agreements?”
Advertisement
But the issue goes further than free trade agreements, he said, pointing out that entering a customs union with the EU would affect the U.K.’s global tariff — the independent system of taxes and duty rates applied to goods imported from other countries. This would be a “huge diminution of the U.K.'s influence in the world to align or take the EU's customs tariff,” Hands added.
Moreover, by signing up to a customs union, the U.K. would also lose its ability to erect its own trade defenses and be forced to implement EU measures like tariffs on steel and electric vehicles, Hands warned.
He also cautioned that closer alignment could complicate relations with the U.S., which has been critical of U.K. ambitions for closer alignment with the EU. “The U.S. is our single largest bilateral trading partner and I don’t think it would be in the U.K.’s interest to mess up that relationship.”
End of CPTPP membership
Liam Fox, a self-proclaimed “staunch euroskeptic” who served as trade secretary in the immediate aftermath of the referendum, between 2016 and 2019, said rejoining the EU or customs union would “mean an end to Britain’s independent trade policy and any strategy influence we have from membership of organizations such as [the Asia-Pacific trade bloc] CPTPP.”
“This vague language from Andy Burnham is all about keeping the Labour left quiet whatever the consequences,” Fox added. “Rejoining the EU would mean being part of Schengen with free movement of people and adoption of the Euro. If that is what Andy Burnham wants, let him make the case for it, stop his mealy-mouthed pandering to his own party and start acting like a real prime minister.”
A third former Tory trade minister — granted anonymity to speak frankly — told MTUK the risks to Britain’s new trade deals was “real” and would “undermine new relationships with some of the fastest growing middle-class economies in the world.”
“As the mature EU markets continue to be a smaller part of U.K. export opportunities, the prime minister should be focusing on supporting U.K. businesses to win export contracts where huge new markets exist,” the former minister argued.

Record numbers going hungry in Yemen amid escalating conflict, WFP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Three in four families go hungry in parts of Yemen from new fighting
GENEVA, Oct 2 - Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the "absolutely devastating" impact of a surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said on Friday.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi group since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022. The renewed conflict could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes.
Within just a few weeks, the fighting has driven the share of households without sufficient food to 74% in government-controlled areas accessible to WFP, the UN hunger body's Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations told reporters in Geneva. The total population of government-held areas is estimated at around 10 million people.
“The effect of this latest flare-up of insecurity on the food security situation threatens to be absolutely devastating,” Hollingworth told reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome.
The Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa, seized the country's entire Red Sea coast last month from Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government, based in the southern port of Aden.
Displaced families are arriving outside Aden and around the mountain city of Taiz without any water or food, as many had to leave everything behind, WFP said.
Prices of basic food staples such as wheat flour and vegetable oil are rising in a country that imports around 90% of its food.
“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth said, adding that frontline areas like Taiz were increasingly hard to access due to the fighting.
WFP said it was scaling up its response but unless it gets around $109 million in funding within a few weeks it will run out of food stocks and money to help the 152,000 newly displaced persons inside the country, as well as the 1.4 million people it is already supporting.
Hollingworth also pointed to the potential ripple effects of disruption to two major chokepoints in the Middle East: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
That, as well as disruption in the Black Sea due to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, risk driving up food and fuel prices and deepening food insecurity globally.
A new analysis published by UN Women on Friday said an additional 11.7 million women and girls across 28 countries including Yemen, Sudan and Lebanon could face food insecurity by the end of the year, due to escalation in the Middle East and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil-industry facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 2, as explosions were followed by a fire at what open-source analysts believe was the massive Samara oil pumping and dispatch complex.
Russian outlet ASTRA, after analyzing eyewitness imagery, reported that the blaze likely broke out at the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station, or LPDS Samara.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents across the region reported drones overhead during the night, while a missile alert was declared in the city of Samara at 5:51 am. A particularly powerful explosion was reported at around 6:30 am.

Russian local authorities did not acknowledge damage to the oil complex. Samara’s mayor said only that the city’s ground-based public transportation had been temporarily suspended.
LPDS Samara is part of Russia’s Transneft pipeline network and functions as a major storage, pumping, and crude-blending hub.

The facility also incorporates the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations and a separate crude-blending station.
Four major trunk pipelines converge at the hub, carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan before it moves farther through Russia’s pipeline system.
Previously, Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Krasnodar region, sparking a significant fire at a fuel storage facility operated by wholesale trader Edelweiss-95.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese boxer Chen Nien-chin (陳念琴) won silver in the women's 65-kilogram division at the Asian Games on Friday, losing to India's Parveen Hooda by a 2-3 split decision in the gold-medal bout.
Chen battled back from a first-round deficit to level the fight in the second round, but three of the five judges scored the decisive third round for Hooda, per ETtoday. The silver medal marks the best Asian Games result of Chen's career.
Chen advanced to the final after defeating Thailand's Suwannapheng 5-0 in the quarterfinals to secure a medal. She then edged North Korea's Hwang Hyo-sun 3-2 in a split decision in the semifinals, reaching an Asian Games final for the first time.
Under the 10-point system, each of the five judges scores every round independently, typically awarding 10 points to the winner and nine to the loser. Each judge totals the points across all three rounds to determine the winner on their scorecard.
In the opening round, all five judges scored Hooda 10-9, leaving Chen trailing 0-5 on the scorecards, ETtoday reported. Chen responded in the second round, with all five judges awarding her a 10-9 win to level the fight at 19-19 on every scorecard.
The gold medal came down to the final three minutes, with the five judges split on the decisive round. Two scored it 10-9 for Chen, while the other three gave Hooda the same margin, resulting in a 3-2 split decision in the Indian boxer's favor.
Chen finished with a 29-28 advantage on two scorecards but trailed 28-29 on the other three, according to ETtoday. The decision gave Hooda the gold and Chen the silver, one judge's vote short of her first Asian Games title.
