Flydubai hijacking: Israel is a nation of heroes - time for the gov't to show courage too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:56 UTC
19:17:56 KST

Israelis are a nation of heroes. That might sound like a slogan, but every so often something happens that reminds us how true this is.
Of all the extraordinary stories to emerge from Wednesday’s flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the one that stands out is the courage of the passengers who realized something had gone terribly wrong, forced their way into the cockpit, and helped subdue the co-pilot, who had allegedly stabbed the captain and appeared to be trying to bring down the plane.
The aircraft plunged thousands of feet; there was chaos onboard, and the passengers had no way of knowing exactly what was happening or whether they had minutes, seconds, or no time at all.
And they acted. They didn’t wait for someone to rescue them or see if everything would resolve itself on its own. They took the initiative and saved lives: not only of the passengers on board, but whatever else the plane could have taken down with it.
When we remember aircraft that have been hijacked or crashed over the years, it is difficult not to appreciate what happened aboard this flight and how there is something deeply Israeli about it.
It is part of this country’s culture: not to stand by and watch events unfold, but to run headfirst into the fire, battle, or the storm and do whatever can be done to save lives.
We have now heard some testimony from passengers aboard the flight. It is frightening and disturbing, particularly as investigators are still trying to understand what exactly happened and what the co-pilot’s motive was. But there is also something heartwarming in hearing how people responded in those terrifying moments.
They literally took charge, and, when we think about it, it is a characteristic we know all too well. Next week, Israel will mark three years since October 7. That terrible day will be seared into our collective memory as one of the greatest failures and tragedies in Israeli history. But, like with the airplane, it too was filled with stories of some of the greatest courage this country has ever seen.
There are many different kinds of heroism, and there is no need to rank them.
But it is impossible to forget the people who woke up that morning, heard that something incomprehensible was happening in the south, understood that people were in desperate need of help, and got into their cars. They took whatever weapons they had, if they had any, and drove straight into the battle.
They did not know what they would find. They did not know how many terrorists had crossed the border, where the army was, or whether they themselves would make it home. They just went.
That, to a large extent, is the story of Israel: a small country whose people are repeatedly confronted with danger and who, when the moment comes, stand up, fight and lead the charge.
A nation prepared to fight
It is worth thinking about that now, just weeks before Israelis go to the polls on October 27.
This election will help determine the direction Israel takes after three extraordinarily difficult years. And whichever government ultimately emerges, it will inherit a country confronting a series of strategic challenges, almost none of which have truly been resolved.
Hamas still controls part of Gaza and retains weapons and military infrastructure. Hezbollah remains a threat to Israel’s north. And Iran remains locked in confrontation over its nuclear program and its wider regional capabilities.
It is true that three years after October 7, Israel has achieved amazing accomplishments, but victory, as we know too well by now, is not measured only by what an army destroys – it is also measured by what a country builds in its place.
And that is where a striking discrepancy has emerged.
Israel’s leaders have been given an extraordinary gift: a population willing to fight, to endure difficult years, and send its children to war knowing the risks and knowing, painfully, that some will not return.
Consider the family of Israel’s ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter. His son Neria was seriously wounded last week in a ramming attack on Route 443 while serving in the reserves. His brother, Moshe, was killed fighting in Gaza in 2023.
Neria had every reason not to continue serving: his brother had been killed, and his family had already sacrificed enough. He could have remained home with his wife and children. He could have spared his parents the anguish of once again worrying about a son fighting on the front.
But he did not. He continued putting on his uniform. He continued reporting for reserve duty. And he continued serving.
Without people like that, Israel would not survive. But courage cannot only be demanded of soldiers and civilians; it must be demanded of politicians as well.
Political courage is different. It is not about charging a cockpit or running toward gunfire. It is about making difficult decisions, accepting risk, challenging traditional assumptions and, most importantly, telling the public where you actually want to take the country.
That is the question Israelis should be asking as they prepare to vote: What is the vision?
Is the future being offered to us simply one of hunkering down, a kind of super-Sparta, stronger and better armed than everyone around us but condemned to fight one war after another?
Or is there another possibility, one that recognizes the threats Israel faces, takes them seriously, and preserves overwhelming military strength, but also searches for a path toward greater security, stability, and eventually something else?
Israel looking for brave leaders
Last week in New York, for example, the US-backed Board of Peace unveiled an ambitious plan for Gaza. Senior officials acknowledged the enormous obstacles standing in the way, including the unresolved dispute over how Hamas will disarm and how Israel will withdraw.
Considering everything that would have to happen for this plan to succeed, skepticism is more than understandable. Is it ambitious and hard to imagine? 100%.
Three years after October 7, with the situation in Gaza still dire – both for its residents and for Israel’s security – this is a thoughtful plan that offers a real chance to change reality on the ground. Considering all the alternatives, isn’t it worth a shot?
But here is the catch: Israelis were not even in the room.
That is what this election campaign should be about. Instead, too much of Israeli politics remains focused on what candidates are against. This person will sit with that party; that person cannot be trusted; this bloc is dangerous, and that bloc is illegitimate.
But what are these politicians for? Where do they want Israel to be in five years?
What is their plan for Gaza? For Lebanon? For the Palestinians? For Israel’s increasingly strained relationship with parts of the Western world? What does victory realistically look like?
Israelis have demonstrated time and again that they are prepared to take extraordinary risks for this country.
The people who stormed the cockpit this week did not wait to be asked. Neither did the Israelis who drove south on October 7. They saw danger. They understood that someone had to act. And despite having no guarantee of what would happen next, they moved forward.
Israel’s political leaders do not need to storm a cockpit. But they do need to show some of the same courage. Instead of spending the next few weeks telling Israelis what they will never do, whom they will never sit with, and why everyone else is dangerous, they should tell us where they want to take this country.
The Israeli people have already shown that they are prepared to be brave. Now they deserve leaders brave enough to offer them a future.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

Flydubai saga captures Israel’s role in a new Middle East - and its old limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:36 UTC
19:17:36 KST

Wednesday’s flydubai saga crammed the new Middle East into a single aircraft.
An Emirati airline carrying Israelis made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia amid war with Iran – and the incident was immediately drawn into an Israeli election campaign dominated by the question of who can keep the country safe.
Talk about one event bringing everything together.
But beyond the frightening drama aboard the plane, the incident also brought something else into focus: how much the region has changed, and where the limits of that change still lie.
Israelis were flying home on an Emirati airline. When their flight turned into a nightmare, they landed in Saudi Arabia, received medical attention and assistance, and were eventually collected by another Emirati aircraft and brought to Israel.
For all the tensions, wars, and political sensitivities, that sequence is worth noting. The absence of Saudi-Israeli diplomatic relations did not prevent the passengers from receiving help or getting home.
Granted, the Saudis refused to let an Israeli aircraft collect them. That matters and is maddening, especially considering the security and intelligence cooperation that does exist between the two countries. But it need not obscure what they did allow, or turn a story of regional cooperation into a tale primarily about rejection.
The new Middle East is imperfect. Wednesday showed, however, that it is also real.
A changing Middle East takes shape
TO APPRECIATE the broader picture, connect the dots from earlier in the week.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, known as MBZ.
According to reports, Netanyahu shared intelligence about Iran’s continued nuclear ambitions, including new construction at the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site, as well as developments involving the Houthis in the Red Sea.
These are issues on which Israel and the Gulf states have overlapping interests. An Iran rebuilding its nuclear capabilities concerns more than Jerusalem. So do the Houthis threatening Red Sea shipping.
But Netanyahu reportedly brought another concern to the meeting, one rooted in Israel’s election campaign.
AP reported that he asked MBZ to deny the Haaretz account that the Emirati leader had warned him about a looming Hamas threat before October 7.
This report has since mushroomed into several accounts of warnings that Netanyahu allegedly received but did not act on before October 7. And all of this has figured prominently in opposition party attacks on him during the campaign. Netanyahu’s office has denied he received any such warning.
The visit thus carried two possible purposes: discussing threats facing the region now and addressing allegations about what Netanyahu knew back then.
That combination is characteristic of this election campaign. Netanyahu wants the public to focus on what he has done to reshape the region since October 7. His opponents want it to focus on what he failed to prevent on that Simchat Torah morning.
A meeting with an important Arab leader can serve the first argument. Reports that the same leader warned him before the attack feed the second.
The UAE confirmed that Sunday’s meeting took place, unlike in May, when it denied Netanyahu’s claim of an earlier visit. That acknowledgment gave him something to point to: evidence that, despite the wars and international criticism, he could still meet a key Arab leader.
The UAE did not, however, deny that a pre-October 7 call had taken place. Netanyahu came away, therefore, with the proverbial half a loaf: confirmation of Sunday’s meeting, but no denial of the earlier warning.
There were also reports that representatives of other Arab countries attended discussions in Abu Dhabi, including Saudi representatives, though the Saudis denied it.
Then, on Tuesday, MBZ’s brother, UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed, traveled to Riyadh and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman.
With the Houthis again threatening Saudi interests, the two Gulf powers had reason to repair ties ruptured by their competing policies in Yemen.
Might the timing – two days after Netanyahu’s meeting with MBZ – have been a coincidence?
It might. But it also might not.
The sequence raises the possibility of wider coordination against threats that concern Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE alike. It does not, however, establish that Netanyahu brokered the Saudi-Emirati rapprochement, or that all three countries agreed on a common policy.
There is enough here to connect some dots. There is not enough to color in the entire picture.
Still, the meetings suggest a region in which governments have reasons to work through their differences because the threats facing them are greater than those differences.
THEN THE flydubai flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai for Tel Aviv.
That flight is the stuff of movies: one pilot stabs another and tries to crash the aircraft before passengers, along with a crew member, intervene and save the day. The plane makes an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Passengers later describe receiving medical attention and assistance there.
For those aboard, this was a terrifying brush with catastrophe. Their survival owed much to the people who intervened and helped bring the aircraft down safely.
What happened next carried its own regional significance: a plane carrying Israelis lands in Saudi Arabia, its passengers receive help, and the UAE sends another aircraft to bring them home.
Each part of that sequence may seem practical and unremarkable on its own. Taken together, however, they describe a regional reality that Israelis should not take for granted.
And that is precisely one of the main achievements of the Abraham Accords: making previously extraordinary things – like a flight from the East on an Arab airline over Saudi Arabia – ordinary.
That does not make Saudi Arabia a party to the Abraham Accords. But it does show that the relationships created by the accords can function in a wider regional setting, even where formal diplomatic ties are absent.
The Saudis nevertheless drew a line, rejecting Israel’s request to send a plane to collect the passengers. Another flydubai plane eventually brought them back home.
That refusal understandably irked Israelis who felt that, after what the passengers had endured, getting them home on an Israeli plane so they felt safe should have overridden political considerations.
Tellingly, Netanyahu chose to stress the Saudi willingness to receive the plane and the hospitality shown to its passengers.
Just a week ago at the UN, he chose to call out by name the leaders of France and Turkey whose words and actions harm the Jewish State, proving he is not shy about doing so when he deems it necessary or politically expedient. He didn’t do so with Saudi Arabia.
There was a practical reason for that restraint: publicly berating the Saudis would hardly strengthen the cooperation that already exists and benefits both sides.
There was also a political reason: Netanyahu has an interest in presenting the region as one in which Israel’s relationships have expanded, even if full normalization with Riyadh remains elusive.
In this case, emphasizing the cooperation also reflected an important part of what happened. The assistance the Saudis did provide showed that the lack of diplomatic relations need not prevent practical help.
But the Saudi refusal to allow Israel to send a plane to retrieve the passengers showed how carefully Riyadh guards the boundary between basic humanitarian help – allowing the plane to land – and a visible gesture toward Israel.
Perhaps the approaching election made the Saudis especially reluctant to allow a scene that Netanyahu could then use in his campaign. An Israeli aircraft retrieving passengers from Saudi soil would have made a striking picture.
It would be a stretch, however, to assume that everything becomes easier after October 27. Saudi reservations about public normalization extend far beyond a reluctance to give Netanyahu a campaign gift.
The limits of regional normalization
THE ATTEMPTED hijacking has also been framed as a test of Israel-UAE ties and the staying power of the Abraham Accords.
That is understandable since the Tel Aviv-Dubai air routes are the accords’ most visible, tangible benefits for the average Israeli. A terrifying incident can shake public confidence in flying that route, and passengers will now understandably want to know what is being done to prevent a recurrence.
But the Israel-UAE relationship will certainly withstand this shock. A relationship that has endured October 7 and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran rests on interests that one attempted hijacking will not shake. If anything, the incident shows the threats both countries face, why they need each other, and how they can help one another.
The regional lesson is broader.
The Saudi refusal showed that significant political barriers to normalization remain, and that Riyadh still insists on keeping its relationship with Israel in the back room rather than bringing it into the front room.
The passengers’ safe return showed, however, that even a relationship confined to the back room can produce practical cooperation when it matters.
The Abraham Accords did not produce a Middle East free of hostility, danger, or diplomatic sensitivities. They did, however, help create a region where Israelis forced to land in an Arab country can receive assistance rather than face unbridled hostility.
Wednesday was a nightmare for the passengers and their families. For the region, however, the response offered something encouraging: evidence that the relationships built up in recent years can deliver practical help when it is needed most.

Taiwan, US organize disaster management forum in New Zealand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:32 UTC
19:17:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan and the US co-sponsored a Global Cooperation and Training Framework workshop about disaster management in the Pacific in New Zealand, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Friday.
The Sept. 29-30 event in Auckland marked the first time Taiwan and the US cooperated on a workshop in New Zealand. They invited member nations of the Pacific Islands Forum, government officials, and disaster response experts.
In her opening speech, Taiwan envoy in New Zealand Joanne Ou (歐江安) said it was important to learn from past experiences to prepare for natural disasters. The practice will not only reduce the impact of a new disaster, but also help speed up the recovery.
As a frequent victim of earthquakes, typhoons, and flooding, Taiwan is interested in sharing its practical disaster prevention experiences with Pacific island nations, Ou said.
US Charge d’affaires Gabrielle Cowan described the Pacific as one of the regions in the world most likely to suffer major disasters. Regional disaster resilience is the result of generations of communities responding to threats and rebuilding after disasters, she said. Cowan named Taiwan as a model for disaster prediction and public participation in disaster prevention.
The ministry said the workshop deepened international partnerships through the exchange of views and the practical use of resources. The experience helped strengthen the potential of the attending countries to prevent and respond to disasters in the Pacific region.

Taiwan government warns of ‘new method’ of transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:24 UTC
19:17:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Mainland Affairs Council said Thursday that a campaign impersonating a Taiwanese distributor of a documentary on forced organ harvesting in China could represent a “new method” of transnational repression.
Since last year, impersonators of Kuan Chien-chung (管建忠) have made threats to an attorney and two organizations, and authorities have brought him in for questioning for each case, said spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) at a press conference.
Every time a victim reported their case, Kuan had to make a statement to the police, Liang said. “The goal is to have him run around exhausted.”
Kuan heads the Taiwanese distributor that brought the Canadian documentary “State Organs” to Taiwan in 2024. Directed by Raymond Zhang, the film examines allegations of state-sanctioned organ harvesting in China targeting Falun Gong followers.
Liang said Kuan has reported the impersonation incidents to police. The council has also worked with the National Police Agency and Ministry of Justice to consolidate the incidents into a single case, which remains under investigation.
The impersonation campaign followed a series of threats against theaters that screened the film.
In late 2024, as “State Organs” was screened nationwide, several theaters received threats, including bomb threats and warnings that their computer systems would be hacked if they did not stop the screening.

First expedition vessel 'stitched' for Northern Maritime Museum in Arkhangelsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:23 UTC
19:17:23 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 2. /TASS/. The first expedition vessel was 'stitched' using traditional technology for the Northern Maritime Museum in Arkhangelsk, the museum told TASS. The vessel will not be an exhibition object. It will be a boat for voyages.
"The Solombala boat, which is traditional for Arkhangelsk, is not a museum exhibit, it is a real boat built specifically for our museum, it is the first expedition vessel in our history," the museum said. "The boat was "stitched" by boat master Mikhail Tsarev in Maymaks at his home shipyard, commissioned by a philanthropist who wished to remain anonymous, and the boat was donated to our museum."
Solombala is a symbol of Arkhangelsk of the 20th century. The boat carries the name of the Solombala historical island, where Peter the Great founded the country's first shipyard.
The newly-made vessel was named the Soyga after a river in the Arkhangelsk Region's Verkhnetoyemsky District. The river is a tributary of the Northern Dvina River. First voyages are planned for the spring and summer of 2027. Presently, the boat is installed in front of the museum entrance on the Northern Dvina embankment.
The Solombala boats with recognizable rounded hull contours and plywood cabins appeared in Arkhangelsk in the late 1950s. They were known as Solombala leisure boats. The boat was 6.22 m long, the width was 1.65 m, the hull was made of pine planks, the frames were made of oak, and the cabin - of plywood. The speed was about 15 km/h, the boat could carry up to 6-8 passengers. The Solombala Shipyard designed the project based on the development by Mikhail Kuroptev, the shipyard's master. The boat used to be equipped with an SM3-12hp diesel engine, popularly called as "top-foot." A stove for heating was normally installed in the cabin.
The Solombala boats were top popular in the 1960s - 1980s. Despite the good capacity, the carrying capacity and the ease of handling, the wooden vessel required constant maintenance. Therefore, by the beginning of the 21st century, wooden Solombala boats became exotic giving way to light and easily-maintained plastic and metal hulls.
The fresh interest in the Solombala boats emerged after the Pomor Shipbuilding Association's shipyard back in 2021 discovered, digitized and published on the web drawings of the Solombala Shipyard's vessels, including those of the Solombala boat.

How can Jordan respond to Israel’s escalation across the West Bank?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:23 UTC
19:17:23 KST

How can Jordan respond to Israel’s escalation across the West Bank?
Settlement expansion, displacement and growing Israeli control would have direct consequences for Jordan.
It is increasingly difficult to regard what is happening in the West Bank as merely a series of measures that the Israeli government justifies on security grounds or as part of counterterrorism operations. Taken together, the cumulative pattern and expanding scope of these measures point to a broader political and territorial trajectory: one aimed at reshaping the West Bank, imposing new facts on the ground, entrenching Israeli control and advancing the de facto annexation of large parts of the territory while simultaneously subjecting Palestinians to mounting pressure that, directly or indirectly, pushes them from their land.
Israeli, journalistic and research reports have documented the intensification of this trajectory through settlement expansion, land confiscation, restrictions on Palestinian movement, control over water resources and grazing areas as well as military operations and repeated internal displacement in several parts of the West Bank.
Considered individually, each of these measures may appear to be a separate issue. Viewed together, however, they reveal a more consequential development: an effort to re-engineer the geography and demography of the West Bank in ways that undermine the prospect of establishing a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.
The question, therefore, is no longer simply what is happening in the West Bank.
The more urgent question is how can Jordan, the Palestinians, the Arab world and the international community prevent this trajectory from becoming a permanent reality.
Jordan Valley at the heart of the equation
The Jordan Valley assumes exceptional importance in this context, not only because of its geographical and security significance but also because of its agricultural and economic importance and its water resources for the Palestinian people.
Reports concerning the construction of a new Israeli barrier, referred to as the “Crimson Thread”, extending roughly 480km (300 miles) from the Golan Heights to the Red Sea, warrant serious Jordanian, Arab and international scrutiny, particularly if such a project is intended to isolate the Jordan Valley and place as much as 83 percent of its total area under Israeli control.
Such a development could in effect sever the West Bank from Jordan and deprive Palestinians of one of their most important agricultural and water resources.
Borders, walls, roads and settlements cease to be merely physical infrastructure when they are combined with control over land and water. They become instruments for reshaping political and demographic geography and weakening the ability of Palestinians to remain on their land.
This is precisely where the Palestinian issue intersects directly with Jordan’s national security.
Jordan faces a different phase
Jordan cannot treat developments in the West Bank as an exclusively Palestinian matter. At its core, this is an issue of Jordanian national security, regional stability and the future of the Palestinian cause.
Any fundamental change to the geographical or demographic reality of the West Bank will inevitably carry direct consequences for Jordan because of geography, history and proximity. And if the eventual outcome is forced displacement, then, as King Abdullah II has repeatedly made clear, such a scenario would amount to a declaration of war on Jordan.
The policy required of Jordan at this stage, therefore, must be proactive: one that anticipates possible scenarios and prepares for them politically, diplomatically, economically and in security terms.
First: Protect Jordanian national unity
Jordan’s first line of defence is its national unity.
At this stage, it is essential to strengthen the concepts of citizenship and the state, consolidate full equality among Jordanians, and reject any discourse or practice that creates divisions on the basis of origin, region or roots.
The Palestinian cause must remain a national, Arab and humanitarian cause. It must not be allowed to become a source of division within Jordanian society.
Responsibility falls on both the state and society to confront hate speech and incitement, apply the law equally and fairly, and protect the national fabric from attempts to exploit regional turmoil to sow division among Jordanians.
One of the gravest outcomes Jordan must prevent is the transfer of the conflict into its own domestic sphere. Relations among Jordanians of different origins, including those of Jordanian and Palestinian heritage, must never become a vulnerable fault line through which those seeking discord, whether from within the country or from abroad, can operate.
National unity, therefore, is not merely a social value. It is an integral component of Jordan’s national security architecture.
Second: Move from diplomacy of protest to diplomacy of pressure and proportionate action
Jordan has accumulated considerable international credibility and diplomatic capital. The present phase, however, requires Jordan to expand the tools at its disposal.
It is no longer sufficient simply to condemn settlement activity, reject annexation or warn against displacement. What is needed is an Arab, Islamic and international diplomatic front capable of translating political positions into practical measures.
In coordination with Palestine and Arab and Islamic states, Jordan should work to:
- Mobilise countries that reject annexation and settlement expansion.
- Support international legal action.
- Push for concrete measures and sanctions not only against settlements but also against state policies that enable and encourage them.
- Systematically document violations.
- Use Arab political and economic relations with influential states more strategically, expanding economic cooperation with countries that adopt firm positions against the Israeli occupation while recalibrating engagement with those that remain reluctant to take clear positions towards Israeli policies.
- Build an international coalition capable of preventing the imposition of irreversible facts by force.
A comparison with Russia’s war in Ukraine is instructive. When Russia occupied large areas of Ukrainian territory, sanctions were not confined to the territories under occupation; they were imposed on Russia itself. The question, therefore, is why a different standard should apply elsewhere.
The international community does not lack resolutions or statements. What it lacks is the conversion of political will into a tangible cost for those who violate international law.
Third: Establish an Arab and Islamic fund for Palestinian resilience
If the objective is to prevent displacement and enable Palestinians to remain on their land, financial support must become a sustained strategic policy rather than seasonal assistance tied to moments of crisis.
One option would be to establish an Arab, Islamic and international fund dedicated to strengthening Palestinian resilience with a mandate to finance specific projects in the West Bank and Gaza, including:
- Protecting land threatened with confiscation.
- Supporting farmers.
- Developing water resources and irrigation networks.
- Assisting affected families.
- Financing housing projects in vulnerable areas.
- Supporting education and health services.
- Assisting municipalities and local councils.
- Providing alternative sources of income to families who have lost employment as a result of Israeli measures.
Resilience is not merely a political slogan. It is a material reality.
Every Palestinian family who remains on its land, every farmer who continues to cultivate his fields and every village that retains access to its water resources represents part of the effort to prevent displacement.
Fourth: Treat the Jordan Valley as a Jordanian national security issue
Jordan should address developments in the Jordan Valley as a permanent strategic file.
A specialised Jordanian mechanism should be established to monitor:
- Settlement expansion.
- Land confiscation.
- The construction of roads, barriers and walls.
- Demographic changes.
- Control over water resources.
- Population movements and displacement.
- Any measures that could permanently alter the status quo.
These developments should be documented through maps, satellite imagery, statistics and official records so Jordan maintains a comprehensive dossier that can be used politically and legally before the international community.
Struggles over land are not determined by force alone. They are also shaped by documentation, maps, law and the ability to present an authoritative, evidence-based account of what is happening.
Fifth: Strengthen Jordan’s national defence architecture
Strengthening Jordan’s ability to protect its security, borders and national interests is not optional.
Jordan is a country with limited resources, but it possesses significant human and institutional expertise. It can further develop an advanced national defence, civil protection and crisis-management architecture.
This could include strengthening national service and training programmes, enhancing civil defence preparedness, protecting critical infrastructure, reinforcing cybersecurity and border security, and improving disaster and emergency management.
Jordan could also draw on the extensive experience of retired military personnel through structured national programmes under the supervision of appropriate state institutions, thereby strengthening the country’s overall defensive readiness.
The strength Jordan requires is the strength of deterrence, protection and preparedness, not an impulse towards an ill-considered confrontation.
Sixth: Prevent Jordan from becoming an “alternative homeland”
This issue must remain at the centre of Jordanian strategic calculations.
Any project that directly or indirectly leads to the depopulation of the West Bank or pushes large numbers of Palestinians towards Jordan is not merely a humanitarian question. It would carry profound political, security and demographic consequences for the kingdom.
Jordan’s position, therefore, must remain unequivocal: Resolving the Palestinian question cannot come at Jordan’s expense; displacement is not a political solution; and Jordan is not an alternative homeland for the Palestinian people.
At the same time, Jordan must preserve the humanitarian and legal dimensions of its response to any forced developments, so that opposition to displacement does not translate into further suffering for civilians.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Here's How Russia Plans to Pay for the Ukraine War in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Russia plans to raise defense spending to a post-Soviet high next year while cutting civilian programs and increasing taxes, signaling that the Kremlin is bracing for a prolonged war in Ukraine despite saying it is ready for peace talks.
The draft 2027 budget unveiled Thursday allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.2 billion) to defense, 26% more than was earmarked for that year in the previous budget and 375% above the pre-war level of 2021.
Defense would account for roughly a third of federal spending next year, setting a post-Soviet record in nominal ruble terms.
Analysts say that Russia still has the resources to keep fighting, but that households, businesses and public services will bear more of the cost.
Economist Boris Grozovsky said Russia’s wartime economy still has a “considerable” financial cushion.
“But the message is clear: everyone will pay for the war, as much as they can. Wherever a little more money appears, the government will come for it, while handing out as little as possible itself,” he wrote in an analysis published by the exiled outlet IStories.
The published defense allocation does not capture the full cost of the war. Russia has released only planned military spending rather than actual outlays since 2022, while classified budget items make the overall bill difficult to establish.
Soaring war costs have put increasing pressure on state finances. The federal budget deficit reached 5.65 trillion rubles ($67.8 billion), or 2.6% of gross domestic product, in 2025.
The government projects a shortfall of 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.6 billion), or 3.2% of GDP, for 2026 before it narrows to 5.4 trillion rubles ($64.8 billion), or 2.2%, in 2027.
In a forecast published before the draft budget was unveiled, economists at Russia’s largest lender Sberbank put next year’s deficit at 2.7% of GDP, questioning whether the government could deliver the spending restraint and higher non-oil and gas revenues needed to meet its earlier target.
This deficit is high by recent Russian standards, but it is still manageable and remains lower than in many European countries, such as France (5.4% of GDP) and Britain (4.3% of GDP).
The projected deficit does not in itself point to an imminent fiscal crisis, but containing it while increasing military spending is becoming more difficult.
The government plans to borrow 6.1 trillion rubles ($73.2 billion) next year, up from 5 trillion rubles ($60 billion) in 2026, to help finance the deficit.
Yet debt servicing is projected to reach 4.6 trillion rubles ($55.2 billion) in 2027, or 9.4% of total federal spending. Those costs remain high because the Central Bank has kept interest rates elevated to contain stubborn inflation that has been fueled by heavy government spending.
To help close the gap, Moscow is also cutting civilian spending and planning another round of tax increases for a third consecutive year.
The draft reduces allocations for healthcare by 5.5%, education by 5.4% and social programs by 6% compared with the amounts previously budgeted for 2027.
Some of Russia's national projects, government programs targeting priorities like healthcare and infrastructure, will also face cuts going forward.
Funding for the Long and Active Life project, which supports health initiatives, would fall by about 20%, from 181.1 billion rubles ($2.17 billion) in 2026 to 145.9 billion rubles ($1.75 billion) next year.
The allocation for the federal cancer program would drop from 44.9 billion rubles ($538.8 million) to 3.9 billion rubles ($46.8 million).
The proposed tax measures are expected to raise an additional 1.5 trillion rubles ($18 billion).
They include a 22% value-added tax on purchases from foreign online retailers and a customs fee of 100 rubles, or about $1.20, on each parcel worth less than 200 euros.
Tax rates on income from sources including deposit interest, dividends and property sales would rise from a range of 13% to 15% to a range of 13% to 22%. The Finance Ministry has also proposed a one-time windfall tax on mining and metals companies.
The changes to taxes on passive income are expected to raise the most revenue, up to 700 billion rubles ($8.4 billion), followed by levies on online purchases, which would bring in another 500 billion rubles ($6 billion).
Analyst Alexandra Prokopenko said the budget showed defense spending growing faster than overall expenditure, squeezing the funds available for other purposes.
In an analysis for Carnegie Politika, she warned that the government may soon be approaching the limits of how much additional revenue it can raise through taxes to fund the war.
That could increase pressure on the Central Bank to support the wartime economy by cutting interest rates to reduce borrowing costs for the government and businesses, as well as increase debt restructuring for struggling companies, she said.

How Brazil's election winner could reshape its institutions as vacancies mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:03:30 UTC
19:03:30 KST

How Brazil's election winner could reshape its institutions as vacancies mount
BRASILIA, Oct 2 - Brazil's next president is set to inherit an unusually large number of appointments to the country's most powerful institutions, with vacancies piled up at the Supreme Court, central bank and economic regulators.
The growing backlog of unfilled posts means the winner of the tight race between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro could gain significant influence over bodies that help shape monetary policy, oversee financial markets and interpret the constitution. The two candidates will face off in the first round of the electoral contest on Sunday, with a runoff later in the month forecast as the most likely outcome.
The vacancies reflect a broader shift in Brazilian politics: an increasingly powerful Congress is using confirmation of nominees as a tool for political leverage, eroding the executive branch's room for maneuver.
A predominantly right-wing Congress has flexed this growing power during Lula's current term by delaying confirmation of a number of his nominees. Lula has also failed to make some nominations.
While nominations once went promptly to Senate committees for approval, many nomination processes stalled during the pandemic, awaiting the Senate president's approval. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre has maintained that practice, concentrating power in the Senate and turning what was once a routine step into a political decision, said a person familiar with the process, who requested anonymity.
The presidential palace and Alcolumbre's office did not respond to requests for comment.
The use of presidential appointments as political leverage has made the executive reluctant to submit nominees without first gauging their Senate prospects, said Rubens Beçak, a law professor at the University of Sao Paulo.
BANK SEATS
At the central bank, two board seats, including the economic policy post that oversees forecasts ahead of rate decisions, have been empty since January, a record length of time for those posts to be left open. Lula has yet to submit nominees.
In April, senators rejected Lula's Supreme Court nominee, Solicitor General Jorge Messias, in a historic setback that extended a vacancy now nearly a year old, the longest since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Securities regulator CVM has had board vacancies since late 2024, while antitrust watchdog Cade, lacking its president and two board members, is near its minimum quorum, delaying merger reviews.
Claudio Couto, a political scientist at the Fundacao Getulio Vargas, called the backlog "deeply problematic," saying it risks concentrating appointments in one administration and politicizing "bodies that are meant to remain nonpartisan."
STRUCTURAL SHIFT
Nominations and bills, once largely negotiated between the president and coalition parties, increasingly hinge on deals among congressional leaders, said Neuriberg Dias, head of legislative watchdog DIAP.
Congress' growing control over spending, he said, has changed the incentives behind executive-legislative bargaining.
Congressional earmarks — which direct funding to local or pet projects — accounted for 7.5% of effective federal discretionary spending in 2018, but swelled to 21% in 2025, according to Planning Ministry data provided to Reuters.
The government's grip on the agenda has in turn weakened. Last year, Congress approved 178 bills introduced by legislators and only 50 from the executive. In 2007, during Lula's second term, the reverse was true: 142 executive bills versus 52 from Congress, according to DIAP data.
The 2026 campaign has slowed nominations further, people familiar with the matter said, as lawmakers wait to see whether Lula wins another term. Voters will also elect all 513 members of the Lower House and two-thirds of the Senate.
With power shifting from the presidency to Congress, the election may decide not only who governs Brazil, but how much room the winner will have to appoint officials and shape key institutions. REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. The Sultan of Brunei, Hassanal Bolkiah, will visit Russia next month, Ambassador to Moscow Husaini Alauddin stated.
Speaking at the opening of an exhibition at the Russian Foreign Ministry dedicated to the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Russia and Brunei, the diplomat said: "Next month, His Majesty, the Sultan of Brunei, will visit Russia."
According to the ambassador, cooperation between the two countries has expanded in various areas over the past 35 years, including defense, energy, interparliamentary cooperation, sports, and religion. "And we believe that we need to continue deepening these ties. We hope to strengthen bilateral cooperation mechanisms in order to interact in a more substantive manner," he added.
The diplomat also emphasized that citizens of Russia and Brunei can visit each other’s countries without a visa. "This underscores the special significance of our relations. We are drawn to Russia not only by its landscapes, but also because we see that we share common values, something that sets you apart from other countries we visit," he noted.

Russia interested in expanding industrial cooperation within EAEU — PM Mishustin

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:02:29 UTC
19:02:29 KST

MINSK, October 2. /TASS/. Russia expects industrial cooperation within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to expand, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said at a meeting between Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko and the heads of delegations participating in a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council.
"The further expansion of industrial cooperation is a key focus of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council. As you know, a supranational mechanism has been launched to support joint projects in this area using funds from the Union budget. Eight initiatives are already being implemented with its support. We expect their number to grow, including because we have made such assistance available to enterprises in the agro-industrial sector. We will focus our efforts on identifying and thoroughly developing projects that take into account the strong competencies of the Union countries," Mishustin said.
According to him, the Intergovernmental Council meeting is also discussing the development of transport infrastructure and a common electricity market, ensuring food security, as well as preparations for new free trade agreements with potential partners of the five EAEU member states.

Hundreds of high schools in France close as new protests against conditions erupt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:02:14 UTC
19:02:14 KST

The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences.
French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycées in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police.
The Ministry of Education said earlier on Friday that 564 schools had "been the subject of actions or disruptions since the start of the day."
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences.
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as "urban violence."
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools, Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
'Held hostage'
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said "the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups," adding that nearly 400 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country were expected to be closed on Friday.
Many high schools have also planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV.
Some 170 students have been wounded while over 100 high schools have suffered "severe damage."
"Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go" to the protests, he added. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger."
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and "pay for repairs."
Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody," 90% of whom were minors," Darmanin told RTL.
'We've won'
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won, our school is closed this morning," said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence. "It makes us even angrier, the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us."
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI), whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency, of being behind the movement.

Six Scottish soldiers buried in France 108 years after their deaths
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:02:14 BST
19:02:14 KST

Six Scottish soldiers buried in France 108 years after their deaths
MOD War Detectives used DNA evidence to identify two of the fallen, four remain unknown though one was identified as having served with the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders whilst the other three likely served with the Gordon Highlanders.
Relatives gathered in France today to witness the burial with full military honours of two Scottish soldiers of World War 1 and four of their unknown comrades.
Private (Pte) George Fleming Brock and Pte Percy Todd, both 11th Battalion, Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, were laid to rest alongside four unknown soldiers 108 years after they were killed in action during the German Spring Offensive in 1918.
Pte Brock of Dunipace, West Falkirk, was serving an architectural apprenticeship with the Stirling firm of Messrs Bruce & Livingston when he enlisted in June 1916. Only a month after joining the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders in France, he was seriously wounded by gunshot and spent several months recuperating in hospital.
He rejoined the battalion in January 1918. Two months later the Germans launched a huge offensive on the Western Front. On 28 March 1918, Pte Brock’s battalion were holding positions in the area of Tilloy-les-Mofflaines, when they were overwhelmed by intense bombardment. It was on this day that Private Brock lost his life, aged just 19.
Pte Todd of Radford, Nottinghamshire, was a draper’s manager at Bryan’s Drapery in Isleworth, London, when he enlisted in November 1915. He was living with his wife, Alice, who he had met eight years earlier at work. Pte Todd was also seriously wounded shortly after joining the battalion, on the first day of the Battle of Arras in 1917. After a long recovery, he rejoined his battalion in February 1918, but lost his life less than two months later during the German Spring Offensive, on 5 April 1918.
In 2023, during an archaeological survey on a site in Tilloy-les-Mofflaines the six men were recovered. Found with them were a variety of artefacts, including regimental insignia from the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, and from the Gordon Highlanders. After extensive historical research and DNA testing, two of these casualties were identified as Private Brock and Private Todd. The two men were buried alongside four others who could not be identified.
The service was organised by the MOD’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), also known as the ‘MOD War Detectives’ who work to identify the recovered remains of British military casualties.
Nicola Nash, MOD War Detective said:
  Private Brock and Private Todd have both been buried today 108 years after they were killed. With half a million British servicemen still missing from World War 1, every identity we make is a huge achievement. It has been a real privilege to give closure to their families and lay these heroes to rest with honour.
David Royle, Recoveries and Ceremonies Manager at CWGC, said:
  For 108 years, these six men lay where they fell on the battlefield. It is a privilege and a source of great pride for the CWGC to have recovered them and worked alongside the JCCC in the effort to restore their identities. While four of these soldiers sadly remain unidentified, they are not forgotten. We will care for their graves, and for those of Private Todd and Private Brock, in perpetuity, ensuring that future generations have opportunity to honour and remember their sacrifice.

Graves of five soldiers killed in Normandy identified
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:01:57 BST
19:01:57 KST

Graves of five soldiers killed in Normandy identified
Five missing soldiers of World War 2 who were killed during the Battle of Normandy now have named graves after Rededication ceremonies were held on 29 and 30 September 26, and 1 October 26.
The graves of five soldiers who went missing during the Battle of Normandy have been identified and were rededicated this week. A commemorative service honouring all five men, was also held at the British Normandy Memorial in Ver-sur-Mer (30 September 26).
Rededication services took place at CWGC St Charles-de-Percy War Cemetery for Private (Pte) George Chapman of 1st Battalion The Herefordshire Regiment (29 September 26), at CWGC Bayeux War Cemetery for Private Vincent Coia of 7th Battalion The Seaforth Highlanders and Lance Corporal (LCpl) Reginald Cyril Dewey of 4th Battalion The Lincolnshire Regiment (30 September 26), at CWGC Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery for Serjeant (Sjt) Frederick Albert Harrison of 1st Battalion The Dorsetshire Regiment and at CWGC Ranville War Cemetery for Corporal (Cpl) Henry Thomas Read of 8th Battalion The Rifle Brigade (1 October 26).
Members of the Chapman, Dewey and Read families were present at their relatives’ rededication service. The Coia and Harrison families were not able to attend, but a poignant message from Reg Harrison, the 95 year old younger brother of Sjt Harrison, was read out at his graveside in Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery.
The message read:
  Although I didn’t know my brother very well, as I was only young when he left home to join the army, I’m very proud of him and what he achieved, and what he went onto do for his King and country. It was soldiers like Fred that helped us win the war, and keep us safe. Always in my thoughts. Your young brother, Reg.
The services were organised by the Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), known as the ‘War Detectives’, and were supported by serving soldiers from 5th Battalion The Rifles, 2nd Battalion The Royal Anglian Regiment and 2nd Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland.
Rosie Barron, JCCC Caseworker, said:
  It has been an honour to have organised these rededication services and to have played a part in giving these families answers as to what happened to their relatives. The local community in Normandy has been very welcoming of both the families and the military party. For them the Battle of Normandy is not just commemorated but celebrated as the moment that they regained their liberty after four long years of occupation. The sacrifices made by these men were not in vain. There are many graves in Normandy which may yet be identifiable with further investigation, so this work will continue into the future.
Reverend Paul Collins CF, Chaplain to 5th Battalion The Rifles, conducted the services.
Reverend Paul Collins said:
  It is my privilege to be able part of these rededication services. These brave soldiers gave their lives in the events following D-Day which led to the liberation of France and the defeat of the Nazis. It is fitting that due to the hard work of the JCCC Commemorations Team and others, we now know who these soldiers were and where they are buried. The graves now bear their names for all those who visit in the future to see and remember.
All five men had previously been commemorated on the Bayeux Memorial to the missing. The CWGC has now replaced their headstones with named markers and will care for them in perpetuity.
Dr James Wallis, Head of Commemorations at the CWGC, said:
  The Commission’s staff consider it a privilege to care for the now-identified graves of these five soldiers who were killed in the aftermath of D-Day during the Battle of Normandy. The impact of loss upon the respective families of these casualties still resonates strongly – so we are thankful to those who instigated each identification and furthermore to the work of partner organisations which has led to this outcome and brought us together today.

Diesel : sous la pression des Etats-Unis, l’exécutif envisage de libérer une part importante de ses réserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:01:09 UTC
19:01:09 KST

Diesel : sous la pression des Etats-Unis, l’exécutif envisage de libérer une part importante de ses réserves
L’exécutif français a proposé aux autres pays européens de mettre sur le marché 100 millions de barils de pétrole brut et de gazole. Une concession majeure envers les Etats-Unis.
French President Emmanuel Macron (C) walks with France's Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noël Barrot (L) as they head to Trump Tower in New York City on Sept. 21, 2026, ahead of a meeting with US President Donald Trump. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUXELLES — Lors de discussions d’urgence vendredi, le gouvernement français a évoqué la possibilité de libérer une partie des stocks stratégiques de pétrole et de gazole, après que l’administration Trump a fait pression sur les pays européens pour qu’ils mettent leurs réserves sur le marché, a appris POLITICO de deux personnes au fait des échanges.
La proposition faite par le gouvernement français lors d’une réunion de hauts responsables européens ce vendredi est que les pays de l’UE libèrent 50 millions de barils de pétrole brut et 50 millions de barils de gazole. Une idée qui fait encore l'objet d'une évaluation technique, a précisé l’un des interlocuteurs.
Cette décision intervient après que le secrétaire américain à l'Energie, Chris Wright, a demandé aux pays européens de libérer 120 millions de barils de leurs stocks sur une période de trois mois afin de lutter contre la hausse des prix du diesel, sous peine de se voir imposer des restrictions à l'importation de diesel américain. Selon ces sources, la proposition de compromis faite vendredi par la France faisait suite à une nouvelle demande adressée par les Etats-Unis au président français Emmanuel Macron, lui demandant de libérer 100 millions de barils de diesel.
Advertisement
L’Elysée a indiqué ce matin qu’Emmanuel Macron avait échangé pendant la nuit avec Donald Trump “pour évoquer la situation énergétique mondiale”, et notamment pour “garantir la disponibilité des produits raffinés au niveau mondial”. La France, qui assure la présidence tournante du G7 “entend réunir dans les meilleurs délais une visioconférence des dirigeants du G7 pour assurer la coordination des mesures à prendre afin de contribuer à desserrer l’étau des prix”.
Lors de l’échange ce vendredi matin, le gouvernement allemand s’est montré réticent à débloquer le moindre baril, selon ces sources. “L'Allemagne et d'autres pays ne veulent pas servir de pions ; ils souhaitent ne libérer leurs stocks que pour de véritables raisons de sécurité d'approvisionnement”, a déclaré l'une d'entre elles à POLITICO, s'exprimant sous couvert d'anonymat afin de pouvoir s'exprimer en toute franchise. L'Allemagne et la France disposent des plus importantes réserves de pétrole et de produits pétroliers en Europe, selon les statistiques officielles de l'UE.
“La France tient à participer et à répondre à cette demande [...] Il est clair que l’UE agira, dans la mesure où ses membres parviendront à s’entendre”, a déclaré une deuxième source. Elle a ajouté qu'il était difficile de savoir si cette libération serait coordonnée conjointement par l’UE ou menée sur une base bilatérale, compte tenu de l’approche “désordonnée” des Etats-Unis, qui ont adressé des demandes différentes à différents pays. “C’est une méthode typiquement américaine : ils ne passent pas par les voies officielles habituelles.”
Le cabinet du ministre Roland Lescure, présent à la réunion vendredi matin, a balayé auprès de POLITICO des “rumeurs” et ne souhaite pas commenter davantage.
Les Etats-Unis montrent une frustration croissante à l’égard des pays de l’UE qui n’ont pas tenu leurs engagements de contribuer à la mise sur le marché de 400 millions de barils, opération coordonnée en début d’année par l’Agence internationale de l’énergie à la suite du déclenchement de la guerre en Iran et de la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz.
Lors de la réunion qui s'est tenue vendredi à Bruxelles, certains représentants européens ont également critiqué la France et l'Allemagne pour ne pas avoir mis sur le marché des réserves pétrolières substantielles, selon l'une des personnes présentes.
POLITICO a rapporté jeudi que les principaux pays de l'UE et le Royaume-Uni souhaitaient répondre aux pressions américaines d'une voix « ferme », tout en cherchant à apaiser les tensions.
Nicolas Camut a contribué à cet article.Il a été initialement publié par POLITICO en anglais et adapté par Alexandre Léchenet.

Cornell University gang rape allegations: case sparks debate among US students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:01:05 UTC
19:01:05 KST

A reopened investigation into an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University is putting fresh attention on how US universities respond to reports of sexual violence.
The case centres on an incident at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024. A 20-year-old Cornell student alleges that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members.
The allegations have resurfaced after the woman filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell, the fraternity and the men involved. She argues that the university did not do enough to protect her or hold those accused accountable.
The lawsuit has also brought renewed attention to messages exchanged by members of the fraternity around the time of the alleged incident.
Cornell University Police provided prosecutors with an image of a Snapchat group used by Chi Phi members. The messages, sent shortly before the alleged assault, reportedly referred to a sexual encounter with the woman in crude terms.
Additional text messages have also been published by CBS News. They reportedly involve one of the defendants and a woman who appears to be the person who made the allegations.
The case is now back in the spotlight as New York state prosecutors reopen their investigation.
For students at Cornell, the developments have raised broader questions about sexual violence and the support available to people who report it.
Jane Wang, a Cornell sophomore, said the case had made her think about the difficulties students can face after an assault and about the support available on campus.
“I think like the main similarity that I found with reading that report was just like the fact that she felt as though afterwards, because of the lack of resources that she had on campus, she had no choice but to eventually drop out, right?”
Wang said she also saw the case as part of a wider problem affecting universities.
“And I think the silver lining of this entire situation is although what happened to Jane Doe was so atrocious and these types of acts that have continued throughout the entire history here at Cornell, but also other universities, is so atrocious,”
For junior Sophia Riley Sim, the questions raised by the case extend beyond Cornell.
“Right now I think we all have the same feeling of where do we go with this? I had questions as a freshman, well, how do we address sexual assault as a university? And now I'm a junior and I'm still asking the same questions of how do we address sexual violence across the nation?”
Cornell has rejected the allegation that it failed to punish those involved. The university has said it supported presenting the case to a grand jury and has agreed to an independent investigation into its handling of the allegations.
The reopened investigation will now determine what further action may follow from the allegations and evidence surrounding the 2024 case.

Kinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:58:19 UTC
18:58:19 KST

Feeld, a UK-based dating app aimed at non-monogamous, queer and kinky users, has reported strong sales growth and paid its largest-ever dividend as it attracts users from more “vanilla” rivals.
Revenues jumped by 32% to £64m following a surge in interest from what it called “open-minded people exploring love, desire, and alternative relationships in a safe, inclusive space”.
Pre-tax profits grew from £9.3m to £11.4m, and the company’s shareholders – including the couple who founded it – shared in a dividend of £3.8m.
Ana Kirova and her partner, Dimo Trifonov, started the business under the name 3nder (pronounced Thrinder), initially targeting couples and singles looking for threesomes.
They were forced to change the company’s name to Feeld owing to a lawsuit from Tinder but it has since experienced rapid growth even as larger rivals have faltered.
Match Group, which owns Tinder and other dating apps such as Hinge and OK Cupid, reported a 5% decline in user numbers earlier this year, amid reports of fatigue with the experience of seeking romance or sex via an app.
But Feeld, which calls itself a dating app “for the curious”, appears to be scooping up some of those users. While this has prompted reports that its edgy image has been watered down by an influx of people with more conventional or monogamous sensibilities, Feeld’s president, Kyle Brennan, said it reflected changing tastes.
“These numbers speak to something bigger than the growth of our business,” said Brennan. “They reflect a broader shift in how people are thinking about connection, with greater openness, curiosity and agency to do things differently.”
Accounts filed at Companies House said rising sales reflected “strong global user growth”, particularly outside the UK, with the rest of the world accounting for £56m of its total £64m in revenues, nearly 90%. Mexico and Spain were Feeld’s fastest-growing regions, while New York, Toronto and Paris led the way among cities, each recording an uplift in user numbers of more than 20%, the company said.
Feeld makes money via the sale of its Majestic memberships, which give users features such as unlimited opportunities to “like” other members, the ability to see who has liked them, and advanced filters to tailor specifications for a potential partner.
It also sells members extra “pings”, a feature that allows members to express interest in someone and send them a message, without having matched with them first.
In 2024, it emerged that some of these features were temporarily vulnerable to manipulation due to security “vulnerabilities” exposed by cybersecurity experts.
Research by the London-based cybersecurity firm Fortbridge found that users could have had sensitive data including messages, private photos and details of their sexuality accessed or even edited.
At the time, Feeld said it had investigated the problems brought to its attention by Fortbridge on 3 March and fixed them by 28 May that year. It said there was no evidence that any customer data had been accessed. It has invested £10.5m in technological upgrades in the past year.
The largest dividend reported in Feeld’s previous accounts was £600,000 in 2024.
As well as its dating platform, Feeld runs in-person social events including a “kinky trivia” night and a “pitch your mate” event, at which guests take to the stage to wax lyrical about why people should date their friends.

UN allocates $160M to 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:57:18 UTC
18:57:18 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The UN on Friday allocated $160 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) to support life-saving assistance in 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises.
The allocation is part of a broader effort to reach 87 million people facing the most severe humanitarian needs this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
“We have 87 million people to reach, and no time to waste,” UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said in a statement.
Fletcher stressed that funding alone would not be enough, urging leaders to “exercise political will to open access, remove obstacles and help us reach people whose lives are on the line.”
Of the funding, $150 million will go to Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Cuba, Mali, Niger, the occupied Palestinian territory, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen.
Afghanistan, the occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen are also among 10 crises where Fletcher has called for urgent diplomatic action to secure humanitarian access.
Another $10 million will address the needs of people with disabilities across the 12 crises.
The latest allocation brings total CERF funding provided so far in 2026 to $483 million.

European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.
