Danish woman fined 200,000 DKK and restricted from keeping dogs over animal mistreatment
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.
Bødskov said Spain partly contributed to the situation by offering legal residence to undocumented migrants. Spain originally expected about 500,000 applications, but more than 1.1 million people applied by the June 30 deadline, according to Euronews.
He said the EU remained vulnerable to sudden large arrivals and needed stronger external borders.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.
Prosecutors seek prison sentence and nightlife ban for Danish man over fatal punch at World Cup event
Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.
Vietnamese president to visit Denmark for talks on green solutions, health and trade
Vietnamese President To Lam and his spouse, Ngo Phuong Ly, will make a state visit to Denmark from October 19 to October 21.
King Frederik and Queen Mary will host a gala dinner for the Vietnamese presidential couple at Christiansborg Palace on October 19.
To Lam and Ngo Phuong Ly will be accompanied by ministers, senior officials and a business delegation, the Danish Royal House said.
The visit marks 55 years of diplomatic relations between Denmark and Vietnam. It will focus on shared interests including green solutions, health, food and trade.
It will be the third state visit hosted by King Frederik since he became king, following visits from Iceland and Egypt. The Danish royal couple has made eight state visits abroad.
The Royal House, the organization supporting Denmark’s monarch and royal family, also highlighted the family’s connection to Vietnam.
Prince Henrik, King Frederik’s father, spent the first five years of his life in Vietnam when the country was part of French Indochina. His family returned to France in 1939. Henrik spoke Vietnamese, Chinese, French and Danish. He died in 2018.
Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess.
Vietnam is a socialist republic led by the Communist Party. To Lam serves as both president and the party’s general secretary, considered the country’s most powerful position.
Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.
The Danish government plans to allocate an additional DKK 22 billion to the Armed Forces in 2027 as part of its upcoming budget proposal, according to Berlingske.
Defense investment is then expected to increase to around DKK 40 billion in 2030.
The government expects Denmark to meet NATO’s target of spending 3.5 percent of GDP on military defense before 2030. According to NATO figures cited by Berlingske, Denmark is already spending 3.4 percent of GDP on defense in 2026 when funding from the Ukraine Fund is included.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said the government’s first budget would require cuts in some areas to finance other priorities.
“There is something we need to have a little less of, so that in return we can invest in the community, in welfare, in security, and in a competitive business sector,” he told Berlingske.
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr said support for Ukraine would continue to form part of defense spending in the coming years.
“This is both about defending Denmark and Europe, while at the same time we also protect welfare. The Danish economy is strong enough to do both,” she said.
Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt said continued donations to Ukraine would require support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
NATO members agreed in 2025 to increase the alliance’s military spending target to at least 3.5 percent of GDP, replacing the previous 2 percent target.

A majority in the Climate, Environment and Technology Committee at Copenhagen Municipality approved a new plan Monday afternoon.
According to it, the city has moved a step closer to introducing a zero-emission zone in part of Vesterbro, where petrol and diesel vehicles would generally not be allowed to drive.
“It is really good that Copenhagen is now getting its first zero-emission zone. It is good for the climate and for reducing local air pollution,” Kristine Ammitzbøll-Bille of De Radikale, the Danish Social Liberal Party, told TV 2 Kosmopol.
The proposal was originally larger but was changed after 768 consultation responses from residents, businesses and interest groups.
Around 80 percent of the responses were either critical or reserved about the plan.
The revised version exempts all of Vesterbrogade, the area around Copenhagen Central Station, Skelbækgade and part of Halmtorvet.
Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.
Fewer trains between Copenhagen and western Denmark until Tuesday morning
Fewer trains will run between parts of Denmark until at least 10 a.m. Tuesday after an overhead wire fell between Sorø and Slagelse.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said Monday afternoon that repairs were underway.
DSB, Denmark’s national passenger rail operator, said InterCityLyn and InterCity trains are still running between Copenhagen and Esbjerg, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
Although the overhead wire fell on the westbound track, trains can still use the other track.
Replacement buses are also running between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. DSB said earlier Monday that it had ordered 50 buses.
The disruption was initially expected to last until 8 p.m. Monday, but Banedanmark later extended the estimate until 10 a.m. Tuesday.
A train that stopped beneath the fallen wire also had to be evacuated. Another train was connected to it and pulled it to the nearest station.
Banedanmark said it would investigate why overhead wires have fallen repeatedly on the same section. A damaged overhead line near Sorø also caused cancellations and delays in mid-September.
“We are well aware that this is not the first time we can see a fallen overhead wire on the same section within a relatively short time,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Smidt Sigsgaard said.
Another overhead wire was also torn down at Copenhagen Airport on Monday, causing reduced service and delays.
DSB and Banedanmark are advising passengers to check Rejseplanen before traveling.
Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.
DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ organization, criticized the government’s plan.
Thomas Sørensen, director of DI’s automotive branch, called it an “own goal to let taxes on electric cars rise from the new year.”
According to FDM, Denmark’s main association for car owners, a VW ID.4 Style could cost around DKK 10,300 more in tax, while a Tesla Model Y Long Range with all-wheel drive could face an increase of nearly DKK 28,000.
Mobility Denmark, an industry association representing the automotive sector, also criticized the proposal.
“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Passengers may also face longer travel times between the two stations.
DSB told Ritzau that trains are still able to run on one track despite the damaged overhead wire.
Around 50 rail replacement buses have been ordered to operate between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. The first buses have already started running.
DSB has also sent staff to the stations in Slagelse and Ringsted to help passengers affected by cancellations and delays.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s rail infrastructure, is at the site and working to repair the fault.
At 2:51 p.m., DSB’s traffic information showed that the company was unable to operate all scheduled trains between the regions.
InterCityLyn and InterCity services between Copenhagen and Esbjerg are still running, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
DSB is advising travelers to check the journey planner before traveling.
Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”
“It is important for safety on the link that the authorities regularly conduct exercises so that we are as well prepared as possible if a serious situation should arise,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police will issue an update through Politi Update, the Danish police public information service, when the bridge reopens Thursday evening.
“We therefore hope for road users’ understanding, and as soon as the exercise is completed, we will reopen the bridge to traffic again,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police said smaller exercises are regularly carried out in cooperation with Swedish authorities, while larger full-scale exercises such as Thursday’s are held less frequently.
Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.
Prosecutors seek prison sentence and nightlife ban for Danish man over fatal punch at World Cup event
Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.

It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.

“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.

Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.
Fewer trains are running between Ringsted and Slagelse until 8 p.m. Monday after an overhead wire fell near Sorø Station, according to DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator.
Passengers may also face longer travel times between the two stations.
DSB told Ritzau that trains are still able to run on one track despite the damaged overhead wire.
Around 50 rail replacement buses have been ordered to operate between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. The first buses have already started running.
DSB has also sent staff to the stations in Slagelse and Ringsted to help passengers affected by cancellations and delays.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s rail infrastructure, is at the site and working to repair the fault.
At 2:51 p.m., DSB’s traffic information showed that the company was unable to operate all scheduled trains between the regions.
InterCityLyn and InterCity services between Copenhagen and Esbjerg are still running, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
DSB is advising travelers to check the journey planner before traveling.
Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”
“It is important for safety on the link that the authorities regularly conduct exercises so that we are as well prepared as possible if a serious situation should arise,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police will issue an update through Politi Update, the Danish police public information service, when the bridge reopens Thursday evening.
“We therefore hope for road users’ understanding, and as soon as the exercise is completed, we will reopen the bridge to traffic again,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police said smaller exercises are regularly carried out in cooperation with Swedish authorities, while larger full-scale exercises such as Thursday’s are held less frequently.
Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

charlotte perriand’s built-in interiors survive inside 1960 paris tower
the preserved rooms show how furniture, structure and everyday life were brought together within an early french residential high-rise.
CHARLOTTE PERRIAND’S APPROACH TO DOMESTIC SPACE
Designed by architect Édouard Albert in 1960, the Albert Tower in Paris’s 13th arrondissement contains a surviving apartment interior shaped by Charlotte Perriand, with built-in storage, a kitchen and furniture designed by the influential architect and designer. Now offered for sale, the property provides a rare glimpse into Perriand’s approach to domestic space within one of France’s early experiments in residential high-rise architecture.
The residence occupies a high floor of the tower, with 102.49 square meters of living space and extensive views across the French capital. Its interior includes an entrance hall with built-in closets attributed to Perriand, a separate kitchen, and a living and dining area. The apartment was once home to Swiss designer Ubald Klug and his wife Helena, a ceramicist. Their home was part of the creative circle around designers such as Jean Prouvé, reflecting the experimental spirit of postwar French design.
ÉDOUARD ALBERT’S FLEXIBLE STEEL STRUCTURE
The interior, listed for sale by the real estate agency Architecture de Collection, gains significance from its relationship to Albert’s construction. The Albert Tower uses a regular metal grid of steel tube columns filled with concrete, supporting reinforced concrete slabs and cross-shaped bracing. Designed to combine lightness and transparency, the structure leaves the facade to reveal its underlying construction. With the supporting elements concentrated in pillars, the plan can be reorganized with relative freedom, giving Perriand’s built-in elements a flexible architectural setting.
The kitchen and entrance storage are particularly revealing. Perriand’s designs are built into the rooms, making storage and other everyday functions part of the architecture. The space shows how architects and designers of the period brought furniture, interiors and structure together.
MODERNIST HIGH-RISE LIVING IN PARIS
Albert’s tower, now listed as a historical monument, was conceived as an experiment in bringing high-rise residential construction into the Parisian context. The metal structure of the building, developed through Albert’s research into steel tubes, reflects his interest in linking construction, economy and architectural expression.
The panoramic position of the apartment makes the relationship between structure and domestic life particularly apparent. Its many windows open toward landmarks including the Eiffel Tower, the Invalides, the Val-de-Grâce, the Sacré-Cœur, the Panthéon and Notre-Dame, while its western exposure brings changing light into the rooms.
Yet the more revealing aspect of the property is closer to eye level. The Perriand-designed elements show how the ambitions of postwar modern architecture could extend where things are stored, how a kitchen is organized and how furniture occupies a flexible plan.
project info:
name: Albert Tower apartment
 architect: Édouard Albert
 interior designer / furniture designer: Charlotte Perriand
 location: Paris 13th arrondissement, France
 year: 1960
 living area: 102.49 square meters
 total area: 106 square meters

A saintly spat and gynaecological gaffe
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil’s beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a black Madonna, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that “messing” with her was “unacceptable”.

Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were “cowards” when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while “women learn to receive a touch from a young age”, referring to gynaecological exams.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that an oil refinery in the Russian city of Volgograd and an oil blending station in Russia's Samara region had been hit.
Overnight on October 2, units of Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka oil refinery in Volgograd, Volgograd region. Explosions and a fire were recorded at the facility.
LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka is one of the largest oil refineries in the Russian Federation. Its refining capacity is about 15 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility produces motor gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuel. It is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
In addition, the Samara linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) in the area of the settlement of Prosvet, Samara region, was hit. A fire was recorded at the facility.
The Samara LPDS is a production facility and a major oil receiving, storage and blending hub. Oil reaches the station via trunk pipelines from Tatarstan, Western Siberia and other oil-producing regions of Russia. The facility blends high- and low-sulfur crude from different fields to produce Urals export-grade crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia's total oil exports. The facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
The results of the strike are being clarified.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that, together with other components of the Defense Forces, it had carried out long-range strikes against four important oil infrastructure facilities in Russia's Samara and Volgograd regions.
Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha Special Operations Center, together with the Unmanned Systems Forces, Special Operations Forces and the Main Intelligence Directorate, struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, as well as the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations near the settlement of Prosvet. Fires were recorded at the facilities following the strikes.
The Volgograd Oil Refinery was also hit in a joint operation with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate. A fire was recorded at the refinery.
NASA's FIRMS satellite service detected fire hotspots near the delayed coking unit and the ELOU-AVT-1 and ELOU-AVT-5 units, which are key processing facilities at the refinery.
As reported, the Transneft hub caught fire in Samara following explosions, while a fire broke out in the area of an oil refinery and chemical plant in Volgograd.

At the age of 100, Zenon Vrublevskyi, a veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, has died
Kyiv • UNN
In Lviv, OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army Zenon Vrublevskyi has died. He survived captivity, Soviet camps, and arrest.
In the 100th year of his life, Zenon Vrublevsky, an OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division, died. This was reported by Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv Regional Military Administration, on Telegram on October 2, UNN writes.
Almost a century of life. And what a life! An OUN underground member, a soldier of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. He experienced captivity and Soviet camps. He fought for Ukraine back when one could pay with freedom or life merely for thinking about its independence
More detailed information about the funeral will be announced later.
Supplement
Zenon Vrublevsky was born in Lviv on March 17, 1927. At the age of 16, he left the gymnasium and secretly, without his parents’ knowledge, volunteered for the Galicia Division. Later, he was the personal driver of Colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic Ivan Rembolovych. During the fighting in the "Brody cauldron," he was taken prisoner and transported to a concentration camp in the Urals. After spending two years there, he managed to escape. In Lviv, he established contacts with the OUN underground.
He was arrested in 1947 and sentenced to 25 years in prison and five years of deprivation of rights, with confiscation of property. He served his sentence in the prisons and camps of Sverdlovsk, Karaganda, Kemerovo, and Vorkuta. After his release, he was forced to live in Vorkuta for several more years. He returned to Lviv in 1960.

Bonds steady as French borrowing costs hit 24-year high and UK 30-year yields top 6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:43:43 UTC
18:43:43 KST

Government bond markets steadied on Friday morning after a sell-off pushed France's 10-year borrowing costs to their highest since 2002, lifted UK 30-year yields above 6% for the first time since 1998 and drove the benchmark US 10-year yield to a 24-year high.
Global bond markets found their footing on Friday morning, with yields slipping back after a turbulent Thursday in which government borrowing costs in Europe and the US hit multi-decade highs.
Yields, which rise when bond prices fall, retreated as Brent crude slipped about 2% to around $99.95 a barrel, tempering fears that the energy shock would keep inflation high and force central banks into more rate hikes.
In the UK, the yield on 30-year government bonds, or gilts, fell to around 5.92% after climbing above 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. The 10-year yield dropped to about 5.37%, below the 19-year high reached earlier this week, while the two-year yield slid more than six basis points to around 4.77%.
Thursday's sell-off also hit British bank shares, with NatWest, Lloyds, HSBC and Barclays falling around 4% to 5%.
The losses deepened after Sky News reported that Chancellor John Healey had summoned bank bosses to a meeting ahead of his 28 October budget, fuelling speculation about new bank taxes.
France in the firing line
France's 10-year yield hit 4.96% on Thursday, its highest since July 2002, before easing to about 4.92% on Friday at about 11 am CEST. The extra yield investors demand to hold French rather than German debt reached over 140 basis points this week, the widest gap since 2012.
That gap jumped 13.9 basis points on Thursday, its biggest daily rise since March 2020, according to Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid.
"The daily moves were reminiscent of the Euro crisis in many respects, with sovereign contagion a big talking point," Reid told clients in a note.
The sell-off came as Paris unveiled a 2027 budget seeking €43 billion in new savings to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP this year to 5% next year. Public debt stands at a post-war record of 119% of GDP, and France plans to borrow a record €340 billion next year.
"Here and there, I hear the prophets of doom promising us worse times ahead. I would like to reiterate here that France's signature is solid," French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said.
France's fiscal watchdog, the High Council of Public Finances, was less upbeat, calling the government's 1% growth forecast for 2027 optimistic and a return below the EU's 3% deficit limit by 2029 very unlikely.
"With a difficult political process ahead, French bonds are likely to remain under pressure, while the threshold for ECB intervention remains high," ING analysts wrote.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polls ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Fresh figuresadded to the inflation worries behind the sell-offas eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, its highest in three years, up from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate published on Friday.
Economists had expected 3.6%, and Spain's annual rate hit 5%.
It was the seventh month in a row above the European Central Bank's 2% target as traders expect the ECB, which raised rates in June and September, to lift its deposit rate by another quarter point to 2.75% by year-end.
US Treasuries retreat from 24-year high
In the US, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.34% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before pulling back to around 5.26%.
Surging energy costs are stoking inflation, while the AI and data-centre boom competes for capital. After a rate hike in September, markets expect at least three more from the Federal Reserve by mid-2027.
"As yields have crept higher, that is going to tighten financial conditions and could increase the risk of a slowdown," said Danny Zaid, portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management.
Overall, the bill is mounting.
Developed economies paid more than $3.3 trillion (€2.9tn) in interest on internationally traded government bonds over the past year, according to the Washington-based Institute of International Finance, which is more than the estimated global spending on defence or AI.

Ousted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has been moved to a military-run hospital in Khartoum for treatment and needs further medical care abroad, his lawyer said Thursday.
Bashir, 82, was ousted by Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2019 after months of mass protests that brought an end to his nearly three-decade rule.
The army and RSF later turned against each other over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the military as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Their dispute erupted into war in April 2023, triggering a devastating conflict that has killed and displaced large numbers of people and left much of Sudan in ruins.
Bashir had been moved from prison to a hospital before the war broke out and was later transferred to the town of Merowe in northern Sudan, where he was placed under military guard.
Bashir was sent to Khartoum for medical tests after developing symptoms that required diagnosis and treatment outside Sudan, his lawyer, Mohamed Alhassan Alameen, told Reuters.
In a statement Wednesday, Bashir’s family said his need for medical treatment outside Sudan "has become critical and urgent, and cannot be delayed any longer," but said they had not received official permission to send him abroad.
It was unclear precisely what condition Bashir was suffering from. Sudan’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several prominent Sudanese Islamist figures also called for his transfer out of the country on social media.
Any such move would likely cause discord within Sudan and could draw international condemnation, as Bashir is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges including genocide. He also faces open cases in Sudan.
During Bashir’s three decades in power, Sudan was listed by the U.S. as a state sponsor of terrorism and was subject to wide-ranging sanctions. Protesters during the popular uprising accused him and his Islamist National Congress Party of widespread corruption and repression.
After his ouster, Bashir was tried on various charges and convicted of corruption and illicit financing, for which he was serving a prison sentence when the war began.

Egypt builds rail link in Sinai, with Israel watching closely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:39:43 UTC
18:39:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt's rail link project in Sinai sets off alarm bells in Israel
Egypt is constructing a new railway to connect the Suez Canal on the Red Sea to the northern Sinai town of Taba near the border with Israel, a project that has raised alarm bells in Israel and prompted calls for tight supervision from Tel Aviv.
The railway, some Israeli media outlets have claimed, would change the demography of Sinai, for years considered a symbol of isolation on the border between Egypt and Israel.
It could also enable the flow of military logistics at high speed, consequently changing the entire regional equation, one Israeli media outlet warned.
Extending over 500 kilometres from al-Ferdan, the world's largest rotating bridge over the Suez Canal, to Taba, the new rail line is Egypt's new attempt to create the infrastructure necessary for the development of Sinai, a territory the size of Israel, Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon combined that has remained largely underdeveloped for decades.
An empty, massive expanse of desert on the Egyptian Israeli border was always viewed as a good sandy buffer against direct contact between the Egyptian and Israeli militaries, bolstering limits to troop deployments on the shared border between the two countries, ones enshrined in the Security Annex of the 1979 peace treaty, analysts said.
But an outsized buffer has come at a heavy cost for Egypt's national security, the same analysts added.
"My belief is that the lack of development in this area for year gave the chance for terrorist groups to take root and grow in it," remarked Gen. Ali Hefzi, the former governor of North Sinai.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that terrorist groups exploited Sinai's sparsely populated geography because of the lack of services in it to expand.
"This is why development is becoming a prerequisite of security in this Egyptian territory," Gen. Hefzi said.
It took the Egyptian army and police a sizeable amount of resources to eradicate a branch of the Islamic State group that popped up in Sinai between 2012 and 2023 and wanted to establish an Islamic caliphate in this territory.
Thousands of Egyptian army personnel and policemen were also either killed or injured over the same decade, during which Egypt tried to uproot the group from Sinai, according to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
Dual goals
Sinai remains generally empty, despite its huge size. Covering almost 6% of Egypt's overall space of 1 million square kilometres, this territory is home to around 600,000 people only.
In the past few years, Egypt accelerated the development of this territory, implementing agricultural and industrial development projects worth tens of millions of dollars.
The same projects also include a new network of roads and educational institutions that try to meet the needs of the territory's residents which have been complaining from the lack of services for years, observers said.
Apart from easing the movement of persons to and from Sinai, the project could also serve as an alternative backup to the Suez Canal for certain types of cargo, thus competing with old Israeli initiatives for a rail link between the Red Sea port of Eilat and the Mediterranean Port of Ashdod, Israeli media declared.
Having been discussed since 1950, the Eilat-Ashdod rail link would be Israel's first attempt to connect the Red Sea with the Mediterranean through an overland route.
According to initial plans, the core section of the project would run from Beersheba/Dimona in southern Israel through the Negev and Arava to Eilat, covering between 180 and 260 kilometres.
The project was approved by the Israeli cabinet in 2012, having received interest from China and other countries for construction and financing.
Egyptian specialists do not underestimate Israeli fears from the new rail link between Suez and Taba sabotaging the planned Eilat-Ashdod link.
The Egyptian project, they say, aims primarily to preserve the competitiveness of the Suez Canal route, contribute to Sinai's development, and protect Egypt's status as an international trade nod at a time of high rivalry.
"The Egyptian project will necessarily negatively affect the planned Israeli project," Wael Qadurra, a former deputy head of the Suez Canal Authority, told TNA.
Egypt's construction of the railway, he added, would make the Israeli project both "useless" and "unfeasible", even as its main objective remains to allow for a speedier transport of goods between Egypt's Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.
Egyptian-Israeli relations at a critical time
The Egyptians are working round the clock to finalise the new Suez-Taba rail link which enjoys support from Sisi and is directly supervised by the minister of transport and the prime minister, according to Israeli media.
The line will pump economic life into Sinai's desert and strengthen Egyptian sovereignty in the region, it adds.
The basic part of the project is in place already, a 100-kilometre line between Suez and the North Sinai town of Bir al-Abd that has returned to work after a five-decade slump since the 1967 Egyptian-Israeli war.
On 30 September, Egyptian Minister of Transport Kamel al-Wazir highlighted the importance of transport and infrastructure projects in Sinai for development in this Egyptian territory.
Commenting on Israeli media reports about the new railway, he added that Egypt has the full right to develop each inch of Sinai.
"Sinai is an inseparable part of the Egyptian homeland," the minister of transport said.
"The primary goal of the road network and the railway [constructed in Sinai] is to serve residents and ease the movement of persons and goods," he told Egyptian television.
The construction of the new rail link comes, meanwhile, at a critical time for relations between Egypt and Israel, analysts said.
These relations are coming under renewed stress against the background of a number of regional developments, including Israel's procrastination to implement the Gaza ceasefire plan which was proposed by US President Donald Trump and approved in Sharm el-Sheikh in October last year, they added.
Israel is also expressing objection to the measures Egypt has taken in Sinai since 2023, including the deployment of additional troops in the border area, in what the Israelis describe as a violation of the Security Annex of the 1979 peace treaty.
However, this tension appears to be only one aspect of complex relations between Cairo and Tel Aviv.
An international newspaper has just revealed that Egypt's former intelligence chief Abbas Kamel visited Israel and met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu days ahead of the October 7, 2023 attacks by Gaza factions to warn him against the imminent attacks.
"Despite political differences and tensions between the two countries, they are capable of maintaining a minimum level of security and intelligence coordination," Gen. Hefzi said. "This coordination is important for finding solutions to problems that emerge between the two sides, not to mention security coordination on the shared border and coordinating aid entry into Gaza."
