Eurozone inflation spikes to 3.8%: Is your country on the worst list?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:39:21 UTC
18:39:21 KST

Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, a three-year high above forecasts. Energy drove the spike. See where prices rose fastest.
Eurozone inflation spiked to 3.8% year-over-year in September, marking the highest rate in three years and topping economists' forecasts of a 3.6% rise.
The jump came almost entirely from one corner of the shopping basket.
Energy costs explained close to half of the inflation rate.
The flash estimate from Eurostat showed prices rising 0.6% in September alone compared with August.
The reading is the highest since September 2023, when inflation ran at 4.3%. It is also almost double the European Central Bank's 2% target, the level the ECB considers consistent with stable prices.
Core inflation told a calmer story. Stripping out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, whose prices swing sharply from month to month, it edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%, exactly in line with forecasts.
That gap leaves the ECB with a central question. Is this an energy shock that will fade, or the start of broader price pressure?
Energy prices drove the eurozone inflation spike
Energy prices rose 18.8% from a year earlier, up from 14.3% in August. In September alone, energy prices climbed 3.9%.
Energy carries a weight of about 9% in the euro area inflation basket. At an 18.8% annual rate, it added roughly 1.7 percentage points to the 3.8% headline figure.
Services inflation rose to 3.2% from 3.0%. Services are the largest piece of the basket, accounting for about 47% of the eurozone inflation basket, and cover items such as rents, restaurants, travel and insurance.
Food, alcohol and tobacco prices increased 1.4%, up from 1.1% in August. Within that group, inflation for unprocessed food such as fresh fruit, vegetables and meat jumped to 4.0% from 2.7%.
Non-energy industrial goods, which include cars, clothing and household appliances, rose 1.1%, down slightly from 1.2%. It was the only major category where annual inflation slowed.
Where was eurozone inflation highest?
Lithuania recorded the highest annual inflation rate in the euro area at 6.1%, up from 5.6% in August.
Bulgaria, which joined the euro on Jan. 1, 2026, followed at 5.6%. Cyprus and Luxembourg both posted 5.2%, ahead of Greece at 5.1% and Spain at 5.0%.
In total, six of the euro area's 21 member countries recorded inflation of 5% or more. Ten countries were at or above the 3.8% euro area average.
At the other end, Malta had the lowest rate at 2.4%, followed by Finland at 2.6% and Latvia at 2.9%. Latvia was the only member country where annual inflation eased in September.
Italy and France saw the sharpest moves among big economies
Inflation accelerated in all four of the euro area's largest economies.
Italy posted the biggest increase among them. Its annual rate climbed to 4.1% from 3.2%, and Italian prices rose 2.0% in a single month, the largest monthly increase in the bloc.
France followed, with inflation rising to 3.4% from 2.6%. As a result, French inflation is now higher than Germany's, where the rate rose to 3.3% from 2.9%.
Spain remained the highest of the four. Its inflation rate reached 5.0%, up from 4.6% in August.
What Eurozone inflation means for the ECB
The ECB raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points on 10 September.
The deposit facility rate now stands at 2.50%. It was the ECB's second increase this year, after a similar move in June.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for households and companies. That tends to slow spending. Over time, slower spending eases pressure on prices.
The ECB's September projections see headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028.
Policymakers meet next on 28-29 October in Frankfurt, with the decision due on 29 October. That meeting will not include new staff projections. The next set arrives in December.
The September data put a fresh warning in front of the ECB. Headline inflation is well above target and still rising.
Prediction markets assign a 91% chance of a further ECB rate hike at the end of the month.

Climate education moves to front burner for UN's COP31 conference in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:46 UTC
18:30:46 KST

Zeynep Ozturhan
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Quality climate education is "probably the most transformative climate adaptation action," according to an expert, who said the UN climate conference COP31, which will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in November, offers a significant opportunity to bring climate education to the center of the global climate agenda.
Youth and Education is one of the 10 priority areas of the COP31 Action Agenda.
Eric Guilyardi, a climate scientist at CNRS-IPSL -- a research federation that groups nine laboratories focused on Earth sciences and climate -- and president of the Office for Climate Education (OCE), spoke to Anadolu about how education can drive climate action.
A lead author on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report, Guilyardi said climate education is not just about transferring scientific knowledge but about equipping young people with the tools they need to think about what kind of world they want to live in.
"There are many reasons why we need young people worldwide to better understand what climate is, how it works, how we are modifying it through our human activities, and what course of action we can think of to limit the changes we are doing and their impact on societies and ecosystems," Guilyardi said.
Noting that climate education is interdisciplinary by nature, spanning from climate science to the humanities, sports and history, Guilyardi said the subject can "fall through the cracks" depending on how an education system is structured.
Quality climate education is 'most transformative' adaptation action
Underlining that teachers are at the heart of climate education, Guilyardi said quality climate education is "probably the most transformative climate adaptation action."
He noted that education systems and teachers must be equipped with both the science and the associated pedagogy, adding that this was the reason OCE was created to bring together climate scientists and educators.
Emphasizing the importance of adapting content to local realities, cultures and education systems, Guilyardi said: “This is absolutely key. The one-size-fits-all approach doesn't work in this field.”
30 to 80 hours of training needed to change teachers' practice
Noting that many teachers feel "a bit lonely" on climate topics they do not fully master, Guilyardi said changing their professional practice requires between 30 and 80 hours of training.
"This education is very different from just awareness. You're not going to have a two-hour conference and that's it. It's not enough to change your professional practice in the classroom," he said.
Guilyardi announced that the fifth edition of the "Teachers' COP" -- a global platform OCE established five years ago -- will be held at COP31 in Antalya this year.
COP31 dedicates a full day to climate education
Guilyardi said it was "extremely exciting" that COP31 in Türkiye is giving such a prominent place to youth and education with a whole day dedicated to the topic, adding that OCE is contributing to and helping organize the day with Turkish authorities.
He noted that COP31 could create a platform to move quality climate education beyond mere awareness, stressing that equipping teachers to overcome anxiety-inducing narratives around climate is critical.
Education now part of NDCs
Noting that disinformation work that started with the Belém Agenda at last year's COP will continue at COP31, Guilyardi said "prebunking" -- equipping young people with the capacity to discern trustworthy information from disinformation on social networks -- has moved higher on the agenda.
Guilyardi described the fact that education is now part of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) -- at the heart of the Paris Agreement -- as a "game-changer" since the last COP, and said OCE would hold several events at COP31 to help countries seize this opportunity.
'Between 3% and 7% receive quality climate education'
Stressing that awareness of climate change is high but not enough on its own, Guilyardi said awareness must be transformed into action through quality climate education, which is different from mere awareness.
"If we look at the different surveys we've been doing in the 30 countries where OCE is working, we estimate at the moment - it varies among countries -- that between 3% and 7% of the young generation receives quality climate education. So we're very far from having a majority that is equipped with quality climate education."
Recalling that climate now appears in more than 50% of national curricula, which was not the case even five years ago, Guilyardi said things are "changing fast."
Drawing attention to the current disconnect between the climate and education arenas, Guilyard said: "We're trying to bring those two worlds together because they really need each other to address today's challenges."

Gandhi's first birthday in free India was no celebration: What happened on October 2, 1947
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:30 UTC
18:30:30 KST

Freedom was just two months old and the country was still struggling to come to terms with Partition when Gandhi’s 78th birthday approached
NEW DELHI: India wanted to celebrate Mahatma Gandhi on October 2, 1947. Gandhi, however, himself wanted no celebration at all.It was his first birthday in an independent India and, as it turned out, his last. Messages, flowers and greetings poured in from India and abroad. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and others came to meet him. But Gandhi, who turned 78 that day, was consumed by what was happening outside the walls of Birla House.Barely seven weeks had passed since Independence. Partition had displaced millions and triggered widespread communal violence across India and Pakistan.So when people wished Gandhi a long life, his response was not one of celebration."Where did the congratulations come in? Would it not be more appropriate to say condolences?" he asked.Later that day, Gandhi told those gathered for his prayer meeting: "For me today is the day of mourning. I am surprised and also ashamed that I am still alive."
A country in flames
Freedom was just two months old and the country was still struggling to come to terms with Partition when Gandhi’s 78th birthday approached.Gandhi had already spent months confronting the violence.
According to the Gandhi Heritage Portal, he left for Noakhali in November 1946 after communal violence erupted there and later began a barefoot march through affected villages, appealing for peace and Hindu-Muslim unity.His peace mission continued even when India became independent. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that Gandhi stayed in riot-hit Calcutta in August 1947 and spent Independence Day fasting and praying rather than taking part in the celebrations.Violence followed Gandhi to Delhi. According to the Gandhi Heritage Portal, when he reached the capital on September 9, 1947, communal violence and refugee camps had made it impossible for him to stay at his usual accommodation at Valmiki Colony, and he moved into Birla House instead.
From there, Gandhi continued holding prayer meetings and appealing for communal peace as tensions gripped the capital.
What Gandhi did on his 78th birthday
According to historian Brijmohan Heda, October 2, 1947, was remembered by those who visited Gandhi that day as one of the most painful days of his life. While the country prepared to celebrate his birthday, Gandhi showed little interest in the celebrations and spent much of the day in prayer and spinning the charkha.
At the morning prayer, Mirabehn decorated the space around Gandhi’s seat at Birla House with flowers arranged in the shape of an Om, the words 'Hey Ram' and a cross. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Ghanshyamdas Birla and Indira Gandhi were among those present.Lady Mountbatten was among those who visited Gandhi later in the day and brought letters and telegrams sent to him from India and abroad.A special radio programme had also been planned to mark his birthday. When asked whether he would listen to the All India Radio programme, Gandhi made his choice clear. He said he would give greater importance to the 'rentio', the spinning wheel, than to the radio.Later in the evening, Gandhi suffered a bout of coughing. His doctors advised him to take penicillin, but he refused, saying Ramanama: the chanting of Lord Rama’s name was his 'sole remedy'.
'Today nobody listens to me'
Consumed by the bloodshed around him, Gandhi used his prayer meeting address on October 2, 1947, to speak openly about his anguish.“Today is my birthday. I do not celebrate my birthday in the usual way. I would say that on this day we must fast, spin and pray. That, in my view, is the most appropriate way of celebrating one’s birthday,” Gandhi said.
“For me today is the day of mourning. I am surprised and also ashamed that I am still alive. I am the same person whose word was honoured by the millions of the country. But today nobody listens to me,” he added. The remarks are recorded in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi.Gandhi then spoke about the growing hostility towards Muslims and questioned what India would become if the violence continued.“You want only the Hindus to remain in India and say that none else should be left behind. You may kill the Muslims today; but what will you do tomorrow? What will happen to the Parsis and the Christians and then to the British?” he said.“Ever since I came to India I have made it my profession to work for communal harmony, and I wish that though our religions are different we may live in amity like brothers. But today we seem to have become enemies,” Gandhi said.Gandhi also said he had given up his earlier desire to live to the age of 125.“I have now stopped thinking about living for 125 years. I have stopped thinking in terms of 100 or even 90 years. I am entering my 79th year today; but even that pains me,” he said.He ended with an appeal against communal hatred: “If you really want to celebrate my birthday, it is your duty not to let anyone be possessed by madness and if there is any anger in your hearts you must remove it.”After the prayer meeting, Gandhi spoke to Sardar Patel in private and asked what “sin” he had committed to be kept alive to witness such horrors, an exchange also recounted by historian Ramachandra Guha.
'If I’m to die by the bullet of a mad man ...'
Just four months later, Gandhi was assassinated in New Delhi.On January 30, 1948, as he walked towards the evening prayer meeting at Birla House, Nathuram Godse approached him and fired three shots at close range. Gandhi died shortly afterwards. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that he was shot while on his way to the prayer ground and received three bullets.
Gandhi was 78 when he was killed. He had spent much of his life speaking against violence and urging Hindus and Muslims to live together peacefully.Just two days before his assassination, Gandhi had spoken about the possibility of being killed."If I’m to die by the bullet of a mad man, I must do so smiling. God must be in my heart and on my lips," he had said on January 28, 1948, according to a contemporary report published by 'The Hindu'.Four months earlier, on his last birthday, Gandhi had already spoken of losing his desire for a long life.The man who had once hoped to live for 125 years had finally seen India become independent. But on his first birthday in free India, the violence surrounding that freedom left him with little reason to celebrate.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

====================================================================================================

Health Care Workers Are Tired of Cleaning Up Palantir’s Mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.
Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.
“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.
The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.
As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.
Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.
HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”
Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”
Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds.
HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback.
“Being Kicked”
On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.
But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says.
Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology.
Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.)
Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry, a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations. Named after the beat-keeping musical instrument, it uses algorithmic forecasts of patient volumes and staffing needs to automatically build nursing schedules. When Timpani launched in 2023, HCA’s top innovation executive Michael Schlosser told WIRED it would save time and money, as well as eliminate favoritism in assigning shifts.
Schlosser said in a paper this past July that Timpani has drastically reduced the number of hours managers spend on scheduling each month, lowered reliance on costly contract nurses to fill shifts, and increased retention. “The efficiency comes from AI generating stronger initial schedules,” he wrote, adding that over 98 percent “include a mix of skill and experiences.”
HCA’s responsible AI policy emphasizes protecting individuals from “physical” or “emotional” harms, and executives have said they spoke to nurses and took an empathetic approach in developing Timpani. In marketing materials, the company features nurses praising the tool for being easy to use and saving them time. Yet other HCA nurses say they feel ignored and disrespected, and they are not the only health care workers who have raised concerns about Palantir’s push into their industry.
Rayus Radiology, a large US imaging chain, began receiving complaints about scheduling errors earlier this year after it introduced a tool also built on Palantir Foundry, according to internal documents viewed by WIRED. The software is designed to populate scheduling fields from doctors’ orders. But in a number of cases, it linked the requests to the wrong patient profiles, listed tests or scans that didn’t match the orders, or made up personal details about patients. Schedulers who work at Rayus suspect that non-standard forms, illegible handwriting, and insufficient human review contributed to the issues.
Rayus spokesperson Kit Crancer says “the broad characterizations” do not fairly reflect its “processes, safeguards, or commitment to safe, accurate, and timely patient care.” He adds that Rayus uses technology “to support, not replace, appropriate human judgment and oversight.”
A Palantir spokesperson declined to comment using their name, but the company has described its software as merely presenting information in a more helpful manner and emphasized that customers are responsible for the data, policies, and decisionmaking.
Palantir Anxiety
Palantir’s sales have nearly doubled recently to almost $2 billion per quarter, as organizations seek its help analyzing data and automating tasks. Soaring costs and staffing shortages have made health care providers especially eager customers. Cleveland Clinic credited Palantir software with boosting patient capacity by forecasting ER discharges and replacing manual coordination.
But Palantir has also received pushback from civil rights activists over its defense and immigration work, as well as the stated political views of cofounders Peter Thiel and Alex Karp. In the UK, Palantir landed a $440 million contract with the National Health Service to try to cut appointment wait times, but nurses and activists have demanded it be canceled over privacy and security concerns.
At HCA, some nurses also want Palantir gone. While studies show AI-based scheduling holds promise, nurses say Timpani has become a source of anxiety. “Everyone checks immediately and every month you hear, ‘Man, why did it schedule me like that?’” Barker says.
Initially, some local managers could edit Timpani’s schedules. Now, nurses must flag problematic shifts to a centralized team at HCA headquarters in Nashville, which reviews appeals without direct communication or room for explanation, according to nurses. If denied, they try to swap shifts, but the chances of success are about only 50 percent, Barker and Retzloff claim.
Barker, who is a National Nurses United leader at an HCA psychiatric center, claims several colleagues quit over Timpani and that workplace injuries have climbed in the first 12 months with the tool. The center’s union of about 500 nurses filed a grievance over the software, arguing HCA is failing to sufficiently honor scheduling preferences. The matter is likely headed to arbitration.
In Timpani’s early days, HCA’s Schlosser acknowledged health care workers can be slow to adopt tech “because they have people’s lives in their hands.” But he envisioned a future where frontline nurses actively pushed for more tools: “Then it’ll be fun.” Three years later, some nurses see little reason to rejoice.

‘No Rules Now’: Putin Orders Civilian Attacks, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:28:50 UTC
18:28:50 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites, President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Friday, Oct. 2.
Zelensky cited intelligence obtained by Ukrainian agencies, including what the FT described as intercepted communications between Kremlin officials. Kyiv has not publicly released the intercepts, and their contents could not be independently verified.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said, referring to the alleged order from Putin.
According to Zelensky, the instruction was issued in September, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and increasingly struck schools, hospitals, telecommunications facilities and data centers.
Zelensky speaks from school bomb shelter
Zelensky spoke to the FT inside the bomb shelter of a Kyiv school struck by a Russian jet-powered drone on Thursday.
The school’s director said 104 students and 60 teachers survived because they reached the underground shelter before the drone hit shortly after 9 a.m.
The drone’s 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead pierced the floor but failed to detonate, Ukrainian authorities said. The impact nevertheless damaged the building and started a fire.
Zelensky later called attacks on educational institutions “a deliberate tactic”, saying Russia was attempting to terrorize civilians and disrupt ordinary life.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
The FT said debris recovered at the school bore markings from Russian manufacturers and handwritten Russian text. Some components were reportedly manufactured in Russia on July 28, while others appeared to be Western-made.
Russia has denied deliberately attacking civilian sites. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the FT that Russian forces do not strike schools or hospitals.
However, Ukraine’s Education Ministry has recorded more than 4,700 attacks on educational institutions since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The World Health Organization has verified more than 3,000 attacks affecting healthcare facilities.
Deliberately attacking civilians or civilian objects constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Russia seeks to pressure civilians
Zelensky said Russia had previously concentrated much of its long-range campaign on military and energy infrastructure, although civilian sites have been repeatedly struck throughout the full-scale invasion.
He alleged that Moscow had now deliberately expanded its target list because Russian forces had failed to achieve their objectives on the battlefield, particularly in the Donbas.
The new campaign seeks “to pressure people,” Zelensky said, describing the strikes as an attempt to frighten civilians, force residents to leave Ukrainian cities and weaken the country’s ability to continue resisting Russia.
On Monday, a Russian drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. Russia also repeatedly attacked the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv on Thursday, damaging a support column, the road surface and a barrier and disrupting transport across the Dnipro.
Recent Russian strikes have also damaged Ukrainian schools, healthcare facilities, warehouses, businesses and communications infrastructure. A Sept. 23 attack damaged Kyiv data centers, disrupting internet service for some residents.
Jet-powered drones strain Ukrainian defenses
Zelensky said Russia had launched around 500 drones over the previous day, approximately half of them jet-powered models that fly considerably faster than conventional Shahed-type drones.
Ukraine intercepted around 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with between 85% and 90% of conventional models, he said.
Russia’s use of jet-powered drones increased eightfold between June and August, according to figures previously released by Ukraine’s Air Force. Their higher speed gives defenders less time to detect and intercept them and can force Ukraine to use comparatively expensive aircraft and missiles.
Zelensky said F-16 fighter jets had proven effective against the new drones. However, around half of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet was spending extended periods outside the country for maintenance and repairs, he said.
Kyiv is seeking Western assistance to move more maintenance work into Ukraine so that aircraft can return to service faster.
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor drone models. Zelensky said one model could enter production at a rate of approximately 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remained in testing.
He identified shortages of suitable engines and insufficient financing as the main obstacles to mass production.
Western pressure ‘not enough’
Zelensky also criticized the US and European governments for failing to apply sufficient economic and diplomatic pressure on Putin to end the war.
Asked whether Ukraine’s partners were doing everything possible to help, he replied: “Not enough, of course not enough.”
Zelensky argued that Russia’s partners had the leverage required to increase the cost of continuing the invasion but lacked the political will to use it fully.

Siegfried Mureșan cabinet rejected in Parliament
Romania remains without a regular government after parliament rejected the government lineup proposed by PM designate Siegfried Mureșan. 182 MPs voted in favour and 15 against. In order to be sworn in, this government needed a minimum of 233 favorable votes. President Nicușor Dan is set to hold a new round of consultations on Monday to find a fourth candidate for prime minister, Radio Romania International reports.
The political crisis in the country has been ongoing for nearly five months. The government of Ilie Bolojan was brought down by a no-confidence vote in May but has remained in office as a caretaker government. The first candidate, Eugen Tomac, withdrew after failing to secure sufficient support, while the proposed cabinet of liberal Adrian Veștea was rejected by parliament.
Following the rejection of two proposed cabinets and the passage of more than 60 days since the first no-confidence motion, the Constitution allows the president to dissolve parliament and call early elections. Nicușor Dan, however, has ruled out such a scenario, arguing that it would deepen instability and delay urgently needed budget adjustments.

Serbian President Vučić resigns to run for prime minister
Parliament Speaker Ana Brnabić assumed the duties of President of Serbia on September 28 after Aleksandar Vučić resigned. Vučić said he was stepping down as President in order to campaign in the early parliamentary elections on October 25 as the Serbian Progressive Party’s candidate for prime minister, N1 reported.

Albania looks to boost revenue from high-end tourism
“Albania will seek to develop high-end tourism following another increase in visitor numbers”, Prime Minister Edi Rama said at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels.
In 2025, Albania recorded 12.47 million visits by foreign nationals, a 6.6% increase compared with 2024, up from nearly 2 million in 2013, when Rama became prime minister. According to Rama, visitors included tourists from Japan, the United States, Latin America, China, Israel and the Middle East, shqiptarja.com reports.
The country will seek not only to attract more visitors but also to expand its luxury tourism segment, draw high-spending tourists, and generate greater revenues from the sector.

Kosovo increasingly relies on foreign workers
Kosovo is increasingly turning to foreign workers to address labor shortages amid continued emigration, particularly among young people of working age, to EU countries, Koha reports.
In 2025, more than 9,000 foreign nationals were granted residence permits, including 5,087 for employment purposes, compared with 2,122 in 2021. Turkish citizens received the largest number of temporary residence permits (3,263), followed by citizens of Serbia, North Macedonia and other countries. Labor shortages are most acute in construction, retail, hospitality, restaurants, and manufacturing.
“Institutions must take measures to retain the existing workforce, encourage emigrants to return, and develop vocational skills”, warned Lulzim Rafuna, President of the Kosovo Chamber of Commerce.
According to the Kosovo Agency of Statistics, the country’s population stood at 1,582,322 in 2025.

The competition supports young people who develop entrepreneurial solutions to social challenges. The supported projects are Plovi Farma, a digital farm management platform; FireFly, an AI-powered platform for autonomous drones designed for the early detection of fires; and Brain Reset Cards, an app offering short cognitive training exercises.
The Audience Award, along with EUR 1,500, went to ReDsponse, a platform connecting blood donors with transfusion services.
The winning teams will also receive three months of mentoring, free workspace at the Science and Technology Park, and the opportunity to participate in the international SIA Summit. Over the past five years, the program has featured 268 social-impact ideas developed by more than 600 young people.

Unknown

2026-10-02
09:21:58 UTC
18:21:58 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf D. A. R. Arnaout and Rania Abushamala
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Israeli opposition parties would win 53 seats against 51 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, said an opinion poll published Friday, less than a month before the Oct. 27 general election.
The survey published by daily Maariv also projected 12 seats for Arab parties and four for the Reservists party led by Yoaz Hendel.
Under the projections, neither Netanyahu’s camp nor the opposition would reach the 61-seat majority needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset or parliament.
Most opposition leaders say they will not rely on Arab parties’ support to form a government, leaving prospects for a governing coalition uncertain.
Maariv said Netanyahu’s bloc gained two seats compared with the previous survey, while the opposition lost two, narrowing the gap between the camps to two seats.
Within Netanyahu’s camp, his Likud party was projected to win 19 seats, followed by extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power with nine.
The ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism would each secure seven seats, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism would take five and Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party four.
Among opposition parties, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar would win 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats 10, and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu nine.
The Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, was projected to secure seven seats, while Mansour Abbas’s United Arab List would take five.
On the poll’s questions on suitability for prime minister, Eisenkot led Netanyahu by 47% to 41%, with the gap narrowing to six percentage points.
Bennett led Netanyahu by 45% to 41%, while Netanyahu led Lieberman 44% to 39%.
Israel’s prime minister is not directly elected. Forming a government depends on securing sufficient parliamentary support.
The poll also found that 67% of Israelis expressed concern about the possibility of a security incident on the scale of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.
Of those surveyed, 43% were moderately concerned and 24% very concerned. Another 26% were not concerned, while 7% were undecided.
Lazar Research conducted the survey among 602 Israeli adults. Its margin of error was four percentage points.

Taiwan received its first two U.S.-made F-16V fighter jets on Oct. 2, as the island democracy upgrades its military capabilities to deter a potential Chinese attack.
The warplanes are part of an $8 billion deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term and scheduled for delivery this year.

Taiwan’s Defense Minister Wellington Koo said on Oct. 2 more F-16Vs would be delivered to Taiwan “before the end of the year,” but did not say how many.
“At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed the tests,” Koo said.
“As for when they will fly back, we will coordinate further with the U.S. side.”

Ambassador to UAE says flydubai incident didn't weaken Israel-Emirati relations - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:37 UTC
18:20:37 KST

Ambassador to the United Arab Emirates Yossi Shelley said the dramatic attack aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv has not weakened the strategic relationship between Israel and the UAE, arguing instead that the Emirati authorities' response has demonstrated the strength of the ties established under the Abraham Accords.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post on Friday, Shelley said he had received what he described as a “very warm” response from Emirati officials and members of the public following the September 30 incident, in which a co-pilot attacked the captain aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, sending the aircraft into a rapid descent before passengers and crew helped regain control.
“I definitely feel a warm embrace,” Shelley told the Post. “Of course there is concern," he said.
Shelley said the response he has received from senior Emirati officials has reinforced his assessment that the relationship between Jerusalem and Abu Dhabi remains deep.
For example, he described calling a senior Emirati business executive around 1 a.m. about the aviation situation and receiving a response shortly afterward.
“I called him at one in the morning, and he called me back at 1:10,” Shelley said. “Who calls you back at 1:10 at night because you have a question about flights tomorrow?”
Investigation being conducted by Israeli, Saudi, Emirati authorities
Shelley said that the investigation into the flydubai incident is being conducted by the relevant authorities in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Israel. On Thursday, the Omani co-pilot was transferred to the UAE for further investigation. “The UAE are investigating, they are doing everything that needs to be done, and we trust them", Shelley said. Israel is preparing to send an investigation team to the country.
Shelly emphasized the importance for Israel of determining whether the attacker acted independently or was sent by someone else.
“We have a very, very big interest, just like everyone else, in knowing whether someone came because somebody sent him, or whether he acted alone,” Shelley said. “We want to know the result because there are implications afterward.”
Shelley said the incident should lead to broader consideration of how flight crews are screened, particularly when airlines operate routes connecting countries that are experiencing political or military tensions.
“When we leave the country and arrive in other countries, they ask us: Where did you come from? What did you bring?” he said. “We need to raise the level and ask the pilots as well: What did you bring and where did you come from?”
He added that authorities should consider the nationalities and backgrounds of pilots when assigning crews to sensitive routes.
“I don’t want to send an Iranian pilot to Israel, or a pilot from a country involved in a war with us,” Shelley said, while stressing that he was speaking about the need for authorities to consider such issues rather than identifying a particular country as responsible for the flydubai incident.
Ambassador expresses gratitude to heroic captain
Shelley also thanked Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was injured in the attack.
Machchhar was stabbed during the incident but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to intervene. Israeli passengers subsequently helped subdue the attacker and prevent the aircraft from crashing.
Shelley said he had spoken with India’s ambassador in the UAE and told him that Israel wanted to find a way to formally thank Machchhar.
“I told him that I want him to speak with the prime minister,” Shelley said. “We really are grateful to him, and of course to all the people who have been talked about and will be talked about.”
Shelley said he had hoped to visit Machchhar personally after the injured pilot was transferred to the UAE, but that logistical and security arrangements had so far prevented the visit.
Not a threat to Abraham Accords
Asked directly what the incident could mean for the Abraham Accords and Israel’s relationship with the UAE, Shelley rejected the idea that the attack could fundamentally damage the partnership.
“Let’s say what it did not do,” Shelley said. “It did not succeed in bringing them down. It tried to break them. It tried to break us. We are strong.”
He pointed to the decision to resume Israeli airline operations to the UAE as evidence that the relationship had not been derailed.
“It did exactly the opposite,” Shelley said of the impact of the incident on the bilateral relationship.
He argued that the UAE’s willingness to allow Israeli carriers to resume operations demonstrated continued confidence in the relationship.
“There is something important here,” Shelley said. “This is not a temporary agreement. It is a way of life. It is a partnership between partners.”
Shelley sought to play down reports of a broader crisis over the resumption of flights between Israel and the UAE.
He said Israeli carriers were expected to begin landing later on Friday and continue operations over the coming days.
“There is no crisis, no major event,” Shelley said.
He described the situation as a matter of establishing new procedures following the incident, including determining how baggage should be handled and screened.
“There are all kinds of things that are part of the setup,” he said. “They don’t want to fall into the second trap.”
The ambassador said the relationship with Abu Dhabi had already endured the unprecedented regional tensions of recent years and that the latest incident would not, in his assessment, change its fundamental trajectory.
“This is a partnership,” he said. “It’s not something temporary.”

Simchat Torah 2026: What exactly are we so joyous about?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:28 UTC
18:20:28 KST

On Simchat Torah, we mark the completion of the annual cycle of Torah reading and the beginning of a new cycle.
Jewish custom is to read the portion of Vezot Habracha and, immediately afterward, to begin reading the first portion, Bereshit, creating an unbroken continuity between the conclusion of the Torah and its beginning.
Rabbi Yaakov ben Rabbeinu Asher wrote about this:
“It is called Simchat Torah because on it we complete the Torah, and it is fitting to rejoice upon its completion. It is customary to begin Bereshit immediately, so that Satan will have no opportunity to accuse us, saying: They have already finished it and do not wish to read it again” (Tur, Orah Hayim, Laws of Lulav, 669).
The conclusion of the Torah and the beginning anew are not two separate things. Precisely because we finish, we hurry to begin again. Had we waited until the following Shabbat to begin reading it again, the conclusion might have seemed like a farewell. Beginning immediately teaches us that the conclusion is not an ending in the sense of parting, but, rather, is meant to make possible a new beginning, with a desire to learn anew.
What exactly am I so happy about?
THIS IDEA takes on special meaning when we consider our relationship to Simchat Torah.
Some people do not feel a sense of connection to the holiday. In particular, someone who does not study Torah regularly might ask: What exactly am I so happy about? What connection do I have to dancing around the Torah scroll when, in my everyday life, I hardly ever open it?
One way to answer this is through a folk tale about a simple villager who was seen dancing with all his might with the Torah scroll, singing, “Your Torah is better for me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.” When people asked him, “But you haven’t opened a book in a long time,” he replied: “If my brother is getting married, shouldn’t I celebrate with him?”
This story carries a profound point. The joy of Simchat Torah is not merely an individual’s personal joy. It is joy about the Torah that exists within the people of Israel; about the connection it creates between the Jewish nation and the Creator of the world; about a Torah-centered world that continues from generation to generation; and about the people within this nation who have devoted their lives to its study. Even if I have not yet found the time and place for it in my own life, the Torah is not foreign to me. It belongs to my family, to my people, to the tradition from which I come. If my brother gets married, I rejoice in his wedding; if the Jewish nation rejoices in the Torah, I, too, share in that joy.
Another way to understand the nature of this joy is this: Dancing with the Torah is not merely an expression of joy that already exists; sometimes, it is the joy itself that creates the connection. When a person dances with the Torah, he brings himself into the joy, even if at first he does not feel a deep connection to Torah study. The very effort to rejoice can open the heart and prepare a person for a new connection with the Torah.
This also has enormous educational significance. A child who sees his father rejoicing with the Torah, dancing with it and expressing his love for it, receives a message far more powerful than any explanation: the Torah is not merely a system of obligations, but something filled with life and joy.
Even if the father has not succeeded in incorporating Torah study into his daily routine, the dancing the child witnesses may influence him years later and awaken in him a desire to become a person of Torah.
AND YET, we can still ask: How can someone who does not feel connected to the world of Torah relate to this joy? How can he dance enthusiastically with something he feels is not a meaningful part of his life?
In his book Pahad Yitzchak on Sukkot, Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner recounts a story about two students of the Hiddushei HaRim, the first Gerrer rebbe. The two students were dancing with tremendous enthusiasm on Simchat Torah. The Hiddushei HaRim looked at them and said to those around him: “Look at these two. One of them will tire before the other.” Indeed, a short while later, one of the students grew weak and stopped dancing, while his friend continued dancing with renewed strength.
When the rebbe was asked how he knew this in advance, he explained:
The student who became tired was dancing out of joy over the Torah he had studied in the past. There is a limit and measure to Torah that has already been attained, and therefore his joy eventually came to an end, and he became tired.
The student who did not grow tired was dancing with joy over the Torah he would study in the future. And since the future has no limit, his joy never ended.
The Hiddushei HaRim added:
“The world thinks that we rejoice on Simchat Torah because we have finished the Torah. But the truth is that we rejoice because we are beginning the Torah anew.”
These words offer a new perspective on Simchat Torah: the joy is primarily about what is yet to come. Someone who studied Torah throughout the year can rejoice over what he has accomplished, but even someone who did not manage to study as much as he had hoped does not need to stand outside the circle of joy. The dancing is not a celebration of past achievements, but of the possibility of beginning again.
We finish so that we can begin
From this perspective, on Simchat Torah we all start from the same place. One person arrives after a year in which he studied a great deal of Torah, while another barely studied at all. One arrives with great accomplishments, while another arrives with a sense of missed opportunities. But when we open the Book of Genesis once again, both stand before the same Torah, the same possibility, the same year that has not yet been written.
Now we understand why, immediately after completing the Torah, we begin the Book of Genesis anew, rather than waiting until the following Shabbat. This is the heart of the matter: we finish so that we can begin. The conclusion is not a point at which we stop and look backward, but the moment from which we set out on a new journey. In this sense, the familiar phrase “Every ending is a new beginning” takes on a particularly profound meaning on Simchat Torah.
On Simchat Torah, we do not need to ask ourselves only how much Torah we studied during the year that has passed. We can ask a different question: How much are we prepared to study in the year that is about to begin?
For Simchat Torah is not only the joy of those who have completed the Torah. It is also, and perhaps above all, the joy of those who are ready to open it anew.
Chag Sameach.■
The writer is the rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.
SIMCHAT TORAH
RABBI SHMUEL RABINOWITZ

Swiss President Guy Parmelin to step down and make way for ‘new blood’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Swiss President Guy Parmelin to step down and make way for ‘new blood’
Swiss Economics Minister Guy Parmelin, who also holds the rotating presidency this year, is stepping down at the end of December after 11 years in government.
Visibly relaxed and with his characteristic sense of humour, the 66-year-old winegrower from Bursins in French-speaking Switzerland announced his resignation to the media in Bern on Friday. Rumours of his resignation had been circulating for some time. There had been repeated speculation about his state of health, with frequent reports that he was suffering from back problems.
However, Parmelin said his decision had nothing to do with his health. After 11 years in government, the member of the right-wing Swiss People’s Party wanted to make way for “new blood in these times of great uncertainty”.
“The passion for the job is no longer as strong as it was at the start,” Parmelin admitted, while ruling out any health issues. However, he stressed that he would continue working until December 31 “at 11:59pm at the very latest”. “After that, I’ll spend six months clearing out my office.”
Explaining that he had spent the summer reflecting, Parmelin believed that at some point “you have to make a decision, and the graveyard is full of people who thought they were indispensable”. “I hope there will be several motivated candidates, including both members of parliament and cantonal elected representatives, when my party opens the call for nominations,” he said.
The People’s Party has already announced that candidates have until October 23 to come forward. The election is due to take place on December 9.
More
Guy Parmelin bows out after a remarkable final act
‘Increasingly burdensome’
At the press conference Swissinfo asked Parmelin what the hardest moment in his career had been. “One of the most difficult moments was the Covid-19 crisis, when we had to announce the closure of many businesses and activities. I saw entrepreneurs who were devastated and afraid they would go bankrupt,” he said. “But when I look at what happened in other countries, I think we came through it relatively well. Nevertheless, it was a very difficult period. I remember meeting people during those two weeks when everything was closed who had tears in their eyes.”
The role of Federal Councillor is very interesting “but increasingly burdensome”, Parmelin acknowledged. “Since 2016, there have been an increasing number of conferences at presidential level. The government must therefore find a way to ensure that Switzerland is not absent from such events.”
He emphasised that Switzerland was ready to rise to the challenges, thanks to sound public finances and innovative businesses. But “nothing can ever be taken for granted”, he warned. Parmelin called on Switzerland not to fall behind.
More
Incoming Swiss president wants new partnerships but deems the US ‘indispensable’
“The world and the geopolitical landscape are changing, and we must adapt. Gone are the days when you could simply make a phone call to arrange a meeting with a leader.” He added that “if we do not adapt, if Switzerland does not take the necessary decisions to avoid falling behind, we risk a rude awakening.”
He experienced such a rude awakening in August 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced a tariff of 39% for Switzerland. “A real hammer blow,” he recalls.
More
Swiss economics minister praises ‘very good’ tariff talks with US
Conversely, Parmelin felt that the government had managed to steer Switzerland through the Covid pandemic “in a gentle manner” by international standards. Schools were closed for only about a fortnight.
Number of successes
Parmelin succeeded Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf in government in December 2015. He first took the reins of the defence ministry before moving to the economics ministry in 2019. He held the rotating one-year presidency on two occasions. In 2021, he guided Switzerland through the Covid crisis and managed the abandonment of negotiations with the EU on a framework agreement.
Rumours of his resignation had been rife in recent weeks. Parmelin will leave having achieved a number of successes, notably the free-trade agreements with India and Mercosur.

Women, girls make up 53% of people facing added food insecurity due to Mideast escalation: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:05 UTC
18:20:05 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Women and girls account for 53% of the projected 22 million additional people who could face food insecurity by the end of this year due to the Mideast escalation and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a UN Women analysis released Friday.
That amounts to an additional 11.7 million women and girls across the 28 countries analyzed, on top of an estimated 208 million who were already food insecure or undernourished, it said.
“When food becomes scarce, women eat less and last,” UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said, noting that women often shift to less nutritious diets or skip meals to prioritize others.
The analysis said disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are increasing energy, fertilizer and transport costs, pushing food prices higher.
According to the analysis, countries such as South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen, and Palestine face more concentrated risks, as multiple sources of vulnerability overlap.
Sudan's female population faces highest risk
In South Sudan, the additional number of women and girls who could face food insecurity represents around 14%, or one in seven, of the country's female population, the highest proportion among the 28 countries analyzed.
Lebanon follows with nearly 4% of its female population potentially facing additional food insecurity.
Women and girls are also expected to account for a particularly high share of those potentially affected in several countries, including 60% in Afghanistan, more than 57% in Yemen, and nearly 56% in Sudan.
The analysis also highlighted employment and financial inequalities that could leave women less able to absorb rising food prices and income losses.
Around 80% of women in Egypt, Iraq, Palestine, Sudan and Syria are outside the labor force, rising to around 95% in Afghanistan and Yemen.
Among employed women, more than 80% are in vulnerable employment in Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Haiti, Mali, and South Sudan.
Financial access also remains limited, with fewer than one in five women in Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, and Yemen owning a bank or mobile money account, according to the analysis.
UN Women called for food and cash assistance alongside nutrition, protection, livelihoods and agricultural support.
It also urged resources to be targeted to places where women and girls face multiple, overlapping risks, and delivered at the right time – including ahead of agricultural seasons.

The government has sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting that the UK is not facing a diesel shortage after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The transport minister Keir Mather said on Friday that the UK has a wide range of sources of the fuel and is in talks with other European countries over the potential release of emergency diesel stockpiles.
“I want to reassure people that they can still go to the pump and fill up with diesel because the supply we have to the UK is inherently resilient,” he said on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. “The flows of diesel into the UK come from a variety of sources, and that is resilient.
“The government’s obligation now is to work really closely with our partners [in Europe] and officials in the US administration to re-stress how important it is to have flows of diesel into the UK. People shouldn’t be concerned about shortages because of the inherent resilience that is built into that system.”
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Earlier this week it emerged that the UK’s biggest refinery, Fawley in Hampshire, is set to shut for up to 10 weeks for planned maintenance. The UK had 18 refineries in the 1980s but now has only four.
On Thursday the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel supplies, after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring prices or face a US supply ban.
The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a record high on Friday, breaking the £2 mark for the first time, according to the motoring body the RAC.
“This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “The average price of a litre of diesel has risen to a record 200.01p and is showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery on to motorists.”
The government has extended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year. Earlier this week the RAC called on the government to extend the freeze into spring.
“We need to give people support where we can,” Mather said on GMB. “The government is not powerless. That is why we have a fuel duty freeze in place at the moment. The chancellor will set out the future of that at the budget, but is very aware of the impact that [high prices] are having on people.”
On Friday, Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said Europe was discussing the question of whether to release emergency reserves of diesel with all members of the International Energy Agency, not only the US.
“This is one of the opportunities that we have; we have used it before, and it is likely that we would use it again,” he told Euronews.

Reporters in the city saw long queues of stationary cars and buses on main roads in the Ukrainian capital as commuters sought alternative routes.
Traffic built up due to the complete closure to traffic in both directions on the Southern Bridge, one of eight connecting the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro River.
The Paton Bridge, further north, was open only one way, city mayor Vitali Klitschko said, but there were no reports that it had been hit.
Russian drones struck the support structures of the Southern Bridge on Thursday. The crossing was temporarily closed while a structural assessment was made.
It reopened to traffic and Metro train services soon afterwards but suffered repeated drone strikes on Thursday night and early on Friday, Klitschko said.
The second on Thursday night damaged a bridge pier, the road surface and a protective concrete barrier along the subway line, he added.
Ukraine has long feared an attack on its major transportation bridges since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment from Russian drones and missiles in recent months, putting the city on near-constant alert and disrupting daily life.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats in the skies sound almost round the clock, urging the city's estimated 3 million people to seek shelter.
Repeated strikes on trains and petrol stations have already hit the rail and road networks.
Political will
The latest Russian attacks killed one person and wounded at least two other people when a 25-storey residential building was hit in southeast Kyiv.
The victim was found as firefighters put out a blaze caused by the blast.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged countries to tighten sanctions to prevent Russia from manufacturing its new jet-powered drones, faster and harder to intercept than previous models, which he said were "critically dependent" on foreign components.

US increasing Middle East military buildup – AP
Washington is sending more warships and troops to the Middle East as US President Donald Trump is considering the resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran after the midterms, AP has reported.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that he has “to make a decision: either Iran signs a very fair deal, or it won’t exist any longer.” In a Time magazine interview published the same day, he said that new attacks on the Islamic Republic were “possible” after the US election on November 3, but declined to reveal any further details.
In its article on Thursday, AP said that a third aircraft carrier and some 9,000 additional service members, including 7,000 sailors and 2,000 marines, are currently on their way to the area of the conflict with Iran.
It would increase the US military presence in the Middle East to more than 20,000, which is “an unusually high number,” it stressed.
The forces on the move include the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, with the cruiser USS Chosin and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships, an unnamed American official told the agency.
With the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington already being deployed, three US aircraft carriers could be in the Middle East simultaneously as early as the end of October, according to the source.
Washington last had as many carriers in the region in April at the height of the American-Israeli missile exchanges with Iran. Before that, it happened back in 2003.
Axios reported on Friday, citing a US official, that it wasn’t yet clear if the USS Theodore Roosevelt would join the two carriers or replace one of them.
Washington also sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar in recent weeks, according to Axios. It was done to make it easier to get permission from Riyadh to use Saudi airspace for possible strikes on Iran, the outlet explained.
When asked by Time if the conflict with Tehran would harm the Republican Party’s chances in the midterms, Trump first acknowledged that “it’s possible,” but then said that “it should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
A poll by AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, which was published on Thursday, suggested that some 70% of Americans disapprove of the war with Iran.
After the initial US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic in late February, Trump claimed that the conflict will be over in a few weeks, but it’s still ongoing, with the diplomatic process remaining in a stalemate.
Trump told Time that he rejected Iran’s latest peace proposal, made during the UN General Assembly last week, because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
In September, Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases were only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

Can AI play a role in reducing inequality?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:06:35 UTC
18:06:35 KST

Can AI play a role in reducing inequality?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
In the debate about how best to regulate artificial intelligence, what about its role in development and aid? Warnings about the potential for exacerbating inequality are rife – but the World Bank argues that the technology could be harnessed for good.
Paschal Donohoe, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer at the World Bank Group, says there are concrete benefits in industries like farming, education and healthcare. "We know that artificial intelligence can play a role in crop productivity. By playing a role in helping farmers better managing what they are planting and harvesting, it has a bigger impact on their productivity and the income they gain. And I saw a very clear example of this in India, where I saw small rice farmers who, through use of artificial intelligence, were given better advice on how rice could be planted and harvested."
He believes developing economies can reap the benefits of AI if it's tailored to their needs – which he refers to as small AI. "That means AI that is more appropriately adjusted to local circumstances, has a higher ability to run offline, will have the ability to operate in environments in which connectivity or electricity may not be at a very high level."
Donohoe says that even as technology transforms daily life, development agencies remain focused on addressing inequality and basic needs like access to clean water, healthcare and education. "By ensuring in dealing with the development of artificial intelligence, that we do not for a moment lose sight of all [those] issues (...) We are recognising the change that is now taking place with AI, and we are making the case that while of course it brings challenges, small AI in particular, harnessed correctly with the right policies around it, can play a positive role."

EU holds crisis meeting as US pressure mounts to release emergency oil stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:05:23 UTC
18:05:23 KST

EU countries and the European Commission are holding talks on Friday that could pave the way for a new emergency oil reserves release, as pressure from Washington mounts. Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Euronews a fresh emergency release is "a possibility".
European countries will meet on Friday to discuss releasing emergency fuel stocks as soaring diesel prices put pressure on governments and the United States urges Europe to act.
Washington has warned European allies to release more diesel supplies or risk a US export ban, a European Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
The talks come as the diesel market tightens ahead of winter, driving up prices for consumers and raising concerns over supplies.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Euronews on Thursday that a new emergency release was "a possibility".
"We are discussing with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the United States, when the right time is to release, because this is one of the opportunities that we have," the Danish commissioner said.
"We've used it before, and we'll likely use it again."
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, confirmed the meeting on Friday.
A spokesperson for Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment said the diesel market was "very tight", resulting in high prices for consumers worldwide.
Ireland is coordinating with EU countries and the European Commission to "take stock of the situation" and "examine appropriate measures" to tackle high prices, the spokesperson said.
The discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency, which coordinated collective action in March to support oil markets following US and Israeli military attacks against Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
IEA chief Fatih Birol has also urged European countries to make use of their diesel stocks.
The reserves have not been tapped since the agency's first emergency oil release in March, when 400 million barrels of oil were put on the market.
Macron speaks to Trump over energy crisis
With pressure mounting, French President Emmanuel Macron held an overnight call with US President Donald Trump to discuss the global energy situation, according to the Elysée.
The French presidency said the two countries shared a "common interest" in coordinated action "without export restrictions".
Macron also discussed the issue with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
The talks stressed "the need to work together to combat rising fuel prices" and "ensure the global availability of refined products", according to the Elysée.
A videoconference of G7 leaders, with France currently holding the presidency, will take place "as soon as possible".
"The aim is to coordinate measures to help ease price pressures and guarantee supplies of crude oil and refined products — both among G7 nations and globally," the Elysée said.
"Coordination efforts are also underway at the European level."
EU holds technical talks on possible emergency release
EU countries will meet on Friday under the Commission's crisis-monitoring and coordination table for energy security.
The forum is used for technical discussions on whether disruptions threaten supplies and what coordinated action may be needed.
An EU source said representatives from France, Germany, Ireland and the UK held a call with the European Commission on 1 October.
The call appears to have preceded Friday morning's technical meeting.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent renewed pressure on European countries on Thursday, urging them to release additional supplies.
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent wrote on X.
"American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage. America is doing its part. We look to our allies to match their commitments with action."
EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the US tone as "rough", saying Washington was not sending "gentle diplomatic messages".
The Trump administration has been considering a 90-day diesel export ban as it seeks to contain domestic fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections.

Julius Bär announces share buyback worth up to CHF600 million
Julius Bär intends to buy back its own shares worth up to CHF600 million ($725 million). The bank has received approval from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) to do so, after the authority announced on Tuesday that it had concluded its investigation into the Signa debacle.
Julius Bär announced on Friday that the share buybacks are now set to begin in the coming weeks and be completed within a year. The implementation will depend on prevailing market conditions. The shares will be purchased via a secondary trading line on the SIX Swiss Exchange.
At the same time, the asset management bank announced a revision to its capital distribution policy. According to this, between 40% and 60% of the IFRS consolidated profit is to continue to be distributed in future. The aim is to pay a progressive dividend per share, provided no exceptional events occur.
With regard to capitalisation, Julius Bär remains committed to maintaining a “solid capital base” with a target Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 15%. As at mid-2026, the bank’s CET1 capital ratio stood at 18.5%.
The revised capital policy reflects the business’s strong capital-generating nature, according to board chairman Noel Quinn, who is quoted in the press release. Surplus capital will be returned to shareholders, while at the same time maintaining the financial strength and flexibility required to achieve the confirmed financial targets for the current 2026–2028 cycle.
Immediate measures relaxed
On Tuesday, FINMA announced that it had concluded its enforcement proceedings against Julius Bär, which had been ongoing for almost two years, relating to the heavy losses on loans to the collapsed property group Signa, owned by the Austrian investor René Benko.
More
Swiss financial watchdog ends Julius Bär proceedings
At the same time, the supervisory authority had eased or lifted certain emergency measures relating to capital and liquidity that had been imposed during the investigation. In an initial response, Julius Bär had already stated that it had immediately applied to FINMA for authorisation to carry out share buybacks.
