BRICS talks energy resilience. Time to make it real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:45:52 UTC
16:45:52 KST

BRICS talks energy resilience. Time to make it real
For the Global South, energy security is no longer a policy talking point – it is a question of survival. With traditional shipping routes rattled by the Middle East conflict, developing countries are being hit by rising costs, broken supply chains, and shortages they did not create.
At the 81st UN General Assembly in September 2026, Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and other leaders from the Global South made that frustration unmistakably clear: poorer nations are being squeezed by a deepening crisis across energy, food, fuel, fertilizer, finance, and logistics.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balen Shah put it starkly: “We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food. And this is not Nepal’s private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask Sri Lanka. Ask any other country in our region and you will hear the same account: hit by the climate we did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start.”
Weeks earlier, on the other side of the world, BRICS leaders gathered in New Delhi had already framed the same problem in strategic terms. Their summit declaration called for stable energy markets, “undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources,” and stronger protection of critical infrastructure.
Events soon put that ambition under strain. Drone attacks disrupted Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, an important route for moving crude to the Red Sea while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. With loadings at Yanbu affected, Saudi Arabia began offering more crude to Asian buyers through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman. The episode showed how quickly even an alternative route can become vulnerable.
BRICS now includes some of the world’s biggest oil producers as well as major importers. Yet membership alone does not guarantee access to another member’s oil when supplies tighten. Producers may have other buyers, while prices and transport conditions can change quickly. The grouping has major oil resources. The harder part is making some of those barrels reliably available to members when supply pressures grow.
What Russian trade reveals
Russia is a useful example of how these energy ties can help during a shortage without guaranteeing supply. As Middle Eastern supplies became less reliable, Russian crude helped India make up some of the shortfall. In July, Russia accounted for a record 50.83% of India’s crude imports, showing how quickly buying patterns can change when supply is disrupted. But the increase in Russian supply did not amount to assured access. As Chinese refiners stepped up purchases, competition for Russian barrels intensified.
A separate analysis estimated India’s Russian crude imports falling to 1.87 million barrels a day in August from 2.79 million in July. Even when BRICS opens another source of supply, its members may still be bidding against one another for the same barrels.
Russian oil, however, now faces another constraint. US President Donald Trump earlier this month signed legislation authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian energy, potentially including India and China. For major buyers such as India and China, sanctions now add another layer of uncertainty to securing Russian barrels.
Trade has also begun to flow the other way. After repeated Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries contributed to domestic fuel shortages, Russia began importing gasoline from India: according to data from Kpler, Russia’s Murmansk port received 40,000 tonnes of gasoline from Nayara Energy, 49% of which is controlled by Rosneft. By late August, Russian gasoline production had fallen to about 70% of domestic consumption as more refineries were forced to temporarily suspend operations or reduce output.
India’s shift toward more Russian crude, and Moscow’s later purchases of Indian gasoline, were both responses to supply disruptions that had already begun to unfold. They showed how quickly energy flows can adjust when circumstances change. BRICS could try to organize some of that flexibility in advance, rather than leaving its members to scramble for alternatives only after a disruption has started. That would make the group’s energy cooperation less reliant on improvisation.
Making stored oil usable in a crisis
One way to reduce that improvisation is to position oil closer to the buyer before it is urgently needed. India already has one such bilateral example. The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) and Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited already have a storage relationship at Mangalore. A May 2026 agreement explores increasing ADNOC crude stored in India to as much as 30 million barrels, including possible new storage at Visakhapatnam and Chandikhol. It also considers Indian strategic crude storage in Fujairah.
The arrangement is bilateral and does not give India a guaranteed right to all the stored crude in a crisis. Even so, it shows that a producer can place oil inside an importing country before a shortage hits. The harder part is agreeing beforehand how much of that oil the buyer could draw on.
One option is a voluntary emergency oil arrangement among interested BRICS members, rather than a common reserve for the entire grouping. Clear ownership is only one part of it. The importing country would also need a defined right to draw an agreed quantity when an emergency occurs. The terms could set how much oil is covered, where it is stored, and how it is priced. They would also spell out who can release it and how the stock is replaced. Refinery compatibility and transport would have to be worked out as well. This would remove some of the uncertainty before markets become even more difficult. India or any other buyer should not be negotiating access after ships have been diverted and prices have already jumped.
India is already working on some of these practical questions outside BRICS. A July India-Japan statement on energy resilience covers stockpiles, emergency response, supplies from third countries, and maritime transport. The India-Japan framework is different, but it shows that many of these operational questions can be worked through in advance. New Delhi therefore does not have to start from scratch. Some of those ideas could now be adapted to voluntary cooperation between BRICS producers and importers.
The test before the next summit
Getting hold of the oil is only part of the problem. The payment also must go through. BRICS finance ministers and central bank governors have already called for better cross-border payment systems. A promised barrel is of little use if the payment cannot be cleared when it is needed. Companies and banks should run payments through the agreed route beforehand and keep a backup ready.
The arrangement should then be put through realistic exercise. The New Delhi Declaration specifically welcomes the work of the BRICS Energy Research Cooperation Platform. There is no need to create another institution. The platform could work with participating oil ministries, national oil companies and storage operators on one or two pilots.
Suppose Hormuz traffic falls further just as a bypass pipeline is damaged and war-risk insurance becomes unavailable. If an importer invokes its agreed right to the oil, how long does it take for the stored crude to reach the refinery? The time it takes would show whether the arrangement is useful in a real emergency.
The New Delhi pledge will matter more if it works when supplies tighten. A member facing a shortage should be able to draw on an agreed volume without having to negotiate the terms again. That is where BRICS can begin to turn its promise of resilient energy flows into something members can use.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Breadcrumb
UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear fallout legacy
The United States needs to take additional steps to remedy the nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands by providing healthcare and releasing secret archives, according to a UN report presented to its human rights body on Thursday.
The US, which administered the Pacific islands after World War Two, conducted 67 nuclear weapons tests in the Marshall Islands from 1946 to 1958, including "Castle Bravo" at Bikini Atoll in 1954
The human cost of these tests has been "severe and lasting", the UN human rights office report said, adding that there has not yet been a just settlement of the claims
"The damage needs to be repaired," Awa Dabo, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva
The UN cited examples of the ongoing impact, such as elevated levels of cancer, displacement from contaminated areas and lasting social stigmas affecting exposed persons who are referred to as "poison people"
The report called for the US to provide remedy in the form of healthcare and to declassify all information pertaining to the nuclear legacy
The US State Department said it had already reached a full and final settlement of all claims with the Marshall Islands in 1986 and said it continues to provide medical and cancer assistance and environmental monitoring programmes for those affected
"The United States has recognised the effects of its nuclear testing program and has accepted and acted on its responsibility to the citizens of the Republic of the Marshall Islands," the State Department said.
Marshallese residents, including Alson Kelen who was displaced from Bikini and lost both parents to cancer, addressed the council and called for a meaningful resolution to the legacy
The Marshall Islands' representative, Senator David Anitok, told the UN body: "The continued denial of an effective remedy has forced us to come before this Council to ask for help"
Washington disengaged from the UN Human Rights Council last year, alleging an anti-Israel bias, and its seat was left empty on Thursday

Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:33:21 UTC
16:33:21 KST

Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
In August 2021, after the withdrawal of U.S. troops, the Taliban, an armed religious and political movement, seized power in Afghanistan. Active fighting has since ended, but life has hardly improved for many Afghans. The Taliban established a Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice and severely curtailed women’s rights. The authorities also tried to block internet access nationwide and ban officials from using smartphones. At the same time, the Taliban declared war on drugs, specifically opium, and it appears to be waging that war quite successfully.
In August 2026, Middle East scholar Ruslan Suleymanov traveled to Afghanistan to see how the country had changed over the past five years. He visited three cities and had dozens of conversations. Meduza has translated his report.
‘Russia? Welcome!’
“Get out of the car!” a Taliban fighter dressed entirely in camouflage tells me firmly, but without aggression, at one of the many checkpoints on the Herat–Kandahar highway. He asks me to follow him.
A local Taliban commander sits on the grass near the highway, surrounded by his aides. He takes his time examining my documents. When he realizes I have a Russian passport, his face lights up with joy, almost elation.
“Oh, Russia! Welcome!” the commander says in Pashto. Only a moment later do I notice that his left leg is missing. A prosthetic leg lies beside him.
He invites me to join him for tea from a thermos and even to stay the night. Hospitality is central to the culture of the Pashtuns, who make up Afghanistan’s ethnic majority and the backbone of the Taliban.
The roughly 500-kilometer (310-mile) journey from Herat in the north, considered Afghanistan’s cultural capital, to Kandahar in the south, where the Taliban movement originated in the mid-1990s, is much the same throughout: poor pavement — in places, very poor — document checks almost every hour, and enthusiasm at the mere mention of Russia.
That enthusiasm is understandable. Russia remains the only country in the world to officially recognize the Afghan government the Taliban formed in September 2021, shortly after seizing power.
For more than 40 years before the Taliban took power, Afghanistan’s roads were the scene of fighting, ambushes, and kidnappings. Today, long-distance travel around the country is relatively safe. Foreigners, however, are still better off traveling with someone local.
In 2026, Afghanistan ranks 11th in the world for terrorism risk, according to Australia’s Institute for Economics and Peace, which compiles the Global Terrorism Index. This is the first time it has fallen outside the top 10 since the ranking began.
In the first years after the Taliban took power, the main source of terrorism in Afghanistan was the Taliban’s bitter enemy, the Islamic State group — specifically its Afghan affiliate, Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISIS-K).
The group became known in Russia in March 2024 following the terrorist attack at Crocus City Hall in Krasnogorsk, outside Moscow, which killed 145 people. U.N. experts estimate that ISIS-K still has around 2,000 fighters. Afghans dissatisfied with the current authorities and people from Central Asia, mainly Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, periodically join its ranks. Over the past five years, ISIS-K has recruited at least 600 volunteers from those countries.
In any case, improved security is one of the few achievements the Taliban can claim over the past five years. That is partly because, before August 2021, the Taliban itself carried out most of Afghanistan’s major terrorist attacks.
How popular is Taliban rule?
In nearly 300 years of statehood, Afghanistan has yet to develop a shared national identity. “We remain a deeply divided community, but we are not yet a nation. Everyone understands the word ‘Afghan’ differently,” Amin, a 31-year-old employee of the nationwide radio station Salam Watandar, tells Meduza.
The main divide is ethnic. Broadly speaking, the country can be divided into Pashtuns in the south and Tajiks, Uzbeks, Hazaras, and others in the north. The government formed by the Taliban is almost 100% Pashtun. The Taliban’s reasoning is simple: the country is led by those who contributed most to the fight against foreign forces from 2001 to 2021. That means exclusively Taliban members and allied groups that fought most actively against the U.S. and its allies.
“Claims that our government supposedly isn’t inclusive are part of an agenda imposed by the West. Afghans are happy with their government,” an ethnic Pashtun employee of the Ministry of Information and Culture told Meduza, asking not to be named. But in private conversations with Meduza, members of six minority groups — Baloch, Qizilbash, Sikhs, Tajiks, Uzbeks, and Hazaras — said they lacked equal rights and equal opportunities to pursue their ambitions in Afghanistan.
Ethnicity, however, is far from the country’s only dividing line. At least 74% of Afghans live in rural areas or are nomads; only 26% live in cities. In rural areas and mountain valleys isolated from the outside world, ways of life have remained unchanged for centuries. The village elder or mullah commands the greatest respect and generally has ties to the Taliban.
That is why, under the previous government, most Afghans heeded Taliban calls to boycott elections. The militants called the elections illegitimate and threatened to cut off the fingers of anyone who went to a polling station. Turnout in Afghanistan’s last presidential election, in September 2019, was less than 20%.
The Taliban’s propaganda about defending Islamic values or fighting foreign invaders, meanwhile, met with understanding, if not approval, among local people.
“The front line used to run through here. Shells were exploding. Today I can grow potatoes and fruit,” Najib, 57, who lives on the outskirts of Lashkar Gah, the capital of Helmand province in southern Afghanistan, tells Meduza.
Najib’s father was killed in the mid-1980s during the Soviet invasion. In the late 1990s, he lost his older brother, who fought for the Taliban against the Northern Alliance — a coalition of northern warlords led by Ahmad Shah Massoud. In 2006, during the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan, his eldest son was killed after accidentally stepping on a mine on the road into Lashkar Gah.
“The war is over. For the first time in more than 40 years, we’re living in peace. That’s all I’ve asked the Almighty for in recent years,” he says. Like Najib, many Afghans are willing to forgive the Taliban for everything else because it has brought long-awaited peace.
‘We have to find a way to survive’
Before the Taliban took power, Helmand was known as Afghanistan’s leading producer of opium poppies. The province accounted for more than half of the country’s opium production.
In April 2022, Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered a crackdown on the drug trade. His decree said offenders would be punished under Sharia, or Islamic law. It did not specify how.
Over four years, the Taliban has achieved impressive results: the area planted with poppies in Afghanistan has fallen by roughly 95%, according to the U.N. In our conversation, Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani went further, insisting that the figure was 98%.
As a result, around five million Afghans across the country have lost a steady source of income. So far, the Taliban has been unable to offer them another way to earn a living legally. Unemployment stands at no less than 75%. More than 90% of the population now lives below the poverty line, and more than 70% of Afghans depend on humanitarian aid.
“We all used to grow poppies. The Taliban themselves controlled the sales and made huge amounts of money from them. We just got what was left over. But we could survive on that,” Ahmad, 62, who also lives in Helmand, near the city of Gereshk, tells Meduza.
He says that now, like many former poppy growers, he has to grow fruit and vegetables and take them into town to sell. “I used to earn up to 20,000 afghanis a month [about $300 at the current exchange rate]. Now I barely make 10,000 [about $150],” Ahmad says.
For many Afghans, that is a substantial amount of money. The U.N. estimates that the country’s average salary is now around $100. Meanwhile, prices keep rising, and inflation had already exceeded 7.5% at the beginning of the year.
Gasoline in Afghanistan now costs around 84 afghanis ($1.20) per liter, liquefied gas costs 66 afghanis ($1) per liter, and beef costs 500 afghanis ($7.60) per kilogram (2.2 pounds). Monthly electricity bills come to nearly 1,000 afghanis ($15.30).
The huge influx of Afghan refugees and migrants from neighboring countries, primarily Iran and Pakistan, has made the situation worse. Over the past three years, more than five million people have been forced to return to Afghanistan at those countries’ insistence, increasing its population by 10%.
Two of Ahmad’s sons, ages 23 and 26, spent several years working in construction in neighboring Pakistan. But Islamabad’s tighter immigration policy forced them to return home in late 2024. They now help their father harvest his crops and sell them at the market in Gereshk.
“Life isn’t getting any easier. We have to find a way to survive. What matters most is that there’s no war,” Ahmad says, alluding to the periodic armed clashes between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which have become more frequent over the past couple of years.
How has the Taliban changed
When the first Afghan state emerged in the 18th century, Kandahar was its first capital. It was also here, in 1994, that graduates of religious schools known as madrasas, mostly from neighboring Pakistan, founded the armed Taliban movement. By 1996, it controlled most of Afghanistan, including Kabul.
Kandahar, now often called the country’s political capital, is home to the headquarters of Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada, who also holds the title amir al-mu’minin, or “commander of the faithful.” He is consolidating his power, which rests on his high standing in the Taliban’s religious hierarchy.
Akhundzada relies on his own military guard and the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, effectively the morality police. The ministry was reestablished in September 2021 in place of the Ministry of Women’s Affairs. It enforces his draconian laws and restrictions, including those imposed on women.
Over the past five years, girls in Afghanistan have been barred from attending school beyond the sixth grade and from pursuing higher education. Women are also banned from beauty salons, fitness centers, parks, and other recreational spaces. The Taliban’s supreme leader has prohibited women from working in government institutions, nongovernmental organizations, and U.N. agencies.
Some Taliban members, mostly in Kabul, do not share the rigid conservatism of their leader, who once turned his own son into a suicide bomber. During the movement’s 20 years underground, some militant leaders lived in countries such as Pakistan and Qatar. They saw that life in a Muslim country could be very different — certainly different from Afghanistan under Taliban rule in 1996–2001.
Some militant leaders are known to have sent their daughters to schools and universities in those countries. These experiences changed Taliban leaders, who became less radical than their predecessors. This is especially true of the movement’s younger generation, those born in the 1980s and 1990s.
In February 2023, for example, Taliban Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani sharply criticized the supreme leader over the ban on education for girls, accusing him of “usurping power.” He later had to leave the country for several months, reportedly because he faced the threat of arrest.
Another member of the Kabul-based Taliban leadership, Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Abbas Stanikzai, also repeatedly called for girls to be allowed to return to school and young women to university. As a result, he was dismissed in May 2024 and later left Afghanistan altogether.
Kandahar itself is more conservative than Kabul. Most women here wear dull purple burqas that cover their faces completely. Boutiques and malls are rare, and most commerce takes place informally at simple stalls or carts on the streets.
Over the past five years, many of the movement’s members most loyal to the supreme leader have moved to this birthplace of the Taliban. Among them is Zabihullah Mujahid, spokesperson for the “Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan” and the Taliban’s public face.
Three years ago, we met in Kabul at the Ministry of Information and Culture, where he is deputy minister. This year, we met at a hotel in Kandahar.
“Education authorities are continuing their efforts. They are trying to create the conditions needed to resolve this issue, which is strictly an internal matter,” Mujahid says when I ask when girls in Afghanistan will be able to return to school beyond the sixth grade.
He says attempts to pressure the Taliban or force it to change any of its restrictions will never succeed. “We urge all countries not to concern themselves with Afghanistan. These are matters for our nation, and they do not concern other states,” Mujahid says, making his reluctance to discuss the subject clear.
He has more to say when asked about the “Islamic Emirate’s” relations with Moscow. “Russia has a very important role in Afghanistan. Russia also plays a very important role in our region, especially economically. You could say that Russia is needed,” Mujahid says. “Moreover, Russia’s recognition of the ‘Islamic Emirate’ government is a very important step that sets an example for everyone else. It shows Western countries in particular that there is no need to be afraid of taking such a step.”
The distance from Kandahar to Kabul is also roughly 500 kilometers (310 miles), but the journey takes a couple of hours less. The pavement is much better here, probably because Taliban officials themselves regularly use this highway.
There was once heavy fighting here, too, and kidnappings were frequent. In July 2007, for example, the Taliban abducted 23 Christian missionaries from South Korea on this road. Two were executed; the others were released more than a month later in exchange for Seoul’s commitment to withdraw its roughly 200 troops from Afghanistan by the end of the year.
Now, the only reminders of the war are the burned-out wrecks of cars and military vehicles occasionally visible beside the highway.
There are checkpoints roughly every 100 kilometers (60 miles), as well as at the entrance to Kabul. At the final checkpoint before entering the Afghan capital, security officers thoroughly inspect the car and record detailed information about every foreigner in a logbook.
As one might expect of a capital, Kabul is different from the rest of Afghanistan. Modern malls, fitness clubs, and fashionable coffee shops from before the Taliban’s return to power are still open. Before the Taliban’s return, those coffee shops were gathering places for Kabul’s cosmopolitan young people, hipsters, and LGBTQ people.
Strangely enough, the Taliban itself no longer shuns the trappings of Western civilization. This sets its members apart from their older comrades who controlled Afghanistan in 1996–2001. Back then, the militants banned music, confiscated photographic equipment and video recorders, forced people to follow a strict dress code, and held public executions in stadiums.
Today’s Taliban members happily take selfies, set up Facebook and Instagram accounts, watch the national cricket team’s matches, and order cappuccinos or lattes at coffee shops.
When Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered Afghanistan’s internet blocked in the fall of 2025 to “prevent immorality,” Taliban leaders in Kabul opposed the move, and service was restored after just three days. In June this year, the supreme leader ordered a ban on smartphones for government employees because, in his view, modern technology threatens Islamic norms and leads to “the destruction of the next generation.” From what I have seen, most officials, and not just in Kabul, still have smartphones.
Unlike in Kandahar, cafes and ordinary eateries in the capital also often show broadcasts from London-based Afghanistan International, the leading anti-Taliban TV channel run by Afghan exiles.
The militants in the Afghan capital also turn a blind eye to many of the restrictions on women imposed by the leadership in Kandahar. Roughly half the women in Kabul, for example, leave their faces uncovered and disregard the requirement to be accompanied in public by a male relative, known as a mahram.
Since August 2024, women in Afghanistan have officially been forbidden even to speak loudly in the street: the supreme leader ruled that “a woman’s voice is a source of impurity.” But this unrealistic rule is barely enforced either.
Perhaps the only thing women really cannot do in the streets is protest against Taliban rule. Immediately after seizing power in August 2021, the militants were shocked by the many protests by young women. Demonstrations took place in all of Afghanistan’s major cities, including Kabul, Herat, Mazar-i-Sharif, and Jalalabad. Typically, each drew between 100 and 300 young women.
This was largely a result of higher levels of education in the country. According to the U.N., primary school attendance among girls in Afghanistan rose from 0% to more than 80% between 2001 and 2021.
Now, at least 80% of the country’s 2.5 million women and girls of school age receive no education. In May and June this year, Afghanistan held entrance exams for public universities. A total of 120,000 applicants took them, without a single woman among them.
Nevertheless, an entire generation has grown up in the country with ideas about freedom, rights, and personal space that are completely different from those of the conservative Taliban. The Taliban, in turn, sees all of this as an intrusion by Western culture.
Can outside pressure influence the authorities?
“My life ended three and a half years ago. I’ll never forget that day. We were on our way to university classes, as usual, but people in uniform with assault rifles stopped us,” Shukriya, 24, tells Meduza, recalling the introduction of Afghanistan’s ban on university education for women in December 2022.
At the time, she was in her third year at Abu Ali ibn Sina (Avicenna) Medical University in Kabul. By now, she could have been working and supporting her loved ones. During decades of unrelenting war, it became commonplace for girls and women to support an entire family financially. But the Taliban’s return to power has made life much harder for women.
“For the first year, I was deeply depressed and thought about killing myself. I couldn’t imagine how to go on living. Even now, I don’t know what will happen to me tomorrow or how to build a life for myself,” Shukriya says. Women now account for up to 80% of all suicides in Afghanistan. Every day, at least one or two Afghan women take their own lives.
She says what kept her from suicide was knowing that she needed to care for her sick father and help raise her two younger brothers. At first, she wanted to work in a beauty salon, but the Taliban banned those, too, in July 2023. These were places where many young Afghan women found work, met, and spent time together.
Only men’s salons now operate openly in Afghanistan. Even the men’s faces on posters advertising these businesses have been painted over. Women’s salons continue to operate only in private homes, and their customers visit in secret, afraid of the “morality police.”
Shukriya now makes dresses to order and sells them through social media. “The money I make barely covers food for the family. But I’m getting more and more orders, and I hope to save as much as I can so I can leave and bring my loved ones with me,” she says.
Education for women and girls is one of the clearest examples of the conflict between urban and rural Afghanistan. Even before the Taliban returned to power, women in rural areas wore burqas, and girls were often kept out of school beyond the sixth grade. While primary school attendance improved dramatically in 2001–2021, average secondary school attendance among girls across Afghanistan never exceeded 40%.
Another source of tension is the Taliban’s particular understanding of Islam. Officially, the Taliban professes Sunni Islam, but its interpretation also incorporates the rules of the Pashtun ethical code, Pashtunwali. Under that code, a woman’s place is “either in the home or in the grave.”
Despite their extraordinary hospitality, Pashtuns fiercely guard their culture against foreign influence. Graffiti on a fence outside the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice in Kabul reads: “The hijab is a shield against the intrusion of foreign culture.”
The Taliban’s draconian laws have baffled even the Muslim world. In January 2023, for example, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the ban on university education for women “has nothing to do with Islam.”
During the Taliban’s first period in power, in 1996–2001, three Muslim countries recognized its government: the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. Today, even those countries do not. Nor does Qatar, which has hosted the movement’s political office since 2013.
At the U.N., Afghanistan is still represented by a diplomat from a state that no longer exists: the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. Taliban spokesperson Mujahid told me this was because “the countries that waged wars in Afghanistan, the countries that occupied Afghanistan, have political influence over the U.N.”
Further isolation appears likely to make life even harder for Afghanistan’s population. Five years of ultimatums and attempts to pressure the Taliban have failed and instead led to a sharp reduction in international humanitarian aid, from $4 billion to $1 billion.
“We want the international community to cooperate with the authorities in Afghanistan, who have ensured security and eradicated corruption, drug trafficking, and other forms of crime,” Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani tells Meduza.
For ordinary Afghans, particularly women and Kabul residents, all the Taliban’s achievements pale beside the restrictions imposed over the past five years. But they, too, see little point in trying to pressure the Taliban from abroad.
“The West was traumatized by its experience in Afghanistan and would rather forget about the country. All it does is try to lecture the Taliban. But they’ll never change. We need some other way to talk to them,” Shukriya says firmly.
“All I want is for people not to forget us or put all the responsibility on the Taliban. The world is responsible for us, too. Otherwise, our lives will become even more hellish,” she says.

Twenty-five years ago: how a public address announcement marked the end of Swissair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Twenty-five years ago: how a public address announcement marked the end of Swissair
“For financial reasons, Swissair is no longer able to operate its flights.” Exactly 25 years ago, on October 2, 2001, this public address announcement at Zurich Airport triggered a national trauma in Switzerland. Swissair was grounded.
Several thousand passengers had already been waiting at Kloten Airport for hours that Tuesday. Across the world, a total of around 20,000 travellers were waiting for their flights, many of whom had already checked in their luggage. Yet for hours, the display board showed only “delayed” for all Swissair flights.
At 3:45pm, Swissair finally informed the media – at that time still by fax – that it would be suspending flight operations with immediate effect. It had been unable to purchase any more fuel, meaning that its 260 aircraft had to remain grounded. At 4:17pm, an airport employee finally announced over the public address system that the airline, once the pride of the nation, had been grounded. Despite the company’s well-known problems, nobody had expected this.
More
Swissair grounding: 15 years on
Aggressive acquisition strategy
The beginning of the end came when voters rejected membership of the European Economic Area (EEA) in 1992. This blocked a bilateral air transport agreement between Switzerland and the European Union. Swissair therefore no longer had free access to the European market and had to reorient itself.
The then CEO, Philippe Bruggisser, set himself the goal of acquiring as many small airlines as possible in order to bring Swissair to a critical mass and circumvent the problem of lack of market access. From 1997 onwards, this aggressive acquisition strategy was officially known as the “Hunter Strategy”.
However, the hunt did not bring Swissair any luck. This was because the acquired airlines, including the Belgian Sabena and the Italian Volare, were not only small but also unprofitable. The “Hunter Strategy” failed miserably.
Bruggisser was forced to step down. In early 2001, Crossair owner Moritz Suter took the helm for a short time. Following the resignation of the entire board of directors, led by its chairman Eric Honegger, Mario Corti, then Nestlé’s chief financial officer, took over.
More
‘Swissair Souvenirs’
He came under pressure, above all from Swissair’s principal bank, UBS, under the leadership of Marcel Ospel. Corti would later hold Ospel responsible for the grounding. “Super-Mario”, as he was known in the media at the time, did attempt to keep the airline in the air with the help of the government and by setting up a rescue company under the Crossair umbrella.
On September 29, however, the government refused to grant a financial guarantee. On October 1, Crossair, under the leadership of André Dosé, finally took over Swissair’s flight operations. The operating companies SAirGroup, SAirLines and Flightlease were placed under debt restructuring proceedings.
No one held to account
But this rescue came too late. On October 2, the grounding took place, which was intended to persuade the government and the banks to reconsider their position.
Reduced operations resumed the very next day thanks to an emergency loan. On April 1, 2002, however, the last Swissair scheduled flight from São Paulo landed in Zurich at 7:15am. With that, the name Swissair came to an end after 71 years of history.
It took years to come to terms with the biggest corporate collapse in Swiss history. Legally, no one was held to account: all 19 former managers and board members who had been charged were acquitted. The financial settlement was only finalised last December – 24 years after the grounding – with the removal of the holding company SAirGroup from the commercial register.

In a statement released late on Thursday, the Iranian Foreign Ministry condemned the illegal and inhumane measures and actions adopted by the US government to disrupt Iran’s commercial exchanges and air transportation with other countries through the extraterritorial enforcement of unlawful US sanctions.
“The ministry emphasizes that these measures not only run counter to the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter and international law, particularly the principle of respect for the national sovereignty of countries, and violate fundamental human rights norms, but also constitute a dangerous scheme aimed at undermining friendly relations among countries, particularly neighboring states,” the Iranian ministry warned.
“In this regard, while recalling the deep historical, religious, cultural and people-to-people ties between the Iranian and Iraqi nations, and appreciating the fraternal relations and good-neighborliness between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Iraq, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs considers the imposed restrictions on civil air travel between Iran and Iraq to be contrary to the common interests and welfare of the two countries,” the statement added.
“Relations between Iran and Iraq go beyond the conventional relations between two neighboring countries and are based on deep people-to-people ties and mutual interests in various fields. The travel of millions of Iranian and Iraqi citizens for economic and commercial activities, pilgrimage to holy sites, tourism, education, and medical treatment necessitates that issues related to transportation and communications between the two nations be managed through an independent, responsible, and forward-looking approach based on common interests,” it also stated.
“The restrictions imposed on air travel between the two countries, in addition to creating serious problems for hundreds of thousands of passengers, pilgrims, patients, students and economic actors from both countries, are in clear conflict with the nature of the strategic relations between Iran and Iraq, which are based on good-neighborly ties,” it noted.
“While respecting the national sovereignty of the Republic of Iraq, the Islamic Republic of Iran calls for appropriate decisions to be adopted in confronting the US economic terrorism and its acts of fomenting discord, in order to remove the restrictions and restore normal conditions for flights operated by the airlines of the two countries, in line with the interests and welfare of the two nations,” the ministry said.

Lithuania tests Ukrainian-developed drone detection system SkyFortress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:31:00 UTC
16:31:00 KST

Lithuania is testing a Ukrainian-developed airspace monitoring system designed to detect low-flying drones and other threats by analysing acoustic and radio signals, the Defence Ministry said Friday.
The pilot deployment of the SkyFortress system is intended to strengthen the first stage of Lithuania’s air defene network – detecting and tracking potential threats before they can be intercepted.
“Air threats are changing rapidly, so we are adapting our solutions accordingly,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said in a statement. “Instead of developing everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine.”
SkyFortress uses artificial intelligence to detect and track low-flying drones and cruise missiles based on acoustic or electromagnetic signatures, the ministry said. The system can classify detected objects in real time.
Under a contract signed this summer, the project also includes processing data collected by the system’s sensors, using libraries of digital acoustic and radio-frequency signatures based on unclassified data, and training personnel, according to the ministry.
Testing will assess the system’s ability to detect and identify low-flying unmanned aircraft in Lithuania.
The deployment comes as Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours have strengthened airspace security amid Russia’s war against Ukraine and an increase in reports of potential air threats in the region.
A drone that entered Lithuania from Belarus was shot down over Lithuanian territory in September by Italian fighter jets stationed in Šiauliai. It was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuania. Similar incidents had previously occurred in Latvia and Estonia.
The Defence Ministry said SkyFortress will contribute to strengthening Lithuania’s broader air defence capabilities, from surveillance and identification to the interception and neutralisation of aerial threats.

louvre-lens turns cuteness into an art history of pink, plush toys and kawaii
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:30:55 UTC
16:30:55 KST

so cute! louvre-lens exhibition unpacks the art of happiness from ancient times until today
through more than 300 works, from ancient cats to rebellious soft toys and the history of pink and glitter, the show examines art's ability to bring us joy and comfort.
LOUVRE-LENS TRACES THE ART AND AESTHETICS OF CUTENESS
Cuteness gets the museum treatment at Louvre-Lens with So Cute! The Art of Happiness, an exhibition tracing how artists and cultures have produced — and occasionally weaponized — the feeling of ‘aww’ from antiquity to the present. Bringing together around 300 paintings, sculptures, photographs, films, objects and installations, the show moves between animals, babies, the color pink, soft toys, glitter and kawaii culture to ask why certain shapes, gestures and materials trigger affection, comfort and the instinct to protect. In other words, the museum is taking cute seriously, without pretending it has always behaved itself.
Curated by Annabelle Ténèze, director of Louvre-Lens, and Émilie Girard, director of the Musées de la Ville de Strasbourg, the exhibition places works from radically different periods into deliberately unlikely conversations. Egyptian cats and ancient babies meet Théodore Géricault, Auguste Renoir, Nicolas Poussin, Jeff Koons and Philippe Katerine, while Cindy Sherman, Rosa Bonheur, Agnès Varda, William Wegman and Pierre et Gilles expand the story through portraits, pets and pop culture. Rather than defining cuteness as a fixed aesthetic, the exhibition treats it as something that shifts with time, geography and whoever happens to be doing the looking.
FROM KAWAII AND PINK TO CUTENESS WITH A DARKER SIDE
One section follows kawaii back well beyond its contemporary overload of mascots and merchandise. The Japanese term emerged centuries ago before developing into the visual vocabulary of rounded forms, oversized heads, large eyes and soft colors now embedded in manga, fashion and advertising. Takashi Murakami appears among the artists extending that language into contemporary art, while an adjacent chapter looks at South Korea’s own culture of cuteness. Elsewhere, pink gets its historical due, alongside works by Cindy Sherman and Ettore Sottsass, whose Ultrafragola mirror makes a fairly convincing case that a color can be both sweet and spectacularly self-aware.
The sugar rush does not last uninterrupted. So Cute! also examines the relationship between adorableness, consumer culture, propaganda, war imagery and social critique, showing how supposedly innocent visual codes can comfort, persuade or unsettle depending on their context. Soft toys move from childhood companions to artistic tools for addressing memory and vulnerability, while the mischievous expressions of characters such as Labubu complicate the idea of the perfectly behaved plushie. The exhibition ends this line of thinking with Pascal Lièvre’s glitter-covered reinterpretations of Louvre icons, where sequins and drag aesthetics turn familiar masterpieces into something brighter, stranger and considerably less reverential.
MATHIS BOUCHER BUILDS A PINK, INTERACTIVE DREAMWORLD
Architect-scenographer Mathis Boucher translates the theme into an environment conceived somewhere between a story and a video game. Visitors pass through a rounded pink entrance into a sequence of dreamlike rooms linked by curves, soft edges and tactile materials including fur, mirrors, bouclé and carpet. Rabbit-shaped magnifying glasses and other ‘treasure objects’ are tucked into the route, while a chapter dedicated to cuteness’ darker side interrupts the fantasy before the exhibition heads towards what the museum describes as a happy ending in a puff of glitter. Argile developed a custom powder tone, dubbed Louvre-Lens Pink, specifically for the scenography.
The visitor is not expected to remain entirely passive in all this softness. A 2.7-meter-wide wheel of emotions greets the public before entry, while interactive labels, a kawaii guide character named Momo, a manga library and a multisensory ‘Symphony of Emotions’ room invite different ways of moving through the show. At the end, visitors can even vote for the work that affected them most. The cheerful scenography also hides a pragmatic layer: almost 90% of its display cases and 80% of its hanging system come from the museum’s reuse program. So Cute! The Art of Happiness runs at Louvre-Lens through January 18, 2027.
project info:
name: Trop mignon! L’art du bonheur | So Cute! The Art of Happiness
 curators: Annabelle Ténèze and Émilie Girard
 location: Louvre-Lens, Lens, France | @louvrelens
 when: September 23, 2026 – January 18, 2027

Apparent drone crashed in Romania amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, causing a fire
Kyiv • UNN
An apparent drone crashed near Plauru in Romania and caused a fire. There were no casualties or damage; the Ministry of Defense is conducting an investigation.
In Romania, during the night of October 2, what was preliminarily identified as a drone was found to have crashed near the border, amid the Russian attack on Ukraine, followed by a fire. This was reported by the country's Ministry of Defense, according to UNN.
During the night of October 1–2, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defense detected new drone attacks on civilian and infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, near the river border with Romania, in the northern part of Tulcea County. "We would like to note that the radar systems of the Ministry of National Defense did not report any unauthorized intrusions into the national airspace during the preceding night," the statement said.

The court extended the preventive measures for Odrex doctors accused of medical negligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The court extended the preventive measures for Odrex doctors accused of medical negligence
Kyiv • UNN
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa upheld the preventive measures against Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska in the case of medical negligence that may have caused the death of Adnan Kivan.
On October 1, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa extended the preventive measures imposed on doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who have been accused of improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker. Both remain subject to a personal recognizance obligation, while Rusakov was also suspended from his position, reports UNN.
After the hearing, the accused Rusakov said that he had resigned of his own accord from the position of head of the surgical department at the Odrex clinic. At the same time, the statement does not make clear exactly when he resigned or whether the relevant documents were added to the court case file.
In addition, the hearing took place with court-appointed defense attorneys present: due to the absence of Rusakov’s and Bielotserkovska’s attorneys, the court appointed a separate defense attorney for each of the accused and continued consideration of the issue of preventive measures.
Will the delay in the Odrex case have consequences for the lawyers?16.09.26, 09:01 • 36933 views
This occurred amid the accused doctors’ attorneys’ regular failures to appear and motions to postpone hearings, which have repeatedly impeded consideration of the case in recent months.
Thus, in September, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa scheduled 13 hearings in the case against the Odrex doctors, but seven of them did not take place or the court was unable to proceed to consideration of the case on its merits. Only six hearings took place in full—less than half.
The presiding judge in the case, Viktor Chaplytskyi, deemed the reasons for the doctors’ attorneys’ regular failures to appear unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. It is to assess whether the defense attorneys’ actions show signs of a disciplinary offense.
Due to the regular postponements, the court has still been unable to proceed to one of the key stages of the trial—the questioning of the medical expert. The court had planned to hear the expert back in May, but at that time Rusakov’s defense raised the issue of changing the venue.
The medical expert is to analyze the documentation, the findings of the examinations conducted, and compliance with treatment protocols, and explain the medical component of the possible causal link between the doctors’ actions and the patient’s death. The court will provide the final assessment of this evidence and the issue of the accused persons’ guilt.
Reminder
Doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, have been accused under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker.
According to the investigation, during Adnan Kivan’s treatment, the medical staff made significant errors, as a result of which the patient developed sepsis that, against the background of his oncological disease, led to his death.

Taiwan receives first new F-16s three years behind plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:13:09 UTC
16:13:09 KST

- Taiwan's Air Force took delivery of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Oct. 2.
- The $8 billion order, approved in 2019, was expected to begin deliveries in 2023 but was delayed by production and software problems.
Taiwan’s Air Force has received the first two of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets bought from the United States, after the aircraft landed at Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung around noon on Oct. 2.
The arrival comes about a month later than expected and roughly three years behind the original schedule. The two jets had been due in Taiwan by late August or early September, but stayed in Hawaii for weeks without explanation, Focus Taiwan reported, after local media said they had turned back shortly after taking off for Guam.
The United States approved the $8 billion sale of 66 F-16 Block 70 jets in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term. Deliveries were supposed to start in 2023 and finish by the end of 2026, but production delays, supply chain problems and software integration issues pushed the schedule back. Lockheed Martin unveiled the first newly built F-16 Block 70 for Taiwan at its plant in Greenville, South Carolina, in March 2025.
The new jets will be based at Chihhang, where they will go through ground inspections while pilots and maintainers convert to the aircraft. Taiwan’s government budgeted NT$247.2 billion, about $8 billion, for the purchase between 2020 and 2026, and says the jets will strengthen air defense along the island’s east coast, the side facing the open Pacific, where Chinese aircraft and ships have operated during large-scale drills around Taiwan.
The Block 70 is the newest production version of the F-16, built at Lockheed Martin’s South Carolina line. It carries the AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, a newer mission computer and updated electronic warfare and communications systems, along with conformal fuel tanks that hug the fuselage to add range without taking up weapons stations. It also has strengthened landing gear to handle heavier takeoff weights and weapons loads.
Taiwan already flies more than 140 older F-16A/B fighters, which have been upgraded to a similar F-16V standard in a program completed in 2023. The 66 new jets will take Taiwan’s F-16 fleet to more than 200 aircraft, giving it the backbone of a force that scrambles almost daily to shadow Chinese military aircraft.
The delivery came about a week after Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. Taiwan is still waiting for U.S. approval of a separate arms package worth about $14 billion that Trump paused after Chinese objections, AFP reported.
Taiwanese officials have said more F-16 Block 70s will arrive before the end of the year, but they have not given a number. Remaining deliveries are expected to stretch into 2027 and 2028.

"There were many warnings and many nights when the system was occupied with clarifying the situation and raising and lowering the alert level. There were many nights of heightened readiness. Hezbollah? It definitely factors into Iran's calculations if Iran enters into a confrontation with Israel," the official said.
According to the defense official, the Iranians are constantly assessing the situation in the US and the extent of Washington's readiness to enter into a confrontation with them, and this affects Tehran's own assessment of the situation.
Economic pressure mounts on Iran
The official also stressed that conditions in Iran are deteriorating and that the effect of US sanctions can be clearly seen.
The number of tankers leaving the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz has been rising, and according to IDF data, an average of 30 to 40 tankers are now passing through each day. That figure reflects levels seen before the war. In other words, Iranian influence in the strait is declining.
The official also noted that the Iranian rial had reached a new low in recent days, with nearly 2.5 million rials now equivalent to one US dollar. At the same time, he clarified that Iran had not yet reached hyperinflation.
The official illustrated the economic situation by citing a critical article in an Iranian newspaper identified with the regime that compared the price of eggs in Iran with the average salary, adding that the cost of living in Iran was now "unbearable."
Compounding the economic pressure is what the official described as a US naval blockade of Iran that began this week. In addition to the sanctions, he said, the measure contains elements that are humiliating for Tehran because it prevents even family visits to neighboring countries.
As a result, the Iranians quickly approached neighboring countries and asked them to restore civilian flights. So far, according to the official, only Iraq has agreed, while there are currently no flights with Azerbaijan.
Israel prepares for risk of escalation
Israeli defense officials assess that Tehran is considering how to respond to the situation, what tools remain available to it, and what form its response should take. As evidence, they point to Iranian efforts to target vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that have so far failed.
The defense establishment believes Iran's range of options has narrowed significantly because of the naval blockade. This comes alongside Iranian attempts to carry out attacks abroad that have also failed, according to the assessment.
Israeli defense officials further assess that unless Iran attempts to break the blockade through a deliberate military move or reaches understandings with the US, it will be forced to contend with worsening domestic problems caused by the sanctions.
The IDF is therefore preparing for the possibility that an Iranian initiative could spiral out of control, such as a cruise missile striking a US vessel and causing fatalities, creating a situation in which it would be unclear how Washington would respond.
Israeli defense officials also assess that if the Iranians conclude that they are about to come under attack, or that the regime is losing ground in its confrontation with the US, they could potentially launch attacks against US assets in Jordan or Israel.
A senior official said the Iranians understand very well what the price of such a move would be, and that this is why they have not attacked Israel.

Singapore EV sales forecast to rise 34.3 pct in 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:12:51 CST
16:12:51 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's electric vehicle (EV) sales are forecast to rise 34.3 percent in 2026 to 34,940 units, lifting EVs' share of total vehicle sales to 54.6 percent, BMI Country Risk and Industry Research said on Thursday.
The Fitch Group unit attributed the growth to government tax incentives, an influx of affordable models produced in the Chinese mainland and the expansion of charging infrastructure.
As of June 2026, EVs accounted for 70 percent of new vehicle registrations, and the BMI expects the trend to continue through 2035, when EVs are projected to make up 44 percent of Singapore's vehicle fleet.
Generous subsidies and rebates, along with measures such as the EV Common Charger Grant, which supports charger installations at private residences, are expected to sustain demand, BMI said. It forecasts EVs will account for 85 percent of total vehicle sales by 2035.
In the first quarter of 2026, EVs accounted for 57.6 percent of new car registrations, or 7,679 vehicles. This was the first time EV sales exceeded those of internal combustion engine and hybrid vehicles. ■

China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:12:44 CST
16:12:44 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On Oct. 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to accommodate the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that Friday's popular departure cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, and Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organization and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
The China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring over 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
The China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains on the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
The China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays with their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which extends from Sept. 23 to Oct. 8. ■

India news: Delhi protesters turn up heat on election chief

What you need to know
- Protesters are gathering in New Delhi's Jantar Mantar to demand the election commission chief's resignation
- They are calling for Gyanesh Kumar to step down amid allegations that voter rolls have been manipulated
- Police tighten security, saying permission to hold the protest had not been granted
Here are the top headlines from India on Friday, October 2:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
IN PICTURES: Thousands protest across Delhi, Mumbai
Thousands show up in Mumbai's Cockroach protest against election chief
Thousands of protesters converged at south Mumbai's Shivaji Park on Friday evening, to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the mass deletion of voters from electoral rolls.
While a protest in Delhi was being led by student bodies and political parties, Mumbai's demonstrations was led by the Cockroach Janta Party which galvanized thousands of Indians earlier a few months ago to force the resignation of former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke posted visuals from the Mumbai protest which showed a sea of demonstrators while he addressed them from a stage.
In another post, Dipke said 'Season 2 begins.'
The protest in India's financial capital began at around 4 p.m. (1030 GST) and is likely to continue into the evening.
Police detain over 700 protesters in Delhi
Delhi Police on Friday detained more than 700 people, including opposition leaders and members of student organizations, News agency PTI reported in and around the grounds of Jantar Mantar, amid a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Activists, opposition leaders and student bodies are demanding Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of electoral rolls, which led to mass deletion of voters.
The detentions were made under prohibitory orders issued earlier on Friday to prevent people from assembling, chanting, demonstrating, or giving speeches.
Authorities had earlier clarified that they had not granted protesters permission to demonstrate in central Delhi.
"My motivation is our future," 19-year-old protester Nidhi Sharma, a Delhi University student, told AFP. "I have to vote."
At the Delhi protest, Mina Giri, 38, said her name had been removed from the rolls even though she has lived in the capital for 15 years and voted in previous elections.
"How could my fundamental right be taken away from me?" she said.
In other news from India
PM Modi speaks with Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke with Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar, who was injured in an alleged mid-air attack on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, lauding him for his bravery and presence of mind.
A video of the conversation, posted on the PM's social media, showed the bandaged captain briefing Modi about the incident and about what gave him the courage to confront the attacking co-pilot.
"I was trying to save my own life, but I knew I could not let all those people die," Machchhar said during a call from his hospital bed.
India trade minister meets counterparts on sidelines of G20 event
India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal met with his counterparts from France, Canada, Saudi Arabia and South Korea to discuss furthering bilateral trade, at a time when India is looking to diversify away from the United States.
The meetings were held on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee.
At the same G20 event, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not think there was "something imminent" on the trade deal with India, News agency PTI reported.
A pending trade deal between New Delhi and Washington has been in a stalemate over threat of new tariffs, sunset clauses and possiblyIndia's use of Russian oil. Greer and Goyal met on Wednesday and said they had a "productive discussion" on the conclusion of an interim trade agreement.
British activist released from Delhi after 9 years in prison
British-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal was released from a prison in Delhi on Thursday after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court. Johal had been in jail for nine years without trial.
The court had ordered Johal's release on September 18 and later warned the government against continued attempts to keep him imprisoned.
Johal was detained on charges of terrorism and targeted killings, and has been a point of diplomatic tensions between India and the UK. While he was acquitted of one terrorism-linked charge in March 2025, eight other charges remain.
Election body orders 'special drive' to enroll 'left out' voters
The Election Commission of India has directed 20 of India's states and union territories to conduct a "special drive" to enroll voters who were "left out" during the controversial revision of electoral rolls. The ECI posted the order, dated October 1, on X on Friday.
"Voter enrollment is a continuous process and any person not yet enrolled in the electoral roll or whose name has got deleted can apply for enrollment at any point of time. The objective of the special drive is to identify and facilitate such electors," the order said.
This comes amid increasing scrutiny of the controversial revision of polling lists and protests in central Delhi over the scale of voters deleted from electoral rolls.
Police deploys water cannons, tear gas at protest site
Protesters began arriving near the heavily barricaded grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi early on Friday morning. DW reporters on the ground witnessed police detaining people, seemingly at random.
Around 11:15 a.m. local time (0545 GMT), a large rally led by the Students' Federation of India (SFI) reached the site. The SFI is a leftist students' body, which, along with others, has been demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's ouster.
Protesters clashed with the police as authorities tried to block the road leading to Jantar Mantar.
Water cannons and tear-gas shell launchers were deployed at the scene, although they have not yet been used.
How does this related to Narendra Modi's BJP?
The protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar are partially being viewed as renewed pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The reason behind it may not be immediately obvious since the Election Commission of India (ECI) is meant to be an independent body. But this might help:
Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, along with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, comprise the Election Commission of India.
They are responsible for overseeing elections and related projects such as the SIR exercise, which is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls.
Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. They have also accused ECI chief Kumar of doing the central government's bidding even though the institute is meant to maintain its independence.
The BJP has dismissed those claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.
Moreover, a 2023 law introduced by the Modi government changed the way the ECI Chief was appointed, giving the government a greater say. Critics have questioned Kumar's credibility and ability to stay independent given the government's heavy role in his appointment.
Why are people protesting?
Pressure on Kumar intensified in September after the Indian Express newspaper reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally raised concerns over aspects of the Special Intensive Revisions (SIR) at least 14 times over the past 10 months.
The objections relate to new voter registrations, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls, filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process and the custody and security of the entire electoral roll itself, the report said.
In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
The Election Commission had dismissed concerns of an internal rift, saying differing views were a "normal" part of deliberations and that all its actions were lawful.
Over 130 million Indian voters have been struck off the draft voters list across 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express report said, putting the ECI in the middle of a national debate over who votes and who doesn't.
Protesters gather in Jantar Mantar to demand Gyanesh Kumar's resignation amid heavy security
Thousands of protesters, activists, opposition members and student bodies are expected to gather in central Delhi's iconic Jantar Mantar grounds today to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Jantar Mantar is an 18th-century observatory and adjoining grounds in central Delhi. Apart from being a protected landmark, the venue serves as the national capital's primary designated zone for public demonstrations and campaigns.
Today's protest is the latest escalation in growing scrutiny of the poll-governing body of the largest democracy in the world — long regarded as one of the country's most trusted independent institutions.
Political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) will not be demonstrating in New Delhi today, according to a clarification posted on X earlier this week.
The group is, however, scheduled to hold a rally against Kumar in Mumbai on Friday, and plans to take the demonstrations nationwide in the coming days.
Visuals coming out of central Delhi showed heavy police and security deployment. Several entry points to the grounds have been barricaded, and authorities have imposed a prohibitory order under Indian law, according to news agency ANI.
Under this order, public meetings, assemblies of five or more people, processions, sloganeering, demonstrations and making speeches without permission are prohibited.
Incidentally, today is the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, informally known as the "father of the nation." Gandhi is known for his non violent demonstrations, marches and hunger strikes, contributing to British India's freedom movement against colonial rule and ultimately leading to India's independence in 1947.
Welcome to our coverage!
Hello, and welcome to DW's India blog!
This is Mahima from Studio Delhi, where the thermometer is beginning to dip with every passing day.
But the heat is still on in the national capital, with protesters gathering at the iconic Jantar Mantar grounds in central Delhi. These are the same grounds which acted as the base for the Cockroach movement a few months ago, leading to the ouster of India's then education minister.
Now, the Chief of India's Election Commission is under fire with protesters demanding his resignation over his role in a controversial revision of electoral rolls which reportedly led to deletion of over 130 million voters across 30 states and union territories.
Authorities have beefed up security in the area, and several metro stations have been shut to limit public access.
DW has multiple reporters on the ground to bring you the latest.

Russia is &quot;creating a new shadow fleet&quot; to finance the war in Ukraine — UK Foreign Office

Russia is "creating a new shadow fleet" to finance the war in Ukraine — UK Foreign Office
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is creating a new shadow fleet of tankers to circumvent sanctions and preserve gas revenues. Britain has imposed sanctions on the vessels and individuals involved.
Russia is attempting to create a new "shadow fleet" of tankers to circumvent sanctions and preserve the revenues from gas exports that the Kremlin uses to finance its war against Ukraine. The Telegraph reports this, citing a statement by the UK Foreign Office, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that Russia has built at least two new tankers, approximately 300 meters long, to transport liquefied natural gas (LNG) through the Arctic; both vessels entered service earlier this year.
The UK Foreign Office believes that the Kremlin has requisitioned a number of other vessels to strengthen its secret fleet, which is increasingly becoming subject to seizure by NATO.
The UK government reported Putin's likely attempt to expand the fleet on Thursday and also announced the introduction of new sanctions against Russia.
The Kremlin is attempting to create a dangerous new "shadow fleet" to circumvent sanctions and maintain revenues from gas exports… The new sanctions package includes several vessels acquired to carry out this task, including those that entered service very recently—in July this year
In addition, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on eight more vessels, including new-generation liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers—the "Alexey Kosygin" and "Konstantin Posyet," which sail under the Russian flag.
These vessels, with a displacement of 127,555 tons, were built in Russia and entered service earlier this year. Both are capable of breaking through ice up to two meters thick, indicating the possibility of their use as part of Russia's advance into the Arctic and the Far North.
The third vessel, the "Pyotr Stolypin," also joined the fleet this year and was sanctioned along with the "Portovyy," "Chaivo," "Avacha," "Bebek-E" (built in 1979), and "Galle Energy"—a 75-foot personnel transport vessel sailing under the flag of Sri Lanka.
To date, the EU has imposed sanctions on approximately 670 vessels, banning them from entering European ports, while the United Kingdom has taken measures against around 600 tankers used to finance Putin's war machine.
It is noted that the sanctions announced on Thursday also target eight individuals involved in the arbitrary detention, torture, and cruel treatment of Ukrainian civilians, including a current employee of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).
Sanctions were also imposed on seven more individuals for their role in the indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children, including those deported by the Russian authorities.

Bailout package for Swiss electricity firms will not be extended
The bailout scheme for systemically important electricity companies in times of crisis will not be extended. On Thursday, parliament declined to consider a proposal to that effect from the government.
Following the House of Representatives, the Senate also rejected the proposal to extend the Federal Act on Subsidiary Financial Assistance for the Rescue of Systemically Important Companies in the Electricity Sector. The Senate thus followed the recommendation of its preparatory committee.
As the government also did not stand by its proposal – to extend the validity of the rescue package by five years until the end of 2031 – a vote was not held. The Act has been limited in duration until the end of 2026 and will therefore expire on December 31, 2026.
More
Explainer: how the Swiss electricity market works
Committee Chair Thierry Burkart emphasised that it is not the government but the companies and their owners who are responsible for taking appropriate precautions for crisis situations.
The so-called rescue package had been brought into force by parliament as a matter of urgency during the autumn session of 2022. This was due to extreme price rises on the energy markets. There were fears that large electricity companies would no longer be able to provide the security deposits required for trading, which would have jeopardised Switzerland’s electricity supply. To date, no federal loans have actually been drawn down.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,537,390 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:37:37 UTC
15:37:37 KST

Russia has lost around 1,537,390 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 2.
The number includes 1,520 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,388 tanks, 25,471 armored combat vehicles, 156,309 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,592 artillery systems, 2,175 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,683 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,810 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.
