Trump administration is redirecting aid under the Ukraine law to Latin America - WP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:36:46 EEST
15:36:46 KST

Trump administration is redirecting aid under the Ukraine law to Latin America - WP
Kyiv • UNN
The Trump administration, over Democrats’ objections, redirected $52 million approved for four countries in Europe and the Middle East. Panama, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia will receive the funds.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, acting contrary to the demands of leading Democrats on the House and Senate foreign affairs committees, has stripped tens of millions of dollars in U.S. military aid from European countries included in a supplemental bill supporting Ukraine and its closest European neighbors, as well as Middle Eastern countries, and will instead provide these funds to conservative governments in Latin America. Three U.S. officials told The Washington Post, UNN reports.
Details
The U.S. State Department informed Congress of its intentions in September, prompting Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen and Democratic Representative Gregory Meeks to suspend the diversion of the funds.
Late on Wednesday, September 30, the administration informed Congress without public disclosure that it was disregarding the suspension and proceeding with the diversion of $52 million to Panama, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia—funds that had been approved for Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia, and Iraq, officials said.
In a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, Shaheen and Meeks called the move a violation of the freeze they had imposed and of statutory requirements governing where the funds could go. The diversion of funding for Slovakia and North Macedonia has drawn particularly strong opposition because the funds were included in a supplemental bill concerning Ukraine, specifically intended for countries affected by the war in Ukraine, the publication reports.
"Both chambers of Congress provided these funds for a very specific purpose: supporting Ukraine and our European allies following Russia's full-scale invasion," they wrote in the letter, a copy of which was obtained by The Post. "The executive branch does not have unlimited authority to redirect these funds to unrelated policy priorities of the administration or countries," the letter states.
In response to questions about the lawmakers' objections, the State Department told The Post that the money would be better used in Latin America in line with Trump's foreign policy doctrine, which calls for a reorientation toward the Western Hemisphere.
"Reprogramming funds from the Middle East and Europe to the Western Hemisphere is consistent with the National Security Strategy," the State Department said in a statement. "Funds used in our region will be directed toward combating narco-terrorism in our hemisphere and will help continue to ensure the security of the Panama Canal," the statement said.
"Funds used in the Western Hemisphere will strengthen the U.S. security partnership and counter adversary military influence in our shared region," the department added.
The State Department did not respond to questions regarding Shaheen and Meeks's assertion that the administration's diversion of funds approved by Congress violates statutory requirements.
Congress approved these funds in 2022 at the beginning of the war in Ukraine. At the time, Washington also relied on non-European countries to end their arms-sale relations with Russia, seeking to isolate the Kremlin.
In addition to assisting Ukraine and its closest European neighbors, the bill was intended to help foreign countries begin purchasing U.S. military equipment instead of Russian equipment, particularly countries that had supplied Ukraine with their older weapons.
Last month, Democratic representatives met with State Department officials to ask how providing funding to Latin American countries could be interpreted as a response to the "situation in Ukraine" or as directing funds to countries "affected by the situation in Ukraine," as stated in the original bill.
The Trump administration "failed" to explain this during briefings for lawmakers or in subsequent written responses to their requests for clarification, Meeks and Shaheen said in their letter to Rubio.
Administration officials "also confirmed that Colombia, Ecuador, Panama and Peru have not provided significant security assistance to Ukraine or to other European allies and partners affected by Russia’s war in Ukraine," they wrote.
Jeremy Shapiro, director of research at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said European countries would view this as a "harbinger" of how the Trump administration will prioritize global affairs.
"This will reinforce the feeling that Europeans could be abandoned if they do not pass a loyalty test or do what the administration wants regarding Iran," he said.

Photos: Major overhaul progresses at Tallinn's Kadriorg Stadium
At Kadriorg Stadium, work is underway across the entire territory, and renovation of the main building as well as construction of the opposite stand of the main arena has begun.
On the main arena, new drainage and irrigation systems are being built for the stadium's grass field, and the track surface has been removed, said Margus Jurkatam, head of the Tallinn Sports Center's Central District
Construction of the opposite stand of the main arena is also underway. In the future, it should accommodate about 5000 spectators.
Construction work on the main arena will be completed in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Renovation of Building A has also begun, and a connecting tunnel between Buildings A and B is being built. Construction work on Building B is in its final stage, and the building's completion deadline is December, Jurkatam said.
Building A is the historical main building of Kadriorg Stadium, while Building B is a completely new building that will house service and changing rooms, conference rooms, and a strength and warm‑up hall.
"A football training arena with a stand is also being built, with a completion deadline in the second quarter of 2027," Jurkatam said.
The completion deadline for the entire complex is January 2028.
ERR wrote in April this year that construction of the stadium will cost €17.1 million without VAT, and the work is being carried out by Nordlin Ehitus OÜ, the winner of the public procurement. With separate procurements, the athletics training arena was renovated by 2021, and by spring 2023 the lighting of the stadium arenas was renewed and its electrical supply improved.

S. Korea's September inflation cools to 2.9 pct on fruit supplies, subsidies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:16:44 CST
15:16:44 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's consumer price inflation cooled down last month, driven by increased fruit supplies and government discount subsidies for the Chuseok holiday, statistical ministry data showed Friday.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.9 percent in September from a year earlier, decelerating from 3.1 percent in the previous month, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
Following the Middle East conflicts, headline inflation fluctuated with 2.2 percent in March, 2.6 percent in April, 3.1 percent in May, 3.2 percent in June, 2.8 percent in July and 3.1 percent in August.
Inflation stayed above the central bank's mid-term inflation target of 2 percent for 13 consecutive months since September 2025.
Amid rising worry about inflationary pressure, the Bank of Korea (BOK) delivered back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3.00 percent.
Prices for agricultural, livestock and fishery products fell 0.3 percent year-on-year in September, fueled by expanded fruit shipments and government discount subsidies for the Chuseok holiday, the South Korean version of Thanksgiving Day.
Agricultural product prices dropped 4.0 percent, pulling down overall inflation by 0.17 percentage points, while those for livestock and fishery products advanced 3.7 percent and 4.5 percent each.
Prices for apple, napa cabbage, peach, grape, spinach and tomato saw a decline, but those for beef, imported beef, pork, mackerel, hairtail and rice gained in single digits.
Processed food prices mounted 2.1 percent in September from a year earlier, faster than a growth of 1.5 percent in the previous month on the back of hikes in factory-gate prices.
Petroleum product prices jumped 14.8 percent last month amid the continued Middle East conflicts.
Computer prices soared 27.4 percent on higher semiconductor costs, and mobile phone prices increased 8.3 percent due to the launch of new smartphones.
Prices for industrial products, including oil products and processed food, advanced 4.2 percent in September from a year earlier after going up 3.7 percent in the prior month.
Service prices swelled 2.7 percent as a result of a surge in international airfares and overseas group travel expenses, which spiked 22.5 percent and 19.3 percent each.
Public service prices, including international airfares, climbed 1.5 percent, while private service prices such as travel expenses picked up 4.3 percent.
Housing rent, including Jeonse and monthly rent, went up 1.3 percent in September compared to the same month of last year.
Jeonse is South Korea's unique contract between two households where a landlord grants the two-year residential right to a tenant, who in turn lends a certain amount of money, or a deposit, to the landlord.
Prices for electricity, natural gas and tap water were up 0.4 percent in September on a yearly basis.
The livelihood items index, which gauges prices for daily necessities, gained 2.5 percent, while the fresh food index, which measures prices for fish, shellfish, fruit and vegetables, dipped 3.3 percent last month.
The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile agricultural and oil products, added 2.7 percent last month, while the OECD-method core price, excluding volatile food and energy costs, was up 2.8 percent. ■

S. Korea abolishes state prosecution service after 78 years, launches new agencies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:16:21 CST
15:16:21 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Korea officially abolished the state prosecution service Friday, ending its 78-year history since its establishment in 1948, while launching new agencies separately in charge of investigation and prosecution.
Under the revised acts, the newly launched public prosecution office will operate under the justice ministry, focusing entirely on indictments and maintaining public prosecution.
The newly established serious crimes investigation agency will be run under the interior ministry and be tasked with directly investigating seven major crime categories and conducting supplementary investigations for crimes targeting vulnerable groups.
Most general criminal investigations will be handled by the police.
Although the prosecution service was disbanded as an institution, the titles of "prosecutor" and "prosecutor general" will remain intact.
Yonhap news agency pointed out that the major overhaul of the criminal justice system stemmed from longstanding domestic criticism over the excessive concentration of power within the prosecution, which critics said led to abusive investigations and indictments.
For a long time, whenever a transition of power occurred in South Korea, the prosecution was consistently plagued by controversies over "targeted investigations" and "politically motivated prosecutions." ■

Greece pushes EU to suspend asylum during mass migration surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:16:14 UTC
15:16:14 KST

Greece pushes EU to suspend asylum during mass migration surges
EU migration pact improvements face criticism for insufficient tools to manage large-scale migration emergencies.
Greece has urged the European Union to allow member states to temporarily suspend asylum applications during periods of mass migration, arguing that current rules cannot handle emergencies such as the surge in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.
The proposal was submitted to EU interior ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Thursday during the Justice and Home Affairs Council, and appeared to draw support from some member states.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3More than 55,000 Sudanese refugees flee to Chad as UN calls for funding
- list 2 of 3French court sentences 13 men over deadliest small-boat crossing to UK
- list 3 of 3Migrant crossings to Europe by sea drop sharply amid heightened risks: IOM
Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris said the EU’s migration pact, which took effect in June, had improved the bloc’s ability to manage migration flows but had not gone far enough.
“In such cases, there should be enhanced border surveillance and suspension of asylum,” he told reporters ahead of the meeting.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink backed the approach, saying mass arrivals like those in Ceuta should be “treated as a border management issue rather than an asylum issue”.
Spain estimates more than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most have since returned, about 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some European capitals for a tougher approach.
Anti-immigration sentiment has remained a potent political force across Europe since more than a million people, many of them Syrians fleeing war, arrived in the bloc in 2015. The influx boosted support for nationalist and far-right parties and pushed many governments towards more restrictive migration policies centred on border controls, deterrence and returns.
Irregular arrivals are down 35 percent this year, while returns rose about 8 percent in the first half of the year.
Several member states argue that although the migration pact has helped reduce arrivals, it still lacks sufficient tools to handle large-scale emergencies, despite containing mechanisms intended for such situations.
Plevris’s proposal comes two weeks after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the commission would present an emergency framework allowing member states to respond to sudden, large-scale arrivals.
EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said international law would still have to be respected. “Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times,” he said. “When movements are engineered and weaponised against us, this is not just a migration issue; it is a security issue … Of course we will always comply with fundamental rights and values.”
Ministers also approved a new return regulation on Thursday allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the EU.
Two European Parliament politicians said Rwanda has held preliminary talks with some EU countries about hosting such a facility, citing discussions with Rwandan officials.
Officials from Greece, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Denmark, known as the Group of Five, met on the sidelines of the council on Thursday. Van den Brink said a technical mission visited the potential host country in early September, and the group aims to identify it by the end of this year, with transfers beginning in 2027.

Over 1,000 adult LEGO fans gathered in Denmark near the toy giant’s birthplace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:15:36 UTC
15:15:36 KST

LEGO reported a net profit of around €1.15 billion in the first half of this year, up 32% on the same period last year, as toymakers increasingly cater to adults buying toys for themselves.
More than 1,000 LEGO fans from 36 countries have gathered in a small Danish town, Skærbæk, near Billund, the toy giant’s hometown, to celebrate their love of the plastic bricks.
At Skærbæk Fan Weekend, Adult Fans of LEGO (AFOLs) find a community around a hobby often associated with children. The fan-run event welcomes people who build their own creations as well as those who collect sets.
“It's a place where AFOLs come together, no matter where they come from, no matter which language they speak, no matter what they believe in,” said Stephan Sander, co-organiser of the event.
“They have just one thing in common and that's the love for the brick.”
Adults have long enjoyed playing with LEGO, but pandemic lockdowns helped rekindle toy buying among adults, industry insiders say.
Some longtime fans also describe a shift in how their hobby is perceived.
Didier Bruel, a 66-year-old French retiree, recalled avoiding the subject when colleagues asked what he had done over the weekend.
“I would be careful not to say that I was doing my LEGO in my basement because they would have looked at me as a bit [of a] bizarre guy,” he said.
Bruel said The LEGO Movie and television programme LEGO Masters helped make the hobby more widely accepted.
“You become kind of a star, right? So it's completely different in the last 20 years”.
Toymakers cater to adult buyers
Adult spending is also boosting toy sales. LEGO reported a net profit of around €1.15 billion in the first half of this year, up 32% on the same period last year.
The trend extends beyond LEGO, with adults also buying plush toys, Hot Wheels cars, Barbie dolls and other collectibles.
These buyers are often described as “kidults”, a portmanteau blending of “kid” and “adult”, referring to grown-ups who buy toys for their own enjoyment.
Nearly 40% of European consumers said they bought toys for themselves or another adult in 2025, according to market research company Circana.
Toymakers such as LEGO have responded with products designed for adults, including elaborate sets costing hundreds of euros, well beyond the average child’s pocket money.
“This is not a fad, this is really a long-term trend,” said Frédérique Tutt, global toy industry advisor at Circana.
“Adults and teenagers are proud of saying 'I am collecting, I'm buying toys, aren't you?'”
Tutt pointed to LEGO’s Formula 1 products and Spice Girls set as examples of how the company appeals to different interests.
“LEGO is targeting every single passion point you might have,” she said.

The death of at least seven miners in the Philippines earlier this week was likely due to gas poisoning, police said Friday as investigation of the deadly incident continues.
The miners died Wednesday night inside a pocket mining tunnel in Benguet on the northern island of Luzon, daily Manila Times reported.
The bodies of the deceased, said to range in age from 18 to 62, were recovered Thursday some 20 meters (66 feet) from the tunnel entrance.
Police did not specify which gas was involved and said they had yet to establish its source.

A referendum on Marine Le Pen: Sunday&#039;s elections to the French senate showed a populist victory is possible in the 2027 presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:11:06 UTC
15:11:06 KST

On Sept. 27, France held partial elections to its upper house of parliament on Sunday, with 178 of the Senate’s 348 seats on the ballot. The main takeaway was an increase from three to 14 in the number of senators representing the right-wing populist National Rally and its allies in the Union of the Right for the Republic. Marine Le Pen has already called the result historic, even if a group of this size is nowhere close to big enough to control the legislative body, which remains capable of blocking her populist initiatives. Far more important is the broader trend. The next major date on the French political calendar is April 18, 2027, when the first round of the presidential election will be held. Sunday's results suggest that Le Pen has a real chance of winning it.
Senate elections as part of the presidential campaign
The vote was undoubtedly a success for Marine Le Pen. Her party and its far-right allies had never before had even a small group in the legislature's upper chamber. Yet Le Pen would be wrong to present Sunday's relative success as the guarantee of a second breakthrough: her victory in the 2027 presidential election.
For one thing, Senate elections in France are not direct. Senators are chosen by an electoral college made up of representatives delegated by municipal councils. As a result, a candidate’s party affiliation matters less than their record and reputation in a particular département.
Second, political debate has historically centered on the National Assembly, while senators tend to be less inclined to make high-profile statements. Only a small number of senators, for example, regularly speak out on foreign policy. Finally, the nature of local representation means that the political makeup of the Senate does not mirror the overall balance of political forces in France. In the previous Senate, for example, the traditional Republican right and the centrist coalition held a solid majority, even though their standing at the national level had long been in decline. That balance will remain largely unchanged in the new Senate.
The Senate’s political makeup does not mirror the overall balance of political forces in France
The reasons for this divergence are clear: politics works to a different rhythm at the local level. Voters may agree with the sharp criticisms of the government and established parties leveled by Le Pen or by her opposite number on the left Jean-Luc Mélenchon, but that does not diminish their trust in a good mayor or municipal councilor, even if that person has spent their entire political career in one of those same established parties.
One important conclusion can nevertheless be drawn already. If Marine Le Pen wins the 2027 presidential election, the Senate could become a significant check on her power, particularly when it comes to her plans to amend the Constitution by referendum. The National Rally’s representation in the upper house has grown from negligible to very weak, while the majority remains in the hands of a coalition of moderate conservatives and centrists. The Senate will of course not systematically obstruct a newly elected president (whoever he or she may be), but the populists’ most radical ideas are unlikely to find much support there.
Meanwhile, the presidential campaign is gradually gathering momentum. Even if it has thus far produced no major surprises, there have been some unexpected turns. Few, for example, could have predicted that throughout September all the candidates would be forced to keep discussing gas station prices. Gasoline now costs more than €2 a liter, with diesel even more expensive, at around €2.40. This poses a major and complex problem for the government.
The main issue: the fuel crisis
There are two Frances. One is the France of large- and medium-sized cities, where people can easily get around on foot, by bicycle or tram, and do not rely on cars every day. Given that many drive electric vehicles, it is easy to see why the fuel crisis does not concern them much.
Then there is provincial France, where people commute dozens of kilometers to and from work every day. For them, there is no alternative to the car, and they tend to be people on low or middle incomes who cannot afford anything fancier than an aging diesel Renault.
For them, rising fuel prices have been deeply painful. In September, fishermen were already protesting the fact that every trip to sea had become much more expensive. The anger of provincial France, sudden and fierce, recently found expression in the Yellow Vest movement of 2018-2020 – a nightmare the political establishment does not wish to see repeated.
Taxes account for roughly 56% of the price of fuel. Several of France’s neighbors have temporarily cut fuel taxes, at least in part, making it possible to fill up in Germany or Italy at prices that are lower, even if they are not back to pre-crisis levels. However, with a budget deficit of 5.1% and public debt at 116%, the French government cannot afford to do the same, since any loss of tax revenue would only worsen the situation. Meanwhile, France’s debt-servicing costs are now higher than even Greece’s, which was on the brink of bankruptcy just 15 years ago.
The government is offering targeted assistance to people who have to drive long distances or, like fishermen and farmers, need fuel for their boats and farm machinery. But these are only partial measures, weighed down by inevitable bureaucratic complications. With no end in sight to the crisis around Iran, oil prices appear set to remain high, and if they do, social tensions will only grow.
Taxes account for 56% of the price of fuel in France
The presidential candidates may prefer to talk about something else, but under the circumstances there is no avoiding the question: “What would you do about fuel prices?” Le Pen is promising to unveil a plan in October that would slash government spending so deeply that fuel excise duties could easily be reduced.
The left-wing Mélenchon, meanwhile, wants to freeze prices and while raising taxes on the wealthy and on the profits of large companies. Édouard Philippe and other centrists are more cautious, as some of them were in government until recently and understand the scale of the budget problems. They see both extremes – left and right – as forms of unrealistic populism. In any case, the fuel crisis has become one of the main themes of the presidential campaign and could remain so for a long time afterward, especially if it triggers social unrest.
Leading the polls
The frontrunner for the first round of the presidential election is indeed Le Pen, and she remains firmly at the top of the polls, with support above 30% in a field where no other candidate tops 20%. At the same time, her numbers are slightly below their summer peak of 36%, and some pollsters now put her at 31–33%.
It is worth noting, however, that Le Pen has yet to reveal the details of her economic program, making a substantive assessment of her presidential ambitions impossible.
Le Pen’s support remains above 30%, while none of her rivals has surpassed 20%
What is known for certain? The key slogan of Marine Le Pen’s campaign will be “national priority.” It should not, however, be understood as a translation of Donald Trump’s America First — it is not about settling scores with France’s neighbors or leaving the EU, and is still less about grandiose foreign-policy ambitions.
National priority means tighter immigration rules, withdrawing from international aid programs, and restricting foreigners’ social rights, particularly when it comes to social benefits and housing support. There is nothing surprising about these plans. Marine Le Pen has long advocated lowering the retirement age back to 60 or cutting VAT by saving money on outlays for migrants. She has also promised to sharply reduce aid to Ukraine.
There are two problems with her plans. First, it would be nice to see the figures and scrutinize the calculations of Le Pen’s economic advisers, because there is reason to suspect that the numbers will not add up. France’s huge budget deficit is largely the result of persistent deficits in the pension and social security systems, but instead of reforming them, Le Pen proposes looking for money elsewhere. Some of her ideas may well prove sensible, but the need for fundamental reforms, which she apparently does not intend to pursue, will not disappear.
Second, attempts to put her promised policies into practice could encounter strong institutional resistance. In traditional populist fashion, Le Pen intends to appeal directly to the people by seeking approval in a referendum, including for constitutional amendments. She has little alternative, since it remains unclear whether her party could secure a majority in the National Assembly (to say nothing of the Senate and the Constitutional Council, which would have to approve any referendum) even if she wins the presidential election.
According to the polls, Le Pen remains comfortably in the lead, but the campaign is still ahead. The various contradictions in her program will not trouble her committed supporters, but they may give pause to those in the protest electorate who have the slightest inclination to look beyond the slogans and examine the details.
The battle for the second round
Le Pen still has no serious rival at the top of the race, as her competitors are vying with one another for the right to face the right-wing populist in the second round. A special place in this competition belongs to Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the candidate of the radical-left party La France Insoumise and a perennial contender in presidential elections, where he has typically won around 20% of the vote. Polls currently put him at 19%, potentially enough to carry him into the second round, where he would face Marine Le Pen an a showdown of polar opposites that could end up tipping to the right.
Mélenchon's unfavorable rating is at almost unprecedented levels: more than 60% of French voters say they would never vote for him. A Trotskyist in his youth, Mélenchon has never concealed his hostility toward capitalism in general and the wealthy in particular. His program essentially calls for taking money from the rich by raising every conceivable tax and redistributing the proceeds to the poor in the name of social justice.
Mélenchon’s prospects of reaching the second round would improve if he could unite the entire left behind him, but the Socialists will hold primaries in October to choose a candidate who will have the backing not only of the party but also of moderate left-wing environmentalist movements and trade unions whose members are tired of Mélenchon’s radicalism. Raphaël Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament currently appears to be the frontrunner among the Socialist candidates. According to polls, he could win around 12% in the first round of the presidential vote. He rejects any alliance with La France Insoumise and could challenge Mélenchon for the support of left-wing voters in April.
Among the centrist and center-right candidates, former prime minister Édouard Philippe currently has the strongest position. Polls put him at around 19% in the first round, on par with Mélenchon. Unlike the Socialists, the centrist camp has no primary planned, and there is no guarantee it will unite behind a single candidate — but if it does, that choice will most likely be made in early 2027, after the current contenders have had a chance to test their public support. Whether Philippe or a different centrist ultimately makes it to the second round, they would prove to be a much more challenging opponent for Le Pen given their potential to unite the electorate against her — as happened in 2017 and 2022, when Le Pen lost to Emmanuel Macron by margins of 32% and 17%, respectively.
So far, then, the Senate elections have brought no definitive clarity to the 2027 presidential race. Marine Le Pen is riding high, but until her opponent in the second round is known, uncertainty will remain. Much will depend on whether she faces a politician who can unite the left and the center, or a polarizing figure like Mélenchon.
Still, one thing is already clear: even if she wins in 2027, Le Pen will not control the institutional checks on presidential power, particularly the Senate. Her promise to hold a referendum to overcome resistance from the political establishment is therefore almost certain to fail, even if she manages to win the presidency.

Ukraine works to restore sanctions on Usmanov, Fridman, prepares list of over 20 Russian oligarchs – Sybiha
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:10:53 EEST
15:10:53 KST

In response to the EU's decision to lift sanctions on Russian businessmen Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, the Ukrainian side has prepared a list to impose restrictions on more than 20 Russian oligarchs, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said.
"It's an outrageous story, removing two Russian oligarchs. […] We fought until the last moment, both publicly and privately, to stop this from happening. […] Our response will again be asymmetric. You removed two oligarchs, we'll add twenty more. We've prepared a list, more than twenty Russian oligarchs. And we'll also keep working to bring these two back. That's our approach now, and we're already at the stage of formalizing it," the minister said.
The Ukrainian side is working to get Usmanov and Fridman sanctioned under national jurisdictions, Sybiha said. A number of countries have already confirmed they will not remove the two from their sanctions lists, according to the foreign minister.
"The president has already approved this, and we're also working at the national level to get Usmanov and Fridman sanctioned under national jurisdictions. Canada has confirmed to us it won't remove them from its list. We have Britain, Japan, Australia. And we'll keep pursuing these two individuals in all other jurisdictions," he said.
Ambassadors and permanent representatives of EU member states, after weeks of discussion, finally decided to extend sanctions over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity for three years instead of the previous six months, but at the cost of exempting Usmanov and Fridman from them at the insistence of Slovakia, France and Luxembourg, as previously reported.
Ukraine imposed personal sanctions on Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman on October 19, 2022. Ukraine's Economy Ministry said at the time that sanctions were introduced that day against 256 individuals — oligarchs from the Forbes list and their associates. The list included Fridman's Alfa Group partners Petr Aven, German Khan and Alexei Kuzmichev, as well as Vladimir Lisin, Leonid Mikhelson, Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, Mikhail Prokhorov, Suleiman Kerimov, Elena Baturina, Yuri Kovalchuk and others.
Ukraine nationalized Sense Bank (formerly Alfa-Bank), a major asset belonging to Fridman and his partners, in the summer of 2023. In 2022, ARMA also received court-ordered management of corporate rights and other assets belonging to IDS Ukraine, a Fridman-linked group and the country's largest producer and distributor of mineral water.
In September 2024, Ukraine's Justice Ministry filed a lawsuit with the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) to seize IDS Ukraine's assets and other Ukrainian assets linked to Fridman in favor of the state. These included shares and stakes in the Myrhorod Mineral Water Plant, the Morshyn Oskar Mineral Water Plant, Industrial and Distribution Systems, Alfa Insurance, and Alfa-Leasing Ukraine. Hearings in the case are ongoing.
Regarding Ukrainian assets belonging to Usmanov and his business partners, the Skoch and Streshinsky families, the HACC already ruled in 2024, following a Justice Ministry lawsuit, to seize them in favor of the state. This involved more than 165,000 tonnes of iron ore products worth an estimated more than UAH 2 billion, as well as 100% of the charter capital of Peter-Service Ukraine LLC, an IT company previously controlled by Usmanov, according to then-Deputy Justice Minister Inna Bahatykh.

Government extends emergency reservist call-ups through November, lowers cap to 200,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:58:17 UTC
14:58:17 KST

The government approved an extension on Wednesday of the emergency framework allowing the IDF to call up reservists under Order 8 through November 30, while reducing the maximum number of call-ups from 240,000 to 200,000, according to a proposal submitted by the Defense Ministry.
Ministers approved two security-related decisions in a telephone vote. The first extends the authority to call reservists into service under Order 8. The second extends by two months the declaration allowing special arrangements for the detention of unlawful combatants.
A legal opinion prepared by the defense establishment devoted considerable attention to the continuing toll on the reserve system. The decision, it said, raises "extremely significant difficulties regarding equality," since the burden on those who actually serve continues to increase while the state has not fulfilled its obligation to ensure equitable conscription across all sectors of the population.
The opinion also noted that the government has not expanded the range of sanctions or sufficiently enforced conscription requirements against draft evaders. The result, according to the opinion, is a situation in which "with one hand the government increases the burden on reservists, and with the other it does not act to enforce the conscription obligation on draft evaders."
Haredi conscription remains central to reserve burden
The issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription also features prominently in the explanation for the continuing need for reservists. According to the IDF's position, expanding the reserve system cannot replace fully utilizing the manpower available through mandatory service, which has a "dramatic impact" on force building.
Call-up orders have been sent to draft-eligible members of the haredi public, and the IDF has stepped up enforcement against draft evaders, but the disparity in the distribution of the burden remains. Despite this, defense officials maintain that the security situation and the IDF's needs do not currently allow the military to end Order 8 reserve call-ups.
In its explanatory notes, the Defense Ministry justified extending the order on the basis of continuing threats, IDF activity in multiple sectors, and operational requirements.
The size of the call-up framework has changed several times over the course of the year. On March 24, amid Operation Roaring Lion and operations against Hezbollah and in other sectors, a framework of up to 400,000 reservists was approved through May 31.
On July 26, a framework of up to 240,000 was approved through September 30. The proposal now approved by ministers will allow up to 200,000 reservist call-ups through November 30, a reduction of 40,000 from the framework expiring on September 30.
The 200,000-call-up framework does not mean that 200,000 reservists may be serving simultaneously. Rather, it is the maximum number of reservist call-ups that may be issued under the order throughout the period.
As a rule, a soldier who is released and subsequently called up again will be counted as an additional call-up, subject to exceptions stipulated in the order. Each call-up will take place only after the available standing forces have been fully utilized and will require individual approval from the head of the IDF Operations Division's Operations Brigade or the official responsible for recruitment and readiness within the brigade.
Nearly three years after October 7, the exceptional use of Order 8 remains necessary, according to the Defense Ministry, because the statutory limitations on reserve service do not allow the IDF to maintain the required force levels for extended periods.
Under the ordinary legal framework, the maximum number of reserve-duty days over a three-year period is 54 days for enlisted personnel, 70 days for commanders, and 84 days for officers. Operational duty may ordinarily be performed once every three years for a period of up to 25 days.
The proposal states that Israel's security needs require maintaining significant troop levels in various sectors for far longer periods, necessitating the continued use of Order 8 call-ups.
The proposal also details steps taken to increase the manpower available to the IDF and ease the burden. Tens of thousands of reservists have been returned from manpower pools to active units, reserve exemptions have been canceled for thousands of soldiers, and the reserve exemption age has been raised to 49 in certain essential professions and units.
In July, a temporary provision stipulated that mandatory service would remain 32 months and would not be shortened to 30 months over the next three years. The defense establishment had originally sought to extend men's mandatory service to 36 months, but the Knesset approved only part of the measure.
According to data attached to the proposal, the total cost of reserve-duty days carried out under Order 8 from January through August stood at NIS 26.7 billion, while the average cost of one day of reserve duty under Order 8 is estimated at approximately NIS 1,000.
The estimated cost of the proposed extension is based on the average volume of reserve-duty days between January and September. If that level continues through October and November, the estimated cost of the additional two months will be approximately NIS 6.6 billion.
Government also extends unlawful combatant detention framework
The second decision submitted for ministers' approval extends the declaration under the Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law. The current declaration expires on September 30, and the government sought to extend it through November 30.
The extension means that the special arrangements introduced during the war regarding the detention of unlawful combatants will remain in force. These include the amount of time allowed before issuing a permanent detention order, the possibility of preventing a detainee from meeting with a lawyer, and the timetable for judicial review.
The ceasefire was signed in October 2025 and intensive ground maneuvers in the Gaza Strip were halted, but according to the Defense Ministry, conditions on the ground still justify extending the declaration.
IDF troops remain in enemy territory, friction continues in various sectors, and dozens of people suspected of involvement in terrorism continue to be detained. Thousands of unlawful combatants remain in detention, including detainees for whom permanent detention orders have not yet been issued and others who have been prevented from meeting with a lawyer.
The legal opinion stated that repeatedly extending the declaration "is not a trivial matter." The number of new detainees has fallen, the ceasefire has already entered into effect, and terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip no longer hold hostages.
Defense officials argue, however, that the IDF remains active on several fronts and that some detainees undergo complex investigations during which it is sometimes necessary to prevent them from meeting with a lawyer.
If the declaration expires, existing decisions preventing detainees from meeting with lawyers would expire immediately. In some cases, authorities would be required to issue a permanent detention order and bring the detainee before a court for judicial review before the investigation had been completed and the necessary factual basis had been established.
Against this background, the legal opinion concluded that although another extension presents difficulties, there is no legal impediment to approving it.
The arrangements currently in force are already narrower than those applied during earlier stages of the war. Under the latest amendment to the temporary provision, which entered into effect on July 1, a permanent detention order for an unlawful combatant must be signed within 18 days of detention, or within 10 days in the case of a minor.
The periods before judicial review were shortened by seven days, and the maximum periods during which a detainee may be prevented from meeting with a lawyer were also reduced.
The Defense Ministry stressed that these are maximum periods and that, in practice, efforts are made to shorten them in accordance with the security situation and the number of new detainees.
Both decisions are being made during an election period, when the government is subject to a heightened duty of restraint. The legal opinions determined that the decisions are urgent, security-related, and limited in duration, and are required because the two existing arrangements expire on September 30.
The opinions therefore concluded that there is no legal impediment to approving them during the election period.

In a statement posted on its official account, the PGSA said on Thursday that several tankers have been hit in the strait in recent days, and that the last three of them were owned or chartered by the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Checks showed that the tankers Al Ruwais, Sinbad and Mersin Prosperity had repeatedly attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz over the past two months.
The authority said the names of all three vessels appear in the latest update of the PGSA non-compliance list. The list covers ships whose status or manner of passage has been found incompatible with the requirements set for safe and authorized transit of the strategic waterway.
This comes as reports said that a supertanker had been hit in the Strait of Hormuz and was burning.
The PGSA has repeatedly warned shipowners and charterers that forcing vessels onto unauthorized routes creates the risk of financial and human losses for the ship, its owner, master and crew, and leads to serious restrictions on any future passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Charterers found to be pressing ships into illegal transit are themselves liable to be added to the non-compliance list, with passage of all their related vessels restricted.
Vessels placed on the list face limits on future transits, including fines, detention or confiscation.
The authority has also cautioned insurers, P&I clubs and classification societies against servicing non-compliant ships, warning of consequences for continued dealings with them.

"Kyiv City Express is running between Kyiv’s banks along its full route and schedule. Despite the enemy attack on the capital, we continue to operate," the Kyiv Circular Railway’s Ukrzaliznytsia social media page reported.

Latvian PM: “We were simply taken for a ride” – 20 million euro cap set per kilometre of Rail Baltica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:53:55 UTC
14:53:55 KST

The Latvian government on Thursday set a maximum cost ceiling of 20 million euros per kilometre for the Rail Baltica railway project, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said following an extraordinary Cabinet meeting.
He explained that, based on a study by independent consultants, the government had decided that costs must not exceed 20 million euros per kilometre. This figure does not include “major structures”, but covers tracks, electrification and signalling needed for “a train to physically run along the main line”.
“These are the costs of the main line; trains are not included,” Kulbergs stressed. According to him, the cost per kilometre had so far ranged from 28 million to 32 million euros.
The Prime Minister said a budget ceiling per kilometre should have been established as early as 2015. Because no such limit was set, the project had entered a “fluid reality”. Changes to technical specifications were allowed, which contributed to the significant increase in the project’s costs, he said.
Kulbergs also said that 
while the airBaltic issue is already extremely costly and complicated, Rail Baltica is “even worse”.
 Under the existing contractual terms, he said, costs have increased by 450 million euros in order to fulfil commitments made when Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) funding was received.
He added that, with the involvement of a consultant, the Ministry of Transport will have to develop a minimum project scenario by December, at which point the actual cost of the first phase should also become clear.
“We need to understand how, with the minimum possible resources, we can achieve a functional railway,” he said.
Kulbergs also stressed that the government had approved the scope of the first phase, which envisages construction of the main-line embankment for a single track, with the possibility of adding a second track in the future, as well as no more than four regional stations.
He also stressed that the main-line construction 
contract signed by Latvia with the E.R.B. Rail JV consortium in December 2023 is highly disadvantageous
 because compensation must be paid even when no construction is taking place, while downtime and cost increases continue.
Kulbergs said someone must be held accountable for the contract.
He argued that the biggest problem with the main-line contract was that professionals capable of defending the state’s interests had not been involved.
“We were simply taken for a ride,” the Prime Minister said.
Kulbergs noted that Estonia and Lithuania had divided their main-line contracts into sections and allowed local construction companies to participate, thereby obtaining lower prices through competitive tenders.
Commenting on possible solutions, he said 
the choices are difficult and negotiations are under way.
 The state must hire professionals to represent its interests and assess the best possible solution, he stressed.
Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) said that when the contract was signed, funding was requested at a time when it was not yet clear how much money would actually be needed.
He stressed that there is insufficient justification for Latvia to cover all the obligations stipulated in the contract, as the country considers a number of cost items disproportionate and inconsistent with the actual situation. It is also necessary to assess how these costs arose.
The minister said specialists and consultants would be sought to prepare the project scope at the minimum technical level.
“Based on the target that has been set – 20 million euros per kilometre – 
it will be possible to determine fairly precise costs, as well as the timeframe within which it can be implemented,”
 Kozlovskis said.
According to the Transport Minister, regardless of future decisions, there is insufficient justification for Latvia to cover all obligations undertaken under the 2023 contract because, in the government’s view, several items are disproportionate and do not correspond to the actual situation.
“And then it must be assessed how they arose – whether this was purely a civil transaction or whether there was some deliberate action that led us to such costs,” Kozlovskis said.
The Prime Minister also said the Baltic states had reached a common position on jointly arriving at the technically minimum solution needed to make the railway functional and “reduce its costs by billions”.
LETA previously reported that in December 2023, Eiropas dzelzceļa līnijas (EDzL) and the E.R.B. Rail JV consortium signed a 3.7 billion euro contract for construction of the Rail Baltica main line.
The E.R.B. Rail JV consortium consists of France’s Eiffage Génie Civil, Poland’s Budimex and Italy’s Rizzani de Eccher.
Main-line construction covers the Rail Baltica route outside the city limits of Riga. The contractor is responsible for building approximately 200 kilometres of Rail Baltica main-line infrastructure, including track substructures and superstructures, earthworks, embankments, railway bridges, roads, underpasses and overpasses, relocation of utility networks, and installation of rails and ballast.
LETA has also reported that the Baltic states have agreed to extend the deadline for the first phase of the Rail Baltica railway project until 2034.
Kulbergs previously said the Baltic states had prepared a final document notifying the European Commission (EC) of their joint agreement on how the Rail Baltica project should proceed.
According to Kulbergs, 
the key elements of the notification include a common agreement on the further implementation of the first phase,
 as well as a joint position on when and how the project should be completed.
“In Brussels, the Baltic states will emphasise that the next funding envelope must include 10 billion euros in European funding for the three Baltic states if this project is to be implemented at all under the current circumstances,” Kulbergs said.
He stressed that the Baltic states need European Union funding because the project cannot be financed from national budgets at a time when the Baltic countries are allocating substantial resources to strengthening the EU’s external border.
It has also been reported that the first phase of the Rail Baltica main line in Latvia is planned within the existing scope, which envisages establishing a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction work at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station to enable Rail Baltica to connect with the existing railway network.
The first phase of Rail Baltica could cost 14.3 billion euros across the Baltic states,
 including 5.5 billion euros in Latvia. However, after indexation, Latvia’s share could rise to six billion euros.
According to the project’s cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros. The previous cost-benefit analysis, conducted in 2017, estimated the total project cost at 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica is intended to establish a European-standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, connecting the Baltic states by rail with the rest of Europe.
The project envisages the construction of a new 870-kilometre European-standard-gauge (1,435 mm) railway line across the Baltic states, with trains capable of reaching a maximum speed of 240 kilometres per hour.

The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:52:00 UTC
14:52:00 KST

The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?
October 30, 2026
Over the past week, three militias from a new alliance, led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), have been fighting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in northern Ethiopia.
The heterogeneous alliance that calls itself the "Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival" brings together seven armed domestic groups that oppose Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
However, the ENDF has painted a picture of an alliance that extends far beyond Ethiopia's borders: Its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the TPLF.
Sudan dismissed the allegation as "baseless." Its military government countered with accusations that Ethiopia was supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia that has been fighting Sudan's army for over three years.
Eritrea said Ethiopia was attempting to shift responsibility for its own internal conflicts onto its neighbors. Cairo, meanwhile, issued a flat denial.
A domestic conflict with "external actors"
Viewing developments in northern Ethiopia as a domestic affair is not the full picture, according to experts.
"While it is primarily a domestic conflict, it certainly has a foreign policy dimension due to the many external actors directly or indirectly involved," said Susanne Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
Stollreiter told DW that these actors have their own interests in the region — interests that could potentially be advanced by the conflict.
"If this conflict escalates, I would even assume that it could truly lead to a kind of conflagration across the region, given the various conflict dynamics here in the Horn of Africa."
Mirroring alliances between Ethiopia and Sudan
Egypt and Sudan have long harbored grievances against Ethiopia because the source country of the Blue Nile dammed the river just before the border.
Sudan has been caught up in a brutal civil war since April 2023. Both sides to the conflict — the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF militia — are believed to have ties to partners that are now fighting on opposing sides in Ethiopia.
On one hand there's the Sudanese government and the TPLF, which was largely defeated in the 2020–22 Tigray War in Ethiopia. Many Tigrayan fighters went into exile in Sudan where they organized as "Army 70" and fought alongside the SAF against the RSF.
"They played quite an important role in the Sudan Armed Forces pushing back against the RSF in eastern Sudan and even into Khartoum. And then that relationship continued," said Magnus Taylor, Deputy Project Manager, Horn of Africa at the think tank International Crisis Group (ICG).
"The issue that the federal government of Ethiopia has is that it appears that Sudan is in a kind of alignment or an alliance with one of the strongest opposition groups in the country."
Tigrayan fighters in Sudan and training camp for Sudan militia in Ethiopia
In May, the Sudanese government hosted high-ranking representatives of the TPLF and leaders of other Ethiopian groups that are critical of Abiy. Some of those groups are now part of the new seven-member alliance.
On the other hand, there's the Ethiopia's central government and the former Sudanese special unit, the RSF.
In February, the news agency Reuters reported on a secret training camp for RSF fighters in the Ethiopian border region of Benishangul-Gumuz. According to the report, the United Arab Emirates provided instructors, funding, and logistical support — claims the UAE denied.
The UAE is closely allied with Ethiopia and, despite denials, is considered the RSF's most important backer.
Is Eritrea involved in the latest conflict?
So far, there are no signs of direct involvement by the Sudanese army or the RSF in the conflict in Ethiopia. There is no evidence of Eritrea's role in the latest escalation either. But there's no shortage of wild speculation.
Eritrea fought alongside Abiy's forces in the Tigray War but the leaders of the two countries had had a falling out by the time the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022.
Experts have long suggested that Eritrea — despite denials — is now supporting the TPLF. Distrust of Abiy runs deep, given his stated ambitions to secure Ethiopia access to the open sea — by force if necessary, such as by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab on the Red Sea.
ICG analyst Magnus Taylor told DW that Eritrean involvement in the latest fighting is plausible.
"I think the Eritreans have used the TPLF and other opposition groups to deter the perceived risk of Ethiopian aggression, whether that's for access to the port or other reasons," Taylor said.
"Having a large physical presence within Tigray or within Afar even would be, I guess, a justification for the Ethiopians to carry out more extensive military operations on Eritrea. The Eritrean tactic is to deter military action, not to invite it."
Asmara has strengthened relations with Cairo this year, and the United States has just let sanctions against Eritrea expire.
Is there a risk of a wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa?
The Horn of Africa borders the Gulf region in the north, which has lost stability due to the Iran war. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are also disrupting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. .
In Somalia, Al-Shabab is regaining ground, cooperating with the Houthis despite wide ideological differences.
"These are important trade routes that are being disputed and fought over and everyone is trying to profit from the unstable situation," Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation, said.
"In this respect, it is no real coincidence that so many actors are now becoming particularly strong again, also because of the absence of the actors who were otherwise protective powers in the region."
The US in particular, but also the Europeans tied down by Russia's war in Ukraine, have less of an eye on the Horn of Africa than before, Stollreiter said.
Have Gulf powers taken sides in Ethiopia?
The UAE and Saudi Arabia, which are accused of supporting different warring parties in Sudan and Yemen, and have polarized the entire region in recent years, are all the more present.
However, ICG's Magnus Taylor does not think that the situation in Ethiopia is at risk of escalating into a proxy war between the Gulf powers.
"While the UAE is a strong backer of Addis Ababa, the Saudis are not strongly backing the TPLF or any other opposition group."
Whether from the Arabian Peninsula, Sudan, or Eritrea — one week after the outbreak of war in Ethiopia, there are no clear signs that the internal conflict is becoming internationalized. However, in the unstable Horn of Africa, that risk is particularly high.

Students and police clash as France struggles to quell school protests
- Riot police clashed with high school students across France over poor classroom conditions and funding cuts, causing injuries and school damage amid rising violence.
- The government plans a below-inflation 1.7 per cent budget increase for education in 2027 but faces widespread protests and criticism for underinvestment.
- Authorities arrested 2,000 people and accused hard-left politicians of inciting unrest, while Amnesty International warned against police brutality towards minors.
AI generated
PARIS – Riot police clashed with high school students in cities across France on Oct 2, as President Emmanuel Macron’s government battled to contain increasingly violent protests over classroom conditions and funding.
Tear gas clouded the streets in the eastern city of Strasbourg, fireworks were aimed at police lines in Marseille in the south and rubbish bins set ablaze in Rennes in the west.
In Paris, where there were also skirmishes, students waved placards reading: “We have a future to build, not to endure.”
Fire damaged the entrances of two Paris high schools – Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east – with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
Six months before the 2027 presidential election, opinion polls consistently show the deep unpopularity of Macron and his centre-right-leaning government. Planned budget cuts, which exacerbate the funding crisis in education, have fuelled the discontent.
Minister says parents should pay reparations
The protests erupted in the Paris region last week but have turned increasingly violent as they spread nationwide.
The Education Ministry said students disrupted lessons at more than 560 schools on Oct 2.
It earlier said 400 high schools – roughly 1 in 10 – were expected to be closed.
Many high schools have planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin told RTL radio that police had arrested 2,000 people, most of them teenagers, since the protests began. He said that parents of those inflicting damage to property should be made to pay reparations.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray urged parents to dissuade their children from protesting in the streets.
“In the streets, the children are in danger,” Geffray told BFM TV.
He said at least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement.
Some 170 students have been wounded while more than 100 high schools have suffered “severe damage”.
Several students in the Paris region whom Reuters spoke to outside high schools earlier in the week said they were staying away from the protests on Oct 2 due to the escalating violence.
Darmanin said the student protest movement had been hijacked by “outsiders”.
Education to get below-inflation budget increase
Students blockading their high schools have voiced anger over overcrowding in classrooms, regular shortages of teachers and dilapidated buildings, blaming years of underinvestment.
“We are 35 per class, we don’t have enough chairs in classrooms, the one hour lunch break (is too short) for everyone to get food,” 15-year-old Kesia told Reuters in the Paris suburb of Pantin before running off as the police used tear gas.
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as “urban violence”.
Under the draft 2027 budget presented by the government on Oct 1, the education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7 per cent to €65.53 billion (S$94.2 billion), excluding teacher pensions.
Education is traditionally the largest budget item, but that changes in 2027 with debt servicing costs expected to reach €74.5 billion, according to the draft Bill.
Hard-left LFI denies stoking protests
Intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Oct 1 that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard left, including members of La France Insoumise (LFI).
Senior LFI lawmakers rebutted the allegations and accused the government of politicising the protests ahead of the election to replace Macron.
Students and rights groups have accused the police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns.
Amnesty International cautioned against the excessive use of police force. “Students must be protected, not beaten with batons,” the advocacy group said on social media platform X.
The Interior Ministry on Oct 2 said that it had opened three investigations into police violence against protesters.
In a sign the protests may spread beyond French borders, some high school students in the city of Liege, in Belgium, began protesting on Oct 1. A city hall spokesperson said high schools were closed on Oct 2. REUTERS, AFP

SINGAPORE, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's overall private residential property price index rose 1.4 percent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter of 2026, accelerating from a 0.5 percent increase in the second quarter, the flash estimate released by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) showed on Thursday.

A total of 4,745 private residential units will be launched under the Confirmed List in the second half of 2026, bringing the full-year Confirmed List supply to 9,320 units, more than 50 percent above the annual average over the past ten years, according to the URA.
This will bring the total supply of private residential units expected to be completed over the next few years to about 60,600 units. ■

Multiple Indian payloads reach orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:19:34 UTC
14:19:34 KST

SpaceX Falcon 9 launches multiple Indian payloads into orbit (representational image)
BENGALURU: Multiple Indian payloads, representing four space startups, reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, which lifted off at 12:02 am IST on Friday (October 2) as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.The mission carried satellites developed by Dhruva Space and TakeMe2Space, along with payloads from SatLeo Labs and EON Space Labs. The payloads will demonstrate technologies for thermal imaging, Earth observation and artificial intelligence (AI)-based data processing in orbit.Dhruva’s LEAP-2 satellite, its second commercial mission using the P-30 satellite platform, was successfully deployed into orbit at 1 am IST. It hosts two in-orbit demonstration payloads: a star tracker developed by France-based Sodern, part of ArianeGroup, and TAPAS-1, developed by SatLeo Labs.SatLeo describes TAPAS-1, or Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions, as India’s first dedicated commercial thermal payload. The CubeSat-category payload uses thermal infrared sensing to capture temperature information that conventional optical satellite imagery cannot directly provide.
The mission will validate its thermal sensing technology, payload performance and data-processing capabilities in orbit.“Most satellites show us what the Earth looks like, TAPAS-1 will show us how it behaves by revealing temperature patterns that ordinary payloads cannot see,” said Shravan Bhati, co-founder and CEO, SatLeo Labs.Dhruva Space also undertook the end-to-end integration of LEAP-2 with the Falcon 9 launch vehicle. The company said this builds on its work on LEAP-1, through which it became the first Indian private company to undertake the launch vehicle integration of its satellite in-house.“This extends our role beyond satellite manufacturing into launch integration and end-to-end mission delivery, reinforcing its full-stack Space engineering approach. LEAP-2 will also be supported by our growing global ground infrastructure, including its owned and operated ground station in Luleå, Sweden; the first non-govt entity owned and operated ground station outside India, authorised by the GoI to provide Ground-Station-as-a-Service,” the firm added.TakeMe2Space’s 14-kg MOI-1A satellite is designed to allow customers to run AI models on Earth-observation data directly in orbit. It carries onboard computing capacity of 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS), 2 TB of storage and a nine-band multispectral imager. Processing imagery in space could reduce the need to transmit large volumes of raw data to Earth, with potential applications in agriculture, mining and supply-chain intelligence.MOI-1A follows TakeMe2Space’s 2024 MOI-TD technology demonstration, which validated onboard AI inference and data processing. The company said it had signed up 23 customers for its in-orbit inference services.MOI-1A also carried MIRA, a 502-g optical telescope developed by EON Space Labs. “A compact optical telescope engineered for space imaging. It delivers high-resolution Earth observation with exceptional stability and thermal robustness,” EON describes the payload.
MIRA is a pathfinder for a planned small satellite constellation. Its flight comes after the loss of the PSLV-C62 mission on Jan 12, which had affected the company’s earlier launch plans.“Satellites collect vast amounts of data, but much of it still has to reach the ground before it can be turned into useful information. With MOI-1A, customers will be able to run their AI models directly in orbit and receive the insights they need, without downloading all the raw imagery. This mission is an important step towards making computing in space a service that businesses can use,” Ronak Kumar Samantray, founder and CEO, TakeMe2Space, said.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Enjoy the last of the warmth? Temperatures in Latvia to reach +20°C this weekend before the weather changes

Unknown Publisher

14:19:30 KST

On Friday and Saturday, sunny spells will frequently alternate with clouds, while the weather will remain dry. Light winds will prevail on both days, meaning fog will thicken in some areas overnight and during the early morning hours, reducing visibility, according to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
Across most of Latvia, overnight temperatures will fall to between +3°C and +8°C, while coastal areas will remain warmer at +8°C to +12°C. During the day, sunshine will warm the air to between +15°C and +20°C.
Sunday will also bring variable cloud cover, although clouds will bring rain to some western areas in the afternoon.
Light to moderate south-westerly and westerly winds will prevail.

Burgas will welcome the international COP31 Bike Ride on 4 and 5 October as the cycling relay makes its way towards the UN Climate Change Conference COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. This year’s route covers more than 22,000 km across three continents and over 20 countries, the Municipality of Burgas said.

What the enemy attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 2 (from 18:00 on October 1), the enemy attacked with 108 Shahed-type attack UAVs (47 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Bryansk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation, the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiyske.

Staff fears grow that BBC will shut its Three and Scotland channels next week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

The BBC has started a redundancy process in its TV and streaming division, heightening staff fears that Matt Brittin will announce the closure of the poorly performing BBC Three and BBC Scotland channels next week.
The corporation’s director general, who has repeatedly said that linear TV and radio services may have to shut as audiences move online, is expected to inform staff on Wednesday of the latest stage of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.
This week, Dan McGolpin, the director of the BBC iPlayer and Channels division, which includes all the corporation’s TV stations, called for expressions of interest across the department in taking voluntary redundancy.
In an email he said the plan to “mitigate the number of [enforced] redundancies” included sounding out staff interest about job-sharing arrangements, a reduction in hours, and “relocating to another BBC base across the UK”.
The move has fuelled speculation that the BBC is about to take the two channels online-only, according to sources, as Brittin focuses on cutting back on TV and radio services and content that delivers the least value for money.
“It is no secret that BBC Scotland and BBC Three are very expensive on a cost-per-viewer basis – a key metric being looked at – and they clearly haven’t achieved what was hoped,” said one insider.
It would be the second time BBC Three has been taken off linear broadcast. The youth-focused channel – which launched in 2003 and generated hits including Gavin and Stacey, Fleabag, Killing Eve and the lockdown hit Normal People – moved online-only in 2016 to save costs.
Since making a comeback to linear TV in 2022, it has struggled as audiences increasingly drift to streaming TV and video platforms such as YouTube. BBC Three recently announced it was canning the high-profile RuPaul’s Drag Race UK owing to financial pressures.
On Tuesday, the channel’s highest-rating show was Stacey Dooley Sleeps Over, which was broadcast in a primetime 9pm slot but only managed an average audience of 74,000.
Typically about 4% of the UK population watch the channel live in a week. Its cost per user hour was 26p in 2023-24 and 18p in 2024-25, the last year the BBC broke out statistics for individual services. This compares with 10p for BBC One that year, 9p for BBC Two and 6p for BBC Four.
BBC Three’s budget was doubled to about £80m when it returned to linear TV, rising to £90m in 2023-24, but it was cut to £66m in 2024-25.
A similar online-only fate is looming for the BBC Scotland television channel, which was launched in 2019 as a dedicated outlet for Scottish programming, separate to the Gaelic-language BBC Alba.
According to the BBC’s latest annual report to 31 March just 12% of people in Scotland watch the channel live. That compares with 54% of the adult population consuming BBC Scotland content each week across BBC TV/iPlayer, BBC Radio and BBC Online.
The BBC Scotland TV channel had a budget of £42m in 2024-25, while its cost per user hour was 13p.
“If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services,” Brittin told BBC One’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme. “When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.”
In June, the BBC announced plans to cut 60 jobs in Scotland, to save £10m. The BBC Scotland channel has received about £250m in funding since its launch but has failed to attract large audiences. Its flagship news magazine programme, The Nine, was scrapped two years ago after some episodes drew as few as 1,700 viewers.
One source believes that completely shutting the TV channel would be too politically difficult for the BBC, and that an online-only future would be a cost-effective and acceptable solution.
Brittin has also suggested radio services could be axed, having already announced that between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.
The corporation has already made a number of cost-saving announcements, including permanently reducing the presenter roster on Radio 4’s Today after the departure of Amol Rajan. It also axed the evening news programme The World Tonight after more than 50 years.
In 2010, Mark Thompson, then director general, proposed shutting the Asian Network and 6 Music. Ultimately both survived following a backlash, although the Asian Network was relocated to Birmingham last year and had its dedicated news bulletins replaced by Newsbeat two years ago.
Cost per user hour, the Asian Network, Radio 1Xtra and Radio 3 are the most expensive of the BBC’s stations.
The BBC said it did not comment on speculation.
