Four hidden trails with medieval roots in the Eastern Alps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

Celtic tribes, Roman soldiers and medieval knights paved the way in the forests of the Eastern Alps. These trails are still there and can be discovered by history lovers during a sunny autumn weekend.
If you like active weekends with hiking and learning, one of the best places to go in Central Europe are the eastern slopes of the Alps.
The lower peaks of the mountains are in Austria, but the foot of the slopes reach Hungary.
It's not only the forests and the mountains which connect the two countries, but also the past, with the mountain bike trails and hiking routes passing through hundreds of years of history.
Velem, Hungary: A small village with rich past
Driving to the village of Velem you can see the white chapel of Saint Vid (or Vitus) from tens of kilometres away.
At an altitude of 589 metres, the chapel is located deep in the forest of the Kőszeg Mountains range, at the end of a moderate hiking trail. It was built in the early 18th century on the ruins of an ancient town.
Celts inhabited the area approximately 2,000 years ago, then the Romans built a watchtower to defend the aqueduct system supplying water to the ancient city of Savaria. If you walk in the forest, the man-made Celtic terraces can still be seen.
The other popular hiking trail from Velem leads to Geschriebenstein, the region's highest peak which is right on the border of Hungary and Austria.
Hiking from Velem is a bit adventurous, but from Austria it is an easy walk.
The third hiking route is the "Springs Trail" (Források útja) that showcases both popular and lesser-known springs in the Kőszeg Mountains. It is 14 kilometres long and features 11 stations.
Kőszeg: The small Hungarian town that prevented the advance of the Ottoman army in 1532
Only a few kilometres from the Austrian border lies Kőszeg, one of the most charming small towns of Hungary. Kőszeg is most famous for Jurisics Castle, a medieval Gothic castle that was in the centre of the siege of Kőszeg in 1532.
The captain of the castle had approximately 50 soldiers joined by 700 Hungarian locals who faced the Ottoman army which wanted to reach Vienna. How did the defenders of the town prevented the advance of the mighty army? The real story remains a mystery but some say the heavy August rains had their say.
Hiking across the mountain from Velem to Kőszeg is a day-long programme, but really worth it. You can pass cold water springs, see the chapel of Saint Vid and visit the Styrian houses used by foresters in the 1800s.
Lockenhaus: Do modern knights ride bicycles?
Lockenhaus knight's castle, once home of the mysterious Templars, is embedded in the beautiful landscape of Austria's Geschriebenstein Nature Park.
The surrounding forest is criss-crossed by mountain bike trails rated from light to extremely hard.
From the nearby town of Rechnitz, the Burgenland Trails shuttle bus helps cyclists take their bikes up to the designated stops. Minibuses equipped for bike transport operate on a regular schedule on weekends and public holidays.
From Geschriebenstein, the highest peak of the region, bikers can reach Lockenhaus, Rechnitz Badesee or Hungary as well.
The bicycle trails are separated from the walking routes, so hikers and bikers do not get in each other's way.
The 13th century castle of Lockenhaus has a remarkable Geoffroy's bat colony that visitors can observe from April to July.
Other feathered castle inhabitants include the majestic kestrels and lightning-fast swifts. And if you are lucky, you can also observe a beaver family by the lake near the castle.
Stadtschlaining: An Austrian town that kept its medieval look
Another 13th century medieval castle in Austria, near the Hungarian border, is Burg Schlaining. Located on the outskirts of Stadtschlaining, it is only 22 kilometres from Lockenhaus on the R1 Jubiläumsradweg bicycle road.
With its medieval centre, Stadtschlaining is situated in a beautiful hilly countryside, and therefore offers possibilities for recreation like walking and bike rides. At the end of the tour, visitors can enjoy the atmosphere of the castle gardens for free.
Stadtschlaining is also the starting point for excursions into the idyllic “weinstrasse” (wine route) of the Südburgenland. Here you can discover charming vineyards with “heuriger” wine taverns and farms which produce cider.

UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:00:02 BST

UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland
The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
- 
    Hundreds of British personnel train with allies from the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to counter rising Russian threat in Exercise Lion Protector 26.
- 
    Training takes place across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea, with Royal Marines conducting the first exercise in the Faroe Islands since the Second World War.
- 
    Comes as the Defence Secretary meets JEF counterparts in Iceland, with Canada and Ukraine also in attendance.
The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
Allies from the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which is led by the UK, have conducted Exercise Lion Protector 26, which saw forces train across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea to protect critical national infrastructure, strengthen joint command and control, and counter emerging threats.
From the data cables that connect the UK to the world, to the energy infrastructure that powers homes and businesses, the North Atlantic and High North are vital to our national security.
It comes as the Defence Secretary today meets with his JEF counterparts at a summit in Keflavik, Iceland, where ministers will progress discussions on Canada’s application for membership of the JEF Framework.
Ministers will also discuss deepening cooperation on countering hybrid threats, furthering industrial collaboration, and support to Ukraine through the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership. As Canada and Ukraine continue to cooperate closely with JEF, Canadian and Ukrainian ministers will also be in attendance.
Part of Exercise Lion Protector 26 saw Royal Marines from the UK’s Special Operations Maritime Task Group conduct the first exercise since the Second World War on the Faroe Islands, alongside Danish forces.
Marines and their Danish allies carried out maritime interdictions, amphibious landings, and vertical ascent training on the Faroes, which was the location of a key Royal Marines deployment during the Second World War.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence.
From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats.
I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.
Lion Protector launched in August with a rehearsal of a multi-national maritime escort operation stretching the length of the Baltic Sea. Warships and aircraft from Denmark, Latvia, Sweden and the UK escorted a Danish vessel carrying military equipment to Latvia, testing the JEF’s ability to coordinate rapidly across sea, land, air, cyber and space.
The UK’s Standing Joint Force Headquarters coordinated activity across the High North and Baltic Sea region, deploying north of the Arctic Circle in Norway to test its ability to command allied forces at speed and range.
JEF is a UK-led coalition of ten like-minded nations comprising high readiness forces configured to respond rapidly to crises in support of NATO security. JEF brings together the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden to secure the Baltic Sea, North Atlantic, Arctic and High North for NATO.
Today’s summit builds on the JEF Leaders’ Summit in Helsinki in March where leaders agreed to reinforce steadfast support to Ukraine through ambitious delivery of the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership.
It also builds on the Prime Minister’s discussions with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Støre this week about the hybrid threat Russia poses.
Exercise Lion Protector 26 comes ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference, both taking place in Oslo in November.

LRT English Newsletter: Seeing red
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – October 2, 2026.
Western media has practically taken over from the Baltics and Eastern Europe in calling out the Russia threat on a near-daily basis. Contrastingly, it is the Baltic officials who are calling for calm nerves.
But let’s go over the role-reversal from the beginning.
For weeks, European intelligence agencies and some Western leaders said Moscow could attack the Baltic states, with prognoses ranging from increased (and, by now, routine) disinformation plays to a boots-on-the-ground attack. These warnings came amid the eerie and unannounced CIA chief visit to Moscow, as well as reported warnings from Washington issued to the Baltic governments about a potential Russian attack.
Western media has therefore been filled with headlines prophesying the impending doom. Playing to the same tune, Moscow has issued (another) nuclear threat, this time focusing on Kaliningrad.
This, along with the rest of the media-political noise, is part of an ongoing campaign to disorient societies, Baltic leaders keep stressing. Intelligence reports also do not indicate anything major happening anytime soon, they say, but there is a threat of sabotage and intelligence operations which have only intensified.
Some analysts and officials are worried about what would happen if Russia launched a few dozen “stray” drones, or something along the lines, but Vilnius-bound Russian tanks are far from likely. In an interview with LRT, Britain’s top navy general also said that he was only worried about Russia doing “something stupid” that would fall under NATO’s collective defence threshold.
Some constructive statements did surface over the past week, including during Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius’ presser with the NATO secretary general, where the latter stressed that NATO isn’t idly sitting by. The words of Lithuania’s PM were later taken out of context, when a Kremlin aide welcomed that the threat from Russia was being toned down by a Lithuanian prime minister himself.
Adding to the chaotic information bubble, the Baltic states – along with France and the United Kingdom – were not invited by Washington to a NATO meeting. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda dismissed it as "artificial hype".
BANS AND SANCTIONS
Lithuania’s government approved a bill that will see additional bans on Belarusian and Russian nationals. If passed by the parliament, they will be banned from buying property near strategic sites. Additionally, people who have performed in occupied or annexed Ukraine will also be banned from performing, or taking part in other public cultural and sports activities. Some things remain unclear, for example, how the idea to have them sign a public statement against the Kremlin would actually play out. In related news, Lithuania has imposed sanctions on Kremlin-linked billionaires that escaped EU-level sanctions.
ECONOMY UPDATES
– The budget deficit is likely to exceed 3 percent next year.
– Lithuania’s historical Snaigė fridge manufacturer is going belly up.
– Lithuania will try to stick to the 2030 Rail Baltica deadline.
– The construction of a Leopard 2 tank plant has begun in Kaunas.
LANGUAGE CHANGES
Some interesting statistics popped up this week since Lithuania intensified efforts to reduce Russian language in schools. Since 2022, the number of Lithuanian school students studying Russian as a second foreign language has fallen by more than 40 percent. There is now also a growing number of kids learning German, French, or Spanish.
FINALLY?
The Catholic Church in Lithuania has decided to investigate the scale of abuse against minors since the country's independence. This landmark decision follows years of successive scandals, in which the priests involved would often face little to no consequences. Observers are naturally calling for the enquiry to be as independent as possible. 
EDITOR’S PICKS:
– US and Lithuanian intelligence services allegedly warned two Russian dissidents of an urgent threat to their lives.
– The Justice Minister has taken another L in trying to block same-sex marriages.
– Shaq was in Lithuania to watch a game and do some promo.
– And young farmers showed off their tractor-driving skills.

Speed up EU health security prep, says NATO chief medic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
SNEAK PEEK
— Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure.
— Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension.
Advertisement
— Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein,with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight.
Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter. This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe.
GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein.
Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference.
Advertisement
Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.”
Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.”
Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.”
Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care.
Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here.
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health.
Advertisement
On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting.
We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said.
Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.”
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
**A message from EFPIA: Fierce competition means the global life science landscape is shifting, demanding a bold response. The Biotech Act is an important signal of the kind of ecosystem Europe wants to create, but it cannot deliver change alone. Europe cannot expect to attract greater investment in medicine innovation while access remains slow and unpredictable. Read more.**
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure.
Recap: France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”
Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response.
Advertisement
Austria is on board: “As Europe… if we do not now see the need to act more [uniformly] and more together, I don't know when we should see it,” said Stefan Eichwalder, director of the health systems division at the Austrian health and social affairs ministry.
It doesn’t mean not doing anything: “It would be dangerous not to act now, but then I think we need to find ways of working together,” he said. Eichwalder added that it was important that national deals — with industry or the U.S. — do “not weaken the position of the EU, and in the end, the position of any member state within the EU.”
The bottom line: Countries should work together “no matter how difficult it is,” he said. “I don't see a solution for Europe to go 27 different different routes.”
Think this through: Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform, said countries should be asking themselves this question: If we were to accept paying higher prices, what can we get in return? “From a first reading of this agreement, France is committing to pay higher prices in return for what exactly? And what are companies committing to delivering in exchange for these higher prices?”
The bigger picture: “Many narratives are going around. Narratives that are used by different sectors to serve specific interests,” Natsis said. “And in this case, this narrative is used to ask and demand higher prices. But again, the question is: if we were to pay these higher prices in Europe… what happens to the other countries? Because if France signs an agreement, if Germany signs an agreement, what about the rest of us?”
Pushing back: Richard Bergström, vice president of European affairs at health data firm IQVIA and former chief of pharma lobby EFPIA, pushed back. “If you read the French deal… there’s a lot of wins for the governments as well,” he told panelists from the audience. “There are requirements on clinical trials, requirements on manufacturing in Europe, and most importantly, there is a gain at the end of life cycle.” It’s a “quite balanced deal,” he added.
Advertisement
OVER IN BRITAIN: The U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal — which is hailed by the Trump administration and industry as a blueprint for other European countries — is running up against some challenges, our colleague Caroline Hug writes in. Four pilots rolled out to try to meet U.S. demands to double medicines spending as a percentage of GDP by 2028 are currently falling short. Britain’s new Science Minister Chris McDonald has signaled the government is willing to try new ideas.
Pilots ongoing: The government — with industry and the U.S. administration — launched the pilots running through September 2027, and the results will inform the next drug-pricing scheme.
The line: “What’s really important here is that we start with what is the objective we want to achieve, rather than the means by which we want to achieve it,” McDonald told Morning Trade U.K. during a fringe event Tuesday at the Labour Party Conference. “I don’t mind trying things, and then if they don’t work, then learning from that and moving on and trying some other things.”
New blood: McDonald replaces former Science Minister Patrick Vallance, who played a key role in the U.K.-U.S. pharma negotiations. One pharma industry figure told MTUK that McDonald “brings rare commercial instinct to the policy debate.”
Deal mode: “It was quite hard to reach an agreement across the entirety of the industry [on pilots],” said Shaun Grady, AstraZeneca U.K. chairman, pointing to varying demands of some pharma companies versus big pharmas like GSK and AstraZeneca which “invest very significantly in the U.K.” He added that conversations are “now moving much more into a bilateral phase where each company will engage with the government.”
BIOTECH ACT
APPROVED: Parliament’s environment committee has confirmed its position on the Biotech Act, with 53 in favor of adopting the opinion led by Nicolás Gonzalez Casares and 11 against. It supported keeping a 12-month extension of patents under certain conditions. Parliament’s legal committee also voted to keep the one-year extension in its opinion.
Advertisement
Coming to the table: The co-leads on the Biotech Act — Vytenis Andriukaitis (S&D) in the health committee and Wouter Beke (EPP) in the industry committee — will meet in Strasbourg next week to try and find a compromise on the patent extensions they can bring back to shadow rapporteurs.
Making progress: Andriukaitis told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of Gastein that political groups will likely have “more compromised solutions” on supplementary protection certificates, cross-border clinical trials and financing for the law by the end of October.” Read more about what he said here.
Feedback: Shadow rapporteurs on the Biotech Act on Thursday submitted their feedback to the co-rapporteurs following a roundtable between MEPs, Commission officials and industry on Tuesday.
Remember: Some MEPs weren’t happy at being offered a roundtable in lieu of an independent assessment on the supplementary protection certificate extension (SPCs) while some NGOs were also upset they didn’t get a seat at the table. Catch up on the controversy here.
UCPM
COMMITTEES BOOST PREPAREDNESS, CIVIL PROTECTION FUND: Lawmakers in the health and environment committee adopted their position on the EU’s next civil protection mechanism (UCPM), which now includes health emergency preparedness and response.
Details: The compromise text boosts the budget of the mechanism from €10 billion to €12.42 billion, earmarking 40% of the funding for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility. The position was approved with 61 votes in favor, nine against and nine abstentions. It will now need to be put to a vote in Parliament.
Advertisement
Sneaky global health reference: The adopted text includes several references to strengthening global health infrastructure. For example, it says that “strengthening cooperation … as well as the global health infrastructure and the World Health Organisation is essential to enhance the global ability to act.”
WHAT WE’RE READING
There have been four more deaths from the West Nile virus in the Netherlands, the NL Times reports.
**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act can be an important step towards Europe’s life sciences future. Done well, it can make clinical research faster, attract more investment to Europe, help biotech companies scale, and ensure Europe is the place where the next generation of medicines is developed. However, it cannot deliver the change that Europe urgently requires in isolation. Access shapes where capital flows right from the start. When market access is slow or fragmented, investors notice and capital follows opportunity elsewhere. Reversing Europe’s decline in research and development investment would require sustained structural reform, stronger action at the Member-State level, and a rethink of how healthcare systems invest in innovation. Europe has both scientific excellence and talent. Now it must create the right conditions for companies to choose Europe as a place to research, develop and deliver new medicines to patients. If we get it right, the reward is higher growth, greater resilience, and better health. The choice is ours. Read more.**

How Switzerland lost 20 percent of its ice in five years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:59:58 UTC
13:59:58 KST

How Switzerland lost 20 percent of its ice in five years
Swiss glaciers have lost more than 5 percent of their ice, threatening the country’s alpine economy.
Switzerland’s glaciers are rapidly receding due to a combination of winters with too little snow and record-high temperatures across Europe this summer, scientists say. In all, one of the world’s top ski destinations has lost nearly one-fifth of its glacial ice in just five years.
In a report (PDF) published by the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (GLAMOS) and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation of the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT) on Thursday, researchers said Swiss glaciers lost 5.5 percent of their ice volume over the hydrologic year ending September 30, 2026, and nearly 20 percent since 2021.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Are Europe’s extreme summers the new normal? What the science says
- list 2 of 3Why Nepal is demanding climate justice and compensation after deadly floods
- list 3 of 3India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
Why is Switzerland, famed for its Alpine terrain and winter sports, losing its glaciers and what does this mean for the country?
Here’s what we know.
What have scientists discovered?
In September, a GLAMOS team visited 23 glaciers in Switzerland to record end-of-summer measurements of ice melt and snow accumulation.
Visiting one glacier named Scex Rouge in the Western Swiss Alps in early September, GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, one of the report’s researchers, told the Reuters news agency that a measuring pole, about four metres (13 feet) high, was drilled into the ice in July to provide the team with a point of reference.
“Now when we have come back here, we saw the pole was out by three metres [10ft]. So just in August and September of this year, even excluding the heatwaves of June and July, we have lost three metres of ice at an elevation of almost 3,000 metres [9,843ft],” he explained.
“This clearly indicates these conditions that we had this summer, they are just inconsistent with the survival of these small glaciers in the Alps,” he added.
Why are glaciers in Switzerland losing ice?
According to the report, the total mean thickness of individual glaciers in Switzerland has fallen by between 2.5 and four metres in 2026. At glacier tongues – narrow glacial extensions of a glacier which project from land into a body of water – it had decreased by as much as 10 metres in some places over the summer.
“We can clearly attribute the massive ice loss to the warming, and thus anthropogenic [caused by humans] climate change. The summer has been the hottest on record in Switzerland. In addition, there was little snow in winter, and therefore the glaciers were poorly protected when the heat started,” GLAMOS chief Huss told Al Jazeera.
He noted that while their measurements have indicated that the melting has affected all glaciers in Switzerland equally, the effects were most visible on smaller glaciers.
“Those shrink very quickly and sometimes even completely disappeared. Also, large glaciers lost an enormous quantity of ice, but they remain impressive,” he added.
The report’s scientists warned that the glaciers also lost a total of about 2.2 trillion litres of water (581 billion gallons) between July and September alone.
“This is more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of all Swiss households,” the report’s researchers said and warned this could impact the country’s future water supply.
What does this mean for Switzerland?
Switzerland is a country known for winter sports and Alpine tourism, which depends on the glaciers. About 4 percent of the country’s entire workforce is employed in the tourism sector.
“This affects tourism and also how we perceive the mountains – they are no longer white but increasingly grey and black,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the water provided by glaciers is also important for the economy. “It is used to fill up hydropower lakes that produce clean energy, and supplies the biggest streams of Europe,” he said.
“We’re not yet seeing the full consequences as glaciers are still around and they contribute water when we need it. But this potential is soon being lost,” he added.
Harry Zekollari, a glaciologist and associate research professor at the Department of Water and Climate at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, shared a similar view.
He stressed that glaciers are important natural water suppliers, as they provide water when people need it most – in summer, when it is hot and dry.
“With climate change, glaciers initially provide more water during summer as they rapidly melt. However, as glaciers become smaller, there is less ice to be melted, and as such the water supply in summer decreases. This peak in water supply has now been passed for glaciers in the European Alps, meaning that we expect glaciers to provide less and less water in the coming years,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Glacier changes can also cause natural hazards, and since most of the ice lost turns into water that reaches the oceans, the consequences of glacier loss [in Switzerland and elsewhere] will be felt for coastlines all around the globe,” he added.
Is there a solution?
Yes. According to Zekollari, in order to save as much glacier ice as possible in Switzerland, the world needs to stabilise rising temperatures as soon as possible.
“Projections for the European Alps and Swiss glaciers show that if we are able to rapidly stop emissions, we may still be able to save about one-third of their ice mass. However, in a case with strong warming, these glaciers are projected to lose more than 90 percent of their volume by 2100,” he said.
He noted that the situation is less grim globally as some glaciers in other regions are more persistent.
“However, even globally, future emissions play a big role and will decide whether we lose about 25 percent of glacier mass by 2100 – that’s the good case, with limited warming – or rather 50 percent – the bad case, with more warming,” he said.
“The losses in the longer term – past 2100 – are even larger due to the long response of glaciers, but also here it is the future warming that decides how much remains. Every 0.1 degree Celsius warming matters.”

The all-Australian supergroup will soundtrack an on-ground tribute to South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow, who told ABC earlier this week he knew "nothing" about plans for him to take a lap of honour around Stadium Australia on Sunday.
The ABC understands that Shark, who performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and company will perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.
Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.
The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred on the NRL's insistence that she perform her 2019 mega-hit Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.
Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment — running close to $1 million — could be put to better use.
"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend $1 million on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.
"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league."
V'landys also said the league would be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, following the Rabbitohs player's departure from the NRL earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.
The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year, and previous acts such as Billy Idol and Tina Turner.
"Our game sells itself," said V'landys.
"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

CANBERRA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Australia's online safety regulator has called for online gaming service providers, including Roblox and Fortnite, to strengthen protections against child sexual exploitation.
Julie Inman Grant, Australia's eSafety commissioner, on Friday released a report showing significant differences in the child safety measures taken by game service providers.
The report found that the providers behind Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam have inconsistent approaches to preventing high-risk games from being accessed by children, warning that such games can create environments for child sexual exploitation or activity that promotes crime or violence.
"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," Inman Grant said.
"Service providers should leverage systems that actually detect and disrupt serious harms before children are exposed to them."
According to the report, the providers of both Fortnite and Minecraft offer protections for child accounts, but generally rely on age information declared by users, allowing users who stated they were adults to access higher-risk features without additional age checks.
It said that Valve, the provider of the game distribution platform Steam, failed to use tools to proactively detect harms on messaging service Steam Chat.
Roblox and Valve reported using only internal datasets to train language detection systems, with neither regularly retraining those models.
Inman Grant said that it is critical for game service providers to adopt meaningful and continuing safety measures to protect young players. ■

New Zealand temperature up 1.36 degrees Celsius over 117 years: statistics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:53 CST
13:29:53 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's average annual temperature increased by 1.36 degrees Celsius over the 117 years to 2025, while rainfall patterns shifted across the country, official data showed on Friday.
The country's average annual temperature has been recorded since 1909, with 2022 being the warmest year on record at an average of 13.76 degrees Celsius. The year 2012 was the last with an average temperature below the 1991-2020 baseline of 12.74 degrees Celsius, Stats NZ reported.
Data from New Zealand's 30 climate stations showed average annual temperatures increased across the country, with temperatures rising fastest in winter and slowest in spring, Stats NZ environment statistics spokesperson Tehseen Islam said in a statement.
Rainfall patterns were more complex. From 1960 to 2025, nine climate stations recorded an increase in average annual rainfall, and six recorded a decrease, Stats NZ said, adding the South Island was generally getting wetter, while rainfall trends varied across the North Island.
Islam said changing rainfall, particularly increased spring rainfall, could affect farmers, fisheries and hydroelectricity generation.
Extreme rainfall also accounted for an increasing share of annual rainfall at 11 of the 30 stations, while three recorded a decrease between 1960 and 2025, according to Stats NZ.
Separately, carbon dioxide concentrations in New Zealand's atmosphere reached 423.1 parts per million in December 2025, up 5.5 percent from December 2016, with methane and nitrous oxide concentrations also showing increasing trends, the department said. ■

Interview: A more stable U.S.-China relationship matters for the world, says U.S. expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:29:13 CST
13:29:13 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- A more stable U.S.-China relationship has effects well beyond the bilateral relationship because the two countries are deeply connected to the global economy and play major roles in international institutions and global governance, a renowned U.S. expert on China affairs has said.
In a written interview with Xinhua, Denis Simon, former senior adviser for China affairs to the president of Duke University, noted that Chinese President Xi Jinping said during the recent state visit to the United States that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world.
"I read this as an attempt to frame the relationship in terms of mutual national interests rather than as a zero-sum contest. Both China and the United States have their own national ambitions and domestic priorities, but those objectives do not necessarily require the other country to fail," said Simon, who also served as executive vice chancellor of Duke Kunshan University in 2015-2020.
"Rather than asking either side to abandon its own national goals, the message is that China's development and America's prosperity can coexist and, under the right conditions, reinforce one another," he said.
Regarding the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences and promises of peace, Simon described the formulation as "an effort to provide a practical framework for managing a relationship in which competition is unavoidable but conflict is not inevitable."
"The key phrase for me is 'competition within bounds.' It recognizes that China and the United States will compete in areas such as technology, trade and strategic influence. The objective is not necessarily to eliminate that competition, but to establish boundaries so that competition does not become confrontation," he said.
Simon said "manageable differences" acknowledges that some disagreements may be very difficult to resolve in the foreseeable future. A stable relationship, therefore, cannot depend on resolving every difference.
"It needs mechanisms that allow the two sides to disagree without allowing individual disputes to destabilize the entire relationship," he said. "If implemented consistently, the framework could shift the emphasis from trying to eliminate competition toward making competition predictable and manageable, while expanding cooperation wherever interests genuinely overlap."
Simon identified economic and trade issues as an obvious area where concrete progress could have immediate effects, while noting that technology and supply-chain questions are more difficult "because they involve both economic and national-security considerations."
"But precisely for that reason, they require sustained dialogue and clearer communication," he said, adding that beyond bilateral issues, cooperation on climate, energy, public health and other transnational challenges could demonstrate that competition does not have to prevent practical collaboration. ■

Rubio unblocks $320 million in military aid to Egypt that had been withheld over human rights concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:22:39 UTC

Top US diplomat Marco Rubio signed off on the waiver but argued that Washington’s concerns over its Middle Eastern ally’s human rights record will remain a point of discussion in full bilateral discussions.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has waived a restriction on $320 million (€284.4 million) in military aid to Egypt that had been previously withheld over human rights concerns, citing Cairo’s help in dealing with Iran since the conflict began earlier this year.
The US State Department said on Thursday that Rubio had signed off on the waiver “in the interest of US national security.”
"The Secretary’s determination reflects the importance of Egypt to US national security interests, and the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States,” the department said.
In a letter sent to lawmakers, Rubio cited, in particular, Egypt’s “helpful role” in the war with Iran. Egypt has been a key mediator between the US and Iran in the efforts to wind down the more than seven-month-long conflict.
The State Department maintained that the Trump administration would continue to raise human rights matters as part of its dialogue with Egypt “on the full range of issues in our bilateral relationship.”
“The waiver determination recognises the importance of maintaining security cooperation with Egypt at a time of significant regional security challenges,” the department said.
The $320 million is part of an annual US contribution of $1.3 billion (€1.16 billion) in economic and military assistance to Egypt. More specifically, it is for foreign military financing, which provides money for recipient nations to purchase US-produced weaponry.
Congress inserted the requirement over concerns about Egypt’s human rights record, which many experts regard as problematic. The State Department itself in recent years has pointed to credible reports of torture, arbitrary arrest, child labour and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
But granting a waiver to Egypt has become routine for both Republican and Democratic administrations. The Biden administration, for example, last issued a waiver in September 2024, citing Egypt’s assistance in US efforts to bring an end to the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.

Danish woman fined 200,000 DKK and restricted from keeping dogs over animal mistreatment
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.
Bødskov said Spain partly contributed to the situation by offering legal residence to undocumented migrants. Spain originally expected about 500,000 applications, but more than 1.1 million people applied by the June 30 deadline, according to Euronews.
He said the EU remained vulnerable to sudden large arrivals and needed stronger external borders.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.
Prosecutors seek prison sentence and nightlife ban for Danish man over fatal punch at World Cup event
Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.
Vietnamese president to visit Denmark for talks on green solutions, health and trade
Vietnamese President To Lam and his spouse, Ngo Phuong Ly, will make a state visit to Denmark from October 19 to October 21.
King Frederik and Queen Mary will host a gala dinner for the Vietnamese presidential couple at Christiansborg Palace on October 19.
To Lam and Ngo Phuong Ly will be accompanied by ministers, senior officials and a business delegation, the Danish Royal House said.
The visit marks 55 years of diplomatic relations between Denmark and Vietnam. It will focus on shared interests including green solutions, health, food and trade.
It will be the third state visit hosted by King Frederik since he became king, following visits from Iceland and Egypt. The Danish royal couple has made eight state visits abroad.
The Royal House, the organization supporting Denmark’s monarch and royal family, also highlighted the family’s connection to Vietnam.
Prince Henrik, King Frederik’s father, spent the first five years of his life in Vietnam when the country was part of French Indochina. His family returned to France in 1939. Henrik spoke Vietnamese, Chinese, French and Danish. He died in 2018.
Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess.
Vietnam is a socialist republic led by the Communist Party. To Lam serves as both president and the party’s general secretary, considered the country’s most powerful position.
Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.
The Danish government plans to allocate an additional DKK 22 billion to the Armed Forces in 2027 as part of its upcoming budget proposal, according to Berlingske.
Defense investment is then expected to increase to around DKK 40 billion in 2030.
The government expects Denmark to meet NATO’s target of spending 3.5 percent of GDP on military defense before 2030. According to NATO figures cited by Berlingske, Denmark is already spending 3.4 percent of GDP on defense in 2026 when funding from the Ukraine Fund is included.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said the government’s first budget would require cuts in some areas to finance other priorities.
“There is something we need to have a little less of, so that in return we can invest in the community, in welfare, in security, and in a competitive business sector,” he told Berlingske.
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr said support for Ukraine would continue to form part of defense spending in the coming years.
“This is both about defending Denmark and Europe, while at the same time we also protect welfare. The Danish economy is strong enough to do both,” she said.
Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt said continued donations to Ukraine would require support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
NATO members agreed in 2025 to increase the alliance’s military spending target to at least 3.5 percent of GDP, replacing the previous 2 percent target.

A majority in the Climate, Environment and Technology Committee at Copenhagen Municipality approved a new plan Monday afternoon.
According to it, the city has moved a step closer to introducing a zero-emission zone in part of Vesterbro, where petrol and diesel vehicles would generally not be allowed to drive.
“It is really good that Copenhagen is now getting its first zero-emission zone. It is good for the climate and for reducing local air pollution,” Kristine Ammitzbøll-Bille of De Radikale, the Danish Social Liberal Party, told TV 2 Kosmopol.
The proposal was originally larger but was changed after 768 consultation responses from residents, businesses and interest groups.
Around 80 percent of the responses were either critical or reserved about the plan.
The revised version exempts all of Vesterbrogade, the area around Copenhagen Central Station, Skelbækgade and part of Halmtorvet.
Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.
Fewer trains between Copenhagen and western Denmark until Tuesday morning
Fewer trains will run between parts of Denmark until at least 10 a.m. Tuesday after an overhead wire fell between Sorø and Slagelse.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said Monday afternoon that repairs were underway.
DSB, Denmark’s national passenger rail operator, said InterCityLyn and InterCity trains are still running between Copenhagen and Esbjerg, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
Although the overhead wire fell on the westbound track, trains can still use the other track.
Replacement buses are also running between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. DSB said earlier Monday that it had ordered 50 buses.
The disruption was initially expected to last until 8 p.m. Monday, but Banedanmark later extended the estimate until 10 a.m. Tuesday.
A train that stopped beneath the fallen wire also had to be evacuated. Another train was connected to it and pulled it to the nearest station.
Banedanmark said it would investigate why overhead wires have fallen repeatedly on the same section. A damaged overhead line near Sorø also caused cancellations and delays in mid-September.
“We are well aware that this is not the first time we can see a fallen overhead wire on the same section within a relatively short time,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Smidt Sigsgaard said.
Another overhead wire was also torn down at Copenhagen Airport on Monday, causing reduced service and delays.
DSB and Banedanmark are advising passengers to check Rejseplanen before traveling.
Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.
DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ organization, criticized the government’s plan.
Thomas Sørensen, director of DI’s automotive branch, called it an “own goal to let taxes on electric cars rise from the new year.”
According to FDM, Denmark’s main association for car owners, a VW ID.4 Style could cost around DKK 10,300 more in tax, while a Tesla Model Y Long Range with all-wheel drive could face an increase of nearly DKK 28,000.
Mobility Denmark, an industry association representing the automotive sector, also criticized the proposal.
“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Passengers may also face longer travel times between the two stations.
DSB told Ritzau that trains are still able to run on one track despite the damaged overhead wire.

DSB is advising travelers to check the journey planner before traveling.
Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”
“It is important for safety on the link that the authorities regularly conduct exercises so that we are as well prepared as possible if a serious situation should arise,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police will issue an update through Politi Update, the Danish police public information service, when the bridge reopens Thursday evening.
“We therefore hope for road users’ understanding, and as soon as the exercise is completed, we will reopen the bridge to traffic again,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police said smaller exercises are regularly carried out in cooperation with Swedish authorities, while larger full-scale exercises such as Thursday’s are held less frequently.
Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.
