A classic coming-of-age novel spurred this writer to 'blow up' her life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Grace Chapple exposes political heart of A Room with a View in new play
When Grace Chapple visited Florence, Italy, in 2022, she was listening to the audiobook of A Room with a View.
Travelling solo for the first time, aged 27, she found herself in the Uffizi Gallery — where Botticelli's The Birth of Venus hangs — feeling unsure what to do with her life.
"I was thinking, 'Do I even know who I am?'" Chapple says.
"You know that first time you're forced to confront yourself alone and how you interact with the world?"
As she wandered the city, a little hungover, so too did the protagonist of the novel: Lucy Honeychurch.
In English author EM Forster's 1908 novel A Room with a View, Lucy visits Italy, chaperoned by her spinster cousin Charlotte Bartlett.
There, she meets the charismatic but strange George Emerson and is wooed by another suitor, the wealthy but condescending Cecil Vyse.
It's the set-up for a love triangle, but Forster's novel was more than a romance; it's Lucy's coming-of-age story, which also pokes fun at turn-of-the-century English society.
That complexity spurred Chapple to adapt it for Sydney's Belvoir St Theatre, where it opens this month before travelling to Melbourne Theatre Company.
"The novel hit me hard," she says. "It found me at the moment in my life where I really needed it."
Listening to A Room with a View in Florence did more than inspire Chapple creatively. It encouraged her to "blow up" her life.
Returning to Sydney, where she had moved from Perth to study playwriting at the National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA), Chapple broke up with her long-term boyfriend.
"When you're stuck on train tracks in life, you need something huge to shake you out of it," Chapple says.
Finding inspiration at home
That year, Chapple's debut play, Never Closer, set during the Troubles, premiered as part of Belvoir's independent 25A program. Two years later, it opened on the theatre's main stage.
A new production from indie company Patalog Theatre will return to Melbourne this month, after earning rave reviews in May.
Never Closer is the story of five schoolfriends reuniting for Christmas Eve at Deidre's house in Northern Ireland in 1987.
Seeing each other a decade after they finished school, with many of them leaving Northern Ireland to work and study, unresolved tensions rise to the surface, especially after Niamh brings home her English fiancé Harry.
It was the play Chapple wrote while studying at NIDA.
She recalls being asked when she applied: "If you had a year left to live, what would you write about?"
She doesn't know why she burst into tears: "I just said, 'My mum'."
Chapple's mum grew up in Northern Ireland and moved to London at 17 to study medicine, where she met Chapple's dad, an Englishman.
"That became the base of the play," Chapple explains.
"But it was mixed in with the fact I had just left home for the first time and was dealing with all these weird feelings about leaving behind my friends and my home and not knowing if there would be a home to go back to.
"It made me think about my mum and how she never went back."
Beneath the period romance
After members of the Belvoir team saw Never Closer during its 25A season, they wanted to know what Chapple was going to do next.
"They were keen to invest in me as an artist," she says.
"They said, 'What else do you have? Is there anything you want to adapt you might be able to turn around quicker than an original?'"
When she listened to A Room with a View earlier that year, Chapple had been struck by its theatricality.
"[Forster] writes in scenes and it's all about relationships," she explains. "The action hinges around conversations."
With buy-in from Never Closer director Hannah Goodwin, Chapple pitched the adaptation to Belvoir artistic director Eamon Flack.
"At first glance it feels like a quite conventional period romance … but the romance is really a vehicle for talking about more exciting political and transgressive topics than we're used to getting out of your Jane Austens," she explains.
Chapple says A Room with a View resonates with a modern audience because Lucy is, like all young people, "learning to think for yourself in a world that is really trying to tell you how to think".
"It's about how dangerous it can be to a dominant culture when people start to break away and carve their own paths.
"It's a journey everyone has to go on of figuring out how to live honestly in this world and be true to the person you are and how much that can cost."
A show about the housing crisis
That question of cost is something Chapple is thinking about with her next project, her second original play, The Landlord, which will feature in Belvoir's 2027 season.
It reunites the writer with Goodwin and Never Closer star Ariadne Sgouros (High Country) and breaks down intergenerational inequality in a story set across two Surry Hill terraces. Both are owned by 65-year-old John — but only one is falling apart.
Chapple started writing The Landlord in 2024, when she was on a research trip to Cambridge University to pore over its archive of Forster's manuscripts and diaries for her A Room with a View.
"[The Landlord] is born out of just all the dehumanising experiences that come from being a renter," she says.
It's a subject many millennial artists are grappling with in their work.
"Every conversation I've had since I moved to Sydney works its way back to the housing crisis eventually," Chapple says.
"Like, someone's got a shitty rental situation or they're getting kicked out or they're paying too much or they're trying to buy and can't."
While it's the subject on everyone's lips, not everyone has Chapple's expertise.
She's approaching the subject armed with a degree in economics.
"I was taught the narratives that are constructed around capitalism that protect it and make it seem like this perfect, inevitable thing," she says.
"I liked the idea of unpicking the narratives I was taught, but for people who didn't study it."
A Room with a View is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from October 3 - November 1 and Melbourne Theatre Company from November 14 - December 19.
Never Closer is at fortyfivedownstairs, Melbourne, from October 15 - November 1.
The Landlord is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from September 25 - October 24, 2027.

Europe war-games life after Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The EU can’t pretend Friedrich Merz isn’t in trouble any longer.
After a string of humiliating election losses where the far right has made historic gains and an internal fight with his own coalition over social care policy, EU partners are starting to plan for the prospect that the German chancellor could be ousted — or at least distracted — in the crucial coming months, according to five diplomats and officials who spoke to POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive talks.
Two European governments have even held internal sessions to game out what the end of Merz’s chancellorship would mean for EU policymaking, two of those familiar with the discussions said.
Advertisement
It’s not a prospect they take lightly. Merz leads the EU’s largest economy and is the chief negotiator for wealthy countries seeking to rein in spending in the bloc’s proposed €2 trillion seven-year budget. He is also a driving force behind EU efforts to save heavy industry.
“Any debate about the German chancellor weakens Germany’s role in the EU and in the world,” said Wilhelm Gebhard, a member of the Bundestag and an official in Merz’s governing CDU party.
With France facing its own far-right surge and a presidential election next year that could hand power to euroskeptic Marine Le Pen, few in Brussels relish the prospect of Germany, historically the EU’s other major player, turning inwards or derailing important negotiations.
The contingency planning, which has seen officials and diplomats brainstorm the situation, comes after months of mixed signals from Berlin on EU policy, including car emissions and a proposed social media ban for children. Even if Merz stays in office, the political turmoil is already complicating Berlin’s work on the EU’s biggest files.
The worst-case scenario for Brussels would be a leaderless Germany, or one with a far-right government. But that is seen as virtually impossible in the short term, with none of the mainstream players seeking new elections while the far-right Alternative for Germany party are leading in the polls.
“All coalition partners know that they have a great deal to lose from early elections,” said Hannah Neumann, an opposition Green MEP who sits on the European Parliament’s security and foreign affairs committees. “My expectation, therefore, is that they will stay together and muddle through.”
Advertisement
While Merz himself could be forced to resign in the face of his growing unpopularity, he would be replaced straight away by a successor from either his center-right CDU party or his center-left coalition partner, the SPD. That should give Brussels confidence “someone will always be in charge,” said one of the diplomats.
Those who know him insist Merz won’t be distracted when it comes to EU affairs.
“Other politicians might say ‘OK, I focus less on EU politics.’ For him it’s just the opposite: It’s an additional incentive to show leadership in Europe,” said a person familiar with the chancellor’s thinking.
In the immediate term, Merz’s political weakness at home could make finding compromise on the bloc’s next seven-year budget harder by pushing the chancellor to double down on Berlin’s hardline stance in search of a win, a further two diplomats warned.
As the leading voice for countries seeking a smaller EU budget, which leaders hope to agree by year-end, Merz has called for cuts of “hundreds of billions of euros.” Germany, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands are pressing for overall reductions, while net recipients such as Poland and Romania want to protect their share.
Advertisement
Nobody who could replace him as chancellor “would be able to be more flexible than Merz is,” said one of the diplomats, but “the risk is he has to show his self-perceived leadership in Brussels in the hope it will help his standing in Germany.”
An envoy from another country said “domestically he is weak [which means] he can’t compromise” and needs to be seen to score a win by slashing the budget as far as possible.
But Merz’s allies say his fight on the world stage is only worthwhile if his coalition partners play along behind the curtain.
“Strength comes not just from grand appearances in Brussels, but above all from stability, reliability and the ability to push through decisions at home. That is precisely what is lacking at the moment,” said CDU Bundestag member Fabian Gramling. “Germany’s influence in Europe also depends on how united and capable of action the federal government appears at home.”
Friedrich Merz is pictured during a meeting with soldiers in Münster, Germany on Oct. 1, 2026. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images
Infighting and indecision
The fractious relationship between the CDU and the SPD has already been undercutting Berlin’s stance on issues of critical national importance.
Throughout 2025, as Brussels renegotiated a planned phaseout of combustion engine cars, in the face of fierce lobbying from Germany’s influential automotive sector, German officials and diplomats were unable to articulate a clear position, with center-right ministers wanting to scrap the green policy and their center-left counterparts pushing to preserve it.
Advertisement
Ultimately Merz’s fellow German conservatives in Brussels — Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European People’s Party chief Manfred Weber — stepped in to kill the proposal at the eleventh hour.
Another key policy area where the coalition struggled to agree a position was on whether children should be banned from social media, a flagship EU-wide proposal from von der Leyen. While Merz personally backed the idea at the start of the year, he and his political allies spent more than six months struggling to land on a specific age limit to lobby for when von der Leyen was consulting with partners, according to officials and diplomats involved in the talks.
Even before the latest crisis, Merz’s domestic troubles were spilling into Brussels at the highest level. Last year, he surprised fellow EU leaders by demanding that a summit scheduled to cover geopolitics and other policy files should instead focus on saving European heavy industry from competition with the U.S. and China.
Germany lost around 124,100 industrial jobs last year, according to an analysis by EY, with the government concerned deindustrialization is helping drive support for Merz’s far-right and far-left rivals. Other capitals share his concerns, but Merz has insisted industry should top the agenda at future summits.
But even inside the chancellor’s own CDU, he has struggled to achieve consensus on what to do about it. As the Commission plans a push against unfair Chinese trade practices, Merz’s fellow party member and foreign minister Katherina Reiche is seen as more protective over the relationship with Beijing, and the German industrial giants like Volkswagen and BASF that trade with it.
In a speech on Thursday commemorating 36 years of German reunification — the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of communist East Germany —the country’s ambassador to the EU, Thomas Ossowski, told fellow envoys and officials that “whenever we celebrate German unity, we celebrate European unity. And we need this unity [now] more than ever.”
Gabriel Gavin reported from Brussels. Frida Preuß reported from Berlin.Jordyn Dahl, Eliza Gkritsiand Carlo Martuscelli contributed to this report.

Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column.

So on the one hand, AI could refuse to shut down and try and blackmail us, but on the other hand, there’s a chance to make some cash by investing in a growth industry. What’s an investor to do?
Despite all the doom and gloom, though, there’s still hope for humanity. This week, the White House signed an accord on “Super Intelligence” — that’s just AI — signed by the likes of xAI CEO Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, as well as noted intelligence fan U.S. President Donald Trump. Egypt declared an Ethiopian diplomat persona non grata and gave him 48 hours to leave the country in retaliation for Ethiopia’s expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, the state news agency MENA reported Thursday.
A senior Egyptian official told MENA that Cairo regretted Ethiopia’s decision to declare a diplomat serving at the Egyptian Embassy in Addis Ababa persona non grata.
The official said Egypt firmly rejects interference in other countries’ internal affairs and maintains a policy of refraining from commenting on domestic developments in Ethiopia and elsewhere in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.
Under the principle of reciprocity, Egypt declared a counselor at the Ethiopian Embassy in Cairo persona non grata and ordered him to leave within 48 hours, the official said.
MENA identified the counselor as Egazi Emelo Borougi.
“The Ethiopian side has a history of attributing its failures in managing its internal affairs and its successive crises to alleged foreign interference, thereby concealing its ongoing problems,” the official said.
Ethiopia earlier ordered the closure of its embassy in the Eritrean capital Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats serving in Addis Ababa persona non grata.
It subsequently declared a diplomat at the Egyptian Embassy in Addis Ababa persona non grata and gave him a deadline to leave the country.

2 new islands appear near Indonesia’s Anak Krakatoa volcano after eruption
The island-like mounds are likely the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s 1883 eruption
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Two new islands have appeared off Anak Krakatoa, potentially the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s catastrophic 1883 eruption.
The formations, discovered following a 25-hour eruption in early September, sit hundreds of metres off opposite sides of Anak Krakatoa – one to the northwest and the other to the southeast – almost on a straight line through the volcano’s crater, according to Indonesia’s Geological Agency.
The agency places one about 760 metres (0.5 miles) off Anak Krakatoa’s northwest coast and the other some 495 metres to the southeast. It has not verified their dimensions or elevation above sea level.
The agency’s preliminary interpretation is that relatively fluid magma released during the continuous eruption reached the surface via an elongated northwest-southeast opening, with erupted material forming two island-like mounds offshore.

CCTV Captures Russian Drone Slamming Into Kyiv School With 104 Children Inside – Warhead Fails to Detonate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:52:07 UTC
10:52:07 KST

A terrifying CCTV video from Kyiv on Thursday captured the moment a Russian drone slammed into a school where more than 100 children had begun their day – another chilling reminder of how Russia’s expanding aerial war is reaching into the places Ukrainian children are supposed to be safest.
At around 9 a.m., a Russian drone struck School No. 12 in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district, smashing through the building, shattering windows and partially destroying a wall and staircase.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside were 104 children and 60 members of staff.
They survived because classes had already moved into the school’s underground shelter after an air raid alert sounded.
But there was another extraordinary stroke of fortune: the Russian drone’s warhead failed to detonate.
The explosive payload was found inside the damaged school after the strike. Had it functioned as designed, the consequences inside a building holding 164 children and staff could have been dramatically more devastating.
Two things stood between the children and a potential catastrophe: Ukraine’s decision to send them underground and the failure of the weapon that struck their school to explode.
No children or teachers were injured.
The 21-second CCTV recording captures the sudden violence of the impact, followed by debris and smoke engulfing part of the school.
“They spare no one,” headteacher Valentyna Chorna said as she surveyed the damage.
Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
“Children are our future, the future of our nation. In order to destroy a nation, of course, they need to destroy children.”
A Relentless Pattern
Thursday’s near-disaster comes amid an intensifying wave of Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with schools, homes and other civilian facilities repeatedly caught in the strikes.
The danger is growing as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones that are more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
That makes the strike on School No. 12 particularly chilling.
This was not simply debris falling from an interception high above the capital. A Russian attack drone crashed directly into the building carrying an explosive warhead.
The weapon failed to complete the destruction it was capable of causing.
The strike came amid a broader pattern of attacks affecting Ukrainian children and educational facilities.
Human Rights Watch reported in September that 314 educational facilities in Kyiv alone had been damaged since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, including at least 107 during 2026.
Across Ukraine, the scale is far greater. UNICEF told the UN Security Council earlier this year that more than 1,780 educational facilities had been verified as damaged or destroyed since 2022, disrupting education for children already entering another year of wartime schooling.
Recent Russian attacks have repeatedly reached places where children live, study and shelter.
On Sept. 29, Russian forces struck Sumy with four glide bombs, hitting a school while pupils were sheltering inside. Children were among those injured, while civilians were killed elsewhere in the city.
A day earlier in Kharkiv, a Russian glide bomb struck a residential area, injuring dozens of people, including children.
For Ukrainian families, everyday routines – walking to school, sitting in class or sleeping at home – continue to unfold under the threat of another missile or drone alert.
Schools under the laws of war
Under international humanitarian law, schools are civilian objects unless and for such time as they are being used for military purposes.
Parties to a conflict are required to distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives and to take feasible precautions to avoid harm to civilians.
Intentionally directing an attack against a school that remains a civilian object can constitute a war crime.
But the repeated destruction and damage inflicted on educational facilities across Ukraine has left children learning under conditions that would have been unimaginable before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has responded by expanding underground classrooms, school shelters and remote education.
At School No. 12 on Thursday, those precautions proved decisive.
More than 100 children were underground when the Russian drone tore into the floors above them.
Had they still been sitting in ordinary classrooms – or had the drone’s warhead detonated as designed — the outcome could have been catastrophic.
Zelensky visits Kyiv school after Russian Shahed strike
President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the school, where he met with the principal and teachers following the morning Russian Shahed strike.
“Most importantly, everyone is alive,” he wrote on X, thanking the school staff for their “clear and coordinated actions,” which he said saved lives.
“Striking schools and kindergartens is a deliberate Russian tactic aimed at making ordinary life a target,” Zelensky wrote.
“And we are working nonstop to strengthen our air defense and increase the production of Ukrainian interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds – in order to protect our cities and communities from such strikes.”

US sends third aircraft carrier to Middle East amid stalemate in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:17:37 UTC
10:17:37 KST

The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as President Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The deployment, which includes a specialist amphibious attack group, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as midterm elections in the US loom large.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation remains a viable option – despite his initial promises that the war would last a matter of weeks.
The group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines. It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, with its two amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to a US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
It is possible the Washington could move to seas off Japan, once the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group arrives.
In a Time magazine interview published on Thursday, Trump raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough”.
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican party chances in November, Trump at first responded: “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide”.
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

AI generated
BRASILIA – Brazilian police are investigating a possible bomb placed in a backpack thrown outside the Supreme Court, the country’s highest tribunal reported on Oct 1, three days before presidential elections begin.
The suspect, who was arrested, “tried to jump the court’s fences” and “threw a backpack on top of a bus stop,” the court said in a statement.
Police restricted access to the site, where an AFP journalist observed around a dozen patrol cars.
A bomb squad was on its way, military police reported, and spokesperson Raphael Broocke told AFP a “rigorous procedure to inspect the object” would take place.
Election campaigning in Latin America’s largest democracy has been tense, with polls showing a dead heat between leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a potential run-off.
The pair will face off in a first-round vote on Oct 4, with Lula projected as slightly ahead of his right-wing rival.
The Supreme Court is highly criticised by the political right, notably for the 2025 conviction of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio’s father – for plotting a coup.
The institution has also become embroiled in a massive fraud scandal that has dominated the final weeks of the presidential campaign.
A man killed himself in a suicide bombing in front of the tribunal in November 2024.
The court was also a target during right-wing rioting on Jan 8, 2023, when Jair Bolsonaro supporters stormed several buildings hosting branches of government.
The Supreme Court later deemed the event an attempted coup against Lula’s presidential victory over Bolsonaro senior that year. AFP

Downing Street said Thursday there could be “no suggestion that anyone is above the rules” after Prime Minister Andy Burnham faced criticism over his comments about Manchester City and the club’s ongoing financial case. 
A No 10 spokesperson told BBC that Burnham had made clear that “the initial judgement is serious” and stressed that the Premier League process must be allowed to continue independently. 
“It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected,” the spokesperson said. “Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” 
The clarification came after Burnham said he would be “really concerned to lose” Manchester City’s owners if they decided to sell the club. 
“They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is,” Burnham said in an interview with the BBC. 
Burnham also said he was “not getting directly involved in the process,” adding that it would be wrong to “jump to a conclusion” because the situation remained “contested by Manchester City.”  
The comments prompted criticism from Conservative and Liberal Democrat politicians, who questioned whether political pressure could be brought to bear on the independent process. 
Manchester City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal against the independent commission’s findings. 
The commission found the club guilty of most of the 115 charges it faced. Among its findings were that City arranged “sham contracts” with commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830 million (nearly $1million). 
The Premier League said Manchester City “systematically broke” its rules for nearly a decade. 
Burnham has also said he was confident that his interactions with City’s owners during his time as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

BERLIN, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, will establish its first dedicated drone regiment in 2027 to adapt to evolving modern warfare, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Thursday.
Speaking during a visit to a military training area in Bergen, Lower Saxony, Pistorius said that the decision was drawn from lessons learned in the conflict in Ukraine.
The planned regiment will deploy both unmanned aerial and ground systems with operational ranges of up to 500 kilometers, and include an electronic warfare company, Pistorius said.
The specialized unit will begin with around 300 troops before expanding to a target strength of 600. ■

Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
01:08:31 UTC
10:08:31 KST

Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
In her statement, Hochul said the decision by Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, not to prosecute the 2024 case, and the questions raised in recent days over the Cornell police department’s investigation of the allegations, have “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time”.
Hochul said James would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
The former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024 filed a lawsuit in September, in a case that has sparked national outrage, roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
Van Houten declined at the time of the alleged assault to bring criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe.
He has maintained that the woman’s first account to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he had never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser.
She is suing seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity and others.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client had not touched the woman or engaged in any drug use.
Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell, a private university, agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carrying 4 astronauts docks with ISS
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:15:06 CST
09:15:06 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft carrying four astronauts for NASA's Crew-13 mission docked with the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday, after a nearly eight-hour journey from launch to the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft lifted off at 11:10 a.m. Eastern Time (1610 GMT) aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It autonomously docked with the ISS at 7:05 p.m. Eastern Time (0005 GMT).
The crew comprises NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
The mission, codenamed Crew-13, marks the 13th crew rotation mission to the ISS conducted by a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft under NASA's Commercial Crew Program.
The crew will spend several months aboard the space station conducting scientific research and technology demonstrations to support future human exploration of the Moon and Mars, as well as studies with potential benefits for people on Earth, according to NASA. ■

US ‘ICE Barbie’ files for divorce from cross-dressing ‘bimbo’ husband
Former US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem has filed for divorce from her husband of 34 years, Bryon Noem, according to court filings seen by multiple outlets.
The former DHS chief, dubbed ‘ICE Barbie’ online over her glamorous appearance while overseeing US President Donald Trump’s controversial immigration crackdown, filed the divorce papers on Monday in Hamlin County in her home state of South Dakota, citing “irreconcilable differences.”
“Kristi Noem has filed for the dissolution of her marriage to Bryon Noem. She has great faith in the South Dakota judicial system and will reserve any further comments for the legal process,” her attorney told People magazine on Tuesday.
The couple married in 1992 and have three adult children – two daughters and a son.
Bryon Noem reportedly acknowledged receiving the divorce papers on April 8, two days after his wife’s legal team signed the complaint.
Shortly before that, reports emerged that he led a double life as a cross-dressing ‘bimbofication’ fetishist – a subculture centered on exaggerated hyper-feminine, Barbie-like aesthetics. The Daily Mail reported in March that Noem had posted multiple pictures of himself in exaggerated forms of drag online during his wife’s roughly 14-month tenure as DHS secretary. He also reportedly spent at least $25,000 on acquaintances from bimbofication forums.
His online activity could have posed a potential blackmail risk for his wife, national security experts cited by the Daily Mail said.
Just weeks before, Trump had fired Noem as DHS secretary over several mounting controversies. He later appointed her to a diplomatic role focused on security cooperation in the Americas.
Her dismissal came a day after Noem was questioned in Congress about an alleged affair with Trump adviser Corey Lewandowski – claims she dismissed as “tabloid garbage.”
Both controversies erupted at a particularly sensitive time for Noem and the DHS, with the department facing public criticism and intense congressional scrutiny following the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents during Trump’s immigration crackdown.

AI is ‘better informed’ than doctors, US health secretary Kennedy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

AI is ‘better informed’ than doctors, US health secretary Kennedy says
Sheryl Gay Stolberg
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has frequently advised Americans not to trust medical experts, said this week that artificial intelligence could offer patients “a second opinion that is much better informed than any doctor in the country” and had the power to “free us from medical tyranny”.
Kennedy made the comments on Sept 29 during a “fireside chat” with Vice-President J.D. Vance at a Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) conference sponsored by companies that have business before his department, as well as AI companies, such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
Kennedy said OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman told him during a recent visit to his office that it would be “malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or to make a prescription without at least checking AI”. Kennedy apparently agreed.
The health secretary’s wholehearted endorsement of AI comes as the Trump administration is facing mounting pressure to do more to regulate the technology. Kennedy’s own department has faced some criticism for moving too rapidly to fund AI projects in healthcare.
“One of the things that is going to change is that we’re never ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,’” Kennedy said during the Sept 29 session.
“If somebody tells you, ‘Masks work, trust the experts,’ AI may tell you otherwise,” he added. “If somebody tells you, ‘Social distancing works, trust the experts,’ AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that.”
When it was finally Vance’s turn to speak, he cracked a joke: “I guess I’m in the wrong summit. I thought this was about weight loss and acid, not AI.”
The MAHA Summit, at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, did indeed address other topics, including some of Kennedy’s core issues: the promise of psychedelic drugs, healthy eating and chronic disease prevention.
Kennedy and other administration officials were not involved in planning the conference; they were invited speakers. But so many appeared – including Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins; Lee Zeldin, who heads the Environmental Protection Agency; and Mehmet Oz, who runs Medicare and Medicaid – that at times it looked like a corporate advertisement with a government imprimatur.
The conference’s tilt towards business, and its sponsorship by companies such as Walmart and Grail, which has an application for a cancer screening blood test pending before the Food and Drug Administration, generated a backlash from some longtime Kennedy supporters.
“It’s all a grift,” said Dr Robert Malone, a critic of mRNA Covid-19 vaccines. Malone served briefly as vice-chair of a vaccine advisory committee appointed by Kennedy, but resigned in March after a judge ruled that he and other committee members lacked essential qualifications.
“Why were none of the founding women of the movement involved?” asked Alex Clark, a podcaster with the conservative group Turning Point USA, referring to the so-called MAHA Moms. One of them, Vani Hari, who calls herself “the Food Babe” and has worked closely with Kennedy, attended as a guest but was not on the programme.
Stefanie Spear, Kennedy’s closest adviser, moderated a session that included Jonathan Neman, a founder of the salad chain Sweetgreen, who marvelled at how Kennedy has changed the conversation around food. Neman said that in 2015, his company briefly promoted an initiative it called Make America Healthy Again.
Coming just five weeks before the midterm elections, the conference shed light on how the MAHA movement has fractured since 2024, when it rallied behind Kennedy and helped power US President Donald Trump’s election victory.
In effect, there are now two MAHAs: corporate, Trump-aligned MAHA, including the conference organisers, and grassroots unaffiliated MAHA, which Democrats are now trying to court. In Michigan on Sept 29, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate, announced a Build a Healthier America agenda.
“Any MAHA anything that is brought to you by Walmart Corporation and the health insurance companies tells you everything you need to know,” El-Sayed, a former public health official in Detroit, said in an interview Monday night.
El-Sayed’s agenda includes plans to address many of the issues that have galvanized MAHA followers: getting toxic substances out of foods, clean water, improving the health of school meals and eliminating pesticides from farming. But he said he did not support Kennedy’s push to discourage childhood vaccination.
The topic of vaccines, central to Kennedy’s work for decades, was conspicuously absent from the conference agenda. So was Dr Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, who has been tangling with the White House over its plan to assert political control over his agency’s grant-making decisions.
Bhattacharya, who was initially scheduled to moderate a panel discussion, disappeared from the final agenda. A spokesperson would not say why.
Journalists were excluded from the conference for the most part, although it was streamed online. Major news outlets that applied for press credentials, including The New York Times, were denied them. In an e-mail, conference organisers said they had “limited space”. But the press section inside the hotel ballroom was empty.
“I cannot understand why the MAHA Summit denied so many press credentials, especially with so many US govt officials on stage,” Helena Bottemiller Evich, founder of an influential newsletter, Food Fix, wrote on the social platform X. She added that while she was granted credentials, “the press area was largely empty and our movement was restricted so I left”.
Reporters and conference guests instead mingled in the grand lobby and restaurant of the hotel, which Trump owned from 2012 to 2022. Among those spotted there was entrepreneur Mark Cuban, whose company Cost Plus Drugs teamed up with Trump on TrumpRx, the president’s plan to reduce the cost of drugs.
Cuban, dressed in a teal T-shirt and dining alone, said he had no idea the MAHA Summit was taking place and had no interest in attending. He was in town for another meeting.
Kennedy’s supporters, including Tony Lyons, who oversees a constellation of MAHA-themed non-profits, including the organiser of the conference, defended the secretary. The MAHA Center, which hosted the conference, said on its website that it did not “coordinate with any government entity” in planning the event.
“People have been going after Bobby Kennedy for many, many years now,” Lyons said during a conversation that included Calley Means, a top Kennedy adviser; Zeldin; and Kyle Diamantas, the acting FDA commissioner.
“They’re going after Bobby Kennedy because they say he’s dangerous,” Lyons added, “and we know what he’s a danger to. He’s a danger to the people who are roadblocks: The people, the companies, the deep-state actors who are roadblocks to real progress.”
The Sept 29 conference came on the heels of another MAHA event, focused on healthcare data, hosted on Sept 28 by the MAHA Institute, another organisation affiliated with Lyons. Kennedy mingled with guests at a private reception Monday night.
One of them, Jeffrey Tucker, who runs the Brownstone Institute, a free-market policy organisation that grew out of a backlash to Covid-19 restrictions, described the scene on X. “Guy at reception last night in DC, confusing me with someone important, started pitching his new medical product that is being considered by the FDA,” Tucker wrote.
“The conversation was not particularly welcomed by me,” he added, “so I said the following: ‘It doesn’t matter if it works or not. All that matters is whether you have the money. Pay the needed millions and it is approved. Pay nothing and it is not approved. That’s how it works.’ To my amazement he said: ‘Yes, that’s it exactly.’” NYTIMES

Time for ASEAN to Revive its Customs Union Vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:38:00 UTC
08:38:00 KST

As tariffs once again become bargaining tools for major powers, one of ASEAN’s key weaknesses is the fragmentation of its market across national tariff regimes. The revival of the Common External Tariff (CET) proposal, rejected four decades ago, raises a fundamental question: can ASEAN move beyond a mere “collection of assembly hubs” to become a higher-value-added economic region and a negotiating actor in its own right?
A Customs Union Proposal Rejected 40 Years Ago
ASEAN’s economic integration has been built on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), agreed in 1992 and implemented through the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme from 1993. The CEPT lowered intra-ASEAN tariffs on goods originating in the region. A CET, by contrast, would require member states to apply a common external tariff schedule to imports from outside ASEAN. Its adoption would take ASEAN beyond a free trade area and towards a customs union.
The CET is not a new idea. In August 1986, exactly 40 years ago, the Philippines, then ASEAN chair, proposed a customs union at the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting. The proposal called for intra-regional tariffs to be reduced gradually within a fixed time frame and for a common tariff to be imposed on imports from outside ASEAN. No consensus emerged: Indonesia opposed the deadline, while Singapore objected that the proposal could result in higher external tariffs. Intra-ASEAN trade then accounted for only about 20 percent of member states’ total trade, and their heavy dependence on external markets made a CET difficult to accept.
AFTA’s Success—and the Borders That Remain
ASEAN instead chose AFTA. This flexible form of integration eliminated most intra-regional tariffs while preserving each member state’s discretion over external tariffs. It supported ASEAN’s model of open regionalism – welcoming foreign investment and imported intermediate inputs while producing for global markets – and helped expand regional production networks. Yet many member states remained concentrated in assembly operations and dependent on external suppliers for key components, advanced materials and research and development. As a result, the value added retained within ASEAN did not rise commensurately with the value of its exports.
Under a fully functioning customs union, goods imported from outside the region could, after paying the common external tariff upon entering ASEAN, circulate freely within the bloc in principle. Certificates of origin and customs clearance procedures currently required for preferential intra-ASEAN trade would, in principle, no longer be necessary. With national tariff borders and rules of origin removed, companies could source the most suitable mix of parts and materials from across ASEAN and allocate production stages accordingly. Lower border costs would encourage intra-regional sourcing, the consolidation of production, and investment in higher-value activities.
Yet the flexibility that was once ASEAN’s strength is becoming a weakness amid intensifying geoeconomic competition. As tariffs, export controls, subsidies, and scrutiny of circumvention become increasingly intertwined with economic security, individual ASEAN members risk accepting different terms in separate negotiations with major powers. If this continues, companies may find it increasingly difficult to treat ASEAN as a single production base. More importantly, if member states continue to bargain separately on critical trade issues, not only regional supply chains but ASEAN centrality itself could be hollowed out.
A CET as a Platform for an Industrial Upgrade
In response to these concerns, the ASEAN Geoeconomics Report 2025 recommended that ASEAN pursue a CET alongside a compatible regional industrial policy. A common tariff alone, however, will not deliver an industrial upgrade; it must be combined with policies that connect the complementary strengths of member states and promote technology adoption, skills development, R&D and intra-regional sourcing. Only then can ASEAN retain more value added and create more high-quality jobs within the region. A CET alone is not sufficient, but it can provide the market foundation for such upgrading.
Realizing this vision will not be easy. ASEAN would have to agree on the treatment of customs revenue, trade-remedy measures and negotiating authority vis-à-vis third countries. It would also have to reconcile the FTAs concluded separately by individual member states. Existing agreements would need either to be consolidated into ASEAN-wide trade agreements or to have their preferential tariff rates and rules of origin harmonized across trading partners and product categories. If national tariff differentials remained, ASEAN would still need origin checks and the collection of tariff differences at internal borders to prevent imports from being diverted through lower-tariff members. The result would fall short of a full customs union.
Even so, ASEAN should not bury the idea once again. As a first step, member states should harmonize tariffs at low levels on critical inputs that cannot be adequately sourced within the region, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and critical minerals. This would not constitute a customs union, but would provide a practical test of whether a transition towards a CET is workable. In parallel, ASEAN should more closely integrate customs procedures, standards and conformity assessment, investment policy, skills development and R&D support. The objective should be to build a regional industrial base linking components and materials with more advanced stages of production.
ASEAN should aim for a customs union that preserves openness to critical inputs, reduces fragmentation within its regional market and encourages companies to invest on an ASEAN-wide basis. It should not become a “tariff fortress” that erects high barriers against the rest of the world. Rather, it should provide the institutional foundation for transforming ASEAN from a “collection of assembly hubs” dependent on cheap labor into an integrated economic region that builds deeper capabilities in technology, components and R&D—and retains more value added at home.
At a time when major powers are once again weaponizing tariffs, a common external tariff and unified negotiating authority would give ASEAN greater collective bargaining power as a single economic bloc. A customs union would be more than a foundation for industrial upgrading; it could also become a powerful shield for ASEAN against tariff coercion.

Saudi-led coalition says Houthis attacked power station for Prophet’s Mosque in Medina

- The conflict escalated after 2026, with Houthi attacks on Saudi territory and a naval blockade, leading to Saudi air strikes and ongoing fighting in Yemen’s Red Sea coast and inland areas.
AI generated
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said on Oct 1 the Iran-aligned group had attacked a power distribution station in Medina that supplies electricity to the Prophet’s Mosque, one of Islam’s holiest sites.
The coalition said the attack put one transformer out of service but did not affect the power network. A Houthi military source, quoted by the Houthi-run Saba news agency, denied the coalition report.
The Houthis later reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and other parts of Yemen, with no immediate Saudi confirmation of the reports.
A spokesperson for Yemen’s armed forces, which are aligned with the internationally recognised government, said coalition forces had attacked what it described as “high-value targets” in the capital Sanaa, without providing further details.
The recent escalation is the most serious fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022.
Hostilities resumed in 2026 after the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in July and began attacking Saudi territory and shipping, while Houthi forces also made major territorial gains along the Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes in Yemen and backed government forces fighting to repel the Houthis.
The Saudi-led coalition said an investigation and examination of drone wreckage confirmed Houthi involvement in planning and carrying out the Sept 29 attack on the Medina power station.
A Houthi military source said the coalition claim was a “lie” intended to cover up what he described as Saudi Arabia’s failure to substantiate its earlier accusation that the Houthis targeted the Muslim holy city of Mecca, Saba reported.
Saudi Arabia said two weeks ago it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered restricted airspace over the city. The coalition described that incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca since 2017, while the Houthis denied targeting Mecca or any other Islamic holy site.
The coalition said the Medina attack was part of what it described as repeated Houthi attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques and “provoke” Muslims worldwide. It said it would continue taking measures to protect the holy sites and pilgrims.
The coalition also said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait. It gave no immediate details on any damage or casualties. Local officials said early on Oct 2 that the Houthis had also targeted the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces command in Aden with several ballistic missiles and drones. There was no immediate comment from the coalition or the Houthis. REUTERS

Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:33:00 UTC
08:33:00 KST

Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered his annual keynote address and answered audience questions at the Valdai Discussion Club’s international forum outside Moscow on Thursday.
During a more-than-three-hour session moderated by foreign affairs expert and RT contributor Fyodor Lukyanov, Putin spoke on a broad range of topics, including tensions with the West, the Ukraine conflict and artificial intelligence.
A world in turmoil and the emergence of a new global balance
The world has reached a pivotal moment shaped by profound transformations in global politics, the economy and demographics, as well as the rapid development of technology, including AI, Putin said.
“We are confident that, in the long term, as we move away from Western hegemony, the global situation will gradually change for the better – toward a more stable, democratic, and free multipolar international order,” he said.
The risk of new conflicts
Technological and social change is fueling a sense of uncertainty and greater international tensions, Putin said. Governments may seek to preserve stability at home by “exporting instability” abroad, while new opportunities “fuel ambitions” and encourage countries to take greater risks.
As a result, “the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, highly likely,” Putin said.
AI could herald an era of ‘digital totalitarianism’
The proliferation of AI could lead to “digital totalitarianism,” shaping individuals and stripping away their individuality through the use of algorithms configured by others, Putin warned.
“Such digital totalitarianism would be just as much of a dead end – as bleak and inhumane – as the totalitarian societies of the past that we know so well,” he said.
Countries and communities must join forces to find broadly acceptable solutions to the challenges posed by AI and other technologies capable of influencing human behavior, identity and thought, Putin said.
While AI can be a useful tool, any final political decision must remain in human hands, he stressed.
Relations with the West
Russia’s current tensions with the West date back to the fall of the Soviet Union, when certain Western leaders sought to further weaken Russia instead of welcoming it into the European security system, Putin argued.
“Despite the many years – and I want to emphasize this, many years – of attempts by the new Russia to become part of so-called Western civilization, in practice they did everything they could to truly isolate and further break apart the Russian Federation itself,” the president said.
“They still say this at various events and gatherings even today: ‘We need to finish breaking up the empire,’” Putin added.
He pointed to NATO’s eastward expansion, which he claimed violated assurances given to Moscow. Putin further argued that European politicians were using escalatory rhetoric toward Moscow to draw attention away from political and economic problems at home.
No saber-rattling around Kaliningrad
The president reiterated that Russia would respond to any potential attack on its Kaliningrad Region, an exclave on the Baltic Sea sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Any assault on Russian territory would “inevitably” be viewed as grounds for using all the weaponry at Moscow’s disposal, he said.
Putin was referring to recent statements by Western officials, including Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who have argued that NATO should be prepared for a potential conflict involving Kaliningrad.
Nuclear weapons as ‘Chekhov’s gun’
The president warned that a conventional war could escalate into a nuclear conflict.
“Today, when the world’s leading powers possess weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, bringing the Earth to a catastrophic state, can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Of course not,” Putin said.
Putin compared the risk posed by the continued existence of nuclear weapons to “Chekhov’s gun,” a dramatic principle attributed to Russian playwright Anton Chekhov that holds that a gun introduced early in a story should eventually be fired.
”We all know the famous saying: if a gun is hanging on the wall at the beginning of a play, by the end it is bound to go off,” the Russian leader said. “We must bear that in mind and prevent it from happening.”
“If we want to live – and everyone wants to live – then, as I once said in a public speech, let’s live in peace. Let’s work together to find ways to make that happen,” he said.
The Ukraine conflict and Russia’s goals
Putin said the Ukraine conflict, which is on track to enter its fifth year next February, is about Russia’s security rather than territorial ambitions. He reiterated Moscow’s demand that Ukraine abandon its plans to join NATO in favor of permanent neutrality.
Russia is ready to end the conflict, but only on terms acceptable to Moscow, he said.

What is celebrated on October 2 in Ukraine and around the world

What is celebrated on October 2 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 2, international and national holidays are observed around the world, including the International Day of Non-Violence and Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Believers commemorate Saints Cyprian, Justina, and Theoctistus.
On October 2, the world observes the UN-sponsored International Day of Non-Violence, World Farmed Animals Day, and World Smile Day. India celebrates Mahatma Gandhi's birthday, while Guinea celebrates Independence Day. According to the new-style church calendar, the hieromartyr Cyprian and the martyr Justina are commemorated, while according to the old style, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorimedon are remembered, reports UNN.
International Day of Non-Violence
An official international UN observance established by a resolution of the General Assembly in 2007. The day is timed to coincide with the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of India's independence movement and the founder of the philosophy and strategy of nonviolent resistance.
The event aims to promote the ideas of peace and tolerance, protect human rights, reject armed aggression, and resolve sociopolitical conflicts through dialogue, education, and civic awareness.
World Day for Farmed Animals (WDFA)
Established in 1983 by the Movement for the Rights of Farmed Animals, it is also timed to coincide with the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who was a consistent advocate of humane treatment for all living things.
The event highlights the problem of the mass industrial raising, slaughter, and suffering of billions of farmed animals worldwide, calling for the humanization of animal husbandry standards, ethical consumption, and the promotion of plant-based food alternatives.
World Smile Day
An unofficial international holiday observed on the first Friday of October since 1999. The holiday was founded by American artist Harvey Ball, who created the famous graphic symbol—a smiling yellow face—in 1963.
The event is held under the motto "Do an act of kindness. Help at least one person smile!" and encourages people to show genuine kindness, engage in positive emotional exchange, and support those experiencing hardship.
Guinea Independence Day
The main national holiday of the West African country, commemorating the events of October 2, 1958, when Guinea became the first among the French colonies of Tropical Africa to reject the French Community project in a referendum and officially proclaim full state sovereignty under the leadership of Ahmed Sékou Touré.
Gandhi Jayanti in India
An official public holiday and one of India's three national days, established in honor of the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi—the "Father of the Nation."
On this day, ceremonial wreath-laying ceremonies, joint prayers by representatives of all the country's religious denominations, and cultural and educational events dedicated to preserving Gandhi's legacy take place near the Raj Ghat memorial in New Delhi.
Grandparents' Day in Italy (Festa dei Nonni)
An official holiday established by the Italian Parliament in 2005 to emphasize the exceptional role of the older generation in raising young people and preserving family values.
The date was chosen for a reason: in the Catholic tradition, October 2 is the feast of the Guardian Angels, symbolically emphasizing the protective and caregiving role of grandfathers and grandmothers in the family.
Day of Remembrance of the Hieromartyr Cyprian, the Martyr Justina, and the Martyr Theoctistus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the hieromartyr Cyprian, the martyr Justina, and the martyr Theoctistus. Cyprian was a renowned pagan magus and sorcerer in Antioch who, using pagan incantations, attempted to seduce the virtuous Christian maiden Justina at the request of a young man named Aglaias.
Seeing that all his magic was powerless against Justina's prayerful sign of the cross, Cyprian believed in Christ, burned his books of sorcery, was baptized, later became a bishop, and, together with Justina, suffered martyrdom under Diocletian in 304.
The blessed Andrew, the fool-for-Christ, is also remembered on this day.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorimedon, who suffered for their faith during the reign of Emperor Probus in the 3rd century in Antioch, displaying unshakable courage during torture.

Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:30:27 UTC
08:30:27 KST

The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell.
Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that the sweeping effort will be “a multiyear transformation” how the Air Force recruits, trains, and develops its maintenance force, suggesting it will be quite a while before that transformation is complete.
“The two-way career field strategy is on track to initiate [an 18-month] pilot test in mid- to late-2027,” said Bell, who added, “It’s going to be a yearslong effort for this to take place.”
The service first revealed its career field transformation plan for maintenance Airmen in January 2025. The strategy called for enlisted Airmen to start out on a generalist track—a single Air Force Specialty Code—where they will focus on applying the most common maintenance skills such as recovering and fueling across multiple airframes. Once Airmen reach the rank of Senior Airman and are preparing to become noncommissioned officers, they would become a specialist in one of six non-aircraft-specific areas:
- Avionics and Electrical, which combines avionics with the electrical side of the Environmental and Electrical (E&E) specialty
- Aerospace Ground Equipment, which will look the same as it does now
- Advanced Mechanical, which combines crew chiefs, fuels, hydraulics, and the flight line side of engine maintenance
- Crew Support Systems, which combines ejection seat systems with the environmental side of E&E
- Fabrication, which combines aircraft structural maintenance, aircraft metals technology, and nondestructive inspection.
- Intermediate-level engines, for maintainers dedicated to intermediate-level engine maintenance.
The New Plan
In the revised plan, the initial phase is similar. It will train maintainers entering the Air Force as aviation maintenance technicians, or AMTs, for their first 18 months of service, focusing on maintenance fundamentals for multiple airframes. The initial phase will also emphasize that the skills they are learning will ground them in the importance of aircraft sortie generation, which is a key focus of the service’s strategy to generate and sustain airpower even if under attack, Bell said.
“We’re an Air Force. We fly, fix, fight, and win. And the first thing that we want to be able to do is make sure that as all of our maintainers come in, they understand what sortie generation is about,” Bell said. “If you can’t get the aircraft off the ground, then what are we really here for?”
Maintenance Airmen will then transition into a specialty track where they will select from one of 14 different specialties, Bell said. The Air Force would not release the new specialty list because it is still refining how it will be organized, according to an Air Force spokesperson. There will be six specialties that are “aircraft-agnostic,” but it’s unclear how they will be different from the original six, the spokesperson said. Another eight specialties will be split among three different aircraft groups:
- Fighter/Atack
- Mobility/Strike
- Tactical Lift/Rotary
Air Force officials refined the plan to offer more specialties after meeting with maintenance Airmen as part of the effort’s feedback-gathering campaign that began in January.
“We stood up 10 different working groups; we brought in almost 280 different maintainers from across the Air Force to help us refine the strategy and the specifics,” Bell said. “It was long list of things that we went through.”
The revised plan offers maintenance Airmen the option to change their specialty, which is currently based on their score on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery test that the majority of enlisted Airmen take while still in high school, Bell said.
“How well they did on that ASVAB test could probably determine what career field they went into and where they were going to spend the next 20 years of their life; something just doesn’t sit right about that,” Bell said. “And if we have the ability to now say, hey, ‘this may be where you scored and which you what you were selected for, but maybe now with a little more maturity, and now that we have shown you some other things, maybe there’s a different path still within the aircraft maintenance career field … maybe you want to choose this specialty over another.’ So, I’m really excited about that aspect of it. There is a little more optionality that also matches up with Air Force needs.”
Eventually, maintainers in the specialty track will have the opportunity to apply for the master aviation technician, or MAT, track—a more specialized pipeline designed to create a smaller force of highly skilled maintainers who will focus on fixing more complex problems on specific aircraft, Bell said.
But the highly selective pipeline is only designed for a “small percentage of maintenance force; that’s going to cultivate them into cross-functional technical experts on a specific aircraft.”
“That small percentage of folks will help us ensure that as people move around, that MAT group of folks will be that core group of folks that we lean on to be those very technical experts to solve some of the hard breaks, the hard problems that might go on the aircraft,” Bell said.
When it was first revealed, the new strategy sparked concerns among current and former Air Force maintainers that the new design could dilute expertise across the career field and reduce local leaders’ ability to solve complex maintenance problems.
“I’m not going to say that that is not a valid concern, but with any change, you’re going to have some amount of pushback to it,” Bell said, adding that that is why the service sought feedback from current maintainers.
“I take all input, and that’s the reason why we have asked the major commands to send me your brightest people who can represent you, who are going to be constructive disruptors,” Bell said.
“To the maintenance Airmen that said, ‘I’m a naysayer and I don’t believe you in this’: give me your input and then help us try to mitigate that,” Bell added. “We can’t continue to do what we’re doing now and think that we’re going to get a different result.”
Critics also question how the Air Force would switch to the new model amid a shortage in maintenance manning.
Bell said that a key benefit of the 2A career field transformation is it will instill in young maintainers the importance of aircraft sortie generation similar to the way Air Force is stressing “airmindedness” in Basic Military Training and tech school to ensure Airmen understand they have a role in generating combat airpower.
“This particular line of effort that we’re doing right now with the two-way career field strategy speaks to retention because we believe that as more maintainers come in and then we train them up in this way, this ability to be sortie generators up front is going to add to their motivation and their reason for being,” Bell said.
“People want to add value, and their ability to be sortie generators early will show that they can add value—that’s why this two-way career field strategy, I believe, is going to be a benefit for us in the retention area.”

Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has dropped out of the final televised debate ahead of a tense first round of voting, accusing the electoral court of "censorship."
The right-wing senator, the son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, announced his withdrawal late on Thursday, just two hours before Brazil's largest television station TV Globo was set to air the programme.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who holds a slight poll lead ahead of Sunday's vote, had already refused to attend, opting to appear on a popular podcast instead.
"I have just decided not to go to Globo's debate due to the censorship imposed on the event by the TSE (the Superior Electoral Court)," Bolsonaro wrote on X.
The court ruled earlier in the evening that TV Globo could not leave an empty chair on the set to represent Lula's absence, according to the decision seen by AFP.
This ruling also prohibits participants from using their speaking time to address the empty chair to highlight the president's no-show.
Polls project a dead heat between the two ideologically opposed candidates in a potential runoff on October 25.
A Datafolha institute poll published Thursday evening gives Lula 48 percent of voting intentions compared with 45 percent for Bolsonaro in the possible second round.
Brazil orders probe into alleged US interference
Also on Thursday, Brazil's attorney general ordered the police to investigate allegations that US President Donald Trump's administration was using government funds to promote a "far-right agenda" in the South American country.
Lula has made Brazil's sovereignty a central campaign theme, warning against "meddling" by Trump, who has backed several right-wing candidates in recent Latin American elections.
Attorney General Jorge Messias called for the probe a day after Britain's The Guardian newspaper published an article alleging that Trump's administration planned to award $1 million to fund civil society groups opposing Brazil's Supreme Court.
The article "raises a serious red flag regarding Brazilian sovereignty," Messias wrote on X.
He said efforts to meddle in Brazilian institutions "cannot be tolerated."
In a separate statement announcing the complaint, the attorney general's office said the Guardian report was "particularly serious, given the ongoing Brazilian electoral process and recent episodes of external pressure on the country's institutions."
Trump was a close ally of Bolsonaro's father, the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after he lost a re-election bid in 2022.
The US administration briefly imposed sanctions against Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes who led the trial against Jair Bolsonaro, which Trump slammed as a "witch hunt" against his ally.

WASHINGTON – RTX’s Raytheon unit won a multiyear contract worth up to US$24.4 billion (S$31.2 billion) to produce Standard Missile-6 interceptors for the US Navy, the service said on Oct 1, as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.
The five-year contract, which includes two additional option years, the Navy said, is meant to provide a steady and reliable supply of the SM-6, a missile that can carry out both offensive strikes and missile defence missions.
The SM-6 award is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued in 2026 to pressure contractors into ramping up output faster. It follows a US$20.7 billion provisional multi-year deal for Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles in late September and a US$58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July.
The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster on increasing output. They are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritise weapons production over shareholder returns.
Industry executives have warned that Congress has not yet appropriated funding for the deals, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.
RTX has said it has invested heavily to keep up with rising demand. It has expanded its skilled workforce, strengthened partnerships across the defence industrial base and automated production, with the aim of significantly increasing output for near- and long-term needs.
Raytheon says the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon that can perform anti-air warfare, anti-surface warfare and ballistic missile defence. It has been fired from a range of Navy ships as well as from land-based launchers. REUTERS
