Putin warns Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in arsenal if any of its territory is attacked
Moscow has told Nato it won’t hesitate to use nuclear arms to defend Kaliningrad against attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal.
In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.
His remarks followed Moscow’s warning to Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia.
Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”.

U.S. designates Russia-linked sanctions-evasion payment network A7 a ‘significant transnational criminal organization’
The U.S. Treasury Department has designated A7, a Russia-linked payment network created to evade sanctions, a “significant transnational criminal organization.”
The designation will make it possible to bar U.S. financial institutions from making any transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents,” foreign shell companies through which the network processes payments for clients in Russia.
The restrictions on A7 were formally imposed as part of sanctions targeting Iran. The Treasury Department said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and central bank used the network’s services.
Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor launched A7 in 2024, with Russia’s Promsvyazbank also taking part. The network consists of hundreds of companies in third countries that process payments for clients in Russia. By Promsvyazbank’s own estimate, A7 processed 7.5 billion rubles in payments in the first half of 2025.
The Russian company A7 itself and A7A5, the ruble-denominated stablecoin it created, have been under U.S. sanctions since August 2025.

Meat industry says it's focused on US trade review, following minister's super proposal
The trade minister has received a rather lukewarm response to his latest proposal to shield Australian farmers from a new round of Trump administration tariffs.
In Wisconsin for a G20 meeting, Don Farrell suggested Australia's wealthy super funds might invest in the US lamb industry, to ultimately help boost sales in America.
Australian lamb is currently subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, which could rise even higher depending on the outcome of a US trade review that's underway.
Asked for his response to Farrell's plan, Australian Meat Industry Council CEO Tim Ryan said the sector was squarely focused on the trade review.
"AMIC maintains that imported lamb is not a cause of injury to the US sheep industry," he said in a statement to the ABC.
"Australian businesses and exporters have already made significant investments in the US lamb supply chain and in developing demand — which ultimately benefits the US industry.
"The Australian and US sheep industry have a history of collaboration across a range of forums for mutual benefit."
Earlier, the superannuation sector pushed back strongly against any moves by the government to dictate how and where it invests its members' money.
Roblox responds to eSafety's call for more action on child safety
Roblox has responded to the eSafety commission's call for large gaming companies to "lift their game" on child safety.
The commission found big differences in how Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam deal with serious harms including grooming, child exploitation, and violent extremist content.
It identified gaps in harmful-content detection, repeat-offender prevention, and information-sharing initiatives.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Roblox says the company prioritises the safety of children.
"We have invested heavily in what eSafety acknowledges is one of the gaming industry's largest Trust & Safety teams, and continue to strengthen our multi-layered safeguards, including advanced detection technologies and mandatory age checks to access chat that no other large online platform has adopted at the scale we have," the spokesperson says.
ATO faces growing calls to reverse credit card payment ban for tax bills
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) is facing mounting calls to reverse its decision to ban credit card payments for tax bills from the end of November.
The ATO announced the surprise move yesterday in response to the Reserve Bank (RBA) outlawing card surcharges, which cost Australians about $1.6 billion a year.
But small businesses are crying foul, arguing they have no option but to absorb the surcharges (or merchants' fees).
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson agrees and has called on the ATO to reverse its decision and allow credit card payments.
"Businesses are expected to absorb these fees, while the ATO avoids them by withdrawing credit card payments," Hanson said in a statement.
"Credit helps businesses manage cashflow and meet tax obligations on time. Removing this option will drive businesses to the wall when they are already doing it tough."
The ATO says the vast majority of Australians do not pay their tax bills using credit cards, and says it would not be appropriate for a government agency to transfer the cost of credit card merchant fees to the community.
Government extends lower fuel quality standards amid Middle East war
Energy Minister Chris Bowen has confirmed the federal government has extended the lower quality standards for fuel as the Middle East war continues.
In March, Labor decided to lower fuel standards to allow more fuel supply into the domestic market in response to higher oil prices.
It allowed high-sulphur fuel, which was restricted a few years ago, to be blended into the Australian fuel supply.
The energy minister says the government intends to keep the lower fuel standards in place until January 2027.
Bowen says it won't affect Australia's emissions.
"It's about sulphur levels and the flashpoint for diesel, so it has no impact on emissions," Bowen says.
"It's about the temperature at which it ignites. It's got no reference to emissions whatsoever."

From yesterday, businesses were banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa.

"This prime minister pretending that somehow there's going to be a discount on his behalf. Well, actually, what's going to happen is everyone will pay more," Taylor says.

Analysis: Albanese leaves grim domestic scene as he flies to the Pacific
Having a Pre-COP meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu is one of those initiatives that probably seemed like a good idea at the time.
No doubt it still has resonance as part of Australia's wider diplomacy in the Pacific, in the battle to limit China's influence. But when Anthony Albanese, still coming down from his New York high, steps onto his plane on Monday bound for Pre-COP, it could feel more like a chore than an opportunity.
Even COP itself, to be held in Turkey from November 9 to 20 and also on Albanese's itinerary, is not expected to break much ground.
Big issues have their high time, seizing public and media attention for brief or long periods. When Labor announced in 2021 that it would bid to host COP (the United Nations' annual climate meeting), climate change was still front and centre. But now — as we (with Pacific countries) are co-hosts with Turkey — global warming has slipped down the public's agenda.
This doesn't mean that, objectively, climate change is any less important. It means other issues have supplanted it on the public's and the media's radar.

The Productivity Commission says its proposal to cut the company tax rate would help with Australia's productivity challenge.

"We did look at the real drop-off that we've seen since the GFC [Global Financial Crisis] in business investment and what we could do to lift that. Company tax reform is one of the sort of the easiest ways, if you like, pathways to doing that."

Spain, Belgium and Poland begin supplying 20mm ammunition — Sybiha

Algeria adopts law imposing death penalty on forest arsonists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:36:47 UTC
05:36:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria adopts law imposing death penalty on forest arsonists
Algerian lawmakers adopted on Thursday a law imposing the death penalty on convicted forest arsonists, after deadly wildfires ripped through swathes of the country in recent weeks.
The official death toll from the blazes, which swept through the country's northeast during the summer, was 12 people, but witnesses have reported the deaths of dozens.
Algeria had upheld a moratorium on the death penalty since 1993, but in August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice minister to amend the penal code to broaden the list of crimes for which capital punishment is allowed.
Lawmakers on Thursday also voted to extend capital punishment to child kidnappings involving torture, sexual assault or mutilation.
"The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes," Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament after the vote.
Despite the moratorium, some death sentences have been handed out, including in terror-related cases, though no executions have been carried out so far.
Tebboune had said that those sentenced to death would be executed once their appeals were exhausted.
The bill received the support of the ruling coalition, while a segment of the opposition objected to it.
"We voted in favour of this bill, given its importance not only legally but also politically and socially for Algerian society," Fatma Zahra Bensafi, an MP for the National Rally for Democracy party, told AFP.
The secular Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) party, however, voted against.
"We are opposed to the death penalty, and this is nothing new for the RCD," said MP Rachid Hassani. "Since its inception, the party has campaigned against capital punishment."
"We believe that the state does not exact revenge or kill," he added. "The state protects citizens."
Under the new law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to "forests, woods or planted or unplanted fields" could face execution.
The same penalty could apply to anyone who "kidnaps a child by any means, tortures them, sexually assaults them and/or mutilates them".
Amnesty International last month urged Algeria not to adopt the law and to refrain from resuming executions.
The rights group described the move as "a deeply retrograde response", adding that authorities should instead "focus on protecting lives, strengthening prevention and emergency response" in the face of reoccurring wildfires.
The justice minister said the Algerian judicial system still provided safeguards for those facing the death penalty, including avenues for appeal or seeking a presidential pardon.
Yet Boudjemaa told parliament the tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", adding that investigations had uncovered links to "foreign parties".
"Targeting the country's environmental and economic assets by deliberately setting fires, at times at the instigation of foreign actors, constitutes a clear form of treason and an attack on the integrity of the national territory," the minister said.
The law is now set to be reviewed by the Senate before being officially ratified by Tebboune.
Forest fires regularly erupt in northern Algeria during the summer, with climate change intensifying their impact due to increasingly frequent droughts and intense heat.
Tebboune has alleged "something criminal" as a cause of the latest summer blazes.

 Einstein correctly described the equivalence of mass and energy as “the most important upshot of the special theory of relativity” (Einstein 1919). Many commentators have observed that he did not write the famous equation (E = mc^2)in his first derivation (Einstein 1905b). Instead, Einstein concluded that if an object, which is at rest relative to an inertial frame, either absorbs or emits an amount of energy (L), its inertial mass will correspondingly either increase or decrease by an amount (L/c^2). The United States imposed sanctions on Russia’s A7 payment system
Kyiv • UNN
Washington blocked the assets of the A7 system, through which Russia conducted international payments. The network claimed a total transaction volume of more than $90 billion.
Washington has imposed sanctions on the A7 system, which Russia used to make payments through international banks in 2024 and 2025. This is reported by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that as of January 2026, A7 claimed to process more than 2,000 transactions daily, with a total transaction volume exceeding 7.5 trillion rubles ($91.5 billion) — approximately 13% of Russia's foreign trade transactions in 2025.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury is dismantling the financial infrastructure that allows Iran and other adversaries to evade sanctions, move illicit funds, and undermine the integrity of the global financial system
Under the sanctions, all property and ownership interests in the A7 network, including transactions involving sub-agents acting on behalf of the A7 network, that are located in the United States or are in the possession or control of U.S. persons, will be blocked.

“What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care,” Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference.
He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike’s death sentence.
“After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now.”
Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre, called the failed execution unprecedented.
“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she told The New York Times.
UN rights chief Volker Turk on Oct 1 urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
“The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished,” his office said on X.
“The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved.”
Pike’s lawyers said earlier that their arguments against the execution had come to pass: “Difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
‘Loudly snoring’
Pike’s case had already attracted scrutiny in the lead-up to her execution date, as she would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Kim Chandler, a media witness with The Associated Press, told CBS News that “Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began” at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
“A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point, she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way,” Chandler said.
Pike later began snoring, witnesses said.
“We just listened... to her snoring and making very loud breathing sounds for almost an hour,” said Catherine Sweeney of WPLN television.
The condemned woman was “loudly snoring, clearly very alive” as the journalists were ushered out of the area, Chandler told CBS.
During a livestream, an ambulance with its lights flashing could be seen leaving the prison.
Established protocol
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol”, adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an “off-site medical facility”.
Governor Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” of the failed execution.
“The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year,” Lee said – apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for Dec 3.
Pike’s case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Following a flurry of legal filings by Pike’s lawyers that delayed the start of the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on the night of Sept 30 cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead.
Pike’s lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer’s killing.
They said her history of childhood sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering”.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. AFP

US judge denies request to find Lindsay Clancy not guilty after mistrial
BOSTON, Oct 1 - A Massachusetts judge who oversaw Lindsay Clancy's murder trial rejected a request on Thursday by her lawyers to declare her not guilty of murder, saying prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a jury to find her responsible for killing her three young children in 2023.
Clancy's lawyers had urged Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth to conclude that prosecutors had failed to prove she could be held criminally responsible for her children's deaths despite suffering from what they said was mental illness. Sullivan declared a mistrial on September 4 after the jury deadlocked.
No one at that trial disputed that Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
But on Thursday, Clancy's lawyers contended that prosecutors failed to present any evidence at the trial proving she had in fact killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan. They also argued that the evidence showed Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.
Sullivan, though, said prosecutors had presented enough physical and circumstantial evidence to allow a jury to conclude that Clancy was the one who strangled the children and was criminally responsible for killing them.
He cited testimony by the prosecution's expert witnesses who "testified that it was their opinion that the defendant did not lack substantial capacity to appreciate the criminality or wrongfulness of her conduct."
"Although the defendant also produced expert witnesses who disagreed with the Commonwealth's experts, it is within the discretion of the fact finder to place little or no weight on that evidence," Sullivan wrote. REUTERS

SpaceX launches Google AI chips into orbit in push toward space-based data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:31:42 UTC
05:31:42 KST

Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality.
The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident. SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time.
SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground. During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs).
The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025. The company aims to develop reliable, solar-powered AI computing infrastructure that can operate continuously in space.
"Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected," Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher, wrote in a blog post following the launch. He called it the first step in a long-term research effort, "exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure."
Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another. Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion.
In low Earth orbit, satellites can "access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth," Alphabet said in the post. Eventually, they expect to be able to "link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit."
The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit.
SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla, Musk's automaker.
Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, "and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy "supercompute in space" in 2027.
Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability.
The Transporter-18 flight was the second major launch in a single day for SpaceX, which also began transporting astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida's Space Coast for NASA with an earlier liftoff on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit.

ICEYE and Nokia to Develop Satellite Communications System for Military Use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:02:13 UTC
05:02:13 KST

Finnish space company ICEYE and Nokia have agreed to jointly develop secure broadband satellite communication systems for government and military customers.
This was reported by ICEYE.
The future system is designed to provide governments with their own secure satellite communications without the need to engage a third-party commercial operator.
The customer will have control over the entire infrastructure — satellites, ground segment, and user terminals. The partners plan to launch the first communications satellites into orbit in 2028.
The system will operate in low Earth orbit and is designed to provide communications coverage over specific mission areas.
The developers envision the system complementing existing military or commercial communications networks. Particular attention will be paid to operations in situations where ground-based networks are damaged, inaccessible, or compromised. This communication system is intended for use by the military, border services, emergency responders, and other government agencies.
As part of the partnership, ICEYE will contribute its expertise in the development and operation of satellite systems, while Nokia will integrate its own secure telecommunications network technologies.
The companies plan to combine the space segment, ground infrastructure, and secure user terminals — all adapted for operation in challenging conditions—into a single system.
“Governments must be able to fully own and control their communications without relying on the terms of service provided by foreign commercial operators… Our collaboration with Nokia allows us to move at the same pace in the field of satellite communications, meeting the deadlines required by governments,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE.
Nokia, for its part, is already developing a separate line of secure communications for defense customers. Specifically, in June 2026, Nokia and KNDS unveiled a solution to provide 5G connectivity for military and unmanned systems based on deployed Banshee networks.
The European Union is simultaneously developing its own secure satellite capabilities. In January 2026, Militarnyi reported on the launch of part of the Govsatcom network, which consolidates the government satellite capabilities of EU countries and is intended to provide secure military and government communications under European control.
In March 2025, the EU held negotiations with SES, Hisdesat, Viasat, and Eutelsat/OneWeb regarding providing Ukraine with backup satellite communications as an alternative to Starlink.
For ICEYE, this is not the first initiative to create a national satellite communications system for the military. In September, ICEYE and the Polish defense group PGZ signed an agreement to jointly develop a MILSATCOM system for the Polish Armed Forces.
In 2022, Ukraine received one of ICEYE’s satellites and access to the company’s constellation data.
In January 2026, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense and ICEYE signed a new agreement to expand the Ukrainian military’s access to the company’s satellite data.

‘Tough’ talks with China have yet to deliver, EU trade chief says

‘Tough’ talks with China have yet to deliver, EU trade chief says
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič tells POLITICO that “our Chinese partners understood” that a deal is urgently needed to preserve Europe’s social fabric and “literally thousands of jobs.”
MILWAUKEE, Wisconsin — China and the EU “are definitely not there yet” on a prospective trade deal, Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told POLITICO Thursday, calling months of talks “constructive, but tough.”
But the EU’s top trade official also emphasized the political pressure he is under to find that elusive common ground with Beijing. “I feel high political interest and, of course, very high expectations from the leaders all across the European Union,” Šefčovič said in an interview on the sidelines of a meeting of G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee.
“I know how politically impatient the European leadership is.”
Advertisement
Šefčovič travels to Beijing Oct. 8 for what he termed a “a super crucial meeting” with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, and said he was optimistic the trip will bear fruit. “You have to believe that you can accomplish something, otherwise you better don’t go.”
The commissioner needs to get results he can present at a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Oct. 15-16, and has said previously that Brussels is ready to restrict Chinese access to the EU market should the talks fail.
The EU and China have been locked in tense negotiations since June. EU leaders have said they can no longer tolerate the flood of Chinese imports inundating the single market, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs.
“I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implication on the future of emblematic European companies — literally thousands of jobs,” Šefčovič reported. “And also the social fabric and social model which was developed in Europe over many, many decades.”
The bloc’s ballooning €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China lies at the heart of the talks. Cutting that deficit would require either reducing imports from China, boosting EU exports, or a mix of the two.
Šefčovič said he hopes to bring a “proof of concept” back from Beijing that addresses three main issues: sudden Chinese export surges in key industrial sectors; tangible ways to increase European goods exports to China; and long-term clarity regarding China’s export curbs on raw materials, especially rare earth elements.
Advertisement
While in Milwaukee, Šefčovič met with Chinese Vice-Minister Li Chenggang. The veteran Slovak commissioner said China understands Europe’s worries: “All the issues we suggested are on the table. I’m not saying that we have clear-cut reassurances that we will solve them, but they are on the table.”
“Some of these topics have been very difficult to put on the agenda in the past. I believe this reflects the understanding of how politically important this is for both of us.”
The bilateral consultations have been divided into four work streams: trade and investment balancing; export controls; intellectual property rights; and reform of the World Trade Organization.
One person with knowledge of the negotiations, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the talks, said the Commission was seeking a settlement with China that would involve a mix of bilateral agreements on certain product categories, coupled with unilateral restrictions on others.
The Commission will present the outcome of the negotiations to EU leaders at their mid-October meeting in Brussels. The leaders will then decide whether the results are satisfactory.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday criticized China for unfairly subsidizing its domestic producers and urged the Commission to deploy more safeguards to protect European industry.
China has also signaled that it’s ready to fight back. Responding to an as-yet-unpublished Franco-German position paper that is expected to urge an upgrade to the EU’s trade defenses, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said China would take “firm action” against any moves to restrict goods from entering the European single market.

New study identifies four unique migraine phenotypes using artificial intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:00:02 UTC
05:00:02 KST

A recent study found that artificial intelligence algorithms can accurately identify people with migraines without relying on any information about their head pain. Published in the journal Neurology, the research suggests that migraines exist on a spectrum of distinct biological and clinical subtypes rather than as a single condition.
Migraine is a common neurological condition characterized by intense, pulsating head pain often accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. The condition frequently causes severe disruptions to daily life, limiting a person’s ability to work or engage in regular activities. The medical field currently diagnoses the disorder based entirely on a patient’s self-reported symptoms during clinical visits.
There are no established biological markers, such as a blood test or a specialized brain scan, to definitively confirm a migraine diagnosis. Because symptoms and treatment responses vary widely among patients, medical professionals debate whether migraine is a single uniform disease. Some researchers suspect it is a spectrum of related syndromes.
These varying syndromes likely result from combinations of genetic vulnerabilities and environmental factors. Previous research into the genetics of migraine has identified many associated DNA variants. However, adding up these individual genetic risks only explains a small portion of how the condition is inherited.
This gap in understanding suggests that genetic factors might interact with each other and with environmental triggers in ways that simple statistical models cannot easily capture. Antonios Danelakis, a researcher at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, led a team to explore these hidden patterns in patient data. They hypothesized that advanced artificial intelligence could capture the full biological footprint of the condition.
To investigate this, the researchers conducted a large study using data from the Trøndelag Health Study in Norway. This massive public health initiative gathered extensive information through physical examinations, blood samples, and self-administered questionnaires. This initial analysis included 43,197 individuals who had provided genetic samples and completed the required health surveys. The participants were classified as either having migraines or being headache-free based on traditional medical criteria.
The team built predictive machine learning models to differentiate the migraine sufferers from the healthy controls. They trained these algorithms using genetic data and general clinical information. This clinical data included details about sleep patterns, cardiovascular health, mental health, socioeconomic status, and regular medication use.
The researchers intentionally excluded any data about the participants’ actual headaches from the computer models. They wanted to test whether the algorithms could detect a migraine diagnosis entirely through other biological and lifestyle markers. The algorithms were trained on one portion of the participants and then evaluated on a separate, unseen group to verify their accuracy.
A specific type of machine learning algorithm performed the best on the test group. The algorithm successfully identified individuals with migraines with a high degree of accuracy. This success indicated that the condition is associated with a wide constellation of clinical and biological markers outside of the head.
The researchers analyzed the algorithm to see which features were most predictive of a migraine diagnosis. The top factors included age, biological sex, neck pain, and nausea. Other highly predictive factors were sleepiness, blood pressure variations, and self-reported mental health status.
Adding genetic data to the clinical data provided only a marginal improvement in the algorithm’s accuracy. The researchers noted that rich clinical data likely already captures the physical manifestations of a person’s genetic risk. Because the clinical data reflects the downstream effects of DNA, the genetic information itself became slightly redundant for diagnostic purposes.
In the second phase of the research, the team conducted another large study focusing on 12,185 individuals who reported experiencing headaches. This time, they used unsupervised machine learning models. Instead of giving the algorithm traditional medical definitions to look for, they allowed the computer to find natural groupings in the data.
The researchers fed the algorithm the participants’ specific headache characteristics, along with the most predictive general health features identified in the first analysis. They used clustering algorithms to see how the patients grouped together mathematically based on shared data points. To better understand these mathematical groupings, the team used an advanced dimensional reduction technique that translated the highly complex data into two-dimensional visual maps.
The unsupervised models divided the participants into two main clusters. The first cluster contained 1,425 individuals, and the algorithm grouped them based on shared traits. When the researchers checked this group against traditional medical guidelines, they found that nearly all of these individuals met the official criteria for a migraine diagnosis.
The second cluster contained 10,760 individuals. Most of the people in this larger group (71%) had non-migraine headaches. This division demonstrated that the artificial intelligence could naturally separate migraine sufferers from other headache patients without being explicitly taught the medical rules.
The researchers then instructed the algorithm to break the migraine cluster down into smaller subgroups. They based this subclustering on the general health features like neck pain and mental health. This process revealed four distinct subtypes of migraine sufferers.
The first subtype consisted entirely of men. The second subtype was characterized by prominent neck pain and an absence of general stomach issues, possibly representing patients whose migraines have a strong connection to neck tension.
The third subtype featured widespread muscle and bone pain, combined with lower self-reported health and higher levels of anxiety and depression. The researchers suggested this group might represent a phenotype where the nervous system is highly reactive to pain. The fourth subtype fit the classic picture of a pulsating migraine but lacked the psychological and widespread physical pain symptoms seen in the third group.
To analyze genetic profiles, the team conducted genome-wide association studies comparing the data-driven migraine group with those labeled as having migraine by traditional criteria. This process scanned genetic variants across tens of thousands of participants to find DNA patterns linked to each group, and found a high degree of overlap in the identified risk loci. When the team compared genetic risk scores across the four subgroups, the machine learning-based genetic risk scores were distinctly different across the subclusters, supporting the idea that these clinical subgroups reflect genuine biological differences.
The study relied on self-reported questionnaires to determine the participants’ initial medical status. Self-reporting can lead to misclassification if participants misremember their symptoms or misunderstand the questions. For instance, people with infrequent migraines might have incorrectly answered negatively to questions about having headaches within the past year, falsely placing them in the healthy control group.
The clinical data was collected between 1995 and 2008. Lifestyle behaviors, mental health trends, and typical sleep patterns have likely shifted since that time, meaning the data might not perfectly reflect a modern population. The genotyping technology used during those years was also less comprehensive than modern laboratory platforms.
The identified relationships between clinical features and migraine subtypes are correlations. The findings do not mean that these general health features directly cause migraines, only that they tend to occur together in specific patterns. The researchers noted that these models need to be validated in entirely different populations before being used in standard medical practice.
Future research should investigate whether these newly identified migraine subtypes respond differently to specific medications. A deeper understanding of these categories could help doctors prescribe targeted treatments rather than relying on a trial-and-error approach. Scientists could also use wearable devices and smartphone applications to track patient symptoms in real time, providing even more detailed data for future algorithms.
The study, “Machine Diagnostics and Machine Phenotyping of Migraine: A HUNT Study,” was authored by Antonios Danelakis, Håkon Kvisle Abildsnes, Fahim Faisal, Marte-Helene Bjørk, Dominic Giles, Knut Hagen, Tjaṧa Kumelj, Manjit Matharu, Parashkev Nachev, Erling Tronvik, Bendik S. Winsvold, and Anker Stubberud.

russia will &quot;liberate&quot; all of Donetsk region earlier than Ukraine and Europe expect - putin

russia will "liberate" all of Donetsk region earlier than Ukraine and Europe expect - putin
Kyiv • UNN
putin said that russia is ready for negotiations, but reaffirmed the demand for Ukraine's neutrality. He also claimed that russia had seized 1,301 km² in September.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin made a number of statements concerning international politics and the war in Ukraine during the plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club on October 1. He tried to absolve his country of responsibility for the peace talks that had reached an impasse and added: "the Russian Federation believes it will liberate the entire territory of the 'Donetsk People's Republic' much earlier than Ukraine and Europe expect," UNN reports.
In addition, Putin tried to convince his compatriots and the international community of the significant successes of the Russian Armed Forces on the battlefield.
What Putin said during the discussion club meeting
Putin tried to convince people that Russia allegedly sought to end the war against Ukraine as soon as possible through negotiations. At the same time, however, he confirmed that Moscow was not abandoning its key demands, including Ukraine's neutral status.
"We would like to end this (the war — ed.) as soon as possible, preferably through negotiations," he said.
At the same time, both Putin himself and his entourage repeatedly put forward demands on the Ukrainian side as part of the talks that are technically impossible to fulfill. For example, the Russian side has consistently and stubbornly demanded that Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy come specifically to Moscow. This is despite the fact that, among others, countries in the East and Turkey have repeatedly expressed their readiness to serve as a venue for peace talks.
The Russian dictator also stated that Ukraine's neutral status remains among Moscow's goals. According to his version, Russia had previously viewed Ukraine as a neutral state, but the situation changed after Ukraine's Constitution enshrined a course toward NATO membership. In practice, Putin once again confirmed that he wants to deprive Ukraine of independence on the international stage and prevent it, as a sovereign state, from making decisions about its own future.
Putin also outlined Moscow's position on the American proposals concerning the end of the war. According to him, they include decisions that are difficult for the Russian side and require compromises. Overall, however, the Kremlin views them as movement toward a possible settlement. However, the Russian leader did not specify exactly which decisions he was referring to. It is entirely possible that he meant potential compromises regarding the end of the war, which he discussed during his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in Anchorage. At the time, Moscow officially claimed that it had agreed with a number of approaches proposed by the American side, although no public comprehensive agreement was announced following the talks.
The Russian dictator separately accused Ukraine of being unwilling to suspend hostilities. He stated that he had allegedly been ready to resume the negotiating process immediately after Russia's parliamentary elections in September, but linked the absence of such dialogue to Ukrainian strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation and on regions of Ukraine occupied by Russia. Putin claimed that Ukrainian servicemen had allegedly deliberately targeted members of electoral commissions, resulting in the deaths of six people. It should be emphasized that Russia's authorities' claim that the strikes specifically targeted members of electoral commissions has not received independent confirmation.
At the same time, Putin spoke about the voting for the State Duma held in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The United Nations emphasized that such electoral processes in occupied Ukrainian territory have no legal basis and do not alter its internationally recognized status.
Putin also stated that, in Moscow's view, a possible peace settlement should address the Russian language and the activities of the church in Ukraine. Russia had previously repeatedly included linguistic, religious, and political issues in its list of demands toward Kyiv.
Putin announced an acceleration of the Russian forces' offensive
During his speech, Vladimir Putin also stated that the pace of the Russian army's advance was allegedly increasing. According to his claim, during September alone, Russian troops established control over 1,301 square kilometers of territory, which he described as approximately 2.5 times greater than the figure for the previous months.
In addition, the Russian leader emphasized that, allegedly, approximately 11% of the territory of Donetsk region, which Moscow illegally incorporated into the Russian Federation, remains under Ukraine’s control. According to him, the Russian leadership believes that the Russian armed forces will be able to seize this territory sooner than Ukraine and European countries expect. However, such statements contradict the actual course of events. In particular, Ukrainian troops are currently successfully conducting Operation "Vivaldi" and liberating occupied territories. The Russians themselves, according to assessments by a number of analysts, have "become bogged down" in Donetsk region and have no progress to boast about.
In his monologue, Vladimir Putin also referred to allegedly existing assessments in Ukraine and Europe according to which Ukrainian forces could hold these territories for another one and a half to two years. However, he did not name the sources of these assessments.

Russian dictator Vladimir Putin called the proposal to stop attacks on vessels in the Black Sea in exchange for Ukraine refraining from attacking Russian oil refineries senseless.

As Ukrinform reported, Russian forces attacked four districts of Dnipropetrovsk region more than 30 times during the day, injuring four people.

How to prepare for daylight saving time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:49:44 UTC
04:49:44 KST

Daylight saving time will kick in this weekend. Here's how to prepare
Daylight saving time is looming for many Australians, meaning half the country will be adjusting to a new time zone.
Here's what you need to know before the clocks change.
When does daylight saving time start?
On Sunday morning.
Each year, daylight saving time kicks in on the first Sunday of October.
This year, that's October 4.
Which states have daylight saving time?
- ACT
- New South Wales
- South Australia
- Tasmania
- Victoria
The Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia do not observe daylight saving time, so clocks will not need to change in those jurisdictions.
Do the clocks move forwards or backwards?
Forwards.
At 2am on Sunday morning, the clocks will move forward to 3am in jurisdictions that observe daylight saving time.
The clocks will go back by an hour when daylight saving time ends in April.
Do I have to do anything?
The clocks in most smart devices will automatically update, so you probably won't have to change the time on your phone.
However, you'll need to adjust the time on your analogue clocks, as well as the clocks on some appliances including ovens and microwaves.
The New South Wales government recommends changing the time before you turn in for the night on Saturday.
"To kickstart your day and avoid any timing issues, set your watch and household clocks that don't automatically update overnight to the new time before you go to bed," the NSW government website says.
Start preparing tonight
The Sleep Health Foundation recommends going to bed 15 to 20 minutes earlier for the three or four nights leading up to the change.
Even though daylight saving time begins in two sleeps, there's nothing stopping you from trying an earlier bedtime tonight.
And while you're at it, plan on waking up a little earlier over the weekend too.
The Sleep Health Foundation says setting your alarm 30 minutes earlier on Saturday and Sunday mornings will help you prepare for an early start on Monday.
Take time to adjust
Loading...
If you can, try to spend a bit of time out in the early morning light to reset your body clock, the New South Wales government says.
And give yourself some grace if things feel a bit off next week, because the Sleep Health Foundation says it can take about a week to adjust to the new time zone.
It offers the following tips to help ease into the change:
- Make your bedroom as bright as possible when you first wake up
- Exercise outside in the mornings
- Avoid exercise just before bed
- Avoid going to bed hungry or too soon after a meal

Police investigating accused paedophile's links to celebrated charity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:29:24 UTC
04:29:24 KST

AFP and Cambodian police probe accused paedophile Mark Dennis's links to Cambodian charity
In short:
Mark Dennis was arrested in January as he returned from Cambodia where he had visited a property at Sunrise Cambodia.
He was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material but was found dead before entering a plea.
ABC Investigations and Background Briefing can reveal Australian and Cambodian police are investigating the former Sunrise chairman and his connections.
Australian and Cambodian police are jointly investigating accused paedophile Mark Dennis's network and links to celebrated charity Sunrise Cambodia, following his death after being charged with possessing child abuse material.
Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse.
ABC Investigations and Background Briefing can reveal the Australian Federal Police and Cambodian National Police have an active child protection investigation into people connected with Mr Dennis.
Mr Dennis was chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia from 2018 to 2020.
He claims to have visited children in the orphanage in Kandal once or twice yearly since 2008.
A spokesperson for Sunrise said it was not aware of any current investigation, and that it had been advised by police that no current or former child in Sunrise's care had been identified in connection with Mr Dennis's arrest.
Mr Dennis was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material after he was arrested at Sydney Airport in January while returning from a trip to Cambodia, where he had visited Sunrise Cambodia in Kandal.
During Mr Dennis's bail hearing the following day, Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch said police found a Dropbox account connected to at least 12 devices.
The prosecutor also alleged Mr Dennis was chatting online with at least two individuals to whom he allegedly expressed sexual interest in children under the age of 18.
Mr Kisch described the offending as "serious" and said Mr Dennis had expressed a "desire to rape" a 16-year-old and possessed an image of a boy aged between six and 10 years old.
Mr Dennis was released from custody on strict conditions, including that he not use the internet or contact anyone under 16, but was found dead in his house under non-suspicious circumstances before entering a plea or the case being tried.
Cambodian National Police head of Transnational Crime Tream, Major General Chhuo Chanthan, exclusively told the ABC in June the cross-border investigation was ongoing as authorities worked together to probe Mr Dennis's network.
"Even though he has died, the investigation is not finished since the people who are involved with him in Cambodia are still alive," Major General Chanthan said.
The Cambodia Ministry of Interior told the ABC in August that the case concerning Mr Dennis was "ongoing and confidential" and that further details could not be provided.
Two weeks after Mr Dennis's death, the AFP's child protection team retained an officer to work full time on the investigation, codenamed Operation Queenstown, which an officer said involved a "substantial amount of material", according to emails seen by the ABC.
Documents from the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, obtained by the ABC under Freedom of Information laws, reveal Mr Dennis denied in an interview with police the allegation he possessed child abuse material, but never entered a formal plea.
A fact sheet among the documents revealed Mr Dennis was charged with using a carriage service to transmit child abuse material by sending Whatsapp messages to two accounts between February 2023 and June 2025, including one account with an Australian number and username "Kanje".
But parts of the fact sheet related to these two accounts were redacted, citing the "current or pending investigation" and "communication the subject of which is under investigation by the Cambodian authorities".
Loading...
An AFP spokesperson said investigations involving alleged offending in foreign countries were "inherently complex" and the organisation worked with international law enforcement partners to "investigate allegations of serious criminal offending".
"As the matter remains ongoing, no further comment is appropriate at this time," the spokesperson said.
The AFP also said "investigators would greatly appreciate" if people with information relevant to Operation Queenstown reported it via its crime portal.
Sunrise was founded by celebrity philanthropist Geraldine Cox in 1993 when she was given land by Cambodia's former prime minister, Hun Sen, and has since supported many disadvantaged children.
There is no suggestion that Ms Cox is personally under investigation or suspected of any wrongdoing.
Sunrise country director Tracey Shelton, who formerly worked as a journalist at the ABC and was appointed ACF director in 2021, said there had been no adverse reports about Mr Dennis during his time as a visitor, donor and director.
Ms Shelton said Mr Dennis had a reputation as a "huge barrister in Sydney, well respected" but stressed Sunrise Cambodia had very strict child protection policies that apply to everyone. She said management had contacted some of the children Mr Dennis sponsored after he was arrested.
The Australian Cambodia Foundation remains responsible for managing bequests to Sunrise Cambodia, according to Sunrise treasurer Hugh Darwell, but Brisbane-based non-government organisation Global Development Group (GDG) is now largely responsible for managing donations from Australia and around the world.
A spokesperson for GDG said it had not been contacted by Operation Queenstown but was alerted to Mr Dennis's arrest at the time, which triggered a review of Sunrise's operations.
"Our aim was to ensure that Sunrise Cambodia had responded appropriately to the news regarding Mark Dennis and that they were following their safeguarding policies and procedures.
"Following our review, we have decided to continue our support for Sunrise Cambodia."
The spokesperson said "all charities should continuously assess and strengthen their safeguarding approach" and "any further information that comes to light will be carefully reviewed and responded to appropriately".
Sunrise has not published a statement on its website about Mr Dennis's alleged offending. Another charity he also donated to, Cambodian Children's Fund, publicly cut ties immediately after charges were laid.
Responding to questions from the ABC this week, Sunrise Cambodia treasurer Hugh Darwell said that after Mr Dennis's arrest, the charity made enquiries to local police and authorities regarding Sunrise children.
"After a period in which they carried out investigations, they advised us that no child in Sunrise's care has been identified in connection with Mr Dennis's arrest," he said.

====================================================================================================

The President of the Government of Spain calls for order based on "the values of advancement and progress"
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:25:00 CEST
04:25:00 KST

8th edition of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum'
The President of the Government of Spain calls for order based on "the values of advancement and progress"
President's News - 2026.10.1
La Toja Island, Pontevedra
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during his speech at the inauguration of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum' (Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has called for order to be based on "the values of advancement and progress", to prevent "others from deciding for us simply because they have more power", whilst pushing ahead with regulation to address the "collapse" of the international order and the multilateral system, economic and trade uncertainty, the climate emergency, and to ensure the responsible deployment of artificial intelligence.
He made this point during his opening address at the 8th edition of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum', held under the theme 'A world in disarray' in Illa da Toxa (Pontevedra) and presided over by His Majesty the King. The forum was attended by the Minister for Finance, Arcadi España, and former Presidents of the Government of Spain Felipe González and Mariano Rajoy, with the President of the Xunta de Galicia, Alfonso Rueda, also taking part.
Pedro Sánchez pointed out that "chaos is not neutral", because "when international law loses its force, the winner is whoever has the most weapons; when markets abandon the rules, the winner is whoever has the most power to impose their conditions; when labour rights are weakened, the winner is whoever holds the stronger hand in negotiations; and when technology advances without limits, the winner is whoever controls the algorithms". The fact is that "disorder has its beneficiaries, and they are almost never those who need protection the most". For this reason he called for order - "a word mistakenly associated for far too long with conservative thinking" - based on "the values of advancement and progress".
In this regard, he explained that "order consists of establishing rules and preventing others from deciding for us simply because they have more power, and in updating those rules in keeping with the spirit of the times", something achieved through "labour rights, the welfare state and market regulation", which, in his view, is "the very essence of democracy".
International order and the multilateral system
Group photograph of the inauguration of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum', presided over by H.M. the King. | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
With this, he said, we must "look to the world that lies ahead and the one we are in" in order to make progress in four areas, such as tackling the "collapse of the international order and the multilateral system", citing the war in Ukraine, the "genocide" in Gaza and the armed conflicts that "claimed more than 150,000 lives worldwide last year alone", seven times more than in 2002, with 117 million people forcibly displaced - three times as many as at the start of this century. "Many because of conflicts, others simply fleeing poverty. The tragedy of irregular migration reminds us of this, and what happened in Ceuta this summer is proof of it," he added, arguing that "no wall or barrier, however high or insurmountable it may be, will be able to contain people's desperation to have a better life".
The head of the Executive stated that the United Nations system is "absolutely essential" and "the best tool we have ever had - and will probably ever have - for tackling global challenges and preventing present and future conflicts", as he argued last week at the UN General Assembly, although it requires "far-reaching reform to reflect today's world", with a "more representative Security Council, more agile and effective organisations, and an international justice system capable of ensuring that crime has consequences and that there is no impunity". "A rule that only the weak must obey is not a rule; it is another form of power", he argued, in defence of multilateralism. "Today we are paying the price for unjust, utterly unjustified and illegal wars which Spain has firmly opposed: Putin's war in Ukraine; Netanyahu's war, with his genocide in Gaza and occupation of Palestinian territory; and the immense mistake of the war in Iran", he lamented.
Economy and trade
Another area in which global turmoil is at play, as cited by Sánchez, is that of the economy and trade, where he emphasised that, in the face of "years of uncertainty and upheaval", Spain "continues to grow and is demonstrating quite commendable resilience", with growth of around 2.6 per cent this year - almost triple the forecast for the euro area - where Spain accounts for 85 per cent of salaried employment, with over 22.5 million national insurance contributors, whilst the proportion of temporary contracts has fallen to 12.3 per cent. "These figures illustrate a model of success in very adverse conditions, but they do not allow us to turn a blind eye to the serious difficulties that still persist", he pointed out, particularly in terms of ensuring access to housing and tackling the housing crisis.
The President of the Government of Spain called on the Lower House of Parliament and the parliamentary groups to show "broad-mindedness" in order to ratify the decrees at this Friday's sitting, following the agreement - "the result of dialogue with the parliamentary groups" - reached on Tuesday. "I ask that we set aside ideology and party politics and focus on an issue that is purely a matter of humanity", he added. However, he referred to other challenges, such as the rise in fuel prices and its impact on the cost of living, with inflation standing at 4.9 per cent in September, due to the impact of energy prices, particularly fuel and gas. "To tackle this 'cost of turmoil', the Government has approved extending protection for families and businesses against the price rises caused by the war in Iran, the pandemic and the invasion of Ukraine, and we will do so again in the face of each and every crisis." With the third Royal Decree-law, a total of more than 12 billion euros is being mobilised, which prevents half of the price rise that would otherwise have occurred, he noted.
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, talks with King Felipe VI at the opening ceremony of the 'La Toja-Vínculo Atlántico Forum' | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
He also criticised the use of tariffs as a "tool of coercion", despite the fact that "in a trade war, there are never any winners, only losers". In response, Spain has advocated a rules-based multilateral trading system, managed by the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which "favours the countries most in need". Within the current framework of trade negotiations between the EU and China, he made it clear that "trade and investment that bring jobs and technology are welcome, but it is imperative to rebalance this relationship between Europe and China, with 'balance and common sense', alongside 'clear and predictable rules'".
Climate emergency
Similarly, the President of the Government of Spain referred to the climate emergency as one of the areas in which it is urgent to reverse the global crisis so as not to take a step backwards, as "climate change kills and impoverishes us", bearing in mind that "Europe is not prepared for the climate emergency; it is warming at twice the global average rate, and its dependence on fossil fuels - exacerbated by wars - makes it doubly vulnerable". In fact, since the start of the war in Iran, Europe has paid an extra 100 billion euros for the fossil fuels it imports - over 3 billion more each week - a figure equivalent to a quarter of all direct grants from the 'Next Generation' funds.
"What Europe built to emerge from the pandemic has been snatched away from us by the chaos of war", he emphasised, which is why Spain advocates "relying less and less on decisions made by others on our behalf" and is therefore promoting renewable energy, which already accounts for nearly 60 per cent of electricity generation. "Sun, water and wind rather than the Strait of Hormuz", he added, particularly given that extreme temperatures in Europe could reduce European GDP by more than 1 per cent and, between 2021 and 2024, the cumulative losses associated with disasters and extreme weather events are estimated at over 200 billion euros for European countries. Consequently, he argued that adaptation and resilience policy should be "the second major pillar of European climate policy, alongside decarbonisation" and that future budgets should include a substantial allocation of resources for adaptation to the climate emergency. In short, "we need the order of reason and science, which are currently being challenged by the chaos leading to the disaster of the climate emergency".
Responsible deployment of artificial intelligence
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, greets the former President of the Portuguese Republic, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, who was awarded a prize at the opening ceremony of the La Toja Forum | Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa
The head of the Executive also called for order to ensure a 'responsible' roll-out of artificial intelligence, with rules that anticipate potential issues and the 'capacity to govern it'. "Yesterday we saw a photo which I personally found clearly inadequate. The US President telling the techno-oligarchs that they must regulate themselves. I believe it is a mistake to put the fox in charge of the hen house. This is not about voluntary agreements between tech oligarchs and self-regulation", but rather about "legal obligations, public scrutiny, social control, government oversight and the assumption of responsibility, including criminal liability", he emphasised. In this vein, he recalled that Spain was the first country to establish an Artificial Intelligence Supervisory Agency and has just presented the AI 360 Plan, a national roadmap focused on responsible deployment to capitalise on all opportunities. Drawing on this "moral authority to champion AI with a humanist ethos", he called for "robust regulatory frameworks" at national, European and multilateral levels to guarantee safety and the protection of human rights.
He also stated that "progress has never meant abandoning the rules; it has meant establishing rules that are equal to the challenges facing each society at any given time". "The powers we are trying to govern have taken on a global scale; there has never been a level of inequality in the history of humanity like the one we are seeing right now", he warned, and therefore argued that, "in the face of the forces of disorder, Spain advocates a Europe with a greater capacity for action", with a "far more ambitious" European budget to address the funding of European public goods (security, defence, the climate emergency, science, the CAP and the social pillar). "Who stands to gain from a world in disarray? The answer is clear: those who know that, when the rules disappear, they can impose their own", he warned, emphasising the need for "fair rules".

Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:23:01 UTC
04:23:01 KST

- Category
- World
Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace
Poland has introduced simplified rules allowing its military to identify and shoot down foreign objects in its airspace without visual confirmation, Gazeta Prawna reported on September 30.
The new procedures took effect on October 1 as Poland adapts its air defense rules to repeated risks from Russian drone and missile attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed that the military had completed preparations for the change.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
UNITED24 Media recently documented a sharp rise in Russian drone and missile incursions near NATO’s eastern flank, with 2026 recording almost as many confirmed and likely Russian-origin incidents as 2024 and 2025 combined. Poland has responded by strengthening air defenses and revising procedures for dealing with unidentified aerial threats.
Under the previous peacetime rules, Polish fighter pilots generally had to approach an unidentified object closely enough to identify it visually before engaging it. Gazeta Prawna noted that the requirement is being replaced by so-called positive identification.
Pilots or commanders will now be able to authorize an interception using information from radars and other surveillance systems, as well as data provided by Ukraine during Russian aerial attacks.
Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Operational Commander General Ireneusz Nowak had reported that the new procedures were fully prepared and being implemented.
“October 1 is always a good moment not only to begin the academic year, but also to introduce new procedures,” Kosiniak-Kamysz stated.
The changes do not require amendments to Polish law and are being implemented at the military level, Gazeta Prawna wrote. The defense minister described the new rules as clear procedures that pilots and other personnel involved in air defense would be expected to follow.
Under existing Polish law, the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces remains responsible for protecting national airspace through the Air Operations Center. The commander can order an intruding object to be shot down or delegate that authority to fighter pilots.
Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk earlier explained that the previous visual-identification requirement was designed to reduce the risk of mistakenly shooting down civilian aircraft during peacetime. Poland’s current security environment, however, required different procedures.
“Until now, we did not use this type of capability because it is usually reserved for a state of war or martial law,” Tomczyk stated.
“Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day, so we have to introduce these changes for both our pilots and the security of the state,” he continued.
Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft and activated air defenses during large Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly when drones and missiles approach its eastern border. The revised rules are intended to give Polish forces more time to respond when unidentified aerial objects enter national airspace.
Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn crossing on Ukraine’s border with Poland, with the blast wave damaging the checkpoint area. Poland scrambled fighter jets and placed air defense and radar units on heightened readiness as the drone approached the border.

Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:19:00 BST
04:19:00 KST

Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
- Published
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.
Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.
Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.
The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.
The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".
Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.
In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.
While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.
The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.
At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.
On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.
Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.
He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.
"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.
While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.
Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.
LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.
Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."
The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.
While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.
Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

The EU rejected the possibility of providing the loan to Kyiv ahead of schedule and is demanding reforms, media report

The EU rejected the possibility of providing the loan to Kyiv ahead of schedule and is demanding reforms, media report
Kyiv • UNN
The EU has refused to provide Ukraine with part of the loan ahead of schedule due to doubts about the deficit assessment and demands for reforms.
The European Union has currently rejected Ukraine’s request to accelerate the disbursement of loan funds to cover an unforeseen deficit in financing military needs for the current year. Bloomberg reports this, citing people familiar with the situation, according to UNN.
The publication notes that the decision followed Kyiv’s unexpected announcement in the summer of an additional funding shortfall of €27 billion ($30.4 billion) due to rising war-related expenditures.
Ukraine appealed to Brussels to accelerate the provision of a €90 billion loan intended to meet the country’s needs through the end of 2027.
The EU has become Kyiv’s largest donor since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, playing a key role in supporting Ukraine ahead of the fifth winter of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
During a tense meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU still had €37 billion available for budget support in 2026. However, she linked this to Kyiv’s progress in implementing key reforms aimed at combating the shadow economy, increasing tax revenues, and bringing legislation closer to EU standards—processes that are currently being stalled in parliament.
"We have identified resources to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and defense needs for 2026," the European Commission and Ukraine said in a joint statement released on Thursday. "We also confirmed the steps necessary to ensure the timely provision of these funds," the parties said, signaling that the EU continues to insist on progress in reforms.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive body, declined to comment further.
According to people who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of the negotiations, the EU questioned some of the figures provided by Ukraine and said that disbursing the loan funds early would only create a new problem for 2027.
It was also suggested that additional funding should be provided by other partners, including Canada, Norway, and Japan. The EU loan was intended to cover only two-thirds of Ukraine’s needs, with the remainder to be provided by partners. According to the statement, €45 billion of the loan earmarked for 2027 will be disbursed "promptly," but not before the beginning of next year; at the same time, work will begin on "identifying additional budgetary and defense needs."
Separately, on Thursday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on the social media platform X that Ukraine and its partners would henceforth "coordinate this work and align their actions every month, ensuring continuous coordination."
This week, the International Monetary Fund estimated that Kyiv would face a funding shortfall of between $30 billion and $35 billion next year, while in 2028 and 2029 the figure would be $17 billion and $2 billion, respectively (according to people familiar with the situation). These figures may change.
IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said on Thursday that the Washington-based Fund was holding active discussions with Ukraine and international partners regarding the potential size of the financing shortfall.
She said the IMF was working with Kyiv to combine the second and third reviews of the $8.1 billion financing program and planned to submit them to the Executive Board by December. Implementation of this plan depends on "obtaining sufficient and credible financing assurances" to cover the shortfall, Kozack said.
