04:14:59 KST

Turkish Super Lig club Trabzonspor hosted Irish side Drogheda United in a friendly, bringing together the sister clubs as Türkiye and Ireland mark 75 years of diplomatic relations.
Thursday’s match at Papara Park marked Drogheda United's first appearance in Türkiye and came as the two countries celebrate longstanding historical and cultural ties.
Before kickoff, players from both teams posed together for a group photo, highlighting the friendship between the clubs.
The first half ended goalless, with Drogheda goalkeeper Fynn Talley making saves from Ahmet Cemil Guren and Metehan Mimaroglu as Trabzonspor sought the opener.
Trabzonspor came close to taking the lead in the 72nd minute when Paul Onuachu dribbled past the goalkeeper and shot from a difficult angle, but Drogheda's defence cleared the ball off the goal line.
Drogheda broke the deadlock in the 86th minute when Shane Farrell sent a free kick into the box and Edwin Agbaje finished from close range with one touch.
Trabzonspor fans applauded the opposing team after the goal, further highlighting the friendly atmosphere surrounding the encounter.
Drogheda United won the match 1-0.
Football friendship rooted in history
Trabzonspor and Drogheda United became sister clubs in 2010, formalising a relationship built around sporting and historical ties.
Trabzonspor said the partnership was inspired in part by similarities between the clubs' crests and the historical connection between Ireland and the Ottoman Empire.
The clubs share similar burgundy-and-blue colours, while Drogheda's coat of arms features a star and crescent, elements also used in Drogheda United's crest.
According to Drogheda United, links between supporters developed earlier, while Trabzonspor fans provided financial support to the Irish club during a period of difficulty in 2008-09.
Both clubs point to humanitarian aid provided by the Ottoman Empire to Ireland during the Great Famine in 1847 as part of the historical foundation of their relationship.
A planned friendly between the clubs in Dublin on March 21, 2013, was cancelled because of heavy rain, making Thursday's encounter their first meeting on the field.
The match comes as Türkiye and Ireland mark 75 years of diplomatic relations, which were established in 1951.

Amnesty Report Documents Morocco's Sustained Spyware Campaign Against Civil Society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:50:00 UTC
03:50:00 KST

Amnesty International has released a new report showing how, despite official denials, Moroccan authorities used surveillance spyware against civil society between 2017 and 2021, and possibly continued to use it later.
The rights watchdog’s report, titled “We start with the verdict”: Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, details how the government deployed Israeli firm NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware to target civil society figures both domestically and abroad in what Amnesty described as “unlawful surveillance attacks.”
“The report presents extensive technical and forensic evidence confirming the DGST acquisition of Pegasus, confirms that civil society members were the primary target of Morocco from the very beginning of their Pegasus use in 2017,” Donncha Ó Cearbhaill, leader of the Security Lab told OCCRP.
According to the findings, the government's deployment of Pegasus evolved in tandem with the technological development in the spyware. Amnesty documented the use of sophisticated attack vectors, ranging from “one-click” phishing links requiring user interaction to advanced “zero-click” exploits capable of compromising devices without any action from the target.
While Pegasus represents the most technically advanced system documented in the report, Amnesty emphasized that it is merely one of the “digital tool[s] among many in Morocco’s repressive surveillance ecosystem.”
The report traces the government's use of digital espionage tools over two decades, citing the mass surveillance system Eagle, acquired in the early 2010s from French firm Amesys; the Remote Control System (RCS) spyware from Italian vendor Hacking Team, used in 2012 against journalists with the citizen media group Mamfakinch; and FinSpy software developed by the Anglo-German company Gamma Group and FinFisher.
As early as 2012, “Morocco was among the first countries where activists and journalists were found to be targeted with advanced spyware tools,” Amnesty said.
The Moroccan government has not responded to OCCRP’s request for comment.
Evidence suggests that national security agencies purchased these spyware systems even earlier. In 2015, emails included in a major leak from Hacking Team revealed that two Moroccan
security agencies, the internal intelligence service, the Direction Générale de la Surveillance du Territoire (DGST) and the National Defence Secrets Committee (CSDN) had contracted with Hacking Team since at least 2009. The records also show that the DGST was licensed to infect up to 2,000 devices, with support for Windows, Mac and mobile devices.
An OCCRP investigation published in July in collaboration with the Paris-based nonprofit Forbidden Stories revealed new evidence of Morocco’s secret service’s use of surveillance technology, particularly how the internal intelligence service DGST were using Pegasus and other surveillance tools to spy on activists.
A whistleblower who worked inside Morocco’s secret services added new evidence to the allegation that the government was behind the spying on a journalist, shedding light on the inner workings of state-backed surveillance operations and how the tool was used. His account was corroborated by other sources with knowledge of Moroccan intelligence operations, and documents.
According to the whistleblower, Moroccan intelligence agents utilized a private intermediary firm to contract with NSO Group, the Israeli cyber-intelligence company that created Pegasus. This arrangement was designed to shield the state from leaving a paper trail directly linking it to NSO Group or the spyware.
The latest evidence stems from a multi-year investigation led by Moroccan journalist Hicham Mansouri, whose own device was infected with Pegasus. Mansouri partnered with Forbidden Stories, the newsroom dedicated to continuing the work of threatened, silenced, or imprisoned journalists. Forbidden Stories organized a media collaboration titled "Pegasus Project: Inside the Moroccan Spying Machine," bringing together 39 journalists across 14 media outlets.
Amnesty’s report builds on this and the 2021 Pegasus Project, a global investigation involving 17 media organizations and coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The landmark reporting revealed that the spyware had been systematically deployed worldwide against journalists, human rights activists, and politicians.
Despite the increasing evidence presented in these publications, the Moroccan government responded to the July reporting with a familiar pattern of denials. Pro-government Moroccan media outlets launched a campaign of disinformation, dismissing the reports as based on “an unverifiable anonymous source, flimsy documentary evidence, and a persistent confusion between technical detection and state attribution.”
The pro-government website Al Barlamane similarly dismissed the investigation as incitement seeking to undermine relations between Morocco and France, stating that the report was published at a time when relations between Rabat and Paris were “undergoing a period of restructuring following successive signs of rapprochement.”
A third website, Le 360, again labelled the evidence as “very fragile,” claiming that the provided evidence was “aggregated under the same biased and politically assumed narrative.”
Corroborating data published in the July investigation, Amnesty’s latest report presents technical evidence that an NSO Group VPN server was deployed within Morocco’s DGST IP range in September 2017. This timeline aligns with earlier testimony and technical leaks from the Pegasus Project that showed DGST officers testing the system on their own phone numbers that same month.
Furthermore, the report says that the Apple iCloud accounts used to target Spanish ministers were the same as those used to target journalist Hicham Mansouri and Claude Mangin, the partner of Naama Asfari, a Sahraoui activist who is imprisoned in Morocco. Since NSO assigns accounts exclusively to single customers, Morocco is the only plausible operator, said Amnesty.
“The forensic evidence and analysis [presented in the report] allows for the high-confidence attribution of Pegasus attacks against Hicham Mansouri and other French-based civil society, the targeting of French and Spanish politicians, and Western Sahara activists as all have been carried out by Morocco's Pegasus system,” said Amnesty's Ó Cearbhaill.

Scientists discover that Earth’s crust has repeatedly rolled over—and it’s still happening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:41:17 UTC
03:41:17 KST

Several times since the age of dinosaurs, the solid part of our planet has rolled over, drowning some continents and lifting others out of the sea.
Our planet is slightly squished, with more mass at the equator. But the movement of Earth’s mantle and rocky crust can make some areas denser than others and throw off the planet’s balance. As a result, these solid outer layers can tilt and slide around the planet’s liquid inner core beneath as the planet works to redistribute its mass. This phenomenon is called true polar wander because it moves the planet’s actual rather than magnetic poles.
Incredibly, a new Science study finds this massive upheaval has happened to our planet at least four times in the past 320 million years. And it’s still ongoing.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Based on satellite measurements, we know that this is happening today, at about 10 centimeters a year, mainly because of melting ice caps,” says Mathew Domeier, a geoscientist at the University of Oslo and lead author of the study.
What scientists didn’t know was whether true polar wander is a slow, steady process that’s always going on or happens in short, rapid bursts. The best evidence scientists had for the phenomenon was from magnetic signals recorded in ancient rocks, but those are sparse and inconclusive. So instead Domeier’s team looked at clues hidden in ancient floods.
Earth’s spin makes both the planet’s rock and water bulge at the equator. When the solid Earth tips out of alignment, it is driven through the watery bulge, and parts of the rock poke out of the water while others get drowned. It looks like sea-level change, but that’s not the case at all, Domeier says: The water stays put while the continents move. Two opposing quarters of the globe flood, while the other two dry out, forming a unique four-leaf-clover pattern.
The team analyzed maps showing where continents lay underwater or dry at 10-million-year time points. The four-leaf-clover pattern appears around 200, 150 and 100 million years ago, and again between 30 and 20 million years ago. The findings, Domeier says, “took me quite by surprise.”
“The particularly elegant aspect of this study is the independent test it provides” for the existing magnetic data, says Giovanni Muttoni, a geologist at the University of Milan, who wasn’t involved in the new research. The strongest signal found, from 150 to 140 million years ago, he notes, matches a period for which magnetic data had already hinted at rapid wander.
“During true polar wander, continents can move rapidly across the climate belts even though their positions relative to one another change much less,” Muttoni says. This rapid movement could reshape ocean currents, upend ecosystems and perhaps even nudge Earth’s magnetic field.
What exactly triggers rapid true polar wander events and how far the poles move during them remains unknown. “Trying to understand why these events happened at these times would be the next logical step,” Domeier says.

03:38:55 KST

TU/ecomotive’s VENTRA electric car concept captures tire dust while driving
the dutch student-built EV captures tire particles close to where they are released, then reuses some inside the cabin.
student-designed EV captures the dust coming off its own tires
Electric cars have done away with exhaust fumes, but they still leave something behind on the road. Every turn of the wheel wears down rubber, while braking releases another stream of fine particles into the air. VENTRA, a new student-built EV from Eindhoven University of Technology, is designed with that overlooked mess in mind.
The car’s most visible feature is a set of bright orange covers wrapped around each wheel. Inside them sits T.R.A.C.E., an electrostatic collection system that pulls tire and brake particles out of the air as the car moves. It is a surprisingly physical solution to a type of pollution that usually disappears into the background.
electrostatic collectors sit close to each wheel
At higher speeds, the movement of the car directs particle-filled air through the collection system. At lower speeds, small fans help draw that air inward. According to simulations by the team at TU/ecomotive, VENTRA can capture around 24 percent of tire particles between 31 and 50 mph (50 and 80 km/h), rising to 42 percent during city driving. The figures come from simulations, so testing on real streets will be the more telling next stage.
Once collected, the material can be removed from the surfaces with water or a vacuum. TU/ecomotive has already found one place for it to go. Some of the particulate matter has been incorporated into an enamel coating inside the cabin, sealing the dark powder into a new material and making an otherwise invisible byproduct physically present inside the car.
a 790-kilogram EV designed to make less tire dust in the first place
VENTRA also approaches the issue through weight. Battery packs make electric vehicles heavier, which can increase the load placed on their tires. The student team built much of the chassis from carbon-fiber-reinforced thermoplastic composite sandwich panels. Its complete chassis weighs about 135 kilograms, compared with roughly 230 kilograms for the conventional construction cited by the team. The finished car weighs 790 kilograms and has an estimated WLTP range of 290 kilometers, or about 180 miles.
The thinking continues on the dashboard. A system called Clean Drive reads steering, braking, and acceleration data, then gives the driver feedback intended to reduce tire and brake wear. VENTRA becomes a study in what happens once automotive emissions move away from the exhaust pipe and toward parts of the vehicle that have been there all along.
VENTRA follows a decade of experimental cars by TU/ecomotive
The project is the eleventh concept car from TU/ecomotive, whose previous prototypes have explored cars made from waste, repairable modular construction, and vehicles designed around longer material lifecycles. VENTRA shifts the question toward what a vehicle leaves behind while it is actually being driven.
European Euro 7 rules introduce requirements addressing brake-particle emissions and tire abrasion, bringing these sources into automotive emissions regulation. VENTRA remains an experimental prototype, though its wheel-level approach gives physical form to an issue that is otherwise easy to miss.
project info:
name: VENTURA
design: TU/ecomotive | @tuecomotive
 institution: Eindhoven University of Technology
 type: electric concept vehicle
 location: Eindhoven, the Netherlands
 year: 2026

Canada fast-tracking oil pipeline designed to diversify economy away from US
The new pipeline could make Canada a major global energy supplier, as Asia looks outside the Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict
Canada will fast track the approval process for a new proposed crude oil export pipeline to its west coast that could generate over C$20 billion (US$14 billion) a year in GDP, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday.
The pipeline, which was announced in July, is a crucial part of Carney’s bid to diversify the economy away from the United States and help lessen the effect of US President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Carney said Ottawa would officially list the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest, which enables it to proceed through a single federal regulatory review process. He said Ottawa aimed to complete the process by September 1, 2027.
“A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports over the next decade … [and] to unlock our full potential as a global energy superpower,” he told reporters in Fort McMurray, hub of Alberta’s oil sands industry.

Treasury sanctions operation targets Iran's auto, rail industries in latest economic attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:37:16 UTC
03:37:16 KST

The Treasury Department on Thursday sanctioned Iran's automotive and rail sectors as part of the Trump administration's wartime effort to hobble Tehran by cutting off its remaining financial lifelines.
Several companies connected to Iran's metals industry, including the Chinese subsidiary of Middle East machinery company HEPCO, are also being designated by the Office of Foreign Assets Control, Treasury said in a news release.
In a separate release, the department announced additional sanctions on the A7 Network, described as a "shadow banking network with ties to Russia used by the Iranian regime to evade sanctions."
The actions are the latest to come from "Operation Economic Outcast," the beefed-up sanctions effort that President Donald Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent touted as Iran's "economic D-Day" when it was unveiled in late August.
As with previous sanctions announcements, it was not immediately clear how much of an impact the new penalties would have on Iran, which has faced heavy sanctions for years. Several entities connected to the A7 Network were previously designated in August 2025.
"The Iranian regime's ability to fund its war machine and inflict terror on the world has been severely diminished thanks to Operation Economic Outcast," Bessent said in Thursday's news release.
"Today's action directly targets Iran's enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime's revenue once and for all," Bessent said.
Treasury alleges Iran's automotive sector is deeply enmeshed with the country's Revolutionary Guard and serves as a "lucrative cash cow" for the regime, despite sustaining annual losses over $1 billion.
In addition to targeting Iran's two main auto companies, OFAC is sanctioning foreign suppliers that continue to export auto parts to Iran. They include UAE-based Integrated Auto Parts LLC, Hong Kong's Hessenberg Co. and Tanex Global Trading Hong Kong Limited, Indonesia's PT Golden Motorcycle International and Turkey-based Troy Trading Arac Parcalari Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi.
Treasury is also designating several Iranian rail companies, alleging Tehran has come to rely on the sector amid an ongoing U.S. naval blockade in the Gulf of Oman. And the department is designating two China-based steel companies, Shanghai Ruimi Import and Export Trade Co., Ltd. and M and R Steel Co., Ltd., among others.
Operation Economic Outcast has drawn questions about whether the U.S. would extend its reach to China, Iran's top trading partner and oil buyer.

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
Police launched a massive operation in the early hours of Sept 27 “due to a range of information” including an alert from a local farmer who became suspicious of the men who she had seen near the base in three vans.
However, the Times newspaper reported that one of the men had also called emergency services shortly before being arrested.
Detectives have confirmed that although petrol was found in the vans used by the men, no improvised explosive device was present.
Burnham said Britain was working closely with the US, whose bombers have in recent months used Fairford to launch missions against Iran, although US President Donald Trump said he would not have released the men, who police said were only freed under stringent conditions.

Putin Raises Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad, Says Russia Monitors Arms Factories in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:11:03 UTC
03:11:03 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that a direct attack on Russia or Kaliningrad exclave would immediately raise the question of using all of Moscow’s weapons, including nuclear, days after Russia previously threatened NATO over the exclave.
Speaking during the annual Valdai Discussion Club forum, Putin also said Russia was monitoring European factories that are producing weapons for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If it comes to a direct attack on Russia, on Kaliningrad, the question of using all the weapons we have will immediately arise,” Putin said, according to translated excerpts published by Clash Report.
“No one currently has weapons like those possessed by Russia,” he claimed.
Insisting that Moscow will not attack Europe
Putin reiterated that Moscow has no initiative to attack Europe, even as Russian drone incursions, airspace violations and sabotage campaigns increase across the EU.
His claims came a week after a Russian military helicopter violated Polish airspace and two days after Estonia concluded that Russian intelligence ordered an arson attack on a defense company supplying Ukraine.
“We don’t intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, or 2050, but if we are attacked, we will have to respond,” he said, adding that “citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that.”
Yet, the First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on CIS Affairs, Viktor Vodolatsky, called for mandatory military training to begin in fifth grade, arguing that Russia must prepare its youth for a possible war with NATO and the EU by 2030.
‘A Deliberate Tactic’: Zelensky Condemns Russian Drone Strike on Kyiv School
From Sept. 1, Russia has already expanded military training for children, including in occupied Ukrainian territories, and raised the share of mandatory instruction to 50% of school time.
During the same address, he said that arms production for Ukraine remains a threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin is monitoring them closely.
“I am not saying that we are going to strike enterprises in the countries supplying weapons to Ukraine, but this is a threat,” Putin said.
In August, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as an attack from NATO itself, particularly because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
Speaking about nuclear weapons, Putin cited a principle associated with Russian writer Anton Chekhov; “If a gun is hanging on the stage, sooner or later it must go off,” he said, repeating the Kremlin’s long-standing claims that the war “was started against us.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has so far rejected every proposal for a direct meeting or a possible ceasefire.
Why Kaliningrad matters
Putin’s assurances contrast with a series of direct threats from Moscow against NATO and its members in recent weeks.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium said it had delivered a position to NATO’s International Secretariat and Belgium’s Foreign Ministry warning that Moscow was ready to deploy its entire arsenal if alliance members tried to isolate Kaliningrad.
The embassy accused NATO of an “aggressive policy” without specifying which actions prompted the warning.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance had responded to Moscow’s informal diplomatic document by reiterating that NATO is an exclusively defensive alliance, simultaneously condemning Moscow’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
The exclave Russia seeks to “protect” is wedged between Lithuania and Poland, both NATO members, and is connected to Russia only by sea. However, it is Russia’s only ice-free Baltic port, which may be particularly important due to Western sanctions imposed on Russia and its shadow fleet vessels.
Kaliningrad also hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet and has Iskander missiles with a range of about 500 kilometers (about 311 miles).
The Suwałki Gap, a roughly 65-kilometer (40 miles) stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border separating Kaliningrad from Belarus remains a big concern for NATO. Should a conflict emerge, Russian forces could try to seize the corridor and cut the Baltic states off from allied reinforcements.
Further threats aimed at NATO and the Baltics
Earlier on Thursday, Russia has also accused the alliance of a reckless course carrying a high risk of direct armed conflict and threatened to strike “decision-making centers” in member countries.
On Sept. 11, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would “disappear from the map” if it lifted its ban on nuclear weapons, claiming NATO would not invoke Article 5 to defend the country as that would mean a “global catastrophe.”
Two weeks later, Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states, the same grievance the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The string of latest threats has raised fears that the Kremlin may be seeking a justification for a direct attack on the Baltic states.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Russia could directly attack another European country, including through a limited ground incursion.
Speaking during a summit in Brussels on Wednesday, Sept. 30, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned Moscow’s rhetoric. NATO’s combined strength exceeds Russia’s, he said, adding that he does not take the nuclear threats seriously.

Ukraine war latest: Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Key developments on Oct. 1:
- Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
- Russian drones strike Kyiv school, key bridge linking eastern, western banks of city
- Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
- Ukrainian pilot dies after MiG-29 fighter shot down by Russian missile
- 'Returning Russia's sick war to where it came from' — Ukraine marks Defenders Day
Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1.
The September figure surpassed previous summer highs of 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August. According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
"This dynamic demonstrates the complete inability of the occupying forces' military leadership to achieve its objectives, as well as the growing accuracy and effectiveness of Ukrainian units' strikes," the General Staff said on Telegram.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The September figure brings Russia's estimated monthly losses closer to that target than at any previous point this year.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
December 2025 marked the first month in which Russian personnel losses exceeded the number of troops Moscow managed to recruit, according to the General Staff. Since then, the manpower balance has remained an increasingly important issue as the Kremlin seeks to sustain the war without announcing a new wave of mobilization.

Russia strikes Kyiv bridge for first time
Two Russian drones struck near the supports of Kyiv's Southern Bridge on Oct. 1, disrupting a key metro link between the city's eastern and western banks, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
This is the first time Russian drones have struck one of the capital's bridges.
The attack took place at around 11:30 a.m. local time, as cars and a metro train continued to cross the bridge. Videos began appearing on social media around the same time, showing a fire on the bridge and a column of smoke rising above it.
Following the strikes, traffic across the bridge was halted as emergency services inspected the site and assessed the damage, the mayor said.
As the train was passing through the area, dust entered the carriage through the ventilation system following the blast wave. Neither passengers nor the driver were injured, and the train's windows and carriage were undamaged. The train was sent to a depot for further inspection, the Kyiv City State Administration said.
Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
A Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv on Sept. 30, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine's State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said on Telegram on Oct. 1.
The strike, which occurred at around 6:18 p.m. local time, sparked a fire that was quickly extinguished. No one was injured in the attack, according to the statement.
The VVR-M research reactor itself and systems important for its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator. Radiation levels remained within the normal background range of 0.16-0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022, when its core was fully unloaded to reduce radiation risks following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. It is currently used only for maintenance of safety-related systems.
The institute is part of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences and conducts research in nuclear physics, atomic energy, and radioecology.
"The drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research was an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes," the regulator said.

A Ukrainian pilot has died after his MiG-29 fighter jet was shot down by a Russian missile whilst performing a combat mission in eastern Ukraine, the country's Air Force said on Oct. 1.

Türkiye-Ukraine free trade pact takes effect, aims for $10B in bilateral business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:46:51 UTC
02:46:51 KST

The free trade agreement between Türkiye and Ukraine came into force to establish a predictable framework and boost the bilateral trade volume to $10 billion in the short term.
The Turkish trade ministry announced on Thursday via the Turkish social media platform NSosyal that the Türkiye-Ukraine Free Trade Agreement entered into force on October 1, 2026.
Türkiye and Ukraine aim to develop commercial relations within a more predictable framework.
Customs duty regulations regarding the trade of goods will take effect on January 1 2027.
The agreement aims to contribute to maintaining trade between the two countries under more predictable rules in current conditions.
The deal, signed on February 3 2022, creates a framework to develop commercial relations in line with the joint goal of reaching a bilateral trade volume of $10 billion in the short term.
The agreement, prepared by considering the sensitive sectors of the parties, includes regulations on services, investments, electronic commerce, trade facilitation, and customs cooperation, in addition to the trade of goods.
Regulations for conducting quota-free bilateral and transit transportation between Türkiye and Ukraine aim to support commercial flows.
As Ukraine's economic integration with the EU advances, the agreement offers a framework to maintain preferential trade opportunities for Turkish and Ukrainian businesses while providing a competitive advantage against third-country suppliers.

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. The West attempted to destroy Russia despite the country's years-long attempt to integrate into Western civilization, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday.
"I want to point out that despite many years of attempts by the new Russia [authorities] to become part of the so-called Western civilization, they [the West] actually did everything to isolate and further dismantle the Russian Federation itself," Putin said at the 23nd annual session of the Valdai International Discussion Club.
According to the Russian president, despite all the internal political changes that have taken place in Russia, the West still viewed it as a key part of the historical Russian Empire.
"This notion is still being raised at various events and gatherings focusing on the motto that 'We need to finish dismantling the Empire,' " Putin added.

The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries, including Algeria, Brazil, China, Egypt, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Iran, Japan, Pakistan, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
Putin has been taking part in the club’s meetings since its establishment in 2004. The first conference was held in Veliky Novgorod, near Lake Valdai, which gave its name to the event. Since 2014, the club’s meetings had been held in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi, but this year the Valdai session has been relocated to the Moscow Region as it is more convenient for most of its participants to get to Moscow.

Dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested over air base security incident

Dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested over security incident at U.S.-run air base in England
Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at the U.S.-run RAF Fairford air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police "under caution," which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions.
On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation "is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles - including possible foreign state involvement," she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.
Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets, but the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under "the strongest grip and the closest control," and British officials had been "talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done."
 U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

French student protests turn violent, schools set on fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:41:35 UTC
02:41:35 KST

French student protesters started fires at two schools, while teachers were inadvertently splashed with petrol at a third, officials have said.
The demonstrations over staff shortages and deteriorating school buildings grew increasingly violent on Thursday.
At Marseille's Victor Hugo high school, teachers were inadvertently splashed when a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. The prosecutor's office had initially said teachers were assaulted and “doused in petrol”.
At another Marseille school, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a fire truck responding to a blaze, police said. The group forced firefighters to leave the vehicle before setting it alight.
Another fire broke out at Nelson Mandela high school in the western city of Nantes, where no injuries were reported. The building was evacuated and students arriving for classes were turned away.
Government holds crisis meeting
The protests and school blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint as the government unveiled unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office held a crisis meeting on the protests, which officials said have left dozens injured and led to hundreds of arrests, most involving teenagers.
In the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, crowds gathered in front of police lines, with one student holding a sign reading: “Can we explain ourselves without being tear-gassed?”
Students have accused police of using heavy-handed tactics, including tear gas. The government has condemned violence during some protests while acknowledging concerns over conditions in high schools.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said troublemakers were moving between schools to incite violence.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said he would meet staff unions, parent groups and student associations on Friday. He also called on schools to switch to remote classes if protesters blocked access.
“Violence will not keep our students from their fundamental right to an education,” Geffray said on X.

Luca Sabbatucci is the new Italian ambassador to Bern
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
19:41:21 CEST
02:41:21 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announces that Luca Sabbatucci has taken up his post today as Italy’s Ambassador to Bern. He was born in Rome on March 5, 1963. He graduated with honors in Political Science with a concentration in international relations from La Sapienza University of Rome in 1988 and completed his military service in the Carabinieri.
                                    
                                       
				   He joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 1990; during the early years of his career, he served in the Diplomatic Protocol Office and the Minister’s Office. In 1992, he was assigned to the embassy in Seoul, where he remained until 1996, when he was appointed Consul in Athens. In April 2000, he returned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as Chief of Staff of the Directorate General for Human Resources. From 2004 to 2008, he served in Ankara as Deputy Chief of Mission. In 2008, he returned to the Ministry and once again oversaw the management of human and financial resources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, first as Deputy Director General and later as Director General for Resources and Innovation. In this role, he completed the process of reorienting Italy’s diplomatic and consular network launched by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, supported reforms aimed at increasing the emphasis on merit in human resources management policies, and promoted the adoption of innovative work methods to ensure their effective implementation. 
   In January 2019, he was appointed Director General for Global Affairs. In this capacity, he was responsible for a wide range of issues, both bilateral and multilateral: from relations with Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Latin America, to Italy’s membership in the G7, the G20, the OECD, the IEA, and other global forums on energy, climate, the economy, and finance.
                                    
                                       
				   In 2022, he served as Chief of Staff to the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, a position he retained following a change in government. On November 15, 2022, in Paris, he served as Permanent Representative to International Organizations, where, among other duties, he chaired the OECD’s External Relations Committee. Since October 1, 2026, he has been Italy’s ambassador to Switzerland.

Fakir consumed lethal dose of cocaine says cops' lawyer
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:59:46 CEST
01:59:46 KST

Abderrahim Fakir, a 42-year-old Moroccan man who died while beinng subdued and pressed to the ground by two police in Bologna on July 19, had consumed a more than lethal dose of cocaine, the officer's lawyer said on the basis of toxicology reports Thursday. 
    The cops are being probed for manslaughter in a case many have likened to that of George Floyd. 
    A lawyer for Fakir's family said, however, that he had only taken half of the amount of cocaine that could have caused his death. 
    Fakir had recently started treatment for mental-health problems. 
    Fakir was referred to a mental health centre (CSM) after being admitted to the emergency room of Bologna's Maggiore Hospital on June 20 because of a psychiatric issue. 
    He went to the centre in the following days, he was assessed and given an initial diagnosis, and a treatment plan was prepared. 
    He had a follow-up appointment early in August to continue his treatment. 
    Fakir died after being pinned to the ground face down. 
    In a video recorded by a local person, Fakir can be held shouting "help" and "enough" as the police try to restrain him, tying his hands and feet together, before he passes out. 
    Other videos have shown that Fakir, who had lived in Italy since he was a child, was in an extreme state of agitation and confusion before the police intervened. 
    Law enforcement had been called to intervene in Bologna's Pilastro quarter because Fakir was suffering from a "psychiatric crisis" and was disturbing the peace and acting erratically, according to initial findings by investigators. 
    He was allegedly threatening people parking a car in a garage. 
    Investigators have opened a probe into involuntary manslaughter and are looking into the conduct of the two police officers who restrained Fakir and four paramedics who were at the scene too. 
    Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi has said that he was confident the cops will be cleared of any wrongdoing. 
    Daily newspaper Il Messaggero reported that a CAT scan ahead of the autopsy suggested that Fakir suffocated following damage to his respiratory tract. 
    Piantedosi also attacked Bologna's centre-left Mayor Matteo Lepore for organizing a demonstration calling for the truth about the case. 
    While that demonstration passed off peacefully, protests in other parts of the city turned into a riot, with 64 police officers injured and massive damage caused. 
    "At the very least, the rally was called without the proper consideration," Piantedosi told La7 television. 
    Lepore, who has said that calling for the truth does not delegimitize the forces of law and order, hit back soon after. 
    "I say to Minister Piantedosi that attacking me, attacking mayors, will not solve any public order problems, not in Bologna or anywhere else," Lepore told ANSA.

Ethiopia: Embassy shut in Eritrea, 10 diplomats expelled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting
October 1, 2026
Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties on Thursday after Ethiopia accused its northern neighbor of involvement in renewed fighting in the Tigray region.
The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry was the first to announce that it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
The Ethiopian embassy in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as part of the rapprochement that culminated in Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.
Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accusing them of "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security." The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.
Hours later, Eritrea's Foreign Ministry called the move "absurd" and said the expulsion of ten of its diplomats from Addis Ababa had effectively shuttered its embassy there.
Eritrea said it therefore had "no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails."
Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters
The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.
The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.
The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.
The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.
It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.
Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.
Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.
Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.
The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.
Edited by: Zac Crellin

====================================================================================================

Google’s dream of AI data centers in space gets its first off-world test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:56:41 UTC
01:56:41 KST

When Elon Musk took SpaceX public in June, a big part of its value proposition came from promises of data centers in space. Skeptics were quick to list all of the hurdles. This afternoon Google’s Project Suncatcher is scheduled to launch hardware in pursuit of the same idea: it will send artificial intelligence processors into orbit onboard—of all things—a SpaceX rocket.
That doesn’t mean Musk’s pitch will become reality anytime soon. If anything, the gulf between Suncatcher and a working data center in orbit suggests how far off that future still is. But as AI’s appetite for electricity tests the patience of communities being asked to feed it, some of the richest tech companies are racing to source their energy needs from space instead.
The test satellite will carry just four processors, which will be used to run Google’s Gemini AI models for 15 minutes at a stretch before they need to shut down and cool off. The ultimate goal is to establish a full-fledged orbital data center, built from constellations of thousands of satellites that will share the work of running AI models and beam their responses back to Earth.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The whole effort has less to do with what could be accomplished out in space than with what’s getting harder to achieve down here on Earth. Data centers are projected to use around 3 percent of the world’s electricity by 2030, roughly double their share today, according to an International Energy Agency report. In orbit, sunlight is abundant and free, and Google says a solar panel there generates up to eight times as much power as it would on the ground. “We have direct access to a wonderful renewable source of energy,” says Alexander Wyglinski, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute.
There’s a political incentive to look beyond U.S. soil, too. As the data-center buildout grows more divisive, blasting that infrastructure into space and away from people’s backyards holds obvious appeal.
But scale is the main question, Google readily admits. The biggest AI data centers that are being built now pack in hundreds of thousands of chips and draw up to a gigawatt of power, several thousand times the output of the International Space Station’s solar arrays. Even getting enough solar panels into orbit would be a massive undertaking at that scale. “It’s going from arrays that are several meters on a side to arrays that are a couple of kilometers on a side,” says Kerri Cahoy, a professor of astronautics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “Launching enough mass to generate the power is huge.”
The problems don’t end once everything is up there, either. Though space is cold, its vacuum is a lousy place to dissipate heat, which is why Suncatcher’s chips must clock out to cool down and why the satellites require specialized radiators. The whole satellite network needs to be resilient to space debris. And the cosmic radiation that Earth’s atmosphere filters out can scramble calculations, forcing systems to catch and correct errors on the fly. “When we talk about satellite platforms, and you put a computer into them, you don’t put [in] a computer like the one you have on your desk,” Wyglinski says.
For months before today’s launch, Google has been anticipating those problems on Earth, shaking spacecraft to simulate the launch and bombarding its chips with proton beams to test their response to radiation. “It's about seeing what works, identifying points of failure and applying those findings to future missions,” says Travis Beals, a senior director at Google, who leads Project Suncatcher.
Even so, scaling up could force Google and SpaceX to confront some stubborn physics. Every chip and solar panel has to be hauled into orbit, and every answer those chips produce has to come back down.
Satellites can transmit data to Earth, but doing so at scale is expensive and difficult. “We don’t have the convenient, easy way to get that data back to the ground,” says Alan George, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Pittsburgh, who heads a National Science Foundation center focused on space computing. During the Cold War, the problem was bad enough that U.S. spy satellites parachuted exposed film back to Earth.
Computers on Earth relay information easily, and lasers have made it possible to do the same between spacecraft. But getting information between Earth and space is another story entirely, so it is best to process some of the information gathered on satellites before it is sent down to Earth. “I like to tell my students the best data compression is answers,” George says. While that logic could apply to AI responses, too, his work putting computers in space tells him that the resource constraints make it hard to match what “you would put down the street in a building.”
Google’s engineers say they began from a similarly skeptical premise. “As a first step, we tried to find reasons that it was impossible,” Beals says, “but we gradually became convinced that it might actually work.”
And then there’s the question that may ultimately decide the whole thing: How will the limited bandwidth and energy savings make up the maintenance costs?
The cost of launching data center satellites and replacing them as they wear out, along with the bottleneck of getting data back down, may eat up whatever the free sunshine saves. The competitors in the first space race were nations jockeying for scientific dominance. Orbital data centers are mainly being pitched by corporations, which tend to prefer profitable ventures. So even if Project Suncatcher solves its technical challenges, those physical limitations could still kill the idea before Google gets anywhere close to a full-blown data center in space.
More often than not, space throws up more challenges than early movers expect. “It’s usually the late entrants who finally figured out how to do it effectively,” Cahoy says. SpaceX itself didn’t reach orbit until half a century after Sputnik.
If she’s right, the company that eventually gets data centers in space to scale may not even have booked its ride to orbit yet.

Shares of Vigor Kobo (維格餅家), a bakery specializing in pineapple cakes and traditional pastries, yesterday plunged 53 percent after announcing that it would delist from the Emerging Stock Board, as the company restructures its business and pursues optimal resource allocation.
At one point, the stock fell to NT$4.88, a record low since its debut on the preparatory board for the nation’s two main bourses in 2012. It closed at NT$4.98, compared with NT$10.64 a day earlier.
Vigor Kobo said in a statement on Wednesday that it decided to delist from the market as its business has largely been impacted by Taiwan’s tourism policy, especially for Chinese tourists, and the overall market environment.
Photo: Chen Wei-chung, Taipei Times
Established in 2003, the company once thrived on an influx of Chinese tourists, with its factory in New Taipei City’s Wugu District (五股) a must-see destination for Chinese tourists visiting Taiwan.
Chinese shareholder Fosun Group (復星集團) acquired a 20 percent stake in the company in 2012, making it the first Chinese firm to receive approval to invest in the nation’s food sector as Vigor Kobo sought to expand its footprint in China.
That boosted Vigor Kobo’s revenue to NT$1.24 billion (US$38.9 million) and earnings per share of NT$7.9 in 2013 and further to NT$1.34 billion and NT$8 respectively in 2014. Its stock soared as high as NT$152 during its heyday.
However, a sharp drop in Chinese visitors to Taiwan due to government policy and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic caused the company to suffer losses for six consecutive years since 2020, while its market capitalization and trading volume on the Emerging Stock Board declined over the period.
Even with the reopening of Taiwan’s borders and the return of foreign tourists following the pandemic, Vigor Kobo’s operations have not recovered to their previous peak.
Last year, the company reported revenue of NT$336 million and net losses of NT$49.21 million, or losses per share of NT$2.05. In the first half of this year, revenue was nearly NT$154 million, and its net loss came in at NT$24.93 million or losses per share of NT$1.04, company data showed.
Vigor Kobo will focus on transforming its operations, expanding its sales channels and developing new businesses, the statement said.
The company would reapply for listing on the Emerging Stock Board once its performance improves, it added.

McDonald’s features ‘Classic Spectrum’ décor at new Ruiguang Road location
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Along Ruiguang Road, a major main road that runs through the heart of Taipei’s Neihu Technology Park (內湖科技園區), a new restaurant with counter seats and small hanging pendant lights by the windows has opened on the first floor of a glass-mirrored office building.
As one walks closer and the automatic sliding glass doors open, a modern restaurant comes into view. It has clean lines, but without a sterile corporate feel. Warm wood-textured furniture and soft lighting create a comfortable atmosphere that invites visitors to step inside.
As soon as one walks in, it becomes clear that the space is about more than coziness. Pops of vibrant red, golden yellow and bright green emerge from different corners of the airy room, adding a sense of fresh, playful energy without overwhelming visitors.
Photo courtesy of McDonald’s
An instantly eye-catching red bench sofa sits in the center of the open-space room, serving as the visual focal point of the restaurant, while two cheerful golden-yellow benches with vertical channel-tufted backrests sit next to it.
Both seating areas are paired with wood-textured tables with gently rounded corners and accented with brightly colored edging. Above some of the tables, oval or rectangular pendant lights cast a warm glow, painted in either golden yellow or classic red.
A dynamic mixture of high and low communal tables, bench seating, counter seating and booth seating areas, mostly in warm mid-tones, fill the remaining space, while the wood-texture tables and chairs create an overall cohesive, balanced and relaxed atmosphere.
Most of the walls are painted in warm mid-tones, but one prominent wall stands out, decorated with simple geometric-shaped wall lights and layers of green in varying shades, creating a distinct, multi-layered contrast that adds depth and visual interest to the overall space.
This is McDonald’s first restaurant in Taiwan that introduces its latest global décor called the “Classic Spectrum,” created in collaboration with FutureBrand. It officially opened to the public on Sept. 21.
The “Classic Spectrum” is a bold and modern take on the global fast-food chain leader’s distinctive branding identity — iconic yellow Golden Arches set against a vibrant red background — tied together with inspiration that comes straight from the signature colors of its core products — golden yellow French fries, the brown mid-tones of a Big Mac, the rich red of ketchup and fresh green of lettuce.
Two partitions creating privacy between the restaurant’s seating area and the ordering and queuing area are a quintessential example of the restaurant’s functional and thoughtful design.
The semi-transparent partitions are accented with horizontal lines in shades of tan and brown, creating a warm and inviting earthy palette. Looking closer, one may experience an “ah-ha moment” upon noticing a rugged line of green and a line of golden yellow with an inverted triangular dip caught in the middle of the shades, and the vivid image of a classic Big Mac — with its flavorful beef patties, melting cheese and crisp lettuce — comes to mind.
The clean geometric lines and color balance — overall subtle cozy shades and layers, fused with hints of the playful vibrant colors of the brand’s signature foods — create a sophisticated, yet relaxing and refreshing environment, inviting customers to “taste” the deliciousness visually before even taking a bite.
Office workers in the surrounding Neihu Technology Park can order ahead using the McDonald’s mobile app to skip lines and pick up their food fast. They can also easily order using the digital self-service kiosks or at the counters. If dining in, they can freely find a seat that suits their needs for the day, whether it be a discussion with colleagues at the communal tables or enjoying a quiet “me moment” at the counter seats by the window.
During the evenings and weekends, local residents from nearby apartments can enjoy the relaxing and playful atmosphere with friends and family, sitting around the red sofa or dining booths, sharing simple good moments together. The specially designed lighting throughout the restaurant also allows customers to clearly see how delicious their meal looks while eating, and ensures food looks great in photographs without light shining straight in their face or casting weird shadows.
In addition to the overall comfortable décor, the “Classic Spectrum” still sneaks subtle fun surprises and practical design details waiting to be explored and uncovered, including a few lively illustrations on tabletops.
Brenda Kou (寇碧茹), vice president of restaurant development group of McDonald’s Taiwan, said although there are different layouts and décor throughout the brand’s restaurants around the world, and local specialty items, such as the popular corn soup in Taiwan, every McDonald’s still feels instantly familiar.
Beneath those differences lie shared core elements, which include “delicious” – enjoyable, satisfying and trustworthy food backed by strict food safety and quality standards, creating simple “feel-good moments” for customers and crew alike, and making the experience convenient and accessible for all, she said.
To keep up with modern lifestyles, McDonald’s has streamlined its ordering, payment and pickup methods, providing flexible options and offering walk-in customers with a welcoming, comfortable and accessible brand experience through carefully designed spatial layouts and décor, Kou said.
As “Classic Spectrum” has plenty of thoughtful touches here and there, everyone who visits the first McDonald’s restaurant in Taiwan with the new décor, located at 208 Ruiguang Rd in Taipei, can easily find a space to relax and enjoy their food.

Chinese invasion unlikely to occur next year: sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

US officials believe a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) instructions for his military to be ready by 2027 to take Taiwan by force, if needed, people familiar with US thinking said.
The main reasons for the belief include delays in military readiness amid the Chinese Communist Party’s anti-corruption campaign, as well as Beijing’s eagerness to see the results of Taiwan’s 2028 presidential election, which some Chinese officials hope could usher in a government more amenable to bringing the nation under Chinese control, according to two US officials, one former US official and a person familiar with the matter.
Beijing might increasingly look to use force in 2028 and beyond if Taiwanese elect a Democratic Progressive Party candidate for a fourth consecutive term, and in particular if President William Lai (賴清德) wins re-election, the people added.
Photo: Reuters
“If that happens, I think 2028 becomes pretty sporty,” said one of the US officials, who like the other sources spoke on condition of anonymity.
The assessment, which has not previously been reported, is a significant update to the years-long understanding among US officials that Xi wanted his military ready to potentially take Taiwan by force next year, the centenary of the founding of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA). China has never ruled out using force to bring Taiwan under its control, but has never publicly confirmed a 2027 readiness order.
In Taipei, Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo (郭雅慧)said in a statement yesterday that under Lai’s leadership, Taiwan will not only strengthen its self-defense capabilities but will also continue to work closely with all international democratic allies, including the US, to maintain the status quo, deter threats through strength, and ensure peace.
"For the sake of its citizens’ freedom, democracy, prosperity, and well-being, Taiwan will not abandon its commitment to democracy and freedom in the face of any military threat," she added.
China’s US embassy and Taiwan’s representative office in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The 2027 benchmark, which analysts say is about Chinese military preparedness rather than a timeline for invasion, has for years created a sense of urgency across multiple US administrations in countering China in the Asia-Pacific region.
The US intelligence community has hinted at Chinese wariness before.
It said in its annual threat assessment in March that China did not, at least at that point, have a plan to invade Taiwan next year and still preferred to wrest control of the nation without the use of force, if possible.
US officials offered mixed assessments of the degree to which China might view the 2028 US presidential election as an important indicator for military action.
While three of the people familiar with the matter said Beijing might also want to evaluate the outcome of the US election, particularly given rising US voter antipathy toward US military action abroad, the first US official said Beijing viewed both Democrats and Republicans as largely aligned on Taiwan.
While China might have a preference in the 2028 US election, “it doesn’t become as decisive a factor in my opinion, as it might have been 15 years ago,” the official said.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the likelihood of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan during his presidency, going so far as to say last year that Xi told him China would not invade while he was in office.
Xi has not rescinded his goal for the PLA to have the capabilities available to take Taiwan by force by next year, officials said.
However, the military did not accomplish as much last year militarily as it probably had intended because of the impact of China’s anti-corruption campaign, the people said.
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has unleashed a sweeping corruption and discipline crackdown. Millions within China’s vast bureaucracy have been investigated, with scores of senior party, government and military officials ensnared and purged.
In the past few years, the PLA has been a target of the campaign. A string of investigations and expulsions has left just two active officials on the formerly seven-member Central Military Commission, including Xi himself, who serves as chair.
China’s military exercises last year were smaller and less threatening compared with the past several years, according to the US official.
While they bounced back a bit this year, the official suggested that Chinese military officials were dissatisfied with their readiness.
China was believed to have drawn a lesson from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, which is the need to move quickly once any invasion begins and avoid getting bogged down in a sustained conflict, the official said.
“There are way too many pieces that aren’t quite in place yet for what would be the most difficult military operation any military has attempted probably since the Allied invasion of Normandy,” the official said.

A debate on a cash handout is pointless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration plans to distribute NT$10,000 in cash to every citizen next year, while the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus on Tuesday said it plans to propose a bill that would provide a NT$20,000 cash handout. Whether to hand out NT$10,000 or NT$20,000 has become the latest point of contention between the ruling and opposition parties, but beyond the political tug-of-war, a much more important question remains: Once the money is spent, what would Taiwan have to show for it?
Universal cash handouts are simple, direct measures that are immediately felt by the public. With prices, rent and the cost of living all rising, a cash payment might provide meaningful assistance to many households. Therefore, universal cash handouts should not be reduced to a binary choice between “handing out money is pandering to voters” and “not giving any money is neglecting people’s livelihoods.”
The problem is that while cash can ease immediate financial pressure, it does little to address structural issues such as wages failing to keep pace with the cost of living, housing affordability for young people, a declining birthrate, long-term care needs and the transformation of small and medium-sized enterprises. The amount of any universal cash handouts offers an additive effect — meaningful institutional reform is what holds the potential for a multiplicative impact.
Rather than repeatedly engaging in a political struggle over how much cash to distribute whenever fiscal conditions allow it, the government should establish a transparent and predictable sharing mechanism for economic dividends that allocates fiscal surpluses into three pots: one for debt reduction to ease the burden on future generations, one for investment in areas such as childcare, housing, long-term care and industrial transformation and one to be shared among the public, depending on fiscal capacity. Universal cash distribution would no longer be one-off handouts, but part of a fiscal system. When the economy is doing well and the government has the capacity, people can share in the gains while the government simultaneously reduces the debt burden on future generations and accumulates long-term investment.
Moreover, the fruits of economic growth do not necessarily find their way into everyone’s pockets. The robust performance of the artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and export-oriented industries does not mean that people working in the restaurant, retail, tourism and traditional industries — or all wage-earning households — are experiencing the same benefits. True, tangible economic growth is not a mere matter of GDP, but whether wages can keep pace with the cost of living, whether young people can afford housing and raise children and whether elderly people can enjoy a secure retirement.
What the ruling and opposition camps should really be competing over is not simply who can hand out more money, but who can ensure that the benefits of economic growth last longer. Whether the amount is NT$10,000 or NT$20,000, any such policy should be guided by three basic principles: It should not increase the government’s debt burden, it should not crowd out existing government programs and it should follow lawful and constitutional budgetary procedures.
Once the cash is spent, it is gone. It is the institutions that remain and can continue to deliver benefits year after year. Rather than fighting over whether next year’s handouts should be NT$10,000 or NT$20,000, the government and the opposition should seize the current wave of economic growth to turn today’s “AI dividend” into tomorrow’s “institutional dividend.”
Chen Ching-yun is a former director of the Legislative Yuan’s Bureau of Legal Affairs.

Fuel surcharge to increase amid rising costs: CAA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

An international fuel surcharge for Taiwan-based carriers is to be raised for the third time this year due to the rising price of oil, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said yesterday.
The surcharge for short-haul international routes is to increase from US$32.50 to US$37.50, while the surcharge for long-haul routes would rise from US$84.50 to US$97.50, the CAA said, adding that it has asked airlines to clearly disclose the changes to passengers.
The adjustment is based on a fuel surcharge mechanism established by the CAA and Taiwan-based airlines in 2005. The mechanism uses the international aviation fuel price announced by state-owned CPC Corp, Taiwan, as the benchmark.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Under the mechanism, no surcharge is imposed when the fuel price is below US$40 per barrel. When the price reaches US$40, but remains below US$50, airlines may charge US$5 for short-haul routes and US$13 for long-haul routes.
For every additional US$10 increase in the benchmark fuel price, the surcharge rises by US$2.50 for short-haul routes and US$6.50 for long-haul routes.
CPC said its international aviation fuel price has risen from US$156.79 to US$177.89 per barrel, moving the benchmark from the 13th to the 15th pricing tier.
The latest increase follows two previous adjustments.
The first took effect on Aug. 9, when the benchmark price rose from US$133.29 to US$147.57 per barrel, moving from the 11th to the 12th tier. The surcharge was consequently raised to US$30 for short-haul routes and US$78 for long-haul routes.
The second took effect on Sept. 7, when the benchmark moved up another tier to the 13th, raising surcharges to US$32.50 for short-haul routes and US$84.50 for long-haul routes.

MOE extends partnership with University of Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

The Ministry of Education (MOE) and the University of Zurich (UZH) have renewed the Taiwan Studies Project, extending the academic partnership over the next five years, the Taiwan Representative Office to Switzerland said.
The new agreement, covering this year to 2031, was signed in Zurich on Wednesday in the latest addition to years of cooperation between the ministry and the UZH’s Institute of Asian and Oriental Studies, the office said in a statement.
“The renewal of the Taiwan Studies Project means that the academic partnership between Taiwan and UZH will now continue into its second decade, providing a sustained institutional framework for Taiwan-related teaching, research and academic exchange in Switzerland,” it said.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Switzerland
The UZH and the MOE jointly launched the Taiwan Studies Project in 2017, with the latter providing funding in an initial two-year agreement, the office said.
Since then, the program has been renewed three times, with the latest five-year renewal activated retroactively on Sept. 1, it said.
Under the leadership of program director Simona Grano, who is also head of UZH Research Area China-Taiwan Relations, the Taiwan Studies supports research and scholarly exchange on Taiwan and its international environment, the office said.
Grano and Lee Chun-yi, associate professor of politics and international relations at the UK-based University of Nottingham, coedited Changing Dynamics in Geopolitics: Implications for Taiwan, published by Palgrave Macmillan last year, it said.
The volume incorporated works on Taiwan’s changing geopolitical environment and its ramifications for the intensifying US-China competition by academics hailing from Europe, the UK, the US and Asia-Pacific countries.
The Department of International and Cross-Strait Education is tasked with handling the Taiwan side of the renewed agreement, as part of its mission to support international scholarly exchanges and promote Taiwan studies programs abroad.
In related news, the UZH Research Area China-Taiwan Relations is to hold a talk on narratives surrounding Hong Kong’s sovereignty transfer in Taiwanese and Chinese-language media, the university said.
The event featuring Lutgard Lams, professor of media discourse analysis at KU Leuven’s Brussels campus, is part of the Zurich Taiwan Lecture Series and would take place at the UZH on Oct. 21, the office said.

Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) yesterday said it is accelerating memorychip capacity expansion amid growing artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand, with its accumulated investment in Taiwan reaching NT$1.6 trillion (US$50.2 billion) as of June.
The company’s investment in Taiwan has surged over the past four years, with recent spending equaling the total invested over the past 25 years, Micron Taiwan chairman Donghui Lu (盧東暉) told a media briefing in Taipei.
“The launch of ChatGPT and the outbreak of COVID triggered increasing demand for memory chips. Since then, demand has gathered pace rapidly, with only a brief pause in 2023 when a major downturn” hit the industry, Lu said.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
At Micron Technology Inc’s earnings call in Boise, Idaho, on Wednesday, the company told investors that memory supply constraints would be even more severe next year and in 2028, prompting more customers to sign long-term supply agreements with the company.
In Taiwan, Micron is scaling manufacturing capacity across its four major sites to meet demand by leveraging the region’s comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem, Lu said.
In Taoyuan, it is transforming an older cleanroom into an advanced facility (Fab 11E), equipped with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems to produce next-generation DRAM chips, he said.
The upgraded fab is slated to begin operations late next year or in early 2028, Lu said.
The new fab’s advanced infrastructure is built to support next-generation lithography, making it fully capable of housing high numerical aperture EUV tools in the future, he said.
The company is building its second high-bandwidth memory chip packaging fab in Taichung’s Houli Science Park, Lu said.
The fab, which is expected to start volume production in the middle of next month, would be the US firm’s largest manufacturing site in Taiwan, he added.
Over the past 13 years, Micron has tripled its footprint in the Houli park and occupies 73 percent of the park, up from just 23 percent when it first established a presence there in 2013, he said.
The company also aims to commence production at its two fabs in Miaoli County in the second half of next year, he added.
As Micron expands its footprint beyond Taiwan, the company is collaborating with Taiwanese supply-chain partners — such as Marketech International Corp (帆宣), a facility monitor and control system provider — to construct cleanrooms and install equipment in Boise, Lu said
L&K Engineering Co (亞翔) is helping build a new advanced memory packaging fab in Singapore, while United Integrated Services Co (漢唐) has been tapped to construct Micron’s new fabs in Hiroshima, Japan, he said.
The company’s other key Taiwanese partners include cleanroom mechatronic engineering leader Acter Group Co (聖暉), advanced packaging equipment specialist Scientech Corp (辛耘) and automated equipment giant Mirle Automation Corp (盟立), Lu said.
