Japan tightens permanent residency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

Japan yesterday toughened requirements for foreigners wanting to obtain permanent residency, as part of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to tighten immigration controls.
Under new rules that would come into effect in stages, foreign residents wishing to stay in Japan permanently will have to prove their annual income is above average and they can carry casual conversations in Japanese.
Application fees would also rise 20-fold.
Photo: AFP
At one immigration office in central Tokyo this week, hundreds of people queued, hoping to wrap up procedures before the price spike.
“I understand that over-accepting foreigners ... might dilute Japan’s unique culture. But at the same time, given its low birthrate and aging population, Japan has to accept foreigners,” said US-born university student Yujie Chono, who was among those waiting.
He said he had been waiting for five hours to file his paperwork.
Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills. Even though Japan has a rapidly aging population and is experiencing labor shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.
“As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness,” Takaichi wrote on X, adding that she was pushing for “orderly coexistence” with foreign nationals.
Programs to attract international workers have fueled public worry. Anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan go to foreigners and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.
Experts and many business leaders warn that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.
“Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment,” the Nikkei said.
Foreigners were a major issue in last year’s upper house election, which saw the sharp rise of the “Japanese first” Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a “silent invasion.”
The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs would be forced to leave Japan if they do not meet the new conditions.
Some foreign residents seek permanent residency to secure long-term stability, employment freedom and to earn trust within Japanese society. Those without permanent residency often have a difficult time seeking mortgages, for example.
The changes might prevent some people from applying for permanent residency, but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.
Under the regulations, the application fee for permanent residency will soar to ￥200,000 (US$1,263) from ￥10,000. Candidates must also show “understanding” of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

Latvia expected to keep EU course as Russia looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:57 UTC
01:40:57 KST

Latvians vote tomorrow in an election dominated by the threat from Russia, and despite progress made by populist and protest parties, they are expected to confirm the country’s pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
The Baltic state is a key pillar of NATO’s eastern defensive flank, and experts said there is widespread support for supporting Ukraine in the war with Russia.
“The stance toward Russia is the main reason for Latvians’ Western, NATO and European anchoring,” a Western diplomat said, adding that it would be hard to imagine major political changes.
Photo: AFP
Polls predict the center-right United List, led by Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, would emerge the largest party in parliament the vote.
However, his center-right coalition, which also brings together the centrist New Unity, nationalist National Alliance and the Union of Greens and Farmers, is expected to emerge weakened from the election.
Security is at the top of voters’ minds in a country bordering Russia.
There is broad consensus on maintaining military spending at nearly 5 percent of GDP and on supporting Ukraine, LaSER analyst Roberts Kits said.
The economy is also a major concern for voters. Latvia is the least affluent of the three Baltic States in terms of living standards. Growth is sluggish, with voters pointing to the cost of living, the state of the healthcare system and the difficulties of public finances.
Complicating this are major regional disparities.
Around Riga, GDP per capita reached 101 percent of the European average in 2024, according to a Brussels report.
However, in other regions this figure does not exceed 50 percent.
As elsewhere in Europe, economic concerns have given a boost to populist parties in the run-up to the election. The Sovereign Power party, critical of aid to Ukraine and increased military spending, is polling at 9 percent — and could reach second place in parliament. Considered pro-Russian by its critics, the party emphasizes Latvia’s economic difficulties. However, the party is isolated politically and barring a huge upset has no chance of entering a future governing coalition.
Another populist party, Latvia First, is also at 9 percent, and its businessman leader, Ainars Slesers, is regularly compared to US President Donald Trump.
The party is winning support with a conservative message and promises of economic revival, and could become an indispensable partner in coalition talks.
Long rallied behind the “Harmony” party, Russian-speakers, who make up about 35 percent of Latvia’s population, no longer vote as a unified bloc.
Harmony, which won several parliamentary elections without ever entering government, disappeared from parliament in 2022 and has very little chance of returning.
“We should not look at Russian-speaking voters as a single bloc with a uniform electoral behavior,” Kits said.
While identity issues have not disappeared, a growing part of this electorate now votes according to economic and social criteria.

“I think it’s too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with any anyone else,” Netanyahu said.
Photo: Israel’s Foreign Ministry / AFP
It was clear that the copilot was suicidal, he added.

A second air crew aboard helped land the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
“We knew there was an attack, because a woman screamed ‘stabbing’ and the plane shook,” Hayun said. “At that moment I ran to the cockpit and the plane dived.”

“One [pilot] was down and one was on the controls, and another person came in with me, I grabbed the assailant and put him in a chokehold, and pulled him out,” he said.
He and a few other people subdued the copilot and then he pulled up the steering control of the plane, Hayun said.
Asked how he knew what to do, Hayun said he watches Air Crash Investigation.
Tzvika Manes, an Israeli bank executive and one of the passengers who helped hold the copilot down, said they used airline earphones to tie the copilot up.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he was nominating Hayun for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, along with Manes, and Manes’ wife Tali — who was first to alert the passengers of the violence in the cockpit — and Shota Musaev, a doctor who treated the wounded captain.
Musaev helped incapacitate the copilot with another passenger, Asaf Rajuan, who was also nominated.
“I’m not a hero,” Rajuan said. “It’s something you do without thinking, running to save your daughter’s life, your family’s life, your wife, and all the staff and people on the plane. You don’t think, you just act.”

Cash handout preparation under way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:32 UTC
01:40:32 KST

The government aims to distribute its planned NT$10,000 (US$314) universal cash payments before the Lunar New Year next year, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said yesterday.
The government has allocated NT$235.7 billion for the cash handout program, and relevant ministries have begun preliminary preparations, Lee told a post-Cabinet meeting news conference in Taipei.
Responding to calls from the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus to increase the handout to NT$20,000 per person, Lee said the government’s proposal is based on three principles: First, it must not increase government borrowing; second, it must not crowd out spending on social welfare, national defense, healthcare or education; and third, it must comply with constitutional and legal requirements.
Photo: CNA
Citing Article 70 of the Constitution and Article 91 of the Budget Act (預算法), Lee said the Legislative Yuan is not permitted to propose measures that would increase government expenditures.
The proposed NT$10,000 payment was decided according to strict fiscal calculations and planning, taking into account the nation’s financial capacity, she said.
Lee urged legislators to review and approve the proposal for next year’s central government budget.
The Executive Yuan submitted the central government budget proposal and related spending plans to the legislature at the end of August, with revenue and expenditure budgeted at NT$3.9266 trillion.
Unlike previous universal cash payments, which were funded through special budgets and involved a streamlined administrative process, the latest proposal is included in the annual budget.
The Ministry of Finance has estimated that it would take about five months to complete the necessary system setup and procurement procedures after the budget is passed by the legislature and is promulgated by the president.
The ministry said it has applied to the Executive Yuan for about NT$100 million from the government’s second reserve fund to begin procurement and preparatory work in advance.
The ministry has already initiated procurement procedures in accordance with the Budget Act, Deputy Minister of Finance Chen Yong-sheng (陳勇勝) said.
Separately, KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said that the KMT caucus’ proposal to distribute NT$20,000 would be funded by the excess tax revenue collected this year, not by borrowing.
Chen said current estimates suggest that excess tax revenue could exceed NT$1 trillion this year, providing a substantial source of funding for the proposed NT$20,000 cash payment.
The government collected more from taxpayers than expected, and after accounting for necessary spending and maintaining fiscal discipline, part of that surplus could be returned to the public, he said, adding: “How does that amount to leaving debt for the next generation?”

EDITORIAL: A meeting of contradictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:31 UTC
01:40:31 KST

The second meeting this year between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in Washington last week was one of grand diplomatic pageantry to showcase the leaders’ supposed personal rapport. However, structural competition and differences persist between the two superpowers.
The 48-hour summit was more symbolic than substantive. The post-summit fact sheets released by the two sides showed that the meeting mostly focused on bilateral trade and tariff agreements, but failed to reach substantive resolutions on many critical issues concerning the global landscape, such as the restrictions on rare earths and advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) risks, and the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Although Beijing intensively deployed cognitive warfare tactics to reiterate that Taiwan is a redline issue ahead of the summit, Taiwan was notably absent from the summit fact sheets. Trump said that the two sides did not spend much time on the nation because Xi was aware of his thoughts and stance, and the US Department of State and US Ambassador to China David Perdue, who also attended the meeting, assured that the US’ Taiwan policy remains unchanged.
The tour of the National Archives Museum also ran into sensitive territory, with the original plan for Xi’s tour to include the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco, an accord that has long been used in support of the argument for Taiwan’s undetermined status, as it only stipulates that “Japan renounces all rights over Taiwan and Penghu” without specifying the disposition of Taiwan. The itinerary reportedly caused complaints from the Chinese delegation, which led to a request for the ad hoc removal of all sensitive documents and shortened Xi’s stay at the museum.
Xi was also showed the US Constitution, Declaration of Independence and Bill of Rights, which should have demonstrated the fundamental difference between the US’ and China’s government systems, individual rights and national sovereignty. Yet, Xi was more concerned with the “Japan issue.”
During the meeting, Xi highlighted the history of the US-China alliance during World War II and said that “the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in a fight against Japanese militarist aggressors,” ignoring the fact that it was the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-led Republic of China (ROC) — not the still-yet-to-be founded Chinese Communist Party-led People’s Republic of China — who had fought alongside the US.
Xi’s distortion of history aimed to erase the historical contribution of the ROC in Taiwan, but it also unveiled his anger with Japan for siding with Taiwan, especially after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s statement last year of Japan’s defense role in a Taiwan contingency. It also highlighted Xi’s anxiety over Japan’s upgrading of defense forces to counter China’s military expansion, with the Xi administration repeatedly stigmatizing the Takaichi government as “neo-militarism.”
Ironically, immediately after Xi’s departure from the US, the White House posted an anti-communist video on social media claiming that “America will never become a communist country, but would defeat communism.”
All of these incidents indicate that, behind the elaborate diplomatic courtesy, the meeting between Trump and Xi was heavy on symbolism and light on major policy breakthroughs.
While Trump faces the upcoming US midterm elections, Xi has prioritized sweeping domestic threats to pave the way for his fourth term and total leadership ahead of the 21st National Congress of the Communist Party of China next year. Last month’s US-China summit was more of a form of “risk management,” depicting the two leaders as seeking “strategic stability,” to prevent miscalculations in escalating US-China competition.
Trump and Xi are to meet twice more — at the APEC leaders’ summit next month and at the G20 summit in December — setting a record of four meetings between the two leaders in one year. A new normal of “high-frequency communication, high-intensity competition” between the US and China is likely to be the trend.
At the same time, pro-China forces will intensify their cognitive warfare, spreading narratives such as “US skepticism” and “Taiwan abandonment” narratives, aiming to divide the US-led democratic alliance and benefit Beijing in acquiring international clout.
For Taiwan, maintaining strategic focus would be of paramount importance.
The nation needs to upgrade its asymmetric defense capabilities and consolidate its position in contributing to global prosperity, such as in high-tech supply chains and First Island Chain security.
Taiwan should also deepen multilateral cooperation with more like-minded countries to develop multilayered regional security networks, and secure international trust as well as the nation’s strategic high ground.

Work on migrant hubs progressing ‘very well’: EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:25 UTC
01:40:25 KST

Work to set up migrant return hubs outside the EU is progressing “very well,” Denmark said yesterday as the bloc’s home affairs ministers met in Luxembourg to discuss further ways to boost deportations.
Denmark — along with Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands — has been exploring options to set up such migrant centers.
“When it comes to return hubs it’s progressing very well,” Danish Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bodskov said. “We are moving in the right direction.”
Photo: Reuters
German Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt said there were “preliminary” talks and that more work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits.
“These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term,” he said, adding that he was hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
The Luxembourg talks come with anti-immigration parties riding high across the bloc, as evidenced by far-right gains in Germany this month.
EU ministers were set to give final approval to tougher new migration rules allowing for the creation of return hubs and granting authorities much broader detention powers. The meeting agenda included discussion on using “enhanced cooperation” with “priority” non-EU countries for returns of people with no right to stay in the bloc.
Proponents said return hubs — which would serve either as the final destination or as transfer centers for those expelled — could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
However, critics question their effectiveness, pointing to the hurdles faced by similar projects and likening them to “legal black holes” that could see migrants stranded in limbo with little oversight.
The UK abandoned a scheme to deport undocumented migrants to Rwanda, while Italian-run facilities to process migrants in Albania have faced legal challenges and a slow uptake.
Greek Minister for Migration and Asylum Thanos Plevris said his country was aiming to open a center next year in an African country “that we have already agreed on,” but could not yet be named.
Two European lawmakers from the Greens group said officials in Rwanda had told them they were negotiating with the five EU countries.
Dutch lawmakers Anna Strolenberg and Tineke Strik oppose return hubs over human rights and other concerns.
“Most likely the first country that a deal will be struck with is Rwanda,” Strolenberg said.

Does avoiding misery make you happy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:21 UTC
01:40:21 KST

In Dr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham, the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another — in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain — until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, Green Eggs and Ham was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it.
Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable.
Consider relationships. Declining to chat with the talkative person sitting next to you on a plane avoids one obvious downside — getting stuck in a boring conversation you can’t gracefully exit. But as psychologist Nicholas Epley shows in an extensive body of research, doing this again and again quietly robs us of interactions we might have found genuinely rewarding, though we’ll never know what we missed.
Photo: AFP
The same instinct to protect ourselves can become more destructive in close relationships, when the misery that we fear is rejection. People who are “rejection sensitive” tend to expect the worst and see signs of the coming apocalypse even in ambiguous behavior, like an unanswered text message. When they think they see rejection coming, they try to avoid it by rejecting first — responding with hostility or pulling away from their partner in a self-defeating effort to protect themselves. As a result, behavior that was meant to ward off rejection ends up provoking it.
In my own research, I surveyed a large sample of adults, asking whether they take too many risks, too few, or roughly the right amount — both overall and across key areas such as work, health and relationships. The results were striking. About half felt they took the right amount of risk. But among the rest, the overwhelming majority felt they took too few — and the reason they gave, again and again, was a desire to avoid miserable emotions like fear and regret.
‘COUNTERFACTUAL THINKING’
One of the great engines of misery is “counterfactual thinking”: our mental habit of imagining how things might have gone differently. While we have the capacity to imagine better and worse outcomes, research shows that we are much more likely to dwell on how things could have been better than to consider how they could have been worse. Such “upward counterfactuals” — the job offer we didn’t take, the romantic connection we didn’t pursue — tend to leave us feeling regretful and dissatisfied with the reality we actually have. This asymmetry punishes those who assiduously avoid every opportunity that might result in pain or heartbreak, because such avoidance inevitably creates a stockpile of upward counterfactuals, all the roads not taken. Psychologists distinguish regrets of commission from regrets of omission; it’s the latter – the things we could have done but didn’t – that haunt us longest.
We don’t only avoid misery by avoiding risky behavior; a whole separate category of avoidance happens purely in the mind. We reach for distraction, numbing, and busyness to keep from thinking about what causes us pain. But you cannot anesthetize sadness without anesthetizing everything nearby. Emotional systems don’t come with a dial that turns down grief while leaving joy untouched; suppress one and the whole range tends to flatten.
The practiced avoider often ends up not happy, exactly, but flat — free of acute suffering, perhaps, but also missing the intensity, curiosity, and aliveness that make the good parts of life feel good. This flatness is easy to mistake for equanimity, since it doesn’t announce itself as pain. The protagonist in Stefan Zweig’s story Fantastic Night lives this numbness for years, until one reckless act cracks it open — and what rushes back in isn’t relief but a flood of feeling, the discovery that his calm had been an absence, rather than peace.
Research on physical pain finds, surprisingly, that focusing on pain can diminish its intensity more effectively than trying to distract from it — and there are parallel, if somewhat more mixed, findings for negative emotions generally. One line of inquiry shows that “affect labeling” — simply putting feelings into words — dampens neural reactions to distress. Another set of studies finds that people instructed to accept a negative emotion, rather than suppress it, recover faster, both emotionally and physiologically.
None of this is an argument for deliberately courting misery, or for treating pain as good in itself. But unhappiness-avoidance, adopted as an organizing life principle rather than an occasional and reasonable caution, is self-undermining. It reduces the kinds of experiences available to us, including those of the “Green Eggs and Ham” variety that may prove incredibly meaningful.
My father, born a German Jew, spent part of the second world war in a French prisoner of war camp. He and the small pack of close friends he made there were hungry enough to dig up worms for food and chew on shoe leather. But he once told me that, due to the companionship and challenge of that ordeal, it was the peak experience of his life. Avoidance of misery rests on a false premise about how happiness actually works. The person who spends a life dodging unhappiness does not arrive, in the end, at a life free from misery. Unhappiness avoided is not happiness gained, but more often just misery in disguise.

Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.

Shipments previously delayed at end customers due to component shortages have returned to normal, providing strong momentum for the second half, Chenming Electronic president Charles Lo (羅志吉) told an earnings conference in Taipei yesterday.
NVIDIA SUPPLIER
Photo: Ou Yu-hsiang, Taipei Times
The company also expects to begin shipments of chassis and rack products for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin 200 platform this quarter, with artificial intelligence (AI) rack-related shipments expected to increase every month throughout the second half if supplies of key components, such as memory chips, are stable, Lo said.
In the first half of the year, the company’s revenue rose 22 percent year-on-year to NT$6.147 billion (US$193 million), and net profit increased 101 percent to NT$570.9 million, or earnings per share of NT$2.78.
Apart from racks and chassis for servers, storage systems, and industrial PCs, the company also produces high-voltage power racks and modular hardware systems, and is expanding into higher-value data center infrastructure, including Level 11 (L11) liquid-cooling system integration, manifolds and containerized modular data centers, Chenming Electronic research and development vice president Calum Chueh (闕仲輝) said.
In the first eight months of this year, server-related products accounted for 73 percent of the company’s NT$7.9 billion revenue, while Level 11 liquid-cooling systems contributed 18 percent, he said.
Based on its order backlog, Chenming Electronic expects its L11 system assembly business, including sidecars, liquid-cooled racks and related products, to continue growing next year, supporting a positive gross margin outlook, Lo said.
Gross margin rose to 21 percent in the first half of this year from 17 percent a year earlier, aided by improved production efficiency and factory performance, the company said.
PLANT INVESTMENTS
To meet increasing demand for racks and liquid-cooling products, Chenming Electronic continues to invest in plants in Taoyuan’s Jhongli District (中壢), Thailand’s Chachoengsao, as well as the Chinese cities of Dongguan and Ningbo, Lo said.
The first phase of its Thailand plant began small-volume production in the fourth quarter of last year, while the second phase is expected to begin production by the end of the year, he said.
The expansion at its Dongguan plant is expected to be completed by the end of this year, he added.
Capital expenditure is projected to stay at about NT$700 million to NT$800 million this year and next year, compared with nearly NT$700 million last year, Lo said.

UAE probes possible terrorism link to flydubai cockpit incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

The United Arab Emirates has launched an investigation into whether a cockpit altercation aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was linked to “terrorist activity” or involved prior planning or direction.
The country’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi had formed a team of specialised public prosecutors to investigate the incident and establish its circumstances and causes.
The probe follows flydubai's announcement that an altercation occurred in the cockpit during flight FZ1073, requiring crew members to intervene and secure the aircraft.
The investigation will examine all circumstances and motives, “including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction”, the ministry said.
UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, state news agency WAM reported. UAE law therefore applies to crimes committed aboard the aircraft even outside the country's territory, it said.
Emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Flight FZ1073, carrying 174 passengers, made an emergency landing on Wednesday at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the Saudi city of Tabuk after the cockpit incident was reported.
Flydubai said crew members secured the plane and diverted it safely to Saudi Arabia. Airport officials said the captain and first officer were injured and taken to hospital, while all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center said its investigation team had begun work and was coordinating with authorities to establish the circumstances, assess aviation safety aspects and collect evidence.
The UAE foreign ministry thanked Saudi authorities for their cooperation and handling of the incident.
Passengers later departed Tabuk aboard an alternative aircraft provided by flydubai.

Ditch the dating app. Meet an Irish town's 83-year-old mystical matchmaker.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:12:37 UTC
01:12:37 KST

For hopeful romantics, a small Irish town and its mystical matchmaker are here to help
Lisdoonvarna, Ireland — For nearly two centuries, a small Irish town has lured singletons to a festival every September that sees hopeful romantics seek their one true love.
The monthlong matchmaking festival that started in 1857 has become a global event, attracting over 60,000 visitors annually to the rugged landscape of County Clare, and specifically to the tiny town of Lisdoonvarna.
The festival even broke into American pop culture, featuring several years ago on the sitcom "Schitt's Creek."
In many ways, it's an old-world solution to modern dating. There is no app and no algorithms, just a chance to meet a match organically, through Irish traditional dancing and music, speed dating — or through the matchmaking skills of 83-year-old local legend Willie Daly.
Daly's grandfather helped start the festival, and his family has been pairing couples for three generations. In his father's and grandfather's day, many Irish towns and villages had traditional matchmakers, but Daly is now believed to be among the last, if not the last, keeping the tradition alive.
If prospective suitors wish to find a match through Daly, they meet with him and fill out a form outlining their hobbies, personality traits, and what they're looking for in a partner. Through his somewhat mystical personal intuition, Daly will then find a match and send the pair off on a first date.
"When I'm walking down the street, often I'd meet people … two or three couples said, 'You fixed us up 30 years ago, or 40 years ago,'" Daly told CBS News last month. "We're lucky here. Now this is a wonderful festival, and it's a great provision of opportunity — the opportunity to get married is very consistent in it. Music and dancing all day long, you know, for 30 days."
In a tattered old book, Daly keeps records of the hopeful matches he's arranged over the years, and local legend has it that if you place two hands on the book, you'll be married within six months.
Daly's image is literally etched on the front of a local watering hole — The Matchmaker Bar, where singles gather every year to drink, dance and try to meet their future spouse — in a testament to his stature in Lisdoonvarna.
CBS News attended the festivities at the pub in September and spoke with young attendees about what they were looking for in an ideal partner.
"I suppose a bit of loyalty, a bit of values, but also a bit of craic, you can't beat a bit of craic," said one young woman, using a common Irish phrase that translates roughly to good fun.
"Someone agricultural. I am agricultural myself … we're farming at home, we have a sheep farm at home. That's what I'm looking for at the moment," an Irishman said about his hunt for love.
Another attendee, Erica, told CBS News she had traveled all the way from Colombia for the festival.
"It's the opportunity to meet people the right way, face-to-face," she said. "Those apps, I mean, I'm not saying that people are hiding anything, but right now, just having the contact, just to sit there and talk to people makes [dating] a whole different event."
American Mary Timby from Colorado came to the village last year and ended up going viral, garnering over 2 million views after posting online about how she found love at the matchmaking festival.
She returned this year, and is now an ambassador for the event.
"I first heard about the festival on 'Schitt's Creek.' It was during COVID. I was huddled in a blanket on my couch and I Googled it and I thought, 'Oh, it's a real festival. Wouldn't it be fun if I just went someday?'" she said.
"My partner is from Ennis, here in County Clare, and we met at The Matchmaking Bar," she said. "I loved the Irish accent, and he just, was funny. He made me laugh and we connected right away, so we exchanged information."
But Timby's story shows that even matchmaking with nearly 170 years of proven success can benefit from modern technology.
"He found me on social media the next day," she said of her match. "And the rest is history."

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Wednesday that it had delivered a "massive strike" by ground-based high-precision weapons and attack drones at a communication center in Kyiv, as well as Ukraine's energy system facilities and the port infrastructure of Izmail in southwestern part of the Odesa region.
The ministry had said in late August that it was preparing a bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure as part of Russia's response to Ukrainian attacks on its fuel and energy facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly last week that Kyiv would make winter deeply painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to agree to an energy truce.
"Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that Russia and Moscow had agreed to halt attacks on energy facilities last month, although both nations swiftly clarified that no formal deal had been finalized.
Trump has also previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.
U.S. NATO envoy: 'Russia is trying to lash out'

The Russian Embassy in Belgium had accused the alliance of escalating the situation around Kaliningrad, a small Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania.
The embassy said NATO's "reckless and irresponsible" approach to Kaliningrad heightens the risk of a direct military confrontation.
It added that Moscow was ready to use its entire military arsenal if NATO tried to block the region, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, said that the alliance was prepared for whatever action Russia may take against a NATO country.
"What we have been very clear in communicating back to the Russian side is that we are a defensive alliance. We will defend every inch of NATO territory but at the same time we are not offensive orientated," Whitaker told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
"This is, you know, a situation where because of the lack of success on the battlefield in Ukraine, I think Russia is trying to lash out, but ultimately ... we are prepared," he added.

Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

Can anyone broker a new peace between Tigray and Ethiopia?
October 2, 2026
Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks.
Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
But this time, the situation looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.
This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.
Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal
The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.
Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.
The final agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF, Mohammed said. It also ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored hardliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace as a military defeat.
Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Abiy's government moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.
"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."
An alliance of former enemies
Mohammed also emphasized that the coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.
It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front, as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region and also ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.
Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.
Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."
She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.
Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.
Could the conflict have been prevented?
Rodrigues also pointed to the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict.
She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.
"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.
The United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants to the negotiating table.
The real cost of war
In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.
"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.
Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.
Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."
Limited prospects for mediation
UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers and Egypt. These are many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.
But, according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."
Rodrigues has a similar opinion, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Scientists are decoding elephant rumble calls, including ‘greetings’ and ‘coos’—hear them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:01:32 UTC
01:01:32 KST

In February 2020 behavioral ecologist Mickey Pardo witnessed the aftermath of an elephant birth. In Kenya’s Samburu National Reserve, he watched as a female African elephant named Matisse called to her newborn with repeated “rumbles”—a kind of deep vocalization he describes as like “an idling truck engine.” Pardo watched as another adult elephant, likely Matisse’s sister, rumbled from a distance before the family came together, uniting with another series of rumbles, as if saying hello.
“It was just really ... fascinating to see this whole sequence,” recalls Pardo, a senior scientist at the research organization ElephantVoices. What these calls might mean, exactly, has long been a mystery. But a new study published on Thursday in Scientific Reports helps to shed some light.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In the study, Pardo and a team of scientists used machine learning to analyze hundreds of rumble recordings from a separate population of African elephants in Amboseli National Park, also in Kenya.
The analysis homes in on several kinds of elephant rumbles: “coo” rumbles to calves, “contact” rumbles made from a distance, “let’s-go” rumbles before group movements, “cadenced” rumbles during rest or meals and two different “greeting” rumbles.
In many cases, the recordings captured overlapping calls, a jumble of rumbles the researchers refer to as “choruses.” To be clear, these calls are not at all like elephants’ iconic trumpet sound. They are low and almost like a growl or thunder.
The researchers used the algorithm to predict the elephants’ behavior based on each recording. It wasn’t entirely accurate, but it did predict behaviors better than chance—suggesting that elephant vocalizations during similar situations may have similar acoustic properties.
“It is pretty exciting that we’re able to train a model to look at an entire chorus and have some interpretation of exactly what’s going on,” says Sara Keen, a study co-author and a senior research scientist at the nonprofit Earth Species Project.
In some cases, different rumbles became progressively similar, a pattern the researchers describe as “vocal convergence.” Scientists have observed this phenomenon in other chatty animals, including parrots and dolphins. Humans, too, are known to mirror one another’s language patterns.
Interestingly, converging appeared “only in the situations where they [the elephants] seem to be coordinating group behavior action,” Keen says. It’s possible that this convergence could indicate agreement, but that theory needs further testing to confirm, she adds.
“This study emphasizes how vital it is to pair new computational analyses with real behavioral observations in the wild,” says Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, who was not involved in the study.
Keen hopes scientists may be able to use similar methods to analyze other animal calls, too, such as for orcas and crows. Many other species are known to perform a kind of “chorusing,” she says, which may make good candidates for future research.
“Animals communicate to influence each other’s behavior, and so you can’t just study the sounds in isolation,” Kershenbaum explains. “But when you combine a rich behavioral dataset with powerful machine learning algorithms, that’s when we can start to get answers to questions like ‘What are the animals saying?’”

People found not guilty by reason of insanity show a surprisingly mixed criminal risk profile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

People who experience severe mental health conditions are frequently overrepresented in the criminal justice system, but their psychiatric symptoms alone do not always explain their legal troubles. A recent study found that standard criminal risk factors, such as antisocial attitudes and having friends involved in crime, are strongly linked to whether a psychiatric patient has been involved in the legal system. The research was published in Law and Human Behavior.
In the past, intervention programs aimed at reducing repeat offenses among people with mental illness focused almost entirely on treating psychiatric symptoms. These medical interventions routinely failed to keep people out of jail. Researchers began to realize that most people with mental illness do not commit crimes because of hallucinations or delusions.
Instead, their criminal behavior is closely linked to the same risk factors that drive crime in the general population. In the fields of criminology and psychology, experts often refer to the central eight criminogenic risk factors. These include a history of antisocial behavior, antisocial personality traits, antisocial friends, substance abuse, family or marital problems, school or work difficulties, a lack of positive recreational activities, and criminal attitudes.
Researchers have consistently found that these non-clinical factors outperform traditional mental health variables in predicting criminal behavior. This means that mental illness alone does not necessarily increase an individual’s risk of breaking the law. Instead, some people with mental illness happen to have co-occurring antisocial tendencies that lead to legal trouble.
While this pattern holds true for general psychiatric patients, a unique subset of individuals occupies a gray area between the mental health and legal systems. These are patients who have been found not guilty by reason of insanity. In these specific cases, a court has determined that the person is not legally responsible for a crime because a mental disease or defect impaired their actions at the time of the offense.
Because their crimes are legally attributed to mental illness, one might assume these individuals lack the general criminal risk factors seen in other offenders. To test this idea, psychology researchers Angelea Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, and their colleagues set out to compare different groups of psychiatric patients. They wanted to see how insanity acquittees stacked up against other patients in terms of criminal attitudes, social support, and psychiatric distress.
The researchers gathered data from 349 participants across three distinct groups. The first group consisted of 74 psychiatric patients who had a history of misdemeanor or felony convictions. The second group included 68 psychiatric patients who had no history of criminal involvement. Both of these groups were recruited from a short-term, private inpatient psychiatric hospital in Texas.
The third group was made up of 207 forensic patients residing in the California state hospital system. These individuals had been found not guilty by reason of insanity and were institutionalized for mandatory psychiatric treatment. To compare the groups, the research team administered a series of self-report questionnaires designed to measure attitudes toward crime, social support networks, and current mental health.
One survey assessed general criminal tendencies, conduct problems, and antisocial personality traits. Another measured the participants’ number of criminal friends and their level of agreement with antisocial attitudes, such as feelings of entitlement or the belief that violence is justified. A third questionnaire evaluated how much support the participants felt they received from family, friends, and romantic partners.
Finally, the participants completed an inventory that measured the severity of their current psychiatric symptoms over the previous week. This included looking at markers for anxiety, depression, and paranoia. The researchers then used statistical models to see if the combination of these traits could accurately distinguish the three types of patients from one another based solely on their survey answers.
The team discovered that patients with mental illness and a history of typical criminal involvement scored the highest on almost all indicators of criminal risk. This group reported having the most criminal associates and the strongest antisocial attitudes. They also reported the lowest levels of perceived positive social support from their families and friends.
The patients found not guilty by reason of insanity presented a more mixed profile. They showed some shared criminal risk factors with the traditional criminal group, scoring higher on general criminal tendencies than the patients with no legal history. However, they did not display the same elevated levels of antisocial attitudes as the group with typical legal involvement.
When it came to social networks, the insanity acquittees actually resembled the patients with no criminal history. Both of these groups reported feeling a comparable level of social support. The researchers suggest that friends and family might remain more supportive of someone whose crime is attributed to a mental health crisis, compared to someone who engages in standard criminal behavior.
In an unexpected twist regarding psychiatric symptoms, the insanity acquittees reported the lowest severity of current mental health distress among all three groups. The researchers suspect this is due to the nature of their hospitalizations. The Texas patients were in a short-term, acute crisis facility, while the California forensic patients had likely been living in a stable, long-term therapeutic environment for an extended period, allowing their symptoms to subside.
Overall, the data showed that criminal risk factors and social support metrics successfully sorted roughly two thirds to three quarters of the participants into their correct legal categories. This predictive accuracy reinforces the idea that criminal attitudes and social environments are defining features of justice-involved populations. The results highlight the need for treatment programs to target these specific criminal risk factors alongside standard psychiatric care.
For example, specialized rehabilitation programs exist to address the concurrent mental health and criminal needs of people in the justice system. Providing this kind of dual-focused therapy could assist forensic patients in developing necessary life skills to optimize their recovery. Preparing these patients for eventual release requires treating the whole person, rather than viewing them solely through a psychiatric lens.
While the study offers a detailed look at forensic and non-forensic patients, the research design relies on data collected at a single point in time. This cross-sectional approach prevents researchers from determining exactly how a person’s mental illness and criminal behavior evolved over time. It is impossible to know whether a patient’s antisocial attitudes developed before or after their psychiatric symptoms began.
The reliance on self-reported questionnaires also introduces the possibility of response bias. Participants might have underreported their antisocial attitudes or exaggerated their mental health symptoms based on what they thought the researchers wanted to hear. Corroborating these self-reports with official legal records or clinician observations in future studies could yield a more comprehensive picture of their behavior.
The sample composition limits how broadly the results can be applied to the general population. The patients from the Texas hospital lacked demographic diversity, being predominantly White and male. Comparing patients across two different states also introduces variations in how different legal systems define and handle insanity acquittals, meaning a patient in California might be treated differently than one in Texas.
A final complication is that 85 percent of the forensic patients in the California sample had additional criminal convictions on top of the charges that led to their insanity acquittals. This high rate of prior criminal behavior blurs the boundary between the strictly psychiatric and the strictly criminal groups. Future investigations could separate insanity acquittees based on their past criminal histories to better understand this unique population.
The study, “Psychiatric Symptoms and Criminogenic Risk in People With Mental Illness: Comparing Patients Across Forensic and Nonforensic Settings,” was authored by Angelea D. Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, Robert D. Morgan, Sean M. Mitchell, and Darci Delgado.

Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
•    The HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme aims to accelerate the transformation of AI R&D projects into impactful practical solutions.
•    Over 30 projects have been approved, backed by a total of HK$1.7 billion.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Artificial intelligence has rapidly evolved from an emerging technology into a cornerstone of Hong Kong's economic transformation strategy. Under the Government's AI+ initiative, further reinforced by the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the HKSAR (2026-2030), the city is stepping up efforts to integrate AI across industries, public services, scientific research, healthcare, finance and smart-city development, with the ambition of becoming a leading innovation hub in the Greater Bay Area and beyond.
At the heart of this strategy is the HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme (AISS), a three-year programme that supports universities, research institutions, enterprises and government departments in harnessing the immense computing power of Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre, the city's largest AI computing facility and a key piece of digital infrastructure. Hong Kong's total computing capacity has now surpassed 5,000 petaFLOPS.
The scheme marks a strategic shift from supporting AI research alone to accelerating real-world applications capable of generating tangible economic and social benefits. .
Against this backdrop, a new generation of researchers, scientists and innovators is translating cutting-edge breakthroughs into practical solutions.
Since the launch of AISS in 2024, more than 50 applications have been received and over 30 projects approved, spanning local universities, R&D centres, government departments, technology companies and start-ups. Total subsidies granted have exceeded HK$1.7 billion.
Speaking at a sharing session featuring approved AISS projects, Daniel Cheung, Acting Commissioner for Digital Policy, highlighted the scheme's role in supporting Hong Kong's broader development goals. "The AISS closely aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan by advancing ‘industries for AI’ and ‘AI for industries,’ promoting the transformation and upgrading of traditional sectors such as finance and healthcare. Since its launch, the AISS has received enthusiastic responses, with subsidised projects demonstrating immense potential in technological innovation and industrial application," he said.
 
Echoing this view, Hendrick Sin, Chairperson of the Committee of AISS, said: "The approved projects not only showcase scientific breakthroughs but are steadily being transformed into practical applications that benefit society and industry, enhancing citizens' quality of life and exemplifying the power of collaborative innovation among government, industry, academia and research."
One of the highlights of the sharing session was a multimodal large language model for medical diagnosis and surgery developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) under the Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Focused on advancing innovation at the intersection of AI and life and health sciences, CAIR has built a comprehensive medical AI ecosystem centred on CARES 3.0, a multimodal medical model equipped with continual learning and trustworthy decision-making capabilities. The platform pioneers a new "copilot" approach to intelligent healthcare.
Among its innovations is EchoCare, an ultrasound foundation model trained on four million ultrasound datasets. Adaptable across a wide range of clinical applications, the model can accurately identify lesions in more than 50 organs. CAIR's technological advances have helped overcome critical technical bottlenecks.
Financial innovation
AI is also reshaping Hong Kong's financial sector. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Cyberport launched the first and second cohorts of the GenA.I. Sandbox in 2024 and 2025 respectively, focusing on use cases in anti-fraud operations, risk management and customer experience enhancement.
Trial results demonstrated significant operational gains across the banking sector. Participating institutions recorded a 30 to 80 percent reduction in preparation time for suspicious transaction reports, while document processing times were cut from one day to approximately five minutes. The technology also reduced risk assessment report production time by 60 percent, enabled more comprehensive risk analysis workflows, and resulted in more than 70 percent of GenAI-generated credit assessments being regarded as useful references by adopting institutions.
Building on this momentum, the HKMA joined forces with Cyberport, the Securities and Futures Commission, the Insurance Authority and the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority to launch GenA.I. Sandbox++ in March 2026, with a strong emphasis on exploring Agentic AI applications.
Moving beyond content generation, selected use cases under Sandbox++ are examining how AI systems can responsibly take on greater autonomy across end-to-end processes, including customer onboarding, payments, insurance claims and customer interactions.
Collaborative Generative AI Platform
Another project demonstrating the breadth of Hong Kong's AI ambitions comes from InfiX.ai, which has independently developed the Collaborative Generative AI (Co-GenAI) Platform. It enables enterprises, research institutions and industry partners to train domain-specific AI models using their own datasets at significantly lower computing costs. By avoiding the centralisation of proprietary data while safeguarding privacy and intellectual property, Co-GenAI allows specialised intelligence distributed across organisations and devices to be connected and integrated into a continuously evolving collaborative intelligence network.
This approach enables AI technologies to be co-created, co-developed and shared among participating organisations. Supported by high-efficiency computing resources, model engineering, knowledge bases and application workflows, the platform offers capabilities ranging from local deployment and model fine-tuning to evaluation, inference services and multi-model collaboration.
Designed as a scalable, secure and controllable AI infrastructure, the platform has applications across sectors including manufacturing, public administration, finance, healthcare and education, helping drive digital transformation and strengthen the broader AI ecosystem.
These three projects illustrate how government support, world-class computing infrastructure and research excellence are converging to address pressing challenges, unlock new opportunities and demonstrate the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for Hong Kong's future.
The city's ambitions are set to grow further with the planned commissioning of the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster in the Northern Metropolis by 2032. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to propel Hong Kong into the ranks of the world's leading centres for computing capacity, strengthening its position as a regional and global AI powerhouse.

Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.
A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.
Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

Ex-Hungarian Minister Detained in $53 Million Graft Probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

Reported by
Black-masked law enforcement officers escorted Balázs Hankó, a former Hungarian culture minister, into a district court on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention over allegations that he masterminded the widespread misappropriation of state funds to benefit the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Hankó was taken into custody after Hungary's Parliament voted 139 to 0 on Monday to strip his legislative immunity. Before surrendering to prosecutors later that evening, he spent the day inside the Parliament building surrounded by his family, framing his pending arrest as political persecution.
"My conscience is clear; this is a political show trial," Hankó said in a video broadcast live on Orbán’s Facebook page before walking out alongside relatives and lawmakers from Fidesz, Orbán's right-wing party, which is now in opposition.
Prosecutors allege that Hankó misused 17.3 billion forints (about $53 million) during his concurrent tenure as president of the National Cultural Fund. According to the prosecutor’s office, between September 2025 and March 2026, Hankó and his associates established a "dual decision-making system" that bypassed legal evaluation procedures to distribute public grants across 1,079 separate instances along electoral and political lines.
The investigation was launched after whistleblowers alleged that the cultural fund was secretly channeling state grants to artists and organizations loyal to Fidesz. In one instance, public money was allegedly used to book a circus for a Fidesz campaign rally, which officials registered as a cultural event. Police previously raided offices housing Fidesz’s internet servers in July as part of the inquiry.
The court order marks one of the most high-profile moves yet in a sweeping anti-graft drive led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose administration took power after defeating Orbán and ending his 16 years in office. Magyar has estimated that systemic corruption under the prior government cost Hungary 8 to 10 percent of its gross domestic product. Writing on social media, Magyar declared that "millions of Hungarians had experienced for the first time what true regime change and equality before the law mean."
Fidesz leaders have fiercely denounced the proceedings, accusing Magyar’s government of authoritarian overreach. János Bóka, the leader of the Fidesz parliamentary group, pledged that the party would hold anyone involved in the prosecution answerable "in court, in politics, and in their finances."
The anti-graft inquiry has expanded beyond Hankó. On Monday, authorities also detained Miklós Seszták, who served as national development minister under Orbán from 2014 to 2018, in connection with a separate bribery investigation. Seszták has denied any wrongdoing.
Prosecutors have not formally charged Hankó beyond the initial suspicion of misappropriation, and he has not been convicted of a crime.
Lawmakers also voted to strip Prime Minister Péter Magyar of his immunity in an unrelated case that predates his time in office.

Pedro Sánchez highlights the Government's commitment to the aerospace and automotive industries during his visit to the Delta Vigo PTL Valladares industrial centre
President's News - 2026.10.1
Vigo (Pontevedra)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, together with the Mayor of Vigo, Abel Caballero, and the President of the Delta Vigo group, Francisco Puga, during their visit to the Delta Vigo PTL Valladares industrial center (Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, highlighted the Government's commitment to the aerospace and automotive industries during his visit to Delta Vigo PTL Valladares, the Delta Group's industrial centre specialising in the manufacture of industrial components and systems for the aerospace sector, in Vigo (Pontevedra). This company, a leading player in the Galician aeronautical industry which works for major international manufacturers, has received support from European funds and is an example of the Government's commitment to the modernisation of Galician industry, technological innovation and quality employment.
The head of the Executive, accompanied by the Government Delegate, Pedro Blanco, and the Mayor of Vigo, Abel Caballero, toured the company's facilities at the Vigo Technology and Logistics Park. As a recipient of European funding, the company has received 4.5 million euros from the PERTE Aerospace and 700,000 euros from the PERTE for the Development of Electric and Connected Vehicles (VEC), both part of the Recovery Plan, as well as 1.84 million euros from the ERDF.
Delta Vigo, which has four plants in Spain, posted a net profit of 3.57 million euros in 2025 and has invested over 60 million euros in R&D&i over the last seven years. The parent company of the Delta Group, founded 80 years ago as a shipyard, has specialised in the manufacture of components and technological products. Delta Vigo Aeroestructuras, together with Delta Illescas, are subsidiaries specialising in the aeronautical and aerospace industries. Of particular note is its collaboration with Airbus on the PEGASO+ project, which is researching the use of new materials and manufacturing techniques with the aim of designing a zero-emission aircraft.
The Government of Spain, through the PERTE VEC programme and its various calls for proposals, has invested more than 80 million euros in the province of Pontevedra. Furthermore, amongst other investments, through the PRTR funds and the National Innovation Agency (ENISA), 12 loans for SMEs and start-ups have been financed, totalling 2.5 million euros. In total, ENISA has invested 41.9 million euros in Galicia.

Flydubai heroes say attacker begged ‘Kill me’ after passengers overpowered him in cockpit
Unknown

15:23:40 UTC
00:23:40 KST

Yaniv Hayun, the Israeli plumber who helped stabilize the Flydubai aircraft after passengers stormed the cockpit, is still struggling to process the midair drama and his unexpected place among its heroes.
“We should celebrate a birthday on this day,” he said Thursday at his home in Ness Ziona after learning that he would receive the city’s Hero Award for his actions. “All the passengers said, ‘We were born again.’”
New footage shows the stabbed Indian pilot receiving treatment, while the attacking pilot is seen restrained:
Later Thursday, Hayun met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the second time. Netanyahu hosted several of the flight’s other rescuers at his office, including Dr. Shota Musaev, who treated the wounded Indian captain, Musaev’s wife Sigalit and Or Pradilov. “The whole world is seeing Israeli heroism,” Netanyahu told them.
He announced that the four would light a torch honoring civilian heroism at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony, which is still about six months away. The composition of Israel’s government, and who will lead it by then, remains uncertain.
Netanyahu said the passengers had acted “with supreme courage, resourcefulness and faith” to prevent a major disaster and save many lives. “I tell the citizens of Israel to learn from you, keep your eyes open and remain vigilant,” he said. “We are in a very sensitive period. Our enemies intend to harm us.”
During the meeting, the passengers offered new details about the moments after they subdued the Omani co-pilot. “We tied the stabbing pilot up with the headphone cord,” they told Netanyahu. “He said, ‘Kill me.’ That means he had failed in his mission and preferred to die.”
‘There was blood everywhere’
Musaev, who treated Capt. Smit Machchhar after he was stabbed during the cockpit struggle, described the scene he encountered. “I saw the terrorist was injured. On the floor, I saw a lot of blood,” he said. “It was the pilot’s blood. We don’t know, maybe he was injured too, the terrorist, but not like the pilot. Everything was cut, his hands, his head, everything. Really deep wounds.”
Musaev said his attention then turned to stopping the bleeding. “I was constantly checking his pulse and seeing what condition he was in,” he said.
The passengers said the most dramatic moments lasted only seconds. “In the end, I came up with the idea of tying him up with the headphone cord, and we tied him because we had no other option,” Musaev said. “Only afterward did they bring us zip ties. The only thing in my head was somehow tying him down so he couldn’t start going wild again.”
Earlier Thursday, Ness Ziona Mayor Shmuel Boxer visited Hayun at home and told him he would receive the city’s Hero Award. Hayun, visibly uncomfortable with the attention, responded: “That will be too much.”
“Why is it too much?” Boxer replied. “You saved dozens of lives. You saved three families from Ness Ziona who were on that plane, and the entire country is thanking you.”
Among previous recipients of the city honor is retired Brig. Gen. Avigdor Kahalani, one of Israel’s best-known heroes of the 1973 Yom Kippur War and one of the few soldiers to receive both the Medal of Valor and the Medal of Distinguished Service.
Hayun said he was not sure what he had done could be called courage. “In moments like that, you operate automatically,” he said.
Boxer said that when he first heard what had happened, he wondered about Hayun’s military background. “Those are actions that come with experience and background,” he said. “To function like that isn’t natural. It’s inconceivable.”
Hayun’s wife, Meital, said people kept asking what her husband did for a living. “I told them, ‘He unclogs sewers,’” she said.
The couple recalled the moments when they felt the aircraft suddenly descending. “At first we thought it was turbulence,” they said. “The plane shook a little at first. Something crazy.”
“This isn’t a joke. It’s a historic event,” Hayun added. “When you think about it, it’s unbelievable.”
He returned to the same thought that had stayed with him since the flight landed safely. “This should be the passengers’ birthday,” he said. “We were all born again.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, was among the Israelis who overpowered the Omani co-pilot alongside Tzvika Mans and Assaf Reguan.
He also responded Thursday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks about his role in the incident. Trump had described Hayun as an Israeli plumber with virtually no aviation experience who recognized what was happening and acted.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with filthy pipes, and he was right. It didn’t offend me.”
Hayun said all he wanted now was to return to his normal life. “In my wildest dreams, I never thought Trump would talk about me and refer to what I did,” he said. “I actually like his humor. The way he described it was funny.”
“I’m no Bruce Lee,” he added. “But I managed to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis, pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Netanyahu admits Flydubai security ‘loophole’
Separately, Netanyahu acknowledged in a Fox News interview that the incident had exposed a loophole in the security procedures governing pilots operating flights to Israel.
“The first thing is you want a background check on pilots,” Netanyahu said. “Even if you have metal detectors, they’re usually for the passengers, and it’s quite possible that pilots just don’t go through that. So obviously, that’s a loophole that has to be corrected.”
Netanyahu also said the Omani co-pilot had undergone radicalization. “We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” he said.
Meanwhile, Indian media reported that Machchhar, the Indian captain attacked in the cockpit, apparently with an emergency axe, had been transferred from Saudi Arabia to Dubai for further medical treatment.
The government of Gujarat announced that it would honor Machchhar for his actions. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised his “unwavering courage,” saying the captain’s actions helped save the lives of the passengers.

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:23:32 UTC
00:23:32 KST

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
- SpaceX launched its 13th long-duration astronaut crew to the International Space Station, carrying two US astronauts, one Canadian, and one Russian for a mission on human health in orbit.
- The Falcon 9 rocket successfully delivered the Crew Dragon capsule into orbit, with a reusable booster returning safely to Earth after launch from Cape Canaveral.
- Crew 13 will conduct biomedical studies on microgravity's effects and join seven ISS occupants, continuing research aboard the US-Russian-led space station operating since 1998 and planned until 2030.
AI generated
CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida - A SpaceX rocket lifted off from Florida on Oct 1 with a crew of two US astronauts, a Canadian astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut headed to the International Space Station (ISS) for a science mission devoted to human health and performance in orbit.
The two-stage Falcon 9 rocket, topped with an autonomously operated Crew Dragon capsule carrying the four-member crew, was launched from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, along Florida’s Atlantic Coast.
A live webcast showed the 25-storey-tall rocket thundering off the launch pad as its nine Merlin engines roared to life in billowing, incandescent plumes of vapour.
Falcon 9’s reusable lower-stage booster separated from the rest of the vehicle within three minutes of launch and flew itself back to Earth for a return landing.
The rocket’s upper stage climbed higher and released into orbit the Crew Dragon carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
“Dragon separation confirmed. Jessica, Luke, Josh, Sergey, welcome to orbit,” SpaceX mission control in Hawthorne, California, told the crew.
The capsule is thrusting itself along an eight-hour orbital voyage to the space station and is set to dock with the orbiting laboratory platform some 400km above Earth around 7pm EDT (7am on Oct 2 in Singapore).
The mission marks the 13th long-duration space station team that NASA has flown aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle since the rocket venture founded in 2002 by Elon Musk began sending US astronauts to orbit in May 2020. The company went public in a record-breaking IPO in July.
The launch also comes days after SpaceX launched its next-generation Starship spacecraft on its first trip to orbit and first commercial satellite deployment, marking the vehicle’s 14th uncrewed test flight since 2023.
Crew 13 is led by geologist-turned-astronaut Watkins, 38, making her second voyage to space and becoming the first NASA astronaut to fly twice aboard a Crew Dragon.
Seated beside her in the pilot’s chair is Delaney, 47, a former test pilot and fighter pilot making his debut in space.
Rounding out Crew 13 are two other spaceflight rookies ranked as mission specialists - Kutryk, 44, a former test and fighter pilot, and Teteryatnikov, 37, an engineer who specialised in the operation of submarines.
The four crewmates are to be welcomed aboard the space station by seven current occupants of the orbital outpost, including the four members of Crew 12 who are due to fly back to Earth as soon as their seven-month-plus mission comes to an end.
The latest arrivals are expected to focus their attention on a series of biomedical and human performance studies, including research on how microgravity affects blood circulation and clotting, and gathering health data to inform future space missions.
The ISS, which spans the length of a football field and ranks as the largest human-made object in space, has been continuously operated by a US-Russian-led consortium that includes Canada, Japan and 11 European countries.
The first hardware for the outpost was launched more than a quarter-century ago. NASA has said it is committed to keeping the space station operating through 2030. REUTERS
